questions.questionText: Calculation: A sample of n = 25 scripts after a process change has mean marking time 18.4 minutes and sample standard deviation 3.0 minutes. Using t* ≈ 2.06 for a 95% CI with df = 24, calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean. (Give to 2 decimal places.)
questions.rationale: The CI for a mean uses mean ± t*×(s/√n). This reinforces the link between variability, sample size and uncertainty in reporting.

questions.questionText: A hypothesis test comparing ‘before’ vs ‘after’ marking time produces p = 0.03. Which statement is correct (using a 5% significance level)?
options: There is a 3% chance the process change caused no difference
If there were truly no difference, results as extreme as these (or more) would occur about 3% of the time due to random sampling variation
The probability the alternative hypothesis is true is 97%
The process change is practically important
questions.rationale: A p-value is calculated under the null hypothesis and describes how surprising the observed data would be if the null were true. It does not directly provide the probability that the null/alternative is true, nor does it guarantee practical importance.

questions.questionText: Scenario: After a change, average marking time decreases by 0.6 minutes and the p-value is 0.01 due to a very large sample size. The service-level target is to reduce average marking time by at least 2 minutes. What is the best conclusion for a quality report?
options: The change is successful because p < 0.05
The change is not successful because p < 0.05 indicates a problem
The change shows a statistically detectable reduction, but it is not practically significant against the 2-minute target
No conclusion is possible because the p-value is too small
questions.rationale: Statistical significance can occur for trivial effects when sample sizes are large. Quality decisions should incorporate practical thresholds, effect sizes and operational impact.

questions.questionText: Which assumption is most important for the validity of a basic two-sample t-test comparing mean marking time between Centre A and Centre B?
options: Each centre must have exactly the same number of scripts
Observations are independent within and between centres (e.g., scripts are not double-counted and not repeated measures of the same script)
Marking times must be integers
Both centres must have identical standard deviations
questions.rationale: Independence is fundamental. Equal sample sizes and integer values are not required. Equal variances may be assumed in some versions, but many workflows use Welch’s t-test which does not require it.

questions.questionText: You have only n = 6 scripts after a change and the marking time distribution looks strongly right-skewed with one extreme value. What is the most appropriate action before claiming a reliable improvement based on a t-test?
options: Proceed with the t-test and ignore the outlier because it is inconvenient
Increase the sample size and/or use a more robust approach (e.g., analyse median and IQR; consider a non-parametric alternative) and report the limitation clearly
Replace the extreme value with the mean to make the data more normal
Remove all values above the mean to reduce skew
questions.rationale: With very small n and strong skew/outliers, t-based inference can be unstable. Best practice is to collect more data, consider robust summaries/tests, and state limitations transparently.

questions.questionText: You want to show stakeholders the estimated difference in mean marking time between ‘before’ and ‘after’ with uncertainty. Which visual is most appropriate?
options: A pie chart of total scripts marked
A bar chart of the mean difference with 95% CI error bars (or an interval plot)
A 3D surface plot
A stacked area chart with no axis labels
questions.rationale: An interval plot (estimate plus CI) directly communicates effect size and uncertainty. The other chart types are unsuitable or likely to confuse a non-specialist audience.

questions.questionText: Write two caveats you would include when reporting a confidence interval or hypothesis test result about a process change in a weekly quality report (e.g., for marking times).
questions.correctAnswer: Any two appropriate caveats, for example: (1) Results depend on assumptions (independence; approximate normality or sufficient sample size). (2) The sample may not be representative of all weeks/centres (mix of scripts or staffing changed). (3) Statistical significance does not guarantee practical significance; consider the size of the effect against targets. (4) Other simultaneous changes (confounders) may explain differences.
questions.rationale: This checks whether learners can communicate limitations and avoid over-claiming—central to stakeholder-friendly reporting.

questions.questionText: Scenario (decision + communication): Before the change, n = 30 scripts had mean marking time 21.0 minutes (sd 4.5). After the change, n = 30 scripts had mean 19.5 minutes (sd 4.0). A two-sample test reports p = 0.04 and the estimated mean reduction is 1.5 minutes. The operational target is a reduction of at least 2 minutes. Write a brief recommendation (3–5 sentences) for a quality meeting that covers statistical result, practical significance and next steps.
questions.correctAnswer: Example recommendation: "The analysis suggests a statistically detectable reduction in mean marking time after the change (p = 0.04), with an estimated reduction of about 1.5 minutes. However, this does not meet the operational target of at least 2 minutes, so the improvement may not be practically sufficient. I recommend continuing data collection for a few more weeks and reviewing distribution/outliers and any confounders (e.g., script mix, staffing levels) before deciding on a wider rollout. We should report both the effect size and an interval estimate to show uncertainty."
questions.rationale: A strong workplace response integrates p-value interpretation with effect size, target-based practical significance, and sensible follow-up actions, communicated in plain language.

formativeAssessments.title: Short Quiz: Choosing and Using Binomial, Normal and Exponential Models in Workplace Risk
formativeAssessments.description: A 12-question quiz on selecting appropriate probability models and carrying out core calculations for defects, demand and downtime in workplace contexts.
formativeAssessments.instructions: Complete after studying the module topics on distributions. Time guidance: 25 minutes. Use a calculator. Show workings for calculation questions (even if you also use Excel/Python). This is low-stakes practice: focus on identifying which model fits and interpreting results.
assessmentCriteria: Correct selection of binomial, normal or exponential models for a given workplace scenario
Accurate probability calculations and correct use of parameters (n, p, μ, σ, λ)
Clear interpretation of results in practical terms (e.g., defect/demand/downtime likelihood)
Reasoned evaluation of distribution choice limitations (fitness-for-purpose, assumptions)

questions.questionText: A quality engineer inspects 30 independently produced items from a stable process. Each item is either defective or not defective. Which model is most appropriate for the number of defectives in the sample?
options: Normal distribution, because quality data are always continuous
Binomial distribution, because it counts successes/failures across a fixed number of trials
Exponential distribution, because it models time between events
Uniform distribution, because any defect count is equally likely
questions.rationale: The binomial model fits a fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes (defective / not defective) and constant probability p. Normal is continuous (though it can approximate binomial in some cases), exponential is for waiting times, and uniform rarely fits defect counts.

questions.questionText:
In a workplace audit, each component has a 3% probability of failing a test (assume independence). A batch sample of 20 components is tested.

Calculate the probability of finding exactly 2 failures.
questions.rationale: This checks correct identification of binomial parameters and substitution into the pmf. The result should be around 0.10; common errors include using (0.97)^{20} or using 2/20 as p.

questions.questionText: A call centre receives calls where each call is either a complaint or not. If the probability a call is a complaint is p = 0.08 and 100 calls are received, what is the expected number of complaints?
questions.rationale: For X ~ Bin(n,p), the expected value is E[X]=np=100×0.08=8. Options 0.08 and 92 confuse probability with expected count; 12.5 would correspond to p=0.125.

questions.questionText:
Weekly demand for a spare part is modelled as Normal with mean μ = 500 units and standard deviation σ = 50 units.

Calculate the z-score for demand x = 580 units.
questions.rationale: A z-score standardises a value relative to the mean and standard deviation. Errors usually come from dividing by variance (σ²) or using (μ−x)/σ.

questions.questionText:
A service desk estimates the time (in minutes) to resolve a routine ticket is Normal with μ = 120 and σ = 15.

Estimate P(T > 150).
questions.rationale: This tests converting to a standard normal and reading/knowing a tail probability. A result near 2–3% is expected; using 0.9772 would be the wrong tail.

questions.questionText: When is the normal approximation to a binomial model generally considered acceptable (rule of thumb)?
options: When n is less than 10, regardless of p
When p is exactly 0.5
When np ≥ 5 and n(1−p) ≥ 5
Only when p is less than 0.01
questions.rationale: A common rule of thumb is that both expected successes and failures should be at least about 5 for the binomial to be reasonably symmetric and well-approximated by a normal distribution.

questions.questionText: A maintenance manager models time between machine breakdowns using an exponential distribution. Which statement best describes a key assumption of the exponential model?
options: Breakdowns become more likely the longer the machine has been running (ageing)
The failure rate is constant over time (memoryless property)
Breakdowns occur only at fixed hourly intervals
The probability of a breakdown is the same for all machines regardless of conditions
questions.rationale: Exponential waiting times assume a constant hazard (failure rate) and are memoryless. Ageing (increasing hazard) would suggest a Weibull model instead.

questions.questionText:
Downtime duration (in hours) after a fault is modelled as Exponential with mean 1.5 hours.

Calculate the probability that downtime lasts more than 2 hours.
questions.rationale: This checks converting mean to rate (λ) and using the survival function for exponential. A common mistake is using 1−exp(−λt), which is P(T≤t), not P(T>t).

questions.questionText:
A site records 12 breakdowns over 2,400 machine-hours. Assuming an exponential model for time between breakdowns, estimate:
(a) the failure rate λ (per hour), and
(b) the mean time between failures (MTBF).
questions.rationale: For a Poisson/exponential process, λ can be estimated as events per unit time and MTBF is the reciprocal. This is a practical parameter estimation step.

questions.questionText: Which distribution choice is most defensible for modelling the number of late deliveries in a week, where each delivery is either late or on time and there are 60 deliveries per week?
options: Exponential, because lateness is a time-related issue
Binomial, because it is a count of late/on-time outcomes across a fixed number of deliveries
Normal, because all workplace data are approximately normal
Cauchy, because it allows extreme values
questions.rationale: This is a fixed number of trials (deliveries) with binary outcomes (late/on time), so a binomial model is appropriate. Exponential is for waiting times; normal may approximate but is not the first-choice model; Cauchy is not suitable for bounded counts.

questions.questionText: A colleague proposes modelling the proportion of defects (which must lie between 0 and 1) using a normal distribution because it is 'simple'. Give two limitations of using a normal distribution for this purpose in a risk report.
questions.correctAnswer: Two limitations: (1) A normal distribution is unbounded and can imply impossible values below 0 or above 1, which can distort tail-risk statements. (2) For proportions near 0 or 1 the distribution is often skewed, while normal assumes symmetry; this can misstate probabilities and confidence intervals (a beta model or a binomial-based approach may be more appropriate).
questions.rationale: This assesses fitness-for-purpose thinking: matching distribution support (allowed values) and shape (skewness) to the real variable, and communicating limitations.

questions.questionText:
A production planner uses a normal model for weekly demand: N(120, 15). Two potential changes are being discussed:
- Change A: increase the mean demand to 130 while keeping σ = 15.
- Change B: keep the mean at 120 but increase σ to 20.

For the risk statement 'probability demand exceeds 150', which change is more likely to increase the exceedance probability, and why?
questions.correctAnswer: Change B is more likely to increase the exceedance probability because increasing σ spreads the distribution and increases upper-tail mass even if the mean stays the same. Increasing the mean (Change A) also increases exceedance probability, but the question asks which is more likely: for tail events far from the mean, higher variability (σ) is often a key sensitivity driver because it materially changes z = (150−μ)/σ and therefore the tail probability.
questions.rationale: This targets sensitivity thinking: exceedance probabilities depend on both location (mean) and spread (standard deviation). Learners should explain in plain terms how σ affects tail risk.

formativeAssessments.title: MCQ Knowledge Check: Monte Carlo Simulation Outputs, Assumptions and Risk Register Communication
formativeAssessments.description: A 12-question knowledge check focused on setting up Monte Carlo logic, interpreting percentiles and exceedance probabilities, and recording assumptions and limitations for stakeholders.
formativeAssessments.instructions: Complete after the simulation and risk register topics. Time guidance: 20 minutes. Most questions are MCQ; a few require short written responses or quick calculations. Aim for clarity over length when writing. This is formative and designed to surface gaps early.
assessmentCriteria: Correct interpretation of Monte Carlo outputs (percentiles, exceedance probability, distributions of outcomes)
Sound recording of assumptions, uncertainty and limitations in risk-register style language
Appropriate judgement about simulation settings (iterations, inputs, distribution choice) and their impact
Ability to identify key sensitivity drivers and communicate them to non-specialists

questions.questionText: In workplace risk analysis, what is the primary purpose of running a Monte Carlo simulation?
options: To replace real data collection entirely
To generate a distribution of possible outcomes by repeatedly sampling uncertain inputs
To guarantee the project finishes on time
To remove the need to document assumptions
questions.rationale: Monte Carlo simulation propagates input uncertainty to produce an output distribution (e.g., cost or schedule). It does not remove the need for data or assumptions, and it cannot guarantee outcomes.

questions.questionText: In Excel, which formula correctly generates one random sample from a Normal distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 15?
options: =NORM.INV(RAND(),100,15)
=NORM.S.INV(100,15)
=NORM.DIST(RAND(),100,15,TRUE)
questions.rationale: NORM.INV(U,μ,σ) converts a uniform random number U from RAND() into a normal variate. NORM.DIST returns a probability (CDF/PDF), not a random draw. The other options are invalid/misused.

questions.questionText: A simulation of total repair cost produces a 90th percentile (P90) of £48,000. Which interpretation is best?
options: There is a 90% probability the cost will be exactly £48,000
The average cost is £48,000
About 90% of simulated outcomes are at or below £48,000 (and about 10% are above), given the model assumptions
The minimum possible cost is £48,000
questions.rationale: A percentile is a threshold. P90 means 90% of simulated outcomes fall below (or equal to) that value under the modelled uncertainty; it is not the mean, not an exact-point probability, and not a minimum.

questions.questionText:
A project plan has a baseline duration of 40 working days. A Monte Carlo simulation of duration gives P50 = 41 days and P80 = 46 days.

If the organisation wants an 80% confidence date, what schedule contingency (in days) should be added to the baseline?
questions.correctAnswer: Use the P80 date as the 80% confidence duration. Contingency = 46 − 40 = 6 working days.
questions.rationale: This checks turning a percentile output into a practical planning action. A common mistake is using P50 for 80% confidence, or subtracting from P50 instead of the baseline.

questions.questionText: A histogram of simulated costs is strongly right-skewed (long tail to the right). Which output statement is most appropriate to include for stakeholders?
options: Because the histogram is skewed, we should only report the mean and hide the percentiles
Skew implies occasional high-cost outcomes; report percentiles (e.g., P50/P80/P90) and an exceedance probability for key thresholds
Skew means the simulation is incorrect and must be discarded
Skew means all outcomes are equally likely
questions.rationale: Right-skew typically indicates low-probability, high-impact outcomes. Percentiles and exceedance probabilities communicate tail risk better than the mean alone.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes the effect of increasing Monte Carlo iterations from 1,000 to 50,000 (keeping the model and inputs the same)?
options: It reduces sampling (Monte Carlo) error and makes estimated percentiles more stable
It reduces the true uncertainty in the real world
It guarantees the model assumptions are correct
It changes the underlying input distributions automatically
questions.rationale: More iterations improve numerical stability/precision of estimates (e.g., percentiles) but do not reduce the real-world uncertainty or validate assumptions.

questions.questionText:
Scenario (risk register practice): You are simulating the monthly cost of warranty claims. Inputs include: number of claims (modelled), average cost per claim (modelled), and a cap on maximum payout per claim. Your simulation shows a 5% chance monthly cost exceeds £120,000.

Write a concise risk register entry (3–5 bullet points) that includes: risk statement, key assumptions, uncertainty notes, and one mitigation action.
questions.correctAnswer:
Example entry:
- Risk: Monthly warranty claim cost may exceed £120,000 (modelled exceedance probability ≈ 5%).
- Assumptions: Claim count follows the chosen discrete model with stable process rate; average cost per claim follows the chosen cost distribution; payout cap applied per claim as specified; independence between claim count and claim severity unless stated.
- Uncertainty/limitations: Outputs reflect model assumptions and available data window; tail costs may be under/over-stated if rare high-severity claims are not well captured; potential correlation (e.g., product batch issues) not modelled could increase tail risk.
- Mitigation: Review and strengthen quality checks/recall triggers for high-risk components and negotiate supplier cost-sharing; update model monthly with latest claims data and re-run sensitivity analysis.
questions.rationale: This assesses whether learners can translate simulation outputs into workplace documentation: a clear risk statement plus explicit assumptions/limitations and a practical mitigation.

questions.questionText: You want to identify which uncertain input most drives simulated project cost. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Change all inputs at once and see if the output changes
Calculate correlation/regression between each input sample and the output, or run a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis
Only look at the minimum simulated cost
Increase iterations until the mean stops changing, then the most important input is the one with the largest mean
questions.rationale: Sensitivity analysis links input variation to output variation. Correlation/regression or structured one-at-a-time methods help identify drivers; changing everything at once is not diagnostic.

questions.questionText: Which is the best example of a simulation modelling error (as opposed to a genuine high-risk outcome)?
options: The simulation shows rare but very high cost outcomes due to a long-tailed input distribution
The simulation uses minutes for one duration input and hours for another without converting units
The output distribution is right-skewed when costs are uncertain
The P90 cost is higher than the mean cost
questions.rationale: Unit inconsistency is a modelling error that can invalidate results. Skewness, long tails, and P90 exceeding the mean can be perfectly valid properties of uncertain cost models.

questions.questionText:
In a Monte Carlo run of 10,000 iterations, 320 simulated outcomes exceed a cost threshold of £100,000.

Estimate the exceedance probability and state it as a percentage.
questions.correctAnswer: Exceedance probability ≈ 320/10,000 = 0.032 = 3.2%.
questions.rationale: This checks translating simulation counts into an estimated probability. Learners should express it clearly for a risk register (e.g., 'about 3.2%').

questions.questionText: For task durations where the team provides a minimum, most likely, and maximum estimate (e.g., 4 days, 6 days, 12 days), which input distribution is typically a good first choice for a simple Monte Carlo model?
options: Triangular distribution
Exponential distribution
Binomial distribution
Standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1
questions.rationale: Triangular is commonly used when only min/mode/max are available. Exponential is for waiting times with constant hazard; binomial is for counts; standard normal does not reflect min/max bounds.

questions.questionText:
A non-specialist stakeholder says: 'So you’re telling me there’s a 10% chance we’ll exceed £200,000. Does that mean we will exceed it once every 10 months?'

Write a brief response (2–4 sentences) that clarifies the meaning and highlights one limitation/assumption.
questions.correctAnswer: A clear response: "It means that, based on the assumptions and input uncertainties we modelled, about 10% of the simulated scenarios were above £200,000. It does not guarantee a pattern like 'once every 10 months' because months are not identical and the real process can change. Also, the 10% figure depends on our input distributions and any correlations we may have simplified or omitted."
questions.rationale: This checks the ability to communicate probabilistic statements accurately and transparently, including the conditional nature of results ('given assumptions') and avoiding deterministic frequency promises.

formativeAssessments.title: Short Quiz: Calibration and Parameter Fitting from Operational Data
formativeAssessments.description: A 12-question quiz focused on building a calibrated model from operational data and checking outputs for units, rounding, tolerance and sensitivity.
formativeAssessments.instructions: Complete after studying the calibration and checking topics. Time guide: 25 minutes. Show working for calculation questions. Use correct SI units where possible and state any assumptions you make. This is low-stakes: use feedback to identify gaps.
assessmentCriteria: Clear statement of variables, assumptions, parameter sources and intended use
Correct selection and application of calibration/parameter-fitting approaches
Accurate unit handling, dimensional sense-checking and appropriate rounding
Sound interpretation of tolerance and sensitivity checks with reproducible calculations

questions.questionText: Which statement best defines model calibration in a workplace mathematical modelling context?
options: Proving a model is correct for all possible future situations
Adjusting model parameters so model outputs match observed operational data within an agreed criterion
Replacing a mathematical model with a descriptive narrative to avoid assumptions
Changing the units in a model so that outputs look reasonable
questions.rationale: Calibration is parameter fitting to observed data (option B). Validation is about fitness-for-purpose, not universal correctness (A). Narratives do not substitute for modelling (C). Unit conversion is not calibration (D).

questions.questionText: You are calibrating a throughput model for a packaging line using three months of shift logs. Which data quality issue most directly threatens calibration validity?
options: The dataset contains both weekdays and weekends
The logs are time-stamped but the clock was not synchronised and the time zone is unknown
The dataset is stored in CSV format rather than Excel
Operators used different coloured pens when filling in paper forms
questions.rationale: If time stamps are unreliable, rates/throughput computed from time differences can be wrong, directly biasing fitted parameters (B). The other items are not inherently calibration-critical (A, C, D).

questions.questionText: Short answer: For a calibrated model used to predict daily energy consumption in a small factory, list THREE items that should appear in the model’s assumptions section to support auditability.
questions.correctAnswer: Any three well-justified assumptions such as: (1) operating hours per day are fixed (e.g., 08:00–18:00) or how variable hours are handled; (2) ambient temperature is treated as constant/averaged or taken from a specified weather source; (3) equipment efficiency is assumed constant over the period (no degradation) or degradation model stated; (4) production mix is assumed representative of historical data; (5) start-up/shut-down energy is included/excluded and why.
questions.rationale: M7-LO1 requires explicit variables, assumptions and intended use. Assumptions must be specific and traceable so a reviewer can judge whether the model is being used appropriately.

questions.questionText: In a simple calibration where you fit a linear model y = a x + b to data, which pair correctly identifies x and y?
options: x is the response/output you are trying to predict; y is the input/control variable
x is the input/predictor variable; y is the response/output variable
x and y can be swapped without changing the fitted parameters
x must always be time; y must always be cost
questions.rationale: Conventionally x is the predictor/input and y is the output/response (B). Swapping changes the fitted parameters unless the relationship is symmetric (C). Variables are not restricted to time/cost (D).

questions.questionText: Scenario (units): A temperature-dependent viscosity model expects temperature in kelvin (K). Your operational dataset records 25.0 °C. What value should be entered into the model, and why does this matter for calibration?
questions.correctAnswer: Enter 298.15 K (25.0 + 273.15). It matters because calibration adjusts parameters to match outputs; if temperature is entered in the wrong unit, the model will be systematically wrong and the fitted parameters will compensate incorrectly, reducing transferability and making validation fail.
questions.rationale: This checks unit correctness (M7-LO2) and highlights how unit errors distort parameter estimation (M7-LO1).

questions.questionText: Calculation (parameter fitting): You are modelling a pump where flow rate Q is approximated by Q = k √(ΔP), with Q in L/min and ΔP in kPa. Using an operational data point ΔP = 36 kPa, Q = 120 L/min, estimate k. (Give units for k.)
questions.rationale: This assesses basic parameter estimation from operational data and correct unit handling. Stating units for k supports auditability and dimensional reasoning.

questions.questionText: Which outcome is the clearest warning sign that your calibrated model may be overfitting the calibration dataset?
options: The model has a small residual error on the calibration dataset but performs poorly on new/hold-out data
The model contains variables with clearly defined units
The model output is reported with consistent rounding
The calibration dataset includes measurement noise
questions.rationale: Overfitting is characterised by excellent fit to calibration data but weak generalisation (A). Units and rounding are good practice, not overfitting (B, C). Noise is common and does not itself prove overfitting (D).

questions.questionText: Short answer: Give TWO practical ways to document parameter sources so that a colleague (or auditor) can reproduce the calibration six months later.
questions.correctAnswer: Any two such as: (1) cite the exact dataset location and version (file name, path, date range, data extract query, hash/checksum); (2) record the fitting method and settings (e.g., least squares, weighting, constraints) and the software/library version; (3) include a table of parameters with units, values, confidence/uncertainty, and source type (measured/fitted/vendor spec); (4) store scripts/notebooks in version control with a tagged release used for calibration.
questions.rationale: M7-LO1 and M7-LO2 emphasise transparency and reproducibility; parameter provenance is central to both.

questions.questionText: Dimensional check: Which expression is dimensionally inconsistent (i.e., cannot be correct because of unit mismatch)?
options: Speed v (m/s) = distance d (m) ÷ time t (s)
Energy E (J) = force F (N) × distance d (m)
Time t (s) = distance d (m) + speed v (m/s)
Pressure P (Pa) = force F (N) ÷ area A (m²)
questions.rationale: You cannot add quantities of different dimensions (metres and metres per second), so (C) fails a dimensional sanity check. The other expressions are dimensionally consistent.

questions.questionText: Scenario (tolerance and rounding): A stakeholder specification says a shaft diameter must be 50.0 ± 0.2 mm. Your model predicts 50.17 mm. If you round to 1 decimal place you would report 50.2 mm. How should you report the result to avoid a misleading tolerance decision, and what is the correct pass/fail conclusion?
questions.correctAnswer: Report using sufficient precision (e.g., 50.17 mm) and state rounding policy; do not round in a way that changes the tolerance decision. With limits 49.8 to 50.2 mm, 50.17 mm is within tolerance (pass). Rounded-to-1dp reporting could misleadingly appear on the boundary.
questions.rationale: M7-LO2 requires correct rounding and tolerance checking. Decisions must be based on appropriate precision, with a documented rounding approach.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes a local (one-at-a-time) sensitivity analysis?
options: Vary one input parameter slightly around a baseline while keeping others fixed, and observe the output change
Randomly vary all parameters across their full plausible ranges and compute output distributions
Change the model structure (equations) and compare the outputs
Only analyse sensitivity when the model has already failed validation
questions.rationale: Local sensitivity perturbs one parameter at a time around a nominal point (A). Option (B) describes global/Monte Carlo style analysis. (C) is model-form uncertainty, not parameter sensitivity. (D) is incorrect practice.

questions.questionText: Scenario (reproducible calculations): Your colleague reruns your calibration and gets slightly different parameter values. Give THREE likely causes and ONE concrete action you would take to ensure reproducibility next time.
questions.correctAnswer: Likely causes (any three): different data extract/filtering (date range, missing values), different software/library versions or solver settings, random initialisation/seed in optimisation, different unit conversions or rounding, or an updated dataset. Action (one): place code and data extract steps under version control, pin package versions (e.g., requirements/lockfile), record random seed, and tag the calibration run with a release and dataset hash.
questions.rationale: This targets M7-LO2: reproducibility, correct rounding/unit handling and traceable calculations, which are essential for reliable calibration work in professional settings.

formativeAssessments.title: MCQ Knowledge Check: Validation, Sensitivity and Audit Readiness
formativeAssessments.description: A 12-question knowledge check emphasising validation evidence, fitness-for-purpose decisions, sensitivity interpretation and version control expectations in professional modelling work.
formativeAssessments.instructions: Time guide: 20 minutes. Answer all questions. For short-answer/scenario questions, keep to bullet points. Use the feedback to identify which validation and audit practices you need to strengthen.
assessmentCriteria: Correct distinction between calibration and validation and appropriate selection of validation methods
Accurate interpretation of tolerance, dimensional and sensitivity results
Evidence-based judgement of fitness-for-purpose against stakeholder requirements
Appropriate documentation practices: validation evidence, version control and corrective actions

questions.questionText: What is the primary purpose of model validation?
options: To tune parameters until the model matches the calibration dataset as closely as possible
To check whether the model is fit-for-purpose for its intended use and stakeholder requirements
To ensure the model contains as many variables as possible
To ensure the model is written in a programming language approved by the organisation
questions.rationale: Validation is about fitness-for-purpose against requirements (B). Parameter tuning is calibration (A). More variables can harm generalisation (C). Language choice is not validation (D).

questions.questionText: A dimensional check is most directly intended to detect:
options: Whether the model is unbiased on a hold-out dataset
Whether terms being added/subtracted have compatible units and the equation makes physical/unit sense
Whether stakeholders agree with the model outputs
Whether the model is fast enough to run within one second
questions.rationale: Dimensional checking catches unit inconsistencies and nonsensical equations (B). Bias/hold-out relates to validation statistics (A). Stakeholder agreement and run-time are different concerns (C, D).

questions.questionText: In a tolerance check, what does it typically mean if a model output is 'within tolerance'?
options: The model is proven correct and does not need version control
The output lies within the agreed acceptable limits for the specified context and measurement precision
The output exactly matches the calibration data with zero error
The model does not require assumptions to be stated
questions.rationale: Within tolerance means it meets agreed limits for that use (B). It does not prove universal correctness (A) and does not imply zero error (C) or remove the need for assumptions (D).

questions.questionText: When is it most appropriate to validate using a hold-out dataset (data not used during calibration)?
options: Always, even if you only have five total data points
When you have sufficient operational data to separate calibration and validation without undermining either
Only when the model has no parameters
Only when stakeholders request a visually appealing report
questions.rationale: Hold-out validation is appropriate when data volume/coverage supports it (B). With very limited data, other validation approaches may be needed (A). Parameter-free models can still be validated (C). Reporting aesthetics are not a method choice (D).

questions.questionText: Scenario (fitness-for-purpose): A stakeholder requires a forecasting model to predict next-day material usage within ±5% on at least 90% of days. On a 30-day validation set, 26 days fall within ±5%. Is the model fit-for-purpose under this requirement, and what should you document?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes: 26/30 = 86.7% is below 90%, so it is NOT fit-for-purpose under the stated requirement. Document the requirement, the validation method and dataset (date range), the calculation (26/30), the shortfall, and proposed corrective actions (e.g., additional predictors, re-calibration with more representative data, or renegotiation of requirement if justified).
questions.rationale: This directly targets M7-LO3: evaluate against stakeholder criteria with documented validation evidence and corrective actions.

questions.questionText: You plot residuals (observed − predicted) against predicted values and notice the spread of residuals increases as predictions increase (a 'fan shape'). This most strongly suggests:
options: Homoscedastic errors (constant variance), so the model is perfect
Heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance), implying errors grow with magnitude and uncertainty treatment may be needed
A dimensional inconsistency in the equation
That the model must be replaced by a completely different programming language
questions.rationale: A fan-shaped residual plot indicates non-constant error variance (B). It is not constant variance (A). Dimensional issues are different (C). Language choice is irrelevant (D).

questions.questionText: A sensitivity summary shows normalised sensitivities: parameter A = 0.10, parameter B = 0.85, parameter C = 0.05. If you can only improve the measurement accuracy of one parameter to reduce output uncertainty, which should you prioritise?
options: Parameter A, because it is the first listed
Parameter B, because it has the largest normalised sensitivity
Parameter C, because it is smallest and therefore easiest to fix
None; sensitivity analysis cannot inform measurement priorities
questions.rationale: The largest normalised sensitivity indicates the output is most responsive to that parameter, so improving B reduces uncertainty most effectively (B). The other options do not follow sensitivity logic.

questions.questionText: Short answer: Provide THREE pieces of evidence you would include in a validation pack to support an audit of a mathematical model used in operations.
questions.correctAnswer: Any three such as: (1) stakeholder requirements/acceptance criteria and intended-use statement; (2) validation dataset description (source, time window, exclusions, data quality checks); (3) validation results (error metrics, tolerance pass rates, plots) with units/rounding policy; (4) dimensional check results; (5) model version identifier (tag/commit hash) and change log; (6) record of corrective actions and re-validation after changes.
questions.rationale: M7-LO3 expects documented validation evidence and audit readiness; this question focuses on what an auditor needs to recreate and trust the validation conclusion.

questions.questionText: Which version control practice best supports traceability of a validated model release used in decision-making?
options: Overwriting the same file name each time to avoid confusion
Tagging a release (or recording a commit hash) and linking it to the exact validation evidence and dataset version
Keeping changes only on a local laptop to prevent others editing the model
Only saving screenshots of results rather than the code
questions.rationale: A tagged release/commit hash linked to validation artefacts gives strong traceability (B). Overwriting files and local-only changes harm auditability (A, C). Screenshots alone are not reproducible (D).

questions.questionText: Scenario (corrective actions): During validation you discover a unit mismatch: one data feed provides mass in pounds (lb) but the model assumes kilograms (kg). List TWO corrective actions and ONE item you would add to the audit trail/change log.
questions.correctAnswer: Corrective actions (two): (1) implement explicit unit conversion (lb to kg) at ingestion with automated tests; (2) update data validation checks to flag unexpected units/ranges and re-run calibration/validation as needed. Audit trail item (one): log the defect, impact assessment (which outputs were affected), the code change reference (commit/tag), and the date/person approving the fix, plus re-validation results.
questions.rationale: This assesses M7-LO3: documenting corrective actions and ensuring validation remains credible after changes, with traceability for audit.

questions.questionText: Which action most directly improves computational reproducibility of model results across different machines?
options: Using more colourful charts in the report
Pinning software/library versions (e.g., using a lockfile) and recording the execution environment details
Deleting intermediate calculation steps to keep the code short
Rounding all values to the nearest whole number
questions.rationale: Environment pinning and recording versions prevents differences caused by dependency updates or numeric changes (B). The other options do not address reproducibility and may reduce transparency/accuracy (A, C, D).

questions.questionText: Calculation (normalised sensitivity): A model output is y = 200 (units). When parameter p increases by 2% (Δp/p = 0.02), the output increases to y = 206. Calculate the normalised sensitivity S = (Δy/y) / (Δp/p).
questions.rationale: Normalised sensitivity compares proportional output change to proportional parameter change. Here the output changes 1.5 times as much (proportionally) as the parameter, indicating high influence.

formativeAssessments.title: Short Quiz: Integrated Model Build, Traceability and Decision Outputs
formativeAssessments.description: A 12-question quiz checking your ability to plan, build and explain a reproducible workplace-style model with clear assumptions, traceability and decision-ready outputs.
formativeAssessments.instructions: Complete this quiz after working through the capstone briefing and example model structures. Allow 25 minutes. Answer all questions. For short-answer questions, keep responses concise but specific (2–5 sentences).
assessmentCriteria: Model structure supports reproducibility and traceable calculations
Appropriate selection and interpretation of analysis/optimisation outputs
Recommendations are evidence-based and recognise constraints
Communication is clear for non-specialists (units, assumptions, visuals)

questions.questionText: You are building a pricing model in Excel for a small wholesaler. Which workbook structure best supports reproducibility and traceability?
options: Put everything on one sheet so users can see all calculations at once
Use separate sheets for Inputs, Calculations and Outputs, with an assumptions log and consistent naming
Hide all calculations and only show final outputs to reduce confusion
Copy and paste values from emails directly into formula cells each week
questions.rationale: Separating inputs, calculations and outputs improves traceability, makes auditing easier, and supports repeatable updates. Hiding calculations or mixing data entry with formulas makes errors harder to spot and reproduce.

questions.questionText: In a Python notebook used for the capstone, which practice MOST improves reproducibility for a team review next month?
options: Hard-code file paths and manually run cells until it works
Add a single screenshot of the final chart to the notebook
Use a requirements file (or environment specification), fixed random seed where relevant, and a clear run order with functions
Remove comments to keep the notebook short
questions.rationale: An environment specification, controlled randomness (when used), and clear execution order allow others to rerun the analysis reliably. Hard-coded paths and manual execution reduce reproducibility.

questions.questionText: Short answer: Give TWO assumptions you would explicitly document in an assumptions log for a workplace pricing model (e.g., setting a selling price for a service package).
questions.correctAnswer: Examples (any two, clearly stated): (1) Demand is assumed to remain within a stated range for the price tested (e.g., 180–220 units/week). (2) Unit variable cost is assumed constant at £X (no bulk discounts). (3) Fixed overheads are assumed £Y per month and do not change with volume in the model range. (4) VAT is excluded/included consistently and stated. (5) Capacity constraint is fixed at Z labour-hours/week. (6) No stockouts/backorders assumed (or explicitly modelled).
questions.rationale: LO1 requires documented assumptions so stakeholders can judge whether results apply. Pricing outputs are only as valid as the assumptions about demand, costs, tax treatment and capacity.

questions.questionText: A manager asks: “What price gives us exactly £12,000 monthly profit, assuming demand stays at 500 units?” Which Excel tool is the most appropriate starting point?
options: Goal Seek (set Profit cell to 12000 by changing Price)
Solver with multiple changing cells and constraints
A PivotTable
Conditional formatting
questions.rationale: Goal Seek is designed for a single target value by changing one input. Solver is more suitable when there are multiple decision variables and constraints (optimisation).

questions.questionText: Calculation: A product sells for £38 per unit. Variable cost is £23 per unit. Monthly fixed costs are £4,800. If you sell 420 units in a month, what is the monthly profit (to the nearest £)?
questions.correctAnswer: Contribution per unit = 38 − 23 = £15. Total contribution = 420 × 15 = £6,300. Profit = 6,300 − 4,800 = £1,500.
questions.rationale: This checks correct use of contribution margin logic in workplace pricing models: Profit = (Price − Variable cost)×Volume − Fixed costs.

questions.questionText: You are optimising weekly production of two items (A and B). Each A uses 2 machine-hours; each B uses 5 machine-hours. You have 100 machine-hours available. Which constraint correctly represents machine capacity?
questions.rationale: A capacity constraint limits resource use: total hours used (2A + 5B) must not exceed 100, hence ≤ 100.

questions.questionText: Scenario: You plot monthly defect rate (%) for 18 months and see a steady decline until month 12, then a sharp increase from months 13–15, then stabilisation. For a recorded team review, what is the BEST description of the turning point?
options: There is no turning point because the final three months are stable
The turning point occurs around month 12–13 where the trend changes direction from improving to worsening
The turning point is month 1 because that is the start of the dataset
The turning point is month 18 because it is the latest month
questions.rationale: A turning point is where the trend changes direction or behaviour. The described shift from decline to sharp increase is around months 12–13.

questions.questionText: Which visual is MOST appropriate to show whether a KPI (e.g., average handling time) is improving month-by-month over a year?
options: Line chart with time on the x-axis and units clearly labelled
Pie chart of each month’s contribution to the annual total
Single stacked bar chart with no axis labels
A table only, with no visualisation
questions.rationale: A line chart is best for time trends and makes turning points visible. Pie charts are not suitable for time series trends.

questions.questionText: Short answer: Describe ONE validation check you would build into your Excel/Python model to catch errors early (be specific about what you would compare or test).
questions.correctAnswer: Examples (any one, specific): (1) Reconcile totals: sum of category volumes equals total volume from source data (difference should be 0). (2) Input sanity checks: flag if negative demand, price below variable cost, or utilisation above 100%. (3) Back-test: run the model on last month’s data and compare predicted vs actual profit within an acceptable tolerance. (4) Unit tests in Python for key functions (e.g., profit calculation) with known inputs/outputs.
questions.rationale: Validation supports trustworthy outputs (LO2/LO1). The check must be defined so it can actually detect common modelling errors (sign errors, missing rows, broken links, wrong units).

questions.questionText: In a technical report for non-specialists, which practice MOST improves clarity and reduces misinterpretation of charts and tables?
options: Remove axis labels to keep visuals clean
Include units, data source, and a one-sentence takeaway directly under each visual
Use as many colours as possible to increase engagement
Only present raw outputs without explanation so readers draw their own conclusions
questions.rationale: Non-specialist audiences need units, context and interpretation. A short takeaway reduces confusion and supports decision-making (LO4).

questions.questionText: Scenario + calculation: Your optimiser suggests producing 60 units of A and 8 units of B. Check whether this violates machine capacity from Question 6 (2 hours per A, 5 hours per B, 100 hours total).
questions.correctAnswer: Hours used = 2×60 + 5×8 = 120 + 40 = 160 hours. This violates capacity because 160 > 100.
questions.rationale: Optimisation outputs must be checked against constraints; if a solution violates constraints, the model setup or solver settings are wrong (LO2).

questions.questionText: Scenario (short answer): After peer review, a colleague says, “I can’t tell which numbers are inputs and which are calculated, and I’m not sure whether prices include VAT.” State TWO concrete changes you would make before final submission.
questions.correctAnswer: Two concrete changes (examples): (1) Create a dedicated Inputs sheet with consistent formatting (e.g., blue cells for inputs) and protect calculation cells; add named ranges or an input table. (2) Add an explicit VAT assumption note (e.g., ‘All prices exclude VAT’) on the cover page/README and on relevant output charts/tables. (3) Add an assumptions log and a data dictionary including units. (4) Add clear labels and references so outputs trace back to inputs.
questions.rationale: This checks the ability to respond to feedback and improve clarity for non-specialists, including assumptions and traceability (LO4 and LO1).

formativeAssessments.title: MCQ Knowledge Check: Uncertainty, Validation and Risk Statements for Workplace Decisions
formativeAssessments.description: A 12-question knowledge check focusing on interpreting uncertainty, choosing appropriate distributions/simulations, validating outputs, and communicating risk and limitations.
formativeAssessments.instructions: Complete this knowledge check after studying uncertainty, sensitivity and validation content. Allow 20 minutes. For the two short-answer items, write 3–6 sentences using plain, workplace-appropriate language.
assessmentCriteria: Correct interpretation of confidence intervals, distributions and probabilities
Appropriate selection of uncertainty methods (CI vs simulation) for the context
Identification of limitations, constraints and practical mitigations
Clear, balanced risk communication for non-specialists

questions.questionText: What does a 95% confidence interval for a mean MOST accurately represent?
options: There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies in this interval for this specific dataset
If we repeated the sampling process many times, 95% of similarly constructed intervals would contain the true mean
95% of individual data points lie inside the interval
The sample mean is wrong 95% of the time
questions.rationale: Confidence intervals are about long-run performance of the method across repeated samples, not the probability of the parameter for a single computed interval.

questions.questionText: All else equal, increasing sample size from n=25 to n=100 will usually make a confidence interval for the mean:
options: Wider, because more data creates more variability
Narrower, because the standard error decreases with larger n
Unchanged, because confidence level determines the width
Invalid, because confidence intervals cannot be used above n=30
questions.rationale: Standard error scales with 1/√n, so more data typically reduces uncertainty in the estimated mean.

questions.questionText: Calculation (95% CI): A process has sample mean 50.0, sample standard deviation 10.0, and n=25. Using t≈2.06, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean?
questions.rationale: Standard error = s/√n = 10/5 = 2. Margin = 2.06×2 = 4.12, so CI ≈ (45.9, 54.1).

questions.questionText: Plain-language interpretation: Your report states “Average weekly demand is 110 units (95% CI: 106 to 114)”. Which explanation is BEST for non-specialists?
options: There is a 95% chance that next week’s demand will be between 106 and 114
We are fairly confident the long-run average weekly demand is between 106 and 114 units, assuming our data and method are appropriate
106 to 114 covers 95% of all weekly demand values
The demand will never be outside 106 to 114
questions.rationale: A CI refers to uncertainty in the estimated mean, not the spread of individual weeks. The best statement also flags assumptions/limitations.

questions.questionText: You are modelling delivery lead times that cannot be negative and occasionally have long delays (a long right tail). Which distribution is often a good first choice to test?
options: Normal distribution (because it is symmetrical and can be negative)
Uniform distribution (because all lead times are equally likely)
Lognormal distribution (because values are positive and can be right-skewed)
Bernoulli distribution (because lead time is yes/no)
questions.rationale: Lead times are typically positive and can be skewed; lognormal often fits that behaviour better than a normal distribution.

questions.questionText: In a Monte Carlo simulation to estimate monthly profit risk, which sequence is MOST appropriate?
options: Pick one ‘best guess’ profit and repeat it 10,000 times
Randomly sample uncertain inputs (e.g., demand, cost), calculate profit each run, then summarise the profit distribution (e.g., percentiles)
Change one input at a time while keeping all others fixed, then pick the largest profit
Only simulate outputs; inputs must stay constant to keep the model stable
questions.rationale: Monte Carlo simulation propagates input uncertainty through the model to produce an output distribution that can be summarised with percentiles, probabilities and ranges.

questions.questionText: Calculation (probability): Weekly demand is approximately Normal with mean 110 and standard deviation 8. If weekly capacity is 120, what is P(demand > 120) approximately? (Use z = (120−110)/8 = 1.25 and Φ(1.25)≈0.894)
options: About 0.894
About 0.106
About 0.500
About 0.006
questions.rationale: P(demand > 120) = 1 − Φ(1.25) ≈ 1 − 0.894 = 0.106, i.e., about a 10.6% risk of exceeding capacity.

questions.questionText: Which statement BEST describes sensitivity analysis in a workplace maths model?
options: A method to make charts more visually appealing
A method to identify which inputs most influence key outputs, by varying inputs and observing output changes
A method to guarantee the model is correct
A method to remove uncertainty from decisions
questions.rationale: Sensitivity analysis explores how changes in assumptions/inputs affect results, helping prioritise what to measure, control or mitigate (LO3).

questions.questionText: Scenario (short answer): Write a balanced risk statement for a manager considering a new price that increases expected profit but may increase the chance of missing weekly capacity. Your statement must include (i) one quantified risk, (ii) one limitation, and (iii) one practical mitigation.
questions.correctAnswer: Example answer: “At the proposed price, expected weekly profit increases by about £1.2k, but there is an estimated ~11% chance demand exceeds our 120-unit capacity (based on recent demand variability). This risk estimate assumes demand remains approximately normal and that recent weeks are representative; a marketing campaign or seasonality could change the distribution. Mitigation: cap promotional volume, add overtime/temporary capacity for peak weeks, and review the estimate weekly with updated actuals.”
questions.rationale: LO3 requires uncertainty plus limitations and mitigations; LO4 requires clear, decision-ready language rather than purely technical outputs.

questions.questionText: During validation you plot residuals (actual − predicted) over time and see a clear upward trend. What does this MOST likely indicate?
options: The model errors are random noise, so the model is well-calibrated
A systematic bias or missing time-related factor (e.g., seasonality, drift) that the model is not capturing
The residual plot proves the model is correct
Residuals trending upward means the data are definitely fraudulent
questions.rationale: A pattern in residuals suggests model misspecification (non-random errors), such as drift or a missing variable, rather than good fit.

questions.questionText: Quality context: A call centre tracks the proportion of calls that breach a service target each day. Which tool is MOST appropriate to monitor whether the process is stable over time?
options: A p-chart (proportion control chart) because the metric is a proportion
A histogram of call durations because it shows the average
A scatter plot of agent ID vs day number
A pie chart of breaches by weekday
questions.rationale: A p-chart is designed for monitoring proportions/defect rates over time and helps identify special-cause variation relevant to operational quality decisions.

questions.questionText: Short answer: For a recorded team review, identify TWO constraints you should explicitly state when presenting an optimisation or pricing recommendation, and explain briefly why each matters.
questions.correctAnswer: Example answer (any two, with why): (1) Capacity constraint (machine-hours/labour-hours): limits feasible output; ignoring it creates unrealistic plans. (2) Minimum margin or price floor: prevents pricing below variable cost/required margin. (3) Demand limit or elasticity range: recommendations may fail if demand response is outside the tested range. (4) Budget constraint: limits spend on inputs/marketing and affects achievable volume. (5) Quality/service constraint: prevents profit optimisation that damages quality KPIs.
questions.rationale: LO2 and LO4 require communicating constraints that determine feasibility and decision risk; stating them prevents overconfident recommendations.

summativeAssessments.title: Final Integrated Workplace Maths Assessment (Diploma)
summativeAssessments.overview: Integrated case study assessing algebra, functions, calculus, optimisation, statistics, probability, simulation and model validation using workplace-style evidence and communication.

components.name: Section A: Controlled Problem-Solving Exam
components.description: 2-hour closed-book exam: algebra, functions/graphs, calculus interpretation, optimisation setup, and model checks with full working and units.

tasks.description: Rearrange formulae; solve for target output/price; show units, rounding and assumptions.
Analyse a function/graph; identify break-even, turning points and constraints; justify recommendation.
Differentiate/integrate given functions; interpret marginal and accumulated change in context.
Formulate an optimisation with objective and constraints; interpret shadow price/sensitivity meaning.
Apply dimensional/tolerance checks and explain rounding/precision impacts on a model output.

components.name: Section B: Practical Case Study Build (Excel or Python)
components.description: Build a traceable model from provided operational data; optimise, analyse uncertainty and report outputs with reproducible logs.

caseBrief.title: Operations Improvement for a Small Manufacturing Line
caseBrief.context: You are supporting a team to set pricing/volume targets, optimise staffing and inventory, monitor quality and quantify delivery risk.

tasks.description: Set up pricing/volume equations; solve for targets; document units, rounding and assumptions.
Graph key relationships; identify trends, intercepts, turning points and operational constraints.
Estimate marginal change from a fitted function; use integration to compute accumulated total over a period.
Use Solver (or equivalent) to optimise profit/cost with constraints; interpret sensitivity and limits.
Clean data; compute summaries and 95% confidence intervals; produce clear visuals for non-specialists.
Fit a distribution; run Monte Carlo to estimate risk of missing a delivery date and cost overrun.
Validate model: dimensional/tolerance checks, sensitivity test of key parameters, reproducibility steps.

components.name: Section C: Team Review Meeting Briefing (Oral Defence)
components.description: 10-min briefing + 5-min Q&A explaining findings, uncertainty, and recommendations using clear visuals and stakeholder language.
prompts: Explain your recommendation and the evidence from graphs and calculations.
Interpret one marginal value and one confidence interval in plain language.
Describe one key risk, its assumptions and how you mitigated or tested it.
Explain one validation or sensitivity check and what it changed (or did not change).

components.name: Section D: Technical Documentation Pack
components.description: Concise documentation pack: methods, assumptions, units/rounding, validation checks, risk register and reproducibility steps for audit.

criteria.name: Algebra, units, rounding and spreadsheet standards
criteria.description: Correct rearrangement/solving; consistent units; justified rounding; clear assumptions and traceable calculations.

levels.descriptor: All methods correct; units and rounding rules explicit; assumptions realistic; audit trail is clear and consistent.
Minor slips only; units mostly correct; rounding mostly justified; assumptions stated; calculations mostly traceable.
Solves standard problems; some unit/rounding inconsistencies; assumptions basic; traceability limited but present.
Frequent algebra errors; missing/incorrect units; unjustified rounding; assumptions unclear; work not traceable.

criteria.name: Functions, graphs and operational interpretation
criteria.description: Accurate graphs and analysis of trends, intercepts, turning points and constraints leading to evidence-based recommendations.

levels.descriptor: Graphs are clear and correctly scaled; interprets features and constraints precisely; recommendation strongly evidenced.
Graphs mostly clear; interpretation correct with minor gaps; recommendation supported with relevant evidence.
Basic graphs and interpretation; identifies some key features; recommendation partially supported.
Graphs unclear/incorrect; misinterprets features; recommendation not supported by analysis.

criteria.name: Calculus: marginal change and accumulation
criteria.description: Correct differentiation/integration (or data-based approximation) and correct contextual interpretation of marginal and total effects.

levels.descriptor: Calculus methods correct and efficient; interpretations precise; links results clearly to decisions and constraints.
Methods largely correct; interpretations mostly correct; links to decisions present with minor weaknesses.
Applies standard rules; interpretation simplistic or partially incorrect; limited decision linkage.
Incorrect or missing calculus; marginal/total concepts misunderstood; no meaningful decision linkage.

criteria.name: Optimisation and sensitivity using Solver (or equivalent)
criteria.description: Correct objective/constraints; appropriate Solver setup; interprets results, marginal values and sensitivity limits.

levels.descriptor: Model formulated correctly; constraints justified; Solver configured appropriately; sensitivity insights are accurate and actionable.
Formulation correct with minor issues; Solver run correctly; sensitivity interpretation mostly accurate.
Basic optimisation works; constraints partly justified; limited sensitivity interpretation.
Incorrect formulation or Solver misuse; results unreliable; sensitivity not attempted or incorrect.

criteria.name: Statistics for quality reporting (summaries, CIs, visuals)
criteria.description: Appropriate cleaning, descriptive statistics and confidence intervals; visuals are clear and suitable for non-specialists.

levels.descriptor: Correct methods and assumptions; CIs interpreted clearly; visuals are well-labelled and communicate quality insights effectively.
Methods correct with minor assumption gaps; CIs mostly correct; visuals clear with minor labelling issues.
Basic summaries produced; CIs attempted but limited; visuals present but may lack clarity or context.
Incorrect summaries/CIs; misleading visuals; results not interpretable for stakeholders.

criteria.name: Probability, distributions and simulation for risk
criteria.description: Appropriate distribution choice/fit and Monte Carlo simulation; quantifies risk with assumptions, uncertainty and limitations recorded.

levels.descriptor: Distribution choice justified; simulation well-constructed; risk metrics clear; assumptions and limitations explicitly recorded.
Approach appropriate; simulation runs correctly; risk metrics mostly clear; assumptions recorded with minor gaps.
Simulation attempted; limited justification; risk metrics basic; assumptions incomplete.
Incorrect probability modelling; simulation invalid or missing; risk not quantified or unsupported.

markingModel.componentWeightingRule: Final grade is the weighted sum of component marks (30/40/15/15). Rubric criteria are applied across relevant evidence in each component.
minimumRequirements: Achieve at least Pass on criteria 'Optimisation and sensitivity' OR 'Statistics for quality reporting' to meet higher-order outcome policy
academicIntegrityControls: Practical files must include calculation log or code cells showing workings
Viva questions verify authorship of model choices and results
Plagiarism detection may be applied to report text and code

mcq.stem: A product price is modelled as Profit = (p − c)q − F, where p is unit price ($/unit), c is unit variable cost ($/unit), q is quantity (units), and F is fixed cost ($). Rearrange to solve for the break-even price p when Profit = 0.
options: p = c + F/q
p = c − F/q
p = (F − cq)/q
p = (c + F)q
mcq.rationale: Set 0 = (p − c)q − F → (p − c)q = F → p − c = F/q → p = c + F/q. Units remain $/unit.

mcq.stem: In a spreadsheet, revenue is R = p·q and demand is q = 1200 − 30p (q in units, p in $/unit). Which expression is the revenue function R(p)?
mcq.rationale: Substitute q into R = p·q: R(p) = p(1200 − 30p) = 1200p − 30p^2.

mcq.stem: A calibration equation is L = k·V, where L is length (mm), V is voltage (V), and k is a calibration constant (mm/V). If L = 250 mm when V = 2.50 V, what is k (rounded to 3 s.f.)?
options: 100 mm/V

mcq.stem: A target output equation is q = (H·r)/t, where H is labour hours (h), r is rate (units/h), and t is cycle time factor (dimensionless). Solve for H in terms of q, r, and t.
options: H = (q·t)/r
H = (q·r)/t
H = (r·t)/q
H = q − r + t
mcq.rationale: q = (H·r)/t → q·t = H·r → H = (q·t)/r. Units: h = (units·1)/(units/h).

mcq.stem: A pricing sheet uses the formula Margin% = (p − c)/p. Solve for price p given cost c and a required margin m (as a decimal).
options: p = c/m

mcq.stem: A cost function is C(q) = 5000 + 12q + 0.04q^2 (C in $, q in units). What is the marginal cost at q = 100?
mcq.rationale: Marginal cost is C'(q) = 12 + 0.08q. At q = 100: 12 + 8 = 20 ($/unit).

mcq.stem: Weekly production output is modelled by q(t) = 200t − 5t^2 (units), where t is weeks. At what week is output maximised?
mcq.rationale: Max occurs when q'(t) = 200 − 10t = 0 → t = 20? Wait: 200 − 10t = 0 → t = 20. But that would be option B. Check: q(t)=200t-5t^2, derivative 200-10t, set to 0 gives t=20. So week 20.

mcq.stem: You use Excel Solver to minimise total cost subject to capacity constraints. Which practice best supports auditability of the optimisation?
options: Paste Solver output values over the original formulas to lock results
Keep the Solver model with named ranges, document constraints, and save a Solver report
Hide intermediate calculation columns to simplify the sheet
Use random starting values each time to test stability
mcq.rationale: Named ranges, documented constraints/objective, and saved Solver reports create a transparent, repeatable optimisation trail for audit.

mcq.stem: If demand D(p) decreases with price p, and you compute dD/dp = −35 units per $ at p = 10, which interpretation is correct?
options: Increasing price by $1 increases demand by about 35 units
Increasing price by $1 decreases demand by about 35 units near p = 10
Demand decreases by $35 per unit near p = 10
Price decreases by 35 units per $ near p = 10
mcq.rationale: A derivative of −35 units/$ means a $1 increase in price corresponds to ~35 fewer units demanded locally.

mcq.stem: A machine’s instantaneous power draw is P(t) = 3t^2 + 2 (kW), with t in hours. What is the energy used from t = 0 to t = 2 hours?
options: 8 kWh
12 kWh
16 kWh
20 kWh
mcq.rationale: Energy = ∫0^2 (3t^2 + 2) dt = [t^3 + 2t]0^2 = (8 + 4) = 12 kWh. (So correct is 12; adjust to option B.)

mcq.stem: A quality team reports sample mean fill volume x̄ = 501.2 ml from n = 36 bottles, with sample standard deviation s = 3.6 ml. Assuming normality, what is the 95% confidence interval for the mean (use t ≈ 2.03)?
mcq.rationale: SE = s/√n = 3.6/6 = 0.6. Margin = t·SE = 2.03·0.6 ≈ 1.22. That matches option B, not A. Correct is 501.2 ± 1.22 ml.

mcq.stem: In Excel, which chart type is most appropriate to communicate the distribution of cycle times to non-specialists?
options: Pie chart
Histogram
Radar chart
3D surface chart
mcq.rationale: A histogram directly shows the frequency distribution of a continuous metric like cycle time.

mcq.stem: You have two independent samples of defect rates from Line A and Line B. Which statistical method best compares their means when variances may differ?
options: Paired t-test
Two-sample t-test assuming equal variances
Welch’s two-sample t-test (unequal variances)
One-way ANOVA with blocking
mcq.rationale: Welch’s t-test is designed for comparing means of two independent groups when variances may be unequal.

mcq.stem: In Python/pandas, which operation most directly produces summary statistics (count, mean, std, quartiles) for a numeric column?
options: df.groupby('col')
df['col'].describe()
df.merge(other)
df.pivot_table(index='col')
mcq.rationale: Series.describe() returns standard descriptive statistics suitable for quality summaries.

mcq.stem: A process capability report includes a bar chart of defects by category. What additional statistic best supports prioritisation for improvement (Pareto principle)?
options: Median defect count
Cumulative percentage line on the same chart
Standard deviation of categories
A correlation matrix of categories
mcq.rationale: A Pareto chart uses bars plus a cumulative percentage line to identify the “vital few” categories.

mcq.stem: From operational data, throughput T(x) follows T(x) = −2x^2 + 40x, where x is staffing level (people). What staffing level maximises throughput?
mcq.rationale: For a quadratic ax^2+bx+c with a<0, maximum at x = −b/(2a) = −40/(2·−2)=10.

mcq.stem: A plot of inventory level vs time shows repeated sharp drops to near zero followed by gradual increases. Which operational interpretation is most plausible?
options: Continuous replenishment with no batch ordering
Batch ordering with periodic stock-outs or near stock-outs
Random measurement noise around a constant mean
Exponential growth in demand
mcq.rationale: Sawtooth inventory patterns typically indicate batch replenishment cycles and potential reorder point issues.

mcq.stem: When presenting a trend analysis in a team review, which statement is the strongest evidence-based recommendation format?
options: “I think we should change the schedule because it feels inefficient.”
“We should change the schedule; everyone agrees.”
“Data show peak queue length occurs at 14:00–16:00; shifting two staff to that window reduces average wait by 18% in the last 8 weeks.”
“Let’s try something different and see what happens.”
mcq.rationale: It ties the recommendation to measured evidence, a defined time window, and quantified impact.

mcq.stem: A constraint in a production model is 0 ≤ x ≤ 500. On a graph, what does this constraint represent?
options: A line with slope 500
A parabola opening upward
A feasible interval on the x-axis from 0 to 500
An unconstrained region for x
mcq.rationale: It restricts x to a bounded interval; graphically it is the segment of the x-axis between 0 and 500.

mcq.stem: A scatter plot of energy use vs output shows energy increases rapidly at high output, with a visible curve upward. Which model form best matches this pattern?
options: Linear: E = a + bq
Quadratic: E = a + bq + cq^2 (c>0)
Constant: E = a
Inverse: E = a + b/q
mcq.rationale: An upward-curving relationship (accelerating increase) is consistent with a positive quadratic term.

mcq.stem: A project task duration is modelled as Normal(μ=10 days, σ=2 days). Approximately what is P(duration > 14 days)?
options: About 50%
About 16%
About 2.5%
About 0.1%
mcq.rationale: 14 is (14−10)/2 = 2 standard deviations above the mean; tail beyond z=2 is ~2.5%.

mcq.stem: Monthly demand follows a Poisson distribution with λ = 3 returns per month. What is P(0 returns in a month)?
mcq.rationale: For Poisson, P(X=0)=e^(−λ)λ^0/0! = e^(−3).

mcq.stem: In a Monte Carlo simulation of total cost, the 95th percentile is $1.2M and the mean is $0.9M. Which risk statement is most appropriate for a risk register?
options: “Total cost will be $0.9M.”
“There is a 95% chance total cost is exactly $1.2M.”
“Based on simulation assumptions, there is ~5% chance total cost exceeds $1.2M.”
“The simulation proves the maximum cost is $1.2M.”
mcq.rationale: The 95th percentile implies ~5% probability of exceeding that value, conditional on model assumptions.

mcq.stem: A schedule risk model assumes task A and task B durations are independent. In reality they share the same resource and are positively correlated. What is the likely impact of ignoring this correlation in simulation?
options: It will typically underestimate the chance of long overall durations
It will typically overestimate the mean duration but not the tail risk
It will make no difference because correlation does not affect sums
It will eliminate uncertainty and make results deterministic
mcq.rationale: Positive correlation increases tail risk (more chance both run long together); assuming independence usually understates the probability of overruns.

mcq.stem: A risk register entry should include assumptions and limitations. Which item is most critical to record for a simulation-based cost risk estimate?
options: The colour theme used in the dashboard
The random seed, distribution choices, and data sources used for parameters
The number of columns in the spreadsheet
The job titles of all meeting attendees
mcq.rationale: Reproducibility and interpretability depend on parameter sources, distributional assumptions, and the ability to rerun the simulation (e.g., seed).

mcq.stem: A flow model uses Q = A·v, where Q is volumetric flow (m^3/s), A is area (m^2), and v is velocity (m/s). A technician enters A in cm^2 without converting. What validation check would most directly detect the error?
options: Dimensional analysis of units for Q
Sorting the data alphabetically
Using a pie chart of A values
Removing all decimals via rounding
mcq.rationale: Dimensional/unit checks reveal inconsistency (cm^2 vs m^2) and resulting incorrect magnitude for Q.

mcq.stem: A sensor specification states ±0.5% tolerance on a 200 kPa reading. What is the absolute tolerance band (kPa)?
options: ±0.5 kPa
±1.0 kPa
±10 kPa
±100 kPa

mcq.stem: A model output y depends on parameter a. When a increases by 1%, y increases by 3%. What is the sensitivity (elasticity) of y with respect to a?
mcq.rationale: Elasticity = (% change in y)/(% change in a) = 3%/1% = 3.

mcq.stem: You are documenting a reproducible calculation in Excel for a regulated report. Which practice best supports reproducibility?
options: Manually type intermediate results to save time
Use formulas with clearly labelled input cells, lock units, and store version-controlled copies of the file
Use circular references to avoid creating extra columns
Turn off automatic calculation and leave it off
mcq.rationale: Clear inputs, consistent units, formula-driven outputs, and version control allow others to reproduce and audit results reliably.

mcq.stem: A computed efficiency is reported as 0.87654. The technical standard requires reporting to 3 decimal places. What should be reported, and why?
options: 0.876, because you always round down for conservative reporting
0.877, because 0.87654 rounds to 0.877 at 3 d.p.
0.880, because rounding to 3 d.p. means rounding to the nearest 0.01
0.8765, because more precision is always better
mcq.rationale: To 3 d.p., look at the 4th decimal place: 0.8765… rounds up to 0.877; this matches standard rounding rules.

sjt.scenario: You are coordinating a maths certification exam session. A proctor reports they saw a candidate briefly looking at a smartwatch during the test. The proctor is unsure whether the device was used to access information, and the candidate denies wrongdoing. The test window is still active for other candidates today.

options.text: Follow the exam incident protocol: document the report, secure any relevant evidence (e.g., proctor statement, seat location, timing), escalate to the exams integrity lead immediately, and apply the standard candidate process (e.g., device removal, continued testing if policy allows).
Ask the proctor to warn the candidate and allow them to continue without recording the incident to avoid unnecessary stress.
Stop the candidate’s exam immediately and fail them on the spot to send a strong message.
Privately interview the candidate yourself during the session to determine intent, then decide whether to log it.

sjt.guidance: In certification settings, consistent application of exam-security policy is critical. The best response preserves evidence, applies documented procedures, and escalates appropriately to protect fairness for all candidates. Overly punitive or undocumented actions increase risk of appeals, inconsistency, and legal challenge.

sjt.scenario: A client school asks for ‘extra hints’ about which topics will appear on an upcoming maths certification exam because they have paid for a premium package. They imply they may switch providers if you don’t help.

options.text: Explain you cannot provide confidential exam content or predictive hints, offer legitimate support (published blueprint, sample items, skills list), and document the request with your manager/compliance team.
Provide general guidance that strongly suggests likely questions based on internal item bank trends, but keep it informal.
Share a few retired items from memory and advise them to focus on similar patterns.
Decline without explanation and end the conversation quickly to avoid conflict.

sjt.guidance: Protecting confidentiality and fairness is central to certification credibility. The preferred approach declines the improper request, provides permitted resources, and records the interaction for governance. Sharing ‘informal’ hints still undermines validity and can constitute misconduct.
