sjt.scenario: You are reviewing item statistics after a pilot. One algebra item shows unusually low performance across all groups and a higher omission rate than comparable items. A subject matter expert insists the item is ‘challenging but fair’ and wants it included unchanged.

options.text: Conduct a structured item review: check keying, wording, distractor plausibility, alignment to the blueprint, and differential performance; propose revisions or removal supported by data and SME input before operational use.
Include the item unchanged because the SME is experienced and the exam needs difficult questions.
Remove the item immediately based only on the low p-value without further investigation.
Split the difference by keeping the item but increasing the time limit to compensate.

sjt.guidance: Strong assessment decisions integrate psychometric evidence and content review. The preferred response investigates root causes (miskey, ambiguity, construct-irrelevance, misalignment) and documents a defensible decision. Relying solely on opinion or a single statistic is risky.

sjt.scenario: A candidate requests accommodations for dyslexia one week before the maths certification exam. They provide partial documentation and ask for extra time and a reader. The accommodations policy requires verification, and testing centers need notice.

options.text: Follow the accommodations process: acknowledge promptly, request the missing documentation, consider interim options allowed by policy, and coordinate with the center to implement any approved adjustments without compromising standardization.
Approve all requested accommodations immediately to be supportive, regardless of documentation, and notify the center later.
Deny the request because it is too close to the exam date and advise them to rebook next cycle.
Offer only extra time (not a reader) as a compromise, without referencing the policy, to keep things simple.

sjt.guidance: Fairness requires timely, policy-based accommodations that are properly verified and operationally feasible. The best approach balances candidate support with exam integrity and consistent treatment by following documented procedures and communicating clearly.

sjt.scenario: A marker messages you saying the rubric for a geometry proof question is ‘too strict’ and they have been awarding partial credit beyond the marking scheme to ‘reward good thinking.’ They already marked 60 scripts this way.

options.text: Pause the marker’s work, clarify the rubric requirements, arrange a quick standardization/calibration check, review the 60 scripts for consistency, and document corrective actions (including retraining if needed).
Tell them to continue as they are, since professional judgment is part of marking and it likely benefits candidates.
Instruct them to follow the rubric from now on but do not revisit the already marked scripts to avoid delay.
Quietly adjust final scores later by scaling to offset any generosity, without discussing it with the marker.

sjt.guidance: Marking reliability depends on standardization and adherence to the marking scheme. The preferred response corrects the issue quickly, re-aligns the marker, and audits impacted scripts to protect fairness and reduce appeal risk. Hidden scaling without transparency is hard to defend.

sjt.scenario: Two departments disagree about changing the exam blueprint: the content team wants more statistics items; the commercial team worries schools will complain about ‘too much data handling.’ You are asked to recommend a path forward under a tight deadline.

options.text: Facilitate a decision using evidence: review stakeholder needs, curriculum standards, performance data, and certification purpose; propose a phased change with clear communication, pilot testing, and impact monitoring.
Side with the commercial team to avoid complaints, since customer satisfaction is the priority.
Side with the content team immediately because they are the subject experts, and announce the change without consultation.
Delay the decision until both teams agree, even if that means missing the release deadline.

sjt.guidance: Blueprint decisions should be defensible, aligned to standards and purpose, and managed with change-control. The preferred option uses evidence, manages risks, and sets a practical implementation plan. Taking sides without analysis or missing deadlines both create avoidable harm.

sjt.scenario: During item writing, you notice a new question uses a real-world context that may disadvantage some candidates (e.g., assumes familiarity with a specific sport or cultural practice). The author argues it makes maths ‘more engaging.’

options.text: Recommend revising the context to a more universally accessible scenario (or removing it) while preserving the mathematical construct, and document the rationale as part of fairness and bias review.
Keep the context because engagement is important and candidates should be exposed to varied situations.
Remove the entire item from the bank immediately without discussion to avoid any risk.
Keep the item but add a glossary explaining the sport/cultural details inside the exam booklet.

sjt.guidance: Contexts should not introduce construct-irrelevant barriers. The preferred response preserves engagement while ensuring accessibility and fairness through revision and documented review. Adding in-exam glossaries can increase reading load and still disadvantage candidates under time pressure.

sjt.scenario: You discover a spreadsheet used to calculate pass/fail decisions includes a formula error affecting one cohort’s results. Some candidates have already been issued certificates, and others were told they failed. Your manager is in meetings all day.

options.text: Immediately follow the incident and data-governance process: validate the error, quantify impact, freeze further communications, notify the responsible governance contact, and prepare a remediation plan (re-issue results, candidate messaging, root-cause prevention).
Quietly fix the spreadsheet and re-run results, then update records without telling anyone to avoid reputational damage.
Wait for your manager to return before doing anything, since it’s a sensitive issue.
Email all affected candidates immediately with an apology before confirming the exact impact, to be transparent quickly.

sjt.guidance: Resulting errors require controlled incident management: confirm facts, stop further harm, escalate, and communicate accurately with an approved plan. The preferred response balances urgency with governance, ensuring messages are correct and actions are auditable.

sjt.scenario: A training partner asks you to share candidate-level performance data (names and detailed topic scores) so they can market targeted remedial courses. They say candidates ‘won’t mind’ and it will help improve outcomes.

options.text: Decline sharing identifiable data, explain privacy obligations, and offer an approved alternative (aggregated, anonymized insights or opt-in consent process) via the proper data-sharing agreement route.
Share the data but remove names, keeping candidate IDs and email addresses so the partner can contact them efficiently.
Share everything requested because the goal is educational improvement and the partner is trusted.
Ignore the request and hope they stop asking.

sjt.guidance: Certification organizations must protect personal data and use clear lawful bases/consent. The preferred option provides a compliant path (anonymization, aggregation, consent, contracts) while maintaining trust and reducing legal and reputational risk.

sjt.scenario: The exam is scheduled to launch in two weeks. A late-stage review finds two items have minor formatting issues (one missing a unit label; one chart axis slightly unclear). Fixing them requires re-exporting and re-QA of the full paper, potentially delaying release.

options.text: Assess risk and severity: propose targeted corrections with controlled re-QA focused on impacted pages/items, confirm no content changes affect psychometrics, and update version control and sign-off documentation.
Launch as-is because the issues are minor and delaying would upset stakeholders.
Delay the full launch until the entire paper is re-exported and fully re-QA’d end-to-end, regardless of the minor nature of the issues.
Ask centers to verbally clarify the missing unit and axis during administration to avoid rework.

sjt.guidance: The best response balances quality and timelines using a controlled change process: fix what affects clarity/fairness, re-QA appropriately, and maintain traceability. Relying on centers to clarify introduces inconsistent administration; ignoring known issues undermines validity.

caseStudies.title: Summit Skills Awards: The £185 Price Cap Spreadsheet
caseStudies.scenario:
At 14:10 on a Thursday, Aisha Khan’s inbox filled with “URGENT” subject lines. The procurement lead at one of Summit Skills Awards’ largest training partners wanted a signed-off exam voucher price—today—stating a hard cap of £185 (gross, including VAT) per candidate. Aisha’s Excel workbook was open on her second screen, but a red flag stared back: the latest cost model used minutes in one section, hours in another, and a hidden rounding cell that changed totals by several pounds.

Organisational context
Summit Skills Awards Ltd is a fictitious UK-based awarding organisation that designs and administers professional maths certification exams for adults and apprentices. It runs around 1,200 exam sessions per year through approved centres, combining remote proctoring, printed candidate packs and digital results processing. The organisation is preparing for an internal audit of its pricing controls.

Background information
Aisha is an Assessment Operations Specialist who owns the monthly “voucher pricing” workbook used by Finance and the Centre Support team. The workbook estimates the net cost per candidate and recommends a gross selling price (including 20% VAT) to approved centres. Last quarter, an internal audit noted three issues: (1) inconsistent unit labelling (minutes vs hours), (2) ad-hoc rounding choices (whole pounds in one sheet; pennies in another), and (3) weak traceability (no change log and several unlabelled cells).

For September’s intake, Summit has forecast 420 candidates (with a plausible range of 380–470). Costs are a mix of fixed monthly charges (platform licence and item bank amortisation) and variable per-candidate charges (remote proctoring, print, postage and support time). Aisha inherited parts of the workbook from different colleagues. A recent edit changed the exam duration from 90 minutes to “1.3 hours” without documenting the conversion.

Challenge description
Aisha must produce a defensible price recommendation that (a) stays under the £185 gross cap, (b) achieves at least a 22% contribution margin on net price, and (c) can pass audit scrutiny. She must decide what to standardise first: units and labels, rounding rules, or spreadsheet structure (named ranges, check cells, and a change log). She also needs to confirm whether the target is feasible given the forecast candidate volume and the centre’s requested minimum of 400 candidates in September.

Data presentation
Key inputs are summarised in Exhibit 1. Exhibit 2 shows the September forecast by centre and the volume constraint (minimum 400 candidates). Exhibit 3 provides the audit extract and the required change-note format.

Decision point
By 17:00, Aisha must send the procurement lead a one-page pricing summary and the workbook for review. Should she (i) patch the existing workbook to meet the deadline, or (ii) rebuild the model using consistent units, explicit rounding and audit-ready spreadsheet standards—even if it risks missing the 17:00 request?
caseStudies.organizationalContext: Summit Skills Awards Ltd is a fictitious UK awarding organisation delivering professional maths certification exams through approved centres. It uses Excel-based costing and pricing models to set voucher prices, and is under increased audit scrutiny for calculation transparency, unit consistency and change control.
caseStudies.backgroundInformation: Aisha Khan, an Assessment Operations Specialist, maintains Summit’s voucher pricing workbook. An internal audit flagged inconsistent units, unclear rounding choices and limited traceability. A new training partner tender imposes a £185 gross price cap and requires evidence of robust calculations. September demand is forecast at 420 candidates (range 380–470), and one partner requires at least 400 candidates.
caseStudies.challengeDescription: Aisha must recommend an exam voucher price that remains under the £185 gross cap, achieves at least a 22% contribution margin on net price, and is transparent and auditable. She must correct unit inconsistencies (minutes vs hours), define rounding/significant-figure rules, and improve spreadsheet layout (references, named ranges, checks and change notes) under tight time pressure.
caseStudies.industryContext: Professional awarding and assessment services (maths certification provider) operating through UK-approved training centres; pricing models must be auditable and consistent with spreadsheet governance standards.

exhibitList.title: Exhibit 1: September Voucher Cost Model Inputs (as used in the workbook)
exhibitList.description: Table of fixed and variable costs, with stated units and the current rounding approach used in different worksheet sections (minutes vs hours; pennies vs whole pounds).

exhibitList.title: Exhibit 2: Candidate Forecast by Centre and Feasibility Constraint
exhibitList.description: Table of forecast candidate volumes by six centres, including a partner requirement of at least 400 candidates in September and a capacity cap per session; suitable for linear inequality checks.

exhibitList.title: Exhibit 3: Audit Extract and Required Change Log Format
exhibitList.description: Document excerpt listing audit findings and a template for recording assumptions, unit conventions, rounding rules, and change notes (who/what/why/when).

keyFacts: The partner tender imposes a maximum selling price of £185 gross (including VAT) per candidate.
VAT is 20% and is applied to the voucher selling price in the workbook.
The target contribution margin requirement is at least 22% on net price.
September candidate forecast is 420 candidates, with a plausible range of 380–470.
One partner requests a minimum of 400 candidates in September.
The exam duration is 90 minutes, but a recent workbook edit recorded it as “1.3 hours”.
Fixed monthly costs include a remote assessment platform licence of £12,500 and item bank amortisation of £3,000 (Exhibit 1).
Remote proctoring is charged at £22.40 per candidate (variable cost) (Exhibit 1).
Invigilator/support time is modelled as 0.15 hours per candidate at £18.60 per hour (Exhibit 1).
Printed formula booklet is 16 pages per candidate at £0.035 per page, with 4% wastage applied (Exhibit 1).
Certificate postage is £1.15 per candidate (Exhibit 1).
The audit previously flagged inconsistent unit labelling and ad-hoc rounding choices across worksheet tabs (Exhibit 3).
The current workbook contains at least one hidden rounding cell that affects totals by several pounds.
Aisha must send a pricing summary and the workbook for review by 17:00 the same day.
misconceptions: Treating £185 gross as the net price (forgetting to remove VAT using net = gross ÷ 1.20).
Converting 90 minutes to 1.3 hours without checking (90 minutes is 1.5 hours).
Rounding intermediate results to whole pounds before multiplying by candidate volume, increasing error propagation.
Mixing units (minutes and hours) in the same formula without conversion, leading to incorrect labour cost.
Applying the 22% margin requirement as cost × 1.22 instead of margin on price: (Price − Cost) ÷ Price.
Using relative cell references where absolute references or named ranges are needed, causing copied formulas to drift.
Ignoring the 4% print wastage factor or applying it twice in the print cost calculation.
decisionPoints: Should Aisha prioritise unit standardisation (minutes vs hours) before adjusting pricing and margin calculations?
Should she implement a single rounding policy (e.g., keep calculations to pennies, round only final price) even if it changes the recommended price?
Should Aisha rebuild the model using named ranges and a structured layout, or patch the existing workbook to meet the 17:00 deadline?
What feasibility check should be performed first to confirm the 22% margin is achievable under the £185 gross cap at 400–420 candidates?
Should Aisha document and lock key assumptions (VAT rate, exam duration, wastage) as controlled inputs with a change log before sharing externally?

terminology.definition: The selling price including VAT. In this case, the partner’s cap is stated as a gross amount, so VAT must be separated to obtain the net price used for margin calculations.
The selling price excluding VAT. Net price is calculated as gross price divided by (1 + VAT rate), and is typically used when comparing against net costs.
The proportion of net price remaining after variable and allocated costs are deducted. It is often expressed as (Price − Cost) ÷ Price and used to test profitability targets.
A spreadsheet practice ensuring every value is labelled and used with the correct measurement unit (e.g., hours, minutes, pounds). Conversions must be explicit to avoid silent errors.
A rounding convention indicating the meaningful digits in a number. Using appropriate significant figures helps communicate precision and prevents overstating certainty in workplace calculations.
The way rounding and measurement errors accumulate through multi-step calculations. Early rounding in a spreadsheet can materially change totals when multiplied by high volumes.
An Excel feature that assigns a readable name to a cell or range (e.g., VAT_Rate). It improves transparency, reduces reference errors, and supports auditing and maintenance.
An Excel cell reference fixed using dollar signs (e.g., $B$2) so it does not change when a formula is copied. It is essential for consistent use of constants and key inputs.
A linear constraint written as an inequality (e.g., candidates ≥ 400 or total sessions ≤ capacity). It is used to test whether targets can be met under stated limits.
A structured record of spreadsheet edits, documenting what changed, who changed it, when, and why. It supports traceability and is commonly required for audit-ready models.

teachingNote.synopsis: This case places learners in the role of Aisha Khan, an Assessment Operations Specialist at Summit Skills Awards Ltd, who must deliver an audit-ready Excel pricing workbook under a same-day deadline. A partner tender imposes a £185 gross (incl. VAT) price cap, while internal policy requires a minimum 22% contribution margin on net price. The existing workbook contains typical workplace risks: inconsistent units (minutes vs hours), ambiguous rounding choices, hidden cells affecting totals, and weak change control. Learners must interpret cost inputs, separate net and gross pricing, rearrange formulae to test margin feasibility, and propose spreadsheet build standards (named ranges, structured inputs/outputs, check cells, and change notes). The case is designed to elicit disciplined quantitative communication (units and labels), appropriate rounding decisions, and simple linear constraints to test whether candidate volume requirements and pricing rules can be satisfied simultaneously—without assuming a single “perfect” spreadsheet layout.
learningObjectives: Explain (Understand) how unit labelling, significant figures and rounding choices affect accuracy and credibility in workplace spreadsheets.
Apply (Apply) algebraic rearrangement to isolate variables (e.g., net price required for a target margin under a price cap).
Analyse (Analyse) a multi-step Excel model to identify sources of error propagation, inconsistent units and weak references.
Evaluate (Evaluate) feasibility of volume and pricing constraints using linear equations and inequalities.
Create (Create) an audit-ready spreadsheet improvement plan using named ranges, structured layout, check cells and a change log.
assignmentQuestions: From the £185 gross cap and 20% VAT, what is the maximum allowable net price per candidate? State your rounding rule and justify it.

Using Exhibit 1, set up the net cost-per-candidate expression (including allocation of fixed costs across volume). Rearrange to determine the net price required to achieve a 22% contribution margin at 420 candidates.
Test feasibility at 400 candidates and 420 candidates: can Summit meet the 22% margin without breaching the £185 gross cap? Clearly state any assumptions and where rounding occurs.
List the top five spreadsheet governance changes Aisha should implement immediately (units, references, named ranges, checks, change log) and explain how each reduces audit risk.
teachingNote.sessionPlan: Total suggested time: 75 minutes. (1) Individual read-through and exhibit scan (10 min). (2) Small-group calculations: net/gross conversion, cost expression, margin feasibility at two volumes (25 min). (3) Plenary: identify unit/rounding risks and error propagation points (15 min). (4) Plenary: spreadsheet build standards—named ranges, layout, checks, and change log (15 min). (5) Wrap-up: decision recommendation under deadline constraints (10 min).
teachingNote.answerGuidance: Q1: Convert gross to net using net = gross ÷ 1.20; learners should state a consistent rounding rule (e.g., keep net to 2 dp, round final gross to partner-friendly increments if required). Q2: Build total cost = fixed_costs/volume + variable_costs; ensure unit conversions are explicit (minutes↔hours), include wastage once, and keep intermediate values unrounded where possible. Margin algebra should use (P − C)/P ≥ 0.22, equivalent to P ≥ C/0.78. Q3: Evaluate feasibility under both volumes; highlight sensitivity of fixed-cost allocation and the impact of rounding and the 90-minute conversion error. Q4: Expected controls include: clearly labelled inputs with units; single input section; named ranges for VAT and key rates; absolute references for constants; check cells (e.g., reconciling minutes and hours); and a change log capturing assumption changes and timestamps.

caseStudies.moduleTitle: Workplace Maths Foundations: Units, Algebra and Spreadsheet Standards
caseStudies.title: QuantPath Certification: The Spreadsheet That Set the Price
caseStudies.scenario:
Aisha Khan stared at the pricing workbook on her screen and then at the email from Finance: “Please confirm the unit assumptions. Last quarter, margins were reported in £ but some costs appear to be in pence.” In three days, QuantPath Certification Services had to send a fixed-price quote to a large employer for 12 cohorts of its “Workplace Maths Foundations” programme. Aisha knew the quote would be audited, and the spreadsheet had become the single source of truth.

**Organisational Context (QuantPath Certification Services)**  
QuantPath is a fictitious UK-based provider of professional maths certification and short workplace programmes. It delivers blended learning (online + invigilated assessments) to employers and training partners. Pricing is built in Excel by the Assessment Operations team and signed off by Finance. Any spreadsheet error can lead to under-pricing, reputational damage, or a failed audit.

**Background Information**  
Aisha is an Assessment Operations Specialist responsible for building cost-and-price models for employer contracts. The current workbook evolved over time: colleagues copied tabs, overwrote formulas, and used “quick fixes” like hard-coded rates. A recent internal audit flagged weak traceability (no change log, inconsistent rounding, and unclear units). The employer tender now requires transparent assumptions: costs must be shown per cohort and per candidate, and the quote must demonstrate how a volume discount still maintains a minimum contribution margin.

Aisha has the latest inputs (Exhibit 1) and a list of audit issues (Exhibit 2). The employer expects **12 cohorts** over a quarter, each cohort planned at **18 candidates**, with a contractual cap of **20 candidates** per cohort.

**Challenge Description**  
Aisha must rebuild the model to be auditable and mathematically sound: (1) standardise units (e.g., £ vs pence; hours vs minutes), (2) apply consistent significant figures/rounding rules, and (3) rearrange formulas to isolate key variables (e.g., “maximum discount allowed” to keep margin ≥ target). She must also test feasibility using inequalities: the team has limited invigilator capacity, and the quote cannot assume impossible staffing.

**Data Presentation (summary from Exhibit 1)**  
Inputs per cohort (planned):
- Venue hire: **£420.00** (fixed)
- Invigilator time: **6.5 hours** at **£28.40/hour** (variable by hours, not candidates)
- Candidate packs: **£3.75 per candidate**
- Certificates: **£1.20 per candidate**
- Payment processing: **2.1% of revenue + £0.20 per candidate**
- Overheads allocation: **12% of (venue + invigilator + packs + certificates)**

Pricing targets:
- List price: **£165 per candidate**
- Minimum contribution margin: **≥ 25% of revenue**
- Proposed volume discount for employer: between **5% and 15%** off list price

Capacity constraints:
- Available invigilator hours for the quarter: **78 hours**
- Each cohort requires invigilator hours = **6.5 + 0.05 × candidates** (additional checks)

**Decision Point**  
Aisha must decide, before sending the draft to Finance, which rounding and unit standards to lock into the spreadsheet, how to structure the workbook for audit (named ranges, checks, change log), and—based on the constraints—whether the employer can be offered 12 cohorts at 18 candidates each, and what the **maximum discount** can be while still meeting the **25% margin** requirement.
caseStudies.organizationalContext: QuantPath Certification Services is a fictitious UK professional maths certification provider serving employer clients. It relies on Excel-based pricing models for cohort-based training and invigilated assessments, with Finance sign-off and increasing audit scrutiny on calculation transparency, units, and change traceability.

A new employer tender requires a defensible, auditable model showing cost build-up, discount logic, and feasibility under invigilator-hour constraints.
caseStudies.challengeDescription: Aisha must rebuild the pricing spreadsheet to standardise units and rounding, document assumptions, and apply algebra to isolate key variables (e.g., discount, required price, minimum candidates). She must also use linear inequalities to test whether the staffing constraint makes the proposed delivery plan feasible, and produce an audit-ready workbook structure with checks and change notes.

QuantPath plans 12 cohorts over a quarter for the employer.
Planned candidates per cohort are 18, with a contractual cap of 20.
Venue hire is £420.00 per cohort (fixed).
Base invigilator time is 6.5 hours per cohort.
Additional invigilator time is 0.05 hours per candidate.
Invigilator hourly rate is £28.40 per hour.

misconceptions: Treating pence as pounds (or vice versa) when copying cost inputs into Excel.
Rounding intermediate calculations (e.g., invigilator cost) too early, causing compounded error in totals.
Applying the 12% overhead rate to revenue instead of the specified cost base.
Forgetting that payment processing includes both a percentage of revenue and a per-candidate fee.
Using relative cell references where absolute references or named ranges are required, leading to incorrect copied formulas.
Assuming 6.5 invigilator hours is fixed and ignoring the 0.05×candidates term in feasibility checks.
Checking feasibility per cohort but not aggregating across 12 cohorts against the 78-hour quarterly limit.
decisionPoints: Should Aisha standardise all money inputs and outputs to £ with two decimal places, while keeping internal calculations at higher precision?
Should Aisha use named ranges and a dedicated ‘Inputs’ tab to reduce referencing errors and improve auditability?
Should Aisha prioritise feasibility (invigilator hours) before optimising discount and margin, or model pricing first?
Should Aisha set the discount at the maximum allowed by margin, or choose a lower discount to create contingency for rounding/error and demand variability?

terminology.definition: A rule for expressing numerical precision. In workplace calculations it controls how many meaningful digits are retained, preventing false precision and helping align reported figures with measurement certainty.
A documented standard stating where and how to round (inputs, intermediate steps, outputs). It reduces inconsistency and helps prevent cumulative rounding error across multi-step spreadsheets.
The way small rounding or measurement errors accumulate through chained calculations. Spreadsheets can amplify these errors if values are repeatedly rounded or referenced inconsistently.
Ensuring all quantities use compatible units (e.g., £ not pence; hours not minutes). Mixing units without conversion is a common cause of pricing and reporting errors.
An Excel feature that assigns a meaningful name to a cell or range (e.g., InvigilatorRate). It improves readability, reduces referencing mistakes, and supports auditing.
A ratio showing profitability before fixed corporate costs: (Revenue − Direct/allocated costs) ÷ Revenue. It is often used as a contractual pricing requirement.
Manipulating an equation to isolate a chosen variable (e.g., discount). This is used to determine the maximum allowable discount that still meets a margin constraint.
A condition expressed with ≤ or ≥ (e.g., total hours ≤ available hours). Used to test feasibility of plans under capacity, budget, or policy limits.
A spreadsheet reference that stays fixed when copied (e.g., $B$2). It is essential when applying one rate or assumption consistently across multiple rows or scenarios.
A simple validation step (totals, bounds, cross-checks) designed to catch obvious errors, such as negative margins, impossible capacities, or unit-scale mistakes.

caseStudies.suggestedApproach:
1) **Define and label units first**: create an Inputs section where every figure has a unit (e.g., £/cohort, £/candidate, hours/cohort). Add a note specifying money is stored in £ (not pence) and time is stored in hours.

2) **Set a rounding and precision rule**: keep internal calculations at full precision (do not round intermediate steps). Round only final outputs for reporting (e.g., price to 2 decimals; margin to 1 decimal point). Document the rule on the sheet.

3) **Build a transparent spreadsheet layout**: separate tabs for Inputs, Calculations, and Outputs. Use named ranges (InvigilatorRate, VenueHire, OverheadRate). Avoid hard-coded numbers inside formulas.

4) **Construct the cost model step-by-step**: compute invigilator hours per cohort = 6.5 + 0.05×candidates; invigilator cost = hours×rate; variable candidate costs = (packs + certificates + 0.20)×candidates; overhead = 12%×(venue + invigilator + packs + certificates). Payment processing percent cost = 2.1%×revenue.

5) **Use algebra to isolate discount**: express price_per_candidate = 165×(1−discount). Write contribution margin as a function of discount and solve for the maximum discount meeting margin ≥ 25%.

6) **Test feasibility with inequalities**: total invigilator hours for quarter = 12×(6.5 + 0.05×candidates). Check whether this is ≤ 78 hours at 18 candidates; if not, solve for the maximum feasible candidates per cohort or maximum cohorts.

7) **Add audit checks and a change log**: include reasonableness checks (margin cannot be negative; discount within 5–15%; candidates ≤ 20). Record changes with date, what changed, and why.
caseStudies.sampleSolution:
Aisha should rebuild the workbook with a clear Inputs tab (all units labelled) and named ranges. She should store all money values in **£** with two decimals displayed, while keeping calculations unrounded until the final output. Time should be stored in **hours**. A visible rounding policy note should state: “No rounding in intermediate steps; final £ outputs to 2 dp; percentages to 1 dp.”

**Feasibility check (invigilator hours):**  
Invigilator hours per cohort = 6.5 + 0.05×candidates. At 18 candidates: 6.5 + 0.9 = **7.4 hours**. Over 12 cohorts: 12×7.4 = **88.8 hours**, which exceeds the available **78 hours**. Therefore, the plan “12 cohorts at 18 candidates” is **not feasible** under current capacity.

Solve the inequality for candidates given 12 cohorts:  
12×(6.5 + 0.05c) ≤ 78  
6.5 + 0.05c ≤ 6.5  
0.05c ≤ 0  
c ≤ 0  
This implies even with zero candidates, 12 cohorts consume 12×6.5 = 78 hours exactly. The additional 0.05×candidates makes any positive candidate count infeasible. Aisha should flag that either (a) invigilator capacity must increase, (b) the number of cohorts must reduce, or (c) the invigilation model must change (e.g., lower base hours or different staffing approach). This is the priority to resolve before pricing.

**Pricing structure (once feasibility is addressed):**  
Set price per candidate P = 165×(1−d). Revenue per cohort = P×c. Build cost per cohort as:
- Venue: 420
- Invigilator: (6.5 + 0.05c)×28.40
- Candidate costs: (3.75 + 1.20 + 0.20)×c
- Overheads: 0.12×(venue + invigilator + (3.75+1.20)×c)
- Payment processing: 0.021×revenue
Contribution margin = (revenue − total_cost)/revenue.

Aisha should implement an Excel ‘Goal Seek’ or algebra block to find the **maximum discount d** satisfying margin ≥ 25% for the agreed feasible cohort plan (c and number of cohorts). She should add checks to prevent discounts outside 5–15% and to warn if any unit assumptions change. Finally, she should include a change log and an outputs dashboard for Finance showing: feasible delivery quantities, price per candidate, total revenue, total cost, and margin (rounded consistently).

teachingNote.synopsis: This practice case places learners in a realistic spreadsheet pricing and feasibility scenario within a fictitious professional maths certification provider. Aisha Khan must produce an audit-ready Excel model for an employer tender while addressing prior audit findings: mixed units, inconsistent rounding, and poor transparency. Learners work with clearly stated inputs to apply workplace maths foundations: unit discipline, significant figures and rounding policy, algebraic rearrangement to isolate key variables (such as discount or price), and linear inequalities to test feasibility under capacity constraints. The case deliberately includes a staffing constraint that forces learners to prioritise feasibility checks before finalising price. The teaching focus is on building trustworthy spreadsheets: separating inputs/calculations/outputs, using named ranges and consistent referencing, documenting assumptions, and adding reasonableness checks and change notes. The case supports formative learning through a structured approach and a sample solution outline rather than a single ‘correct’ numeric answer.
learningObjectives: Remember/Understand: Define and apply consistent units and labelling for workplace calculations (Bloom: Understand).
Apply: Implement significant figures and rounding rules appropriately and explain how rounding errors propagate across spreadsheet steps (Bloom: Apply).
Apply/Analyse: Rearrange pricing and margin equations to isolate a variable such as discount or required price (Bloom: Analyse).
Analyse: Use linear equations and inequalities to test feasibility of delivery targets under capacity constraints (Bloom: Analyse).
Apply: Build a transparent spreadsheet structure using named ranges, separation of inputs/calculations/outputs, and audit checks (Bloom: Apply).
assignmentQuestions: What unit and rounding standards should be applied in the workbook, and at which steps should rounding occur (inputs, intermediate calculations, outputs)?
Using the invigilator-hours relationship, is the plan for 12 cohorts at 18 candidates feasible under a 78-hour quarterly capacity? Show the inequality and interpretation.
How would you structure the Excel workbook to improve auditability (tabs, named ranges, checks, change log)? Provide a brief layout plan.
Which equation(s) would you rearrange to solve for the maximum allowable discount given a minimum contribution margin of 25%, and what variables must be clearly defined?
teachingNote.sessionPlan: 60–75 minutes total: (1) 10 min individual read and highlight units/constraints; (2) 15 min unit/rounding policy and error-propagation discussion; (3) 20 min feasibility inequality work (pairs); (4) 15 min spreadsheet standards (named ranges, layout, checks); (5) 5–15 min debrief linking to audit needs and tender risk.
teachingNote.answerGuidance: Q1: Expect a documented rounding policy; avoid rounding intermediate values; keep internal precision; round final £ to 2 dp and % to 1 dp; explicitly label £, hours, candidates. Q2: Compute hours per cohort and total; recognise base hours already consume full capacity at 12 cohorts; interpret infeasibility and propose options (increase capacity/reduce cohorts/change model). Q3: Inputs/Calculations/Outputs separation; named ranges; no hard-coded constants; absolute references; validation checks (discount bounds, candidate caps, negative margin flags); change log with date/author/reason. Q4: Define price per candidate as function of discount; define revenue; define margin formula; rearrange or use Goal Seek; ensure consistent cost base for overheads and inclusion of percent + per-candidate processing fees.

caseStudies.suggestedTiming: Deploy after learners have covered units and rounding basics and have practised simple Excel formulas; use as a mid-module practice to integrate algebra, inequalities, and spreadsheet audit standards.

caseStudies.learningApplication: Applies M1-LO1 through M1-LO4 by requiring unit labelling, rounding decisions, algebraic rearrangement for pricing variables, transparent spreadsheet construction with traceable changes, and feasibility testing using linear inequalities.

caseStudies.moduleTitle: Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making
caseStudies.title: Northbridge Assessment Services: Pricing a Maths Exam Under Capacity Constraints
caseStudies.scenario:
Aisha Patel stared at the draft slide deck for tomorrow’s operations review, knowing one chart could trigger a costly decision. Northbridge Assessment Services’ Maths Certification exam had never been more popular—yet the test centre calendar was already near full. Aisha’s task was deceptively simple: recommend next quarter’s exam fee and decide whether to add evening sittings. The wrong recommendation could either leave revenue on the table or create a backlog of frustrated candidates.

Northbridge Assessment Services Ltd (NAS) is a UK-based certification provider delivering vocational Maths Certification exams through three regional test centres. The organisation runs standardised, computer-based sittings with trained invigilators and a central quality team. NAS competes on reliability and clear candidate communications, and its senior team expects operational decisions to be evidenced with simple, readable graphs suitable for non-specialist stakeholders.

Over the last six months, NAS adjusted the exam fee several times to manage demand. Aisha, an Operations Analytics Specialist, plotted “price (£)” against “monthly candidates (people)” and fitted a linear function that the team found intuitive: Q = 820 − 1.6P (Exhibit 1). The relationship was used informally in pricing discussions, even though it was based on a limited price range.

Next quarter, NAS expects an additional uplift of around 260 candidates per month due to two new employer partnerships and a marketing push. Aisha proposes modelling this as a shift in the intercept: Q_next = 1080 − 1.6P (Exhibit 2). However, NAS’s current schedule is capped at 12 daytime sittings per month, 50 seats each (maximum 600 candidates). Running extra evening sittings would add fixed costs and higher marginal staffing costs after the first 600 candidates (Exhibit 2). The Head of Operations wants a recommendation that is “financially sound, operationally feasible, and easy to explain in one graph”.

Aisha can see multiple options: raise the list price to keep demand under 600 and avoid evenings; keep price lower to maximise volume but pay for evening capacity; or propose a two-tier approach (standard fee plus capped employer vouchers) that creates a piecewise demand picture. Whatever she chooses, she must present clear axes, units, and a break-even/threshold explanation (Exhibit 3).

Tomorrow morning, Aisha must decide which pricing and capacity option to recommend for next quarter—and what single graph (or pair of graphs) will make the decision obvious without oversimplifying the constraints.
caseStudies.organizationalContext: Northbridge Assessment Services Ltd (NAS) is a fictitious UK vocational certification provider delivering Maths Certification exams via three regional test centres. Operations are scheduled monthly, with seating capacity, invigilation staffing, and room hire driving cost and throughput decisions. Senior leaders require decisions to be supported by clear spreadsheet-style charts with labelled axes and units for non-technical audiences.
caseStudies.backgroundInformation: NAS has used recent pricing experiments to estimate a practical demand relationship between exam fee (P, £) and monthly candidate volume (Q, people). Based on six months of data, Aisha fitted a linear model Q = 820 − 1.6P. For the coming quarter, a marketing campaign and employer partnerships are expected to increase baseline demand by approximately 260 candidates per month, which Aisha models as Q_next = 1080 − 1.6P. Capacity is currently limited to 600 seats per month (12 sittings × 50 seats). Exceeding 600 requires evening sittings with additional fixed and marginal costs.
caseStudies.challengeDescription: Aisha must recommend a next-quarter exam fee and capacity plan using functions and graphs. She needs to quantify thresholds (e.g., the price at which demand hits 600), show break-even or profitability implications, and explain any turning points or constraints (including piecewise costs when evening sittings are added). The recommendation must be communicated through clear, appropriately scaled charts suitable for a team review meeting.

exhibitList.title: Exhibit 1: Historical pricing and demand (last 6 months)
exhibitList.description: Dataset used to fit a linear demand model. Columns: Month, Price P (£), Candidates Q (people). Data: M1 380, 210; M2 360, 245; M3 340, 280; M4 320, 310; M5 300, 345; M6 280, 375. Fitted model used internally: Q = 820 − 1.6P.

keyFacts: The organisation is Northbridge Assessment Services Ltd (NAS), a fictitious UK certification provider.
Aisha Patel is an Operations Analytics Specialist preparing for an operations review meeting.
Historical fitted demand model is Q = 820 − 1.6P, where P is price in £ and Q is candidates per month.
Historical dataset includes P=380 with Q=210 candidates.
Historical dataset includes P=280 with Q=375 candidates.
Next-quarter uplift is modelled as +260 candidates/month in the intercept, giving Q_next = 1080 − 1.6P.
Monthly daytime capacity is 600 seats, calculated as 12 sittings × 50 seats.
If Q ≤ 600, monthly cost is C = 45,000 + 18Q.
If Q > 600, an additional fixed £9,000 is incurred plus marginal £20 per candidate above 600.
Revenue is modelled as R = P × Q_next.
Profit is Π = R − C(Q_next).
The Head of Operations asks for a recommendation that is feasible and explainable in one graph.
misconceptions: Treating the intercept (e.g., 1080) as a maximum possible revenue rather than baseline demand at P=0.
Mixing units on axes (plotting price and candidates without clear labels/units, leading to misinterpretation).
Ignoring the capacity constraint and applying the simple cost model C = 45,000 + 18Q for Q>600.
Assuming the linear demand model is valid far outside the observed price range (e.g., very low or very high fees).
Confusing break-even (Π=0) with the capacity threshold (Q=600).
Using the wrong independent variable (plotting P as dependent and Q as independent without clarity).
Failing to represent piecewise behaviour on a graph (single straight line where a ‘kink’ should appear).
decisionPoints: Should Aisha recommend a price that deliberately keeps Q_next at or below 600 to avoid evening sittings?
Should NAS add evening sittings and accept Q_next above 600 if it improves overall contribution margin?
Should Aisha propose a single-price policy or a capped/tiered approach that creates piecewise demand in practice?
What is the priority for the meeting: maximising profit, avoiding operational complexity, or maintaining access/volume?

terminology.definition: A relationship where each input value maps to exactly one output value. In the case, price (input) determines expected candidates (output) via a fitted model.
The variable chosen as the input that drives change in another variable. Here, exam price P is treated as independent when modelling demand.
The output variable that changes in response to the independent variable. Here, monthly candidates Q (or Q_next) depends on price P.
The rate of change of the output with respect to the input on a straight-line graph. In Q = 1080 − 1.6P, demand falls by 1.6 candidates per £1.
The value where a graph crosses an axis. In the demand model, the intercept (e.g., 1080) represents the modelled demand when price is set to £0.
The point where profit equals zero (revenue equals total cost). It is not the same as reaching capacity; it is a financial threshold.
A practical upper limit on output due to resources. NAS’s current schedule limits monthly throughput to 600 seats without adding evening sittings.
A function defined by different rules over different input ranges. NAS’s cost changes after Q exceeds 600, creating a ‘kink’ in the cost/profit relationship.
A point where a curve switches from increasing to decreasing (or vice versa), often linked to optimisation. Profit versus price may have a turning point indicating an optimal price.
Choosing axis ranges and intervals so the graph is readable and not misleading. Poor scaling can exaggerate or hide differences relevant to decision-making.

discussionPrompts: To what extent is a linear demand function appropriate for NAS’s pricing decisions, and how might you communicate limitations without undermining confidence in the analysis?
How might Aisha visualise the capacity constraint (600 seats) so that non-specialists understand both the operational threshold and the financial implications?
Compare and contrast two graphs Aisha could present: (1) candidates versus price and (2) profit versus price. Which better supports the decision, and why?
To what extent should the recommendation prioritise maximising profit versus minimising operational complexity (e.g., avoiding evening sittings), given the data provided?
How might a two-tier or capped-voucher approach change the ‘function’ being modelled (including piecewise behaviour), and what would you want to see in the chart(s) to make this clear?
caseStudies.participationCriteria: Quality participation is defined as: (1) an initial post that references at least one exhibit quantitatively (e.g., uses the demand function, identifies the 600-seat threshold price, or compares outcomes at two prices) and explains the reasoning in plain language; (2) at least two replies that build on peers by challenging an assumption, improving a proposed graph/axis choice, or offering an alternative representation (table, chart, or narrative caveat); and (3) professional communication—clear units, correct terminology (gradient, intercept, break-even, constraint), and explicit acknowledgement of uncertainty/limitations in the fitted model.

teachingNote.synopsis: This discussion case places learners in the role of an operations analytics specialist at a fictitious Maths Certification provider facing a practical pricing and capacity decision. Learners use a fitted demand function to interpret inputs/outputs (price and candidates), then connect operational constraints (seat capacity) to financial outcomes using a piecewise cost function. The case is designed to practise graph selection and construction standards: labelled axes, units, sensible scaling, and clear threshold annotations (capacity line, break-even, and any turning points in profit). The decision context encourages a recommendation note suitable for a team review meeting, balancing rigour with clarity for non-specialists. The ambiguity is intentionally low: the models and constraints are provided, but multiple reasonable recommendations can be defended depending on priorities (profit, simplicity, access/volume, and risk of modelling error).
learningObjectives: Interpret (Understand) linear functions to explain operational meaning of inputs and outputs in demand modelling (M2-LO1).
Plot and present (Apply) operational datasets and fitted functions with correct axes, units, and scaling for non-specialists (M2-LO2).
Calculate and explain (Apply) gradients, intercepts, and key thresholds such as capacity and break-even from graphs and formulas (M2-LO3).
Analyse and recommend (Analyse/Evaluate) an operational decision using constraints and turning points, producing a short, defensible recommendation narrative (M2-LO4).
assignmentQuestions: Using Exhibit 2, at what price does Q_next reach the 600-seat capacity? What does this threshold mean operationally?
Using Exhibit 3 (or your own calculations), compare profit and feasibility for at least two candidate prices (e.g., £280 and £340) and state which option you would recommend.
What graph(s) would you include in a one-slide summary to the Head of Operations, and what specific annotations (thresholds, labels, caveats) would you add?
Where does piecewise behaviour appear in this case, and how should it change the way Aisha communicates costs and constraints?
teachingNote.sessionPlan: 60–75 minutes total: 10 min individual review of Exhibits 1–3; 15 min small-group calculations/graph choices; 25 min plenary discussion using prompts (focus on thresholds and graph clarity); 10–15 min wrap-up linking functions, constraints, and recommendation writing.
teachingNote.answerGuidance: Q1: Solve 1080 − 1.6P = 600 ⇒ P = £300; below £300 demand exceeds capacity, triggering evening sittings and the higher-cost regime. Q2: Compute Q_next, revenue, piecewise cost, and profit for selected prices; justify recommendation based on stated priority (profit vs simplicity vs access). Q3: Strong answers choose either (a) profit vs price with a vertical line/marker at P=£300 and clear units, or (b) candidates vs price plus a horizontal capacity line at 600; include brief caveat about linear fit and observed price range. Q4: Piecewise cost after Q>600; graphs should show a kink/step in cost/profit or clearly indicate that costs change beyond the capacity threshold.

caseStudies.estimatedDuration: 60–75 minutes (plus optional 20 minutes for learners to recreate charts in Excel).
