Model Assurance.technicalNote: Validation evidence may include hold-out testing, back-testing, residual diagnostics, and structured review against acceptance criteria and stakeholder requirements.

Model Assurance.definition: Check that equations and spreadsheet formulas are consistent in physical dimensions and units, such as metres, seconds, or pounds. It helps detect missing conversion factors, incorrect constants, and impossible results before deeper validation.
Model Assurance.exampleSentence: A quick dimensional analysis caught a hidden seconds-to-hours mistake that made the predicted flow rate 3,600 times too high.
Model Assurance.technicalNote: A practical approach is to annotate each variable with units, ensure both sides of an equation match, and track conversions explicitly in spreadsheet cells.

Model Governance.definition: Judgement that a model or calculation meets stakeholder needs for accuracy, scope, and decision impact. It considers assumptions, uncertainty, and tolerances, and may accept simplifications if they do not change the decision.
Model Governance.exampleSentence: Although simplified, the staffing model was fit-for-purpose because it correctly ranked options within the agreed decision tolerance.
Model Governance.technicalNote: Fitness-for-purpose is usually expressed through acceptance criteria: required accuracy, coverage of operating conditions, acceptable uncertainty, and the consequences of wrong decisions.

Model Analysis.definition: Assessment of whether output variation stays within allowed limits when inputs vary within specified tolerances. It links measurement accuracy and process variation to model predictions, supporting pass/fail decisions and robust design.
Model Analysis.exampleSentence: Tolerance analysis confirmed the calculated clearance stayed positive even when all dimensions drifted to their worst-case limits.
Model Analysis.technicalNote: Worst-case stacking and statistical tolerancing are common; choice depends on independence assumptions and the cost of failure versus conservatism.

Documentation & Audit.definition: Calculation workflow that another person can rerun and obtain the same result using the same data and version. It requires clear inputs, fixed units, documented rounding, and transparent steps, often via spreadsheets or scripts.
Documentation & Audit.exampleSentence: To make the estimate reproducible, we locked the input sheet, recorded data sources, and saved the exact model version used.
Documentation & Audit.technicalNote: Reproducibility is strengthened by separating inputs from logic, avoiding manual overrides, using named ranges, and keeping an execution log (including software versions).

Documentation & Audit.definition: System for tracking changes to models, spreadsheets, and datasets over time, including who changed what and why. It supports audit, rollback, and collaboration, and helps ensure validation evidence matches the correct model version.
Documentation & Audit.exampleSentence: We used version control to tag the validated release and to trace later changes back to the engineer who made them.
Documentation & Audit.technicalNote: Even without specialist tools, a controlled folder structure, semantic version numbers, and a change log can provide basic version control for spreadsheets.

Uncertainty & Error.definition: Acronym for Uncertainty Quantification, meaning the methods used to estimate and communicate how unsure a model result is. In this module it includes rounding, measurement error, and assumption uncertainty.
Uncertainty & Error.exampleSentence: Add a short UQ section to the report so stakeholders understand how input errors change the final recommendation.
Uncertainty & Error.technicalNote: UQ outputs are often reported as ranges, confidence or prediction intervals, or probability statements tied to decision thresholds.

Modelling workflow.definition: An Excel or Python workbook that can be rerun by someone else to get the same results, using saved inputs, clear steps, and consistent formulas or code.
Modelling workflow.exampleSentence: We submitted a reproducible workbook so reviewers could rerun the pricing model and verify every output from the raw data.
Modelling workflow.technicalNote: In Python, reproducibility often includes pinned package versions, fixed random seeds, and scripts/notebooks that run end-to-end without manual edits.

Modelling workflow.definition: A clear record showing how results were produced, including data sources, formulas or code, intermediate steps, and changes, so calculations can be checked and justified later.
Modelling workflow.exampleSentence: The audit trail links each dashboard figure to a worksheet cell, data extract date, and the calculation used.
Modelling workflow.technicalNote: Audit trails may include calculation logs, cell comments, named ranges, change history, and documented data cleaning steps for traceability.

Reporting and documentation.definition: A written list of modelling choices taken as true, such as prices, demand rules, capacity limits, or rounding, so readers understand what drives the results and where they may fail.
Reporting and documentation.exampleSentence: Our documented assumptions include a fixed energy tariff, no overtime, and a 2% scrap rate based on last quarter’s quality data.
Reporting and documentation.technicalNote: Good assumptions include units, source or rationale, and a sensitivity note describing how results change if the assumption is wrong.

Optimisation.definition: A mathematical model that finds the best decision under a chosen goal, such as minimising cost or maximising profit, while following rules and limits from the workplace problem.
Optimisation.exampleSentence: The optimisation model selects production quantities that maximise margin while keeping machine hours and defect rates within agreed limits.
Optimisation.technicalNote: Common forms include linear programming, nonlinear optimisation, and integer programming; many workplace tasks are solved using Excel Solver or Python libraries.

Statistics and inference.definition: An abbreviation for confidence interval, meaning an estimated range for an unknown value, reported with a confidence level such as 90%, 95%, or 99%.
Statistics and inference.exampleSentence: Report the CI alongside the point estimate so stakeholders can see the likely spread in the predicted cost per unit.
Statistics and inference.technicalNote: Always specify the confidence level and the target parameter (e.g., mean, proportion, difference) when reporting a CI.

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Workplace Maths Foundations: Units, Algebra and Spreadsheet Standards

terms.definition: Checking that every quantity in a calculation uses compatible units (for example, metres with metres), and converting where needed, so spreadsheet formulae and reported results make physical and business sense.
terms.exampleSentence: Before sharing the pricing sheet, we checked unit consistency so the material cost per kg was not mixed with cost per tonne.
terms.technicalNote: A quick check is to write units beside each input and ensure units cancel correctly in each formula; this is similar to dimensional analysis.

terms.definition: A way to state how precise a number is by counting meaningful digits from the first non-zero digit. It helps you report results that match the accuracy of your measurements and inputs.
terms.exampleSentence: Because the length was measured to three significant figures, the final area was also reported to three significant figures in the spreadsheet.
terms.technicalNote: When multiplying or dividing, results are often rounded to the least number of significant figures among the inputs; for addition and subtraction, decimal places are usually the limiting factor.

terms.definition: Agreed methods for reducing digits in a number (for example, rounding to decimal places or significant figures) so results are consistent, appropriate for the data quality, and clearly documented in workplace calculations.
terms.exampleSentence: We applied the rounding rules stated in the notes so all unit costs were shown to the nearest penny across the workbook.
terms.technicalNote: Different rounding conventions (such as round half up or bankers’ rounding) can produce different totals; spreadsheets may use specific defaults that should be documented for audit.

terms.definition: The way small input errors and rounding differences spread through multi-step calculations and spreadsheets, sometimes growing larger in later results. Understanding it helps you choose sensible precision and identify risky formula chains.
terms.exampleSentence: We reviewed error propagation because a 0.5% measuring error in thickness noticeably changed the final cost estimate after several steps.
terms.technicalNote: In spreadsheets, floating-point representation can introduce tiny rounding differences; repeated operations, subtraction of similar numbers, or long dependency chains can amplify these effects.

terms.definition: Changing the form of an equation without changing its meaning, so a chosen variable is isolated on one side. In workplace pricing and production models, this lets you solve for targets directly in Excel.
terms.exampleSentence: Using algebraic rearrangement, we rewrote the pricing formula to solve for required volume given a fixed contribution margin target.
terms.technicalNote: Common steps include adding or subtracting the same term on both sides, factoring, and dividing by a non-zero coefficient; record assumptions such as non-zero rates or valid ranges.

terms.definition: Methods for pointing a formula to the correct inputs, using relative, absolute, or mixed cell references and meaningful names for key cells or tables. Good referencing reduces errors and improves transparency during updates.
terms.exampleSentence: We used Excel referencing and named ranges so the VAT rate cell stayed fixed when copying the formula down the column.
terms.technicalNote: Absolute references use dollar signs (for example, $B$2). Named ranges and structured references can make formulae more readable, but require consistent workbook design and governance.

terms.definition: A clear record of how a spreadsheet produces results, including structured layout, labelled units, stated assumptions, and traceable change notes. It supports checking, explaining decisions, and meeting audit or governance requirements.
terms.exampleSentence: The manager asked for a spreadsheet audit trail so reviewers could see why the rounding choice changed the reported gross price.
terms.technicalNote: Auditability improves with consistent input/output sections, version control, protected cells, and documented formula logic; Excel tools like Trace Precedents/Dependents can support reviews.

terms.definition: Relationships written with variables to the power of one, using equals (=) for exact conditions and inequality signs (≤, ≥, <, >) for limits. They are used to test feasibility under simple workplace constraints.
terms.exampleSentence: We modelled capacity with linear equations and inequalities to confirm the weekly production target was feasible within labour-hour limits.
terms.technicalNote: Feasibility means there exists at least one solution that satisfies all constraints simultaneously; graphing the feasible region or checking boundary values helps identify limiting constraints.

terms.definition: Gross price is the full price including additions such as tax or fees, while net price is the amount after removing tax, discounts, or other deductions. Spreadsheets should state which is used and why.
terms.exampleSentence: The invoice used the gross price, but our profit model needed the net price so tax was not counted as revenue.
terms.technicalNote: Definitions vary by context (for example, net of VAT versus net of discounts). Always label assumptions and rates used so results can be audited and compared across reports.

terms.definition: The amount each unit sold contributes towards covering fixed costs and profit, usually calculated as selling price minus variable cost per unit. It is used to assess pricing decisions and production targets.
terms.exampleSentence: After updating material costs, we recalculated the contribution margin to decide whether the new net price still met the profitability requirement.
terms.technicalNote: Contribution margin can be stated per unit, as a total, or as a ratio. When modelling, keep units clear (for example, £/unit) and separate variable from fixed costs.

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making

terms.definition: A function is a rule or relationship that assigns exactly one output value to each input value. In workplace modelling, functions link variables such as hours worked to cost, or units sold to revenue.
terms.exampleSentence: We used a function in Excel to show how weekly labour hours affect total staffing cost for scheduling decisions.
terms.technicalNote: Functions are often written as f(x), where x is the input and f(x) is the output; domain and range describe allowable inputs and resulting outputs.

terms.definition: The independent variable is the input you choose, set, or observe to see its effect on an outcome. It is usually plotted on the horizontal (x) axis and may include time, volume, or price.
terms.exampleSentence: Price was treated as the independent variable so the team could compare how different prices changed predicted demand.
terms.technicalNote: In operational analysis, the independent variable is not always controllable (for example, time); it is simply the variable used to explain variation in the output.

terms.definition: The dependent variable is the output that changes in response to the independent variable. It is usually plotted on the vertical (y) axis and may represent cost, revenue, throughput, defects, or waiting time.
terms.exampleSentence: Total cost was the dependent variable, rising as production volume increased during the month-end throughput run.
terms.technicalNote: Dependent variables should be reported with clear units and appropriate scales so non-specialists can interpret the size and practical impact of changes.

terms.definition: A linear function is a straight-line relationship where the output changes by a constant amount for each one-unit change in the input. It is often written as y = mx + c in workplace graphing.
terms.exampleSentence: A linear function helped estimate delivery cost because each additional mile added roughly the same amount to the total charge.
terms.technicalNote: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept; linear models are most suitable when the rate of change is approximately constant over the relevant range.

terms.definition: A quadratic function is a curved relationship where the output depends on the square of the input, commonly written as y = ax² + bx + c. It can show a turning point, useful for optimisation and capacity discussions.
terms.exampleSentence: We fitted a quadratic function to show how overtime first improves output, then reduces it as fatigue increases.
terms.technicalNote: The turning point (vertex) occurs where the rate of change switches sign; depending on a, the curve has a maximum or minimum, which can support operational recommendations.

terms.definition: An exponential function models growth or decay where the rate of change is proportional to the current value, often written as y = a·b^x or y = a·e^(kx). It suits compounding, learning curves, or depreciation.
terms.exampleSentence: An exponential function described the increase in subscriber numbers early on, then the team compared it with capacity constraints.
terms.technicalNote: If b > 1 (or k > 0) the function grows; if 0 < b < 1 (or k < 0) it decays. Logarithms can linearise exponential data for checking fit.

terms.definition: The gradient (slope) measures how steep a line is and gives the rate of change: the rise in y divided by the run in x. In operations, it can represent marginal cost, throughput change, or price sensitivity.
terms.exampleSentence: The gradient showed that every extra unit produced added £1.20 to variable cost, which affected the pricing discussion.
terms.technicalNote: For a linear function y = mx + c, the gradient is m. Units matter: it is measured as ‘units of y per unit of x’.

terms.definition: An intercept is where a graph crosses an axis. The y-intercept is the output when the input is zero, often representing a fixed or baseline amount. The x-intercept can indicate a threshold such as zero profit.
terms.exampleSentence: The y-intercept suggested a £5,000 fixed cost even with zero output, which helped explain overheads to non-specialists.
terms.technicalNote: In y = mx + c, c is the y-intercept. The x-intercept is found by setting y = 0 and solving for x, which is common in break-even analysis.

terms.definition: The break-even point is the input level where two quantities are equal, commonly where total revenue equals total cost. On a graph, it is the intersection point and marks the minimum output or sales needed to avoid loss.
terms.exampleSentence: From the graph, the break-even point was about 820 units per week, so the manager adjusted the production target upward.
terms.technicalNote: Break-even can be found by solving the relevant equations (for example, revenue function = cost function). Some situations have multiple break-even points, especially with non-linear cost or revenue.

terms.definition: A fitted function is a mathematical relationship chosen to match an operational dataset as closely as practical. It helps summarise patterns, estimate missing values, and support forecasting when shown clearly on a labelled graph with units and sensible scales.
terms.exampleSentence: We added a fitted function in Excel to the scatter plot so the team could forecast next month’s throughput.
terms.technicalNote: Fitting is often done using regression or spreadsheet trendlines, commonly minimising squared errors between observed and predicted values; fit quality should be checked to avoid misleading recommendations.

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Calculus Essentials: Marginal Change and Accumulation

terms.definition: An exponential function models growth or decay where the rate of change is proportional to the current value, often written as y = a·b^x or y = a·e^(kx). It suits compounding, learning curves, or depreciation.
terms.exampleSentence: An exponential function described the increase in subscriber numbers early on, then the team compared it with capacity constraints.
terms.technicalNote: If b > 1 (or k > 0) the function grows; if 0 < b < 1 (or k < 0) it decays. Logarithms can linearise exponential data for checking fit.

terms.definition: The rate of change describes how quickly one quantity varies as another changes, often measured “per unit” (for example, cost per item or energy per hour). It links real workplace data to calculus.
terms.exampleSentence: We tracked the rate of change of energy use per extra unit produced to see when efficiency started falling.
terms.technicalNote: Average rate of change uses two points; instantaneous rate of change is captured by the derivative at a point.

terms.definition: A derivative is the calculated instantaneous rate of change of a function at a specific input value. In workplace models it represents “marginal” effects, such as extra cost for producing one more unit.
terms.exampleSentence: The derivative of the cost function at 1,000 units estimated the marginal cost for the next unit of output.
terms.technicalNote: If y depends on x, the derivative dy/dx carries units of “units of y per unit of x”, which supports unit checking.

terms.definition: Differentiation is the process of finding a derivative from a function or dataset. It is used to model marginal change, such as how throughput, cost, or energy use responds to small increases in production.
terms.exampleSentence: Using differentiation in Excel, we estimated how fast scrap cost increased when the line speed was raised.
terms.technicalNote: Rules commonly used include the power rule for polynomials and the exponential rule; spreadsheet models often approximate derivatives with finite differences.

terms.definition: Marginal cost is the additional cost caused by producing one more unit of output. In calculus-based models, it is often represented by the derivative of total cost with respect to quantity produced.
terms.exampleSentence: We used marginal cost to decide whether an extra production run would still be profitable at current material prices.
terms.technicalNote: If C(q) is total cost, marginal cost is dC/dq; it may vary with q due to overtime, waste, or capacity limits.

terms.definition: An integral is a value that represents accumulation across a range, such as total energy used over time or total resource use over units produced. It is often interpreted as the area under a rate curve.
terms.exampleSentence: The integral of the power-demand curve over the shift gave an estimate of total energy consumption.
terms.technicalNote: Definite integrals have limits (from a to b) and produce a total quantity; the result’s units combine rate units with the integration variable’s units.

terms.definition: Integration is the process of finding an integral to calculate total change or accumulation. It is used to convert a rate model, like throughput per hour, into a total amount over a time period.
terms.exampleSentence: After modelling flow rate by hour, we used integration to estimate the total volume pumped during the weekend.
terms.technicalNote: In spreadsheets, integration is commonly done numerically from sampled data rather than symbolically, especially when the function is not known exactly.

terms.definition: The trapezium rule is a numerical method for estimating a definite integral by splitting a curve into trapezia and adding their areas. It is useful when you have discrete spreadsheet data points.
terms.exampleSentence: Using the trapezium rule on the hourly demand data, we approximated total consumption without fitting a complex curve.
terms.technicalNote: Accuracy improves as step size decreases; for smooth functions the error is proportional to the square of the step size.

terms.definition: A polynomial function is a function made from terms like ax^n added together, where n is a whole number. Polynomials are common in workplace curve fits because they are easy to differentiate and integrate.
terms.exampleSentence: We used a polynomial function to approximate cost versus volume, then differentiated it to estimate marginal cost.
terms.technicalNote: Higher-degree polynomials can overfit data and behave poorly outside the observed range, so plausibility checks are important.

terms.definition: Dimensional consistency means an equation’s units work correctly throughout, so you only add or compare like units and the result has sensible units. It helps catch spreadsheet and calculus mistakes early.
terms.exampleSentence: We checked dimensional consistency to confirm the integral converted kilowatts over hours into kilowatt-hours, not an impossible unit.
terms.technicalNote: Dimensional checks are especially useful after differentiation or integration because units change (for example, £ vs £/unit and kW vs kWh).

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver

terms.definition: A controllable input in an optimisation model, representing a choice you can change (such as production quantities). In Excel Solver, decision variables are the changing cells adjusted to improve the objective.
terms.exampleSentence: We set weekly output of products A and B as decision variables so Solver could maximise total contribution.
terms.technicalNote: Decision variables may be continuous, integer, or binary depending on operational rules and Solver settings.

terms.definition: A formula that measures what you want to optimise, such as maximising profit or minimising waste. It converts decision variables into a single value that Solver tries to make as large or small as possible.
terms.exampleSentence: Our objective function calculated total profit from unit margins multiplied by quantities, then Solver maximised it.
terms.technicalNote: Objectives can be linear or non-linear; Solver’s method choice depends on the objective and constraint structure.

terms.definition: A rule that limits the allowed values of decision variables, often written as an equation or inequality. Constraints represent real-world restrictions such as budgets, capacity, demand, or quality limits in an optimisation model.
terms.exampleSentence: We added a labour-hours constraint so the solution could not exceed the weekly staffing capacity.
terms.technicalNote: In Solver, constraints may be ≤, ≥, =, and may also enforce integer or binary requirements.

terms.definition: A constraint that is exactly met at the optimal solution and therefore limits further improvement of the objective. Binding constraints often indicate bottlenecks because relaxing them can change the optimal objective value.
terms.exampleSentence: The machine-time constraint was binding, so increasing capacity by one hour raised profit in the Solver results.
terms.technicalNote: Binding status is typically identified by zero slack (or zero surplus) in Solver’s reports.

terms.definition: The estimated change in the objective value when a constraint’s right-hand side increases by one unit, assuming the model structure stays the same. It helps quantify trade-offs and the value of extra resources.
terms.exampleSentence: The shadow price of £12 per hour showed the expected profit increase if we could buy one more hour of labour.
terms.technicalNote: Shadow prices are dual values and are most reliable within the allowable increase/decrease range given in sensitivity outputs.

terms.definition: An Excel add-in that finds optimal values for decision variables to maximise or minimise an objective function while meeting constraints. It supports common optimisation types, including linear, non-linear, and integer programming models.
terms.exampleSentence: After defining the objective and constraints, we ran Excel Solver to choose quantities that maximised profit.
terms.technicalNote: Common methods include Simplex LP for linear models and GRG Nonlinear for smooth non-linear models.

terms.definition: A method for checking how an optimal solution and key outputs change when inputs, coefficients, or constraints change. In Excel Solver, sensitivity outputs help interpret marginal values, bottlenecks, and trade-offs for decisions.
terms.exampleSentence: We used sensitivity analysis to see whether changing material costs would alter the recommended product mix.
terms.technicalNote: For linear models, Solver’s sensitivity report includes reduced costs, shadow prices, and allowable ranges.

terms.definition: A structured comparison of alternative sets of assumptions, constraints, or targets to see how the optimal solution changes. It supports transparent justification of a chosen option by documenting inputs, results, and risks.
terms.exampleSentence: We ran a high-demand scenario and a low-demand scenario, then compared profits and constraint pressure before choosing the plan.
terms.technicalNote: Good practice includes keeping a calculation log, versioning spreadsheets, and clearly labelling scenario inputs and outputs.

terms.definition: An inequality that compares two linear expressions, such as 2x + 3y ≤ 100. In optimisation, linear inequalities are commonly used to express resource limits and define the feasible region of solutions.
terms.exampleSentence: The budget limit became a linear inequality, ensuring total spend stayed below £10,000 for all allowed production plans.
terms.technicalNote: A set of linear inequalities forms a convex feasible region, which enables efficient solution by linear programming methods.

terms.definition: A small numerical difference caused by storing and calculating numbers in limited binary precision, as spreadsheets do. Rounding errors can accumulate across many formulas and slightly alter optimisation results or constraint checks.
terms.exampleSentence: A floating-point rounding error made the total appear to exceed the limit by 0.000001, so we adjusted tolerances and audited formulas.
terms.technicalNote: Errors arise from representation (e.g., 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary) and propagation through operations; model auditing and tolerances reduce risk.

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Statistics for Quality Reporting in Excel or Python

terms.definition: The process of preparing raw quality data for analysis by fixing errors, standardising units and formats, handling missing values, and removing duplicates, using Excel tools or Python code to produce a reliable dataset.
terms.exampleSentence: Before calculating any statistics, we cleaned the inspection log by removing duplicates and standardising all measurements to millimetres.
terms.technicalNote: In Excel this may use Power Query steps; in Python it often uses pandas operations such as type casting, imputation, and de-duplication with documented rules.

terms.definition: Summary numbers that describe a dataset’s typical value and variation, such as mean or median, standard deviation and interquartile range, often used in routine quality reports before any inference is made.
terms.exampleSentence: The monthly report starts with descriptive statistics so managers can see the average defect rate and how much it varies.
terms.technicalNote: Good practice includes reporting sample size (n) and using robust summaries (median, IQR) when distributions are skewed or contain outliers.

terms.definition: Statistics that describe a typical or central value in a dataset, such as the mean, median, and mode, used to summarise process performance in quality reporting.
terms.exampleSentence: We used the median as the measure of centre because a few extreme batches were pulling the mean upwards.
terms.technicalNote: For skewed data, the median is often more robust than the mean; trimmed means can also reduce sensitivity to extremes.

terms.definition: Statistics that describe how variable the data are, such as range, variance, standard deviation, and interquartile range, helping explain whether a process is stable or inconsistent.
terms.exampleSentence: Even though the average was on target, the standard deviation showed the process spread was too wide for the tolerance.
terms.technicalNote: Standard deviation assumes a mean-based summary, while IQR is more robust when outliers or skewness are present.

terms.definition: A marker added to a record when a value is unusually far from the rest of the data under a stated rule (for example, beyond 1.5×IQR or 3 standard deviations), prompting review.
terms.exampleSentence: The dashboard highlights any outlier flags so the shift supervisor can check whether the reading was a measurement error.
terms.technicalNote: Outlier rules should be agreed in advance; for process monitoring, consider domain limits, robust z-scores, and whether the outlier is a special cause.

terms.definition: A range calculated from sample data that is likely to contain the true process mean or proportion at a stated confidence level (for example, 95%), provided the sampling method and model assumptions are reasonable.
terms.exampleSentence: We reported a 95% confidence interval for the defect rate to show the uncertainty, not just a single percentage.
terms.technicalNote: For a mean with unknown variance, the interval commonly uses the t-distribution; interpretation is about the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability for one fixed parameter.

terms.definition: A formal method for deciding whether sample evidence is strong enough to reject a ‘no change’ claim about a process, using a test statistic and p-value, while controlling the chosen significance level.
terms.exampleSentence: After the equipment update, we ran a hypothesis test to check whether the mean fill weight had genuinely increased.
terms.technicalNote: Common outputs include p-value, test statistic, degrees of freedom, and an effect estimate; reporting should state the null and alternative hypotheses and any test assumptions.

terms.definition: A condition that must be approximately true for a statistical method to be valid, such as independent observations, stable measurement, or normally distributed residuals; assumptions should be stated and checked before reporting conclusions.
terms.exampleSentence: The team noted the independence assumption might be violated because multiple measurements came from the same machine run.
terms.technicalNote: When assumptions fail, consider transformations, robust methods, resampling, or revised sampling plans; at minimum, document the risk to interpretation and decisions.

terms.definition: A constraint on how data are collected that affects how far results can be generalised, including small sample size, non-random selection, low sampling frequency, or dependence between observations from the same batch or shift.
terms.exampleSentence: We added a note on sampling limits because the data came from one week only and may not represent seasonal variation.
terms.technicalNote: Sampling limits influence confidence interval width and test power; documenting them supports ethical reporting and prevents over-claiming process improvements.

terms.definition: A single-page, stakeholder-friendly display of key quality metrics and charts, built in Excel or Python, with clear titles, units, filters, and brief narrative notes so non-specialists can interpret results quickly.
terms.exampleSentence: The dashboard shows the defect trend, the latest confidence interval, and a short note explaining what changed after the trial.
terms.technicalNote: Effective dashboards use consistent scales, avoid misleading chart types, and connect to a refreshable data pipeline with documented calculations for audit.

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Probability, Distributions and Simulation for Risk

terms.definition: A method for checking how an optimal solution and key outputs change when inputs, coefficients, or constraints change. In Excel Solver, sensitivity outputs help interpret marginal values, bottlenecks, and trade-offs for decisions.
terms.exampleSentence: We used sensitivity analysis to see whether changing material costs would alter the recommended product mix.
terms.technicalNote: For linear models, Solver’s sensitivity report includes reduced costs, shadow prices, and allowable ranges.

terms.definition: A mathematical description that assigns probabilities to the possible values of a random variable, allowing you to model uncertainty and calculate the likelihood of defects, demand levels, or downtime in workplace decisions.
terms.exampleSentence: We selected a probability distribution for weekly demand so the simulation could estimate stockout risk under uncertainty.
terms.technicalNote: Distributions may be discrete or continuous and are often defined by parameters (for example, mean and standard deviation).

terms.definition: A discrete probability model for the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, where each trial has the same probability of success, such as counting defects in a batch of items.
terms.exampleSentence: Using a binomial distribution, we estimated the chance that more than five units in the lot would be defective.
terms.technicalNote: Parameters are n (number of trials) and p (success probability); mean = np and variance = np(1−p).

terms.definition: A continuous, bell-shaped distribution defined by a mean and standard deviation. It is widely used to model measurement variation and aggregate outcomes, and to approximate some discrete processes under suitable conditions.
terms.exampleSentence: We modelled delivery time as a normal distribution to estimate the probability of missing the service-level target.
terms.technicalNote: Standardising with z = (x−μ)/σ enables use of standard normal tables; the central limit theorem supports many approximations.

terms.definition: A continuous distribution used to model the time between random events that occur at an average constant rate, such as time to failure or time between breakdowns in operational downtime analysis.
terms.exampleSentence: Assuming exponential failures, we calculated the probability that a machine would run for two hours without stopping.
terms.technicalNote: It is memoryless: P(T>t+s | T>t) = P(T>s); parameterised by rate λ with mean 1/λ.

terms.definition: A risk analysis method that repeatedly samples random inputs from chosen probability distributions to produce many possible outcomes, helping estimate the likelihood and impact of schedule delays or financial overruns.
terms.exampleSentence: The Monte Carlo simulation produced a range of project costs, showing a 20% chance of exceeding the approved budget.
terms.technicalNote: Key settings include number of iterations, random seed, correlation assumptions, and whether sampling uses simple random or variance-reduction techniques.

terms.definition: A structured log used to record workplace risks, including their causes, likelihood, impact, owners, controls, and planned actions. In modelling work, it should also document assumptions, data sources, and uncertainty in estimates.
terms.exampleSentence: We updated the risk register with the simulation’s worst-case schedule outcomes and the assumptions behind our downtime model.
terms.technicalNote: Good practice includes version control, clear risk ratings, and traceability from model outputs to decisions and mitigations.

terms.definition: A chosen condition or simplification used in a calculation or simulation, such as independence of events, a specific distribution shape, or fixed parameter values. Assumptions should be recorded so results can be reviewed and challenged.
terms.exampleSentence: Our key assumption was that defects were independent, so the binomial model would be suitable for estimating rework risk.
terms.technicalNote: Assumptions can be structural (model form) or parametric (input values) and should be tested via sensitivity checks where possible.

terms.definition: Methods for measuring and communicating uncertainty in inputs and results, such as ranges, probabilities, or intervals. In workplace simulations, it supports transparent decisions by showing how confident you are and what could change outcomes.
terms.exampleSentence: Uncertainty quantification helped us present a likely cost range and explain why the tail risk increased when demand variability rose.
terms.technicalNote: Uncertainty can be aleatory (randomness) or epistemic (lack of knowledge); both should be reflected in modelling choices and reporting.

terms.definition: A distribution-free approach that adds uncertainty bounds to predictions by creating prediction sets with a guaranteed long-run coverage rate, under suitable data conditions. It can support risk reporting when you do not trust a parametric distribution.
terms.exampleSentence: We used conformal prediction to provide a 90% coverage interval for next week’s demand without assuming it was normally distributed.
terms.technicalNote: Coverage guarantees typically require exchangeability; methods include split conformal and cross-conformal, and outputs may be intervals or sets depending on the target.

moduleTermLists.moduleTitle: Mathematical Modelling: Calibration, Validation and Sensitivity

terms.definition: A method for checking how an optimal solution and key outputs change when inputs, coefficients, or constraints change. In Excel Solver, sensitivity outputs help interpret marginal values, bottlenecks, and trade-offs for decisions.
terms.exampleSentence: We used sensitivity analysis to see whether changing material costs would alter the recommended product mix.
terms.technicalNote: For linear models, Solver’s sensitivity report includes reduced costs, shadow prices, and allowable ranges.

terms.definition: Methods for measuring and communicating uncertainty in inputs and results, such as ranges, probabilities, or intervals. In workplace simulations, it supports transparent decisions by showing how confident you are and what could change outcomes.
terms.exampleSentence: Uncertainty quantification helped us present a likely cost range and explain why the tail risk increased when demand variability rose.
terms.technicalNote: Uncertainty can be aleatory (randomness) or epistemic (lack of knowledge); both should be reflected in modelling choices and reporting.

terms.definition: Process of adjusting model parameters so the model’s outputs match observed operational data, while keeping assumptions and intended use explicit. Calibration aims to reduce error without overfitting and should be documented for audit.
terms.exampleSentence: We calibrated the throughput model using last quarter’s data, then froze parameters before running the next set of scenarios.
terms.technicalNote: Common approaches include least-squares fitting, maximum likelihood estimation, and constrained optimisation with parameter bounds informed by physics or policy.

terms.definition: Independent checking that a calibrated model is fit for its intended purpose by comparing predictions with new data or known behaviour. Validation records evidence, limitations, and corrective actions so results are defensible to stakeholders.
terms.exampleSentence: Validation compared the model’s predicted scrap rate to a new month of data and documented the remaining bias.
terms.technicalNote: Validation evidence may include hold-out testing, back-testing, residual diagnostics, and structured review against acceptance criteria and stakeholder requirements.

terms.definition: Judgement that a model or calculation meets stakeholder needs for accuracy, scope, and decision impact. It considers assumptions, uncertainty, and tolerances, and may accept simplifications if they do not change the decision.
terms.exampleSentence: Although simplified, the staffing model was fit-for-purpose because it correctly ranked options within the agreed decision tolerance.
terms.technicalNote: Fitness-for-purpose is usually expressed through acceptance criteria: required accuracy, coverage of operating conditions, acceptable uncertainty, and the consequences of wrong decisions.

terms.definition: Check that equations and spreadsheet formulas are consistent in physical dimensions and units, such as metres, seconds, or pounds. It helps detect missing conversion factors, incorrect constants, and impossible results before deeper validation.
terms.exampleSentence: A quick dimensional analysis caught a hidden seconds-to-hours mistake that made the predicted flow rate 3,600 times too high.
terms.technicalNote: A practical approach is to annotate each variable with units, ensure both sides of an equation match, and track conversions explicitly in spreadsheet cells.

terms.definition: Assessment of whether output variation stays within allowed limits when inputs vary within specified tolerances. It links measurement accuracy and process variation to model predictions, supporting pass/fail decisions and robust design.
terms.exampleSentence: Tolerance analysis confirmed the calculated clearance stayed positive even when all dimensions drifted to their worst-case limits.
terms.technicalNote: Worst-case stacking and statistical tolerancing are common; choice depends on independence assumptions and the cost of failure versus conservatism.

terms.definition: Calculation workflow that another person can rerun and obtain the same result using the same data and version. It requires clear inputs, fixed units, documented rounding, and transparent steps, often via spreadsheets or scripts.
terms.exampleSentence: To make the estimate reproducible, we locked the input sheet, recorded data sources, and saved the exact model version used.
terms.technicalNote: Reproducibility is strengthened by separating inputs from logic, avoiding manual overrides, using named ranges, and keeping an execution log (including software versions).

terms.definition: System for tracking changes to models, spreadsheets, and datasets over time, including who changed what and why. It supports audit, rollback, and collaboration, and helps ensure validation evidence matches the correct model version.
terms.exampleSentence: We used version control to tag the validated release and to trace later changes back to the engineer who made them.
terms.technicalNote: Even without specialist tools, a controlled folder structure, semantic version numbers, and a change log can provide basic version control for spreadsheets.

terms.definition: Acronym for Uncertainty Quantification, meaning the methods used to estimate and communicate how unsure a model result is. In this module it includes rounding, measurement error, and assumption uncertainty.
terms.exampleSentence: Add a short UQ section to the report so stakeholders understand how input errors change the final recommendation.
terms.technicalNote: UQ outputs are often reported as ranges, confidence or prediction intervals, or probability statements tied to decision thresholds.

terms.definition: A rule that limits the allowed values of decision variables, often written as an equation or inequality. Constraints represent real-world restrictions such as budgets, capacity, demand, or quality limits in an optimisation model.
terms.exampleSentence: We added a labour-hours constraint so the solution could not exceed the weekly staffing capacity.
terms.technicalNote: In Solver, constraints may be ≤, ≥, =, and may also enforce integer or binary requirements.

terms.definition: A range calculated from sample data that is likely to contain the true process mean or proportion at a stated confidence level (for example, 95%), provided the sampling method and model assumptions are reasonable.
terms.exampleSentence: We reported a 95% confidence interval for the defect rate to show the uncertainty, not just a single percentage.
terms.technicalNote: For a mean with unknown variance, the interval commonly uses the t-distribution; interpretation is about the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability for one fixed parameter.

terms.definition: A mathematical description that assigns probabilities to the possible values of a random variable, allowing you to model uncertainty and calculate the likelihood of defects, demand levels, or downtime in workplace decisions.
terms.exampleSentence: We selected a probability distribution for weekly demand so the simulation could estimate stockout risk under uncertainty.
terms.technicalNote: Distributions may be discrete or continuous and are often defined by parameters (for example, mean and standard deviation).

terms.definition: A risk analysis method that repeatedly samples random inputs from chosen probability distributions to produce many possible outcomes, helping estimate the likelihood and impact of schedule delays or financial overruns.
terms.exampleSentence: The Monte Carlo simulation produced a range of project costs, showing a 20% chance of exceeding the approved budget.
terms.technicalNote: Key settings include number of iterations, random seed, correlation assumptions, and whether sampling uses simple random or variance-reduction techniques.

terms.definition: A distribution-free approach that adds uncertainty bounds to predictions by creating prediction sets with a guaranteed long-run coverage rate, under suitable data conditions. It can support risk reporting when you do not trust a parametric distribution.
terms.exampleSentence: We used conformal prediction to provide a 90% coverage interval for next week’s demand without assuming it was normally distributed.
terms.technicalNote: Coverage guarantees typically require exchangeability; methods include split conformal and cross-conformal, and outputs may be intervals or sets depending on the target.

terms.definition: An Excel or Python workbook that can be rerun by someone else to get the same results, using saved inputs, clear steps, and consistent formulas or code.
terms.exampleSentence: We submitted a reproducible workbook so reviewers could rerun the pricing model and verify every output from the raw data.
terms.technicalNote: In Python, reproducibility often includes pinned package versions, fixed random seeds, and scripts/notebooks that run end-to-end without manual edits.

terms.definition: A clear record showing how results were produced, including data sources, formulas or code, intermediate steps, and changes, so calculations can be checked and justified later.
terms.exampleSentence: The audit trail links each dashboard figure to a worksheet cell, data extract date, and the calculation used.
terms.technicalNote: Audit trails may include calculation logs, cell comments, named ranges, change history, and documented data cleaning steps for traceability.

terms.definition: A written list of modelling choices taken as true, such as prices, demand rules, capacity limits, or rounding, so readers understand what drives the results and where they may fail.
terms.exampleSentence: Our documented assumptions include a fixed energy tariff, no overtime, and a 2% scrap rate based on last quarter’s quality data.
terms.technicalNote: Good assumptions include units, source or rationale, and a sensitivity note describing how results change if the assumption is wrong.

terms.definition: A mathematical model that finds the best decision under a chosen goal, such as minimising cost or maximising profit, while following rules and limits from the workplace problem.
terms.exampleSentence: The optimisation model selects production quantities that maximise margin while keeping machine hours and defect rates within agreed limits.
terms.technicalNote: Common forms include linear programming, nonlinear optimisation, and integer programming; many workplace tasks are solved using Excel Solver or Python libraries.

terms.definition: An abbreviation for confidence interval, meaning an estimated range for an unknown value, reported with a confidence level such as 90%, 95%, or 99%.
terms.exampleSentence: Report the CI alongside the point estimate so stakeholders can see the likely spread in the predicted cost per unit.
terms.technicalNote: Always specify the confidence level and the target parameter (e.g., mean, proportion, difference) when reporting a CI.

moduleLessonPlans.moduleTitle: Workplace Maths Foundations: Units, Algebra and Spreadsheet Standards

lessons.lessonTitle: Units, significant figures and rounding rules in workplac...
objectives: Select and apply correct units (including conversions) for at least 8 of 10 workplace quantities in a short scenario, documenting units next to inputs and outputs in a spreadsheet.

Apply significant-figure and rounding rules to multi-step calculations by keeping guard digits during intermediate steps and rounding only final reported values, achieving ≥80% accuracy on a rounding practice set.

Demonstrate basic error/uncertainty propagation in spreadsheets by comparing outcomes when rounding at each step vs rounding at the end, and explain the difference in 2–3 sentences using a provided template.

Rearrange a pricing or production formula to isolate a target variable (e.g., price, break-even volume, or required output), and implement the rearranged formula correctly in Excel using cell references.

Record assumptions, rounding choices, and units in a workplace-style spreadsheet (input section, calculation section, output section) using a checklist, meeting at least 5 of 6 documentation criteria.

activities.title: Setup + Diagnostic Check: Units, rounding, and algebra readiness
activities.description: Learners complete a short auto-marked diagnostic (10 questions) covering unit identification, decimal places vs significant figures, and one-step rearrangement. Feedback routes learners to optional review links based on results.
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-marked quiz with immediate feedback and adaptive remediation links (micro-review cards).
resources: Remediation micro-cards: Units, Sig figs, Algebra basics (PDF/HTML)
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to point to targeted remediation resources by question/topic.
Set expectations: diagnostic is for learning, not grading; encourage honest attempt.
studentActions: Complete diagnostic independently.
Open remediation links for any topic scoring below 70%.

activities.title: Mini-lesson: Units, significant figures, and rounding rules used at work
activities.description: Short instructional segment introducing: unit consistency, conversion factors, when to use decimal places vs significant figures, and workplace rounding policies (reporting vs calculation). Includes 2 embedded “check your understanding” questions.
activities.teachingMethod: Concise video or interactive reading with embedded knowledge checks and worked examples (e.g., mm↔m, kWh, $/unit).
resources: Video/interactive lesson: Units + sig figs + rounding rules
One-page reference sheet: rounding rules + sig-fig decision guide
instructorActions: Model a consistent notation standard (units in headers, symbols defined, avoid ambiguous abbreviations).
Emphasize the workplace habit: keep guard digits in calculations; round for reporting.
studentActions: Take notes using a provided template (Key term → Rule → Example).
Answer embedded checks and review explanations for any incorrect items.

activities.title: Demonstration: How rounding errors propagate in multi-step spreadsheets
activities.description: Guided walkthrough of a small spreadsheet that calculates total cost and unit price across multiple steps. Learners toggle between (A) rounding every step and (B) rounding only final outputs, then compare differences and identify where drift appears.
activities.teachingMethod: Screen-recorded demo + downloadable spreadsheet with pre-built toggles (e.g., ROUND() on/off) and highlighted calculation chain.
resources: Short guide: Excel ROUND vs cell formatting (2-page)
instructorActions: Explicitly distinguish: rounding a value (ROUND function) vs displaying fewer decimals (formatting).
Call out the ‘weak links’ in a calculation chain (repeated multiplication/division, subtraction of close numbers).
studentActions: Open the spreadsheet and replicate the toggle steps shown.
Record the output differences and note which step causes the biggest change.

activities.title: Applied practice: Units + rounding + uncertainty check (with answer key)
activities.description: Learners complete a structured practice set in a spreadsheet: (1) convert units for 6 inputs, (2) compute outputs using full precision, (3) apply a stated rounding policy to final outputs, (4) run a simple sensitivity check by changing one input by ±1% and observing output change. Learners then compare to an auto-check tab or provided key.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided, scaffolded spreadsheet exercise with step-by-step prompts, self-checks, and an audit checklist (units, assumptions, rounding).
resources: Audit checklist: units, assumptions, rounding, reproducibility
instructorActions: Provide a ‘minimum acceptable documentation’ example (what good looks like).
Ensure the self-check reveals *where* an error occurs (step-level feedback), not only final correctness.
studentActions: Complete each section (Inputs → Calcs → Outputs) following prompts.
Use the checklist to verify units/rounding and correct any discrepancies.

activities.title: Mini-lesson: Algebraic rearrangement for pricing/production targets (then map to Excel)
activities.description: Instruction and examples on isolating variables (inverse operations, maintaining equality, factoring). Then shows how the rearranged form becomes a clear Excel formula using named inputs or cell references. Includes a worked example: solve for required volume given fixed costs, variable cost, and target profit.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example teaching: show symbolic rearrangement → annotate units → translate into Excel syntax; includes 1 embedded check.
instructorActions: Model writing the formula with units before rearranging (dimensional sanity check).
Emphasize documenting assumptions (e.g., linear cost, constant variable cost, no taxes/discounts unless stated).
studentActions: Complete the embedded check by selecting the correct rearranged form.
Annotate the example with units for each term (e.g., $ = $ + ($/unit × units)).

activities.title: Applied practice: Rearrange and implement a target-variable formula in Excel (documentation required)
activities.description: Learners choose 1 of 2 workplace scenarios (pricing or production). They: (1) rearrange a given formula to isolate a target variable, (2) implement the rearranged equation in Excel, (3) add units in headers and a short assumptions/rounding note, (4) verify with a quick ‘back-substitution’ check (plug result into original equation to confirm).
activities.teachingMethod: Choice-based applied task with a submission-ready spreadsheet and a rubric-style checklist; self-validation via back-substitution.
instructorActions: Provide an optional hint path (stepwise rearrangement) and an ‘expert path’ (minimal hints).
Include a common-error gallery after completion (e.g., sign errors, misplaced parentheses, unit mismatch).
studentActions: Select a scenario and complete the rearrangement and Excel build.
Run the back-substitution check and correct until the difference is within a stated tolerance (e.g., ≤0.1%).

activities.title: Formative wrap-up: Quick quiz + reflection + discussion post prompt
activities.description: A short auto-marked quiz checks application of rounding policy, identification of unit inconsistency, and correct rearrangement. Learners then write a brief reflection and (optionally) post to the forum using a provided prompt.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes retrieval practice + metacognitive reflection; optional peer discussion for self-study cohorts.
instructorActions: Set quiz to show worked solutions after submission (or after deadline if needed).
Seed the discussion board with 1 model post demonstrating strong unit/assumption documentation.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review worked solutions.
Write a 3–5 sentence reflection and optionally post one takeaway or question to the forum.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Alignment to Bloom (Apply): Keep the lesson centered on doing—converting units in context, applying rounding policies, implementing formulas in Excel, and validating results. Use worked examples sparingly and transition quickly to guided practice.

Online self-study design: Each content segment should be short (≤15 minutes) and immediately followed by an action (toggle a spreadsheet option, complete a conversion, run a check). Provide instant feedback via auto-marked items and spreadsheet self-check tabs.

Reproducibility and workplace standards: Reinforce a consistent spreadsheet structure: Inputs (with units) → Calculations (no hard-coded numbers) → Outputs (rounded for reporting). Require learners to document assumptions (e.g., linear model, constant rates) and rounding policy (e.g., ‘round final unit price to 2 dp; keep full precision internally’).

Error checking habits: Teach ‘unit sanity checks’ (dimensional consistency), ‘reasonableness checks’ (order of magnitude), and ‘back-substitution’ (confirm rearranged solutions). Encourage learners to use guard digits and to avoid premature rounding.

Assessment use: Use the diagnostic to route learners to remediation rather than to judge. Use the wrap-up quiz to strengthen retrieval and reveal persistent misconceptions (ROUND vs formatting, sig figs vs dp, sign/parentheses in rearrangement).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
If learners are progressing quickly: shorten the unit/sig-fig segment by allowing them to skip directly to practice after passing embedded checks; add an extension to the sensitivity check (±5% and compare nonlinearity if present).

If learners are progressing slowly: pause after each spreadsheet step with a mandatory self-check (units present? correct conversion factor? parentheses correct?); offer the hint path for rearrangement with one operation per line.

Recommended time boxes: Diagnostic (10) should not exceed 12 minutes; if it does, advise learners to submit and use remediation links. Practice blocks are the core—protect the 20-minute rounding/units practice and 15-minute rearrangement/Excel practice. Encourage a brief break if needed between Activities 4 and 5 without extending total time.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility/low bandwidth: Provide a text-based version of videos (step list + screenshots) and a CSV version of spreadsheets; allow use of Google Sheets with equivalent functions.
Math support: Offer a scaffolded rearrangement template (one inverse operation per line) and a ‘common rearrangements’ cheat sheet (solve for x in ax+b=c; solve for x in c=abx).
Challenge/extension: Add an uncertainty/CI-style extension: treat one input as measured ± tolerance and compute best/worst-case outputs (min/max) without rounding until the end.
Language support: Include a glossary with examples for key terms (significant figures, assumption, tolerance, sensitivity) and allow learners to annotate in their first language alongside symbols.

Neurodiversity/time management: Provide a printable checklist and suggested micro-deadlines (e.g., ‘finish inputs by minute 35’), and reduce cognitive load with consistent spreadsheet layout across tasks.

Prior Excel experience differences: Provide two starter files—(A) fully labeled with cell names and prompts, (B) minimal prompts for advanced learners; include optional guidance on absolute vs relative references.
commonMisconceptions: More decimal places automatically means more accuracy (confusing precision with accuracy).
Rounding at every intermediate step is ‘safer’ than rounding only final reported results (premature rounding increases error).
Excel cell formatting (displaying fewer decimals) is the same as rounding the stored value (ROUND function changes the value; formatting does not).
Significant figures and decimal places are interchangeable rules (they apply in different reporting contexts).
Unit conversion errors such as multiplying when you should divide (or mixing mm, cm, m) won’t matter much in the final result (they can create 10×/100× errors).
Algebraic rearrangement can be done by ‘moving terms across the equals sign’ without applying inverse operations to both sides (leads to sign/operation mistakes).
Parentheses are optional in Excel formulas (missing parentheses changes order of operations).
If a rearranged formula gives a number, it must be correct (skipping validation like back-substitution and unit checks).
Assumptions are optional ‘extra notes’ rather than part of calculation quality and reproducibility.
discussionPrompts: Describe a time (real or hypothetical) when a unit mismatch could cause a costly workplace error. What simple spreadsheet convention would prevent it?
When should an organization round: at each step, at key milestones, or only for final reporting? Propose a rounding policy for a pricing spreadsheet and justify it.
In your practice file, which step created the biggest difference between ‘round each step’ vs ‘round at the end’? Why do you think that step is sensitive?
Share one algebra rearrangement checkpoint you used (e.g., units check, back-substitution, reasonableness). How did it help you catch or prevent an error?
What assumptions were implicit in the pricing/production scenario (e.g., linear costs, constant rates)? Which assumption is most likely to fail in real operations?

instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to point to the exact refresher based on incorrect choices.

Open any suggested refresher link(s) if flagged by the quiz feedback.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: isolating variables with units and assumptions
activities.description: Short instructional segment focused on applying algebraic rearrangement in workplace contexts. Includes 2 worked examples: (1) pricing: Revenue = Price × Quantity; (2) production: Output = (MachineRate × Time) × Yield. Emphasis on: keeping units attached to variables, stating assumptions, and avoiding premature rounding.
activities.teachingMethod: Chunked video (3–4 minutes each) + downloadable notes with step-by-step rearrangement and unit annotations.
resources: Video: Algebraic rearrangement in pricing/production (12 min total)
Key terms sheet: algebraic rearrangement, assumption, CI (confidence interval concept as an uncertainty note, if applicable later)
instructorActions: Model explicit notation: variable = value [units].
Include a brief callout on integrity: what to record when inputs are estimates (assumptions/limitations).
studentActions: Watch the mini-lecture.
Annotate guided notes with units and any assumptions mentioned.

activities.title: Demonstration: translating rearranged algebra into an auditable Excel layout
activities.description: Screen-capture demonstration building a transparent sheet: sections for Inputs, Assumptions, Calculations, Outputs. Shows named ranges (e.g., Price, Quantity, Yield), correct anchoring ($A$1) vs relative references, and a simple change log. Demonstrates formatting conventions: units column, rounding policy note, and cell comments for assumptions.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided screencast + pause points where learners replicate steps in a starter workbook.
resources: Starter Excel workbook (.xlsx) with blank template sections
Checklist: Inputs/Calculations/Outputs separation; named ranges; change notes; units/rounding/assumptions

Show Excel tools for traceability: Trace Precedents/Dependents (or equivalent).
studentActions: Download and open the starter workbook.

activities.title: Guided practice: rearrange and implement (pricing target)
activities.description: Learners rearrange a pricing model and implement it in Excel with documentation. Scenario example: Target profit requires solving for Price given Costs, Quantity, and Margin assumptions. Learners: (1) rearrange formula on paper/notes, (2) implement in Excel using named ranges, (3) document units and rounding policy, (4) add one change note entry.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example-to-independent transfer: first half scaffolded with prompts, second half requires learner completion with self-check answers.
resources: Practice brief (PDF): pricing target scenario + given inputs
Answer key for algebra rearrangement (revealed after attempt)
Self-check rubric (units, references, documentation, change note)
instructorActions: Provide ‘hint layers’ in the LMS: Hint 1 (units), Hint 2 (algebra step), Hint 3 (Excel formula structure).
Ensure answer key is gated (accessible only after learners submit or click ‘I attempted’).
studentActions: Rearrange the provided formula to isolate the target variable (Price).
Implement the formula in Excel using named ranges and correct anchoring.
Record units, rounding choice (where and why), and assumptions in the designated sheet area.

activities.title: Break / reset
