activities.title: Case analysis: production target + audit trail improvements
activities.description: Learners analyse a partially completed spreadsheet that contains typical issues (mixed units, hard-coded constants, unclear assumptions, inconsistent rounding). They must: (1) identify at least 5 issues, (2) fix at least 3, (3) add change notes explaining corrections, and (4) run a reverse-check by substituting the computed result back into the original equation to verify correctness.
activities.teachingMethod: Error-spotting and correction task with a structured ‘issue log’ table (issue, risk, fix, evidence).
resources: Reference: rounding guidance (when to round; display vs calculation)
instructorActions: Seed the case with realistic workplace errors (e.g., hours vs minutes; percent as 0.2 vs 20).
Include an exemplar issue log entry to model expected detail and integrity language (limitations/uncertainty).
studentActions: Audit the case spreadsheet and record issues in the issue log.
Correct at least three issues and document changes.
Perform a reverse-check and units check, noting results in the workbook.

activities.title: Formative assessment: applied quiz + spreadsheet checkpoint
activities.description: Learners complete an auto-graded quiz (algebra isolation + Excel reference interpretation) and upload/submit a screenshot or exported PDF of their workbook sections (Inputs/Calculations/Outputs + assumptions + change note). Feedback focuses on correctness, transparency, and reproducibility.
activities.teachingMethod: Mixed-format formative assessment: auto-graded items + rubric-based checklist for the uploaded evidence (can be self-graded or instructor/TA graded depending on platform).
resources: Submission instructions (export to PDF / screenshot guidance)
Rubric checklist aligned to MLOs (references, named ranges, units, rounding, assumptions, change notes)
instructorActions: Configure quiz explanations for each item (why the correct algebra/reference is correct).
Set rubric criteria to mirror module standards: transparency, integrity, unit consistency, reproducibility.
studentActions: Complete the quiz.
Submit required workbook evidence (or complete the self-check rubric if instructor grading is not used).
Review feedback and note one improvement to apply next lesson.

activities.title: Wrap-up reflection: integrity and transparency prompt
activities.description: Learners write a short reflection (3–5 sentences) responding to prompts about assumptions, rounding, and auditability. They also post (or privately journal, if no forum) one ‘rule’ they will follow in future spreadsheets (e.g., never hard-code a constant inside a formula).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection with a model answer and optional peer discussion board.
instructorActions: Provide a model response that demonstrates professional tone and transparency language (e.g., “Assumption: yield stable at 92% based on last quarter; limitation: may vary by batch”).
If a forum is used, provide 2–3 reply stems to encourage constructive peer feedback.
studentActions: Write and submit reflection (forum post or private journal).
If in a forum, reply to one peer with a suggestion to improve transparency.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson to keep learners operating at Apply level: each concept (rearrangement, referencing, named ranges, documentation) should be immediately used in an Excel task with observable outputs. Emphasize professional integrity by making documentation non-optional: require explicit units for every input/output, a visible rounding policy (display vs calculation), and written assumptions/limitations. Use ‘audit lens’ language throughout (e.g., “Could another person reproduce this result?” “Can we trace every output back to inputs?”). Provide scaffolded supports (hint layers, gated solutions) that reduce cognitive load early, then fade supports in the second half. Include verification habits as part of the workflow: (1) units/dimensional check; (2) reverse-check by substituting the computed variable back into the original equation; (3) Excel trace precedents/dependents to confirm references. Encourage learners to avoid hard-coded values inside formulas; instead, store constants as inputs with labels, units, and rationale. For transparency, standardize layout: Inputs (clearly labeled), Assumptions (with rationale/source), Calculations (no hidden constants), Outputs (with units), and Change Log (what/why/date/version). Ensure accessibility: captions for videos, downloadable transcripts, and keyboard-navigable templates.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep mini-lecture segments short and task-driven (no more than ~12 minutes before learners must do something in Excel). In the 20-minute guided practice, recommend learners spend ~8 minutes on algebra rearrangement and ~12 minutes implementing and documenting in Excel; prompt them to stop at the 10-minute mark if still rearranging and use Hint 1/2. For the case analysis, timebox issue-spotting to 6 minutes, fixing to 10 minutes, and verification to 2 minutes. If learners finish early, direct them to the optional stretch: add a sensitivity cell (e.g., vary Yield by ±2%) and note how that would be communicated honestly. If learners are behind, allow them to skip non-critical formatting polish and prioritize: correct formula + correct references + units + assumptions + one change note.
adaptationOptions: Math support pathway: provide an optional ‘algebra steps’ worksheet with intermediate steps pre-written and blanks to fill (scaffold), plus extra practice on sign changes and dividing/multiplying both sides.
Excel support pathway: provide a short add-on tutorial on absolute/relative references and named ranges with 3 micro-exercises and immediate feedback.
Advanced extension: require learners to implement a two-step rearrangement (variable appears on both sides) and document a limitation if an iterative/circular approach is needed.

Low-bandwidth option: offer downloadable PDFs of screenshots + transcripts, and allow learners to complete calculations in a free spreadsheet tool (e.g., LibreOffice/Google Sheets) while still meeting documentation standards.
Accessibility: provide captioned videos, transcripts, high-contrast template, and instructions that do not rely on color alone to indicate inputs/outputs.
Language support: provide a glossary with plain-language definitions and example sentences for ‘assumption’, ‘limitation’, ‘rounding policy’, and ‘audit trail’.
commonMisconceptions: Treating units as optional labels rather than constraints (e.g., adding values in different units without conversion).
Algebra sign errors during rearrangement (especially when moving terms across the equals sign or dividing by negative values).
Confusing ‘solve for x’ algebra with Excel assignment (thinking the left side of an equation can be typed as-is into a cell).
Using hard-coded numbers inside formulas (reducing transparency and making auditing/updates error-prone).
Misusing percent values in Excel (20% vs 0.2 vs 20) and not documenting the chosen representation.
Rounding too early in the calculation chain (changing results materially) instead of rounding for display at the end; failing to record rounding choice.
Assuming relative references will behave correctly when copied, or forgetting to anchor constants with absolute references when appropriate.
Believing named ranges automatically improve correctness (they improve readability, but can still refer to the wrong cell if defined incorrectly).
Not performing a reverse-check/validation step and assuming a plausible number means the model is correct.
discussionPrompts: Where in your spreadsheet could a reviewer misunderstand your intent, and what single note (units, assumption, or change comment) would prevent that?
When is it acceptable to round in the middle of a calculation, and how would you disclose that choice transparently?
Give an example of an assumption in your model that could materially change the output. How would you label it as an assumption (not a fact)?
What is the risk of hard-coding constants inside formulas in a workplace setting (handover, audit, updates)?
How does a units check catch errors that a quick ‘looks reasonable’ check might miss?
If two analysts get different answers from the same model, what documentation elements (named ranges, change log, assumptions table) would help reconcile the difference fastest?

lessons.lessonTitle: Use Excel referencing, named ranges and structured layout...
objectives: Create a structured Excel calculation sheet that uses relative and absolute references correctly (e.g., $A$1) with at least 90% accuracy on a reference-selection check.

Define and use at least 3 named ranges (inputs, rates, capacities) to make formulas readable and auditable, and demonstrate traceability by locating each value’s source within 15 seconds using Excel’s tracing tools.
Implement a simple change-note/audit section (date, change, reason, author) and record at least 2 documented assumption statements (units, rounding rule, constraint source).

Model a workplace production target as a linear equation/inequality system (at least 2 constraints) and determine feasibility (feasible/not feasible) with supporting spreadsheet evidence (units, calculations, and stated assumptions).
Communicate one evidence-based recommendation (e.g., adjust target or capacity) using the model outputs, explicitly noting at least one limitation/uncertainty in the assumptions.

activities.title: Warm-up: Spreadsheet transparency + references quick check
activities.description: Learners complete a short interactive checkpoint reviewing relative vs absolute references, unit labels, and where assumptions belong in a workplace sheet. Includes 5 micro-items (multiple choice + drag-and-drop) and immediate feedback explaining why each choice supports auditability.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with immediate feedback; primes attention to integrity/traceability standards before building.
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to explain audit implications (e.g., why hard-coded numbers reduce transparency).
Review item analytics after release to identify common errors for a follow-up announcement.
studentActions: Complete the 5-item check and review explanations for any incorrect answers.
Note one personal ‘watch-out’ (e.g., forgetting to lock a tax rate cell).

activities.title: Micro-lecture: Audit-ready spreadsheet layout (inputs → calculations → outputs)
activities.description: Short video + annotated slides introducing a standard worksheet structure: clearly separated input block (with units), calculation block, output block, and an assumptions/change log area. Covers why named ranges and structured layout support professional integrity and reproducible calculations.
activities.teachingMethod: Direct instruction with worked mini-examples showing ‘bad’ vs ‘good’ spreadsheet practices.
resources: Template rubric: Transparency & audit checklist (1 page)
instructorActions: Provide a consistent standard (colors, labels, unit column, rounding note line) and explain the rationale.
Explicitly connect layout choices to the module competencies (integrity, diligence, checking assumptions/units).
studentActions: Watch the video and download the checklist.
Identify two layout features they will adopt (e.g., input cells shaded, units column).

activities.title: Demonstration: Named ranges, structured formulas, and trace tools
activities.description: Guided demonstration (video walkthrough) building a small cost/production calculator: define named ranges (e.g., UnitPrice, MaterialCost, MaxHours), create formulas using names, and use Trace Precedents/Dependents and Evaluate Formula to confirm traceability. Demonstrates documenting units and rounding rules in-cell comments or a designated assumptions table.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked example with stop-and-try prompts every 2–3 minutes (learner pauses video to replicate steps).
instructorActions: Model ‘think-aloud’ checks: units, reasonableness, and where each number comes from.
Show at least one common error (hard-coded constant inside formula) and then correct it using a named range.
studentActions: Follow along and reproduce the named ranges and formulas in their own copy.
Use trace tools to verify at least one output cell’s dependency chain.

activities.title: Guided practice: Build an audit-ready sheet section (inputs + change notes)
activities.description: Learners construct an inputs block and a change-note/assumptions section in Excel from a prompt. Requirements: units column, data source column (e.g., ‘given by supervisor’, ‘policy v2.1’), rounding rule note, and a simple change log with two entries. Learners then self-check against the transparency checklist.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured practice with a checklist and exemplars; learners compare their work to a model after attempt.
instructorActions: Provide clear completion criteria and a model artifact for self-verification.
Offer optional ‘challenge’ criteria (e.g., add data validation dropdowns for units).
studentActions: Create the inputs and change-note areas in Excel using the scenario data.
Self-assess using the checklist and revise until all required items are met.

activities.title: Micro-lecture: Linear equations/inequalities for feasibility under constraints
activities.description: Short lesson translating workplace constraints into linear inequalities (e.g., labor hours ≤ capacity, material use ≤ stock, production ≥ target). Emphasizes documenting assumptions (time per unit, scrap rate) and checking units. Includes one worked example of determining feasibility by testing values and interpreting constraints in context.
activities.teachingMethod: Concept-to-application explanation with a single worked example and unit-check callouts.
resources: Key terms card: linear equation, inequality, constraint, assumption, CI
instructorActions: Highlight that feasibility is about satisfying ALL constraints simultaneously.
Demonstrate unit consistency checks (e.g., hours/week vs minutes/unit) and show how to convert cleanly.
studentActions: Translate two written constraints into inequalities in their notes.
Answer two embedded checks (e.g., ‘Which direction is the inequality?’) with feedback.

activities.title: Case practice: Test a production target in Excel using inequalities
activities.description: Learners complete a scenario-based task: given selling price, variable cost, available labor hours, and a target output, they model constraints as inequalities and test whether the target is feasible. They must: (1) use named ranges for all inputs, (2) keep units visible, (3) avoid hard-coded constants in formulas, (4) add an ‘Assumptions’ table (including at least one uncertainty/limitation), and (5) conclude feasible/not feasible with one recommendation.
activities.teachingMethod: Authentic task with scaffolded steps; learners produce an artifact and compare to a solution outline.
resources: Solution outline + common error checks (revealed after submission/self-declare completion)
instructorActions: Provide a clear marking guide aligned to MLOs (references, named ranges, transparency, feasibility logic, assumptions).
Ensure the solution outline explains reasoning, not just final numbers (supports integrity and reproducibility).
studentActions: Build the constraint calculations and a feasibility indicator (e.g., TRUE/FALSE per constraint plus an overall status).
Write a short recommendation statement in the sheet (e.g., ‘Target not feasible; increase capacity by X hours or reduce target to Y units’), including one limitation/uncertainty.

activities.title: Formative check + reflection forum post
activities.description: Learners complete a 6-question quiz (mix of spreadsheet and inequality application) and then write a short reflection/discussion post: what assumption mattered most, and how they ensured traceability. Encourages professional transparency about limitations and uncertainty.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes knowledge check plus metacognitive reflection to reinforce integrity and diligence standards.
instructorActions: Enable auto-feedback with explanations, including unit/assumption reminders.
Respond to a sample of posts emphasizing good documentation habits and correcting recurring issues.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review explanations.
Post a brief reflection identifying one assumption, one traceability method used, and one improvement for next time.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design and facilitation should prioritize ‘apply’ outcomes: learners must produce a working spreadsheet artifact and use it to test feasibility, not merely define terms. Use a gradual release pattern (model → guided build → independent case) and embed integrity cues throughout: (1) separate inputs/calculations/outputs, (2) visible units and consistent conversions, (3) named ranges to reduce ambiguity, (4) no hard-coding of constants in formulas, (5) explicit assumptions and rounding rules, and (6) traceability checks using Excel auditing tools. Provide exemplars of both poor and strong practice to make auditability concrete. In feedback, comment first on transparency/traceability (can another person reproduce and audit the result?) before commenting on numeric accuracy; this aligns to the module competencies. Encourage learners to state limitations (e.g., time per unit is an estimate, scrap rate not measured) and avoid overclaiming certainty when making recommendations.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Timebox videos to the listed durations and include ‘pause-and-do’ markers during demonstrations so learners alternate between watching and applying (reduces passive viewing). If learners finish early, direct them to extension tasks: add data validation for inputs, conditional formatting for violated constraints, or sensitivity checks (e.g., vary labor minutes/unit by ±10%). If learners run long, allow them to complete the case practice first (core apply objective) and return to optional enhancements later; the minimum viable deliverable is a readable, named-range-based constraint model with documented assumptions and a feasibility conclusion.
adaptationOptions: For learners new to Excel: provide a pre-built workbook with the layout already created; they only add named ranges and formulas. Include a short optional primer on $-locking and cell referencing.

For advanced learners: add an extension requiring a one-way sensitivity check (e.g., how much can labor minutes/unit increase before infeasibility) and document results as a limitation/uncertainty note.
For learners with accessibility needs: provide step lists with keyboard-only instructions for defining named ranges and using trace tools; ensure videos have captions and transcripts.
For learners with math anxiety: offer a ‘constraint translation’ scaffold table (words → symbols → units) and a partially completed inequality set to reduce cognitive load.

For limited software access: offer an alternative using Google Sheets with equivalent features (named ranges, protected ranges, formula auditing via dependent/precedent highlighting) and a submission format that captures formulas (shared link or exported workbook).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing relative vs absolute references (e.g., failing to lock a rate cell, causing incorrect copied formulas).
Believing named ranges are optional ‘labels’ rather than tools that improve auditability and reduce formula ambiguity.
Hard-coding numbers inside formulas (e.g., =A2*1.15) while still claiming transparency; this hides assumptions such as tax/markup rates.
Reversing inequality direction when translating constraints (e.g., using ≥ for capacity limits) or forgetting that all constraints must be satisfied simultaneously.
Mixing units (minutes/unit with hours/week) without conversion, leading to apparently ‘feasible’ results that are dimensionally incorrect.
Interpreting a single satisfied constraint as overall feasibility, rather than checking every constraint and documenting which one binds/violates.
Rounding too early in intermediate steps, causing small but meaningful feasibility differences; or failing to state rounding rules at all.
discussionPrompts: Which spreadsheet choice most improved auditability in your work (named ranges, layout, change log, trace tools)? Explain how it would help a colleague review your calculation.
Share one assumption you documented (e.g., minutes per unit, scrap rate). What evidence supports it, and what uncertainty remains?
In your case model, which constraint was most likely to ‘bind’ (be the limiting factor), and how did you identify it from your sheet?
Describe one common way someone could accidentally (or intentionally) mislead with a spreadsheet in this scenario. What design feature prevents that?
If your target was infeasible, propose one operational change (capacity, efficiency, target adjustment). What would you need to measure or verify before implementing it?

lessons.lessonTitle: Linear equations and inequalities to test feasibility of ...
objectives: Given a workplace scenario with stated constraints, set up at least 2 linear inequalities (with correct units) and determine whether a proposed production target is feasible.
Rearrange a linear equation to solve for an unknown target variable (e.g., required output, hours, cost) and report the result with appropriate units and rounding.
Apply significant figures and rounding rules to multi-step spreadsheet calculations and justify (in 1–2 sentences) when to round during vs. at the end of a workflow.
Identify and correct at least 3 unit/rounding/assumption issues in a provided spreadsheet excerpt, documenting corrections in an assumptions log.

activities.title: Orientation + Diagnostic Check: Units, Rounding, Constraints
activities.description: Learners complete a short diagnostic to activate prior knowledge: (a) choose correct units for given quantities, (b) round values to specified significant figures, (c) interpret a simple constraint statement (e.g., “no more than 40 hours”). Immediate feedback directs learners to optional review links.
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-graded diagnostic quiz with targeted feedback and remediation links.
resources: Quick reference sheet: significant figures + rounding rules
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to route learners to specific review sections based on missed items.
Set a mastery threshold (e.g., 70%) and recommend remediation if below.
studentActions: Complete the diagnostic quiz and review feedback.
Open recommended remediation links if needed.

activities.title: Mini-Lecture: Linear Equations/Inequalities as Workplace Constraints
activities.description: Short, structured content on translating statements into inequalities, solving linear equations for a target, and documenting assumptions/units. Includes examples: capacity limits, labor-hour limits, and budget ceilings. Emphasizes feasibility (satisfies all constraints) and showing work clearly in a spreadsheet context.
activities.teachingMethod: Video (8–10 min) + guided notes + embedded checks (2–3 knowledge checks).
instructorActions: Model translating 3 workplace statements into inequalities and highlight key words (at least, at most, no more than).
Explicitly model writing units next to each variable (e.g., x = units/day; h = hours/week).
Include one example where units reveal an error (e.g., mixing hours and minutes).
studentActions: Watch the mini-lecture and complete guided notes.
Answer embedded checks and review explanations.

activities.title: Demonstration: Significant Figures, Rounding, and Error Propagation in Spreadsheets
activities.description: Walkthrough showing how rounding choices affect downstream results (e.g., cost per unit, total cost, required output). Demonstrates best practice: keep full precision in intermediate cells, round for reporting, and document rounding rules. Includes a simple sensitivity check by changing a rounded input vs. full-precision input and comparing outputs.
activities.teachingMethod: Screen-recorded spreadsheet demo with pause-and-try prompts.
instructorActions: Demonstrate: (1) setting cell formats vs. actual stored values, (2) where to apply ROUND(), (3) how early rounding can change feasibility decisions.
Narrate an explicit rule-of-thumb: round only for display/reporting unless a standard requires rounding at a specific step.
Show a simple ‘difference’ cell to quantify rounding impact (e.g., Output_full - Output_rounded).
studentActions: Follow along in the workbook and reproduce the demo steps.
Pause at prompts to predict outcomes before revealing results.

activities.title: Guided Practice: Solve for Targets + Test Feasibility Under Constraints
activities.description: Learners complete a sequence of scaffolded tasks in a spreadsheet: (1) rearrange a linear equation to solve for a production target, (2) translate 3 constraints into inequalities, (3) evaluate whether a proposed target satisfies all constraints, and (4) document assumptions/units in an assumptions log tab. Automated checks confirm correctness of setup and final feasibility conclusion.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example → faded guidance → independent completion with auto-check cells.
resources: Answer key for final values (released after attempt)
instructorActions: Provide a worked example for the first item, then remove steps progressively.
Include prompts requiring units in text (e.g., “Report x in units/day”).
Configure auto-checks to validate both numeric results and inequality direction (where possible).
studentActions: Complete each task in order, using the assumptions log to note units, rounding decisions, and any given constraints.
Use auto-check feedback to correct errors and resubmit within the workbook.

activities.title: Case Analysis: Rounding-Driven Decision Risk (Feasibility Borderline)
activities.description: A short scenario where the feasibility of a target is borderline (e.g., capacity limit is close). Learners compare two spreadsheet approaches: early rounding vs. end rounding. They determine whether the target is feasible under each approach, explain the discrepancy, and recommend a standard for reporting and decision-making. Learners post a brief justification to the course discussion board (or reflective journal in fully self-paced mode).
activities.teachingMethod: Scenario-based analysis with structured prompts and a short written recommendation.
resources: Two mini-workbooks (Approach A: early rounding; Approach B: end rounding)
Discussion board or reflection journal prompt
instructorActions: Provide a rubric snippet for the recommendation: must mention units, rounding stage, and assumption transparency.
Seed the forum with 1–2 exemplar responses showing concise, evidence-based reasoning.
studentActions: Compute feasibility under both approaches and identify the turning point causing the change.
Post a 100–150 word recommendation (or journal entry) citing at least one numerical comparison.

activities.title: Formative Assessment: Applied Quiz (Equations, Inequalities, Units, Rounding)
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz requiring application: solve for a target from a linear formula, choose correct inequality direction from a constraint statement, and select the best rounding approach for a multi-step spreadsheet. Includes one item asking learners to identify an assumption that must be documented.
activities.teachingMethod: Randomized item bank with immediate feedback and second-attempt option.
resources: Formula/units quick reference (available during quiz if desired)
instructorActions: Use an item bank with common distractors (e.g., reversing inequality, rounding too early).
Allow one retry and require learners to review feedback before retaking.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback explanations.
Retake (if needed) and note 1–2 personal error patterns.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson around ‘decision accuracy’ in workplace maths: learners are not only solving equations/inequalities, but verifying feasibility and defending results with units, assumptions, and rounding choices. In an online self-study format, make checking behaviors visible and repeatable: (1) always label variables with units, (2) translate constraints into inequalities before calculating, (3) keep full precision in intermediate spreadsheet cells, (4) round for reporting according to a stated rule/standard, and (5) run a quick sensitivity check when results are close to a limit. Provide frequent low-stakes checks (auto-feedback) and require short written justifications in the case analysis to reinforce diligence and attention to detail. Ensure examples include at least one ‘borderline feasibility’ case where rounding changes the decision, so learners experience why documentation and reproducible calculations matter.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners struggle early (diagnostic <70%), recommend they spend an extra 10–15 minutes on the optional micro-review before continuing. Keep the mini-lecture brisk and example-heavy; shift time to guided practice where application occurs. In the guided practice, suggest a timebox per task (e.g., 6–8 minutes each) and instruct learners to move on after two correction attempts, then consult the answer key/explanations. For faster learners, add an extension: create an additional constraint and test how it changes feasibility. For learners who are slower, prioritize correct inequality setup, units, and a clear feasibility conclusion over completing every optional prompt.
adaptationOptions: Provide two versions of the practice workbook: a scaffolded version (step-by-step prompts, partial formulas) and a standard version (minimal prompts).
Offer accessibility supports: captions/transcripts for videos, keyboard-navigable spreadsheets/templates, and screen-reader-friendly PDFs.
Allow learners to submit explanations as audio (1–2 minutes) instead of text for the case analysis reflection.
Include an optional ‘units clinic’ mini-activity: matching quantities to units and converting common workplace units (minutes↔hours, g↔kg) before starting inequalities.
For advanced learners: add a tolerance/sensitivity extension asking them to compute the maximum rounding error allowed before a feasibility decision flips.
commonMisconceptions: Reversing inequality direction when translating phrases like “no more than,” “at least,” or “minimum required.”
Treating an equation as a constraint when it should be an inequality (or vice versa).
Mixing units within a formula (e.g., hours and minutes) without converting, leading to seemingly plausible but incorrect results.
Rounding intermediate results too early, then assuming the final answer is still accurate enough for a feasibility decision.
Confusing cell formatting (displayed decimals) with the underlying stored value in spreadsheets.
Assuming more decimal places always means more accuracy, without considering significant figures and measurement precision.
Failing to document assumptions (e.g., constant rate, linearity, fixed cost) and then being unable to reproduce or defend calculations.
discussionPrompts: Describe a time when rounding could change a workplace decision (e.g., meeting a limit, passing a threshold). Where should rounding happen, and why?
A target is feasible only if it satisfies all constraints. What is one practical method you can use in a spreadsheet to ensure you didn’t miss a constraint?
When results are close to a constraint boundary, what quick sensitivity check would you run to confirm the decision is robust?
Which is riskier in your context: rounding too early or rounding too late? Support your view with a short numerical example.
What assumptions are hidden in using a linear model for production or cost, and how would you document them for a team review meeting?

lessons.lessonTitle: Units, significant figures and rounding rules in workplac...
objectives: Identify and correctly apply significant-figure and rounding rules (including when to delay rounding) in at least 8/10 workplace-style calculations.

Build a simple multi-step Excel calculation that records units, assumptions, and rounding choices, and demonstrate (by comparison) how rounding at different steps affects final outputs within a stated tolerance.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design the lesson around ‘workplace reproducibility’: every calculation should be traceable (inputs), interpretable (units), defensible (assumptions), and checkable (validation tests). In self-study mode, build this through (1) explicit modeling (demo spreadsheet structure), (2) immediate feedback (auto-graded quizzes, embedded checks), and (3) checklists/rubrics that prompt diligence.

Emphasize the difference between display formatting and changing stored values in Excel, because it directly affects error propagation. Encourage learners to keep full precision in intermediate cells and to round only for reporting unless a business rule requires otherwise (and then document it). Reinforce algebraic rearrangement as a reversible process: every rearranged formula should be verified by ‘plug-back’ into the original relationship and by unit consistency. Finally, normalize the habit of adding a simple sensitivity/tolerance (or CI-style bounds) check to detect fragile outputs caused by small input changes or rounding.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep micro-lessons short and action-oriented (≤12 minutes) and move quickly into spreadsheet application. Use clear stop points: (1) after the rounding demo, (2) after Practice 1 comparison, (3) after rearrangement mini-check. If learners are progressing slowly, advise completing only one scenario in Practice 2 (either pricing or production) and prioritizing correct documentation (units/assumptions/rounding) over extra features. If learners finish early, extend by adding an additional sensitivity run (e.g., ±10%) and summarizing the most sensitive input in one sentence.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility: Provide captions/transcripts for videos and a high-contrast spreadsheet theme; allow keyboard-only navigation instructions for Excel tasks.
Math support scaffold: Offer a rearrangement ‘recipe’ sheet (inverse operations, common fraction/percent transformations) and a partially completed example with missing steps.
Spreadsheet support scaffold: Provide a version of the template with named ranges already created and comments showing where to enter formulas.
Extension (advanced): Ask learners to implement a sensitivity table (one-variable or two-variable) and interpret which inputs drive output variance most.
Alternative tool option: Allow Google Sheets equivalents (ROUND, named ranges/defined names if available) for learners without Excel, while keeping the same documentation standards.
Language support: Provide a glossary with plain-language definitions and an example Calculation Note written in simple, concise sentences.
commonMisconceptions: Rounding at every intermediate step is always ‘more accurate’ than rounding only at the end (often the opposite for final accuracy).
Cell formatting to 2 decimal places changes the stored value (formatting changes display only; ROUND changes stored results used downstream).
Significant figures and decimal places are the same concept (they are different and used for different reporting requirements).
Units don’t matter as long as the numbers ‘look right’ (unit inconsistency can silently produce incorrect results).
Algebraic rearrangement can be done by ‘moving terms across the equals sign’ without applying inverse operations consistently (leads to sign/bracket errors).
Percentages can be used directly in formulas without converting (e.g., using 20 instead of 0.20).
A model that matches one test case is correct (needs plug-back verification, unit checks, and reasonableness/sensitivity checks).
discussionPrompts: When (if ever) is it appropriate to round intermediate values in a workplace spreadsheet? Give one example and state the assumption behind it.
What’s your personal checklist for validating a pricing/production model before sharing it with a colleague?
Share one unit-check you used today (e.g., $/unit × units = $). Where in the model did it catch—or could it catch—an error?
In your Practice 1 comparison, how large was the difference between ‘round each step’ vs ‘round at the end’? Was it within tolerance? What tolerance did you use and why?
Which input in the sensitivity/tolerance (or CI-style range) check had the biggest impact on the output, and what does that imply for data collection accuracy?

Step 3 (Integrity note): Write a short change note describing what was changed, why, and any limitation/uncertainty (e.g., assumes linear relationship; rounding at output only).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Keep the lesson firmly at Bloom ‘apply’ by prioritizing doing over describing: learners must (1) perform rearrangements, (2) implement formulas correctly in Excel, and (3) document decisions for audit.

Use worked examples early, then fade support: provide step prompts in the first practice problem and reduce them in the second so learners must choose correct operations and spreadsheet structure independently. Reinforce professional integrity by requiring explicit assumptions and limitations; avoid presenting results as exact when rounding or model simplifications exist.

Emphasize error-prevention routines: separate inputs from calculations, use named ranges to reduce reference mistakes, avoid hard-coded constants in formulas, and use trace tools to verify dependencies. Treat unit checks and sensitivity checks as normal workflow (not “extra”) and require learners to record check outcomes in the workbook.

Feedback should be diagnostic: when learners fail a check cell, direct them to likely causes (parentheses/order of operations, sign errors, wrong absolute/relative reference, missing unit conversion, rounding too early). Encourage learners to correct systematically: verify algebra on paper/notes, verify units, then verify Excel references.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Timebox video/demos (do not exceed the planned 30 minutes total for lecture+demo). If learners stall during practice, prompt a 3-step recovery sequence: (1) confirm algebraic isolation steps, (2) confirm units and conversions, (3) use Trace Precedents to inspect references.

If learners finish early, add an extension: introduce a second sensitivity input (two-way check) or require an additional output formatting rule (e.g., currency with 2 decimals, rates with 1 decimal). If learners are behind, allow them to complete only Task A plus the validation section, then attempt Task B later; the quiz can still be completed to consolidate key concepts.
adaptationOptions: Provide two workbook versions: scaffolded (with step-by-step rearrangement prompts and partially built named ranges) and standard (blank structure requiring full setup).
Offer alternative tools for accessibility: allow Google Sheets equivalent functions and named ranges; provide PDF screenshots for learners with limited Excel access.
Add an optional “algebra refresher” micro-lesson (5–8 minutes) focused on inverse operations and common rearrangement pitfalls.

For advanced learners: include a challenge requiring Goal Seek to confirm the rearranged solution matches a numeric target and to document why formula-based solutions may be preferable for auditability.
Support neurodiverse learners with consistent page layout, chunked instructions, and a single ‘Next step’ indicator per task; provide a completed example after a first attempt.
For learners with math anxiety: include a ‘check values’ approach (plug the isolated variable back into the original equation) and encourage use of units as a confidence scaffold.
commonMisconceptions: Treating rearrangement as ‘moving terms across the equals sign’ without applying inverse operations to both sides, leading to sign and division errors.
Misplacing parentheses in Excel so the implemented formula does not match the intended algebra (order of operations errors).
Mixing units (e.g., hours vs minutes; $ vs $/unit) or omitting necessary unit conversions, then trusting the numeric output.
Rounding too early in intermediate steps, which compounds error and reduces transparency; confusing display formatting with actual rounding of values.
Hard-coding constants (tax rate, conversion factors) inside formulas, making spreadsheets non-auditable and hard to update.
Using relative references where absolute references are required (or vice versa), causing formulas to break when filled down/across.
Assuming named ranges automatically prevent errors; misunderstanding scope (worksheet vs workbook) or using ambiguous names.
Believing a single ‘correct-looking’ output is sufficient without sensitivity/reasonableness checks or documentation of assumptions/limitations.
discussionPrompts: Where in your spreadsheet should rounding occur, and how would you justify that choice to an auditor or supervisor?
What is one assumption in the production/pricing model that could materially change the result if violated? How would you disclose it clearly?
When you find an error in a workbook used for decisions, what should a transparent change note include (and what should it avoid)?
How do named ranges improve integrity and traceability, and what new risks do they introduce if used poorly?
Describe a quick sensitivity check you would run before sharing a result. What output behavior would make you distrust the model?

Moderate for correctness of constraint reasoning and respectful, audit-minded language.

Reply to one peer with a question about units/assumptions or a suggestion to improve transparency.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson as an applied, artifact-producing workflow rather than a concept lecture. The core evidence of learning is the spreadsheet: it should be readable, checkable, and defensible.

Key instructor moves for online self-study:
- Make expectations visible: provide an acceptance-criteria checklist (inputs/calcs/outputs separation, named ranges, no hard-coded numbers, units everywhere, assumptions tab, change log entry).
- Model professional integrity language: 'Given…, assume…, constraint is…, therefore…'. Require learners to state limitations of linearity (e.g., constant rates, no setup time, no scrap) and to identify uncertainty (e.g., variability in labour efficiency).
- Prioritise traceability: demonstrate Trace Precedents/Dependents and a self-check cell (alternate calculation or reconciliation). Emphasise that trace tools help follow logic but do not guarantee correctness—units and assumptions still need checking.
- Embed unit discipline: include unit labels adjacent to every input, and encourage unit-consistent naming (e.g., LabourRate_perHour, MaterialAvailable_kg). Prompt learners to verify dimensional consistency (hours vs units/hour).
- Prevent common spreadsheet failure modes: discourage merged cells in calculation areas, discourage overwriting formulas, and require that changes be recorded in the Change Log with date, reason, and impact.
- Feedback strategy: when marking or auto-checking, comment first on transparency (can another person audit it?), then on mathematical correctness, then on communication quality (recommendation and assumptions).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Use short cycles of watch → do → check. Recommended pacing within the self-study environment:
- After each video segment, insert a mandatory pause point with a micro-task (e.g., 'Create 3 named ranges before continuing').
- Timebox Practice 1 to 15 minutes; if learners exceed 20 minutes, direct them to the exemplar comparison and a troubleshooting list (absolute references, Name Manager, unit labels).
- In the case task, encourage a constraint-by-constraint build: implement one inequality check, validate it with a quick sanity test (extreme target values), then proceed.
- Provide optional extension tasks (conditional formatting flags, simple chart of feasible range) so faster learners stay engaged without delaying core outcomes.
adaptationOptions: Support: Provide a partially completed workbook where only named ranges and two constraints must be added; include step-by-step screenshots for each action (Name Manager, trace tools).
Support: Offer a glossary pop-up for key terms (constraint, assumption, confidence interval/CI if mentioned in workplace context) and a unit-conversion mini-sheet if learners struggle with units.
Accessibility: Ensure videos are captioned, provide transcripts, and supply keyboard-only instructions for Excel actions (where possible).
Platform flexibility: Allow Google Sheets equivalents (named ranges, data validation, formula auditing alternatives) with a mapping guide for learners without Excel.
Challenge: Add a second product with two decision variables and multiple constraints; ask learners to identify the binding constraint(s) and propose a change to make an infeasible plan feasible.
Challenge: Require sensitivity checks: vary one input (e.g., labour hours available) by ±10% and record the impact on feasibility, documenting the uncertainty and limitations.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing relative and absolute references, causing constraints or rates to shift when formulas are filled down/across.
Using hard-coded numbers inside formulas (magic numbers) instead of referencing input cells or named ranges, reducing auditability.
Assuming that if the output 'looks right' the sheet is correct; skipping unit checks, assumption statements, and trace/reconciliation checks.
Treating constraints as equations (using = instead of ≤/≥), which can incorrectly eliminate feasible solutions.
Flipping an inequality incorrectly when rearranging (especially when multiplying/dividing by a negative number).
Rounding too early in intermediate calculations, which can change feasibility outcomes near constraint boundaries.
Mixing units (e.g., minutes vs hours, kg vs g, $/unit vs $/batch) without explicit conversion and labeling.
Believing Trace Precedents/Dependents guarantees correctness; it only shows relationships, not whether assumptions and units are valid.
discussionPrompts: Post your feasibility conclusion (feasible/not feasible) and name the binding constraint. What evidence in your sheet supports that this constraint is binding?
Which assumption in your model is most likely to fail in a real workplace (e.g., constant labour rate, no downtime, perfect yield)? How would that affect your recommendation?
What change note did you add to your workbook? If someone audited your file later, would they be able to reproduce your result and understand why the change was made?
Where did you apply rounding, and why there (not earlier)? Describe one risk of rounding earlier in the calculation chain.
If the target is infeasible, propose one operational change (increase capacity, reduce target, substitute materials) and show which inequality would become satisfied as a result.

lessons.lessonTitle: Linear equations and inequalities to test feasibility of ...
objectives: Given a short workplace scenario, write a linear equation or inequality representing a production target and at least two constraints (e.g., labour hours, material availability) with correct units (≥90% accuracy).

Solve a one-variable linear equation and a one-variable linear inequality from a production context, and interpret the solution set as feasible/not feasible against stated constraints (correct interpretation in 4/5 cases).

In a spreadsheet-style, multi-step calculation, apply appropriate significant figures and rounding rules (including when to delay rounding) and justify rounding choices in a notes/assumptions field (meets a provided checklist).

Identify and correct at least three unit, assumption, or rounding issues in a provided “messy” calculation log, documenting fixes so another person could reproduce the result (3/3 issues corrected with clear documentation).

activities.title: Diagnostic warm-up: Units, sig figs, and inequality quick check
activities.description: Learners complete a short auto-graded quiz (8–10 items) to activate prior knowledge: unit consistency (e.g., minutes vs hours), significant figures vs decimal places, rounding (round half up), and interpreting inequality symbols in context (e.g., “at least”). Immediate feedback explains each answer.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with instant feedback; learners note two personal focus areas for the lesson (e.g., rounding too early, unit conversion).
resources: One-page reference: Significant figures & rounding rules
instructorActions: Provide quiz with targeted feedback for common errors (unit mismatch, rounding too early, misreading ‘at most/at least’).
Include a brief note directing learners to the relevant reference sections based on their score.
studentActions: Complete the quiz without notes first, then review feedback.
Write down two error patterns to watch for during practice.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: Translating workplace constraints into linear inequalities
activities.description: Short content segment explaining how to model constraints and targets using linear equations/inequalities. Includes: defining variables with units, keywords (“at least,” “no more than,” “must be between”), and documenting assumptions (e.g., constant rate, negligible waste). Ends with two worked examples (one feasible, one infeasible).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture + guided notes; learners pause to answer two embedded “check-for-understanding” questions.
resources: Guided notes template (fillable PDF or doc)
Worked example sheet (with units and assumption box)
instructorActions: Model variable definition format: x = units produced per day (units/day).
Explicitly connect each inequality to a real constraint (capacity, budget, time).
Emphasize documenting assumptions and units beside every quantity.
studentActions: Fill in guided notes (variables, constraints, assumptions).
Answer embedded checks and compare with provided solutions.

activities.title: Demonstration: Spreadsheet standards—units, rounding, and error propagation
activities.description: Walkthrough of a 6–8 cell spreadsheet calculation (e.g., labour cost per batch and maximum batches) showing how rounding at intermediate steps can change feasibility decisions. Demonstrates: keeping full precision in intermediate cells, rounding only for reporting, using units in column headers, and adding an Assumptions/Notes cell. Includes a before/after comparison of early-rounding vs end-rounding outcomes.
activities.teachingMethod: Screencast demonstration with annotated cells and a short ‘spot the issue’ pause.
resources: Checklist: Spreadsheet documentation standards (units, rounding, assumptions, reproducibility)
instructorActions: Show a clear naming convention (e.g., Input_, Calc_, Output_ sections).
Highlight where rounding belongs (display vs stored value).
Explain how small rounding changes can flip an inequality outcome near a constraint boundary.
studentActions: Follow along by opening the spreadsheet and replicating steps.
Pause at the ‘spot the issue’ moment to identify what causes the discrepancy.

activities.title: Guided practice: Solve and test feasibility (equations + inequalities)
activities.description: Learners work through 4 scaffolded problems. Each problem requires: (1) define variable with units, (2) write equation/inequality, (3) solve, (4) test feasibility against a given constraint, (5) state conclusion in a sentence. Problems increase in complexity and include one inequality that requires careful interpretation of “at most/at least.”
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example fading: first problem mostly worked, then decreasing hints; auto-check final answers plus a solution walkthrough for each step.
resources: Practice set (4 problems) with hint buttons
Optional algebra refresher: solving linear equations/inequalities
instructorActions: Provide structured answer format with fields: Variable, Model, Solve, Check units, Feasibility statement, Assumptions.
Include unit checks as required steps (not optional).
studentActions: Complete problems using the structured format.
Self-check against solutions and annotate one correction per problem if needed.

activities.title: Case analysis: Production target decision with constraints and assumptions
activities.description: Scenario (workplace-style): A small workshop has a daily labour limit and material limit; each unit requires a fixed amount of labour and material. Learners must determine whether a proposed production target is feasible, and if not, compute the maximum feasible output and identify the binding constraint. Must document assumptions (constant rates, no downtime, waste factor if stated) and units throughout.
activities.teachingMethod: Applied problem-solving using a decision memo template; learners compare their decision to a model memo.
instructorActions: Prompt learners to explicitly state which constraint is binding and why.
Require a final sentence that references units and rounding (e.g., ‘max = 47 units/day (rounded down to whole units)’).
studentActions: Complete the memo with calculations and a clear recommendation.
Identify at least one risk if assumptions fail (e.g., variability in labour time).

activities.title: Formative Assessment 1: Feasibility and inequality interpretation check
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz (6–8 items) focusing on applying linear inequalities to feasibility. Includes one item where the inequality direction changes due to multiplying/dividing by a negative number (conceptual check), and one item on interpreting a solution set (e.g., x ≤ 12 means ‘no more than 12 batches’).
activities.teachingMethod: Mastery check with targeted remediation paths based on wrong-answer patterns.
resources: LMS quiz with feedback by misconception
Remediation mini-lesson: inequality sign flips and interpretation
instructorActions: Configure feedback to point to specific misconceptions (wording interpretation, sign flip, unit mismatch).
Recommend a retry after remediation for mastery.
studentActions: Complete quiz and review feedback.
Redo missed items after remediation notes.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 2: Spreadsheet audit—rounding, sig figs, and unit corrections
activities.description: Learners receive a ‘messy’ calculation table (spreadsheet screenshot or file) with embedded errors: inconsistent units, rounding too early, missing assumptions, and incorrect sig figs in reported results. Task: identify and correct at least three issues and rewrite the final reported value with appropriate significant figures and a short note on rounding and assumptions.
activities.teachingMethod: Error-spotting and correction to build diligence and attention to detail; rubric-based self-check.
resources: Rubric/checklist: units, rounding stage, sig figs, assumptions, reproducibility
instructorActions: Provide an annotated answer key that explains why each issue matters (error propagation, feasibility decisions).
Encourage learners to keep intermediate precision and round only in final reporting cell.
studentActions: Mark and correct issues, then compare with the annotated key.
Record one personal rule they will apply in future spreadsheets (e.g., ‘never round intermediate cells’).

activities.title: Wrap-up reflection: Assumptions and constraints in one paragraph
activities.description: Learners write a short reflection: one example of an assumption they used today, one constraint that bound the solution, and one rounding/units practice they will adopt to prevent errors in multi-step calculations.
activities.teachingMethod: Metacognitive consolidation (can be optional forum post in self-study mode).
instructorActions: Provide a model reflection response and a brief rubric (clarity, units, rounding rationale).
If a forum exists, seed with 2–3 strong examples and invite peer replies.
studentActions: Write the paragraph and save it to their learning journal or post to the forum (if available).
Reply to one peer (optional) with a question or improvement suggestion.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson to repeatedly force the ‘units–model–solve–check–communicate’ loop. Because the Bloom level is Apply, keep explanations brief and allocate most time to worked application with structured templates.

Key teaching moves:
- Require variable definitions with units before any algebra (e.g., x = units/day). This reduces common modelling errors and supports reproducibility.
- Make constraints explicit and literal: tie each inequality to a physical limitation (time, material, budget). Ask learners to label constraints (C1 labour, C2 material).
- Emphasize feasibility as a decision, not just a number: learners must conclude ‘feasible/not feasible’ and justify with a comparison to constraints.
- Rounding and significant figures: teach ‘compute with full precision, round for reporting.’ Show at least one boundary case where early rounding changes a feasibility call.
- Documentation: enforce a minimal documentation standard (assumptions box + units on every quantity + rounding note). This directly targets the competency of diligence and attention to detail.

For self-study delivery, provide: (1) immediate feedback quizzes, (2) model solutions that show reasoning steps, not only final answers, and (3) checklists learners can self-audit against.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Aim for ~30 minutes input (mini-lecture + demo) and ~55 minutes application/assessment.
- If learners score <70% on the diagnostic, advise spending an extra 5–10 minutes on the refresher resources before continuing.
- During guided practice, suggest a time box of ~5 minutes per problem; if stuck after 2 minutes, use hints rather than guessing.
- Case analysis should be completed in one pass; if it exceeds 15 minutes, learners should write the decision memo first (claim + constraint check) and then refine calculations.
- Encourage a final 2–3 minute self-audit using the checklist: units consistent, assumptions stated, rounding applied at the end, inequality interpreted in words.
adaptationOptions: Support (scaffolded): Provide partially completed models (variable defined, inequality set up) and ask learners to finish solving and interpreting; include a glossary pop-up for ‘constraint’ and ‘assumption.’
Support (numeracy/fluency): Offer an optional micro-lesson on rearranging linear equations and handling inequality sign flips, with 5 extra practice items and feedback.
Support (accessibility): Provide captions/transcripts for videos, high-contrast spreadsheet screenshots, and an editable text-only version of the messy spreadsheet audit.
Extension (challenge): Add a second constraint and require identifying the binding constraint(s) and computing slack (e.g., unused labour hours) after finding the maximum feasible output.
Extension (rounding sensitivity): Ask learners to compare outcomes under different reporting rules (e.g., whole units only vs one decimal) and explain which is appropriate and why.
Language support: Provide a keyword-to-inequality translation table (at least ≥, at most ≤, between inclusive) with 2 contextual examples per term.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing significant figures with decimal places (e.g., thinking 2.50 has two significant figures).
Rounding too early in multi-step calculations, causing materially different final values and incorrect feasibility decisions.
Mixing units within the same calculation (minutes used with hours, grams with kilograms) without converting consistently.
Interpreting inequality wording incorrectly (e.g., treating ‘at least’ as ≤ instead of ≥).
Forgetting that multiplying/dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
Treating an inequality solution as a single value instead of a range/set of feasible values.
Reporting a maximum feasible production number with inappropriate rounding direction (e.g., rounding up when outputs must be whole units).
Failing to state assumptions, leading to models that appear precise but are not defensible or reproducible.
discussionPrompts: In the case analysis, which constraint was binding and how did you determine it from your calculations (not intuition)?
Share one example where rounding early could change a feasibility decision. What rule will you adopt to prevent this in spreadsheets?
What assumptions did you make about production rate or resource use? Which assumption is most risky in a real workplace context, and why?
When should results be rounded down vs rounded to nearest? Provide a production example where rounding up would be inappropriate.
How do you document units in spreadsheets so that someone else can audit your work quickly? Describe a layout or naming convention you prefer.

lessons.lessonTitle: Units, significant figures and rounding rules in workplac...
objectives: Apply unit checking and unit conversions in a multi-step workplace spreadsheet so that every input and output cell includes a stated unit (in a header or adjacent “Units” column) with 0 unit inconsistencies across the sheet.

Apply significant figures and rounding rules to intermediate and final spreadsheet results by selecting an appropriate rounding strategy (no rounding / round at end / controlled rounding at key steps) and justifying it in an “Assumptions & Rounding” note field for at least 3 calculated outputs.

Quantify rounding/error propagation in a multi-step calculation by comparing at least two rounding strategies and reporting the absolute and percent difference between final outputs, including a brief interpretation of which strategy is acceptable for the stated context/tolerance.

Rearrange at least two workplace formulae (pricing or production targets) to isolate a target variable and correctly implement the rearranged forms in Excel using cell references, with units and assumptions documented.

Perform and record at least two verification checks (dimensional check, reasonableness/spot-check with hand calculation, sensitivity check by varying one input) and identify any resulting corrections to units, rounding, or assumptions.

activities.title: Orientation + download workspace (template + datasets)
activities.description: Learners open the lesson workbook template and review the required spreadsheet standards used in this program (units column, assumptions/rounding notes, reproducible formulas, and check cells). They confirm they can edit formulas and see example documentation fields.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided walkthrough video (screen recording) + brief checklist to ensure learners set up the template correctly before calculations.
instructorActions: Provide a clean template with pre-labeled columns: Inputs, Units, Value, Formula, Rounding rule, Assumptions, Checks.
Ensure the template includes one completed example row showing expected documentation quality.
studentActions: Download and open the workbook template.
Confirm they can see and edit formulas; complete the setup checklist.

activities.title: Mini-lesson: units, significant figures, rounding rules (workplace emphasis)
activities.description: Learners study short content segments that connect units, significant figures, and rounding to workplace risk: incorrect procurement quantities, pricing errors, and inconsistent reporting. Content highlights: (1) units as part of the number, (2) significant figures vs decimal places, (3) rounding rules (nearest, up/down), (4) when to round (end vs controlled steps), (5) Excel display formatting vs actual stored value.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture video with embedded self-check questions after each concept (auto-feedback).
resources: One-page reference: significant figures and rounding rules
instructorActions: Include at least 4 embedded questions with explanations (e.g., ‘How many significant figures in 0.004560?’).
Use workplace-flavoured examples (inventory, production yield, pricing).
studentActions: Watch the micro-lecture and answer embedded checks.
Add 2–3 key reminders into the workbook ‘Notes’ tab (personal checklist).

activities.title: Demonstration: rounding/error propagation in a multi-step spreadsheet
activities.description: A worked example shows how small rounding decisions can change a final result. Learners see three strategies side-by-side: (A) no rounding until the final output, (B) rounding every step, (C) rounding only at defined reporting points. The demonstration also models documentation: units, assumptions, and a simple sensitivity check (vary one input by ±1%).
activities.teachingMethod: Screen-recorded build-along: instructor constructs the sheet and narrates decision points (where rounding is applied and why).
instructorActions: Show at least one ‘gotcha’: formatting to 2 decimals changes appearance but not downstream calculations.
Model a check cell that computes percent difference between strategies (e.g., =ABS(A-B)/A).
studentActions: Follow along in the starter tab (pause and replicate).
Annotate the sheet: where rounding occurred and what rule was used.

activities.title: Practice: choose and justify rounding + measure impact (propagation)
activities.description: Learners complete a structured task using provided data (e.g., material usage → cost → unit price → profit). They implement two rounding strategies and compare final outputs. They must document units for each variable, state assumptions (e.g., ‘costs in AUD’, ‘wastage rate assumed constant’), and report absolute/percent differences in a summary box.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided independent practice with step-by-step prompts and immediate ‘check values’ revealed after each stage (progressive disclosure).
resources: Auto-check cells (conditional formatting: green if within tolerance)
instructorActions: Provide milestone check ranges (not just final answers) to support debugging.
Define an acceptable tolerance for numeric matching (e.g., within ±0.1%) and explain why tolerance is used.
studentActions: Complete Stage 1–4 calculations with units and notes.
Compute and record: final output under Strategy A vs B, absolute difference, percent difference, and a short interpretation.

activities.title: Break + reflection: build a personal ‘calculation diligence checklist’
activities.description: Learners pause and create a quick checklist they can reuse in workplace spreadsheets: unit checks, reasonableness, rounding policy, and assumptions log. They add it to the workbook Notes tab (or a downloadable template).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection prompt (text-based) with an optional forum post for peer comparison.
instructorActions: Provide 6–8 checklist starters (e.g., ‘Have I documented the unit in the header?’).
If a forum exists, post an example checklist and invite learners to adapt it.
studentActions: Draft a 6–10 item diligence checklist.
Optionally post 2 items to the discussion board that they think prevent the most costly errors.

activities.title: Mini-lesson: algebraic rearrangement for pricing/production targets
activities.description: Learners review rearrangement steps (inverse operations, maintaining equality, handling negatives, brackets) and then connect to common workplace formulae. Example focus: Profit = (Price − VariableCost) × Quantity − FixedCost. Rearrange to isolate Price or Quantity given a target profit. Emphasis: carry units through the rearrangement and note assumptions (e.g., constant variable cost).
activities.teachingMethod: Concept explanation + two worked examples (one to isolate Price, one to isolate Quantity) with quick self-check questions.
instructorActions: Explicitly show unit reasoning (e.g., profit in $; quantity in units; therefore (profit+fixed)/quantity has units $/unit).
Include one common error demonstration (e.g., missing brackets when dividing).
studentActions: Work through the examples and answer the self-check questions.
Copy the final rearranged formulas into the workbook ‘Algebra’ tab with a one-line unit statement.

activities.title: Practice case: implement rearranged formulae in Excel with documentation
activities.description: Learners complete two Excel tasks: (1) Given a target profit and costs, calculate required Price; (2) Given a target output and cycle time, calculate required production rate or number of shifts. They must implement formulas using cell references, include units, and record rounding choices (e.g., rounding up to whole units or whole shifts).
activities.teachingMethod: Independent case practice with automated validation: unit check prompts + ‘sanity check’ expected ranges.
resources: Excel function tips: ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, ABS
instructorActions: Provide expected value ranges (not exact values) to encourage verification rather than copying.
Include a required documentation rubric snippet: units present, assumptions stated, rounding justified, checks completed.
studentActions: Rearrange (on paper or in a notes cell) then implement in Excel using references.
Add at least 2 check cells (dimensional note + reasonableness check or sensitivity check).

activities.title: Formative assessment: accuracy + diligence check (auto-mark + reflection)
activities.description: A short formative quiz tests application: identify correct rounding approach, choose correct sig figs, detect a unit mismatch, and select the correct rearranged formula. Learners then complete a brief reflection: one error they caught and how they caught it (units, rounding, or assumptions).
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-marked quiz (6–8 items) + 2-sentence reflective response (self-mark guidance).
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to explain why distractors are wrong (especially unit and bracket errors).
Review item analytics to identify widespread misconceptions for future remediation content.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review explanations for any incorrect items.
Write a brief reflection and update their diligence checklist if needed.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design for ‘apply’ by keeping content short and pushing time into spreadsheet execution and verification. Require visible evidence of diligence: (1) units recorded adjacent to values, (2) assumptions/rounding choices written in plain language, (3) at least two check cells per task (dimensional/units check, reasonableness check, or sensitivity check).

In online self-study, reduce cognitive load with progressive disclosure: reveal milestone checks after learners attempt each stage. Emphasize that Excel number formatting changes display, not underlying precision; learners should use functions (e.g., ROUND/ROUNDUP/ROUNDDOWN) only when a rounding decision is justified by reporting needs, tolerances, or real-world constraints (whole units/shifts).

Model error propagation concretely: side-by-side outputs under different rounding strategies and a percent-difference cell. Encourage learners to adopt a default policy: keep full precision in intermediate steps unless a step represents a real-world discrete action (e.g., ordering whole items) or a defined reporting requirement (e.g., currency to cents). When teaching rearrangement, anchor each step to both algebra and units (dimensional reasoning) to catch bracket/sign mistakes.

Feedback should prioritize process over final numeric match: if a learner’s result differs, guide them to audit units, brackets, and rounding points before recalculating. Provide brief ‘debug pathways’ (e.g., check units → check brackets → check cell references → check rounding/formatting).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
If learners are slower with Excel, allow them to complete only one rounding strategy in the 20-minute propagation practice, then add the second strategy afterward. For stronger learners, keep the timings but add an extension sensitivity check (±5% on one input) during the 15-minute algebra-to-Excel case.

Maintain momentum by time-boxing: 15 minutes maximum for the first concept block before learners touch the spreadsheet; 20 minutes maximum for the main practice before a brief break/reflection. Encourage learners to stop after each milestone and use the check cells before moving on—this prevents compounding errors that can derail pacing.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded version: provide partially completed formulas with missing components (e.g., missing brackets or a missing division) so learners focus on units/rounding decisions rather than starting from blank cells.
Advanced extension: require a simple sensitivity table (Data Table or manual +/- scenarios) and a short note on which input drives the largest output change and why.
Accessibility: provide the workbook in both Excel and Google Sheets formats, plus a text-only alternative where learners can compute with a calculator and fill a table of units/rounding/assumptions.
Math support: include an optional ‘rearrangement steps’ guide with highlighted inverse operations and a checklist for sign/bracket handling.

Language support: provide a mini glossary for key terms (significant figures, tolerance, assumption, CI as confidence interval) and sentence starters for documenting assumptions (e.g., ‘Assume ___ remains constant because ___.’).
Low-bandwidth option: offer downloadable PDFs of worked examples and a non-video step list mirroring the demonstration.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing significant figures with decimal places (e.g., thinking 0.00450 has 2 significant figures instead of 3).
Believing that rounding at every step always improves accuracy; in multi-step calculations it can increase cumulative error.
Assuming Excel formatting (e.g., showing 2 decimals) changes the stored value used in later formulas.
Mixing units silently (e.g., hours vs minutes; mm vs m) and trusting the spreadsheet because it produces a number.
Dropping brackets during rearrangement or Excel entry, especially when dividing a sum (e.g., using (P+F)/q + c vs P+F/q + c).
Sign errors when moving terms across the equals sign (particularly with ‘Price − Cost’ structures).
Treating rounding rules as purely mathematical rather than context-driven (currency, discrete items, safety tolerances).
Using incorrect cell referencing in Excel (relative vs absolute references) leading to correct-looking but wrong copied formulas.
discussionPrompts: In your workplace (or a realistic scenario), when is it appropriate to round intermediate values, and when should rounding only occur at the final output? Give one example and explain the risk of the wrong choice.
Describe one unit-check habit that would have prevented a real or plausible error (e.g., mixing minutes and hours). How would you implement that habit in a spreadsheet template?
A colleague says: ‘If it shows 2 decimals, it’s rounded.’ How would you respond, and what quick test in Excel would you use to prove your point?
Which is more dangerous in your opinion: a rounding mistake or a unit mistake? Defend your answer with a short scenario.
When rearranging formulas for targets (price/quantity), what is your most reliable method to avoid bracket and sign mistakes?

moduleLessonPlans.moduleTitle: Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making

lessons.lessonTitle: Interpret linear, quadratic and exponential functions to ...
objectives: Given a workplace scenario (e.g., staffing vs output, cost vs units, demand vs price), identify the function’s input (independent variable) and output (dependent variable) and state both with correct units in 1–2 sentences.

Classify a relationship as linear, quadratic, or exponential from a short description and/or a plotted dataset, and justify the choice using at least one observable feature (constant rate of change, turning point, or multiplicative growth).

Calculate and interpret key parameters in context (e.g., linear slope and intercept; quadratic turning point direction; exponential growth/decay factor) and describe what they mean operationally (rate, baseline, constraint/peak).

In Excel or Python, plot an operational dataset and an appropriate fitted function (trendline/model) on the same chart with labelled axes, units, title, and an appropriate scale, producing a visual that a non-specialist can read.
Apply a quality-check routine to verify units, axis scaling, and calculation accuracy (at least 3 checks) and correct at least one deliberate error in a provided “messy” graph or formula.

activities.title: 1) Lesson launch: What does a graph say to a workplace audience?
activities.description: Short setup explaining why functions/graphs are used in operational decision-making. Learners review a one-slide example of a confusing chart (missing units, misleading scale) and list what makes it hard to trust.
activities.teachingMethod: Prompted reflection (asynchronous): learners write 2–3 bullet points in a note or forum post on clarity and trustworthiness (units, scale, labels).
resources: Slide image: ‘Bad chart’ example (missing units, truncated axis)
Downloadable lesson workbook (Excel) and/or starter notebook (Python)
instructorActions: Provide a clear success criterion: ‘A good operational chart lets a non-specialist answer: what, how much, and in what units?’
Include an example response showing attention to detail (units, scale, assumptions).
studentActions: Inspect the chart and note at least two issues affecting interpretation.
State one improvement they would make (e.g., add units, start axis at zero, clarify time period).

activities.title: 2) Micro-lecture: Inputs/outputs and three function families used at work
activities.description: Concept video/reading covering: function as input→output; independent/dependent variables; units; and when linear, quadratic, exponential models appear in operations (costing, learning curves, growth/decay). Includes quick “spot the function type” checks.
activities.teachingMethod: Segmented instruction with embedded checks: after each segment, learners answer a single multiple-choice question with immediate feedback.
resources: Key terms card: Function, Exponential function, Fitted function, CI (introduced as ‘uncertainty range’ for later lessons)
instructorActions: Use consistent variable naming (e.g., x=input, y=output) and always include units (e.g., x in hours, y in units produced).
Emphasize ‘model choice should match mechanism + data shape,’ not memorization.
Flag that confidence intervals (CI) will be used later to communicate uncertainty; for now, focus on clear visuals and correct interpretation.
studentActions: Take notes on: key visual features of each function type and common operational examples.
Complete the embedded checks and review feedback for any incorrect responses.

activities.title: 3) Demonstration: Plotting data + fitted function in Excel or Python (with units and scale)
activities.description: Guided walkthrough showing how to import a small operational dataset, create a scatter plot, add a fitted function (Excel trendline or Python regression/curve fit), and format for non-specialists (labels, title, units, scale).
