instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Focus this lesson on analysis and professional practice rather than procedural calculus. In an online self-study format, reduce cognitive load by providing computed derivative/integral outputs and directing attention to: (1) meaning, (2) units, (3) plausibility, and (4) documentation. Use a consistent routine throughout the lesson: 
- Step 1 (Context): What are f and x? What do they represent operationally?
- Step 2 (Units): Derivative units = units(f)/units(x); Integral units = units(f)·units(dx).
- Step 3 (Interpretation): Write a complete sentence: ‘At x = …, the rate/accumulation means … per …’.
- Step 4 (Plausibility): Apply at least two checks (sign, magnitude vs typical range, boundary behaviour, compare to average, quick back-of-envelope).
- Step 5 (Transparency): Record assumptions, rounding rule, and at least one limitation/uncertainty statement.
Emphasise integrity: learners should practise stating when an output is not trustworthy (e.g., extrapolation beyond calibrated range, missing variables, noisy data). Reward careful checking and clear logs as much as correct interpretation. Provide model wording for limitations and encourage reproducible documentation (clear variable definitions, units in headers, and consistent rounding).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Target a brisk pace in the first 25 minutes to establish the interpret-units-plausibility-log routine (Diagnostic 10 + Micro-lecture 15). If learners are slower, advise them to (a) skim the transcript instead of video and (b) complete only the first 4 items of the units practice, then return later. The longest, highest-value segment is the Case Analysis (20 minutes); encourage learners to protect this time because it integrates all lesson goals. For faster learners, suggest completing a second case scenario or adding an extra plausibility check (e.g., sensitivity to rounding or parameter uncertainty) in the log. Keep the final 10 minutes for the formative critique quiz; it consolidates misconceptions and provides feedback to guide revision.
adaptationOptions: Low bandwidth / accessibility: Provide transcripts for videos, downloadable PDFs, and a non-Excel alternative (Google Sheets or static tables) while keeping the same unit/plausibility prompts.

Math anxiety / lower readiness: Offer a ‘guided’ version of the case log with sentence starters (e.g., ‘Units of dC/dq are ___ because…’) and fewer simultaneous checks (require 1 plausibility check instead of 2).

Advanced learners: Add an extension prompt to perform a simple sensitivity check (e.g., vary an input by ±5% in the spreadsheet and comment on how the derivative/integral output changes) and document it in the log.
Language support: Provide a glossary box with sample interpretation sentences and a bank of verbs (increase/decrease/accumulate) to improve precision in explanations.
Neurodiversity/time management: Chunk tasks into checklists with estimated times; allow completing the case analysis in two sittings (interpretation first, log completion later).
Workplace relevance: Allow learners to substitute one scenario with a mini-example from their own workplace, provided they include units, assumptions, and a limitation statement.
commonMisconceptions: Believing the derivative has the same units as the original function (forgetting it is ‘per unit of the independent variable’).
Treating integration as ‘rate’ instead of accumulation, or forgetting that integrating over time changes kW to kWh (or L/min to L).
Assuming the area/integral must be positive; not recognising that signed area can be negative depending on the function and interval.
Confusing average rate (e.g., C/q) with marginal rate (dC/dq) and using one as if it were the other.
Reporting excessive precision (too many decimal places) without considering measurement uncertainty, model limitations, or audience needs.
Ignoring domain/calibration limits—accepting derivative/integral outputs even when evaluated outside the valid range of the model or data.
Thinking plausibility checks are optional ‘extra’; not realising they are part of professional diligence and auditability.
discussionPrompts: You’re asked to report a marginal cost estimate to management. What is the minimum information (units, assumptions, range, rounding) you would include to make it transparent and defensible?
Describe a plausibility check you trust most (sign, magnitude, comparison to average, boundary behaviour). Why is it effective in your context?
A colleague reports energy use by writing ‘The integral equals 15 kW’. How would you explain the issue clearly and professionally, and what unit should it be?
When is it appropriate to say ‘this derivative/integral result is not reliable’? Give one example of a limitation that would change your decision-making.
How do rounding choices affect downstream decisions (e.g., budgeting, capacity planning)? Share a rounding rule you would adopt for technical documentation.

activities.title: 4) Guided practice: compute marginal cost and total resource use (with validation)

They must produce: (1) a marginal cost table across q values; (2) a total cost/resource summary for an interval; (3) a validation block that includes units, sign/magnitude reasoning, and at least one numerical cross-check.

resources: Workbook practice instructions (inside the file and in LMS)

Run validation checks: (a) unit consistency; (b) compare C’(q) to ΔC/Δq at a nearby interval; (c) compare two methods of accumulation (antiderivative vs trapezoid) and comment on differences.

activities.title: 5) Case analysis: audit and repair a flawed worksheet (integrity & diligence focus)

activities.title: 6) Formative assessment and reflection: plausibility, units, and documentation

Reflection prompt (LMS text box or workbook 'Reflection' cell block)

activities.title: 7) Wrap-up: checklist for next lesson and file hygiene
activities.description: Learners finalize the workbook: ensure units filled, log completed, and formulas reproducible. They export a PDF of key outputs (optional) and save versioned files (e.g., MOD103_L12_v1.xlsx). A short exit checklist prepares them for subsequent optimization/model validation work.

resources: Exit checklist (5 items) embedded in LMS

Offer an optional forum prompt for peer sharing of best validation checks.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this self-study lesson to force analysis (plausibility/units/auditability), not just rule application. Every computational step should have an interpretive counterpart: (1) What does this derivative/integral mean in context? (2) What units must it have? (3) What sign/magnitude is plausible? (4) How can I cross-check it?

Emphasize professional integrity and transparency by requiring learners to:
- State assumptions explicitly (domain of q, parameter meaning, constant pricing assumptions, step size for numerical integration).
- Keep full precision internally and document rounding policy; prohibit rounding mid-calculation.
- Maintain an audit trail (calculation log + cell-cited error notes). Make “traceable and reproducible” a graded expectation in later module assessments.

Use Excel as a modelling environment, not a black box. Encourage formula auditing (Show Formulas, Trace Precedents), named ranges, and consistent unit columns. Provide two independent methods for at least one quantity (e.g., antiderivative vs trapezoid; analytic derivative vs finite difference) to normalize validation as standard practice.

Feedback should explain reasoning: when an answer is wrong, direct learners to the violated principle (units, bounds, or interpretation), not only the algebraic step. Include at least one example where the computation is correct but the conclusion is not justified (e.g., extrapolation beyond model validity).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
If learners struggle early (diagnostic score <70%), recommend: spend 5 extra minutes on the refresher clip and complete only the polynomial part of the practice before attempting the exponential extension.

For on-time learners: keep the demonstration to 1× speed but require pausing at checkpoints to verify formulas in formula view—this prevents passive watching.

If running short on time: in Activity 4, allow either (a) antiderivative-with-bounds OR (b) trapezoid accumulation, but still require the three plausibility checks and documentation.

If learners finish early: add an extension—change step size in trapezoidal accumulation and comment on sensitivity; or vary a parameter and describe how marginal cost changes (qualitatively) and why the units remain consistent.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for all videos; ensure workbook instructions are screen-reader friendly and avoid color-only error flags (add text warnings).
Math support: offer an optional 'rule card' with derivative/integral rules for polynomials/exponentials and one fully worked example before the guided practice.

Excel support: provide a beginner pathway with pre-built table structure and only require editing formulas in highlighted cells; advanced pathway requires learners to build the table from scratch with named ranges.
Language support: include a glossary block in the workbook defining marginal cost, accumulation, bounds, and units; allow learners to submit reflection in bullet points.
Challenge option: require both analytic and numerical integration and a brief comparison statement about approximation error and step size.
Bandwidth/tech constraints: allow Google Sheets equivalent template and instructions; provide a PDF alternative for reading content, with Excel steps summarized as static screenshots.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing marginal cost (derivative, $/unit) with total cost (function value, $) or with average cost (C(q)/q).
Treating the derivative as a finite difference without acknowledging approximation, step size, or where it is evaluated.
Forgetting that a definite integral requires bounds; reporting an antiderivative expression as if it were a numeric total.
Misinterpreting integral units (e.g., thinking the result has the same units as the integrand rather than integrand-units × variable-units).
Applying exponential differentiation incorrectly (e.g., mixing up d/dq[e^{kq}] = k e^{kq}, or mishandling base-10 exponentials).
Using premature rounding in intermediate Excel cells, producing materially different totals and hiding discrepancies.
Excel reference errors (relative vs absolute references) that silently change formulas down a table.
Assuming any positive-looking number is plausible without checking magnitude against context, units, or bounds.
Ignoring domain/validity limits (extrapolating the model beyond the stated range and presenting results without limitations).
discussionPrompts: Which plausibility check (units, sign/magnitude, or numerical cross-check) caught the most important issue in your work today, and why?
When your analytic integral and trapezoidal accumulation disagreed, what did you conclude about step size, rounding, or implementation—what evidence supported your conclusion?
What is one assumption in the scenario that, if wrong, would most undermine the interpretation of marginal cost? How would you document that limitation professionally?
Share a screenshot snippet (or describe) one Excel auditing tool you used (Show Formulas, Trace Precedents). How did it improve transparency or reduce error risk?
If a stakeholder asked, 'How confident are you in this total resource estimate?', what uncertainty/limitations would you report without over-claiming precision?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson to foreground analysis over procedure: learners should spend more time validating outputs than performing long symbolic manipulations. Use authentic units and require learners to state what each quantity represents (e.g., ‘P(t) is kW at time t in hours’). Reinforce an ‘audit mindset’: every result must have (1) units, (2) an interpretation tied to context, (3) at least one plausibility check (sign/magnitude/boundary), and (4) documented assumptions/limitations. In feedback, avoid only marking answers right/wrong—reference the checking process (e.g., ‘Your unit check is missing; add a line showing kW·h = kWh’). Encourage transparent rounding: keep full precision during calculations, then round at reporting with a stated rule (e.g., 3 s.f. or to measurement tolerance). Provide hint ladders so learners can self-correct without immediately seeing final answers; this supports independent online study while maintaining rigor. Where possible, include “deliberate errors” in examples to normalise checking behaviour as professional diligence rather than remediation.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 25–30 minutes brisk (warm-up + micro-lecture) to activate prior knowledge and set expectations for analysis. Allocate the largest uninterrupted block (25 minutes) to the case analysis; advise learners to timebox: 5 minutes to scan and flag issues, 10 minutes to correct with unit checks, 10 minutes to complete the calculation log and interpretation. If learners fall behind, they should prioritise: (1) identifying flaws with reasons, (2) unit-consistent corrected result, (3) at least 5 log entries—over perfect algebraic simplification. Offer an optional extension (not required for the 90 minutes): complete a second case or add a sensitivity/plausibility estimate using a rough average approximation to cross-check an integral.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility: provide transcripts/captions for all videos and a screen-reader-friendly version of the case pack; allow responses in typed text or annotated PDF.
Scaffolding: offer a ‘unit pipeline’ checklist (Given quantity → units → operation → resulting units → interpretation) and a partially completed calculation log for learners who need structure.
Challenge: add an extension prompt asking learners to compare two modelling assumptions (e.g., linear vs piecewise constant rate) and discuss how results and limitations change.
Language support: provide a glossary box for key terms (rate of change, accumulation, marginal, tolerance) with one workplace sentence each.
Math support: include a short optional refresher on derivative/integral rules used in the cases, but keep the core task focused on analysis/validation.
Assessment flexibility: allow multiple attempts on quizzes with item pools; for the reflection, allow audio submission for learners who express themselves better verbally.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing average rate of change with instantaneous rate (treating Δy/Δt as y′(t) without context).

Believing an integral ‘always increases’: forgetting that the integral of a negative rate can decrease an accumulated quantity (or that accumulated energy should be non-negative if power is non-negative).
Dropping or inventing units during differentiation/integration (e.g., thinking integration ‘removes’ units rather than multiplying by the unit of the variable).
Ignoring the variable’s unit (seconds vs hours) and failing to convert, leading to magnitude errors by factors of 60 or 3600.
Assuming any computed value is plausible because the algebra is correct; neglecting sign, boundary behaviour, and order-of-magnitude checks.
Premature rounding during intermediate steps, causing avoidable discrepancies; not stating rounding rules or precision expectations.
Treating constants and scaling factors incorrectly (e.g., forgetting that integrating k·f(t) gives k·∫f(t)dt).
Interpreting a derivative or integral without specifying what quantity is changing/accumulating (missing ‘per unit time’ or ‘total over interval’ language).
discussionPrompts: In your chosen case, what was the first red flag that the derivative/integral output was not plausible (units, sign, magnitude, or interpretation)? Explain your reasoning.
Share one calculation-log entry you wrote that improved transparency. What assumption did you document, and how could it change the decision someone makes from the result?
Pick one: throughput, cost, or energy. Describe a real workplace situation where confusing rate with accumulation would cause a practical error. How would you prevent it with a check?
What rounding rule is most defensible in technical documentation: fixed decimal places, significant figures, or rounding to measurement tolerance? Justify with an example.

If two analysts get slightly different answers but both are dimensionally consistent, what evidence would you request to decide which is more trustworthy (logs, assumptions, domain checks, sensitivity checks)?

lessons.lessonTitle: Differentiate and integrate polynomial and exponential fu...
objectives: Given a polynomial or exponential cost/resource function C(q) with stated units, compute the marginal quantity (derivative) analytically and implement it in Excel so that marginal values are correctly produced across a column for q (quantity) values.

Using Excel outputs, analyse marginal (derivative) and accumulated (integral) results for plausibility by performing at least two validation checks (units/dimensions, sign and monotonicity, boundary-value check, and/or order-of-magnitude reasonableness).

Compute total resource use or total cost over an interval [q1, q2] by integrating a polynomial/exponential rate function, and verify the result by comparing (i) analytic integration to (ii) numerical approximation (e.g., trapezoidal rule) in Excel, explaining any discrepancy.
Document assumptions, rounding decisions, and limitations in a calculation log (including units, source of constants, and interpretation notes) to produce a reproducible, auditable worksheet.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 1: Read-the-output diagnostic (marginal vs total, units)
activities.description: Auto-graded diagnostic quiz (8–10 items) based on screenshots of Excel tables/graphs. Learners identify whether a column represents C(q), C′(q), or ∫C′(q)dq; select correct units; and flag at least one implausible output (e.g., negative marginal cost when the context implies increasing cost). Immediate feedback is provided after submission.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with immediate feedback to surface misconceptions before computation.
instructorActions: Configure quiz with targeted distractors (average vs marginal, wrong units, missing constants).
Provide feedback that links each wrong choice to a specific check (units/sign/boundary).
Post a brief note: learners should keep a running 'checks list' for later activities.
studentActions: Complete the diagnostic quiz independently.
Record two personal 'watch-outs' (e.g., unit mismatch, confusing marginal with average) to apply later.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: Marginal change and accumulation as audit-ready quantities
activities.description: Short segmented lesson (video + notes) connecting calculus outputs to professional practice: marginal cost C′(q) as a rate, total cost difference ΔC as an accumulation, and what makes a calculation transparent (units, assumptions, rounding, reproducibility). Includes two worked examples: (1) polynomial cost and (2) exponential resource use.
activities.teachingMethod: Direct instruction with worked examples and embedded 'pause-and-predict' questions.
resources: Downloadable notes (formulas for derivatives/integrals of polynomials and exponentials)
instructorActions: Emphasise interpretation: derivative units = (output units)/(input units); integral units = (rate units)×(input units).
Model transparency: state assumptions explicitly (domain of q, positivity, parameter source).
Show one intentional error (unit mismatch) and how a check detects it.
studentActions: Watch segments and answer embedded 'pause-and-predict' questions in notes.
Add at least one check to their personal checklist (e.g., boundary-value check at q=0).

activities.title: Demonstration: Building a derivative + integral worksheet in Excel (polynomial & exponential)
activities.description: Guided screencast building an audit-ready Excel sheet: define inputs and units, compute C(q), compute analytic C′(q) in cells, approximate derivative by finite differences for comparison, and compute accumulated total over an interval using both analytic integral and trapezoidal approximation. Demonstration includes formatting for transparency (named ranges, unit column, and a calculation log tab).
activities.teachingMethod: Worked demonstration with explicit narration of assumptions, checks, and documentation steps.
resources: Excel template file (starter: columns for q, C(q), analytic C′(q), numeric C′(q), analytic total, trapezoid total)
instructorActions: Demonstrate a consistent structure: Inputs → Model → Outputs → Checks → Log.
Show how to compare analytic vs numeric derivative (absolute/relative difference column).
Model dimensional checks by adding a 'Units' column and commenting units in headers.
Demonstrate rounding discipline: keep full precision internally, round only for reporting with a stated rule.
studentActions: Follow along in the template workbook and reproduce the demonstrated formulas.
Pause to replicate each section before continuing.
Note where each plausibility check is implemented in the sheet.

activities.title: Break / cognitive reset
activities.description: Short offline break. Learners are prompted to return and re-open the workbook, then run a quick 'sanity scan' (scan headers, units, and signs) before proceeding.
activities.teachingMethod: Spaced learning and attention reset to reduce error rates in later computation.
instructorActions: Provide a prompt: 'When you return, re-check units in headers and confirm q-step size.'
studentActions: Step away briefly.
Return and do a 30-second scan for units, correct cell references, and q increments.

activities.title: Guided Practice: Compute marginal cost and total resource use (with checks)
activities.description: Learners complete an applied task in Excel using two functions (one polynomial, one exponential). They compute marginal cost/resource rate, then compute total over a specified interval. They must run and record at least two checks: (1) dimensional/unit consistency, and (2) plausibility (sign, monotonicity, boundary-value, or comparison to numeric approximation). An automated self-check (hidden key cells or conditional formatting) flags common errors (wrong exponent rule, incorrect absolute references, wrong step size).
activities.teachingMethod: Guided problem-solving with scaffolded prompts and immediate automated feedback in the workbook.
resources: Practice workbook (same template, new parameters and prompts)
Hint bank (collapsed sections: derivative rules, exponential rules, trapezoid setup)
instructorActions: Provide stepwise prompts that require analysis (e.g., 'Which check is most sensitive to step-size errors?').
Include a 'debug pathway' for learners who get a mismatch (check units → check references → check derivative rule → check interval/step).
Ensure the task requires interpretation (not just computation), e.g., identify where marginal cost increases fastest.
studentActions: Fill in formulas for analytic derivative and integral for both functions.
Compute numeric derivative and trapezoidal totals and compare to analytic results.
Record two checks and outcomes (pass/fail + explanation) in the calculation log tab.

activities.title: Case Analysis: Plausibility, tolerance, and sensitivity mini-audit
activities.description: Learners audit their own worksheet (or a provided 'buggy' version). They identify at least two issues (e.g., unit mismatch, missing constant of integration/incorrect baseline, inappropriate rounding, step-size too large, parameter without source). Then they perform a small sensitivity check by varying one parameter (e.g., growth rate in the exponential) and describing how marginal and total outputs change, including what remains invariant dimensionally.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured self-audit using a rubric: detect, explain, correct, and document.
resources: Buggy workbook option (intentional errors) OR self-audit rubric
Sensitivity check instructions (use a 2–3 row parameter table or slider cell)
instructorActions: Provide a short rubric with point-by-point expectations (what counts as a valid check and a valid limitation statement).
Model one example of a strong limitation statement (e.g., 'Assumes continuous q; discrete batch sizes may change interpretation of marginal cost').
studentActions: Identify and correct at least two issues (in their own sheet or the buggy sheet).
Run a one-parameter sensitivity change and interpret the effect on outputs (direction + relative magnitude).
Update the calculation log with corrections and a limitation note.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 2: Exit ticket (analysis + documentation)
activities.description: Short submission/quiz: learners answer 4 prompts and upload (or paste) key cells from their log. Prompts: (1) state units for C(q), C′(q), and accumulated total; (2) report one plausibility check and evidence; (3) explain a discrepancy between analytic and numeric results (if any) and what caused it; (4) state one assumption and one limitation relevant to the context.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes exit ticket focused on analysis and professional transparency.
resources: Example of an acceptable assumption/limitation statement
instructorActions: Set clear criteria for completion (must include units + one check + one assumption + one limitation).
Provide automated feedback stems for common issues (e.g., 'Derivative units must divide by the input unit').
studentActions: Complete the exit ticket prompts.
Submit required excerpts (units, check evidence, assumption/limitation) from the calculation log.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson so learners must interpret and validate, not only compute. In every example, require explicit units in headers and a short written interpretation of what the derivative/integral means in context (rate vs accumulation). Emphasise professional integrity: (1) keep a transparent calculation log (assumptions, parameter sources, rounding rules), (2) separate model inputs from formulas, (3) make checks visible (comparison columns, conditional formatting), and (4) report limitations/uncertainty honestly (e.g., step-size effects, continuous approximation, parameter sensitivity). Encourage learners to triangulate results: analytic derivative/integral vs numerical approximations in Excel, plus boundary and sign checks. When giving feedback, link each error to the specific check that should have caught it (units, monotonicity, boundary value, or magnitude).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Target a brisk pace in the first 45 minutes (diagnostic + concepts + build). If learners fall behind during the demonstration, recommend skipping cosmetic formatting and focusing only on (a) correct formulas, (b) a comparison column (analytic vs numeric), and (c) the log entries. During guided practice, use a timebox: 10 minutes to complete derivatives, 10 minutes for totals (analytic + trapezoid), 5 minutes for checks/log. Faster learners can extend by adding a parameter table for sensitivity or by testing two different step sizes to see numeric convergence; slower learners should use the hint bank and complete one function (polynomial) fully before starting the exponential.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded template: provide a version with cell references and structure pre-built (learners only enter derivative/integral formulas) for those needing additional support.
Challenge extension: include a piecewise function or an exponential with a shift (e.g., C(q)=a·e^(kq)+b) requiring careful handling of constants and interpretation of baseline cost.
Accessibility: offer a text-only walkthrough of the screencast, high-contrast workbook formatting, and keyboard-only navigation tips.
Alternative tool pathway: allow learners who cannot access Excel to use Google Sheets with equivalent formulas and a simplified numeric integration method.

Language support: provide a bilingual key-terms sheet (Function, derivative, integral, marginal cost) and sentence frames for assumptions/limitations (e.g., 'Assumes ___ because ___. This may not hold when ___').
Error-reduction support: provide a 'debug checklist' flowchart (units → references → formula rule → interval/step → rounding/reporting).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing marginal cost (derivative) with average cost (C(q)/q) or with total cost difference (ΔC).
Forgetting that derivative units are output-units divided by input-units (e.g., $/unit), leading to dimensionally impossible interpretations.
Treating the integral of a marginal function as the total cost without accounting for a baseline/constant of integration (mixing 'total' with 'total change').
Applying the exponential derivative rule incorrectly (e.g., d/dq[e^(kq)] = e^(kq) instead of k·e^(kq)).
Numeric approximation errors: using an inconsistent step size, off-by-one ranges in trapezoidal sums, or mixing endpoints incorrectly.
Rounding too early in intermediate cells, causing mismatches between analytic and numeric comparisons and hiding errors.
Misreading Excel order of operations or misplacing parentheses in formulas (especially with exponentials).
Assuming a model must always produce increasing marginal cost; ignoring contexts where marginal may decrease or plateau and failing to justify expected behaviour.
discussionPrompts: Which single check (units, boundary value, monotonicity/sign, or numeric-vs-analytic comparison) would catch the most serious errors in your worksheet, and why?
If your analytic integral and trapezoidal total differ, how can you determine whether the discrepancy is due to step size, a formula error, or rounding?
What is one assumption you made about the quantity variable q (continuity, range, discreteness), and how would violating it change the interpretation of marginal cost?
How would you explain (to a non-specialist stakeholder) the difference between 'marginal cost at q=50' and 'total cost from q=0 to 50' using units and a one-sentence interpretation?
Where should rounding occur in a professional calculation log, and what risks arise if you round intermediate results?

moduleLessonPlans.moduleTitle: Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver

lessons.lessonTitle: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver to...
objectives: Identify and label (in an Excel model) the decision variables, objective function, and at least three constraints for a given operational scenario with correct units and assumptions.

Configure Excel Solver (variable cells, objective, constraint directions, and solving method) to obtain an optimal solution for a constrained optimisation problem and verify feasibility by checking constraints numerically.
Interpret Solver outputs to classify constraints as binding/non-binding and explain at least two operational bottlenecks or trade-offs using the final values and slack.

Use the Sensitivity Report (shadow prices and reduced costs) to explain marginal change for one constraint and one decision variable, including the valid range/allowable change where the interpretation holds.
Produce a transparent calculation log (assumptions, units, rounding) that enables another reviewer to reproduce the Solver result without additional guidance.

activities.title: Start-up: lesson map, prerequisites check, and Solver readiness
activities.description: Self-study orientation page (or short video) that outlines the optimisation workflow: define variables → write objective → translate constraints → build Excel model → run Solver → validate → interpret sensitivity. Includes a checklist to confirm Solver Add-in is enabled and a quick prerequisite refresher (functions/graphs from MOD3).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-content + checklist; learners confirm setup before proceeding to avoid downstream errors.
instructorActions: Provide a clear workflow diagram and explicit success criteria for the lesson.
Include troubleshooting notes for common Solver add-in issues and version differences.
studentActions: Enable Solver add-in and confirm it appears in the Data tab.
Complete the prerequisite readiness checklist (self-confirmation).

activities.title: Core concepts: translating a scenario into an optimisation model
activities.description: Interactive mini-lesson on key terms (decision variable, objective, constraint, feasible region, binding constraint) and how to convert a word problem into an Excel-ready mathematical structure. Includes two embedded “analyse” checks: (1) classify statements as objective vs constraint, (2) spot missing units/assumptions in a draft model.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked examples with embedded knowledge checks that require justification (not just selection).
resources: Interactive content page (H5P or LMS equivalent)
Key terms glossary (Decision variable, Constraint, Excel Solver, optimisation model, CI)
instructorActions: Use one consistent scenario (e.g., two-product production planning) throughout the lesson to reduce cognitive load.
Model diligence: explicitly show units beside every coefficient and constraint limit.
studentActions: Complete embedded checks and read feedback explanations.
Annotate the scenario with variable names, units, and constraint types (≤, ≥, =).

activities.title: Demonstration: build and run a Solver model end-to-end (with audit trail)
activities.description: Step-by-step video demonstration of building an Excel model: decision variable cells, objective cell formula, constraint calculations, and a clearly labelled assumptions table. Run Solver, select an appropriate solving method (Simplex LP for linear), and generate the Answer + Sensitivity Reports. Demonstration includes a “calculation log” tab showing assumptions, units, rounding decisions, and checks (e.g., constraint residuals/slack).
activities.teachingMethod: Pause-and-do prompts every 2–4 minutes; learners replicate steps in parallel using a provided template.
resources: Completed solution file (locked until after practice, or provided as optional check)
instructorActions: Explicitly narrate why each Solver setting is chosen (especially solving method and constraints).
Show validation checks: confirm objective improves, confirm constraints satisfied, confirm units are consistent.
studentActions: Follow along and replicate the model structure in their own copy of the template.
Pause at prompts to enter formulas and label units/assumptions.

activities.title: Guided practice: complete a new optimisation model and validate feasibility
activities.description: Learners complete a second scenario (similar structure, different numbers/constraints) using a scaffolded worksheet. Tasks: (1) define variables and units, (2) write objective and constraint formulas, (3) configure Solver, (4) run Solver and record results, (5) validate with a constraint check table (left-hand side vs right-hand side, slack, and flagged violations). Includes an auto-check rubric: feasibility, correct constraint directions, correct variable ranges (e.g., non-negativity), and transparent calculation log completeness.
activities.teachingMethod: Scaffolded completion + self-check rubric; emphasis on error detection and correction (analyse-level).
resources: Troubleshooting guide (common Solver messages and fixes)
instructorActions: Provide targeted hints (progressive reveal): first about structure, then about formulas, then about Solver settings.
Include feedback for typical errors (e.g., wrong constraint sign, objective set to value cell not formula cell).
studentActions: Complete the workbook steps and run Solver.
Use the constraint check table to diagnose any infeasibility and iterate until feasible/optimal.

activities.title: Case analysis: interpret Answer & Sensitivity Reports for marginal values and bottlenecks
activities.description: Learners analyse a provided Solver output (Answer + Sensitivity Reports) and answer prompts: identify binding constraints, interpret slack, interpret one shadow price (marginal value of relaxing a constraint) and one reduced cost, and state the allowable range caveat. Learners then write 3–5 sentences translating the math into an operational recommendation (e.g., which resource is the bottleneck and what improvement is worth considering).
activities.teachingMethod: Guided interpretation questions that force linkage from report fields → operational meaning → limitation (range validity).
resources: PDF/Excel excerpt of Answer and Sensitivity Reports
Shadow price & reduced cost “cheat sheet” (definitions + interpretation template)
Short example of an evidence-based recommendation paragraph
instructorActions: Provide a structured response template: Claim → Evidence (report value) → Implication → Validity range.
Prompt learners to check units of shadow prices (objective units per constraint unit).
studentActions: Complete the interpretation questions and write a recommendation paragraph.
Check that interpretations include units and the allowable increase/decrease constraint.

activities.title: Formative assessment (auto-marked): diagnose model and interpretation errors
activities.description: Short quiz with scenario snippets and Solver outputs. Item types: (1) identify mis-specified decision variable cells, (2) choose correct constraint direction, (3) decide if a shadow price statement is valid given allowable range, (4) spot a units/rounding issue in a calculation log excerpt.
activities.teachingMethod: Immediate feedback with targeted remediation links back to the relevant section of the lesson.
instructorActions: Design distractors based on real Solver mistakes (not superficial errors).
Attach feedback that explains why an option is wrong (unit inconsistency, range misuse, infeasible constraints).
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback for any incorrect items.
Re-attempt missed items after reviewing remediation content (if allowed).

activities.title: Wrap-up: reflection and reproducibility checklist
activities.description: Learners complete a short reflection and final check: confirm assumptions table, unit labels, Solver settings recorded, and constraint residuals shown. Learners save/export their calculation log (or screenshot key tabs) for auditability.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured self-reflection (written) aligned to diligence/attention-to-detail competency and audit-ready documentation expectations.
instructorActions: Provide a model checklist and an exemplar of a transparent log.
Emphasise that interpretation is only as reliable as the documented assumptions and unit consistency.
studentActions: Complete the reproducibility checklist against their own file.
Write a brief reflection on one modelling decision and one validation check they performed.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design the lesson around an explicit, repeatable modelling workflow to support self-study: (1) translate scenario to variables/objective/constraints, (2) implement in Excel with labelled units, (3) run Solver with justified settings, (4) validate feasibility and reasonableness, (5) interpret sensitivity within allowable ranges, (6) document for audit.

Because the Bloom target is Analyse, embed tasks that require learners to detect, classify, and justify (e.g., diagnose why a constraint is binding, explain a trade-off using shadow prices, identify whether a marginal interpretation is valid given allowable changes). Prioritise diligence and attention to detail by requiring: a units column, an assumptions table, and a constraint check table (LHS, RHS, slack, violation flag). Provide frequent “pause-and-check” prompts and immediate feedback, since there is no live instructor.

Use a consistent scenario first (worked example), then a near-transfer scenario (guided practice) to reinforce structure while still requiring analysis. Include troubleshooting for common Solver errors (infeasible, unbounded, wrong method) and encourage learners to keep Solver settings and versions recorded in a log tab for reproducibility.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Keep the concept segment tight (15 min) and move quickly into building/analysing models. In the demo, insert mandatory pause points every few minutes so learners actively replicate steps rather than watch passively. If learners are behind during guided practice, advise they: (a) complete the model structure first, (b) run Solver even if unsure, (c) use the constraint check table to locate the error, then iterate.

Optional time-flex: learners who finish early should attempt an extension—add a new constraint (e.g., minimum demand) or change a parameter and predict which constraint will become binding before rerunning Solver. Learners who need more time can skip the extension and focus on producing a correct, well-documented baseline model and one correct sensitivity interpretation.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded pathway: provide a version of the practice workbook with the objective and constraint formulas partially filled, requiring learners to complete only missing parts and interpret outputs.
Reduced-cognitive-load pathway: provide a smaller model (2 variables, 2 constraints) before moving to the full scenario; keep the same workflow and documentation requirements.

Challenge pathway: require integer constraints (if context-appropriate) or add a scenario twist (e.g., capacity expansion option) and ask learners to compare outcomes and explain differences in binding constraints.
Accessibility: provide video transcript, captions, and a text-only step list; ensure colour is not the only indicator in constraint violation flags (use icons or conditional formatting with labels).
Math-support: include a brief refresher on slope/marginal change and how it relates to shadow price units; provide a template sentence starter for interpreting marginal values.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing decision variable cells with calculated cells (e.g., selecting total profit as the changing cell range).
Entering constraints with the wrong inequality direction (≤ vs ≥) or constraining the wrong cell (e.g., constraining per-unit usage instead of total usage).
Omitting non-negativity constraints, leading to unrealistic negative production/allocations.
Using the wrong solving method (e.g., GRG Nonlinear for a linear model) and misinterpreting results or encountering avoidable convergence issues.
Assuming a non-binding constraint has ‘no effect ever’ rather than ‘no effect at the optimum within the current model’.
Interpreting shadow prices as universally valid, ignoring allowable increase/decrease ranges from the Sensitivity Report.
Misreading reduced cost (thinking it is profit/cost directly rather than the amount the objective coefficient must improve for a non-basic variable to enter the solution, in linear models).
Failing to track units, causing incorrect coefficients (e.g., mixing hours and minutes, or kilograms and grams) and therefore invalid optimisation results.
Rounding too early (in coefficients or intermediate calculations), producing different optima or constraint violations; not documenting rounding rules in the calculation log.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the primary bottleneck in your model, and what evidence (slack/binding status/shadow price) supports that claim?
If you could increase one resource by 1 unit, which would you choose and why? Include units and reference the shadow price and its allowable range.
Find one assumption in the scenario that, if wrong, would most change the optimal solution. How would you test sensitivity to that assumption in Excel?
Your Solver result recommends a surprising decision (e.g., produce none of a product). What checks would you run to confirm the result is not due to a modelling error?
How would you explain the trade-off shown by the Sensitivity Report to a non-technical stakeholder in a team review meeting?

lessons.lessonTitle: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver to...
objectives: Given an operational scenario, define at least 2 decision variables with correct units and specify an objective function (maximise or minimise) in an Excel model with transparent cell references/named ranges.

Construct a constrained optimisation model in Excel Solver by correctly entering the objective cell, variable cells, and at least 3 constraints (including non-negativity), and select an appropriate solving method (Simplex LP vs GRG Nonlinear) based on model structure.
Analyse Solver output to identify binding vs non-binding constraints, locate the bottleneck resource(s), and justify the conclusion using reported constraint slack and/or status.

Interpret marginal values from Solver sensitivity outputs (e.g., shadow prices / reduced costs where applicable) to explain at least 2 trade-offs and recommend one operational change supported by numerical evidence and correct units/rounding.

activities.title: 1) Lesson orientation + prerequisite check (MOD103 refresh)
activities.description: Self-study kickoff: learners review what an optimisation model needs (decision variables, objective, constraints) and complete a quick prerequisite check on reading formulas and basic function graphs. Emphasis on diligence: units, assumptions, and calculation accuracy.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice (micro-quiz) + checklist priming for accuracy (units/assumptions/rounding).
resources: One-page 'Accuracy Checklist' (units, signs, rounding, variable ranges)
instructorActions: Provide the micro-quiz with automated feedback explaining why each option is correct/incorrect.
Provide an accuracy checklist and require learners to keep it open during model building.
studentActions: Complete the prerequisite micro-quiz and review feedback.
Open/save the accuracy checklist for use during the lesson.

activities.title: 2) Modelling translation: from words to an Excel optimisation structure
activities.description: Interactive mini-lesson (video + guided notes) on translating a short scenario into: decision variables (with units), objective function, and constraints (capacity, demand, budget, time). Learners label each constraint type and write it in inequality form before touching Solver.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked example + annotation: learners pause video to fill a modelling table (Variable | Unit | Meaning; Constraint | Unit | Inequality; Objective | Unit).
resources: 8–10 min captioned video: 'Model components and units'
Guided notes template (fillable PDF or Word): modelling table
Scenario text: 'Production mix with labour and material limits'
instructorActions: Model explicit unit-checking (e.g., hours/product × products = hours).
Call out typical sign-direction errors and how to sanity-check constraints using extreme values.
studentActions: Complete the modelling table with units for each term.
Write each constraint in inequality form and briefly note what would violate it.

activities.title: 3) Demonstration: Building the Excel sheet + Solver setup (transparent logs)
activities.description: Step-by-step demonstration (screen capture) creating a clean Excel layout: inputs, decision variable cells, calculated totals (LHS of constraints), objective cell, and a 'calculation log' area documenting assumptions and units. Learners follow along in a provided template and replicate the structure.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided imitation with pause points; emphasis on reproducible structure (named ranges, consistent units, no hard-coded constants in formulas).
resources: Screen-capture demo (10–12 min) showing Solver parameters and method choice
Quick reference: 'Which Solver method?' (Simplex LP vs GRG Nonlinear)
instructorActions: Demonstrate setting: Set Objective, By Changing Variable Cells, Add constraints, Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative.
Explain how to detect linearity (formulas) to justify Simplex LP vs GRG Nonlinear.
Demonstrate creating a short calculation log: date/version, assumptions, units, rounding rule.
studentActions: Open the template and mirror the layout from the demo.
Enter Solver settings exactly as shown and save a versioned file name (e.g., L2_v1).

activities.title: 4) Guided practice: Solve, verify, and audit the model
activities.description: Hands-on build-and-solve cycle. Learners complete the missing formulas, run Solver, and then perform an audit: (1) verify constraints are satisfied, (2) check units, (3) confirm objective formula references decision variables, (4) document assumptions and rounding. Learners correct at least one intentional 'trap' (e.g., mismatched unit or reversed inequality) embedded in the template.
activities.teachingMethod: Deliberate practice with immediate feedback: automated 'check cells' compare expected totals and flag common errors (signs/units/references).
resources: Excel template with built-in checks (conditional formatting flags)
Answer key panel unlocked after attempt (showing correct Solver parameter setup and expected objective value range)
instructorActions: Provide automated feedback rules (e.g., highlight if a constraint LHS exceeds RHS; warn if objective cell does not depend on variables).
Encourage learners to keep a short audit trail: what changed, why, and what was rechecked.
studentActions: Complete formulas, run Solver, and record the optimal variable values and objective value.
Use the checklist to audit constraints, units, and references; fix any flagged issues and re-solve.
Write 2–3 bullet notes in the calculation log describing the correction(s) made.

activities.title: 5) Interpreting results: binding constraints, slack, and bottlenecks
activities.description: Short lesson on reading Solver results (Answer Report or output table): determine which constraints are binding (bottlenecks), quantify slack, and explain operational meaning. Learners classify each constraint as binding/non-binding and justify using slack values and the solution point.
activities.teachingMethod: Explain–apply: mini-explanation followed by structured analysis prompts applied to the learner’s own solution.
resources: Short explainer (5 min): 'Binding vs non-binding constraints'
instructorActions: Provide a decision rule: binding if slack ≈ 0 (within tolerance) and constraint active at optimum.
Highlight tolerance/rounding issues: near-zero slack may be numerical, so interpret with Solver precision settings.
studentActions: Generate an Answer Report (or read constraint table) and list binding constraints.
State the bottleneck resource(s) and quantify slack for non-binding constraints (with units).

activities.title: 6) Sensitivity and trade-offs: marginal values for decision-making
activities.description: Learners interpret sensitivity outputs (where applicable) to explain marginal change: shadow price for resources (constraints) and reduced cost (variables). They test one 'what-if' change (e.g., +1 unit of a binding resource) and compare predicted vs recomputed objective change, noting any limits of validity.
activities.teachingMethod: Prediction–check cycle: use sensitivity output to predict impact, then modify input and re-run Solver to validate within allowable range.
resources: Mini-guide: 'Shadow price, reduced cost, allowable increase/decrease' (plain language + units)
Optional note: 'Sensitivity reports only for linear models (Simplex LP)'
instructorActions: Instruct learners to state marginal values with units (e.g., profit per additional labour hour).
Prompt learners to compare predicted change to actual re-optimised change and explain discrepancies (range limits/nonlinearity/tolerance).
studentActions: Record shadow price(s) and interpret at least one in context.
Run a small what-if change and compare predicted vs actual objective change; document conclusion in calculation log.

activities.title: 7) Formative assessment: Results interpretation and recommendation
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz + short written justification. Quiz focuses on identifying decision variables, binding constraints, and interpreting a marginal value. Learners also submit a brief recommendation (3–5 sentences) grounded in their Solver output and sensitivity evidence.
activities.teachingMethod: Formative assessment with targeted feedback and an evidence-based recommendation prompt.
resources: 10-item auto-graded quiz (mix of numeric, MCQ, and interpretation)
Short-response submission box with rubric (clarity, correct units, evidence, rounding)
instructorActions: Provide automated feedback explanations for each quiz item.
Provide a rubric emphasizing: correct units, correct identification of bottleneck, and transparent evidence from reports.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback for any missed concepts.
Submit a short recommendation referencing at least one binding constraint and one marginal value (with units).

activities.title: 8) Wrap-up + next-step preview (link to team review communication)
activities.description: Learners consolidate: create a one-screen summary (variables, objective, binding constraints, marginal insight) suitable for an audit trail and team review. Preview next lesson: integrating calculus-based marginal reasoning with Solver-based optimisation and presenting findings.
activities.teachingMethod: Reflective synthesis: concise ‘executive summary’ for operational decision-making.
resources: One-slide summary template (PowerPoint/Google Slides) or LMS text box
Checklist: 'What to include in an optimisation recommendation'
instructorActions: Provide the summary template and model an example of clear, audit-ready wording.
Direct learners to the module forum prompt (optional) for peer comparison of bottlenecks and trade-offs.
studentActions: Complete the one-screen summary and save/export (PDF).
Optionally post one key insight to the forum prompt.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design for analysis (not just button-clicking): require learners to justify each modelling choice (variables, objective, constraint direction) and to interpret outputs (binding constraints, marginal values) in operational language. Use an explicit accuracy routine aligned to the competency: (1) units check on every term (dimensional consistency), (2) sign/inequality sanity check using extreme values (e.g., set all variables to zero; test a clearly infeasible point), (3) reference check to avoid hard-coded constants in formulas, (4) rounding rule: avoid rounding intermediate cells; round only reported results with stated precision.

For online self-study, embed frequent pause points with prompts (e.g., 'Before you run Solver, predict which constraint will bind and why'). Provide immediate feedback through spreadsheet check cells and auto-graded items. Emphasise transparency and reproducibility: encourage named ranges, versioned file saves (v1, v2), and a calculation log capturing assumptions, Solver method choice, and any corrections made after error flags.

When addressing sensitivity: clarify applicability. Sensitivity reports (shadow prices, reduced costs, allowable ranges) are meaningful primarily for linear models solved with Simplex LP; for GRG Nonlinear or integer constraints, use scenario testing and local marginal reasoning instead. Require units on marginal values (e.g., $ per labour-hour) and a statement of validity limits (allowable increase/decrease or 'local to current solution').
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Keep the first 30 minutes moving: learners should reach a runnable Solver setup by minute ~35 (end of Activity 3). If learners stall, direct them to the template’s 'minimum viable model' tab and then return to full build. Allocate the largest block (Activity 4) to hands-on solving and auditing; if time is tight, prioritise: correct constraints + verified feasibility + identification of binding constraints, then treat sensitivity as an extension.

Suggested self-study rhythm: 8–12 minute content chunks, then an action (edit spreadsheet, run Solver, record output). Encourage learners to time-box debugging: 5 minutes to diagnose with checklist, then consult the unlocked answer panel and note what was wrong in the calculation log.
adaptationOptions: Support for learners needing more scaffolding: provide a fully worked example spreadsheet alongside the starter template, with commentary bubbles explaining each formula and unit check.

Extension for advanced learners: add an additional constraint (e.g., minimum contractual demand) or an integer/binary decision (setup/no-setup) and ask learners to compare how interpretation changes when sensitivity reports are unavailable.

Accessibility: provide captioned videos, a text-only walkthrough of Solver steps, and an alternative dataset in CSV compatible with screen readers; ensure colour-based flags also include text warnings.

Math confidence support: include a pre-filled modelling table with blanks only for inequality direction and units; provide a glossary pop-up for key terms (decision variable, constraint, shadow price, reduced cost).
Challenge option (analysis-focused): require learners to run two scenarios (resource increase vs demand change) and argue which yields higher marginal benefit, citing computed outcomes and limits.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing decision variables with parameters/inputs (e.g., treating labour hours available as a variable rather than a constraint bound).
Reversing inequality direction (e.g., using ≥ when capacity is a maximum) or mixing up LHS/RHS when entering Solver constraints.
Objective cell not actually depending on the changing variable cells due to hard-coded numbers or incorrect references.
Assuming 'Solver found a solution' implies it is correct—ignoring feasibility (constraint violations), tolerances, and unit consistency.
Misinterpreting slack: thinking a large slack means the constraint is important, when it actually indicates the constraint is not currently limiting.
Treating shadow prices as globally valid regardless of allowable ranges or model type; applying sensitivity interpretations to nonlinear/integer problems without scenario re-solving.
Rounding intermediate values, which can change binding status and reported marginal values; failing to state rounding precision in documentation.
Using the wrong solving method (e.g., GRG for a linear model) and then expecting a sensitivity report or consistent marginal outputs.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint was binding in your solution, and how can you justify it using slack and units (not just 'Solver says so')?
If you could increase only one resource by 1 unit, which would you choose and why? Use a marginal value (shadow price or scenario test) to support your choice.
Describe one modelling assumption you made (e.g., linearity, divisibility of products) and explain how violating it might change the recommendation.
Where did you find the highest risk of a unit mismatch in this model? What specific unit check helped you detect or prevent it?
Compare two learners’ solutions (or your v1 vs v2): did the same constraint remain the bottleneck? If not, what modelling or data difference caused the shift?
When would you distrust a near-zero slack value? What Solver settings or rounding choices could produce misleading ‘almost binding’ constraints?

lessons.lessonTitle: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver to...
objectives: Identify and classify constraints in an Excel optimisation model as binding or non-binding using Solver Answer Report outputs (final value vs. constraint RHS) with 100% correct classification on a provided case.

Interpret Solver Sensitivity Report fields (shadow price, reduced cost, allowable increase/decrease) to explain at least two operational trade-offs and one bottleneck in a short written justification (150–200 words) using correct units.

Validate Solver results by completing an audit-ready calculation log that documents decision variables, objective, constraints, Solver method/settings, and a minimum of three accuracy checks (units, rounding, and feasibility) with no missing fields.

Perform a one-parameter what-if change to a constraint RHS, predict the direction of objective change using marginal values, and verify by re-solving; report the prediction error within ±5% for the provided linear case.

activities.title: Warm-up diagnostic: Reading a Solver result snapshot
activities.description:
Learners view a screenshot of an Excel Solver Answer Report (objective value, variable values, constraints table). They answer 5 quick prompts: (1) Which constraint(s) are binding? (2) Which decision variable is at its lower/upper bound? (3) Is the solution feasible? (4) What units should the objective be in? (5) What single check would you do first to verify accuracy?

Immediate feedback is provided after submission, with a short explanation for each prompt.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice + error-spotting to activate prior knowledge and foreground attention-to-detail habits.
resources: Key terms mini-glossary: decision variable, constraint, objective, binding constraint
instructorActions: Provide the report snapshot with clearly labelled units (or intentionally missing units for learners to infer).
Configure auto-feedback explaining how to detect binding constraints (Final Value equals Constraint RHS within tolerance).
Include a reminder that feasibility checks precede interpretation.
studentActions: Answer the 5 prompts individually.
Review feedback and note one personal accuracy rule to apply in later tasks (e.g., “always check units on objective cell”).

activities.title: Concept mini-lecture: Marginal values, bottlenecks, and sensitivity limits
activities.description:
A short, segmented lesson (5–7 minutes video or equivalent reading) explains: (1) binding vs. non-binding constraints as bottlenecks, (2) shadow price as marginal value of relaxing a constraint, (3) reduced cost as “what must improve” for a non-basic variable to enter the solution, (4) allowable increase/decrease as the range where marginal values remain valid, and (5) when sensitivity reports are valid in Excel (linear models solved with Simplex LP).

Learners complete a 6-item “fill the gap” note-catcher to ensure active processing and correct terminology.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture with guided notes; emphasis on interpreting outputs rather than running Solver.
resources: Worked example handout (one-page): interpreting shadow price with units
instructorActions: Use consistent units throughout (e.g., profit in $/week, labour in hours/week) and state them explicitly.
Add a callout on rounding/tolerances (e.g., treat 9.999999 as 10 within tolerance).
Include a caution slide: Sensitivity Report not produced/valid for GRG Nonlinear in the same way.
studentActions: Watch/read the segment and complete the note-catcher.
Pause to rewrite one definition in their own words (shadow price or reduced cost) including units.

activities.title: Guided demonstration: Building the interpretation trail (objective → variables → constraints → sensitivity)
activities.description:
Step-by-step walkthrough (screen recording or interactive click-through) of a prepared Excel model: setting decision variable cells, objective cell, constraints, and Solver options; running Solver; generating Answer and Sensitivity Reports; then interpreting results in an “Interpretation & Audit Log” tab.

Focus: how to create a transparent calculation trail suitable for audit/team review (inputs, assumptions, Solver settings, outputs, checks).
activities.teachingMethod: Worked example + modelling of expert checking behaviour (units, assumptions, feasibility, and reproducibility).
resources: Excel template workbook (with Solver-ready model + Audit Log tab)
Solver settings checklist (Simplex LP, Assume Linear Model, Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative)
instructorActions: Model ‘stop-and-check’ moments: units on each constraint, sign/direction (≤, =, ≥), and variable bounds.
Demonstrate how to document Solver settings and the time/date/version in the audit log.
Show how to interpret one shadow price statement in plain language for an operations meeting.
studentActions: Follow along without editing yet; jot down the 3 checks the demonstrator performs.
Download/save the template workbook locally (or in OneDrive) to prepare for practice.

activities.title: Guided practice: Run Solver, then analyse bottlenecks and trade-offs
activities.description:
Learners open the template workbook and complete a structured task:
1) Verify units and assumptions (objective units, constraint units, non-negativity).
2) Run Solver with specified settings.
3) Generate Answer + Sensitivity Reports.
4) In the Audit Log tab, record: decision variables, objective value, binding constraints, slack values, and at least two interpretations using shadow prices/reduced costs.
5) Complete three validation checks: (a) feasibility (all constraints satisfied), (b) reasonableness (variables within expected magnitude), (c) rounding/tolerance note (how many decimals reported and why).

Auto-check cells in the workbook flag missing entries and common errors (e.g., mismatched units, forgetting to generate reports).
activities.teachingMethod: Scaffolded independent practice with immediate, criterion-based feedback aligned to ‘analyse’ (interpretation and validation).
resources: Excel workbook with embedded instructions and auto-checks
Answer key (released after submission or time delay)
Quick reference: How to read Answer Report vs Sensitivity Report
instructorActions: Embed hints in the workbook (progressive disclosure) rather than giving full solutions upfront.
Provide a troubleshooting sidebar: enabling Solver add-in, selecting Simplex LP, dealing with ‘Solver could not find a feasible solution’.
Ensure auto-check logic tolerates minor rounding differences.
studentActions: Run Solver and populate the Audit Log completely.
Write two evidence-based interpretations (e.g., “Labour is the bottleneck: +1 hour/week increases profit by $X within allowable range”).
Correct any flagged issues until the workbook indicates completion.

activities.title: Case analysis: Predict–change–verify using marginal values
activities.description:
Learners conduct a controlled what-if analysis:
- Scenario A: Increase one binding constraint RHS by a small amount (within allowable increase).
- Scenario B: Increase beyond the allowable increase.
For each scenario, learners:
1) Use the shadow price to predict the change in objective (show units).
2) Re-run Solver to compute the actual new objective.
3) Compare prediction vs actual and explain discrepancies, explicitly referencing allowable increase/decrease and/or basis changes.

A short response box prompts a bottleneck statement: “The constraint most limiting profit/waste is ___ because ___.”
activities.teachingMethod: Analytical reasoning with verification; connects sensitivity theory to operational decision-making.
instructorActions: Choose increments that clearly illustrate ‘within range’ vs ‘outside range’ behaviour.
Prompt learners to track all changes in the audit log (what changed, why, and outcomes).
Provide an exemplar explanation focusing on units and validity range.
studentActions: Compute predictions using shadow price and document assumptions.
Re-solve and record results.
Explain why Scenario B prediction may fail (basis/active set changes; marginal values no longer constant).

activities.title: Formative assessment: Interpreting Solver outputs (application to operations)
activities.description:
An 8-question quiz mixing multiple-choice and short answer:
- Identify binding constraints from a report snippet.
- Interpret a shadow price statement with correct units.
- Determine whether a proposed constraint change is within allowable range.
- Spot an audit/logging omission that would prevent reproducibility.

Includes two “attention to detail” items (units and rounding).
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes check for understanding with targeted feedback and links back to content segments.
resources: Feedback bank keyed to common errors
instructorActions: Provide feedback that explains why distractors are wrong (especially unit and range errors).
Tag each item to objectives for learner self-tracking.
studentActions: Complete the quiz independently.
Review feedback and note one area to revisit (reports, validity range, or audit checks).

activities.title: Wrap-up: Audit-ready checklist and discussion forum prompt
activities.description:
Learners complete a 5-item checklist in the workbook/LMS: (1) units consistent, (2) Solver settings recorded, (3) binding constraints identified, (4) at least one marginal interpretation written with units, (5) prediction vs actual comparison completed.

They then post (or draft) a brief forum response to one prompt about bottlenecks and trade-offs, using evidence from their Sensitivity Report.
activities.teachingMethod: Metacognitive closure + communication practice for team review contexts.
instructorActions: Provide a model forum post structure: claim → evidence (report field) → unit-aware interpretation → limitation (allowable range).
Encourage concise, evidence-based language suitable for operational meetings.
studentActions: Submit the checklist.
Post or draft a 3–5 sentence evidence-based comment referencing one report value and its units.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson to move learners from ‘running Solver’ to analysing and validating results. Because the Bloom level is analyse, prioritise interpretation, comparison, and justification over procedural clicking.

Key instructional moves:
- Always anchor interpretations in (a) which constraint is binding, (b) what the relevant marginal value is (shadow price/reduced cost), and (c) the validity conditions (allowable increase/decrease; linearity; correct Solver method).
- Make attention-to-detail explicit and assessable: require units on every interpretation sentence; require Solver settings and version/time in the audit log; require a feasibility check before discussing “optimality”.
- Use “predict–verify–explain” to expose the limits of marginal analysis: within allowable ranges, predictions should match closely; outside, learners should explain basis/active constraint changes rather than treating it as an arithmetic mistake.
- If the module includes non-linear models later, flag early that Excel’s Sensitivity Report behaves differently and that interpretation must be method-appropriate.

Feedback guidance:
- When learners misinterpret shadow prices, respond with a structured template: ‘If we relax constraint X by 1 [unit], the objective changes by Y [objective-unit] provided the change stays within [allowable range] and the model assumptions hold.’
- When learners get inconsistent results, first check: (1) Solver method (Simplex LP), (2) constraints entered correctly (direction and RHS), (3) decision variable bounds/non-negativity, (4) objective cell reference, (5) units and scaling (e.g., hours vs minutes).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Target completion times are based on a prepared template. If many learners are new to Solver, allow them to spend up to +10 minutes in Guided Practice by shortening the Case Analysis (Scenario B can become optional). Suggested pacing checkpoints:
- Minute 10: Warm-up complete; learners can correctly identify at least one binding constraint.
- Minute 40: Demonstration finished; learners have the template open and Solver enabled.
- Minute 65: Guided Practice complete; audit log populated and reports generated.
- Minute 80: Case analysis predictions and re-solve completed for Scenario A (Scenario B if time).
- Minute 88: Quiz submitted; Minute 90: checklist done.

If learners finish early, offer an extension: add a new realistic constraint (e.g., minimum production requirement), re-solve, and update the audit log with the new bottleneck and trade-offs.
adaptationOptions: Low-bandwidth route: provide a downloadable PDF pack (report snippets + worked example) and allow learners to complete interpretations without running Excel; they can still meet analysis objectives via report reading and prediction tasks.

Solver access issues: offer an alternative using a pre-solved workbook containing Answer/Sensitivity Reports so learners can focus on analysis; optionally allow LibreOffice/Google Sheets users to complete the interpretation portions with supplied outputs.
Additional scaffolding: include a partially completed Audit Log with sentence starters (e.g., “Constraint ___ is binding because …”; “Shadow price means … per …”) and a units checklist.

Increased challenge: require learners to justify which constraint to invest in (e.g., buy extra labour hours vs machine time) using shadow prices AND allowable ranges, and to write a short recommendation memo (200–250 words).

Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for videos, keyboard-only navigation guidance for Excel steps, and colour-independent indicators (icons/text) for binding constraints rather than colour alone.
commonMisconceptions: Treating any ‘non-zero’ slack as binding (binding means slack = 0 within tolerance; small numerical residues may be rounding).
Interpreting shadow price as a total value rather than a marginal per-unit rate, or omitting units (e.g., ‘+$50’ instead of ‘+$50 per labour-hour’).
Using shadow prices outside the allowable increase/decrease range and expecting predictions to remain accurate.
Assuming Sensitivity Report interpretations apply to non-linear or incorrectly configured Solver runs (e.g., using GRG Nonlinear instead of Simplex LP for a linear model).
Confusing reduced cost with profit contribution or believing a negative reduced cost always means “bad” without reference to max/min and variable bounds.
Failing to check feasibility first (discussing “optimal” results when constraints are violated due to wrong inequality direction or missing constraints).
Mismatched units/scales (hours vs minutes; per day vs per week) causing incorrect objective magnitudes and misleading bottleneck conclusions.
Rounding too early in intermediate calculations, leading to inconsistent Solver results and non-reproducible logs.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the primary bottleneck in your model, and what specific evidence from the Answer/Sensitivity Report supports that claim (include the report field and units)?
If you could relax only one constraint by a small amount, which would you choose to improve the objective most, and how does the allowable increase/decrease affect your recommendation?
Describe a situation where a shadow price-based prediction would fail. What would you check in your Solver outputs to detect that the marginal value is no longer valid?
What is one assumption in your model that, if wrong, would most undermine the decision recommendation? How would you document and test it (dimensional/tolerance/sensitivity check)?
In a team review meeting, how would you explain reduced cost to a non-technical stakeholder in two sentences without losing mathematical accuracy?
