lessons.lessonTitle: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver to...
objectives: Given a word problem and dataset, identify and label (in a model map) the decision variables, objective function, and at least 3 operational constraints with correct units and inequality direction.

Build a constrained optimisation model in Excel (decision variable cells, objective cell, constraint formulas) and configure Solver settings (method, variable bounds, non-negativity) to obtain an optimal solution that matches an instructor check within ±0.5% on the objective value.

Analyse Solver outputs (Answer + Sensitivity reports) to determine which constraints are binding, interpret at least two shadow prices/reduced costs in operational terms, and state one trade-off supported by the report values.

Perform and document at least 5 accuracy/audit checks (units, signs, rounding, feasibility, constraint satisfaction, and assumption notes) in a calculation log so another learner can reproduce the result.

activities.title: Orientation + diagnostic: What is the model?
activities.description: Self-check warm-up using a short scenario (e.g., product mix with labour/material limits). Learners classify statements as decision variables/objective/constraints and choose correct units. Immediate automated feedback highlights unit mismatches and inequality direction errors.
activities.teachingMethod: Interactive diagnostic quiz with feedback; retrieval practice to activate prior knowledge (functions/constraints from earlier modules).
instructorActions: Provide a scenario with deliberately tricky units (e.g., hours vs minutes, kg vs g).
Configure automated feedback that explains why each item is variable/objective/constraint and flags unit issues.
Include a brief note on how this connects to Solver (objective cell, variable cells, constraint formulas).
studentActions: Complete the diagnostic and review feedback until they can correctly label all components.
Write a one-sentence model summary: 'Maximise/minimise ___ by choosing ___ subject to ___'.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: Translating constraints into Excel formulas (audit-ready)
activities.description: Concept lesson focusing on: (1) model structure (decision variables → computed totals → objective), (2) constraint types (≤, ≥, =), (3) feasibility vs optimality, (4) dimensional checks, and (5) what Solver reports mean (binding constraints, shadow price, reduced cost, allowable increase/decrease). Includes pause points for quick reflection questions.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture video with embedded checkpoints and a downloadable ‘model-to-sheet’ checklist.
resources: Glossary: decision variable, constraint, objective, binding, shadow price, reduced cost
instructorActions: Explain a consistent spreadsheet layout convention (Inputs/Decisions/Calculations/Outputs/Checks).
Model at least two dimensional checks (e.g., 'units of LHS must match units of RHS').
Emphasise diligence: checking signs, absolute/relative references, and documenting assumptions.
studentActions: Watch the video and answer embedded questions (e.g., identify correct inequality direction).
Download and skim the checklist; highlight 3 checks they often forget.

activities.title: Guided demonstration: Build and solve a constrained model in Excel Solver
activities.description: Step-by-step screencast building a product-mix (or waste-minimisation) model: define decision variable cells, compute resource usage, set objective, add constraints, choose solving method (Simplex for linear; GRG for nonlinear), enforce non-negativity, and run Solver. Demonstration includes creating a calculation log and a 'constraint satisfaction' table.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked example with ‘pause and replicate’ cues; show both the process and the verification steps.
instructorActions: Demonstrate clean cell naming or consistent range labels for audit traceability.
Show how to add a constraint-check block (LHS, RHS, slack, status) and use conditional formatting to flag violations.
Explain what to do if Solver returns 'no feasible solution' or 'stopped at current solution' (diagnose constraints, bounds, method).
studentActions: Replicate the build in their own copy, pausing as prompted.
Run Solver and save: (1) Solver Parameters screenshot, (2) Answer Report, (3) Sensitivity Report (if available).

activities.title: Independent practice: Rebuild with partial scaffolding + verification
activities.description: Learners rebuild the model from a new but similar dataset (numbers changed; same structure). They must complete missing formulas, configure Solver, and complete a verification checklist: feasibility, unit consistency, and constraint satisfaction. Auto-check cells validate key outputs (objective value, binding constraints list).
activities.teachingMethod: Deliberate practice with fading support; immediate feedback via auto-checks and hints.
instructorActions: Provide tiered hints (formula pattern → cell reference tips → full formula) to support different needs.
Embed validation rules (e.g., conditional formatting) that highlight unit/sign errors and constraint violations.
Include an 'audit note' prompt requiring learners to state assumptions (e.g., divisibility, linearity).
studentActions: Complete the model build and solve it.
Fill the calculation log: assumptions, Solver method choice, and checks performed.
Record which constraints are binding and the slack values for non-binding constraints.

activities.title: Case analysis: Interpreting sensitivity outputs for trade-offs and bottlenecks
activities.description: Learners analyse a provided Solver Sensitivity Report and answer structured questions: identify bottlenecks (binding constraints), interpret shadow prices as marginal value of resources, interpret reduced costs for non-produced items, and state a recommendation (e.g., whether to buy extra capacity) within the allowable range. Focus is on analysis and justification, not just reporting numbers.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided analysis using prompts; learners translate report metrics into operational decisions with evidence statements.
resources: Worked commentary (released after submission or self-check)
instructorActions: Provide a structured template for responses: 'Metric → meaning → decision implication → limitation (allowable range)'.
Include one intentionally misleading interpretation example for learners to critique (e.g., using shadow price outside allowable range).
Emphasise rounding discipline and correct sign interpretation.
studentActions: Answer analysis questions and write one recommendation supported by at least two report values.
Identify one risk/limitation (e.g., validity only within allowable increase/decrease, linear assumptions).

activities.title: Formative assessment: Solver setup + interpretation checkpoint
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz: (1) choose correct Solver method and settings for a described model, (2) identify binding constraints from a mini-report, (3) compute and interpret a marginal value decision (shadow price) with an allowable range constraint.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes formative quiz with targeted feedback; error-based learning (feedback explains why distractors are wrong).
instructorActions: Design distractors aligned to common misconceptions (global optimum assumption, sign errors, allowable range misuse).
Provide feedback that directs learners to the exact step/checklist item to fix.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback.
Note one personal 'next time I will check ___' action in their log.

activities.title: Wrap-up: Audit-ready submission pack + reflection
activities.description: Learners compile an ‘audit pack’: solved workbook, Solver Parameters screenshot, reports, and a completed calculation log. They answer a short reflection: which check caught an error (or would have), and which constraint is the key bottleneck and why.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection; optional forum post for peer comparison in self-study cohorts.
instructorActions: Provide clear submission/archiving naming conventions (date_version_initials).
Offer an optional forum prompt and a model reflection example.
Encourage learners to keep a reusable template for future modules/assessments.
studentActions: Save/export required artifacts and complete the reflection.
Optionally post one insight (e.g., a bottleneck interpretation) and respond to one peer.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Align every step to analysis-level thinking by requiring learners to justify model structure choices and interpret outputs for decisions (not just run Solver). Use an explicit ‘model map → spreadsheet layout → Solver configuration → verification → interpretation’ workflow. Emphasise diligence and attention to detail by making checks non-optional: (1) units/dimensions on every constraint, (2) sign and inequality direction, (3) constraint satisfaction table (slack/status), (4) rounding policy (store full precision, present rounded), (5) reproducibility (document Solver method, options, and variable bounds). When teaching sensitivity, insist on operational translation: shadow price is a marginal value valid only within allowable ranges; reduced cost indicates what must change for a non-basic variable to enter the solution (in linear models). Include troubleshooting branches: if infeasible, isolate constraints; if nonlinear/GRG, discuss local optimum risk; if sensitivity report unavailable, explain why (e.g., nonlinear or integer constraints) and how to do a simple one-at-a-time what-if instead. Provide worked examples plus a scaffolded practice to fade support and promote transfer.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 25 minutes brisk (diagnostic + mini-lecture) to reserve time for hands-on build and analysis. During the 20-minute demonstration, insert two mandatory pause points where learners must replicate before continuing. If learners fall behind, prioritise: (1) correct decision variable cells and objective, (2) correct constraints and non-negativity, (3) feasibility checks, then (4) sensitivity interpretation. Offer an optional extension (outside the 90 minutes) to explore what-if analysis beyond allowable ranges or to add an additional constraint and re-optimise.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility: provide transcripts, keyboard-only navigation guidance, and a high-contrast Excel template; ensure all charts/conditional formatting have text equivalents.
Support for novices: offer a fully guided ‘click-by-click’ version of the practice workbook with additional hint layers and pre-named ranges.

Challenge/advanced: add a new constraint (e.g., minimum demand, machine overtime cost) and ask learners to predict which constraint becomes binding before solving; require a short sensitivity-based recommendation with a cost-benefit calculation.
Low-bandwidth: provide a static PDF walkthrough with screenshots and a lightweight CSV dataset; allow submission of calculated results without video viewing.
Math-anxious learners: include a short ‘common errors’ checklist and encourage incremental verification after each formula block rather than end-of-task checking.
Learners using alternative tools: allow Google Sheets for model build, but require a documented method for optimisation and a manual sensitivity/what-if (noting limitations vs Excel Solver).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing decision variables with calculated totals (e.g., treating resource usage cells as variables).
Using inconsistent units across constraints (hours vs minutes; kg vs g), leading to plausible-looking but wrong solutions.
Reversing inequality direction (≤ vs ≥) or misplacing RHS/LHS in constraints.
Assuming Solver always finds the global optimum (especially with GRG/nonlinear problems) and not checking for local optimum risk.
Forgetting to apply non-negativity or appropriate bounds, allowing negative production/allocations.
Misinterpreting shadow price sign or meaning (e.g., treating it as valid for any size increase, ignoring allowable increase/decrease).
Treating non-binding constraints as irrelevant rather than considering slack as potential capacity or resilience.
Misreading reduced cost as 'profit' or 'importance' rather than the marginal change needed for a variable to enter the optimal basis (linear models).
Changing data but not re-running Solver or not updating constraint references, producing outdated results.
Rounding intermediate calculations too early, causing constraint violations or incorrect binding status.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the bottleneck (binding) in your solution, and what operational action would you take to relieve it?
A resource has a positive shadow price. Under what conditions would buying more of that resource be a good decision, and when would the sensitivity report stop being valid?
If a constraint has large slack, what might that indicate about the system (overcapacity, incorrect assumptions, missing constraints, or demand limits)?
How would you explain ‘reduced cost’ to a non-technical manager deciding whether to introduce a new product option?
What verification check (units, feasibility, rounding, constraint satisfaction, assumption log) most improves trust in your model—and why?
If Solver returns an infeasible solution, what is your step-by-step diagnostic plan before changing the model?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Keep the lesson anchored to analysis (not just button-clicking). Require learners to (1) classify constraints (binding vs non-binding), (2) interpret marginal values with correct units, and (3) justify recommendations with evidence from Solver reports.

Emphasise diligence and auditability throughout: build a ‘checking culture’ by repeatedly prompting unit checks, sign/direction checks (≤, ≥), and plausibility checks (e.g., do outputs violate capacity?). Use transparent calculation logs: learners should be able to explain where every number comes from and reproduce results.

Teach Solver as a modelling tool: Solver will optimise whatever you tell it, including incorrect models. Therefore, model validation comes before and after solve: verify formulas, confirm constraints represent the real-world rules, and confirm the solution is feasible.

Sensitivity interpretation should be taught with boundaries: explain that shadow prices/allowable ranges are typically meaningful for linear, continuous models; if learners later use integer constraints or nonlinear relationships, sensitivity outputs may be missing or misleading. Encourage small ‘what-if’ re-solves to validate directionality.

For online self-study delivery, embed frequent checkpoints (pause-and-do), auto-feedback, and progressive hints. Ensure materials are downloadable, include screenshots for key Solver dialogs, and provide alternate instructions for Windows/Mac Excel where menus differ.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
If learners are new to Solver, allow them to spend up to +10 minutes by shortening the case analysis write-up (keep the extraction of binding constraints and one shadow price mandatory). If learners progress quickly, extend the case analysis by asking them to test a parameter change within the allowable range and compare predicted vs actual objective change.

Use a checkpoint rule: by minute 40, every learner should have a feasible solved model; if not, direct them to the ‘Solver configuration’ quick guide and the model health indicator. By minute 75, learners should have generated the Sensitivity Report and extracted at least one shadow price with units.

Keep the reflection short; do not let posting replace the analysis work. Require evidence (table/screenshot) to prevent unsupported claims.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded pathway (support): Provide a fully completed model structure with only Solver configuration left to do; include a guided checklist for each constraint and a unit-labeling template.

Challenge pathway (extension): Add one additional constraint (e.g., minimum service level or emission cap) and have learners predict which constraint will become binding before solving, then verify via reports.
Accessibility/low bandwidth: Offer a text-and-screenshot version of videos and a PDF walkthrough; ensure the workbook works offline and avoids heavy embedded media.
Math support: Provide a brief primer linking shadow price to marginal change (derivative intuition) with one numeric example using units.
Excel support: Provide separate mini-guides for (a) enabling Solver, (b) named ranges, (c) absolute/relative references, (d) generating reports.
Assessment accommodations: Allow an alternative submission—a written interpretation using a provided Solver report screenshot—if learners cannot run Excel Solver on their device.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing decision variables with parameters (treating fixed inputs like prices/capacities as ‘changing cells’).
Believing Solver guarantees the global optimum in all cases (especially for nonlinear or non-convex problems).
Assuming Sensitivity Report shadow prices and allowable ranges are valid for integer constraints or nonlinear models (they are often not).
Misinterpreting the shadow price sign or units (e.g., reading it as total profit rather than $ per unit of constrained resource).
Thinking non-binding constraints ‘don’t matter’ and can be deleted (they may matter under different scenarios or parameter changes).
Entering a constraint with the wrong inequality direction (≤ vs ≥) or comparing mismatched units (minutes vs hours, units/day vs units/week).
Over-rounding decision variables or objective values early, causing constraint violations or misleading recommendations.
Confusing reduced cost with profit contribution; misreading it without considering whether the variable is at zero and the model type.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the primary bottleneck in your solution? What evidence (slack + shadow price) supports your claim?
Interpret one shadow price with units. What real operational decision could it inform (e.g., overtime hours, machine capacity, supplier quota)?
Within the allowable range, what change would you recommend first to improve the objective, and why is that recommendation safe only within that range?
What is one assumption in your model that, if wrong, would most undermine the recommendation? How would you test or validate it?
If you had to present this result in a team review meeting, what two tables/screenshots would you include to make the calculation auditable and persuasive?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Focus this lesson on evaluation (not just running Solver). Require learners to (1) cite specific report fields, (2) state validity conditions (e.g., allowable ranges), and (3) document limitations and uncertainty. Reinforce professional integrity by modelling careful language: 'Within the allowable increase of X, the shadow price suggests…' and 'This conclusion depends on linearity/constant coefficients.' Emphasize collaborative behaviours by structuring explanations as if for a team review: claim → evidence → limitation → invitation to challenge. Use worked examples where one interpretation is intentionally wrong (e.g., using a shadow price for a non-binding constraint) and have learners diagnose the error. Keep self-study friction low: provide a pre-built workbook with clearly named sheets, locked formula areas where appropriate, and auto-checks for key numbers; reserve open-response items for evaluation and justification. Align feedback to auditability: if a learner cannot reproduce the result from the log, the submission is incomplete even if the numeric answer is correct.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 25–30 minutes brisk (diagnostic + mini-lesson) to get learners into the workbook quickly. If learners stall on Solver setup, direct them to the demonstration and the settings checklist before they spend time troubleshooting. The 25-minute practice block is the core: encourage completing Parts A–C first (binding/shadow/reduced cost), then Parts D–E (allowable ranges + limitations). For the case evaluation, time-box scenario runs to ~5 minutes each and reserve at least 5 minutes for writing the decision memo with explicit citations. If running behind, prioritize: binding vs non-binding + one shadow price interpretation + decision memo with two evidence points and two limitations (minimum viable evaluation).
adaptationOptions: Excel/Solver support: Provide an alternate 'Solver-ready' version of the workbook with Solver parameters pre-filled; learners focus on interpretation and evaluation rather than setup.
Accessibility: Offer a text-based walkthrough with screenshots and keyboard navigation tips; ensure videos have captions and transcripts.
Math confidence scaffolding: Provide a simplified dataset with fewer constraints/variables for the first run, then a 'stretch' dataset for the case.
Advanced extension: Add a third scenario that forces a different binding constraint set; ask learners to explain the shift in bottleneck structure and implications for investment.
Language support: Provide sentence frames for evaluation (e.g., 'Constraint ___ is binding because…', 'Within allowable increase ___, the marginal value is…', 'Limitation: … therefore we should…').
Collaborative option (if cohort-enabled): Pair learners asynchronously to exchange decision memos using a critique protocol (clarify → challenge → suggest → revise).
commonMisconceptions: Treating shadow price as valid for any size change, ignoring allowable increase/decrease and the fact it is a local marginal value.
Interpreting a shadow price for a non-binding constraint (or assuming all constraints have meaningful shadow prices).
Confusing reduced cost with 'cost to produce' rather than the marginal objective improvement required for a variable at zero to become positive (for maximization) within the current basis.
Assuming the 'best' objective value is automatically the best decision without checking feasibility, operational realism of constraints, or risk/uncertainty.
Failing to record Solver settings/method and therefore producing results that cannot be audited or replicated.
Overstating precision: reporting point estimates as certainties and omitting CI/uncertainty notes for estimated inputs.
Believing sensitivity reports apply to nonlinear models or to Solver runs not using appropriate methods (e.g., misunderstanding when Sensitivity Report is available/meaningful).
discussionPrompts: Which Solver output field (slack, shadow price, reduced cost, allowable range) is most persuasive in a team decision meeting—and why? Provide one example of a responsible claim and one overconfident claim.
A colleague proposes increasing capacity by an amount beyond the allowable increase shown. How would you respond, and what additional analysis would you propose?
Describe a realistic operational reason for adding a new constraint that could reduce the objective value but improve decision quality (e.g., service level, compliance, safety).
How would you document uncertainty for one key input (e.g., demand) using a CI or range, and how would that change your recommendation or risk notes?
What would make you distrust a Solver result even if the objective value is high (e.g., missing constraints, unrealistic coefficients, non-reproducible setup)? List two red flags.

activities.teachingMethod: Evidence-based evaluation: learners judge robustness and explicitly document uncertainty/limitations to meet professional integrity and transparency expectations.
resources: Example risk notes (good vs weak examples)

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Keep the lesson anchored to Bloom ‘evaluate’: learners must defend a choice, not merely produce an optimum. Repeatedly separate (1) numerical optimality from (2) decision quality under real constraints and uncertainty. Require transparency: every scenario run should have a Solver settings record, a calculation log (units, assumptions, cell references), and a note on feasibility/interpretability. Emphasise diligence: prompt learners to check units, signs, and non-negativity; use reasonableness checks (e.g., totals match constraints; decisions align with business logic). Build integrity by modelling careful claims: use conditional language, document limitations, and include risk notes in a workplace-style risk register. Support collaborative behaviours in an online self-study context by using optional peer discussion prompts that invite critique of assumptions/constraints and encourage learners to revise based on feedback. When providing feedback (automated or written), prioritise: (a) missing/weak constraint rationale, (b) incomplete logs, (c) unjustified scenario selection, and (d) unacknowledged sensitivity or uncertainty.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners move quickly, extend Activity 6 by adding a third sensitivity check (e.g., change two parameters simultaneously) and ask for a stronger mitigation plan in the risk register. If learners move slowly or struggle with Solver setup, allow them to use the provided partially completed workbook and focus on evaluation: interpreting binding constraints, documenting assumptions, and writing a justified recommendation. Encourage a ‘stop-and-check’ moment after each Solver run: confirm constraints, confirm units, record settings, then proceed—this prevents late-stage rework. Recommend learners pause the demonstration video at each step and replicate immediately rather than watching end-to-end.
adaptationOptions: Provide a ‘scaffolded’ workbook version with decision variable cells pre-identified and named ranges already created; learners only add constraints and complete the evaluation/log sections.
Provide an ‘advanced’ extension: add an integer/binary constraint (e.g., choose to open/close a line) and ask learners to discuss how this changes evaluation and Solver method choice.
Accessibility: offer captions/transcripts for all videos; provide keyboard-only navigation notes for Excel; ensure PDFs are screen-reader friendly.

Tool constraints: if learners lack desktop Excel, provide instructions for Excel Online (where possible) plus an alternative: a pre-solved dataset for evaluation and memo-writing so the evaluation outcomes can still be achieved.
Language support: offer sentence starters for risk notes and justification (e.g., ‘This recommendation is sensitive to…’; ‘Constraint X is included because…’).
Math confidence support: include a short optional refresher on interpreting marginal change/binding constraints and a glossary of Solver terms with examples.
commonMisconceptions: ‘The highest objective value is automatically the best choice’ (ignoring feasibility realism, robustness, and uncertainty).
Assuming Solver always finds the global optimum (especially if the model is nonlinear or method choice is inappropriate).
Confusing decision variables with parameters (editing costs/prices instead of the variable cells Solver should change).
Forgetting non-negativity constraints, leading to nonsensical negative production/allocation decisions.
Interpreting binding constraints incorrectly (e.g., thinking a constraint is binding just because it exists, not because it is tight at the solution).
Changing multiple things between scenarios without documenting, making comparisons invalid or non-auditable.
Treating sensitivity results as definitive predictions rather than ‘what-if’ analysis dependent on assumptions and parameter uncertainty.
Rounding intermediate calculations early, which can change Solver results and reduce reproducibility.
Not recording Solver settings/constraints, making the solution impossible to audit or reproduce later.
discussionPrompts: When would you choose a slightly lower-profit scenario over the maximum-profit scenario? Give two concrete, quantitative reasons (e.g., robustness, risk exposure, constraint realism).
Which constraint in your model is most ‘business-critical’ and why? What evidence from your scenario runs supports that claim?
Describe one uncertainty that could flip your preferred scenario choice. How would you monitor it in practice?
If Solver reports an infeasible solution for a scenario, what are the first three checks you would perform (before changing the model)?
How should you document assumptions so that a colleague can reproduce your work and challenge your reasoning constructively?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Keep the lesson anchored on evaluation (judgement with evidence), not calculation alone. Require learners to (1) cite specific Solver outputs (shadow price, reduced cost, allowable increase/decrease), (2) state units and interpretation in plain language, and (3) explicitly name limitations (validity ranges; model assumptions such as linearity/divisibility; sensitivity outputs not extrapolated beyond allowable ranges). Reinforce professional integrity by making transparency non-optional: every claim in the decision note should link to a captured output or logged assumption. For collaborative behaviours, structure critique as evidence-based questions (e.g., 'Which field supports that?' 'Is this within allowable range?') and require a revision note that shows how feedback changed the solution or strengthened the justification. When CI appears, treat it as a decision-confidence input: learners should explain how uncertainty could flip the preferred scenario and what monitoring/contingency is appropriate.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners struggle, shorten the case-analysis to two scenarios (A and B) and keep Scenario C as an extension. Maintain the full 20 minutes for independent interpretation practice because it prevents downstream errors in evaluation. Encourage a strict timebox: 10 minutes to scan each scenario for feasibility/objective change, then 5 minutes to compare trade-offs, then 10 minutes to write the decision note and 5 minutes to complete the risk register entry. For faster learners, add an optional task: test a parameter change just outside the allowable range and explain why sensitivity guidance may fail.
adaptationOptions: Provide two workbook versions: (1) scaffolded with highlighted Sensitivity Report fields and sentence starters; (2) unscaffolded for advanced learners.
Offer transcript-only and image-based walkthroughs for low-bandwidth access; include alt-text for report screenshots.
Allow submission in multiple formats (typed memo, annotated slides, or structured form) as long as evidence citations and calculation logs are included.
Add an accessibility-friendly 'numbers-only' Sensitivity Report table (no embedded images) for screen readers.

Extension for advanced learners: introduce a non-linear variation (GRG Nonlinear) and ask learners to evaluate whether sensitivity outputs are trustworthy and what alternative checks (scenario reruns, manual perturbation tests) are needed.
commonMisconceptions: Treating a shadow price as a guaranteed gain for any size increase in a constraint, rather than a marginal value valid only within the allowable range.
Ignoring units/sign: reporting a shadow price without specifying $/unit of constraint or misreading negative values as 'bad' without interpretation.
Assuming non-binding constraints have zero relevance; learners may miss that they can become binding under scenario changes.
Misinterpreting reduced cost as 'profit' or 'importance' rather than the required improvement for a variable to enter the solution (in linear models).
Changing coefficients beyond allowable increase/decrease while still claiming the same sensitivity conclusions.
Confusing feasibility with optimality (a feasible solution is not necessarily the best).
Believing Solver outputs are self-justifying and omitting calculation logs, assumptions, or limitations (weak audit trail).
Interpreting CI as certainty (or as a single value) rather than an interval describing uncertainty and decision risk.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the primary bottleneck in your base model, and what operational action would you recommend to relieve it? Use the shadow price and allowable range to support your claim.
Under what conditions would you distrust the Sensitivity Report and rerun scenarios instead of relying on marginal values? Name at least two red flags.
A teammate argues your chosen scenario is 'overfitted to the current coefficients.' How do you respond using allowable increase/decrease and a documented limitation?
How did the CI (uncertainty) in Scenario C affect your confidence in the recommended option, and what would you record in the risk register?
What is one transparency practice you used (or failed to use) that would matter in an audit or handover to another analyst?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Keep the lesson centred on evaluation rather than mechanics: learners should justify a choice under constraints, not merely produce a Solver output. Reinforce professional integrity and transparency by requiring reproducible logs (inputs changed, Solver settings, constraints rationale, outputs) and explicit uncertainty/limitations in a risk register. Prompt diligence: units on every constraint/input, constraint direction (≤/≥/=), non-negativity, and reasonableness checks (e.g., does the solution violate real-world logic even if mathematically feasible?). When learners encounter infeasibility or unexpected results, treat it as a learning moment: model how to diagnose (check constraint signs/units, bounds too tight, wrong objective cell, decision variable range) and how to document the fix. Encourage collaborative behaviours even in self-study via structured explanation templates and optional peer review: explaining reasoning and welcoming challenge is part of the assessed competency. If sensitivity/answer reports are used, explicitly note their assumptions and limitations (e.g., linear models; not reliable for integer/nonlinear settings) and require learners to state when they cannot rely on them.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Use visible checkpoints to avoid spending too long troubleshooting late in the lesson: by minute 25 learners should have a working base scenario with a completed log entry; by minute 55 all three scenarios should have run and be recorded; by minute 70 the comparison table should be complete and a provisional recommendation chosen; the last 20 minutes are for the quiz and writing a concise decision memo. If learners get stuck, direct them to the troubleshooting guide and require a minimal diagnostic log entry (what failed, what they checked) before attempting fixes—this preserves momentum and supports auditability. Provide an optional 'extension' (e.g., add an extra constraint or compare Solver methods) only if the three scenarios and documentation are complete.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded pathway: provide a version of the workbook with named ranges, pre-built constraint blocks, and guided prompts; advanced pathway: learners build the model layout from a blank sheet and must justify each constraint’s origin.
Accessibility: provide text-based click-path instructions alongside screencasts; ensure worksheets are screen-reader friendly with clear labels and avoid colour-only meaning in tables.
Tool flexibility: allow Google Sheets + OpenSolver (or alternative) where Excel Solver is unavailable, but require the same documentation artifacts (scenario table, run log, risk notes).

Reduced cognitive load: limit to 2 decision variables and 3 constraints for learners needing support; enrichment: add an additional scenario with a new constraint (e.g., minimum service level) and require a short note on feasibility/ethics.
Language support: provide sentence starters for the decision memo (e.g., 'I recommend Scenario B because… Evidence: … Assumptions: … Risks/limitations: … Reproducibility: …').
Extra practice for diligence: provide a 'buggy model' optional exercise where learners identify and correct unit mismatches, wrong inequality direction, or missing non-negativity constraints.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming Solver’s output is automatically correct or realistic without checking units, constraint direction, and reasonableness.
Confusing decision variables with inputs/parameters (e.g., treating capacity or cost as a variable to optimise rather than a constraint/input).
Misinterpreting constraints (using ≥ instead of ≤, or mixing hours with minutes/seconds), leading to infeasible or nonsensical solutions.
Forgetting non-negativity or appropriate bounds, allowing negative production/resource allocations that inflate the objective artificially.
Believing a higher objective value always means the better scenario, ignoring risk, assumptions, feasibility under uncertainty, or compliance constraints.
Using Sensitivity Report outputs in contexts where they are not valid (e.g., integer or nonlinear models) without stating limitations.
Changing multiple inputs at once during scenario testing and then being unable to attribute outcome changes (poor experimental control).
Rounding intermediate calculations too early, causing constraint violations or misleading comparisons across scenarios.
discussionPrompts: Which scenario did you choose and what is the single strongest piece of evidence (objective value, binding constraint, feasibility) supporting your recommendation?
What assumption in your model, if wrong, would most likely change your chosen scenario? How did you record this in your risk register?
Identify one constraint that became binding in your preferred scenario. Why does that matter for operational decision-making?
Describe one diligence check you performed (units, rounding, constraint direction, bounds). What error did it prevent or reveal?
If a colleague challenged your recommendation, what calculation log detail would you show first to make your work reproducible and auditable?
When (if ever) is it appropriate to prefer a slightly lower objective value? Give a scenario-based justification (risk, compliance, uncertainty, stakeholder needs).

activities.title: Orientation & success criteria: What ‘good evaluation’ looks like
activities.description: Learners review lesson goals, the evaluation rubric (evidence-based recommendation + transparency), and a short glossary (Constraint, CI). CI is framed as a practical ‘confidence interval-style’ range for inputs/outputs (where applicable) and compared with Solver’s allowable ranges (which are not probabilities). Learners download the case workbook and the calculation-log template.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-content page + annotated screenshots + checklist. Includes a 2-minute ‘what you will submit’ walkthrough emphasizing integrity and transparent reporting.
instructorActions: Provide a clear definition of ‘evaluate’ (compare alternatives using criteria and evidence) tied to module learning outcomes.
Include an example of an acceptable recommendation paragraph that cites Solver outputs (shadow price, binding constraint, allowable range).
Flag the integrity expectations: no cherry-picking results; report limitations and uncertainty explicitly.
studentActions: Open/download the workbook and templates.
Skim the rubric and highlight the three required evidence types for the final recommendation.
Answer a quick self-check: ‘What is the difference between a constraint and an assumption?’

activities.title: Guided demonstration: Reading Solver Answer & Sensitivity Reports for marginal values and bottlenecks
activities.description: Step-by-step guided walkthrough using an embedded screencast and an annotated workbook. Learners locate binding constraints, interpret shadow prices as marginal objective change per unit of RHS change (within allowable range), and interpret reduced costs for decision variables not in the solution. The demo explicitly contrasts Solver allowable ranges with probabilistic CI language (to prevent misinterpretation).
activities.teachingMethod: Screencast with pause points + ‘try it now’ prompts. Each pause point asks the learner to compute/interpret one value and then reveal the worked answer.
resources: Annotated screenshots: Shadow price, reduced cost, allowable ranges
instructorActions: Model the language of transparent interpretation: ‘Within the allowable increase of X, increasing constraint RHS by 1 increases objective by Y.’
Provide a short ‘sanity check’ routine: confirm feasibility, check signs/units, confirm binding constraints, confirm objective direction (max/min).
Embed a warning box: allowable ranges are not probabilities; do not label them as 95% CI.
studentActions: Run Solver (or open the provided reports if Solver is unavailable) and locate the Answer Report and Sensitivity Report.
Identify which constraints are binding and record them in the calc log with the exact cell references.
Write two sentences interpreting one shadow price and one reduced cost using correct units and ‘within range’ wording.

activities.title: Independent practice: Bottleneck diagnosis and trade-off explanation
activities.description: Learners complete a structured worksheet: (1) list binding constraints, (2) rank bottlenecks by shadow price magnitude (and sign), (3) explain one trade-off between two constraints, (4) propose one operational action (e.g., add capacity, change mix) that is supported by sensitivity evidence and is valid only within allowable ranges.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided practice with progressively reduced scaffolding: first item is fully worked, second has hints, third is independent. Includes auto-check fields where feasible.
instructorActions: Provide hints that direct attention to the correct report columns (e.g., shadow price vs. slack) and to units/scale.
Include an ‘integrity checkpoint’ prompt: ‘What would make this interpretation invalid?’ (forces mention of allowable ranges/model assumptions).
Offer an optional extension: interpret a negative shadow price and explain what it means operationally.
studentActions: Complete the bottleneck ranking and trade-off explanation in the workbook.
Paste key values (shadow prices, allowable ranges, slack) into the calc log with cell references or report line identifiers.
Write a 3–5 sentence explanation suitable for a team review meeting (clear, challenge-welcoming tone).

activities.title: Case analysis (evaluate): Compare two alternative scenarios and choose a justified option
activities.description: Learners evaluate two scenarios: Scenario A modifies one constraint RHS (e.g., capacity increase); Scenario B modifies an objective coefficient (e.g., cost/benefit change) or introduces a new constraint. Learners compare objective value, feasibility, and whether the change stays within sensitivity allowable ranges. If outside range, they must rerun Solver and explain why sensitivity predictions may not hold. Deliverable: a recommendation with evidence + constraints rationale + risk notes.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured decision memo: criteria table (objective, feasibility, robustness, operational realism, risk/limitations) + evidence citations from Solver reports and logs.
resources: Decision memo template (within calc log): 'Scenario Evaluation'
instructorActions: Provide scenario instructions that force evaluation (not just calculation): learners must justify using explicit criteria and cite Solver evidence.
Add a ‘collaboration cue’ box: ‘State one question you would ask a teammate to challenge your conclusion.’
Include a worked example of a limitation note (e.g., linearity, data dated, integer restrictions ignored).
studentActions: Compute/confirm results for Scenario A and Scenario B (using Solver or provided outputs).

Fill the comparison table and decide which scenario to recommend, explicitly referencing at least three Solver evidence points (e.g., binding constraints, shadow price, allowable range breach, reduced costs).
Write 3 risk-register style entries: assumption, potential impact, mitigation/next check, and whether a CI-style uncertainty estimate exists (if provided).

activities.title: Formative assessment 2: Integrity-focused evaluation check (auto-mark + reflection)
activities.description: A short quiz checks interpretation accuracy and integrity behaviours: identifying incorrect shadow price statements, distinguishing allowable ranges vs CI/probability claims, selecting the best evidence for a recommendation, and spotting missing transparency items in a sample calc log. Ends with a reflection prompt to revise one part of the learner’s own calc log.
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-mark quiz (8–10 items) + immediate feedback explanations. Reflection requires updating the learner’s log (self-correction).
instructorActions: Design distractors around common misconceptions (e.g., treating allowable increase as a 95% CI).
Provide feedback that explains reasoning, not just correctness, and prompts revision of learner work.
Tie results to next steps: what to revisit if score < 70%.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback carefully.
Revise one section of the calc log (e.g., add missing constraint rationale or correct an interpretation statement).
Note one ‘challenge question’ they would welcome from a reviewer.

activities.title: Wrap-up: Submission-ready decision statement and next-step plan
activities.description: Learners finalize a concise recommendation statement and a ‘next data/checks’ plan. They confirm that the calc log contains model version, Solver settings, constraints rationale, and limitations/uncertainty notes. Optional: post a discussion-board entry for peer challenge (asynchronous).
activities.teachingMethod: Exit ticket: one-paragraph recommendation + two-bullet next steps. Optional forum post for peer review culture.
instructorActions: Provide a model ‘audit-ready’ exit ticket example (concise, evidence-based, transparent about limits).
Encourage a collaborative tone: invite critique, specify what would change the recommendation.
Remind learners to keep all Solver reports exported/saved for traceability.
studentActions: Submit the exit ticket paragraph and verify log completeness against the checklist.
Optionally post their recommendation and one question for challengers in the forum.
Bookmark one concept to revisit (shadow prices, reduced costs, or allowable ranges).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the self-study lesson so learners must justify, not just compute. Keep evaluation anchored to explicit criteria (objective value, feasibility, robustness within allowable ranges, operational realism, and risk/limitations). Use worked examples sparingly and place ‘pause-and-try’ checkpoints immediately after each concept (shadow price, reduced cost, allowable ranges). Reinforce professional integrity by requiring: (1) exact references to Solver outputs (report line/cell), (2) explicit ‘valid within allowable range’ language, (3) a limitations/uncertainty section that is not optional, and (4) a versioned calculation log (date/time, scenario label, Solver settings). Encourage collaborative behaviours through prompts that simulate team review: learners write explanations that welcome challenge and include at least one question they would ask/accept from a peer. Provide feedback that emphasizes reasoning quality (units, directionality, conditions) and flags overconfident claims (e.g., presenting sensitivity ranges as probabilistic certainty).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners finish early: add the extension to test a change outside the allowable range, rerun Solver, and write a short note explaining why sensitivity predictions broke (basis change). If learners are slower: allow them to use the provided Solver reports rather than running Solver, and focus on interpretation and justification (the evaluate-level target). Keep the case analysis (25 min) protected; shorten the independent practice by 5 minutes only if needed, but do not remove the requirement to write a recommendation with evidence and limitations. Use time-boxed checkpoints: by minute 30 learners should have identified binding constraints; by minute 55 they should have a completed bottleneck explanation; by minute 80 they should have a scenario choice with three cited evidence points.
adaptationOptions: Solver-access alternative: provide pre-generated Answer and Sensitivity Reports (PDF/embedded tables) so learners can complete evaluation tasks without Excel Solver.

Scaffolded vs. advanced track: offer a ‘guided’ worksheet with sentence starters for interpretations, and an ‘advanced’ worksheet requiring learners to craft stakeholder-facing explanations with minimal prompts.
Accessibility: provide screen-reader friendly tables of the Sensitivity Report and captions/transcripts for screencasts; ensure color is not the only indicator for binding constraints.
Math support: include a mini-remediation pop-up on marginal change (derivative intuition) and units, connecting shadow price to marginal value conceptually.

Challenge extension: add an integer or binary decision variant (not solvable with standard sensitivity) and ask learners to explain why sensitivity outputs may be unavailable/invalid and what to do instead.
Language support: provide a glossary of reporting verbs (interpret, justify, qualify, caveat) and an exemplar ‘team review’ paragraph structure.
commonMisconceptions: Treating ‘allowable increase/decrease’ as a probabilistic confidence interval (CI) (e.g., assuming 95% certainty) rather than a range where the current basis remains optimal.
Interpreting shadow price as always valid regardless of how much a constraint changes (ignoring allowable ranges and basis changes).
Confusing slack with shadow price (e.g., assuming a nonzero slack means a high marginal value, or assuming binding constraints always have positive shadow prices).
Misreading reduced cost: thinking it is a penalty added to the objective rather than the improvement needed for a non-basic variable to enter the solution (for max/min).
Forgetting the direction of optimisation (max vs min), leading to reversed interpretation of signs and ‘better/worse’ conclusions.
Assuming Solver output is automatically ‘correct’ without checking model setup (units, cell references, constraints applied, non-negativity, variable types).
Reporting a single optimal number without documenting assumptions, limitations, or the scenario version, undermining auditability and professional integrity.
Believing that a higher objective value always means the better operational choice, ignoring feasibility realism, risk, and robustness.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the true bottleneck in your baseline model, and how do you know from the Sensitivity Report (cite the specific evidence)?
Write a recommendation you could say in a team review meeting that explicitly invites challenge. What question would you want a colleague to ask you?
Describe one change that looks beneficial from shadow price logic but becomes questionable when you consider allowable ranges or operational realism. What would you do next?
Where could your model be misleading (linearity, ignored integer restrictions, data quality, timing)? Write one risk-register entry with a mitigation step.
If Scenario A improves the objective but increases reliance on a single binding constraint, is it still the best choice? What trade-off criterion matters most in your context?
How would you explain the difference between Solver allowable ranges and a statistical CI to a non-technical stakeholder without overstating certainty?

lessons.lessonTitle: Alternative optimisation scenarios and justify a chosen o...
objectives: Set up an Excel Solver optimisation model (decision variables, objective cell, and at least 3 constraints) and solve it, achieving a Solver status of “Optimal” or correctly diagnosing “Infeasible/Unbounded” within the provided case file.

Evaluate at least three alternative optimisation scenarios by comparing objective value, constraint tightness (binding vs non-binding), feasibility, and practical risk/assumption impacts, documenting results in a transparent calculation log.

Justify a recommended scenario in a short decision memo (150–250 words) that includes: constraints rationale, key assumptions, uncertainty/limitations, and at least two risk register entries relevant to implementation.

Perform and record at least two diligence checks (units/scale check, rounding policy, constraint direction/sign check, or sensitivity/tolerance check) and explain how they affect confidence in the recommendation.

activities.title: Diagnostic warm-up: audit-readiness check
activities.description: Learners open the provided Excel case file and complete a quick diagnostic checklist: identify decision variables, objective, constraints, units, and where a calculation log will be maintained. Includes 5 auto-check questions (MCQ/short answer) focused on constraint direction, units, and feasibility cues. This sets expectations for transparency and evaluation-level thinking.
activities.teachingMethod: Self-check diagnostic quiz embedded in the LMS with immediate feedback; guided file-orientation prompts inside the spreadsheet.
resources: LMS diagnostic quiz (5 items with feedback)
Excel case file (baseline model template + empty log table)
instructorActions: Provide the case file with pre-labelled ranges and a blank calculation log table.
Configure the LMS quiz with feedback that points to the exact spreadsheet location for each concept (objective cell, constraint table, units row).
Post an optional Q&A thread: 'Lesson 11 Setup Issues' for troubleshooting.
studentActions: Download/open the case file and locate objective/decision cells and the constraint table.
Complete the diagnostic quiz and review feedback for any incorrect items.
Create (or confirm) a named area for the calculation log (timestamp, scenario name, Solver settings, results, notes).

activities.title: Concept mini-lecture: evaluating scenarios with integrity and transparency
activities.description: A short video/reading introduces an evaluation framework for optimisation scenarios: feasibility first, then objective value, then constraint rationale, then implementation risk. Emphasises professional integrity: honest reporting of assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations; and diligence: unit checks, rounding policy, and reproducibility.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture (8–10 min) + guided notes (5–7 min) with a worked example of an audit log entry and a risk register entry.
resources: Micro-lecture video: 'Scenario Evaluation & Audit Logs' (10 min)
Risk register template (2-column: risk, mitigation; plus assumptions/limitations)
instructorActions: Explicitly model how to write a constraint rationale (why it exists, source, units, and consequence if violated).
Include a short segment on uncertainty/limitations (e.g., demand variability, parameter estimation).
Provide an exemplar ‘good’ and ‘weak’ scenario justification for comparison.
studentActions: Watch/read the mini-lecture and complete guided notes.
Copy the exemplar audit-log structure into their spreadsheet log table.
Draft one constraint rationale sentence for a chosen constraint in the case file.

activities.title: Demonstration: Excel Solver setup + reproducible calculation logs
activities.description: A step-by-step screen recording shows setting decision variables, objective, constraints, and Solver options (Simplex LP vs GRG Nonlinear; non-negativity; precision/tolerance). Demonstrates how to capture Solver outputs, interpret status messages, and log settings/results for audit.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided demonstration with pause-and-try prompts; learners replicate each step in their own file and compare to a checkpoint screenshot.
resources: Solver status interpretation quick guide (Optimal/Infeasible/Unbounded/Not Solved)
instructorActions: Demonstrate at least one common failure mode (e.g., missing non-negativity constraint) and how to detect it via outputs.
Show how to save a Solver scenario/run configuration or document it (method, tolerance, constraints list).
Provide a reproducibility reminder: document any manual edits and parameter changes.
studentActions: Replicate the Solver setup and run the baseline optimisation.
Record the baseline scenario in the calculation log (scenario name, Solver method, objective value, binding constraints, notes).
Confirm feasibility and sanity-check units (e.g., hours, dollars, kg) before proceeding.

activities.title: Guided practice: run and compare three constrained scenarios
activities.description: Learners evaluate three pre-defined scenario variants in the case file (e.g., tighter capacity constraint, added waste limit, changed demand/price range). For each, they run Solver, capture results, and complete a comparison table: objective value, feasibility, binding constraints, and a short ‘what changed and why it matters’ note.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured hands-on practice with embedded prompts and auto-check cells (e.g., flags when constraints are violated or units mismatch).
resources: Excel case file with 3 scenario tabs (or toggles) and comparison table
Embedded auto-checks (constraint violation flags, unit consistency prompts)
Short checklist: 'Before you trust the number…' (units, rounding, constraint directions)
instructorActions: Provide scenario definitions with a real-world rationale (why the constraint changes).
Include a minimal 'hint path' (where to look if infeasible; which constraints to review first).
Ensure auto-check feedback explains what to verify rather than giving only the answer.
studentActions: Run Solver for Scenario A, B, and C and log each run (including Solver settings).
Complete the comparison table and identify which constraints become binding in each scenario.
Perform at least two diligence checks and record outcomes (e.g., confirm units/scale; avoid premature rounding; verify constraint direction signs).

activities.title: Case analysis: choose and defend a recommendation with risk notes
activities.description: Learners synthesise results to select the best scenario for a stakeholder (profit maximisation or waste minimisation depending on the case). They must justify not only the best objective value but also feasibility robustness, constraints rationale, and practical risks/limitations. They add at least two entries to a workplace-style risk register and explicitly state uncertainty and limitations.
activities.teachingMethod: Decision-oriented analysis using a structured template (claim → evidence → constraints rationale → risk/limitations → recommendation).
resources: Risk register mini-template (risk, likelihood/impact optional, mitigation, owner/date)
Rubric (criteria: transparency, correctness, evaluation quality, integrity/limitations)
instructorActions: Provide a scoring rubric aligned to evaluation: comparison quality, defensibility, transparency, and honesty about limitations.
Model language for uncertainty (e.g., 'Results assume linear costs; if costs are stepwise, objective may be overstated').
Encourage learners to consider stakeholder constraints (policy, compliance, service level) beyond the numeric optimum.
studentActions: Write a decision memo recommending one scenario with evidence from the comparison table.
Add at least two risk register entries tied to assumptions/uncertainty (e.g., demand variability; parameter estimation; capacity reliability).
Note at least one limitation and its likely direction of impact (over/under-estimate).

activities.title: Formative assessment + reflection: self-review against the evaluation rubric
activities.description: Learners complete a short formative quiz (interpretation + critique items) and then perform a self-review of their memo/logs using the rubric. Optional: post a 3–4 sentence summary to the discussion board and respond to one peer by challenging an assumption respectfully and suggesting an improvement.
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-graded quiz + rubric-based self-assessment checklist; optional asynchronous peer interaction to support collaborative behaviours.
resources: Formative quiz (8–10 items: status messages, binding constraints, constraint rationale, integrity/limitations)
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to point to specific conceptual corrections (e.g., feasibility vs optimality).
Provide an example of constructive challenge language for peer replies.
If facilitating, sample a few posts and highlight strong transparency practices (without grading peers).
studentActions: Complete the formative quiz and review explanations for any missed items.
Self-assess the calculation log and memo against the rubric; revise one element (e.g., clearer constraint rationale or added limitation).
Optionally post and reply in the forum using collaborative, evidence-based critique.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design the lesson around evaluation rather than mere Solver operation. Require learners to (1) establish feasibility, (2) compare scenarios using multiple criteria (objective value, binding constraints, robustness, stakeholder fit), and (3) justify a recommendation with transparent evidence. Reinforce professional integrity by making uncertainty/limitations non-optional: learners must state assumptions and what could break them. Reinforce diligence by embedding check routines (units, sign/direction of constraints, rounding policy, and reproducibility). Encourage collaborative behaviours in an online self-study context via structured, respectful challenge prompts and optional peer reply templates.

Instructor focus points:
- Always separate “best number” from “best decision.” Ask: What constraints are binding? Are they realistic and sourced? What risks arise if parameters shift?
- Model auditability: scenario naming conventions, timestamped logs, Solver method/tolerance recorded, and clear notes on parameter changes.
- Use error-driven learning: show an infeasible or unbounded run and a systematic troubleshooting path (review constraint directions, missing non-negativity, inconsistent units, objective mis-specified).
- Emphasise reproducibility: learners should be able to re-run and get the same result; discourage manual overwrites without logging.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Aim for brisk execution in the first 40 minutes (setup + baseline + first scenario) to leave enough time for evaluation and justification.
- If learners get stuck on Solver setup (beyond ~5 minutes), direct them to the checkpoint screenshots and the 'known-good' baseline settings section of the file.
- If infeasibility arises, cap troubleshooting to ~7 minutes before using the hint path: check non-negativity, constraint directions, and unit scaling.
- Protect time for the case analysis (15 minutes): this is where Bloom level “evaluate” is met. If behind schedule, reduce scenario count from three to two but keep the memo + risk notes requirement.
- Extension (if ahead): add a quick sensitivity/tolerance check (e.g., tweak a key parameter ±5% and note whether the recommendation changes).
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded path (support): provide a step-by-step Solver setup checklist with exact cell references; pre-fill one scenario log entry as a model for learners to emulate.

Advanced path (challenge): add a fourth scenario requiring a different Solver method (e.g., GRG Nonlinear) or an additional constraint (service level / minimum production) and require a brief comment on method choice and potential local vs global optimum concerns.
Accessibility: offer a keyboard-only navigation guide for Solver and ensure all videos have captions and transcripts; provide an alternate PDF walkthrough with screenshots.
Low-bandwidth/offline: supply a lightweight version of the case file and a text-only demo guide; allow learners to submit a screenshot of Solver settings instead of video engagement.
Math confidence support: include a short optional refresher on interpreting marginal trade-offs conceptually (binding constraints as ‘scarce resources’) without requiring dual values/shadow prices.
Language support: provide sentence stems for memos (claim–evidence–limitation–recommendation) and a glossary for key terms (decision variable, constraint, objective, feasibility, CI/uncertainty).
commonMisconceptions: Assuming Solver’s ‘Optimal’ means the solution is practical or implementable without checking constraint realism and assumptions.
Confusing feasibility with optimality (e.g., treating an infeasible model as ‘no solution exists in real life’ rather than a modelling/specification issue).
Forgetting non-negativity or using incorrect constraint directions (≤ vs ≥), leading to unrealistic negative production/allocations or reversed limits.
Mixing units or scales (hours vs minutes, $ vs $000s), causing distorted objectives and misleading comparisons across scenarios.
Rounding decision variables too early, which can violate constraints or change binding status and invalidate comparisons.
Believing Solver always finds the global optimum regardless of method/settings; not recognising differences between Simplex LP and nonlinear methods.
Treating constraints as arbitrary numbers without documenting the rationale/source, making the model non-auditable.
Recording only the final objective value and ignoring binding constraints, solver settings, and parameter changes—preventing reproducibility and transparency.
Assuming a higher objective value always dominates, ignoring risk/uncertainty, robustness, and stakeholder or compliance requirements.
discussionPrompts: When should a real-world limit be modelled as a hard constraint versus a penalty in the objective? Give one example and justify your choice.
Your best objective scenario is feasible but relies on a tight (binding) capacity constraint. What risks does that create, and what mitigation would you record?
What is one assumption in your model that, if wrong, would most likely change the recommended scenario? Explain the direction of impact.
If a peer challenges your recommendation by pointing out a different key constraint, what evidence from your log would you use to respond transparently?
How do you decide an appropriate rounding policy for decision variables, and how can rounding change feasibility or the ‘best’ scenario?
Describe one diligence check you performed (units, signs, tolerance, reproducibility). What would have gone wrong if you skipped it?

objectives: Identify (with 100% accuracy in a checklist) which constraints are binding vs non-binding from Solver results and explain the operational meaning of each binding constraint in 1–2 sentences.

activities.title: Orientation + success criteria (what “good evaluation” looks like)
activities.description: Learners review the lesson goals, the evaluation rubric (what must be justified and documented), and a short reminder of the key terms: constraint and CI (confidence interval). Includes a 3-item diagnostic poll/check to activate prior knowledge: binding constraint, shadow price meaning, and when sensitivity can mislead.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-content page with rubric + interactive diagnostic questions and immediate feedback explanations.
instructorActions: Publish the rubric and an annotated exemplar showing strong transparency (assumptions, units, Solver settings, limitations).
Provide automated feedback for each diagnostic option explaining why it is correct/incorrect.
studentActions: Review the rubric and exemplar once before starting tasks.
Complete the diagnostic check and note any weak areas to focus on.

activities.title: Demonstration: Reading Solver Answer + Sensitivity Reports for decisions
activities.description: Guided walkthrough (video + transcript) showing how to locate binding constraints, interpret shadow prices and reduced costs, and translate them into operational language (bottlenecks/trade-offs). The demo explicitly flags limitations (e.g., integer/nonlinear models, large changes beyond allowable ranges) and models professional transparency in reporting uncertainty.
activities.teachingMethod: Step-by-step screencast with pause points; learners follow along in Excel using the same template.
resources: Excel template: 'MOD104_L12_BaseModel.xlsx' with Solver already configured
One-page 'Sensitivity fields cheat-sheet' (shadow price, reduced cost, allowable ranges)
instructorActions: Narrate the interpretation using units (e.g., '$ per hour', 'profit per unit capacity') and connect to constraints as bottlenecks.
Explicitly model how to write a limitation note (e.g., 'valid only within allowable increase/decrease').
studentActions: Open the template and reproduce the report generation (Answer + Sensitivity).
Pause at marked points to write down: (1) one bottleneck, (2) one trade-off, (3) one limitation.

activities.title: Guided practice: Margin and bottleneck interpretation (with self-check)
activities.description: Learners complete a structured worksheet: (A) label each constraint binding/non-binding, (B) interpret 2 shadow prices with valid ranges, (C) interpret 1 reduced cost and what change would make a variable enter the solution, (D) translate findings into a short recommendation sentence for a manager. Includes an auto-check key for numeric entries and a model answer for the written translation.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example fading: early items are partially filled; later items require full learner completion.
resources: Auto-check answer key (embedded quiz or downloadable key)
instructorActions: Provide a model ‘manager-ready’ sentence frame (e.g., 'The bottleneck is __; adding 1 unit of __ increases objective by __ within __ range.').
Include common pitfalls callouts in the worksheet margins (units, validity ranges, misreading reduced cost sign).
studentActions: Complete the worksheet using their generated Sensitivity Report.
Use the self-check to correct errors and annotate what they changed and why (audit mindset).

activities.title: Case analysis: Evaluate two alternative scenarios and choose one
activities.description: Learners evaluate a base model plus two scenario changes, then choose and justify one option. Scenario examples (select two): (1) increase a binding capacity constraint by a specified amount; (2) tighten a quality/service constraint; (3) change an objective coefficient (cost/profit); (4) add a risk buffer informed by a CI (e.g., demand forecast uncertainty). Learners must decide whether sensitivity results are sufficient or if Solver must be rerun, then produce a justification with quantified impacts and risk notes.
activities.teachingMethod: Decision memo format with evidence requirements: numbers + interpretation + limitations + recommendation.
resources: Risk register template (assumptions, uncertainty/CI note, limitations, mitigation)
instructorActions: Design scenarios so at least one exceeds allowable ranges, forcing learners to evaluate validity and rerun Solver.
Provide a checklist for integrity/transparency: document Solver settings, cite ranges, note uncertainty, avoid overclaiming.
studentActions: Run/compare scenarios (using sensitivity when valid; rerun Solver when not).
Complete a 1-page decision memo recommending one option with: objective impact, bottleneck/trade-off explanation, and risk/uncertainty notes referencing CI where relevant.

activities.title: Formative assessment: Scenario justification quiz + audit-log checkpoint
activities.description: A short graded (or completion-based) check aligned to Bloom ‘evaluate’: learners answer 6–8 items including two short responses. Items require judging whether a claim is justified by sensitivity output, selecting the best recommendation given constraints, and identifying missing transparency elements in a provided (flawed) calculation log.
activities.teachingMethod: Immediate feedback with rationale; short responses compared against a rubric and exemplars.
resources: Flawed calculation log excerpt for critique
instructorActions: Configure feedback to explain why an interpretation is invalid (e.g., outside allowable range; integer constraint present).
If instructor-reviewed, use a lightweight rubric focusing on evidence, validity range, and limitation notes.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback.
Revise their decision memo/log if the quiz reveals a validity or transparency issue.

activities.title: Collaboration simulation: Peer-review your reasoning (asynchronous) + reflection
activities.description: Learners post a short version of their recommendation (3–5 sentences + one screenshot/table) to a discussion board and respond to one peer using a structured critique protocol: ask one clarifying question, challenge one assumption, and suggest one improvement. They then add a brief reflection: what they changed (or would change) after feedback and what limitation they will state explicitly.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured peer review to build collaborative behaviours and transparent quantitative communication.
resources: Screenshot guide (how to capture Solver report snippets)
instructorActions: Provide sentence starters for constructive challenge (e.g., 'What evidence supports…?', 'Does this hold if…?').
Moderate for tone and ensure feedback focuses on reasoning, not the person; highlight 1–2 strong examples in a weekly roundup.
studentActions: Post recommendation with evidence and limitation note.
Reply to one peer using the protocol and update their own work based on insights.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Align all tasks to evaluation by requiring learners to (1) judge validity of sensitivity-based claims, (2) compare scenarios, and (3) defend a recommendation with explicit limitations. Emphasise professional integrity: learners must state units, allowable ranges, Solver configuration, and when results may not generalise (e.g., nonlinear/ integer constraints, large parameter shifts, model misspecification). Build transparency habits by requiring a calculation log and a risk register entry (assumptions + uncertainty, including CI where applicable). Support collaborative behaviours in an online self-study context using structured peer-review prompts and a critique protocol that normalises challenge and revision. Use exemplars that show both strong reasoning and strong limitation statements; explicitly model what ‘overclaiming’ looks like and how to correct it. Keep cognitive load manageable by providing a cheat-sheet for sensitivity fields and using worked-example fading before open-ended scenario evaluation.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners are slow in Excel, allow them to watch the demo at 1.0x and pause frequently; the key is accuracy, not speed. Use time boxes: 15 minutes max for generating reports (Activity 2), 20 minutes for worksheet completion (Activity 3), and 25 minutes for scenario evaluation (Activity 4). If behind, prioritise: binding constraints identification + one scenario comparison + a clear limitation note (core of evaluation). If ahead, add a third scenario or require a brief 'what would change my recommendation?' sensitivity reflection.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility: provide transcripts, downloadable PDFs, and an alternative to screenshots (copy/paste tables) for low-bandwidth learners.
Math/Excel scaffolding: offer a pre-built Solver file with named ranges and a guided ‘click path’ checklist; advanced learners use a blank template and configure Solver themselves.
Language support: provide sentence frames for recommendations and limitation notes (e.g., 'Valid only if…', 'Within allowable range…').

Challenge extension: include a scenario with integer constraints and require learners to explain why the Sensitivity Report is unavailable/not meaningful, then propose an alternative analysis approach (rerun scenarios, what-if tables, simulation).
Confidence/CI integration: for learners less comfortable with statistics, provide a short primer on interpreting a CI and a worked example of adding a conservative buffer based on uncertainty.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming shadow prices apply for any size change; ignoring the allowable increase/decrease validity range.
Confusing a non-binding constraint with an unimportant constraint (it may become binding under a scenario).
Interpreting reduced cost as a ‘penalty paid’ rather than the required improvement in an objective coefficient for a non-basic variable to enter the solution (sign errors are common).
Believing Solver always finds the global optimum; not checking model type (nonlinear) or starting points, or not validating with scenario reruns.
Treating sensitivity outputs as meaningful for integer/binary decision models (where standard sensitivity results may be missing or misleading).
Reporting marginal values without units or operational interpretation (e.g., '$ per unit of capacity').
Overstating certainty: failing to document assumptions, data quality issues, forecast uncertainty (CI), or model limitations in the log/risk register.
discussionPrompts: Which constraint is the true bottleneck in your model, and what operational action does the shadow price suggest—within what valid range?
Where did sensitivity analysis save you time, and where did it fail (forcing a Solver rerun)? What sign told you it was invalid?
What is one limitation you would explicitly state to a stakeholder to avoid overclaiming from the optimisation results?
If a teammate challenges your recommendation, which single piece of evidence from the Solver reports best defends it—and what caveat must accompany it?
How did you incorporate uncertainty (e.g., CI on demand or processing time) into your recommendation or risk register entry?

objectives: Set up an Excel Solver model for a constrained optimisation problem by correctly defining decision variables, objective cell (max/min), and at least 4 constraints (including units and non-negativity), achieving a feasible solution in ≤2 Solver runs.
