instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the lesson so learners must repeatedly justify choices (mean vs median, outlier handling, test selection) and interpret outputs in context, not merely compute them. Use a consistent dataset across activities to reduce extraneous load and highlight how cleaning decisions propagate to inference. Emphasise professional integrity: require explicit statements of assumptions, sampling limits, and uncertainty; discourage binary ‘pass/fail’ thinking based solely on p-values. For the Excel/Python split, keep learning outcomes identical and provide parallel templates so learners can focus on analysis rather than interface friction. Build in frequent checkpoints (intermediate answer checks and interpretation questions) because errors in units, SD type (sample vs population), and rounding often cascade. Encourage reproducibility: in Excel, require labelled cells and formula transparency; in Python, require a single-run notebook with fixed seeds (if used) and clear package versions if feasible. When giving feedback (via automated keys or exemplars), prioritise explaining why an interpretation is valid/invalid and how to communicate results to non-specialists without overstating certainty.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Time-box each segment and make completion criteria explicit (e.g., ‘You are done when your report table includes n, mean/median, SD/IQR, an OutlierFlag column, and a labelled visual’). If learners are behind after the demonstration, suggest skipping optional enhancements (e.g., extra visuals) and proceeding to the core guided practice outputs. If learners finish early, offer an extension: rerun the case analysis using an alternative assumption (equal vs unequal variances) and compare conclusions, or compute an effect size and relate it to tolerance. For self-study, include estimated times on each resource and a “minimum path” (core tasks) versus “deepening path” (extensions).
adaptationOptions: Support for novices: provide partially completed templates (Excel workbook with formulas started; Python notebook with TODO markers) and a test-selection decision tree (paired vs two-sample).

Challenge for advanced learners: add a sensitivity check—repeat analysis with and without flagged outliers and compare CI/test conclusions; require a short justification of which version to report and why.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for videos, high-contrast templates, and allow submission of written interpretations without requiring audio/video responses.

Tool flexibility: allow Google Sheets as an alternative to Excel (with equivalent formulas) or pure pandas/scipy in Python; keep grading focused on reasoning and interpretation rather than exact tool commands.

Language support: provide sentence stems for stakeholder reporting and a glossary with plain-language definitions; encourage learners to draft interpretations first, then translate into technical terms.
Pacing flexibility: offer a ‘core dataset’ (n≈25) and an optional ‘larger dataset’ (n≈200) for learners who want to see how sample size affects CI width and test sensitivity.
commonMisconceptions: Confidence interval misconception: believing a 95% CI means there is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this specific computed interval (rather than the long-run coverage interpretation).
P-value misconception: interpreting p-value as the probability the null hypothesis is true, or as the probability results occurred ‘by chance’ in a literal sense.
Equating non-significance with ‘no effect’ rather than ‘insufficient evidence given this sample size/variability’.
Treating statistical significance as automatically practically important, ignoring tolerance/impact size.
Automatically deleting outliers without investigation or documentation; confusing ‘outlier’ with ‘error’.
Using population SD (STDEV.P) when sample SD (STDEV.S) is needed for inference; mixing SD with standard error.
Rounding intermediate steps too early, causing mismatches and inaccurate reported results.
Ignoring units or mixing unit systems, leading to incorrect summaries and misleading visuals.
Assuming normality is always required, rather than considering sample size, robustness, and visual diagnostics.
Choosing the wrong test design (paired vs independent samples) based on the scenario structure.
discussionPrompts: When you flag an outlier, what evidence would you need to justify excluding it from a quality report—and how would you document that decision transparently?
How would you explain a 95% confidence interval to a non-specialist stakeholder without using the word ‘probability’ incorrectly?
A process change yields p = 0.04 but the estimated mean difference is far smaller than the tolerance. What should the team do next, and how should this be reported?
Your result is not statistically significant (p = 0.12), but the CI still includes values that would be practically concerning. How would you communicate risk and uncertainty?
What sampling limits in your context could make your conclusions unreliable (e.g., non-random sampling, short time window, operator effects), and how could you mitigate them in a follow-up study?
Which is more informative for stakeholders in your scenario: a p-value, a confidence interval, or both? Why?

lessons.lessonTitle: Confidence intervals and simple hypothesis tests for proc...
objectives: Given a before/after process dataset, compute and interpret a 95% confidence interval for a key metric (mean or proportion) and state what it does and does not imply about the process change.

Select and run an appropriate simple hypothesis test (e.g., two-sample t-test or test for difference in proportions) in Excel or Python, and report p-value, test statistic, and a plain-language conclusion tied to the business question.

Document at least 4 assumptions/sampling limits (e.g., independence, representativeness, normality/large-n, constant measurement method, time-related confounding) and explain how each could affect the validity of conclusions.

Differentiate statistical significance from practical significance by calculating an effect size (e.g., mean difference and/or percent change) and comparing it to a stated decision threshold or engineering tolerance.

Create a stakeholder-friendly chart or mini-dashboard (1–3 visuals) that communicates the change, uncertainty, and recommendation using clear labels, units, sensible axes, and 3–5 sentences of narrative commentary.

activities.title: Kick-off case: “Did the process change improve quality?”
activities.description: Learners review a short scenario (e.g., a manufacturing step change intended to reduce defect rate or increase fill weight). They identify the metric, the comparison (before vs after), and what decision a stakeholder needs to make. Learners write a 2–3 sentence problem statement and list what evidence would be persuasive to a non-specialist.
activities.teachingMethod: Problem framing + guided prompts (self-study worksheet).
resources: Case handout (PDF/HTML) with context, metric definition, and decision question
Dataset (CSV) with before/after samples; optional second dataset with a confound (e.g., shift change)
instructorActions: Provide a concise case narrative and clarify success criteria (decision-focused reporting).
Provide a worked example of an acceptable problem statement (separate from the main dataset).
studentActions: Draft a decision-oriented problem statement (who, what metric, what change, what decision).
List at least 2 possible limitations or confounders (e.g., seasonality, operator mix, measurement drift).

activities.title: Concept build: Confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, assumptions, and practical significance
activities.description: Learners watch/read a structured micro-lesson covering: CI interpretation (parameter vs sample), hypothesis test logic (H0/H1, p-value), practical vs statistical significance, and the integrity lens (what to report, what not to claim). Includes a short “spot the overclaim” segment to reinforce transparency.
activities.teachingMethod: Chunked micro-lecture with retrieval pauses and integrity checkpoints.
resources: Micro-lecture video (10–12 min) or annotated reading
One-page reference sheet: CI/test selection guide + assumption checklist
instructorActions: Explicitly model language for uncertainty (e.g., 'estimate', 'evidence suggests', 'within sampling error').
Highlight common misinterpretations (CI ≠ probability the true mean is inside; p-value ≠ probability H0 is true).
studentActions: Answer 4 embedded retrieval questions (auto-check) on CI and p-values.
Rewrite one overclaim statement into an honest, stakeholder-appropriate statement.

activities.title: Tool demonstration (choose one track): Excel or Python workflow for before/after analysis
activities.description: Guided demonstration showing end-to-end analysis for a process change: importing data, checking basic summaries, selecting test (two-sample t-test or proportion test), computing CI for the difference, and generating a clear visual (before/after with CI/error bars). Includes reproducibility steps (documenting settings, rounding rules, and versioning).
activities.teachingMethod: Walkthrough with pause-and-try steps; learners follow along in their chosen tool.
resources: Excel workbook template (tabs: Data, Summary, CI_Test, Charts, Dashboard)
Python notebook template (pandas, scipy/statsmodels, matplotlib/seaborn) with TODO cells
Short video clips: (A) Excel t-test/CI and error bars, (B) Python CI and plots
Reproducibility checklist (file naming, cell locking, code comments, seed usage if applicable)
instructorActions: Provide two parallel tracks (Excel/Python) that produce comparable outputs.
Call out where assumptions enter (e.g., equal variances choice; normal approximation conditions).
Demonstrate how to avoid misleading charts (axes, units, baseline, annotation of n).
studentActions: Follow the workflow to generate preliminary CI/test output and one draft plot.
Record chosen method and justification (1–2 sentences) in the analysis notes.

activities.title: Guided practice: Interpret results with assumptions, sampling limits, and practical significance
activities.description: Learners complete a structured analysis worksheet: (1) compute/confirm CI and hypothesis test, (2) interpret in plain language, (3) compute effect size and compare to a practical threshold, (4) list assumptions/limits and their likely direction of impact, and (5) decide what they would recommend next (e.g., more data, run chart, stratification).
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example fading: high scaffolding at start, then independent completion.
resources: Decision threshold examples (e.g., “≥1% defect reduction is operationally meaningful”)
Optional quick check: normality/robustness note (rules of thumb for n, outliers)
instructorActions: Provide an answer key for one section only (e.g., assumptions list) to reduce over-reliance.
Emphasize integrity: require learners to state at least one limitation even when results look strong.
studentActions: Complete the worksheet fields (numbers + narrative).
Flag one assumption most at risk in the scenario and propose one mitigation (e.g., stratify by shift).

activities.title: Break / reset
activities.description: Short break. Learners are prompted to stand up, then return and re-open their output with a ‘stakeholder lens’.
activities.teachingMethod: Timeboxed pause to support attention and reduce cognitive overload.
resources: Reminder checklist: “What would a non-specialist need to trust this?”
instructorActions: Provide a clear resume cue: next task is creating a dashboard-ready message.
studentActions: Pause and reset; return ready to refine communication.

activities.title: Create: Stakeholder-friendly chart or mini-dashboard + narrative commentary
activities.description: Learners design a 1-page output (Excel dashboard tab or a single report figure in Python) that includes: (a) before vs after comparison chart with CI/error bars or a CI band, (b) a small table of key stats (n, mean/proportion, difference, CI, p-value), and (c) a concise narrative: what changed, how sure we are, practical significance, and limitations/next steps. Must include clear labels, units, and a non-misleading axis choice.
activities.teachingMethod: Product-oriented creation with a rubric and exemplars (create-level synthesis).
resources: Dashboard/report rubric (clarity, correctness, transparency, visual integrity, audience fit)
Exemplar good dashboard and a ‘fixed’ version of a misleading one
Style guide: units, rounding rules, annotation conventions (n, CI level, timeframe)
instructorActions: Provide rubric-aligned exemplars and a ‘minimum viable dashboard’ template.
Prompt inclusion of uncertainty and limitations (not optional).
studentActions: Build the dashboard/report figure and write 3–5 sentences of commentary.
Run a self-check: labels/units, axis integrity, rounding, assumptions/limits stated, recommendation present.

activities.title: Formative check + peer challenge prompt (asynchronous collaboration)
activities.description: Learners complete a short auto-graded quiz (method selection + interpretation) and submit their dashboard/report output. Optional peer-review: learners post one figure and respond to one peer using a structured ‘challenge and improve’ protocol (question the assumption, request clarification, suggest one improvement). This targets collaboration behaviours in an online self-study context.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes retrieval + structured peer feedback to reinforce transparency and reasoning.
resources: Auto-graded quiz (6–8 items) covering CI/test interpretation and common pitfalls
Submission dropbox (PDF/image export of dashboard or notebook render)
instructorActions: Configure auto-feedback for quiz misconceptions.
Provide one example of respectful challenge language and what ‘good feedback’ looks like.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback for any incorrect items.
Submit dashboard/report output; optionally give one peer a rubric-based improvement suggestion.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson as a build-from-evidence workflow: (1) frame the decision, (2) compute CI/test, (3) interpret with uncertainty, (4) communicate visually and ethically. Because the delivery mode is online self-study, provide two parallel tool pathways (Excel and Python) with equivalent checkpoints and outputs. Use scaffolds that fade: start with templates (problem statement, interpretation sentence starters, dashboard layout), then require learners to make choices (test selection, threshold for practical significance, chart type) with justification.

Emphasize professional integrity and transparency by requiring explicit statements of assumptions, sampling limits, and what the analysis cannot conclude (e.g., correlation vs causation; possible confounding in before/after comparisons). Model non-overclaiming language and include a mini-activity where learners rewrite misleading statements. Reinforce reproducibility: insist learners record data source, timeframe, n, any exclusions, tool settings, and rounding rules. Encourage collaborative behaviour asynchronously via structured peer challenge: learners must explain reasoning, welcome critique, and integrate at least one feedback point into a revised chart or commentary when possible.

Maintain stakeholder focus: every output should answer a decision question in plain language, with visuals that are readable and not misleading (clear units, sensible axes, CI level shown, annotation of sample size). When learners struggle, steer them to the rubric: correctness first, then clarity, then narrative concision.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Target a steady cadence with frequent ‘pause-and-produce’ moments.

- If learners are slower/new to tools: advise spending up to +10 minutes by reducing optional peer review and using the provided dashboard template and pre-built formulas/code cells.
- If learners are faster/experienced: add an extension during the creation activity—e.g., stratify by shift/line, add a second visual (run chart over time), or compare results under an alternative assumption (equal vs unequal variances) and note any change in conclusions.
- Suggested time checks: by minute 25 learners should have a computed CI/test output; by minute 55 they should have a completed interpretation worksheet; by minute 80 they should have a dashboard draft; last 10 minutes for polish, quiz, and submission.
adaptationOptions: Tool-choice adaptation: provide equivalent Excel and Python resources; allow submission in either format (PDF export or notebook HTML).
Scaffolding adaptation: offer (A) fully worked template with blanks to fill, (B) partially worked template, (C) open-ended build-from-scratch option for advanced learners.
Accessibility: provide alt-text guidance for visuals, color-blind-safe palettes, and a table-based alternative summary for learners who cannot rely on charts.
Math readiness: include a short optional refresher on standard error and the link between CI width and sample size; provide a ‘rules of thumb’ card for when t-based methods are reasonable.
Language support: provide sentence frames for transparent reporting (e.g., “Estimated change is __ with 95% CI __ to __; results depend on __; practical impact relative to threshold __ is __.”).
Challenge/extension: introduce an optional sensitivity check (remove one outlier or use median/bootstrapped CI) and ask learners to compare conclusions and document the change.
commonMisconceptions: Interpreting a 95% confidence interval as “there is a 95% probability the true value lies in this interval” (instead of a repeated-sampling coverage statement).
Treating a non-significant p-value as proof of “no effect,” rather than “insufficient evidence given the sample size/variability.”
Equating statistical significance with practical importance; ignoring effect size and decision thresholds.
Assuming overlapping 95% CIs automatically imply no significant difference (overlap rules are not that simple, especially across different designs).
Ignoring independence/representativeness (e.g., using repeated measures from the same machine/operator as if they were independent samples).
Choosing a test mechanically without checking conditions (small n with heavy skew/outliers; unequal variances; proportion tests with low counts).
Using misleading visuals: truncated y-axes without justification, missing units, unclear timeframes, or omitting sample size and CI level.
Rounding too early or inconsistently, causing small differences to disappear or appear; failing to document rounding rules in technical reporting.
Overclaiming causality in before/after comparisons without considering confounding process changes.
discussionPrompts: Your CI excludes zero but the effect is smaller than the operational threshold. What should you recommend, and how would you explain it to a non-specialist?
Your p-value is > 0.05 but the estimated effect would be valuable if real. What additional data or design change would you propose (and why)?
Which assumption is most fragile in a before/after process change study: independence, comparability of conditions, or measurement stability? Defend your choice.
What is one sentence you should avoid saying to stakeholders about p-values or confidence intervals, and what is a better replacement sentence?
How could a chart be ‘technically correct’ but still misleading? Identify one risk in your own dashboard and how you mitigated it.
A teammate challenges your conclusion, pointing out a possible confound (e.g., shift mix changed). How do you respond and update your report while maintaining integrity?

lessons.lessonTitle: Stakeholder-friendly charts or dashboards that explain st...
objectives: Clean a provided quality dataset (handle missing values, consistent units, correct data types) and document at least 3 assumptions made in a short data-cleaning log.

Compute and present measures of centre and spread (mean, median, standard deviation and/or IQR) plus an outlier flag using a stated rule (e.g., 1.5×IQR or z-score threshold) with results reproducible in Excel or Python.
Create a stakeholder-friendly chart set (minimum 2 visuals) that communicates a trend and highlights turning points/constraints, using correct titles, labels, units and an appropriate chart type.

Assemble a one-page dashboard (or single notebook output page) that combines summary metrics, a trend view and an outlier view, and includes a concise narrative (100–150 words) suitable for a non-specialist audience.
Self-evaluate the dashboard using a quality-report checklist (accuracy, units, clarity, interpretation) and revise at least 2 elements based on feedback from an exemplar comparison or rubric prompts.

activities.title: Kick-off: Lesson brief, success criteria and dataset orientation
activities.description: Learners open the lesson workspace (Excel workbook template or Python notebook) and the provided quality dataset (CSV). They review the dashboard requirements and the marking checklist: must include measures of centre/spread, an outlier flag, at least two visuals, and a short narrative. Learners identify what the stakeholder cares about (e.g., defect rate, cycle time, yield) and note units and time period.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-briefing with a checklist and a quick 'what does the stakeholder need?' prompt to prime purposeful creation.
resources: Excel template (dashboard_skeleton.xlsx) OR Python notebook template (dashboard_skeleton.ipynb)
Glossary: Measures of centre, Outlier flag, Dashboard, CI
instructorActions: Provide a clear definition of the end product (one-page dashboard + narrative) and non-negotiables (units, labels, outlier rule stated).
Model diligence expectations: verify units, check for missing/invalid values, sanity-check summary numbers.
Offer two tool pathways (Excel or Python) with equivalent outcomes.
studentActions: Open the dataset and scan columns, units and date/time fields.
Record the stakeholder question they will answer (one sentence).
Confirm they can run the template (enable macros if needed; run notebook cells).

activities.title: Concept build: From statistics to stakeholder story (charts, CI and outliers)
activities.description: Short content segment on choosing charts for operational quality reporting: KPI cards, line charts for trends, boxplots/histograms for distribution, and control-style thinking (without full SPC). Emphasis on clear labeling, consistent units, and explaining outliers. Introduce confidence intervals (CI) as uncertainty around an estimate and show how to avoid over-claiming (e.g., overlapping CIs).
activities.teachingMethod: Interactive reading/video with embedded checkpoints asking learners to select the best chart type for a scenario and to interpret a CI statement.
resources: Mini-lesson slides or reading (PDF/HTML): 'Quality Reporting: What to show and why'
instructorActions: Emphasize that dashboards are decisions tools, not data dumps; every visual should answer a question.
Explicitly connect outlier handling to integrity: do not delete outliers without justification; flag and investigate.
Provide 2–3 examples of strong vs weak chart labeling (missing units, unclear time base, truncated axes).
studentActions: Answer embedded checks: pick a chart for a trend vs distribution question; identify what’s wrong with a poorly labeled chart.
Write a draft 'message headline' for their dashboard (one sentence).
Note which CI display they might use (error bars, shaded band, or CI table note).

activities.title: Guided demonstration: Build the summary table + outlier flag (Excel/Python)
activities.description: Walkthrough showing (a) cleaning steps (type conversion, missing handling), (b) measures of centre/spread, and (c) an outlier flag using a declared rule. Excel route may use formulas (AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, QUARTILE.INC, IQR) and helper columns; Python route may use pandas describe(), quantiles, and boolean flags. End with a small, tidy summary table ready for dashboard use.
activities.teachingMethod: Tool-aligned screencast (choose Excel or Python) with pause-and-do prompts every 2–3 minutes.
resources: Screencast: 'Summary stats + outlier flag in Excel' (10–12 min)
Screencast: 'Summary stats + outlier flag in Python/pandas' (10–12 min)
Outlier rule options card (IQR and z-score)
instructorActions: Model explicit assumption statements (e.g., 'Missing cycle_time treated as not recorded; excluded from mean but counted in missing-rate KPI').
Model accuracy checks: recompute one metric two ways; spot-check with a small filtered sample.
Name the outlier rule in the output (e.g., 'Outlier = value < Q1−1.5×IQR or > Q3+1.5×IQR').
studentActions: Follow along to create the same summary table in their chosen tool.
Implement an outlier flag column and verify it marks expected extreme values.
Add a short note in their log: rule used, why chosen, and any data exclusions.

activities.title: Practice sprint 1: Clean, summarise, and validate (diligence focus)
activities.description: Independent build time. Learners complete cleaning and summary outputs for the dataset, then run validation checks: units consistent, no negative times/defects, reasonable ranges, missing-rate calculated, and outlier count plausible. Learners create a small 'data quality' box on the dashboard (e.g., N, missing %, outlier count).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured practice with a required checklist and optional extension tasks for faster learners.
resources: Validation checklist (units, types, missing, duplicates, range checks)
instructorActions: Provide a minimum viable target: at least 4 stats + outlier flag + missing-rate.
Encourage learners to annotate formulas/cells or code comments to explain reasoning.
Offer troubleshooting notes for common tool issues (date parsing, text-to-number).
studentActions: Clean and summarise the dataset, completing the log (at least 3 assumptions).
Run validation checks and fix any issues found.
Create a compact summary block ready to be referenced by charts/dashboard elements.

activities.title: Practice sprint 2: Create the stakeholder dashboard (create-level product)
activities.description: Learners assemble a one-page dashboard that includes: (1) KPI cards (e.g., average, median, defect rate, outlier count), (2) a trend chart over time with turning points annotated, and (3) an outlier/distribution view (boxplot, histogram, or highlighted points). Learners add a CI element where feasible (e.g., mean with 95% CI error bars by week/month) or include a clear note explaining uncertainty if CI is not implemented. Finish with a 100–150 word narrative and an action-oriented recommendation.
activities.teachingMethod: Creation task with a rubric and a 'stakeholder lens' constraint: no more than 6 elements, plain-language labels, and consistent units.
resources: Dashboard rubric (clarity, accuracy, relevance, integrity, design)
Annotation guide: turning points and constraints
CI how-to (Excel error bars / Python seaborn+matplotlib or plotly)
instructorActions: Remind learners to avoid clutter: fewer visuals with clearer messages.
Require explicit units on every axis and metric; require time granularity stated (daily/weekly/monthly).
Prompt evidence-based recommendations: connect recommendation to a shown turning point, outlier cluster, or constraint.
studentActions: Build the dashboard page/output with at least 2 visuals and KPI metrics.
Add clear titles, labels, units, and brief annotations for key changes.
Write the narrative commentary and a recommendation for the stakeholder.

activities.title: Formative assessment: Self-check + exemplar comparison + revision
activities.description: Learners complete a short auto-graded quiz (accuracy and interpretation) and then compare their dashboard to an exemplar using the rubric. They must revise at least two items (e.g., fix units, change chart type, clarify narrative, correct outlier rule statement, add CI note). This simulates collaborative feedback by requiring learners to anticipate and respond to critique prompts.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes formative quiz followed by guided self/peer-simulation review using structured prompts.
resources: Formative quiz (10 questions): units, chart selection, outlier interpretation, CI meaning
Revision prompt sheet: 'If a teammate challenged X, how would you respond?'
instructorActions: Provide targeted feedback per quiz item (explanations, not just correct answers).
Ensure exemplar shows transparent assumptions and outlier handling.
Require revisions to be logged (what changed, why).
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review explanations for any incorrect items.
Use the rubric to identify 2 improvement areas in their dashboard.
Implement the improvements and note changes in their revision log.

activities.title: Wrap-up: Team review simulation (collaboration behaviours) and export
activities.description: Learners prepare a short 'team review meeting' response: three bullet points explaining their findings, one anticipated challenge question, and a brief response grounded in the dashboard evidence. They export the dashboard (PDF/image or notebook HTML) and save the cleaning/revision logs.
activities.teachingMethod: Asynchronous role-play via scripted prompts to practise explaining reasoning and welcoming challenge.
instructorActions: Prompt respectful, evidence-based phrasing: 'Based on the chart..., we recommend...' and 'A limitation is...'.
Reinforce professional reporting norms: versioning, clear file names, reproducible steps.
Encourage learners to keep a 'questions to investigate next' list.
studentActions: Write the three bullets + challenge question + response.
Export and save their dashboard and logs.
Optional: post their Q&A in the discussion forum if available.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson around a tangible artefact: a one-page dashboard that must be accurate, interpretable, and decision-oriented. Because the delivery mode is online self-study, embed guidance directly into templates (cell comments, notebook markdown, checklists) and use frequent pause-and-do prompts.

Prioritise diligence: require learners to (1) state assumptions, (2) verify units and ranges, and (3) run at least one independent check (e.g., recompute a metric via pivot/groupby versus formula/function). Treat outliers as signals to investigate, not automatic deletions; the key is transparent rules and clear communication.

Support collaborative behaviours through structured critique prompts even without live peers: learners should explain reasoning, anticipate challenges, and revise based on rubric/exemplar comparison. Provide an exemplar that includes both strong design and explicit caveats (limitations, missing data, CI interpretation).

Keep the create-level emphasis: learners must make choices (chart types, layout, outlier rule, narrative focus) and justify them. Evaluate success by whether a non-specialist could answer 'What happened? Why might it matter? What should we do next?' from the dashboard alone.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Timebox creation: aim for a 'minimum viable dashboard' by minute ~60 (KPI block + one trend chart + one outlier/distribution view). Use the last 30 minutes to label/annotate, add CI or uncertainty note, and improve narrative clarity.

If learners fall behind: skip CI implementation and instead add an explicit uncertainty note (e.g., small sample size, missingness) while keeping correct summary stats and clean visuals. If learners finish early: add interactivity (Excel slicers or plotly filters), segment by shift/line/product, or add a CI band/error bars by time period.

Encourage micro-checkpoints every 10 minutes: (1) Are units consistent? (2) Are axes labeled? (3) Is the outlier rule written on the dashboard? (4) Does each visual have a takeaway annotation?
adaptationOptions: Tool pathway choice: provide parallel instructions and templates for Excel-only and Python-only learners; allow submission in either format with the same rubric.
Scaffold for novices: pre-built cleaning steps (or starter code) with blanks for learners to complete; provide a dashboard wireframe with placeholders for titles/units.
Extension for advanced learners: implement 95% CI for mean by week/month; add segmented dashboards by category (shift/line/product) and discuss practical vs statistical significance.
Accessibility adaptations: require colour-blind safe palettes, larger fonts for KPI cards, high-contrast themes, and alternative text/captions for exported visuals.
Math support: offer an optional refresher on IQR, standard deviation, and CI interpretation with short practice questions and immediate feedback.
Language support: provide a narrative sentence starter bank (e.g., 'The median cycle time increased after…', 'Outliers are concentrated in…') and a glossary of plain-language terms.
commonMisconceptions: Believing dashboards must include every available metric; confusing comprehensiveness with clarity.
Mixing units or time bases (e.g., minutes vs seconds; daily vs weekly) and still interpreting trends as comparable.
Treating the mean as always the best ‘typical’ value even when distributions are skewed; ignoring the median/IQR.
Assuming outliers are always errors to remove rather than values to flag and investigate; failing to state the outlier rule used.
Misinterpreting confidence intervals as '95% of data lie in this range' instead of uncertainty around an estimate (e.g., mean).
Using misleading chart practices (truncated axes without justification, 3D charts, excessive decimal places, cluttered legends).
Confusing correlation in operational data with causation; presenting recommendations without linking to evidence shown in the visuals.
Assuming a visually large change is meaningful without considering sample size, missingness, or variability.
discussionPrompts: Which single question does your dashboard answer for a non-specialist stakeholder, and how do your visuals directly support that answer?
What outlier rule did you choose (IQR or z-score), why is it appropriate for this dataset, and what would change if you used a different rule?
Where do you see a turning point or constraint in the trend chart, and what operational explanation is plausible (without over-claiming causation)?
If a teammate challenged your calculation (e.g., mean/median, missing handling), what specific check would you show to defend or revise your result?
What is one limitation of your analysis (missing data, small samples, measurement issues), and how did you communicate that limitation on the dashboard?
How did you decide whether to include a confidence interval, and what would you say to a stakeholder who interprets it incorrectly?
What change would make your dashboard easier to read in under 30 seconds (fewer visuals, better titles, clearer units, stronger annotation)?

lessons.lessonTitle: Confidence intervals and simple hypothesis tests for proc...
objectives: Given a pre/post process dataset, compute and report a 95% confidence interval (CI) for the mean (or proportion) change in Excel or Python, including units and correct rounding.

Select and run an appropriate simple hypothesis test for a process change (e.g., one-sample or two-sample t-test; proportion test where applicable) and interpret the p-value and decision in plain language for non-specialists.
Produce an “assumptions + sampling limits” statement (minimum 4 items) that transparently identifies data conditions, potential biases, and limitations affecting the CI/test validity.

Distinguish statistical significance from practical significance by defining a practical threshold (e.g., minimum meaningful improvement) and concluding whether the change is operationally meaningful.

Create a stakeholder-friendly chart or mini-dashboard that communicates the change and uncertainty (CI/error bars), with clear labels, units, and 2–4 sentences of narrative commentary suitable for a quality report.

activities.title: Set-up, success criteria, and integrity checklist
activities.description: Learners review the lesson goal: move from calculations to a stakeholder-ready story. They download the dataset and choose a tool path (Excel or Python). They read a short checklist on professional integrity: show uncertainty, state assumptions, document steps, and avoid overclaiming.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided self-study orientation with a short “what good looks like” example and a quick checklist.
resources: CSV dataset: process_metric_pre_post.csv (includes metric, date/batch, group=pre/post, sample size notes)
Starter Excel workbook template (tabs: Data, Calculations, Charts, Dashboard)
Starter Python notebook template (cells scaffolded for CI/test/chart)
instructorActions: Provide two tool pathways (Excel/Python) with equivalent outcomes.
Show an exemplar screenshot of a finished dashboard (blurred values) highlighting labels, units, CI bars, and a short narrative.
Embed a reminder: learners must report assumptions and sampling limits, not just p-values.
studentActions: Download/open the dataset and select Excel or Python pathway.
Read the integrity checklist and note 2 items they often forget (e.g., units, sampling bias).

activities.title: Concept build: CI + hypothesis test for process change (with practical significance)
activities.description: Learners study a concise explainer that links: (1) estimating change with a CI, (2) testing change with a hypothesis test, and (3) deciding whether the change matters operationally (practical significance). Includes assumptions (independence, approximate normality/CLT, stable measurement system) and sampling limits (small n, convenience sampling, missing data).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lesson with worked example narratives (good vs misleading) and embedded comprehension checks.
resources: Short reading/video (8–10 minutes): “CI vs p-value vs practical significance”
Mini glossary: confidence interval, hypothesis test, sampling limit, dashboard, assumption
instructorActions: Present a single worked scenario: ‘Process change intended to reduce defect rate / cycle time’.
Include two ‘integrity flags’: (a) claiming causation without design evidence, (b) hiding uncertainty.
Add 3 auto-check questions with immediate feedback (e.g., interpret a CI, interpret a p-value).
studentActions: Complete embedded checks (auto-graded) and review feedback.
Write down a practical significance threshold they might use in their workplace context (e.g., ≥1.0 minute reduction, ≥0.5% defect reduction).

activities.title: Tool demonstration: compute CI and run a simple test (Excel or Python)
activities.description: Step-by-step demonstration in the chosen tool to: clean/filter pre/post samples, compute summary statistics, compute a CI for the mean (or mean difference), run a t-test (or appropriate simple test), and capture results in a reproducible table (with units and rounding).
activities.teachingMethod: Guided walk-through using a scaffolded template; learners pause at checkpoints to replicate results.
resources: Excel: Data Analysis Toolpak instructions + formulas for CI (t critical, standard error) + T.TEST
Python: pandas + scipy.stats (t.interval / ttest_ind or ttest_rel as appropriate) + matplotlib/seaborn starter code
Reproducibility checklist (n, missing values handled, parameters chosen, rounding rule)
instructorActions: Model transparent reporting: show the exact test used, alpha level, and why it matches the design (paired vs independent).
Emphasize sampling limits: demonstrate what changes when n is small or when outliers exist.
Provide a ‘checkpoint table’ of expected intermediate values so learners can self-verify.
studentActions: Replicate the calculation steps in their tool using the template.
Fill in the results table: n_pre, n_post, mean_pre, mean_post, estimated change, 95% CI, p-value, and chosen practical threshold.

activities.title: Practice: interpret results + write assumptions, sampling limits, and practical significance statement
activities.description: Learners draft a short quality-report paragraph (120–180 words) interpreting the CI and test, explicitly stating assumptions and sampling limits, and concluding on practical significance. They must include at least one limitation and one recommendation for next data collection or validation.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured writing with sentence starters and a marking checklist; self-check against a model answer.
resources: Interpretation sentence starters (e.g., “We estimate the average change is … with a 95% CI of …”)
instructorActions: Provide a rubric snippet: accuracy, transparency, practical significance, and stakeholder clarity.
Include prompts that require humility and integrity (e.g., “What would make this conclusion unreliable?”).
Offer an optional extension: if assumptions seem weak, suggest a nonparametric alternative or bootstrap CI (conceptual, not required).
studentActions: Write the paragraph and complete the assumptions/limits checklist (minimum 4 items).
Compare their paragraph to the model and revise one sentence to improve clarity or transparency.

activities.title: Create: stakeholder-friendly chart/mini-dashboard with narrative callouts
activities.description: Learners build a single-page view that a non-specialist could understand in under 60 seconds. Minimum requirements: (1) a chart comparing pre vs post (or trend over time) with CI/error bars or uncertainty band, (2) clear title, labels, units, sample sizes, (3) an annotation stating estimated change and CI, (4) a short narrative box (2–4 sentences) including assumptions/limits and practical significance conclusion.
activities.teachingMethod: Performance task (create) using a template layout; learners make design choices and justify them.
resources: Dashboard layout template (Excel tab or notebook markdown block)
Chart style guide (do/don’t examples: avoid 3D, include units, readable scales, honest axes)
instructorActions: Provide 2–3 recommended chart options (e.g., dot plot with CI bars; bar chart with error bars; line chart with pre/post marker + CI).
Remind learners to avoid misleading visuals (truncated axes without disclosure; omitting n).
Encourage reproducibility: keep calculations linked to data, avoid manual copy/paste values without notes.
studentActions: Build the chart and assemble the mini-dashboard page.
Add the narrative callout including: estimated change, 95% CI, p-value (if used), practical threshold, and one limitation.
Run a final self-audit: units, labels, n, assumptions, and rounding consistency.

activities.title: Formative assessment: self-review + optional peer challenge response
activities.description: Learners complete a short formative check aligned to the lesson objectives and then perform a structured self-review of their dashboard using a rubric. Optional: post a screenshot/export to the course forum and respond to a peer ‘challenge question’ to practice collaborative behaviours (welcoming critique and integrating feedback).
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-graded quiz + rubric-based reflection; optional asynchronous peer review for collaboration practice.
resources: Formative Quiz 1 (5 items): CI interpretation, test selection, p-value meaning, practical vs statistical significance, assumptions
Dashboard rubric (clarity, integrity, uncertainty, assumptions/limits, practical significance, reproducibility)
Forum prompt template: “One thing I’m confident about / One thing I’m unsure about”
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to address common misconceptions (e.g., CI probability misinterpretation).
Provide a ‘revision loop’: learners identify 1 improvement and update their dashboard.
Model respectful challenge language for peer review (e.g., ‘What assumption supports…?’ ‘How sensitive is…?’).
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback for any missed items.
Use the rubric to identify and implement 1 concrete improvement to their dashboard.
Optional: post their dashboard and respond to one peer question, acknowledging feedback and stating what they changed (or why not).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Keep the lesson anchored in quality-reporting decisions rather than calculation mechanics: learners should finish with a communicable artifact (dashboard + narrative) that demonstrates integrity. Emphasize the logic chain: (1) quantify change (estimate + CI), (2) evaluate evidence (simple test), (3) communicate uncertainty and limitations (assumptions + sampling limits), and (4) decide if it matters (practical significance threshold).

For online self-study, provide tight scaffolds (templates, checkpoint values, sentence starters) and multiple verification points so learners can self-correct without live instructor intervention. Embed transparency as a required deliverable: learners must show n, units, and at least one limitation. Reinforce reproducibility habits: calculations linked to data, documented parameters (alpha, test type), and consistent rounding rules.

Support collaborative behaviours asynchronously: include optional peer review prompts that explicitly invite challenge (“What assumption could fail?”) and require learners to integrate at least one piece of feedback into a revision. Avoid overclaiming: repeatedly distinguish ‘evidence of a change in this sample’ from ‘proof the process change caused improvement’ unless the design supports causal claims.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Target completion is 90 minutes, but expect variance by tool familiarity.
- If learners are strong in Excel/Python: reduce the demo to 10–12 minutes by letting them jump to the checkpoint table, and spend extra time (5–10 minutes) improving the dashboard narrative and limitations.
- If learners are new to tools: keep the full demo and allow the dashboard to be minimal (one chart + one text box) as long as it includes CI/uncertainty, units, n, and assumptions.
- Encourage a two-pass approach: (1) get a correct CI/test result quickly using the template, (2) refine communication quality (labels, narrative, practical significance, limitations).
- Timeboxing tip: if stuck on chart formatting after 7–8 minutes, move on to narrative and return later—communication can compensate for simpler visuals.
adaptationOptions: Tool choice: Provide equivalent step-by-step guides for Excel and Python; allow submission in either format (workbook export or notebook PDF/HTML).
Math support: Offer an optional ‘formula sheet’ with t critical values explanation and an annotated example of standard error and CI construction.
Accessibility: Provide a high-contrast, colorblind-safe chart palette and require non-color cues (markers/labels) for categories.
Cognitive load reduction: Supply a pre-cleaned dataset version for learners who struggle with missing values/outliers, while still requiring them to state sampling limits.
Extension for advanced learners: Add an optional bootstrap CI comparison, sensitivity check (remove outliers / change alpha), or a second visualization (trend line with annotated turning point).
Language support: Provide sentence frames for reporting uncertainty and limitations; allow learners to record an audio explanation instead of writing (then transcribe key numbers).
commonMisconceptions: Misinterpreting a 95% CI as “there is a 95% probability the true value is in this specific interval” rather than a long-run coverage statement.
Treating p-value as the probability the null hypothesis is true, or as the probability results are due to ‘chance’ in a colloquial sense.
Equating statistical significance with practical/operational importance (ignoring effect size and practical thresholds).
Assuming overlapping confidence intervals automatically mean ‘no difference’ (or non-overlap guarantees significance) without considering the correct comparison method.
Using the wrong test design (paired vs independent) or ignoring independence assumptions (e.g., repeated measurements treated as separate samples).
Hiding sampling limits: assuming the sample represents the process when there may be convenience sampling, missing shifts, or measurement system issues.
Creating misleading visuals (truncated y-axis without disclosure, missing units, missing sample sizes, or using 3D/overdecorated charts).
Over-rounding results so that the CI/test decision or practical significance conclusion becomes ambiguous.
discussionPrompts: Your dashboard shows a statistically significant change but a small effect. What practical threshold did you choose, and how would you justify it to operations or quality stakeholders?
Which assumption is most likely to fail in your dataset (independence, normality/CLT, stable measurement, random sampling)? What evidence do you have, and what would you do next to reduce risk?
How would you communicate uncertainty to a manager who asks for a single ‘yes/no’ answer? Draft one sentence that is honest but still decision-oriented.
If a peer challenges your chart as potentially misleading (axis scaling, missing n, unclear units), what would you change first and why?
What sampling limit could most change your conclusion (small n, missing time periods, outliers, process drift)? Propose one additional data collection step to address it.

lessons.lessonTitle: Stakeholder-friendly charts or dashboards that explain st...
objectives: Given a raw quality dataset, compute and report (with correct units) at least 3 measures of centre/spread (e.g., mean, median, SD or IQR) and create an outlier flag using a stated rule (e.g., 1.5×IQR or z-score threshold) in Excel or Python with ≤1 calculation/labeling error.

Create at least 2 stakeholder-friendly visuals (e.g., histogram/box plot and time-series/run chart) that include clear titles, axis labels, units, and an annotation highlighting one key operational insight (trend, shift, turning point, or constraint).

Construct a one-screen dashboard (or single report page) that integrates summary statistics, outlier counts, and visuals, and includes a concise narrative (≤120 words) that explains findings and uncertainty (CI where appropriate) for a non-specialist audience.
Apply a self-check protocol (units, assumptions, rounding, and chart integrity) to identify and correct at least 3 issues in a draft report/dashboard before submission.

Provide and incorporate peer feedback by making at least 2 specific improvement actions (e.g., relabeling, changing chart type, revising narrative, correcting an assumption) documented in a short revision note.

activities.title: Orientation + success criteria (What ‘stakeholder-friendly’ looks like)
activities.description: Self-study micro-lesson introducing the end product: a single-screen dashboard/report page summarising quality data with measures of centre/spread, outlier flags, and clear visuals. Includes an exemplar and a checklist (titles/units, readability, message-first narrative, uncertainty/CI, and traceable assumptions).

instructorActions: Provide exemplars and a clear definition of stakeholder audience (non-specialist, time-limited).
Emphasise diligence: units, assumptions, and reproducibility as grading priorities.
State required deliverable format options: Excel dashboard tab or Python notebook export (HTML/PDF).
studentActions: Download the checklist and save it for use during the build.
Identify 2 features that make the exemplar easy to understand (e.g., labels, narrative, minimal clutter).

activities.title: Tool demonstration: cleaning + summaries + outlier flag + CI (Excel or Python path)
activities.description: Guided demonstration showing a complete workflow on a sample dataset: importing, handling missing values, standardising units, computing mean/median/SD (or IQR), generating an outlier flag using a stated rule, and producing a simple CI for a mean (or proportion) where appropriate. Demonstration also shows how to structure calculations so they feed a dashboard (named ranges/tables in Excel; functions and tidy dataframe in Python).

Quick reference: Outlier rules (IQR and z-score) + CI cheat sheet
instructorActions: Model ‘thinking aloud’ about assumptions (e.g., independence, stable process period) and units.
Demonstrate how to document the chosen outlier rule and why it was selected.
Show one example of a common error and how to catch it (e.g., wrong units, percent vs proportion).

Follow the demonstration to reproduce the workflow on the provided dataset.

activities.title: Hands-on build 1: Clean, summarise, and flag outliers (core calculations)
activities.description: Learners perform the workflow independently on a new but similar dataset (or a new subset/time window). Output must include: (1) a clean data table, (2) measures of centre/spread, (3) an outlier flag column, and (4) a small summary table for dashboard use (e.g., N, mean, median, SD/IQR, outlier count, and % outliers). A short self-check is completed at the end.

resources: Validation hints: expected ranges for mean/median and outlier percentage
Self-check protocol (units, assumptions, rounding, missing data handling)
instructorActions: Provide benchmark ranges and a troubleshooting guide (e.g., if your mean is outside X–Y, check unit conversion).
Encourage documenting decisions: missing values treatment and outlier rule.
Remind learners to keep formulas/code transparent for auditability.

Compute centre/spread measures and create an outlier flag using a stated rule.
Complete the self-check protocol and correct any issues found.

activities.title: Break / cognitive reset
activities.description: Short pause to reduce fatigue before designing visuals and narrative.
activities.teachingMethod: Offline pause with a quick reminder: return and build visuals that answer stakeholder questions.
instructorActions: Prompt learners (in the lesson page) to stand up, then return with one stakeholder question in mind.
studentActions: Take a short break and return ready to design visuals.

activities.title: Hands-on build 2: Create stakeholder-friendly visuals + one-screen dashboard/report page
activities.description: Learners design and assemble a one-screen dashboard (or single report page) that includes: a summary table, at least 2 charts (distribution + time/trend or comparison), and concise narrative commentary including a confidence interval statement where appropriate. Learners must label axes with units, add an annotation that highlights a key insight, and ensure the visuals are readable (font size, colour choices, minimal clutter).
activities.teachingMethod: Creation task with a layout scaffold: ‘Top-left: KPI tiles; Top-right: trend; Bottom-left: distribution; Bottom-right: outliers/notes’. Learners choose chart types that best match the message.
resources: Chart selection guide (when to use run chart vs bar chart vs box plot/histogram)
Plain-language reporting stems (e.g., “We are 95% confident that…”)
instructorActions: Provide accessibility reminders (colour-blind friendly palette, avoid tiny labels).
Reinforce message-first reporting: each chart should answer a question.
Encourage including uncertainty only when meaningful and correctly interpreted.
studentActions: Build at least 2 charts with titles, axis labels, and units.
Assemble the one-screen dashboard/report page.
Write a ≤120-word narrative summarising the key message, including CI language if used.

activities.title: Collaborative review (asynchronous): Peer feedback + revision note
activities.description: Learners post a screenshot/export of their dashboard (and a short note of assumptions/outlier rule) to a discussion board. They give structured feedback to at least one peer using ‘Glow/Grow’ (one strength, one improvement). Learners then revise their own dashboard and write a brief revision note listing at least 2 changes made in response to feedback.
activities.teachingMethod: Asynchronous peer critique with a rubric-aligned feedback form focusing on clarity, correctness, and stakeholder relevance.
instructorActions: Seed the forum with one sample post and model constructive critique.
Moderate for tone and accuracy; correct misconceptions in a summary reply.
Encourage learners to welcome challenge and show evidence of revision.
studentActions: Post dashboard image/export and assumptions/outlier rule.
Provide one peer with specific feedback tied to checklist criteria.
Revise dashboard and document at least 2 changes in a revision note.

activities.title: Formative assessment: Quality reporting checkpoint (auto-graded + reflection)
activities.description: Two-part formative check: (A) short auto-graded quiz (interpret CI statement, choose correct chart, identify labeling/unit errors, spot outlier-rule misapplication); (B) reflection prompt: ‘List 3 diligence checks you performed and what you corrected.’
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-graded quiz for immediate feedback + short written reflection for metacognition and diligence habits.
instructorActions: Provide targeted feedback messages keyed to common errors (units, CI interpretation, chart choice).
Use results to post a ‘Top 5 fixes’ announcement to the class.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review explanations.
Submit a short reflection describing checks performed and corrections made.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson around a concrete creation deliverable (one-screen dashboard/report page) and make the quality criteria explicit early (checklist + exemplars). Keep the cognitive load manageable by splitting the build into two phases: (1) trustworthy calculations (cleaning, summaries, outlier flag, CI) and (2) communication (charts, annotations, narrative). Model diligence by repeatedly externalising a verification routine: units check, reasonableness check (benchmark ranges), and assumption logging (missing data handling and outlier rule). For collaborative behaviour in an online self-study context, require structured peer feedback that is rubric-aligned and revision-oriented; assess the revision note, not just the initial post, to incentivise integrating feedback. Encourage multiple correct tool paths (Excel or Python) while keeping outputs comparable via common required elements (summary table, outlier count, two charts, narrative, labels/units). Emphasise that outlier flags are for investigation and transparent reporting—not automatic deletion—unless a justified data-quality reason is documented.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners are moving slowly: reduce chart scope to two high-value visuals (run chart + box plot) and use the provided template to avoid layout overhead; keep the narrative to 3 sentences (finding, evidence, implication). If learners are moving quickly: add a slicer/filter (Excel) or interactive widget (Python) for product line or time window; include a second CI (e.g., difference in means between two shifts) and annotate a turning point with a brief operational hypothesis. Maintain momentum by enforcing ‘stop-and-check’ moments at minute ~25 (after summaries) and minute ~70 (after dashboard assembly) using the checklist. Encourage learners to timebox polishing (fonts/colours) to the final 5 minutes of the build segment so correctness and clarity come first.
adaptationOptions: Excel support track: provide a pre-built pivot table and chart placeholders; learners focus on correct measures, labeling, and narrative rather than chart construction from scratch.
Python support track: provide starter functions for summary stats, outlier flagging, and CI; learners focus on selecting and formatting visuals (e.g., seaborn/matplotlib templates).

Accessibility: offer a high-contrast colour palette, guidance on font sizes, and allow submission as a simple annotated report page (table + charts) if dashboards are difficult to view on small screens.
Extension for advanced learners: require a brief sensitivity check comparing two outlier rules (IQR vs z-score) and discuss how conclusions change (or don’t).
Language support: provide sentence stems for narrative commentary and a glossary for key terms (measures of centre, outlier flag, dashboard, CI) with plain-language definitions.
Anxiety/low-confidence support: allow learners to submit a ‘draft dashboard’ for low-stakes feedback before posting to peers; encourage using benchmark ranges to build trust in results.
commonMisconceptions: Treating an outlier flag as an instruction to delete data rather than a prompt to investigate and report transparently.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error (and therefore producing incorrect confidence intervals).
Interpreting a 95% CI as ‘95% of data fall in this interval’ rather than ‘we are 95% confident the parameter lies in this interval’ (under repeated sampling logic).
Using inconsistent units (e.g., mixing seconds and minutes) or omitting units on axes, leading to misleading visuals and summaries.
Choosing chart types that don’t match the question (e.g., pie chart for time trends; bar chart of averages without showing variation or sample size).
Over-rounding or excessive decimal places that either hide meaningful differences or create false precision.
Assuming correlation/association in operational data proves causation without additional evidence or process context.
Misreading box plots/histograms (e.g., thinking the box shows the full range; misunderstanding quartiles).
discussionPrompts: What single question should your dashboard answer for a non-specialist stakeholder, and which two visuals best answer it?
When you flag outliers, what are at least two plausible real-world causes (process issue vs measurement/data entry issue), and how would you recommend investigating?
Where could unit inconsistency creep into your workflow (collection, import, transformation, charting), and what checks prevent it?
How would you explain your confidence interval in one sentence to a stakeholder, and what decision could it inform (or not inform)?
If a peer challenges your chart choice or outlier rule, what evidence (not opinion) can you use to justify or revise your approach?
What is one change you made after feedback that materially improved clarity or correctness, and why did it matter to the stakeholder?

lessons.lessonTitle: Confidence intervals and simple hypothesis tests for proc...
objectives: Given a before/after process dataset, compute and interpret a 95% confidence interval for the mean change (Excel or Python) and state the parameter, units, and practical meaning in 1–2 sentences.

Select and run an appropriate simple hypothesis test for a process change (e.g., one-sample or two-sample t-test, paired t-test), report the test statistic and p-value, and clearly state assumptions and sampling limits using a provided checklist.

Evaluate statistical vs practical significance by comparing effect size (absolute and/or percent change) to a stated business threshold and summarise the decision with uncertainty language (e.g., “evidence suggests…”, “results are inconclusive because…”).

Create a stakeholder-friendly chart or mini-dashboard that communicates the process change with clear labels, units, confidence interval visualisation, and a concise narrative commentary (≤120 words) including limitations and next-step recommendations.
Apply professional integrity and collaborative behaviours by using a review checklist to critique a draft dashboard (self-check or peer-check) and implement at least 2 improvements based on feedback.

activities.title: Diagnostic warm-up: CI & hypothesis test quick check
activities.description: Self-marking quiz to activate prior knowledge: identify which test to use (paired vs independent), interpret a CI, interpret a p-value, and spot missing labels/units on a chart. Includes one question on ethical reporting (what not to claim from a non-significant result).
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with immediate feedback; learners correct their own misconceptions before building new work.
instructorActions: Provide an auto-marking quiz with explanations that explicitly contrast statistical vs practical significance.
Flag common errors in the feedback text (e.g., 'CI is not the probability the mean is in the interval').
studentActions: Complete the quiz independently.
Review explanations and note 1 concept to watch for during the lesson.

activities.title: Micro-lesson: Assumptions, sampling limits, and honest uncertainty statements

activities.teachingMethod: Chunked video (3–4 minutes each) with embedded pauses to write a one-sentence interpretation and a limitation statement.

Model integrity language (e.g., 'Our sample suggests…', 'We cannot rule out…').

Download the checklist and keep it open for later tasks.

activities.title: Tool demonstration: CI and test for a process change (Excel or Python path)

Steps include: data cleaning checks, choosing the correct test (paired vs two-sample), computing CI for mean difference, running hypothesis test, and creating a simple CI plot (error bars/forest-style).

activities.title: Guided practice: Analyse, interpret, and document assumptions/limits

They compute CI and run a simple hypothesis test, then fill in a structured reporting block: assumptions met/not met, sampling limits, practical threshold, and a plain-language conclusion. Includes an integrity check: identify at least one limitation that could change the conclusion.

activities.title: Create task: Build a stakeholder-friendly chart or mini-dashboard with narrative
activities.description: Learners design a one-page visual (Excel dashboard sheet or Python-rendered report) aimed at non-specialist stakeholders. Required elements: clear title with context, labeled axes with units, sample size, CI visualization, a short narrative (≤120 words) stating the conclusion, assumptions, sampling limits, and practical significance, plus one recommendation for next steps (e.g., collect more data, check measurement system).

activities.title: Collaborative review simulation: Critique, challenge, improve
activities.description: Learners perform a structured review using the checklist (self-review or peer-review in a discussion board if available). They must identify: one strength, two clarity issues (labels/units/audience fit), one statistical integrity concern (assumption/overclaiming), and then implement at least two improvements and log what changed.
activities.teachingMethod: Checklist-based critique to practise welcoming challenge and integrating feedback; models team review meeting norms asynchronously.

instructorActions: Provide example critique comments that are specific and respectful.
If a forum is used, set expectations: focus on reasoning, not the person; require evidence-based suggestions.
