Revise the dashboard and complete the revision log.

activities.title: Exit ticket: Integrity statement + next step
activities.description: A 2-minute submission: (1) one sentence stating the conclusion with uncertainty and practical significance, (2) one limitation, and (3) one next data/analysis step to reduce uncertainty.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-reflection to consolidate learning and reinforce transparent reporting habits.
instructorActions: Provide automated exemplars showing strong vs weak integrity statements.
Use exit ticket responses to identify patterns for the next lesson (e.g., assumption confusion).
studentActions: Submit the three-part exit ticket.
Save final dashboard/report as a portfolio artifact.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Keep the lesson anchored to quality-reporting decisions rather than procedures alone: every calculation should lead to a stakeholder-facing claim that is appropriately cautious. Emphasise a repeatable reasoning chain (goal → parameter → method → assumptions → result → interpretation → recommendation). Model professional integrity by explicitly distinguishing: statistical significance (p-value/CI excludes 0) vs practical significance (effect compared to a business threshold). Require units, sample size, and data provenance on visuals to prevent accidental misrepresentation. For online self-study, build in ‘pause-and-do’ points, self-check keys, and exemplars of good narrative language. Reinforce collaboration norms through the critique activity: learners practise explaining reasoning, inviting challenge, and making documented revisions. Use a consistent reporting template to reduce cognitive load so learners can spend effort on interpretation, limitations, and communication design (Bloom: create).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners are slower with tools, recommend completing the demo first in their chosen tool and using the provided template for the create task; they can customise styling later. If learners are ahead, offer an extension: add a second visual (e.g., distribution/boxplot before vs after) and a sensitivity check (remove one outlier and compare conclusions). Timebox the create task: 10 minutes to draft the visual layout, 10 minutes to refine labels/CI display, 5 minutes to craft and edit the ≤120-word narrative. Encourage learners to stop after each section and run the checklist rather than polishing at the end.
adaptationOptions: Tool choice: provide parallel Excel and Python pathways with equivalent outputs and a common reporting template so learners can use their stronger tool.
Scaffolding: offer a partially completed dashboard template (pre-built chart + placeholders) for learners who need support; advanced learners start from a blank canvas.
Accessibility: provide high-contrast chart palettes, alt-text guidance for visuals, and a text-only reporting option for low-bandwidth users.
Language support: supply interpretation sentence stems and a glossary pop-out for key terms (confidence interval, hypothesis test, assumption, sampling limit).
Challenge extension: add an optional comparison of equal-variance vs unequal-variance two-sample t-test (or bootstrap CI) and ask learners to justify the choice.
Anxiety reduction: allow learners to submit either a narrated screen recording (2 minutes) or a written narrative (≤120 words) explaining the same findings.
commonMisconceptions: Interpreting a 95% confidence interval as 'there is a 95% probability the true mean is in this specific interval' rather than a long-run method statement.
Treating a non-significant p-value as proof of 'no effect' instead of 'insufficient evidence given the data and assumptions'.
Equating statistical significance with practical importance and omitting business thresholds or effect sizes.
Choosing the wrong test (paired vs independent) because the learner focuses on equal sample sizes rather than how the data were collected.
Ignoring assumptions and sampling limits (e.g., independence violated by repeated measures; measurement system changes; convenience sampling).
Over-rounding intermediate values, leading to mismatched CI/test outputs or irreproducible results.
Misleading visuals: truncated axes without warning, missing units, unclear baselines, or using chart types that hide uncertainty.
Reporting only p-values without confidence intervals and without a plain-language conclusion tied to the operational question.
discussionPrompts: You have p = 0.03 but the estimated improvement is smaller than the business threshold. What should you recommend, and how would you phrase it to avoid overclaiming?
Your 95% CI for the mean change includes 0, but most observations improved. What could explain this, and what additional data or analysis would help?
Which assumption is most fragile in operational data (independence, normality, equal variances), and how can you check it pragmatically in Excel/Python?
What is one sampling limit in your workplace (or a realistic scenario) that could bias a process-change conclusion? How would you disclose it in a report?
Compare two visuals: a bar chart of means vs a plot showing means with confidence intervals. Which better supports transparent decision-making and why?
In a team review meeting, how would you respond if someone challenges your chart as 'confusing' or your conclusion as 'too cautious'?

lessons.lessonTitle: Stakeholder-friendly charts or dashboards that explain st...
objectives: Clean a provided quality dataset in Excel or Python by handling missing values, validating units, and generating an outlier flag column using a stated rule (e.g., IQR or z-score), with zero unresolved data-type errors.
Compute and report measures of centre and spread (mean, median, standard deviation, IQR) for at least two key quality variables, ensuring correct units and clearly stated assumptions.

Create a stakeholder-friendly chart set (minimum: one distribution chart and one trend/over-time chart) with accurate titles, axis labels, units, and annotations that highlight at least one trend and one constraint/turning point.

Build a one-page dashboard (Excel sheet or Python export) that combines summary metrics, outlier counts, and visuals, and add a concise narrative (80–150 words) that communicates findings and recommended next steps to non-specialists.

activities.title: Orientation + success criteria (dashboard brief)
activities.description: Learners review the lesson brief and the stakeholder scenario: a quality manager needs a weekly summary of defect rate and process measurements. Learners inspect the success criteria checklist (labels, units, assumptions, outliers, chart clarity, narrative). They choose tool path: Excel or Python.
activities.teachingMethod: Brief guided reading with a checklist and tool-choice branching (Excel vs Python).
instructorActions: Present a clear definition of 'stakeholder-friendly' (non-technical language, minimal chart clutter, explicit units, direct recommendations).
Provide the rubric/checklist upfront to anchor quality expectations.
studentActions: Download dataset and checklist.
Select Excel or Python track and open the provided starter template (Excel workbook or Jupyter notebook).

activities.title: Demonstration: from raw data to summary + outlier flags
activities.description: Walkthrough (video or annotated notebook) showing a clean workflow: data type checks, missing values, unit sanity checks, outlier rule selection (IQR or z-score), and producing a tidy summary table. Emphasis on diligence: verifying assumptions and calculation accuracy.
activities.teachingMethod: Model a worked example with pause points prompting learners to predict the next step and to check units/assumptions.
resources: Screen-capture demo (Excel) OR annotated Python notebook demo
Outlier flag reference card (IQR and z-score formulas)
instructorActions: Explicitly state why a chosen outlier rule fits the scenario (routine quality reporting vs investigation).
Model 'double-checking' habits: spot-check 3 rows, verify units, confirm no silent type coercion.
studentActions: Watch/step through the demo and answer embedded checkpoints (e.g., 'Which unit looks inconsistent?' 'Which column has mixed types?').
Record the chosen outlier rule and rationale in notes.

activities.title: Guided practice: clean, summarise, and flag outliers
activities.description: Learners apply the workflow to the provided dataset. Output requirements: (1) cleaned table, (2) summary metrics table (centre/spread), (3) outlier flag column and outlier count by week/line (as applicable).
activities.teachingMethod: Step-by-step task list with optional hints; immediate self-check against expected intermediate outputs (not final answers).
resources: Excel functions sheet (AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, QUARTILE, IF) OR Python snippets (pandas describe, quantile, numpy)
Expected intermediate checks (e.g., row counts before/after cleaning, number of missing values)
instructorActions: Provide 'hint tiers' (light hint → stronger hint → worked snippet) to support self-study without giving away the full solution.
Include a self-check table: expected cleaned row count range and expected outlier-count range (to catch major mistakes).
studentActions: Perform cleaning steps and document assumptions (e.g., how missing values were handled).
Generate summary metrics and outlier flag; verify at least two spot-checks manually (random rows).

activities.title: Design lab: build stakeholder-friendly visuals (trend + distribution)
activities.description: Learners create at least two visuals: (1) a time trend chart (e.g., weekly mean/median with target line and optional CI band), (2) a distribution chart (histogram/box plot) to show spread and outliers. Learners must add clear titles, units, and a short annotation highlighting a turning point/constraint.
activities.teachingMethod: Design constraints + exemplars: learners compare 2 good and 2 poor charts, then build their own under specific requirements.
resources: Visualization requirements card (titles, units, baseline/targets, accessible colours)
Optional: CI quick guide (what a CI communicates, when to include)
instructorActions: Prompt learners to choose chart types based on message (trend vs spread) rather than habit.
Warn against misleading choices (truncated axes, overplotting, excessive decimals) and require units on axes.
studentActions: Create and format the two charts, including target lines/thresholds where relevant.
Add one annotation that explains a trend/turning point and one that flags an outlier implication (investigate vs ignore).

activities.title: Create task: assemble a one-page dashboard + narrative for non-specialists
activities.description: Learners assemble a single view (Excel dashboard sheet or Python-exported HTML/PDF image) containing: KPI tiles (e.g., mean/median, defect rate, outlier count), the two charts, and a compact summary table. They write an 80–150 word narrative: what happened, why it matters, and recommended next actions. Includes a 'team review' simulation: learners respond to two scripted stakeholder questions.
activities.teachingMethod: Authentic performance task with a rubric; reflection prompts simulate collaborative review (explain reasoning, welcome challenge, integrate feedback).
resources: Dashboard layout template (Excel) OR notebook section scaffold (Python)
Narrative template (What? So what? Now what?)
Two scripted stakeholder questions (e.g., 'Are outliers driving this?' 'Can we trust this week’s change?')
Rubric aligned to MLOs (clarity, accuracy, diligence, stakeholder fit)
instructorActions: Require learners to state assumptions and units within the dashboard (small footnote section).
Provide a short 'stakeholder language' glossary (avoid jargon; define CI/outlier in plain language).
studentActions: Assemble the dashboard and export/save it.
Write the narrative and answer the two stakeholder questions in 2–4 sentences each, referencing the visuals.

activities.title: Formative check + self-review (quality assurance pass)
activities.description: Learners complete a short formative quiz/check (auto-graded where possible) and a dashboard QA checklist: units, labels, axis scales, assumptions, outlier rule stated, calculations verified, narrative clarity. Learners then revise one element based on checklist results.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes verification: quick quiz + structured self-critique leading to one concrete improvement.
resources: Formative quiz (8–10 items) on outliers, centre/spread, CI interpretation, and chart integrity
instructorActions: Design quiz feedback to explain why wrong options are wrong (especially CI and outlier misconceptions).
Prompt a single focused revision to promote iteration (Bloom: create → improve).
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback.
Apply at least one improvement to the dashboard (e.g., add units, adjust axis, clarify narrative).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson as an authentic ‘produce a quality report’ task rather than a calculation drill to match Bloom’s Create level. Keep the learner’s attention on communication quality and statistical integrity: (1) require explicit assumptions (time window, missing-value treatment, outlier rule), (2) enforce units everywhere (axis labels, KPI tiles, table headers), and (3) build in verification habits (spot-checks, row counts, intermediate checkpoints). For online self-study, provide branching supports: Excel and Python templates that mirror the same steps; layered hints; and intermediate expected ranges (counts, missing values) to catch major workflow errors without revealing full solutions. Embed a simulated ‘team review’ by giving two stakeholder challenge questions and requiring short evidence-based responses—this targets collaborative behaviours even in self-study (explain reasoning, welcome challenge, integrate feedback via revision). Emphasize chart ethics: avoid misleading axes, overprecision, and decorative clutter; highlight practical interpretation (what action should a manager take?).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners are ahead: shorten the demo to 6–8 minutes (skim) and spend more time iterating the dashboard (add a CI band, segmentation by line/shift, or a filter/slicer). If learners are behind: complete only one variable end-to-end (clean → summarise → outliers → 2 charts → dashboard) before expanding to additional variables. Encourage timeboxing: 10 minutes max on cleaning decisions before using the hint tier; 15 minutes on visuals before checking exemplars; 10 minutes on narrative drafting before refining. A practical rule: do not move to dashboard assembly until the summary table and outlier counts match the intermediate self-check ranges.
adaptationOptions: Tool choice adaptation: Provide parallel instructions for Excel (tables, PivotTables, slicers) and Python (pandas, seaborn/matplotlib) with identical required outputs.

Scaffolded vs extension track: Scaffold includes a pre-cleaned dataset and focuses on visualization + narrative; extension requires learners to justify an outlier rule choice and include a CI or uncertainty statement.
Accessibility: Offer high-contrast chart theme, colorblind-safe palette, and require patterns/labels in addition to colour for outlier points; provide alt-text guidance for exported dashboard images.
Math support: Provide a ‘concept card’ explaining mean/median/SD/IQR in plain language plus one worked example; allow calculator checks for a small sample to validate code/Excel formulas.
Challenge/advanced: Ask learners to compare mean vs median sensitivity to outliers and to present both on the dashboard with a recommendation for routine reporting.

Language support: Provide sentence stems for narrative (“The process shifted after…”, “This matters because…”, “Next, we recommend…”) and a glossary translating jargon (CI, outlier) into non-technical terms.
commonMisconceptions: Treating outliers as errors to delete by default rather than flags for investigation; confusing ‘outlier’ with ‘impossible value’.
Believing the mean is always the best ‘typical’ value even when the distribution is skewed or contains outliers (median may be more representative).
Misinterpreting a confidence interval as ‘most data fall in this range’ rather than uncertainty about an estimated parameter (e.g., mean).
Using misleading chart scales (e.g., truncated y-axis) that exaggerate small changes or hiding variability by over-smoothing.
Forgetting units on axes/KPIs or mixing units (e.g., mm vs cm) leading to incorrect comparisons and summaries.
Assuming correlation or time co-movement implies causation; making recommendations not supported by the displayed evidence.
Overprecision: reporting too many decimals, implying false accuracy in a stakeholder-facing report.
discussionPrompts: If you could include only two visuals for a non-specialist manager, which would you choose and why (trend vs spread vs outliers)?
When would you report the mean, the median, or both? What would you say to justify your choice to a stakeholder?
Your dashboard shows a spike and several outliers in the same week. What are three plausible explanations, and what data would you request next?
How can chart design mislead even when calculations are correct? Identify one design risk and how you mitigated it.
What is an appropriate plain-language explanation of an outlier flag and a confidence interval for a weekly quality report?
A stakeholder challenges your conclusion: ‘Is this change real or just noise?’ What evidence from your summaries/visuals supports your response?

moduleLessonPlans.moduleTitle: Probability, Distributions and Simulation for Risk

lessons.lessonTitle: Calculate probabilities using binomial, normal and expone...
objectives: Select and justify an appropriate probability model (binomial, normal, or exponential) for a workplace scenario (defects, demand, or downtime) by identifying the random variable, key assumptions, and required parameters.

Compute and interpret at least two probabilities (e.g., tail probability, interval probability) using binomial, normal, and exponential models, with correct units and parameter definitions, and state any approximations used.

Analyse a Monte Carlo simulation output (histogram, percentile table, summary statistics) to estimate schedule/financial risk metrics (e.g., P50, P90, probability of overrun) and explain what each metric means in context.
Record simulation assumptions, uncertainty sources, and limitations in a structured workplace-style risk register entry, including a confidence/uncertainty statement and traceable calculation notes.

activities.title: Lesson launch: risk framing, integrity, and expectations
activities.description: Students review a short scenario: a project manager asks for the probability of missing a delivery date due to machine downtime and variable task duration. Students identify what information is missing and what would need to be assumed. Emphasis: professional integrity—explicitly reporting assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations.
activities.teachingMethod: Prompted reflection (self-check) + optional forum post to surface assumptions and unknowns before calculations.
instructorActions: Provide the scenario and a checklist of what 'transparent quantitative work' looks like (units, parameters, assumptions, limitations, versioning).
Provide an example of an acceptable short response naming unknowns and assumptions without overclaiming.
studentActions: List 3–5 pieces of missing information and 2–3 assumptions they might need to proceed.
Optional: post one assumption and one limitation to the course discussion board.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: choosing distributions for workplace events
activities.description: Conceptual overview linking common workplace questions to distributions: binomial for counts of defects in n trials, normal for aggregated variation/measurement (with caveats), exponential for time-to-failure/downtime with constant hazard. Students complete quick checkpoints on identifying random variables and parameters (n, p, μ, σ, λ).
activities.teachingMethod: Interactive micro-lecture with embedded retrieval questions focused on model selection and assumptions (analysis-level: why this model vs another).
resources: Short video or narrated slides (10–12 min)
instructorActions: Explicitly contrast 'model convenience' vs 'model fit' and require stating assumptions (independence, identical trials, constant rate, approximate normality).
Include at least one counterexample for each model (e.g., exponential not appropriate if hazard changes over time).
studentActions: Complete embedded checks: identify the correct model and parameters for 4 short scenarios.
Write one sentence per scenario justifying the choice and naming a key assumption.

activities.title: Guided practice: computing probabilities with units and assumptions
activities.description: Students work through three short workplace problems (one per model) with worked-solution scaffolds: (1) Binomial: probability of ≥k defects in n items given defect rate p. (2) Normal: probability demand exceeds capacity given μ and σ (or measurement error interval). (3) Exponential: probability downtime exceeds t given mean time between failures or rate λ. Each problem includes a 'check units/parameters' step and an 'assumptions and limitations' step.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example fading: first problem mostly worked, second partially worked, third mostly student-completed; immediate feedback after each step.
resources: Guided worksheet (fillable PDF or LMS page)
Answer key with reasoning and common pitfalls
instructorActions: Provide dual method options (formula + spreadsheet function) and show parameter mapping (e.g., λ in 1/hour; mean = 1/λ).
Embed 'sanity checks' (bounds 0–1, monotonicity, expected direction, unit consistency).
studentActions: Compute each probability and interpret it in a workplace sentence (what it means and what it does not mean).
Complete the assumptions box for each model (independence, constant rate, approximate normality, etc.).
Perform a quick self-check: does the probability change in the expected direction if parameters change?

activities.title: Demonstration: Monte Carlo simulation for schedule/financial risk
activities.description: Students follow a step-by-step demo of a simple Monte Carlo model (e.g., 3-task schedule with uncertain durations, or cost with uncertain inputs). They observe how changing an assumption (distribution choice or parameter) shifts outputs. Focus: reading outputs (histogram, cumulative curve, percentiles, CI) and connecting them to risk questions (probability of overrun, P80 date/cost).
activities.teachingMethod: Guided walkthrough (video/screencast) + pause-and-predict prompts to promote analysis of input-output relationships.
resources: Simulation template (Excel/Sheets) or hosted notebook with fixed seed option
Output interpretation guide (P50/P80/P90, exceedance probability, simple CI explanation)
instructorActions: Use consistent terminology: percentile vs probability; clarify what a CI applies to (e.g., mean estimate vs outcome distribution).
Show at least one sensitivity change (e.g., increasing σ or changing λ) and ask learners to predict the effect before revealing results.
studentActions: Run (or replay) the simulation and capture key outputs: mean/median, P90, and probability of exceeding a threshold.
Answer 3 pause-and-predict questions about how outputs should change if an input changes.

activities.title: Case analysis: converting outputs into a risk register entry
activities.description: Students create one risk register entry based on the Monte Carlo results. They must: define the risk statement, quantify likelihood/impact (using simulation outputs), document assumptions and uncertainty, and note limitations/next data to collect. Emphasis: transparency and auditability (what model version, which distributions, units, sample size/iterations).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured template completion with exemplars; analysis focus on translating quantitative evidence into decision-ready documentation.
resources: Risk register template (fields: risk, metric, probability, impact, assumptions, uncertainty/CI, limitations, controls, owner, date/version)
instructorActions: Provide an annotated example that models honest reporting (e.g., 'based on assumed triangular durations; limited historical data; results sensitive to σ').
Prompt learners to separate 'model output' from 'decision' (avoid false certainty).
studentActions: Populate the risk register template using their simulation outputs (include P90 and probability of overrun).
Write a 2–3 sentence uncertainty statement (what is uncertain, why, and how it affects confidence).

activities.title: Formative assessment 1: auto-graded quiz + targeted feedback
activities.description: An auto-graded quiz checks model selection, parameter interpretation, and output analysis. Includes one item requiring identification of an incorrect assumption/units mismatch, and one item interpreting a percentile from a Monte Carlo output table.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes retrieval and application with immediate explanations; questions designed to diagnose misconceptions.
resources: Feedback bank mapped to misconceptions (units, λ vs mean, normal approximation conditions, percentile interpretation)
instructorActions: Configure feedback to explain why distractors are wrong (not just why the key is right).
Set mastery option (e.g., 2 attempts) and recommend review links based on missed items.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback for any incorrect responses.
Note one personal 'watch-out' item to apply in future calculations (e.g., always state units for λ).

activities.title: Wrap-up reflection: integrity and diligence checklist
activities.description: Students complete a short checklist and reflection: what assumptions did you make, what limitations remain, and how would you communicate uncertainty to a manager? Reinforces professional integrity and attention to detail.
activities.teachingMethod: Metacognitive reflection to consolidate habits (units, assumptions, verification, documentation).
resources: One-page checklist (units, parameters, assumptions, validation/sanity checks, documentation)
Optional forum prompt for sharing one best practice
instructorActions: Provide a model reflection response that is concise and workplace-appropriate.
Encourage learners to keep a personal 'assumption log' for the module.
studentActions: Complete the checklist and write 3 bullets: (1) a key assumption, (2) a limitation, (3) a verification step they used.
Optional: post one verification step to the discussion board.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the lesson to repeatedly cycle through: (1) identify the workplace question, (2) choose a model with explicit assumptions, (3) compute/interpret, (4) document limitations and uncertainty. Because Bloom level is analyse, prioritise 'why this model and what does the output mean' over mechanical calculation. Embed frequent micro-checks that force parameter identification (n/p, μ/σ, λ/mean) and unit statements (e.g., λ = 0.2 per hour). In the Monte Carlo portion, emphasise interpretation literacy: percentiles (P90 means 90% of simulated outcomes are below this value), exceedance probability, and the difference between uncertainty in an estimate (CI for mean) vs spread of outcomes (distribution). Model professional integrity: show an example where the model is sensitive to an assumption and demonstrate how to report that sensitivity rather than hiding it. Encourage diligence: sanity checks (probabilities in [0,1], directionality, boundary cases), and traceability (record inputs, version/date, and iteration count).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Maintain a brisk pace in the first 20 minutes to establish the model-selection framework, then slow down for the 20-minute guided practice (most error-prone). If learners struggle, advise pausing after each distribution problem to verify: random variable definition, parameter units, and whether the assumption set is plausible. In the Monte Carlo demo, keep the model simple (few inputs) to avoid cognitive overload; spend more time interpreting outputs than building the simulation mechanics. If time runs tight, shorten the demo (15→10) but keep the risk register activity intact, as it directly aligns to the PLO and integrity competency.
adaptationOptions: Maths support path: provide an optional 'distribution basics' refresher (mean/variance, z-scores, exponential memoryless property) and a formula sheet with parameter definitions.
Low-bandwidth option: offer static screenshots of simulation outputs plus a pre-generated output table so learners can still complete the analysis and risk register tasks without running the file.
Accessibility: ensure videos have captions and transcripts; provide spreadsheet templates that are screen-reader friendly and avoid colour-only encoding in charts.
Extension for advanced learners: add a sensitivity analysis task (tornado chart or input correlation) and require a short recommendation about which assumption to validate first.
Language support: include sentence starters for risk register fields (e.g., 'Assuming ___, the probability of ___ is estimated as ___. Limitation: ___').
Anxiety-reducing assessment: allow two quiz attempts with item-level feedback and a short remediation link after each objective domain.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing distribution choice: using normal for counts with small n or skewed outcomes without checking conditions; using binomial when trials are not independent or p is not constant.
Parameter mix-ups: treating λ as a mean time (it is a rate), or using mean time between failures directly as λ instead of λ = 1/mean (with correct time units).
Misinterpreting percentiles: believing P90 means a 90% chance the outcome equals that value, rather than 90% of outcomes fall below it.
Equating simulation variability with model uncertainty: assuming more iterations reduces real-world uncertainty (it only reduces Monte Carlo sampling error).
Forgetting units and context: mixing hours and days, or reporting a probability without specifying the time window (especially for exponential).
Assuming a confidence interval describes where most outcomes lie (confusing CI of an estimate with prediction/outcome distribution spread).
Overstating precision: reporting too many decimal places and failing to state assumptions/limitations in a workplace communication.
discussionPrompts: In a workplace risk register, what is the minimum set of assumptions you would document for a binomial vs exponential model? Why do they differ?
A manager asks for a single 'most likely' completion date. How would you use Monte Carlo outputs to respond without hiding uncertainty?
Share one example of a unit/parameter mistake that could materially change a risk estimate (e.g., λ per day vs per hour). How would you prevent it?
When (if ever) is it acceptable to use a normal approximation? What checks would you apply before doing so?
What limitation in your simulation would you prioritise validating with real data first, and what data would you collect?

lessons.lessonTitle: Calculate probabilities using binomial, normal and expone...
objectives: Select an appropriate probability model (binomial, normal, or exponential) for a given workplace risk scenario and justify the choice by stating the underlying assumptions and data requirements.

Calculate and interpret at least three workplace-relevant probabilities (e.g., defect rate, demand exceedance, downtime occurrence) using binomial, normal, and exponential models, including correct units and parameter meanings.

Analyse Monte Carlo simulation outputs by extracting key risk metrics (P50/P80/P90, mean, standard deviation, and a 95% CI where applicable) and explaining what each metric implies for schedule/financial risk decisions.
Create a workplace-style risk register entry that records assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and recommended actions based on probability-model calculations and simulation outputs.

activities.title: Warm-up: Model recognition + integrity check
activities.description: Learners complete a short diagnostic that presents 6 micro-scenarios (defects per batch, call arrivals, time-to-failure, demand variability, etc.). For each, they: (1) choose binomial/normal/exponential/other, (2) identify required parameters and units, and (3) list one key assumption and one limitation. Immediate feedback explains why each model fits (or doesn’t) and highlights common assumption pitfalls.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with immediate, explanatory feedback to activate prior knowledge (prereqs MOD4/MOD5) and foreground professional integrity (assumptions/limitations).
resources: One-page 'Model selection cues' handout (binomial vs normal vs exponential)
instructorActions: Provide scenarios that resemble workplace contexts (quality, operations, demand).
Configure feedback to explicitly address assumptions, units, and when a model is inappropriate.
studentActions: Complete the diagnostic and review feedback.
Note two personal 'watch-outs' (e.g., unit errors, assumption gaps) for use later in the lesson.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: From workplace question → distribution → probability statement
activities.description: Short, segmented content (3–5 minutes each) that shows how to translate a workplace risk question into a probability statement: defining the random variable, choosing a distribution, setting parameters with correct units, and writing the event of interest. Includes quick checks on: binomial conditions (fixed n, independent trials, constant p), normal modeling (mean/SD; standardization), and exponential modeling (rate λ; memoryless property).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lectures with embedded 'stop-and-think' questions; emphasis on diligent checking (units, assumptions, parameter interpretation).
instructorActions: Use consistent notation (e.g., X~Bin(n,p), X~N(μ,σ²), T~Exp(λ)).
Model an 'assumption log' after each example (what must be true for this to be valid).
studentActions: Watch segments and answer embedded checks.
Write one probability statement per model (e.g., P(X≥k), P(X>threshold), P(T≤t)).

activities.title: Guided practice: Workplace probability calculations (binomial, normal, exponential)
activities.description:
Learners work through three structured problems with progressively less scaffolding:
1) Binomial defects: compute P(X≥k) and interpret as a quality risk.
2) Normal demand: compute exceedance probability and relate to stockout/capacity risk.
3) Exponential downtime: compute P(T≤t) and interpret as likelihood of failure within a window.
Each problem includes an explicit checklist: define variable, list assumptions, check units, compute, interpret in context, state limitation/uncertainty.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example → completion → independent attempt; automated hints focus on common errors (e.g., unit mismatch, wrong tail, incorrect parameterization).
resources: Optional spreadsheet template with built-in functions (BINOM.DIST, NORM.DIST, EXPON.DIST)
instructorActions: Provide answer ranges and reasoning steps, not just final numbers.
Include a 'units + parameters' table for each model (p is unitless; μ, σ share units with X; λ is 1/time).
studentActions: Complete calculations and compare to automated checks.
Write a 2–3 sentence interpretation for each result (what it means for defect/demand/downtime likelihood).

activities.title: Demonstration: Reading Monte Carlo outputs + confidence intervals
activities.description: Learners explore a prepared Monte Carlo output (schedule or cost) presented as: histogram/density, cumulative distribution, summary table (mean, SD, P50/P80/P90), and a sampling error/CI panel (e.g., CI for the mean or for a percentile when available). They answer prompts to diagnose what the distribution shape implies (skew, tail risk), identify which metric best supports a risk decision, and explain the meaning and limitation of a 95% CI in simulation context (iteration count, convergence).
activities.teachingMethod: Interactive data walkthrough using a 'notice–interpret–justify' protocol: learners first identify features, then interpret, then justify a decision metric.
resources: Interactive dashboard (embedded) OR downloadable spreadsheet with simulated outputs
Short reading: 'Percentiles vs mean for risk decisions' (1 page)
Glossary: Monte Carlo simulation, CI, percentile, tail risk
instructorActions: Provide a version with fixed random seed for consistency.
Explicitly connect output interpretation to transparency: what can/can’t be concluded from the simulation.
studentActions: Extract P80/P90 and compare to a threshold (budget or deadline).
Answer 5 guided questions about skew, tail risk, and CI meaning.

activities.title: Case analysis: Quantify risk and write a risk register entry
activities.description: Scenario-based task (workplace style): Learners receive a short project brief with uncertain task durations/cost drivers plus one discrete risk driver (e.g., rework defects). They must (a) use a distribution model for the discrete driver (binomial) or downtime (exponential) to estimate a probability, (b) interpret the provided Monte Carlo summary (P50/P80/P90 and CI info) to quantify schedule/financial risk, and (c) complete a risk register entry capturing assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and mitigation/monitoring actions.
activities.teachingMethod: Authentic assessment-style task emphasizing analysis and professional documentation; learners synthesize model outputs into a decision-ready register entry.
resources: Case packet (1–2 pages) with data and simulation summary
Risk register template (table with required fields)
instructorActions: Provide a rubric-aligned checklist: assumptions stated, units correct, metric justified, limitation noted, action proposed.
Include an exemplar that shows concise, transparent language (e.g., 'Based on 10,000 iterations…').
studentActions: Complete the risk register entry (fields: risk statement, likelihood, impact, metrics used, assumptions, uncertainty/CI, limitations, response).
Self-check against the rubric checklist before submitting/saving.

activities.title: Formative assessment: Analysis-focused quiz + reflection
activities.description: Auto-marked quiz (10–12 items) mixing calculation and interpretation: choosing a model, identifying assumption violations, interpreting P90 and CI statements, and spotting unit/parameter errors. Ends with a brief reflection prompt: 'What assumption, if wrong, would most change your conclusion?' Learners receive targeted feedback and recommended remediation links.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes formative assessment with diagnostic feedback and adaptive release of remediation resources.
resources: LMS quiz bank (Formative Assessment 1 for MOD106 Lesson 2)
Remediation links to specific mini-lecture segments and practice items
instructorActions: Configure feedback by misconception category (tail selection, parameter units, CI interpretation, model fit).
Set mastery thresholds and allow retakes to support self-study pacing.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback.
Write a 1–2 sentence reflection identifying the most sensitive assumption/limitation in their case analysis.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design for analysis (not just computation): repeatedly ask learners to (1) identify the random variable and units, (2) justify distribution choice with conditions/assumptions, (3) interpret probabilities/percentiles as workplace risk statements, and (4) document uncertainty and limitations transparently.

Use a consistent routine across tasks:
- Define: What is X or T? What are units?
- Choose: Why binomial/normal/exponential? Which assumptions must hold?
- Compute: Show parameter meanings (n, p, μ, σ, λ) and check reasonableness.
- Interpret: Translate to a decision-relevant sentence (e.g., “There is a 12% chance of exceeding budget”).
- Document: Record assumptions, CI/uncertainty, and limitations in risk-register language.

Emphasize professional integrity: discourage false precision, require explicit iteration count/source for Monte Carlo outputs, and require learners to note when inputs are estimates or when independence/constant-rate assumptions are questionable. Promote diligence by embedding unit checks (λ as 1/time; σ in same units as X), tail-direction checks (≥ vs ≤), and sanity checks (probabilities in [0,1], extreme percentile behavior).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Target completion times (self-study): Warm-up 10 min (cap at 12), mini-lecture 15 min (cap at 18), guided practice 20 min (cap at 25), simulation demo 15 min (cap at 18), case analysis 20 min (cap at 25), quiz 10 min (cap at 12). If learners exceed the cap, suggest moving on and returning after the quiz feedback identifies weak areas. Encourage a two-pass approach: first pass for completion, second pass (optional) to deepen interpretation and improve risk-register wording.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolding support: Provide a partially completed risk register entry (pre-filled risk statement and units) for learners who struggle with documentation.
Alternative tools: Offer both spreadsheet-based and calculator-only paths for probability computations; include step-by-step screenshots for spreadsheet functions.
Language support: Provide a glossary with plain-language definitions and sentence starters for interpretations (e.g., 'This means that…', 'Assuming…, the likelihood is…').

Extension (advanced): Add an optional sensitivity check—compare how P90 changes when σ increases by 10% or when λ changes due to improved maintenance; ask learners to update the limitations section accordingly.
Accessibility: Provide transcripts for videos, downloadable static versions of dashboards, and keyboard-navigable quizzes.
Remediation path: If quiz score <70%, direct learners to a focused mini-set on (a) tail selection and (b) parameter/unit interpretation, then allow a retake.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up model conditions: using binomial when trials are not independent or when p changes across items/time.
Confusing normal distribution parameters (σ vs σ²) or standardizing incorrectly (wrong z formula or sign).
Treating exponential λ as a time rather than a rate (1/time), leading to unit-inconsistent results.
Misreading tails: calculating P(X≤k) when the question asks for exceedance P(X≥k), or forgetting continuity correction when using normal approximations (if introduced).
Interpreting a 95% CI as '95% of outcomes fall in this range' rather than uncertainty about an estimated statistic (e.g., mean/percentile) given finite simulation runs.
Assuming Monte Carlo output is exact: ignoring sampling error, iteration count, convergence, or input uncertainty.
Overstating conclusions: failing to record limitations (data quality, assumption validity, model fit) in the risk register.
discussionPrompts: A colleague reports: 'There is a 95% chance the project finishes between day 48 and 55' based on a 95% CI for the mean. What’s wrong with this statement, and how would you rewrite it transparently?
In your workplace (or a familiar context), where might the binomial independence assumption fail? What would be the practical effect on risk estimates?
When is P90 more decision-relevant than the mean for schedule or cost risk? Give an example and explain the trade-off.
What is one unit/parameter check you now always perform before trusting a probability result (binomial/normal/exponential)?
If a Monte Carlo histogram is strongly right-skewed, what does that imply about using mean vs percentiles for risk communication?
What limitation should always be included when reporting probabilities from estimated inputs (e.g., p, μ, σ, λ) rather than known parameters?

lessons.lessonTitle: Calculate probabilities using binomial, normal and expone...
objectives: Given a workplace scenario (defects, demand, or downtime), select an appropriate probability model (binomial, normal, or exponential) and justify the choice by checking required assumptions (e.g., independence, constant rate, appropriate measurement scale).

Compute and interpret at least three probabilities relevant to risk questions (e.g., P(X≥k) defects, P(demand exceeds capacity), P(downtime exceeds t)) using binomial, normal (including standardisation), and exponential models with correct units and clear notation.

Analyse a Monte Carlo output summary (mean, SD, percentiles, probability of exceeding a threshold, and a 95% confidence interval for an estimate) to quantify schedule/financial risk and explain what the CI does and does not mean.

Create a concise workplace-style risk register entry that documents inputs, assumptions, uncertainty (including CI/percentiles), limitations, and a recommended action/next step, demonstrating professional integrity and transparency.

Perform a reasonableness check on results (order-of-magnitude, bounds 0–1 for probabilities, unit consistency) and identify at least one potential source of error or misinterpretation in the modelling or simulation.

activities.title: Orientation + prior knowledge checkpoint (distribution choice)
activities.description: Learners review the lesson map (what will be analysed today) and complete a short interactive diagnostic: three micro-scenarios where they choose binomial/normal/exponential and select which assumption must be checked. Immediate feedback explains why each model fits/doesn’t fit.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with immediate feedback and short corrective explanations; learners are prompted to articulate assumptions explicitly before seeing the answer.
resources: One-page ‘Model selection’ reference sheet (binomial vs normal vs exponential)
instructorActions: Provide feedback keyed to assumptions (independence, fixed n, constant rate, continuous vs discrete).
Flag common unit/notation issues in feedback (e.g., rate per hour vs per minute).
studentActions: Complete the diagnostic quiz and note two personal ‘watch-outs’ (e.g., forgetting units, misreading ‘at least’).
Download/save the model selection reference sheet for later use.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: analysing workplace questions with binomial/normal/exponential
activities.description: Short, segmented content (read/watch) focused on analysing problem structure: what is random, what is being counted/measured, and what assumptions must hold. Includes worked examples emphasising interpretation (not just computation) and unit checks.
activities.teachingMethod: Segmented direct instruction with ‘stop-and-think’ prompts after each model; worked examples highlight assumption checks and interpretation of results in workplace language.
resources: Worked example notes (PDF) with step-by-step solutions
Formula sheet (binomial CDF, z-standardisation, exponential survival function)
instructorActions: Explicitly model a ‘professional integrity’ script: state assumptions, show units, and note limitations (e.g., normal may allow negative values).
Include at least one ‘sanity check’ per example (bounds, scale, quick approximation).
studentActions: Annotate each example with: (1) why this distribution, (2) key assumption, (3) what the probability means in context.
Pause at prompts to predict the direction/size of an answer before seeing it.

activities.title: Guided practice: multi-part probability analysis (3 scenarios)
activities.description: Learners solve three workplace-styled tasks (one per distribution). Each task requires: identify variables/units, choose model, compute probability, and write a 2–3 sentence interpretation with a reasonableness check. Automated checking provides numeric tolerance and rubric-based feedback for interpretation.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example fading: first task provides a scaffold template; second provides partial hints; third is mostly independent. Feedback targets both calculations and interpretation quality.
resources: Interactive problem set (LMS) with embedded calculator/spreadsheet support
Optional spreadsheet template with built-in functions (BINOM.DIST, NORM.DIST, EXPON.DIST or equivalents)
instructorActions: Provide scaffold prompts: ‘Define X’, ‘State assumptions’, ‘Check units’, ‘Interpret for a manager’.
Include common-error feedback (e.g., using PDF instead of CDF; confusing ‘within’ vs ‘beyond’).
studentActions: Complete all three scenarios and submit final interpretations.
Run a self-check: confirm probabilities are between 0 and 1 and units match (e.g., hours with hours).

activities.title: Mini-lecture + micro-demo: Monte Carlo outputs, percentiles, and confidence intervals
activities.description: Learners explore how simulation outputs are summarised for risk: mean, SD, P(exceed threshold), P90/P95, and a 95% confidence interval for an estimated probability or mean. Emphasis is on analysing what the output implies for decisions and how uncertainty should be reported transparently.
activities.teachingMethod: Annotated walkthrough of a prepared simulation summary table/plot; short ‘interpret this output’ pauses to keep the focus at Bloom level ‘analyse’.
resources: Pre-generated Monte Carlo output summary (table + histogram/CDF plot)
Short note: ‘CI for an estimate vs percentile interval for outcomes’
instructorActions: Highlight the distinction between: (a) uncertainty in outcomes (percentiles), and (b) uncertainty in estimates (CI due to finite simulations/data).
Model transparent reporting language (e.g., ‘Estimated probability… with 95% CI…; assumes…; limitations…’).
studentActions: Answer two embedded ‘pause questions’ interpreting P90 vs 95% CI.
Identify one missing assumption that would be needed before trusting the simulation.

activities.title: Case analysis: interpret simulation output and write a risk register entry
activities.description: Learners receive a brief case (e.g., project task duration or cost risk) with a Monte Carlo output summary. They must: (1) quantify risk using at least two metrics (e.g., P(delay > 5 days) and P90 completion time), (2) interpret a CI provided for an estimate, and (3) produce a risk register entry documenting assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and an action/owner suggestion.
activities.teachingMethod: Authentic performance task using a structured template; rubric focuses on analytical interpretation, transparency, and diligence (units/assumptions/checks).
resources: Monte Carlo output pack (summary stats + plot + short ‘inputs used’ list)
instructorActions: Provide a rubric and an exemplar ‘strong’ risk register entry (with redacted numbers) to show expected level of transparency.
Include checklist prompts: units, assumptions, limitations, verification/sanity checks.
studentActions: Complete the risk register entry (one row) and submit.
Self-assess against the checklist before final submission.

activities.title: Formative assessment: analytic vs simulation interpretation quiz
activities.description: Two-part quiz aligned to the lesson objectives: Part A tests correct setup and calculation for binomial/normal/exponential questions; Part B tests interpretation of a Monte Carlo output (percentiles, exceedance probability, and CI) and identification of missing/weak assumptions. Instant feedback explains both the correct choice and why distractors are tempting.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes mastery check with targeted feedback and optional retry; emphasis on analysis and interpretation rather than lengthy computation.
resources: LMS quiz bank (Formative Assessment #1 or #2 for the module, adapted to this lesson)
Feedback glossary for key terms (Monte Carlo simulation, risk register, assumption, CI)
instructorActions: Configure feedback to address integrity/diligence: highlight where assumptions/units were missing even if numbers were correct.
Offer branching remediation links based on item performance (e.g., ‘Review exponential survival’).
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback notes.
Choose one remediation link if score is below the target threshold (e.g., 80%).

activities.title: Wrap-up reflection: uncertainty statement and next-step planning
activities.description: Learners write a short ‘manager-ready’ uncertainty statement (3–5 sentences) summarising one key result from the case analysis, including a quantified metric (probability/percentile), a stated assumption, and one limitation. They then select one next step (e.g., collect better data, validate distribution choice, increase simulation runs).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection to consolidate professional reporting habits; optional peer viewing in an asynchronous forum if enabled.
instructorActions: Provide sentence frames that enforce transparency (e.g., ‘Assuming __, we estimate __; 95% CI __; limitation __.’).
If a forum is used: provide a short moderation guide and a ‘good example’ post.
studentActions: Submit the uncertainty statement and chosen next step.
Optionally read one peer response and note one improvement idea for their own reporting.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson to keep learners at Bloom level ‘analyse’: every computation should feed a judgement about model fit, assumptions, and meaning. Use a consistent analysis routine across tasks: (1) define the random variable and units, (2) justify distribution choice by checking assumptions, (3) compute the quantity asked, (4) interpret in workplace language, (5) run a sanity check, (6) document uncertainty/limitations.

Because the delivery mode is online self-study, embed frequent ‘stop-and-think’ questions and immediate feedback. Feedback should not only correct arithmetic but also address professional integrity: penalise (in rubric/feedback) missing assumptions, unit mismatches, and overconfident language (e.g., presenting simulated estimates as exact). Encourage transparent phrasing: ‘estimate’, ‘under assumptions’, ‘based on N runs/data’. Ensure all provided examples include explicit units and a short limitations note.

When introducing confidence intervals, be explicit about what is random: the CI describes uncertainty in the estimate (given finite data or finite simulation runs), not a percentile range for outcomes. Reinforce the difference by pairing CI questions with percentile questions in the same screen. Finally, connect the outputs to action: a risk register entry must include an implication (trigger/threshold) and a next step (mitigation, monitoring, or data improvement).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Target pacing (90 min total): 0–10 diagnostic; 10–25 models mini-lecture; 25–45 guided practice; 45–55 Monte Carlo outputs mini-lecture/demo; 55–75 case analysis + risk register; 75–85 quiz; 85–90 reflection.

If learners are behind at minute 45: complete only two of the three guided practice scenarios (prioritise the one matching their workplace context), then proceed to the Monte Carlo/case analysis since it links directly to the PLO and integrity competency.

If learners finish early: add an extension prompt—compare an analytic estimate (e.g., normal approximation) to the simulation estimate and explain any discrepancy in terms of assumptions, sampling error, and model limitations.
adaptationOptions: Maths support (foundational): provide a step-by-step scaffold template for each distribution (define X, parameters, CDF/survival, interpret) and an optional ‘z-table refresher’ or calculator walkthrough.
Advanced learners: add an extension comparing analytic vs simulated results, asking for sensitivity analysis (e.g., vary rate λ or defect probability p) and comment on robustness of decisions.
Accessibility: provide all videos with captions and a text-only equivalent; ensure plots have alt-text descriptions and tables are screen-reader friendly.
Low-tech option: offer a PDF-based case with pre-computed simulation summaries so learners can focus on interpretation and risk register writing without running software.
Language support: include a glossary and sentence starters for transparent uncertainty reporting; allow submissions in bullet points to reduce writing load while maintaining required elements.
Assessment flexibility: allow a second attempt on formative quizzes with item-level feedback and a short remediation path based on missed concepts.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming normality by default, even for bounded or highly skewed quantities (and ignoring that normal models can imply impossible negative values).
Using the binomial model when trials are not independent or when p changes across trials (e.g., learning effects, changing supplier quality).
Confusing probability density (PDF) values with probabilities; forgetting to use CDF/survival for interval or tail probabilities.
Mixing up ‘at least’ vs ‘at most’ and mishandling complement rules (e.g., P(X≥k) vs 1−P(X≤k−1)).
For exponential models: not checking the ‘constant rate’ assumption; misunderstanding the memoryless property and applying it where it doesn’t fit.
Interpreting a 95% confidence interval as ‘95% of outcomes fall in this range’ rather than ‘uncertainty in the estimate’.
Treating Monte Carlo output as exact truth; failing to report simulation run size, input assumptions, or estimation uncertainty.
Unit errors (rate per hour used with minutes; cost per day mixed with per week) and not performing basic bounds/sanity checks.
discussionPrompts: Pick one of today’s models (binomial/normal/exponential). What is one assumption that is often violated in real workplace data, and how would that violation bias risk estimates?
In the Monte Carlo case, which metric would you report to a manager: mean, P90, or probability of exceeding a threshold? Justify your choice based on decision needs and risk appetite.
Write a two-sentence statement that reports a result with integrity: include an assumption, an uncertainty measure (percentile or CI), and one limitation.
When two methods disagree (analytic approximation vs simulation), what are the first two checks you would perform before changing the decision?
What information would you add to the risk register to make your analysis auditable by someone else (e.g., data source, version, number of simulation runs, parameter estimates)?

lessons.lessonTitle: Calculate probabilities using binomial, normal and expone...
objectives: Select an appropriate probability model (binomial, normal, exponential) for a workplace defect/demand/downtime scenario and justify the choice by explicitly stating assumptions (e.g., independence, constant rate, measurement scale).

Calculate and interpret at least two workplace-relevant probabilities using binomial, normal or exponential models (including correct parameterisation and units), achieving ≥80% accuracy on a self-check quiz.
Analyse Monte Carlo simulation outputs (mean/median, percentiles, probability of threshold exceedance) to quantify schedule or financial risk and explain what each metric implies for decision-making.

Compute and correctly interpret a confidence interval (CI) or simulation uncertainty band for an estimated risk metric (e.g., P(delay > 5 days)) and state at least two limitations that affect reliability.
Produce a concise risk register entry that records risk statement, quantitative result, assumptions, uncertainty/CI, limitations, and recommended action/escalation criteria.

activities.title: Diagnostic warm-up: model recognition + units check
activities.description: Learners complete a short diagnostic quiz (auto-marked) with 6 items: identify whether binomial/normal/exponential is appropriate, pick correct parameters, and flag unit/assumption issues. Immediate feedback includes brief explanations and links to the relevant section of the lesson.
activities.teachingMethod: Retrieval practice with immediate feedback; misconception-focused distractors (e.g., rate vs mean, p vs q, σ vs variance).
instructorActions: Configure quiz with targeted distractors that diagnose common errors (wrong λ units, normal used for small n, confusing CI with percentile range).
Enable item-level feedback and point learners to specific timestamps/sections in the lesson content.
Collect analytics to identify which items most learners miss for later cohort messaging.
studentActions: Complete the diagnostic quiz independently.
Review feedback and note two personal focus areas (e.g., exponential parameterisation, interpreting percentiles).

activities.title: Mini-lecture: choosing and parameterising distributions ethically
activities.description: Interactive micro-lesson (text + short video clips) covering: (1) binomial conditions and parameters (n, p), (2) normal modelling and z-scores (μ, σ) including when normal approximations are/aren’t justified, (3) exponential downtime model (rate λ, mean 1/λ), and (4) professional integrity: documenting assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations; checking units and plausibility.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-examples + decision tree prompts; embedded “stop-and-think” questions that require learners to articulate assumptions before revealing solutions.
resources: Worked example set (3 scenarios: defects, demand, downtime)
instructorActions: Present a decision pathway: data type → trial structure → time-to-event → candidate distribution.
Model transparent reporting language (e.g., 'Assuming independent trials and constant defect probability…').
Include quick plausibility checks (e.g., probability bounds, unit consistency, parameter reasonableness).
studentActions: Work through embedded questions and compare their assumption statements to exemplars.
Save the decision tree and add one personal example from their workplace (or a provided context).

activities.title: Demonstration: Monte Carlo outputs, percentiles, and CI in a spreadsheet
activities.description: Guided demonstration using a provided spreadsheet template: run a Monte Carlo simulation for a simple schedule risk (task durations with variability), then extract outputs: mean/median, P(total duration > threshold), P(cost > budget), P90, and an uncertainty estimate/CI for a probability via repeated batches or a binomial CI on simulated exceedance counts.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided walkthrough with 'pause-and-do' steps; emphasis on interpreting outputs and checking for stability with more iterations.
resources: Spreadsheet template (Excel/Google Sheets) with RNG and summary table
instructorActions: Demonstrate how to compute: exceedance indicator, estimated probability, and a CI (e.g., Wilson interval) from the simulated exceedance count.
Show how iteration count affects stability (e.g., compare 1,000 vs 10,000 runs).
Highlight integrity points: label assumptions, input sources, and limitations directly in the model notes.
studentActions: Open the template, run the simulation, and reproduce the summary metrics.

activities.title: Practice set: distribution calculations in workplace contexts
activities.description: Learners complete a structured problem set with instant solution reveal after attempting: (A) Binomial—probability of ≥k defects in a batch; (B) Normal—probability demand exceeds capacity; (C) Exponential—probability downtime exceeds a threshold time and expected downtime. Answer key with annotated reasoning (not just final numbers)

activities.title: Case analysis: interpret simulation outputs and draft a risk register entry
activities.description: A mini-case provides: simulation summary table (mean, P50, P80, P90, exceedance probability for a deadline/budget), histogram, and a stated iteration count. Learners analyse what the outputs imply for schedule/financial risk, identify limitations (input quality, independence, distribution choice, iteration adequacy), and complete a risk register entry including assumptions and uncertainty/CI.

activities.title: Formative assessment: mixed items + integrity check
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz (8–10 items) covering: model selection, parameterisation, probability calculation, interpretation of Monte Carlo percentiles vs CI, and a short constructed-response prompt: 'State two assumptions and two limitations you would record for this analysis.'
activities.teachingMethod: Mastery check with immediate feedback; constructed response evaluated with a checklist (self-mark or instructor-sampled review depending on course setup).
instructorActions: Set quiz feedback to explain *why* distractors are wrong (especially CI vs percentile misunderstandings).
Provide a checklist for the short response so learners can self-assess quality of documentation.

activities.title: Wrap-up: action checklist + next-step plan
activities.description: Learners complete a 2-minute exit ticket: (1) one distribution they still confuse and why, (2) one unit/assumption check they will apply next time, (3) one sentence they would use to communicate uncertainty professionally to a stakeholder.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-reflection to consolidate learning and reinforce professional integrity norms.
instructorActions: Provide 2–3 exemplar responses that model concise, transparent communication.
Use responses to post a brief cohort-wide clarification on the most common remaining confusion.
studentActions: Submit the exit ticket.
Save their uncertainty sentence for reuse in future risk register entries.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design for analysis-level learning by requiring learners to (a) justify model choice, (b) interpret outputs in context, and (c) critique assumptions/limitations. In self-study mode, embed frequent ‘stop-and-think’ prompts that force an assumption statement before calculation, and use item-level feedback to correct misconceptions immediately. Emphasise professional integrity: learners should document where numbers come from, what was assumed (independence, constant rate, normality), and how uncertainty is expressed (percentiles vs CI). Include explicit unit checks (λ in 1/time; σ in same units as variable). For Monte Carlo interpretation, repeatedly distinguish: distribution of outcomes (percentiles) vs uncertainty in an estimate (CI). Encourage learners to test stability by increasing iterations and noting whether key metrics materially change. Provide exemplars of risk register wording and require linkage from conclusions to specific outputs (e.g., P90, exceedance probability, CI).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep early sections brisk: the diagnostic should be timed and low-stakes (10 minutes) to surface gaps. If learners struggle with model selection, direct them to the decision tree before allowing them to proceed to the practice set. During the spreadsheet demo, recommend pausing after each metric is produced (mean/percentiles/exceedance/CI) so learners can replicate immediately. For practice problems, suggest a 2-pass approach: first pass for setup (assumptions + parameters), second pass for computation and interpretation. In the case analysis, allocate time explicitly: ~8 minutes interpreting metrics, ~7 minutes writing assumptions/limitations, ~5 minutes completing the risk register entry. Encourage a short break between the practice set and case analysis if learners feel cognitive overload.
adaptationOptions: Provide two tool pathways: spreadsheet template (default) and an optional Python/R notebook for learners with coding experience.
Offer scaffolded and unscaffolded versions of the problem set (scaffold includes parameter boxes and hints; unscaffolded is exam-style).
Include accessibility supports: captions/transcripts for screencasts, screen-reader friendly PDFs, and high-contrast charts for histograms.
For learners needing more support, supply a filled example of the assumptions/units checklist and a partially completed risk register entry to finish.
For advanced learners, add an extension: compare normal approximation to binomial exact; run sensitivity analysis on p/λ and report which assumption drives risk most.
commonMisconceptions: Treating the normal model as universally applicable (ignoring discreteness, skew, or small sample sizes) and failing to justify approximation conditions.
Confusing binomial parameters (using n as probability or mixing p and 1−p), or forgetting the ‘fixed number of trials’ requirement.
Mis-parameterising the exponential distribution (mixing rate λ with mean 1/λ) and/or using inconsistent time units (hours vs days).
Interpreting a percentile (e.g., P90 outcome) as a confidence interval about the mean, or interpreting a CI as covering 90% of outcomes.
Assuming simulation output is ‘exact’ and not recognising Monte Carlo error; failing to check stability with more iterations.
Ignoring dependency between tasks/events (assuming independence by default), leading to under/over-estimation of risk.
Reporting a single number without documenting assumptions, data sources, limitations, or uncertainty (violating transparency expectations).
discussionPrompts: You are given defect counts per batch and a target of ‘≤2 defects’. What makes a binomial model defensible here, and what workplace factors would break its assumptions?
A stakeholder asks: ‘Is P90 the same as a 90% confidence interval?’ How would you explain the difference in one or two sentences?
When modelling downtime with an exponential distribution, what evidence would you look for to support or reject the ‘constant rate’ assumption?
In a Monte Carlo schedule simulation, which is more decision-relevant: the mean, the median, or P90? Defend your choice for a risk-averse manager.
What are two limitations you would always record in a risk register for simulation-based estimates, even when the model seems reasonable?
Describe a unit check you would perform that could prevent a major reporting error in a risk analysis (give a concrete example).

lessons.lessonTitle: Calculate probabilities using binomial, normal and expone...
objectives: Given a workplace scenario (defects, demand, downtime), select an appropriate probability model (binomial, normal, or exponential) and justify the choice by stating assumptions (e.g., independence, constant rate, approximate symmetry).

Compute required probabilities for each model (e.g., P(X≤k) for binomial, P(a≤X≤b) for normal with standardisation, P(T>t) for exponential) with correct parameter identification, units, and rounding; achieve ≥80% accuracy on an auto-marked check.

Analyse Monte Carlo simulation outputs (histogram/summary table) to estimate a risk metric (e.g., P(cost>budget), P(finish date>deadline), P(downtime>threshold)) and extract a 90% confidence interval (CI) for the key outcome.

Document the simulation and analytical results in a workplace-style risk register entry that includes assumptions, uncertainty (CI/percentiles), limitations, and a transparency note on data quality/model fit.
Critique (identify and correct) at least two issues in a provided worked solution related to unit consistency, parameter misuse, or overconfident reporting of simulation results.

activities.title: Orientation: lesson goals, integrity expectations, and setup

Download: Risk register template (spreadsheet or doc)

Note the lesson success criteria and how performance will be checked.

activities.title: Model selection refresher (binomial, normal, exponential) with workplace cues

activities.title: Monte Carlo outputs: interpret risk, percentiles, and CI
activities.description: Learners are given a pre-run Monte Carlo output (histogram + summary: mean, SD, P50, P90, P95, and a 90% CI for mean or for a key percentile depending on tool). activities.teachingMethod: Data interpretation task using provided simulation results; learners explain decisions using probability-of-exceedance and percentile language.

Short explainer: CI vs percentile interval (1 page)
Threshold definitions: budget cap and deadline date
instructorActions: Clarify terms: percentile (distribution of outcomes) vs CI (uncertainty in estimate due to finite simulation/data).
Prompt learners to state the risk metric explicitly (e.g., P(Cost>1.2M)).
Encourage transparent language: 'Based on 10,000 trials…' and note limitations.
