lessons.lessonTitle: Uncertainty using confidence intervals, distributions or ...
objectives: Compute and interpret a confidence interval (CI) for a workplace metric (mean, proportion, or difference in means) and write a 3–5 sentence uncertainty statement that correctly explains the CI in plain language, including units and rounding rules.

Build a reproducible Excel or Python workflow that (a) imports/records inputs, (b) documents assumptions and units, (c) performs CI or simulation-based uncertainty analysis, and (d) generates an audit-ready output table and chart.

Evaluate at least three key assumptions (e.g., independence, distribution choice, sample representativeness, stationarity) and record their likely impact on results plus practical mitigations in an “Assumptions & Limitations” log.

Create a balanced risk statement that combines point estimate + CI (or simulated quantiles), explicitly states limitations, and proposes at least two mitigations or next data-collection steps appropriate for a workplace stakeholder.

activities.title: Start-up: Capstone uncertainty brief + exemplar scan
activities.description: Learners review the lesson brief and a 1-page exemplar output (risk statement + CI chart + assumptions log). They identify the required components for an audit-ready uncertainty section in a workplace report.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked exemplar with guided noticing prompts (self-study worksheet) focusing on integrity: units, rounding, assumptions, and limitations.
resources: PDF: Exemplar one-page uncertainty summary (CI + risk statement)
Checklist: “Audit-ready uncertainty section” (units, rounding, assumptions, versioning, data source)
Starter dataset (CSV) with a workplace-style metric (e.g., defect rate by shift or demand samples)
instructorActions: Provide an exemplar that includes transparent notes (why a CI method was chosen, what was assumed, what was not claimed).
Include a short checklist that maps directly to the lesson objectives and assessment criteria.
studentActions: Mark (highlight) where the exemplar shows units, rounding, assumptions, limitations, and mitigations.
Answer 3 guided questions: What is being estimated? What uncertainty method is used? What claims are avoided?

activities.title: Mini-lecture (asynchronous): Confidence intervals, simulation, and honest reporting
activities.description: Short instructional segments explain: what a CI is (and is not), when to use t-interval vs proportion CI, and when simulation (bootstrap/Monte Carlo) is preferred. Emphasis on transparent communication and avoiding over-precision.
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lectures (3–5 minutes each) with embedded knowledge checks and immediate feedback explanations.
resources: Video 1: CI interpretation and common pitfalls (5 min)
Video 2: Choosing a method (t, z, proportion, bootstrap) (5 min)
Video 3: Turning results into a risk statement + mitigations (5 min)
instructorActions: Use one consistent running example with units (e.g., minutes, $/unit, % defective) and show how rounding changes messaging.
Model integrity language: distinguish evidence from assumptions; state what the data cannot support.
studentActions: Complete embedded checks and note at least two misconceptions they previously held (from provided list).
Select a method (CI type or simulation) for the provided dataset using a decision table.

activities.title: Demonstration: Build a reproducible uncertainty workflow (Excel or Python)
activities.description: Step-by-step walkthrough building an audit-ready workbook/notebook: data tab, calculations tab, assumptions log, outputs (CI/quantiles), and a stakeholder-ready chart plus risk statement. Includes how to keep a traceable calculation log.
activities.teachingMethod: Screencast with pauses for “Do it now” replication steps; includes both Excel path and Python path (learner chooses one).
resources: Excel template (tabs: Data, Calc, Assumptions_Log, Outputs, Version_Log)
Python notebook template (cells: imports, data load, assumptions dict, CI/sim functions, outputs)
Guide: Setting rounding, units, and named ranges (Excel) / setting random seed (Python)
Reference: Common CI formulas and bootstrap outline
instructorActions: Demonstrate a clean structure: inputs clearly separated from calculations; outputs protected/labelled; version/date noted.
Show at least one built-in check (unit check, sanity range check, or reconciliation against a manual calculation).
Explicitly narrate limitations (e.g., small n, non-random sampling) and how they affect interpretation.
studentActions: Follow along and reproduce the structure using the provided template.
Implement one integrity check (e.g., conditional formatting for impossible values, or assert statements in Python).
Fill in at least two entries in Assumptions_Log during the demo (not after).

activities.title: Create task: Produce your own uncertainty section + risk statement (capstone build)
activities.description: Learners create an uncertainty analysis deliverable for a workplace-style scenario (pricing/optimisation/quality). They compute a CI or simulation interval, generate a chart, and write a balanced risk statement with limitations and mitigations. Output must be reproducible and auditable.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided build with a rubric-aligned checklist; learners choose one of two difficulty tracks (standard vs stretch).
resources: Scenario options (choose 1): (A) quality defect rate, (B) demand forecasting mean with CI, (C) process time reduction difference in means
Rubric checklist: reproducibility, uncertainty correctness, integrity, communication quality
Sentence starters for risk statements (plain language) + examples of acceptable limitations
Optional extension: Bootstrap CI / Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis
instructorActions: Provide a ‘minimum viable deliverable’ definition (what must be present to pass) and a stretch goal list (e.g., sensitivity analysis, alternative CI method comparison).
Offer an annotated “common errors” note that learners can consult while building (self-remediation).
studentActions: Choose a scenario and build/complete the workbook or notebook so it runs end-to-end without manual patching.
Compute and report: point estimate, CI (or 5th–95th quantiles), and a chart with labelled axes/units.
Write: (1) a 3–5 sentence risk statement, (2) at least three limitations/assumptions with impact, (3) at least two mitigations/next steps.

activities.title: Formative Assessment: Integrity + uncertainty checkpoint (auto-check + self-audit)
activities.description: Learners complete a short auto-graded quiz plus a self-audit using the provided checklist to verify correctness, documentation, and reproducibility. They fix any identified issues (rounding, labels, CI interpretation, missing assumptions).
activities.teachingMethod: Two-part formative: (1) auto-graded conceptual quiz, (2) self-audit checklist with required corrections before proceeding.
resources: Quiz (8–10 items): CI interpretation, method choice, rounding/units, assumptions
Self-audit checklist: run-from-top reproducibility, units/labels, assumptions log completeness, seed/versioning
Answer key with explanations and “fix-it” guidance
instructorActions: Configure feedback to be diagnostic (why an answer is wrong, what change to make in the workbook/notebook).
Prompt learners to re-run their analysis after any fix (ensuring the workflow remains reproducible).
studentActions: Complete quiz and review explanations for any incorrect items.
Run the self-audit, record 1–3 fixes made, and re-export the final output (PDF/screenshot of Outputs + risk statement).

activities.title: Wrap-up: Reflection + discussion post (stakeholder communication)
activities.description: Learners reflect on what uncertainty means for decision-making and post a concise stakeholder-facing summary (or save as a private reflection if no forum is used).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection prompt; optional peer review using two-comment protocol (clarity + integrity).
resources: Discussion board prompt set (or private reflection template)
Peer feedback micro-rubric (2 criteria: clarity, transparency)
instructorActions: Provide an example of a high-quality post that is clear, cautious, and actionable (no overclaiming).
If a forum is available, seed the board with one ‘good’ and one ‘problematic’ risk statement for critique.
studentActions: Post (or write) a 120–180 word summary: estimate + uncertainty + key assumptions + mitigations.
If forum-enabled: give feedback to 1 peer using the micro-rubric.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Emphasise professional integrity as a mathematical skill: learners must separate what the data show (estimate + interval) from what they assume (sampling, independence, distributional form, process stability). Repeatedly model ‘claim discipline’: avoid stating that the true value is inside the interval with a given probability; instead explain the long-run CI procedure and what the interval suggests for decision risk. Insist on units and sensible rounding at every output point (tables, charts, narrative). Build auditability habits: (1) inputs clearly labeled with source/date, (2) calculations traceable (named ranges or well-labeled cells; functions documented), (3) a version log or run log, and (4) reproducibility (Excel: no hidden manual steps; Python: fixed seed and re-runnable notebook). Encourage method choice justification: t-interval for mean with small n and approximate normality; proportion CI methods (e.g., Wilson) when n is moderate; simulation/bootstrapping when assumptions are weak or the statistic is complex. Require mitigations that are practical (collect more data, stratify sampling, validate measurement system, sensitivity analysis on key inputs) rather than vague. Provide feedback focused on two axes: technical correctness (interval computed/selected correctly) and communication integrity (limitations and assumptions made explicit, no overconfidence).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the create task (30 min) protected: if learners fall behind, direct them to complete the ‘minimum viable deliverable’ first (one correct CI/simulation interval + one chart + assumptions log + short risk statement). If time is tight, reduce scenario choice to one default dataset and provide a pre-built chart scaffold. For faster learners, add a stretch requirement: compare two interval methods (e.g., t vs bootstrap) and explain differences, or run a one-parameter sensitivity analysis and report how the interval shifts. Use time-box prompts in materials (e.g., “Stop at 12 minutes: confirm your workflow runs end-to-end”). Encourage learners to spend no more than 5 minutes polishing visuals before correctness and documentation are complete.
adaptationOptions: Template scaffolding levels: (A) fully structured Excel/Python template with placeholders; (B) partially structured (tabs/cells created but formulas missing); (C) blank build for advanced learners.
Method choice flexibility: allow either CI (analytic) or simulation/bootstrap interval, provided learners justify the choice and communicate limitations.
Accessibility: provide step-by-step written instructions mirroring the screencast; ensure charts use accessible colour palettes and include data labels/alt text guidance.
Math support: provide a ‘formula bank’ and a short optional refresher on standard error vs standard deviation, plus a calculator-check example.

Data complexity adjustment: offer smaller/cleaner dataset for learners who need it; offer a messy dataset with missing values/outliers for stretch learners (requiring documented cleaning assumptions).
Language support: provide sentence frames for risk statements and limitation wording (e.g., “This estimate assumes…, which may…; to reduce this risk we will…”).
commonMisconceptions: Interpreting a 95% CI as “there is a 95% probability the true value lies in this interval” for the already-collected data (instead of a long-run coverage statement).
Believing higher confidence automatically gives a narrower interval (it generally widens as confidence increases).
Confusing standard deviation with standard error, leading to incorrect CI widths.
Using a normal/z interval by default regardless of small sample size, skewness, or unknown variance.
Treating a CI as describing where 95% of individual data points lie (confusing CI with prediction interval).
Ignoring units and rounding, producing false precision (e.g., reporting $12.34567 or 0.123456 defects/unit).
Assuming independence or random sampling without checking the data collection process (e.g., repeated measures, batch effects, shift-based clustering).
Failing to set a random seed or document simulation settings, making results non-reproducible.
Overstating conclusions (e.g., claiming a process ‘meets spec’ without considering uncertainty and limitations).
Not documenting data cleaning choices (e.g., removing outliers) and thereby hiding impactful assumptions.
discussionPrompts: Your stakeholder asks: “So what’s the chance the true defect rate is above 2%?” How would you respond ethically using your CI/simulation results without overstating what the CI means?
Which assumption in your analysis is most fragile (sampling, independence, distribution, stationarity, measurement accuracy)? What specific action would you take next week to reduce that risk?
If you changed the confidence level from 95% to 90% (or 99%), how would your recommendation change, if at all? When is it appropriate to use a different confidence level in a workplace context?
Describe one unit/rounding decision you made (e.g., dollars to cents, minutes to seconds). How did that decision affect clarity or perceived certainty?
What would an auditor or manager need to reproduce your result six months from now? List the minimum artifacts (data source, version log, assumptions log, seed, formulas/code).

lessons.lessonTitle: A reproducible Excel or Python workbook solving a workpla...
objectives: Build a reproducible Excel or Python workflow that can be rerun end-to-end from raw data to final outputs (tables/plots) with no hard-coded intermediate values, evidenced by a successful “restart-and-run” test.

Create an explicit Assumptions & Limitations log (minimum 6 entries) that documents units, data sources, rounding rules, and model/measurement limitations, and link it to the calculations or code sections where each assumption is used.
Implement at least 3 audit/quality checks (e.g., unit checks, reasonableness bounds, reconciliation totals, sensitivity checks) and record results in a dedicated “Checks” sheet or notebook section.

Produce a 1-page technical report (or equivalent notebook narrative) and a 5-slide deck for non-specialists that includes: key result(s), method summary, at least 1 visual, units, uncertainty statement (e.g., CI or sensitivity range), and a clear decision recommendation.
Revise the workbook/report based on at least 5 items of structured feedback (self-checklist + peer/instructor-style prompts), documenting what changed and why in a change log.

activities.title: Orientation: Capstone deliverable expectations (reproducibility + transparency)
activities.description: Learners review a brief overview of what “reproducible” and “auditable” mean in workplace maths deliverables. They examine the marking criteria focus for Lesson 6: traceability, assumptions, unit discipline, uncertainty reporting, and communication to non-specialists. Learners set up a working folder structure (raw_data / outputs / report / slides) or notebook section structure.
activities.teachingMethod: Short video or narrated slides + checklist. Emphasise ‘restart-and-run’ and ‘someone else can follow your steps’ as the performance standard.
instructorActions: Provide a clear definition and examples of non-reproducible vs reproducible work (hard-coded numbers, hidden steps, overwritten cells, manual filtering).
Explain minimum evidence required: assumptions log, checks sheet, change log, and final outputs.
studentActions: Download/clone the starter template (Excel or Python notebook).
Create a project folder structure and rename the file with versioning (e.g., MOD108_L6_v1).

activities.title: Case analysis: Deconstruct an exemplar (what makes it audit-ready?)
activities.description: Learners open an annotated exemplar workbook/notebook and identify features that support integrity and diligence: named ranges, consistent units, input/output separation, transparent formulas, CI/sensitivity statements, and clear visuals. They answer short prompts to label where assumptions and checks appear and how uncertainty is communicated.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided annotation activity with embedded questions (auto-graded or self-check). Learners compare their annotations to an answer key.
resources: Annotated exemplar (Excel + PDF export, or notebook + HTML export)
Auto-check quiz or self-check answer key
instructorActions: Highlight 3–5 ‘must-have’ patterns: Inputs tab, Calculations tab, Outputs tab; Checks tab; Assumptions log; consistent units/rounding; narrative that matches figures.
Model how to spot red flags (unlabeled units, magic numbers, unexplained exclusions).
studentActions: Mark up the exemplar: list at least 5 audit-ready features and 3 red flags that were avoided.
Complete quick questions to confirm understanding (e.g., where CI is computed and how it’s explained).

activities.title: Demonstration: Build the audit trail (assumptions + change log + calculation map)
activities.description: Learners follow a step-by-step walkthrough to add (or refine) three structures in their own capstone file: (1) Assumptions & Limitations log with links to calculation areas; (2) Change log documenting revisions; (3) Calculation map showing data flow from inputs to outputs (sheet diagram in Excel or markdown section in Python).
activities.teachingMethod: Screen-recorded demo with pauses for ‘do this now’ checkpoints. Provide a completed reference version for comparison.
resources: Assumptions & Limitations log template (with required fields: ID, statement, rationale, source, unit, location link, impact)
Calculation map example (flow diagram or numbered pipeline steps)
instructorActions: Demonstrate how to write assumptions in testable language (e.g., ‘Assume scrap rate = 2.0% based on Q3 QA report’).
Show how to link assumptions to formulas/cells or code cells and how to reference assumption IDs in comments.
studentActions: Create/populate an assumptions log with at least 6 entries relevant to their chosen pricing/optimisation/quality scenario.
Add a change log and record at least 2 anticipated revisions they expect to make after checks/feedback.

activities.title: Practice: Implement quality checks (units, reasonableness, reconciliation, sensitivity)
activities.description: Learners implement at least three checks appropriate to their project type. Examples: unit consistency checks (e.g., $/unit vs $/kg), bounds checks (non-negative demand, capacity limits), reconciliation totals (inputs vs outputs), and sensitivity checks (vary a key assumption ±5–10% and show effect on decision). Learners record pass/fail and notes in a dedicated Checks section.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided build with a menu of check patterns. Learners choose checks that match their model and document the logic and outcome.
resources: Checks pattern library (Excel formulas; Python snippets)
instructorActions: Explain that checks are not ‘extra’; they are evidence of diligence and reduce workplace risk.
Provide exemplars for ‘good’ check statements: what is checked, expected range, actual result, action if failed.
studentActions: Implement ≥3 checks and record results (including at least 1 unit-related check).
If a check fails, fix the model and note the fix in the change log.

activities.title: Create communication outputs: 1-page report + 5-slide deck (for non-specialists)
activities.description: Learners draft a concise report and slide deck that translate the technical work into an accessible recommendation. Required inclusions: key KPI/result with units; method in plain language; at least one visual; uncertainty/limitations statement (CI or sensitivity range); and a clear decision recommendation (what to do, expected impact, risks).
activities.teachingMethod: Template-driven writing: learners fill a structured outline and export figures directly from their workbook/notebook outputs to avoid copy/paste errors.
resources: 5-slide deck template (problem → method → results → uncertainty/limits → recommendation)
instructorActions: Model how to describe uncertainty without undermining credibility (e.g., ‘95% CI for mean defect rate: …; decision robust to ±10% demand change’).
Emphasise alignment: numbers in slides must match workbook outputs and use consistent rounding.
studentActions: Draft the report and slides using their current outputs, ensuring units and rounding rules are consistent throughout.
Insert at least one chart/table that is directly generated from the model outputs.

activities.title: Formative assessment: Reproducibility test + self-audit submission
activities.description: Learners run a structured self-audit: (1) restart-and-run test (close/reopen file; clear outputs; rerun pipeline); (2) checklist verification (assumptions, checks, units, uncertainty statement, consistent rounding); (3) export/share audit pack (PDF report + slides + workbook/notebook). They submit a short self-audit note describing what they verified and what remains uncertain.
activities.teachingMethod: Self-check + upload. Provide an automated checklist form and a rubric-aligned reflection prompt.
resources: Submission instructions (what files, naming conventions, export format)
instructorActions: Provide explicit pass criteria (e.g., no broken links; assumptions log complete; checks documented; outputs regenerate).
Offer an optional ‘common failure modes’ troubleshooting guide.
studentActions: Complete the restart-and-run test and record results.
Submit workbook/notebook + report + slides + self-audit note.

activities.title: Feedback integration plan (asynchronous peer-style prompts)
activities.description: Learners respond to structured feedback prompts (either from a discussion forum peer review, instructor bank, or self-generated “critical friend” questions). They identify at least 5 improvements and log them as planned revisions, prioritised by risk (highest risk to decision first).
activities.teachingMethod: Asynchronous prompt set. Learners post (or privately answer) prompts and create a short action list tied to rubric criteria.
resources: Peer feedback prompt bank (clarity, assumptions, uncertainty, visuals, decision readiness)
instructorActions: Provide 8–10 high-quality prompts that simulate workplace challenge (audit, stakeholder questions).
Encourage learners to treat challenge as collaboration: revise, don’t defend.
studentActions: Answer feedback prompts and list ≥5 changes to implement next.
Update change log with planned revisions and rationale.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Lesson 6 sits at Bloom ‘create’: learners must assemble a coherent, rerunnable quantitative product and communicate it responsibly. Prioritise (1) reproducibility, (2) auditability, and (3) stakeholder-ready communication.

Key teaching moves:
- Make quality visible: require explicit artefacts (Assumptions log, Checks sheet, Change log). Learners often believe “my math is correct” is enough; the workplace standard is “my process is inspectable.”
- Use model-based examples: show two versions of the same analysis—one with hidden steps and one audit-ready—so learners feel the difference.
- Treat uncertainty as professional integrity: insist every headline result has an uncertainty or robustness statement (CI, sensitivity, or limitations) and that limitations are written in decision-relevant terms.
- Enforce unit discipline: require units on every key input/output and spot-check unit consistency; encourage dimensional reasoning to catch errors.
- Align narrative to outputs: teach learners to generate figures/tables directly from model outputs to reduce transcription errors.

For online self-study:
- Provide templates and short, checkpointed demos (pause-and-do) to reduce cognitive load.
- Use auto-check questions (e.g., ‘where is assumption A3 used?’) and submission checklists to simulate instructor presence.
- Encourage versioning (v1, v2) and periodic exports (PDF/HTML) so learners can roll back and demonstrate improvement over time.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Timebox build activities tightly and prioritise “minimum viable audit pack” first:
- By minute 30: assumptions log + change log exist (even if incomplete).
- By minute 45: at least 3 checks implemented and recorded.
- By minute 70: report + slides drafted with placeholders for any missing outputs.
- Final 20 minutes: run reproducibility test and fix the most critical issues.

If learners are behind: reduce slide polish (fonts/graphics) and focus on correctness, traceability, units, and uncertainty statements. If ahead: add an extra sensitivity analysis, a CI visualisation, or a second stakeholder view (operations vs finance).
adaptationOptions: Tool choice flexibility: allow Excel-only, Python-only, or hybrid workflows; provide parallel templates and equivalent check patterns for both.
Scaffolded vs independent: offer a ‘guided track’ with pre-filled headings and examples in each template cell/markdown section; offer an ‘open track’ with only rubric criteria for advanced learners.
Accessibility: provide captioned demos, transcripts, high-contrast slide/report templates, and keyboard-navigable spreadsheets/notebooks.
Math support: include optional refreshers on confidence intervals, Solver setup, and unit conversion; link to quick practice sets for learners who need reinforcement.

Extension for advanced learners: implement parameterised scenarios (best/base/worst), Monte Carlo simulation (optional), or automated report generation (e.g., Python to PDF/HTML; Excel PowerQuery + pivot outputs).
Language support: provide a plain-language glossary for key terms (assumption, limitation, CI, sensitivity) and sentence starters for uncertainty and recommendation statements.
commonMisconceptions: “Reproducible” means the same person can redo it; in practice it means someone else can run it end-to-end with minimal guidance and get the same outputs.
Assumptions are obvious and don’t need writing down; in professional work, undocumented assumptions are treated as missing evidence and increase risk.
Confidence intervals (CI) are guarantees that 95% of future values fall in the interval; CI typically describes uncertainty around an estimated parameter (e.g., mean), not prediction spread.
Rounding is cosmetic; inconsistent rounding across workbook/report/slides can change decisions and undermines trust.
Unit errors are rare; in workplace settings, unit inconsistency is one of the most common causes of incorrect conclusions.
Checks are only needed if you suspect errors; checks are standard diligence and part of an auditable workflow.
A polished slide deck can compensate for weak model transparency; stakeholders may accept clear visuals initially, but audits and follow-up questions require traceable calculations.
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption in your model, if wrong, would most change the decision? How did you test sensitivity to it?
Where could a unit mismatch plausibly occur in your workflow, and what specific check did you implement to catch it?
How did you communicate uncertainty (CI, sensitivity range, limitations) without confusing a non-specialist reader? Share your exact sentence.
What is one place you were tempted to hard-code a value? How did you redesign the workflow to keep it reproducible?
If an auditor asked you to justify one data cleaning step (e.g., outlier removal), what would you show them and what limitation would you disclose?
Compare two visuals you could use for the same result (e.g., bar chart vs line chart). Which is more decision-useful for your audience and why?
Describe one piece of feedback you received (or simulated) that materially improved your solution. What changed in the model or report as a result?

lessons.lessonTitle: Produce a concise technical report and slide deck for non...
objectives: Draft a 150–250 word executive summary that states the problem, key quantitative findings (with units), and a recommendation with at least one explicit limitation or uncertainty statement.

Create 2 stakeholder-ready visuals (chart/table) from project data/model outputs that correctly label units, identify at least one turning point/constraint, and include one uncertainty communication element (e.g., CI band, error bars, or qualitative uncertainty note).
Assemble a 3–5 slide mini-deck that follows a clear narrative (context → evidence → recommendation) and includes an assumptions/constraints slide with at least 3 items relevant to the capstone model.
Produce an audit-ready calculation log (or spreadsheet notes) that documents assumptions, rounding choices, and unit checks for at least 3 key calculations used in the report/deck.
Revise one section of the draft report/deck using a structured peer-feedback protocol (or provided simulated peer comments), explicitly stating what changed and why.

activities.title: Quality bar warm-up: non-specialist communication checklist
activities.description: Learners review a one-page checklist for technical integrity in workplace maths outputs (units, assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, audit trail) and quickly self-audit their current capstone draft or sample artifact. They identify 3 gaps to fix during the lesson.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided checklist + quick self-audit. Learners select ‘must-fix’ items to focus effort and avoid polishing low-impact areas.
resources: Sample 1-page report excerpt (good vs weak example)
instructorActions: Provide checklist with brief examples of acceptable wording for assumptions/limitations and uncertainty.
Upload two contrasting examples (annotated) showing why one is audit-ready and one is not.
Prompt learners to capture 3 prioritized fixes in a workspace note (LMS journal or doc).
studentActions: Run the checklist against their current draft or the sample artifact.
Record 3 prioritized gaps (e.g., missing units on a chart, unclear assumption, overconfident recommendation).

activities.title: Mini-lesson: report + slide narrative for non-specialists
activities.description: A short, structured lesson on converting analysis into a decision-oriented story: framing the question, selecting only decision-relevant metrics, stating constraints, and using plain-language uncertainty statements. Includes a simple template for a 1-page technical report and a 3–5 slide deck.
activities.teachingMethod: Template-based instruction using worked micro-examples (before/after phrasing) focused on integrity and clarity rather than more computation.
resources: 1-page report template (headings: Purpose, Data/Method, Findings, Recommendation, Assumptions/Limitations)
Rubric excerpt aligned to MLOs (clarity, units, assumptions, limitations, evidence, audit trail)
instructorActions: Explain the ‘decision first’ structure and how to keep maths transparent (what was done, not every step).
Model plain-language uncertainty phrasing (e.g., ‘estimated range’, ‘likely’, ‘based on historical data’).
Highlight where to place constraints/turning points (e.g., capacity limit, diminishing returns).
studentActions: Download/open templates.
Map their capstone topic into the template headings (bullet points only).
Identify one non-specialist stakeholder persona (e.g., operations manager) to guide tone and detail.

activities.title: Demonstration: visuals with units, turning points, and uncertainty
activities.description: Walkthrough of making two stakeholder-ready visuals from analysis outputs: (1) a trend or marginal-change plot highlighting a turning point/constraint; (2) a summary chart/table that includes uncertainty (CI/error bars) or a clearly stated limitation when CI is not appropriate. Focus is on labeling, annotation, and avoiding misleading scales.
activities.teachingMethod: Screen-recorded demonstration with pause points: learners replicate steps in Excel (or Python) and compare against a reference output.
resources: Screen recording: Excel charting + annotation + error bars/CI
Reference visuals (PNG/PDF) with annotations: units, assumptions note, constraint callout
Optional: Python notebook snippet for CI and plots (for learners using Python)
instructorActions: Show how to label axes with units and include source/time window in a caption.
Demonstrate highlighting a constraint (e.g., capacity line) and marking a turning point (e.g., optimum point).
Demonstrate one acceptable uncertainty method: CI band/error bars, or a limitation statement if CI not defensible.
studentActions: Recreate at least one demonstrated visual using their own outputs (or provided data if not ready).
Add a one-sentence caption stating what the visual shows and why it matters for the decision.

activities.title: Build sprint: 1-page report + 3–5 slide mini-deck (draft)
activities.description: Learners draft the core artifacts: (a) a concise report (1 page maximum) and (b) a short slide deck (3–5 slides). Required inclusions: two visuals with units; at least three assumptions/constraints; one explicit limitation/uncertainty statement; a recommendation linked to evidence.
activities.teachingMethod: Time-boxed production with embedded self-checkpoints (stop at 10 and 20 minutes to verify required elements and avoid overbuilding).
resources: Audit trail mini-log template (assumption, unit check, rounding, source link)
instructorActions: Provide a ‘minimum viable draft’ target (what must exist by minute 25).
Provide exemplar sentence stems for assumptions and limitations (e.g., ‘Assumes demand pattern in Q1–Q4 is stable…’).
Encourage learners to prioritize correctness/clarity over design polish.
studentActions: Draft executive summary (150–250 words) and insert two visuals with captions.
Create 3–5 slides following the storyboard: Context, Evidence, Recommendation, Assumptions/Constraints (optional: Next steps).
Complete audit log entries for at least three key calculations/metrics used.

activities.title: Peer challenge simulation: respond, revise, and document changes
activities.description: Learners practice collaborative professional behaviour by responding to critique. In self-study mode, they use either (a) a discussion-board swap if available, or (b) instructor-provided ‘simulated peer comments’ that challenge assumptions, units, and overclaims. Learners revise one section and write a brief change log: what changed and why.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured critique protocol: Clarify → Challenge → Improve. Learners practice acknowledging uncertainty and defending decisions with evidence without becoming defensive.
resources: Simulated peer feedback cards (e.g., ‘Where did this unit come from?’, ‘Is this a constraint or a preference?’, ‘CI vs variability?’)
Feedback response template (Claim → Evidence → Change decision)
Optional LMS discussion forum prompt for real peer exchange
instructorActions: Provide 6–10 common critique comments aligned to competencies (integrity, diligence, collaboration).
Model a high-quality response that integrates feedback and documents the revision.
Remind learners to revise the artifact, not just reply to comments.
studentActions: Select 2 critique comments (real or simulated) and draft professional responses.
Revise one report paragraph or one slide to address critique (e.g., add unit label, qualify claim, add constraint).
Write a 3–5 bullet change log noting what changed and why.

activities.title: Formative assessment: submission + self-evaluation against rubric
activities.description: Learners submit the draft report and mini-deck (or export to PDF) plus the audit log and change log. They complete a short self-evaluation aligned to the MLOs (tick + short justification). Auto-feedback or instructor feedback (if enabled) focuses on integrity, clarity, and decision relevance.
activities.teachingMethod: Formative checkpoint emphasizing transparency and revision readiness. Self-evaluation primes learners for the next iteration and final capstone submission.
instructorActions: Configure the LMS form to require: units check, assumptions list, uncertainty/limitations statement, and audit log attachment.
Provide brief automated feedback rules or a short feedback guide (what ‘meets standard’ looks like).
If offering instructor feedback, focus comments on the top 2 risks to validity or communication.
studentActions: Export and submit report + slides + audit log + change log.
Complete the self-evaluation with one improvement target for the next lesson/work session.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Center this lesson on creation and revision: learners are not doing more maths; they are making their maths usable, auditable, and decision-relevant. Reinforce professional integrity by requiring explicit uncertainty/limitations statements and separating what the data show from what is inferred. Reinforce diligence by embedding unit checks, assumption logging, and rounding documentation in the workflow (not as an afterthought). Reinforce collaboration by using a critique protocol that normalizes challenge and requires learners to integrate feedback into an improved artifact.

In online self-study delivery, clarity of templates and exemplars is critical. Provide ‘good vs weak’ examples with annotations showing why a choice is misleading or strong (e.g., unlabeled axis, truncated y-axis, missing timeframe, unjustified CI). Use time-boxed checkpoints to prevent learners from over-polishing design while core integrity elements are missing. Encourage a stakeholder persona so learners choose the right level of detail and avoid jargon; require a brief method statement that is honest but non-technical (e.g., “We used historical data from Jan–Dec and fit a simple trend model; results assume similar operating conditions.”).

Feedback guidance: when learners respond to critique, require them to (1) acknowledge the issue, (2) state the evidence/rationale, (3) revise or justify transparently, and (4) document the change. This models audit-ready professional practice.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep early segments brisk to maximize build time. If learners are behind on analysis outputs, allow them to use provided sample data for the visuals so they can still practice the reporting skill. During the 25-minute build sprint, enforce two micro-checkpoints (at ~10 and ~20 minutes): first confirm required components exist (headings, two visuals, assumptions/limitations), then improve clarity (captions, stakeholder wording). If learners get stuck on formatting, redirect to content integrity (units, assumptions, uncertainty, constraint) and postpone styling. For the critique/revision segment, limit to revising one high-impact section to ensure a concrete improvement is completed within time.
adaptationOptions: Support (scaffolding): Provide partially completed templates with sentence starters for executive summary, assumptions, and limitation statements; allow learners to fill blanks using their data.
Support (skills gap): Offer an alternative ‘visuals pack’ (ready-made charts) so learners can focus on captions, units, and interpretation if chart-building is a barrier.
Accessibility: Provide templates compatible with screen readers, require alt-text for visuals, and allow audio narration instead of dense slide text.
Tool flexibility: Permit Excel or Python; accept screenshots/exports as evidence if learners cannot embed charts cleanly.
Extension (advanced): Require one additional slide or appendix section quantifying sensitivity (e.g., change in recommendation if key assumption shifts by ±10%) and a brief explanation.
Language support: Allow bilingual glossary for key terms (constraint, assumption, CI) and encourage plain-language rewriting using a readability target (e.g., short sentences, defined acronyms).
commonMisconceptions: Treating a confidence interval (CI) as a guarantee that future results will fall in that range, rather than an estimate about a parameter under assumptions.
Reporting results without units or mixing units across visuals/tables (e.g., hours vs minutes, $ vs $000) leading to incorrect interpretation.
Confusing constraints (hard limits like capacity or budget) with preferences (soft goals), which weakens recommendations.
Overstating causality from observational trends (e.g., ‘X caused Y’) when the analysis only supports association.
Assuming more decimals implies more accuracy; rounding should match measurement precision and decision needs.
Using visually misleading charts (truncated axes, inconsistent scales) that exaggerate differences.
Believing an audit trail must include every calculation step; instead it should document key assumptions, sources, and checks sufficient to reproduce critical results.
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption, if wrong, would most change your recommendation—and how will you disclose that to a non-specialist stakeholder?
Where does your model/output show a turning point (diminishing returns, optimum, threshold), and how will you visually communicate it without jargon?
What is your primary constraint (capacity, budget, time, quality tolerance), and how does it limit the feasible recommendation set?
How will you explain uncertainty: will you use a CI/error bars, a sensitivity note, or a limitation statement—and why is that choice appropriate for your data?
Identify one place you might be unintentionally misleading (wording, chart scale, omitted units). What will you change to improve transparency?
What feedback would you most want from a peer reviewer (e.g., unit check, logic check, stakeholder clarity), and what question will you ask them?

lessons.lessonTitle: Uncertainty using confidence intervals, distributions or ...
objectives: Compute and report an appropriate 95% confidence interval for a workplace metric (mean, proportion, or defect rate) and state the key assumptions (distributional, sampling, independence) in a short, auditable note.

Create a reproducible Excel workbook or Python notebook that separates Inputs, Assumptions, Calculations, and Outputs, includes unit checks, and produces traceable results (cell references or code functions) suitable for audit.

Evaluate uncertainty using (a) a confidence interval and (b) a simple simulation or distribution-based approach, then compare what each method captures and what it misses in a brief limitations section.

Write a balanced risk statement that communicates uncertainty to non-specialists, including: the metric, CI, practical meaning, limitations, and at least two actionable mitigations linked to controllable levers.
Apply a structured self-audit (rounding, units, assumptions, reproducibility) to identify and correct at least three issues in a draft workbook/notebook before submission.

activities.title: Entry task: Audit a flawed uncertainty statement (micro-case)
activities.description: Learners review a short “quality report excerpt” with common problems (misinterpreted CI, missing units, hidden assumptions, unclear rounding). They annotate what is wrong and propose a corrected version in 3–5 bullet points.
activities.teachingMethod: Worked-example critique: learners practice professional integrity by spotting omissions and overclaims, then rewriting for transparency.
resources: Annotation tool in LMS (or prompt with text entry)
instructorActions: Provide the flawed excerpt and the audit checklist in the LMS.
Include an answer key showing 6–8 typical issues and one strong rewritten model statement.
In discussion-enabled cohorts, seed one thread: “Which flaw is most dangerous in your workplace context?”
studentActions: Identify at least 5 issues (e.g., CI misinterpretation, missing assumptions, unit ambiguity).
Rewrite the statement to be accurate and appropriately cautious.
Optional: post one improvement to the forum and reply to one peer.

activities.title: Micro-lesson: Confidence intervals, distributions, simulation, and ethical reporting
activities.description: Short, segmented content covers: what a CI means (and does not mean), choosing a CI (mean vs proportion), when normal/t/bootstrapping is appropriate, and how simulation complements CIs. Emphasis on transparency: assumptions, data limitations, and avoid overprecision.
activities.teachingMethod: Interactive micro-lecture with 2 embedded checks (1-minute self-check questions) to maintain attention in self-study mode.
resources: 8–10 minute video or reading with examples
Embedded LMS quiz: 2 conceptual questions (CI interpretation; assumptions)
instructorActions: Provide a CI decision guide and a plain-language interpretation template (audience: non-specialists).
Make explicit the integrity standard: claims must match evidence; uncertainty must be shown, not hidden.
Ensure examples show units and rounding rules (e.g., defects per 1,000 units; currency to cents).
studentActions: Complete the two embedded checks and review feedback.
Download the interpretation template and keep it open for later activities.
Note (in their workbook/notebook) which CI type will fit their chosen capstone scenario.

activities.title: Demonstration: Build a reproducible structure (Excel or Python) with a traceable calc log
activities.description: Step-by-step demonstration of a reproducible layout. Excel path: create sheets for Inputs, Assumptions, Calculations, Outputs, and a Calc Log table with timestamp/version notes; use named ranges; add unit columns and data validation. Python path: notebook with sections, functions, fixed random seed, requirements, and a run-all check; produce a single summary table and chart.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided build: learners pause after each segment to replicate the structure in a starter file; emphasis on traceability and audit-ready design.
resources: Starter dataset (CSV) with a workplace-style metric (e.g., defect counts, cycle times, or sample measurements)
Excel starter template (.xlsx) OR Python notebook starter (.ipynb)
Reproducibility checklist (Inputs/Assumptions/Calcs/Outputs; units; rounding; version notes)
Short screencast: “Named ranges + unit checks” OR “Random seeds + run-all reproducibility”
instructorActions: Model a clean separation of inputs vs calculations (no hard-coded constants inside formulas).
Demonstrate at least one unit check (e.g., converting minutes to hours; per-batch to per-unit).
Show how to document assumptions directly next to outputs (e.g., CI method, distribution choice, independence).
studentActions: Create (or update) their workbook/notebook structure to match the template.
Implement at least one unit check and one rounding rule (documented).
Add an Assumptions table with at least 4 entries (what, why, impact if violated, how checked/mitigated).

activities.title: Guided build practice: Produce CI + simulation (or distribution) and draft a risk statement with mitigations
activities.description: Learners complete the core capstone component: compute a CI for a chosen metric, run a simple simulation or distribution-based scenario (e.g., Monte Carlo for cost/defects/time), and generate an output page with a balanced risk statement. They must include limitations and at least two practical mitigations tied to controllable actions.
activities.teachingMethod: Scaffolded create-task: prompts are provided, but learners generate their own outputs (tables/charts/statement) and make justified method choices.
resources: Prompt sheet with two scenario options: (A) Quality metric CI (mean/proportion) or (B) Pricing/production uncertainty scenario
Risk statement template (fillable): Metric + CI + interpretation + limitations + mitigations
Optional helper formulas/snippets: Excel CONFIDENCE.T / T.INV.2T / binomial CI approach; Python scipy/statsmodels snippets
Example output screenshot (for formatting expectations, not numbers)
instructorActions: Provide clear acceptance criteria: (1) CI computed correctly and labeled with units; (2) method justified; (3) simulation documented (seed/iterations); (4) limitations stated; (5) mitigations actionable.
Offer two difficulty tracks: “guided” (more hints) and “challenge” (choose method and justify).
If running as a facilitated cohort, provide a ‘common pitfalls’ post halfway through the lesson.
studentActions: Choose a scenario and compute a 95% CI with correct interpretation wording.
Run a simulation/distribution-based analysis (minimum: define inputs, distribution/assumptions, produce a percentile range).
Create an Outputs page (or notebook cell section) with one chart and one summary table.
Write a 120–180 word risk statement including at least 2 mitigations (e.g., extra sampling, process control limits, supplier checks, buffer stock, pricing guardrails).

activities.title: Formative assessment: Self-audit for integrity, reproducibility, and uncertainty communication
activities.description: Learners complete a short formative check: (1) a 6-item quiz on CI interpretation, rounding, and assumptions; (2) a self-audit checklist applied to their own workbook/notebook to identify and fix issues before submission.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes assessment with immediate feedback plus an applied checklist to reinforce diligence and attention to detail.
resources: LMS quiz (6 items) with automated feedback
Self-audit checklist (downloadable): units, rounding, assumption visibility, traceability, reproducibility run-all, limitation statements
Correction log mini-template (What changed / Why / Evidence)
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to explain why wrong options are wrong (especially CI misconceptions).
Provide a model ‘correction log’ example to normalize iteration and error-finding.
Track common missed items to inform feedback in the next lesson/module touchpoint.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback for any incorrect items.
Apply the self-audit checklist and fix at least 3 issues in their file (document in correction log).
Save/export an audit-ready version (e.g., versioned filename).

activities.title: Wrap-up: Publish a concise ‘audit note’ and plan next capstone steps
activities.description: Learners write a brief audit note summarizing: what was built, key assumptions, key outputs (CI and/or simulation range), limitations, and next actions. Optional: post to discussion board for peer learning.
activities.teachingMethod: Reflection-to-action: reinforces transparency and prepares for capstone submission standards.
resources: Optional forum thread: “One assumption I documented that changed my conclusion”
instructorActions: Provide an exemplar audit note (concise, plain language, includes units).
If forum-enabled, encourage responses that focus on clarity and integrity (not just ‘looks good’).
studentActions: Write and save the audit note in the workbook/notebook (or LMS text entry).
Optional: post one key limitation and one mitigation to the forum.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the lesson around ‘create for audit’: learners are not only computing uncertainty, they are producing an artifact that can be rerun and defended. Emphasize (1) separation of concerns (Inputs/Assumptions/Calcs/Outputs), (2) transparent uncertainty reporting (CI or simulation range plus plain-language meaning), and (3) professional integrity (no stronger claims than the data justify). Use short, concrete templates: a CI interpretation sentence starter (e.g., “Based on this sample and method, we estimate…; if repeated, 95% of such intervals would contain…”), and a limitations/mitigations pair (“Limitation: convenience sample; Mitigation: expand sampling frame next cycle”). Encourage learners to show their work with traceable references (named ranges in Excel; functions and run-all cells in Python) and to record a correction log to model diligence. When giving feedback (asynchronous), comment first on claim accuracy and assumption visibility, then on computation and formatting. Reinforce that a clean risk statement is part of the math deliverable, not an extra.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Timebox the first 25 minutes (entry task + micro-lesson) so most time is spent creating the workbook/notebook. If learners fall behind, prioritize: (1) reproducible structure, (2) one correct CI with units and interpretation, (3) a limitations + mitigations risk statement; treat simulation as an extension if needed. For faster learners, add an extension: compare two CI methods (t vs bootstrap, or Wald vs Wilson for proportions) and note how conclusions change. Recommend learners use a ‘stop-and-check’ rhythm every 10 minutes: units, references, rounding, and whether the written claim matches the numeric evidence.
adaptationOptions: Tool choice: Provide parallel tracks (Excel-only and Python-only) with equivalent outputs and rubrics.
Scaffolding: Offer a fully scaffolded template (prebuilt sheets/sections) for learners needing support; offer a blank template plus requirements list for advanced learners.
Accessibility/low bandwidth: Provide a text-based walkthrough and screenshots as an alternative to video; ensure templates are usable with screen readers (clear headings, table structures).
Math readiness: Include an optional refresher card on standard error vs standard deviation, and when to use t vs normal approximations.
Language support: Provide sentence stems for risk statements and limitations; allow learners to submit the risk statement in bullet points if writing fluency is a barrier.
Challenge extension: Require sensitivity analysis on one assumption (e.g., change distribution or sample size) and document impact on the CI/risk conclusion.
commonMisconceptions: Interpreting a 95% confidence interval as: “There is a 95% probability the true value lies in this specific computed interval.”
Confusing standard deviation (variability of data) with standard error (variability of the estimated mean/proportion).
Using a normal (z) interval automatically for small samples or skewed data without checking assumptions or considering t/bootstrapping.
Reporting a CI without units, context, or the statistic it applies to (mean vs proportion vs rate).
Over-rounding (or inconsistent rounding) that changes decisions, while not documenting rounding rules.
Hard-coding constants inside formulas/cells (breaking traceability) rather than placing them in an Inputs/Assumptions section.
Running simulations without documenting iterations, random seed, or input distributions, then presenting outputs as precise forecasts.
Treating simulation percentiles as guarantees rather than conditional results based on assumptions.
Equating ‘no evidence of difference’ with ‘evidence of no difference’ when CIs overlap or include a target value.
discussionPrompts: What is one sentence you would remove from the flawed report because it overclaims certainty, and how would you rewrite it?
Which assumption in your CI (independence, random sampling, approximate normality) is weakest in a real workplace setting, and what mitigation is realistic?
When would you choose simulation over a confidence interval, and what extra transparency does simulation require to be ethical?
What rounding rule is appropriate for your metric (money, time, defect rate), and how could rounding change a decision threshold?
What does your CI mean for a manager deciding today—what action would change if the interval were wider or shifted?
Name one limitation you included that might feel uncomfortable to report, and explain why including it improves professional integrity.

formativeChecks.question: Short Quiz: Integrated Model Build, Traceability and Decision Outputs
MCQ Knowledge Check: Uncertainty, Validation and Risk Statements for Workplace Decisions

lessons.lessonTitle: A reproducible Excel or Python workbook solving a workpla...
objectives: Build (or refactor) an Excel workbook or Python notebook for a workplace pricing/optimisation/quality problem that is fully reproducible (inputs separated from calculations, steps traceable, outputs regenerable) and includes an assumptions log (minimum 5 assumptions) with units and sources.

Implement at least 3 integrity checks in the model (e.g., unit checks, reasonableness bounds, reconciliation totals, Solver/optimizer constraint checks) and document what each check verifies and what action to take if it fails.

Create two stakeholder-ready visuals (one summary chart and one uncertainty/variation visual such as a confidence interval plot) with correct titles, units, captions, and interpretation written for non-specialists.
Produce a concise technical report (max 1 page) and a 5–7 slide deck that communicate method, results, assumptions, and limitations, including explicit rounding rules and uncertainty statements.

Revise the workbook/notebook and report artifacts based on structured feedback (peer, simulated peer, or rubric-based self-review), documenting at least 3 changes made and why they improve clarity, accuracy, or auditability.

activities.title: Success criteria & capstone deliverables map
activities.description: Self-study orientation that clarifies what “reproducible” and “auditable” mean in this capstone context. Learners review a one-page rubric excerpt and a deliverables checklist, then select which track they are completing (Excel pricing/optimisation/quality or Python). They set a concrete target for what they will finish in the next 90 minutes (e.g., assumptions log + two visuals + draft slide deck).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture (read/watch) + goal-setting prompt
resources: MOD108 Lesson 9 checklist (reproducibility, assumptions, visuals, reporting)
Rubric excerpt: transparency, units, uncertainty, limitations
instructorActions: Provide a short annotated checklist showing minimum acceptable evidence (e.g., where assumptions are logged, how to trace a number to inputs).
Include two model screenshots: one “good audit trail” and one “hard to audit,” with callouts.
studentActions: Choose Excel or Python pathway and open their current capstone file.
Write a one-sentence goal for the session and identify the single biggest risk to reproducibility in their current file.

activities.title: Transparency toolkit: assumptions, units, rounding, and uncertainty statements
activities.description: Learners study a short content segment covering: (1) documenting assumptions (what, why, source, impact), (2) unit discipline (dimensional consistency and unit conversions), (3) rounding policy vs internal precision, and (4) honest uncertainty language (confidence intervals, limitations, sensitivity). Includes mini-examples of good/bad reporting statements for non-specialists.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided notes + worked micro-examples with self-check questions
resources: Assumptions log template (table with columns: Assumption, Rationale, Source, Unit, Sensitivity/Impact, Review date)
instructorActions: Embed 3 quick self-check items with immediate feedback (e.g., identify missing units, rewrite an overconfident claim).
Model one strong limitation statement tied to a specific assumption.
studentActions: Complete the 3 self-check items and correct their own wording where needed.
Draft 2–3 assumption statements relevant to their chosen problem and note where each will be placed in their report/slide deck.

activities.title: Demonstration: making a model reproducible (Excel or Python audit trail)
activities.description: Step-by-step walkthrough of a reference solution structure. Excel path: Inputs sheet → Calc sheet (named ranges, consistent units) → Outputs/Dashboard sheet + a Calculation Log tab (date, change, rationale). Python path: notebook sections (imports, data loading, cleaning, analysis, checks, outputs), fixed random seed if applicable, and saving figures/tables. Emphasises traceability: every reported number can be traced to a formula/code cell and an input source.
activities.teachingMethod: Screen-recorded demo with pause-and-try prompts
resources: Reference Excel workbook template (with Calculation Log + Checks section)
Reference Jupyter notebook template (with checkpoints and export cells)
Short video: ‘Trace any number in 3 clicks’ (Excel) / ‘From cell to output table’ (Python)
instructorActions: Provide a downloadable template and explicitly label what must be customized vs left as-is.
Highlight common reproducibility breakers (hard-coded numbers in formulas, overwritten cells, untracked data cleaning).
studentActions: Follow along and apply at least one structural improvement to their own file (e.g., separate inputs, add checks block, add assumptions table).
Add one calculation log entry describing the change they made.

activities.title: Build sprint: implement assumptions log + integrity checks + traceable outputs
activities.description: Focused creation time. Learners implement: (a) an assumptions log (minimum 5 assumptions), (b) at least 3 integrity checks (units/reasonableness/reconciliation/constraint check), and (c) traceable outputs that will be used in the report and slides. Learners are prompted to annotate key formulas/cells (Excel) or key code blocks (Python) to explain reasoning and units.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided independent build with timeboxed checkpoints
resources: Integrity checks menu (examples for pricing, optimisation, and quality contexts)
Annotation guide (how to comment cells, label units, document data sources)
Optional sample dataset (for learners who need a starting point)
instructorActions: Provide three timed checkpoints (at minute 8/16/24) with ‘minimum evidence’ targets (e.g., ‘5 assumptions logged’, ‘3 checks implemented’, ‘one output table ready’).
Include troubleshooting notes for common issues (Excel Solver infeasible; Python missing package; CI calculation pitfalls).
studentActions: Populate the assumptions log with sources/units and mark 1–2 high-impact assumptions for sensitivity or caution in reporting.
Implement 3 checks and record what ‘pass’ looks like, plus what they will do if a check fails.
Ensure at least one key output (price, optimum plan, defect rate summary, CI) is generated from the model without manual retyping.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 1: Reproducibility & integrity self-audit (rubric-based)
activities.description: Learners complete a structured self-audit and mini-quiz aligned to professional integrity: traceability, unit consistency, assumption documentation, and uncertainty reporting. They must identify two weaknesses in their current workbook/notebook and write a concrete fix for each.
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-graded quiz + checklist submission (pass/fail evidence)
resources: Self-audit checklist (traceability, inputs/calc/outputs separation, units, rounding, checks, assumptions, limitations)
Evidence capture instructions (screenshots or exported notebook sections)
instructorActions: Configure auto-feedback that explains why each item matters for audit and stakeholder trust.
Provide ‘if you scored below X’ remediation links back to templates and the demo segment.
studentActions: Complete the quiz and checklist, then capture evidence (e.g., screenshot of assumptions log and checks block).
Write two targeted improvements they will make next (specific file location + exact change).

activities.title: Communicate for non-specialists: draft report + slide deck with two visuals
activities.description: Learners create: (1) a one-page technical report and (2) a 5–7 slide deck. Must include: problem statement, method summary, key results with units, two visuals (one summary + one CI/uncertainty visual), explicit assumptions and limitations, and a short ‘What to do next’ recommendation. Emphasis: clarity, brevity, and honest uncertainty statements.
activities.teachingMethod: Template-driven authoring with exemplars
resources: Slide deck template (title, context, results, uncertainty, assumptions/limitations, recommendation)
Exemplar visuals gallery (good labels, captions, CI interpretation notes)
instructorActions: Provide an exemplar report/slide pair and annotate where units, assumptions, and limitations appear.
Include a ‘language check’ box: replace overconfident claims with calibrated statements.
studentActions: Insert two visuals generated directly from their model and add captions interpreting them in plain language.
Write one limitation that links to a specific assumption and one sentence on how that limitation could be reduced (e.g., better data, process change, sensitivity analysis).

activities.title: Formative Assessment 2: Feedback integration (simulated peer review + revision log)
activities.description: Learners receive either (a) simulated peer comments (pre-written critique aligned to common issues) or (b) optional asynchronous peer-review prompts (if a forum is used). They must respond by making at least 3 improvements and logging them in a revision log (what changed, where, why).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured critique + revision log entry
resources: Simulated peer feedback set (choose 5 comments relevant to Excel/Python)
Revision log template (Change, Location, Reason, Impact on accuracy/clarity/auditability)
instructorActions: Provide 2–3 ‘typical reviewer voices’ (non-specialist manager, auditor, technical peer) to force audience-aware revisions.
Mark completion based on evidence of change (revision log + updated artifact).
studentActions: Select 3 feedback points to act on and implement the changes immediately.
Record the changes in the revision log and export updated report/slides (PDF) or save notebook outputs.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Keep the lesson anchored in ‘professional integrity’ rather than just formatting. Reproducibility should be taught as a workflow: clean separation of inputs/calculations/outputs, traceable steps, and explicit assumptions that can be challenged. Encourage learners to treat checks as first-class model components (not optional): each check should have a purpose, a pass criterion, and a documented response if it fails. For non-specialist communication, coach learners to lead with the decision and the magnitude (with units), then justify briefly, then state uncertainty and limitations without undermining credibility. Reinforce that confidence intervals describe uncertainty under assumptions; learners must state those assumptions and avoid overconfident causal language. In self-study delivery, embed frequent ‘pause-and-try’ prompts and provide exemplars plus non-exemplar counterexamples to make quality criteria visible. Use the formative assessments to force evidence capture (screenshots/exports) so learners practice audit-ready documentation.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Timebox the build sprint aggressively (25 minutes) with three checkpoints; learners often over-polish visuals or over-debug Solver/code. If they are behind at minute 40, instruct them to prioritize: (1) assumptions log (minimum 5), (2) three checks, (3) one traceable output table, then add visuals and narrative. If ahead, add a stretch goal: sensitivity test of one high-impact assumption (e.g., vary demand by ±10% or recompute CI with alternative method) and report how conclusions change. For learners with limited time, allow the slide deck to be drafted from the report headings (copy + tighten) rather than creating entirely new content.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded pathway: provide a nearly-complete Excel/Python template where learners only replace inputs and add 2 assumptions + 1 check, then gradually require the full minimum (5 assumptions, 3 checks).

Challenge pathway: require automated output export (Excel: Power Query refresh + dashboard; Python: save figures/tables to /outputs and generate a brief markdown/PDF report), plus a small sensitivity analysis on one assumption.

Accessibility: provide captioned videos, transcripts, high-contrast templates, and allow submission as Word/PDF with alt-text for figures; ensure screen-reader-friendly headings in the report template.
Low-bandwidth: offer static annotated screenshots instead of video demos; allow offline work with later upload of PDFs and screenshots.
Tool flexibility: allow Google Sheets instead of Excel, or a Python script (.py) instead of a notebook, as long as traceability and assumptions documentation are equivalent.
Math support: provide optional CI calculation helper (Excel functions or Python snippet) and a ‘units conversion’ mini-reference for common workplace measures.
commonMisconceptions: Believing that more decimal places in the final report increases accuracy (confusing precision with accuracy); failing to state rounding rules.
Treating Solver/optimizer outputs as ‘the truth’ even when constraints are violated, the solution is infeasible, or the model assumptions are unrealistic.
Assuming a confidence interval means ‘there is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval’ without clarifying the frequentist interpretation and underlying assumptions.
Leaving units implicit (mixing percent vs proportion, hours vs minutes, dollars vs thousands of dollars) and not performing dimensional consistency checks.
Hard-coding numbers into formulas/cells or manually editing outputs, breaking reproducibility and auditability.
Using charts without clear titles, axis labels, units, or captions—leading non-specialists to misinterpret the message.
Stating conclusions without limitations (or listing generic limitations not tied to specific assumptions or data quality issues).
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption in your model, if wrong, would most change the decision recommendation—and how did you communicate that risk to a non-specialist?
What integrity check in your workbook/notebook would catch the most damaging mistake (units, constraints, reconciliation, or reasonableness)? Why?
How did you decide what to round in the report versus what to keep at full precision in calculations? Provide one example.
If a stakeholder challenges your result (‘That price seems too high’ / ‘That defect rate seems too low’), what evidence in your audit trail helps you respond transparently?
How would your recommendation change if the confidence interval were wider than expected? What action would you propose (more data, process change, or model revision)?
