lessons.lessonTitle: Produce a concise technical report and slide deck for non...
objectives: Draft a 1–2 page technical report section (Findings + Recommendations) that includes at least 3 visuals, correct units, explicit assumptions/constraints, and a limitations statement aligned to the project brief.

Create a 5–7 slide deck for non-specialists that translates model outputs into 2–3 actionable recommendations, with one slide explicitly communicating uncertainty (e.g., CI, error bands, or scenario range) and one slide stating constraints/turning points.
Apply a quality-assurance checklist to verify unit consistency, rounding rules, and calculation accuracy, and record at least 5 audit-log entries (what was checked, result, and any fix).
Use a structured feedback rubric to critique a sample report/deck (or a peer’s draft) and implement at least 2 concrete revisions that improve clarity, transparency, or evidential support.

activities.title: Capstone communication target: what “done” looks like
activities.description: Self-study orientation to the lesson deliverable: a concise report section plus a short slide deck for non-specialists. Learners review success criteria tied to professional integrity (assumptions/limitations), diligence (units/rounding checks), and collaboration (responding to critique). Learners download templates and skim the rubric.
activities.teachingMethod: Short pre-recorded video + rubric walkthrough + quick LMS checklist confirmation.
resources: Report template (1–2 page section template: Findings/Recommendations/Limitations)
Slide deck template (5–7 slides with placeholders for visuals/uncertainty/constraints)
Marking rubric (clarity, evidence, transparency, visuals, actionability)
QA checklist (units, rounding, assumptions, CI interpretation, chart labeling)
instructorActions: Provide a brief video clarifying audience (non-specialists), required components, and common failure modes (missing units, hidden assumptions, overstated certainty).
Post downloadable templates and a rubric annotated with examples of ‘meets’ vs ‘exceeds’.
Set expectations for evidence: each recommendation must cite at least one metric/visual/model output.
studentActions: Download templates/rubric/QA checklist.
Identify the primary audience persona (e.g., operations manager) and write a one-sentence purpose statement for their deck/report.

activities.title: Micro-lesson: communicating uncertainty, assumptions, constraints, and CI to non-specialists
activities.description: Learners study a focused lesson on ethical reporting: distinguishing statistical vs model uncertainty, writing assumptions vs constraints, and explaining confidence intervals (CI) without jargon. Includes guidance on chart titles, axis units, and plain-language qualifiers (e.g., ‘estimated’, ‘likely range’).
activities.teachingMethod: Interactive reading with embedded knowledge checks (auto-marked) and 2 short rewrite examples (before/after).
resources: Interactive notes: Assumption vs constraint vs limitation
CI explainer (95% CI interpretation + common misstatements)
Visual labeling guide (units, sources, time windows, sample size)
Rewrite examples: overconfident claim vs transparent claim
instructorActions: Include 2–3 ‘translation’ examples turning technical output into stakeholder-ready statements.
Emphasize integrity: state what the model does NOT capture and where uncertainty is highest.
Provide a mini-glossary for key terms: constraint, assumption, CI.
studentActions: Complete embedded checks (e.g., identify whether a statement is an assumption or constraint).
Rewrite two claims from technical to non-specialist language including uncertainty phrasing.

activities.title: Annotated exemplar: how to integrate visuals, turning points, and constraints into a narrative
activities.description: Learners review an exemplar report section and slide deck with annotations showing: where units appear, how turning points are described (e.g., capacity threshold), how constraints are surfaced, and how uncertainty/CI is visualized and interpreted. Includes a short ‘spot-the-issue’ task (find 5 problems in a flawed slide).
activities.teachingMethod: Walkthrough video + clickable annotations + short diagnostic task with automated feedback.
resources: Exemplar report section (PDF) with margin notes
Flawed slide exercise (missing units, misleading CI, unclear takeaway)
instructorActions: Model the reasoning chain: data → metric → visual → interpretation → recommendation → implication.
Highlight turning points/thresholds and link them to constraints (budget, capacity, SLA).
Show a transparent calculation log snippet (what changed, why, and impact on outputs).
studentActions: Take notes using a provided ‘Narrative Planner’ (claim, evidence, qualifier, action).
Complete the ‘spot-the-issue’ task and compare to the answer key.

activities.title: Build: draft Findings + Recommendations with evidence and transparency
activities.description: Learners draft their own 1–2 page section (or the equivalent block inside their capstone report): 2–3 key findings, 2–3 recommendations, each tied to at least one visual or model output. Must explicitly include (a) units, (b) assumptions, (c) constraints, (d) one uncertainty statement (e.g., CI or scenario range), and (e) limitations. Learners also identify at least one turning point (threshold where decision changes).
activities.teachingMethod: Guided writing with prompts + template completion + optional sentence starters.
resources: Learner’s own project dataset/model outputs (Excel/Python exports)
instructorActions: Provide prompts that force specificity (e.g., ‘What decision should change? By how much? Under what condition?’).
Encourage tight structure: each paragraph begins with a takeaway, not a method description.
Remind learners to document rounding and units at the point of use (tables, axes, and text).
studentActions: Draft 2–3 findings and 2–3 recommendations with linked evidence.
Add an ‘Assumptions & Constraints’ box and a ‘Limitations & Uncertainty’ box.
Mark one turning point/threshold and explain its operational meaning.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 1: QA + audit log, then Formative Assessment 2: feedback and revision
activities.description: Two-part formative sequence. Part A: learners run a QA checklist on their draft (units, labels, CI wording, rounding, consistency between text and visuals) and create/update an audit log with at least 5 entries. Part B: learners apply a feedback rubric to either (i) a peer draft via discussion board exchange, or (ii) a provided ‘near-miss’ sample if peers are unavailable. Learners then implement at least 2 revisions and record what changed and why.
activities.teachingMethod: Checklist-driven self-assessment + rubric-based peer/simulated review + targeted revision loop.
resources: Audit log template (date, item checked, issue found, fix, impact)
Feedback rubric (clarity, evidence, transparency, visuals, actionability)
Peer review protocol (2 strengths, 2 questions, 2 suggestions)
instructorActions: Provide clear pass criteria for QA (e.g., ‘no unlabeled axes’, ‘every metric has units’, ‘CI interpretation statement included’).
Moderate or seed discussion board threads with example feedback that is specific and respectful.
Require revision notes: each change must reference feedback or QA finding (traceability).
studentActions: Complete QA checklist and write at least 5 audit-log entries.
Give rubric-based feedback to a peer OR critique the near-miss sample using the rubric.
Revise draft and add a short ‘revision note’ list (minimum 2 implemented changes).

activities.title: Polish: assemble the slide deck + final self-check and reflection
activities.description: Learners finalize a 5–7 slide deck that aligns with the report narrative. Slides must include: (1) context/problem, (2) key findings visual, (3) turning point/constraint slide, (4) uncertainty/CI slide, (5) recommendations with expected impact and conditions. Learners complete a final self-check and write a brief reflection on one integrity choice they made (e.g., a limitation they disclosed) and one diligence action (e.g., unit correction).
activities.teachingMethod: Template-based production + submission checklist + short reflection prompt.
resources: Final submission checklist (alignment, labeling, uncertainty, assumptions, constraints)
instructorActions: Provide a final checklist emphasizing alignment: no slide claim without evidence; no evidence without interpretation.
Suggest time-boxing for polishing (avoid endless formatting).
Offer optional ‘accessibility’ guidance (font sizes, color contrast, alt text for charts).
studentActions: Assemble and polish the deck with required slides and labels.
Complete final checklist and a 3–5 sentence reflection.
Save/export in required format (PDF/PPT) and ensure links to data/model outputs are traceable.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this as a create-level lesson by forcing learners to produce authentic artifacts (report section + slide deck) and to iterate based on critique. Emphasize professional integrity: learners must distinguish assumptions (chosen simplifications), constraints (hard limits like capacity/budget/policy), and limitations (what the analysis cannot conclude). Require uncertainty communication (e.g., CI or scenario ranges) and prohibit overclaiming; use explicit language models (‘estimated’, ‘within the observed range’, ‘based on n=…’). Build diligence through a mandatory QA checklist and an audit log; treat the audit log as an assessable practice for transparency and repeatability. Support collaboration in an online self-study context via structured peer review (or a robust solo alternative using a near-miss sample) with a rubric and required revision notes. Throughout, keep the audience non-specialist: prioritize interpretation, decision thresholds/turning points, and actionable recommendations over methods. Encourage evidence chaining: every recommendation should trace to a metric/visual/model output and note conditions under which it holds.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Time-box production to prevent learners getting stuck on formatting: (1) draft content first (claims + evidence + qualifiers), (2) then visuals, (3) then slide polish. If learners are behind at minute 45, direct them to complete only two findings and two recommendations but ensure they still include assumptions, constraints, and one uncertainty statement. If ahead, add an extra improvement cycle: tighten slide titles into takeaway statements and add a sensitivity/scenario note to the uncertainty slide. Encourage a strict ‘one pass QA’ before peer feedback, then a short ‘two-change minimum’ revision sprint after feedback.
adaptationOptions: Solo pathway (no peers available): use the provided near-miss sample for rubric critique, then apply the same rubric to self-assess and revise your own work.
Scaffolded writing supports: provide sentence frames for recommendations (Action + Impact + Conditions + Evidence) and a word bank for uncertainty language.
Reduced cognitive load: allow learners to start from a partially completed template with placeholders for units, assumptions, constraints, and CI interpretation.
Extension for advanced learners: add a one-slide appendix explaining method choices (e.g., why a CI was computed, or why a constraint binds) while keeping the main deck non-technical.
Accessibility adjustments: offer high-contrast slide themes, guidance on colorblind-safe palettes, and require descriptive chart titles/alt text for visuals.
Language support: allow learners to submit a brief glossary box translating 5 technical terms into plain language for stakeholders.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing assumptions with constraints (e.g., treating ‘demand is stable’ as a constraint rather than a simplifying assumption).
Misinterpreting a 95% CI as ‘95% chance the true value is in this interval’ without clarifying the frequentist meaning or the practical takeaway.
Overstating conclusions (implying causation from correlation, or claiming certainty from a model estimate).
Omitting units on axes/tables or mixing units (e.g., per day vs per week) leading to incorrect comparisons or recommendations.
Treating visuals as decoration rather than evidence (charts without a stated takeaway, or takeaways not supported by the chart).
Ignoring turning points/thresholds (e.g., capacity limits) and presenting linear recommendations that fail when constraints bind.
Rounding inconsistently (text vs table vs chart) so figures appear contradictory or untrustworthy.
Hiding limitations in vague language (‘data issues’) instead of stating specific impacts (missing periods, small n, measurement error).
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption in your analysis has the greatest potential to change your recommendation? How would you test or monitor it in the workplace?
What is your key turning point (threshold) where the best decision changes? How would you explain it to a non-specialist in one sentence?
Where is uncertainty highest in your outputs, and how will you show it (CI, scenario band, sensitivity table) without overwhelming the audience?
Pick one recommendation: what evidence supports it, what constraint could block it, and what ‘next data’ would reduce uncertainty?
What is one place you could unintentionally mislead a stakeholder (through units, rounding, or chart choice), and how will you prevent that?

lessons.lessonTitle: Uncertainty using confidence intervals, distributions or ...
objectives: Construct a 95% confidence interval (CI) for a workplace metric (e.g., defect rate, mean cycle time) in Excel or Python, stating the distribution/assumptions used and reporting units and rounding rules.

Create a reproducible analysis workbook/notebook that separates Inputs, Assumptions, Calculations, and Outputs, includes a transparent calculation log (e.g., parameter table, formula map, code cells), and can be rerun to reproduce identical results (including fixed random seed where applicable).
Evaluate uncertainty using either (a) an analytical CI, (b) distribution fitting, or (c) Monte Carlo simulation, and compare at least two methods for consistency and limitations.

Write a balanced risk statement (3–6 sentences) that interprets uncertainty for a non-specialist stakeholder, explicitly listing limitations, confidence level, key assumptions, and at least two practical mitigations.
Implement at least three diligence checks (units check, reasonableness check, and sensitivity/spot-check) and document the outcome of each check in the workbook/notebook.

activities.title: Capstone Setup: What “reproducible + transparent” looks like

activities.title: Uncertainty toolkit refresher: CI types, assumptions, and integrity cues
activities.description: Interactive mini-lesson covering: interpreting CI correctly; selecting CI approach (z/t for mean, CI for proportion, bootstrap, or simulation); when normality is reasonable; what to disclose (sample size, missing data, independence); and how to avoid misleading certainty (rounding, significant figures, units).

activities.title: Demonstration: Building a traceable CI + optional simulation in Excel/Python

activities.title: Guided build: Create your uncertainty section (CI/distribution/simulation) + checks
activities.description: Learners build their own uncertainty analysis end-to-end: compute CI (or simulation interval), produce a simple visual (e.g., histogram of simulated outcomes, error bars), and implement three diligence checks with documentation. Includes prompts to compare two methods when possible (e.g., analytic CI vs bootstrap).

Include ‘if-then’ guidance: if n is small or data skewed, recommend t/bootstrapping or transformation and disclosure.

Add/confirm at least 3 documented assumptions and 3 documented checks (what was checked + outcome).
Generate one visual that supports the risk interpretation (CI bar, distribution plot, or simulation histogram).

activities.title: Case analysis: Turn uncertainty into a balanced risk statement + mitigations
activities.description: Learners translate their computed uncertainty into a short stakeholder-facing risk statement. They must include: confidence level, what parameter the interval refers to, key limitations, and at least two practical mitigations (process changes, data collection improvements, buffer/contingency, monitoring).
activities.teachingMethod: Worked examples + structured writing frame (fill-in template), then apply to their own project context.
resources: Risk statement writing frame (prompt + sentence stems)
Examples: good vs misleading risk statements (annotated)
instructorActions: Provide examples that avoid overclaiming and explicitly note limitations (sampling bias, seasonality, independence).
Prompt learners to align mitigations with the dominant uncertainty driver (measurement noise vs model uncertainty vs process variability).
studentActions: Draft a 3–6 sentence risk statement in the Outputs section of their workbook/notebook.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 1: Uncertainty method and interpretation check
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz focusing on CI interpretation, method selection, and identifying missing disclosures. Includes one item where learners choose the correct risk statement from options.
activities.teachingMethod: Auto-graded LMS quiz with immediate feedback and targeted remediation links.
resources: Remediation links to the mini-lesson sections
instructorActions: Configure feedback keyed to misconceptions (e.g., CI meaning, t vs z, normality assumptions).
Use item analytics to identify widespread issues for a follow-up announcement.

activities.title: Formative Assessment 2: Reproducibility + audit trail submission and self-review
activities.description: Learners run a final self-audit using a short rubric: reproduce results from a fresh run (or reopened Excel), confirm fixed seed for simulation, verify units/rounding, and ensure the calculation log is complete. They submit a ‘checkpoint’ export (PDF + file) or a link (notebook) depending on platform.
activities.teachingMethod: Rubric-based self-assessment with a required evidence checklist; optional peer forum post for feedback.
resources: Submission checklist (file naming, version, run instructions)
instructorActions: Provide clear pass criteria for the checkpoint (e.g., can a third party rerun it?).
Offer a ‘minimum acceptable’ example submission and a ‘gold standard’ example.
studentActions: Re-run their analysis (or refresh calculations) and confirm outputs match prior results.
Submit the checkpoint artefact and (optional) post one question or improvement idea in the forum.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the lesson around authentic workplace reporting standards: uncertainty is not an afterthought but a decision-support feature. Require learners to (1) show method choice, (2) document assumptions/limitations, and (3) produce an interpretable risk statement with mitigations. In self-study delivery, embed frequent ‘pause-and-apply’ prompts and provide templates that enforce structure (separate Inputs/Assumptions/Calculations/Outputs/Log). Emphasise professional integrity: learners must avoid overstating certainty, must disclose when assumptions are weak (small n, non-random samples, seasonality), and must keep an audit trail (date/version, data source, parameter settings, random seed). Encourage two-method triangulation when feasible (analytic CI + bootstrap/simulation) to build healthy skepticism and improve checking behaviour. Give concrete exemplars of good documentation: naming conventions, unit labeling, rounding policy, and explicit limitations phrased for non-specialists. Where possible, include automated feedback keyed to common errors (SE vs SD, wrong distribution, missing n, CI misinterpretation).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 30 minutes moving (setup + refresher + demo) so learners reach hands-on creation quickly. Insert explicit pause points in the demo at: (a) CI computed, (b) assumptions table populated, (c) log completed—learners should not proceed until each is done. The 25-minute build is the core; suggest learners spend ~15 minutes getting a correct interval and ~10 minutes on checks/visual/log. If learners finish early, prompt extension: add bootstrap/simulation validation, add sensitivity to key inputs, or rewrite the risk statement for two different stakeholders (operations vs finance). If learners fall behind, allow them to use the provided sample dataset to complete the workflow first, then swap in their own data later.
adaptationOptions: Tool pathway choice: provide parallel instructions for Excel-only learners and Python learners; allow submission in either format if it meets reproducibility criteria.
Scaffolding: offer a ‘minimum viable’ CI route (analytic t/z CI) and an advanced route (bootstrap/simulation + comparison).
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for videos, screen-reader-friendly PDFs, and high-contrast template formatting; ensure charts have descriptive titles and alt-text guidance.
Math support: include an optional refresher on standard error vs standard deviation and on proportion vs mean intervals with extra practice items.
Challenge extension: require two uncertainty methods (analytic + bootstrap), include a short sensitivity analysis (±10% on key input), and add a brief recommendation section tied to mitigations.
Pacing support: provide a time-boxed checklist and a ‘common fixes’ troubleshooting guide for learners who get stuck on functions, degrees of freedom, or simulation setup.
commonMisconceptions: Interpreting a 95% CI as ‘there is a 95% chance the true value is in this specific computed interval’ rather than a long-run procedure statement.
Using standard deviation instead of standard error in the CI formula (or forgetting the sqrt(n) term).
Defaulting to a z-interval regardless of small sample sizes or unknown population variance (ignoring t-distribution).
Assuming normality automatically without checking context (skewed data, outliers, bounded rates) or without disclosing the assumption.
Reporting CI endpoints without units, or mixing units (e.g., minutes vs hours) across inputs and outputs.
Over-rounding or under-rounding in a way that changes interpretation (e.g., rounding CI endpoints to whole units when precision matters, or showing excessive decimals implying false certainty).
Treating simulation outputs as deterministic while failing to set a random seed or record simulation parameters (number of trials, distribution choice).
Believing ‘narrow CI = model is correct’ without considering bias, measurement error, or non-representative sampling.
Hiding limitations to make results look stronger, instead of practicing transparent reporting and mitigations.
discussionPrompts: Your CI is wide. What are two plausible drivers (data quantity, process variability, measurement noise, sampling bias), and which mitigations would you propose for each?
Which assumption in your analysis is the riskiest (most likely to be violated)? How would violating it change the decision?
Write two versions of your risk statement: one for an operations manager and one for a finance stakeholder. What changes and what stays the same?
When would you choose bootstrap/simulation over an analytic CI in a workplace setting? Provide a concrete example.
What does ‘reproducible’ mean for your chosen tool (Excel or Python), and what evidence would convince an auditor that your results are traceable and honest?

lessons.lessonTitle: A reproducible Excel or Python workbook solving a workpla...
objectives: By the end of the lesson, learners will compile a reproducible Excel workbook or Python notebook that runs end-to-end without manual rework (e.g., no hidden steps), producing final outputs (price/optimal decision/quality summary) from raw inputs in ≤2 clicks (Excel: Refresh/Calculate; Python: Run All).

By the end of the lesson, learners will document at least 6 explicit assumptions (including units, data source, time period, constraints, rounding rule, and model limitations) in a dedicated ‘Assumptions & Limitations’ section and cross-reference them in calculations/outputs.

By the end of the lesson, learners will create one confidence interval (CI) relevant to their project (e.g., mean defect rate, mean cycle time, demand estimate) and interpret it correctly in plain language for a non-specialist audience.

By the end of the lesson, learners will produce a concise deliverable set: (a) a ≤1-page technical summary and (b) a 3–5 slide deck including at least 2 visuals, with clearly labeled axes, units, and a stated limitation/uncertainty statement.

By the end of the lesson, learners will apply structured peer feedback (or rubric-based self-review if working solo) to implement at least 3 concrete improvements (e.g., clearer units, corrected formula, added audit trail, improved chart labeling), documented in a change log.

activities.title: Capstone Build Target: What ‘Reproducible + Auditable’ Means
activities.description: Self-study orientation to the lesson’s output: a single workbook/notebook that can be audited. Learners review a short checklist covering integrity (honest uncertainty), diligence (units/assumptions checks), and collaboration (inviting challenge, integrating feedback). Learners select which project track they’re completing (pricing, optimisation, or quality).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture video + downloadable checklist; learners pause to select their project track and confirm required outputs.
instructorActions: Provide an explicit definition of reproducibility (run end-to-end from raw inputs) and auditability (traceable steps, clear assumptions).
Explain minimum evidence expected: inputs, calculation trail, outputs, and uncertainty/limitations.
Offer track-specific examples (pricing/optimisation/quality) without prescribing a single solution.
studentActions: Choose a project track and open their current draft workbook/notebook.
Download the checklist and mark current status (green/yellow/red) for each item.
Write a one-sentence ‘build target’ (e.g., ‘Run All produces updated optimal plan + chart + CI summary’).

activities.title: Demonstration: Setting Up Traceable Calculations (Excel or Python)
activities.description: Guided demonstration of how to structure work so another person can follow and reproduce it. Excel path: inputs sheet, calc sheet, outputs/dashboard sheet, named ranges, cell comments, and a calculation log tab. Python path: parameter cell, data import, cleaning, analysis, visuals, and an ‘Assumptions’ markdown section; ensure deterministic outputs (seeds if needed).
activities.teachingMethod: Walkthrough video with pause points; learners mirror the structure in their own file.
resources: Short guide: ‘Units, Rounding, and Naming Conventions’
instructorActions: Model a clean file structure and naming convention (tabs/sections clearly labeled).
Demonstrate at least one traceability technique (Excel: precedents/dependents; Python: function blocks + comments).
Highlight where and how to record assumptions (not buried in code/cells).
studentActions: Restructure their project file into Inputs → Calculations → Outputs (and Log) sections.
Add labels and units to all key inputs and outputs.
Create/insert an ‘Assumptions & Limitations’ section (even if incomplete).

activities.title: Build Sprint 1: Make the Model Run End-to-End
activities.description: Focused build time. Learners implement or repair the end-to-end workflow: from raw inputs to final outputs. Emphasis on removing hidden steps (manual edits, hard-coded values, copied results). Learners add a ‘Change Log’ entry for each major fix.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided practice with a step list; learners stop at checkpoints and compare to a rubric.
resources: Optional: Excel Solver setup guide / Python optimisation or stats snippet pack
instructorActions: Provide checkpoint criteria (what should be visible/working by minute 10/20/25).
Offer common fix patterns (replace hard-coding with references/parameters; validate units).
Encourage learners to add brief comments explaining non-obvious formulas or code blocks.
studentActions: Run the full workflow (Excel: recalc/refresh; Python: Run All) and confirm outputs update from inputs.
Remove or flag hard-coded constants (convert to parameters; label units).
Record at least 2 changes in a Change Log (what changed + why + impact).

activities.title: Quality Check: Units, Assumptions, and Error Traps
activities.description: Learners perform a structured audit pass: unit consistency, rounding policy, assumption completeness, and simple error traps (sanity checks, boundary checks, and ‘does this number make sense?’ checks).
activities.teachingMethod: Self-check protocol using a checklist and automated tests where possible (Excel data validation; Python assertions).
resources: Optional: Python assertion examples / Excel data validation examples

Explain that transparent limitations are part of integrity (state what you cannot conclude).
studentActions: Add at least 3 error traps (e.g., conditional formatting for impossible values; assertion for non-negative quantities).
Complete the Assumptions table to at least 6 items, each with a short justification.
Confirm and document a rounding rule (where applied and why).

activities.description: Short pause to reduce cognitive load; learners step away briefly before writing and visual design tasks.
activities.teachingMethod: Timed break with a reminder of the next deliverable: report + slides for non-specialists.
resources: Timer prompt (built into the LMS page)
instructorActions: Prompt learners to return with one priority: explain results clearly to a non-specialist.
studentActions: Take a break; return ready to write and simplify.

activities.title: Build Sprint 2: CI + Visuals + Plain-Language Interpretation
activities.description: Learners add one confidence interval (CI) relevant to their project, generate at least two visuals, and write plain-language interpretations (what it means, what it does not mean). Focus on labeling (units, time period) and stating limitations/uncertainty transparently.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided build with exemplars; learners implement and then paraphrase for non-specialists.
resources: Chart checklist (titles, units, axes, source notes)
Example phrases: ‘What we can conclude / cannot conclude’
instructorActions: Provide one CI example per track (pricing/demand estimate; optimisation performance measure; quality defect rate/time).

Create at least two visuals (e.g., trend, histogram, sensitivity, before/after comparison) with correct labeling.

activities.title: Formative Review: Rubric-Based Peer Feedback (or Solo Self-Review) and Revision Plan
activities.description: Learners conduct a structured review using a simplified rubric. If a peer forum is available, they exchange one screenshot + link/file and provide feedback using ‘Glow/Grow’ plus one specific question challenging an assumption. If working solo, they do a rubric-based self-review and generate a revision plan. Learners implement at least 3 improvements and record them in the Change Log.
activities.teachingMethod: Asynchronous forum post (preferred) or self-review worksheet; focus on collaborative behaviours (explain reasoning, welcome challenge, integrate feedback).
instructorActions: Provide norms for professional critique (specific, evidence-based, respectful).
Offer sample feedback stems (e.g., ‘I can trace X to Y, but I can’t trace Z because…’).
Encourage learners to ask one assumption-challenge question.
studentActions: Post one draft artifact (screenshot + short summary + one question) or complete the solo self-review.
Provide feedback to at least one peer (if available) or simulate peer review by applying the rubric strictly to their own work.
Implement ≥3 improvements and document them in the Change Log (before/after notes).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: This lesson sits at Bloom ‘create’: learners must produce an integrated, reproducible artefact plus communication deliverables. Keep the emphasis on (1) traceability (auditable steps), (2) integrity (explicit uncertainty/limitations), and (3) diligence (units, assumptions, checks). For online self-study, structure content into short demonstrations followed by build sprints with clear checkpoints and tangible outputs. Encourage learners to externalize reasoning: label inputs, comment complex steps, and write interpretations aimed at non-specialists. Reinforce that a correct-looking answer is insufficient if it cannot be reproduced or audited. When facilitating asynchronously, prioritize quick, rubric-aligned feedback on a small number of high-impact issues (units, hard-coding, missing assumptions, misinterpreted CI) rather than rewriting the learner’s solution. Provide exemplars of ‘good enough’ documentation so learners don’t over-document trivial steps while under-documenting key assumptions and limitations.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Use time-boxing: learners should not spend more than 25 minutes perfecting calculations before moving to traceability and documentation. If a learner is stuck on optimisation/statistics implementation, they should (a) freeze the model version, (b) document the limitation, and (c) proceed to reporting with what works, then return for refinement. Fast finishers: add sensitivity analysis (e.g., varying key parameters) and update visuals/interpretation accordingly. Learners behind pace: use the provided template and focus on minimum viable reproducibility—inputs labeled, calculations traceable, one CI, two correctly labeled charts, and a brief limitation statement.
adaptationOptions: Excel-only pathway: provide an ‘Audit-Ready Template.xlsx’ with pre-built tabs (Inputs/Calcs/Outputs/Assumptions/Change Log) and optional Solver setup notes; reduce coding load.
Python-only pathway: provide a notebook scaffold with headings, function placeholders, and a ‘Run All’ validation cell; learners fill in analysis steps.

Reduced math complexity option: allow learners to use a simpler model (e.g., linear pricing equation or single-metric quality CI) provided they meet reproducibility, documentation, and reporting requirements.
Accessibility support: provide narrated captions/transcripts for demos; offer a text-only step list; ensure templates are screen-reader friendly (clear headings, logical tab order).
Confidence-building option: provide a worked example dataset so learners can test the pipeline before swapping in their own data.
Challenge extension: require a second uncertainty statement (e.g., scenario range or bootstrap CI) and a brief sensitivity chart showing which assumptions most affect the result.
commonMisconceptions: ‘Reproducible’ means the file opens successfully—rather than producing the final outputs from raw inputs without manual steps or hidden edits.
Hard-coded values in formulas/code are acceptable ‘because they came from the data’—instead of parameterizing and labeling them with units and source.
Confidence intervals mean ‘most data points fall in this range’ rather than ‘the true parameter (e.g., mean) is likely in this range under assumptions.’
If Solver/optimiser returns a solution, it must be correct—ignoring constraints, infeasibility, local optima, or unrealistic assumptions.
Units can be inferred from context—leading to mixing monthly vs yearly, minutes vs hours, or currency vs currency-per-unit without noticing.
Rounding is purely cosmetic—rather than affecting decisions, totals, and audit trails (and needing a stated rule).
A report for non-specialists should remove uncertainty to sound confident—rather than stating limitations transparently as part of professional integrity.
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption, if wrong, would most change your decision/recommendation? How would you test or monitor it at work?
Show one output number and trace it back to the raw input(s). Where could an auditor get confused, and how will you fix that?
Write your CI interpretation in one sentence for a non-specialist. What does it NOT mean?
If a stakeholder challenges your result (e.g., ‘That price seems too high’ or ‘That defect rate seems too low’), what evidence in your workbook/notebook supports your reasoning?
What is one limitation you will state explicitly on your slides, and what is the practical impact of that limitation on decision-making?
What feedback did you receive (or what did the rubric reveal) that led to the biggest improvement in clarity or correctness?

activities.title: Build: One-page technical report draft (non-specialist but precise)

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Keep the lesson anchored to a decision a non-specialist must make. Treat mathematics as evidence, not the story: learners should lead with a claim, support it with quantified evidence (with units), and include caveats (assumptions, limitations, uncertainty).

Reinforce professional integrity explicitly: (1) separate what is observed vs modelled, (2) report uncertainty (CI) in plain language, (3) avoid causal language unless justified, (4) document assumptions and constraints that could change the recommendation.

Support diligence with required micro-checks: unit checks, rounding rationale, and a traceable calculation log. Encourage an audit mindset: every reported figure should be reproducible from a referenced cell/formula or code output.

Model collaborative behaviours in an asynchronous format by using structured feedback tools: a rubric, comment bank, and required revision log. Emphasise that responding to critique is part of the deliverable quality, not an add-on.

When learners struggle, ask: 'What decision does the manager need to make on Monday morning?' and 'What would change your recommendation?' These questions naturally elicit constraints, assumptions, and sensitivity to uncertainty.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
If learners are behind: prioritise (a) completing the one-page report with units/assumptions/CI/constraint, then (b) converting it into 5 slides. The deck can reuse text from the report, but the report should not be a copy of the slides.

If learners are ahead: add a sensitivity note (e.g., how the recommendation changes if demand is ±10%) or add a second visual only if it reduces ambiguity. Extend the revision log to include a brief 'before/after' screenshot of one improved slide.

Suggested timeboxing within long activities: during the 25-minute report build, spend 10 minutes on structure headings, 10 minutes on results + uncertainty, 5 minutes on assumptions/constraints/rounding checks. During the 15-minute deck build, spend 3 minutes per slide with a hard stop.

Encourage learners to stop at the end of each build activity and run the checklist once rather than perfecting wording too early.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded templates: provide a 'fill-in-the-blanks' report version for learners who need more structure; provide an 'open' template for advanced learners.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for videos; allow submissions as narrated slides, text-only report with embedded chart image, or screen-reader-friendly documents.
Tool flexibility: allow Excel-only (charts + Solver outputs + CI from formulas) or Python (pandas summaries + CI + matplotlib) as long as units and audit trail are clear.
Reduced cognitive load option: learners use the provided dataset/model output pack rather than their own capstone data if they are still assembling inputs.

Extension for advanced learners: include a brief methods appendix (≤150 words) describing the optimisation/statistical approach and why it is appropriate, plus one additional limitation about model form or data quality.
Language support: provide sentence starters for recommendations, limitations, and CI phrasing; provide a glossary with plain-language definitions of constraint/assumption/CI.
commonMisconceptions: Treating a confidence interval as a guarantee that future values will fall within the interval, or confusing CI with data range/standard deviation.
Reporting point estimates without uncertainty, limitations, or assumptions (implying unjustified certainty).
Mixing units (e.g., per hour vs per day, $ vs $,000) or omitting units on charts/axes and in text.
Over-precision: copying many decimals from spreadsheets rather than rounding to decision-appropriate precision and stating rounding rules.
Claiming causation from correlational operational data or from a fitted model without appropriate justification.
Hiding key constraints (capacity, budget, service level) until the end, or not explaining how constraints shape the recommendation.
Assuming Solver/optimisation output is automatically valid without checking feasibility, boundary solutions, or sensitivity to assumptions.
Using visuals that look 'technical' but are not interpretable by non-specialists (unclear titles, no takeaway, cluttered legends).
Not maintaining an audit trail (reported numbers cannot be traced back to a calculation, cell, or code output).
Treating feedback as subjective preference rather than evidence of audience needs; revising wording without fixing underlying clarity/correctness issues.
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption in your model/report would most change the recommendation if it were wrong? How will you disclose it clearly?
What is the main constraint in your scenario (capacity, budget, quality, time)? How does it shape the feasible solution space?
Write one sentence that explains your confidence interval to a non-specialist. What misunderstanding might they still have?
Where could unit errors occur in your workflow (data import, conversion, charting, Solver inputs)? What checks will you implement?
What is one limitation you are tempted to omit because it weakens the recommendation? How can you state it professionally without undermining trust?
If a peer challenged your result as 'too optimistic,' what evidence would you show first (data trend, turning point, sensitivity, CI)?
What would you remove from your slides to make the message clearer while keeping the analysis honest and transparent?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson to produce a tangible capstone artefact: an audit-ready ‘Uncertainty & Risk’ section. Keep the cognitive focus at Bloom ‘create’ by having learners build within their own project file rather than only reproducing a worked example.

Emphasise professional integrity throughout:
- Separate calculation from interpretation. Require learners to label units, sample size, confidence level/iteration count, and data window next to every output.
- Model cautious, defensible language (e.g., ‘We estimate…’, ‘Under the assumption…’, ‘This does not account for…’). Explicitly prohibit overconfident claims (e.g., ‘We are 95% sure the mean is exactly…’).
- Make assumptions visible at the point of use: each distribution choice, parameter estimate, and independence/representativeness claim should appear in an Assumptions table and be referenced in the narrative.

Support reproducibility and auditability:
- In Excel: encourage named ranges, consistent tab structure (Inputs → Calculations → Outputs → Log), and a Calculation Log that records method/version/date.
- In Python: require a fixed random seed for simulation, clear function blocks, and a single ‘Run all’ path that regenerates outputs.

Feedback should prioritise: (1) missing units/labels, (2) undocumented assumptions, (3) incorrect CI interpretation, (4) rounding too early, and (5) non-reproducible simulation settings.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
If learners are behind: recommend the minimum viable deliverable—produce one CI (mean or proportion) plus a complete risk statement with assumptions/limitations/mitigations; postpone simulation to the next session.

If learners are on track: complete CI plus a basic Monte Carlo simulation (1,000–5,000 iterations) and add a simple percentile summary (P5/P50/P95) chart.

If learners are advanced: add sensitivity analysis (one-way or tornado chart), compare CI vs simulation results, and refine the narrative for a non-technical stakeholder (two-paragraph executive summary + technical appendix note).

Timeboxing tip for self-study: stop building at minute ~70 and reserve the final 20 minutes for self-audit and writing; most integrity issues are reporting/documentation, not computation.
adaptationOptions: Excel-first pathway: provide a partially completed workbook with placeholders for CI inputs, simulation parameters, and a pre-formatted risk statement table.
Python-first pathway: provide a notebook scaffold with function stubs (ci_mean(), simulate_profit()) and TODO markers for assumptions and narrative text.
Low-confidence learners: restrict to one uncertainty method (CI only) and use a guided template with sentence starters and a completed example to imitate.
High-confidence learners: require both a CI and a simulation, plus a short comparison explaining why results differ and which is more decision-relevant.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for demos, high-contrast templates, and allow submissions as PDF exports plus a text risk statement.
Different project contexts: offer three mini-datasets (quality, pricing, operations) so learners can match uncertainty methods to their capstone theme.
Support for math gaps: include an optional remedial micro-lesson on t vs z, standard error, and the difference between CI for mean vs prediction interval.
commonMisconceptions: Interpreting a 95% confidence interval as: ‘there is a 95% probability the true mean is in this particular interval’ (instead of a long-run method statement).
Assuming a confidence interval predicts where the next observation will fall (confusing CI with a prediction interval).
Believing a narrower CI is always ‘better’ without considering bias, data quality, or violated assumptions.
Using normal-based CI formulas automatically, even with small n, skewed data, or non-independent samples.
Treating Monte Carlo simulation output as ‘truth’ without documenting distribution choices, parameter uncertainty, or random seed/reproducibility.
Rounding intermediate calculations (inflates error and makes audit trails inconsistent).
Mixing units (e.g., monthly vs annual demand; percent vs proportion; dollars vs thousands of dollars) and then interpreting results as comparable.
Reporting a single point estimate without uncertainty while still making strong decisions or recommendations.
Failing to distinguish assumptions (chosen modelling simplifications) from limitations (constraints of data/method) and mitigations (actions to reduce risk).
discussionPrompts: When would a confidence interval be more appropriate than a simulation for your capstone problem, and why?
What is the single most decision-threatening assumption in your model (e.g., independence, representativeness, distribution shape), and how could you test or reduce that risk?
How would you explain your uncertainty result (CI or P5/P95) to a non-specialist manager in two sentences without overselling certainty?
If an auditor asked ‘Show me where this number came from,’ which part of your workbook/notebook provides the clearest traceability—and what is still missing?
What mitigation would you recommend if the downside scenario (e.g., P5 profit, upper CI defect rate) occurs, and what early indicator would you monitor?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson as a build-and-document session rather than a concept-only session. Keep the focus on observable artefacts: an Assumptions Register, a traceable calculation path, and a plain-language uncertainty/limitations statement. Model professional integrity explicitly: show how to avoid overstating certainty, how to phrase limitations without undermining credibility, and how to document what you did so someone else can reproduce it. For self-study delivery, provide: (1) templates, (2) an annotated exemplar, and (3) a rubric that converts abstract expectations (“transparent”) into checkable items (“units on all outputs/charts”, “assumptions table with sources”). Reinforce diligence through repeated micro-checks: units, rounding rules, and ‘60-second trace’ (can the learner locate the origin of each key number quickly). Reinforce collaboration behaviours by structuring critique: learners must point to evidence and propose a concrete improvement, and then record what they changed in response (version note/change log).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Timebox the guided build (25 min) with a ‘must-do first’ order: (1) create Assumptions Register, (2) label units/rounding on key outputs, (3) add calculation log/traceability, (4) add uncertainty/limitations. If learners finish early, offer stretch tasks: add a sensitivity table (best/base/worst), add a data validation check, or add a short ‘audit trail’ section (solver settings, data refresh timestamp). If learners are behind, allow a minimal submission: 3 assumptions + units on top 3 outputs + one clear limitation statement, then expand later.
adaptationOptions: Excel vs Python pathway: provide parallel templates (Excel tables + named ranges; Python Markdown tables + functions) so learners can meet the same objective in different tools.
Accessibility/low bandwidth: offer a text-based walkthrough with screenshots in place of video; ensure all templates are downloadable and screen-reader friendly.
Scaffold for struggling learners: provide a partially completed Assumptions Register with sentence starters (e.g., 'Assuming ___ because ___; if violated, output likely ___').
Extension for advanced learners: require a second uncertainty method (e.g., CI + scenario analysis) and a short note comparing which is more decision-relevant.
Language support: provide a glossary for key terms (assumption, documented assumptions, CI) and plain-language alternatives for technical phrases.
Confidence-building option: allow learners to critique only the exemplar (not share their own work) while still completing the revision step in their file.
commonMisconceptions: “Reproducible” means the file opens—rather than someone else being able to re-run the workflow and regenerate the same outputs with stated inputs/settings.

Confidence interval misunderstanding: treating a 95% CI as '95% probability the true value is in this specific interval' without clarifying the repeated-sampling interpretation (or using CI language at all).
Hiding assumptions in narrative text only, instead of documenting them in a structured register with units, sources, and impact.
Mixing or omitting units (e.g., dollars vs thousands of dollars; hours vs minutes) and then reporting results without unit labels.
Over-rounding intermediate calculations (causing drift) or rounding inconsistently between spreadsheet cells, charts, and written report.
Assuming Solver/optimisation output is 'the answer' without recording constraints, tolerances, or sensitivity to starting values.
Presenting limitations as an afterthought (‘data is limited’) instead of specifying what is limited and how it could affect the decision.
Treating peer feedback as subjective preference rather than evidence-based critique that can improve clarity, accuracy, and auditability.
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption, if wrong, would most change your recommendation? How would you test or monitor it in the workplace?
Pick one key number in your output: can you trace it back to a source and calculation path in under 60 seconds? What step is currently weakest?
Write a one-sentence explanation of your CI (or uncertainty range) for a non-specialist. What wording avoids overstating certainty?
What did you choose to exclude from the model (a limitation), and why was that reasonable given the project constraints?
If a colleague challenged your result, what evidence (logs, sources, units, version notes) would you show first?
What change did you make after critique, and how did it improve transparency or reproducibility?

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design this lesson to prioritise creation with integrity: learners are not just producing artefacts (report/deck) but demonstrating trustworthy quantitative communication. Use a “claim–evidence–qualifier” norm throughout: every recommendation must be paired with quantified evidence (with units) and a qualifier that states constraints, assumptions, and uncertainty. In self-study delivery, embed frequent checkpoints that force diligence (e.g., ‘units required’ fields, rounding rule fields, CI interpretation prompts) rather than relying on instructor observation.

Emphasise the difference between constraints (external limits that bind the solution, e.g., capacity, budget, regulatory thresholds) and assumptions (simplifications or choices, e.g., linearity, stationarity, normality, constant marginal cost). Require learners to explicitly label which is which. For uncertainty, coach learners to report confidence intervals as ranges for plausible values under stated assumptions, not as guarantees; model cautious language (‘consistent with’, ‘suggests’, ‘within X–Y range’).

To support collaborative behaviours in an online self-study format, simulate peer review with standardised reviewer prompts and require a change log. This makes the revision process visible and assessable (transparency) and encourages welcoming challenge.

When giving any instructor feedback (asynchronous), focus on: (1) unit and label correctness, (2) whether evidence directly supports the claim, (3) whether limitations could change the decision, and (4) whether visuals are interpretable by non-specialists (titles that answer a question, captions that state the takeaway).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 20 minutes brisk (exemplars + micro-lesson) to free time for production. If learners stall in analysis, direct them to extract only three ‘anchor facts’ first: one trend, one turning point/threshold, one binding constraint—each with a number and units—then build visuals from those. For the creation block, enforce a ‘summary-first’ workflow: draft the executive summary and recommendation in 5 minutes, then fill in evidence, visuals, and caveats. Reserve the final 10–15 minutes for revision; do not let drafting consume all time, as iteration is part of the learning outcome at the Create level.
adaptationOptions: Accessibility/tech option: provide both Excel and Google Sheets versions of templates; allow learners to submit visuals as screenshots if export tools are limited.
Scaffolded path (support): offer a partially completed report/deck with placeholders and sentence stems (e.g., ‘Given ___ (units), we recommend ___ because ___; however ___’).
Extension path (challenge): require an additional sensitivity check (e.g., alternative assumption or parameter) and a slide that compares outcomes under two scenarios with a brief risk note.
Language support: provide a glossary for key terms (constraint, assumption, CI, marginal change) and a bank of non-specialist synonyms (e.g., ‘limit’, ‘range’, ‘best estimate’).
Neurodiversity/time management: provide a timed checklist with micro-deadlines (e.g., ‘minute 35: three anchor facts completed’) and allow pausing the lesson with resume markers.
commonMisconceptions: Treating a constraint as an assumption (or vice versa), leading to incorrect statements about what can or cannot be changed operationally.
Interpreting a confidence interval as ‘the probability the true value is in this range’ without stating assumptions or the repeated-sampling meaning.
Overclaiming causation from observational trends (e.g., assuming a trend implies a policy caused the change) without qualifiers.
Omitting units in charts/tables or mixing unit bases (per day vs per week; dollars vs thousands) and then drawing incorrect comparisons.
Reporting excessive precision (too many decimals) or inconsistent rounding across tables and slides, creating apparent contradictions.
Equating ‘Solver found a solution’ with ‘the solution is feasible in the real world’ without checking binding constraints, model assumptions, or data quality.
Using visuals that look polished but are not interpretable (missing titles that answer a question, unlabeled axes, truncated scales that mislead).
discussionPrompts: What is the single most decision-relevant constraint in your scenario, and how did it shape (or limit) your recommendation?
Choose one figure in your deck: what is the non-specialist takeaway in one sentence, and what is the most important caveat (assumption/limitation) to state alongside it?
Where could a unit or rounding mistake most easily occur in your workflow, and what specific check did you use to prevent it?
How did you communicate uncertainty (e.g., CI, model error, data gaps) without undermining usefulness—what wording did you use?
If a stakeholder challenged your conclusion, what additional evidence or sensitivity check would you run first, and why?

resources: Short-response submission prompt + rubric (clarity, completeness, transparency)

activities.title: Wrap-up reflection: What evidence would convince an auditor?
activities.description: Learners complete a brief reflection checklist: identify one improvement to their audit trail, one sensitivity risk, and one limitation statement they would include in documentation. They optionally post one insight or question to the forum.
activities.teachingMethod: Metacognitive reflection to consolidate evaluation criteria and professional behaviours (welcoming challenge, integrating feedback).
instructorActions: Seed the forum with 2–3 model responses demonstrating constructive critique.
Summarize common issues in an announcement (e.g., rounding too early, missing units).
studentActions: Complete reflection checklist.
Optionally post one takeaway or one question for clarification.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Design intent (Evaluate level): Learners are not just performing checks; they must judge adequacy against stakeholder requirements and justify decisions with evidence. Make the ‘decision point’ explicit: a model can be calibrated yet still not fit-for-purpose.

Emphasize professional integrity and transparency:
- Require explicit limitation statements (what the model does NOT support) and uncertainty language that avoids false precision.
- Reward honest reporting of failed checks and corrective actions rather than ‘hiding’ issues.

Teach reproducibility as a habit, not a tool:
- If learners cannot use Git, use a manual versioning convention (v0.1, v0.2) and a change log. The learning goal is traceability and auditability.
- Require a minimal reproducibility package: inputs, assumptions, step-by-step run instructions, outputs, and a version identifier.

Quality-control thinking:
- Dimensional checks: focus on derived units and implicit conversions (e.g., hours vs seconds; kPa vs Pa; mm vs m).
- Tolerance checks: distinguish between measurement tolerance, acceptance tolerance, and numerical tolerance.
- Rounding: teach guard digits and rounding at the end; highlight when intermediate rounding biases tolerance pass/fail.

Feedback strategy (online self-study):
- Use immediate feedback for concept checks; use rubric-based feedback for the decision memo/README. Provide at least one annotated exemplar showing how to cite evidence.
- Use forum prompts to normalize challenge and correction (“Here is what I missed; here is what I changed”).
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions:
Keep early segments brisk to protect time for evaluation tasks:
- 0–10 min: Diagnostic only; do not reteach yet.
- 10–35 min: Micro-lecture + demo (25 min total). If learners struggle, direct them to the scaffolded lab path rather than extending lecture time.
- 35–60 min: Guided lab is the core. If time is tight, require sensitivity on 3 parameters only and provide a pre-filled template for one parameter as an example.
- 60–75 min: Case decision memo: timebox drafting (10 min) + quick self-check against rubric (5 min).
- 75–85 min: Formative assessment; if needed, allow completion after the 90-minute lesson as an asynchronous continuation.
- 85–90 min: Reflection—keep to 5 minutes; it is a closure habit, not a second assignment.

Optional extensions (outside 90 minutes): add multi-parameter sensitivity (e.g., tornado chart), or compare two validation datasets and discuss domain shift.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded vs standard lab path: scaffolded includes hints, unit-conversion reminders, and partially completed sensitivity tables; standard requires learners to construct checks from the checklist.
Accessibility: provide transcripts for all videos, screen-reader-friendly templates, and downloadable PDFs; ensure spreadsheets have clear labels and avoid color-only cues.
Low-bandwidth option: replace videos with annotated slides + text walkthrough; provide a lightweight CSV-based lab instead of a large spreadsheet.
Math support: include a mini-remediation link on dimensional analysis basics and significant figures, plus a short practice set with solutions.
Advanced learners: add a challenge to propose a CI-style checklist (pre-run checks, automated unit tests, reproducibility checks) and draft pseudo-tests or validation assertions.
Anxiety reduction: allow multiple quiz attempts; make the decision memo ‘draft’ optional for peer review before final submission.
commonMisconceptions: “If it’s calibrated, it’s validated.” (Calibration fits parameters to data; validation tests performance for intended use and conditions.)
“Passing tolerance means the model is correct.” (It may pass a narrow criterion yet fail dimensional logic, generalization, or stakeholder use-case constraints.)
“Rounding at each step is fine.” (Intermediate rounding can change pass/fail decisions and distort sensitivity rankings.)
“Units are just labels.” (Unit errors can silently create orders-of-magnitude mistakes; dimensional checks are logic checks, not formatting.)
“Sensitivity analysis equals uncertainty quantification.” (Sensitivity indicates influence; uncertainty requires distributions/measurement error and propagation.)
“Reproducibility is optional if results look reasonable.” (Auditability requires traceability of inputs, assumptions, and versions.)
“Version control is only for programmers.” (Any quantitative work needs change tracking; manual versioning can still meet the principle.)
“More decimals = more accurate.” (False precision undermines integrity; reporting must match measurement and model uncertainty.)
discussionPrompts: A stakeholder asks for ‘the most accurate number possible.’ How do you respond while maintaining integrity about uncertainty and limitations?
What is the minimum evidence you would require before declaring a model fit-for-purpose for (a) exploratory analysis vs (b) safety-critical decisions?
When tolerance checks fail but dimensional checks pass, what are the most likely root causes and corrective actions?
How can early rounding change a validation conclusion? Provide a concrete example (even a simple one).
Which is more concerning for audit: an incorrect result with thorough documentation, or a correct result with poor documentation? Defend your view.
If a sensitivity check shows one parameter dominates output, what actions should be taken (measurement, documentation, stakeholder communication, model redesign)?
What should a reproducibility README contain so another analyst can reproduce your results without contacting you?

activities.description: Learners receive a short technical excerpt containing model outputs, stated units, a tolerance requirement, and a rounding rule. The excerpt includes deliberate issues (unit mismatch, inconsistent significant figures, missing assumption, and an ambiguous tolerance statement). Learners must (1) identify issues, (2) correct or propose corrections, and (3) write an audit-friendly note describing what was changed and why. Auto-check compares against a rubric of required findings; learners also self-check against an ‘expected issues’ list after submitting.
activities.teachingMethod: Error-spotting and corrective-action writing aligned to evaluation (judge adequacy, justify corrections).
resources: Rubric checklist: units, tolerance, rounding, assumptions, reproducibility
Short answer submission box (LMS) with model solution reveal after attempt
instructorActions: Provide a clear rubric that rewards justification and traceability, not just ‘getting the number’.
In feedback, distinguish between: error, limitation, and acceptable assumption.
Encourage learners to cite the requirement when deciding if rounding is acceptable.
studentActions: Annotate the excerpt (digitally) to flag at least 5 issues.
Submit a corrected mini-note including: corrected units, revised rounding approach, and a corrective action entry (what/why/impact/version).
Compare work to the model answer and revise notes if needed.

activities.title: Case analysis: Fitness-for-purpose decision with sensitivity evidence + version control plan
activities.description: Scenario: A stakeholder needs a model output for a decision with specified accuracy/tolerance and a defined operating range. Learners are given (a) stakeholder requirements, (b) calibration summary, (c) a one-way sensitivity table (parameter perturbations and output change), and (d) an issue log showing a recent change. Task: Evaluate fitness-for-purpose and choose one decision: Accept, Accept with conditions, or Reject. Learners must justify using sensitivity evidence (material drivers), limitations/uncertainty, and propose a corrective action + version control entry (including how CI checks would prevent regression).
activities.teachingMethod: Decision-based evaluation using a structured decision note and evidence triangulation.
resources: Stakeholder requirement brief (acceptance criteria + operating range)
Template: Validation Decision Note + Version/CI checklist
instructorActions: Design the case so evidence is mixed (some checks pass, others borderline) to require evaluation.
Provide exemplars for all three possible outcomes (accept/conditional/reject) to show that reasoning quality is the target.
Highlight professional integrity: clearly separate what is known, inferred, and unknown.
studentActions: Complete the Validation Decision Note (1–2 short paragraphs + bullet evidence).
Identify the top 2 sensitive parameters and propose at least one mitigation (e.g., tighter measurement, narrower operating range, additional validation).
Write a version control entry and propose 2 CI-style checks (e.g., dimensional assertion test, regression tolerance test).

activities.title: Formative assessment 1 (module-provided): Validation and reproducibility quiz
activities.description: Auto-marked quiz focused on evaluating evidence quality: selecting appropriate checks, interpreting sensitivity/tolerance results, identifying rounding pitfalls, and choosing the most audit-ready documentation. Includes scenario-based MCQs and 1–2 short numeric items (with unit handling).
activities.teachingMethod: Scenario-based retrieval practice with immediate explanatory feedback.
resources: Feedback explanations with links back to lesson sections
instructorActions: Ensure feedback explains why tempting distractors are wrong (e.g., ‘calibration success implies validity’).
Monitor item analytics to identify concepts to revisit in announcements or office hours.
studentActions: Complete the quiz in one sitting to simulate decision pressure.
Review feedback for any missed items and note one action to improve future validation notes.

activities.title: Wrap-up: Personal validation checklist and commitment to transparency
activities.description: Learners finalize a personal ‘validation checklist’ (10–12 items) they will reuse in later lessons (units, tolerance, sensitivity, reproducibility, versioning, CI checks, and uncertainty statement). They also write a 2–3 sentence reflection: what evidence they tend to overlook and how they will correct that habit.
activities.teachingMethod: Metacognitive consolidation: convert lesson criteria into a reusable checklist.
resources: Editable checklist template (doc or LMS page)
instructorActions: Provide a model checklist that is minimal but sufficient for audit (avoid overly long lists).
Encourage wording that is testable (e.g., ‘Units verified for every equation’ rather than ‘Check units’).
studentActions: Save a completed checklist for future modules/assessments.
Submit (or privately record) the short reflection.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Align the lesson to Bloom ‘evaluate’ by consistently framing tasks as decisions against criteria, not as computation-only. Use a claim–evidence–limit structure throughout: learners should state (1) what they conclude (e.g., model is fit/unfit), (2) what evidence supports it (dimensional/tolerance/sensitivity results), and (3) what remains uncertain or out-of-scope. For online self-study, embed frequent low-stakes checks (stop-and-think questions, predict-then-reveal moments) to maintain engagement and reduce passive watching.

Emphasize professional integrity: model language that avoids overstating certainty (e.g., ‘within tested range’), and require explicit documentation of assumptions, data version, model version, and rounding rules. When discussing version control and CI, keep it practical: focus on traceability (what changed and why) and on a small set of automated checks that would catch unit regressions, rounding-induced threshold flips, and sensitivity regressions. Feedback should reward justification quality and auditability (clarity, reproducibility) as much as numeric correctness.

If instructors interact asynchronously (forums/announcements), prompt learners to post one validation decision note and challenge at least one peer note respectfully by asking for missing evidence or clarifying assumptions. Provide a short moderation rubric: be specific, cite criteria, propose improvements.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 25–30 minutes brisk: diagnostic + core framework so learners have the evaluation lens early. In the demonstration, timebox each check (units → tolerance → rounding → reproducibility) and avoid extended algebra; link to optional deep-dive notes instead. Allocate the most time to the two evaluation tasks (flawed report repair and case decision), as these best match ‘evaluate’ and the linked PLOs. If learners are running long, allow them to submit bullet-point decision notes (claim/evidence/limits) rather than polished prose, but do not drop the version control + corrective action element. Encourage learners to pause after each major activity and update their personal checklist (micro-consolidation prevents cognitive overload).
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded vs. open-ended pathway: provide a guided worksheet with prompts (for learners needing structure) and an optional blank template (for advanced learners).
Tool choice: offer both spreadsheet and notebook versions of the worked example; ensure answers are tool-agnostic (focus on reasoning and documentation).
Low-bandwidth alternative: provide downloadable PDFs of the case, datasets in CSV, and a text-based walkthrough transcript of the demonstration video.
Accessibility supports: captions/transcripts for all media; ensure unit notation is screen-reader friendly; avoid conveying meaning by color alone in sensitivity tables.
Extension for advanced learners: add a brief prompt to propose an additional validation test (e.g., benchmark comparison or cross-validation) and justify cost/benefit.
Numeracy support: include an optional refresher micro-lesson on significant figures, rounding at thresholds, and unit conversions with 3 practice items.
Time-flex option: allow the 20-minute case analysis to be split into two passes—first decide (5 minutes), then justify with evidence and version/CI plan (15 minutes).
commonMisconceptions: “If the model is calibrated, it is validated.” (Calibration fit does not guarantee predictive validity or fitness in the intended operating range.)
“Dimensional checks are only about converting units.” (Dimensional consistency is about physical/mathematical validity; unit conversion is only one part.)

“Tolerance and uncertainty are the same.” (Tolerance is an acceptance criterion; uncertainty is a property of estimates/measurements and must be reported, not treated as a pass/fail threshold by default.)
“Rounding is cosmetic and can be done at the end without consequences.” (Rounding strategy can change pass/fail near thresholds and affect reproducibility.)
“Sensitivity analysis proves causation or correctness.” (Sensitivity shows responsiveness to inputs; it does not validate model structure.)
“Version control is only for code.” (Data, parameters, assumptions, and documentation versions must also be traceable for audit.)
“CI is irrelevant to maths models.” (Automated checks can enforce units, regression tolerances, and reproducibility to prevent silent errors.)
discussionPrompts: What is the minimum set of evidence you would accept to declare a model ‘fit-for-purpose’ for a high-stakes decision? What changes for low-stakes use?
Describe a situation where a model passes tolerance checks but should still be rejected. What limitation or missing evidence drives your decision?
When a result is close to a threshold, how should rounding be handled and documented to maintain integrity and reproducibility?
Which is more persuasive in an audit: a single strong validation test or multiple weaker checks? Explain how you would balance breadth vs depth of evidence.
How would you design two CI-style automated checks for this module’s models to prevent unit mistakes and rounding/tolerance regressions?
What language would you use to report uncertainty without undermining stakeholder confidence—while remaining honest?

If sensitivity analysis shows one parameter dominates, what are two concrete corrective actions you could take (data collection, constraint, redesign, documentation) and how would you record them in version control?

objectives: Apply dimensional analysis to identify and correct at least 3 unit/scale inconsistencies in a provided model output table, with all corrections justified in writing.
