activities.title: 1) Orientation + success criteria checkpoint
activities.description: Learners review the lesson goals, the stakeholder requirements brief, and the validation rubric. They complete a quick self-check: identify what evidence is needed to claim a model is fit-for-purpose (not just “works on my machine”).
activities.teachingMethod: Advance organizer + checklist-based priming to focus attention on evaluation criteria and evidence standards.
instructorActions: Provide a clear rubric emphasizing evidence-based judgment (units, tolerance, sensitivity, reproducibility).
Define what constitutes acceptable documentation (minimum audit trail).
studentActions: Read the requirements brief and rubric.
Complete the self-check: list 3 types of evidence they must produce by the end of the lesson.

activities.title: 2) Mini-lecture: Fitness-for-purpose, validation evidence, and integrity in reporting
activities.description: Short content segment explaining: (a) fitness-for-purpose as a stakeholder-relative claim, (b) distinction between calibration and validation, (c) uncertainty/limitations reporting as professional integrity, (d) what “reproducible calculation” means in practice (inputs, environment, rounding rules, and verification).
activities.teachingMethod: Micro-lecture with embedded “stop-and-think” prompts that require learners to choose the strongest evidence statement among options.
resources: Slide deck PDF: key terms (fitness-for-purpose, reproducible calculation, version control, CI)
instructorActions: Emphasize that validation is not a one-time checkbox; it is an evidence-backed claim with scope/limits.
Model transparent language: what is known, uncertain, and out-of-scope.
studentActions: Watch/read the mini-lecture materials.
Answer the embedded prompts and note any criteria they expect to use later for a pass/fail decision.

activities.title: 3) Demonstration: Running dimensional, tolerance, and sensitivity checks with reproducibility evidence
activities.description: Guided walkthrough in an interactive notebook/spreadsheet: (a) unit consistency checks (dimensional analysis and unit conversions), (b) tolerance checks (allowed deviation bands), (c) one-way sensitivity sweep and interpreting a tornado plot, (d) reproducibility artifacts: fixed seed where relevant, recorded rounding rules, and linking results to version control + CI output.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided worked example + “annotate the evidence” approach (learners tag each step with what it proves for an audit).
resources: Sample dataset + parameter definitions with units
Example Git commit history screenshot (or lightweight version log)
Example CI run log (pass/fail) and what it guarantees/does not guarantee
instructorActions: Show at least one deliberate unit error and demonstrate how the check detects it.
Explicitly connect each check to a validation claim (e.g., tolerance pass ≠ model validity outside the tested range).
Point out what CI confirms (repeatable execution) versus what it cannot confirm (scientific correctness).
studentActions: Follow along in the notebook/spreadsheet (or watch if they cannot run it).
Highlight/annotate: where units are verified, where tolerance bounds are enforced, where sensitivity conclusions are drawn, and where reproducibility is evidenced.

activities.title: 4) Guided practice: Find-and-fix validation issues (units, rounding, tolerance breaches)
activities.description: Learners independently inspect a model output pack containing a few planted issues: unit mismatch, inconsistent rounding leading to apparent tolerance breach, and an assumption not documented. They correct issues and record each correction as a “corrective action” with justification and impact assessment.
activities.teachingMethod: Error analysis + structured troubleshooting: learners must (1) detect, (2) diagnose cause, (3) implement fix, (4) document evidence.
resources: Correction log template (issue → evidence → fix → verification → impact)
Rounding/precision policy sheet (significant figures vs decimal places)
instructorActions: Provide a worked example for the first issue only (to set expectations).
Offer an optional hint path (progressive disclosure) for learners who get stuck.
Ensure the correction log template prompts integrity statements (what changed, why, what remains uncertain).
studentActions: Identify at least 3 issues and complete the correction log entries.
Recompute affected values and confirm whether tolerance status changes after correct rounding/units.

activities.title: 5) Break / reset
activities.description: Short pause to reduce cognitive load. Learners are prompted to write a one-sentence interim judgment: “If I had to decide now, would I trust this model for the stated purpose? Why/why not?”
activities.teachingMethod: Deliberate pause + retrieval cue to consolidate evaluation criteria before the case decision task.
instructorActions: Encourage learners to keep the judgment tentative until all evidence is assembled.
Remind learners that uncertainty statements are part of high-quality work.
studentActions: Take a break.
Write the one-sentence interim judgment for later comparison.

activities.title: 6) Case analysis: Fitness-for-purpose decision with audit-ready documentation
activities.description: Learners receive a short case: a calibrated model is proposed for a stakeholder use (e.g., estimating material usage/cost under specified operating conditions). Learners must decide pass/conditional pass/fail by weighing dimensional checks, tolerance compliance, sensitivity implications, and documented limitations. They produce a mini validation report including: decision, evidence summary, limitations/uncertainty, version identifier, and corrective actions required for conditional pass.
activities.teachingMethod: Evidence-based decision-making using a rubric; learners must justify decisions against explicit stakeholder requirements and audit criteria.
resources: Case packet: stakeholder requirements + model summary + test results
Decision rubric (pass/conditional pass/fail) aligned to MLOs
instructorActions: Ensure the case includes trade-offs (e.g., acceptable tolerance but high sensitivity to an unmeasured parameter).
Provide exemplar language frames: “Fit for purpose within X range; not validated for Y; uncertainty dominated by Z.”
studentActions: Select a decision (pass/conditional pass/fail).
Complete the mini validation report, explicitly mapping each requirement to evidence (or noting missing evidence).

activities.title: 7) Formative assessment: Scenario-based evaluation + reproducibility/VC/CI check
activities.description: Auto-graded quiz plus one short constructed-response item. Quiz focuses on: interpreting sensitivity outputs, detecting unit errors, choosing correct rounding, and identifying what CI evidence supports. The constructed-response asks learners to state a fitness-for-purpose decision and cite 2–3 pieces of validation evidence with one limitation/uncertainty statement.
activities.teachingMethod: Mastery check with immediate feedback; constructed-response graded with a simple rubric (evidence + integrity + clarity).
resources: Answer key with rationales (released after attempt)
instructorActions: Configure feedback to explain why distractors are wrong (e.g., “CI passing does not validate scientific assumptions”).
Flag patterns of errors for follow-up announcements (common unit/rounding mistakes).
studentActions: Complete the quiz and review feedback.
Submit the short justification (3–6 sentences) using the rubric checklist.

activities.title: 8) Collaboration simulation: Challenge-and-improve reflection (asynchronous)
activities.description: Learners draft a short ‘response to reviewer’ note. They choose one potential critique (e.g., missing assumption, sensitivity too narrow, tolerance justified poorly) and write how they would address it, what they would change in the documentation, and what evidence they would add. If a discussion board is available, they post and optionally reply to one peer using respectful challenge language.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection to practice collaborative behaviours: explaining reasoning, welcoming challenge, integrating feedback into improved solutions.
resources: Optional discussion board prompt + reply sentence starters
instructorActions: Provide sentence starters for constructive challenge (e.g., “What evidence supports…?”, “Have you considered…?”).
If facilitated, spotlight 1–2 strong examples emphasizing integrity and auditability.
studentActions: Write a brief ‘response to reviewer’ note.
Optionally post/reply in the forum, focusing on evidence and clarity rather than opinion.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Keep the lesson anchored on evaluation (judgment with evidence), not computation for its own sake. Repeatedly ask: “What claim are you making, and what evidence supports it?” Use the rubric as the central organizing tool so learners practice making defensible pass/conditional pass/fail decisions. Model professional integrity by demonstrating how to document limitations and uncertainty without undermining credibility—clear scope statements increase trust. Emphasize diligence via micro-habits: unit checks at every boundary (inputs/outputs), explicit rounding rules, and verification steps recorded in an audit trail. For reproducibility, require learners to capture minimal but sufficient metadata (data source, parameter set, environment/version identifier, and rerun instructions). When introducing version control and CI, be explicit about their role: they support traceability and repeatability, not correctness of assumptions. Reinforce collaborative behaviour even in self-study by using the ‘reviewer critique’ simulation: learners practice responding to challenge constructively and improving documentation/analysis based on feedback.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Aim for brisk movement through concepts and more time on evaluation tasks. If learners are slow in the demonstration (Activity 3), allow them to watch-only and reserve hands-on time for Activity 4 where evidence is generated. In Activity 4, suggest a timebox: 8 minutes to scan for issues, 10 minutes to fix/log, 2 minutes to verify. For Activity 6, recommend drafting the decision first (1 minute), then filling evidence mapping (12 minutes), then writing limitations/corrective actions (5 minutes). If short on time, keep Activity 8 to a private reflection (no forum) but do not drop the constructed-response in Activity 7, as it best targets the Evaluate level.
adaptationOptions: Low-coding pathway: Provide a spreadsheet-based version of the notebook with prebuilt sensitivity tables and plots; learners focus on interpretation and decision-making.
High-support scaffolding: Offer an “evidence bank” checklist (units verified where? tolerance limits defined where? sensitivity range justified where?) to guide the validation report.
Extension for advanced learners: Add a two-parameter sensitivity or scenario analysis and ask learners to compare conclusions to the one-way sensitivity (does the decision change?).
Accessibility: Provide captions/transcripts for all media; ensure tables have headers and are screen-reader friendly; offer downloadable PDFs of plots with alt-text descriptions.
Language support: Provide sentence frames for limitations/uncertainty statements and for constructive peer challenge/reviewer response.
Assessment flexibility: Allow the constructed-response to be submitted as bullet points (claim → evidence → limitation → corrective action) to reduce writing load while preserving evaluative rigor.
commonMisconceptions: Conflating calibration with validation (assuming a well-fitted model is automatically fit-for-purpose).
Believing that passing CI or reproducing the same numbers guarantees the model is scientifically correct.
Treating dimensional consistency as optional or assuming software will ‘handle units’ automatically.
Assuming rounding is a cosmetic step; not realizing rounding policy can change tolerance pass/fail outcomes.
Interpreting sensitivity results as proving causation or global robustness (one-way sensitivity over a narrow range does not guarantee stability elsewhere).
Thinking tolerance bands are universal rather than stakeholder- and context-dependent requirements.
Hiding limitations/uncertainty to appear confident, rather than documenting them transparently for audit and safe decision-making.
Assuming version control is only backup, not an audit mechanism linking results to exact inputs and code state.
discussionPrompts: What minimum evidence would you require to claim a model is fit-for-purpose for a safety-critical decision versus a rough budgeting estimate?
When (if ever) is it acceptable to report results without uncertainty bounds or limitations? What are the risks?
A model passes tolerance checks but is highly sensitive to a parameter that is poorly measured. Would you pass, conditionally pass, or fail? What corrective action would you require?
How can rounding policy create apparent tolerance failures or hide real ones? Give an example of a rounding rule you would document.
What does a ‘green’ CI pipeline actually tell you, and what does it not tell you, about model validity?
Describe a constructive challenge you could raise about someone else’s validation report that focuses on evidence rather than opinion.

activities.title: Orientation: What does it mean to ‘evaluate’ a model?

Focus: what constitutes reproducibility (data + code/spreadsheet + environment + version), how version control supports auditability, and how CI (continuous integration) can automate checks (units tests, regression tests, tolerance checks) for models.

Example CI pipeline screenshot or short screencast (2–3 minutes)

activities.title: Demonstration: Evaluating a model output with a validation checklist
activities.description: Guided walkthrough of a worked example where model outputs contain intentional issues: unit mismatch, hidden assumption, over-rounding, tolerance breach, and an unstable parameter. Learners observe how to identify issues, record evidence, and decide whether the model is fit-for-purpose.

resources: Worked example file (spreadsheet or Jupyter notebook)

They run or interpret one-at-a-time sensitivity results for 3 parameters, rank parameter influence, and decide pass/conditional-pass/fail with recommended corrective actions (e.g., recalibration, tighter input measurement, model revision, further testing).

Decision worksheet (pass/conditional-pass/fail + evidence + corrective action log)
instructorActions: Provide a rubric describing what counts as sufficient evidence for each decision category.
Offer an optional ‘challenge’ section showing how a stakeholder change (tighter tolerance) flips the decision.

Make a fitness-for-purpose decision and propose at least 2 corrective actions with rationale.

activities.title: Formative assessment: Audit-ready validation summary + version-control change note
activities.description: Learners produce a short validation package: (1) validation summary (what was checked, evidence, limitations), (2) reproducibility statement (inputs, tool/version, run instructions), and (3) a version-control style change note documenting a corrective action (e.g., unit fix, rounding rule update) and its impact. Auto-scored components check completeness; a model answer supports self-evaluation.
activities.teachingMethod: Template-driven submission with checklist scoring and guided self-marking against an exemplar.
resources: Version-control change note template (e.g., commit message format)
instructorActions: Provide an exemplar and a ‘minimum audit trail’ checklist.
Configure automated checks for required fields and common omissions (units, assumptions, tolerance definition).
studentActions: Submit the validation package (templates).
Self-mark using the scoring guide and record one improvement to apply next time.

activities.title: Consolidation: Reflection and optional collaboration prompt
activities.description: Learners reflect on how evaluation decisions can change with stakeholder requirements and what transparency looks like when results are borderline. Optional forum prompt encourages collaborative behaviours: explain reasoning, welcome challenge, integrate feedback.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection (short response) + optional asynchronous discussion thread with a ‘challenge and refine’ norm.
resources: Forum thread: ‘Borderline tolerance—what would you report?’
instructorActions: Post a model ‘constructive challenge’ reply demonstrating respectful critique and revision.
If facilitated, summarise common themes and highlight strong evidence-based justifications.
studentActions: Write a 3–4 sentence reflection: what evidence mattered most and what they would do to improve reproducibility.
Optionally post one decision and respond to one peer using the sentence stems.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the lesson around evaluation-as-judgement, not just calculation. Require learners to (a) state criteria (stakeholder requirements/tolerances), (b) present evidence (dimensional/unit checks, tolerance results, sensitivity ranking), and (c) make a defensible decision (pass/conditional-pass/fail) with limitations. Use ‘think-aloud’ demonstrations to model professional integrity: explicitly flag uncertainty, boundary conditions, and assumptions; avoid overclaiming (e.g., ‘validated’ vs ‘consistent with tests under these conditions’). Reinforce diligence by embedding micro-checkpoints: units on every quantity, definitions of tolerance (absolute vs %), rounding tied to measurement resolution, and reproducibility essentials (inputs, versions, run steps). To cultivate collaborative behaviours in self-study, provide optional forum structures and peer-feedback stems and encourage learners to revise their decision after critique. Align feedback to an audit mindset: would another person reproduce the result and understand the decision trail?
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep early concept input brisk (no more than ~22 minutes combined for orientation + key terms) and shift quickly to evidence-based evaluation tasks. Time-box the case analysis (20 minutes) with a visible checklist so learners don’t get stuck perfecting calculations at the expense of making and justifying a decision. Provide ‘stop points’ after the demonstration and guided practice where learners can either continue or take an optional deep-dive (e.g., extra sensitivity plots). If learners fall behind, prioritise: (1) making a fitness-for-purpose decision with evidence, (2) documenting limitations and reproducibility, then (3) extended sensitivity exploration.
adaptationOptions: Provide two tool tracks: spreadsheet-based and Jupyter notebook-based, with equivalent datasets and answer checks.
Add scaffolding for learners who need it: partially completed checklists, unit tables, and a worked sensitivity example; gradually remove supports in later lessons.
Offer extension tasks for advanced learners: multi-parameter sensitivity (tornado chart), simple uncertainty propagation, or designing a CI test suite for regression/tolerance checks.
Accessibility supports: captions/transcripts for all screencasts, screen-reader-friendly templates, and downloadable materials in accessible formats.
Allow alternative demonstration of competence: audio-recorded justification of the fitness-for-purpose decision instead of written (where appropriate), while still requiring the key evidence fields.
For learners with limited time, provide a ‘minimum viable audit package’ template that focuses on essential evidence, assumptions, and versioning.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing verification (correctly implemented calculations) with validation (adequate representation for the intended purpose).
Assuming dimensional consistency alone guarantees the model is correct or fit-for-purpose.
Mixing absolute tolerance and percentage tolerance, or applying tolerance to the wrong quantity (input vs output).
Believing rounding is merely formatting; not recognising that rounding policy can change pass/fail decisions near tolerance boundaries.
Assuming sensitivity checks prove causality or global importance; overlooking that one-at-a-time sensitivity can miss interactions and nonlinearity.
Thinking ‘reproducible’ means ‘I can rerun it on my computer’, while omitting data versions, parameter sets, environment/tool versions, or run instructions.
Treating version control as only for software code; not applying it to spreadsheets, datasets, and model documentation changes.
Overstating certainty (e.g., claiming the model is ‘validated’ without stating the tested range, limitations, and residual uncertainty).
Assuming CI is only for large teams; missing its value for individual assurance via automated checks and regression detection.
discussionPrompts: A model output meets tolerance only after rounding to fewer decimals. Is it fit-for-purpose? What rounding policy and evidence would you cite?
What is the minimum evidence you would include in an audit-ready validation summary for a stakeholder who will make safety-critical decisions?

Your sensitivity ranking shows one parameter dominates output uncertainty. What corrective action is most appropriate: recalibrate, measure inputs more precisely, revise the model structure, or widen tolerances? Justify.
Describe a transparent way to report a ‘conditional-pass’ decision so stakeholders understand limitations and residual risk.
How would version control and CI change your confidence in the model over time as data and assumptions are updated?
When a peer challenges your unit choice or tolerance definition, what is a constructive way to respond and integrate feedback into a revised solution?

activities.title: Guided Practice: Dimensional + Tolerance Checks on a Provided Model Output

activities.title: Case Analysis: Sensitivity Check + Fitness-for-Purpose Decision
activities.description: Learners analyse a short scenario: a stakeholder needs a model for a specific operating range and decision threshold. Using provided baseline inputs, learners run one-at-a-time sensitivity (±x%) on 3–5 inputs, interpret which inputs drive the decision metric, and evaluate whether the model is fit-for-purpose given validation results, sensitivity, and limitations. Deliverable: a one-page decision memo (accept/reject/accept-with-conditions) with quantified uncertainty and corrective actions.
activities.teachingMethod: Decision-focused evaluation: learners must justify a recommendation using explicit criteria, not just compute results. Uses a rubric aligned to integrity, diligence, and transparency.
resources: Case brief: Stakeholder requirements + acceptance criteria
Decision memo template + rubric (fitness-for-purpose, evidence quality, uncertainty reporting, corrective actions)
instructorActions: Provide a rubric with ‘must-have’ elements: criteria quoted, evidence referenced, uncertainty stated, limitations stated, rounding rule declared, reproducibility steps listed.
Include exemplar phrases for honest limitation reporting (e.g., ‘Valid within range…, not validated for…’).
studentActions: Run OAT sensitivity and summarize results (table or tornado-style ranking).
Make a fitness-for-purpose decision and justify it against stakeholder criteria.
Propose at least one corrective action (e.g., recalibrate with new data, add unit test/CI check, adjust rounding policy, tighten input controls).

activities.title: Collaborative Forum Task: Peer Challenge and Improvement Plan (formative)
activities.description: Learners post a brief excerpt (150–250 words) from their decision memo: recommendation + top 2 evidence points + one limitation. They then respond to two peers using a structured ‘challenge respectfully’ protocol: ask one clarifying question, identify one potential risk/assumption, and suggest one improvement to reproducibility/version control/CI checks. Learners revise their memo based on feedback (documenting what changed).
activities.teachingMethod: Structured peer review to build collaborative behaviours: explain reasoning, welcome challenge, integrate feedback. Uses sentence starters and a feedback checklist.
resources: Peer feedback checklist (assumptions, units, rounding, uncertainty, evidence traceability, versioning)
instructorActions: Moderate with a light touch: highlight one strong example of transparent limitation reporting and one strong example of reproducibility documentation.
Intervene only to correct harmful misconceptions (e.g., confusing validation with calibration) and to enforce respectful critique norms.
studentActions: Post excerpt and limitation statement; include a link/reference to evidence table location (even if local).
Provide two peer replies following the protocol.
Add a short revision note: ‘Changed X because Y; impact on decision Z.’

activities.title: Wrap-up: Exit Ticket + Personal QA Checklist
activities.description: Learners complete a 5-question exit ticket (auto-marked + one short response) focused on evaluation decisions: which evidence is sufficient, when to reject a model, and how to document version control/corrective actions. They finish by saving a personal ‘QA checklist’ they will reuse in later modules.
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes formative assessment with immediate feedback; commitment-to-action checklist.
instructorActions: Configure feedback to direct learners to revisit specific segments (units, tolerance, sensitivity, version control, CI checks).
Collect anonymized analytics (most-missed items) to inform next lesson’s remediation notes.
studentActions: Complete exit ticket and review feedback.
Save a personalized QA checklist (top 5 checks they will always perform).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Focus the lesson on evaluation decisions, not just computation. Require learners to (a) state stakeholder criteria, (b) present validation/sensitivity/tolerance evidence, (c) quantify uncertainty or bounds, and (d) explicitly decide accept/reject/accept-with-conditions. Reinforce professional integrity by rewarding clear limitation statements and uncertainty reporting; penalize overclaiming. Use an ‘evidence table’ and a decision memo rubric to make expectations concrete and auditable. Model diligence: insist units are shown in every key step and that rounding is declared and applied consistently (avoid premature rounding during intermediate calculations unless required). For reproducibility, teach learners to record inputs, assumptions, run steps, and output identifiers (version/tag). Treat version control and CI-style checks as quality safeguards: a small set of automated checks (units/bounds/regression of key outputs) can prevent silent errors and support transparent corrective actions. For collaboration, structure peer feedback with a protocol that normalizes challenge and requires integrating feedback via a documented revision note.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the warm-up and wrap-up strictly time-boxed (10 and 5 minutes) to protect the two 20-minute evaluation blocks. If learners fall behind, prioritize: (1) completing one full dimensional check example, (2) one tolerance bound comparison, and (3) a defensible fitness-for-purpose recommendation with at least one stated limitation. Offer optional extensions (e.g., additional sensitivity inputs or a simple regression test) only after the decision memo is drafted. Encourage learners to use the provided templates rather than creating new formats during the 90 minutes to reduce cognitive load and keep attention on evaluation quality.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolding for developing learners: provide a partially completed evidence table with units pre-filled and a guided calculation path for the first tolerance check; allow use of a calculator-only path without plotting for sensitivity.

Extension for advanced learners: add a second sensitivity method (e.g., normalized sensitivity coefficients or scenario analysis across operating ranges) and require a brief comment on interaction effects/limitations of OAT sensitivity.
Tool flexibility: offer both spreadsheet and notebook versions; allow learners to submit either, provided reproducibility requirements (inputs, assumptions, steps, version identifier) are met.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for videos, screen-reader-friendly templates, and a text-only alternative to plots (ranked sensitivity table).

Language support: include a glossary card for key terms (fitness-for-purpose, reproducible calculation, version control, CI) and sentence starters for limitation reporting and audit-style documentation.
commonMisconceptions: “If the model is calibrated, it is validated.” (Calibration fits parameters; validation tests performance against independent or fit-for-purpose criteria.)
“Sensitivity analysis tells me which parameter is most important in reality.” (It indicates influence within the tested range/assumptions; results are conditional.)
“Dimensional checks are only for physics problems.” (Any quantitative model with units/scales benefits; unit errors are common in business/engineering contexts.)

“Rounding should always be done only at the final step.” (Often true, but documentation may require consistent reporting precision; intermediate rounding can be mandated or can introduce error—must be stated and controlled.)
“Version control is just for programmers.” (Any model/spreadsheet needs traceable changes for auditability and reproducibility.)
“CI is too advanced for maths models.” (Simple automated checks—bounds, unit assertions, regression checks—are CI-like and highly practical.)
“Passing one acceptance criterion means the model is fit-for-purpose.” (Fitness-for-purpose is a holistic judgement across criteria, uncertainty, operating range, and limitations.)
discussionPrompts: What minimum validation evidence would you require before recommending a model for operational decision-making, and why?
When is it ethically necessary to recommend ‘reject’ or ‘accept-with-conditions’ even if the model appears numerically accurate on a small test set?
How should tolerance bounds and sensitivity results change the way you communicate uncertainty to stakeholders (e.g., thresholds, safety margins, disclaimers)?
Which is more dangerous in practice: a unit error or an undocumented assumption? Defend your view with an example.
What CI-style checks would you implement first for this model to prevent silent failures (e.g., unit mismatch, output drift, broken assumptions)?
Share one example of a constructive peer challenge you received (or gave) and how it improved the final recommendation or documentation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Model fitness-for-purpose against stakeholder requirement...
objectives: Given a short stakeholder brief and operational dataset, construct a calibrated mathematical model (equation/algorithm) and document variables, units, assumptions, parameter sources, and intended use in a one-page Model Card.

Apply at least three validation checks (e.g., residual inspection, dimensional/unit check, tolerance/rounding check, holdout test) and record evidence and pass/fail decisions aligned to stakeholder fitness-for-purpose criteria.

Create an audit-ready change record by implementing a version control approach (e.g., semantic file naming + change log, or Git commits) that captures what changed, why, who/when, and the impact on results.

Propose and document at least two corrective actions when validation fails (e.g., revise assumptions, re-calibrate, adjust data handling, constrain parameter ranges) and justify them transparently, including uncertainty/limitations.

activities.title: Start-up: retrieval quiz + integrity checkpoint
activities.description: Self-marking quiz (8–10 items) reviewing: calibration vs validation, assumptions, fitness-for-purpose, rounding rules, and what counts as audit evidence. Learners then complete a 2-minute integrity checkpoint: identify one limitation they must disclose when modelling from operational data (e.g., missing values, measurement error).
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes retrieval practice to activate prerequisites and surface misconceptions before creation tasks; immediate feedback explanations included.
resources: One-slide integrity checklist: 'What must be disclosed?'
instructorActions: Configure quiz with feedback explanations keyed to common errors.
Review quiz analytics to identify items needing a clarifying announcement/video note.

Write a short note (2–3 sentences) naming one likely limitation and how it will be disclosed in documentation.

activities.title: Mini-lecture: fitness-for-purpose and validation evidence (what auditors look for)
activities.description: Short, structured content explaining how stakeholder requirements translate into acceptance criteria (accuracy threshold, operating range, response time, safety margin), and what constitutes defensible validation evidence (tests performed, data splits, residual patterns, unit checks, reproducibility, rounding/tolerance statements). Includes a quick contrast table: calibration evidence vs validation evidence.
activities.teachingMethod: Concept-then-criteria approach: present definitions, then operationalize them as checkable acceptance criteria and evidence artifacts.
instructorActions: Provide a worked exemplar showing weak vs strong evidence statements.
Explicitly model transparent language (e.g., 'valid within range X–Y; outside this range not tested').
studentActions: Complete the worksheet by converting a sample stakeholder brief into 3–5 acceptance criteria.
Highlight (or note) which criteria can be tested with available data and which require assumptions or additional data.

activities.title: Demonstration: audit trail and version control for models (spreadsheet/notebook friendly)
activities.description: Step-by-step demonstration of a lightweight version control workflow appropriate for self-study: (1) structured folder layout, (2) semantic file naming (v0.1, v0.2…), (3) CHANGELOG entries with impact statements, and (4) reproducibility checklist (inputs, code/formulas, outputs). Optional branch: short intro to Git commit messages if learners use Git.
activities.teachingMethod: Show-and-replicate: learners pause the demo to set up their own project structure and first change log entry.
instructorActions: Provide downloadable templates and a completed example (gold standard).
Embed prompts in the video: 'Pause and do this now' checkpoints.
studentActions: Create the folder structure and start a change log.
Record an initial entry: model purpose, dataset version, and starting assumptions.

activities.title: Create task: build and calibrate a model from operational data + Model Card draft
activities.description: Learners use a provided dataset to build a calibrated model aligned to a stated use-case (e.g., forecasting within a range, estimating a parameter, or mapping input-output). They must: define variables with units, state assumptions, identify parameter sources (estimated from data vs external), and produce a calibrated result (parameters + fit summary). They complete a one-page Model Card draft capturing intended use and constraints.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided creation with scaffolds: a template Model Card and a minimal required output checklist; learners choose tool (spreadsheet or notebook).
resources: Calibration starter notebook (optional) and/or spreadsheet starter file
Checklist: required artefacts (model equation, parameters, assumptions, units)
instructorActions: Provide two pathways (spreadsheet + notebook) with equivalent outcomes.
Include a 'minimum viable model' example to reduce cognitive load, but require learner-produced final parameters and documentation.
studentActions: Fit/calibrate the model and record parameter estimates with appropriate rounding.
Complete Model Card sections: variables/units, assumptions, parameter sources, intended use, constraints/operating range.

activities.title: Case analysis: validation + sensitivity checks and corrective actions (write-up)
activities.description: Learners run validation checks against acceptance criteria (from Activity 2) and perform at least one sensitivity check (e.g., ±5% parameter perturbation, alternative data filtering rule, or holdout split). They must document evidence (tables/plots) and decide pass/fail per criterion. If any criterion fails, learners propose corrective actions and document them as planned changes (not silent fixes).
activities.teachingMethod: Evidence-first reasoning: learners must justify conclusions using recorded checks, not intuition; emphasis on transparent limitations and uncertainty.
resources: Validation checklist (dimensional/unit, residuals, tolerance/rounding, holdout test, edge cases)
Sensitivity analysis quick guide (one-at-a-time and scenario-based)
instructorActions: Provide threshold examples (e.g., acceptable error bands) and remind learners they must be tied to stakeholder needs, not generic norms.
Offer an exemplar of a corrective action note that includes rationale and expected impact.
studentActions: Complete 3+ validation checks and record evidence (screenshots, tables, metrics).
Run 1 sensitivity check and summarize which assumptions/parameters most affect outputs.
Draft 2 corrective actions with rationale and risks (including what remains uncertain).

activities.title: Formative assessment: submit Model Card + Validation Log + Change Log (audit-ready bundle)
activities.description: Learners assemble an audit-ready bundle: Model Card (final), Validation Evidence table (with pass/fail decisions), and version control artefacts (CHANGELOG entries or Git log). Auto-rubric checks for completeness plus short instructor rubric for reasoning quality (where applicable). Learners complete a self-review: identify one place they could be more transparent.
activities.teachingMethod: Performance-based formative assessment aligned to 'create': learners submit authentic artefacts; self-check rubric promotes professional integrity and reproducibility.
resources: Rubric: fitness-for-purpose alignment, evidence quality, transparency, reproducibility, version control quality
instructorActions: Set up LMS submission with required components and rubric.
If feedback is provided: comment on (a) clarity of assumptions, (b) linkage between criteria and evidence, (c) audit trail completeness.
studentActions: Submit the three artefacts as a single PDF/zip (as specified).
Complete the self-review prompt and note one improvement to make in the next iteration.

activities.title: Asynchronous wrap-up: peer-review simulation prompts + next-step plan
activities.description: Learners respond to discussion-board style prompts (or private reflection if no forum): explain one modelling decision, invite challenge, and state how they would integrate feedback. They also write a 3-step next iteration plan (what to test next, what data to request, what to refactor) and record it in the change log as a planned entry.
activities.teachingMethod: Collaborative behaviours in self-study: structured prompts simulate team review meetings; emphasis on explaining reasoning and welcoming challenge.
resources: Discussion prompts (LMS) or reflection journal template
instructorActions: Provide sentence starters for constructive critique and response (e.g., 'What evidence supports…?', 'What would change your mind?').
Optionally curate 2–3 anonymized exemplar responses.
studentActions: Post (or write) a brief explanation of one key decision and one open question.
Add a planned next-step entry to the change log to reinforce version control habits.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Align every task to the two MLOs by requiring learners to produce auditable artefacts (Model Card, Validation Evidence table, Change Log) rather than only computations. Emphasize integrity and transparency: learners must explicitly disclose assumptions, uncertainty, operating range, and known limitations; reward clear 'not validated beyond X' statements. Use exemplars that contrast weak vs strong documentation (e.g., 'model is accurate' vs 'MAE=1.2 within 10–50 units; fails at >50 due to sparse data'). To support creation at diploma level, provide scaffolds (templates, checklists) while preserving learner agency (choice of model form/tool, choice of sensitivity scenario). Reinforce reproducibility: require inputs, parameter sources, rounding rules, and rerunnable steps; discourage copy-paste results without traceability. Build collaborative behaviours via structured peer-review simulation prompts: learners must explain reasoning, invite challenge, and specify how they would integrate feedback, even in self-study mode.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Keep the first 35 minutes brisk (quiz + two short content blocks) to maximize time for artefact creation. If learners stall during calibration, direct them to the 'minimum viable model' path: fit a simple baseline model, document assumptions, then iterate. Timebox validation: 3 checks only, then add more if time remains. If running long, reduce sensitivity analysis to one perturbation scenario but require a clear written interpretation. Encourage learners to stop at the 80-minute mark to assemble the audit bundle; incomplete bundling is a common failure in self-study.
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded route: provide a partially completed Model Card (variables/units prefilled) so learners focus on calibration, validation evidence, and corrective actions.
Extension route: require two sensitivity methods (one-at-a-time + scenario/Monte Carlo) and a brief discussion of parameter identifiability.
Tool flexibility: offer equivalent workflows in spreadsheet and Python/R notebook; accept either with the same documentation requirements.
Accessibility: all videos with captions/transcripts; provide templates compatible with screen readers; allow submission in markdown or doc format.
Math support: optional refresher micro-lesson on residual plots, error metrics (MAE/RMSE), and rounding/significant figures tied to tolerance.
Support for anxious learners: provide a 'checkpoints' timeline and an exemplar change log entry list to reduce uncertainty about expectations.
commonMisconceptions: Calibration and validation are the same step (students may treat a good fit on training data as proof of fitness-for-purpose).
High R² automatically implies the model is fit-for-purpose (ignores operating range, error tolerances, bias, and stakeholder criteria).
Assumptions are optional or can remain implicit (reduces transparency and auditability).
Version control is only for software code (ignores spreadsheets, datasets, and documentation changes).
Rounding can always be done at the end without consequence (ignores tolerance propagation and reproducibility).
Sensitivity analysis only means changing one parameter slightly (ignores interaction effects and scenario-based uncertainty).
If validation fails, the fix should be applied silently (instead of documenting corrective actions and their impact).
Dimensional/unit checks are ‘administrative’ rather than a mathematical validation tool.
discussionPrompts: Which stakeholder requirement most strongly determines your fitness-for-purpose criteria, and how did you translate it into a measurable acceptance threshold?
What is the most consequential assumption in your model? If it were wrong, what direction would your recommendations change?
Show one piece of validation evidence (metric/plot/check). What alternative explanation could a teammate raise, and how would you respond?
Where does your model perform poorly (range/conditions), and how will you disclose that limitation in technical documentation?
Describe one corrective action you would take after a failed validation check. What new risk might that corrective action introduce?
What change log entry would you expect to see if someone modified the dataset cleaning rule? What would make that change auditable?

lessons.lessonTitle: Develop a calibrated mathematical model from operational ...
objectives: Given an operational dataset and a modelling brief, create a calibrated mathematical model by (a) defining variables and parameters, (b) stating at least 5 explicit assumptions, (c) documenting parameter sources, and (d) specifying intended use and boundaries in a short model spec (≥250 words).

Implement a reproducible calculation workflow (spreadsheet or notebook) that includes labelled units for all inputs/outputs, clear cell/code annotations, and a repeatable calibration procedure (one-click rerun / single “Run all” path).

Validate model outputs by completing (and submitting) a dimensional consistency check, a tolerance/rounding check (including a rounding policy), and a sensitivity check (at least 3 parameters varied), with results summarised in a table.

activities.title: Set-up, expectations, and integrity checkpoint

activities.description: Short video segments with embedded questions cover: selecting a functional form, separating variables vs parameters, sourcing parameters, stating assumptions, and defining intended use and out-of-scope conditions. studentActions: Answer embedded questions (classification + short response).

activities.title: Demonstration: Reproducible calculations, units, rounding, and CI basics
activities.description: Walkthrough demonstrates (a) setting up a single source of truth for inputs, (b) unit labelling and unit checks, (c) calibration steps that can be rerun, (d) avoiding premature rounding, and (e) computing a CI (concept + minimal procedure) for a key output or parameter estimate.
activities.teachingMethod: Guided screencast with ‘pause-and-do’ prompts; emphasis on workflow design (reproducibility) rather than only results.

Add unit labels to all provided template inputs/outputs.

activities.title: Practice: Build and calibrate your model from operational data
activities.description: Learners create a calibrated model. Auto-check items (e.g., unit completeness, required fields completed)

Complete the model spec: variables, assumptions (≥5), parameter sources, intended use and limits.

Plotting guide (simple tornado plot / sensitivity table)
instructorActions: Provide a worked micro-example of a dimensional check and a sensitivity table.
Prompt learners to flag any violated assumptions or suspicious outputs and to write what they would do next (e.g., collect more data, revise model form).
Auto-feedback on common issues (missing units, rounding too early, sensitivity not tied to decision variable).

Define tolerances for key inputs and test output stability; implement rounding policy at final reporting stage only.

activities.title: Case analysis / role-play (asynchronous): Team review recommendation with transparency statement
activities.description: Learners write a brief recommendation as if presenting at a team review meeting. activities.teachingMethod: Structured professional communication task; learners adopt the role of analyst reporting to stakeholders, using an integrity rubric to avoid overconfidence.

instructorActions: Provide sentence frames that model honest uncertainty reporting (e.g., 'Within X–Y range, we recommend…').

activities.description: Short auto-graded quiz (units, assumptions vs parameters, rounding, CI interpretation, sensitivity meaning) plus a 2-question reflection: (1) What assumption is most decision-critical? (2) What would you do next to improve validation?
activities.teachingMethod: Low-stakes retrieval practice with immediate feedback; reflection to consolidate ‘create-level’ outputs into transferable habits.
instructorActions: Configure quiz feedback to explain why incorrect choices are wrong (especially units/rounding/CI).
Collect common errors (from quiz analytics) to inform next lesson’s remediation materials.
studentActions: Complete quiz and review feedback explanations.
Submit reflection responses for their learning log.

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design the lesson around producing artefacts (model spec, reproducible workflow, validation tables, recommendation) rather than passive watching, since the Bloom level is create. Use scaffolding that fades: provide templates and worked micro-examples early, then require independent completion. Continuously foreground professional integrity: learners must separate what the data shows, what the model assumes, and what is unknown. Require units everywhere (inputs, intermediate terms, outputs) and treat missing units as a correctness failure, not a formatting issue. Encourage ‘auditability’: a reader should be able to rerun the calibration and reproduce outputs from the same dataset. Build in deliberate checkpoints where learners must (a) state assumptions before fitting, (b) justify rounding policy, and (c) interpret sensitivity results in relation to the decision variable (not just compute them). When teaching CI, keep it method-appropriate and focus on interpretation: what the interval means, what it does not mean, and how it should constrain claims. Provide immediate feedback on common failure modes: premature rounding, mixing tolerance with uncertainty, and treating calibration error metrics as proof of validity.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Target completion times: Orientation (≤5 min), mini-lecture (≤15 min), demo (≤15 min), build/calibration (20–30 min), checks/sensitivity (15–25 min), recommendation (5–10 min), quiz/reflection (3–5 min). If learners are behind after 35 minutes, advise using the provided functional-form option rather than deriving their own, and focus on completing the reproducibility + validation artefacts. If learners are ahead, add the optional extension: compare two model forms (e.g., linear vs piecewise) and justify selection using residual patterns and sensitivity implications. Encourage learners to timebox calibration iterations (e.g., max 2 refits) to avoid overfitting and to preserve time for validation checks.
adaptationOptions: Tool choice: offer spreadsheet-only and notebook-based pathways with equivalent outputs; allow learners to submit either.
Scaffolding levels: provide hint tiers (light/medium/explicit) and an optional ‘partially completed’ template for learners with weaker prerequisites.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for all videos; ensure templates are screen-reader friendly (clear labels, no color-only encoding).
Math support: include a short remedial sidebar on units/dimensional analysis and on interpreting CIs (with 2–3 simple examples).
Challenge extension: require a second sensitivity method (scenario set or normalized sensitivity coefficients) and a short justification of why one-at-a-time may miss interactions.
Language support: provide sentence starters for assumptions, limitations, and uncertainty statements; allow submission of bullet-point model specs.
Assessment flexibility: allow an audio-recorded recommendation (≤90 seconds) instead of written for learners with writing barriers, while still requiring the validation table artefacts.
commonMisconceptions: ‘Calibration proves the model is correct’: learners may confuse good fit with validity outside the calibration data range.
Units are optional if the numbers look right: learners may omit units or mix unit systems, causing silent errors.
Rounding can be done at any stage: learners may round intermediate values and unintentionally change calibration/sensitivity outcomes.
Tolerance and uncertainty are the same: learners may treat engineering tolerance bands as statistical uncertainty (or vice versa).
A CI means ‘95% of future values will be inside’: learners may misinterpret CIs as prediction intervals or as guarantees.
Sensitivity analysis is just changing inputs without interpreting decision impact: learners may compute variations but not link them to the key recommendation.
One-at-a-time sensitivity captures all risk: learners may ignore parameter interactions and nonlinearity effects.
More parameters always improve the model: learners may overfit by adding complexity without validation rationale.
If a unit cancels algebraically, it can be ignored: learners may miss that intermediate unit checks reveal conceptual mistakes.
discussionPrompts: Which single assumption in your model is most ‘decision-critical’ and why? What evidence would you collect to test it?
Where did you draw the line between what the data supports and what you inferred from the model form?
What rounding policy did you adopt, and how did it change (or not change) your reported outputs?
Share one example where a unit check revealed (or could reveal) a modelling mistake. What was the correction?
How did sensitivity results change your confidence in the recommendation? Which parameter(s) dominated and what does that imply operationally?
Write a transparency statement: what is the biggest limitation of your model, and what is the likely direction of bias if that limitation is violated?
If a stakeholder asks for a single number (no uncertainty), how would you respond while maintaining professional integrity?

lessons.lessonTitle: Model fitness-for-purpose against stakeholder requirement...
objectives: Construct a calibrated mathematical model from a provided operational dataset by defining variables, stating at least 5 explicit assumptions, citing parameter sources, and producing a reproducible calculation (spreadsheet or notebook) with consistent units.

Evaluate model fitness-for-purpose against a stated stakeholder requirement by selecting and computing at least 2 validation metrics (e.g., MAE, RMSE, MAPE, residual checks) and writing a 150–250 word justification of whether the model is acceptable for the intended use.

Create an audit-ready validation record by completing a Model Card that includes: intended use, scope/limitations, validation evidence, rounding policy, uncertainty statement, and corrective actions taken after a critique scenario.

Implement simple version control practices by producing a minimal version history (at least 3 entries) that documents changes, rationale, and impacts on outputs, and by naming files/versions consistently.

activities.title: Diagnostic warm-up: Calibration vs validation + integrity check

Includes one scenario question on professional integrity (e.g., reporting uncertainty and limitations). Immediate feedback explains why each option is correct/incorrect.

activities.title: Demonstration: Building a calibrated model with transparent assumptions
activities.description: Short walkthrough video (or step-by-step annotated slides) demonstrating how to: define variables and units, log assumptions, select a simple model form, calibrate parameters from operational data, and record parameter sources. The demonstration explicitly shows: (a) unit consistency checks, (b) a rounding policy, (c) a minimal version history entry after changing a parameter source.
activities.teachingMethod: Cognitive apprenticeship: instructor models expert thinking aloud (why this metric, why this assumption, what limitation must be disclosed).
resources: Demo file (spreadsheet or notebook) with cells/sections clearly labelled (Inputs/Assumptions/Calibration/Validation/Sensitivity)

Show a 'before/after' version note (v1.0 → v1.1) and what changed in outputs.

activities.title: Guided build (core create task): Calibrate + validate your model and draft the Model Card
activities.description: Learners build their own small calibrated model from a provided operational dataset and stakeholder requirement brief. Required outputs: (1) model definition (variables/units), (2) assumptions log (≥5 items), (3) calibrated parameters with sources, (4) validation metrics (≥2) with residual/constraint commentary, (5) a short sensitivity check on at least 1 parameter, (6) a first-pass Model Card draft. Learners must include an explicit uncertainty/limitation statement and a reproducibility note (how to re-run).
activities.teachingMethod: Guided creation with scaffolds: partially completed template + step prompts; learners generate an original, auditable artefact.

instructorActions: Provide scaffold prompts in the starter file (e.g., 'Assumption A1: …; Impact if violated: …; How to test/monitor: …').
Include an optional 'hint path' for calibration (e.g., least squares steps) and an optional 'manual path' (graphical fit) to accommodate varied backgrounds.
studentActions: Calibrate the model parameters from the dataset and record parameter sources.
Compute validation metrics and interpret whether errors meet stakeholder thresholds.
Run a simple sensitivity check (e.g., ±5% on one parameter) and record the impact on the key output.
Draft the Model Card sections up to 'Validation & Sensitivity' and save as Version v1.0.

activities.title: Asynchronous team-review simulation: Challenge, respond, correct, and version
activities.description: Role-play via written responses. Learners receive two simulated reviewer comments (e.g., 'Your model overfits outside the operating range' and 'Where is your evidence that this assumption holds?'). Learners must: (1) respond respectfully with reasoning and evidence, (2) make one corrective action (e.g., restrict scope, adjust rounding policy, add validation split, revise assumption/limitation), (3) update the Model Card and version history (v1.1) documenting what changed and why. Emphasis: collaborative behaviours—welcoming challenge and integrating feedback into improved solutions.
activities.teachingMethod: Structured reflection + revision cycle to practice transparent communication and audit-friendly change documentation.
resources: Response framework: Claim → Evidence → Limitation → Action
instructorActions: Provide comment scenarios that target typical weak points: scope creep, hidden assumptions, missing units, and unjustified thresholds.
Include a model response exemplar that demonstrates professional tone and transparency.
studentActions: Write two short responses (4–6 sentences each) to the reviewer challenges.
Implement one corrective change to model/documentation and update the version history to v1.1.
Revise the uncertainty/limitations statement to align with the new scope and evidence.

activities.title: Formative check and submission pack: Fitness-for-purpose decision + audit readiness
activities.description: Learners complete a final self-check using a rubric and submit (or save for portfolio) the 'submission pack': model file + Model Card + version history. Includes a short auto-graded exit quiz focused on fitness-for-purpose decisions, correct rounding, and what constitutes sufficient validation evidence. Learners must answer one prompt: 'Is the model fit-for-purpose? Yes/No/Conditional—justify.'
activities.teachingMethod: Rubric-based self-assessment + exit ticket to consolidate the create-level artefact into an auditable deliverable.
resources: Fitness-for-purpose rubric (4 criteria: requirement alignment, validation evidence, transparency/limitations, reproducibility/versioning)
Submission checklist (files, naming convention, required sections)
instructorActions: Align rubric language with module competencies (integrity, transparency, collaboration).
Provide automated feedback for quiz plus a 'next steps' path: if score <70%, direct to specific remediation sections.
studentActions: Run the rubric checklist and fix any missing audit items (units, assumptions, sources, version entry).
Complete the exit quiz and write the fitness-for-purpose decision statement.
Save/export the submission pack using consistent naming (e.g., MOD107_L8_Model_v1.1).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance: Design this lesson as an artefact-creation cycle: learners should leave with a calibrated model plus an audit-ready documentation trail, not just calculations. Continuously reinforce professional integrity: (1) separate what is known from what is assumed; (2) report uncertainty and limitations explicitly; (3) avoid overclaiming validity beyond the operating range. Use the Model Card as the backbone to unify modelling, validation, and communication. To cultivate collaborative behaviours in a self-study environment, embed structured 'reviewer challenge' prompts and require learners to revise their work (version bump) rather than merely explain it. Insist on reproducibility: clear units, labelled inputs/outputs, consistent rounding policy, and a version history that records rationale and impact. Provide exemplars that show both strong practice and common documentation failures (missing sources, silent scope changes). Encourage learners to treat fitness-for-purpose as a decision under constraints—often 'conditional acceptance' with boundaries is the most honest outcome.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: Timebox tightly to preserve the create task (25 minutes) and revision cycle (15 minutes). If learners fall behind, prioritise: (1) clear intended use + assumptions, (2) at least two validation metrics, (3) a concise limitation statement, (4) a version entry documenting one corrective change. Optional depth (only if on track): additional residual diagnostics, cross-validation split, or multi-parameter sensitivity. Recommend learners work in two passes: Pass 1 (build v1.0 quickly with placeholders), Pass 2 (tighten evidence, wording, and audit trail to v1.1).
adaptationOptions: Scaffolded vs independent path: provide a fully guided spreadsheet with formulas pre-built for learners needing support; offer a blank template (or coding notebook) for advanced learners.
Multiple validation metric choices: allow learners to choose metrics aligned to the stakeholder brief (e.g., MAE for interpretability, RMSE for penalising large errors) while requiring justification.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for videos, screen-reader friendly templates, and an alternative text-only walkthrough of the demonstration.

Extension task for high performers: add an out-of-sample validation split and document how the fitness-for-purpose decision changes; include a second sensitivity factor (e.g., data noise or tolerance bounds).

Language support: provide sentence stems for limitations and uncertainty (e.g., 'This model is valid within…', 'Primary sources of uncertainty include…', 'If assumption A fails, expected impact is…').
commonMisconceptions: Calibration proves the model is valid (confusing fitting parameters with independent validation).
A high overall goodness-of-fit automatically implies fitness-for-purpose (ignoring operating range, constraints, and decision risk).
Assumptions do not need to be written if they seem 'obvious' (hidden assumptions undermine auditability and integrity).
Version control is only for software code (not for spreadsheets, parameter tables, or documentation changes).
Rounding is cosmetic and can be done at any step (premature rounding can change calibrated parameters and validation metrics).
Sensitivity analysis equals uncertainty quantification (sensitivity shows responsiveness to inputs; uncertainty needs explicit sources and bounds).
If validation fails, the only option is to discard the model (often the honest action is to restrict scope, state limitations, or adjust intended use).
discussionPrompts: What minimum evidence would convince you a model is fit-for-purpose for this stakeholder brief, and why that evidence (not others)?
Which assumption in your model is most risky? How would you monitor or test it in operation?
When is a 'conditional' fitness-for-purpose decision more professionally honest than a simple yes/no?
What change did you make after the reviewer challenge, and how did you document its impact in your version history?
How does your rounding policy affect reproducibility and trust in the reported results?
If two models meet the error threshold, what non-error factors (interpretability, robustness, auditability) should decide which to recommend?

lessons.lessonTitle: Develop a calibrated mathematical model from operational ...
objectives: Create a calibrated mathematical model from a provided operational dataset by defining at least 3 variables, 1–3 parameters, and documenting at least 5 explicit assumptions and the intended use in a one-page “model card”.

activities.title: Guided practice: calibrate parameters and report CI with correct units

instructorActions: Clarify sensitivity vs uncertainty: sensitivity is conditional on the model and local perturbations.

instructorActions: Provide clear submission requirements (file types, naming, what must be reproducible).

instructorNotes.pedagogicalGuidance:
Keep the lesson anchored in the two assigned MLOs by treating documentation and checking as core mathematical work, not add-ons. Because Bloom level is “create,” allow multiple plausible model forms provided learners justify choices and clearly bound intended use. Emphasize professional integrity: learners must explicitly separate (a) observed data facts, (b) modelling assumptions, and (c) inferred conclusions. Require units on every variable/parameter and make unit-checking a gating step before calibration interpretation. For reproducibility, enforce a simple standard: a third party should be able to re-run the artifact from raw data to final outputs without hidden steps. Use exemplars that show honest reporting of limitations (e.g., ‘CI assumes independent errors; violated if time-series autocorrelation exists’). Encourage diligence via structured checklists (dimensional, tolerance, rounding, sensitivity), and frame validation as an ongoing process rather than a one-time pass/fail.

In an online self-study setting, embed frequent micro-checks with immediate feedback, and provide “acceptable answer bands” rather than single numeric keys to reduce frustration due to solver/tool differences. Provide sentence stems for transparent reporting (assumptions, limitations, uncertainty statements) to support learners who are new to technical writing.
instructorNotes.pacingSuggestions: If learners are on pace: keep Activity 3 to 20 minutes by using the provided calibration template and focusing on one CI method (analytic or bootstrap). If learners are ahead: add an extension to Activity 6 comparing two perturbation sizes (e.g., ±1% vs ±10%) and commenting on linearity/locality. If learners are behind: allow them to use the exemplar functional form and focus on completing a correct model card + validation checklist rather than exploring alternate models. Recommended time controls: stop calibration after obtaining stable parameters (don’t chase marginal fit improvements), and prioritize (1) correct units, (2) explicit assumptions, (3) reproducible steps, (4) a clear sensitivity ranking.
adaptationOptions: Tool choice: offer both spreadsheet and notebook workflows; learners pick the tool that matches their confidence while meeting the same reporting requirements.
Scaffolded vs open-ended model form: provide a suggested functional form for learners needing support; allow advanced learners to justify an alternative model and compare fit/validation outcomes.
Accessibility: provide captions/transcripts for demos, a screen-reader-friendly model card template, and colorblind-safe sensitivity charts (patterns + labels).
Math support: supply a CI ‘cookbook’ (step list) plus an optional deeper note on assumptions behind t-based intervals and when bootstrap is preferable.
Challenge extension: ask advanced learners to add a brief note on potential overfitting and propose a simple hold-out validation or cross-validation plan (conceptual is acceptable).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing calibration with validation (believing a good fit automatically means the model is valid for decision-making).
Treating assumptions as optional or ‘obvious,’ leading to undocumented constraints that undermine transparency.
Misinterpreting a 95% CI as ‘95% probability the parameter is in the interval’ without acknowledging modelling assumptions and frequentist interpretation limitations.
Ignoring or inconsistently applying units (e.g., mixing hours and seconds or using unitless parameters when they should carry dimensions).
Believing sensitivity analysis measures uncertainty directly (rather than the model’s output responsiveness to input/parameter changes).
Over-rounding intermediate values, causing drift in outputs and irreproducible results; or rounding inconsistently across tables/figures.
Assuming reproducibility only means ‘I can re-run it,’ rather than ‘someone else can re-run it’ with clear steps and no hidden manual edits.
discussionPrompts: Which assumption in your model has the highest risk of being wrong in real operations, and how would that bias your recommendations?
Share one validation/tolerance check that failed (or nearly failed). What did you change: the model form, the parameter estimate, the data preprocessing, or the stated intended use?
How did you decide on rounding rules for parameters and outputs? What is the consequence of rounding too early vs too late in your workflow?
Post your sensitivity ranking (top 3 drivers). If you had budget to improve measurement of only one input, which would you choose and why?
What would you include in a ‘limitations’ section to be transparent without undermining stakeholder trust (i.e., honest but decision-relevant reporting)?
