slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)
content: List units for: rate, time, quantity, cost, revenue, profit
Convert one value (your choice) into a new unit correctly
Do a 3-step calculation using guard digits throughout
Recalculate rounding each step; compare final outputs
Explain difference using: “Early rounding changes ___ because ___”
Complete checklist: inputs/units, outputs/units, assumptions, notes
content.notes:
Guide learners to create a simple spreadsheet scenario of their own (or use workplace-like numbers): e.g., output rate, shift length, unit cost, selling price, fixed cost. The focus is the process, not the context.

Encourage structured checking:
1) Unit audit: can every number be read with a unit?
2) Conversion audit: are conversion factors visible?
3) Rounding audit: is rounding applied only at the reporting stage?

Probing questions:
- Which step in your model is most sensitive to rounding?
- If a colleague challenged your answer, what evidence is visible in the sheet?

Common misconception: writing a reflection that is descriptive but not causal. Push for cause-and-effect language: rounding location changes intermediate values, which changes later multiplications/divisions.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD101 spreadsheet standards and calculation tasks
Marks often depend on units and documentation, not just answers
Avoid mixing units within one formula (convert first)
Avoid ROUND() in every step; round only reported outputs
Avoid missing brackets when translating algebra into Excel
Avoid unclear sheets: no input/output separation or assumptions
content.notes:
Position the lesson as directly transferable to assessment criteria: clarity, auditability, and correctness. Explain that assessors typically look for evidence of method: labelled units, coherent layout, and justified rounding.

Offer practical advice: when you submit work, imagine it is being checked by someone who cannot ask you questions. Your spreadsheet must answer those questions itself.

Probing questions:
- If your final answer is wrong, could an assessor still award method marks from your spreadsheet?
- Would a unit check have caught the error earlier?

Misconception: “If the final value matches, presentation does not matter.” In workplace and assessed contexts, transparent method is a key outcome.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Units are part of the number: label inputs and outputs clearly
Convert once, early, and keep a consistent calculation unit set
Use significant figures to match measurement precision
Keep guard digits; round only the final reported result
Rearrange formulas carefully and translate brackets into Excel
content.notes:
Reinforce that these are habits to apply in every spreadsheet, not rules for a single topic. Encourage learners to save a personal spreadsheet template with: sections (inputs/calculations/outputs), a notes area, and a rounding/unit checklist.

Exit questions:
- What is one unit conversion you will stop doing “in your head” and start documenting?
- Where in your spreadsheets will you record rounding choices so they are visible to others?

Close by reminding learners that careful units, rounding, and documentation are what make calculations reliable and defensible in workplace settings.

content.title: Algebraic rearrangement for workplace pricing

Maths Certification

content.notes: Welcome learners and set expectations for an applied session: we will take familiar workplace formulae (pricing, break-even, yield) and practise rearranging them to isolate a chosen variable. Emphasise that the end goal is not only correct algebra, but also a spreadsheet that an auditor can follow: clear inputs, transparent calculations, units stated, rounding justified, and a simple change note. Ask: where in your workplace do you solve “backwards” for an unknown (e.g., target price, required volume, required input)?

slides.title: Learning objectives

content.title: Learning objectives
content: Rearrange 3+ workplace formulae to isolate a target variable
Show correct algebra steps and state units for each variable
Build an Excel sheet using correct references and named ranges

Validate using units check and a reverse check against original formula
content.notes: Clarify what “apply” means at Bloom’s level: you should be able to do the method reliably, not just recognise it. Stress that correct answers without correct method (steps, units, checks) are not sufficient in workplace settings. Introduce the idea that every rearrangement should end with two confirmations: dimensional plausibility (units) and behavioural plausibility (reverse check).

slides.title: How to use this lesson (self-study)

content.title: How to use this lesson (self-study)
content: Read each rule, then copy one example by hand
Rebuild each example in Excel using named ranges
Add units, rounding notes, and assumptions as you build
Run the self-checks before you trust the output
Keep a short change note when you edit your model
content.notes: Explain a practical workflow: (1) do the algebra on paper first to reduce spreadsheet errors, (2) implement once in Excel, (3) test with known values, (4) document decisions as you go rather than at the end. Highlight a common self-study pitfall: learners often jump into Excel and then ‘debug’ algebra via trial and error. Encourage deliberate practice: one formula at a time, with a deliberate check step. Ask: what would a colleague need to understand your sheet if you were off sick?

slides.title: Core idea: isolate the variable you need

content.title: Core idea: isolate the variable you need
content.content: To isolate a variable, perform the same operation to both sides to undo how the variable is combined with others. Keep the formula equivalent at every step. Treat units as part of the meaning, not decoration.
content.notes: Unpack the phrase “undo how the variable is combined”. If the variable is multiplied by something, you divide by that thing; if it is inside brackets multiplied by a factor, you divide first and then deal with the brackets. Reinforce equivalence: each line should be true whenever the original line is true. Mini-example to speak through: if TotalCost = Fixed + (Rate × Hours), and you need Hours, first subtract Fixed, then divide by Rate. Ask: what is the final operation applied to the target variable in the original expression?

slides.title: Rearrangement rules you will use repeatedly

content.title: Rearrangement rules you will use repeatedly
content: Add/subtract: move terms by doing the opposite to both sides
Multiply/divide: undo by dividing/multiplying both sides
Brackets: remove by dividing first, then expanding if needed
Fractions: clear by multiplying both sides by the denominator
Powers/roots: use inverse operations (square ↔ square root)
Do one change per line to reduce mistakes
content.notes: Model the discipline of ‘one change per line’. Many errors come from doing two or three moves at once, then losing track of sign changes or factors. Address misconceptions: (1) ‘moving a term across the equals’ is shorthand, not a rule—what you are really doing is applying the same operation to both sides; (2) cancelling only works with multiplication/division, not addition. Probing questions: Which operation is “closest” to the target variable? Are you allowed to divide by that term (i.e., can it be zero)?

slides.title: Units and rounding: make meaning explicit

content.title: Units and rounding: make meaning explicit
leftColumn: State units for every input and output
Check dimensional consistency line-by-line
Use % as a decimal in Excel (e.g., 20% = 0.20)
Prefer rounding at outputs, not mid-calculation
rightColumn: Record where rounding occurs and why
Use sensible display vs calculation precision
Note currency rounding rules (e.g., 2 dp for £)
Flag assumptions (e.g., constant rate, linear cost)

Encourage learners to choose a rounding point intentionally (often at the final output) and document it. Ask: if you round earlier, could it bias the result up or down?

slides.title: Spreadsheet layout for transparency

content.title: Spreadsheet layout for transparency
content: Separate: Inputs, Calculations, Outputs (clear headings)
Use consistent units next to values (e.g., £/unit, hours)
Keep formulas simple; avoid hidden constants in formulas
Add an assumptions table near inputs
Add a change note: what, when, why, who
Use cell styles to distinguish input cells
content.notes: Explain why separation matters: it reduces accidental overwriting and makes review faster. Ask: if an auditor only had your spreadsheet, could they identify inputs without clicking into formulas?

slides.title: Excel implementation: references and named ranges

content.title: Excel implementation: references and named ranges
content: Relative refs for copied rows; absolute refs for fixed cells
Lock with $ (e.g., $B$2) when a cell must not move
Use 2+ named ranges for key inputs (e.g., VAT, Markup)
Prefer names for rates and constants to improve readability
Test with known values and a second test case
Avoid hard-coding rates inside formulas
content.notes: Demonstrate the difference: if you copy a unit-price formula down a list of products, product-specific cells should move (relative), but VAT rate should not (absolute or named range). Explain named ranges: they reduce errors like selecting the wrong cell and they read like the algebra. Typical errors to warn about: (1) mixing percentages written as 20 rather than 0.20, (2) copying formulas that reference the wrong row, (3) using absolute references everywhere, making the model inflexible. Probing question: which values should change when you copy the formula, and which must stay fixed?

slides.title: Worked example 1: isolate cost from selling price

content.title: Worked example 1: isolate cost from selling price
leftColumn: Given: SP = C × (1+M) × (1−D) × (1+VAT)
Goal: isolate C (cost per unit, £/unit)
Step 1: divide by (1+VAT)
Step 2: divide by (1−D)
Step 3: divide by (1+M)
rightColumn: Rearranged: C = SP /((1+VAT)(1−D)(1+M))
Excel: =SellPrice/((1+VAT)*(1-Disc)*(1+Markup))
Named ranges: VAT, Disc, Markup
Units: SP £/unit, C £/unit; rates unitless
content.notes: Talk through why division is appropriate: C is multiplied by several factors, so undo multiplication by dividing. Stress bracket discipline in Excel; missing brackets is a top cause of wrong answers. Use a quick numeric check in narration: if SP is £120, VAT 20%, D 10%, M 25%, then C should be lower than £120—if you get higher, you have likely inverted a factor. Misconception: learners sometimes subtract VAT (SP−VAT) rather than divide by (1+VAT). Ask: why is VAT removed by division, not subtraction, when VAT is a percentage of the net?

slides.title: Worked example 2: break-even quantity

content.title: Worked example 2: break-even quantity
content.notes: Define variables clearly in speech: P = selling price (£/unit), VC = variable cost (£/unit), FC = fixed cost (£), Q = units (units). Reinforce the units cue: FC/(P−VC) gives £ divided by (£/unit) = units, which is correct. Discuss the condition P > VC: if contribution margin is zero or negative, break-even is impossible. Excel mapping: inputs as named ranges Price, VarCost, FixedCost; formula =FixedCost/(Price-VarCost). Probing questions: what happens if Price equals VarCost? How would you handle that in Excel (e.g., IFERROR with a meaningful message)?

Reinforce the units cue: FC/(P−VC) gives £ divided by (£/unit) = units, which is correct. Discuss the condition P > VC: if contribution margin is zero or negative, break-even is impossible. How would you handle that in Excel (e.g., IFERROR with a meaningful message)?

slides.title: Worked example 3: required input for target output

content.title: Worked example 3: required input for target output
leftColumn: Given: Good = Input × Yield
Goal: isolate Input (units of input material)
Step: divide both sides by Yield
Rearranged: Input = Good / Yield
rightColumn: Excel: =TargetGood/YieldRate
YieldRate must be decimal (e.g., 92% = 0.92)
Assumption: yield constant over the batch
Reverse check: Input×Yield returns TargetGood
content.notes: Explain yield as a proportion: a 92% yield means 0.92 good units per 1 input unit. Highlight the common spreadsheet error: typing 92 rather than 0.92, which makes required input far too small. Encourage documenting the assumption that yield is stable; in practice it may vary with batch size, operator, or machine settings. Ask: if yield drops, should required input rise or fall? Use this as a sense-check before trusting the formula.

slides.title: Practice prompts (do in Excel)

content.title: Practice prompts (do in Excel)
content: Rearrange: Revenue = Price × Quantity to isolate Quantity
Rearrange: Total = Fixed + Rate×Hours to isolate Hours
Rearrange: SP = C×(1+M)×(1+VAT) to isolate M
Build a sheet with Inputs/Calcs/Outputs blocks
Use 2 named ranges and correct $ references
Test with two sets of values and record outcomes
content.notes: Encourage learners to write the rearranged algebra next to the Excel formula (e.g., in a note cell) to keep the link clear. For the markup rearrangement: M = SP/(C(1+VAT)) − 1; discuss where the “minus 1” comes from (undoing +1 after dividing). Suggest simple test values to catch mistakes: choose numbers where you can estimate mentally (e.g., VAT 20%, C £50, M 25% gives net before VAT £62.50, after VAT £75). Probing questions: are your output units correct? do your results move in the expected direction when an input increases?

slides.title: Self-check and documentation checklist

content.title: Self-check and documentation checklist
content: Units check: do the units match on both sides?
Reverse check: substitute result into original formula
Rounding: where do you round and why there?
Assumptions: list at least two and keep them visible
Change note: what changed, when, why (and by whom)
Sanity check: does the answer look plausible?
content.notes: Teach the reverse check explicitly: after solving for the target variable, plug it back into the original formula using the same inputs; you should reproduce the given output (within rounding tolerance). Discuss tolerances: currency outputs may differ by 1p due to rounding decisions—document this. Give a misconception to avoid: ‘it matches for one test so it must be right’—errors can hide until you try a second case. Suggest a second test chosen to stress the model (e.g., a high discount, a low yield, or a near-zero margin). Ask: if someone challenged your result, what evidence inside the sheet would you point to?

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
leftColumn: Supports MOD101 spreadsheet standards tasks
Evidence: algebra steps + working Excel model
Evidence: units, assumptions, rounding, change note
Evidence: validation (units + reverse check)
rightColumn: Mistake: subtracting a percentage instead of dividing
Mistake: wrong brackets in Excel changes order of ops
Mistake: 20 typed instead of 0.20 (percent handling)

content.content:
Maths Certification

Lesson 3: Use Excel referencing, named ranges and structured layout
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Introduce this lesson as a practical spreadsheet standards session. Emphasise that the aim is application: learners will build a small, auditable model rather than memorise Excel features. Set expectations: they should work alongside Excel, pausing often to replicate steps. Prompt: “When you copy a formula, do you know exactly which parts should change and which must stay fixed?” Highlight that good referencing and layout reduce errors and make work reviewable by others.

slides.title: Learning objectives (apply)

content.title: Learning objectives (apply)
content: Use relative/absolute refs correctly when copying formulas
Create 3+ named ranges to make formulas readable and traceable
Add change notes and record key assumptions (units, rounding)
Model a target with 2+ constraints and test feasibility in Excel
Write one recommendation and state a limitation/uncertainty
content.notes: Explain how success will be judged in practical terms. For referencing: they should be able to justify every dollar sign, not guess. For named ranges: stress audit value—another person should locate each input quickly using tracing tools. For assumptions/change notes: position these as professional controls, not ‘extra admin’. For constraints/feasibility: link to algebra they already know (inequalities) and show that Excel is used to evidence the logic with units. For the recommendation: clarify it must be evidence-based (numbers from the model) and include at least one limitation (e.g., processing time estimates). Ask: “If your spreadsheet were handed to a colleague, could they verify it in five minutes?”

slides.title: How to use this lesson

content.title: How to use this lesson
leftColumn: Read each concept, then pause
Replicate steps in a blank workbook
Keep units visible in labels
rightColumn: Test by copying formulas across/down
Use tracing tools to verify sources
Record assumptions and changes as you go
content.notes: Guide learners towards an iterative workflow: build a small piece, test it, then continue. Reinforce that copying formulas is the fastest way to reveal incorrect references. Encourage them to keep units in column headers or labels (e.g., hours/unit, units/week). Demonstrate a habit: after entering a formula, immediately click it and use Trace Precedents—if the arrows point somewhere unexpected, fix the layout or references before adding more complexity. Probing questions: “What would break if this table expands by one row?” and “Could you explain your workbook to someone without scrolling for two minutes?”

slides.title: Relative vs absolute references

content.title: Relative vs absolute references
leftColumn: Relative: A1 changes when copied
Best for repeating patterns in a table
Risk: accidental drift from the true input
rightColumn: Absolute: $A$1 stays fixed
Use for constants, rates, capacities
Mixed: $A1 or A$1 locks one dimension
content.notes: Explain referencing as a coordinate system: copying a formula applies an offset. Relative references move by the offset; absolute references ignore it. Give a quick mental test: “If I copy this one column right, should the input move with me?” If yes, it should usually be relative (or partially relative). If no, lock it with $. Clarify mixed references with a typical use: a multiplication table or cost matrix where the row header stays fixed while the column changes (or vice versa). Common misconception: learners often lock the wrong cell because they think $ means ‘important’ rather than ‘fixed when copied’. Ask learners to predict before copying: “Where should this reference point after I fill down five rows?”

slides.title: Reference types and copy behaviour

content.title: Reference types and copy behaviour
content.notes: Talk through each row and connect it to typical spreadsheet tasks. Relative is for repeating calculations by row (e.g., revenue per line). Absolute is for a single input used everywhere (e.g., VAT rate, hourly cost rate, capacity). Mixed is for two-dimensional structures: one axis is a list you move through, the other is a header you keep fixed. Demonstrate the F4 key (or Fn+F4 on some laptops) cycling through reference modes and remind learners to check the result in the formula bar. Quick check question: “If I copy this formula across columns, which part should remain anchored—row, column, or both?”

slides.title: Named ranges for readable formulas

content.title: Named ranges for readable formulas
content: Named range = label for a cell or block of cells
Use for inputs, rates and capacities used in many formulas
Choose clear names: Target_A, MachHrsPerUnit_A
Create via Name Box or Formulas > Define Name
Audit via Name Manager and Go To (F5)
Avoid spaces and ambiguous names like Data or Rate
content.notes: Explain that named ranges reduce ‘mystery cell’ formulas and help reviewers understand the model without clicking multiple cells. Use a mini before/after: “=B6*$E$2” becomes “=Units_A*LabourRate”. That readability supports debugging and external review. Clarify scope briefly: workbook-level names are easiest for beginners; sheet-level names can cause confusion if duplicated. Mention that names should encode meaning and, where helpful, the unit (e.g., MachHrsPerUnit_A). Common misconception: learners sometimes name an entire column when they only need a single input cell; this can create unexpected results when the range includes blanks. Ask: “If I printed just the formula, would the name tell me what it represents and its unit?”

slides.title: Structured layout for calculation sheets

content.title: Structured layout for calculation sheets

rows: Max hours, max materials, budget limits

content.notes: Emphasise the professional principle: separate inputs from calculations from outputs. This reduces the chance of accidentally overwriting formulas and makes auditing faster. Point out that consistent formatting is not cosmetic—it signals where users are allowed to type. Suggest practical controls: data validation for inputs (e.g., non-negative targets), and consistent number formats (e.g., 2 decimal places for hours). Common misconception: mixing inputs into the calculation area because it is ‘convenient’—this makes later changes error-prone. Probing question: “If someone asked you to change one assumption, could you do it without searching the entire sheet?”

slides.title: Audit trail and traceability tools

content.title: Audit trail and traceability tools
content: Add a change log: date, change, reason, author
Write assumptions: units, rounding rule, constraint source
Use Trace Precedents/Dependents to follow links
Use Evaluate Formula to step through calculations
Use comments/notes for non-obvious choices
Aim: locate each input source within 15 seconds
content.notes: Explain auditability as the ability to answer: “Where did this number come from?” and “Who changed this, and why?” Give an example assumption statement: “Processing times are averages from Jan–Mar logs; rounded to 0.1 hour.” Stress that constraints must have a source (e.g., “Machine hours from shift rota: 2 machines × 40 h/week”). Demonstrate how tracing tools support this: Trace Precedents should lead from an output cell back to named inputs; Evaluate Formula is especially helpful when IF statements hide logic. Common misconception: using comments as a substitute for a change log; comments explain, but they do not record change history. Ask: “If an auditor challenged a capacity value, could you show the source immediately?”

slides.title: Worked example: production target inputs

content.title: Worked example: production target inputs
content.notes: Frame this as a realistic planning question: the workplace has targets for two products, and limited machine and labour hours each week. Reinforce units in every row; this prevents common mistakes such as mixing minutes and hours. In Excel, advise placing these in the Inputs/Rates/Capacities sections with consistent shading. Suggest naming key cells: Target_A, Target_B, MachHrsPerUnit_A, MachHrsPerUnit_B, LabHrsPerUnit_A, LabHrsPerUnit_B, MachCapacity, LabCapacity. Probing question: “Before any calculation, can you already predict which constraint might be tight?”

slides.title: Worked example: formulas using named ranges

content.title: Worked example: formulas using named ranges
content: Name the input cells (Targets, times/unit, capacities)
Machine hours used =Target_A*MachA +Target_B*MachB
Labour hours used =Target_A*LabA +Target_B*LabB
Keep formula cells separate from inputs (no hard-coded numbers)
Copy patterns carefully; lock only what must stay fixed
Use Trace Precedents to confirm each term links to inputs
content.notes: Walk through building the two resource-use calculations. Emphasise that named ranges make the formula self-explanatory, and they reduce errors when you insert rows/columns later. If learners prefer cell references initially, show the ‘upgrade’ path: build with cell refs, then apply names and watch the formula update to names automatically. Stress the discipline: do not type 0.4 into a formula; link to the rate cell so changes flow through. Misconception to address: believing named ranges automatically make a model correct; they improve readability, but you still must check logic and units. Ask: “If the machine time for Product B changes, how many formulas should you need to edit?” (Target answer: one input cell.)

slides.title: Worked example: feasibility from constraints

content.title: Worked example: feasibility from constraints
content: Constraint 1: machine used ≤ machine capacity
Constraint 2: labour used ≤ labour capacity
Compute gaps: capacity - used (keep units: hours/week)
Flag with IF: =IF(gap>=0,"OK","Over")
Example result: machine used 96 > 80, labour used 52 ≤ 60
Overall feasibility: Not feasible (machine constraint)
content.notes: Connect this explicitly to linear inequalities: you are testing whether the target point (A=120, B=80) lies inside the feasible region. Show the arithmetic behind the example so learners can sanity-check: machine used = 120×0.4 + 80×0.6 = 48 + 48 = 96 hours; labour used = 120×0.3 + 80×0.2 = 36 + 16 = 52 hours. Stress that feasibility is determined by all constraints simultaneously; one failure makes the plan infeasible. Common misconception: treating ‘close’ as ‘feasible’—in operations, exceeding capacity is a real violation unless you explicitly model overtime. Probing questions: “Which constraint is binding here?” and “What change would restore feasibility with the smallest adjustment?”

slides.title: Worked example: recommendation and limitation

content.title: Worked example: recommendation and limitation
content: Recommendation: reduce target, add capacity, or change mix
Example: keep A=120; solve for max B by machine capacity
Max B = (MachCapacity - 0.4*A)/0.6 = 53.3 units
So B must drop from 80 to 53 (or add 16 machine hours)
State limitation: times/unit are estimates and may vary by shift
Record decision and rationale in the change log
content.notes: Model the recommendation as a transparent response to the constraint. Demonstrate the simple rearrangement as algebra in context: 0.4A + 0.6B ≤ 80, so B ≤ (80 − 0.4A)/0.6. With A=120, B ≤ 53.3, which you might round down to 53 units if units must be whole. Alternatively, compute extra capacity needed: 96 − 80 = 16 machine hours. Emphasise that the recommendation must reference outputs (used hours, gaps) and must acknowledge uncertainty (e.g., processing times depend on operator skill, product mix, downtime). Common misconception: giving a recommendation without stating what assumption drives it. Ask: “If machine time per unit is 10% higher than assumed, what happens to feasibility?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
content: Build the sheet using the structured sections (Inputs to Outputs)
Define 3+ named ranges and rewrite formulas using them
Add 2 assumptions with units and a source for each constraint
Create a change log and record two edits you make today
Test a new target mix and decide feasible/not feasible
Write one recommendation plus one limitation of your model
content.notes: Encourage learners to treat this as a mini deliverable: a clean workbook someone else could use. Suggest a self-check routine: (1) click an output, trace precedents to confirm only input cells feed it; (2) copy formulas across/down and confirm no reference drift; (3) change one input (e.g., capacity) and see if outputs update logically. Invite reflection: “Which part took most time—getting the maths right, or making it auditable?” Address a common barrier: learners may avoid documenting assumptions because they feel unsure; reassure them that stating uncertainty is a strength, not a weakness. If learners finish early, prompt them to add conditional formatting to highlight ‘Over’ constraints.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD101 spreadsheet modelling/standards submission
Marks often reward clarity: layout, traceability, assumptions
Common error: hard-coded numbers inside formulas
Common error: missing $ locks when copying across/down
Common error: capacities without units or source
Common error: recommendation not linked to model outputs
content.notes: Explain that assessment typically judges both correctness and professionalism: can the model be checked, reused, and defended? Expand on each mistake: hard-coding hides assumptions and breaks change control; missing absolute references causes silent errors when copied; missing units leads to invalid comparisons (e.g., hours vs minutes); unsourced capacities reduce credibility; and recommendations must cite evidence (e.g., ‘machine gap is −16 hours’). Offer a final pre-submission checklist: review Name Manager, check that all inputs are in one place, and use Evaluate Formula on at least one key output. Ask: “If an assessor changes one input, do all dependent outputs update without manual edits?”

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Use $ to control what changes when formulas are copied
Named ranges make models readable and faster to audit
Separate inputs, rates, capacities, calcs and outputs
Document assumptions and maintain a simple change log
Test feasibility by checking each constraint with units shown
content.notes: Reinforce that spreadsheet skill here is about controlling risk: reference discipline prevents accidental errors, structured layout prevents confusion, and documentation supports accountability. Encourage learners to keep practising with small models before scaling up. Prompt a final self-question: “Could I defend every number in this workbook—where it came from, what unit it uses, and what would happen if it changed?” Suggest next steps: apply the same structure to another workplace scenario (budgeting, staffing, materials) while keeping the same standards.

Prompt: “When someone says ‘we can make 55 by Friday’, what maths checks would you run before agreeing?”

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Set up ≥2 linear inequalities from constraints, with units
Test whether a proposed target is feasible under constraints
Rearrange a linear equation to solve for an unknown target
Apply significant figures and justify when to round
Fix unit/rounding/assumption issues in a spreadsheet excerpt
Use: study → practise → self-check as you progress

slides.title: From constraints to linear inequalities

content.title: From constraints to linear inequalities
content: A constraint limits or requires a quantity
Define variables clearly: name, meaning, unit
Translate wording into symbols: ≤, ≥
Multiply rate × quantity to match the resource unit
Feasible means all inequalities are satisfied together
content.notes:
Model the translation process explicitly. Start with a sentence such as: “Each unit takes 1.5 hours, and we have 90 hours.” Explain that the *rate* (hours per unit) multiplied by the *quantity* (units) gives total hours, which must be no more than availability.

Mini-example (verbal): If x is units/day, and each unit needs 0.2 kg of material, then material used is 0.2x kg/day; if stock is 30 kg, you write 0.2x ≤ 30.

Probe: “What word cues suggest ≤ (at most, no more than) versus ≥ (at least, minimum)?”

Misconception: writing ‘=’ when the situation is a limit. In feasibility, equality is a special case, not the default.

slides.title: Units and interpreting feasibility results

content.title: Units and interpreting feasibility results
content: Convert units first (e.g., minutes to hours)
Attach units to coefficients (e.g., 2 kg per unit)
Check feasibility by substituting the proposed target
If a target breaks any constraint, it is not feasible
Non-integer results need a rounding decision with a reason
content.notes:
Emphasise that unit errors are among the most common sources of incorrect feasibility decisions. Demonstrate a quick conversion: 90 minutes = 1.5 hours; if you treat 90 as hours, you inflate capacity by 60×.

Explain interpretation: substituting a proposed value is often faster than solving inequalities fully, especially when the question is “is this target feasible?”.

Rounding principle preview: if you calculate a maximum feasible quantity as 97.14 units and units must be whole, rounding up to 98 would breach a constraint. In feasibility contexts, rounding direction matters.

Probe: “If the maths gives you 12.3 staff needed, what does your organisation do—round up, down, or negotiate inputs?”

slides.title: Rearranging linear equations for targets

content.title: Rearranging linear equations for targets
content: Use a linear model: total = fixed + rate × quantity
Isolate the unknown with inverse operations
Keep units visible at each step
Use brackets carefully when substituting values
Validate by substituting your answer back into the model
content.notes:
Frame rearranging as ‘undoing’ operations in reverse order, but stress that learners should write each step to avoid spreadsheet-style hidden errors. Demonstrate the structure: if C = 350 + 8.75q, then q is found by subtracting 350, then dividing by 8.75.

Discuss unit sense-checking: dividing £ by (£/unit) should give units. Encourage learners to check dimensional consistency as an error trap.

Probe: “If you got q = £97, what does that tell you immediately?” (Unit mismatch suggests an algebra/unit error.)

Misconception: treating rounding as purely cosmetic—here it can change feasibility.

slides.title: Rounding and significant figures in spreadsheets

content.title: Rounding and significant figures in spreadsheets
leftColumn: Round during: display to users
Round during: currency to 2 dp per policy
Round during: when a step is a stated requirement
Round during: to avoid false precision in inputs
rightColumn: Round at end: multi-step calculations
Round at end: when rounding affects later results
Round at end: keep full precision in hidden cells
Round at end: then report to required s.f. or dp
content.notes:
Explain the tension: rounding early can reduce noise, but it can also accumulate error across multiple steps (especially with repeated multiplication). A robust spreadsheet approach is to keep full precision in calculation cells and round only in output/reporting cells, unless a policy requires intermediate rounding (e.g., invoicing rules).

Provide a mini-example: If you round 97.142… to 97.1 and then multiply by £8.75, your final cost changes slightly; across thousands of units, that difference can be material.

Probe: “Where in your own spreadsheets do you round—inputs, intermediate results, or final outputs—and why?”

Common mistake: using formatting (showing 2 dp) but assuming the underlying value is rounded; Excel formatting does not change stored values unless ROUND() is used.

slides.title: Worked example: feasibility with inequalities

content.title: Worked example: feasibility with inequalities
content: Let x = packs produced per shift (packs)
Labour: 1.5 h/pack, 90 h available → 1.5x ≤ 90
Material: 2 kg/pack, 110 kg available → 2x ≤ 110
Minimum order: x ≥ 40 packs
Proposed target: x = 55 packs
Check gives 82.5 h and 110 kg → feasible
content.notes:
Walk through the reasoning slowly. First define x with meaning and unit; learners often skip this and then struggle to interpret the inequality. Next, show how each constraint becomes a statement about total resource use.

Do the substitution explicitly: 1.5×55 = 82.5 hours, which is within 90 hours; 2×55 = 110 kg, which exactly matches stock. Explain that ‘equals the limit’ is still feasible (it is tight, leaving no slack).

Probe: “Which constraint is binding here?” (Material is binding because it hits the limit.) “What operational risk does a binding constraint create?” (Any waste/delay breaks feasibility.)

Misconception: seeing one satisfied constraint and concluding feasibility. Reinforce: all constraints must be satisfied simultaneously.

slides.title: Worked example: solve for a maximum target

content.title: Worked example: solve for a maximum target
content: Cost model: C = 350 + 8.75q (£), q in units
Subtract fixed cost: 850 = 8.75q
Whole units only → q_max = 97 units (round down)
Check: cost at 97 is £1,198.75, within budget
content.notes:
Explain what each term means in workplace language: £350 is the fixed setup cost (paid even for zero output), and £8.75 per unit is variable cost. The goal is to find the maximum output that does not exceed the budget.

Highlight the rounding logic: rounding down protects feasibility. Ask learners to test the ‘temptation’ to round to 98 and verify it breaks the constraint: 350 + 8.75×98 = £1,207.50, which exceeds £1,200.

Probe: “If units could be produced in half-units (e.g., hours billed), would the rounding rule change?” This helps learners connect rounding to the nature of the quantity.

Common mistake: forgetting the fixed cost and solving 1200 = 8.75q, which overstates capacity.

slides.title: Worked example: audit a spreadsheet excerpt

content.title: Worked example: audit a spreadsheet excerpt

rows: Rounded labour hours each line item
£ sign missing; treated as plain number

content.notes:
Treat this slide as an audit checklist. Explain that spreadsheet errors are often not ‘maths mistakes’ but modelling and communication mistakes: unclear units, inconsistent rounding, and undocumented assumptions.

For each row, briefly expand:
- Minutes vs hours: show how 90 hours vs 1.5 hours is a 60× difference.
- Early rounding: explain that rounding each row can bias totals up or down depending on direction.
- Currency: without units, a value like 1200 could be £, minutes, or units.
- Efficiency: assuming 100% implies no downtime; in many workplaces, 85–95% is more realistic.

Probe: “Which of these issues would be hardest to spot if you inherited the spreadsheet?”

Misconception: believing formatting (e.g., showing £) is optional. In workplace maths, labels and formats are part of accuracy.

slides.title: Assumptions log template (with examples)

content.title: Assumptions log template (with examples)
content.notes:
Explain what an assumptions log is: a short, explicit record of modelling choices that are not given in the data but are necessary to complete the calculation. Stress that this is not bureaucracy; it protects you when decisions are questioned later.

Demonstrate how to write an assumption in a testable way (e.g., “Efficiency set to 90% based on last month’s average”). Encourage linking each assumption to a cell in the spreadsheet (so reviewers can find it).

Probe: “If a manager challenges your result, which assumption would you check first?”

Common mistake: writing vague assumptions such as “numbers are accurate” instead of specific operational statements.

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
leftColumn: Write 2 inequalities for a time + material constraint
Test whether a target value satisfies both constraints
Rearrange: Total = fixed + rate×q to solve for q
Decide: round during or at end, with a reason
rightColumn: Which constraint is most limiting, and how do you know?
What units did you track, and where could they slip?
If results are non-integer, what rounding is safest?
What 2 assumptions would you log for your scenario?
content.notes:
Encourage learners to create their own small scenario (or use a familiar workplace process) to make practice meaningful: for example, packing orders, call handling, or machine time allocation. Remind them that feasibility is a logical ‘AND’: all constraints must hold.

If learners struggle, suggest a scaffold:
1) Define x with units.
2) Write one constraint at a time, checking units match.
3) Substitute the proposed target.
4) Summarise feasibility in one sentence.

Probe: “How would you explain your conclusion to a non-technical colleague in 15 seconds?”

Misconception: learners may think reflection questions are optional; explain that they build the justification skill needed for workplace reporting.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Use these methods in MOD101 planning and spreadsheet tasks
Show your inequalities and define variables with units
Do not mix minutes/hours or g/kg without converting
Avoid rounding up when checking maximum feasible targets
Document assumptions (efficiency, wastage, whole units)
Check results by substituting back into the equation(s)
content.notes:
Explain how these skills typically appear in assessment: learners may be given a workplace planning sheet and asked to justify feasibility, compute a required target, and clean up spreadsheet logic. Stress that marks are often awarded for method and justification, not only the final number.

Expand on pitfalls:
- Unit mixing: can produce ‘plausible-looking’ but wrong answers.
- Rounding up: can turn a safe plan into an infeasible one.
- Missing assumptions: makes the work hard to audit and easy to challenge.

Probe: “If you had to pick one habit to reduce errors immediately, what would it be: unit labels, substitution checks, or an assumptions log?”

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Define variables with meaning and units before forming inequalities
Translate limits into ≤ or ≥ and test feasibility by substitution
Rearrange linear equations to solve for workplace targets
Round deliberately: protect feasibility and avoid early rounding bias
Audit spreadsheets for units, rounding rules, and hidden assumptions
content.notes:
Close by reinforcing the decision-making theme: the mathematics supports operational choices, so clarity and auditability matter. Encourage learners to keep a personal checklist: variables + units, constraints as inequalities, substitution check, rounding rule, assumptions log.

Final probe: “What is one check you will add to your next spreadsheet before sharing it with someone else?”

Address confidence: remind learners that errors are normal, but systematic checking (units, substitution, and assumptions) is how professionals reduce risk.

slides.title: Units, significant figures and rounding at work

content.title: Units, significant figures and rounding at work
content: Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD101 — Workplace Maths Foundations
Lesson 5: Units, significant figures and rounding rules
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Introduce the lesson as a set of workplace habits rather than abstract rules. Emphasise that small numerical choices (units, significant figures, where you round) can create material differences in quotes, stock planning, capacity estimates, and KPI reporting. Set expectations: we will focus on application—how to produce calculations that are correct, auditable, and reproducible in a spreadsheet. Prompt: Where have you seen rounding cause disagreement (in invoices, time sheets, reports)? Clarify that throughout the lesson we will distinguish between (1) calculation precision and (2) reporting precision.

slides.title: Orientation: what you will be able to do

content.title: Orientation: what you will be able to do
content: Apply s.f. and rounding rules correctly in workplace calculations
Build an Excel model showing units, assumptions, and rounding
Run unit checks; fix inconsistent units in pricing/production models
Rearrange formulae to isolate a target variable; implement in Excel
Validate a model with units, reasonableness, and tolerance checks
How to use: study → practise in Excel → self-check your outputs
content.notes: Explain that these objectives align to ‘apply’ on Bloom’s taxonomy: you are expected to use rules reliably, not just describe them. Encourage a workflow: (1) understand the rule, (2) apply it to a realistic calculation, (3) check the result, and (4) document what you did. Probing questions: What does “correct” mean in your workplace—nearest penny, nearest unit, three significant figures, or a tolerance band? When should a spreadsheet show rounded values, and when should it keep full precision? Flag a common misconception: learners often think “more decimal places” always means “more accurate”. Accuracy depends on measurement quality and appropriate rounding.

slides.title: Units as an error-checking tool

content.title: Units as an error-checking tool
content: Treat units as part of the number, not optional decoration
Only add/subtract quantities with the same unit
Multiplying/dividing combines units (e.g., £/unit × unit = £)
Write units beside each input and each key output in Excel
Do a quick unit check before trusting any spreadsheet result
Flag red alerts: mixed time bases, hidden conversions, unitless rates
content.notes: Talk through dimensional consistency: a correct formula must make sense in units even before you calculate any numbers. Example: If labour cost is £/hour and you multiply by hours, the result must be £. If your result comes out as £/hour, you have likely missed the hours term or used the wrong cell. Stress the workplace value: unit checks catch errors that ‘look plausible’ numerically. Ask: If you double the quantity, should this output double? Which outputs should not change? Common misconceptions: (1) adding £/month to £/year without converting, (2) treating percentages inconsistently (5 vs 0.05), (3) confusing kW (rate) and kWh (energy). Encourage learners to label inputs with both a unit and a short description: “Setup time (min)” is clearer than “Time”.

slides.title: Common prefixes and quick conversions

content.title: Common prefixes and quick conversions
content.notes: Explain that many unit errors are simple powers-of-ten mistakes. Reinforce a consistent method: write the conversion as a fraction equal to 1, then multiply. Example: converting 2500 mm to m: 2500 mm × (1 m / 1000 mm) = 2.5 m. This prevents ‘guessing’ whether to multiply or divide. Probing question: If you convert from a smaller unit (mm) to a larger unit (m), should the number increase or decrease? It should decrease. Highlight a frequent spreadsheet pitfall: mixing kW and W in the same calculation without converting. Encourage learners to standardise units early (e.g., all lengths in metres, all times in hours) and clearly state that standard in the spreadsheet.

slides.title: Significant figures vs decimal places

content.title: Significant figures vs decimal places
leftColumn: Significant figures (s.f.) count meaningful digits
Use for measured/estimated values (precision-based)
Leading zeros do not count (0.00456 = 3 s.f.)
Keeps similar relative precision across magnitudes
rightColumn: Decimal places (d.p.) are digits after the decimal point
Use for reporting formats (money often 2 d.p.)
Fixed d.p. can overstate precision for large numbers
£12.30 has 2 d.p. (and 4 s.f.)
content.notes: Clarify the decision rule: use significant figures when the measurement precision is the key constraint (e.g., a sensor reading, a sampled average), and use decimal places when a reporting convention is required (e.g., currency to the nearest penny). Work a quick check aloud: how many s.f. are in 1500? Answer depends on context—could be 2, 3, or 4 if trailing zeros are not specified; writing 1.500×10^3 removes ambiguity. Probing question: Why might reporting 123456.789 to 2 d.p. be misleading? Because the extra decimals suggest a precision you do not have. Misconception to address: learners often round to 2 d.p. everywhere because “Excel shows two decimals”; display format is not the same as rounding the underlying value.

slides.title: Rounding rules and when to delay rounding

content.title: Rounding rules and when to delay rounding
content: Delay rounding until the final reporting step where possible
Keep full precision in intermediate steps and in stored inputs
Basic rule: 0–4 down, 5–9 up (unless told otherwise)
× and ÷: final result uses the fewest significant figures
+ and −: final result uses the fewest decimal places
Always state the required precision (e.g., £0.01, 3 s.f.)
content.notes: Explain why delaying rounding matters: rounding introduces small errors; repeated rounding can accumulate and change decisions (e.g., pass/fail thresholds, margin calculations). Stress the difference between (1) rounding for display and (2) rounding the value used in later calculations. Give a mini-example: if unit cost is 8.030487…, rounding to 8.03 before scaling up to 250 units can shift the total by several pence. Address rounding ‘ties’: many workplaces use “round half up”, but some finance systems use “bankers’ rounding” (half to even). Learners should follow organisational policy when specified. Probing questions: What precision is needed for a purchase order vs an engineering tolerance? When is it acceptable to round intermediate values (e.g., regulatory reporting, fixed pricing rules)?

slides.title: Excel modelling: documenting units and rounding

content.title: Excel modelling: documenting units and rounding
content: Separate inputs, workings, and outputs (clear layout)
Add a Units column for each key input and intermediate value
Name key cells/ranges (e.g., Price, FixedCost, VarCost)
Log assumptions and rounding choices in a visible notes area
Use ROUND for reporting; keep raw values for calculations
Build checks: units, reasonableness, and sensitivity/tolerance
content.notes: Explain that good spreadsheets are readable by someone else (or by you in three months). Demonstrate the principle: an input table might have columns ‘Value’, ‘Unit’, ‘Source/assumption’, ‘Last updated’. Named ranges reduce errors and make formulas self-explanatory, but warn that names must be managed carefully to avoid duplicates or misleading labels. Clarify practical rounding in Excel: using cell formatting to show 2 d.p. does not change the stored number; using ROUND() does. Probing question: Which is safer for intermediate steps—formatting or rounding? Usually formatting, unless the business rule requires rounding at that step (e.g., billing per line item). Common misconception: “If it looks right, it is right”—visual plausibility is not validation.

Demonstrate the principle: an input table might have columns ‘Value’, ‘Unit’, ‘Source/assumption’, ‘Last updated’. Named ranges reduce errors and make formulas self-explanatory, but warn that names must be managed carefully to avoid duplicates or misleading labels. Clarify practical rounding in Excel: using cell formatting to show 2 d.p. does not change the stored number; using ROUND() does. Probing question: Which is safer for intermediate steps—formatting or rounding? Usually formatting, unless the business rule requires rounding at that step (e.g., billing per line item). Common misconception: “If it looks right, it is right”—visual plausibility is not validation.

slides.title: Worked example: effect of rounding too early

content.title: Worked example: effect of rounding too early
content.notes: Walk through the scenario: a batch costs £987.65 and yields 123 units. Unit cost is £987.65 ÷ 123 = £8.0304878… If you round this to £8.03 and then price a 250-unit order, you get £8.03 × 250 = £2007.50. If you keep precision and round only at the end: £8.0304878… × 250 = £2007.62195 → £2007.62. Explain that £0.12 may be immaterial once, but it can matter over many orders, or when checking against tolerances. Probing questions: Which value is ‘more correct’ for internal costing? Which is appropriate for invoicing? Misconception: rounding “should not matter”; it matters whenever results are compared to thresholds or aggregated at scale.

slides.title: Worked example: unit check in a pricing model

content.title: Worked example: unit check in a pricing model
leftColumn: Fixed cost: £/month
Variable cost: £/unit
Volume: unit/month
Price: £/unit
rightColumn: Revenue = Price × Volume → £/month
Variable cost = VarCost × Volume → £/month
Contribution = Price − VarCost → £/unit
Break-even = FixedCost ÷ Contribution → units
content.notes: Explain how unit checks guide formula building. Start by asking learners to predict units before calculating: ‘Revenue’ must be £/month if price is £/unit and volume is unit/month. Show how inconsistencies surface: if someone inputs volume as units/week while fixed cost is £/month, the break-even will be wrong unless you convert weeks to months. Probing question: In your organisation, what is the standard time base—per shift, per week, per month? Make it explicit in the spreadsheet headings. Common misconceptions: (1) treating ‘units’ as interchangeable across products (e.g., items vs cases vs pallets), (2) using percentages without stating “of what” (e.g., 12% of revenue vs 12% of cost), (3) mixing VAT-inclusive and VAT-exclusive figures.

slides.title: Worked example: rearrange a formula for Excel

content.title: Worked example: rearrange a formula for Excel
content: Profit = (P − V)Q − F  (P=price, V=var cost, F=fixed)
Solve for Q:  Q = (Profit + F) / (P − V)
Solve for P:  P = (Profit + F)/Q + V
Excel with names: =(TargetProfit+FixedCost)/(Price-VarCost)
Use brackets to control order; test with simple numbers
Check units: £ ÷ (£/unit) = units
content.notes: Model the algebra step-by-step, narrating each transformation: add F to both sides, then divide by (P−V). Emphasise that rearrangement errors often come from missed brackets or sign mistakes. Recommend a validation habit: after rearranging, substitute easy values (e.g., set Profit=0 and see if Q becomes the break-even point). In Excel, named cells make the formula readable, but brackets are still essential. Probing questions: What happens if Price equals VarCost? (Denominator becomes zero; break-even is impossible.) What does a negative Q imply? (Likely a sign error or an infeasible model.) Reinforce dimensional reasoning: if the units do not reduce to “units”, the formula is wrong even if Excel returns a number.

slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)
content: Round 0.009876 to 2 s.f.; then to 4 d.p. (compare meaning)
Choose: should you round VAT per line or only the invoice total?
Spot the issue: Fixed cost £/year, volume units/month (fix it)
Rearrange: Revenue = Price × Quantity to isolate Quantity
In Excel, add a Units column and a “check” cell for each output
Reflect: where could early rounding change a decision at work?
content.notes: Encourage learners to write their answers and check them against unit logic. For the rounding item: 0.009876 to 2 s.f. is 0.0099; to 4 d.p. is 0.0099 as well, but the interpretation differs—s.f. communicates measurement precision, d.p. communicates formatting. For VAT, highlight that many accounting systems round at line level due to legal or system constraints; others round at invoice total—learners must follow policy and document it. For the unit mismatch, illustrate a fix: either convert fixed cost to £/month (÷12) or volume to units/year (×12), then re-run checks. For the Excel checks, suggest simple flags such as “IF(ABS(CheckValue)<Tolerance,"OK","Investigate")”.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: spreadsheet model build, documentation, and validation
Common error: rounding mid-calculation without stating the rule
Common error: mixing units (week/month; kW/kWh; % vs decimal)
Common error: hard-coding numbers instead of using inputs/names
Common error: missing brackets gives correct-looking wrong results
Common error: no checks (units, reasonableness, sensitivity range)
content.notes: Explain what assessors typically look for in workplace maths submissions: not just a correct final number, but evidence of a controlled method. Encourage learners to include a brief calculation note: what data sources were used, what units were assumed, what precision was required, and where rounding occurred. Discuss ‘auditability’: can another person reproduce your result from your spreadsheet and notes? Probing question: If a manager challenges your output, can you point to three independent checks that support it? Highlight that sensitivity checks can be simple: vary a key input by ±5% and see whether the output behaves as expected. Reinforce that good practice reduces rework and increases trust.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Units are part of the calculation; use them to detect errors
Use s.f. for measurement precision; use d.p. for reporting needs
Delay rounding unless a business rule forces earlier rounding
Make Excel models readable: units, assumptions, named inputs
Validate outputs with unit, reasonableness, and tolerance checks
content.notes: Close by linking the five takeaways to daily workplace tasks: quoting prices, budgeting, production planning, and performance reporting. Reiterate the mindset: precision is a design choice—decide it, apply it consistently, and document it. Probing questions for consolidation: What is one unit check you will add to your next spreadsheet? What rounding rule will you adopt (and where will you record it)? Encourage learners to revisit their own work spreadsheets and identify one place where early rounding or missing units could be creating hidden error.

slides.title: Algebraic rearrangement for pricing models

content.title: Algebraic rearrangement for pricing models
content.content:
Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD101 — Workplace Maths Foundations
Lesson 6: Algebraic rearrangement to isolate variables in pricing
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Introduce the lesson focus: taking a business equation (pricing, cost, profit, revenue, volume) and rearranging it to make one variable the subject, then implementing it correctly in Excel.

Position this as an “apply” lesson: learners are expected to use a method, not just recognise terms. Emphasise that in workplace spreadsheets, correctness is judged by whether the formula reproduces a check value and remains robust when inputs change.

Prompt: “When you open someone else’s spreadsheet, what makes you trust it?” Use this to foreshadow transparency (layout, units, assumptions, checks, audit trail).

slides.title: Orientation: objectives and study approach

content.title: Orientation: objectives and study approach
content: Rearrange equations to isolate a target variable
Implement rearranged forms in Excel with correct brackets
Build a clear sheet: Inputs, Calculations, Outputs
Use named ranges and correct relative/absolute references
Document units, rounding rules, and key assumptions
Run and record unit and reasonableness/sensitivity checks
content.notes:
Explain how to use the lesson:
1) Read the algebra steps slowly and rewrite them by hand.
2) Recreate the worked examples in Excel (do not copy/paste only).
3) Compare your output to a check value (100% match).
4) Stress-test the sheet by changing one input at a time.

Clarify what “correct brackets” means: Excel follows a strict order of operations; if the algebra says divide the entire numerator by Q, you must use parentheses.

Probing questions:
- “If your Excel result is ‘close’, what are the likely causes?”
- “How would you make your workbook easy to review by someone else?”

Common misconception: believing algebraic steps are ‘obvious’ so documentation is unnecessary. In audits, undocumented assumptions are treated as errors.

slides.title: Isolating a variable: what and why

content.title: Isolating a variable: what and why
content: Make the target variable the subject (alone on one side)
Use inverse operations to undo additions, products, powers
Keep equality: whatever you do to one side, do to both
Aim for a form that maps cleanly into an Excel formula
Check: substitute back to verify the original equation holds
content.notes:
Define “the subject”: the variable you want to calculate directly (e.g., price P, volume Q, unit cost c).

Explain the workplace rationale: in pricing and production, we often know the target outcome (profit, break-even, revenue) and must solve for the decision variable.

Mini-example (verbal): If Total = Fixed + Variable×Q, and you want Q, you subtract Fixed first, then divide by Variable.

Probing questions:
- “Which operations would you undo first in (P−VC)×Q−FC?”
- “Why is substitution-back a stronger check than ‘it looks right’?”

Misconception to address: rearrangement is not ‘moving terms across the equals sign’; it is applying inverse operations consistently.

slides.title: A reliable rearrangement method

content.title: A reliable rearrangement method
content: Step 1: write the equation clearly; define each symbol
Step 2: remove additions/subtractions around the target
Step 3: remove multiplication/division around the target
Step 4: handle brackets and fractions last, carefully
Step 5: simplify and label units for the solved variable
Step 6: verify by substituting values back into original
content.notes:
Talk learners through a disciplined sequence: isolate by “peeling the onion”. You undo the outermost operations first.

Example to narrate:
Profit = (P − VC)×Q − FC
To isolate P: add FC, divide by Q, then add VC.

Explain why the order matters: if you divide before adding FC, you change the structure of the equation.

Probing questions:
- “What is the outermost operation acting on P in the profit equation?”
- “If Q is in the denominator, what does that imply about sensitivity?”

Common errors:
- Dividing only one term instead of the whole numerator.
- Forgetting that subtraction changes sign when rearranging.

slides.title: Excel translation: brackets and operator order

content.title: Excel translation: brackets and operator order
content: Excel order: brackets, powers, ×/÷, then +/−
Use brackets to match algebraic grouping exactly
Prefer named ranges to reduce cell-address mistakes
Test with a known check value before extending the model
Avoid hidden constants; keep all inputs in the Inputs block
content.notes:
Explain PEMDAS/BODMAS in the Excel context: Excel will multiply and divide before addition and subtraction, so missing parentheses often produces plausible-but-wrong outputs.

Mini-example:
Correct: =((TargetProfit+FixedCost)/Q)+VarCost
Incorrect: =(TargetProfit+FixedCost)/Q+VarCost is fine; but
Incorrect: =(TargetProfit+FixedCost)/(Q+VarCost) changes meaning.

Emphasise “check value”: choose one test case with known expected output and confirm a 100% match before copying formulas.

Probing questions:
- “Which part of your formula is the numerator?”
- “If you remove parentheses, does Excel still compute what you intend?”

Misconception: “Excel knows what I mean.” It only follows syntax and operator precedence.

slides.title: Spreadsheet layout for transparency

content.title: Spreadsheet layout for transparency
leftColumn: Inputs/Assumptions at top-left
Units shown in a dedicated column
One input per cell; no hard-coded numbers in formulas
Assumptions table: source, date, owner
rightColumn: Calculations in a separate block
Outputs grouped and clearly labelled
Use consistent formats (%, currency, decimals)
Include check cells near outputs (PASS/FAIL)
content.notes:
Explain why layout is not cosmetic: it prevents errors, supports review, and makes models easier to maintain.

Give a practical rule: if a value can change, it belongs in Inputs. If it is derived, it belongs in Calculations. If it is a decision or a result to report, it belongs in Outputs.

Mini-example:
- Input: VAT rate (e.g., 20%)
- Calculation: net-to-gross conversion
- Output: gross price

Probing questions:
- “If a manager asks ‘what if volume drops by 10%?’, where do you change it?”
- “Could someone find every assumption without opening formulas?”

Common misconception: mixing inputs and calculations “to save space” increases the chance of overwriting formulas.

slides.title: Named ranges and cell references

content.title: Named ranges and cell references
content: Use named ranges for key inputs (e.g., Price, Volume, VC)
Relative refs (A1) copy-change; absolute refs ($A$1) lock
Lock constants and tables; keep scenario inputs relative
Use consistent direction for copying (down rows or across)
Audit: trace precedents/dependents to confirm links update
content.notes:
Explain the practical difference:
- Relative reference: changes as you copy the formula.
- Absolute reference: stays fixed.

Example to narrate:
If you have a table of months across columns, you may lock the row for a rate: =B5*$A$2 (rate in A2).

Named ranges reduce cognitive load and are easier to review, but warn learners to keep names simple and unique (avoid spaces if your organisation’s standards require it).

Probing questions:
- “When you copy this formula down 12 rows, what should change?”
- “If you see #REF!, what does that tell you about a deleted cell?”

Misconception: using named ranges means you can ignore reference behaviour. Named ranges help readability; they do not replace good structure.

slides.title: Documenting units, rounding, and assumptions

content.title: Documenting units, rounding, and assumptions
content.notes:
Explain that documentation is part of the calculation, not an optional extra.

Units:
- A unit check is impossible if units are not visible.
- Encourage writing “£/unit” rather than only “£” where relevant.

Rounding:
- Differentiate between rounding for presentation (outputs) and rounding within calculations (only when a business rule demands it, such as billing to nearest penny).
- Mini-example: keep full precision in unit cost calculations; round final invoice value to 2 decimals.

Assumptions:
- State what is assumed constant (e.g., fixed costs) and over what time period.

Probing question: “If someone reviewed this in six months, could they reproduce the result without asking you?”

Common misconception: rounding early “makes it cleaner”. It often introduces compounding error.

slides.title: Worked example 1: solve for price to hit profit

content.title: Worked example 1: solve for price to hit profit
content: Given: Profit = (P−VC)×Q − FC
Isolate P: P = (Profit+FC)/Q + VC
Inputs: Profit £, VC £/unit, Q units, FC £
Excel: =((Profit+FC)/Q)+VC
Check: substitute P back to confirm Profit matches exactly
content.notes:
Walk through slowly with numbers to make it concrete.

Example values (you can narrate these):
- Target Profit = £12,000
- FC = £8,000
- VC = £15/unit
- Q = 2,000 units

Compute P:
P = (12,000 + 8,000)/2,000 + 15 = 10 + 15 = £25/unit.

Then verify:
Profit = (25−15)×2,000 − 8,000 = 20,000 − 8,000 = £12,000.

Emphasise units at each step:
- (Profit+FC) is £
- divided by Q gives £/unit
- plus VC (£/unit) remains £/unit

Probing questions:
- “What happens to required price if volume halves?”
- “Which inputs have the biggest effect on price?”

Common errors:
- Using (Profit+FC)/(Q+VC) due to missing brackets.
- Forgetting VC is per unit and adding it in the wrong place.

slides.title: Worked example 2: solve for volume with discount

content.title: Worked example 2: solve for volume with discount
content: Given: Revenue = P×Q×(1−d)
Isolate Q: Q = Revenue / (P×(1−d))
Inputs: Revenue £, P £/unit, d as decimal, Q units
Excel: =Revenue/(Price*(1-Disc))
Check: compute Revenue from Q and confirm exact match
content.notes:
Explain why discount needs careful handling: d must be a decimal (e.g., 0.10 for 10%). A frequent error is entering 10 rather than 10%.

Narrated numbers:
- Revenue target = £90,000
- Price P = £50/unit
- Discount d = 10% (0.10)
Then Q = 90,000 / (50×0.9) = 90,000 / 45 = 2,000 units.

Verification:
Revenue = 50×2,000×0.9 = £90,000.

Highlight sensitivity:
- As d increases, (1−d) decreases, so Q must increase for the same revenue.

Probing questions:
- “If discount rises from 10% to 15%, what direction does Q move?”
- “What unit should Q have, and how do you know?”

Common errors:
- Writing =Revenue/Price*(1-Disc) (missing parentheses changes meaning).
- Using d as 10 instead of 0.10/10%.

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
content: Rearrange: TC = FC + VC×Q to isolate Q and VC
Rearrange: Profit = Revenue − Cost to isolate Cost
Build a 3-block sheet: Inputs, Calculations, Outputs
Add named ranges for at least 5 key inputs
Run a unit check and a one-variable sensitivity check
Write a short change note: what you checked and limits
content.notes:
Encourage learners to do this in Excel, not just on paper.

Suggested approach:
1) Do the rearrangement by hand and label units.
2) Implement the Excel formula using named ranges.
3) Create a check cell that recomputes the original equation.

Unit check guidance:
- Confirm each term in an addition has the same unit.
- Confirm multiplication/division leads to expected units.

Sensitivity check guidance:
- Change one input by +10% and observe whether the output moves in the expected direction.
- Record: input changed, expected direction, actual direction, any explanation.

Probing questions:
- “Where in your sheet could a reviewer see every assumption?”
- “If your output changes in the wrong direction, what will you inspect first?”

Common misconception: sensitivity checks require advanced tools. For this lesson, simple one-at-a-time changes are sufficient.

- Confirm multiplication/division leads to expected units.

Sensitivity check guidance:
- Change one input by +10% and observe whether the output moves in the expected direction.
- Record: input changed, expected direction, actual direction, any explanation.

Probing questions:
- “Where in your sheet could a reviewer see every assumption?”
- “If your output changes in the wrong direction, what will you inspect first?”

Common misconception: sensitivity checks require advanced tools. For this lesson, simple one-at-a-time changes are sufficient.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports spreadsheet-based pricing/production calculations
Mistake: algebra correct but Excel brackets change meaning
Mistake: mixing units (%, decimals, £ vs £/unit)
Mistake: hard-coded numbers in formulas break scenarios
Mistake: rounding inside calculations without a business rule
Avoid by adding check cells and a brief audit trail
content.notes:
Connect to typical module expectations: a reviewer should be able to follow your logic, update inputs, and obtain updated outputs without repairing formulas.

Expand each mistake with a quick diagnostic:
- Brackets: compare your Excel formula structure to your algebra line-by-line.
- Units: create a units column and ensure every input/output has one.
- Hard-coding: use Excel’s ‘Find’ to look for numbers in formulas.
- Rounding: inspect whether ROUND() appears mid-calculation; justify it.

Probing questions:
- “If your sheet is copied to another workbook, will named ranges still behave?”
- “How would you prove to a marker that your model is robust?”

Misconception: a correct final number is enough. In assessment and practice, method and traceability are part of correctness.

slides.title: Transparent layout: inputs, processing, outputs

content.title: Transparent layout: inputs, processing, outputs
content: Separate Inputs, Calculations, and Outputs (IPO)
Keep inputs grouped and referenced, not duplicated
One direction flow: left-to-right or top-to-bottom
Use clear labels and units next to every key value
Avoid hard-coding numbers inside formulas
Add whitespace to make sections visually distinct
content.notes: Walk through why IPO matters: it reduces errors and makes review faster. Explain ‘referenced, not duplicated’: if unit cost appears in two places, one will eventually be wrong. Stress the “no hard-coding” rule: numbers inside formulas hide assumptions and defeat auditing. Mini-example to say aloud: instead of =B10*1.2, place 1.2 in an input cell labelled ‘Waste factor (multiplier)’ and reference it. Probing questions: If a colleague changed the labour rate, could they find it in 5 seconds? If you print the sheet, are units still clear?

slides.title: Named ranges and cell styles

content.title: Named ranges and cell styles
leftColumn: Named ranges: label key inputs once
Readable formulas, e.g., =Units*UnitCost
Names reduce wrong-cell references
Use short, consistent naming rules
rightColumn: Cell styles: visual meaning (Input/Calc/Output)
Inputs shaded; outputs highlighted
Consistent number formats and units
Avoid using colour without a legend
content.notes: Explain how named ranges support transparency: a formula like =TargetUnits*LabourHrsPerUnit is self-explanatory compared with =C6*$F$14. Show practical naming rules: no spaces (use underscores), start with a letter, include units in the label if helpful (but keep the name simple). Contrast naming with styles: names help the formula reader; styles help the sheet reader. Misconception: learners sometimes name everything; instead, prioritise ‘key drivers’—rates, capacities, conversion factors, and targets. Prompt: Which 5–10 values, if changed, would alter most outputs? Those are prime candidates for names.

slides.title: Relative vs absolute references

content.title: Relative vs absolute references
leftColumn: Relative: A1 changes when copied
Use for row-by-row calculations
Example: =B2*C2 copied down a table
Works best with consistent structure
rightColumn: Absolute: $A$1 stays fixed when copied
Use for shared constants and rates
Example: =B2*$E$1 copied down
Mixed: $A1 or A$1 for row/column lock
content.notes: Teach this as a copying problem: ‘What should move when I fill down/right?’ Demonstrate mixed references with a simple grid: a multiplication table where the top row is fixed (A$1) and the first column is fixed ($A1). Common misconception: learners lock cells ‘just in case’, which breaks reuse and makes errors harder to spot. Probing question: If I copy this formula 20 rows down, what do I want to remain constant? Encourage use of F4 (Windows) / Cmd+T (Mac, depending on settings) to cycle reference types, but emphasise understanding over shortcuts.

slides.title: Audit-ready assumptions and change log

content.title: Audit-ready assumptions and change log
content.notes: Explain that workplace spreadsheets often become evidence: someone will ask ‘why is this number like that?’ Assumptions must be visible and dated where appropriate. Give guidance on what counts as an assumption: anything not directly measured in the problem (e.g., efficiency rate, standard pack size, overtime not allowed). Stress that units are part of assumptions: £/hour vs £/day changes results drastically. Common misconception: adding assumptions in an email or separate document—teach learners to keep them in the workbook, preferably in a dedicated Assumptions/Change Log sheet plus brief notes beside key inputs/outputs.

slides.title: Worked example: set up an IPO sheet structure

content.title: Worked example: set up an IPO sheet structure
content.notes: Narrate a step-by-step build: create section headers, reserve space, then enter labels before numbers. Explain why you keep calculations separate: it allows you to inspect logic without scrolling through mixed content. Mention practical details: freeze panes so headers and input labels remain visible; use consistent decimal places; align units in a dedicated column. Probing question: If someone prints this, can they tell which cells they are allowed to edit? Reinforce that ‘Checks’ is a normal part of modelling, not an optional extra.

slides.title: Worked formulas (1): correct referencing patterns

content.title: Worked formulas (1): correct referencing patterns
content.notes: Explain each formula in words before showing the Excel version: this reduces ‘symbol blindness’. Point out where errors often occur: adding scrap as +5 rather than +5%; mixing kg and tonnes; multiplying by cost twice. Encourage naming intermediate calculations too (e.g., TotalLabourHrs) when they are reused, but avoid naming every cell. Ask learners to check dimensional consistency: units * hours/unit = hours; hours * £/hour = £. That unit check is a powerful error detector.

slides.title: Worked formulas (2): copying with $ references

content.title: Worked formulas (2): copying with $ references
content.notes: Focus on the ‘fill’ test: after writing a formula, copy it to where it will be used and see if the references behave. Demonstrate the failure mode: forgetting $ in a lookup range causes the lookup table to ‘slide’ and return wrong results with no obvious error. Encourage learners to use Excel’s ‘Show Formulas’ view temporarily to see patterns. Probing question: If you copied this formula one column right, which parts should change and which must not? Tie this back to good structure: consistent tables make relative references safe and predictable.

slides.title: Verify accuracy: trace tools and self-checks

content.title: Verify accuracy: trace tools and self-checks
content: Use Trace Precedents to see what feeds a cell
Use Trace Dependents to see what a cell affects
Check for hard-coded numbers in formulas
Add a self-check: expected vs actual difference
Flag failures with IF() and clear warning text
Re-run checks after any input change
content.notes: Explain how tracing supports debugging: if an output is wrong, trace back to see the chain of inputs and intermediate steps. Demonstrate a self-check pattern: ‘Check = OutputTotal - (LabourCost + MaterialCost + Overhead)’ and then a status cell ‘=IF(ABS(Check)<0.01,"OK","CHECK LINKS")’. Discuss tolerance and rounding: if values are rounded for display, checks should use underlying values or include a tolerance. Common misconception: learners rely only on ‘it looks right’. Encourage deliberate checks: does increasing a unit cost increase total cost? If not, the model is broken.

slides.title: Feasibility using linear constraints

content.title: Feasibility using linear constraints
content: Write each constraint as an inequality
Compute LHS from target units and input rates
Compare LHS to available capacity (RHS)
Use consistent units on both sides
Overall feasible only if all constraints pass
Summarise as Feasible / Not feasible
content.notes: Teach the underlying maths explicitly: constraints are typically linear in this context (e.g., hours = units × hours/unit). Give three common constraint types: resource (labour/material), demand (max units), and policy (e.g., overtime not allowed, minimum batch). Stress unit alignment: hours compared to hours, kg to kg, units to units—never compare unlike quantities. Probing questions: Which constraint is ‘tightest’ (closest to the limit)? If we change the target, which constraint fails first? This builds intuition for sensitivity without requiring advanced optimisation.

slides.title: Worked feasibility check for a production target

content.title: Worked feasibility check for a production target
content.notes: Explain how to implement this in Excel: create a small constraint table in the Outputs section. For each row, compute the LHS in units (hours, kg, units). Then compute a result cell such as ‘=IF(LHS<=RHS,"PASS","FAIL")’. For the overall result, use AND(): ‘=IF(AND(Result1="PASS",Result2="PASS",Result3="PASS"),"FEASIBLE","NOT FEASIBLE")’. Common misconception: treating MIN() output as ‘feasibility’. MIN() limits an output but does not prove all resources are within capacity—hence the explicit constraint checks.
