content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Create an IPO sheet for a 1-product cost model
Name 8 key inputs (rates, limits, factors, target)
Write 6 formulas using correct relative/$ references
Add 4 assumptions with units and rounding rules
Add one dated change note in a Change Log tab
Add 3 constraint checks and an overall status cell
content.notes: Guide learners to pick any familiar context (e.g., printing flyers, baking items, assembling kits) as long as it has a unit cost and at least three constraints. Encourage them to test the model by changing one input at a time and observing whether outputs behave logically. Probing questions: If I double the target units, which costs double and which do not? If I reduce available labour hours, does feasibility change as expected? Remind them to inspect formulas for hidden constants and to use trace tools on at least one output and one constraint row.

slides.title: Linear equations and inequalities to test feasibility

content.title: Linear equations and inequalities to test feasibility
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD101 — Workplace Maths Foundations: Units, Algebra and Spreadsheet Standards
Lesson 8: Linear equations and inequalities to test feasibility
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners to Lesson 8. Frame this as a practical modelling lesson: you will turn workplace statements (targets and limits) into linear equations/inequalities, solve them, and then decide whether a plan is feasible.

Emphasise the applied focus (Bloom: apply): we are not doing algebra for its own sake; we are using algebra to make operational decisions (e.g., can we meet a target given labour and materials?).

Prompt: “When someone says ‘we must produce at least…’ what mathematical symbol should you think of? When they say ‘we cannot exceed…’ what symbol?”

slides.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson
leftColumn: Model a target and 2+ constraints with correct units
Solve 1 equation and 1 inequality; interpret feasibility
Apply sig figs and rounding rules in multi-step calcs
Fix unit/assumption/rounding issues in a messy log
rightColumn: Study: read slides and examples carefully
Practise: do the prompts using working or a spreadsheet
Check: compare decisions to constraints and units
content.notes:
Clarify success criteria in plain terms.

For objective 1, stress that correctness includes: (a) a defined variable, (b) a clear unit, and (c) constraints written as inequalities with the right direction.

For objective 2, stress interpretation: solutions are not just numbers; they represent allowable production quantities. Learners should be able to say “feasible” or “not feasible” and why.

For objective 3, remind learners: spreadsheet outputs often look precise but are only as accurate as the rounding decisions. Delaying rounding is a professional habit.

For objective 4, explain that ‘messy logs’ are common in workplaces—your job is to make calculations auditable and reproducible.

Probing question: “Which is harder in practice: solving the inequality, or deciding what the inequality should be? Why?”

slides.title: From scenario to model: choose variable and units

content.title: From scenario to model: choose variable and units
content: Define a single variable, e.g. x = units produced per day
Write the unit next to x (units/day, hours/day, kg/day)
Convert all rates to consistent units before modelling
State basic domain constraints: x ≥ 0; sometimes x is whole
Separate: target statements vs resource limit statements
content.notes:
Walk learners through the modelling habit:

1) Define x with a unit. If x is “bottles produced”, the unit is bottles/day (or bottles/shift). Without the unit, later steps become guesswork.

2) Do unit alignment early. Many feasibility mistakes come from mixing minutes and hours, or grams and kilograms. Encourage writing conversions explicitly (e.g., 3.6 min/unit = 0.06 h/unit).

3) Domain matters. If x counts physical items, it is usually a whole number. If x is time or mass, it can be continuous. This affects rounding and the final decision.

4) Classify statements:
- Targets: “at least”, “no fewer than”, “minimum” → typically ≥
- Limits: “no more than”, “at most”, “cannot exceed” → typically ≤

Common misconception: treating the target as an equality (x = 500) when the requirement is ‘at least’ (x ≥ 500).

Probing question: “What would x represent in a service context (e.g., appointments), and would it need to be whole?”

slides.title: Equations vs inequalities: when to use each

content.title: Equations vs inequalities: when to use each
leftColumn: Equation (=) sets an exact requirement
Often used for break-even or exact totals
Solving gives a single value for x
Check solution makes sense with units and domain
rightColumn: Inequality (≤, ≥) sets allowable limits
Used for capacity, budgets, safety limits
Solving gives a range (solution set) for x
Feasible means meeting all inequalities at once
content.notes:
Explain that workplace requirements rarely demand an exact single value; they usually define acceptable ranges.

Mini-examples:
- Equation: “Total pay is £480 for x hours at £12/h” → 12x = 480.
- Inequality: “Overtime must be no more than 8 hours” → x ≤ 8.

Stress interpretation:
- An equation solution is a candidate.
- An inequality solution is a set of candidates.

Misconception to address: learners sometimes ‘flip’ the meaning of ≥ and ≤ when rearranging, or think the solution to multiple constraints is the union (either/or). In feasibility, it is the intersection (all constraints simultaneously).

Probing question: “If one constraint says x ≤ 600 and another says x ≤ 700, which one actually limits you?”

Probing question: “If one constraint says x ≤ 600 and another says x ≤ 700, which one actually limits you?”

slides.title: Solving linear equations and inequalities (1 variable)

content.title: Solving linear equations and inequalities (1 variable)
content: Simplify: collect like terms and keep units visible
Isolate x using inverse operations (same both sides)
For inequalities, reverse sign only when × or ÷ by negative
Write the solution as a set, e.g. x ≥ 500
Sense-check: does the solution fit the scenario?
content.notes:
Teach the ‘same operation on both sides’ rule, and then highlight what changes for inequalities.

Key point: the inequality direction only flips when multiplying/dividing by a negative number. In most production contexts, coefficients are positive, so flipping is not common—but learners must know the rule.

Mini-example for flipping:
If -2x ≥ 10, then dividing by -2 gives x ≤ -5 (sign reverses).

Sense-checking: ask learners to plug in a simple test value.
If they conclude x ≥ 666 from a labour capacity constraint, test x = 1000: does that exceed available hours? If yes, the inequality direction is wrong.

Probing question: “What quick test value could you substitute to check your inequality direction?”

slides.title: Feasibility means meeting all constraints together

content.title: Feasibility means meeting all constraints together
content: List all constraints as inequalities in x
Solve each inequality to find its allowable range
Intersect ranges: keep only values meeting every constraint
Include domain rules: x ≥ 0, and whole numbers if required
Conclude: feasible range, or not feasible if empty
content.notes:
Emphasise the logic: feasibility is an AND condition.

Explain intersection in everyday language: “x must be big enough to hit the target AND small enough to fit within every limit.”

Mini-example:
- Target: x ≥ 500
- Labour: x ≤ 666.7
- Materials: x ≤ 750
Intersection: 500 ≤ x ≤ 666.7 (then apply whole-number rule if needed).

Misconception: choosing the “best-looking” constraint and ignoring others. Another misconception is reporting only the maximum value and not the feasible interval.

Probing question: “If your intersection gives x ≤ 400 and target says x ≥ 500, what does that mean operationally?”

slides.title: Rounding and significant figures in feasibility work

content.title: Rounding and significant figures in feasibility work
content: Avoid early rounding in multi-step calculations
Keep full precision in working; round at final reporting
Round to match data quality (sig figs or decimal places)
For capacity limits, round down to stay within constraints
Record rounding rules used in a notes/assumptions field
content.notes:
Explain why rounding is not just presentation—it changes decisions.

Key guidance:
- Delay rounding: if you round intermediate values, small errors can accumulate and shift a feasibility boundary.
- Match precision to inputs: if a time-per-unit is given to 2 significant figures, reporting 6 significant figures is misleading.

Introduce a professional rule-of-thumb for feasibility:
- If a value is a maximum allowed by a constraint (e.g., maximum units given labour), rounding up can make the plan infeasible. Therefore, round down for safe feasibility decisions when x must be an integer.

Mini-example:
If x ≤ 666.67 units and x must be whole units, the largest feasible x is 666, not 667.

Probing question: “When might rounding down be too conservative, and what could you do instead (e.g., refine the inputs)?”

slides.title: Make your spreadsheet calculation reproducible

content.title: Make your spreadsheet calculation reproducible
content: Label every quantity with units (in headers or cell notes)
State assumptions: shift length, scrap rate, batch sizes
Show key conversions (min→h, g→kg) rather than hiding them
Flag which values are rounded and at what stage
Write a brief decision statement: feasible/not feasible and why
content.notes:
Frame this slide as workplace standard: someone else should be able to re-run your logic and get the same result.

Explain what “reproducible” looks like in a spreadsheet:
- Units in column headings: “Time per unit (min)” not just “Time”.
- Explicit conversion cells: e.g., a cell that divides minutes by 60.
- Assumptions field: e.g., “Assume 1 shift = 8.0 h, no downtime included.”
- Rounding field: e.g., “Final output rounded down to whole units due to item count.”

Common issues:
- Hidden conversions inside formulas, making auditing hard.
- Assumptions implied but not stated (e.g., “x must be whole”).

Probing question: “If a colleague challenged your result, which single note would help you defend it?”

slides.title: Worked example 1: translate a production brief

content.title: Worked example 1: translate a production brief
content: Scenario: fill x bottles/day of sanitiser
Target: at least 500 bottles/day → x ≥ 500
Labour: 3.6 min per bottle; 40 h/day available
Labour constraint: 3.6x ≤ 40×60 (minutes/day)
Material: 0.40 L per bottle; 300 L/day → 0.40x ≤ 300
content.notes:
Talk through the modelling choices slowly and explicitly.

First, define x: “x is the number of bottles filled per day.” This makes the interpretation of x immediate.

Then translate each statement:
- “At least 500” becomes x ≥ 500.
- Labour is given as minutes per bottle, but availability is hours per day. Show the conversion choice: either convert 40 hours to minutes (40×60 = 2400 min) or convert 3.6 min to hours. Either is fine as long as you are consistent.

Explain the labour constraint structure:
(time per bottle) × (bottles per day) ≤ (minutes available per day)
So 3.6x ≤ 2400.

For material:
(0.40 L/bottle) × (bottles/day) ≤ (L/day)
So 0.40x ≤ 300.

Probing questions:
- “What unit does 3.6x have?” (Answer: minutes/day.)
- “Why is the labour statement a ≤ rather than ≥?”

Misconception: writing 3.6 + x ≤ 2400 instead of multiplication. Reinforce that rates multiply by quantities.

slides.title: Worked example 2: solve and interpret feasibility

content.title: Worked example 2: solve and interpret feasibility
content: Solve labour: 3.6x ≤ 2400 → x ≤ 666.67
Solve material: 0.40x ≤ 300 → x ≤ 750
Combine with target x ≥ 500
Feasible range (continuous): 500 ≤ x ≤ 666.67
If x must be whole: feasible integers 500 to 666
content.notes:
Narrate the solving steps and then spend most time on interpretation.

Labour constraint:
3.6x ≤ 2400
Divide by 3.6 (positive, so inequality direction stays the same):
x ≤ 666.67

Material constraint:
0.40x ≤ 300
x ≤ 750

Now interpret intersection with the target:
- The target sets a minimum.
- Labour and material set maxima.
- The tightest maximum dominates (here, labour at 666.67).

Explain domain decision:
If x represents countable bottles, x is an integer. Therefore the maximum feasible is 666 (round down). Make it explicit that rounding to 667 would violate labour.

Probing questions:
- “Which constraint is binding? How can you tell?”
- “Would producing x = 650 be feasible? Check each inequality.”

Common misconception: learners sometimes take the larger maximum (750) and ignore the tighter one.

slides.title: Worked example 3: rounding in a multi-step check

content.title: Worked example 3: rounding in a multi-step check
content.notes:
Use this table to model good ‘spreadsheet-style’ working.

Explain what is being rounded and why:
- Keep the division result as 666.666… in working.
- You may display 666.67 for readability, but the operational maximum is 666 because bottles are whole.

Highlight the key professional judgement: rounding direction depends on context.
- For a maximum capacity, rounding down avoids exceeding the limit.
- If you were estimating a minimum requirement (e.g., minimum staff needed), rounding up might be appropriate.

Ask learners to consider: “If the labour time 3.6 min/bottle is itself an estimate, should we build in a margin (e.g., treat it as 3.7)?” This introduces the idea of conservative planning.

Common mistake: rounding x ≤ 666.67 to x ≤ 667 without checking that 667 violates 3.6x ≤ 2400 (because 3.6×667 = 2401.2 min).

slides.title: Worked example 4: fix a messy calculation log

content.title: Worked example 4: fix a messy calculation log
leftColumn: Unit mismatch: minutes used with hours available
Rounded x to 667 and claimed feasible
No statement that x must be a whole number
Checked each constraint separately, not together
rightColumn: Convert units explicitly (40 h = 2400 min)
Use floor: max feasible whole x = 666
Add domain note: x ∈ Z, x ≥ 0
Intersect constraints; report feasible range
content.notes:
Present this as an audit mindset: you are improving someone else’s work so it is correct and traceable.

For each issue, model documentation language a learner could copy into a spreadsheet notes cell:
- “Converted labour availability to minutes to match 3.6 min/bottle.”
- “x is a count of bottles; therefore x must be an integer. Rounded down to remain within labour limit.”
- “Feasible set is the intersection of all constraints, not a separate pass/fail per constraint.”

Probing questions:
- “Which error is most likely to cause a costly real-world decision?”
- “How would you show the intersection in a spreadsheet—what cells would you create?”

Misconception: believing that if a value meets ‘most’ constraints it is acceptable. In feasibility, a single violated constraint makes it infeasible.

slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)
content: Write x and units for a scenario: x chairs/day; target x ≥ 120
Add 2 constraints: labour 12 min/chair; max 20 h/day
Solve and state the feasible range (include whole-number rule)
Explain where you would delay rounding and why
Spot 3 issues: missing units, early rounding, hidden conversion
content.notes:
Encourage learners to pause and actually do the work.

Guide for the chair scenario (without fully giving the answer upfront):
- Convert 20 h/day to minutes (or convert 12 min to hours).
- Form inequality: 12x ≤ 20×60.
- Solve for x, then intersect with x ≥ 120.
- Apply whole-number rule: x is a count.

Reflection prompts:
- “If your maximum feasible x is below 120, what options might a workplace consider?” (e.g., add labour hours, reduce time per unit, adjust target.)

For error-spotting, suggest learners annotate each fix:
- What was wrong?
- What did you change?
- How can someone verify it?

Common misconception: treating ‘notes/assumptions’ as optional. In workplace maths, it is part of the deliverable.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes to avoid

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes to avoid
content: Supports: MOD101 feasibility modelling and spreadsheet standards
Show variable definitions, units, and constraints clearly
Use intersection of constraints; do not report one constraint only
Do not round mid-calculation unless justified
Document assumptions so another person can reproduce results
Check inequality direction with a quick test value
content.notes:
Connect explicitly to typical module assessments, even if learners see different formats (quiz, workbook, or portfolio evidence). The assessed skill is usually not the algebra alone, but the modelling clarity and decision justification.

Expand on each mistake:
- “One constraint only”: learners sometimes compute the maximum from labour and stop, forgetting materials or minimum target.
- “Mid-calculation rounding”: emphasise that it can flip feasibility near boundaries.
- “No assumptions”: without stating x must be whole, two people can legitimately report different answers.

Probing questions:
- “If you had to defend your feasibility decision to a manager, which three lines would you show first?”
- “What is your personal checklist before submitting a spreadsheet?”

content: Translate words to maths: targets (≥) and limits (≤)

Solve each constraint, then intersect to find feasibility
Apply domain rules (x ≥ 0; whole numbers for item counts)

- Can you write constraints with correct units?

slides.title: Units, significant figures and rounding in spreadsheets

content.title: Units, significant figures and rounding in spreadsheets
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD101 Workplace Maths Foundations
Lesson 9 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome. This lesson is about producing workplace spreadsheets that other people can trust: every number has a stated unit, calculations are dimensionally consistent, and rounding is applied deliberately rather than accidentally. As you work through, imagine a colleague inheriting your spreadsheet in six months’ time—would they understand what each cell means, and could they reproduce your logic?

Key message: units, significant figures, and rounding are not “presentation”; they are part of correctness and auditability.

slides.title: Learning objectives

content.title: Learning objectives
content: Check units and convert units across a multi-step spreadsheet
Apply sig figs/rounding with a justified strategy for 3 outputs
Compare rounding strategies and quantify absolute and % difference
Rearrange 2 workplace formulae and implement correctly in Excel
Perform 2+ verification checks and correct units/rounding/assumptions
content.notes:
These objectives are all “apply” level: you are expected to do, not just describe. Keep returning to two questions: (1) What is the unit of this cell? (2) What precision is appropriate for the decision being made?

When you justify rounding, make it specific: for example, “Final output reported to 2 dp because invoices are in pence; intermediate values kept unrounded to avoid compounding error.” A common misconception is thinking that choosing 2 dp is automatically ‘more accurate’—accuracy depends on the measurement quality and the context tolerance, not the number of decimals.

slides.title: How to use this lesson

content.title: How to use this lesson
content: Watch: follow the unit and rounding rules on each slide
Practice: build a mini-sheet and label units for every cell
Check: run dimensional, reasonableness and sensitivity checks
content.notes:
Work actively: pause and try each step in Excel (or your spreadsheet tool). Create a simple sheet with: inputs, intermediate calculations, and outputs; then add a Units column or unit headers.

When you “check”, do not only look for Excel errors (#DIV/0! etc.). We are checking for silent errors: wrong unit conversions, inconsistent assumptions, and rounding that changes decisions.

Probing question: if an output changes by 1% when you alter an input by 1%, is that expected? If not, why not?

slides.title: Unit discipline in workplace spreadsheets

content.title: Unit discipline in workplace spreadsheets
content: Give every numeric cell an explicit unit (header or Units col)
Keep one unit system per block (e.g., all lengths in metres)
Write conversions in cells, not in your head
Treat unitless ratios separately (e.g., yield, VAT rate)
Use dimensional checks to catch wrong formula structure
content.notes:
Units are part of meaning. A cell containing “25” is ambiguous; “25 kg” or “25 m” is usable. In workplaces, many spreadsheet failures come from implicit units (someone assumes mm, another assumes m).

Practical approach: add a Units column next to Inputs and Outputs, and for intermediate calculations use clear headings (e.g., “Mass flow (kg/s)”). If you are using tables, add a Units field per column.

Dimensional check idea: in a formula like Cost = Quantity × Unit price, you should see (kg) × (£/kg) = (£). If you end up with (£·kg) or (kg/£), something is structurally wrong.

Common misconception: “If Excel gives a number, it must be correct.” Excel does not know units; you must impose that structure.

slides.title: Conversion factors you can audit

content.title: Conversion factors you can audit
content.notes:
A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, expressed in different units. The key is direction: multiplying by 1000 converts kg → g, but dividing by 1000 converts g → kg.

In spreadsheets, make conversions explicit:
- Have a cell that contains the conversion factor (labelled with units if helpful).
- Then compute: value_in_target = value_in_source * factor.

Mini-example: If A2 = 2.4 (kg), and B2 = 1000 (g per kg), then C2 = A2*B2 gives 2400 g. Ask yourself: do the units cancel correctly?

Common misconception: relying on “moving the decimal point”. That is fragile and hard to audit later.

slides.title: Significant figures vs decimal places

content.title: Significant figures vs decimal places
leftColumn: Significant figures: counts meaningful digits
Linked to measurement precision
Example: 0.004560 has 4 sig figs
Good for science/engineering reporting
rightColumn: Decimal places: digits after the decimal point
Linked to currency/format conventions
Example: £12.50 has 2 dp
Good for finance and billing outputs
content.notes:
These are different ideas. Significant figures relate to how precisely something is known (measurement quality). Decimal places relate to how you present numbers (often driven by policy, e.g., currency in pence).

Mini-examples:
- 12.50 has 4 significant figures (1,2,5,0) and 2 decimal places.
- 0.01250 has 3 significant figures (1,2,5) and 4 decimal places.

Probing questions:
- Is your input measured to the nearest 1 mm, 0.1 mm, or estimated? That drives sig figs.
- Is your output used for payment, compliance reporting, or internal planning? That drives formatting/rounding rules.

Common misconception: “Trailing zeros don’t matter.” They can matter when they indicate precision (e.g., 12.50 vs 12.5).

slides.title: Rounding strategies and when to use them

content.title: Rounding strategies and when to use them
content.notes:
Your choice should be driven by purpose and tolerance. In many workplace cases, “round at end” is best: keep full precision internally, then round the final outputs to the required reporting level.

Controlled rounding is used when the real process rounds: for example, materials ordered in whole packs, or labour billed in 15-minute blocks. In that case, rounding is not a mathematical preference—it is a business rule.

Excel tip: distinguish between formatting and calculation.
- Formatting changes display only.
- ROUND() changes the stored value used in downstream calculations.

Probing question: where in your process does rounding happen in reality—measurement, ordering, billing, or reporting?

slides.title: Worked example: unit audit for a mini-sheet

content.title: Worked example: unit audit for a mini-sheet
leftColumn: Before: numbers without units
Mixed mm and m in one formula
Conversions done mentally
Outputs labelled only in a chart
rightColumn: After: Units column for inputs and outputs
Single base unit per section (e.g., m, kg, s)
Explicit conversion cells with factors
Dimensional check noted next to key outputs
content.notes:
Imagine a simple workplace sheet: calculating material cost from length, width, thickness, density, and price per kg.

Typical failure pattern:
- Length entered in mm, width in m, thickness in mm, then volume computed as L*W*T without conversion. The spreadsheet runs, but volume is wrong by factors of 1000 or 1,000,000.

Walkthrough you can replicate:
1) Create an Inputs table with Value and Units.
2) Choose base units (e.g., convert all lengths to metres).
3) Add conversion lines: “Length (m) = Length (mm) * 0.001”.
4) Compute volume (m^3) and mass (kg), then cost (£).
5) Write a dimensional check note: (m^3)×(kg/m^3)=kg; (kg)×(£/kg)=£.

Probing question: if you doubled thickness, which outputs should double? If they do not, what is wrong?

slides.title: Worked example: rounding impact on final outputs

content.title: Worked example: rounding impact on final outputs
content.notes:
This table illustrates error propagation: rounding at every intermediate step can drift away from the full-precision result.

How to create this in Excel:
- Build one column of calculations with no ROUND() applied.
- Copy the calculation chain into a second column and apply ROUND(value,2) at each step.
- Compare the final outputs using:
  Abs diff = ABS(final_A - final_B)
  % diff = Abs diff / final_A

Interpretation depends on tolerance. A difference of £0.43 may be acceptable for an internal estimate but not acceptable for invoicing if the contract requires exact billing rules.

Common misconception: “Rounding each step is safer.” It often increases cumulative error unless it matches a real-world rounding rule.

slides.title: Worked example: rearrange and implement formulae

content.title: Worked example: rearrange and implement formulae
content: Example A: Revenue = price × quantity → quantity = revenue/price
Example B: Time = units/rate → rate = units/time
Use brackets to control order of operations
Use cell references; avoid typing numbers into formulae
Document units and assumptions beside each rearranged formula
content.notes:
Rearranging formulae is common in workplaces: targets are often set on an output, and you need to solve for an input.

Example A (pricing target): If revenue target is £50,000 and price is £125/unit, then quantity = 50000/125 = 400 units. Unit check: (£)/(£/unit) = unit.

Example B (production rate): If you must produce 960 units in 8 hours, rate = 960/8 = 120 units/hour. Unit check: (units)/(hours) = units/hour.

Excel implementation guidance:
- Use parentheses explicitly even when you “know” precedence.
- Use absolute references for constants you will copy (e.g., $B$2).
- Keep a nearby note cell: “Assumptions & rounding: output rate rounded to nearest whole unit/hour for staffing.”

Common misconception: rearranging changes units. Units must still balance; if they do not, the rearrangement or the original formula is wrong.

slides.title: Practice: build and test your own mini-sheet

content.title: Practice: build and test your own mini-sheet
content: Create 5 inputs with units and 3 outputs with units
Add at least 2 explicit unit conversion steps
Choose a rounding strategy for 3 outputs; justify in a note
Compare 2 rounding strategies; compute abs and % difference
Rearrange 2 formulae to solve for a target variable
Record 2 corrections you made after checking
content.notes:
Keep the mini-sheet realistic: choose something like costing, staffing, production targets, or material usage.

Suggested structure:
- Inputs: quantity, unit price, time, rate, waste %, VAT rate (unitless).
- Outputs: total cost (£), required hours (h), required quantity (units).

When comparing strategies, ensure you are changing rounding behaviour, not just cell formatting. Use ROUND() for deliberate rounding.

Probing questions:
- Which inputs are measured vs fixed constants?
- Where would rounding occur in the real process (ordering, billing, reporting)?

slides.title: Verification checks you should always run

content.title: Verification checks you should always run
leftColumn: Dimensional check: do units cancel to the right unit?
Reasonableness check: quick hand estimate or spot-check
Sensitivity check: vary one input by 1–10% and observe change
Cross-check: compare to historical/benchmark figures
rightColumn: What changed after checks (units, formula, rounding, assumptions)?
Which outputs are most sensitive, and why?
Is the rounding consistent with tolerance and policy?
What would you tell a colleague to watch for?
content.notes:
Verification is how you catch silent errors.

Dimensional check: write the unit algebra as text next to key outputs. If your ‘cost’ output ends up in (£·kg), the formula is structurally wrong.

Reasonableness check: do a rough calculation with rounded numbers. If Excel says 12,874 and your estimate is ~1,300, investigate immediately.

Sensitivity check: change one input (e.g., price per kg) by +5%. Does total cost change by about +5% (if that input is proportional)? If not, what other dependencies exist?

Common misconception: only checking the final cell. Many errors occur upstream; check the chain.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: spreadsheet standards tasks (units, assumptions, audit trail)
Common error: confusing display formatting with true rounding
Common error: mixing unit systems within one calculation block
Common error: rounding inputs that are exact constants
Common error: no stated tolerance/context for rounding choice
Common error: rearranged formula missing brackets in Excel
content.notes:
This lesson supports assignments where your spreadsheet is judged on correctness and professional standard, not just getting an answer.

Formatting vs rounding: showing 2 dp does not prevent Excel using full precision; equally, using ROUND() changes downstream results. Choose deliberately.

Mixing units: if some cells are in mm and others in m, the sheet must convert to one base unit before combining values.

Rounding inputs: do not round exact constants (e.g., 1000 g per kg) unless a policy requires it. Instead, keep them exact and round outputs.

Excel brackets: rearranged formulae often fail due to missing parentheses. Encourage yourself to test with a known scenario where you can predict the result.

slides.title: Summary

content.title: Summary
content: State units for every value; convert explicitly and consistently
Use dimensional checks to validate formula structure
Choose and justify a rounding strategy based on context/tolerance
Quantify rounding impact with absolute and percent differences
Verify with reasonableness and sensitivity checks; document changes
content.notes:
If you take one habit from this lesson, make it this: never leave a number without a unit or a reason for its precision.

Before you finish any workplace spreadsheet, ask:
- Can someone else identify the unit of every input/output immediately?
- Have I documented assumptions and where rounding occurs?
- Have I demonstrated that rounding does not change the decision?

In your own practice, keep a small “Checks performed” section on the sheet—this turns your work from a personal calculation into an auditable tool.

slides.title: MOD102 — Functions and graphs

content.title: MOD102 — Functions and graphs
content: Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD102 — Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making
Lesson 1: Interpret linear, quadratic and exponential functions
Duration: 1h 30m (online self-study)
content.notes:
Welcome. In this lesson we focus on interpreting three common function types used in operational settings: linear, quadratic and exponential. The emphasis is on application: identifying inputs/outputs with units, classifying patterns from words or plots, interpreting parameters in context, producing a readable chart in Excel or Python, and applying quality checks.

As you work through, keep asking: “What quantity can I control or choose?” (often the input) and “What quantity responds?” (often the output). Also keep units visible at all times—most interpretation errors are unit errors in disguise.

slides.title: Orientation: goals and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: goals and how to use this lesson
leftColumn: Identify input x and output y, each with units
Classify: linear, quadratic, or exponential
Interpret key parameters in context
Plot data plus a fitted model in Excel/Python
rightColumn: Read/watch each concept slide actively
Pause to sketch the expected graph shape
Replicate the worked examples on your device
Apply the quality-checks before moving on
content.notes:
The left column is what you should be able to do by the end, using workplace-style examples (staffing, costs, demand, outputs). The right column is the study method: this lesson works best when you frequently stop and predict what the graph should look like before calculating.

Probing questions to self-ask: If x increases by 1 unit, what tends to happen to y? Does the change in y look additive (constant differences), does it speed up then slow down (turning point), or does it scale by a factor (constant percentage change)?

Common misconception: treating the “thing on the horizontal axis” as automatically the independent variable. In real work, you must justify which variable is the input (decision/control) and which is the output (response).

slides.title: What you will produce by the end

content.title: What you will produce by the end
content: A 1–2 sentence input/output statement with correct units
A justified function choice using a visible graph feature
Parameter meanings: rate, baseline, peak/constraint
One chart: data + fitted model, labelled for non-specialists
A quality-check list with at least 3 checks applied
At least one corrected error in a messy graph or formula
content.notes:
These outputs align directly with operational reporting: you are practising how to communicate a model, not just compute it. A strong answer is readable by someone who is not a mathematician.

When you write your 1–2 sentence statement, aim for: “As [input, with units] changes, [output, with units] changes; x is the input because…, y is the output because…”. The justification can be brief but must be explicit.

Misconception to avoid: thinking “a chart is self-explanatory”. In professional contexts, unlabeled axes, missing units, or unclear scales can make correct calculations useless.

slides.title: Inputs, outputs and units in workplace settings

content.title: Inputs, outputs and units in workplace settings
content: Input (independent): the variable you set or observe first
Output (dependent): the variable that responds to the input
State both with units (e.g., hours, £, units/day, %)
Template: “y (units) depends on x (units) because …”
Check: does changing x plausibly cause/drive changes in y?
content.notes:
In operations, the independent variable is often a decision lever (staff count, price, production time) or a time index. The dependent variable is an outcome (output, cost, defects, demand). Always attach units immediately; it prevents later mistakes when interpreting slopes or growth factors.

Mini-examples:
- Staffing vs output: x = number of staff (people), y = units produced per day (units/day).
- Demand vs price: x = price (£), y = quantity demanded (units/week).
- Energy use vs temperature: x = outside temperature (°C), y = kWh per day (kWh/day).

Probing questions: If I swapped x and y, would the story still make sense? Which variable would I naturally put on the horizontal axis for decision-making? A frequent error is to treat “time” as the input even when the real driver is a policy change or workload level.

slides.title: Recognising linear, quadratic and exponential patterns

content.title: Recognising linear, quadratic and exponential patterns
content: Use differences, turning points, and ratios to classify quickly.
content.notes:
Classification is about observable behaviour, not memorising formulas. A linear relationship adds or subtracts by roughly the same amount for each step in x. A quadratic changes direction once (a single turning point). An exponential scales: each step multiplies by a similar factor, often described in percentages.

How to test with data:
- Differences: compute y(i+1) − y(i). If these are roughly constant, linear is plausible.
- Ratios: compute y(i+1) / y(i). If these are roughly constant, exponential is plausible.
- Turning point: look for y increasing then decreasing (or vice versa), suggesting quadratic behaviour.

Misconception: assuming “curved” automatically means exponential. Many quadratic relationships are curved too; the turning point is the giveaway.

slides.title: Linear parameters: slope and intercept in context

content.title: Linear parameters: slope and intercept in context
content: Model: y = mx + c (m slope, c intercept)
Slope m: change in y for a 1-unit increase in x
Units of m: (units of y) per (unit of x)
Intercept c: predicted y when x = 0 (a baseline)
Negative m means y decreases as x increases
Sense-check m using two points: m = Δy/Δx
content.notes:
Slope is the operational “rate”: output per worker, cost per unit, miles per hour, etc. Always state the slope with units, because the unit tells you the meaning. For example, “15 units/day per person” is interpretable; “15” alone is not.

Intercept is often misunderstood. It is the model’s predicted output at x = 0, which may or may not be meaningful in the real situation. Example: a delivery firm might have a base cost even at zero parcels (c > 0). But if x = 0 is impossible (e.g., ‘0 workers’), the intercept is still a mathematical parameter; treat it cautiously.

Probing questions: If x increases by 10, can you estimate y quickly using the slope? Does the intercept represent a fixed cost or initial level? Common mistake: reading the intercept off a graph where the axis does not include x = 0.

slides.title: Non-linear parameters: quadratic vs exponential

content.title: Non-linear parameters: quadratic vs exponential
leftColumn: Quadratic: y = ax² + bx + c
a sets direction: a>0 opens up, a<0 opens down
Turning point (vertex) gives min or max output
Vertex often represents a capacity optimum or peak
rightColumn: Exponential: y = A·b^x (or A·e^(kx))
A is the starting level at x=0
b is the growth/decay factor per 1 unit of x
0<b<1 decay; b>1 growth (multiplicative change)
content.notes:
This slide is about what parameters mean operationally.

Quadratic: The sign of a tells you whether you are looking for a maximum (opens down) or a minimum (opens up). In operations, a turning point can represent an optimal price (peak profit), a best staffing level (peak throughput before congestion), or a minimum cost point.

Exponential: The key operational idea is percentage change. If b = 0.9, you have a 10% decrease per 1 unit of x. If b = 1.05, you have a 5% increase per 1 unit of x. Learners often confuse “add 10%” with “multiply by 1.10”; emphasise the multiplicative factor.

Probing questions: What does “per unit of x” mean here—per day, per £, per kilometre? Is x continuous or counted in whole steps? Common mistake: using an exponential model when the context has a natural maximum (which may require a different model).

slides.title: Plot and fit a model in Excel or Python

content.title: Plot and fit a model in Excel or Python
leftColumn: Excel: Insert → Scatter (points only)
Add Trendline: linear/quadratic/exponential
Show equation and R² (use with caution)
Label axes with units; add a clear title
rightColumn: Python: plot scatter (matplotlib/seaborn)
Fit: polyfit (linear/quadratic) or log-fit exp
Plot fitted curve on same axes as data
Include labels, units, and sensible axis limits
content.notes:
The aim is a chart that a non-specialist can read and trust. Start with a scatter plot to show the raw relationship. Only then add a fitted model curve/line. Ensure the fitted line is visible and not implied.

Excel notes: Trendlines can be convenient, but do not let the tool choose the story for you. Pick the model based on context and features, not just R².

Python notes: For linear/quadratic, polynomial fitting is straightforward (degree 1 or 2). For exponential, a common method is to fit a line to ln(y) vs x (only valid when y>0). Mention this limitation explicitly.

Misconceptions: (1) Using a line chart that connects points in time order when x is not time. (2) Using a truncated axis to exaggerate changes. (3) Choosing exponential just because R² is slightly higher.

slides.title: Quality-check routine for graphs and calculations

content.title: Quality-check routine for graphs and calculations
content: Units: do all terms and parameters have correct units?
Axes: labels, units, title, and readable tick marks
Scale: does the axis range hide patterns or distort them?
Model: does the chosen type match the visible feature?
Spot-check: compute y at 1–2 x values and compare to data
Reasonableness: do predictions break constraints (e.g., negatives)?
content.notes:
Treat this as a minimum professional standard before submitting any analysis.

Explain each check:
- Units: slopes must be “output per input”. Exponential factors are unitless, but x must be clearly defined (per day, per week, per £).
- Axes and scale: missing units is a common reason stakeholders misinterpret magnitude. Also check whether the scale compresses or exaggerates trends.
- Model-feature match: if your relationship has a turning point, a simple exponential is unlikely to be appropriate.
- Spot-check: take two observed x values, compute predicted y from the model, and see if the model is in the right ballpark.
- Reasonableness: outputs like demand or defects cannot be negative; if your model predicts negatives in the relevant range, flag it.

Probing question: If you handed this chart to a manager with no context, what would they misunderstand first?

slides.title: Worked example: staffing and daily output (linear)

content.title: Worked example: staffing and daily output (linear)
content: Scenario: output changes by a near-constant amount per worker.
content.notes:
Step 1 (identify variables): x is staff (people). y is output (units/day). The units matter: output per day is already a rate.

Step 2 (check for linearity): Differences are constant: +15 units/day for each +1 person. That is a clear linear feature.

Step 3 (calculate slope): m = Δy/Δx = (145 − 100) / (8 − 5) = 45/3 = 15. Units: (units/day) per person.

Step 4 (find intercept): Use y = mx + c with a point, e.g., 100 = 15·5 + c, so c = 25. Model: y = 15x + 25.

Interpretation: Each additional worker is associated with ~15 extra units/day. The intercept suggests a baseline of 25 units/day at x=0, which may represent fixed output from automation or may be outside the feasible range—so state that limitation.

Probing questions: Would you expect linearity to continue indefinitely (e.g., space limits, congestion)? What real constraint might introduce curvature at higher staffing?

slides.title: Worked example: complaints falling by 20% weekly

content.title: Worked example: complaints falling by 20% weekly
content: Let x = weeks since change (weeks), y = complaints/week
Given: week 0 has 50 complaints; each week is 80% of last
Exponential factor b = 0.8 (a 20% reduction per week)
Model: y = 50 × 0.8^x
Predict week 3: y = 50 × 0.8^3 = 25.6 complaints/week
Interpretation: reductions slow in absolute terms over time
content.notes:
This scenario is written in multiplicative language (“20% each week”), which strongly signals an exponential model.

Walkthrough:
- Identify variables with units: x is weeks (input index). y is complaints per week (output rate).
- Convert percentage to factor: “reduce by 20%” means multiply by 1 − 0.20 = 0.80.
- Build the model: starting level A = 50 at x = 0, so y = 50·0.8^x.
- Compute a prediction: 0.8^3 = 0.512, so y ≈ 25.6. In context you might round to 26 complaints/week, but keep the exact value for calculation steps.

Key interpretation: Exponential decay reduces by equal percentages, not equal counts. The absolute drop from week 0 to 1 is 10, but from week 5 to 6 it is much smaller.

Common misconception: writing y = 50 − 0.2x (that would be linear and implies a constant drop of 0.2 complaints per week, which is not the meaning).

slides.title: Practice: classify and justify from short scenarios

content.title: Practice: classify and justify from short scenarios
content: A: Output rises by 12 units/day for each extra worker
B: Profit rises with price, peaks, then falls after £20
C: Stock level decreases by 5% each day
D: Processing time drops, then rises as load gets very high
For each: state x and y with units; choose type; cite a feature
Self-check: can you sketch the curve shape before fitting?
content.notes:
Suggested answers (focus on justification):
- A is linear: constant rate of change (+12 per worker). x = workers (people), y = output (units/day).
- B is quadratic (or at least “has a turning point”): the peak indicates a maximum. x = price (£), y = profit (£/week, for example).
- C is exponential decay: constant ratio (multiply by 0.95 each day). x = days, y = stock (units).
- D suggests a turning point (often quadratic-like): performance improves then deteriorates due to congestion/queuing effects. x = load (jobs/hour), y = time (minutes/job).

Probing questions: What wording clues indicate multiplicative change (“%”, “factor”, “doubles”)? Where is the turning point operationally—an optimum, a capacity limit, or a pricing peak?

Misconception to watch: assuming any “peak” must be quadratic. Real data may be noisy; your job is to justify the simplest plausible model based on features and context.

slides.title: Practice: correct at least one “messy” output

content.title: Practice: correct at least one “messy” output
content: Error 1: axes lack units (e.g., “Time” but not days/weeks)
Error 2: slope reported without units (e.g., “m = 15”)
Error 3: exponential written as y = A + b^x (wrong form)
Error 4: axis truncated, exaggerating change near baseline
Choose one error to fix, then rerun your quality checks
Write one sentence: what the corrected chart now implies
content.notes:
This is about professional checking habits.

How to approach:
1) Pick one issue and correct it fully (not partially). For example, add axis units and update any text that references those units.
2) If correcting a formula: exponential models multiply, they do not add a powered term. Typical correct forms are y = A·b^x or y = A·e^(kx).
3) If correcting a scale: ensure the axis range supports honest comparison. A truncated y-axis is not always wrong, but it must be clearly justified and should not mislead.

Probing questions: If someone skim-reads your chart in 10 seconds, what conclusion will they draw? Would that conclusion still be valid after your correction?

Common misconception: thinking presentation errors are “cosmetic”. In decision-making, they can change choices (e.g., overestimating a growth rate).

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD102 tasks: model data, plot clearly, interpret params
Include: x/y with units, model choice, parameter meaning
Show chart with data + fitted function on the same axes
Attach your quality-check list and the correction you made
Avoid: choosing by R² alone; explain the visible feature instead
Avoid: extrapolating beyond feasible ranges without caveats
content.notes:
In the module assessment, markers typically look for a coherent chain: clear variable definitions → justified model choice → correct parameter interpretation → readable visual → evidence of checking.

Common pitfalls:
- High R² but wrong story: e.g., fitting a quadratic to fundamentally exponential growth because it “fits” the limited range.
- Missing units: especially on slope and on axes.
- Overconfident intercepts and forecasts: if x=0 is outside the data range, say so. If forecasts imply negatives or exceed capacity, flag that the model is not valid there.

Probing questions: If a stakeholder asked “so what does your slope mean in practice?”, could you answer in one sentence with units? If asked “why exponential?”, can you point to the ratio/percentage feature?

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Define x and y with units before choosing any model
Linear: constant differences; slope is a rate with units
Quadratic: a turning point indicates a max/min operational level
Exponential: constant ratios; factor b encodes % change per x unit
Plot data + model clearly, and run unit/scale/spot-check routines
content.notes:
As you continue in MOD102, keep returning to these basics. Most modelling errors are not advanced mathematics problems—they are definition, unit, or interpretation problems.

Final self-questions:
- Did I name x and y in plain language and include units?
- Did I justify model type using an observable feature?
- Can I explain each parameter in operational terms (rate, baseline, peak, factor)?
- Would my chart be interpretable to a non-specialist without me narrating it?

slides.title: Plot operational data and fitted functions

content.title: Plot operational data and fitted functions
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD102 — Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making
Lesson 2: Plot operational datasets and fitted functions
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners and situate the lesson within MOD102. Emphasise that this is an applied session: the goal is not just to “make a chart”, but to produce a decision-ready graphic with a defensible fitted function.

Briefly preview the workflow: (1) tidy data, (2) scatter plot with correct labels and scale, (3) fit a line and report the equation, (4) interpret gradient and intercept in operational terms, (5) use cost and revenue lines to find and check break-even.

Probing question to open: “When you see a chart in a report, what makes you trust it?”

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Create a scatter plot with labels, units, title, fair scale
Fit a linear function and report the equation with rounding
Interpret gradient and intercept with correct operational units
Find break-even and verify it by substitution and on the plot
How to use: watch → practise in tool → self-check your output
content.notes:
Frame the objectives as observable outputs. For Objective 1, stress that “fair scale” means the chart does not exaggerate or hide variation; if an axis is truncated, there must be a reason stated.

For Objective 2, clarify what “appropriate function” means here: we are focusing on linear relationships (trendline/regression). If the data are clearly non-linear, the correct action is to say so and justify a different model, but this lesson assesses linear fitting.

For Objective 3, remind learners that units come from ‘rise over run’. If y is £ and x is units, the gradient is £/unit.

For Objective 4, stress verification: break-even is not just a computed number; you should check it in the functions and, where possible, visually confirm the intersection on the chart.

Probing question: “Which objective is most likely to be marked down by presentation errors rather than maths errors?”

slides.title: Why scatter plots for operational datasets

content.title: Why scatter plots for operational datasets
content: Operational data usually come as paired measurements (x, y)
Scatter plots show relationship, spread, and possible outliers
They support modelling: choose a function that matches the pattern
They help detect non-linearity before fitting a line
They make assumptions visible (e.g., constant rate of change)
content.notes:
Explain that operational decisions often depend on relationships: demand vs price, throughput vs labour hours, cost vs output. A scatter plot is the correct first step because it respects the raw paired structure and does not imply continuity where it is not warranted.

Mini-example: If weekly units sold (x) and marketing spend (y) have a few extreme weeks, a line chart can mislead by implying time continuity is the main story; scatter reveals the relationship and outliers.

Common misconception: learners sometimes choose a line chart because the data are in two columns and Excel suggests it. Reinforce: for modelling y as a function of x, start with scatter.

Probing question: “What visual clues would make you doubt that a straight line is appropriate?”

slides.title: Chart-quality checklist (use before submission)

content.title: Chart-quality checklist (use before submission)
content.notes:
Talk learners through each checklist item as a ‘minimum standard’ for operational reporting.

Title: Encourage specificity, e.g., “Total cost vs units produced (January sample)” rather than “Graph”.

Axes: Units must be explicit. If you are plotting ‘Cost’, do not omit currency. If time is in minutes, do not label as hours.

Scale: Explain that truncation can be legitimate (e.g., focusing on a narrow operating range), but must be stated. Otherwise it is treated as misleading.

Markers: In many operational datasets, points overlap; learners may need transparency, smaller markers, or jitter. If a trendline is used, it must not visually hide the data.

Equation: Stress that the equation should be usable on its own. If the line is “Cost = 1800 + 12Q”, units should be interpretable: 1800 is £, 12 is £/unit.

Probing question: “Which checklist item is easiest to do last, but most costly to forget?”

slides.title: Choosing axes and scale without distortion

content.title: Choosing axes and scale without distortion
content.content: Choose x and y to match the operational question, then set a scale that shows all relevant data without exaggerating changes. Truncating an axis can be acceptable only if you state the reason and it does not change the conclusion.
content.notes:
Expand the idea of ‘matching the operational question’. Typically, x is the driver/input (units produced, hours worked) and y is the outcome (cost, revenue, defects). If the question is “How does cost change with output?”, output belongs on the x-axis.

Explain truncation with a concrete comparison: if costs range from £9,800 to £10,200, starting the y-axis at £9,700 may make sense to show variation; starting at £0 is not wrong but may hide differences. However, truncating from £9,800 to £10,200 can exaggerate a small change; therefore you must justify it.

Common misconception: learners assume axes must always start at zero. Clarify: bar charts should usually start at zero; scatter plots and line charts can start elsewhere if justified.

Probing questions: “If I change only the y-axis limits, can the ‘story’ of the chart change?” and “What range would a manager need to see to make a decision?”

slides.title: Fit a linear function on the chart

content.title: Fit a linear function on the chart
leftColumn: Excel: Insert → Scatter (markers only)
Excel: Add Trendline → Linear
Excel: Show equation and R² on chart
Excel: Format labels, units, and decimals
rightColumn: Python: plot scatter with matplotlib
Python: fit line with numpy.polyfit or sklearn
Python: overlay fitted line and annotate equation
Python: control rounding and axis formatting
content.notes:
Clarify that both tools achieve the same modelling goal; choice depends on context and learner preference.

Excel guidance: After adding a linear trendline, explicitly tick “Display Equation on chart” and (optionally) “Display R-squared value”. Explain what R² is used for here: a quick sense of fit, not a guarantee of causation.

Python guidance: Provide a simple pattern:
- Read data (pandas DataFrame)
- Scatter: plt.scatter(x, y)
- Fit: m, c = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
- Line: yhat = m*x + c; plt.plot(x, yhat)
- Annotate: plt.text(..., f"y = {m:.2f}x + {c:.0f}")

Common misconceptions:
- Fitting the line to the wrong variables (swapping x and y changes units and meaning).
- Reporting too many decimals because the software prints them.

Probing question: “If you swap x and y, what happens to the units of the gradient?”

slides.title: Interpret gradient and intercept in context

content.title: Interpret gradient and intercept in context
content: Gradient m is the rate of change: m = Δy/Δx
Units of m are (units of y) per (units of x)
Intercept c is y when x = 0 (if x=0 is meaningful)
Interpretation must match the operational process
Avoid extrapolating beyond the observed x-range
content.notes:
Explain gradient using a plain-language operational reading: “For each additional unit produced, total cost increases by about m pounds.” Then connect this to variable cost.

Intercept: Discuss when it is meaningful. In cost models, the intercept can represent fixed costs (rent, baseline staffing). In other contexts, x=0 may be impossible (e.g., temperature scale choices), so the intercept is a mathematical parameter but not an operational state.

Mini-example: If y is ‘revenue (£)’ and x is ‘units sold’, the intercept should be near £0 if there are truly no sales at x=0; a large intercept may indicate modelling issues or data problems.

Common misconception: learners say “the intercept is the starting value” without checking whether x=0 is within the data range.

Probing question: “Is x=0 inside your dataset? If not, how confident are you in c?”

content.title: Worked example data (excerpt)
content.notes:
Introduce a realistic scenario: a small operation records total weekly cost (including fixed overhead) at different output levels. The full dataset should contain at least 10 rows; we show an excerpt to keep the slide readable.

Provide the full dataset verbally for learners to practise (you can also supply it as a downloadable file in your platform):
Q: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200
Cost (£): 2050, 2290, 2520, 2770, 3000, 3240, 3480, 3710, 3950, 4200

Explain that these values are approximately linear, but not perfectly so (normal in operational data). This makes it suitable for a linear fit and for discussing residual variation.

Probing question: “Do you expect cost to be perfectly linear in real operations? What could cause departures?”

slides.title: Worked example: build the scatter plot

content.title: Worked example: build the scatter plot
content: Put Q in one column and Cost in the next (no blank rows)
Insert a scatter plot (markers only), not a line chart
Add title and label axes with units (Q, £)
Set axis limits to show all points clearly
Check readability: marker size, gridlines, font size
content.notes:
Walk learners through a disciplined build process.

Data layout: stress that Excel trendlines and Python scripts both depend on clean numeric columns. Common data issues: currency symbols stored as text, thousands separators, and missing values.

Chart choice: explain why markers-only scatter is preferred initially—lines can imply intermediate values or a time sequence that is not present.

Axes: suggest explicit labels, e.g., x-axis “Units produced, Q (units)” and y-axis “Total cost, C (£)”. Encourage learners to avoid ambiguous labels like “Value”.

Scaling: remind learners not to crop points. If there is a compelling reason to zoom in, say so in a caption or notes.

Probing questions: “Can someone read your chart in greyscale?” and “If printed, is it still legible?”

slides.title: Worked example: fit line and report equation

content.title: Worked example: fit line and report equation
content: Add a linear fit and display the equation on the chart
Example fit: C = 1800 + 12.0Q
State units: 1800 (£), 12.0 (£ per unit)
Round sensibly (match data precision; avoid false accuracy)
Interpret: fixed cost ≈ 1800; variable cost ≈ 12 per unit
content.notes:
Explain that the numerical values shown are illustrative of what learners should obtain from the provided dataset; minor differences are acceptable depending on rounding and tool.

Rounding guidance: If costs are recorded to the nearest £10, reporting 12.0374 is not sensible. Encourage 2–3 significant figures for parameters unless a marking rubric specifies otherwise.

Units: model how to write them clearly:
- C(Q) = 1800 £ + (12.0 £/unit)·Q
This makes the dimensional meaning explicit.

Interpretation: tie back to operations. Fixed cost could be rent and baseline staffing; variable cost could be materials and piecework labour.

Common misconception: learners interpret R² as “accuracy”. Clarify it only describes how much variation the linear model explains within this dataset.

Probing question: “If the intercept is negative, what might that tell you about the model or data range?”

slides.title: Break-even point from cost and revenue

content.title: Break-even point from cost and revenue
content: Let Revenue be R = 25Q (price £25 per unit)
Break-even occurs where R = C
Solve: 25Q = 1800 + 12Q → Q = 138.5 units
Round to 139 units if only whole units are feasible
Verify by substitution and by checking the line crossing
content.notes:
Explain the operational meaning: break-even is the output level where profit is zero; above it the operation makes a surplus (before other constraints).

Work the algebra slowly:
25Q = 1800 + 12Q
(25−12)Q = 1800
13Q = 1800
Q = 138.46...

Rounding decision: If you cannot sell half a unit, round up to 139 to ensure revenue meets or exceeds cost. Encourage learners to state the rounding rule they chose.

Verification: show the substitution check:
At Q=139: R = 25×139 = £3475; C = 1800 + 12×139 = £3468 → small positive margin.
Also discuss graph check: the intersection should occur near Q≈140 if axes are scaled sensibly.

Assumptions to state: constant unit price, constant variable cost, linearity over range, no capacity limits, no step costs.

Probing question: “Which assumption is most likely to fail first in a real operation?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)
content: Make your own plot using a 10+ row dataset you choose
Apply the checklist: labels, units, title, fair scale
Fit a line and report m and c with units and rounding
Write 2 sentences: what do m and c mean operationally?
Create a revenue line and compute break-even; then verify
content.notes:
Encourage learners to practise with data that are meaningful to them: e.g., hours worked vs output, distance vs fuel cost, units shipped vs delivery cost. The dataset must have at least 10 rows to make the fit non-trivial.

Self-check method:
- Can a reader reproduce your equation from the chart annotation?
- Do the units make sense when multiplied/divided?
- Does your break-even value sit within the observed range? If not, note that it is extrapolation.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD102 task: chart + fitted line + interpretation
Common pitfall: missing units on axes or in equation write-up
Common pitfall: misleading scale or unexplained axis truncation
Common pitfall: over-precise parameters (too many decimals)
Common pitfall: interpreting c when x=0 is outside data range
content.notes:
Position this lesson as directly supporting typical assessed outputs in MOD102: producing a publishable chart, reporting the fitted function, and drawing operational conclusions.

Expand each pitfall with an example:
- Units: “Cost = 1800 + 12Q” is incomplete unless we state £ and units.
- Scale: a y-axis starting at 1700 can be fine, but if it changes the perceived steepness, you must justify the choice.
- Precision: software may output many decimals; mark schemes often penalise ‘false accuracy’.
- Intercept: if your Q values start at 50, claiming c is the cost at zero units requires a caveat.

Probing question: “Which of these mistakes would cause a correct calculation to be graded poorly?”

content.title: Interpret linear, quadratic and exponential functions
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD102 — Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making

Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners to Lesson 3. Position this lesson as the bridge between recognising a function form and using it for operational meaning and prediction. Emphasise the Bloom’s level (apply): we are not only defining terms; we are using them to interpret workplace-style data, create readable graphs, fit a model, and check for errors.

Probing questions:

- Who is the audience of your graph: a specialist or a non-specialist decision-maker?

Common misconception to pre-empt: learners often jump straight to calculations before clarifying variables and units; highlight that this is the most frequent cause of nonsense results.

slides.title: Orientation: what you will do in this lesson

content.title: Orientation: what you will do in this lesson
content: Identify inputs/outputs and units in workplace scenarios
Interpret parameters: slope, intercept, vertex, growth/decay factor
Plot data clearly in Excel or Python using a 6-point checklist
Fit a model and predict within-range values with correct units
Run diligence checks: units, rounding, scale, reasonableness
Workflow: read → plot → fit → interpret → check
content.notes:
Talk through the workflow as a repeatable routine learners can use beyond this lesson. Stress that interpretation is not “maths for its own sake”: each parameter should map to an operational statement someone could act on.

Mini-example: “If slope is 2.5 minutes per order, what does that mean for staffing when orders increase by 20?”

Probing questions:
- What would ‘100% correctness’ mean for units in your context?
- How might a good graph prevent a poor decision?

Misconception: learners sometimes treat plotting as presentation only; reinforce that plotting is an analytical step to choose model type and spot anomalies.

slides.title: Step 1: identify variables and units

content.title: Step 1: identify variables and units
content: Input (independent): what changes or is chosen (x)
Output (dependent): what responds or is measured (y)
Write units for x and y before using any formula
State domain limits (e.g., time ≥ 0, items are whole numbers)
Check: does y’s unit match the context and the equation?
Always label axes as “quantity (unit)”
content.notes:
Explain that this step is the foundation for every later objective. Give a concrete operational scenario: x = hours since shift start (h), y = cumulative units packed (units). Clarify that “independent” does not mean “more important”; it means it is the variable you treat as the driver for the model.

Mini-examples:
- If y = 50 + 3x and x is “weeks”, then 3 has units “items per week” and 50 has units “items”.
- If x is “temperature (°C)” and y is “defect rate (%)”, then the slope has units “percentage points per °C”.

Probing questions:
- What is a plausible range for x in this workplace setting?
- If x doubled, would y realistically double, more than double, or less?

Common misconceptions:
- Forgetting that intercept has units of y.
- Using “x” and “y” in a graph without naming the real quantities and units.

slides.title: Linear functions: meaning of slope and intercept

content.title: Linear functions: meaning of slope and intercept
content: Form: y = mx + c
m: constant rate of change (units of y per unit x)
c: baseline value when x = 0 (units of y)
Positive/negative m shows increase or decrease with x
Useful when change is steady over the observed range
Interpretation must reference the real quantities, not x/y
content.notes:
Expand on operational meanings: slope m is often productivity rate, cost per unit, speed, or conversion factor. Intercept c might represent fixed cost, starting stock, or initial reading.

Mini-example: y = 120x + 500, where x = days and y = litres processed. Interpret: “Each day adds 120 litres; we start at 500 litres already processed/available.” Ask learners to decide which story makes sense.

Probing questions:
- What would x = 0 represent in your scenario, and is it meaningful?
- If x cannot be 0 (e.g., x is distance travelled), should you still interpret c literally?

Common misconceptions:
- Treating c as ‘nothing’ if it looks inconvenient; instead, question whether x=0 is within the domain.
- Confusing slope with total change rather than change per unit.

slides.title: Quadratic functions: curvature and turning point

content.title: Quadratic functions: curvature and turning point
content: Form: y = ax² + bx + c
a controls curvature: a>0 opens up, a<0 opens down
Vertex is the turning point (max or min)
Vertex x-value: x = -b/(2a)
Use when there is an optimum or diminishing returns
Interpret y-values near vertex as best/worst performance
content.notes:
Explain why quadratics appear operationally: learning curves that plateau then drop, profit vs price (too low/too high), throughput vs staffing (overstaffing causes coordination losses), projectile-like motion, etc.

Mini-example: y = -2x² + 40x + 100, x = staff on shift, y = units/hour. Interpret: increasing staff helps at first, but after a point it reduces output due to congestion/coordination.

Guide learners to interpret the vertex:
- Compute x* = -b/(2a) (staff level at peak).
- Compute y* by substitution (peak output).

Probing questions:
- What would it mean if the vertex occurs at a non-integer x (e.g., 7.5 staff)?
- Is the quadratic believable across all x, or only within a limited range?

Common misconceptions:
- Assuming the vertex is always a maximum (it depends on sign of a).
- Ignoring units: the vertex x-value has units of x.

slides.title: Exponential functions: growth, decay, and factors

content.title: Exponential functions: growth, decay, and factors
content: Form: y = A·b^x (or y = A·e^(kx))
A is initial level when x = 0 (units of y)
b is growth/decay factor per 1 unit of x (unitless)
If b>1 growth; if 0<b<1 decay
Percent change per x-step: (b−1)×100%
Use when change is proportional to current level
content.notes:
Connect exponential to operational realities: demand growth, depreciation, learning/forgetting, decay of backlog after a fix, or sensor discharge.

Mini-example: y = 800·0.85^x where x = weeks, y = remaining faults. Interpret: start with 800 faults; each week 15% are resolved (on average), so remaining faults shrink multiplicatively.

Discuss the difference between additive and multiplicative change:
- Linear: add the same amount each step.
- Exponential: multiply by the same factor each step.

Probing questions:
- If you see the same absolute drop each week, is exponential appropriate?
- What does “per unit of x” mean if x is measured in months rather than weeks?

Common misconceptions:
- Treating b as having units; it is dimensionless.
- Confusing A with ‘maximum’; A is the value at x=0, not a cap.

slides.title: Choosing a model from a plot and context

content.title: Choosing a model from a plot and context
leftColumn: Straight-line pattern
Single peak or trough
Curves up/down faster over time
Same % change per step
rightColumn: Linear: constant rate
Quadratic: turning point
Exponential: accelerating change
Exponential: multiplicative trend
content.notes:
Use this slide as a decision rule: you rarely start with the equation; you start with a scatter plot and the story. Encourage learners to plot first, then choose the simplest model that fits the pattern within the data range.

Mini-demonstration (verbal):
- If y increases by +5 each day: linear.
- If y increases by +5%, +5%, +5%: exponential.
- If performance improves then worsens: quadratic.

Probing questions:
- What operational mechanism could cause a turning point?
- If the plot is noisy, what feature still helps you choose the model?

Misconception: thinking a high-degree polynomial is “better” because it can fit more closely. Reinforce: operational decision-making values interpretability and robustness, not just fit.

slides.title: Graph-quality checklist (Excel or Python)

content.title: Graph-quality checklist (Excel or Python)
content: Title states what, where, and period (if relevant)
Axes labelled as quantity (unit), not just x and y
Scale shows pattern without hiding variation
Markers/lines readable; legend only if multiple series
Data range and domain sensible (no misleading extrapolation)
Optional: add fitted curve and show equation with units
content.notes:
Expand each checklist point with guidance learners can apply immediately.

1) Title: “Weekly energy use (kWh), Warehouse A, Jan–Mar”.
2) Axes: “Time (weeks)” and “Energy use (kWh)”.
3) Scale: discuss zero baseline where appropriate (e.g., bar charts) versus line/scatter where zooming may be justified—explain the choice.
4) Readability: avoid clutter; prefer scatter for raw data, line only when sequence matters.
5) Range/domain: emphasise that predictions should be within observed x-range unless explicitly justified.
6) Fitted curve: if you show an equation, it must correspond to plotted variables and units.

Probing questions:
- Could a colleague read approximate values directly from your chart?
- What could be misinterpreted if the y-axis is truncated?

Common misconceptions:
- Using a line chart for unordered categories.
- Forgetting units, making the chart unusable for decisions.

slides.title: Fitting a function and making a prediction

content.title: Fitting a function and making a prediction
content: Plot scatter first; choose linear/quadratic/exponential
Excel: Add Trendline → set type → display equation and R²
Python: use regression/curve_fit; keep variables and units clear
Report fitted equation with defined x and y meanings
Predict only within data range; include units and rounding
Justify: why this model is reasonable for this process?
content.notes:
Teach fitting as a transparent process, not a button-click. Explain what R² does and does not tell you: it summarises fit to the observed data but does not validate the causal story or suitability outside range.

Excel guidance (spoken):
- Use a scatter plot.
- Add trendline and compare types.
- Ensure the trendline uses the correct x values (not category index).

Python guidance (spoken, conceptual):
- Linear regression: y = mx + c via least squares.
- Quadratic: include x² term.
- Exponential: fit y = A·b^x or take logs if appropriate, but note log-transform changes error structure.

Probing questions:
- If two models have similar R², which would you choose and why?
- What does a prediction mean operationally (staffing, cost, output)?

Common misconceptions:
- Extrapolating because “the equation allows it”.
- Reporting an equation without defining what x and y represent.

slides.title: Worked example: linear rate from operations data

content.title: Worked example: linear rate from operations data
content.notes:
Walk learners through interpreting and fitting a linear model.

Step-by-step narrative:
1) Identify variables: x = time since shift start (hours), y = cumulative units packed (units).
2) Compute slope from two points: from (0,120) to (6,300):
   m = (300−120)/(6−0) = 180/6 = 30 units per hour.
3) Intercept: at x=0, y=120 units (already packed or pre-counted stock). So model: y = 30x + 120.
4) Interpretation in plain language: “Packing increases by about 30 units each hour; at shift start the count is 120 units.”
5) Within-range prediction: at x=5 hours, y = 30·5 + 120 = 270 units.

Probing questions:
- Does it make sense to have 120 units at time 0? What might it represent?
- If a break occurs at hour 3, would a single linear model still be reasonable?

Common misconceptions:
- Treating m as “units” rather than “units per hour”.
- Predicting for x=12 hours without considering shift length.

slides.title: Worked example: quadratic optimum (staff vs output)

content.title: Worked example: quadratic optimum (staff vs output)
content.notes:
Use this to demonstrate a turning point and operational interpretation.

Step-by-step narrative:
1) Variables and units: x = staff on shift (people), y = output rate (units per hour).
2) Shape: output rises then falls; this suggests a quadratic with a maximum.
3) Fitting (tool-based): in Excel, add a polynomial trendline (order 2). In Python, fit y = ax² + bx + c.
4) Interpret the vertex: the staff level at peak output is x* = -b/(2a). Emphasise that x* has unit “people”.
5) Translate to an operational decision: “Beyond about x* staff, coordination effects reduce throughput.”

Probing questions:
- If x* is 8.6 staff, what should you do in practice?
- What other factors could explain the drop at 10 staff (space, equipment limits)?

Common misconceptions:
- Assuming the fitted maximum is exact; it is an estimate.
- Ignoring that the quadratic may be valid only from 4 to 10 staff.

slides.title: Worked example: exponential decay (backlog reduction)

content.title: Worked example: exponential decay (backlog reduction)
content.notes:
Show learners how to recognise a constant percentage decrease.

Step-by-step narrative:
1) Variables: x = weeks since fix deployed (weeks), y = open tickets (tickets).
2) Check ratios: 400/500 = 0.8; 320/400 = 0.8; 256/320 = 0.8.
   The same factor repeats → exponential decay.
3) Model: y = 500·0.8^x.
4) Interpretation: start with 500 tickets; each week, tickets reduce to 80% of previous (20% resolved net).
5) Prediction within range: at week 2.5,
   y = 500·0.8^2.5 ≈ 500·0.572 = 286 tickets (rounded appropriately).
6) Discuss rounding and reporting: tickets are whole numbers; round to nearest whole ticket.

Probing questions:
- What operational assumption is implied by a constant factor each week?
- Would it be sensible to predict to week 20? Why/why not?

Common misconceptions:
- Using linear decrease because the numbers “look like they drop by 100 then 80…”.
- Reporting 286.3 tickets without context-aware rounding.

leftColumn: 1) Name x, y and units for a scenario you know

4) Spot 2 errors: units, axis scale, rounding, domain

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD102 tasks: graphing, fitting, interpretation, prediction
Marking focus: units, labels, parameter meaning, justified model choice
Avoid: missing units on axes or in reported equation
Avoid: extrapolation beyond data without justification
Avoid: choosing model by R² alone, ignoring process meaning
Avoid: rounding inputs early and compounding error
content.notes:
Explain how these skills typically show up in assessed work: learners might be given a dataset and asked to (i) choose a model, (ii) fit it, (iii) interpret parameters in context, and (iv) predict a value with justification.

Elaborate on “justified model choice”: the argument should reference both the plot shape and the operational mechanism (steady rate vs multiplicative change vs optimum).

Mini-scenarios of mistakes:
- A correct line but axes labelled “x” and “y”: loses marks because it is unusable.
- A beautiful curve fit that predicts negative tickets: fails reasonableness.

Probing questions:
- If your intercept is negative, what might that imply about the model or x=0 meaning?
- What would you write to justify that a prediction is within-range and reasonable?
