content.title: Orientation: outcomes and study route
leftColumn: Create labelled scatter plots from CSV data (Excel or Python)

Reflective prompt: what would count as “good enough” evidence for someone else to trust your graph and your break-even calculation?

slides.title: Scatter plots for operational datasets

content.title: Scatter plots for operational datasets
content: Use scatter plots for two quantitative variables (x, y)
Put the driver/input on x (e.g., volume, hours)
Put the response/output on y (e.g., cost, energy)
One dot per observation; do not connect dots by default
Add legend only when comparing multiple series
Aim for a chart readable by a non-specialist
content.notes:
A scatter plot is appropriate when both variables are numeric and you want to see a relationship (trend, curvature, clusters, outliers). Operational datasets often include time, volume, labour hours, machine utilisation, costs, defects, or throughput.

Why not a line chart? Excel line charts typically treat x-values as categories, which can distort spacing and therefore the perceived relationship. In contrast, an XY scatter plot uses a true numeric x-axis.

Mini-example: If x is “shift length (hours)” and y is “units produced”, a scatter plot can show diminishing returns at longer shifts.

Probing questions: What is your explanatory variable (what drives change)? What would an outlier mean operationally: a data error, or an unusual event worth investigating?

slides.title: Axes, units and scaling choices

content.title: Axes, units and scaling choices
content: Label both axes with variable name and unit
Choose scales that show the pattern without exaggeration
Use sensible tick marks; avoid cramped labels
Start at zero when it aids interpretation (often for costs)
Avoid 3D effects and unnecessary gridlines
Check that units match the CSV (e.g., £, k£, minutes)
content.notes:
Axis labelling and scaling are where many otherwise-correct analyses fail. Always include units: “Cost (£)” is not the same as “Cost (k£)”. If the dataset is in thousands, say so explicitly.

Starting at zero: for many operational quantities (cost, volume), a zero baseline prevents misleading visual comparisons. However, if you are investigating small variations around a large baseline (e.g., temperature), a non-zero start may be justified—if you explain it.

Common misconception: “If the trendline is correct, labels do not matter.” In real decision-making, labels and units are part of correctness.

Probing questions: Could someone read your chart without the dataset? If you changed £ to k£, what would happen to your gradient’s units and interpretation?

slides.title: Linear fit: gradient and intercept meaning

content.title: Linear fit: gradient and intercept meaning
content: Linear model: y = mx + c
Gradient m: change in y per 1 unit increase in x
Intercept c: estimated y at x = 0 (may be extrapolated)
State units: m is (y-unit per x-unit); c is (y-unit)
Report to 2–3 significant figures with rounding noted
Check if linearity is reasonable before relying on m, c
content.notes:
A fitted line summarises the average relationship between x and y. Interpreting m and c correctly is essential.

Example interpretation: If y is “Total cost (£)” and x is “Units produced”, then m is an estimated variable cost per unit (e.g., £/unit). c is an estimated fixed cost (e.g., £) if a fixed-cost interpretation is sensible.

Caution: c is not automatically “fixed cost”. If x=0 is outside the observed range, then c is extrapolated and may not be operationally meaningful. You can still report it, but you should comment on this limitation.

Probing questions: What is one operational reason your relationship might not be linear (capacity limits, overtime premiums, bulk discounts)? If the points curve, what would a linear fit do to your decision?

slides.title: Fitting a line: Excel vs Python workflow

content.title: Fitting a line: Excel vs Python workflow
leftColumn: Import CSV → select x,y → Insert → Scatter (markers)
Add axis titles/units; format scales for readability
Add Trendline (Linear) and show equation and R²
Use LINEST to capture m and c in cells for reporting
rightColumn: Read CSV in pandas; check types and missing values
Plot scatter in matplotlib with labels, units and title
Fit with polyfit or LinearRegression; extract m and c
Plot fitted line; compute and report break-even point
content.notes:
Choose the tool that best fits your context. Excel is fast for small datasets and reporting; Python scales better, is reproducible, and reduces manual transcription errors.

Excel detail: Trendline gives a displayed equation, but you should still extract m and c via LINEST (or SLOPE and INTERCEPT) so your report is traceable and less error-prone than copying text from the chart.

Python detail: a typical workflow is pandas for data handling, matplotlib for plotting, and either numpy.polyfit(x, y, 1) or sklearn LinearRegression for fitting.

Probing questions: Which approach better supports auditability in your workplace? If someone changed the CSV, how easily could you regenerate the chart and results?

slides.title: Worked example data: volume vs total cost

content.title: Worked example data: volume vs total cost
content: Goal: plot total cost (£) against production volume (units)
Then fit a linear cost function from the plotted data
content.notes:
Treat this as if it arrived as a CSV export from an operations system. Before plotting, do a quick sense-check: costs rise with volume, and the increments are roughly similar—suggesting a near-linear relationship with some noise.

If you are using Excel: enter the two columns, ensure they are numeric, and avoid storing numbers as text (look for left-alignment and green triangles).

If you are using Python: load into a DataFrame, confirm dtype is numeric, and check for missing values.

Probing questions: What would you do if one cost value decreased when volume increased? Would you remove it, correct it, or keep it and explain it?

slides.title: Worked example: create the scatter plot

content.title: Worked example: create the scatter plot
content: Insert → Scatter (only markers), not a line chart
Title: "Total cost vs production volume"
Axis titles: Volume (units); Total cost (£)
Format axes: sensible min/max; clear tick spacing
Use consistent number formats (e.g., £0, no mixed decimals)
Keep design simple; avoid clutter
content.notes:
In Excel, highlight both columns, then Insert → Scatter → markers only. If your chart shows evenly spaced categories rather than numeric spacing, you have likely created the wrong chart type.

Formatting guidance: choose axis limits that include all points with a small margin. For this example, x might run 0–550 and y might run 0–3500. Use a currency format for the y-axis.

In Python, the equivalent is: plt.scatter(volume, cost); plt.xlabel('Volume (units)'); plt.ylabel('Total cost (£)'); plt.title('Total cost vs production volume').

Probing questions: If you showed this chart to a manager with no maths background, what would they immediately conclude? Is that conclusion warranted from the data?

slides.title: Worked example: fit line and extract m and c

content.title: Worked example: fit line and extract m and c
content: Add linear trendline; display equation on the chart
Or use LINEST to compute m and c from the data table
Example fit: y = 4.50x + 1.00×10^3
Gradient m = £4.50 per unit; intercept c = £1000
Round to 2–3 s.f.; keep units attached to values
Check fit quality (R²) and any visible curvature
content.notes:
Trendline equation is a convenient summary, but treat it as a starting point, not the final evidence. Use LINEST in Excel to retrieve the gradient and intercept directly from the data; this reduces the risk of copying the wrong equation.

Explain units explicitly. Here, m has units £/unit because y is £ and x is units. This is not optional: without units, the gradient cannot be interpreted operationally.

In Python, fitting could be:
- m, c = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
Then report m and c with appropriate rounding.

Misconception to address: a high R² does not prove causation; it only indicates the line explains variation in y within this dataset.

Probing questions: If you doubled the x-unit (e.g., from units to hundreds of units), how would m and c change numerically and in units?

slides.title: Break-even point from fitted cost function

content.title: Break-even point from fitted cost function
content: Assume selling price p = £6.00 per unit
Revenue R(x) = px; Cost C(x) = 4.50x + 1000
Solve R(x) = C(x) to find break-even x
Break-even x = 667 units; break-even y = £4000
State assumptions and rounding decisions explicitly
Note if break-even uses extrapolation beyond observed x
content.notes:
Break-even is where profit is zero, i.e., revenue equals cost. Using the fitted cost line turns noisy data into a usable decision rule.

Work it through carefully:
6x = 4.50x + 1000
1.50x = 1000
x = 666.666… units
Then y = 6x = £4000 (exactly, given the chosen numbers). In a report, keep the unrounded value for calculations and round at the end. State your rounding rule (e.g., “rounded to the nearest unit”).

Assumptions matter: constant selling price, constant variable cost per unit, and the relationship remains linear near the break-even point. If your dataset only covers 100–500 units, x=667 is an extrapolation; you must flag this and treat the result as less certain.

Probing questions: What operational factors might change the variable cost beyond 500 units (overtime, second shift, maintenance)? How would that affect the credibility of this break-even?

slides.title: Quality checks: avoid common errors

content.title: Quality checks: avoid common errors
content: Use XY scatter; do not treat numeric x as categories
Verify axis labels and units against the CSV header
Check scale choices do not distort the message
Spot-check 2–3 plotted points against the dataset
Re-type equation carefully; confirm sign and decimals
Sense-check m and c against operational reality
content.notes:
Adopt an error-checking routine as part of your method. Many “incorrect” submissions are correct mathematically but have basic presentation or transcription errors.

Practical checks:
- Pick two data rows (e.g., x=200, y=1900) and confirm the dot appears in the right place.
- If your gradient suggests £45 per unit instead of £4.5, check whether your y-axis is in £ or k£.
- If the intercept is negative for a cost model, ask whether that is plausible or whether the linear model is being forced beyond its valid range.

Misconception: “Excel will choose the right settings.” Excel optimises for general use, not for statistical integrity or operational clarity.

Probing questions: If you handed your chart to a colleague, what is the single most likely misunderstanding they could have? How could you prevent it with a small change?

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
leftColumn: Import a CSV with 10–30 rows of operational data
Create a scatter plot with labels, units, and title
Fit a linear model; report m and c to 2–3 s.f.
Compute a break-even point for a chosen price/target
rightColumn: Does the trend look roughly linear in your x-range?
Are all units consistent across data, plot, and model?
Did you justify rounding and assumptions in words?
Could a non-specialist act on your chart confidently?
content.notes:
Choose a dataset where a linear relationship is at least plausible: examples include cost vs volume, energy vs machine hours, output vs labour hours (within a limited range), or delivery time vs distance.

When you compute a break-even, define your pricing or revenue rule clearly. If price depends on volume (discounting), then a simple linear break-even may be inappropriate—flag this and either restrict the range or explain why a different model is needed.

Write 2–3 sentences of interpretation, not just numbers. For instance: “Variable cost is approximately £m per unit over 100–500 units. At £p selling price, break-even occurs at x units; this is an extrapolation and should be validated with additional data.”

Probing questions: What would you need to collect to reduce uncertainty—more x-range, better measurement, or different variables?

slides.title: Assessment connection and pitfalls to avoid

content.title: Assessment connection and pitfalls to avoid
content: Supports MOD102 assignment: data plot + fitted function + decision
Prioritise clarity: labels, units, scales, and short interpretation
Show working: Excel cells/LINEST or Python code and outputs
Report m, c, and break-even with units and s.f. stated
Avoid mixing units (e.g., hours vs minutes) across calculations
Avoid uncritical extrapolation; always comment on data range
content.notes:
Your assessed work is judged on both correctness and communication. A technically correct model with missing units or unclear axes is not fit for operational decision-making.

Evidence expectations: include either a screenshot of the Excel chart plus the LINEST results, or a reproducible Python snippet that loads data, fits the model, and generates the chart. Add a brief narrative explaining what the gradient and intercept mean in context.

Common pitfalls:
- Copying the displayed trendline equation and then using different rounded values in calculations without stating it.
- Failing to specify whether costs are in £ or k£.
- Presenting a break-even outside the data range with no caution.

Probing questions: If a marker asked “How do you know you used the right chart type and the right units?”, what would you point to in your submission?

content.title: MOD102 Functions and graphs: Lesson 5
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD102 — Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making
Lesson 5: Interpret linear, quadratic and exponential functions
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome to Lesson 5. The focus is on applying function models to operational data: recognising whether a relationship is best described as linear, quadratic or exponential, interpreting what the parameters mean in context, and presenting a fitted graph clearly and responsibly.

As you work, keep returning to a practical question: “If I show this to a non-specialist manager, will they understand what changes, by how much, and under what assumptions?” A common misconception is that the ‘best’ model is the one with the highest R²; in operational settings, interpretability, correct units, and plausible behaviour over the relevant domain are equally important.

slides.title: Learning objectives

content.title: Learning objectives
content: Classify linear/quadratic/exponential from graph or data
Justify choice using 2 observable features
Interpret inputs/outputs and parameters with units
Create a labelled plot with fitted model in Excel or Python
Do diligence checks and report a recommendation + limitation
content.notes:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to do five things reliably.

First, classification: given a graph or a short dataset, decide whether linear, quadratic or exponential is most appropriate.

Second, justification: you must be able to point to at least two visible/compute-able features—such as constant first differences (linear), a turning point or constant second differences (quadratic), or a constant ratio / multiplicative change (exponential).

Third, interpretation: you will explain what the input and output represent, and what key parameters mean in context, including units. This is where many technical answers fail: learners can fit an equation but cannot explain what ‘0.08 per week’ means.

Fourth, communication through plotting: a clear plot with correct axis labels, units, sensible scaling, and a fitted model.

Fifth, diligence: before you report, you will check units, scale, domain assumptions, and parameter reasonableness, then produce a brief quality-check note. Ask yourself: “What could a stakeholder misunderstand if they only look at the chart?”

content: Read the model cues, then study the three worked examples

Pause to predict the model type before seeing the answer
Write 3–5 sentences interpreting parameters in a scenario
Complete the practice prompts and self-check your reasoning
content.notes:
Approach this lesson as a cycle: predict → test → explain → check.

When you see a dataset, make an initial prediction (linear/quadratic/exponential) before you compute anything. Then verify using differences or ratios.

When you create a plot, do not treat it as decoration; it is evidence. The learning goal is that a plot plus a short explanation is enough for an operational decision conversation.

A useful habit: after fitting a model, always write a 3–5 sentence narrative that includes (1) what changes with what, (2) the rate/growth factor with units, (3) what the intercept or baseline means, and (4) one limitation about domain or assumptions.

slides.title: Model families in operational data

content.title: Model families in operational data
content.content: Operational relationships often follow additive change (linear), curved change with a turning point (quadratic), or multiplicative change (exponential). The model choice affects forecasts, thresholds, and how you communicate risk and uncertainty.
content.notes:
In operations, model choice is not only a maths decision; it influences what actions you take.

Linear models imply a constant absolute change: ‘each extra unit of input adds the same amount of output’. This is common for costs proportional to activity, or time increasing steadily with quantity.

Quadratic models capture curvature and can include a turning point: performance may improve up to a point then worsen (or the reverse). This can represent an optimal setting (maximum profit, minimum waste) within a usable range.

Exponential models represent multiplicative change: ‘each period multiplies by a constant factor’. This is typical for compound growth (demand growth) or decay (reliability loss, depreciation, contamination reduction).

Probing question: if you extended the relationship slightly beyond the data, would your chosen model still behave plausibly? A common misconception is that any curve can be “made to fit” and therefore is acceptable; in operations, implausible extrapolation can be costly.

slides.title: Classifying by observable features

content.title: Classifying by observable features
content: Use two cues: one from the graph and one from the numbers
content.notes:
This table is your fast classification toolkit. The aim is to justify your choice using observable evidence.

Graph cue: linear looks straight; quadratic bends and may have a clear minimum/maximum; exponential either accelerates upward (growth) or drops quickly then levels (decay).

Numeric cue: with equally spaced x-values, linear relationships show constant first differences in y. Quadratics show roughly constant second differences (differences of differences). Exponentials show an approximately constant ratio between successive y-values (or a constant percentage change).

Important: real workplace data is noisy. You are rarely looking for perfect equality; you are looking for a stable pattern.

Probing questions:
- Are x-values equally spaced? If not, differences need adjusting (rate per unit x).
- Are you mixing units (e.g., minutes and hours) causing ‘false’ non-constant differences?

Common misconception: learners sometimes use ‘curved’ to mean exponential automatically. Quadratic and exponential are both curved; you need the right cue (turning point or ratios).

slides.title: Interpreting parameters and units

content.title: Interpreting parameters and units
content: Always interpret parameters in words and confirm the units

rows: rate of change per 1 unit x

content.notes:
Interpretation is where ‘apply’ level work shows: you connect symbols to operations.

Linear: m is a rate. If y is cost (£) and x is hours, m is £/hour. A frequent error is describing the slope as “£” rather than “£ per hour”. c is the predicted y when x = 0; sometimes this is a fixed cost, but sometimes x = 0 is outside the meaningful domain (for example, a queue length cannot be negative).

Quadratic: rather than memorising all coefficient meanings, focus on operationally meaningful features: curvature direction (sign of a), and the turning point (vertex). The vertex is often the ‘optimal’ setting (minimum cost, maximum output), but only if it lies within the realistic domain.

Exponential: b is the multiplier for each 1-unit increase in x. If b = 1.05, that is 5% growth per unit x. If b = 0.92, that is 8% decay per unit x. b is unitless; the unit sits in the definition of ‘per unit x’ (per day, per month, per cycle).

Probing question: if you change x by 2 units, how does the interpretation change? Linear doubles the change; exponential squares the multiplier (b²).

slides.title: Plot–fit–explain: a repeatable workflow

content.title: Plot–fit–explain: a repeatable workflow
content: 1) Define x and y with units and a realistic domain
2) Make a scatter plot; avoid joining points by default
3) Inspect cues: differences, turning point, ratios
4) Fit a model (trendline/regression) and record equation
5) Label axes, units, scale, and add a descriptive title
6) Run checks and write a short quality-check note
content.notes:
This workflow is designed to prevent two common failures: (1) a correct equation presented badly, and (2) a neat graph built on incorrect assumptions.

Step 1: define x and y. Be explicit: “x = months since installation (months)”, “y = % machines functioning (%)”. Decide the domain: are negative x-values possible? Is extrapolating beyond 12 months reasonable?

Step 2: scatter plots are standard for observed paired data. Line charts that connect points can imply continuity or time-series structure that may not exist.

Step 3: classification cues help you choose a sensible model family before fitting.

Step 4: fitting: in Excel, you can add a trendline and display the equation (and R²). In Python, you might use numpy/polyfit for linear/quadratic, or log-transform/curve fitting for exponential. Emphasise: the method is less important than interpreting outputs correctly.

Step 5: labelling is not optional. A plot without units cannot be audited. A poor axis scale can exaggerate or hide changes.

Step 6: quality checks: treat them as part of professional practice. Ask: “If someone acted on this, what could go wrong if I made a mistake?”

slides.title: From fitted graph to decision message

content.title: From fitted graph to decision message
content: State what changes, by how much, and over what range
Quantify a forecast with units and a time/input horizon
Identify a key feature: rate, turning point, or factor
Give one recommendation linked to the evidence
State one limitation or assumption (domain, noise, causality)
Avoid claiming precision beyond the data quality
content.notes:
Operational stakeholders usually need: (1) the direction and size of the effect, (2) what happens if we change an input, and (3) what we should do next.

Your message should explicitly connect the fitted model to a decision. Examples:
- Linear: “Each extra operator-hour adds about 12 units of output, up to 80 hours/week.”
- Quadratic: “Profit peaks at about £12 per item; prices above that reduce volume enough to lower profit.”
- Exponential: “Stock shrinks by about 8% per month; after 6 months we expect ~60% remaining.”

Limitations matter. Common ones:
- Domain: the model only applies within observed x-range.
- Assumptions: constant conditions (no new process, no seasonality).
- Data quality: measurement error, small sample.
- Causality: correlation does not prove the input causes the output.

Probing question: if a manager asked “how sure are we?”, what would you point to—data spread, residuals, and whether the model form makes operational sense.

slides.title: Worked example: linear labour cost vs hours

content.title: Worked example: linear labour cost vs hours
content: Cues: constant difference; interpret slope as £ per hour
content.notes:
Step 1: Check the pattern. Hours increase by 10 each time; cost increases by 160 each time. Constant first difference strongly suggests a linear relationship.

Step 2: Compute slope. Slope m = change in cost / change in hours = 160 / 10 = 16 (£ per hour).

Step 3: Find intercept. Use one point, e.g., (10, 260): 260 = 16(10) + c → c = 100. So the model is y = 16x + 100.

Step 4: Interpret in context. The slope 16 £/h is the variable labour cost rate. The intercept £100 is the baseline cost when hours are zero—often a fixed call-out cost, setup cost, or minimum shift cost.

Step 5: Sense-check. Does “0 hours costs £100” make operational sense? Sometimes yes (fixed charge), sometimes no (data may not include low-hour cases). If it does not make sense, you still may keep the model for x within the observed range and explain the limitation.

Common misconception: treating the intercept as always ‘fixed cost’. It is only meaningful if x = 0 is meaningful and within scope.

slides.title: Worked example: quadratic profit vs price

content.title: Worked example: quadratic profit vs price
content: Cues: turning point; rising then falling output indicates a vertex
content.notes:
Step 1: Look for a turning point. Profit rises from £8 to £12, then falls from £12 to £16. This ‘up then down’ pattern suggests a quadratic with a maximum.

Step 2: Interpret the vertex. The best observed point is around price £12 with profit about £11.4k/day. In a fitted quadratic, the vertex gives the estimated best price (within the data range).

Step 3: What does curvature mean operationally? At low prices, margin is low; as price increases, margin improves faster than demand drops—up to a point. Beyond the vertex, demand reduction dominates and profit declines.

Step 4: Caution on causality. The data shows association; other factors (competitor pricing, seasonality) may also affect profit. Your recommendation should acknowledge this.

Step 5: Recommendation + limitation example: “Set price near £12 short-term, but validate with more days and segment by weekday.”

Common misconception: assuming the vertex is a ‘true’ optimum. In practice it is an estimate conditional on stable conditions and adequate data coverage near the peak.

slides.title: Worked example: exponential decay in usable stock

content.title: Worked example: exponential decay in usable stock
content: Cues: near-constant ratio; interpret factor as % loss per month
content.notes:
Step 1: Check ratios (multiplicative change). 920/1000 = 0.92; 846/920 ≈ 0.92; 778/846 ≈ 0.92. A roughly constant ratio suggests exponential decay.

Step 2: Write a model. Using A = 1000 at month 0 and b ≈ 0.92 per month: y = 1000·(0.92)^x.

Step 3: Interpret the factor. b = 0.92 means each month we retain about 92% of usable stock, i.e., around 8% becomes unusable per month (shrinkage, spoilage, damage).

Step 4: Forecast carefully. For month 6: y = 1000·(0.92)^6 ≈ 606 units. Emphasise this is conditional on the decay rate staying similar.

Step 5: Misconception to address. Learners often say “it drops by 80 units each month” by looking at early differences (1000 to 920). In exponential decay, the absolute drop shrinks over time even if the percentage loss stays constant.

Probing question: if the process improved so b became 0.96, what would that mean operationally, and how quickly would benefits accumulate?

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
content: For 3 datasets, classify model and cite two observable cues
Write a 3–5 sentence interpretation including units
Create one Excel/Python plot with fitted model and labels
Do 3 checks: units, scale, domain, parameter reasonableness
State one recommendation and one limitation for a stakeholder
content.notes:
Use these prompts to consolidate skill, not to memorise rules.

1) Classification practice: for each dataset, explicitly write two cues. Example structure: “I choose exponential because ratios are stable and the curve steepens/levels.”

2) Interpretation practice: include units in every parameter description. If you cannot attach a unit, pause and ask what the variable actually measures.

3) Plotting practice checklist (aim for 4/5):
- Scatter plot appropriate for paired observations
- Axes labelled with variable names and units
- Appropriate scale (not misleading; readable)
- Descriptive title and legend (if multiple series)
- Equation shown or reported, with parameters clearly identified

4) Diligence checks: choose at least three and document them as a short quality-check note. Examples:
- Units: are x and y consistent (hours vs minutes)?
- Scale: does the axis start at zero, and if not, is that justified?
- Domain: did you avoid extrapolating beyond observed data without warning?
- Parameters: do signs and magnitudes make sense (e.g., negative costs)?

Reflection question: what would you change in your explanation so a non-specialist would not misread the intercept or overtrust the forecast?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports: operational modelling mini-report (graph + narrative)
Pitfall: choosing model by R² only, ignoring operational logic
Pitfall: missing units on slope/factor or misreading intercept
Pitfall: extrapolating beyond the data without warning
Pitfall: unclear plots (no labels, poor scale, no context)
content.notes:
This lesson directly supports typical module assessment tasks where you submit a fitted graph and a short interpretation aimed at operational decision-making.

Markers usually reward: (1) justified model choice, (2) correct parameter interpretation with units, (3) clear and auditable presentation, and (4) evidence-based recommendation plus a transparent limitation.

Common pitfalls to avoid:
- R² as the only criterion: a slightly lower R² model may be more plausible and safer to use.
- Intercept errors: interpreting c as a real baseline when x = 0 is outside the domain.
- Unit drift: mixing days and weeks, or using percentages inconsistently (0.08 vs 8%).
- Extrapolation: making confident statements beyond observed conditions.
- Presentation gaps: no axis labels, missing units, or truncated axes that distort perception.

Probing question: if a colleague had to audit your work next month, could they reproduce your model and understand your assumptions from the chart and notes alone?

slides.title: Key takeaways

content.title: Key takeaways
content: Linear: constant difference; slope is a rate with units
Quadratic: curvature with a turning point (vertex) in-range
Exponential: constant ratio; factor is % change per x-unit
Plot clearly, fit appropriately, and explain in plain language
Run diligence checks and state one limitation with any forecast
content.notes:
Keep these takeaways as a mental checklist.

When classifying, always use at least two cues—ideally one from the graph shape and one from differences/ratios.

When interpreting, treat units as your error-detection system: if the units do not make sense, your model or your variable definitions are likely wrong.

When communicating, your goal is not to impress with algebra; it is to support a decision with transparent evidence, clear labelling, and honest limitations.

Self-question: if you removed the equation from your graph, could your written explanation still convey the key operational insight? If not, strengthen your narrative.

Maths Certification

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Create clear scatter plots with labels, units, scale and title
Fit a linear model and display the equation on the plot
Interpret slope and intercept in operational terms with units
Find and verify a break-even point from a graph or equation
Use: watch/learn → replicate steps → practise → self-check
content.notes:
Explain that the lesson is structured as a workflow: (1) plot raw data correctly, (2) fit a simple model, (3) interpret what the model means operationally, (4) use the model to answer a break-even question.

Clarify what “clear” means: someone outside your discipline can read the chart without asking what x and y represent. Probe: “If I removed your spoken explanation, would your plot still make sense?”

Common misconception to pre-empt: thinking the graph is ‘finished’ once points appear. In operational work, the communication quality (labels/units/scales/title) is part of correctness.

slides.title: Operational datasets: choosing x and y

content.title: Operational datasets: choosing x and y
content: x: driver (e.g., units, hours, distance, throughput)
y: response (e.g., cost, energy, defects, time)
Each point is one observation (same conditions if possible)
Check units and time period consistency before plotting
Look for range, outliers, and missing values
content.notes:
Develop the idea of operational causality/logic: we usually place the controllable or explanatory variable on x (inputs), and the outcome on y (outputs). Give a mini-example: x = machine hours per day; y = daily electricity cost.

Stress comparability: a scatter plot assumes each point is a comparable observation. Ask: “Are these all the same product mix? Same shift pattern? Same tariff?” If not, the relationship may look weaker because multiple processes are mixed.

Common misconceptions: (1) swapping x and y because it ‘looks nicer’; (2) mixing units (minutes and hours) in one column; (3) plotting totals for different time windows (weekly vs monthly) without normalising.

slides.title: Create a scatter plot: Excel vs Python

content.title: Create a scatter plot: Excel vs Python
leftColumn: Excel: insert → Scatter (markers only)
Select x and y columns explicitly
Add axis titles and chart title
Format axes: min/max, units, decimals
rightColumn: Python: use pandas to load and inspect data
Use matplotlib/seaborn scatterplot
Set labels: variable name + unit
Set limits/ticks for readable scale
content.notes:
Narrate that the plotting principles are identical regardless of tool: show points, label axes with names and units, choose an appropriate scale, and write a descriptive title.

Excel guidance: emphasise choosing ‘Scatter’ not ‘Line’. Learners often pick a line chart, which implies equal spacing and an ordered sequence; scatter is correct for paired measurements.

Python guidance (optional detail for learners who choose Python): typical workflow is pandas read_csv, then plt.scatter(x, y). Mention that seaborn can automatically style and handle data frames.

Probing question: “What would go wrong if we used a line chart and the x-values are not evenly spaced?”

Python guidance (optional detail for learners who choose Python): typical workflow is pandas read_csv, then plt.scatter(x, y). Mention that seaborn can automatically style and handle data frames.

Probing question: “What would go wrong if we used a line chart and the x-values are not evenly spaced?”

slides.title: Chart quality: labels, scales, and titles

content.title: Chart quality: labels, scales, and titles
content: Axis label format: Name (unit), e.g., Output (units/day)
Use sensible axis limits; avoid misleading truncation
Keep decimals meaningful; avoid over-precision
Title should state relationship and context
Add legend only if there are multiple series
content.notes:
Explain that in operational decision-making, charts are evidence. Poor labelling or misleading scales can lead to poor decisions.

Discuss truncation: starting y-axis at a non-zero value can exaggerate changes. This is sometimes acceptable, but should be justified and clearly indicated. Ask: “Does the chosen y-axis start change the impression of variability?”

Decimals: if costs are to the nearest pound, don’t show four decimal places; it implies false accuracy.

Title guidance: include what, where, and when if relevant (e.g., “Total cost vs output, Line A, Jan–Mar”). Common misconception: titles like “Graph 1” communicate nothing.

slides.title: Linear model and parameter meaning

content.title: Linear model and parameter meaning

rows: Predict y given x within observed range
How much variation the line explains

content.notes:
Talk through the line y = mx + b as a compact operational story.

Slope (m): emphasise units. If y is £ and x is units produced, m is £/unit, interpretable as marginal cost. Invite learners to say the slope as a sentence: “For each additional unit, cost increases by about £m.”

Intercept (b): interpret as the model’s predicted cost at zero output—often a proxy for fixed cost. Caution: x = 0 may be outside the data and not physically meaningful (e.g., a machine cannot run at zero output if it still uses standby power). This is a key misconception: learners treat b as ‘true fixed cost’ without checking context.

R²: position as a diagnostic, not a grade. A high R² does not prove causation; a low R² may still be useful if the purpose is rough planning.

slides.title: Break-even from a fitted model

content.title: Break-even from a fitted model
content: Define the net measure: profit, contribution, or net output
Set net = 0 and solve for the unknown (often x)
Check result is within a realistic operating range
Verify by substitution back into the equation
State the answer with units and sensible rounding
content.notes:
Explain break-even as “the point where gains and costs balance”. In operations, it might be profit = 0, or net output = 0 (e.g., output minus demand gap).

Model-based method: if Profit(x) = Revenue(x) − Cost(x), set Profit(x) = 0 and solve. Reinforce that this is an algebraic use of the fitted function.

Verification: show learners how to avoid algebra slips—substitute the x value back in and confirm that net is approximately zero, noting rounding.

Probing questions: “Does your break-even x fall below your minimum feasible production run?” and “If you round x to a whole unit, does profit become slightly positive or negative?”

Probing question: “If the pattern were not linear (e.g., costs rose faster at high output), what operational reasons might explain that (overtime, maintenance, scrap)?”

slides.title: Worked example: fit and show the trendline

content.title: Worked example: fit and show the trendline
content: Plot x vs y as a scatter chart (markers only)
Add linear trendline; tick 'Display Equation'
Optional: tick 'Display R-squared value'
Check equation form y = mx + b matches axes units
Do not force intercept to zero unless justified
content.notes:
Walk through Excel steps in more detail:
- Select the two columns (ensure x is first, y is second).
- Insert → Scatter → “Scatter with only Markers”.
- Right-click a data point → Add Trendline → Linear.
- Tick “Display Equation on chart” and optionally “Display R-squared value”.

If using Python, narrate an equivalent approach: fit a line (e.g., numpy.polyfit or sklearn LinearRegression) and then annotate the plot with the equation.

Key misconception: forcing intercept = 0 because it ‘seems logical’. Explain that this can distort slope and worsen predictions unless you have a strong physical/operational reason and data near zero to support it.

slides.title: Worked example: interpret slope and intercept

content.title: Worked example: interpret slope and intercept
content: From the pattern, m ≈ 12 £/unit (variable cost)
Intercept b ≈ 5000 £ (baseline/fixed cost estimate)
Interpretation: Cost(£) ≈ 12×Output + 5000
State meaning in a sentence, not just the equation
Use model for interpolation; be cautious with extrapolation
content.notes:
Use the dataset to justify the fitted parameters: each +100 units adds about +£1200, so slope is about £12 per unit. Then infer intercept: at x = 100, y ≈ 6200, so b ≈ 6200 − 12×100 = 5000.

Model sentence: “Each additional unit increases total cost by around £12, and there is an estimated £5000 baseline cost even at zero output.”

Units emphasis: m is £/unit; b is £. Ask: “If your slope came out in units of ‘£’, what does that tell you about your axis set-up?”

Extrapolation caution: explain why predicting at x = 2000 units might be risky (capacity limits, step-costs, different suppliers).

slides.title: Worked example: compute break-even output

content.title: Worked example: compute break-even output
content: Assume revenue = 18 £/unit; Cost = 12x + 5000 (£)
Set Profit = 0: 6x − 5000 = 0 → x = 833.33 units
Check: Profit(833.33) ≈ 0 (£), rounding may shift sign
Report: break-even ≈ 834 units (nearest whole unit)
content.notes:
Talk through each transformation slowly to model good algebraic hygiene.

Explain why we define profit as revenue minus cost, then substitute the fitted cost function. Highlight that profit inherits units of pounds, so setting profit = 0 means “no profit or loss”.

Verification: substitute x = 833.33 into Profit(x) = 6x − 5000 to show it returns 0 (within rounding). Then discuss rounding: in real operations you can’t produce 0.33 of a unit, so 833 units might yield a small loss and 834 a small profit. Invite learners to check: Profit(833) and Profit(834).

Common misconception: solving for the x-intercept of the cost line (where cost=0) instead of the profit line (where profit=0). Ask: “Which function’s zero actually represents break-even?”

content.title: Practice and reflection
content: Create your own scatter plot from a dataset you have access to
Label axes with names + units; choose sensible scale and title
Fit a linear trendline; record m and b with units
Write one operational sentence for m and one for b
Set up a break-even equation and verify by substitution
content.notes:

- Are the units consistent throughout?
- Does the intercept make operational sense or indicate missing variables?

If learners struggle, suggest they start by computing two-point slopes manually to estimate the gradient before relying on a trendline.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD102 assignment: modelling an operational dataset
Common error: using a line chart instead of a scatter plot
Common error: missing units in labels and equation interpretation
Common error: forcing intercept or over-trusting R²
Common error: break-even from cost=0, not profit=0
content.notes:
Explain how this lesson feeds into typical assessment tasks: producing a professional plot, fitting a model, interpreting parameters with units, and answering a decision question (often break-even).

Expand each mistake with consequences:
- Line chart: implies order and equal x-spacing; can mislead.
- Missing units: makes slope/intercept meaningless; markers lose operational value.
- Forcing intercept: can bias slope; might ‘look right’ but be wrong.
- Over-trusting R²: a high value doesn’t validate assumptions; check residual patterns and context.
- Break-even confusion: break-even concerns net (profit/contribution), not raw cost.

Probing question: “If you presented this to a manager, what single question would they ask first—and does your chart already answer it?”

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: A good scatter plot communicates variables, units, and context
A fitted line gives a usable model: y = mx + b
Slope and intercept must be interpreted with correct units
Break-even comes from net = 0 and must be verified

slides.title: MOD102 Lesson 7: Interpreting function models

content.title: MOD102 Lesson 7: Interpreting function models
content: Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD102 — Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making
Lesson 7: Interpret linear, quadratic and exponential functions
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners and set expectations for an applied session: the goal is not to memorise formulas, but to choose an appropriate model for an operational relationship, interpret what the parameters mean, and communicate results clearly in a chart.

Frame the lesson around workplace decision-making: managers rarely ask for “a quadratic”; they ask “what happens to output if we add two more staff?” or “when does profit peak?”. Emphasise that the same dataset can be plotted well or poorly, and that chart quality directly affects decision quality.

Probing questions:
- When you see a graph in a report, what makes you trust it?
- What is the cost of choosing the wrong model type in operations?

Common misconception to flag early: “If the points look roughly like a line, it must be linear.” Stress that exponential growth can look linear over short ranges, and that checking residuals and context matters.

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
leftColumn: Select model type for a scenario; justify with 2 cues
Explain parameters with units: slope/intercept, vertex, growth
Plot data + fitted model in Excel/Python with labels + caption
Run 3+ chart quality checks and record what you verified
rightColumn: Study: read slides, then replay key parts slowly
Do: recreate the worked example in Excel or Python
Check: compare your chart to the quality checklist
Reflect: what decision could this model support?
content.notes:
Talk learners through how to use the lesson in a self-study mode: (1) understand model cues, (2) practise interpreting parameters with units, (3) produce one clean chart with evidence of checks.

Clarify what “justify with two cues” means. For example, saying “it looks curved” is vague; better cues are “there is a turning point” (quadratic) or “each week is about a constant percentage change” (exponential).

Emphasise units: in operational contexts, unit mistakes are among the most common and costly errors. Slope is not “3.2”; it is “3.2 units per hour” (or similar).

Probing questions:
- What would count as strong evidence that the model choice is reasonable?
- Which is more important for stakeholders: perfect fit or clear interpretation?

Misconception to address: learners often treat plotting as cosmetic. Reframe plotting as a quality assurance step that can reveal data errors (swapped columns, outliers, wrong units).

slides.title: Choosing a model: quick diagnostic cues

content.title: Choosing a model: quick diagnostic cues

rows: Cost vs units at fixed unit cost
Profit vs price; defects vs speed

content.notes:
Explain that model selection is a modelling decision, not a pattern-matching game. Encourage learners to combine: (1) context knowledge (“is there a physical limit?”), (2) relationship features (constant rate vs turning point vs multiplicative change), and (3) evidence from a plot.

For linear: stress “additive” change—each +1 in x adds about the same amount to y.

For quadratic: highlight that the defining feature is the turning point; this often appears in optimisation problems (maximum profit, minimum cost).

For exponential: stress “multiplicative” change—each step multiplies y by about the same factor, so the absolute increases get bigger over time.

Probing questions:
- If you double x, do you expect y to double, or to change by a fixed amount?
- Is there a reason the relationship should peak or bottom out?

Common misconception: believing quadratic means “anything curved”. Point out that many curves are not quadratic; the turning-point structure is the key cue.

slides.title: Interpreting linear parameters in context

content.title: Interpreting linear parameters in context
content: Linear form: y = mx + c (m = constant rate of change)
Slope m = Δy/Δx; units are 'y-units per x-unit'
Intercept c = y when x = 0 (check if x=0 makes sense)
Sign of m shows increase (+) or decrease (−) as x grows
Use linear when rate is roughly constant over the x-range
content.notes:
Walk through meaning, then insist on units. If y is “units produced” and x is “hours”, then m is “units per hour”. If y is “£ cost” and x is “items”, m is “£ per item”. Learners often omit this, but it is what makes the model interpretable.

Discuss the intercept carefully: x=0 may be outside the operational range. Example: for “cost vs output”, x=0 can represent fixed cost (rent, setup). For “temperature vs time since switch-on”, x=0 is meaningful. For “profit vs price”, x=0 price is meaningless; intercept should not be over-interpreted.

Probing questions:
- If x increases by 10, what does the model predict happens to y?
- Is x=0 inside the data range? If not, should we interpret c?

Common misconceptions:
- Confusing slope with “steepness” only, not “rate with units”.
- Thinking a high R² guarantees a causal relationship. Emphasise: regression fits association, not causation.

slides.title: Interpreting quadratic parameters in context

content.title: Interpreting quadratic parameters in context
content: Quadratic form: y = a(x − h)^2 + k (vertex at (h, k))
Vertex gives turning point: maximum (a<0) or minimum (a>0)
a controls curvature: larger |a| = steeper rise/fall
Axis of symmetry: x = h; values mirror either side
Use quadratic for 'increase then decrease' or U-shaped patterns
content.notes:
Explain vertex form as the most interpretable for decision-making: (h, k) tells you the input level where performance is best or worst.

Operational examples:
- Profit vs price: there may be a price that maximises profit; set h as the best price.
- Defect rate vs machine speed: defects may be low at moderate speed but rise when too slow (idle issues) or too fast (quality loss).

Units matter: h has x-units (e.g., £, mph, hours), and k has y-units (e.g., £ profit, % defects). Parameter a has units of y per x², which learners often find unintuitive—frame it as “how quickly performance deteriorates as you move away from the optimum.”

Probing questions:
- What does being 1 unit away from h do compared with 2 units away?
- Is a maximum/minimum plausible in the real process, or is another model needed?

Common misconception: treating any U-shape as symmetric in reality. Real systems may be skewed; quadratic symmetry is an assumption to evaluate.

slides.title: Interpreting exponential parameters in context

content.title: Interpreting exponential parameters in context
content: Exponential form: y = a·b^x (or a·e^{kx})
a is value at x=0; units match y
b is factor per 1 x-unit; b=1.05 means +5% each step
k is continuous growth rate; % change ≈ 100·k per x-unit
Doubling/halving time depends on b or k, not current y
Use exponential for multiplicative change, not additive change
content.notes:
Make the contrast explicit: linear adds a constant amount; exponential multiplies by a constant factor. Provide a quick numeric mini-example:
- Linear: start 100, add 5 each week → 100, 105, 110, 115.
- Exponential: start 100, grow 5% each week → 100, 105, 110.25, 115.76.
Same first step, different long-term behaviour.

Explain b and k both describe growth, but in different time interpretations. If data are in weekly steps, b is intuitive (factor per week). If modelling continuous processes, k is useful.

Units: a has y-units, b is unitless, k has “per x-unit”. Learners often attach units to b incorrectly.

Probing questions:
- Are changes better described as “+10 per week” or “+10% per week”?
- Does the process have a saturation point (suggesting logistic rather than exponential)?

Common misconception: assuming exponential forever. Emphasise model validity is limited to the observed range and realistic constraints.

slides.title: From dataset to fitted model and chart

content.title: From dataset to fitted model and chart
content: Start with a tidy table: one row per observation, units included
Choose x (input) and y (output); do not swap cause and effect
Make a scatter plot of raw data before fitting any model
Fit model: Excel Trendline or regression in Python (e.g., numpy)
Check fit: residual pattern; curvature suggests wrong model type
Add labels, units, sensible scales, and a one-sentence caption
content.notes:
Give learners a repeatable workflow that they can apply to any operational dataset.

Excel guidance (talk-through):
- Put x in the first column and y in the second, include headers with units.
- Insert → Scatter (markers only).
- Add Trendline: Linear / Polynomial (order 2) / Exponential.
- Tick “Display Equation” and “Display R-squared”.

Python guidance (talk-through):
- Use pandas to load data; plot scatter with matplotlib.
- Linear/quadratic: numpy.polyfit(x, y, deg=1 or 2).
- Exponential: fit log(y) vs x if y>0, or use scipy curve_fit.

Explain residuals in plain language: residual = actual − predicted. If residuals are randomly scattered, the model structure may be reasonable; if they curve systematically, reconsider the model.

Probing questions:
- What is your x variable, and why does it make sense as the input?
- If you extrapolate, what operational constraint might break the pattern?

Excel guidance (talk-through):
- Put x in the first column and y in the second, include headers with units.

slides.title: Worked example: choose the model type

content.title: Worked example: choose the model type

rows: Similar units/hour; no turning point in range
Has a maximum; increases then decreases
Active users vs weeks after launch

content.notes:
Model choice is an argument. For each row, make the justification explicit and tied to features.

For labour hours vs units: ask learners to consider assumptions—constant staffing, constant process conditions, no bottlenecks. Discuss where linear may fail (fatigue, learning curve, machine capacity).

For profit vs price: explain why turning points arise: price affects demand; profit is revenue minus costs; the combination often yields a peak. Note that the exact form might be more complex, but quadratic is a useful local approximation around a peak.

For users vs weeks: stress that marketing-driven growth can be multiplicative early on. Also introduce a reality check: exponential growth is unlikely to continue indefinitely; saturation suggests alternative models later.

Probing questions:
- What measurement would help you confirm “constant % change”?
- Which variable is controllable (decision variable), and which is outcome?

Common misconception: “Quadratic means two variables multiply.” Clarify it is about squared dependence and turning-point behaviour, not multiplication of two different variables.

slides.title: Worked example dataset: time vs output

content.title: Worked example dataset: time vs output
content.notes:
Use this small operational dataset to practise the full cycle: plot raw data, fit a model, and interpret parameters.

Step-by-step guidance:
1) Start by plotting as a scatter plot (not a line chart). Ask: does the pattern look roughly straight, U-shaped, or accelerating?
2) Try a linear fit first because it is the simplest interpretable model. In Excel, add a linear trendline and display the equation.
3) Interpret parameters in context. If the fitted model is approximately y = mx + c:
- c (units) is baseline output at time 0 h (setup output/starting point).
- m (units per hour) is the production rate.
4) Reality check: Does the intercept make sense operationally? At 0 h, could there be 12 units already completed (e.g., carry-over or initial stock), or is this a data definition issue?

Probing questions:
- What does “time = 0” represent in your process?
- Would you expect output to be zero at time zero? Why/why not?

Common misconception: assuming time must start at zero for the model to be valid. It does not; the intercept is tied to the chosen zero point.

slides.title: Worked example: improve a chart before sharing

content.title: Worked example: improve a chart before sharing
leftColumn: Line chart implies continuity through missing times
Axes unlabeled; hours/units missing from titles
y-axis starts high, hiding early low output
Trendline shown but equation and R² missing
rightColumn: Use scatter for observations; add fitted line separately
Axis titles: Time (h) and Output (units)
Start y at 0 (or justify truncation clearly)
Show equation + R²; add a plain-language caption
content.notes:
Treat this slide as a before/after critique, because charting errors are common in operational reporting.

Explain why a line chart can mislead: it visually implies values exist between measured times and can hide that data were sampled irregularly.

Discuss axis truncation: sometimes it is defensible (to show small changes), but only if clearly signposted. In self-study materials, encourage learners to default to y=0 unless there is a strong reason not to.

Explain what R² is and is not: it summarises fit for that model form, but it does not prove the model is appropriate, and it does not guarantee good predictions outside the data range.

Model communication: an equation without units can still confuse non-specialists. Encourage adding one sentence: “Output increases by about m units per hour over 0–4 h.”

Probing questions:
- If a supervisor saw this chart, what might they misread?
- What single change would most improve trust in the chart?

Common misconception: believing that adding a trendline automatically makes a chart ‘analytical’. The analytical quality comes from correct choices and clear labelling.

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Pick a model for each scenario and list 2 supporting features
Interpret y=3.2x+15: meaning and units of 3.2 and 15
Interpret y=−0.5(x−4)^2+20: vertex and max/min meaning
Interpret y=120·1.08^t: meaning of 120 and 1.08
Create a plot: raw points + fitted model, with labels and units
Write a caption: what, source/timeframe, and key message
content.notes:
Encourage learners to write their answers as if explaining to a non-specialist colleague.

For the linear prompt, insist on units: if x is “hours”, then 3.2 is “units per hour”; 15 is “units at 0 hours”. Ask learners to state what evidence would make the intercept plausible.

For the quadratic prompt, have them explicitly state whether it is a maximum or minimum (because of the negative sign). Then connect it to a decision: “Best performance occurs when x=4 (units of x).”

For the exponential prompt, require a percent interpretation: 1.08 means “8% increase per time unit”. Ask what time unit t represents (days, weeks, months) and how that changes interpretation.

For the plotting prompt, reinforce: raw data must be visible, axes must have units, and the caption should communicate the implication, not just describe the picture.

Probing questions:
- Which interpretation would you trust more: with units or without?
- What would make you reject your fitted model even if R² is high?

Common misconception: writing captions that merely restate the title. A good caption states the main takeaway and any important caveat.

slides.title: Chart quality checks to document

content.title: Chart quality checks to document
content: Axis titles include quantity and unit; legend matches series
x-axis increases left→right; y-axis increases bottom→top
Scale choice does not distort change; avoid unnecessary 3D
No misleading truncation; if truncated, state it clearly
Data points visible; do not hide scatter with thick lines
Record checks: version, date, source, and model form used
content.notes:
Frame quality checks as part of professional practice: they protect you and your organisation from avoidable errors.

Expand each check with an example:
- Missing units: “Time” is ambiguous (minutes? hours? weeks?).
- Swapped axes: a very common spreadsheet error; the story can reverse.
- Distorting scales: a stretched y-axis can exaggerate changes; a compressed one can hide them.
- Truncation: can be acceptable for stable processes (e.g., temperature control), but must be transparent.
- Point visibility: if points are hidden, viewers cannot judge variability or outliers.

Documentation matters in operational settings: another analyst should be able to reproduce the chart. Encourage learners to keep a short “chart QA log” (even a few bullet notes) that states what they checked.

Probing questions:
- Which of these errors could change a decision?
- How would you explain your scale choice to an auditor or manager?

Common misconception: “My audience won’t notice.” Decision-makers may not notice, but they will still be influenced by misleading visuals.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD102 applied task: model an operational relationship
Marks reward: correct model choice, justified with evidence
Include units in parameter interpretations and axis labels
Report fit quality (R²/residuals) and note limitations
Common errors: forcing linear; mixing % change with absolute
Common chart errors: swapped axes, missing units, truncated y-axis
content.notes:
Position this lesson as directly supporting an applied modelling-and-communication task typical of MOD102: you will be expected to justify model choice, interpret parameters in plain language, and produce a chart suitable for a workplace report.

Explain what assessors typically look for:
- A defensible reason for choosing linear/quadratic/exponential (context + visual evidence).
- Parameter interpretations that include units and are tied to the scenario.
- A chart that is readable, honest, and reproducible.
- Brief discussion of limitations: range of data, potential confounders, and whether extrapolation is safe.

Expand on the “mixing % and absolute change” error: learners often describe exponential growth as “+10 each week” when it is actually “+10% each week”, which leads to incorrect forecasts.

Probing questions:
- What would you write as a limitation for each model type?
- If you had to present this in one slide to management, what would you keep?

Common misconception: thinking the assessment is mainly about calculation. Stress that communication quality (labels, units, justification) is central.

slides.title: Summary: what you should now be able to do

content.title: Summary: what you should now be able to do
content: Choose model type using features: constant rate, turning point, % change
Explain parameters with units, tied to the operational context
Plot raw data plus a fitted model, with clear labels and caption
Quality-check charts for axes, units, scales, and transparency
Prefer simple, interpretable models unless evidence demands complexity
content.notes:
Close by reinforcing transfer: learners should be able to take an unfamiliar workplace relationship and make a reasoned modelling choice, not just replicate a worked example.

Invite learners to self-evaluate against the learning objectives:
- Can you give two concrete cues for why a model is appropriate?
- Can you interpret parameters without slipping into “math-only” language?
- Does your chart stand alone—could a non-specialist understand it without you narrating?
- Did you document at least three quality checks?

Encourage a final reflection: modelling is iterative. It is acceptable to start with a linear model, check residuals, and then revise to quadratic/exponential if the evidence supports it.

Probing questions:
- Which model type do you personally overuse, and why?
- What is one habit you will adopt to prevent charting errors?

Common misconception to address in the wrap-up: “The model is the truth.” Emphasise: the model is an approximation for a purpose, within a range, under assumptions.

slides.title: Operational datasets and scatter plots

content.title: Operational datasets and scatter plots
content: Operational data often comes as paired measurements (x, y)
Use a scatter plot to show relationship, not categories
Each point is one observation (shift, order, day, batch)
Choose x as the driver; y as the outcome you care about
Check you have enough variation, not repeated x values only
Keep raw data visible in the sheet/notebook for audit
content.notes: Define an operational dataset as measurements collected from a process: e.g., units produced vs labour hours, throughput vs waiting time, demand vs price, mileage vs fuel used. Reinforce why scatter plots are appropriate: they preserve the paired nature and show spread, clusters, and potential outliers. Probing question: “What is your hypothesised driver (x) and why—does it cause y, or is it just associated?” Common misconceptions: (1) using a line chart for unordered observations (implies time order); (2) swapping x and y accidentally (changes interpretation of slope units); (3) hiding raw data so results cannot be checked.

slides.title: Axes, units, and scaling conventions

content.title: Axes, units, and scaling conventions
content: Axis labels must include name and units, e.g., Time (hours)
Scale should show the data range with sensible padding
Avoid truncated axes unless you justify the choice
Use an informative title: what, where, and when
Use a legend only when you have multiple series
Use consistent number format (e.g., £, 2 d.p., thousands)
content.notes: Explain that good graphs reduce cognitive load: the reader should not infer units or context. Give mini-examples: “Output (units/day)” vs “Output” (ambiguous); “Cost (£)” vs “Cost”. Discuss scale choices: starting at zero can be helpful for magnitude comparisons, but for relationships it may compress variation—either choice is acceptable if you explain it and avoid misleading impressions. Ask: “If I changed the y-axis from 0–3000 to 2000–2600, what story would the chart tell?” Misconceptions: (1) truncating axes to exaggerate change; (2) mixing units (minutes on axis, hours in equation); (3) overusing legends instead of direct series names.

slides.title: Fitting a linear function: what it means

content.title: Fitting a linear function: what it means
content.content: A linear fit finds the straight line y = mx + c that best matches your data. In Excel and Python this is typically least squares: it minimises the total squared vertical errors from the line. The fitted line is a model for prediction and comparison, not a guarantee of causality.
content.notes: Unpack ‘best matches’ in plain language: among all possible straight lines, the software chooses the one that makes the points, on average, as close as possible vertically. Clarify what is being minimised (squared residuals) and why (penalises large errors, yields a unique solution under typical conditions). Probing question: “If your data shows curvature or a threshold effect, what might a linear fit hide?” Misconceptions: (1) assuming a good fit proves a causal relationship; (2) believing the line must pass through the origin; (3) extrapolating far beyond the observed x range without stating the risk.

slides.title: Interpreting m and c (with units)

content.title: Interpreting m and c (with units)
content.notes: Walk through unit logic slowly because it drives correct interpretation. If y is cost (£) and x is volume (units), then m is £/unit: a variable cost or marginal cost estimate. If y is output (units) and x is labour hours, m is units/hour: productivity. For c, discuss whether x=0 is meaningful; sometimes it is (fixed costs), sometimes it is not (e.g., “temperature at 0 customers” might be meaningless). Probing questions: “Does x=0 exist in your process?” and “Would you expect y to be non-zero at x=0?” Misconceptions: (1) quoting m without units; (2) interpreting a negative intercept as ‘impossible’ rather than as a sign the linear model is only valid in a range; (3) treating high R² as proof the model is appropriate for decisions.

slides.title: Break-even: graphical vs algebraic method

content.title: Break-even: graphical vs algebraic method
leftColumn: Plot cost and revenue on the same axes
Find where the lines intersect
Read x and y using gridlines
Fast sense-check for reasonableness
rightColumn: Set Cost(x) = Revenue(x)
Solve for x (break-even volume)
Compute y by substituting x
Use tolerance to reconcile with graph
content.notes: Explain break-even as the point where profit changes sign: below it, costs exceed revenue; above it, revenue exceeds costs (under the model). Emphasise why we use both methods: the graph helps spot mistakes (wrong units, wrong slope), while the algebra provides precision. Demonstrate tolerance thinking: if the graph gives 171 and algebra gives 171.4, that is consistent within ±0.5 units. Probing question: “Which method would you trust if they disagree by 10 units—and what would you check first?” Misconception: confusing break-even in x (volume) with y (value), or using the wrong equation (e.g., setting profit to revenue).

content: Excel: add Trendline → Linear → show equation and R²

content.notes: Excel guidance: right-click data series → Add Trendline → Linear; tick “Display Equation on chart” and “Display R-squared value”. slides.title: Worked example: calculate and plot break-even

content.title: Worked example: calculate and plot break-even
content: Cost model: C(x) = 1200 + 8x  (C in £, x in units)
Revenue model: R(x) = 15x  (R in £)
Algebra: set 1200 + 8x = 15x
Break-even x = 1200/7 = 171.4 units (≈171)
Break-even y = 15×171.4 = £2571 (approx.)
Graph: intersection should match within ±0.5 units
content.notes: Explain each term operationally: £1200 is fixed cost (e.g., setup, rent, salaried staff allocation), £8/unit is variable cost, £15/unit is selling price. Emphasise unit consistency: x is units, not batches; price and costs must be per same unit. For spreadsheet calculation: show that you can compute x directly using the formula x = fixed_cost / (price − variable_cost), or use Goal Seek to set Profit(x)=0. For graph-based estimation: plot both lines over a relevant x-range (e.g., 0–300 units), then read off the intersection using gridlines. Probing question: “What happens to break-even if variable cost rises to £9/unit?” Misconceptions: (1) using y-values from the wrong axis; (2) calculating y using the cost function rather than revenue (both should match at break-even, but rounding can reveal errors); (3) ignoring that break-even volume may need rounding up to a whole unit in practice.

slides.title: Checking routine for plots and thresholds

content.title: Checking routine for plots and thresholds
content.notes: Frame checking as part of professional practice: you are producing evidence for an operational decision, so you must be able to defend it. Give a mini-scenario: if x is hours and someone typed minutes, slope changes by a factor of 60—your check should catch this instantly. Explain rounding: chart labels may show 8.1 when the underlying slope is 8.056; calculations should use the precise value to avoid drift in break-even. Probing questions: “Does the sign of m make operational sense?” and “If I double x, would y roughly double under your model?” Misconception: learners often treat ‘close enough’ as subjective; instead, define a tolerance (e.g., ±0.5 units) and apply it consistently.

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Pick a dataset (≥15 rows) with x driver and y outcome
Create a scatter plot with title, labels, units, scale

content.notes: Encourage learners to use their own operational context, but provide alternatives if they do not have data: e.g., monthly demand vs price, production volume vs total cost, deliveries vs fuel spend, calls handled vs staffing hours. Probing questions: “What decision would change if your break-even moved by 10%?” and “What would you monitor to see if the model is drifting over time?” Misconception: writing a recommendation that repeats calculations without stating an action; push for a clear threshold and decision rule.

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD102 tasks: plotting, fitting, and thresholds
Marking often rewards clarity: units, titles, and context
Common error: wrong chart type or swapped x and y
Common error: interpreting m without units or meaning
Common error: break-even mismatch not investigated

content.notes: Explain what assessors typically look for: not just a correct number, but a transparent chain from data → plot → model → interpretation → decision. slides.title: Gradients, intercepts and break-even calculations

content.title: Gradients, intercepts and break-even calculations
content: Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD102 — Functions and Graphs for Operational Decision-Making
Lesson 9: Gradients, intercepts and break-even calculations
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners to Lesson 9 in MOD102. Frame the session as a decision-focused use of graphs: you are not only extracting numbers (gradient, intercept, intersection) but also interpreting what they mean operationally, with units, assumptions, and limits. Emphasise that the target Bloom level is analyse: you will justify recommendations from graph evidence rather than only compute values. If learners feel less confident, reassure them that the method is consistent: identify variables and units, read or calculate key features, then translate into a decision statement.

slides.title: Learning objectives

content.title: Learning objectives
content: Calculate gradient and y-intercept from a graph, with units
Find break-even point(s) from cost–revenue or input–output graphs
Identify trends, turning points and constraints, and justify impact
Write a 120–180 word recommendation using graph evidence + limitation
Collaborate online: invite challenge and revise using peer feedback
content.notes: Briefly unpack each objective in practical terms. (1) Gradient is the rate of change; intercept is the baseline when the input is zero—both must be stated with units, for example £/unit or units/hour. (2) Break-even is an intersection; it may be one point, multiple points, or none depending on the shapes. (3) Analysis goes beyond reading: you will explain how a turning point changes a decision (e.g., ‘increasing output beyond 75 units reduces profit’). (4) Recommendations must cite specific graph features and include a limitation such as uncertainty, measurement error, or a confidence interval if data-based. (5) Collaboration is assessed as a process: show reasoning, ask for critique, and integrate at least one comment—do not treat peer input as optional.

slides.title: How to use this lesson (self-study)

content.title: How to use this lesson (self-study)
leftColumn: 1) Review key terms (gradient, intercept, intersection)
2) Watch/read the worked examples slowly
3) Pause to compute before revealing each step
4) Track units at every step
rightColumn: 5) Do practice prompts and self-check your answers
6) Draft a short recommendation note (120–180 words)
7) Post reasoning and invite challenge from peers
8) Revise using at least one peer comment
content.notes: Position this as an active lesson rather than passive reading. Encourage a ‘stop-and-solve’ routine: before reading the solution, learners should attempt each calculation using their own method. Stress that units are not decoration: they are part of the meaning and often reveal errors (e.g., confusing £/unit with units/£). For the online element, suggest a simple pattern for posting: ‘My result is…, because…, assumptions…, does anyone disagree with…?’ Then, when revising, learners should explicitly reference what changed due to the peer comment (e.g., rounding decision, constraint identified, or alternative interpretation).

slides.title: Linear graphs: the model behind the picture

content.title: Linear graphs: the model behind the picture
content.content: Many operational relationships are approximated as linear: y = mx + c. The gradient m is the change in y for each 1 unit change in x, and c is the y-value when x = 0. Your interpretation must always state the variables and units.
content.notes: Explain that graphs are models: a straight line implies a constant rate of change. Reinforce variable meaning: x is typically the input/driver (time, quantity produced, miles travelled), y is the outcome (cost, revenue, output). Mini-example verbally: if x = hours and y = items produced, m = 30 items/hour means each extra hour adds 30 items, assuming conditions remain stable. Common misconception: learners sometimes say the intercept is ‘the starting point’ even when x = 0 is not operationally meaningful (e.g., ‘cost at 0 units’ might exist as fixed cost, but ‘speed at 0 time’ might not). Probing question: ‘If x cannot be 0 in the real process, what does the intercept represent—if anything?’

content.title: Gradient vs y-intercept: calculation and meaning

rows: c = y − mx (use a known point)

content.notes: Talk through each row with a concrete operational interpretation. Emphasise that the gradient is a ‘per’ measure (e.g., £ per unit, units per hour, kWh per day). Misconception to surface: using two points that are not actually on the line (reading inaccurately from a graph) will produce a wrong gradient—encourage using clearly marked points or grid intersections. For intercept, stress the method: calculate m first, then substitute. Probing questions: ‘What would a negative gradient mean for staffing or inventory?’ and ‘When would a non-zero intercept be expected in cost modelling (fixed costs)?’

slides.title: Break-even: intersection as a decision threshold

content.title: Break-even: intersection as a decision threshold
content: Break-even occurs where two graphs have equal y-values
On cost–revenue graphs: break-even where revenue = cost
Graph method: locate intersection, then read x (and y) values
Algebra method: set equations equal and solve for x
State assumptions: linearity, constant price/cost, steady demand
Round sensibly: discrete units vs continuous measures
content.notes: Clarify the interpretation: break-even is usually an x-value (quantity, customers, hours) at which profit is zero. If learners only read the y-value, they miss the operational question (‘how many units do we need to sell?’). Highlight multiple intersections: with non-linear functions you may have two break-even points, creating a profitable interval between them. Also note ‘no intersection’ cases (always loss or always profit within the domain). Rounding: if x is units produced, you cannot produce 38.46 units—so you may need 39 to cover costs; if x is hours of machine time, decimals may be acceptable. Probing question: ‘If you round down, what risk are you taking?’

slides.title: Beyond numbers: trends, turning points, constraints

content.title: Beyond numbers: trends, turning points, constraints
content: Trend: overall increase/decrease; relate to operational drivers
Turning point: change in direction (max/min) on a curve
Constraint: domain/range limits or operational caps/floors
Check realism: do not extrapolate beyond the plotted domain
Explain decision impact: what changes if x exceeds a constraint?
Justify with evidence: quote approximate values from the graph
content.notes: Explain that analysis requires linking shape to decisions. Trend example: a steadily rising cost trend indicates variable costs; a flattening output trend could indicate diminishing returns. Turning point: for profit curves, the maximum indicates an ‘optimal’ operating level, but only within feasible constraints. Constraints are often operational: capacity, staffing limits, legal thresholds, minimum order quantities. Common misconception: treating a smooth curve as valid for all x; remind learners that graphs are typically based on a range of observed or feasible values. Probing questions: ‘What is the meaningful domain here?’ and ‘If demand is capped at 60 units/day, how does that alter your recommendation even if profit would rise beyond 60?’
