slides.title: Derivative as marginal rate (what it tells you)

content.title: Derivative as marginal rate (what it tells you)
content.content: A derivative gives the instantaneous rate of change of an output with respect to an input. In applied terms it is a marginal quantity, such as £ per additional unit or kWh per additional day. Units come from ‘output units ÷ input units’ and should be checked first.
content.notes:
Extend the idea of ‘instantaneous’ by contrasting it with an average rate (finite difference). If learners are uneasy with “instantaneous”, describe it as the slope of the tangent line at a point.

Mini-example (verbal): if R(t) is an energy-use rate in kWh/day, then R’(t) is how quickly that daily rate is increasing, in kWh/day².

Common misconceptions to surface:
- Confusing the derivative with the original function (e.g., reporting C(q) when asked for C’(q)).
- Treating the derivative as unitless.

Probing questions:
- “If q is measured in thousands of units, what happens to the units of C’(q)?”
- “Should marginal cost ever be negative in your scenario? If not, why might Excel show a negative value?”

slides.title: Definite integral as accumulation (area under curve)

content.title: Definite integral as accumulation (area under curve)
content.content: A definite integral accumulates a quantity over an interval, interpreted as ‘area under the curve’. If the integrand is a rate (per unit time, per unit output), the integral returns a total. Units multiply: ‘(output units) × (input units)’.
content.notes:
Stress that interpretation depends on what the function represents:
- If R(t) is a rate (e.g., kWh/month), then ∫ R(t) dt gives total kWh over the period.
- If C(q) is a cost per unit at output level q (a marginal/unit cost curve), then ∫ C(q) dq gives total cost for producing from q1 to q2.

Clarify bounds: learners must state the interval and apply it (upper minus lower). Many spreadsheet errors come from calculating an antiderivative but forgetting the evaluation at both limits.

Common misconceptions:
- Forgetting that an indefinite integral requires “+C”, whereas a definite integral does not.
- Mixing units so the integral result is not meaningful (e.g., integrating £ when q is also ‘£’).

Probing question: “If the integrand is always positive, what sign must the definite integral have? What would make it negative?”

Clarify bounds: learners must state the interval and apply it (upper minus lower). Many spreadsheet errors come from calculating an antiderivative but forgetting the evaluation at both limits.

Common misconceptions:
- Forgetting that an indefinite integral requires “+C”, whereas a definite integral does not.
- Mixing units so the integral result is not meaningful (e.g., integrating £ when q is also ‘£’).

Probing question: “If the integrand is always positive, what sign must the definite integral have? What would make it negative?”

slides.title: Rules for polynomials and exponentials

content.title: Rules for polynomials and exponentials
leftColumn: d/dx (ax^n) = a·n·x^(n−1)
Differentiate/integrate term-by-term
Careful with brackets and negative powers
rightColumn: d/dx (a·e^(kx)) = a·k·e^(kx)
∫ a·e^(kx) dx = (a/k)·e^(kx) + C
Excel uses EXP( ) for e^x
Base-10: a·b^x needs LN(b) factor
content.notes:
Emphasise pattern recognition: learners should identify whether the function is a sum of powers (polynomial) or has an exponential form (EXP).

Clarify the “base-10” point: if a function is a·b^x, then derivative is a·b^x·LN(b). This is a frequent exam and spreadsheet trap.

Mini-example to illustrate LN(b): if y = 5·2^t, then y’ = 5·2^t·LN(2).

Misconceptions:
- Treating e^(kx) as e^k·x (incorrect splitting of exponentials).
- Forgetting to multiply by k when differentiating e^(kx).

Probing question: “If k is negative, what do you expect the function to do over time? How should that affect your integral totals?”

slides.title: Implementing calculus in Excel (transparent formulas)

content.title: Implementing calculus in Excel (transparent formulas)
content.content: Use explicit cell references and keep formulas auditable.
content.notes:
Explain the modelling discipline:
- Keep inputs (parameters and x-values) in clearly labelled cells.
- Use absolute references ($) for parameters that should not change when copied.
- Separate ‘model’ cells (inputs) from ‘results’ cells (outputs).

Explain the integral row: in Excel you typically implement a definite integral by computing an antiderivative F(x) at b and a, then subtracting. This keeps formulas simple and visible.

Add a practical auditing technique: place the formula in a neighbouring cell as text using apostrophe ' (e.g., ' =0.4*A2+5) so reviewers can see it even if Show Formulas is off.

Probing question: “If you copy your derivative formula down a column, which parts should stay fixed (absolute) and which should update (relative)?”

slides.title: Worked example 1: polynomial unit-cost curve

content.title: Worked example 1: polynomial unit-cost curve
content: C(q)=0.2q^2+5q+100 (£/unit); q in units produced
Differentiate: C'(q)=0.4q+5 (change in £/unit per unit)
At q=50: C'(50)=25 (£/unit per unit)
Integrate for total cost: ∫0^50 C(q)dq
Antiderivative: F(q)=0.0666667q^3+2.5q^2+100q
content.notes:
Frame the interpretation carefully:
- Here C(q) is a unit-cost (or marginal cost) curve in £/unit that depends on production level q.
- The derivative C’(q) is NOT a cost; it is the rate at which unit cost changes as output rises.
- The definite integral ∫ C(q) dq gives total cost for producing units across the interval, provided C(q) is interpreted as cost per unit.

Walk through the differentiation:
- d/dq(0.2q^2)=0.4q
- d/dq(5q)=5
- d/dq(100)=0

Walk through the integration term-by-term and emphasise the power increase by 1.

Reasonableness prompts:
- “C(q) is positive for all q here; should the integral ever be negative?”
- “C’(50)=25: does it make sense that unit cost is increasing at q=50?”

Common mistake to highlight: integrating 0.2q^2 as 0.1q^3 (forgetting /3).

slides.title: Example 1: Excel cell plan and check values

content.title: Example 1: Excel cell plan and check values
content.content: One-row setup for q=50 with formulas visible.
content.notes:
Explain how to use this layout in practice:
- Keep q in a single input cell (A2) to support sensitivity testing.
- B2 is the model output at q (unit cost at that production level).
- C2 is the derivative at q; remind learners it has different units.
- D2 is the antiderivative evaluated at q; E2 is the definite integral with a=0.

Encourage learners to add explicit lower bound cells for generality (q0 and q1), then compute F(q1)-F(q0). This helps prevent the “forgot the lower limit” error.

- Using 0.0666667 as an approximation: acceptable if rounding is stated; better is =0.2/3.
- Writing =0.2*A2^2+5*A2+100 without understanding order of operations (it is fine here, but not always).

Probing question: “If you change q to 60, which cells should update automatically? How will you confirm the updates are correct?”

slides.title: Worked example 2: exponential resource rate

content.title: Worked example 2: exponential resource rate
content: R(t)=120·e^(0.03t) (kWh/month); t in months
Differentiate: R'(t)=3.6·e^(0.03t) (kWh/month^2)
Integrate total use: ∫0^12 R(t)dt
Antiderivative: F(t)=120/0.03·e^(0.03t)
Total: F(12)-F(0)=1,733.33 kWh (approx.)
content.notes:
Give a clear physical interpretation:
- R(t) is a consumption rate. Integrating over time returns total energy consumed.
- The derivative R’(t) tells you how quickly the monthly consumption rate is rising.

Step-by-step reasoning:
- Differentiation: derivative of EXP(0.03t) is 0.03·EXP(0.03t). Multiply by 120.
- Integration: divide by 0.03 because ∫ e^(kt) dt = (1/k)e^(kt).

Numerical approximations:
- e^0.36 ≈ 1.43333, so R(12)=120×1.43333≈172.
- Total ≈ 4000×(1.43333−1)=1733.33.

Misconceptions:
- Writing EXP(0.03)*t instead of EXP(0.03*t).
- Forgetting the /0.03 in the antiderivative.

Probing question: “If t were measured in years instead of months, how would the 0.03 parameter need to change to represent the same growth?”

slides.title: Plausibility checks for derivatives and integrals

content.title: Plausibility checks for derivatives and integrals
leftColumn: Units/dimensions: do units match the interpretation?
Sign and shape: does output increase/decrease as expected?
Boundary check: values at t=0 or q=0 sensible?
Numerical estimate: compare to finite difference or TRAPZ
rightColumn: Write units beside each result cell (e.g., kWh/month^2)
Graph f(x) and f'(x); check slope matches derivative sign
Evaluate at bounds; confirm integral uses both limits
Use small Δx: (f(x+Δ)-f(x))/Δ as a check
content.notes:
Teach analysis as a repeatable routine, not an afterthought.

1) Units/dimensions
- Encourage learners to annotate units directly in the worksheet (adjacent cells).
- If units do not work, the formula is almost certainly wrong.

2) Sign and shape
- If f(x) is increasing, f’(x) should be mostly positive over that region.
- If f’(x) is increasing, the curve should be getting steeper.

3) Boundary checks
- At t=0, R(0)=120. If the worksheet gives 0 or 120e^0.03, there is a bracket error.

4) Numerical estimates
- Finite difference derivative: choose a small step (e.g., Δ=0.01 or Δ=0.1) and compare.
- Numerical integral: trapezium rule can validate the analytic result; discrepancy should shrink as step size shrinks.

Probing questions:
- “Which check would detect a missing ‘/0.03’ most quickly?”
- “What would the graph look like if you accidentally used 0.3 instead of 0.03?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection tasks

content.title: Practice and reflection tasks
content: Compute f'(x) and ∫ from given bounds for 2 new functions
Show formulas in Excel and label units for every result
Run 3 checks: units, sign/shape, numerical estimate
Debug a buggy sheet: references, brackets, exponents, bounds
Record at least 2 corrections and the assumption behind each
Write a log entry: rounding rule, validity range, limitations
content.notes:
Provide guidance for self-paced practice without needing a live activity sheet:

Suggested function set learners can create themselves:
- Polynomial: f(x)=3x^3−2x+7 on [0,2]
- Exponential: f(t)=50·e^(−0.2t) on [0,10]

Debugging prompts (what to look for):
- Relative vs absolute reference: did a copied formula drift to the wrong parameter cell?
- Missing parentheses: EXP(0.03*A2) vs EXP(0.03)*A2.
- Wrong operator precedence: 1/0.03*EXP(...) is fine, but 1/(0.03*EXP(...)) is not.
- Bounds omitted: computing F(b) but not subtracting F(a).

Calculation log coaching:
- Require three elements: (i) statement of method, (ii) assumptions, (iii) uncertainty/limits.
- Encourage a simple template: “Given…, I computed…, I checked…, therefore…”.

Probing question: “If a numerical estimate disagrees with your analytic derivative by 20%, is that a maths error or a step-size choice? How would you decide?”

slides.title: Assessment connection and common errors

content.title: Assessment connection and common errors
content: Supports: MCQ quiz on marginal change and accumulation (Excel)
Supports: MCQ check on limits, units, and reasonableness
Common error: wrong cell referencing when copying formulas
Common error: missing parentheses in powers/EXP expressions
Common error: bounds missing or swapped in definite integrals
Common error: units mismatch and undocumented rounding
content.notes:
Make the link to assessment explicit:
- The MCQs typically test conceptual interpretation (units, signs) as well as mechanics (correct rule application).
- Learners often lose marks not because the calculus is wrong, but because the spreadsheet implementation is opaque or inconsistent.

Expand on each common error with a quick diagnostic:
- Referencing: if results change unexpectedly when copied down, inspect $ usage.
- Parentheses: if R(0) is not equal to the parameter a in a·e^(kt), suspect EXP brackets.
- Bounds: if ∫ is negative for a positive function, check order a and b.
- Units: if derivative has same units as original, something is being misinterpreted.

Probing question: “Which error types are easiest to catch with a graph, and which require unit checking?”

slides.title: Summary

content.title: Summary
content: Derivatives give marginal change; units are ‘output ÷ input’
Definite integrals accumulate totals; units multiply over interval
Polynomials: power rules; exponentials: EXP with k factor
Excel: keep formulas visible, references controlled, bounds explicit
Always analyse outputs with units, shape expectations, and checks
content.notes:
Close by reinforcing transfer to new problems:
- The specific functions will change, but the workflow should remain stable: compute → interpret → check → document.

Invite learners to self-evaluate against the learning objectives:
- “Can you reproduce the worked examples in Excel without looking?”
- “Can you explain, in one sentence, what your derivative means in units?”
- “Can you identify at least two ways your worksheet could be misleading to a reviewer?”

Encourage learners to keep their calculation log as an artefact for future modules: it demonstrates sound quantitative practice, not just final answers.

slides.title: Derivative vs integral: what the output means

content.title: Derivative vs integral: what the output means
leftColumn: Derivative: dy/dx is an instantaneous rate of change
Units: (units of y) ÷ (units of x)
Use when: asking “how fast is it changing now?”
Example: dC/dq = marginal cost (£ per unit)
rightColumn: Integral: ∫ y dx is an accumulated total over a range
Units: (units of y) × (units of x)
Use when: asking “how much in total over time/space?”
Example: ∫ P dt = energy used (kWh)
content.notes: Narrate the contrast as two different questions: derivatives answer ‘speed/slope right now’, integrals answer ‘total amount collected’. Stress that learners often mix them up because both use the same symbols and functions; the deciding factor is the question being asked and the units. Mini-check: if x is time in hours and y is power in kW, then dy/dx would be kW per hour (a rate of change of power), whereas ∫y dx would be kWh (energy). Ask: if the business wants monthly energy consumption, which tool fits and why?

slides.title: Dimensional consistency: unit rules you must apply

content.title: Dimensional consistency: unit rules you must apply
content: Write units for every variable before differentiating/integrating
If y in U_y and x in U_x, then dy/dx in U_y/U_x
If y in U_y and x in U_x, then ∫ y dx in U_y·U_x
Constants keep their units; pure numbers are unitless
Never add/subtract terms with different units
content.notes: Explain dimensional analysis as a non-negotiable safety check. Walk through a quick example: if C(q) is in £ and q is in units, then C'(q) must be £/unit—if a learner reports £/hour, something has been mis-defined. Emphasise that integration ‘brings in’ the unit of the integration variable: integrating a rate over time must multiply by time units. Common misconception: treating the differential dx as “just notation” rather than something carrying units. Probing question: if you integrate 50 litres/min over 2 minutes, what unit must the answer have, and why?

slides.title: Plausibility checks for calculus outputs

content.title: Plausibility checks for calculus outputs
content: Baseline check: compare to a known typical value
Range check: compare to min/max possible in the context
Sign check: should it be positive, negative, or zero here?
Trend check: does monotonicity match the situation?
Back-of-envelope check: rough average × width of interval
content.notes: Frame plausibility as ‘sanity checking with numbers’. Give an example: if throughput is usually 80–120 items/hour, a computed 900 items/hour needs scrutiny. Explain sign and monotonicity: if cumulative output N(t) cannot decrease during production, then N'(t) should not be negative for periods of active production; if it is, either the model includes scrap/returns or there is an error. Back-of-envelope check is powerful: approximate integral as average value times interval length and see if the exact result is in the same ballpark. Probing question: what would you do if your calculated answer is off by a factor of 60 (minutes vs hours)?

slides.title: Calculation log template (for reproducibility)

content.title: Calculation log template (for reproducibility)

rows: No downtime; model fits observed period
At t=5, 90 items/h; round to 2 s.f.

content.notes: Explain that the calculation log is a professional habit: it turns private working into an auditable record. Encourage learners to write the log as they work, not after. Highlight what makes it ‘reproducible’: someone else can see definitions, units, domain, method, and checks, and obtain the same result. slides.title: Worked example 1: throughput from cumulative output

content.title: Worked example 1: throughput from cumulative output
content: Given N(t)=120t−3t^2, where N in items and t in hours
Interpretation: N'(t) is throughput rate (items/hour)
Differentiate: N'(t)=120−6t (items/hour)
At t=5 h: N'(5)=120−30=90 items/hour
Plausibility: compare to baseline 100 items/hour (close)
Sign check: N'(t)>0 for t<20 h, so OK for 0–8 h
content.notes: Walk learners line-by-line: we start with a cumulative quantity N(t), so the derivative has a natural operational meaning: instantaneous throughput. Show a quick quantitative check: at t=0, rate is 120 items/hour; at t=8, rate is 72 items/hour; is that credible for a shift? Ask: what would it mean if N'(t) became negative during the shift—would that be modelling returns, or an invalid model domain?

slides.title: Worked example 2: marginal cost and unit checking

content.title: Worked example 2: marginal cost and unit checking
content: Given C(q)=500+12q+0.02q^2, C in £ and q in units
Interpretation: C'(q) is marginal cost (£ per unit)
Differentiate: C'(q)=12+0.04q (£/unit)
Unit check: each term in C'(q) must be £/unit
Plausibility: average cost ≈ C(200)/200=£18/unit (close)
content.notes: Explain that marginal cost is a derivative used for decision-making (e.g., whether to accept an additional order). Make the unit logic explicit: 12q must be in £, so 12 must carry £/unit; similarly 0.02q^2 must be in £, so 0.02 must carry £/unit^2. This helps learners see that coefficients can have units. For plausibility, compare marginal vs average cost: in a convex cost function, marginal cost at q=200 should be higher than average cost, which we observe (20 vs about 18). Probing questions: if a learner reported 20 £ (no ‘per unit’), what is missing? If C'(q) came out negative at high q, what would that imply about the model?

slides.title: Worked example 3: energy from power (integration)

content.title: Worked example 3: energy from power (integration)
content: Given P(t)=5+0.5t, P in kW and t in hours, 0≤t≤4
Energy used: E=∫[0 to 4] P(t) dt (kWh)
Dimensional check: kW × h = kWh (correct)
Back-of-envelope: avg P≈6 kW, so E≈6×4=24 kWh
Sign/range: P(t)>0, so E must be positive
content.notes: Reinforce the accumulation meaning: power is a rate of energy use, so integrating over time gives total energy. Many learners confuse kW and kWh; explicitly state the difference: kW is ‘how fast’, kWh is ‘how much’. slides.title: From total to marginal: what a derivative tells you

content.title: From total to marginal: what a derivative tells you
content: Derivative = instantaneous rate of change at a point
For cost C(q), C'(q) is marginal cost at output q
Interpret as “£ per extra unit” near q
Units: if C is £ and q is units, C' is £/unit
Marginal ≠ average cost C(q)/q
In Excel, compute C'(q) then evaluate at chosen q
content.notes:
A derivative gives the slope of the total function at a specific point. In business or operations language, it answers: “If I increase output slightly from this level, how much does total cost change?”

Stress the local nature of marginal: it is a ‘nearby’ approximation, not necessarily the change from 0 to q.

Mini-example (verbal): If C(60) = £2,340 and C'(60) = £39/unit, that does not mean the 60th unit costs £39 exactly, nor that total cost is 60×39. It means around q=60, adding one more unit is predicted to add about £39.

Misconceptions:
- Confusing marginal cost (derivative) with average cost (C/q).
- Treating derivative as a finite difference over a large interval.

Probing questions:
- If C'(q) is negative, what would that imply about total cost as q increases?
- What would the graph of C(q) look like if C'(q) is increasing?

slides.title: Derivative rules used in this lesson

content.title: Derivative rules used in this lesson

rows: Do not forget the k factor

content.notes:
These are the only rules you need for the polynomial and exponential functions in this lesson. The key operational idea is that differentiation is linear: you can split sums into separate derivatives.

Excel-specific emphasis:
- Use ^ for powers and EXP() for exponentials. Avoid typing e^x directly.
- Bracketing is crucial: x^(n-1) is not the same as x^n-1.

Common error patterns:
- Writing derivative of EXP(kx) as EXP(kx) (missing the multiplier k).
- Dropping coefficients (e.g., derivative of 0.2x^2 written as x).

Probing question: If k is small (e.g., 0.01), how should that affect the marginal values compared to the original exponential?

slides.title: Excel setup for derivative calculations

content.title: Excel setup for derivative calculations
content: Place x (q, t, etc.) in one cell; store parameters separately
Use parentheses: =a*n*(x^(n-1))
Exponential: =A*k*EXP(k*x)
Avoid hard-coding; reference parameter cells or named ranges
Show units and rounding rules next to each output
Add a finite-difference check as a reasonableness test
content.notes:
This slide is about spreadsheet engineering choices that reduce errors.

Talk through a clean layout:
- Inputs area: x (the independent variable) and parameters (a, b, A, k, etc.).
- Outputs area: total function value, derivative (marginal), and checks.

Finite-difference check (mini-example): If C(q) is in a cell, approximate marginal as:
- (C(q+h) − C(q)) / h with a small h (e.g., 0.01 or 0.1).
Then compare it to the analytic derivative C'(q). They should be close if h is small and the formula is correct.

Misconceptions:
- Using too large an h and expecting exact agreement.
- Mixing units (e.g., q in thousands of units but treating it as units).

Probing questions:
- What value of h would be ‘small enough’ in your context?
- If the finite-difference check disagrees, what will you inspect first: brackets, coefficients, or cell references?

slides.title: From marginal to total: what an integral gives you

content.title: From marginal to total: what an integral gives you
content.content: Integrating a marginal function accumulates small changes into a total. The total change from x0 to x1 is the definite integral ∫x0→x1 m(x) dx. To get an absolute total, add the constant of accumulation: Total(x1)=Total(x0)+∫x0→x1 m(x) dx.
content.notes:
Keep the meaning clear: derivatives take you from totals to rates; integrals take you from rates back to totals.

Two distinct outputs:
1) The integral over an interval gives a change (a difference), not necessarily the full total.
2) The constant of accumulation is the ‘starting value’ at x0 (e.g., known cost at baseline output).

Mini-example (conceptual): If marginal cost is £30/unit between q=10 and q=11, then the cost increase across that one-unit interval is about £30. Over many units where marginal changes, the integral sums these varying increments.

Misconception to highlight: learners often report ∫ m(x) dx as “the total cost”, forgetting that it is total change relative to a baseline.

Probing question: In a spreadsheet, where will you store Total(x0), and how will you stop it being accidentally overwritten?

slides.title: Plausibility checks for derivatives and integrals

content.title: Plausibility checks for derivatives and integrals
content: Units: derivative is “per x”; integral removes “per x”
Sign: negative marginal implies decreasing total over that region
Monotonicity: rising marginal suggests convex total cost curve
Magnitude: compare with MC(midpoint)*Δx as a quick estimate
Boundary: ∫x0→x0 m(x) dx must equal 0
Log checks: what you tested, result, and any fix made
content.notes:
These checks are part of the learning outcomes: you are expected to critique outputs, not just calculate them.

Explain each check with a short illustration:
- Units: If MC is £/unit and Δq is unit, the product is £. If your integral result is still “£/unit”, something is wrong.
- Sign: If m(x) is positive throughout, the integral over a positive-width interval must be positive.
- Monotonicity: If C(q)=0.2q^2+…, then C'(q) is linear increasing; if you see a decreasing marginal, you likely mis-specified the power.
- Magnitude: Use a midpoint approximation as a sanity check (not as the final method).

Common pitfalls:
- Forgetting that changing the unit scale (e.g., q measured in 1000s) changes the derivative magnitude.
- Assuming “bigger numbers are better”; instead ask whether the value is plausible relative to baseline costs.

Probing questions:
- Which check would catch a missing k in an exponential derivative fastest?
- If your marginal is correct but the integral seems too large, what interval-width issue might exist?

slides.title: Worked example: polynomial total cost to marginal cost

content.title: Worked example: polynomial total cost to marginal cost
content.notes:
Walk learners through building this in Excel with cell references.

Suggested layout:
- Put q in cell B2.
- Put coefficients (0.2, 15, 100) in separate cells (e.g., B5:B7) or named ranges.
- Compute total cost: =a*(B2^2)+b*B2+c.
- Compute marginal: =2*a*B2 + b (or directly =0.4*B2+15 for this specific a).

Interpretation emphasised:
- The marginal at q=60 is a local prediction for q=61 relative to q=60.
- Average cost at q=60 is C(60)/60; it answers a different question.

Common mistakes:
- Differentiating 0.2q^2 as 0.2q (forgetting the 2).
- Evaluating the derivative at the wrong q because of a mistaken cell reference.

Probing questions:
- If q doubles, what happens to MC(q) here, and why?
- What does it mean if MC(q) crosses zero (hypothetically) in a cost model?

slides.title: Worked example: exponential resource use to marginal

content.title: Worked example: exponential resource use to marginal
content: Resource use: R(t)=500*EXP(0.03*t)+200 kWh/day
Excel total: =500*EXP(0.03*t)+200
Marginal: R'(t)=500*0.03*EXP(0.03*t)
Excel marginal: =500*0.03*EXP(0.03*t)
At t=10: ≈ 20.25 kWh/day^2 (rate of increase in daily use)
Check: for k>0, marginal is positive and increasing with t
content.notes:
Clarify the variable: here t is time (days). R(t) is already a rate (kWh per day). Therefore R'(t) has units ‘kWh per day per day’ (kWh/day²). That often feels unfamiliar, so emphasise the meaning: how quickly the daily use is changing over time.

Guide learners through evaluation:
- Put t in a cell (e.g., B2=10).
- Compute R(t) and R'(t) in separate cells.
- Use a quick check: compute R(10) and R(11) and compare R(11)-R(10) to R'(10)×1 day. They won’t match exactly, but they should be in the same range.

Common misconceptions:
- Reporting the derivative with the wrong units (writing kWh/day instead of kWh/day²).
- Treating the additive constant (+200) as affecting the derivative.

Probing questions:
- If the 0.03 were 0.003, what would happen to marginal values?
- Why does an exponential model produce an ever-increasing marginal?

slides.title: Worked example: integrate marginal cost over an interval

content.title: Worked example: integrate marginal cost over an interval
content.notes:
This example links the two directions: the marginal function is the derivative of the total cost from the earlier polynomial example.

Emphasise the structure learners must replicate:
1) Identify the interval [q0, q1].
2) Integrate MC(q) to get an antiderivative F(q).
3) Compute the change ΔC = F(q1) − F(q0).
4) If asked for an absolute total at q1, add C(q0).

Excel guidance:
- Keep q0 and q1 as input cells (e.g., B2 and B3) so the interval can change.
- Consider writing the antiderivative using those cells: =(0.2*B3^2+15*B3)-(0.2*B2^2+15*B2).

Checks:
- Units: MC is £/unit, dq is unit, result is £.
- Boundary: if q1=q0, the formula should return 0 for ΔC.

Misconceptions:
- Forgetting to subtract F(q0).
- Adding C(q0) when the question only asks for the change.

Probing question: How would you modify your sheet if the baseline were C(0) instead of C(50)?

This example links the two directions: the marginal function is the derivative of the total cost from the earlier polynomial example.

Emphasise the structure learners must replicate:
1) Identify the interval [q0, q1].
2) Integrate MC(q) to get an antiderivative F(q).
3) Compute the change ΔC = F(q1) − F(q0).
4) If asked for an absolute total at q1, add C(q0).

Excel guidance:
- Keep q0 and q1 as input cells (e.g., B2 and B3) so the interval can change.
- Consider writing the antiderivative using those cells: =(0.2*B3^2+15*B3)-(0.2*B2^2+15*B2).

Checks:
- Units: MC is £/unit, dq is unit, result is £.
- Boundary: if q1=q0, the formula should return 0 for ΔC.

Misconceptions:
- Forgetting to subtract F(q0).
- Adding C(q0) when the question only asks for the change.

Probing question: How would you modify your sheet if the baseline were C(0) instead of C(50)?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Build C(q)=0.05q^3+2q^2+40q+500 and compute MC(q)
Evaluate MC at q=20, 40, 60 with correct units
Given MC(q)=8+0.6q, find ΔC from q=10 to q=25
If C(10)=1200, compute C(25) using the constant of accumulation
For each result, log 3 checks: units, sign, magnitude vs baseline
Attempt both MCQs after you have a working spreadsheet
content.notes:
Encourage learners to create one workbook with separate sections for each prompt. The key is reproducibility: inputs at the top, outputs and checks below.

Suggested reflection questions:
- Which part felt most error-prone: differentiation, integration, or interpretation?
- When your answer looked ‘wrong’, which plausibility check flagged it first?

Magnitude check examples learners can use:
- Compare ΔC to MC(midpoint)×(q1−q0).
- Compare C(25)−C(10) to what a simple linear model would predict.

Common issues to watch:
- Cubic derivative: 0.05q^3 differentiates to 0.15q^2 (not 0.05q^2).
- Forgetting to keep consistent units if q is in batches (e.g., q=20 batches vs 20 items).

Link to formative checks:
- Advise learners to attempt the MCQs twice: once immediately, once after revising their spreadsheet based on errors.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Directly supports MOD103 MCQs on marginal change and accumulation
Use the audit checklist: transparency, assumptions, limitations
Pitfall: derivative of EXP(kx) missing the multiplier k
Pitfall: reporting ΔC as C(q1); forgetting the baseline constant
Pitfall: mixing average cost with marginal cost in interpretation
Submission tip: include a visible checks log and rounding rule
content.notes:
Make the assessment link explicit: marks are typically lost on interpretation, units, and transparency—not only on calculus steps.

Expand on “audit checklist” expectations:
- No hidden steps: formulas should be visible and traceable.
- Clear labelling: units in headings; parameter definitions.
- Assumptions stated (e.g., model validity range, constant prices).
- Rounding policy (e.g., currency to 2 dp; intermediate values unrounded).

Explain why the pitfalls matter:
- Missing k in EXP(kx) can change the marginal by an order of magnitude.
- Confusing ΔC and C(q1) leads to double-counting or missing baseline costs.

Probing questions:
- If someone audits your file, can they reproduce your answer by changing inputs only?
- Where in your workbook do you explicitly state limitations (e.g., extrapolation risk)?

slides.title: Derivative and integral outputs: plausibility and units

content.title: Derivative and integral outputs: plausibility and units
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD103 — Calculus Essentials: Marginal Change and Accumulation
Lesson 9 (1h 30m)
content.notes:
Introduce the lesson as practical sense-checking of calculus outputs, not symbol manipulation. Emphasise workplace contexts where a model, spreadsheet, or colleague provides a derivative/integral result and your job is to judge whether it is credible.

Frame the session around two recurring questions: (1) Does the sign and magnitude make sense in context? (2) Do the units work out? Stress that at Bloom’s “analyse” level we are evaluating outputs using multiple checks, not just computing them.

Prompt: “If you were signing off this result for a client or audit, what evidence would you need?”

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Judge sign and size of outputs using 2+ reasoned checks
Check dimensional consistency; state resulting units accurately
Keep an audit-ready calculation log: assumptions, units, rounding
Use Excel to estimate marginal and accumulated quantities from data
Spot quality issues (rounding, units, hidden settings) and fix them
Study flow: learn concepts → try examples → do the two quizzes
content.notes:
Explain how to use the lesson in a self-study mode: read each slide, pause to do the small calculations (even roughly), then compare with the notes. Encourage learners to keep a running ‘calculation log’ document alongside the lesson and treat it as part of the learning, not an extra.

Clarify what “reasoned checks” means: not just “it looks big/small”, but checks anchored in trend (does it align with nearby values or a plot?), bounds (can it exceed a maximum/minimum?), and contextual constraints (capacity, conservation, physical limits, business rules).

Probing question: “Which objective feels most unfamiliar: units, plausibility, Excel, or documentation?”

slides.title: Derivative vs integral: rate and accumulation

content.title: Derivative vs integral: rate and accumulation
leftColumn: Derivative: dY/dX is marginal change (a rate)
Looks at local behaviour around a point
Sign shows increasing (+) or decreasing (−)
Units: (units of Y) per (units of X)
rightColumn: Integral: ∫Y dX is total accumulation
Adds up contributions across an interval
Sign depends on whether values are above/below zero
Units: (units of Y) × (units of X)
content.notes:
Talk through the mental model: derivatives answer “how fast is it changing right now?”, integrals answer “how much in total over time/space?”. Use everyday examples: speed as derivative of distance; distance as integral of speed.

Highlight a common misconception: learners sometimes treat a derivative value as a total change. Reinforce that a derivative needs a ‘small interval’ to become an approximate change (e.g., ΔY ≈ (dY/dX)ΔX).

Probing questions: “If dC/dx = £3/unit, is that the total cost?” “If ∫P(t)dt = 18 kWh, is that a power?”

slides.title: Plausibility checks for sign and magnitude

content.title: Plausibility checks for sign and magnitude
content: 1) Sign: does the direction match the story and the graph?
2) Trend: compare with nearby slopes/areas; look for smoothness
3) Bounds: capacity limits, non-negativity, conservation constraints
4) Scale: compare to typical/average values and known benchmarks
5) Units: wrong units often create wrong magnitudes
6) Sensitivity: would small input changes cause huge output swings?
content.notes:
Explain each check with a mini-example.

Sign: If cumulative output increases with time, dQ/dt should be ≥ 0. A negative derivative suggests either a data issue, a reversed axis, or that Q is not cumulative output but perhaps backlog.

Trend: If a process is stable, slopes between adjacent points should not jump wildly without a reason (e.g., shift change, outage). Encourage learners to sketch a quick plot or use an Excel scatter plot.

Bounds: Use hard constraints: maximum machine rate, maximum power draw, physical impossibilities (negative mass). Show how a bound can immediately flag an error: if an 8 kW heater allegedly used 40 kWh in 3 hours, it violates the bound 8×3=24 kWh.

Scale: Compare marginal to average: if average cost is £10/unit and marginal cost is £200/unit, you need a strong explanation.

Sensitivity: Very large derivatives can be real, but often indicate a unit mismatch (seconds vs hours) or a decimal error.

Probing question: “Which check would you apply first if you had 10 seconds?”

slides.title: Dimensional consistency: common derivative/integral units

content.title: Dimensional consistency: common derivative/integral units
content: Use units algebra: treat d/dx like “per x”, and ∫ like “times x”.

rows: Q in items, t in min
P in kW, t in h
v in m/s, t in s

content.notes:
Demonstrate the method explicitly: write the units next to each symbol and simplify like fractions.

For derivatives: (units of numerator)/(units of denominator). For integrals: (units of integrand)×(units of variable of integration).

Point out common pitfalls:
- Mixing time units (s, min, h) without converting first.
- Treating “°C” as needing special calculus rules; for unit checking it behaves like a unit label.
- Confusing kW (a rate) with kWh (an amount).

Probing questions: “If t is in seconds but you report kWh, what conversion is missing?” “If C is in £000 and you forget, what happens to dC/dx?”

slides.title: Calculation log: make your work auditable

content.title: Calculation log: make your work auditable
content: Assumptions: what you treat as constant, linear, negligible
Units: each variable’s units; show conversions explicitly
Rounding: when and why; keep full precision until the end
Method: formula used (difference, trapezoid), interval choice
Tools: Excel functions, Solver/Analysis settings, data source
Limits: uncertainty, data quality, model validity range
content.notes:
Explain that an audit-ready log is a professional habit: it protects you when results are questioned and makes your work reproducible.

Give a compact template learners can copy:
- Inputs: list values, units, and where they came from.
- Conversions: e.g., “10 min = 10/60 h”.
- Computation: exact formulas (cell references if in Excel).
- Checks: at least two plausibility checks and a units check.
- Output: final value with units and sensible significant figures.

Misconception to address: “I can tidy rounding as I go.” Emphasise cumulative rounding error, especially for numerical integration.

Probing question: “If someone re-ran your spreadsheet in six months, what might they not know?”

slides.title: Excel workflow: marginal and accumulated from data

content.title: Excel workflow: marginal and accumulated from data
content: Plot data first to see trend and possible outliers
Marginal estimate: forward/central difference from neighbours
Accumulation: trapezoidal rule across the full interval
Keep units in headers; convert time units before computing
Use absolute cell refs for constants; label all assumptions
Write 2–4 sentences: rate vs total and how they relate
content.notes:
Talk through a practical Excel approach without relying on advanced tools:

1) Plot: A quick scatter plot often reveals a transposed column, a missing value, or a non-monotonic “cumulative” measure.

2) Derivative estimate (marginal):
- Forward difference at the start: (Y2−Y1)/(X2−X1).
- Central difference in the middle: (Y3−Y1)/(X3−X1), usually more stable.

3) Trapezoidal integration:
- For each interval i: area_i = (Yi + Yi+1)/2 × (Xi+1 − Xi).
- Sum areas with SUM().

4) Interpretation sentence structure:
- “The derivative estimate is about … per …, meaning ….”
- “The integral over … is …, meaning the total ….”
- “They relate because the integral adds up the rate over time.”

Quality note: remind learners to check whether Excel is displaying rounded values while using full precision internally; your log should record the displayed rounding versus stored values if it matters.

slides.title: Worked example 1: throughput rate from cumulative output

content.title: Worked example 1: throughput rate from cumulative output
content: Estimate dQ/dt at 20 min and check plausibility vs capacity.
content.notes:
Walk learners through the marginal estimate at 20 minutes.

Option A (central difference around 20): use points at 10 and 30 minutes.
- dQ/dt at 20 ≈ (Q(30)−Q(10)) / (30−10)
- = (360−120)/20 = 12 items/min.

Option B (nearest-interval slope): around 20 the slope is 13 items/min (10→20) and 11 items/min (20→30), so 12 items/min is a sensible “middle”.

Plausibility checks:
- Sign: positive, consistent with increasing cumulative output.
- Bounds: if the line’s rated capacity is 15 items/min, 12 is plausible.
- Trend: slopes vary moderately; no sudden spikes that suggest a data error.

Ask learners: “If someone reported −12 items/min at 20 min, what are the first two things you would check in the spreadsheet?” (Axis direction, whether Q is cumulative or net of rejects, unit conversions.)

slides.title: Worked example 2: energy from power via integration

content.title: Worked example 2: energy from power via integration
content: Compute ∫P(t)dt using trapezoids; check against a max bound.
content.notes:
Explain what the integral represents: the area under the power–time curve is energy.

Units check:
- Power is kW = kJ/s (rate).
- Integrating over hours gives kWh (an amount of energy).

Plausibility checks:
- Bound: maximum possible energy if power stayed at 8 kW for 3 h is 24 kWh. Our 18.5 kWh is below the bound, so feasible.
- Trend: power declines after hour 1; total energy should be less than 8×3.

Common misconception: treating the average of the power readings (e.g., (5+8+6+4)/4) and multiplying by 3 h without considering spacing. Here spacing is equal, so it’s close, but the trapezoid method is explicit and general.

Probing question: “If the time points were 0, 0.5, 2, 3 hours, what changes in your Excel formula?”

slides.title: Worked example 3: marginal cost and reasonableness

content.title: Worked example 3: marginal cost and reasonableness
content: Marginal cost near 110: dC/dx ≈ (1060−1000)/(120−100)
So dC/dx ≈ £60/20 = £3 per unit
Check vs average cost at 110: about £1,030/110 ≈ £9.36
Check bounds: if materials ≥ £2/unit, £3 is plausible
Flag if dC/dx < 0 unless strong reason (rebates, errors)
content.notes:
Narrate the steps and explicitly label units at each stage.

Interpretation: “Near 110 units, producing one extra unit increases total cost by about £3.” Stress “about” because it is an estimate over a finite interval.

Why the average-cost comparison helps: average cost includes fixed costs spread across units; marginal cost often reflects variable cost. It is therefore reasonable for marginal cost to be below average cost when fixed costs are significant.

Bounds/context: bring in simple constraints. If the bill of materials is at least £2/unit, a marginal cost of £0.20/unit is suspicious; if labour and energy are also variable, £3 could be reasonable.

Misconception: “If marginal cost is lower than average cost, it must be wrong.” Correct: it often indicates economies of scale or fixed-cost dilution.

Probing question: “What business scenario could produce a negative marginal cost over a short range, and what evidence would you need to accept it?” (e.g., volume discount rebate applied at a threshold; check the contract terms and whether C includes rebates.)

slides.title: Practice and reflection: quick plausibility tests

content.title: Practice and reflection: quick plausibility tests
leftColumn: A) dQ/dt = 900 items/min for a manual line
B) ∫P dt = 30 kWh from an 8 kW device over 3 h
C) dC/dx = −£4/unit when output increases
D) ∫v dt gives 120, but you report it as m/s
rightColumn: Which check fails first: sign, trend, bounds, or units?
What minimum info would you request to verify it?
What correction would make it reproducible in Excel?
Write a 2–4 sentence interpretation for one scenario
content.notes:
Guide learners to respond systematically rather than guess.

A: Bounds/scale likely fails first; ask for time units (per second vs per minute), and whether 900 is per hour. Also check whether Q is items or “item-batches”.

B: Bounds fails: 8 kW × 3 h = 24 kWh max if 8 kW is a hard cap. Either the cap is wrong, time is longer, or units are inconsistent (maybe P in kW but time in minutes).

C: Sign plausibility: negative marginal cost needs a strong contextual story (rebates, error correction, or C includes net revenue). Ask to see raw data, definitions, and whether C is “net cost” after credits.

D: Units check: integral of velocity is distance (m), not m/s.

Encourage learners to write their answers as they would in a calculation log: short, explicit, and with units.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports both MCQs on marginal change, accumulation, and checks
MCQ focus: units, sign, bounds, and interpreting Excel outputs
Mistake: mixing s/min/h or kW/W without conversion
Mistake: rounding early; use full precision then round at end
Mistake: hidden Excel settings (Solver, iteration, manual calc)
Fix: document settings + formulas; provide a reproducible method
content.notes:
Explain how the formative quizzes test thinking, not just arithmetic: many questions are designed so that a wrong unit or sign leads to an obviously implausible conclusion.

Expand on “hidden settings”:
- Calculation mode set to Manual can leave stale results.
- Solver can retain constraints/options that change outputs.
- Iterative calculation (circular references) can change results if iteration limits differ.

Give learners a practical reproducibility checklist:
- Include screenshot or note of calculation mode.
- Avoid hard-coded numbers inside formulas where possible.
- Use named ranges or clearly labelled constants.

Probing question: “If someone cannot reproduce your answer, is it more likely a maths error or a process/documentation error?”

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Derivatives are rates; integrals are totals (rate vs accumulation)
Always check sign, scale, bounds, and trend before trusting outputs
Units algebra catches many errors quickly and reliably
Excel: use differences for marginal, trapezoids for accumulation
Document assumptions, units, rounding, and settings for audit
content.notes:

Invite learners to self-assess: “Could you defend your result to a sceptical colleague using at least two checks plus a units argument?” Encourage them to revisit the worked examples and rewrite the interpretation sentences in their own words.

If time, suggest a personal habit: whenever you compute a derivative/integral output, immediately write one line: “Value, units, and why it is plausible.” This builds the analysis mindset the module aims for.

Invite learners to self-assess: “Could you defend your result to a sceptical colleague using at least two checks plus a units argument?” Encourage them to revisit the worked examples and rewrite the interpretation sentences in their own words.

If time, suggest a personal habit: whenever you compute a derivative/integral output, immediately write one line: “Value, units, and why it is plausible.” This builds the analysis mindset the module aims for.

slides.title: Marginal change via derivatives

content.title: Marginal change via derivatives
content: If C(q) is total cost, then MC(q)=dC/dq
Units: if C is £ and q is units, MC is £/unit
Derivative is local: valid near the chosen q value
Sign matters: negative marginal needs explanation
Curvature matters: d²C/dq² shows rising or falling marginal
content.notes: Walk through meaning: the derivative is the slope of the cost curve at a point, not an average over a range. Link to economic interpretation: increasing marginal cost corresponds to convex total cost. Clarify that second derivative is not required for all tasks, but is a powerful plausibility lens. Mini-example: if C(q)=1000+5q then MC(q)=5 everywhere (constant marginal). If C(q)=1000+q^2 then MC(q)=2q (rises with q). Misconception to address: learners often treat MC(q) as an average cost; challenge with: “If average cost is £10/unit, can marginal be £2/unit? When might that happen?”

slides.title: Accumulation via definite integrals

content.title: Accumulation via definite integrals
content: If MC(q) is marginal cost, total change is ∫ MC(q) dq
Use limits: ∆C=∫[q1,q2] MC(q) dq
Units: (£/unit)×(unit)=£, so totals align
Antiderivative gives an exact value when available
Numerical integration provides a cross-check in Excel
content.notes: Explain the integral as “adding up many small marginal pieces” from q1 to q2. Emphasise that definite integrals produce a number with the correct total units; this is a key unit-consistency test. Clarify the role of the constant of integration: it cancels in a definite integral, but matters if reconstructing total cost from marginal plus a baseline. Probing questions: “If MC is roughly £12/unit across a 40-unit range, what ballpark total change do you expect?” and “How could an incorrect limit (swapping q1 and q2) show up in the sign of ∆C?”

slides.title: Rules you will use most

content.title: Rules you will use most
content.notes: Reinforce that polynomial terms are handled term-by-term, while exponentials “reproduce themselves” under differentiation/integration, scaled by b. Connect parameters to units: if q is measured in units of output, then b must have units of 1/unit so that bq is dimensionless (required for EXP). Common error: forgetting to multiply by b when differentiating EXP(bq), or forgetting to divide by b when integrating. Quick check: if b is small (e.g., 0.02), the exponential grows gently; if b is large (e.g., 2), it explodes quickly—does your context support that?

slides.title: Excel implementation essentials

content.title: Excel implementation essentials
content: Keep an Inputs block: q, parameters, and their units
Use POWER(q,n) or q^n; use EXP(b*q) for exponentials
Use absolute refs for parameters (e.g., $B$2) where needed
Display units beside outputs (not inside formulas)
Graph C(q) and MC(q) to spot shape errors early
content.notes: Explain a robust spreadsheet layout: separate inputs/parameters from outputs to reduce accidental edits and improve transparency. Encourage naming key cells (e.g., q, a, b) to make formulas readable, but caution learners to verify names map to the correct cells. Mention numeric stability: exponentials can overflow for large bq; set reasonable input ranges. Mini-example formula patterns: if q is in B5 and a in B2, a·q^2 is =$B$2*B5^2; k·EXP(bq) is =$B$3*EXP($B$4*B5). Probe: “If you copy this formula down a column, which references must stay fixed, and why?”

slides.title: Plausibility and validation checks

content.title: Plausibility and validation checks
content.notes: Explain each check with a concrete method. Finite difference: choose a small step h (e.g., 1 unit) and compute (C(q+h)−C(q−h))/(2h); it should be close to the analytic derivative if h is small and the function is smooth. Trapezoid: create a grid of q values from q1 to q2, compute MC at each, and sum Δq*(MC_i+MC_{i+1})/2 using SUMPRODUCT; it should match the antiderivative-based definite integral to within rounding/discretisation error. Misconceptions: (1) using too-large h and concluding the derivative is “wrong”; (2) using inconsistent Δq steps in trapezoid. Probe: “If your trapezoid estimate differs by 15%, is that more likely a grid issue, a formula error, or a units issue?”

slides.title: Calculation log for auditability

content.title: Calculation log for auditability
content: Record at least 6 entries, each dated/labelled
State parameter sources (given, assumed, or estimated)
Note units and any conversions (e.g., kWh to MWh)
Justify rounding choices and displayed precision
List checks performed and whether they passed
Document limitations and uncertainty clearly
content.notes: Describe the log as a short table in the spreadsheet (or a separate sheet) with columns such as: Step, Description, Value/Formula, Units, Source, Rationale. Provide a mini-example entry: “Assumed b=0.02 1/unit based on last quarter’s data; sensitivity to b tested at 0.015–0.025.” Emphasise that ‘limitations’ can be simple and honest: measurement error, model form uncertainty (polynomial vs exponential), and extrapolation beyond observed q. Probe: “Which assumption, if wrong, would most change your marginal value at q=100?”

slides.title: Example 1: polynomial cost and marginal cost

content.title: Example 1: polynomial cost and marginal cost
content: Total cost: C(q)=1200+8q+0.04q^2  (C in £)
Marginal: MC(q)=8+0.08q  (units: £/unit)
Excel: =8+0.08*q_cell
Sense-check: MC rises linearly as output increases
content.notes: Talk through interpretation: the fixed cost (£1200) disappears in the derivative; only variable components drive marginal cost. Highlight that the quadratic term creates increasing marginal cost, consistent with congestion or capacity strain. Show how to compute in Excel using cell references: if q is in B5, the marginal formula is =8+0.08*B5. Then ask learners to validate with finite difference: compute C(49), C(51) and estimate slope (C(51)−C(49))/2; it should be ~12. Common mistake: differentiating 0.04q^2 as 0.08q^2 (forgetting the power rule reduces exponent). Probing question: “What would MC be at q=0, and does that make operational sense?”

slides.speakerNotes: Talk through interpretation: the fixed cost (£1200) disappears in the derivative; only variable components drive marginal cost. Then ask learners to validate with finite difference: compute C(49), C(51) and estimate slope (C(51)−C(49))/2; it should be ~12. Common mistake: differentiating 0.04q^2 as 0.08q^2 (forgetting the power rule reduces exponent). Probing question: “What would MC be at q=0, and does that make operational sense?”

slides.title: Example 2: integrate marginal to total change

content.title: Example 2: integrate marginal to total change
content: Use MC(q)=8+0.08q to compute cost change
Antiderivative: 8q+0.04q^2, evaluate at 60 and 20
Trapezoid check on q grid should be close to 448 £
content.notes: Explain that we are computing change in total cost between two production levels, not total cost itself. Connect to the earlier C(q): because MC is the derivative of C, integrating MC over [20,60] must equal C(60)−C(20) (a strong consistency check). In Excel, demonstrate both methods: (1) exact: compute F(q)=8q+0.04q^2 in two cells and subtract; (2) trapezoid: set up q from 20 to 60 in steps (e.g., 5), compute MC at each q, then sum Δq*(MC_i+MC_{i+1})/2. Provide an explicit trapezoid pattern in words: “multiply step size by average of adjacent MC values, then sum.” Misconception: forgetting that limits matter and accidentally integrating from 60 to 20, producing −448. Probe: “If your trapezoid result is 430, is that acceptable? What step size would you change first?”

Provide an explicit trapezoid pattern in words: “multiply step size by average of adjacent MC values, then sum.” Misconception: forgetting that limits matter and accidentally integrating from 60 to 20, producing −448. Probe: “If your trapezoid result is 430, is that acceptable? What step size would you change first?”

slides.title: Example 3: exponential resource use and marginal

content.title: Example 3: exponential resource use and marginal
content: Energy use: E(q)=50*EXP(0.02q)  (kWh total)
Marginal: dE/dq=1*EXP(0.02q)  (kWh/unit)
At q=100: dE/dq=EXP(2)≈7.39 kWh/unit
Unit check: 0.02 must be in 1/unit so 0.02q is unitless
Shape check: E and dE/dq both increase; curvature is positive
content.notes: Explain why exponentials are used: compounding effects such as inefficiency growth or thermal losses can cause marginal use to rise faster than linearly. Show the differentiation carefully: derivative of 50*EXP(0.02q) is 50*0.02*EXP(0.02q)=1*EXP(0.02q). Stress the dimensional argument: EXP() requires a dimensionless input; therefore, if q is “units produced”, the 0.02 parameter must be “per unit produced”. In Excel: =50*EXP(0.02*B5) and derivative =EXP(0.02*B5). Validation idea: compute finite difference using E(101) and E(99), then compare to derivative at 100. Common mistake: writing EXP(0.02)*q, which changes the model entirely. Probe: “If you measured q in hundreds of units instead of units, what must happen to the 0.02 parameter?”

slides.title: Practice: build and test your spreadsheet

content.title: Practice: build and test your spreadsheet
content: Choose one polynomial and one exponential function with units
Compute marginal at two q values; interpret each meaningfully
Integrate marginal over an interval; state q1, q2 and units
Run 2 validations: finite-diff and trapezoid numerical check
Do unit checks on 3 formulas; fix any mismatches
Write a 6-entry calculation log with assumptions and limits
content.notes: Give guidance on selecting values: keep q in a realistic range to avoid extreme exponential values. Encourage learners to create a small dashboard cell that flags failures (e.g., “Derivative check error %”). Suggest a structure: Sheet 1 ‘Model’, Sheet 2 ‘Checks’, Sheet 3 ‘Log’. Probing questions for reflection: “Which check was most informative?” “Did your marginal values change more in the polynomial or exponential case?” “Where did units nearly go wrong (e.g., interpreting q in hours vs units)?” Common issue to pre-empt: learners compute an integral but forget it represents a change, not necessarily the full total from zero.

slides.title: Formative quizzes and common errors

content.title: Formative quizzes and common errors
leftColumn: Quiz 1: Marginal change & accumulation (Excel)
Quiz 2: Limits, units, reasonableness checks
Focus: interpreting outputs, not just computing
Show working: formulas, limits, and units
rightColumn: Forgetting b in d/dq of EXP(bq)
Missing limits or reversing q1 and q2
Unit mismatches (e.g., q in hours, b in 1/unit)
No validation: trusting one number without checks
content.notes: Position the quizzes as practice for disciplined modelling: correct calculus, correct spreadsheet logic, and correct interpretation. Explain that many errors are ‘silent’—Excel returns a number even when the model is wrong. Encourage learners to annotate: label axes on charts, label unit columns, and write the definite integral in the sheet near the calculation. Probing question: “If you could only do one validation check under time pressure, which would you choose and why?” Also note that assessment items often test conceptual traps: e.g., confusing average and marginal, or treating EXP parameter b as unitless.

slides.title: Key takeaways

content.title: Key takeaways
content: Derivatives give marginal change at a point with per-unit units
Definite integrals accumulate marginal values over explicit limits
Excel needs clear inputs, fixed references, and visible units
Plausibility + validation checks catch most modelling errors
A short log makes your work transparent and auditable
content.notes: Close by reinforcing the ‘analysis’ mindset: you are responsible for judging outputs, not merely producing them. Invite learners to revisit their spreadsheet and identify one improvement in clarity (labelling, units, structure) and one improvement in robustness (additional check, sensitivity). Final probing question: “What is your strongest piece of evidence that your marginal and total results are correct?”

content.title: MOD103 Calculus Essentials — Lesson 11
content.content: Derivative and integral outputs: plausibility and dimensional checks (1h 30m)
content.notes: Welcome. In this lesson we focus on interpreting the *outputs* of calculus—numbers from derivatives and integrals—in workplace settings such as cost, throughput, and energy use. The key shift is from “can I differentiate/integrate?” to “does this result make sense, with the right units, and within realistic operating ranges?”. Keep linking every output back to the original quantities and their units.

slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study
content: Interpret derivatives as marginal rates with correct units
Verify dimensional consistency for derivative and integral outputs
Apply at least two plausibility tests to calculus results
Complete a short calculation log with assumptions and limits
Critique and correct common interpretation errors
Sequence: learn → worked examples → practise → quizzes
content.notes: Aim to produce *complete sentences* that interpret results (not just calculations). A good workflow is: (1) identify what depends on what, (2) write units for each variable, (3) compute derivative/integral, (4) derive the output units, and (5) run plausibility checks. When you reach the quizzes, treat them as diagnostic: if you miss a question, identify whether the issue is (a) calculus procedure, (b) units, or (c) interpretation language. Probing question: if I hide the algebra and only show you a number with units, can you still explain what it means?

slides.title: Derivative outputs: marginal change

content.title: Derivative outputs: marginal change
content: Derivative: f'(x) is change in f per small change in x
Units: (units of f) ÷ (units of x)
Interpretation sentence: “At x=…, f changes by … per 1 x”
Use for marginal cost, marginal throughput, power (rate of energy)
Derivative is local; it need not match the average over a range
content.notes: A derivative value is a *marginal rate*: what happens “right now” at a specific operating point. Always attach the operating point (e.g., at 100 units/day). Units are your first defence against misinterpretation: if cost is £ and output is units, then marginal cost is £/unit. Common misconception: learners state “the cost is 12” instead of “the cost increases by £12 per additional unit”. Another misconception is treating a derivative as a total (e.g., calling £/unit a total cost). Probing questions: What is the dependent variable? What is the independent variable? If x increases by 1 (in its units), what happens to f?

slides.title: Integral outputs: accumulation over a range

content.title: Integral outputs: accumulation over a range
content: Integral: ∫ f(x) dx accumulates f across an interval of x
Units: (units of f) × (units of x)
Definite integral gives a total between two limits
Use for total energy from power, total cost from marginal cost
Integral is not a rate unless divided by the interval length
content.notes: An integral aggregates contributions over time, distance, or quantity produced. Emphasise the *limits*: totals depend on the interval (e.g., 0 to 8 hours). Units flip compared with derivatives: if power is kW and time is h, then energy is kWh. A very common error is saying “the integral is the rate”; it is the *total*, unless you explicitly compute an average by dividing by the interval width. Probing question: if we double the time interval while holding the rate similar, should the integral roughly double?

slides.title: Quick unit rules for calculus outputs

content.title: Quick unit rules for calculus outputs
content.notes: This table is your ‘dimensional consistency checklist’. Before trusting any result, derive the output units *from first principles*. Notice the pattern: derivatives reduce a dimension (divide by the independent variable’s unit), integrals add a dimension (multiply by it). If the units do not match the story you are telling, something is wrong—either the model, the variables, or the interpretation. Mini-example: if someone reports ∫P dt in “kW”, you can immediately flag the mismatch because integrating a rate over time cannot stay a rate.

slides.title: Plausibility tests for derivative and integral results

content.title: Plausibility tests for derivative and integral results
content: Sign check: should it be positive, negative, or zero here?
Magnitude: compare with typical operating ranges or benchmarks
Boundary behaviour: what happens at x=0, max capacity, long time?
Compare to average rate over a nearby interval
Cross-check with a simple estimate or graph shape
content.notes: Plausibility is about reasoning, not perfection. Use at least two tests each time. Sign: if producing more should not reduce total cost (in your context), a negative marginal cost is suspicious and needs explanation (e.g., rebates, by-product sales). Magnitude: if marginal cost is £12/unit but average is £2/unit, ask why—maybe high fixed costs distort the average, or maybe an algebra/units slip occurred. Boundary behaviour: does your model predict nonsense at q=0 or very large q? If so, record the valid range. Probing questions: If you increase output slightly, would costs really fall? If time goes to zero, should accumulated energy go to zero?

slides.title: Transparent reporting: the calculation log

content.title: Transparent reporting: the calculation log
content: State variables, units, and operating point (e.g., q=100 units)
Record data sources and any conversions (min, h, kW, kWh)
Write assumptions (steady conditions, valid range, linearity)
Note rounding choices and intermediate precision
Add at least one uncertainty/limitation statement
content.notes: A calculation log is how you make your work auditable. Imagine a colleague revisiting your result in six months: they need to know what you assumed and what you ignored. Examples of limitations: “Model fitted on q=50–150 only; extrapolation beyond 150 may be unreliable” or “Power readings sampled every 30 minutes; short spikes are not captured”. Rounding: keep extra precision during calculations, round at the end, and record the rounding rule. Probing question: what piece of missing information would most change your conclusion?

slides.title: Worked example: marginal cost at a throughput level

content.title: Worked example: marginal cost at a throughput level
content: Model: C(q)=500+8q+0.02q², C in £, q in units
Differentiate: C'(q)=8+0.04q (marginal cost)
Interpret: “At 100 units, +1 unit raises cost by ~£12”
Plausibility: MC > 0 and rises with q due to q² term
content.notes: Walk through the modelling meaning: £500 is fixed cost, 8q is linear variable cost, and 0.02q² captures increasing marginal costs (e.g., overtime, inefficiency). Show that C'(q) inherits units £/unit. Emphasise the approximation language: the derivative describes a *small* change near q=100, not a jump of 50 units. Check reasoning: since the quadratic term is positive, marginal cost increases as q increases; that matches many real systems approaching capacity. Probe: what would C'(q) be at q=0, and does that make sense for your context?

slides.title: Worked example: energy rate vs total energy

content.title: Worked example: energy rate vs total energy
leftColumn: Rate model: P(t)=3+0.5t kW
At t=2 h: P(2)=4 kW
Meaning: instant power draw at 2 hours
Units check: kW is kWh per hour
rightColumn: Total energy: E=∫₀² P(t) dt
E=∫₀² (3+0.5t) dt=7 kWh
Meaning: energy used during first 2 hours
Units check: kW×h = kWh
content.notes: Use this to cement the difference between a rate and an accumulation. Power (kW) tells you how fast energy is being used; energy (kWh) tells you how much was used over a period. Derive E explicitly: ∫(3+0.5t)dt = 3t + 0.25t²; evaluate from 0 to 2 gives 6 + 1 = 7 kWh. Common errors to address: (1) reporting the integral in kW, (2) describing P(2)=4 kW as ‘4 kWh used’, and (3) forgetting limits on the definite integral. Probe: if we extended the interval to 4 hours, should energy be more than double 7 kWh, and why?

rows: Valid for q≥0; grows with q

Supports: MCQ on limits, units, and reasonableness checks

slides.title: Summary: what to do with calculus outputs

content.title: Summary: what to do with calculus outputs
content: Derivatives give marginal rates: change per unit of input
Integrals give totals: accumulated quantity over an interval
Units come from divide (derivative) or multiply (integral)
Plausibility: check sign, magnitude, boundaries, vs averages
Report transparently: assumptions, sources, rounding, limits
content.notes: The overall skill is critical interpretation: you are validating that a calculus output is meaningful, correctly dimensioned, and credible. Build the habit of writing the interpretation sentence immediately after computing a value, then running at least two reasonableness checks before you move on. content.title: Lesson 12: Differentiate and integrate functions
content: Programme: Maths Certification

slides.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson
content: Compute derivatives and definite integrals for given functions

Study flow: read → worked examples → build in Excel → self-check

Explain that the lesson is structured to mirror real workflow: (1) do the calculus symbolically so you know the “ground truth”, (2) implement in Excel so it is reproducible, (3) validate so errors are caught early.

slides.title: Derivatives as marginal change

content.title: Derivatives as marginal change
content: Derivative = instantaneous rate of change of a function
If C(q) is cost, C'(q) is marginal cost at output q
Interpret C'(q) as slope of the tangent to C(q)
Derivative units: (cost units) per (output unit)
Polynomials: use the power rule term-by-term
Exponentials: d/dx[e^{kx}] = k e^{kx}
content.notes:
Talk through why marginal cost is a derivative: it answers “how much extra cost for a very small increase in output right now?” Distinguish marginal from average: average cost is C(q)/q; marginal is C'(q).

Mini-example (mental maths): If C(q)=q^2, then C'(q)=2q. At q=10, marginal cost is 20 (cost per unit). Ask: is that the same as average cost (which would be 10)? No.

Units are your first defence against nonsense: if q is in tonnes and C is in £, then C'(q) must be £/tonne. If your spreadsheet shows £, something is wrong.

Common misconceptions:
- Differentiating a constant incorrectly (it becomes 0).
- Forgetting the chain rule factor k in e^{kx}.
- Interpreting marginal cost as the cost of the “next full unit” rather than a local rate.

slides.title: Integrals as accumulation (definite integrals)

content.title: Integrals as accumulation (definite integrals)
content: Definite integral accumulates a rate over an interval
If r(t) is rate, ∫a^b r(t) dt gives total from a to b
Bounds matter: reversing bounds changes the sign
Integral units: (rate units) × (time/output units)
FTC link: ∫a^b f'(x)dx = f(b) − f(a)
Include constants correctly when finding antiderivatives
content.notes:
Frame integrals as “adding up” continuously: area under a curve with a purpose. If r(t) is kWh per hour (kW), integrating over hours gives kWh.

Explain the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) as a powerful cross-check: if you can integrate C'(q), you should get C(b)−C(a) (up to any fixed-cost constants).

Probing questions:
- If the rate is always positive, what must be true about the total integral?
- If the time interval doubles, what would you expect to happen to the total, approximately?

Common misconceptions:
- Dropping bounds (doing an indefinite integral when a definite total is required).
- Forgetting to evaluate the antiderivative at both bounds.
- Confusing “total cost” with “change in cost” when a fixed cost is present.

slides.title: Rules for polynomial and exponential functions

content.title: Rules for polynomial and exponential functions
content.content: Use these rules to compute marginal (derivative) and total (integral).
content.notes:
Use the table as a “pattern library”. For polynomials, emphasise term-by-term processing: learners often try to apply the power rule to an entire sum.

For exponentials, stress the chain rule: derivative of e^{kx} is not e^{kx}; it is k e^{kx}. Similarly, integration divides by k.

Mini-checks:
- If k is small (e.g., 0.03), then growth is gentle; derivatives should reflect that.
- If n is 2, power rule gives 2x, not x^2.

Common misconception: confusing e^{kx} with k^x (different function entirely). If the model is written with e, keep it as exp() in Excel to avoid formatting ambiguity.

slides.title: Plausibility checks for calculus outputs

content.title: Plausibility checks for calculus outputs
leftColumn: Units/dimensions
Sign and magnitude
Numerical cross-check
rightColumn: Do units match the question (e.g., £/unit, kWh)?
Is result sensible vs inputs and context?
Approximate with finite differences / trapezoids
content.notes:
Make clear that checking is not optional: in applied settings, the main skill is detecting when a result cannot be right.

1) Units/dimensions: treat units like algebra. If you integrate a rate, you must multiply by the interval’s unit. If you differentiate cost by output, you must get cost per output.

2) Sign and magnitude: if cost increases with output, marginal cost should not be negative over the relevant range. Magnitude check: compare marginal cost to average cost and to neighbouring values.

3) Numerical cross-check: use a small step h and compute (C(q+h)−C(q))/h, or use trapezoidal accumulation in Excel for integrals. The symbolic and numerical results should be close when h is small.

Probing questions:
- If your derivative says marginal cost is £0.02/unit at high output, what business story could justify it?
- If your integral produces a negative total energy use, which assumption is most likely wrong: bounds, sign, or units?

slides.title: Worked example: polynomial cost model

content.title: Worked example: polynomial cost model
content: Model: C(q)=5q^2+20q+100 (£), q in units
Marginal cost: C'(q)=10q+20 (£/unit)
Change in cost 10→30: ∫10^30 (10q+20)dq
Antiderivative: 5q^2+20q, evaluate 10 and 30
content.notes:
Walk slowly through each step and narrate the meaning:
- C(q) includes a fixed cost of 100. When we compute C(30)−C(10), the fixed cost cancels, which is why the change is based on variable terms.
- The derivative gives marginal cost at a point; the definite integral of marginal cost across a range gives the change in total cost across that range.

Highlight the FTC cross-check explicitly: since C'(q) is the derivative of C(q), ∫ C'(q)dq over [10,30] must equal C(30)−C(10). If it does not, there is an algebra mistake.

Common pitfalls to surface:
- Differentiating 20q as 20q (it should be 20).
- Integrating 10q as 10q^2 (missing the 1/2 factor).
- Forgetting that bounds 10→30 represent a change; starting from 0 would answer a different question.

Probing question: What does it mean if MC at q=30 is 320 but average cost at q=30 is much smaller? (Answer: costs are accelerating; later units are more expensive.)

slides.title: Worked example: exponential rate and accumulation

content.title: Worked example: exponential rate and accumulation
content: Rate model: r(t)=200e^(0.03t) (units/hour), t in hours
Rate change: r'(t)=6e^(0.03t) (units/hour^2)
Total output 0→8: Q=∫0^8 200e^(0.03t) dt
Check: Q positive and near 200×8=1600 (growth increases total)
content.notes:
Explain the modelling choice: r(t) is an instantaneous rate (like throughput per hour). Integrating gives total produced over the time window.

Emphasise the chain rule/integration factor: derivative multiplies by 0.03; integral divides by 0.03. Learners often forget this and end up off by a factor of ~33.

Do the plausibility check in words:
- If the rate were constant at 200 units/hour for 8 hours, total would be 1600.
- Because the rate increases over time (positive exponent), total should be higher than 1600, so ~1807 is plausible.

Units check:
- r(t): units/hour.
- dt: hour.
- Integral: units (hours cancel).

Probing questions:
- What would Q be if the exponent were negative (decay)?
- If you accidentally used e^(0.3t), how would your plausibility check reveal the mistake?

slides.title: Excel implementation patterns (reproducible formulas)

content.title: Excel implementation patterns (reproducible formulas)
content.content: Use labelled inputs and consistent references for transparency.

rows: k in B1, A in B2
Absolute for params, relative for t

content.notes:
Coach spreadsheet hygiene as a mathematical skill:
- Put every parameter (A, k, coefficients, bounds) in its own input cell with a unit label.
- Use absolute references ($B$1) for parameters so copying formulas does not silently change assumptions.
- Use relative references (A5) for time/output values so the model scales down the sheet.

Explain why numerical methods appear here: even when you can integrate symbolically, trapezoids provide a robust cross-check and also handle cases where no simple antiderivative is used in the module.

Common spreadsheet misconceptions:
- Hard-coding constants inside formulas prevents auditing.
- Rounding intermediate values can significantly distort derivatives and integrals.
- Misaligned ranges in SUMPRODUCT produce plausible-looking but wrong totals.

Probing questions:
- If you copy the r(t) formula down, which parts must stay fixed?
- How would you modify trapezoids if time steps are not equal?

slides.title: Debugging a flawed Excel model: common errors

content.title: Debugging a flawed Excel model: common errors
content: Units mismatch (e.g., minutes in t but k per hour)
Wrong bounds (integrating 0→b when asked a→b)
Hard-coded constants inside formulas
Relative refs used for parameters (copied wrong)
Early rounding hides errors and distorts slopes
EXP used incorrectly (e.g., EXP(k)*t not EXP(k*t))
content.notes:
Present debugging as systematic, not guesswork. Encourage a repeatable sequence:
1) Check units first (most powerful filter).
2) Check signs and monotonicity (should the curve rise or fall?).
3) Cross-check a few rows manually (spot check).
4) Replace complex formulas with helper cells (make logic visible).

Expand each error with a quick illustration:
- Minutes vs hours: if t is in minutes but k is per hour, the exponent is 60× too large.
- Wrong bounds: a total over 10→30 is a change; 0→30 answers a different operational question.
- EXP misuse: EXP(k)*t implies linear scaling after exponentiation; EXP(k*t) is exponential growth/decay.

Probing questions:
- Which of these errors would still produce ‘reasonable-looking’ numbers?
- How can you structure your sheet so bounds cannot be missed (e.g., named cells a, b)?

content.notes:

content: Derivative models marginal change; units reveal meaning

content.title: Derivative and integral outputs: plausibility & units
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD103 — Calculus Essentials: Marginal Change and Accumulation
Lesson 13 (1h 30m)
content.notes: Position this lesson as a bridge between “doing calculus” and “trusting calculus outputs”. Emphasise the workplace focus: throughput, cost, and energy are common contexts where the wrong choice (differentiate vs integrate) leads to believable-looking but wrong answers. Remind learners that Bloom’s level here is analyse: they will justify method choice, check dimensional consistency, and critique plausibility (not just compute).
