slides.title: Orientation: objectives and study route

content.title: Orientation: objectives and study route
leftColumn: 1. Choose diff vs integ; justify with rate vs accumulation
2. Compute derivative/integral units with 100% consistency
3. Check plausibility: sign, size, domain, boundaries
4. Produce an audit-trail calculation log (5+ entries)
rightColumn: Watch/read: concepts and decision rules
Work through: three short worked examples
Practise: quick scenarios + self-check prompts
Check: MCQs (incl. Excel) and review mistakes
content.notes: Explain how to use the lesson in a self-study pattern: (1) understand the decision rule (rate vs accumulation), (2) confirm units before trusting any number, (3) apply plausibility checks, (4) document decisions as if another analyst must audit the work. Probing questions: What is the “thing that changes”? What is it changing with respect to? If time doubled, should the output double (accumulation) or change in another way (rate)? Misconception to address: learners often treat derivatives and integrals as purely symbolic operations, forgetting they encode a physical/economic interpretation.

slides.title: Core idea: rate of change vs accumulation

content.title: Core idea: rate of change vs accumulation
leftColumn: Differentiate to get a rate at a point
Inputs: a quantity as a function of x
Outputs: per-unit-x change
Language: marginal, instantaneous, sensitivity
rightColumn: Integrate to get an accumulated total over x
Inputs: a rate as a function of x
Outputs: total amount added up
Language: total, cumulative, area under the curve
content.notes: Make the conceptual contrast explicit: derivative answers “how fast is it changing now?”; integral answers “how much has built up over an interval?”. Mini-examples: If C(q) is total cost in £, then dC/dq is £ per unit (marginal cost). If P(t) is power in kW, then ∫P(t)dt over hours is energy in kWh. Probing questions: When you report the result, does it need ‘per hour’ (derivative) or not (integral)? Common misconception: “integration undoes differentiation” is true algebraically but not a decision rule; the modelling question determines the operation.

slides.title: Core tool: method choice in 3 questions

content.title: Core tool: method choice in 3 questions
content: Is the given quantity already a rate (per time, per unit)?
Do you need a point rate or a total over an interval?
What are the input and output units expected in the report?
If x increases, should the result accumulate or respond instantly?
Do boundaries matter (0 to T, q1 to q2)? State them.
Write a 2–3 sentence justification before calculating.
content.notes: Walk learners through a disciplined pre-calculation routine. Example prompt: “We are given throughput r(t) in items/hour and asked for items produced between 09:00 and 12:00; this is accumulation, so integrate r(t) from 9 to 12.” Then contrast: “We are given total energy E(t) in kWh and asked for instantaneous power at 10:00; power is the rate of change of energy, so differentiate E(t).” Misconception: confusing average rate over an interval with instantaneous rate at a point—reinforce that averages use Δ/Δ, not d/d.

slides.title: Core idea: units of derivatives and integrals

content.title: Core idea: units of derivatives and integrals

rows: y in U as f(x in V)
Rate r in U per V

content.notes: Emphasise that units are a built-in error detector: if the units do not match the intended quantity, the method is wrong or something is missing (such as a time conversion). Clarify the constant-factor point: a dimensionless constant changes the size, not the unit; a constant with units changes the unit (e.g., tariff converts kWh to £). Probing questions: If x is measured in minutes but you thought hours, what happens to the units and magnitude? Common misconception: treating “dx” as decorative—reinforce it carries the unit of x.

slides.title: Core workflow: dimensional consistency check

content.title: Core workflow: dimensional consistency check
content: Step 1: Declare units for every variable and parameter
Step 2: Confirm x-unit in the derivative/integral (dx)
Step 3: Compute output units symbolically (before numbers)
Step 4: Convert units once, explicitly (e.g., min to h)
Step 5: Re-check units after simplification and rounding
Fail fast: if units mismatch, stop and fix the model
content.notes: Teach this as a repeatable workflow learners can apply in Excel or by hand. Mini-example: If r(t)=120 items/hour and you integrate over t in minutes, you must convert: items/hour × minutes = items·minutes/hour, not items—so convert minutes to hours (divide by 60). Probing questions: Where in your working did the unit conversion occur? Can another person locate it quickly? Misconception: assuming spreadsheets “handle units automatically”; they do not unless you enforce conversions.

slides.title: Core idea: plausibility checklist for outputs

content.title: Core idea: plausibility checklist for outputs

rows: Using t<0 or q outside spec

content.notes: Explain plausibility as an analysis skill, not guesswork. Encourage learners to build a “sanity range” from context: a small machine cannot consume industrial-scale energy; costs should not be negative if fixed costs exist; throughput cannot be negative unless modelling returns/defects explicitly. Probing questions: What is the maximum possible throughput given capacity? What happens at the start time—should the model allow an instantaneous jump? Misconception: believing a mathematically valid expression is automatically physically valid—domain and boundaries encode reality constraints.

slides.title: Worked example 1: choose derivative or integral

content.title: Worked example 1: choose derivative or integral
content: Given: P(t)=1.2+0.3t kW, t in hours from start
Task A: energy used from t=0 to t=4
Task B: power increase rate at t=4
A uses ∫ P(t) dt (accumulation over time)
B uses dP/dt (rate of change of power)
content.notes: Talk through the interpretation before any calculus: power is already a rate (kW = kJ/s up to scaling), so integrating over time gives energy. For Task A: ∫0^4 (1.2+0.3t) dt = [1.2t+0.15t^2]0^4 = 4.8+2.4 = 7.2 kWh. Highlight units: kW·h = kWh. For Task B: dP/dt = 0.3 kW per hour (kW/h), constant; at t=4 it is still 0.3 kW/h. Probing question: If time interval doubles, should energy roughly double? Yes, accumulation suggests so (subject to changing rate). Common misconception: differentiating to get energy because “energy is related to power”; correct relation is E is the integral of P over time.

slides.title: Worked example 2: units for 4 expressions

content.title: Worked example 2: units for 4 expressions
content.notes: Work line-by-line and insist learners say the units out loud. (1) C(q) is a total; differentiating gives a per-unit quantity. (2) r(t) is a rate; integrating over time returns a total count. (3) E(t) already has accumulated units; differentiating returns a rate again, and show the equivalence kWh/h = kW (important for interpreting results). (4) The 0.8 factor is dimensionless; it scales energy but does not change units—contrast with multiplying by a tariff like 0.30 £/kWh, which would convert energy to cost in £. Probing question: Which of these results could sensibly be negative, and under what modelling assumptions (e.g., net flow could be negative)? Common misconception: writing “kW/h” when you mean “kWh” (rate vs accumulation confusion).

slides.title: Worked example 3: spotting flaws in outputs

content.title: Worked example 3: spotting flaws in outputs
content: Flaw 1: ∫0^2 r(t)dt gives negative total with r(t)≥0
Flaw 2: Units end as £·hours (missing conversion or dx unit)
Flaw 3: Used q=-5 in cost model valid only for q≥0
Flaw 4: Derivative spikes at t=0 but system starts smoothly
Flaw 5: Magnitude off by ×60 (minutes treated as hours)
content.notes: Present these as typical errors from real submissions. For Flaw 1, remind learners: if the integrand is non-negative over the interval, the definite integral cannot be negative; the error is often reversed limits or a sign slip. For Flaw 2, explain that “£·hours” indicates you integrated a £ value with respect to time without a justification—perhaps you meant integrate a £/hour rate. For Flaw 3, emphasise domain: models are conditional on assumptions (e.g., q is quantity produced, cannot be negative). For Flaw 4, connect boundary behaviour to physical reality: a spike may indicate division by (t) or a log at 0; you may need a shifted model or a domain restriction t>0. For Flaw 5, highlight the classic time-base conversion mistake and show how to detect it via magnitude and units. Probing question: Which flaw would you catch first if you only had 10 seconds? Encourage: check units and sign first.

content: 1) Given cost rate £/hour: find total cost over 8 hours

slides.title: Marginal change vs accumulation (with units)

content.title: Marginal change vs accumulation (with units)
leftColumn: C(q): total cost as a function of quantity q
C′(q): marginal cost (rate of change of cost)
Units: if C is £ and q is units, C′ is £/unit
Interpretation: slope of C at a specific q
rightColumn: r(q): rate function (e.g., energy per unit)
∫ r(q) dq: total accumulation over quantities
Units: if r is kWh/unit, integral is kWh
Interpretation: area under r from q1 to q2
content.notes: Clarify the conceptual difference: derivatives describe instantaneous rate (marginal), integrals describe total accumulation over an interval. Emphasise dimensional analysis: units should transform predictably (differentiate divides by q-units; integrate multiplies by q-units). Mini-example: If C(q) is in £ and q in tonnes, then C′(q) must be £/tonne; if you see £·tonne, it is wrong. Misconception to address: learners often treat C′(q) as a ‘new cost function’ without relating it back to slope/rate. Ask: “If marginal cost is rising with q, what does that imply about economies of scale?”

slides.title: Differentiation rules you will use most

content.title: Differentiation rules you will use most
content.notes: Walk through why each rule holds at a practical level. For exponentials, emphasise the chain rule constant k and its units: if q is ‘units produced’, then k must be 1/unit so that kq is dimensionless. Common error: differentiating e^(kq) as e^(kq) (forgetting the k). Another common error: confusing e^(kq) with k^q; highlight that b^q is differentiated using ln(b). Probing question: “If k has units of 1/unit, what does a larger k do to the curvature of the cost function?”

slides.title: Integration rules for totals over an interval

content.title: Integration rules for totals over an interval
content.notes: Explain integrals as ‘total change’ and as ‘area under the curve’. Reinforce the definite integral process: find antiderivative, then apply bounds, not the other way around. Emphasise the constant of integration is irrelevant for definite integrals but matters for indefinite ones. Common misconception: learners sometimes divide by k incorrectly (multiplying instead). Quick check: differentiate your antiderivative to see if you recover r(q). Probing question: “If r(q) is always positive on [q1,q2], what must be true about the definite integral?”

slides.title: Implement derivatives in Excel (fill down safely)

content.title: Implement derivatives in Excel (fill down safely)
content: Put q values in a column (e.g., A2:A102)
Enter C(q) in B using cell references to q
Enter C′(q) in C using the analytic derivative formula
Use $ for constants (absolute references) where needed
Check first and last rows after filling down
Label units in headers (e.g., £, units, £/unit)
content.notes: Demonstrate best practice spreadsheet structure: one column per concept (q, C, C′). Explain relative vs absolute referencing: constants such as a, k, n should live in named cells (e.g., E2:E4) and be referenced as $E$2 so fill-down does not drift. Mini-example: if C(q)=a q^2 + b, and a is in $E$2, formula in B2 could be =$E$2*A2^2 + $E$3. Then C′(q)=2a q becomes =2*$E$2*A2. Probing question: “If you copy the derivative formula down and it changes ‘a’ to the next row, how will the error show up in the marginal column?”

slides.title: Worked example 1: polynomial cost and marginal cost

content.title: Worked example 1: polynomial cost and marginal cost
content: Given C(q)=1200+8q+0.02q^2  (C in £, q in units)
Differentiate: C′(q)=8+0.04q  (units £/unit)
Excel (q in A2): =8+0.04*A2
Sanity check: C′ increases linearly with q
Boundary check: at q=0, C′(0)=8
content.notes: Walk the class through each term: constant differentiates to 0, 8q to 8, 0.02q^2 to 0.04q. Emphasise how units behave: 0.02 has units £/unit^2 so that 0.02q^2 yields £; therefore 0.04q yields £/unit. Ask learners to interpret: “Why might marginal cost rise with output?” (e.g., capacity constraints, overtime). Common mistake: forgetting that 2×0.02=0.04. Excel note: use decimal constants carefully and consider storing 0.02 in a cell to reduce transcription errors. Validation prompt: “Does it make sense that marginal cost at q=0 is £8/unit even though there is a fixed cost of £1200?”

slides.title: Worked example 2: exponential rate and total over [q1,q2]

content.title: Worked example 2: exponential rate and total over [q1,q2]
content: Given r(q)=3e^(0.01q)  (kWh/unit), q in units
Integrate: R(q)=300e^(0.01q)  (kWh)
Excel analytic: =300*(EXP(0.01*q2)-EXP(0.01*q1))
Units check: (kWh/unit)×(unit)=kWh
Sign check: r(q)>0 ⇒ total must be >0
content.notes: Explain the chain rule in reverse for integration: ∫3e^(0.01q)dq = 3/0.01 e^(0.01q) = 300e^(0.01q). Highlight that 0.01 must have units 1/unit so the exponent is dimensionless. Stress careful handling of bounds and that the result is a total energy amount in kWh. Probing questions: “If q2 increases, what happens to the total—linearly or faster?” “If you mistakenly used 3*EXP(0.01*q) without dividing by 0.01, how would the magnitude look compared to expectations?”

slides.title: Verify by trapezoidal rule in Excel

content.title: Verify by trapezoidal rule in Excel
content: Create q grid: q0, q1, …, qn with step h
Compute r(qi) in a column using EXP()
Trapezoid: total ≈ h*[0.5r0 + r1 + … + 0.5rn]
Excel pattern: =h*(0.5*B2 + SUM(B3:Bn) + 0.5*B(n+1))
Compare to analytic: discrepancy shrinks as h decreases
Explain mismatch: curvature and step size drive error
content.notes: Explain trapezoidal rule as approximating the area under r(q) with trapezia. Emphasise that for convex functions like exponentials, trapezoidal rule tends to overestimate (though the direction can depend on curvature; for convex, trapezoids lie above the curve). Encourage learners to test two step sizes (e.g., h=10 and h=1) and observe convergence towards the analytic result. Common spreadsheet pitfall: mixing h units or forgetting the 0.5 weights at endpoints. Probing questions: “If your trapezoidal estimate is wildly different, what are the first three things you check?” (grid spacing, endpoint weights, referencing the right range).

slides.title: Plausibility checks for derivative and integral outputs

content.title: Plausibility checks for derivative and integral outputs
leftColumn: Units/dimensions match labels and expectations
Sign: positive/negative aligns with the context
Monotonicity: trends match the function shape
Boundary values: check q=0 and at stated limits
rightColumn: Order of magnitude: compare to a rough estimate
Cross-check: derivative vs finite differences ΔC/Δq
Cross-check: analytic integral vs trapezoidal estimate
Graph: quick plot exposes many errors immediately
content.notes: Teach validation as a repeatable habit, not an optional extra. Give a quick finite-difference check: approximate C′(q) ≈ [C(q+h)−C(q)]/h for small h and compare to the analytic derivative value; they should be close if implemented correctly. Emphasise boundary checking: if C(q) is total cost, C(q) should rarely be negative; if r(q) is a rate, it should not flip sign unless justified. Encourage plotting: a chart of q vs C, q vs C′, and q vs cumulative integral often reveals reference errors, incorrect exponents, and sign mistakes. Probing question: “Which check would catch a missing ‘0.01’ in EXP(0.01q) fastest?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-paced prompts)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-paced prompts)
content: Differentiate: C(q)=500+12q−0.03q^2 (interpret units)
Find q where C′(q)=0 and explain the meaning
Integrate: r(q)=2q+5 from q=10 to q=40
In Excel, compare analytic vs trapezoid with h=5
List two checks you used and what they confirmed

content.notes: Guide learners to treat these as short ‘lab tasks’. For the polynomial, note the negative quadratic term implies marginal cost falls with q after some point; ask whether that is realistic and what model limitations might be. For C′(q)=0, discuss interpretation: stationary point in total cost vs marginal cost; be careful—depending on context, it could indicate a minimum/maximum or a modelling artefact outside valid range. For the integral, encourage doing it both by hand and in Excel to reinforce process. slides.title: Assessment connection and common errors to avoid

content.title: Assessment connection and common errors to avoid
content: Supports: MCQ on marginal change and accumulation (Excel)
Supports: MCQ on limits, units and reasonableness checks
Avoid: missing chain-rule constants in exponentials
Avoid: misapplied $ references when filling down formulas
Avoid: mixing q units (e.g., items vs thousands of items)
Avoid: reporting totals without stating interval [q1,q2]
content.notes: Explain how quiz items typically test both method and interpretation: correct derivative/integral form, correct units, and correct reading of Excel output. Probing questions: “When would average cost over [q1,q2] be more meaningful than marginal cost at q2?” “How could a unit conversion error hide inside a plausible-looking chart?”

slides.title: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver

content.title: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD104 — Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver
Lesson 1 | Duration: 1h 30m | Bloom’s level: Analyse
content.notes:
Introduce the purpose of the lesson: translating an operational problem into a transparent Excel model and using Solver to obtain and interpret an optimum.

Position this within MOD104: we are not doing calculus here; we are operationalising optimisation concepts in a spreadsheet and learning to justify results with evidence (constraints, slack, sensitivity outputs).

Prompt learners: “When you see a business decision with limits, what are the controllables (decisions) and what are the limits (constraints)?” Emphasise that most errors come from model structure (units, wrong cell ranges) rather than the Solver button itself.

slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study
content: Label decision variables, objective and 3+ constraints with units
Configure Solver: objective, variable cells, constraints, method
Check feasibility numerically; identify binding vs non-binding
Use Sensitivity: shadow price and reduced cost with valid ranges
Create a reproducible log: assumptions, units, rounding choices
Workflow: read → build → solve → interpret → quiz checks
content.notes:
Frame these as practical competencies. Learners should be able to open a blank workbook and produce a model that another person can audit.

Clarify what “analyse” means here: not just obtaining a number, but diagnosing what drives the solution (bottlenecks, trade-offs, marginal values).

Encourage an iterative approach: first build a correct calculation model (formulas), then use Solver, then interpret and document. If Solver fails, you return to structure and units rather than repeatedly changing methods.

Probing questions:
- “Where in your sheet can someone see: what we can choose, what we want, what limits us?”
- “If I changed one availability by 1 unit, can you predict the impact direction before running Solver?”

slides.title: What Solver is doing (conceptually)

content.title: What Solver is doing (conceptually)
content: Chooses values for decision variables within allowed bounds
Maximises or minimises a single objective cell
Satisfies constraints expressed as equalities/inequalities
Assumes a model form: linear, smooth nonlinear, or heuristic
Returns an optimal solution if the model is well-specified
content.notes:
Explain Solver as an optimisation engine that searches feasible solutions (those meeting constraints) and improves the objective.

Stress the dependency: Solver only “knows” your model through formulas. If formulas are wrong, Solver will optimise the wrong thing perfectly.

Clarify model classes:
- Linear (Simplex LP): objective and constraints are linear in variables.
- Nonlinear (GRG): differentiable nonlinear relationships.
- Heuristic (Evolutionary): complex or non-smooth problems; slower and less certain.

Common misconception: “Solver is broken” when it is actually an infeasible model (constraints cannot all be satisfied) or inconsistent units.

Ask: “What would make a solution infeasible in your scenario?” (e.g., demanding more resources than available).

slides.title: From maths model to Excel layout

content.title: From maths model to Excel layout
leftColumn: Decision variables: quantities we control
Objective: measure to maximise/minimise
Constraints: limits that must hold
Non-negativity / integrality (if required)
rightColumn: Variable cells (one cell per decision)
Objective cell using SUMPRODUCT
LHS calculations compared to RHS limits
Tick “Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative”
content.notes:
Walk through translation: each mathematical symbol needs a clear cell location.

Decision variables: typically a small block of cells, labelled with units (e.g., units/week). Keep them separate from data.

Objective: build from data and variables. For linear product mix, objective is often profit = SUMPRODUCT(profit per unit, units).

Constraints: compute left-hand side usage (e.g., labour hours used) using SUMPRODUCT of coefficients and units; compare to right-hand side availability.

Non-negativity is usually required (you cannot produce negative units). Integrality is only needed when fractional decisions are impossible (e.g., whole staff). Warn that integer constraints make problems harder.

Probing question: “If I change a decision variable by 1, which cells should change, and which should not?”

slides.title: Units, assumptions, and a calculation log

content.title: Units, assumptions, and a calculation log
content: State units for every row/column (hrs, kg, £, units/week)
List assumptions (e.g., constant profit per unit, no wastage)
Keep inputs, decisions, and outputs in separate sections
Use named ranges or clear labels to reduce range mistakes
Record rounding policy and whether variables must be integers
content.notes:
Emphasise reproducibility: a reviewer should be able to follow the logic without asking you what a cell means.

Explain why units matter: mixing “minutes” and “hours” silently invalidates constraints. Encourage writing units directly in adjacent cells.

Examples of assumptions to log:
- Linear proportionality: resource usage scales with units produced.
- Coefficients are stable across the relevant range.
- No set-up times, no volume discounts, no interaction effects.

Common misconception: “Assumptions are optional.” In optimisation, assumptions define the model’s validity; without them, results are not defensible.

Practical tip: Add a small “Model log” box with date, version, and key assumptions. Ask: “Could someone rebuild the model from your sheet alone?”

slides.title: Configuring Solver: the essential settings

content.title: Configuring Solver: the essential settings

rows: Selecting a label cell, not the formula cell
Including constraint LHS cells as variables
Wrong direction (<= vs >=) or mismatched units
Using Evolutionary for a linear model (slow, noisy)

content.notes:
Talk learners through the Solver dialogue in the order shown. Reinforce that each item links to a specific block in the spreadsheet.

Objective cell: should contain a single formula (often SUMPRODUCT). Remind learners to confirm it updates when variables change.

Variable cells: should be only the decision variables. A frequent error is accidentally including the objective cell or intermediate calculations.

Constraints: Encourage writing constraints first on the sheet (as inequalities with LHS and RHS), then mirroring them in Solver. This makes checking feasibility easy.

Method selection:
- Use Simplex LP if all formulas are linear in the variables.
- Use GRG for smooth nonlinear (e.g., diminishing returns with powers/logs).
- Use Evolutionary only when you must (non-smooth, discontinuous, or complex).

Probing question: “How would you justify your method choice to a marker?”

slides.title: Feasibility, slack, and binding constraints

content.title: Feasibility, slack, and binding constraints
content: Feasible means every constraint is satisfied numerically
Check each constraint: LHS value versus RHS limit
Slack = RHS − LHS for “≤” constraints (if feasible)
Binding constraint has zero slack at optimum
Non-binding has positive slack; it is not limiting
Bottlenecks are typically the binding resource constraints
content.notes:
Explain feasibility as a pass/fail property: before discussing “optimal”, confirm the solution obeys the rules.

Demonstrate slack carefully:
- For LHS ≤ RHS, slack = RHS − LHS.
- For LHS ≥ RHS, slack = LHS − RHS (be explicit; direction matters).
- For equality constraints, slack should be 0 (within tolerance).

Discuss binding vs non-binding:
- Binding constraints are active at the optimum and often determine the solution shape.
- Non-binding constraints have unused capacity; relaxing them will not improve the objective (locally).

Common misconception: “If slack is small, it is binding.” In practice, rounding and Solver tolerances can give tiny residuals; define an acceptable tolerance (e.g., 1e-6) and document it.

Probing questions:
- “Which constraint would you relax first to improve profit, and why?”
- “If a constraint has slack, what operational action does that suggest?” (e.g., unused material).

slides.title: Sensitivity report: what it tells you

content.title: Sensitivity report: what it tells you
content: Shadow price: objective change per +1 unit of a constraint RHS
Valid only within allowable increase/decrease range
Reduced cost: improvement needed for a zero variable to enter
Ranges show where the current basis stays optimal (LP case)
Interpret only for Simplex LP with a valid Sensitivity Report
Use it to justify marginal recommendations, not big changes
content.notes:
Set expectations: sensitivity analysis is local. It helps answer “What if we change a constraint a little?” without re-solving, but only within stated ranges.

Explain shadow price in operational terms: the marginal value of one more unit of a scarce resource (e.g., one more labour hour). If labour is binding, its shadow price may be positive in a maximisation problem.

Explain reduced cost: if a product is not produced (decision variable at 0), reduced cost tells you how much its unit profit would need to improve (or cost decrease) before it becomes worthwhile, given current constraints.

Important caveats:
- If you used GRG/Evolutionary, Excel may not provide a meaningful Sensitivity Report.
- Integer constraints invalidate standard LP sensitivity interpretation.

Probing question: “If a shadow price is £12 per labour hour, what would you pay for an extra hour, and why might you pay less than £12 in practice?” (hint: ranges, step changes, realism).

Probing question: “If a shadow price is £12 per labour hour, what would you pay for an extra hour, and why might you pay less than £12 in practice?” (hint: ranges, step changes, realism).

slides.title: Worked example: data for a product mix model

content.title: Worked example: data for a product mix model
content.notes:
Introduce a realistic but simple linear programming scenario: choose weekly production quantities of A and B to maximise profit subject to limited labour and material.

Decision variables:
- x_A = units of Product A per week
- x_B = units of Product B per week

Objective:
Maximise Profit = 30 x_A + 50 x_B

Constraints:
- Labour: 2 x_A + 4 x_B ≤ 100
- Material: 3 x_A + 2 x_B ≤ 90
- Non-negativity: x_A, x_B ≥ 0

Ask learners to sanity-check coefficients: “Which product is more labour-intensive per unit? Which uses more material?” This anticipates which constraint might bind.

Common misconception: treating availability as per day while decisions are per week. Reinforce consistent time basis.

slides.title: Worked example: build the sheet and solve

content.title: Worked example: build the sheet and solve
content: Enter variable cells for A and B (start with 0 and 0)
Objective cell: =SUMPRODUCT(profit_row, variable_row)
Compute Labour used: =SUMPRODUCT(labour_row, variables)
Compute Material used: =SUMPRODUCT(material_row, variables)
Add constraints: Labour_used<=100 and Material_used<=90
Solve with Simplex LP; verify LHS values meet each limit
content.notes:
Speak through a clean layout:
- Put data coefficients in a small table.
- Put decision variables in a dedicated row/column adjacent to products.
- Put constraint calculations in separate cells with labels and units.

Demonstrate a quick “before Solver” test: manually type x_A=10, x_B=10 and check labour/material used update correctly. If formulas do not update, Solver will not work.

In Solver, also set:
- “Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative” (unless you explicitly model lower bounds).
- Add any upper bounds if operationally needed (e.g., demand caps). Explain that without demand constraints, Solver may push production up until a resource binds.

After solving, explicitly check feasibility:
- Read the computed Labour_used and Material_used numbers.
- Compare to 100 and 90; compute slack.

Probing questions:
- “Which constraint hit its limit?”
- “If the solution has A=0, what might that indicate about profitability per scarce resource?”

slides.title: Worked example: interpreting sensitivity outputs

content.title: Worked example: interpreting sensitivity outputs
leftColumn: Shadow price (e.g., Labour)
Meaning: £ change per +1 labour hr
Use only within allowable increase/decrease
If constraint non-binding, shadow price is 0
rightColumn: Reduced cost (e.g., Product A at 0)
Meaning: profit increase needed to produce A
If variable >0, reduced cost is 0
Interpretation changes if constraints/basis changes
content.notes:
Guide learners to locate the Sensitivity Report fields:
- For constraints: Shadow Price, Allowable Increase, Allowable Decrease.
- For variables: Reduced Cost, Objective Coefficient, Allowable ranges.

Provide a mini-interpretation template:
1) Identify whether the constraint is binding (slack = 0). If not binding, shadow price should be 0.
2) If binding, interpret the shadow price as a marginal value: “One extra unit of RHS increases objective by …”
3) Check the allowable range before using that statement.

For reduced cost:
- If Product A is at 0, a positive reduced cost in a maximisation problem indicates A is currently unattractive; its unit profit must rise by that amount (or its resource usage fall) to enter.

Common misconceptions:
- Treating shadow price as valid for large changes (it is not).
- Applying sensitivity results when integer constraints were used.

Probing questions:
- “Which is more valuable: +1 labour hour or +1 kg material? What evidence supports your claim?”
- “What operational change could reduce a reduced cost: raise price, reduce labour, reduce material, or all three?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection (with self-checks)

content.title: Practice and reflection (with self-checks)
content: Draft a model for 3 products and 3 resources (choose units)
Write objective and each constraint in plain English
Build the sheet: variables, objective, LHS calculations, RHS
Run Solver twice: once with a wrong direction to spot impact
Answer the MCQ quiz: building and interpreting a Solver model
Answer the MCQ: sensitivity, scenarios, recommendations
content.notes:
Provide guidance on the practice without needing a case study:
- Invent a small scenario: three products (P1–P3), limited labour hours, machine time, and raw material. Use realistic magnitudes so solutions are not extreme.

Reflection prompts:
- “Which part took longest: formulas, constraints, or Solver settings?”
- “How did you detect the wrong-direction constraint? What changed?”

Encourage learners to validate by inspection:
- If you reverse a constraint (≤ becomes ≥), you often see either infeasibility or an implausible solution (e.g., forcing minimum resource usage).

MCQ linkage:
- Treat the quizzes as diagnostics: if you miss items, return to the slide that addresses that skill (e.g., slack/binding, sensitivity caveats).

Common misconception: believing the first feasible solution is optimal. Reinforce that feasibility is necessary but not sufficient.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD104 optimisation workbook and write-up justification
Marks often depend on clarity: labels, units, and assumptions
Common error: wrong variable range or selecting constants
Common error: constraint direction reversed or wrong RHS units
Common error: using GRG/Evolutionary for an LP sensitivity task
Common error: reporting results without feasibility checks/slack
content.notes:
Explain what assessors typically look for: a transparent model plus interpretation. Getting the numeric optimum is not the whole task; you must justify why it is credible.

Expand each mistake:
- Wrong variable range: leads Solver to “change” LHS cells directly, bypassing the logic.
- Wrong direction: turns a capacity limit into a minimum requirement.
- Units mismatch: the most common hidden flaw (hours vs minutes; per day vs per week).
- Wrong method: if you need sensitivity outputs, Simplex LP is required and the model must be linear.
- Missing feasibility checks: always show LHS, RHS, and slack values in the final sheet.

Probing question: “If a colleague challenged your result, what three screenshots or cells would you show first to defend it?” (suggest: variables, constraint table with slack, Solver settings).

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: A Solver model is decisions + objective + constraints in cells
Correct units and assumptions are as important as the optimum
Configure Solver carefully: objective, variables, constraints, method
Verify feasibility and use slack to find bottlenecks
Sensitivity explains marginal trade-offs within stated ranges
content.notes:
Close by reinforcing a repeatable workflow:
1) Structure the sheet so the logic is visible.
2) Validate formulas with manual test values.
3) Configure Solver to match the model type.
4) Check feasibility numerically and interpret binding constraints.
5) Use sensitivity cautiously and only within allowable ranges.

Invite learners to self-assess against the objectives:
- “Can you point to the three elements on your sheet in under 10 seconds?”
- “Can you explain, in words, why the optimal solution looks the way it does?”

Encourage saving a template layout they can reuse in later lessons and assignments.

content.title: Set up constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver
content: Maths Certification
MOD104 — Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver
Lesson 2: Constrained optimisation models in Excel Solver
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
In this lesson you will build and analyse constrained optimisation models using Excel Solver. Ensure the Solver add-in is enabled (File > Options > Add-ins > Manage: Excel Add-ins). Keep Excel open alongside the lesson so you can pause and replicate each step.

This lesson sits at an analysis level: you are not only setting up a model, but also diagnosing what the results mean (binding constraints, bottlenecks, and marginal values).

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.notes:
Treat the lesson as a repeated cycle: (1) understand the modelling idea, (2) implement it in a small Excel layout, then (3) interpret the outputs using evidence (slack, binding status, marginal values).

As you work, keep asking: What are my controllable choices (decision variables)? What is the single performance measure I am optimising (objective)? What are the real-world limits that must never be violated (constraints)?

Common misconception: learners often start with Solver and only later decide what the model means. Reverse that: define the scenario and units first, then let Solver do the arithmetic.

slides.title: What constrained optimisation means in practice

content.title: What constrained optimisation means in practice
content: Choose variable values to optimise one goal under limits
Objective function: the metric to maximise or minimise
Constraints: resource, policy, demand, or technical limits
Feasible solution: satisfies every constraint
Optimal solution: feasible plan with best objective value
content.notes:
Constrained optimisation is decision-making with trade-offs. You are choosing values you control (e.g., production quantities, staffing hours, shipment volumes) to improve a single goal, while respecting limits.

Mini-example: if x is units produced, you might maximise profit = 5x subject to labour hours 2x ≤ 40 and x ≥ 0. Solver is doing what you would do algebraically, but at scale and with multiple variables/constraints.

Probing questions:
- Which quantities are decisions, and which are fixed inputs?
- If a constraint is removed, does the problem become unrealistic?

Misconception to address: “More constraints always makes the model better.” Extra constraints can encode incorrect assumptions and distort results; each constraint must be justified by the scenario.

slides.title: Model components and how they appear in Excel

content.title: Model components and how they appear in Excel
content.notes:
This slide is your translation key from the mathematical model to the spreadsheet.

Decision variables should be a small, clearly labelled block. Avoid scattering decision cells across the worksheet; it makes errors harder to detect and ranges harder to select in Solver.

Your objective should be a single cell containing a formula. A frequent mistake is typing an objective value directly into the objective cell (a constant), which gives Solver nothing to optimise.

Constraints should be implemented as: (1) a calculated left-hand side (LHS) total and (2) a right-hand side (RHS) limit value. This makes constraints auditable.

Probing question: If I change a single input coefficient, do all dependent totals update automatically without editing formulas?

slides.title: Build a transparent worksheet model

content.title: Build a transparent worksheet model
content: Put decision variables in a labelled Inputs block
Use named ranges for key cells to reduce reference errors
Calculate each constraint LHS with clear, auditable formulas
Label units in headers (kg, hours, ) and keep them consistent
Create a Slack cell: Slack = RHS - LHS for each constraint
content.notes:
Transparency is a quality standard: another person should be able to inspect your worksheet and understand the model logic without opening Solver.

Named ranges: use the Name Box (left of the formula bar) or Formulas > Define Name. For example, name the decision cells x and y, and name limits FlourLimit, LabourLimit. In formulas, =0.3*x + 0.5*y is more readable than =0.3*$B$4 + 0.5*$C$4.

Use Slack = RHS - LHS as a diagnostic. If Slack is negative, your solution is infeasible (the constraint is violated). If Slack is zero (or extremely close, allowing for rounding), the constraint is binding.

Misconception: “If Solver says ‘Solved’, the model must be correct.” Solver can solve an incorrect model perfectly. Your job is to validate that formulas represent the scenario and that units are consistent (e.g., not mixing minutes and hours).

slides.title: Choosing Simplex LP vs GRG Nonlinear

content.title: Choosing Simplex LP vs GRG Nonlinear
leftColumn: Simplex LP: linear objective and linear constraints
Fast and reliable; provides Sensitivity report
Best for product mix, blending, transport, linear scheduling
Avoid IF/MIN/MAX; keep relationships proportional
rightColumn: GRG: nonlinear formulas (powers, products, EXP, logs)
May find a local optimum; starting values can matter
No standard Sensitivity report like LP shadow prices
Use when relationships come from calculus-based models
content.notes:
Method choice should be justified by structure, not preference.

Linear means: every term looks like constant × variable, and variables are added/subtracted. Examples: 3x + 2y is linear; x*y, x^2, IF(x>0,...) are nonlinear.

Why this matters: Simplex LP gives you strong diagnostic outputs (Sensitivity report) that support LO4 (trade-offs). GRG is appropriate when the real relationship is nonlinear, but you must be more cautious about interpretation (and you typically need to test multiple starting points).

Probing questions:
- Do any formulas multiply decision variables together?
- Are there step-changes or IF statements that create kinks?

Note: integer/binary decisions introduce another class of problem; Excel may remove Sensitivity outputs when integer constraints are used.

slides.title: Enter the model in Solver (checklist)

content.title: Enter the model in Solver (checklist)
content: Set Objective: select the objective cell and choose Max/Min
By Changing: select the decision variable cell range
Add constraints using LHS cells and RHS limit cells
Include non-negativity: tick option or add x,y  0 constraints
Choose method (Simplex LP or GRG) and click Solve
Request reports: Answer; Sensitivity (Simplex only)
content.notes:
Work systematically through the Solver dialogue box.

Objective cell: ensure it contains a formula that changes when decision cells change. A quick test before running Solver: manually change x and y slightly and confirm the objective updates.

Constraints: prefer selecting a calculated LHS cell rather than placing a complex formula directly inside the Solver constraint entry. This keeps the constraint visible on the sheet.

Non-negativity: ticking “Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative” is convenient, but only safe if all decision variables truly cannot be negative. If any variable could take negative values (e.g., net flows), you must handle bounds explicitly.

Common mistake: selecting the wrong variable range (e.g., including totals or limit cells). This causes Solver to change values that should be fixed inputs.

slides.title: Using Solver reports to diagnose results

content.title: Using Solver reports to diagnose results
leftColumn: Answer report: binding if slack = 0 (capacity fully used)
Slack > 0 means unused capacity (non-bottleneck)
Check solution status and final objective value
Verify on-sheet totals match the reported solution
rightColumn: Sensitivity (LP): shadow price = value of +1 unit RHS
Reduced cost: gain needed for a zero variable to enter
Allowable inc/dec: range where marginal values stay valid
State units explicitly (e.g., /kg, /hour)
content.notes:
The Answer report supports LO3: identifying binding constraints and bottlenecks.

Binding constraints are the active limits at the optimum. In operational terms, these are where the organisation is ‘up against the wall’. The bottleneck is often a binding resource constraint with a meaningful shadow price.

The Sensitivity report supports LO4: explaining trade-offs numerically. Shadow price answers: ‘If I had one more unit of this resource, how much would the objective improve?’ Reduced cost answers: ‘If this activity is currently zero, how much would its profitability need to improve before it becomes worthwhile?’

Important nuance: shadow prices and reduced costs only hold within the “allowable increase/decrease” ranges. Beyond that range, the set of binding constraints can change, so the marginal values change.

Probing questions:
- Which constraint has the largest positive shadow price? What real action could change it?
- If a constraint has slack, why might it still matter operationally (e.g., risk, variability)?

slides.title: Worked example: Bakery product mix data

content.title: Worked example: Bakery product mix data
content.notes:
This is a standard linear product-mix model: choose quantities of two products to maximise profit under resource and demand limits.

Be explicit about units: flour is in kilograms per unit, labour is in hours per unit, profit is pounds per unit. When you later read a shadow price for flour, its unit will be  per kg.

Before building Excel, do a ‘reasonableness scan’:
- Which product is more profitable per kg of flour? (profit divided by flour coefficient)
- Which is more profitable per hour of labour?

These quick ratios do not replace Solver, but they help you anticipate what might become binding and detect suspicious results.

slides.title: Worked example: Build the worksheet

content.title: Worked example: Build the worksheet
content: Create decision cells for x and y and assign names
Objective cell: =2.5*x + 3.2*y
FlourUsed: =0.3*x + 0.5*y; compare to 60
LabourUsed: =0.2*x + 0.25*y; compare to 40
Create Slack cells for flour and labour (RHS - LHS)
Keep all coefficients in input cells, then reference them
content.notes:
A robust layout is: Inputs (coefficients and limits) at the top-left, Decision variables nearby, Calculations (LHS totals) below, and Checks (slacks) beside each constraint.

Even though the formulas shown here are simple, still store coefficients (2.5, 3.2, 0.3, 0.5, etc.) in cells rather than hard-coding them in formulas. This makes scenario testing easy and reduces transcription errors.

Mini-example of transparency: if flour per muffin is in cell B8 named FlourMuffin, then FlourUsed can be =FlourMuffin*x + FlourScone*y. Someone auditing your sheet can immediately see what is driving FlourUsed.

Misconception: “Named ranges are optional.” They are not strictly required, but they substantially reduce mistakes when models become larger than two variables.

slides.title: Worked example: Configure Solver

content.title: Worked example: Configure Solver
content: Objective: Profit cell, set to Max
Variable cells: x and y decision cells
Constraints: FlourUsed  60; LabourUsed  40
Constraints: x  160; y  120; and x,y  0
Select Simplex LP for this linear structure
Solve and produce Answer and Sensitivity reports
content.notes:
Enter constraints exactly as stated by the scenario, then validate them against your computed LHS cells.

A common slip is reversing the inequality direction (typing  instead of ). Another is applying the wrong RHS (e.g., using 40 as a flour limit by mistake). Your Slack cells help detect this: if your initial ‘guess’ values violate constraints, slack becomes negative.

Because this model is linear, choose Simplex LP. If you choose GRG by mistake, you may still get a solution, but you lose the LP sensitivity information that you need for trade-off analysis.

Probing question: Which constraints are ‘physical’ (resources) versus ‘market’ (demand caps)? How might each be changed in practice?

slides.speakerNotes:
Enter constraints exactly as stated by the scenario, then validate them against your computed LHS cells.

A common slip is reversing the inequality direction (typing  instead of ). Another is applying the wrong RHS (e.g., using 40 as a flour limit by mistake). Your Slack cells help detect this: if your initial ‘guess’ values violate constraints, slack becomes negative.

Because this model is linear, choose Simplex LP. If you choose GRG by mistake, you may still get a solution, but you lose the LP sensitivity information that you need for trade-off analysis.

Probing question: Which constraints are ‘physical’ (resources) versus ‘market’ (demand caps)? How might each be changed in practice?

slides.title: Worked example: Interpret and justify changes

content.title: Worked example: Interpret and justify changes
content: Optimal: x=160, y=24; objective (profit) 476.80
Binding: flour (slack 0) and muffin cap (slack 0)
Non-binding: labour slack 2 hr; scone cap slack 96 units
Bottleneck: flour; labour not limiting so shadow price  0/hr
Flour shadow price  6.40/kg; +4 kg  +25.60 profit
Muffin cap shadow price  0.58 per unit (trade-off vs scones)
content.notes:
Start with LO3: use slack to classify constraints.

- Flour is binding (slack 0): all flour is used, so it is a bottleneck.
- Labour has slack (2 hours unused): increasing labour alone will not improve profit; the marginal value is effectively zero at this solution.
- Demand cap on muffins is binding: the model would like to sell more muffins, but cannot under the cap.

Now LO4: interpret marginal values with units.

Flour shadow price  6.40 per kg means: if you can obtain 1 additional kg of flour (and nothing else changes), expected profit increases by about 6.40, within the valid range. Here, the ‘+4 kg’ statement is linked to the idea that only the first few extra kg matter before another constraint (labour) would become binding; beyond that point, the marginal value changes.

Muffin cap shadow price  0.58 per extra muffin allowed means: relaxing the muffin upper bound slightly increases profit, but less strongly than buying flour. This occurs because, with flour fixed, extra muffins displace some scones; the shadow price captures that trade-off.

Probing questions:
- If flour costs 4 per kg to buy, is purchasing extra flour worthwhile? Show the net gain.
- Why is the value of relaxing the muffin cap not equal to 2.50? What must be given up to make space for extra muffins?

Misconception: learners often treat shadow prices as ‘always true’. Emphasise the allowable range: once the set of binding constraints changes, the shadow price no longer applies.

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
leftColumn: Rebuild the model using your own layout and named ranges
Change limits (e.g., flour=65) and predict the new mix
Add a new constraint (e.g., minimum scones) and re-solve
Complete both MCQ quizzes and review any incorrect answers
rightColumn: Are units consistent in every coefficient and constraint?
Which constraints are binding, and what is your slack evidence?
What single change gives best marginal improvement, and why?
When would GRG be required for your formulas?
content.notes:
Use the practice prompts to move from following steps to analysing consequences.

Prediction before running Solver is important: it forces you to reason about structure. For example, if you increase flour from 60 to 65, ask yourself: will muffins increase (they are already at a cap), or will scones increase, or will the binding set change?

When you add a minimum-production constraint (e.g., y  30), pay attention to what becomes binding and how profit changes. This is a common real-world policy constraint.

After the MCQs, do not just note the correct option; identify the reason your chosen option was tempting. That ‘near-miss’ logic is often the misconception that would later cause modelling errors.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD104 Solver workbook task and written justification
State variables, objective, constraints, and method choice clearly
Use Solver reports: binding constraints, slack, and marginal values
Avoid hard-coded coefficients inside formulas; reference input cells
Avoid missing non-negativity and incorrect inequality directions
Report trade-offs with correct units and sensible rounding
content.notes:
In a typical submission, markers look for two things: (1) a correct model and (2) a defensible interpretation. A correct spreadsheet without a clear explanation of bottlenecks and trade-offs will not meet the analysis standard.

Evidence matters: do not merely assert that ‘flour is the bottleneck’. Quote the slack (0) and, where applicable, the shadow price and its units.

Rounding: present operational recommendations with sensible precision. For example, 6.40/kg is already two decimal places; if you compute 25.60 additional profit for 4 kg, keep the same currency precision.

Frequent errors to flag:
- Using GRG on a linear model and then wondering where Sensitivity output is.
- Omitting upper bounds (demand caps), leading to unrealistic ‘infinite’ production.
- Selecting totals/limits as variable cells, allowing Solver to ‘cheat’ by changing constraints.

slides.title: Summary

content.title: Summary
content: Define decision variables with units, then write an objective formula
Convert each constraint into a visible LHS and RHS limit on-sheet
Solver requires: objective cell, variable cells, constraints, method
Use slack/status to identify binding constraints and bottlenecks
Use shadow prices (LP) to quantify trade-offs and recommendations
content.notes:
You should now be able to go from a narrative operational scenario to a structured Solver model, and then explain the result using evidence.

If you feel unsure, revisit your worksheet transparency first: clear inputs, named decision variables, calculated LHS totals, and slack cells. Many ‘Solver problems’ are actually worksheet-structure problems.

Looking ahead in the module, these skills support more complex models (more variables/constraints, scenario analysis, and more nuanced recommendations). As models grow, disciplined layout and unit checking become even more important.

content.notes:

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Classify binding vs non-binding constraints from Answer Report (100%)
Explain 2 trade-offs + 1 bottleneck from Sensitivity Report (150–200w)
Produce an audit-ready calculation log with 3 accuracy checks
Run a one-RHS what-if; predict objective change within ±5%
Study path: watch → build → interpret → check → quiz
content.notes:
Work through the lesson in the order shown: first understand model structure, then learn how to read Solver reports, then practise validation and what-if analysis.

Clarify what “analyse” means here: you are not only executing Solver, but interpreting outputs, judging reliability, and translating numbers into operational implications.

Two common misconceptions to challenge early:
- “If Solver gives an answer, it must be correct.” (Models can be mis-specified.)
- “Sensitivity values always predict outcomes.” (They are local and conditional.)

As you proceed, keep a document open for your calculation log. Treat it as a running lab notebook: decisions, settings, and checks recorded as you go.

slides.title: What a Solver optimisation model contains

content.title: What a Solver optimisation model contains
content: Decision variables: cells Solver can change
Objective: formula to maximise or minimise
Constraints: limits expressed as formulas ≤, =, or ≥
Feasible region: solutions that satisfy all constraints
Linear vs non-linear models determine Solver method
Reports support interpretation and audit evidence
content.notes:
A Solver model is a spreadsheet translation of an optimisation problem. Decision variables should represent controllable choices (e.g., units produced, staffing hours, shipment quantities). The objective should be a single quantified performance measure (profit, cost, time, emissions), calculated from the decision variables.

Constraints are not “data”; they are statements about reality and policy (capacity, demand caps, minimum service levels, budget limits). In Excel, they are usually set up as left-hand side (LHS) formulas compared to right-hand side (RHS) limits.

Probing questions:
- If you change a decision variable by 1 unit, does the objective formula respond correctly?
- Are your constraints written so that the LHS changes when decisions change?

Misconception to address: putting constants on the LHS (or hard-coding decision values) prevents Solver from exploring options. Encourage use of formulas like SUMPRODUCT to link decisions to constraints cleanly.

slides.title: Binding vs non-binding constraints (Answer Report)

content.title: Binding vs non-binding constraints (Answer Report)
content: Compare Answer Report: Final Value (LHS) vs Constraint RHS
Binding if Final Value = RHS (within Solver tolerance)
Non-binding if ≤ constraint has slack > 0 (Final < RHS)
Non-binding if ≥ constraint has surplus > 0 (Final > RHS)
Equality constraints are always binding
Record slack/surplus and units for each constraint
content.notes:
The Answer Report is your primary tool for classifying constraints. A binding constraint is “active” at the optimum: it is tight and limits improvement in the objective, at least locally. A non-binding constraint has slack (for ≤) or surplus (for ≥), meaning it is satisfied with room to spare.

Be careful with the phrase “Final Value = RHS”: Solver works with tolerances. In practice, treat a constraint as binding if the difference is extremely small relative to the scale (e.g., |LHS−RHS| < 0.001 for hour-based constraints, or within a defined tolerance you justify in your log).

Mini-example:
- Labour ≤ 100 hours; Answer Report shows Final Value 100 → binding.
- Machine ≤ 80 hours; Final Value 70 → slack 10 → non-binding.

Probing questions:
- Does a constraint look binding only because of rounding in the display?
- Are you mixing units (minutes vs hours) such that “slack” is misread?

Misconception: learners sometimes label a constraint binding because it is “important in real life”. Binding/non-binding is a mathematical property at the current optimum, not a judgement of managerial importance.

slides.title: Sensitivity Report: shadow price and reduced cost

content.title: Sensitivity Report: shadow price and reduced cost
content: Shadow price: objective change per +1 unit of a constraint RHS
Reduced cost: improvement needed for a zero variable to enter
State units explicitly (e.g., £ per labour hour)
Shadow prices are valid only within allowable RHS ranges
Shadow price often zero when a constraint is non-binding
Reduced cost depends on objective direction and sign rules
content.notes:
The Sensitivity Report is available for linear models solved with Simplex LP. It provides marginal values that support decision-making.

Shadow price (dual value): interpret as “the value of relaxing this constraint by one unit”, holding the optimal basis constant. For a maximisation model with a ≤ constraint, a positive shadow price means extra RHS increases objective.

Reduced cost: for a variable at zero in the optimal solution (non-basic), the reduced cost tells you how much its objective coefficient would need to improve (increase for maximisation, decrease for minimisation) before it becomes worthwhile to include.

Mini-example language you can reuse in your justification:
- “The shadow price of labour is £5 per hour, so an extra hour of labour capacity is worth about £5 in profit, within the valid range.”

Common misconceptions:
- Treating shadow price as a global rule (it is local).
- Reporting shadow prices without units.
- Forgetting that signs can differ for ≥ constraints or minimisation models.

Probing question:
- Which is more informative for a bottleneck: slack, shadow price, or both together?

slides.title: Allowable ranges and when marginal values fail

content.title: Allowable ranges and when marginal values fail
content: Allowable inc/dec: RHS range where the optimal basis stays same
Within range: new objective ≈ old + (shadow price × ΔRHS)
Outside range: re-solve; shadow price may change
Multiple RHS changes: effects are not reliably additive
Degeneracy can make shadow prices unstable
Record assumptions when using marginal predictions
content.notes:
Allowable increase/decrease is the safeguard for using shadow prices. It defines the interval over which the current set of binding constraints and active variables remains optimal. Within this interval, the linear approximation using the shadow price is appropriate.

Explain degeneracy simply: sometimes multiple constraints intersect so that small changes can switch which constraint is “effectively” active, causing discontinuities or unstable marginal values. You may see shadow prices of zero even for a binding constraint in degenerate cases.

Probing questions:
- Is your proposed change (e.g., +10 hours) within the allowable increase?
- Are you changing just one RHS, or several? If several, why are you still using single-parameter sensitivity?

Practical teaching tip: if learners are unsure, advise re-solving and treating the shadow price as an initial prediction to be validated, not a final answer.

slides.title: Validation: build an audit-ready calculation log

content.title: Validation: build an audit-ready calculation log
content: Log: variables, objective, constraints, outputs and file versions
Record Solver method and key settings used
Check 1: units consistency across inputs, formulas and reports
Check 2: rounding policy and its feasibility impact
Check 3: feasibility check for every constraint (LHS vs RHS)
Save Answer/Sensitivity reports as part of the audit trail
content.notes:
An audit-ready log is a structured record that lets another person reproduce and trust your result. Treat it like a lab report: what you did, with what settings, and why the outcome is credible.

What to record for Solver settings (minimum):
- Solving method (Simplex LP for linear problems).
- Options: “Assume Linear Model”, “Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative”, and any tolerances you adjusted.
- Decision variable range and objective cell.

Three checks explained with examples:
1) Units: if profit is £/unit and labour is hours/unit, RHS must be hours (not minutes). Unit mismatches are the most common hidden error.
2) Rounding: if you round decision variables to whole units after solving, re-check feasibility. A solution can become infeasible after rounding.
3) Feasibility: independently compute each constraint LHS from the decision variables and confirm it satisfies the inequality.

Probing question:
- If you were asked to justify your model to a colleague, what single screenshot or table would you provide first?

slides.title: Worked example: set up a linear model in Excel

content.title: Worked example: set up a linear model in Excel
content: Scenario: mix Products A and B to maximise weekly profit
Decision cells: x_A and x_B (units/week)
Objective cell: =30*x_A + 20*x_B
Resource LHS: labour=2*x_A+1*x_B; machine=1*x_A+2*x_B
Constraints: labour≤100; machine≤80; x_A≤50; x_A,x_B≥0
Solver: Simplex LP; tick “Assume Linear Model”
content.notes:
Walk learners through a clean spreadsheet layout:
- Put decision variables in clearly labelled cells (e.g., B4 for x_A, B5 for x_B).
- Keep parameters (profits per unit, resource coefficients, capacities) in a small table so formulas reference cells, not hard-coded numbers.

Implementation guidance:
- Use SUMPRODUCT for scalability: e.g., Profit = SUMPRODUCT(profit_row, decision_vector).
- For each constraint, compute an LHS cell using SUMPRODUCT(resource_row, decision_vector).

Solver setup steps (narrate slowly):
1) Set Objective: profit cell; choose “Max”.
2) By Changing Variable Cells: decision vector.
3) Add constraints: each LHS cell ≤ RHS cell; add x_A ≤ 50; tick non-negativity (or add explicit ≥0 constraints).
4) Select “Simplex LP”; tick “Assume Linear Model”.

Common misconceptions:
- Selecting GRG Nonlinear for linear models (works sometimes, but reports differ and sensitivity may be unavailable).
- Forgetting non-negativity, leading to negative production values.

Probing questions:
- Which cells will change when Solver runs, and which must remain fixed?
- Can you trace each constraint LHS back to the decision variables?

slides.title: Worked example: classify constraints from Answer Report

content.title: Worked example: classify constraints from Answer Report
content.notes:
Explain that these values are read directly from the Solver Answer Report (Constraints section). The logic is mechanical:
- Labour: LHS equals RHS → binding. This is a candidate bottleneck.
- Machine: LHS 70 vs RHS 80 → slack 10 hours → non-binding.
- Demand cap A: LHS 40 vs RHS 50 → slack 10 units → non-binding.

Stress the need for units: “70 of what?” If machine time is in hours, label it. If it is in minutes, the RHS must also be minutes.

Tolerance note: if learners see values like 99.99999 vs 100, they should treat it as binding and document the tolerance used.

Probing questions:
- If machine has slack, would buying more machine time help profit? Why or why not?
- If demand cap A is non-binding, what does that imply about product mix and profitability?

Common mistake: classifying based on intuition rather than report values. The assessment criterion requires 100% correct classification from the provided outputs.

slides.title: Worked example: interpret Sensitivity Report meaning

content.title: Worked example: interpret Sensitivity Report meaning
leftColumn: Trade-off: labour shadow price values extra capacity
Trade-off: reduced cost shows profit needed to add a product
Use allowable ranges to bound recommendations
Write impacts in operational language, not Solver jargon
rightColumn: Bottleneck: binding constraint with positive shadow price
Non-bottleneck: slack constraint often has zero shadow price
Check if shadow price is stable (non-degenerate basis)
Propose action: expand bottleneck or redesign constraints
content.notes:
Use a concrete numerical illustration (you can narrate this even if learners’ numbers differ):
- Suppose labour shadow price = £5 per labour hour, allowable increase = 20 hours.
  Interpretation: within +0 to +20 hours, each extra hour increases profit by about £5.
- Suppose machine shadow price = £0 with 10 hours slack.
  Interpretation: machine is not currently limiting; extra machine time has no marginal value.
- Suppose reduced cost for x_B is £3 (in a maximisation model) and x_B is 0.
  Interpretation: Product B would need an extra £3 profit per unit (or equivalent cost reduction) to be produced.

Help learners write the required 150–200 words:
- Start with the bottleneck and its unit value.
- Add at least two trade-offs (e.g., “invest in labour vs do not invest in machine”; “improve margin of B vs keep current mix”).
- Close with a condition: “valid within allowable range” and “re-solve if policy changes”.

Misconception: “highest shadow price always means expand that resource.” Correct this: expansion must be feasible, within the allowable range, and cost-effective compared to the shadow price.

Probing questions:
- What is the maximum you should be willing to pay for an extra labour hour?
- Why is a binding constraint sometimes associated with a zero shadow price?

  Interpretation: machine is not currently limiting; extra machine time has no marginal value.
- Suppose reduced cost for x_B is £3 (in a maximisation model) and x_B is 0.
  Interpretation: Product B would need an extra £3 profit per unit (or equivalent cost reduction) to be produced.

Help learners write the required 150–200 words:
- Start with the bottleneck and its unit value.
- Add at least two trade-offs (e.g., “invest in labour vs do not invest in machine”; “improve margin of B vs keep current mix”).
- Close with a condition: “valid within allowable range” and “re-solve if policy changes”.

Misconception: “highest shadow price always means expand that resource.” Correct this: expansion must be feasible, within the allowable range, and cost-effective compared to the shadow price.

Probing questions:
- What is the maximum you should be willing to pay for an extra labour hour?
- Why is a binding constraint sometimes associated with a zero shadow price?

slides.title: Worked example: one-parameter RHS what-if

content.title: Worked example: one-parameter RHS what-if
content: Change one RHS: labour from 100 to 110 (+10)
Predict: ΔObjective ≈ shadow price_labour × 10
Confirm +10 is within allowable increase before trusting prediction
Re-solve with new RHS and record the new objective value
Compute % error: (predicted−actual)/actual × 100
Target: |error| ≤ 5% for this linear case
content.notes:
Demonstrate the full loop: predict first, then verify by re-solving.

Example workflow (illustrative numbers):
1) Original optimal profit = £1,500.
2) Sensitivity report: labour shadow price = £5/hour; allowable increase = 20.
3) Proposed change: +10 hours, which is within the allowable increase.
4) Prediction: new profit ≈ 1,500 + (5×10) = £1,550.
5) Re-solve with labour RHS = 110; suppose Solver returns £1,540.
6) Error = (1,550−1,540)/1,540 = 0.65% → acceptable.

Teach why error may not be exactly zero even in linear cases:
- Display rounding, Solver convergence tolerances, or slight basis changes near boundaries.

Common mistakes:
- Using the shadow price when the allowable increase is smaller than the proposed change.
- Forgetting that the shadow price is per unit of RHS (e.g., per hour), not per 10 hours.
- Changing multiple constraints at once and still using a single shadow price.

Probing questions:
- If the allowable increase were only 5 hours, what would you do?
- If the shadow price were negative, what would that imply about increasing RHS?

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
content: Classify 4 constraints as binding/non-binding from a report snippet
Explain one shadow price in a sentence with correct units
Identify one bottleneck using both slack and shadow price
Complete an audit log template with all Solver settings
Run one RHS what-if and compare predicted vs actual objective
Reflect: what would make sensitivity results unreliable?
content.notes:
Encourage deliberate practice: learners should pause the lesson and do each prompt in Excel, not just mentally.

Suggested self-check approach:
- For binding/non-binding: make a two-column list (constraint name; binding?); justify with LHS vs RHS.
- For shadow price sentence: force yourself to include “per” and the unit (e.g., “£ per hour”).
- For bottleneck: require two pieces of evidence: (1) binding status and (2) positive shadow price.

Reflection prompts you can narrate:
- “If I doubled a capacity, would my shadow price logic still hold?”
- “Did I solve with the correct method (Simplex LP), and do I actually have a linear model?”
- “Did I make any manual edits to decision cells after solving?”

Common misconception: learners often equate “binding” with “highest impact”. Stress that binding is necessary but not sufficient; the shadow price captures marginal impact.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD104 Solver model write-up and recommendations
Use Answer/Sensitivity reports as evidence, not just screenshots
Mistake: using shadow price outside allowable range
Mistake: missing or inconsistent units in interpretations
Mistake: post-solve rounding without re-checking feasibility
Submission standard: audit log + checks + saved report outputs
content.notes:
Position this lesson as directly supporting assessed work where you must justify decisions and provide an audit trail. Even when the task is “find the optimum”, marks are typically earned for model quality, interpretation, and validation.

Explain what assessors look for:
- Traceability: can they see where each number came from?
- Correct interpretation: particularly of shadow prices and reduced costs.
- Decision relevance: translating Solver outputs into operational recommendations.

Expand the common mistakes:
- Shadow price misuse: If your RHS change exceeds the allowable increase/decrease, you must re-solve and you should not present the marginal prediction as reliable.
- Units: A correct number with incorrect units is treated as incorrect interpretation.
- Rounding: If decisions must be integers, either use integer constraints or re-check after rounding; do not assume feasibility remains.

Probing question:
- If you had to defend your model in a professional meeting, what would be the first weakness someone might challenge?

slides.title: Summary: what you should now be able to do

content.title: Summary: what you should now be able to do
content: Set up variables, objective and constraints with correct Solver method
Classify binding vs non-binding constraints from Answer Report outputs
Use Sensitivity fields to explain trade-offs and identify bottlenecks
Validate results with an audit log and feasibility/units/rounding checks
Predict and verify one-RHS what-if changes using shadow prices
content.notes:
Reinforce that the technical skill (running Solver) is only part of optimisation work. The higher-value skill is analysis: interpreting reports, explaining trade-offs, and producing a defensible audit trail.

Suggested final self-test questions:
- Can you explain, in one minute, why the solution is optimal and feasible?
- Can you identify the bottleneck and quantify its marginal value with units?
- Can you show a complete calculation log with no missing fields?

Direct learners to complete the formative MCQs next, treating any incorrect answers as prompts to revisit the relevant slide: Answer Report classification, Sensitivity interpretation, or what-if validity conditions.

content.notes: Position this lesson as the bridge between mathematical optimisation and operational decision-making in a spreadsheet. Remind learners that Excel is the tool; the model structure and interpretation are the core skills. Prompt: "When you see a word problem, what is the first thing you try to optimise, and what usually limits you?"

slides.title: Learning objectives and how to use this lesson

content.title: Learning objectives and how to use this lesson
leftColumn: Map decision vars, objective, 3+ constraints with units
Build model + Solver to match check within ±0.5%
Use reports: binding constraints, shadow prices, trade-offs
Log 5+ audit checks so others can reproduce results
rightColumn: Watch: focus on model map and Excel layout
Practise: rebuild example from scratch (no copy/paste)
Check: run MCQs, then revisit any weak steps
Reflect: write one trade-off justified by report values
content.notes: Frame the lesson workflow: understand the problem structure, implement it correctly, then interrogate the outputs. Explain the ±0.5% tolerance as a realism check: small differences can arise from rounding, solver options, or using different cell references, but large differences typically signal a modelling error. Ask: "Which objective is easier to get right—the formula or the units? Why?" Highlight a common misconception: learners often jump to Solver before confirming that constraint left-hand sides (LHS) and right-hand sides (RHS) share the same units.

slides.title: From word problem to model map

content.title: From word problem to model map
content: Decision variables: controllable quantities (with units)
Objective: maximise/minimise one measurable metric
Constraints: operational limits or requirements (inequalities)
Write every constraint as LHS ≤/≥/= RHS with units shown
Check directions: “at most” (≤), “at least” (≥), “exactly” (=)
Add non-negativity and any explicit bounds (e.g., 0–500)
content.notes: Walk learners through translating language into mathematics. Use micro-examples: "Produce x units" implies x is a decision variable; "profit" or "cost" indicates an objective; "machine hours available" signals a capacity constraint. Reinforce that units act as a diagnostic tool: if LHS is hours and RHS is units, something is wrong. Probing questions: "What would you physically measure on-site for each constraint?" and "If you increased one decision variable by 1, which constraints become tighter?" Misconception to address: treating given numbers (like demand) as decision variables rather than parameters.

slides.title: Model structure in Excel: what goes where

content.title: Model structure in Excel: what goes where
content.notes: Explain why a consistent spreadsheet layout matters: it reduces reference errors and makes auditing feasible. Encourage a standard template: variables at the top, objective below, then a block of constraints with LHS, sign, RHS, and slack. Clarify that Sensitivity reports require a linear model and Simplex LP; learners often expect sensitivity output for nonlinear models. Prompt: "If I asked you to hand this file to a colleague, could they see the model structure in 30 seconds? What would you change to make that true?"

slides.title: Common constraints and their Excel patterns

content.title: Common constraints and their Excel patterns
leftColumn: Capacity: do not exceed available resources
Demand/targets: meet minimums or exact totals
Balance: inputs equal outputs (flow conservation)
Logical bounds: upper/lower limits per variable
rightColumn: SUMPRODUCT(coeffs, vars) <= limit
SUMPRODUCT(...) >= minimum or = target
SUM(inflows) - SUM(outflows) = 0
lower <= variable <= upper (or separate constraints)
content.notes: Provide plain-language interpretation: capacity is "what we cannot do more than"; demand/targets are "what must be achieved"; balance is "nothing disappears"; bounds are "policy or physical limits". Mini-example: if Product A uses 2 machine hours and Product B uses 3, then total machine hours is 2*A + 3*B, implemented via SUMPRODUCT. Probing question: "Which constraint types typically become binding in a profit maximisation problem, and why?" Misconception: writing constraints with the inequality direction reversed, which can silently produce an ‘optimal’ but operationally impossible plan.

slides.title: Solver setup checklist (do this every time)

content.title: Solver setup checklist (do this every time)
content: Set Objective: correct cell and Max/Min selection
By Changing Variable Cells: only decision variable cells
Add constraints: LHS references, correct signs, RHS limits
Tick non-negativity; add bounds for realism if needed
Select method: Simplex LP (linear), GRG (smooth), Evo (discrete)
Request reports: Answer; Sensitivity if Simplex LP is valid
content.notes: Explain method choice in operational terms: Simplex LP is fast and provides sensitivity information but assumes linearity; GRG handles smooth nonlinearities but sensitivity differs; Evolutionary is for non-smooth or discrete choices but may be slower and less stable. Teach learners how to detect linearity: all formulas must be linear in the decision variables (no products of variables, no IF branching on variables, no exponentials of variables). Probing question: "If you changed a variable by 10%, would every constraint LHS change by a constant multiple?" Common misconception: including intermediate calculated cells as changing cells, which breaks the model logic.
