slides.title: Worked example: data for a product-mix model

content.title: Worked example: data for a product-mix model
content.notes: Introduce the example as a canonical linear programme: choose quantities of A and B to maximise total contribution, limited by three resources. Clarify that contribution is not a constraint here; it defines the objective coefficients. Ask learners to sanity-check coefficients: "Which product is more machine-intensive? Which is more material-intensive?" Common misconception: mixing up coefficients and limits (e.g., placing 240 under A instead of under the resource limit column). Also flag that the word ‘contribution’ implies revenue minus variable cost, not total profit including fixed costs, unless stated.

slides.title: Worked example: build the model in Excel

content.title: Worked example: build the model in Excel
content: Create variable cells for quantities of A and B
Objective cell: =SUMPRODUCT(contribution, quantities)
Compute each constraint LHS via SUMPRODUCT of resource use
Place RHS limits next to LHS; show units in headers
Add slack cells: RHS − LHS (helps checking feasibility)
Name ranges or use absolute references to avoid drift
content.notes: Talk through a recommended layout: a small decision block (A, B), then an objective row, then a constraints table. Demonstrate why slack is useful: negative slack means infeasible; zero slack often indicates binding. Encourage learners to label units explicitly in the sheet (e.g., 'hrs/week'). Probing question: "If you copied this sheet down for 10 products, where would reference errors most likely occur?" Misconception: calculating LHS using manual addition across cells, which is error-prone and harder to scale than SUMPRODUCT.

slides.title: Worked example: run Solver and validate the solution

content.title: Worked example: run Solver and validate the solution
content: Set objective to Max and select the objective cell
Set changing cells to the A and B quantity cells
Add constraints: each resource LHS <= corresponding limit
Apply A>=0, B>=0; add upper bounds if specified
Choose Simplex LP; solve and keep the solution
Recalculate objective; confirm constraints satisfied exactly
content.notes: Emphasise validation immediately after solving: do not trust the output until you have checked constraint satisfaction and objective calculation outside Solver (e.g., a duplicate objective formula). Explain why Simplex LP is appropriate: all coefficients are constants and all relationships are linear. Ask: "If your solution uses fractional units, is that operationally acceptable? If not, what changes?" (This previews integer constraints and the effect on sensitivity reporting.) Common misconception: thinking that a feasible solution is automatically optimal because Solver found it quickly; learners must still verify settings and model correctness.

slides.title: Interpret Solver reports: what to look for

content.title: Interpret Solver reports: what to look for
leftColumn: Binding constraint: slack = 0 at optimum
Non-binding: slack > 0, does not limit the optimum
Shadow price: objective change per +1 unit of RHS
Reduced cost: value needed for variable to enter solution
rightColumn: Binding constraints are the active bottlenecks
Extra capacity has no value when non-binding
Use £ per extra hour/kg to value expansions
Use reduced cost to justify excluding an option
content.notes: Explain interpretation in operational language. Example phrasing: "A shadow price of £12 per machine hour means one extra hour increases maximum contribution by £12, within the allowable range." Stress the condition: shadow prices are local marginal values, valid only within the reported allowable increase/decrease. Probing questions: "Which resource would you invest in expanding first, based on shadow prices?" and "If a variable has a negative reduced cost in a maximisation, what does that tell you about its attractiveness?" Misconception: treating shadow prices as permanent ‘true’ values outside the allowable range or under major model changes.

slides.title: Accuracy and audit checks (your calculation log)

content.title: Accuracy and audit checks (your calculation log)
content: Units check: every LHS and RHS match (hrs with hrs, kg with kg)
Direction check: ‘at most’ uses ≤, ‘at least’ uses ≥
Objective check: recompute using an independent formula
Feasibility check: all slacks >= 0 for ≤ constraints
Constraint check: record max violation (should be ~0 within tolerance)
Assumption notes: linearity, divisibility, no fixed costs, etc.
content.notes: Position the calculation log as a reproducibility tool: another learner should be able to follow your log and obtain the same objective value within the allowed tolerance. Expand on numerical tolerances: due to floating-point arithmetic, you may see tiny violations (e.g., 1E-9), which are acceptable if clearly documented. Encourage learners to screenshot Solver settings and keep a versioned file name. Probing question: "If your model gives a different optimum after you copy a formula, which audit check would detect the error fastest?" Misconception: equating a neat-looking answer with a correct model; audit evidence is part of the skill at Bloom ‘analyse’ level.

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-paced)
content: Write a model map for the product-mix example (vars, obj, 3 constraints)
Build the sheet from scratch; avoid using any provided template
Run Solver; compare your objective to a check value (±0.5%)
Identify binding constraints and explain why they bind
State one trade-off using a shadow price and its allowable range

Misconception: skipping interpretation and moving straight to ‘the numbers’; in operational contexts, interpretation is what makes optimisation useful.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: assessed spreadsheet model + interpretation write-up
Marks typically reward: model clarity, correct Solver setup, audit trail
Common error: wrong inequality direction or mismatched units
Common error: using GRG on a linear model (no Sensitivity report)
Common error: changing cells include totals or formulas (not variables)
Common error: overclaiming shadow prices beyond allowable ranges
content.notes: Explain how assessment criteria usually map to professional practice: a correct model that cannot be understood or reproduced is not considered high quality. Reinforce that sensitivity interpretation must be appropriately qualified (allowable ranges, linearity assumptions). Ask: "If an assessor re-runs your Solver, will they get the same result? What evidence have you provided to ensure that?" Provide a corrective strategy for each mistake: e.g., if units mismatch, label every row/column; if method is wrong, justify Simplex LP for linear models; if changing cells are wrong, highlight variables with a consistent colour and lock other cells.

slides.title: Model anatomy in Excel (what goes where)

content.title: Model anatomy in Excel (what goes where)
content.content: A Solver model is a set of linked cells with clear roles.
content.notes:
Explain that good modelling starts with spreadsheet design, not Solver. The key is separation of roles: variable cells should be in one contiguous range; parameters should be clearly labelled and protected from accidental editing.

Mini-example: If x1 and x2 are product quantities, profit per unit is a parameter; total profit is the objective; total labour used is a constraint LHS; labour capacity is the RHS.

Common misconceptions:
- Treating a computed cell (e.g., total labour) as a decision variable.
- Hard-coding numbers into formulas (makes auditing and sensitivity harder).

Probing questions:
- If a parameter changes (e.g., capacity), which cells should update automatically?
- Could another person identify your decision variables in 10 seconds?

slides.title: Decision variables vs fixed parameters

content.title: Decision variables vs fixed parameters
leftColumn: Unknown quantities to choose (e.g., units to produce)
Must be in variable cell range
Often have bounds (≥0, integer)
Drive objective and constraints
rightColumn: Given inputs (e.g., capacities, times, profits)
Should not be in variable range
May change in scenarios, not during solve
Used to calculate LHS and objective
content.notes:
Emphasise the conceptual distinction: variables are choices; parameters describe the environment. In Excel, the operational distinction is: variable cells are the only cells Solver changes.

Mini-example: ‘Overtime hours allowed’ is a parameter (management policy). ‘Overtime hours used’ could be a decision variable if you allow the model to choose it. Learners often confuse these.

Probing questions:
- If you are “allowing” overtime, is overtime a decision or a limit?
- What happens if you accidentally include a parameter cell in the variable range?

slides.title: Writing constraints correctly (units and direction)

content.title: Writing constraints correctly (units and direction)
content: Build each LHS as a formula, usually SUMPRODUCT
Match units on both sides (e.g., hours ≤ hours available)
Use correct direction: ≤ for capacity, ≥ for demand
Add non-negativity bounds unless negative is meaningful
Equality constraints (=) remove flexibility; use sparingly
Check slack: LHS vs RHS should be interpretable
content.notes:
Explain that a constraint is a mathematical statement linking decision variables to limits. In Excel this becomes a computed LHS cell compared to a parameter RHS cell.

Units: model errors often come from inconsistent units (minutes vs hours, weekly vs monthly). Encourage writing units in labels (e.g., “Labour hours used (h/week)”).

Direction: capacity is typically ‘used ≤ available’. Demand satisfaction is typically ‘produced ≥ required’. If a direction is wrong, Solver can “cheat” by making production negative or by violating operational logic.

Common misconceptions:
- Thinking ‘≤’ is always correct.
- Using ‘=’ for capacity because it “looks neat”, forcing wasteful production.

Probing questions:
- What does slack mean operationally in your context (idle time, spare budget)?
- When would negative decision variable values make real-world sense?

slides.title: Configuring Solver (objective, variables, method)

content.title: Configuring Solver (objective, variables, method)
content: Set Objective: select target cell and Max/Min/Value
By Changing: select contiguous decision variable range
Add constraints: LHS cells linked to RHS limit cells
Select method: Simplex LP, GRG Nonlinear, Evolutionary
Options: tick Assume Linear, Make Unconstrained ≥ 0
Solve and request Answer and Sensitivity reports
content.notes:
Talk through Solver as a translation step: you are telling Excel which cell represents the objective, which cells it can change, and what limits must hold.

Method choice guidance:
- Simplex LP: linear objective and linear constraints (most common for product mix, blending, allocation).
- GRG Nonlinear: smooth nonlinear formulas (e.g., multiplication of variables, nonlinear cost curves).
- Evolutionary: non-smooth, discontinuous, or integer-heavy models; slower and less transparent.

Stress that Sensitivity Report is generally available for linear models solved with Simplex LP; if learners pick the wrong method, they may lose sensitivity outputs.

Probing questions:
- How can you tell from your formulas whether the model is linear?
- What would you change if Solver returns “no feasible solution”?

slides.title: Worked example data (product mix)

content.title: Worked example data (product mix)
content.content: We maximise profit subject to labour and machine capacity.
content.notes:
Frame the scenario: two products compete for two scarce resources. The decision is quantities of A and B (continuous, unless you later impose integrality).

Explain the modelling interpretation:
- Profit is contribution per unit (assumed constant).
- Labour and machine requirements are per unit (assumed linear scaling).
- Capacities are total available for the planning period.

Assumptions to surface (important for audit readiness):
- Divisibility: allowing fractional units may be unrealistic.
- Certainty: capacities and profits are treated as known.

Probing questions:
- What would you add if there is a minimum demand for Product A?
- How would the model change if products must be integers?

slides.title: Build the worksheet (layout and formulas)

content.title: Build the worksheet (layout and formulas)
content: Enter xA and xB in a labelled variable cell block
Compute profit: =SUMPRODUCT(profit_row, x_range)
Compute labour used: =SUMPRODUCT(labour_row, x_range)
Compute machine used: =SUMPRODUCT(machine_row, x_range)
Reference capacities from separate parameter cells
Create a small check area: slack = capacity − used
content.notes:
Speak as if guiding a screen build: keep variables together, keep parameters together, and keep calculations traceable.

Explain why SUMPRODUCT is preferred: it scales to many products/resources without rewriting formulas and reduces reference mistakes.

Encourage robust referencing:
- Use absolute references or named ranges for parameter blocks.
- Avoid mixing constants inside formulas (e.g., “=2*$B$5 + 1*$B$6”).

Common misconceptions:
- Putting capacities directly into Solver rather than referencing a cell (harder to scenario test).
- Omitting slack checks and only relying on Solver’s “feasible” claim.

Probing questions:
- If you change the profit of Product A, which cells should update?
- Can you detect a constraint direction error just from your slack signs?

slides.title: Run Solver for the example (set-up)

content.title: Run Solver for the example (set-up)
content: Objective: Total profit cell, set to Max
Changing cells: xA:xB decision variable range
Constraints: Labour used ≤ Labour capacity
Constraints: Machine used ≤ Machine capacity
Tick non-negativity (xA, xB ≥ 0)
Method: Simplex LP; Solve; keep solution
content.notes:
Reinforce the mapping: objective is one cell; variables are the cells Solver can change; constraints are comparisons between LHS formula cells and RHS limit cells.

If the solution seems odd, diagnose systematically:
- Check formulas first (are LHS cells correctly linked to xA and xB?).
- Check constraint direction (≤ vs ≥).
- Confirm the objective cell references the variable cells.

Common misconception: learners add constraints on the variable cells instead of on the LHS usage cells (e.g., mistakenly constraining xA ≤ 100 when 100 is labour hours, not units).

Probing questions:
- What does “Assume Linear Model” change about the solve process?
- Why might Solver give different answers if you start with different initial guesses in nonlinear models?

slides.title: Interpret the Answer Report (feasibility first)

content.title: Interpret the Answer Report (feasibility first)
content: Confirm Solver status: found optimal solution
Record objective value and variable values with units
Check each constraint: LHS, RHS, and slack
Binding if slack = 0; non-binding if slack > 0
Verify 0 violations; investigate any “not satisfied”
Translate results into operational statements
content.notes:
Teach a disciplined reading order.

1) Status line: “Solver found a solution” is not enough; you want “optimal” and feasible.
2) Decision variables: state them with units (e.g., units/week). Avoid copying raw numbers without context.
3) Constraints: explain slack operationally (unused hours, unused budget). If slack is negative, you have a violation or a sign convention problem.

Operational implications examples:
- Binding labour: labour is a bottleneck; extra labour could raise profit.
- Non-binding machine: spare machine capacity; investing in more machines may not help yet.

Common misconceptions:
- Calling a constraint “binding” because it is important conceptually, not because slack is zero.
- Ignoring a small violation caused by precision/rounding.

Probing questions:
- Which resource is the bottleneck and how can you tell?
- If a constraint is non-binding, is it irrelevant? When might it become binding?

slides.title: Use Sensitivity Report for recommendations

content.title: Use Sensitivity Report for recommendations
content.content: Interpret shadow prices and ranges only within valid limits.

rows: Δ objective per +1 RHS unit (binding only)
RHS can rise by this amount with same basis
Check if recommendation range is valid
RHS can fall by this amount with same basis
Improvement needed for variable to enter solution

content.notes:
Explain sensitivity as ‘local’ analysis around the optimum for linear models. The shadow price is a marginal value: how much the objective would improve if you relax a binding constraint by one unit, holding everything else consistent.

Make the units explicit:
- If objective is £ profit and RHS is labour hours, shadow price is £/hour.
- Learners should state this in recommendations (e.g., “An extra labour hour is worth about £X profit, within Y hours”).

Allowable ranges are crucial:
- Shadow prices are only reliable within the allowable increase/decrease, because beyond that the set of binding constraints can change.

Mini-example recommendation structure:
- Identify highest positive shadow price among binding constraints.
- Propose expanding that capacity first, up to the allowable increase.
- Justify rounding: e.g., “Shadow price £4.67/hour, rounded to £4.70/hour to match reporting precision.”

Common misconceptions:
- Using shadow prices for non-binding constraints (often zero).
- Applying shadow prices far beyond the allowable range.
- Treating reduced cost as a “penalty” without linking it to the objective coefficient.

Probing questions:
- If two constraints are binding, can both have positive shadow prices? What does that imply?
- What would you conclude if the shadow price is zero for a binding constraint (degeneracy)?

slides.title: Practice and reflection (do, then verify)

content.title: Practice and reflection (do, then verify)
leftColumn: Rebuild the model with your own cell layout and labels
Add a minimum demand constraint for one product
Solve and identify binding constraints from slack
Write one capacity-expansion recommendation using units
rightColumn: Variables are separate from parameters and clearly named
All constraints show 0 violations in the Answer Report
Method choice matches model type (LP vs nonlinear)
Recommendation respects allowable increase/decrease
content.notes:
Encourage active practice: learners should not only replicate the example but introduce one modification (e.g., a minimum demand). That forces them to think about constraint direction and feasibility.

Guide reflection:
- Ask them to explain in words what changed in the solution when the new constraint was added.
- Ask whether the new constraint became binding and what slack means now.

Common misconception: adding constraints until Solver fails, then randomly changing numbers. Instead, diagnose infeasibility by checking whether constraints logically conflict (e.g., minimum demand exceeds combined capacity).

Probing questions:
- What is your evidence that your solution is feasible?
- Which constraint would you relax first if the model becomes infeasible, and why?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: MOD104 optimisation workbook and quiz questions
Mistake: wrong changing-cell range (includes parameters)
Mistake: constraint direction wrong (≤ vs ≥) or units mixed
Mistake: using Simplex on nonlinear formulas (bad reports)
Mistake: interpreting shadow prices outside allowable range
Mistake: no audit trail (cannot justify or reproduce results)
content.notes:
Position the lesson as directly supporting typical assessed tasks: building an Excel optimisation model, documenting it, and interpreting Solver reports to justify decisions.

Expand on each common mistake with a quick fix:
- Changing-cell range: keep variables in one contiguous block; colour-code.
- Direction/units: add units in headers; do a quick “reasonableness” test (e.g., if x=0, are LHS values 0?).
- Wrong method: check linearity by scanning for variable*variable terms, IF statements, or nonlinear functions.
- Shadow price misuse: always cite the allowable range alongside the marginal value.
- Audit trail: include a calculation log with dated checks and brief notes.

Probing questions:
- If a marker changes one parameter, will your workbook update cleanly?
- What would you show to defend your recommendation to a manager?

content: A Solver model is objective + variables + constraints + parameters
Feasibility first: 0 violations, then interpret optimality
Binding constraints indicate bottlenecks; slack indicates capacity

Audit checks make your optimisation result credible and reusable

Encourage learners to complete the MCQ checks after a short break, and to revisit any step where they relied on “trial and error” rather than a clear modelling rationale.

content.title: Orientation and learning outcomes
content: Identify binding constraints, shadow prices, reduced costs
Use allowable ranges to judge 'safe' parameter changes

slides.title: Solver reports: what they are for

content.title: Solver reports: what they are for
content: Answer Report: solution values, objective, constraint slack
Sensitivity Report: prices/costs and allowable ranges (LP only)
Use Simplex LP to generate sensitivity outputs
Treat reports as evidence: what changed, what stayed tight
Export/keep reports with timestamp for audit
content.notes:
Explain the practical workflow: after running Solver, you can request reports. The Answer Report is broadly available and gives you the chosen decision variable values, the objective value, and slack/surplus for constraints. The Sensitivity Report is only produced for linear programmes solved using Simplex LP, and typically not available (or not meaningful) for integer, nonlinear, or evolutionary methods.

Stress the “evidence” mindset: reports are not decoration; they are the justification for decisions. Encourage learners to think like an auditor: Can you show what the objective was, what constraints were active, and how sensitive the result is to key assumptions?

Common misconception: learners treat the Sensitivity Report as automatically valid regardless of Solver settings. Make explicit: if you used GRG Nonlinear or set integer constraints, do not rely on shadow prices and allowable ranges without further checking.

Probing questions: Which Solver method did you use, and why? If you cannot produce a Sensitivity Report, what alternative approach can you use (e.g., scenario re-solves, data tables)?

Common misconception: learners treat the Sensitivity Report as automatically valid regardless of Solver settings. Make explicit: if you used GRG Nonlinear or set integer constraints, do not rely on shadow prices and allowable ranges without further checking.

Probing questions: Which Solver method did you use, and why? If you cannot produce a Sensitivity Report, what alternative approach can you use (e.g., scenario re-solves, data tables)?

slides.title: Binding versus non-binding constraints

content.title: Binding versus non-binding constraints
content: Binding: slack = 0, limits the optimum
Non-binding: slack > 0, not currently restricting
Binding does not mean 'important forever'
Multiple binding constraints can exist at one optimum
Check signs: '≥' constraints use surplus, not slack
content.notes:
Define binding in operational terms: a binding constraint is “tight” at the optimum, so relaxing it slightly could improve the objective (subject to other constraints). A non-binding constraint has unused capacity (slack), so small increases in capacity typically do not change the optimum.

Clarify slack vs surplus: for a “≤” constraint, slack = RHS − LHS; for a “≥” constraint, you may see “surplus” (LHS − RHS). Learners often misread a surplus value as slack and reverse the meaning.

Explain why “binding” is not a permanent label: if prices change, demand changes, or you add constraints, a previously non-binding constraint can become binding and vice versa.

Mini-example (verbal): if your labour constraint has slack of 5 hours, adding 1 hour of labour will not change the solution (locally); but reducing labour by 6 hours will likely force a different plan.

Probing questions: If a constraint is non-binding, what two actions could still make it relevant? (e.g., reduce RHS, change objective coefficients).

slides.title: Shadow prices vs reduced costs

content.title: Shadow prices vs reduced costs
leftColumn: From constraints
Value of +1 RHS unit (within range)
Zero for non-binding constraints
Units: objective per constraint unit
rightColumn: From variables
Penalty for forcing variable into solution
Zero for variables used in optimum
Shows objective change needed to enter
content.notes:
Teach the interpretation contrast clearly.

Shadow price (dual value): how much the objective would improve if you increase a constraint’s RHS by one unit, assuming you stay within the allowable RHS range. Emphasise the units: “£ per labour hour”, “£ per kg of material”, etc. A non-binding constraint typically has shadow price 0 because extra capacity is not currently valuable.

Reduced cost: for a variable at zero (or at a bound), the reduced cost tells you how much the objective coefficient must improve (for maximisation) before that variable becomes positive in the optimal solution, holding the current basis. It is an “opportunity cost” of including that variable.

Common misconceptions:
- Shadow price is not the “average value” of a resource; it is marginal and local.
- Reduced cost is not “cost reduction achieved”; it is a threshold for attractiveness.

Probing questions: If a product has reduced cost of −3 in a profit maximisation model, what does that imply about its unit profit? If labour has a shadow price of 13, what business question can you answer with it, and what caveat must you add?

slides.title: Allowable ranges and what they do not mean

content.title: Allowable ranges and what they do not mean
content: Allowable inc/dec show where current basis stays optimal
RHS ranges: valid region for shadow prices
Objective ranges: where reduced costs remain valid
Outside range: re-solve; prices/costs may change
Ranges are local, not forecasts under uncertainty
content.notes:
Explain “basis stays optimal” in plain language: the same set of binding constraints (and which variables are at zero vs positive) remains optimal. Within that region, the shadow prices and reduced costs are valid approximations.

Separate two range types:
- RHS allowable increase/decrease: how far you can change a constraint limit before the shadow price changes (or before a different constraint becomes binding).
- Objective coefficient allowable increase/decrease: how far you can change a variable’s profit/cost coefficient before the solution structure changes.

Emphasise the evaluation step: if your proposed scenario change exceeds an allowable range, you cannot simply multiply the shadow price by the change; you must re-run Solver.

Common misconception: treating allowable ranges as “worst/best case” uncertainty bounds. They are not probabilistic; they are structural stability limits.

Probing questions: If the allowable increase for labour RHS is 8 hours and you propose adding 20 hours, what is the correct method? What do you expect could happen to the binding set?

slides.title: Audit trail: what to log for replication

content.title: Audit trail: what to log for replication
content: Inputs table with sources, units, and version/date
Decision variable cells named and bounded
Objective formula shown and cross-checked
Constraints listed with rationale and cell references
Solver settings: method, tolerances, integer options
Saved outputs: reports, screenshots, file path, timestamp
content.notes:
Frame this as professional practice: optimisation outputs often inform spend, staffing, pricing, or capacity decisions, so you need a transparent record that another analyst (or an external reviewer) can reproduce.

Explain what “replication” means: opening the workbook, understanding what each number represents, running Solver with the same settings, and obtaining the same solution and reports.

Give concrete examples of what learners should write:
- “Labour hours per unit from time-and-motion study v3, dated 12/02/2026.”
- “Decision variables in cells B12:B13, non-negativity enforced.”
- “Objective in B15 = SUMPRODUCT(profit_per_unit, quantities).”
- “Constraints: labour use (B18) <= 100; material use (B19) <= 80; rationale: weekly capacity.”
- “Solver: Simplex LP; Assume Linear Model ticked; Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative ticked.”

Common mistake: learners record the final numbers but not the Solver configuration, making results irreproducible.

Probing questions: If you were absent, what would a colleague need to rerun your model correctly? What might change if they choose GRG Nonlinear instead of Simplex LP?

slides.title: Risk register: link limits to Solver outputs

content.title: Risk register: link limits to Solver outputs
content: Assumption: linearity/divisibility; note if violated
Data quality: stale costs/capacity; link to input sources
Range limits: shadow prices valid only within RHS range
Model form: omitted constraints; watch for infeasibility
Alternative optima: zero allowable change may signal this
Document mitigations and when to rerun Solver
content.notes:
Introduce the risk register as a structured way to state: (1) what could invalidate the recommendation, (2) where it shows up in outputs, and (3) what you will do about it.

Provide examples learners can adapt:
- Assumption risk (model form): “Linearity assumed; volume discounts ignored. If discounts apply, re-model with piecewise costs.” Link: Solver method and linear model assumption.
- Data risk: “Unit profits based on last quarter; may drift.” Link: inputs table with dates, and scenario analysis changing profits within allowable ranges.
- Sensitivity applicability risk: “Shadow price for labour (£/hr) valid only within allowable increase/decrease.” Link: Sensitivity Report RHS range.
- Feasibility risk: “New policy constraint could make model infeasible.” Link: Solver status messages and infeasibility when adding constraints.
- Alternative optimum risk: “Allowable change of 0 may indicate multiple optima/degeneracy.” Link: Sensitivity ranges and Solver report behaviour.

Common misconception: listing generic risks without tying them to model evidence. Require the link: each risk note should reference a specific output or Solver status.

Probing questions: Which assumption, if wrong, would change your recommendation most? What evidence would trigger a rerun?

slides.title: Worked example: product mix model set-up

content.title: Worked example: product mix model set-up
content: Decision vars: units of A and B (≥0)
Maximise total profit subject to labour and material limits

table.notes:
Walk learners through translating the table into an LP model.

Define decision variables clearly: x_A = units of A, x_B = units of B.
Objective (maximise profit): Maximise 30x_A + 20x_B.
Constraints:
- Labour capacity: 2x_A + 1x_B ≤ 100.
- Material capacity: 1x_A + 2x_B ≤ 80.
- Non-negativity: x_A, x_B ≥ 0.

Explain how to implement in Excel:
- Place x_A and x_B in cells (e.g., B6:C6).
- Compute labour used with SUMPRODUCT of labour coefficients and quantities.
- Compute material used similarly.
- Compute objective with SUMPRODUCT of profits and quantities.
- In Solver: Set Objective (profit cell) to Max; By Changing Variable Cells (x_A, x_B); Add constraints; choose Simplex LP.

Probing questions: What are the units of each coefficient? If profit were instead “contribution margin”, what would need to change in your narrative? What real-world factors might make non-negativity unrealistic (e.g., returns), and how would you handle that?

slides.title: Lesson 7: Optimisation scenarios and justified choice

content.title: Lesson 7: Optimisation scenarios and justified choice
content: Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD104 — Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver
Lesson: Alternative optimisation scenarios and justify a choice
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
In this lesson you will move beyond finding a single ‘best’ Solver solution and instead evaluate multiple optimisation scenarios. In practice, constraints, capacities, and input parameters are rarely fixed; decision-makers need to know how the solution changes when assumptions change.

Emphasise that the learning focus is evaluative (Bloom: evaluate): you will compare scenario outputs, assess robustness using sensitivity checks, and justify a recommendation with evidence and clear limitations.

If learners are new to Excel Solver: reassure them that the technical steps are straightforward, but the higher-value skill is documenting what you did so the model can be audited and reproduced.

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Build a Solver model with objective, variables and 3+ constraints
Save Solver settings/log for audit and reproducibility
Run 3 scenarios and compare objective, feasibility and variables
Do 2 sensitivity checks and capture risks in a risk register
Write a 150–250 word decision memo with results and risks
content.notes:
How to use this lesson in self-study: (1) read the core concepts first, (2) follow the worked example in Excel, pausing to replicate each step, (3) complete the practice prompts, and (4) attempt the two MCQ checks.

Clarify the difference between ‘doing Solver’ and ‘doing optimisation professionally’. Professional practice includes: clear labelling of cells, consistent units, a record of assumptions, and a traceable record of Solver settings.

Probing questions to frame the lesson:
- If a stakeholder tightens a constraint, which decision variables change most?
- When does a higher objective value become unacceptable due to risk?
- What evidence would convince an auditor that your result is reproducible?

Common misconception to surface early: learners often think ‘the Solver answer’ is final. Instead, Solver provides conditional answers given assumptions and constraints; your role is to evaluate alternatives and justify a decision.

slides.title: Scenarios, sensitivity and robustness

content.title: Scenarios, sensitivity and robustness
content: Scenario: purposeful change to constraints, bounds or structure
Sensitivity check: small parameter change to test stability
Robust solution: remains acceptable under plausible changes
Compare: objective value, feasibility, and key variables
Document: what changed, why, and what stayed constant
content.notes:
Explain scenario analysis as ‘what-if with intent’: you change something that might realistically change in the real system (e.g., capacity cut, new policy limit, tighter service requirement). Sensitivity checks are typically smaller, plausibility-based perturbations (e.g., ±5% on resource availability) to see whether the recommendation is fragile.

A useful rule for learners: scenarios help you compare options; sensitivity helps you trust (or doubt) an option.

Highlight feasibility: a scenario can be infeasible if constraints conflict. Infeasibility is not a failure; it is evidence that the requirement set cannot be met simultaneously.

Ask learners to consider: if a scenario increases profit but violates a constraint, is that a ‘better’ solution? (Answer: no—constraint violations mean it is not an admissible solution.)

Misconception: ‘robust’ does not mean the objective never changes. It means the decision remains defensible because changes are modest, predictable, or manageable.

slides.title: Configuring Solver with an audit trail

content.title: Configuring Solver with an audit trail
content: Decision variables: changing cells with clear names and units
Objective: single cell formula to maximise or minimise
Constraints: include 2+ business limits plus non-negativity
Method: Simplex LP for linear; GRG for smooth non-linear
Save/load model range and keep Solver reports as evidence
Record: version, timestamp, scenario label, and assumptions
content.notes:
Talk through a minimal but audit-friendly setup. Decision variables should be in a dedicated block, labelled (e.g., xA, xB) with units (units produced, hours allocated). The objective should be a single cell that references those variables (e.g., total profit = SUMPRODUCT(profit, quantities)).

Constraints should be explicitly written on the sheet (left-hand side and right-hand side), not only inside Solver. This allows a reader to see the model logic without opening Solver.

Non-negativity: either tick ‘Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative’ or add explicit constraints x ≥ 0. Emphasise that non-negativity is a modelling assumption, not just a Solver option.

Audit trail options:
- Use Solver’s Load/Save to store the model in a cell range.
- Save Solver Answer Report (and Sensitivity Report for LP).
- Maintain a simple log: scenario name, what changed, objective value, and file version/date.

Misconception: screenshots alone are not reproducible; a saved model range plus documented cell references is much stronger evidence.

slides.title: A simple scenario comparison framework

content.title: A simple scenario comparison framework
content: Baseline: current assumptions and constraints
Scenario A: tightened constraint (e.g., less labour available)
Scenario B: added bound (e.g., capacity limit on a product)
Keep a scenario table: change, objective, x-values, notes
Flag feasibility and binding constraints for each scenario
content.notes:
Introduce a repeatable process learners can reuse in assignments:
1) Define a baseline model and confirm it solves correctly.
2) Change one modelling element at a time for each scenario.
3) Re-solve and capture: objective value, key decision variables, and whether any constraints are binding.

Explain why ‘one change at a time’ matters: it supports attribution. If you change three assumptions at once, you cannot explain why the solution moved.

Binding constraints: help learners interpret. If a constraint is binding, it is actively limiting the optimum; non-binding constraints have slack. Binding constraints are often where managerial attention goes (e.g., invest in extra capacity, renegotiate supply).

Probing questions:
- Which scenario is best if profit is the only criterion?
- Which scenario is best once risk and feasibility are considered?
- Which constraint is the main bottleneck, and can it realistically be relaxed?

slides.title: Risk register for scenario robustness

content.title: Risk register for scenario robustness
content.notes:
Use this slide to teach learners how to convert ‘uncertainty’ into something actionable. A risk register is not just for compliance; it is a thinking tool.

Explain each column:
- Risk/assumption: what might be wrong or change.
- Impact: how that would change feasibility or optimality.
- Mitigation/response: what you will do now (scenario tests, data collection, contingency plan).
- Monitor/trigger: what evidence would tell you to revisit the decision.

Connect to sensitivity checks: each sensitivity check is often a mitigation for a risk (e.g., profits are uncertain → test ±10%).

Probing questions:
- Which risk could flip your recommended scenario?
- Which risk is most likely vs most harmful?
- What is a realistic trigger you can actually measure?

Misconception: listing risks without monitoring actions is not robust evaluation; it is merely a disclaimer.

slides.title: Worked example data: product mix model

content.title: Worked example data: product mix model
content.notes:
Set up a realistic but simple product-mix model in Excel.

State the full model verbally so learners can translate it into a worksheet:
- Decision variables: xA and xB (units to produce).
- Objective: maximise total profit = 30·xA + 20·xB.
- Constraints (baseline):
  1) Labour: 2·xA + 1·xB ≤ 100 hours
  2) Material: 1·xA + 2·xB ≤ 80 kg
  3) Demand cap: xB ≤ 50 units
  4) Non-negativity: xA, xB ≥ 0

Encourage learners to build a clear layout:
- Inputs (profits, coefficients, limits)
- Decision variable cells
- Calculated LHS for each constraint
- A check column for slack (RHS − LHS)

Probing question: which resource is likely to be the bottleneck, labour or material, and why?

Common mistake: mixing units (hours vs days, kg vs tonnes) without converting; this silently breaks optimisation results.

slides.title: Worked example: Solver setup and baseline run

content.title: Worked example: Solver setup and baseline run
content: Set objective cell: Total profit = SUMPRODUCT(profit, x)
By changing: xA and xB decision variable cells
Add constraints: labour <=100; material <=80; xB<=50
Ensure xA>=0 and xB>=0 (or tick non-negativity)
Select Simplex LP; Solve; save Answer Report
Save model range and label it 'Baseline v1'
content.notes:
Walk learners through the exact Solver fields and how to avoid common configuration errors.

Key teaching points:
- Confirm the objective cell contains a formula, not a hard-coded value.
- Ensure the ‘By Changing Variable Cells’ range includes only decision variables.
- For linear problems, Simplex LP is appropriate; using GRG can still work but may be slower and less transparent.

After solving, interpret the solution in plain language: “Produce xA units of A and xB units of B to maximise profit while respecting labour, material, and demand limits.”

Reproducibility steps:
- Save the Solver model to a cell range (Solver → Load/Save).
- Save the Answer Report and keep it with your file.
- Record scenario name, date/time, and what constraints were used.

Probing questions:
- Which constraints are binding at the solution (slack = 0)?
- If a constraint has slack, does that mean it is unimportant?

Misconception: learners sometimes ‘solve’ without checking feasibility. Always check constraint LHS values against RHS on-sheet.

slides.title: Worked example: scenario comparison results

content.title: Worked example: scenario comparison results
content.notes:
Use the table to model how to communicate results succinctly. Explain what changed in each scenario and what stayed constant.

Interpretation guidance:
- Baseline produces more A than scenarios because A is profit-rich and uses less material per profit than B in this setup.
- Tightening labour (Scenario A) reduces the objective and shifts the mix slightly towards B because B uses fewer labour hours per unit.
- Adding a capacity cap on A (Scenario B) forces substitution into B, lowering the objective further.

Feasibility check: confirm each scenario remains feasible (constraints satisfied). If learners get different numbers, prompt them to check:
- Did they change the correct RHS cell?
- Did they accidentally overwrite a formula with a number?
- Are variable cells correctly referenced in constraint formulas?

Probing questions:
- Which scenario would you recommend if the A capacity cap is likely?
- Which scenario is more sensitive to errors in the profit estimates?

Use the table to model how to communicate results succinctly. Explain what changed in each scenario and what stayed constant.

Interpretation guidance:
- Baseline produces more A than scenarios because A is profit-rich and uses less material per profit than B in this setup.
- Tightening labour (Scenario A) reduces the objective and shifts the mix slightly towards B because B uses fewer labour hours per unit.
- Adding a capacity cap on A (Scenario B) forces substitution into B, lowering the objective further.

- Did they change the correct RHS cell?
- Did they accidentally overwrite a formula with a number?

leftColumn: Run Scenario C: material <= 75; record new solution
Sensitivity 1: change profit A by -10%; does x change?

content.notes:
This is where learners practise evaluation rather than calculation.

Guidance for Scenario C (material tightened): remind learners to change only one element and keep the rest identical to baseline, then log results with a new label.

Sensitivity checks: stress that the purpose is diagnostic, not to ‘find a better answer’. If the optimal decision variables change drastically after a small parameter change, the solution is fragile and needs stronger risk management or a different modelling approach.

Encourage learners to write down, for each run:
- what changed,
- why it is plausible,
- the new objective,
- the new x values,
- feasibility and binding constraints.

Probing prompts if learners are stuck:
- If the objective changes but x stays the same, what does that suggest?
- If x changes, what does that suggest about trade-offs and bottlenecks?

Common mistake: learners perform multiple changes at once (e.g., change profit and constraints). Require discipline: one change per test.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: scenario comparison + decision memo recommendation
Include Solver settings record and labelled scenario log/table
State feasibility; do not compare infeasible solutions

content.notes:
Explain what a strong submission looks like: it tells a coherent story from model → scenarios → robustness → recommendation.

Decision memo expectations (150–250 words): learners should cite quantitative results (objective values and key variable changes), explain constraint rationale (why these limits exist), and explicitly discuss at least two risks/limitations with mitigation or monitoring.

Common mistakes to warn about:
- Missing non-negativity (allowing negative production/allocation).
- Treating Solver output as ‘correct’ without checking constraint satisfaction.
- Using inconsistent units across coefficients and RHS values.
- Reporting only the objective value without the decision-variable implications.
- Forgetting to save the Solver model; results become non-auditable.

If learners have access to the Sensitivity Report (LP), remind them it is only valid under linearity and within allowable ranges; it is not a substitute for scenario testing.

Encourage learners to use the MCQs as diagnostic tools: review explanations and revisit the slides where they missed concepts.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: A Solver solution is conditional on assumptions and constraints
Scenario analysis compares structured model changes
Sensitivity checks test whether a recommendation is fragile
Auditability needs saved settings, labelled runs, and clear logs
Justification requires numbers plus risks, limits, and actions
content.notes:
Reinforce the evaluative mindset: you are not optimising for its own sake; you are supporting a defensible decision.

Invite learners to self-assess against the objectives:
- Can you rebuild the model from your saved settings alone?
- Can you explain why each scenario differs in outcome?

content.title: Solver results and sensitivity outputs
content.content:
Maths Certification

Lesson 8: Solver results and sensitivity outputs to interpret marginal values
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners to Lesson 8, which focuses on evaluating Solver outputs rather than building models from scratch. Emphasise that at Bloom’s ‘evaluate’ level, the goal is to justify decisions using evidence from Solver’s Answer and Sensitivity reports, including limitations.

Frame why this matters: in operational settings, the optimisation result is only the start—decision-makers need to know (1) what is constraining performance, (2) how stable the recommendation is under change, and (3) what risks and assumptions sit behind the numbers.

Prompt: “If your manager asks ‘what should we change first to improve profit?’, what part of the Sensitivity Report answers that most directly?”

slides.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson
content: Identify binding constraints and rank bottlenecks by shadow price
Use reduced costs and ranges to judge if changes alter the solution
Compare scenarios using objective, feasibility, realism and risk

Study flow: read → replicate in Excel → attempt checks → review
content.notes:
Talk learners through the four learning objectives as a workflow:
1) Diagnose the current optimum (binding constraints and bottlenecks).
2) Test stability (reduced costs; allowable ranges for coefficients and RHS).
3) Evaluate alternatives (scenario thinking and explicit criteria).
4) Document for audit (so another analyst can reproduce results).

Explain ‘audit-ready’: it does not mean perfect forecasting; it means reproducible steps, referenced outputs, and clearly stated assumptions.

Probing questions:
- “What evidence would you attach to prove a constraint is binding?”
- “When is it unsafe to use shadow prices for ‘what-if’ calculations?”

slides.title: When sensitivity outputs are valid

content.title: When sensitivity outputs are valid
content.content: Sensitivity reports apply to linear programmes solved by Simplex LP. They assume a fixed model structure and changes within allowable ranges. Integer, nonlinear, or large structural changes require re-solving and may invalidate marginal values.
content.notes:
Clarify the scope conditions learners often miss:
- Sensitivity Report is produced for linear models (Simplex LP). If you used GRG Nonlinear or Evolutionary, the report may be absent or not meaningful.
- Even in LP, sensitivity is local: it describes marginal effects near the optimum, not global behaviour.
- The ‘model structure fixed’ assumption means: same decision variables, same constraints (except small RHS changes), same linearity.

Common misconception: treating shadow price as universally true for any size change. Reinforce: it is only guaranteed within the allowable increase/decrease for the RHS.

Ask: “If you add a new constraint (e.g., emissions cap), is that a ‘within-range’ change or a structural change?”

slides.title: Constraint section: how to read it

content.title: Constraint section: how to read it
content.notes:
Explain each field in plain language with a quick mental model: the constraint is a ‘gate’ limiting the solution.
- Final value is what you used.
- RHS is what you have.
- Slack is what remains.
- Shadow price is the value of one more unit of RHS, holding the rest constant.

Units: shadow price has units of objective per unit of constraint. If objective is profit (£) and RHS is labour hours, shadow price is £/hour.

Sign: in maximisation with ≤ constraints, shadow prices are typically non-negative. If learners see negative values, discuss whether it is a ≥ constraint, a minimisation objective, or a modelling sign convention issue.

Probing question: “If slack is 10, what should you expect the shadow price to be—and why?”

slides.title: Decision variable section: stability signals

content.title: Decision variable section: stability signals
content.notes:
Explain reduced cost carefully because it is a frequent stumbling block:
- For a maximisation problem, a non-basic variable at 0 with reduced cost −2 means its profit must increase by 2 (units of objective per unit) before it becomes attractive enough to enter the solution.
- For variables already positive in the optimal solution (basic variables), reduced cost is 0.

Link to evaluation: reduced cost and allowable ranges tell you whether a proposed pricing/cost change is likely to matter. If the change sits fully inside the allowable range, you can usually argue the current decision mix remains optimal (though objective value changes).

Ask: “If a product is currently not produced, what two numbers in the report tell you how far it is from being selected?”

slides.title: Interpretation rules and misconceptions

content.title: Interpretation rules and misconceptions
leftColumn: Binding: slack = 0 (within tolerance)
Bottleneck: highest shadow price among binding constraints
Reduced cost: how much coeff must improve to enter
Ranges: limits where marginal values stay valid
rightColumn: Slack > 0 can occur with a positive shadow price (degeneracy)
Shadow price is not a forecast beyond its RHS range
Reduced cost is not a 'loss' if the var is used
Ranges ignore structural changes (new constraints/vars)
content.notes:
Use this slide to teach ‘rules of thumb’ and then immediately challenge them with edge cases.

Degeneracy note: sometimes Solver reports a binding constraint (slack 0) with shadow price 0, or a non-binding constraint with non-zero shadow price due to numerical tolerance or degeneracy. Advise learners to treat very small slacks (e.g., 1E-9) as effectively zero and to sanity-check by slightly perturbing RHS and re-solving.

Misconception check:
- “If I increase RHS by 100, can I multiply shadow price by 100?” Only if 100 is within allowable increase.

Probing question: “Which is more convincing in a decision note: quoting a shadow price alone, or quoting it together with the allowable RHS range?”

slides.title: Worked example: identify binding constraints

content.title: Worked example: identify binding constraints
content.notes:
Walk learners through the mechanics of identification:
1) Locate the constraint section.
2) Mark constraints with slack = 0 as binding (here: Labour, Material).
3) Confirm non-binding constraints have shadow price 0 (here: both demand caps).

Interpretation: Labour and Material are the active ‘bottlenecks’ at the optimum; demand is not currently limiting.

Explain the sign and units explicitly:
- Labour shadow price +12 £/h means: within the allowable RHS range, 1 extra hour of labour increases optimal profit by about £12.
- Material shadow price +8 £/kg means: within range, 1 extra kg increases profit by about £8.

Probing question: “If you could buy either 1 more hour of labour or 1 more kg of material, which is more valuable at the margin—and what additional information would you need before acting?” (Expected: cost to acquire; allowable range; operational feasibility.)

slides.title: Ranking bottlenecks and reporting correctly

content.title: Ranking bottlenecks and reporting correctly
content: Step 1: list binding constraints (slack = 0)
Step 2: rank by absolute shadow price (objective units/RHS unit)
Step 3: report sign and units (e.g., +12 £ per labour hour)
Step 4: cite allowable RHS range as validity limit
Step 5: note feasibility/realism of relaxing the constraint
content.notes:
Teach learners how to fill the required template without ambiguity:
- Ranking: usually sort by shadow price magnitude because it indicates marginal leverage. In maximisation with ≤ constraints, values are typically positive; still, instruct them to keep the sign.
- Units discipline: write “£/hour”, “£/kg”, “minutes per unit profit” etc depending on the model.
- Validity: learners must mention the allowable increase/decrease for the RHS (even if not shown on the slide) because otherwise the recommendation is not defensible.

Mini-example sentence for a decision note: “Labour is the primary bottleneck: shadow price +£12 per hour (valid for RHS changes within the allowable range), exceeding Material at +£8 per kg.”

Common error: ranking by slack size rather than shadow price. Slack tells you ‘unused’, not ‘value of more’.

slides.title: Worked example: reduced costs and ranges

content.title: Worked example: reduced costs and ranges
content.notes:
Explain what learners can conclude, and what they cannot:
- A and B are produced (positive final values); reduced cost 0 is expected.
- Product C is not produced; reduced cost −2 means its unit profit must increase by £2 (from £18 to £20) before it is worth entering the plan, holding everything else fixed.

Use the ranges to judge ‘material change’:
- If A’s profit changes from £30 to £33, it remains within £20–£35, so the optimal basis is expected to remain the same; objective value updates, but the mix may not.
- If C’s profit increases to £21, this exceeds its allowable increase; the current basis may change. The correct action is to re-run Solver and compare.

Probing question: “If marketing proposes a £1 discount on B (profit down by £1), do you expect the production plan to change? What evidence supports your answer?” (Expected: £1 is within B’s allowable decrease of 4 if current coeff is 20 → down to 16.)

content.title: Evaluating alternative scenarios explicitly

rows: Prefer highest net gain with feasible delivery

content.notes:
Show learners how to move from report-reading to evaluation.

Explain the asterisk: the quick calculation (shadow price × change) is a local approximation and only defensible if the RHS change is within allowable increase/decrease and the model stays linear.

Teach explicit criteria (from the learning objective):
- Objective value: expected net benefit, not just gross benefit.
- Feasibility: can you actually acquire labour/material in time?
- Operational realism: does it require retraining, downtime, quality impacts?
- Risk: uncertainty in parameters; dependency on assumptions.

Probing questions:
- “What additional data do you need to turn +£60 gross gain into a net recommendation?” (Cost per labour hour, overheads, recruitment constraints.)
- “Why is S3 flagged as ‘must re-solve’ rather than using a quick marginal estimate?”

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: scenario evaluation and justified recommendations tasks
Include Solver settings: method, tolerance, linearity assumptions
Reference outputs: report names, cell ranges, timestamps
Common error: using shadow price beyond allowable RHS range
Common error: ignoring units/sign or mixing profit and cost
Common error: no risk note or missing assumptions/uncertainty
content.notes:
Explain what ‘good’ looks like in assessed work: a marker should be able to reproduce your result without asking questions.

Elaborate on the most frequent mistakes:
- Validity misuse: learners multiply shadow price by a large change without checking allowable ranges.
- Unit slippage: reporting ‘12’ without “£/hour”, or forgetting that a cost-minimisation shadow price often flips sign interpretation.
- Over-claiming: presenting sensitivity as certainty. Encourage careful language: “within the allowable range, the model implies…”.

Risk note expectations: even a basic confidence interval (if provided in the task data) should be recorded, alongside limitations (e.g., linear cost assumption, no integer constraints).

Probing question: “If two scenarios have similar objective value, which criterion becomes decisive, and how would you evidence it?”

slides.title: Lesson 9: Alternative optimisation scenarios

content.title: Lesson 9: Alternative optimisation scenarios
content.content:
Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD104 — Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver
Lesson: Alternative optimisation scenarios and justification
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
In this lesson we move beyond “find the optimum once” and focus on evaluation: comparing alternatives and justifying a recommendation with evidence. In practice, the most useful optimisation work is scenario-based: stakeholders change limits, prices, or add new constraints, and you need to show how (and why) the optimum responds.

As you work, keep the end-product in mind: a clear recommendation that is auditable. That means (1) a tidy model with units, (2) a transparent log of Solver settings and scenario changes, (3) a comparison of at least three scenarios, and (4) diligence checks that catch typical modelling errors.

Probing question to frame the lesson: if two scenarios have similar objective values, what other evidence would make one option preferable?

slides.title: Learning objectives

content.title: Learning objectives
content: Set up Solver with ≥2 variables, 1 objective, ≥3 constraints + units
Compare ≥3 scenarios; maintain a transparent settings log
Evaluate using outputs (objective, binding constraints, reports)
Apply diligence checks; correct ≥2 issues before recommending
content.notes:
Treat these objectives as a checklist for your own work. “Set up Solver” is not only clicking the right buttons: it includes making the spreadsheet legible, ensuring decision variables and constraints are correctly referenced, and stating units so results are interpretable.

Scenario comparison requires more than rerunning Solver. You need to record what changed, what stayed constant, and what Solver settings were used (method, tolerances, iteration limits). If you ever have to defend your result, the log is your evidence.

Evaluation at this level means you justify a choice, not merely report numbers. You will use objective value, binding constraints, and (where appropriate) Answer/Sensitivity reports. Finally, diligence checks are part of professional practice: many “wrong answers” are actually avoidable setup or reporting errors.

Question: which objective will be most challenging for you—building the model, comparing scenarios, or writing the justification—and why?

slides.title: How to use this lesson

content.title: How to use this lesson
content: Work through core ideas, then replicate the worked Excel model
Create a calculation log and label units on the sheet
Run scenario changes and save Solver reports/screenshots
Complete the two MCQ quizzes to check interpretation
Draft a 150–250 word justification for your chosen scenario
content.notes:
This is designed for self-study, so your pacing matters. After each core slide, pause and check your spreadsheet matches the principle being discussed (for example: are your units visible; can another person follow your formulas?).

For the worked example, save separate file versions per scenario (or clearly separated worksheet tabs). Screenshots of Solver settings and the Results dialogue are acceptable evidence if reports are unavailable.

Use the quizzes diagnostically: if you miss a question, identify whether the issue is conceptual (e.g., misunderstanding binding constraints) or procedural (e.g., where to find the report). Your final draft justification should read like an evidence-based recommendation to a decision-maker: what you chose, what trade-offs you accepted, and what could change the conclusion.

Probing question: what would a “transparent log” need to contain so that someone else could reproduce your result exactly?

slides.title: Why run alternative scenarios?

content.title: Why run alternative scenarios?
content: One model can answer many 'what if?' questions
Scenarios test robustness when inputs or limits change
Compare trade-offs, not just the highest objective value
Document changes so results are auditable and repeatable
Use evidence: objective, binding constraints, feasibility status
content.notes:
A single optimisation run answers one question under one set of assumptions. Scenario-based optimisation acknowledges that assumptions are uncertain: resource availability shifts, unit contributions change, and new constraints (policy, safety, emissions) appear.

Evaluation involves looking for stability: does your recommendation remain sensible when key inputs vary? For example, if a small decrease in a resource limit causes a large drop in objective value, your solution may be fragile and require contingency planning.

Also note that “best” is rarely only the maximum objective. You may prefer a slightly lower objective if it reduces risk, uses less of a scarce resource, or avoids dependence on a tight constraint.

Common misconception: treating scenarios as informal tinkering. In academic and professional settings, you must be able to show precisely what changed and why.

Question: which inputs in a typical optimisation problem are most uncertain—limits, coefficients, or the model structure itself?

slides.title: Build a clean Solver model

content.title: Build a clean Solver model
leftColumn: Separate inputs, decisions, calculations, outputs
Use named ranges; keep formulas transparent
Include a units column or in-cell unit labels
Add a scenario/log area (date, changes, comments)
rightColumn: Set Objective: Max/Min the objective cell
By Changing: decision variable cells
Add constraints with correct ≤/≥/= directions
Choose method (Simplex LP, GRG, Evolutionary)
content.notes:
Good optimisation is mostly good spreadsheet design. If inputs, decisions, and calculations are mixed together, errors become hard to spot and harder to explain. A practical pattern is: (1) inputs table with units, (2) decision variable cells, (3) calculated left-hand sides (LHS) for each constraint, (4) objective calculation, (5) outputs summary.

On the Solver side, the most frequent setup errors are selecting the wrong objective cell, selecting a range that includes labels (not just variable cells), and entering a constraint in the wrong direction. Always read each constraint out loud: “LHS must be less than or equal to RHS”.

Method choice matters. Simplex LP is appropriate for linear models; GRG is for smooth nonlinear; Evolutionary is for non-smooth or discontinuous problems. If you choose a method inconsistent with the model type, you may get misleading or slow results.

Probing question: how could you tell, from looking at formulas, whether Simplex LP is suitable?

slides.title: Constraints, feasibility and meaning

content.title: Constraints, feasibility and meaning
content: Every constraint needs a clear meaning and units
Non-negativity: decision variables ≥ 0 unless allowed negative
Feasibility: Solver may return 'no feasible solution'
Binding constraints are tight at optimum; others have slack
Check directions: ≤ is not the same as ≥
Avoid hidden constraints from rounding or formatted cells
content.notes:
Constraints are not just mathematical limits; they represent real conditions (capacity, demand, policy, safety). If you cannot explain a constraint in words and with units, it is unlikely to be correct.

Non-negativity is a modelling choice. In many production/allocation problems, negative quantities are nonsensical. In other contexts (e.g., net flows, deviations), negatives may be valid—so do not apply non-negativity automatically without thinking.

If Solver reports infeasibility, resist the temptation to “force” a solution. Instead: (1) check each constraint direction, (2) check that RHS units match LHS units, (3) remove constraints one-by-one to identify the conflicting one, and (4) document what you changed.

Binding versus slack is central to explanation. A binding constraint is one you have fully used; it often explains why increasing a variable further is impossible.

Common misconception: “non-binding constraints do not matter”. They still matter as conditions of feasibility and may bind under a different scenario.

Question: what would be an example of a rounding decision that accidentally makes a feasible solution infeasible?

slides.title: Evidence from Solver outputs

content.title: Evidence from Solver outputs
content.notes:
Your scenario evaluation should be evidence-led. Start with the objective value, but do not stop there: two scenarios can have similar objectives while using resources very differently.

Decision variable values must be reported with units and appropriate precision. If you round, you must re-check constraints using the rounded numbers—rounding can push the LHS just over the RHS.

Binding/slack information supports your narrative: “We are limited by labour, not material” is a meaningful interpretation. When available (linear, continuous models solved with Simplex), the Sensitivity Report provides shadow prices and allowable ranges. Use it carefully: if you have integer constraints, nonlinear relationships, or the Evolutionary method, sensitivity outputs may be unavailable or invalid.

Always capture the Solver status text. “Solver found a solution” is not the same as “Solver found an optimal solution”. For example, Solver may stop due to iteration limits.

Probing question: if the objective increases but a previously slack constraint becomes binding, what does that suggest about risk in that scenario?

slides.title: Worked example: baseline model constraints

content.title: Worked example: baseline model constraints
content.notes:
We will use a simple product-mix model with two decision variables: x = units of Product A, y = units of Product B. The objective is to maximise total profit, calculated in one cell as Profit (£) = 30x + 20y.

The table shows the minimum set of constraints you should be comfortable implementing in Excel: two resource constraints, one demand/upper-bound constraint, and non-negativity.

When building the sheet, create separate LHS cells that calculate each expression using the current x and y values. This is preferable to typing algebra directly into Solver because it is visible and checkable.

Mini-check: verify units. If labour is “hours per unit”, the LHS is “hours”, and the RHS must also be “hours”. A common error is to mix “minutes” on one side and “hours” on the other.

Probing question: if the demand cap were removed, what practical risk might appear even if the maths still works?

slides.title: Worked example: implement in Excel Solver

content.title: Worked example: implement in Excel Solver
content: Enter x and y in two cells; set initial values (e.g., 0)
Objective cell: Profit = 30x + 20y (label as £)
Create LHS cells for each constraint using x,y formulas
Open Solver: set objective, variables, then add constraints
Select Simplex LP if all formulas are linear
Record settings, assumptions, and units in your calculation log
content.notes:
As you implement, focus on traceability. Use cell references (or named ranges) everywhere rather than hard-coding values inside formulas. For instance, store profit per unit for A and B in input cells, then compute Profit as (profit_A * x) + (profit_B * y). This makes scenarios easy: you change one input, not several formulas.

In Solver, confirm: (1) you are maximising (not minimising), (2) the changing cells are only x and y, and (3) each constraint references the correct LHS cell and RHS limit cell.

If you use Simplex LP, ensure the model is linear: no IF statements, no products of decision variables, no powers. If nonlinearity is present, use GRG and note that sensitivity information may not be available.

Your calculation log should include: date/time, scenario name, what changed, objective cell address, variable cell addresses, method, and any Solver options used (e.g., “Make unconstrained variables non-negative”).

Common misconception: thinking the model is “done” once Solver runs. The model is only credible once you can explain and reproduce it.

slides.title: Worked example: compare scenarios in a log

content.title: Worked example: compare scenarios in a log
content.notes:
This slide models how your scenario log should look: each row is a controlled change. The discipline is to change one thing at a time (where possible), so you can attribute differences in the outcome to a specific assumption.

Interpretation is as important as calculation. Ask: which constraint is driving each scenario? For example, in Scenario 2 the increased contribution from A makes it attractive to push x up to the labour limit with y dropping to zero.

Important nuance: the baseline problem can have multiple optimal solutions (alternative (x,y) pairs with the same objective). Solver may return different optimal points depending on starting values. This is not an error, but it must be explained. A good practice is to rerun with different starting values and note whether the objective stays the same.

Diligence check: after Solver returns a solution, compute and display each constraint LHS next to the RHS to confirm all inequalities are satisfied (especially if you report rounded values).

Probing question: if Scenario 3 (CO2 cap) has a lower objective, what might still justify choosing it?

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
leftColumn: Change one limit: which constraint becomes binding?
Change one profit: does the product mix switch? why?
Add a new constraint: can you keep feasibility?
Explain your choice: what evidence supports it?
rightColumn: Units consistent in inputs, formulas, and outputs?
Rounding: do constraints hold after rounding?
Direction checks: ≤/≥ correct and matches wording?
Reasonableness: are values plausible and non-negative?
content.notes:
Use these prompts to practise both technical and evaluative skills. When you change one limit, do not just report the new optimum—identify which constraint becomes binding and what that means operationally (for example, “material becomes the bottleneck”).

When you change a profit coefficient, look for a “corner switch”: the optimal solution may jump from one corner point to another. This is a key idea behind sensitivity, even if you do not compute shadow prices.

For adding a constraint, deliberately try one that makes the model infeasible (e.g., a very tight cap). Then practise diagnosing infeasibility: remove constraints temporarily, check unit consistency, and review inequality directions.

The right-hand column is your diligence checklist. You are expected to find and correct issues before finalising. Typical issues include: (1) objective is total profit but reported as profit per unit, (2) a constraint uses the wrong cell reference, (3) rounding makes labour exceed the limit by a small amount.

Reflection question: what is the strongest single piece of evidence that your chosen scenario is “better”, and what evidence is missing or uncertain?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MCQs on model setup, reports, and scenario comparison
Write 150–250 words using evidence from Solver outputs
Explain why each constraint is included and how it affects choice
Add ≥2 risk/uncertainty notes (data, demand, costs, policy)
Common errors: wrong objective, missing units, wrong constraint sign
If infeasible: diagnose, revise, and document resolution steps
content.notes:
The MCQs will test whether you can recognise correct Solver setup and interpret outputs. For the written justification, aim for a clear structure: (1) recommendation (which scenario and why), (2) quantitative evidence (objective value and key constraints), (3) constraint rationale (why those limits are appropriate), and (4) risks/uncertainties that could change the decision.

Two useful risk notes are: data uncertainty (e.g., contribution margins may change) and model limitation (e.g., linearity assumption, ignoring set-up costs, ignoring minimum batch sizes). Another is feasibility risk: a scenario that relies on a constraint being exactly met can be brittle in practice.

Common mistakes to avoid:
- Using the wrong objective (e.g., maximising revenue instead of profit).
- Forgetting non-negativity, leading to nonsensical negative quantities.
- Entering a constraint as ≥ when it should be ≤.
- Reporting results without confirming constraints are satisfied after rounding.

Probing question: if your preferred scenario has the highest objective but relies on a very tight constraint, how would you communicate that risk in your justification?

slides.title: Summary

content.title: Summary
content: Define decisions, objective and constraints with explicit units
Run several scenarios and keep a transparent Solver settings log
Use binding constraints and reports to justify recommendations
Check feasibility, directions, rounding and reasonableness
Choose the best-supported option, not only the highest £
content.notes:
To conclude, scenario-based optimisation is a workflow: build a sound model, test plausible alternatives, and then evaluate evidence to make a defensible recommendation.

If you take one practical habit away, make it this: always maintain a calculation log that someone else could use to reproduce your results. This is what distinguishes a one-off spreadsheet answer from credible analytical work.

Before you finalise any recommendation, run the diligence checks systematically. Many marks (and real-world decisions) are lost through avoidable errors: unit mismatches, incorrect inequality directions, and careless rounding.

Self-check question: if you were given your own spreadsheet with no explanation, what would you need to see (labels, units, log entries, outputs) to trust the recommendation?

slides.title: Solver outputs: what each report is for

content.title: Solver outputs: what each report is for
content: Answer Report: solution values and which constraints bind
Sensitivity Report: marginal values and stable ranges
Objective value: what you optimise (profit, cost, time)
Decision variables: what Solver is allowed to change
Constraints: limits that may create bottlenecks
Interpretation: translate outputs into operational actions
content.notes: Clarify the division of labour: the Answer Report answers ‘what is the optimum now?’; the Sensitivity Report answers ‘how fragile is this optimum to small changes?’. Reinforce that sensitivity is tied to linear models (Simplex LP) and is not produced for all Solver methods. Probe: If you only had the Answer Report, what questions would remain unanswered about robustness? Misconception to address: learners often treat sensitivity as a prediction tool for large changes; stress it supports ‘within-range’ reasoning.

slides.title: Key sensitivity terms you must interpret

content.title: Key sensitivity terms you must interpret

rows: Value of 1 extra unit of resource
Penalty/benefit of forcing a variable in
Check why a product is zero
Range where shadow/reduced cost stays valid

content.notes: Walk through each term as a ‘sentence you can say’. Example phrasing: ‘An extra hour of machine time is worth £X in profit, provided the change is within Y hours.’ Emphasise units: the shadow price is in objective units per constraint unit (e.g., £ per labour-hour). Probe: What is the unit of reduced cost in a profit-maximisation problem? Common misconception: interpreting reduced cost as a ‘cost to produce’; instead it is an opportunity cost relative to the current optimum.

slides.title: Binding constraints and bottlenecks

content.title: Binding constraints and bottlenecks
content: Binding: LHS equals RHS at the optimum (no slack)
Non-binding: slack exists; relaxing may change nothing
Bottleneck: binding constraint with high shadow price
At least two bottlenecks should be named if present
Use Solver output, not intuition, to label bottlenecks
Report both the constraint and what it represents
content.notes: Explain that ‘binding’ is a mathematical condition; ‘bottleneck’ is the operational interpretation. A constraint can be binding but not strategically important if its shadow price is zero (degeneracy can occur), so learners must always check the shadow price alongside binding status. Probe: If a constraint is non-binding, what is its shadow price usually? (Often zero.) Misconception: thinking the largest RHS is the bottleneck; the bottleneck is about marginal value, not size.

slides.title: Shadow prices: interpreting marginal impact

content.title: Shadow prices: interpreting marginal impact
content: Shadow price = change in objective per +1 unit of RHS
Valid only within allowable increase/decrease for RHS
Positive in maximisation: more resource increases value
Negative implies more resource worsens the objective
Zero shadow price: resource not scarce at optimum
Outside range: re-solve; marginal value may change
