Clarify that the sign depends on model direction and formulation; encourage learners to interpret sign with care rather than memorising. Probe: Why might a shadow price be negative in a minimisation problem? Misconception: treating shadow price as ‘total value of the constraint’; it is marginal, not total.

content.title: Reduced costs: why some variables are zero
content: Reduced cost shows impact if a zero variable is forced up
For maximisation: negative reduced cost hurts objective
For minimisation: positive reduced cost raises total cost
If variable is positive, reduced cost is typically zero
Use allowable ranges to judge coefficient stability
Large changes to coefficients require re-solving

In maximisation, a reduced cost of -5 means forcing one unit of that variable decreases profit by 5 (within linear assumptions). Probe: What change would be needed to make a non-produced product attractive? Misconception: confusing reduced cost with accounting cost; stress it is an optimisation concept linked to the objective coefficient.

content: State model purpose and objective in one sentence
Define decision variables with units and bounds
Justify each constraint and data source

content.notes: Frame this as professional practice: your spreadsheet must be reviewable by someone who did not build it. Suggest a simple structure: a ‘ReadMe’ sheet (purpose, scope, units), an ‘Inputs’ sheet (dated sources), a ‘Model’ sheet (formulas), and a ‘Results’ sheet (reports pasted as values with timestamps). Probe: If a colleague re-runs Solver and gets a different result, what information would they need to reproduce your outcome? Misconception: thinking screenshots are sufficient; emphasise versioning, dates, and explicit Solver settings.

slides.title: Limitations: convert sensitivity into risks

content.title: Limitations: convert sensitivity into risks
content: Linearity: marginal values assume linear relationships
Stability: only valid within allowable ranges
Rounding: small changes may flip binding status
Data freshness: old inputs can invalidate conclusions
Model scope: missing constraints can distort shadow prices
Record each as risk with trigger and mitigation
content.notes: Explain the ‘risk register’ mindset: each limitation becomes an entry with (a) what could go wrong, (b) what signal indicates the risk is active, and (c) what you would do. Link explicitly to sensitivity ranges: if the planned change exceeds allowable increase, that is a trigger to re-solve and re-check feasibility. Probe: Which limitation is most likely to affect your workplace scenario—data freshness or missing constraints? Misconception: listing generic limitations without linking to model outputs; require a specific reference (e.g., allowable increase on labour RHS is only 10 hours).

slides.title: Worked example: reading bottlenecks from output

content.title: Worked example: reading bottlenecks from output
content.notes: Talk through interpretation step-by-step. First, identify binding constraints: Labour hours, Machine time, Storage space. Second, identify bottlenecks by combining binding with meaningful shadow price: Labour and Machine are the bottlenecks; Storage is binding but has zero marginal value (possible degeneracy or an alternative optimal basis). Third, convert to action statements: ‘An extra labour-hour is worth £12 up to 10 hours; after that, re-optimise.’ Probe: Why might Storage be binding but have shadow price 0? Discuss degeneracy or multiple binding constraints where one is redundant at the margin.

slides.title: Worked example: baseline vs scenario decision

content.title: Worked example: baseline vs scenario decision
leftColumn: Baseline objective: £4,800
Binding: labour, machine
Labour shadow price: 12 (range +10)
Feasible with current limits
rightColumn: Scenario: +8 labour hours
Predicted gain: 8×12 = £96 (within range)
Binding may shift after +10; re-solve if exceeded
Recommend if labour cost < £12 per hour
content.notes: Model the evaluation logic: (1) Is the scenario change within allowable range? Yes: +8 is within +10, so the shadow price can be used. (2) What is the expected objective change? £96 increase, holding other assumptions constant. (3) What is the economic decision rule? If the marginal benefit (£12/hour) exceeds the marginal cost of buying labour hours, it is attractive. Probe: What additional evidence would you cite besides shadow price? (Binding status, allowable range, and feasibility.) Misconception: assuming the predicted gain is guaranteed; remind learners it holds under linearity and within the stated range.

slides.title: Worked example: audit-ready justification paragraph

content.title: Worked example: audit-ready justification paragraph
content.content: In the baseline Solver run (Simplex LP), labour hours and machine time are binding constraints. The Sensitivity Report shows shadow prices of 12 and 8, meaning each additional hour increases profit by £12 and £8 respectively, within allowable RHS increases of 10 and 25. Therefore, we recommend purchasing up to 8 additional labour-hours, as this remains within the sensitivity range, improves the objective by an estimated £96, and preserves feasibility; beyond +10 hours, the model must be re-solved because the marginal values may change.
content.notes: Teach learners how to write for audit: name the run, method, what binds, the numerical evidence, the validity condition (allowable range), and the recommendation with a decision rule. Encourage them to include units and to avoid vague phrases like ‘Solver says’. Probe: Does the paragraph state (a) what changed, (b) why it is valid, and (c) what you would do if conditions are not met? Misconception: omitting the ‘within allowable range’ condition, which is essential to responsible interpretation.

slides.title: Solver model: the three essential building blocks

content.title: Solver model: the three essential building blocks
content: Decision variables: the controllable quantities
Objective: maximise or minimise a single metric
Constraints: limits, requirements, or logical rules
Linking formulas connect variables to totals
Set variable bounds (e.g., non-negativity)
Choose method: Simplex LP vs GRG vs Evolutionary
content.notes: Expand each block with a concrete mental model: decision variables are your “levers”, the objective is the “score”, constraints are “rules of the game”, and formulas are the accounting that enforces consistency. Stress a common misconception: typing constraints into Solver without having correct spreadsheet formulas does not create a valid model—Solver only sees cell relationships. Mini-example: two products x1 and x2; profit = 5x1 + 4x2; labour = 2x1 + x2 ≤ 100; material = x1 + 2x2 ≤ 80; demand x2 ≥ 10; x1, x2 ≥ 0. Ask: “Which cells would you change if the labour limit increases by 10%?” This checks whether learners can locate variables and parameters.

slides.title: Binding vs non-binding constraints (tightness)

content.title: Binding vs non-binding constraints (tightness)
leftColumn: Binding: LHS equals RHS at the solution
Uses all of a scarce resource (zero slack)
Often explains why optimum stops increasing
Relaxing it may improve objective value
rightColumn: Non-binding: slack exists at the solution
Not limiting the objective at the optimum
Relaxing it does not change the solution
Still important for feasibility and compliance
content.notes: Explain tightness in plain language: binding constraints are the “active bottlenecks” at the optimum; non-binding constraints are currently not restricting. Show how to compute slack: for ≤ constraints, slack = RHS − LHS; for ≥ constraints, surplus = LHS − RHS. Misconception to address: learners sometimes assume “non-binding means irrelevant”; correct this by noting that a constraint may become binding in a different scenario (e.g., if demand rises). Probing questions: “Which constraint would you negotiate to relax?” and “Which constraint would you never relax due to regulation or ethics?”

Encourage a simple scenario log: scenario name, changed parameters, Solver method, status, objective value, binding constraints, notes. Probing question: “If you had to defend this model to an auditor, what would you show them first?”

slides.title: Diligence checks to increase confidence

content.title: Diligence checks to increase confidence
content: Units/scale check: £, hours, tonnes, per week vs per day
Constraint direction check: ≤, ≥, = matches wording
Sign check: are coefficients and totals positive/negative?
Rounding policy: when to round and to how many decimals
Tolerance/sensitivity: does small change flip the decision?
content.notes: Explain that diligence checks are not optional “extra steps”; they are safeguards against silent spreadsheet errors. Provide mini-examples: (1) Units: demand entered as 500 (per month) but production is per week—your optimum will look feasible but is not. (2) Direction: ‘must meet demand’ is ≥, not ≤. (3) Rounding: rounding decision variables can break feasibility (e.g., integer-like quantities). (4) Sensitivity: try ±5% on a key limit or profit coefficient and see if the recommended scenario changes. Ask: “Which check would most likely catch an error that still produces an ‘Optimal’ status?”

content.notes: Walk through the spreadsheet layout: keep parameters (coefficients, limits) separate from variable cells to make scenarios easy. Mention absolute/relative references: use $ signs for parameters so formulas copy correctly. Explain method choice: Simplex LP is for linear models (no multiplication of variables, no IF with non-linear effects), GRG is for smooth non-linear, Evolutionary for discontinuous or complex. Common misconception: selecting GRG for a linear model can still work but may be slower and can confuse interpretation. Probing question: “Which formulas in your sheet would prove the model is linear?”

slides.title: Worked example: interpret Solver outcomes correctly

content.title: Worked example: interpret Solver outcomes correctly
content: Optimal: all constraints satisfied; objective at best found
Infeasible: constraints conflict; no solution satisfies all
Unbounded: objective can improve without limit
Check binding constraints via slack/surplus values
Record final variable values and objective with units
Note any Solver warnings and your fix in the log
content.notes: Explain diagnosis tactics. For infeasible: temporarily relax or remove one constraint at a time to identify the conflict; check sign and direction; confirm bounds (e.g., x ≥ 0) are intended. For unbounded: usually missing a limiting constraint (e.g., no upper bound on production) or wrong sign in objective. Clarify that “Optimal” is conditional on the model and Solver settings; it does not guarantee real-world optimality if assumptions are wrong. Probing question: “What is the most plausible real-world reason your model could be unbounded?” (Answer: a missing capacity/resource limit or missing non-negativity/bounds.)

slides.title: Decision memo and risk register essentials

content.title: Decision memo and risk register essentials
leftColumn: Memo: state recommendation and why
Cite binding constraints and key assumptions
Note limitations and uncertainty explicitly
Refer to evidence: objective and feasibility
rightColumn: Risk 1: parameter error (units/scale); mitigation
Risk 2: resource not available; contingency plan
Rate likelihood/impact qualitatively (L/M/H)

content.notes: Clarify that the memo is short but structured: a clear recommendation, then justification grounded in constraints and scenario comparisons, then limitations. Provide a sentence scaffold learners can reuse: “I recommend Scenario B because it increases the objective by £X while keeping all constraints feasible; the binding constraint shifts to material, which is controllable via [action].” For risks, stress specificity: “material shortage” is too vague; “supplier lead time exceeds 2 weeks, reducing available material by 15%” is testable. Probing question: “What would make your recommendation ethically or operationally unacceptable even if it is optimal?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection: your scenario work

content.title: Practice and reflection: your scenario work
content: Build the model and solve until status is Optimal
Create 3 scenarios by changing one assumption each
For each: record objective, status, slack, binding set

content.notes: Guide learners to keep scenario changes “one-at-a-time” initially (ceteris paribus) to attribute effects. Suggest scenario types: increase a capacity limit, change a unit profit/cost, add a policy constraint (e.g., minimum output), or tighten a regulatory limit. For diligence checks, encourage them to deliberately try a “fault injection”: flip a constraint direction and observe infeasibility, then fix it—this builds diagnostic skill. Reflection questions: “Which constraint felt most ‘real’ in practice, and which felt like a modelling convenience?” and “Which result surprised you, and why?”

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports: optimisation scenario evaluation and memo tasks
Show a clear calculation log for reproducibility
Do not report objective without units and time basis
Avoid mixing per-unit and total values in constraints
Do not ignore infeasible/unbounded; diagnose and explain
Do not overclaim: optimal in model ≠ optimal in reality
content.notes: Explain how markers typically judge this work: correctness of model set-up, quality of evidence, and quality of reasoning. Emphasise that transparency often differentiates strong submissions: screenshots of Solver parameters, a neat scenario table, and a short but precise memo. Probing question: “If someone else opened your file, could they reproduce your numbers in under five minutes?”

content.title: Solver results and sensitivity outputs
content: Programme: Maths Certification

Lesson 12: Solver results and sensitivity outputs to interpret marginal…

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Use flow: read → interpret → test scenarios → document
LO1: Classify binding vs non-binding constraints; explain meaning
LO2: Interpret shadow price, ranges, reduced cost in an example
LO3: Compare 2 scenarios and justify a recommended option
LO4: Produce a calculation log with settings, assumptions, limits
content.notes:
Work through the lesson in three passes. Pass 1: focus on ‘what does this field mean?’ Pass 2: apply to the worked example and practise writing 1–2 sentence operational interpretations (this is often where marks are won/lost). Pass 3: evaluate scenarios: quantify the objective impact, identify the bottleneck(s), then add risk/uncertainty notes.

As you proceed, ask yourself: ‘If I had to brief an operations manager using only these Solver outputs, what would I say and what would I avoid claiming?’ A common misconception is treating sensitivity numbers as universal truths; they are local (valid in a range) and assumption-dependent.

slides.title: Reading Solver output: where to find binding constraints

content.title: Reading Solver output: where to find binding constraints
content: Check Solver status: “Solution found” and method used
Answer Report: Final Value and Objective Cell value
Constraints section: Slack tells binding vs non-binding
Binding constraint: Slack = 0 at the optimum
Non-binding constraint: Slack > 0; RHS not fully used
Sensitivity Report appears only for Simplex LP (linear)
content.notes:
Start with the status message: you need a valid optimum for interpretation. In the Answer Report, ‘Final Value’ gives the chosen decision variable levels, and the objective cell value gives the optimum objective.

To identify binding constraints, focus on Slack: Slack is the unused capacity (for ≤ constraints) at the reported optimum. Slack = 0 means the constraint is tight and is actively restricting the solution; Slack > 0 means there is spare capacity. Operationally, binding constraints are your bottlenecks—if you could relax one slightly, the objective might improve.

Probe yourself: If Slack is 0, can I explain in plain language what resource/limit is fully used? If Slack is positive, can I explain what extra capacity remains?

Misconception to avoid: assuming a non-binding constraint is ‘unimportant’. It may become binding under scenario changes (e.g., if you increase another resource).

slides.title: Shadow price: marginal value of a constraint RHS

content.title: Shadow price: marginal value of a constraint RHS
content: Shadow price = change in objective per +1 unit of RHS
Usually non-zero only for binding constraints
Units: objective units per constraint unit (e.g., £ per hour)
For maximisation, positive shadow price means RHS is valuable
Interpret as marginal value, not average value
Valid only within the allowable increase/decrease range
content.notes:
A shadow price tells you how much the objective would improve if you could increase the right-hand side (RHS) of a constraint by 1 unit, holding the model structure fixed. This is a marginal concept: it is about the ‘next unit’ of capacity, not the value of all capacity.

Example language: ‘An extra hour of labour is worth £20 in profit, provided we stay within the valid range stated in the report.’ That final clause matters.

Check units carefully. If your objective is profit (£) and your constraint is hours, the shadow price is £/hour.

Misconception to avoid: reading shadow price as the cost you should pay. It is a maximum willingness-to-pay implied by the model; real procurement costs, overtime premiums, and feasibility issues may differ. Use it as an input to evaluation, not as a final decision rule.

slides.title: Allowable increase/decrease: when the marginal value holds

content.title: Allowable increase/decrease: when the marginal value holds
content: Allowable inc/dec gives the RHS range with same basis
Within range: objective change ≈ shadow price × RHS change
Outside range: basis changes; re-run Solver to re-optimise
Small changes can still change mix, even if basis is stable
Ranges are local; do not extrapolate far beyond them
Range 0 can indicate degeneracy or multiple optima issues
content.notes:
The allowable increase/decrease is Solver’s way of saying ‘this marginal value is valid only here’. Within that interval, the set of binding constraints (the simplex basis) remains the same, so the shadow price stays constant.

Use the approximation explicitly: ΔObjective = (shadow price) × (ΔRHS), but only if the proposed ΔRHS stays within the allowable range. If you go outside the range, you must re-run Solver; otherwise, your quantified impact is not defensible.

Important nuance: even within the range, the decision variable values typically change—what stays stable is the marginal relationship captured by the shadow price.

Misconception to avoid: thinking allowable ranges are ‘confidence intervals’. They are structural ranges for the current optimal basis, not statistical uncertainty bounds.

slides.title: Reduced cost: whether a zero variable should enter

content.title: Reduced cost: whether a zero variable should enter
content: Reduced cost applies to decision variables at 0 in solution
Maximisation: negative reduced cost means “not worth producing”
Its magnitude = profit increase needed to make it enter
If coefficient change is within range, solution basis stays
If coefficient change exceeds range, re-optimise
Reduced cost is not a penalty term; it is an optimality signal
content.notes:
Reduced cost explains why a variable is zero at the optimum. For a maximisation model, a negative reduced cost means: if you force this variable up from zero (by 1 unit), the objective would worsen by that amount at the margin, given current shadow prices of resources.

The most useful interpretation is threshold-based: ‘This product would need at least £15 more profit per unit (or equivalent cost reduction) before it becomes part of the optimal plan.’ This directly supports scenario evaluation when you consider changing objective coefficients.

Misconception to avoid: treating reduced cost as a ‘real cost’ you pay. It is an implied opportunity cost from the optimisation structure, not an accounting entry.

slides.title: Documentation and when sensitivity is invalid

content.title: Documentation and when sensitivity is invalid
content: Log: assumptions, units, decision vars, and objective definition
Log: constraint rationale, data sources, and RHS justifications
Record Solver settings: Simplex LP, options, and precision
Sensitivity is invalid for integer/binary or nonlinear methods
Invalid if model structure changes (new vars/constraints added)
Invalid if changes exceed allowable ranges; re-solve is required
content.notes:
A transparent calculation log is part of good optimisation practice: it allows another person (or future you) to reproduce, audit, and challenge the analysis. In academic work, it also demonstrates that your evaluation is grounded in traceable evidence.

Sensitivity reports are only produced (and meaningful) for linear, continuous models solved with Simplex LP. If you used GRG Nonlinear, Evolutionary, or you imposed integer/binary constraints, the classic shadow price/reduced cost interpretations do not hold in the same way.

Also distinguish: changing a parameter value (RHS, objective coefficient) versus changing the model structure (adding a constraint, changing a coefficient matrix entry, adding logical constraints). Structural changes require a full re-optimisation and make prior sensitivity outputs obsolete.

Probing question: ‘If I presented this recommendation, could someone ask “what exactly did you assume?” and I can point to the log line where it is stated?’

slides.title: Worked example set-up (product mix LP)

content.title: Worked example set-up (product mix LP)
content: Decision variables: units of A, B, C (continuous, ≥ 0)
Maximise profit subject to labour, material, and demand limits
Constraints: Labour ≤100; Material ≤80; Demand: B ≤60
content.notes:
We will use a small product-mix linear programme because it produces clear binding constraints and a meaningful reduced cost.

Model statement:
Maximise Z = 50A + 40B + 35C
Subject to:
(1) Labour: 2A + 1B + 1C ≤ 100
(2) Material: 1A + 2B + 3C ≤ 80
(3) Demand: B ≤ 60
A, B, C ≥ 0

Excel build guidance (typical layout): put A, B, C in three adjacent decision cells; compute total profit with SUMPRODUCT(profits, decision_cells). For each constraint, compute a left-hand side (LHS) with SUMPRODUCT(resource_use, decision_cells) and link the RHS to a clearly labelled parameter cell.

Solver settings to narrate: Set Objective = profit cell; To: Max; By Changing Variable Cells = A,B,C; Add constraints as above; select Simplex LP; tick ‘Assume Linear Model’ and ‘Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative’ as appropriate.

Probing question: are the units consistent (hours vs units) and are coefficients plausible? Sensitivity analysis is only as credible as the modelling assumptions.

slides.title: Worked example: binding vs non-binding constraints

content.title: Worked example: binding vs non-binding constraints
content: Optimal solution: A=40, B=20, C=0; Profit = £2,800
Binding if Slack=0; explain each binding constraint in 1–2 lines
content.notes:
From the Answer Report, we read the decision variables and then check each constraint’s Slack.

Operational interpretations (model-based):
• Labour is binding (slack 0): all 100 labour hours are fully allocated; labour is a bottleneck at the optimum.
• Material is binding (slack 0): all 80 material units are fully allocated; material is also a bottleneck.
• Demand for B is non-binding (slack 40): the plan produces 20 units of B, well below the demand limit of 60, so demand does not restrict the optimum under current resource limits.

Checklist for 100% accuracy:
1) For every constraint, record Slack.
2) Mark binding if Slack = 0.
3) Write a plain-language meaning: ‘fully used’ vs ‘spare capacity’.
4) Avoid claiming causality beyond the model (e.g., ‘customers do not want B’ is not implied; only that demand is not currently limiting).

Common misconception: students sometimes call a constraint ‘binding’ because it feels important. Only the reported Slack determines binding status at the current optimum.

slides.title: Worked example: interpret sensitivity outputs

content.title: Worked example: interpret sensitivity outputs
content: Marginal value uses: ΔProfit = shadow price × ΔRHS (within range)
Reduced cost explains why C=0 and how much profit must rise
content.notes:
Interpret three elements and explicitly state the valid range.

1) Labour shadow price = £20 per hour, allowable increase 60 and decrease 60.
Meaning: If you can increase labour from 100 up to 160 hours, each extra hour is worth about £20 additional profit (locally). If labour drops below 40 hours, the current marginal relationship no longer applies because the optimal basis would change.

2) Material shadow price = £10 per unit, allowable increase 60 and decrease 30.
Meaning: Increasing material from 80 up to 140 units adds about £10 profit per extra unit. If material falls below 50 units, the optimal plan changes and you must re-run Solver to quantify effects.

3) Demand constraint for B has shadow price 0 with a large allowable increase.
Meaning: relaxing the demand cap above 60 does nothing now because demand is not restricting the solution. However, the allowable decrease is 40: if you reduce the demand limit below 20, it becomes binding and the objective will change—so ‘0’ is not a general statement about demand, only about the current range.

4) Reduced cost for C = −15.
Meaning: product C is excluded because, at current resource scarcity, it would need an extra £15 profit per unit (from £35 to at least £50) before it becomes attractive to produce.

Misconceptions to avoid:
• Treating 1E+30 as ‘infinite in reality’—it only means ‘not binding within typical variation’.
• Ignoring signs: negative reduced cost (max problem) is a ‘needs improvement’ signal.
• Forgetting to state the range every time you quote a marginal value.

slides.title: Worked example: evaluate scenarios and recommend

content.title: Worked example: evaluate scenarios and recommend
leftColumn: Scenario A: labour RHS +10 (100→110)
Within range: +10 ≤ 60, so shadow price applies
Predicted ΔProfit = 20×10 = +£200 (to £3,000)
Bottleneck logic: relaxes a binding constraint (labour)
rightColumn: Scenario B: raise profit of C by +£20 (35→55)
Exceeds threshold: +20 > 15, basis likely changes
Sensitivity no longer valid; must re-run Solver
Risk: C uses high material; may tighten material bottleneck
content.notes:
This slide demonstrates the evaluation structure expected at Bloom’s ‘evaluate’ level: quantify, explain bottlenecks, and note uncertainty.

Scenario A (RHS change within allowable range): we can defensibly quantify impact using the shadow price. We also explain why: labour is binding, so extra labour directly relaxes a bottleneck. If you want to go further, you can compute the new mix (not required for the marginal estimate): with Labour=110 and Material=80, the optimal mix shifts but the predicted profit change remains +£200 within the valid range.

Scenario B (objective coefficient change beyond allowable increase): we cannot defensibly quantify impact from the current sensitivity report. The reduced cost tells us C becomes potentially profitable to include, but once the coefficient change exceeds the allowable range, the set of binding constraints/variables can change. The correct workflow is to re-run Solver and then re-interpret the new Answer/Sensitivity reports.

Recommendation (based on evidence available now): prefer Scenario A if you need an immediate, quantifiable improvement with clear assumptions. Scenario B could be promising, but it carries model risk (requires re-optimisation) and operational risk (it may intensify the material bottleneck because C is material-intensive).

Probing questions:
• If labour costs £x per hour, what is your maximum willingness-to-pay given the £20/h shadow price?
• What additional real-world constraints (set-up time, minimum batch sizes) might invalidate the continuous LP assumption?

slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-check)
content: From an Answer Report, list binding constraints and meanings
Given a shadow price and ΔRHS, compute ΔObjective (if valid)
Check if proposed change exceeds allowable range; decide re-solve
Interpret a reduced cost: coefficient change needed to enter
Write 2-sentence recommendation: impact, bottleneck, risks
Complete: MCQ Sensitivity… and Short Quiz on Solver models
content.notes:
Treat this as retrieval practice. For each prompt, write your answer in full sentences, not fragments—assessment typically rewards clarity of interpretation.

Mini-drill you can do quickly: invent a small ΔRHS (e.g., +5 units), check it is within allowable increase, compute ΔObjective, then write an operational statement: ‘An extra 5 units of material increases profit by about £50, provided material stays within the stated sensitivity range.’

Reflection questions:
• When you see a shadow price of 0, do you immediately conclude ‘irrelevant’? What would make it relevant under a different scenario?
• What is the difference between ‘within allowable range’ and ‘realistically feasible’ (e.g., can you actually buy that extra capacity)?

Common misconception: students compute ΔObjective correctly but forget to state the validity condition (within range, linear/continuous model). In evaluation tasks, the condition is part of the answer.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: optimisation report sections on results and evaluation
Use a binding/non-binding checklist with Slack evidence
Always state units and valid ranges for marginal values
Do not use Sensitivity with integer/binary or nonlinear Solver
Avoid extrapolating beyond allowable ranges; re-optimise instead
Submit a calculation log: settings, assumptions, limitations
content.notes:
In typical optimisation coursework, marks often split between (i) correct identification/interpretation and (ii) quality of justification and transparency. Use Solver outputs as evidence: quote Slack, shadow prices, and reduced costs with units.

Frequent marking issues:
• Confusing ‘slack’ (unused capacity) with ‘shadow price’ (marginal value).
• Quoting a shadow price but not stating the allowable range.
• Reporting a sensitivity output when the model used integers (e.g., ‘number of trucks’)—Excel may not provide a Sensitivity Report, and if it does via approximation, the classic interpretation is not valid.
• Making strong claims like ‘we should definitely invest’ without noting uncertainty (data quality, linearity assumptions, omitted constraints).

A good calculation log reads like a lab book: dated steps, what changed, why, and what you concluded, including any non-validity warnings.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Binding constraints have Slack=0; they indicate bottlenecks
Shadow price is marginal objective gain per +1 RHS unit
Allowable ranges define where marginal values are valid
Reduced cost explains why a zero variable stays out of solution
Document assumptions and settings; re-solve when validity fails
content.notes:
Keep these five points as your interpretation template. In practice, aim to write results in the pattern: (1) what Solver says (field + value), (2) what it means operationally (one sentence), (3) validity conditions (ranges/model type), and (4) decision implication (scenario choice or next step).

If you can reliably do that, you are operating at the intended ‘evaluate’ level: you are not only reading numbers, but judging how far they can support decisions.

slides.title: MOD104 Lesson 13: Alternative optimisation scenarios

content.title: MOD104 Lesson 13: Alternative optimisation scenarios
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD104 — Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver
Lesson 13: Alternative optimisation scenarios and justify a chosen option
Estimated study time: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome. In this lesson we move beyond “finding an optimum” to evaluating competing optimisation scenarios and defending a recommendation. In practice, managers rarely ask for a single optimal number; they ask what happens if a limit changes (capacity, demand, waste, budget), and whether the recommended plan is robust enough to implement.

As you work, keep two mindsets active: (1) technical correctness (units, constraints, feasibility, Solver settings) and (2) decision quality (transparent logging, scenario comparison, risk and limitations). A key misconception is that an optimisation output is automatically “the answer”. The output is only as credible as the model design, the documentation, and the diligence checks you apply.

slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and study route

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and study route
content: Build a Solver model: vars, objective, ≥4 constraints + units
Reach a feasible optimum in ≤2 Solver runs
Keep a log so others reproduce the objective within ±0.5%
Compare ≥2 scenarios; justify a choice using evidence and risk
Add ≥3 risks + mitigations; record uncertainty and limitations
Critique outputs: spot ≥3 errors and maintain a change history
content.notes:
These outcomes reflect “evaluate” level work: you are judging the quality of solutions, not just producing them.

Two practical standards underpin the lesson:
1) Efficiency: aim to reach feasibility quickly (within two Solver runs). That usually means you set up clean formulas, choose an appropriate solving method (e.g., Simplex LP for linear models), and start from a sensible initial guess.
2) Reproducibility: another learner should be able to open your spreadsheet, follow your log, use the same Solver settings, and obtain essentially the same objective value. If they cannot, the model is not yet academically robust.

As you read each slide, ask: “If I handed this file to a colleague, could they audit it? Could they re-run it? Would they trust it?”

slides.title: Why run alternative scenarios?

content.title: Why run alternative scenarios?
content: Scenarios change inputs or limits, while keeping the model structure
They test robustness when data, policy, or capacity shifts
Use a baseline case as the reference point for comparisons
Prefer small, explicit changes before combining multiple changes
A scenario is not a guess: it should have a rationale and units
content.notes:
A scenario is a disciplined “what-if” experiment. The structure of the model (decision variables, objective formula, constraint formulas) stays the same; what changes are parameters such as capacities, demand ceilings, waste limits, costs, or service-level targets.

A strong baseline is essential. Without it, you cannot interpret whether a scenario improvement is meaningful or merely an artefact of a modelling change.

When learning, change one driver at a time (e.g., only waste limit, then only demand). Later you can test combined changes, but combined changes make it harder to attribute cause.

Probing questions:
- Which parameters are genuinely uncertain versus policy-controlled?
- Which constraints are likely to tighten in real operations?
- If the optimum changes a lot for a small parameter change, what does that imply about risk?

Common misconception: treating a scenario as a narrative (“suppose demand rises”) without specifying numbers, units, and why that change is plausible.

slides.title: Solver model anatomy in Excel

content.title: Solver model anatomy in Excel
leftColumn: Decision variables (quantities to choose)
Objective (maximise or minimise)
Constraints (limits, targets, rules)
Outputs (slack, utilisation, KPIs)
rightColumn: Changing cells range
Set Objective cell + Max/Min
Add constraints + variable bounds
Reports, checks, charts and logs
content.notes:
A Solver model has four parts. First, decision variables are the cells Solver is allowed to change (for example, quantities produced per week). Second, the objective is a single cell that computes what you want to maximise or minimise (profit, cost, emissions, time). Third, constraints operationalise reality: capacity limits, contractual demand limits, quality standards, and non-negativity.

Fourth, you need outputs for interpretation: constraint slack, utilisation rates, and any secondary KPIs that matter (e.g., waste generated, overtime, service level). Learners often stop at the objective value, but evaluation requires understanding what is binding and why.

Mini-example: if you maximise profit subject to a waste cap, a high profit might still be undesirable if it uses the waste cap completely and leaves no buffer, increasing operational risk.

Misconception to challenge: “Constraints are optional.” In optimisation, constraints are the model; without them you are not modelling the real decision problem.

slides.title: Constraint quality and feasibility checks

content.title: Constraint quality and feasibility checks
content: Write constraints with explicit units (e.g., hrs/week, kg/week)
Include x ≥ 0 (and integer/binary rules when appropriate)
Keep constraints formula-driven; avoid hard-coded totals
Check feasibility by relaxing limits before seeking an optimum
Confirm every constraint reflects a real rule or physical limit
Watch for hidden duplicates or contradictions between limits
content.notes:
High-quality constraints are measurable, unit-consistent, and traceable to a real-world rationale.

Units are a frequent source of error: minutes versus hours, tonnes versus kilograms, £ versus pence. A quick audit technique is to annotate each parameter cell with its unit and ensure every constraint sums like-with-like.

Non-negativity is not automatic unless you specify it. If a variable represents quantities produced, shipments, staffing, or budgets, negative values are usually meaningless and can create nonsensical “optimal” solutions.

Feasibility checking is an academic integrity step. If Solver reports infeasible, do not keep clicking “Solve” blindly. Instead, relax one tight limit temporarily to confirm the formulas are correct, then re-tighten.

Probing questions:
- Which constraints are “must-not-violate” and which are negotiable?
- If you relax one constraint, does the solution behaviour make sense?

Common misconception: adding many constraints always improves realism. Redundant or contradictory constraints can make models unstable and difficult to audit.

slides.title: Calculation log essentials (for reproducibility)

content.title: Calculation log essentials (for reproducibility)

rows: Prevents silent unit and scope errors
Why each limit exists; where it comes from

content.notes:
Your calculation log is the difference between a private spreadsheet and an academic artefact.

At minimum, record: (1) assumptions and units, including any conversions (e.g., “labour is in hours; input data in minutes divided by 60”), (2) constraint rationale, so a reader knows whether a limit is a policy, a physical capacity, or a contract, (3) Solver settings, including the chosen algorithm (Simplex LP, GRG Nonlinear, Evolutionary), plus any key options, (4) version and timestamp, so your outputs can be matched to a specific file state, and (5) rounding choices.

Important nuance: rounding before optimisation can change the feasible region and the optimum. A common better practice is to optimise on full precision, then round decision variables only at the end, followed by a feasibility re-check.

Probing questions:
- Could someone rebuild my model from the log alone?
- If they get a different objective value, can we diagnose why quickly?

slides.title: Scenario comparison and recommendation logic

content.title: Scenario comparison and recommendation logic
leftColumn: Objective value change vs baseline
Feasibility + which constraints bind
Sensitivity/robustness (buffers, ranges)
Operational risk and implementability
rightColumn: Is the improvement material and credible?
What becomes the bottleneck, and is it stable?
Does a small change flip the decision?
What could fail in delivery, and what is the cost?
content.notes:
To evaluate scenarios, compare more than the objective value.

First, quantify the change versus baseline (absolute and percentage). Second, assess feasibility and identify binding constraints. Binding constraints often define the real bottleneck, and bottlenecks can shift across scenarios (e.g., waste becomes binding instead of labour).

Third, consider robustness. In linear models, sensitivity information (e.g., shadow prices and allowable ranges) can indicate how fragile the solution is to parameter error. Even without formal sensitivity reports, you can check robustness by making small perturbations (±5–10%) and seeing whether the chosen plan changes.

Fourth, evaluate operational risk: does the solution run at 100% of a limit with no slack? Does it require perfect forecasts? Does it rely on continuous (fractional) outputs that are not implementable?

A disciplined recommendation answers: “Which scenario do we choose, why, and what checks remain before implementation?”

slides.title: Risk register notes (minimum set)

content.title: Risk register notes (minimum set)
content: Assumption risk: key parameter wrong; mitigate via ±10% checks
Data quality risk: stale/noisy data; mitigate with source validation
Model form risk: wrong structure; mitigate by alternative model run
Implementation risk: rounding/integer needs; mitigate with re-check
Ethics/integrity risk: selective reporting; mitigate by baseline lock
content.notes:
A risk register is not bureaucracy; it is part of responsible quantitative practice.

You need at least three risks, but notice how each risk includes a mitigation or sensitivity check. For assumption risk, choose the parameter that drives results most (often the binding constraint coefficient or profit/cost coefficient) and run a controlled perturbation (e.g., ±10%).

For data quality risk, identify whether inputs come from reliable sources, how often they are updated, and whether they reflect the same time period as the decision. A model using last year’s demand to plan next month’s production is vulnerable.

Model form risk asks whether the mathematical structure is appropriate: are relationships truly linear? Are there missing constraints (e.g., minimum batch sizes, setup times)? A mitigation is to test an alternative formulation or add a constraint and see if conclusions change.

Ethics/integrity risk is often overlooked: do you report only the best scenario? A mitigation is to “lock” the baseline and maintain a change history so comparisons are fair.

Probing question: If your recommendation is implemented and fails, what is the most likely modelling-related reason?

slides.title: Worked example: product-mix data (weekly)

content.title: Worked example: product-mix data (weekly)
content.notes:
We will use a simple product-mix optimisation to demonstrate scenario evaluation. Decision variables are:
- x_A = units of Product A per week
- x_B = units of Product B per week

Objective: maximise weekly profit = 30·x_A + 50·x_B.

Constraints (with units):
- Machine hours: 2·x_A + 3·x_B ≤ 200 (hrs/week)
- Labour hours: 1·x_A + 2·x_B ≤ 140 (hrs/week)
- Waste: 3·x_A + 4·x_B ≤ 220 (kg/week)
- Demand: x_A ≤ 50 and x_B ≤ 40 (units/week)
- Non-negativity: x_A, x_B ≥ 0

Mini-check: notice each constraint is a ‘rate × quantity’ sum with a clear unit. Encourage yourself to label these directly in Excel next to the formulas.

Common misconception: treating demand limits as forecasts rather than explicit bounds. In this model, “Max demand” is an upper bound; if you want to enforce meeting demand, you would model minimums instead.

slides.title: Worked example: set up Solver (step-by-step)

content.title: Worked example: set up Solver (step-by-step)
content: Create variable cells x_A and x_B (units/week)
Compute totals for profit, machine hrs, labour hrs, waste
Set objective: maximise total profit cell
Add constraints for capacities, waste, and demand upper bounds
Add x_A ≥ 0 and x_B ≥ 0 (and integer if required)
Use Simplex LP when formulas are linear
content.notes:
Build the spreadsheet so that Solver is only changing x_A and x_B; everything else should be formula-driven.

Practical build sequence:
1) Put x_A and x_B in clearly labelled cells with units.
2) Create totals using SUMPRODUCT-style formulas (e.g., MachineUsed = 2*x_A + 3*x_B).
3) Create an objective cell Profit = 30*x_A + 50*x_B.
4) Add constraints exactly as written, referencing the totals and the limit cells.

Solver method selection matters. This is a linear programming model (all relationships are linear), so Simplex LP is appropriate. A common error is using GRG Nonlinear out of habit, which can still solve some linear problems but may be slower and less transparent.

To achieve feasibility quickly: start with x_A = 0, x_B = 0 (always feasible with ≤ constraints), then solve once. If you get infeasible, do not iterate randomly—inspect which constraint formula is wrong or which unit conversion is inconsistent.

Probing question: if you changed the waste limit cell, would every related formula update automatically?

slides.title: Worked example: baseline solution interpretation

content.title: Worked example: baseline solution interpretation
content: Optimal solution: x_A = 20, x_B = 40
Objective value: Profit = £2,600 per week
Waste is binding: 3·20 + 4·40 = 220 kg (0 slack)
Machine slack: 200 − (2·20 + 3·40) = 40 hrs
Labour slack: 140 − (1·20 + 2·40) = 40 hrs
content.notes:
Interpretation is where evaluation begins.

The baseline solution uses Product B at its demand limit (40 units). Waste becomes the binding constraint: you cannot increase production further without exceeding 220 kg/week. Machine and labour are not limiting here, because both have 40 units of slack in their respective units.

This tells you something operationally important: investing in more machine hours will not raise profit unless waste capacity (or waste intensity per unit) also changes.

A useful habit is to compute and display slack explicitly in the spreadsheet. This makes it harder to misread the model and supports scenario reasoning.

Common misconception: “Slack means the constraint is irrelevant.” Slack only means it is non-binding at the optimum under current assumptions. Under a scenario change (e.g., higher demand for B), that same constraint can become binding.

Probing questions:
- If waste handling costs rise, which product becomes less attractive?
- If waste capacity is uncertain, is a zero-slack plan operationally safe?

slides.title: Worked example: two alternative scenarios

content.title: Worked example: two alternative scenarios

rows: Waste binds; B at demand cap
More A feasible; check waste data certainty
Profit drops; consider marketing or substitution

content.notes:
Scenario 1 loosens the binding constraint (waste). The model responds by increasing production of A once B is already at its demand cap. Profit rises meaningfully (here, about 8.5% vs baseline). Evaluation question: is the +10% waste capacity realistic (e.g., extra disposal contract, process improvement), and what is the cost or risk of achieving it?

Scenario 2 tightens a key market constraint: reduced demand for Product B. Profit falls. The bottleneck may shift away from waste because B is no longer consuming as much waste. This is a realistic business interpretation: market conditions can be more constraining than operations.

When you compare scenarios, keep the baseline spreadsheet untouched and save scenario versions separately (or use a scenario manager with a clear log). Otherwise, you risk contaminating comparisons.

Probing questions:
- Which scenario is more plausible: increasing waste capacity or losing demand?
- Does the recommendation change if you require integer units?
- Is the “best profit” scenario also the “best operationally” scenario?

slides.title: Critique output and log corrections (example)

content.title: Critique output and log corrections (example)

rows: Machine in mins; limit in hrs gives odd utilisation
Convert mins→hrs; log conversion and rerun
Negative x appears, profit rises unrealistically
Changing limit cell has no effect on solution
Reference limit cell in constraint; record formula change
Apply rounding rule; re-check feasibility; log rounding

content.notes:
This slide models the diligence expected at Bloom’s ‘evaluate’ level: you are not only solving, you are auditing.

Unit mismatch: If your machine utilisation seems impossible (e.g., >100% but Solver says feasible), suspect units first. Always label inputs with units and run a quick “dimensional sanity check”.

Missing non-negativity: Solver may exploit negative quantities to satisfy constraints while increasing the objective in a mathematically valid but real-world invalid way. Non-negativity is a modelling decision, not a default.

Hard-coded limits: If a scenario change does nothing, it often means your constraint uses a typed number rather than referencing the limit cell. That breaks scenario analysis and reproducibility.

Over-precision: Solver often returns decimals. If the real system needs whole units or batches, you must either impose integer constraints or apply rounding with a documented feasibility re-check.

Change history guidance: note what changed, why, when, and the effect on the objective and feasibility. This is both good scholarship and good professional practice.

slides.title: Practice and reflection (self-paced)

content.title: Practice and reflection (self-paced)
content: Rebuild the model from Slide 9 data in your own spreadsheet
Solve baseline; confirm binding constraint and slack values
Run two new scenarios: one tighter, one looser constraint
Complete a calculation log with settings, version, timestamp
Write a short justification choosing one scenario (evidence-based)
Add 3 risk notes, each with a mitigation or sensitivity check
content.notes:
Treat this as a mini-lab.

For your two scenarios, choose changes that are meaningful and interpretable. Examples: reduce waste limit by 5–15% to model stricter regulation; increase demand cap for Product A to test a marketing push; reduce machine capacity to model downtime; increase profit for B to model pricing.

When justifying your choice, do not rely on a single number. Use the structure: recommendation → key numbers → bottleneck explanation → robustness/risk → next check.

Reflection prompts:
- Which input do you feel least confident about, and why?
- Did your recommendation change when you tightened one constraint slightly?
- If you had to explain your model to a non-technical manager, what would you show first?

Common pitfall: running many scenarios but failing to keep a clean baseline and change log. Quality of comparison matters more than quantity of scenarios.

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD104 portfolio: Solver model + scenario justification
Use your log and risk notes as evidence of diligence
Avoid: unclear units, missing bounds, and hard-coded constraints
Avoid: changing multiple drivers without a baseline reference
Avoid: reporting only the best scenario without limitations

content.notes:

Markers (and practitioners) look for: transparent modelling choices, reproducibility, and a defensible argument. A high objective value with weak documentation is not strong work.

Common mistakes to address early:
- Units not stated or inconsistent across formulas.
- Missing non-negativity or integer constraints where needed.
- Constraints typed as numbers rather than linked to cells.

Use the MCQs as a diagnostic. If you miss an item, return to the relevant slide and then check your own spreadsheet for the same issue. The goal is not just correctness, but consistent, auditable practice.

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Scenario analysis changes parameters, not the model structure
A credible Solver result requires unit-consistent constraints
Reproducibility needs a clear calculation log and version control

Maintain integrity by critiquing outputs and logging changes
content.notes:

Final probing question to self-assess: If someone challenged your recommendation, could you point to specific cells, constraints, Solver settings, and scenario comparisons that support your conclusion?

content.title: Solver results and sensitivity outputs
content: Maths Certification
MOD104 — Optimisation with Calculus and Excel Solver
Lesson 14
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
In this lesson we focus on interpreting Excel Solver outputs rather than building a model from scratch. The emphasis is evaluative: you will use evidence from Solver reports to (1) diagnose operational bottlenecks, (2) quantify marginal values using sensitivity measures, and (3) make a justified recommendation between optimisation scenarios.

As you progress, keep a clear separation between (a) what the reports state, (b) what you infer, and (c) what you recommend. This separation is essential for an audit-ready decision note.

slides.speakerNotes:
In this lesson we focus on interpreting Excel Solver outputs rather than building a model from scratch. The emphasis is evaluative: you will use evidence from Solver reports to (1) diagnose operational bottlenecks, (2) quantify marginal values using sensitivity measures, and (3) make a justified recommendation between optimisation scenarios.

As you progress, keep a clear separation between (a) what the reports state, (b) what you infer, and (c) what you recommend. This separation is essential for an audit-ready decision note.

slides.title: Orientation and study route

content.title: Orientation and study route
content: What you'll learn: binding constraints and bottlenecks
Interpret shadow price, slack, reduced cost, allowable ranges
Test scenarios and justify a recommendation with calculations
Create an audit-ready decision note with settings and outputs
Study path: watch/read → replicate → attempt checks
Download Answer + Sensitivity reports to follow along
content.notes:
Work through the lesson in three passes. Pass 1: read the key definitions and locate each field in the Solver reports. Pass 2: replicate the worked example, pausing to compute slack, shadow price impacts, and validity ranges by hand so you can detect implausible outputs. Pass 3: attempt the formative checks under timed conditions.

Probing questions to keep in mind: Which constraints are actually limiting performance right now? If I could ‘buy’ one more unit of a resource, what is it worth and for how long is that valuation valid? What would I write down so that someone else can reproduce my result in six months’ time?

Common misconception: treating sensitivity values as universal “truths”. They are local marginal claims with explicit validity conditions.

slides.title: Which Solver output answers which question?

content.title: Which Solver output answers which question?
content.content: Use the right report for the decision question you are answering.
content.notes:
The Answer report is your primary evidence source for Learning Objective 1: it tells you which constraints bind at the optimum via ‘Slack’ and often an explicit ‘Binding’ status. It also provides the final decision variable values and objective value.

The Sensitivity report is the core for Learning Objective 2: shadow prices (marginal value of RHS changes), reduced costs (how far a zero variable is from entering the solution), and allowable increase/decrease (the validity window for marginal claims).

The Limits report is frequently misunderstood: it is about feasibility bounds for decision variables while holding others fixed, not about marginal objective impacts. It can support reasonableness checks but does not replace sensitivity analysis.

Audit point: always record the Solver method (e.g., Simplex LP), and any options such as ‘Assume Linear Model’ and ‘Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative’. Sensitivity outputs are only meaningful under specific solver/model conditions.

slides.title: Binding constraints and bottlenecks

content.title: Binding constraints and bottlenecks
content: Binding constraint: slack = 0 at the optimum
Non-binding: slack > 0; relaxing it will not change solution
Bottleneck = binding constraint limiting objective improvement
Use units: e.g., machine-hours, labour-hours, kg, £
Evidence: cite LHS, RHS and slack from Answer report
Write 3–5 sentences linking bottleneck to operations impact
content.notes:
A constraint is binding when the solution sits exactly on its boundary; operationally, you have fully used that resource or fully met a requirement. Non-binding means you have unused capacity (positive slack) for a ≤ constraint. Emphasise units: slack is in the same units as the constraint (hours, tonnes, etc.), while the objective is typically £ or utility.

Bottleneck language must be precise: ‘Machine time is the bottleneck’ is only defensible if the machine-time constraint binds (slack 0). It is possible to have multiple bottlenecks simultaneously (multiple binding constraints), especially in linear programmes.

Mini-example prompt: If labour has slack of 12 hours, what happens if you add 5 more labour hours? (Answer: nothing, unless labour becomes binding under a different scenario.)

Common misconceptions:
- Confusing “important” constraints with binding constraints. A safety constraint might be non-binding today yet critical.
- Assuming only one constraint can be binding.

Probing questions: What resource is fully utilised? If you could add 1 unit of a binding resource, what would you do with it in the current solution?

slides.title: Shadow price and allowable range

content.title: Shadow price and allowable range
content: Shadow price = Δobjective per +1 unit of RHS (within range)
Sign matters: + means extra resource improves objective
Allowable inc/dec define where the shadow price is valid
Outside range, basis may change; re-solve before claiming value
If constraint non-binding, shadow price is usually 0
State range: RHS ∈ [RHS-AD, RHS+AI]
content.notes:
Shadow price is the linear-programming analogue of a derivative: it estimates the marginal change in the objective when you relax or tighten a constraint RHS by one unit, holding the current optimal ‘structure’ (basis) fixed. Always say what ‘one unit’ is: one machine-hour, one kg of material, one staff-hour.

Crucially, Solver reports a shadow price with an allowable increase and allowable decrease for the RHS. Your marginal claim is only valid within that interval. Outside it, the set of binding constraints may change, so the marginal value changes.

Explain sign conventions carefully. In a maximisation problem with a ≤ resource constraint, a positive shadow price means additional resource increases maximum profit. A zero shadow price typically indicates the constraint is non-binding at the optimum.

Probing questions:
- If the shadow price is £13.33 per machine-hour, what is the predicted profit change for +4 hours? What must you check before multiplying?
- If the allowable increase is 0, what does that suggest about the solution structure?

Common misconception: using shadow price to value very large changes (e.g., doubling capacity). That is exactly when you should re-optimise and compare solutions.

slides.title: Reduced cost for decision variables

content.title: Reduced cost for decision variables
content: Reduced cost applies to variables at 0 (non-basic variables)
It is the profit improvement needed before the variable enters
For max problems: negative reduced cost = needs higher profit
Reduced cost = 0 for variables produced in the optimum
Cross-check: rc = c - Σ(a·shadow price)
Do not use reduced cost if model is not linear/Simplex
content.notes:
Reduced cost answers: ‘Why is this activity not used in the optimal solution?’ If a decision variable is zero, reduced cost measures how much its objective coefficient would need to improve for it to become attractive, given current shadow prices.

Interpretation (maximisation): if reduced cost is −£1.66 for a product currently at 0, its unit profit would need to increase by £1.66 (or its resource usage decrease equivalently) before producing it becomes optimal, assuming the current basis remains valid.

Mini-example using dual prices: suppose the shadow price of machine hours is £13.33/hr and labour is £3.33/hr. A proposed product C uses 1 machine-hour and 1 labour-hour per unit. The implied resource value is £16.66 per unit. If product C’s unit profit is £15, then rc = 15 − 16.66 = −£1.66, so it is not selected.

Common misconceptions:
- Interpreting reduced cost for variables that are not at 0 (it will be 0 for basic variables).
- Forgetting the direction changes for minimisation models.

Probing question: What business levers can change reduced cost—price, unit cost, or process redesign (resource coefficients)?

slides.title: When sensitivity results apply (and when not)

content.title: When sensitivity results apply (and when not)
leftColumn: Model is linear; solved with Simplex LP
Same set of binding constraints (same basis)
Only one RHS or coefficient changes at a time
No integer/binary restrictions
rightColumn: Non-linear model or GRG used
Integer constraints: sensitivity is invalid/unavailable
Large changes beyond allowable ranges
Multiple simultaneous changes without re-solving
content.notes:
Treat sensitivity analysis as a local approximation around the current optimum. The key phrase to use in your writing is ‘within the allowable range’. This is not pedantry; it is the condition under which the reported shadow prices and reduced costs are guaranteed to remain correct.

If your model includes integer decisions (e.g., number of vehicles, whether to open a facility), the Sensitivity report is generally not provided or is not meaningful because the objective response is no longer linear and continuous.

If you need to evaluate combined changes (e.g., +10 machine-hours and +5 labour-hours together), a safe rule is to re-solve the model for the combined scenario and compare outcomes. Sensitivity analysis can still guide which scenarios are worth testing first, but it does not replace re-optimisation.

Probing questions:
- Which Solver method did you use, and why is that relevant for sensitivity?
- Are your decision variables divisible in reality? If not, what risk does that create?

Common misconception: believing that ‘allowable increase/decrease’ refers to acceptable business tolerance. It refers to the mathematical region where the same optimal basis remains optimal.

slides.title: Worked example: Answer report evidence

content.title: Worked example: Answer report evidence
content.content: Maximise profit with two products and three constraints.
content.notes:
State the model (verbally) before interpreting the table: decision variables are quantities A and B; objective is maximise profit; constraints represent machine capacity, labour capacity, and a demand limit on B.

From the slack column, machine-hours and labour-hours are binding (slack 0). Demand for B is non-binding (slack 5 units), meaning the optimum does not come close to the demand ceiling.

How to write the required 3–5 sentences (template learners can adapt):
1) ‘At the optimum, machine-hours and labour-hours constraints are binding because slack is 0 hours for both (LHS=RHS).’
2) ‘This indicates all available machine and labour capacity is fully utilised.’
3) ‘The demand constraint for product B is non-binding with 5 units slack (10 used vs 15 allowed), so demand is not currently limiting output.’
4) ‘Operationally, capacity (machine and labour hours) is the bottleneck rather than market demand.’

Probing question: If both machine and labour bind, which should you prioritise expanding first? (Lead into shadow prices.)

slides.title: Worked example: Sensitivity interpretation

content.title: Worked example: Sensitivity interpretation
content: Optimal plan: A=20, B=10; profit £800
Shadow prices: machine £13.33/hr; labour £3.33/hr
Demand(B) slack 5 ⇒ shadow price £0 per unit
Machine RHS 50: valid for 35–80 (−15, +30)
Labour RHS 40: valid for 25–47.5 (−15, +7.5)
Predict Δprofit: ΔZ = shadow price × ΔRHS (if valid)
content.notes:
Interpret the numbers as marginal values. A shadow price of £13.33/hr for machine time means: if you could increase machine capacity by 1 hour, profit would increase by about £13.33, provided the increase is within the allowable range and other parameters remain unchanged.

Demonstrate a calculation: adding 4 machine-hours (within +30) predicts Δprofit ≈ 4 × 13.33 = £53.32. Then emphasise the condition: this is valid only if the basis does not change.

Explain the allowable range in plain language: ‘As long as machine capacity stays between 35 and 80 hours, the marginal value £13.33/hr remains correct for small changes.’ Repeat for labour.

Important nuance: these marginal values assume you change one RHS at a time. If you simultaneously add machine and labour, the combined effect may differ; re-solve to confirm.

Probing questions:
- Why is the demand shadow price zero here? What would need to change for demand to become valuable?
- Labour has a positive shadow price but smaller than machine. What does that imply about where scarcity is most costly?

slides.title: Worked example: Compare scenarios and recommend

content.title: Worked example: Compare scenarios and recommend
content.content: Use marginal values to screen options, then justify a choice.
content.notes:
Model the evaluative reasoning explicitly. First, screen scenarios using shadow prices and validity ranges. Machine expansion looks most valuable in gross terms. Labour expansion is beneficial but far smaller. Expanding demand for B has no value because demand is not binding.

Then introduce economic comparison: if extra machine hours cost £12/hr, the net gain is (13.33 − 12) × 10 = £13.30, which is small and may be wiped out by uncertainty.

This is where you add the required brief risk note. Examples of appropriate limitations:
- The marginal values assume linearity and the same binding set; if expansion changes the product mix, re-optimise.
- Costs and achievable capacity may be uncertain; a small net gain is sensitive to estimation error.
- If capacity comes in discrete blocks (e.g., buying a new machine), the continuous shadow price is only a guide.

Probing questions:
- What additional information would you need to make a robust recommendation (e.g., cost of capacity, demand variability)?
- If you could only choose one action, which has the strongest evidence and why?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: From your model, list each constraint with slack and status
Identify the bottleneck and justify in 3–5 sentences
Use shadow prices to value +1 unit of each scarce resource
Test one change beyond range; explain why re-solving is needed
Draft a decision note: settings, outputs, scenario log, limits
content.notes:
Encourage learners to use their own spreadsheet model from earlier lessons or create a small two-variable LP. The goal is not the complexity of the model; it is the quality of interpretation and justification.

Suggested workflow for the practice:
1) Capture the Answer report and highlight slack values. Write the bottleneck explanation using units.
2) Capture the Sensitivity report and compute at least two ‘what-if’ changes using ΔZ = shadow price × ΔRHS.
3) For the ‘beyond range’ test, deliberately choose a ΔRHS larger than allowable increase (e.g., +50 hours). Write a short explanation: ‘Shadow price no longer valid; must re-solve; expect different binding constraints.’
4) Start building your audit-ready decision note as you go; do not leave documentation to the end.

Probing questions:
- What would convince an external reviewer that your scenario claim is valid?
- Where could unit errors occur in your worksheet (hours vs minutes, £ vs pence)?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
leftColumn: MCQ: interpret slack, shadow price, reduced cost, ranges
Quiz: build model, choose method, read reports
Assignments: scenario comparison and recommendation
Skill: audit-ready decision documentation
rightColumn: Omitting units or mixing £/unit and £/hour
Claiming shadow price outside allowable range
Treating non-binding constraints as bottlenecks
No settings/versioned outputs in submission
content.notes:
Make explicit how this lesson supports assessment: the quizzes test recognition and interpretation of report fields, while longer assignments typically require scenario evaluation and a justified recommendation.

Stress that marks are often lost on ‘presentation of evidence’ rather than mathematics. For example, a correct shadow price used outside its allowable range should be treated as incorrect because the claim is unjustified.

Audit-ready expectations (what to include in submissions):
- A clear statement of objective, decision variables, and units.
- Solver method (e.g., Simplex LP) and key options.
- Dated/versioned Answer and Sensitivity reports (or screenshots) matching the submitted numbers.
- A limitation statement: when the sensitivity results do not apply.

Probing question: If you changed any coefficient after generating the report, how would a reviewer detect that? (They should not have to; your versioning should make it obvious.)

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Use slack to classify constraints and locate bottlenecks
Shadow prices quantify marginal value, but only within ranges
Reduced cost explains why a zero variable is not chosen
Scenario claims need validity checks and transparent logs
Audit-ready notes require settings, reports, and limitations
content.notes:
Reinforce the evaluative mindset: Solver outputs are not merely numbers to report; they are evidence to support a decision under explicit assumptions.

A useful closing check learners can apply to any optimisation write-up: can you point to a specific cell in a Solver report for every important claim you make? If not, the claim is likely an untested inference.

Forward-looking link: in more complex models (non-linear, integer, stochastic), you will often need to replace sensitivity outputs with systematic scenario re-solving and robustness checks. The discipline you practise here—units, evidence, validity ranges, and documentation—still applies.

slides.title: Clean and summarise quality data in Excel or Python

content.title: Clean and summarise quality data in Excel or Python
content.content:
Program: Maths Certification
Module: MOD105 — Statistics for Quality Reporting in Excel or Python
Lesson 1 • Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners to MOD105 Lesson 1. Position this lesson as the foundation for all later statistical reporting: if the data are not credible, the statistics are not credible. Emphasise Bloom level ‘analyse’: learners will diagnose data problems, choose appropriate summaries, and interpret inferential outputs rather than merely compute them. Briefly preview the tool flexibility: every method can be done in either Excel or Python, and the logic is identical even when the clicks/commands differ.

slides.title: Orientation: what you will learn and how to study

content.title: Orientation: what you will learn and how to study
content: You will clean a raw dataset and keep an audit log
You will choose centre/spread measures that fit the data
You will flag outliers and decide what to do with them
You will build a 95% CI for a process mean with limits
You will run a t-test and report stats vs practical impact
Study loop: watch → practise → self-check → re-run
content.notes: Explain the study loop explicitly: (1) read/watch the concept, (2) replicate the worked example with your own file, (3) answer the practice prompts, then (4) re-run the same workflow faster, aiming for fewer errors. Reinforce that ‘cleaning decisions’ are part of the deliverable: in quality contexts you must be able to justify exclusions and transformations. Probing questions: What would happen if two analysts cleaned the same file—would they produce the same result? If not, what documentation would reduce ambiguity?

slides.title: Data cleaning in quality reporting: the goal

content.title: Data cleaning in quality reporting: the goal
content: Make data fit for purpose, not perfect
Preserve traceability: original vs cleaned values
Separate errors from rare but real process events
Prefer flags over deletions until justified
Record each rule: why, how, and impact on N
content.notes: Clarify that cleaning is a decision process: you are balancing bias, variance, and operational realism. Distinguish between (a) data-entry/measurement errors (e.g., impossible temperature), (b) valid extreme values caused by special causes, and (c) structural issues (units, formats). Stress traceability: ideally keep a raw copy and create new columns for cleaned values or flags. Common misconception: “cleaning means removing outliers.” Instead, outliers are a later analytic step and may be the most important observations in quality improvement.

content.title: Common data issues and typical treatments
content.notes: Walk through each row with a brief concrete example: missing diameter measurements, negative cycle time, thickness recorded in mm and inches, duplicate inspection records, and ‘12,5’ stored as text due to locale settings. Explain that treatment depends on purpose: a control chart may handle missing differently than a capability study. Probing question: Which issues change your estimate of the mean versus your estimate of variation? Highlight a misconception: removing duplicates is not always correct—sometimes repeats are legitimate repeated measures; you need a defined key (e.g., part_id + timestamp + station).

Probing question: Which issues change your estimate of the mean versus your estimate of variation? slides.title: Audit log: minimal structure that meets QA needs

content.title: Audit log: minimal structure that meets QA needs
content: Column/field affected
Rule applied (exact logic)
Reason (spec, physics, process knowledge)
Before/after counts (N changed, flags raised)
Who/when/tool version
Notes on assumptions and follow-up actions
content.notes: Explain that an audit log is a reproducibility tool and a governance tool. In Excel, this can be a separate sheet; in Python, a markdown cell or a structured list/dictionary written to CSV. Encourage precise logic: not “removed outliers” but “flagged values with |z|>3; retained for reporting; excluded for mean estimate.” Probing question: If your manager asks ‘why is N smaller this week?’, can your audit log answer in one minute? Common mistake: documenting only what you did, not why you did it.

leftColumn: Mean + SD
Sensitive to outliers
Best for symmetric data

Robust to outliers

content.notes: Explain that ‘best’ depends on the question: if you need inference for a mean (e.g., CI/t-test), mean/SD connect directly to those methods, but only if assumptions are reasonable. Probing questions: What does your customer experience—typical or average? Is the cost driven by extreme values? Misconception to address: “median is always better because it ignores outliers.” Sometimes outliers are the main risk, and the mean captures their impact.

slides.title: Outlier flags: rules and decision options

content.title: Outlier flags: rules and decision options
content: z-score rule: flag if |z| > 3 (or agreed threshold)
IQR rule: < Q1−1.5×IQR or > Q3+1.5×IQR
Flags are not automatic deletions
Investigate: measurement, data entry, special cause
Decide: retain, exclude, or report separately
Document the decision and its effect on results
content.notes: Clarify when each rule is appropriate: z-scores assume roughly normal data and use mean/SD; IQR is distribution-robust and works well with skew. Stress that outlier ‘handling’ is a business decision informed by statistics and process knowledge. Give examples: a one-off machine jam causing a long cycle time may be a special cause worth investigating, not deleting. Common misconception: selecting a rule after seeing results (p-hacking). Encourage pre-specifying the threshold and reporting sensitivity (e.g., results with and without flagged points).

slides.title: 95% confidence interval for a process mean

content.title: 95% confidence interval for a process mean
content: Interpretation: plausible range for the true mean
Formula: mean ± t* × (s/√n)
Use t* with df = n−1 when σ is unknown
Report n, mean, s, CI bounds, units
State at least 3 assumptions/limits explicitly
content.notes: Teach interpretation carefully: a 95% CI is about the procedure’s long-run coverage, not the probability the specific mean lies in the interval (avoid that wording). Explain components: standard error shrinks with √n; t* is larger for small n. Provide assumptions/limits examples: (1) sampling method represents the process of interest, (2) observations are independent (watch for batching or repeated measures), (3) approximate normality of the mean (either the data are roughly normal or n is reasonably large), (4) measurement resolution and gauge error (tolerance vs instrument). Probing question: If you sample 10 consecutive parts, are they independent?

slides.title: t-tests: statistical vs practical significance

content.title: t-tests: statistical vs practical significance
leftColumn: Statistical significance
Uses p-value vs α (e.g., 0.05)
Answers: is there evidence of change?
Sensitive to sample size
rightColumn: Practical significance
Uses effect size vs spec/tolerance
Answers: does the change matter?
Link to risk, cost, capability
content.notes: Explain the decision split: p-value addresses evidence, not importance. A tiny shift can be ‘significant’ with large n; a meaningful shift can be ‘non-significant’ with small n. Provide a quality example: mean thickness drops by 0.01 mm; p<0.01 but tolerance is ±0.5 mm, so impact may be negligible. Conversely, a 0.2 mm shift might be practically important even if p=0.08 with n=12—this suggests more data may be needed. Emphasise reporting: include the estimated difference, CI if possible, and compare to spec.

content.notes: Talk through a realistic dataset: 200 inspection rows with columns such as part_id, timestamp, thickness, unit, operator, station. content: Load with pandas; inspect dtypes and missingness
Standardise units using vectorised conversion
Flag impossible values with boolean conditions

Summarise: mean, median, SD, IQR after cleaning

content.notes: Describe a minimal, reproducible workflow: read_csv, then df.info() and df.isna().sum() to diagnose. Emphasise dtype pitfalls: numeric columns read as object due to stray characters. Test change: one-sample or two-sample t-test
