content.notes: Provide a coherent story: a process change (new cutting tool) aims to reduce mean burr height. Step 1: flag outliers (e.g., burr height spikes due to tool damage). Step 2: show that the mean shifts substantially when including spikes, while the median is stable—this motivates robust reporting. Step 3: compute a 95% CI for the post-change mean and interpret it as a plausible range for the true process mean. Step 4: run a two-sample t-test comparing pre vs post groups; remind learners to check equal/unequal variance options (Welch is safer when unsure). Probing questions: Are the samples independent (different parts) or paired (same part measured twice)? Which test matches that design?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD105 assignment: cleaned dataset + statistical report
Marks often lost on missing audit trail and unclear rules
Do not delete rows without a documented rationale
Avoid mixing units or rounding away meaningful variation
Report both p-value and effect size vs spec/tolerance
Check tool outputs: correct test type and correct inputs
content.notes: Explain typical grading expectations: evidence of a reproducible workflow, clear documentation, and correct interpretation in plain language. Highlight frequent pitfalls: (1) cleaning after running the stats (reverse order), (2) changing thresholds until results look ‘good’, (3) misusing a paired t-test when samples are independent (or vice versa), (4) ignoring independence (e.g., using repeated readings as separate data points), and (5) presenting confidence intervals without units. Suggest a submission checklist: raw file preserved, cleaned file saved, audit log included, and a short narrative of decisions.

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Cleaning is analysis: define rules, flag issues, and log decisions
Pick summaries that match distribution and reporting purpose
Outlier rules flag candidates; process knowledge drives actions
CIs quantify uncertainty; always state assumptions and limits
t-tests need interpretation: statistical evidence vs practical impact
content.notes: Reinforce the through-line: quality reporting is credibility plus clarity. Encourage learners to keep templates: an audit log format, a standard summary table, and a standard reporting sentence for CIs and tests. Remind learners that the next lessons will build on these outputs, so disciplined workflow now prevents compounding errors later.

slides.title: Summary statistics and when to use them

content.title: Summary statistics and when to use them
leftColumn: Mean: sensitive to extremes
Median: robust to outliers
SD: spread around mean
IQR: spread of middle 50%
rightColumn: Use mean+SD for stable, symmetric data
Use median+IQR for skewed or tailed data
Always report units and sample size (n)
Check distribution before strong conclusions
content.notes: Explain each statistic in plain language. Mean answers 'typical if values are balanced'; median answers 'typical middle value'. SD assumes a mean-centred notion of spread and is strongly influenced by extreme values. IQR focuses on the central mass and is more stable under outliers. Stress that 'use' depends on both purpose and data shape. Common misconception: 'Median is only for non-normal data'—in fact, it is often useful whenever robustness matters. Ask: 'If you have a single extreme value, which summary changes more: mean or median?'

A flag is not automatic deletion

Mean CI: x̄ ± t* × (s/√n) when SD unknown
Mean difference CI compares before vs after samples
State assumptions: independence and stable measurement

Discuss assumptions: independent observations, consistent measurement system, and approximate normality or sufficient n via CLT. p-value: evidence against “no change” model

content.notes: Frame tests as decision-support, not truth machines. Explain null and alternative in plain language: 'assume no change; how surprising is the observed difference?' Common misconception: 'p<0.05 means the change is important'—importance must be judged against tolerances and business impact. Ask: 'What is the smallest change that matters operationally in your setting?'

content.title: Common risks and verification checks
leftColumn: Unit mismatch (e.g., cm vs mm)

rightColumn: Recompute via a second method (tool or formula)

content.notes: Walk through how these failures happen in practice. Unit mismatch often arises when combining files from different sources; show how a 10× scaling error can look like a 'process shift'. Missing values: Excel may ignore blanks, Python may treat strings as objects; both can distort n and SD. Outlier removal: removing extremes can artificially reduce SD and inflate perceived capability. Verification checks should be quick and repeatable: (1) independent recomputation (e.g., Excel formula vs PivotTable; pandas vs manual check), (2) spot-check several random rows, (3) sensitivity analysis, and (4) keep a simple change log. Probing question: 'If your mean changes after you “clean” data, how will you explain why?'

slides.title: Worked example: CI and t-test in Excel vs Python

content.title: Worked example: CI and t-test in Excel vs Python
leftColumn: Excel: mean AVERAGE(range)
Excel: SD STDEV.S(range)
Excel: CI via t*×s/√n
Excel: t-test T.TEST(range1,range2,2,3)
rightColumn: Python: df['x'].mean(), .std(ddof=1)
Python: df['x'].quantile([.25,.75])
Python: scipy.stats.t.interval(...) or statsmodels
Python: scipy.stats.ttest_ind(x1,x2,equal_var=False)
content.notes: Explain what each line does and the key options. In Excel, show how to compute n with COUNT(range) (ignores blanks), then standard error s/√n, then find t* with T.INV.2T(0.05, n-1). Clarify that T.TEST’s fourth argument controls variance assumption: 3 is Welch (unequal variances), often safer for before/after samples. In Python, remind learners to use ddof=1 for sample SD, and to drop missing values explicitly: x = df['x'].dropna(). content.title: Orientation: how to use this lesson

slides.title: What “clean” quality data means

content.title: What “clean” quality data means
content: Complete: missing values handled explicitly, not ignored
Valid: values fall in realistic ranges and permitted codes
Consistent: units, formats, and categories match definitions
Unique: duplicates removed or justified (true repeats vs errors)
Traceable: every edit is logged and reversible
content.notes: Define each dimension with a quality context: e.g., a temperature reading of 850°C might be valid in one process and impossible in another—validity needs domain knowledge. Give a mini-example: ‘Length’ recorded as 12.3 (cm) in one row and 0.123 (m) in another; both are numerically plausible but inconsistent. Ask: Which problems bias your mean, and which mainly affect variability or counts? Misconception: deleting missing values is always safe—if missingness is systematic (e.g., night shift), deletion can bias results.

slides.title: Reproducible cleaning: Excel vs Python

content.title: Reproducible cleaning: Excel vs Python
leftColumn: Excel: keep raw tab unchanged; work on a copy
Excel: use Power Query steps where possible
Excel: record filters, rules, and formulas used
Excel: save a change log table (what, why, when)
rightColumn: Python: keep raw file; create a cleaned dataframe
Python: code cells show each transformation
Python: validate with asserts (ranges, types, uniques)
Python: export cleaned data + script/notebook
content.notes: Emphasise that reproducibility is about someone else rerunning your process, not about memory. In Excel, Power Query is preferable because it records transformations; if using manual steps, create a log table (timestamp, field, rule, count affected). In Python, stress small, readable steps and validation checks (e.g., ensure no negative cycle times). Probing question: If an auditor asked ‘how many rows changed and why?’, could you answer in one minute?

slides.title: Summarise centre and spread

content.title: Summarise centre and spread
content: Mean: sensitive to outliers; best for roughly symmetric data
Median: robust centre when skew or outliers are present
SD: typical spread around mean; pairs naturally with mean
IQR: middle 50% spread; pairs naturally with median
Interpret with units and context (e.g., seconds, mm, %)
content.notes: Explain why pairing matters: mean with SD assumes a distribution where those summaries are informative; median with IQR is safer for skewed quality metrics (e.g., repair times). Mini-example: if most cycle times are 45–55s but one is 300s, mean inflates while median stays stable. Ask: What operational story could generate an extreme value—special cause, data entry error, or different product? Misconception: SD is ‘always’ the measure of variability; in quality reporting, IQR is often more defensible for skewed data.

slides.title: Outlier flags: choose a rule you can justify

content.title: Outlier flags: choose a rule you can justify
content.notes: Stress that an outlier flag is a starting point for investigation, not permission to delete. Explain the difference between ‘statistical’ outliers and ‘engineering’ nonconformance. Probing questions: If you remove flagged points, how do your mean and SD change? Are the flagged rows concentrated by operator, machine, supplier, or shift? Misconception: treating outlier removal as routine ‘cleaning’; it can manufacture improvements that are not real.

slides.title: 95% confidence interval for a process mean

content.title: 95% confidence interval for a process mean
content: Goal: estimate a plausible range for the true process mean
Formula: mean ± t*SE, where SE = SD/√n
95% level: long-run, 95% of such intervals contain the mean
Assume independent data; normality helps, n≥30 often OK
CI is not: “95% chance the mean is in this range”
Be explicit about sampling limits and representativeness
content.notes: Walk through interpretation carefully: the parameter is fixed; the interval varies with repeated samples. Use a mini-example: n=50, mean=10.2 mm, SD=0.5 mm → SE≈0.071; with t≈2.01, CI≈10.2±0.14 → (10.06, 10.34). Ask: What would make independence false (e.g., repeated measures on the same part, time series drift)? Misconception: assuming a narrow CI proves the process meets spec; the CI is about the mean, not individual units or defect rates.

slides.title: Hypothesis tests for a process change (t-tests)

content.title: Hypothesis tests for a process change (t-tests)
content: One-sample: compare mean to target or historical baseline
Two-sample: compare before vs after (independent samples)
State H0/H1 and choose one- or two-sided before testing
Report p-value and an effect size (mean diff, Cohen’s d)
Set a practical threshold (e.g., ≥0.5 mm improvement)
Decision: evidence level + uncertainty + key limitations
content.notes: Explain the logic: a small p-value suggests the observed difference is unlikely under H0, but does not measure importance. Give a mini-example: p=0.03 with a mean change of 0.05 mm may be statistically detectable yet irrelevant if your practical threshold is 0.5 mm. Ask: What is the consequence of a false positive vs a false negative in this process? Misconception: treating p<0.05 as a guarantee; also, changing sidedness after seeing results (‘p-hacking’). Note assumptions: approximate normality of means, independence, and (for classic two-sample) similar variances unless using Welch’s t-test.

rows: Correct entry or set to NA

Probing question: For each fix, ask ‘could this change shift the mean?’ If yes, note it explicitly and consider reporting with and without the corrected rows. Misconception: believing a cleaned dataset is ‘true’; it is an evidence-based reconstruction.

content: Compute n, mean, median, SD, IQR for key measure
Choose outlier rule; flag rows but do not delete by default
Create a plot: histogram/boxplot to check skew and tails
Build 95% CI for mean using t and SE = SD/√n

slides.title: Practice: clean and summarise your dataset

content.title: Practice: clean and summarise your dataset
content: Pick a raw dataset (≥50 rows) with a measurable quality metric
List 5+ expected issues to check (missing, range, units, dups)
Create a cleaning log: rule, rows affected, and rationale
Compute mean/median/SD/IQR; add units and rounding rule
Flag outliers using IQR or z-score; note counts and IDs
Write 2 sentences: what changed after cleaning, and why
content.notes: Encourage learners to choose a metric with real meaning: cycle time, thickness, defect count per batch, tensile strength, etc. Suggest a simple structure for the log: Step number, field, check, action, rows affected, and comment. Probing questions: Are missing values random, or concentrated by time/machine/operator? Do duplicates represent retests (valid) or double entry (invalid)? Misconception: assuming rounding is cosmetic—rounding decisions can imply false precision; align decimals with measurement resolution and stakeholder needs.

slides.title: Practice: write a stakeholder-ready report paragraph

content.title: Practice: write a stakeholder-ready report paragraph
content.content: Template: “After cleaning [n] records (removing/fixing [x] issues), the process average was [mean] [units] (median [median]). Variability was [SD] [units] (IQR [IQR]); we flagged [k] potential outliers using [rule], retained for investigation. A 95% CI for the mean was [L, U], and a [one/two]-sample t-test gave p=[p] for a mean change of [Δ] [units], which [meets/does not meet] the practical threshold of [T] [units], subject to [key assumption/limit].”
content.notes: Explain that this paragraph is a ‘translation layer’ between analysis and decision-making. Point out good practice: include units everywhere; state what you did to the data; avoid causal language unless the design supports it. Prompt: Which parts of the paragraph would you change for a non-technical reader—would you replace ‘t-test’ with ‘statistical comparison’? Common misconception: overstating certainty (“proved”, “guaranteed”). Encourage careful verbs: “suggests”, “is consistent with”, “provides evidence of”.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports: data-cleaning log, summary stats, CI, t-test write-up
Show reproducibility: screenshots of steps or executable notebook
Avoid: deleting outliers without justification and sensitivity check
Avoid: p-value-only conclusions; include effect size + threshold
Avoid: claiming CI is a 95% probability statement
Check: assumptions, independence, and units consistency
content.notes: Explain how assessors will look for transparency: a clear chain from raw data to cleaned data to outputs to conclusions. Suggest including a short ‘assumptions and limitations’ section: sampling method, representativeness, possible autocorrelation, and measurement resolution. Probing question: If a peer reran your work, would they get identical figures? Misconception: thinking ‘more statistics’ earns marks—clarity, correctness, and defensible decisions matter more than complexity.

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Cleaning is analytical: document decisions and their impact
Use mean/SD or median/IQR to match data shape and purpose
Outlier flags support investigation; they do not justify deletion
CIs quantify uncertainty; interpret them with assumptions stated
t-tests need practical significance and honest limitations

Ask learners to self-audit: What is the weakest link in your chain—data quality, method choice, assumptions, or communication? slides.title: A practical workflow for cleaning quality data

content.title: A practical workflow for cleaning quality data
content: State the measurement, unit, and intended precision
Check data types: numbers stored as text, dates, categories
Scan for missing values, duplicates, and impossible values
Check units and scaling (e.g., cm vs mm) before analysis
Create a log of edits: what changed, why, and by whom
Keep raw data unchanged; analyse a cleaned copy
content.notes: Explain that cleaning is a reproducibility task: another analyst should be able to justify and replicate your steps. Give a mini-example: a thickness reading of “0.8” could be 0.8 mm or 0.8 cm; without unit checking, summary statistics are meaningless. Ask: If you delete a row, can you defend that decision in an audit? Highlight a common misconception: ‘Cleaning’ is not ‘making the data look nice’; it is correcting known errors and documenting uncertainty. In Python, this is often a pipeline (read → validate → transform → analyse). In Excel, it is often a structured set of helper columns plus a notes cell describing changes.

slides.title: Choosing summaries: robust vs sensitive statistics

content.title: Choosing summaries: robust vs sensitive statistics
leftColumn: Mean: best for symmetric data without extreme values
SD: typical spread around the mean (same unit as data)
Range: quick sense of spread, but driven by extremes
Use mean ± SD when normality is plausible
rightColumn: Median: robust centre when data are skewed
IQR: spread of middle 50%, robust to outliers
Use median + IQR for skewed or heavy-tailed data
Report both if you need robustness and comparability
content.notes: Clarify that ‘robust’ means not overly influenced by a few extreme points. Provide a mini-example: with values 10, 10, 10, 10, 30 the mean is 14 but the median is 10—very different ‘typical’ values. Ask: In your process, what causes occasional extreme measurements (start-up, changeover, sensor faults)? Misconception: learners often think the mean is always ‘better’ because it uses all data; remind them it can be misleading when data are skewed or contaminated. Reinforce unit discipline: SD and IQR share the measurement unit; variance does not.

slides.title: Flagging outliers: rules and decision principles

content.title: Flagging outliers: rules and decision principles
content: IQR rule: outlier if < Q1−1.5×IQR or > Q3+1.5×IQR
Z-score rule: flag if |z| > 3 (or agreed threshold)
Treat rules as flags, not automatic deletions
Decide: retain, investigate, or exclude (with a reason)
Exclude only for clear data integrity faults, not “bad news”
Document impact: report summaries with and without the point
content.notes: Stress the distinction between an extreme but real event (a true process upset) and a bad datum (mis-key, wrong unit, instrument failure). Use a mini-example: a fill volume of 612 mL might be a real overfill (process issue) or could be 512 mistyped. Ask probing questions: What is physically possible given the equipment limits? Is there corroborating evidence (batch record, calibration log)? Common misconception: ‘Outlier = remove’. Instead, teach a three-way action: retain (real), investigate (uncertain), exclude (proven error). Encourage sensitivity reporting: show how mean/SD change if the flagged point is removed—this is often what stakeholders need.

slides.title: 95% confidence intervals: meaning and assumptions

content.title: 95% confidence intervals: meaning and assumptions
content: A 95% CI estimates a plausible range for a population mean
For small n, use t-based CI: x̄ ± t*×(s/√n)
State assumptions: independence, stable process, sampling method
CLT helps as n grows; with small n, check shape/outliers
CI width reflects variability and sample size, not “certainty”
If data are autocorrelated, CI is often too narrow
content.notes: Translate the CI meaning carefully: it is not ‘95% of values lie here’ and it is not a probability statement about a fixed mean after the fact. A good phrasing: ‘If we repeated this sampling many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean.’ Ask: Are your measurements consecutive in time? If yes, independence may be violated due to autocorrelation, making the interval overconfident. Discuss practical implications: a narrow CI might still be unhelpful if it sits near a specification limit. Misconception: learners often treat CI overlap as a hypothesis test; explain that overlap rules are not exact and depend on design.

slides.title: Hypothesis testing for process change (t-tests)

content.title: Hypothesis testing for process change (t-tests)
content: Define question: has the mean changed from a baseline/target?
Set H0 and H1, choose α (often 0.05) before testing
Check design: one-sample vs two-sample; paired vs unpaired
Compute test statistic and p-value (software does this)
Report effect size or practical threshold, not just p-value
State limits: non-random samples, small n, multiple testing
content.notes: Walk through the logic: a p-value is the probability of data this extreme (or more) assuming H0 is true; it is not the probability that H0 is true. Emphasise the difference between statistical and practical significance: a 0.5 mL change could be ‘significant’ with large n but irrelevant to customers, while a 5 mL change might be operationally critical even if p>0.05 with small n. Probe: What change would matter in your process (a meaningful threshold)? Common misconception: failing to reject H0 means ‘no difference’—instead, it means ‘insufficient evidence with this data and design’.

slides.title: Worked example: cleaning decisions to document

content.title: Worked example: cleaning decisions to document
content: Scenario: bottle fill volumes (mL), n=24, target 500 mL

rows: Keep as NA; exclude from calc

content.notes: Use this slide to model what ‘good documentation’ looks like: not just what you did, but how you decided. Explain that different workplaces will have different policies; the key is consistency and traceability. Ask: Which of these issues is most common in your context—missingness, unit errors, duplicates, or extremes? Highlight that missing data handling is not trivial: deleting rows changes n, which changes SD, SE, and CIs. For unit/scaling, emphasise that you should only correct values when you have supporting evidence (e.g., a known decimal shift error).

slides.title: Worked example: compute summaries (Excel vs Python)

content.title: Worked example: compute summaries (Excel vs Python)
leftColumn: Excel: =AVERAGE(A2:A25)
Excel: =MEDIAN(A2:A25)
Excel: =STDEV.S(A2:A25)
Excel: IQR =Q3−Q1 via QUARTILE.INC
rightColumn: Python: df['x'].mean(), .median()
Python: df['x'].std(ddof=1)
Python: q1,q3=np.percentile(x,[25,75])
Python: iqr=q3-q1; range=x.max()-x.min()
content.notes: Explain that these are ‘sample’ formulas: STDEV.S and ddof=1 match the sample SD used in t-based inference. Prompt: Why does ddof matter? Because the sample SD is an estimate and needs a small correction to be unbiased under normality assumptions. Clarify rounding: agree a rule before reporting (e.g., mean to 1 decimal mL, SD to 2 decimals, CI endpoints to 1 decimal). Misconception: learners sometimes mix STDEV.P with t-based CI, producing inconsistent inference. In Excel, show how to compute Q1 and Q3: QUARTILE.INC(range,1) and QUARTILE.INC(range,3).

slides.title: Worked example: flag outliers (Excel vs Python)

content.title: Worked example: flag outliers (Excel vs Python)
leftColumn: Excel: Q1=QUARTILE.INC(x,1); Q3=... ,3
Excel: IQR=Q3-Q1; Lower=Q1-1.5*IQR
Excel: Upper=Q3+1.5*IQR
Excel: Flag with IF(x<Lower,1,IF(x>Upper,1,0))
rightColumn: Python: q1,q3=np.percentile(x,[25,75])
Python: iqr=q3-q1; lower=q1-1.5*iqr
Python: upper=q3+1.5*iqr
Python: flag=(x<lower)|(x>upper)
content.notes: Explain that the output is a flag column, not an automatic filter. Encourage learners to add a second column for ‘decision’ (retain/investigate/exclude) and a third for ‘reason’. Ask: If the flagged point is real, what process story could explain it (e.g., manual top-up, valve sticking, start-up)? Misconception: using the same data to set thresholds and then claiming ‘objective’ removal; remind them thresholds are rule-based but still require judgement. Also note that the IQR rule is more robust than z-scores when the data are skewed.

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI and t-test (both tools)

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI and t-test (both tools)
leftColumn: Excel CI: x̄±T.INV.2T(0.05,n-1)*s/SQRT(n)
Excel: =CONFIDENCE.T(0.05,s,n) gives margin
Excel t-test: =T.TEST(range1,range2,2,3) as needed
Always report CI, p-value, and practical threshold
rightColumn: Python CI: scipy.stats.t.interval(0.95,df=n-1,loc=xbar,scale=s/√n)
Python t-test: scipy.stats.ttest_1samp or ttest_ind
For unequal variances, use Welch (ttest_ind, equal_var=False)
Add effect: mean diff and % of spec/target
content.notes: Talk through when to use which test: one-sample compares to a target or historical baseline; two-sample compares before/after groups; paired compares matched items (e.g., same machine before and after adjustment). Emphasise assumptions: approximate normality of the mean (often okay via CLT if independence holds), and independence between observations; for two-sample tests consider equal variance vs Welch. Probe: If your data are collected every minute, what assumption is most at risk? (Independence.) Misconception: ‘p<0.05 proves improvement’; instead, it indicates evidence against H0, not proof, and does not quantify operational benefit. Encourage a stakeholder-friendly statement: ‘Estimated increase is 2.1 mL (95% CI 0.4 to 3.8); statistically significant at 5%, but still within the allowed tolerance.’

slides.title: Practice and reflection: apply to your own dataset

content.title: Practice and reflection: apply to your own dataset
content: Pick n≥20 measurements from one process and define unit/precision
List 3 data checks you will run before any statistics
Compute mean, median, SD, IQR, range; apply a rounding rule
Flag outliers using 1.5×IQR; decide retain/investigate/exclude
Construct a 95% CI for the mean; state assumptions explicitly
Write one sentence for a non-specialist on what the CI implies
content.notes: Encourage learners to pause and actually do the steps, even if with a small dataset. Provide prompting questions: What is the sampling method—random, convenience, consecutive? Are measurements from one shift only? What might that do to generalisability? Ask them to compare mean vs median: if they differ, what does that suggest about skew or contamination? Common misconception: writing assumptions as boilerplate; push them to link assumptions to their real sampling process. If learners do not have workplace data, suggest using a simulated dataset (e.g., 25 values around a target with one injected extreme) to practise the workflow.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports quality reporting tasks: summary + CI + test narrative
Show your cleaning log and justify any exclusions
Use sample SD (STDEV.S / ddof=1) for inference tasks
Do not interpret p-value as size or importance of effect
Avoid false precision: round consistently and keep units visible
State design limits: bias, autocorrelation, and small n
content.notes: Connect this lesson to typical module outputs: a short report that includes descriptive statistics, an interval estimate, and a simple comparison/target test with interpretation. Explain what markers usually look for: transparent workflow, correct function choices, consistent units, and cautious interpretation. Misconception: learners often hide data cleaning because it feels ‘messy’; in assessment and industry, transparency is a strength. Another common error: mixing population and sample formulas, or reporting a CI without stating n and assumptions. Probe: If your sample is not random, what can you still say responsibly? (Describe your sample, avoid strong population claims, and frame results as indicative.)

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Clean first: units, types, missingness, and documented decisions
Use mean/SD for symmetric data; median/IQR for robust summaries
Outlier rules flag candidates; process context decides action
95% CIs quantify mean uncertainty but rely on design assumptions
t-tests need p-value plus practical significance and limitations
content.notes: Close by reinforcing that the ‘analysis’ skill is connecting outputs to process meaning and data integrity. Invite learners to reflect: Which assumption is hardest to justify in your context—independence, randomness, or stable process conditions? Encourage them to keep a reusable template: a cleaning checklist, a summary stats block, and standard wording for CI and hypothesis test interpretation aimed at non-specialists. Remind them that the next step in quality analytics is often visualisation and control charts, where independence and time structure become even more important.

slides.title: Clean and summarise quality data in Excel or Python

content.title: Clean and summarise quality data in Excel or Python
content.content:
Program: Maths Certification
Module: MOD105 — Statistics for Quality Reporting in Excel or Python
Lesson 5 • Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners and set expectations: this lesson moves from “having data” to “having defensible evidence”. Emphasise that quality reporting depends on two things: (1) trustworthy data (cleaning + documentation) and (2) appropriate summary/inference (centre/spread, outliers, confidence intervals, and t-tests). Remind learners they may use either Excel or Python; the statistical reasoning is the same. Probing question: what is worse in a quality context—missing a real process change, or acting on a false alarm—and how could poor data cleaning trigger either outcome?

slides.title: Orientation: what you will be able to do

content.title: Orientation: what you will be able to do
content: Fix ≥3 issues in a raw dataset and write a 5+ point cleaning log
Compute mean, median, SD, IQR and flag outliers (IQR or z-score)
Build a 95% confidence interval and state key assumptions
Run a t-test for a process change and write a 5–7 sentence summary
Do 3 diligence checks to reduce risk of misleading conclusions
content.notes: Briefly connect each objective to a real reporting task. Cleaning log: not bureaucracy—your “audit trail” for why figures can be trusted. Centre/spread: mean and SD can be distorted by outliers; median and IQR are more robust. Confidence intervals: focus on interpretation (range of plausible means) and assumptions (independence, approximate normality, sample size). T-tests: statistical significance is not the same as practical significance; you will report the difference in means and its impact. Diligence checks: units, rounding, and formula/reference errors are common sources of incorrect decisions. Ask: when you read a dashboard, which of these steps do you assume has already been done?

slides.title: How to use this lesson (watch, practice, check)

content.title: How to use this lesson (watch, practice, check)
content: Watch/read: concepts + rules of thumb for quality datasets
Practice: replicate steps in Excel or Python on provided data
Check: compare against solutions and update your cleaning log
Reflect: can you justify each decision to a stakeholder?
content.notes: Encourage an iterative workflow: do not clean everything at once; clean, summarise, then revisit anomalies. In self-study, the key habit is to “pause and reproduce”: after each concept, do one concrete action (e.g., compute IQR, flag outliers). If learners have no provided dataset, they can use any ≥30-row quality dataset (dimensions, weights, defect counts, cycle times). Probing question: if someone challenged your results, what evidence would you show first—your outputs, or your cleaning log?

slides.title: Core idea: common data issues in quality datasets

content.title: Core idea: common data issues in quality datasets
content: Missing values: blanks, NA, placeholders like 999 or '—'
Impossible values: negatives, beyond physical or spec limits
Inconsistent units: mm vs cm, °C vs °F, mixed decimal separators
Duplicate records: repeated IDs or repeated timestamps
Text-as-number: '12.0' stored as text, leading/trailing spaces
content.notes: Explain that “data issue” means “analysis risk”. Missing values can bias estimates if missingness is not random. Impossible values often come from sensor faults or data entry errors—treat as a signal to investigate, not just to delete. Inconsistent units are especially dangerous because calculations still run but become meaningless. Duplicates can double-count defects or inflate sample size, giving false confidence (n appears larger). Text-as-number causes silent failures in Excel (AVERAGE ignores text) and in Python (object dtype breaks numeric ops). Probing questions: What is an impossible value in your domain? How would you distinguish a true extreme from a data error?

slides.title: Core idea: cleaning decisions and a simple log

content.title: Core idea: cleaning decisions and a simple log
content.notes: Use this slide to model what a cleaning log looks like: issue, explicit rule, action, and reason. Stress: the goal is consistency and transparency, not perfection. Discuss alternatives: for missing values you might drop rows (listwise deletion) if missingness is small and random; you might also impute mean for symmetric data, but median is safer with skew. For duplicates, sometimes you should aggregate (e.g., two readings in same minute) rather than delete—state the rule. In Excel, a log can be a separate sheet; in Python, a markdown cell or a text file in the repo. Probing question: which decision above could change the mean the most, and why?

slides.title: Core idea: workflow in Excel vs Python

content.title: Core idea: workflow in Excel vs Python
leftColumn: Excel: Filter, Remove Duplicates, Text to Columns
Excel: IFERROR, VALUE, TRIM/CLEAN for coercion
Excel: PivotTable for quick summaries
Excel: Data Analysis ToolPak for t-tests/CI

Python: .drop_duplicates(), .astype(), .str.strip()

Ask: which tool better suits your workplace constraints (access, audit, repeatability), and how will you compensate for its weaknesses?

slides.title: Core idea: centre, spread, and outlier rules

content.title: Core idea: centre, spread, and outlier rules
content: Mean: sensitive to outliers; best for symmetric data
Median: robust centre for skewed or contaminated data
SD: spread around mean; assumes a roughly stable scale
IQR: Q3−Q1; robust spread for skew/outliers
Outlier (IQR): <Q1−1.5×IQR or >Q3+1.5×IQR
Outlier (z): |x−mean|/SD > 3 (rule of thumb)
content.notes: Teach “choose statistics that match your data behaviour”. In quality data, a single sensor glitch can distort the mean and SD, so median/IQR are often more reliable for monitoring and reporting. Clarify that outlier flags are not automatic deletions: they are prompts for investigation (e.g., special cause vs data error). Mention that z-score rules assume something close to normality and can be misleading in skewed distributions. Practical Excel notes: QUARTILE.INC/EXC, AVERAGE, STDEV.S; in Python: series.mean(), median(), std(ddof=1), quantile([0.25,0.75]). Probing question: if you remove an outlier, how will you justify it in the log?

slides.title: Core idea: 95% confidence interval for a mean

content.title: Core idea: 95% confidence interval for a mean
content: Goal: plausible range for the true process mean
CI: x̄ ± t* × (s/√n), using df = n−1
Assumptions: independent data, stable process, approx normal x̄
Sampling limits: avoid tiny n; n≥30 is a common rule of thumb
Interpretation: 95% of such intervals would contain μ
content.notes: Emphasise interpretation: the CI is about the mean parameter, not about individual values. Address a common misconception: “There is a 95% probability that μ is in this interval” is not strictly correct in frequentist terms; the correct statement is long-run coverage under repeated sampling. Explain why the t critical value is used (unknown population SD). Discuss normality: for larger n, the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal (CLT), but strong autocorrelation or drifting processes violate independence and stability. Excel: CONFIDENCE.T or manual t value via T.INV.2T and compute margin; Python: use scipy.stats.t.interval with sample mean and SEM. Probing question: what process behaviour would make this CI untrustworthy even with n=50?

slides.title: Core idea: choosing a t-test for process change

content.title: Core idea: choosing a t-test for process change
content: Two-sample t-test: different units/parts in each group
Paired t-test: same unit measured before and after change
Report: p-value + difference in means (effect size)
Practical significance: compare effect to spec or tolerance
Assumptions: independence, approx normal residuals, stable variance
content.notes: Help learners choose the correct design: if the same machine/part is measured twice, pairing removes between-unit variability and increases power. For independent groups (before vs after but not matched), two-sample is appropriate; consider Welch’s t-test when variances differ. Clarify “effect size” here: the raw difference in means is often the most interpretable in quality contexts (e.g., −0.8 mm). You can mention standardised effect (Cohen’s d) as optional, but do not let it replace the practical comparison to spec limits. Misconception to address: a small p-value does not mean a large effect, and a large p-value does not prove no effect (may be underpowered). Probing question: if p=0.04 but the mean shift is 0.02 mm, what would you recommend?

For independent groups (before vs after but not matched), two-sample is appropriate; consider Welch’s t-test when variances differ. Clarify “effect size” here: the raw difference in means is often the most interpretable in quality contexts (e.g., −0.8 mm). You can mention standardised effect (Cohen’s d) as optional, but do not let it replace the practical comparison to spec limits. Misconception to address: a small p-value does not mean a large effect, and a large p-value does not prove no effect (may be underpowered). Probing question: if p=0.04 but the mean shift is 0.02 mm, what would you recommend?

content.title: Worked example: cleaning and logging (before/after)
content.notes: Walk through the idea that “before/after” should be traceable. Explain how you would detect each issue: min/max checks reveal negatives; frequency tables show 999 placeholders; unit checks compare typical ranges; duplicates detected by ID+timestamp keys; text numbers seen via Excel alignment or pandas dtypes. Stress documentation: each change must be recorded with a rule, not a one-off judgement. In Excel, show how to create helper columns (e.g., unit conversion) rather than overwriting raw data; keep a raw tab and a clean tab. In Python, keep the raw dataframe unchanged and create a cleaned copy. Probing question: which of these issues could inflate the SD the most, and how would that affect your outlier flags?

slides.title: Worked example: summary stats and outlier flag

content.title: Worked example: summary stats and outlier flag
content: Compute Q1, Q3, IQR; then lower/upper fences
Flag: outlier=TRUE if outside fences; do not delete by default
Compare mean vs median to assess skew/outlier influence
Excel: QUARTILE.*, IF(OR()), AVERAGE, STDEV.S
Python: quantile(), describe(), boolean mask for flags
content.notes: Demonstrate a concrete mini-workflow: after cleaning, compute quartiles and IQR; calculate fences; create an outlier column. Ask: if the mean is much larger than the median, what does that suggest about the distribution, and which summary would you prefer for a stakeholder report?

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI and a two-sample t-test

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI and a two-sample t-test
content: CI: compute x̄, s, n; then margin = t* × (s/√n)
State assumptions: independence, stable process, approx normal x̄
t-test: choose two-sample or paired based on data structure
Report: p-value, mean difference, and practical impact vs spec
Write a 5–7 sentence stakeholder-ready conclusion
content.notes:
Provide a narrated example structure learners can copy:
1) “We analysed n=… observations from before/after …”
2) “After cleaning (rules summarised in log), the mean was …”
3) “A 95% CI for the mean was … to …, assuming independence and stable process.”
4) “A two-sample/paired t-test gave p=…; the mean difference was ….”
5) “This shift is/is not practically meaningful because … relative to tolerance/spec.”
6) “Therefore we recommend … (monitoring, confirmatory sampling, investigate root cause).”
Explain why confidence intervals complement p-values: CI shows magnitude and uncertainty. Probing question: if the CI for the difference includes 0 but mostly lies in the practically important region, what is your next step?

content.title: Practice and reflection: quick prompts
content: List 3 issues you expect in your dataset before opening it
Create a 5+ bullet cleaning log while you work
Compute mean, median, SD, IQR; interpret mean vs median
Flag outliers using IQR rule; inspect the flagged rows
Write 2 sentences on assumptions you cannot fully verify
content.notes: Encourage learners to treat this as a rehearsal for assessment: capture your decisions as you go, not at the end. Suggest a minimum set of checks: count rows before/after cleaning; count missing values per column; check min/max after unit conversion. Reflection is about limits: you often cannot prove independence from a spreadsheet; you infer it from sampling design. Prompt learners to articulate uncertainty honestly (e.g., “measurements are time-ordered; mild autocorrelation may exist”). Probing question: which assumption (independence, stability, normality) is most likely to fail in your context, and how would that failure bias your conclusion?

content.title: Assessment connection: what this lesson supports
content: Supports: data cleaning log + summary stats + inference report
Common mistake: deleting outliers without a documented rule
Common mistake: mixing units or rounding too early
Common mistake: wrong t-test (paired vs independent)
Common mistake: p-value only, no effect or practical meaning

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Clean systematically and document rules in a short log
Use centre/spread that fit your data; flag outliers transparently
Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty; state assumptions clearly

slides.title: Clean and summarise quality data

content.title: Clean and summarise quality data
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD105 — Statistics for Quality Reporting in Excel or Python
Lesson 6: Clean and summarise quality data in Excel or Python
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners and position the lesson in the module: we are moving from describing data to making defensible statistical statements for quality reporting. Emphasise that the focus is analysis: choosing appropriate summaries, handling outliers transparently, and communicating uncertainty.

Set expectations: we will use the same statistical ideas whether you work in Excel or Python; what changes is the tool syntax. Ask learners: “When you report a mean, what assumptions are you implicitly making about the data?”

slides.speakerNotes:
Welcome learners and position the lesson in the module: we are moving from describing data to making defensible statistical statements for quality reporting. Emphasise that the focus is analysis: choosing appropriate summaries, handling outliers transparently, and communicating uncertainty.

Set expectations: we will use the same statistical ideas whether you work in Excel or Python; what changes is the tool syntax. Ask learners: “When you report a mean, what assumptions are you implicitly making about the data?”

slides.title: Orientation: what you will be able to do

content.title: Orientation: what you will be able to do
content: Choose mean/median and SD/IQR for n=20–50 quality data
Flag potential outliers (IQR or z-score) and justify action
Build a 95% CI for a mean (or mean difference) with assumptions
Run a one- or two-sample t-test and explain results plainly
Use an integrity checklist: units, rounding, assumptions, versioning
Workflow: watch → practise in tool → self-check your outputs
content.notes:
Frame the learning objectives as a workflow used in real quality reporting: (1) tidy and summarise, (2) check unusual values, (3) quantify uncertainty, (4) test a change, (5) document so someone else can reproduce.

Clarify that outlier “flagging” is not automatic deletion. A common misconception is “outliers must be removed”; instead, we treat them as prompts for investigation (measurement error? special cause? data entry?).

Probe: “If two analysts use the same file, could they get different results? What steps would prevent that?”

slides.title: From raw quality data to reporting numbers

content.title: From raw quality data to reporting numbers
content: Start with data integrity: correct types, units, and missing values
Summarise centre and spread to describe typical performance
Check distribution shape before choosing mean/SD vs median/IQR
Flag outliers to trigger investigation, not automatic removal
Add uncertainty: confidence intervals for process estimates
Support claims of change with a hypothesis test and context
content.notes:
Explain the end-to-end logic: quality data is collected to make decisions (is the process stable? did a change help?). Each step builds credibility.

Mini-example: if defect rates are recorded as percentages sometimes (5%) and sometimes as proportions (0.05), a mean is meaningless unless units are standardised first.

Misconception to challenge: “The summary statistics are the analysis.” In quality reporting, the summary is only the start; decision-making needs uncertainty and clear assumptions.

Ask: “Which of these steps would you prioritise if you only had 10 minutes before a meeting?”

slides.title: Choosing centre and spread

content.title: Choosing centre and spread
content.notes:
Teach the decision rule: don’t choose mean/median by habit—choose based on what the data look like and what decision you must support.

Explain what “robust” means: median and IQR change less when one value is extreme. Give a quick numeric illustration: values 10, 10, 10, 10, 50 → mean=18, median=10; which better reflects ‘typical’?

Highlight that SD is tied to the mean and assumes a meaningful average; IQR is percentile-based and works well for skew.

Probe: “If a stakeholder asks ‘what’s normal performance?’, which summary would you pick and what would you show alongside it (e.g., a histogram/boxplot)?”

slides.title: Outlier rules: flagging vs deciding

content.title: Outlier rules: flagging vs deciding
content: IQR rule: flag if x < Q1−1.5×IQR or x > Q3+1.5×IQR
z-score rule: flag if |(x−mean)/SD| > 3 (common threshold)
Use IQR when skewed; z-scores assume SD is meaningful
Always check units, data entry, and measurement system first
Decide: investigate, retain with note, or exclude with justification
Report what rule you used and the impact on results
content.notes:
Make the distinction explicit: rules create a shortlist for review; they do not prove a value is “wrong”.

Explain why IQR is preferred under skew: quartiles are less pulled by extreme values. Explain why z-scores can mislead when the SD is inflated by the same outliers you are trying to detect.

Give a practical investigation checklist: check raw record, instrument calibration, re-measure if possible, confirm the unit, confirm time period/batch.

Common misconception: removing outliers to ‘improve’ a mean. This is cherry-picking unless justified (e.g., confirmed transcription error).

Probing questions: “If you remove one point, does your conclusion change? If yes, how will you communicate that sensitivity?”

slides.title: 95% confidence intervals for a process mean

content.title: 95% confidence intervals for a process mean
content: 95% CI estimates a plausible range for the true process mean
Formula: mean ± t* × (SD/√n) for small samples
Assume independence; data roughly normal or n large enough
CI width shrinks with larger n and lower variability
State sampling limits: timeframe, shift, line, material, operator
Do not interpret as: “95% of values fall in this range”
content.notes:
Explain interpretation carefully: in repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean. It is not a probability statement about this specific interval unless using a Bayesian framing.

Discuss assumptions in quality contexts: independence can fail when readings are sequential (autocorrelation), or when multiple readings come from the same batch (clustering). Normality is often reasonable for means with moderate n, but strongly skewed data may need transformation or non-parametric alternatives (beyond today’s scope).

Mini-example narrative: “We sampled 25 parts from Line A, Day shift, last week; our CI only supports that context.”

Probe: “What would make you distrust the CI even if the calculation is correct?”

slides.title: t-tests for process change: choose the right one

content.title: t-tests for process change: choose the right one
leftColumn: One-sample t-test
Compare mean to target μ0
Example: mean fill vs 500 ml
Needs SD and n from one sample
rightColumn: Two-sample t-test
Compare means of two conditions
Example: before vs after change
Use Welch if variances differ
content.notes:
Position t-tests as tools for evidence about a change, not a replacement for process understanding. Clarify the null hypothesis (no difference) and alternative (difference or directional).

Explain practical vs statistical significance: with low variability, tiny differences can be “significant” but irrelevant; with high variability, meaningful changes may not reach p<0.05 with small n.

Common misconception: p-value is the probability the null is true. Correct it: p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours if the null were true.

Probe: “If your p-value is 0.06, what would you do next in a quality investigation?”

slides.title: Worked example: summary stats in Excel vs Python

content.title: Worked example: summary stats in Excel vs Python
content.notes:
Walk through a realistic dataset context: e.g., 30 measurements of cycle time (seconds) for one machine and one operator. Emphasise ‘sample SD’ (ddof=1) because we are estimating population variability.

Point out Excel pitfalls: using STDEV.P by mistake; mixing empty cells and zeros; non-numeric entries stored as text. In Python, warn about NaN handling and the need to confirm units before computing.

Probing questions: “How would you check quickly whether Excel is treating a column as numbers or text?” and “What does ddof=1 change conceptually?”

slides.title: Worked example: IQR outlier flags and action

content.title: Worked example: IQR outlier flags and action
content: Step 1: Compute Q1, Q3, and IQR from the sample
Step 2: Lower bound = Q1−1.5×IQR; upper = Q3+1.5×IQR
Step 3: Flag points outside bounds; count how many
Step 4: Investigate each flag: entry error, unit, special cause
Step 5: Recompute summaries with/without flagged points
Step 6: Write a 2–3 sentence justification for reporting choice
content.notes:
Provide a concrete micro-scenario: 25 thickness readings; two are unusually high. Demonstrate how to compute bounds and identify the specific values.

Model the 2–3 sentence justification:
- “Two points were flagged by the IQR rule. Review of the log shows a gauge calibration issue on that hour; we exclude those two readings from the process mean report but retain them in an appendix as evidence of a special cause.”
Or
- “Flagged points correspond to a deliberate material change. We retain them and report median/IQR rather than mean/SD.”

Common misconception: using the rule to ‘clean’ until the data look normal. Emphasise transparency and traceability.

Probe: “If your conclusion changes depending on excluding an outlier, how would you communicate that to a non-specialist?”

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI and t-test reporting

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI and t-test reporting
content: Given n=25, mean=10.2, SD=0.8 (units stated)
Interpret: plausible range for true mean in this sampling context
One-sample t-test vs target 10.0: report t, df, p-value
Decision: reject/fail to reject; add practical significance
Plain-language line: “Difference is small and not meaningful”
content.notes:
Do the calculation in narrative: SE=0.8/5=0.16. With df=24, t*≈2.06, margin≈0.33, CI≈[9.87, 10.53]. Emphasise rounding appropriately and keeping units.

For the t-test: t=(10.2−10.0)/0.16=1.25; p-value likely >0.2 (two-sided). Use this to illustrate ‘fail to reject’ and that it does not prove equality—only that evidence is insufficient.

Show how to communicate to stakeholders: avoid jargon; connect to tolerance/specification if appropriate (but distinguish CI for mean from conformance rates).

Probe: “If the CI includes the target, does that automatically mean the process meets requirements?” (Answer: not necessarily; specs apply to individual units, not the mean alone.)

content.title: Reproducibility and integrity checklist
content.notes:
Explain why this slide matters for quality reporting: reproducibility is part of integrity. If someone cannot reproduce your figures, your conclusions are fragile.

Expand each row with a brief example: mixing mm and cm creates a bimodal distribution that looks like a process shift; zeros for missing values drag down the mean and inflate SD.

Misconception: rounding improves accuracy. Clarify: rounding improves presentation, but premature rounding changes results.

Probe: “If you had to hand your analysis to another site tomorrow, what would they need to rerun it exactly?”

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD105 assignment: quality report with tool outputs
Include screenshots/cell refs or code cells for reproducibility
Common mistake: reporting mean/SD on skewed data without comment
Common mistake: deleting outliers without investigation evidence
Common mistake: CI/test without assumptions and sampling limits

content.title: MOD105 Lesson 7: CIs and simple hypothesis tests
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD105 — Statistics for Quality Reporting | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome. In this lesson we focus on two closely linked tools for before/after process reporting: (1) confidence intervals (CIs) to quantify uncertainty around an estimated change, and (2) simple hypothesis tests to evaluate whether the observed change is unlikely under a “no change” assumption. The emphasis is not only computation, but interpretation for quality and business decisions. Keep the ‘before/after’ framing in mind: we are usually trying to decide whether a process change improved a key metric and whether the improvement is meaningful in practice.

slides.title: Orientation: what you will do

content.title: Orientation: what you will do
content: Compute and interpret a 95% CI for a mean or proportion
Run a simple test: two-sample t or diff in proportions
Report test statistic, p-value, and plain-language conclusion
List 4+ assumptions and how violations threaten validity
Compare statistical vs practical significance using effect size
Create a 1–3 visual mini-dashboard with narrative commentary
content.notes: How to use this lesson in self-study: first, read each concept slide and pause to paraphrase it in your own words. Next, follow the worked example steps and replicate them in either Excel or Python (choose one tool and stick with it initially). Then do the practice prompts using your own small dataset or a fabricated one. Finally, check yourself: can you state what the CI does NOT mean (common error), and can you connect the p-value to the business question rather than to ‘truth’? Probing questions: What decision will be made from this analysis? What threshold defines ‘good enough’? What data limitations could flip your conclusion?

slides.title: Confidence intervals: what they are

content.title: Confidence intervals: what they are
content: A CI is a plausible range for a population parameter
For change: CI can be for (After − Before)
A 95% CI comes from a method with 95% long-run coverage
Narrower CIs mean more precision, often from larger n
CIs support decision-making better than a single point estimate
content.notes: Build intuition: a CI is about the unknown population value, not about variability of individual observations. For before/after, the parameter of interest is often the mean difference (e.g., average cycle time reduction) or difference in proportions (e.g., defect rate reduction). Stress the repeated-sampling meaning: if you repeated the same sampling process many times, about 95% of the computed intervals would contain the true parameter. Misconception to address explicitly: it is NOT correct to say ‘there is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this specific interval’ in the strict frequentist interpretation. Practical teaching tip: ask learners to point to the business-relevant question—‘How big could the improvement plausibly be?’—and show how the CI answers that.

slides.title: CI interpretation: does vs does not imply

content.title: CI interpretation: does vs does not imply
leftColumn: Does: range of plausible values for the true change
Does: quantifies uncertainty from sampling variation
Does: show direction and magnitude, not just yes/no
Does: allow comparison to a decision threshold
rightColumn: Does not: guarantee the true value is in this one interval
Does not: prove the process change caused the difference
Does not: fix bias from poor sampling or confounding
Does not: describe spread of individual observations
content.notes: Use a short mini-example: ‘Our 95% CI for mean time reduction is −1.8 to −0.4 minutes.’ This suggests the true average reduction is likely between 0.4 and 1.8 minutes (negative sign indicates reduction, depending on your definition). Then ask: does this prove the new process caused the improvement? No—other changes (staffing, seasonality, measurement changes) could explain it. Another misconception: learners often treat the CI endpoints as ‘worst case’ guarantees; emphasise that endpoints still come from assumptions and sampling. Probing questions: What could shift the entire interval (bias)? What would happen to the CI if you doubled sample size?

slides.title: Hypothesis tests: the basic workflow

content.title: Hypothesis tests: the basic workflow
content: State H0: no change; H1: change (or improvement)
Choose test: means (t-test) or proportions (z/χ²)
Check assumptions and sampling plan before testing
Compute test statistic and p-value from the sample
Conclude with context: evidence strength, not certainty
Report effect size alongside p-value
content.notes: Frame the logic: the p-value is the probability of data as or more extreme than observed, assuming H0 is true. It is not the probability H0 is true. Reinforce: we choose a test based on data type and study design—two independent samples (before and after from different items) versus paired data (same units measured twice). If learners have paired before/after for the same item, the paired t-test is more appropriate; if not, two-sample t-test. For proportions, use a two-proportion z-test (or χ² test). Probing question: What is the ‘unit’ being sampled (orders, parts, customers), and are the before/after samples comparable?

slides.title: Test selection guide for before/after data

content.title: Test selection guide for before/after data
content.notes: Explain the design column carefully: ‘independent groups’ means the before and after observations are not naturally matched (e.g., different batches). ‘Same units twice’ means a paired structure (e.g., same machine measured pre/post calibration). Note that Excel’s Data Analysis Toolpak supports t-tests (including paired), but not a dedicated two-proportion z-test as a single menu item; learners can compute it using formulas or use Python. In Python, statsmodels and scipy can handle these tests. The last row is marked with an asterisk to signal it is beyond “simple” in this lesson; mention it as awareness only. Probing question: If you mistakenly use an independent t-test on paired data, what happens to your uncertainty (typically larger than necessary) and power?

slides.title: Assumptions and sampling limits to document

content.title: Assumptions and sampling limits to document
content: Independence: observations not influencing each other
Representativeness: sample reflects the process of interest
Normality or large-n: CLT supports mean/proportion methods
Stable measurement: same definitions, tools, and thresholds
No time confounding: seasonality or mix shifts not driving change
Constant process except intervention: avoid multiple changes
content.notes: For each assumption, give a concrete risk. Independence: if one operator produces many consecutive items, defects may cluster—standard errors become too small, giving false confidence. Representativeness: if you only sample day shift after the change but all shifts before, you confound shift with intervention. Normality/large-n: t-tests are fairly robust, but extreme skew with small n can distort results; for proportions, ensure expected counts are not tiny. Stable measurement: if the defect definition changed, apparent improvement might be reclassification. Time confounding: promotions, demand surges, new suppliers, or staffing changes can mimic an intervention. Probing questions: What changed besides the process? How were samples chosen? Would an external auditor agree the ‘before’ and ‘after’ are comparable?

slides.title: Practical vs statistical significance

content.title: Practical vs statistical significance
content: Statistical: p-value below α suggests evidence vs H0
Practical: effect size exceeds a decision threshold
Effect size examples: mean diff, % change, risk diff
Use tolerances: e.g., must save ≥1.0 min per unit
A tiny effect can be significant with large n
A large effect may be non-significant with small n
content.notes: Make the distinction explicit: statistical significance is about detectability given noise and sample size; practical significance is about whether the change matters. Provide a numeric mini-example: saving 0.1 seconds per unit may yield p<0.001 with millions of units, but may be operationally irrelevant. Conversely, saving 2 minutes with n=8 might yield p=0.08—potentially important but uncertain; the CI may still include meaningful improvements. Encourage learners to pre-specify a decision threshold (engineering tolerance, SLA, cost savings target) before looking at results. Probing question: If your CI includes both ‘no improvement’ and ‘meets threshold’, what action would you recommend (collect more data, pilot longer, or accept risk)?

slides.title: Worked example setup: before/after cycle time

content.title: Worked example setup: before/after cycle time
content: Metric: cycle time (minutes) for a transaction
Before sample: n1=30, mean=12.4, sd=2.1
After sample: n2=28, mean=11.1, sd=1.9
Question: did the change reduce mean cycle time?
Threshold: practical target is ≥1.0 min reduction
content.notes: Introduce a realistic scenario: a process change (template, automation, training) aims to reduce cycle time. Clarify that these are independent samples (not paired), so we use a two-sample t-test (typically Welch’s, which does not assume equal variances). State the parameter: μ_after − μ_before; reduction implies a negative value. Ask learners to predict direction before calculating. Also highlight that we will report both uncertainty (CI) and evidence (p-value) and then compare to the practical target of 1.0 minute. Probing question: If the after period had a different transaction mix (more complex cases), how might that bias the observed mean?

slides.title: Worked example: CI, test, and interpretation

content.title: Worked example: CI, test, and interpretation
content: Effect: mean diff = 11.1 − 12.4 = −1.3 min
Compute 95% CI for (After − Before) using Welch method
Run one-sided or two-sided t-test to match the question
Report: t, df, p-value, and CI in one results paragraph
Decision: compare CI and −1.0 min practical threshold
content.notes:
Walkthrough guidance (tool-agnostic):
1) Compute the effect size first: −1.3 minutes.
2) Compute the standard error for Welch’s two-sample t: SE = sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2). Then compute df using the Welch–Satterthwaite approximation.
3) 95% CI: (mean diff) ± t* × SE.
4) Hypothesis test: if the business question is specifically ‘reduce’, a one-sided test is defensible only if pre-specified; otherwise use two-sided.
Excel guidance: use Data Analysis Toolpak ‘t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Unequal Variances’ for a two-sided p-value; adjust carefully if you need one-sided (common mistake: halving p without checking sign).
Python guidance: scipy.stats.ttest_ind with equal_var=False gives t and two-sided p; compute CI separately or via statsmodels.
Interpretation model paragraph (learners can copy): ‘Average cycle time decreased by 1.3 minutes. The 95% CI for the true mean change is [L, U] minutes (after minus before). The t-test gives t(df)=..., p=.... This provides (or does not provide) evidence of a reduction. Compared with the −1.0 minute target, the interval (does/does not) support achieving the threshold.’
Misconceptions: (a) claiming causality; (b) concluding “no difference” from p>0.05; instead discuss uncertainty and whether CI includes meaningful effects.

slides.title: Communicating results: mini-dashboard essentials

content.title: Communicating results: mini-dashboard essentials
content: Visual 1: before vs after mean with 95% CI error bars
Visual 2: dot/box plot to show spread and outliers
Optional: effect vs threshold line (practical target)
Label units, time window, and sample sizes on the chart
Add 3–5 sentences: change, uncertainty, recommendation
content.notes: Emphasise stakeholder readability: one graphic should answer ‘what changed and by how much’, another should show variability and whether the data are messy or skewed. For error bars, specify they are 95% CIs for the mean (not min/max). For spread plots, discourage truncated y-axes that exaggerate differences unless clearly justified; sensible axes maintain trust. Provide a model narrative (adaptable): ‘After the intervention, mean cycle time fell from 12.4 to 11.1 minutes (n=30 vs n=28). The estimated mean change is −1.3 minutes; the 95% CI indicates the true reduction is plausibly between … and …. This supports/does not support meeting the ≥1.0 minute target. Recommendation: proceed/extend pilot/collect more data, noting [top assumption risk].’ Probing question: If an executive only reads the chart title and one sentence, what should they learn?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Pick a metric: mean (time) or proportion (defect rate)
Compute effect size and a 95% CI for the change
Run the appropriate test and capture t/z and p-value
Write 4 assumptions/limits and a risk for each
Decide practical significance vs your threshold
Draft a 4-sentence stakeholder summary
content.notes:
Encourage learners to use a small dataset they can access (workplace, open data, or simulated). Provide a suggested structure:
- Dataset: 20–50 observations per period is enough for practice.
- If using a proportion: count defects and total units in each period.
Self-check questions:
1) Did you define the parameter correctly (after − before, or before − after)?
2) Does your CI direction match your narrative (sign errors are common)?
3) Did you match the test to the design (paired vs independent)?
4) Are you overclaiming causality?
5) Does your recommendation change if you consider confounding (e.g., different product mix)?
Extension prompt (optional): redo the analysis with a longer time window and compare how CI width changes.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
leftColumn: Supports: before/after quality report assignment
Expected: CI + test + effect size + assumptions
Expected: chart(s) with narrative recommendation
Expected: tool output clearly referenced (Excel/Python)
rightColumn: Mistake: interpreting p-value as P(H0 true)
Mistake: claiming ‘95% probability’ for one CI
Mistake: ignoring design (paired vs independent)
Mistake: skipping practical threshold and effect size
content.notes: Position this lesson as a template for the typical reporting task: quantify change, quantify uncertainty, test against a no-change baseline, and communicate decision relevance. If learners are submitting screenshots/outputs, remind them to label what the software produced (t, df, p) and to state the hypotheses in words. Address frequent marking issues: missing units, missing time windows, inconsistent direction (sometimes they compute before − after but write after − before), and over-reliance on p-values. Probing question: If a stakeholder challenges your conclusion, what evidence would you show first—effect size and CI, or p-value—and why?

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: CIs quantify plausible change sizes; interpret with care
Tests quantify evidence vs ‘no change’, not practical value
Assumptions and sampling choices can dominate conclusions
Effect size + threshold links statistics to decisions
Clear visuals and narrative make results actionable
content.notes: Close by reinforcing the hierarchy for decision-making: start with the business question and threshold, then effect size and CI, then the hypothesis test as supporting evidence. Remind learners that documentation of assumptions is not a formality; it is how you communicate risk and credibility. Final reflective questions: What would you do differently in data collection to reduce uncertainty? What is the smallest change that matters in your context, and have you made that explicit?

slides.title: Stakeholder-friendly charts and dashboards

content.title: Stakeholder-friendly charts and dashboards
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD105 Statistics for Quality Reporting
Lesson 8 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome to Lesson 8 in MOD105. In this session you will move from “doing the statistics” to “reporting the statistics” in a way that non-specialists can trust and act on. The emphasis is on creating outputs (charts and a one-page dashboard) that are accurate, clearly labelled, and reproducible in either Excel or Python. Keep the end-user in mind throughout: a stakeholder wants to know what changed, when it changed, whether it is unusual, and what constraints or caveats apply.

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome to Lesson 8 in MOD105. In this session you will move from “doing the statistics” to “reporting the statistics” in a way that non-specialists can trust and act on. The emphasis is on creating outputs (charts and a one-page dashboard) that are accurate, clearly labelled, and reproducible in either Excel or Python. Keep the end-user in mind throughout: a stakeholder wants to know what changed, when it changed, whether it is unusual, and what constraints or caveats apply.

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Use: watch/skim, practise in Excel or Python, then self-check
Clean data; log at least 3 assumptions
Compute centre/spread; add an outlier rule and flag
Build 2+ visuals: trend plus turning points/constraints
Assemble a one-page dashboard with a 100–150 word narrative
Self-evaluate with a checklist and revise 2+ elements
content.notes:
How to study: first, read through the concepts to understand what “stakeholder-friendly” means in practice. Next, replicate the worked steps on a dataset (provided in your course area). Finally, use the checklist to critique your own dashboard as if you were the stakeholder.

As you work, continually ask: “Could someone reproduce my numbers?” and “Could someone misinterpret this chart?” A common misconception is that a visually attractive dashboard is a good dashboard; in quality reporting, credibility comes from correct units, traceable calculations, and careful framing of uncertainty and constraints.

slides.title: What stakeholders need from charts

content.title: What stakeholders need from charts
content: A clear question: what decision does this support?
Trust: correct units, definitions, and consistent time periods
Signal vs noise: what changed and how big is it?
Context: targets, capacity limits, or policy constraints
Action: where to look next, not just “interesting patterns”
content.notes:
Stakeholders typically do not want every statistic; they want an answer to a decision-oriented question (e.g., “Is the defect rate improving, and are there any concerning spikes?”). You build trust by being explicit about units and definitions: for example, “minutes per unit” versus “hours per batch” cannot be compared without conversion.

Probe: If you removed all annotations, would the chart still be interpretable? Another misconception is assuming stakeholders share your statistical vocabulary. Replace jargon with plain language (e.g., “typical value” instead of “central tendency”) while keeping technical correctness in the background calculations.

slides.title: Data cleaning for quality reporting

content.title: Data cleaning for quality reporting
leftColumn: Missing values: delete, impute, or label as missing
Units: convert to one standard unit
Types: date as date, numbers as numeric, categories as text
Duplicates: decide rule for removal or aggregation
rightColumn: Log assumptions: what you changed and why
Keep raw data: never overwrite original source
Check ranges: impossible values and typos
Document scope: time window and exclusions
content.notes:
This slide frames cleaning as a reporting responsibility, not just a technical task. For missing values, the choice depends on meaning: if a sensor failed, imputing could hide reliability issues; if a value is genuinely “not applicable”, it should remain missing.

Mini-example: If a column mixes “ms” and “s”, convert everything to seconds and note the conversion factor. If dates import as text in Excel, convert using DATEVALUE (or Power Query). In Python/pandas, use pd.to_datetime and errors='coerce' to detect bad entries.

Probing questions: Which cleaning choice could most change the story of your dashboard? What evidence supports your assumption? Common mistake: silently dropping rows reduces sample size and can bias the trend.

slides.title: A simple data-cleaning log (example)

content.title: A simple data-cleaning log (example)
content.notes:
Use a log like this to make your work auditable. The log is not busywork: it tells a reviewer what you did, what you assumed, and what you checked.

In Excel, keep the log on a separate tab with a timestamp and your initials. In Python, keep a markdown cell or a small dataframe printed as part of the notebook output.

Misconception to address: “I can remember what I did.” In practice, you will not, and neither will a stakeholder or marker. The evidence/check column is where you demonstrate you did not guess—e.g., you cross-referenced downtime logs, equipment specifications, or range checks.

slides.title: Centre, spread, and reproducible calculations

content.title: Centre, spread, and reproducible calculations
content: Centre: mean (average) and median (typical value)
Spread: standard deviation and/or IQR
Use consistent rounding rules; state precision
Excel: AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, QUARTILE.INC
Python: df.mean(), median(), std(), quantile()
Report n (sample size) after cleaning
content.notes:
Mean and median answer different questions: the mean is sensitive to extreme values, while the median is robust when there are outliers or skew. Spread measures tell you variability; without spread, a single centre measure can be misleading.

Reproducibility means someone can copy your method and get the same numbers. That requires: (1) stating whether you use sample or population standard deviation (in Excel, STDEV.S vs STDEV.P), (2) stating which quartile definition you used (Excel QUARTILE.INC vs EXC), and (3) reporting n after any exclusions.

Probing question: If your mean and median differ a lot, what does that suggest about the distribution or outliers?

slides.title: Outlier rules and how to flag them

content.title: Outlier rules and how to flag them
content: IQR rule: outlier if < Q1 − 1.5×IQR or > Q3 + 1.5×IQR
Z-score: outlier if |z| > threshold (often 3)
Choose rule to match data shape and stakeholder risk
Flag, do not delete, unless you have a justified reason
Explain: outlier may be error or real special-cause variation
content.notes:
An outlier rule is a consistent way to highlight unusual points. The IQR rule is robust and works well for skewed data; z-scores assume something closer to a symmetric distribution and can be misleading with heavy tails.

In Excel, compute IQR as Q3−Q1, then compute lower/upper bounds and use IF to label “Outlier” vs “In range”. In Python, compute q1=df[col].quantile(0.25), q3=..., then bounds and a boolean flag.

Key teaching point: an outlier is not automatically “wrong”. In quality reporting, it can indicate a process change, a constraint breach, or a special cause worth investigating. Ask: “If I remove it, what story am I hiding?”

slides.title: Choosing stakeholder-friendly chart types

content.title: Choosing stakeholder-friendly chart types
leftColumn: Trend over time: line chart with clear time axis
Comparison: bar chart with ordered categories
Distribution: histogram or box plot for spread/outliers
Relationship: scatter plot with labelled units
rightColumn: Avoid: 3D charts and dual axes without justification
Label: units, timeframe, and definitions in subtitle
Annotate: turning points, constraints, target lines
Use colour sparingly; ensure readability in greyscale
content.notes:
Your goal is not to use many chart types, but to match the chart to the question. For turning points, annotate the event (e.g., “New supplier introduced”) rather than forcing the viewer to guess.

Misconception: dual-axis charts are “efficient”. They often confuse scale and imply relationships that are not real. If you must use two axes, justify it and consider an alternative such as two aligned small multiples.

Probing questions: What is the single message of each chart? If a stakeholder has 20 seconds, what do they take away? Would the chart still work printed in black and white?

slides.title: Worked example: clean and compute metrics

content.title: Worked example: clean and compute metrics
content: Step 1: profile columns (types, ranges, missingness)
Step 2: standardise units and parse dates
Step 3: compute mean, median, SD, IQR and n
Step 4: compute outlier bounds and add a flag column
Step 5: record 3+ assumptions in the cleaning log
content.notes:
Walkthrough guidance (apply to your provided dataset):
1) Profile: in Excel, use filters, COUNTBLANK, MIN/MAX; in Python, use df.info(), describe(), isna().mean().
2) Standardise: decide the canonical unit (e.g., seconds). Convert all values to that unit and retain the original column if you need traceability.
3) Metrics: compute n after exclusions. Report mean/median with the same rounding (e.g., 2 decimal places) and state the rounding choice.
4) Outliers: implement the IQR rule and create a new column OutlierFlag = TRUE/FALSE.
5) Assumptions: examples include how you treated missing values, why you chose a time window, and how you handled duplicates.

Common pitfall: mixing cleaned and uncleaned columns in calculations. Ensure all reported metrics use the same cleaned variable.
