slides.title: Worked example: build two visuals with meaning

content.title: Worked example: build two visuals with meaning
content: Visual 1: trend line with target and turning-point annotation
Use consistent time bins (daily/weekly/monthly) and state choice
Visual 2: box plot or histogram showing spread and outliers
Title states metric, unit, and timeframe
Caption notes any constraints (capacity, spec limit, downtime)
content.notes:
Trend visual: choose a time bin that matches decision cadence. For operational quality, weekly is often readable; daily can be too noisy, monthly can hide short disruptions. Add a target line (e.g., “Target defect rate ≤ 2%”) and annotate known changes.

Distribution visual: a box plot quickly shows median, IQR, and outliers; a histogram shows shape and potential multimodality. Whichever you choose, label units and ensure axis scales do not exaggerate differences.

Mini-example annotation: “Week 6: maintenance shutdown (reduced throughput)” or “Week 9: new test protocol”.

Misconception: “Turning points must be statistically significant.” In dashboards, you can flag turning points descriptively, as long as you do not overclaim causality.

slides.title: Worked example: one-page dashboard narrative

content.title: Worked example: one-page dashboard narrative
content.content: Write a 100–150 word summary that states the trend, notes any outliers, and explains constraints or assumptions in plain language. Avoid causal claims unless you have evidence.
content.notes:
Use a structure that stakeholders can scan:
- Sentence 1: what metric, unit, and timeframe.
- Sentences 2–3: the main trend and any turning point.
- Sentence 4: what the outlier flag shows and how many points were flagged.
- Sentence 5: constraints/assumptions (e.g., missing data periods, unit conversions).
- Final sentence: what action or investigation is recommended.

Example (about 120 words; adapt to your data):
“Across Jan–Jun 2026, the median cycle time was 42.5 s (n=1,248), with a gradual improvement from March onwards. A step-change is visible in week 10, aligning with the introduction of the revised inspection workflow. Variation remained moderate (IQR 8.1 s), although 17 readings were flagged as outliers using the 1.5×IQR rule; most occurred during two short periods of unplanned downtime. Values were standardised to seconds from mixed ‘ms’ and ‘s’ entries, and missing readings were retained as missing rather than imputed. Further review should focus on downtime root causes and whether the week 10 change can be replicated across shifts.”

Common mistake: writing vague commentary (“performance improved”) without magnitude, timeframe, or units.

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: List 3 cleaning assumptions and argue why each is reasonable
Recompute metrics using a different rule (IQR vs z-score)
Does the story change? If yes, explain why
Identify 2 turning points; write annotations for each
Rewrite chart titles so a non-specialist understands in 5 seconds
Peer/self review: what could be misread at a glance?
content.notes:
Use these prompts as a self-study checkpoint. The aim is to stress-test your reporting choices.

Guidance: When comparing IQR and z-score flags, do not pick the method that “looks nicer”. Pick the method that fits your data and the decision risk. If a stakeholder would act on an outlier alert (e.g., stop production), you must avoid both excessive false alarms and missed signals.

Probing questions: Which assumption is the most fragile? What additional data would strengthen it? If your chart were shown without you present, what is the most likely misunderstanding?

slides.title: Quality-report checklist for dashboard revision

content.title: Quality-report checklist for dashboard revision
content.notes:
This checklist is your mechanism for improvement. Use it twice: first on your initial dashboard, then after revisions to confirm you genuinely improved it.

For “reproducible”, an easy win is to remove manual edits that cannot be repeated (e.g., typing over values). In Excel, prefer Power Query steps and formula columns; in Python, prefer functions or clearly labelled notebook cells.

Revision requirement: identify at least two elements to change (e.g., fix a missing unit, change a chart type, adjust binning, rewrite narrative to remove implied causality). A misconception is that revision is cosmetic; here, revision is about reducing the risk of misinterpretation.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: dashboard/report assignment in MOD105
Marking focus: correctness, clarity, reproducibility, insight
Common mistake: no cleaning log or assumptions not stated
Common mistake: charts lack units/timeframe or have vague titles
Common mistake: outliers deleted without justification
Common mistake: narrative exceeds 150 words or is too technical
content.notes:
Connect your work directly to assessment criteria: you are being assessed not only on calculations but on your ability to communicate them responsibly.

Common errors to pre-empt:
- Presenting mean/SD without noting skew or outliers; consider including median/IQR as well.
- Using default Excel chart titles like “Chart 1”. Replace with a sentence-style title that includes the metric, unit, and period.
- Omitting sample size (n). After cleaning, n often changes and affects credibility.

Probing question: If a marker or stakeholder tried to recreate your results, what would they need that you have not provided?

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Clean data transparently; keep a short, auditable cleaning log
Report centre and spread, plus n, with reproducible methods
Flag outliers using a stated rule; interpret before acting
Use chart types that match the question and label everything
A good dashboard pairs metrics, visuals, and a concise narrative
content.notes:
The central idea is credibility: stakeholders trust reports that are transparent, consistent, and easy to interpret. Your dashboard should tell a coherent story supported by well-chosen visuals and defensible statistics.

Before you finish, do a final “stakeholder read”: can someone unfamiliar with the dataset answer (1) what happened, (2) when it changed, (3) how unusual it is, and (4) what constraints apply? If not, revise titles, annotations, and narrative until those answers are obvious.

slides.title: Confidence intervals and simple hypothesis tests

content.title: Confidence intervals and simple hypothesis tests
content.content:
Maths Certification • MOD105 Statistics for Quality Reporting
Lesson 9 • Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners and position the lesson within MOD105. Emphasise that this session connects statistical outputs (CI and p-values) to quality reporting decisions. Set expectations: you will compute intervals/tests, state assumptions and limits, and communicate uncertainty to stakeholders. Prompt: “When you see a p-value in a report, what decision do you think it is meant to support?” Highlight that the lesson is tool-agnostic: Excel or Python are both acceptable routes.

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome learners and position the lesson within MOD105. Emphasise that this session connects statistical outputs (CI and p-values) to quality reporting decisions. Set expectations: you will compute intervals/tests, state assumptions and limits, and communicate uncertainty to stakeholders. Prompt: “When you see a p-value in a report, what decision do you think it is meant to support?” Highlight that the lesson is tool-agnostic: Excel or Python are both acceptable routes.

slides.title: Orientation: learning objectives

content.title: Orientation: learning objectives
content: Compute and report a 95% CI for a mean/proportion change
Run a suitable simple test and interpret the p-value plainly
Write an assumptions + sampling limits statement (4+ items)
Separate statistical from practical significance via a threshold
Create a chart/dashboard with CI/error bars and brief narrative
content.notes: Walk through each objective as a deliverable you could place into a quality report. Stress that marks (and workplace credibility) often come from communication and transparency, not just calculation. Ask: “Which objective feels most unfamiliar: the maths, the software, or the writing?” Address a common misconception: a confidence interval is not a statement about individual observations; it is about an unknown parameter (e.g., mean change).

slides.title: How to use this lesson (self-study)

content.title: How to use this lesson (self-study)
content: Read concept slides for definitions and decision rules
Follow worked examples in Excel or Python step-by-step
Pause to answer practice prompts before viewing notes
Draft your assumptions + limits text as you work
Finish with a chart and 2–4 sentences of narrative
content.notes: Guide learners to actively produce artefacts: a CI statement, a test decision statement, and an assumptions paragraph. Encourage keeping a ‘reporting template’ they can reuse. Probing question: “Could someone else reproduce your result from your notes?” Clarify that rounding, units, and plain language are assessed skills. Misconception to address: copying software output verbatim is rarely sufficient; learners must translate it into stakeholder-ready statements.

slides.title: Core idea: what a 95% confidence interval means

content.title: Core idea: what a 95% confidence interval means
content: CI estimates a plausible range for a population parameter
95% refers to long-run coverage over repeated samples
Wider CI = more uncertainty (often small n or high spread)
Report: estimate, CI bounds, units, and sample size
Avoid: “95% of data lie in the interval”
content.notes: Explain with a repeated-sampling story: if we repeatedly sampled and built CIs, about 95% would contain the true mean change. Emphasise that once computed, the interval is fixed; the parameter is unknown. Mini-example: “Mean change = 1.8 seconds, 95% CI [0.6, 3.0] seconds” signals improvement with uncertainty. Probing questions: “What would make the CI narrower without changing the process?” and “Why do we include units?”

Probing questions: “What would make the CI narrower without changing the process?” and “Why do we include units?”

slides.title: Selecting a simple test for process change

content.title: Selecting a simple test for process change
content.notes: Teach selection by matching the data structure first (paired vs independent), then outcome type (continuous vs proportion). Clarify that “pre/post” often implies pairing by the same unit (machine, operator, customer). Misconception: learners frequently run a two-sample test on paired data, inflating variability and losing power. Probing question: “What does ‘paired’ mean in your context—same item measured twice, or just two time periods?” If learners are in Python, note that packages differ (scipy.stats ttest_rel vs ttest_ind; statsmodels for proportions).

slides.title: Hypothesis tests: p-values and decisions

content.title: Hypothesis tests: p-values and decisions
content: H0: no change (mean/proportion difference = 0)
H1: change exists (two-sided) or improvement (one-sided)
p-value: data compatibility with H0, not P(H0 true)
If p < 0.05, reject H0 (evidence of change)
Always state direction and magnitude, not p alone
content.notes: Explain that tests formalise “is this change likely due to sampling noise?” but they do not measure importance. Stress writing decisions in plain language: “We have evidence of a reduction in mean cycle time” rather than “p=0.03.” Clarify two-sided vs one-sided: one-sided must be justified before looking at data (e.g., only improvements are plausible and relevant). Misconception: p=0.049 and p=0.051 are not qualitatively different; avoid ‘cliff-edge’ thinking. Probing question: “What would you conclude if p is small but the estimated change is tiny?”

slides.title: Statistical vs practical significance

content.title: Statistical vs practical significance
leftColumn: Statistical: CI excludes 0 or p < alpha
Driven by n, variability, and effect size
Answers: “Is change detectable?”
Can flag trivial changes as significant
rightColumn: Practical: exceeds a meaningful threshold
Threshold set by cost, safety, service, or specs
Answers: “Is change worth acting on?”
May matter even if not statistically significant
content.notes: Define a practical threshold (minimum meaningful improvement, MMI) as an operational requirement, not a statistical one. Example: “At least 2 seconds reduction per job is required to meet capacity.” Then link to the CI: if the entire CI is above 2 seconds improvement, you have strong evidence of practical benefit; if it straddles 2, the decision is uncertain. Probing questions: “Who sets the threshold?” and “What is the opportunity cost of acting on a false improvement?” Misconception: ‘not significant’ does not mean ‘no effect’; it may mean ‘insufficient evidence given the sample’.

slides.title: Assumptions + sampling limits (minimum 4 items)

content.title: Assumptions + sampling limits (minimum 4 items)
content: Sampling: how units were chosen; any convenience sampling
Independence: repeated measures, batching, time trends
Distribution: outliers/skew; t-test robustness with n
Measurement system: instrument drift, rounding, missingness
Scope: only applies to similar conditions (shift, product mix)
content.notes: Coach learners to write this as a transparent paragraph in a report, not as an afterthought. Provide a sentence stem: “Results assume …; limitations include …; therefore conclusions are most applicable to …”. Explain that independence is often violated in process data due to autocorrelation (time-ordered data), and that pairing can mitigate some variability but not time trends. Probing question: “What is the most plausible bias that could make the improvement look larger than it is?” Common misconception: assuming normality of raw values rather than normality of differences (for paired t-tests).

Provide a sentence stem: “Results assume …; limitations include …; therefore conclusions are most applicable to …”. slides.title: Worked example setup: pre/post paired data

content.title: Worked example setup: pre/post paired data
content: Scenario: 12 operators measured before and after training
Metric: mean call handling time (seconds) per operator
Compute differences: after − before (negative is faster)
Goal: estimate mean change with a 95% CI
Then test H0: mean change = 0 (two-sided)
content.notes: Introduce realistic context: training intervention; same operators measured twice implies a paired design. Explain why we use differences: it removes between-operator variability and focuses on within-operator change. Clarify sign conventions; choose one and keep it consistent in reporting. Probing question: “If you swapped to before − after, how would your interpretation change?” Emphasise that the CI/test should be applied to the difference vector, not to before and after separately.

Explain why we use differences: it removes between-operator variability and focuses on within-operator change. Clarify sign conventions; choose one and keep it consistent in reporting. slides.title: Worked example: compute CI and test in Excel/Python

content.title: Worked example: compute CI and test in Excel/Python
content: 1) Create Diff = After − Before for each paired unit
2) Mean diff and SD(diff); note n and units
3) 95% CI: mean ± t* × SD/√n (df = n−1)
4) Excel: T.INV.2T(0.05,n-1) and formulas
5) Python: scipy.stats.t.interval or statsmodels
6) Paired t-test: Excel t-Test: Paired or ttest_rel
content.notes: Walk the calculation conceptually: standard error is SD(diff)/sqrt(n), t* comes from the t distribution with df=n−1. In Excel, show the pattern: mean = AVERAGE(diff_range); sd = STDEV.S(diff_range); se = sd/SQRT(n); tcrit = T.INV.2T(0.05,n-1); CI = mean ± tcrit*se. For the test, explain that a paired t-test is equivalent to a one-sample t-test on differences against 0. Python note: scipy.stats.ttest_rel(before, after) returns statistic and p-value; ensure order aligns with your sign convention. Misconception: using population SD (STDEV.P) instead of sample SD (STDEV.S). Probing question: “What does the CI tell you that the p-value does not?”

slides.title: Practice & reflection prompts

content.title: Practice & reflection prompts
content: Choose the correct test for: paired, independent, vs target
Write a 1–2 line CI statement with units and rounding
Write a plain-language p-value decision for a stakeholder
List 4+ assumptions/limits specific to your data source
Set a practical threshold and conclude operational impact
Sketch a chart: mean change with 95% CI error bars
content.notes: Encourage learners to pause and actually draft text, not just think about it. Provide a reporting template prompt: “Estimated mean change was X units (95% CI [L, U], n=__). This suggests …”. For rounding, suggest 1–2 decimal places guided by measurement resolution (e.g., seconds to 0.1s if system records tenths). content.notes: Teach a simple framing script: “We are monitoring [metric] in [unit] for [scope/time], to decide [action].” Explain that charts fail when they answer a different question from the stakeholder’s. content.notes: Clarify that units matter: mean/median have the same unit as the metric; SD and IQR also share the metric’s unit. Ask: “If I add one extreme value, which statistics move most?” Misconception to address: reporting mean alone is enough; stakeholders need spread to understand reliability and risk.

slides.title: Outlier flags: rules and interpretation

content.title: Outlier flags: rules and interpretation
content: IQR rule: outlier if x < Q1−1.5×IQR or x > Q3+1.5×IQR
z-score rule: outlier if |(x−mean)/SD| exceeds threshold (e.g., 3)
State the rule on the chart or in a footnote
Outlier ≠ error; verify before removal
Count and report outliers; show impact on mean/SD if relevant
content.notes: Explain why we flag outliers: to prompt investigation, not to “clean until tidy”. Provide a mini-example: a single long delay could be a special cause (machine failure) or a data entry error; both need different actions. Discuss when to prefer IQR: skewed distributions and non-normal data. Discuss z-scores: most meaningful when data are approximately normal. Probing questions: “What is the operational story behind an extreme point?” and “Would a stakeholder prefer to see extremes hidden or highlighted?”

content.title: Choose the right visual for the question
leftColumn: Distribution: histogram
Distribution: box plot
Compare groups: side-by-side box plots
Show outliers: box plot + points
rightColumn: Over time: run chart (line)
Detect shifts: median line + annotations
Spot seasonality: weekly/monthly aggregation
Compare periods: small multiples (same scales)

Ask: “If you only had one chart, would you prioritise distribution or time—and why?”

content: Use clear titles: metric + unit + time window
Label axes; avoid abbreviations unknown to stakeholders
Keep scales honest; avoid truncated y-axis for rate/level plots
Use colour sparingly; ensure accessible contrast
Annotate one insight: trend, shift, turning point, constraint

content.notes: Explain that stakeholders judge trust quickly: unclear labels or odd scales raise suspicion even if results are correct. slides.title: Worked example: stats and outlier flag

content.title: Worked example: stats and outlier flag
content: 1) Check data types, missing values, and units
2) Compute mean, median, SD and/or IQR (state choice)
3) Compute Q1 and Q3; derive IQR and fences
4) Add Outlier_Flag (TRUE/FALSE) using the rule
5) Summarise: n, outlier count, min/max (with units)
content.notes:
Walk through implementation in both tools.
Excel path: use AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S; QUARTILE.INC for Q1/Q3; IQR=Q3−Q1; Lower=Q1−1.5*IQR; Upper=Q3+1.5*IQR; Outlier_Flag=OR(x<Lower, x>Upper). Show learners how to lock cell references with $ when copying formulas.
Python path (pandas): df['x'].mean(), median(), std(ddof=1); quantile(0.25/0.75); compute fences; df['Outlier_Flag']= (x<lower) | (x>upper).
Explain common errors: mixing population vs sample SD, quartile method differences, forgetting units, and silently treating text numbers as strings. Ask: “If you changed the quartile method, would your outlier count change—and would that matter for decisions?”

slides.title: What a confidence interval tells you

content.title: What a confidence interval tells you
content: Parameter: population mean change, μΔ
Estimate: sample mean change, x̄Δ
95% CI: plausible range for μΔ from this sample
CI width reflects variability and sample size
CI is not a guarantee for each individual case
Always report units and the direction of change
content.notes:
Clarify ‘parameter vs statistic’: μΔ is the unknown true mean change across the process (e.g., all future jobs), while x̄Δ is what we observed in our sample.

Key interpretation: a 95% CI is a range of values for μΔ that are consistent with the data and assumptions. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the parameter is in the interval (that is a Bayesian interpretation).

Common misconception: learners often say “95% of observations lie in the CI”. Correct this: the CI is about the mean change, not individual changes.

Mini-example: If CI is (−5.2 s, −2.4 s), every plausible mean change indicates improvement (negative change if defined as After−Before).

Prompt: What would it mean for decision-making if your CI crosses 0?

slides.title: 95% CI for a mean change (paired data)

content.title: 95% CI for a mean change (paired data)
content.content: For before/after on the same units, compute changes Δ = After − Before. Then CI = x̄Δ ± t* × (sΔ/√n), with df = n−1. Interpret in one sentence with the parameter, units, and practical meaning.
content.notes:
Speak through the workflow: (1) verify the data are paired (same item/person measured twice), (2) create a change column Δ, (3) summarise x̄Δ, sΔ, n, (4) use the t critical value for df=n−1.

Explain why t (not z): population standard deviation is unknown and estimated from the sample.

Interpretation template (encourage learners to reuse): “We estimate the true mean change in [units] is between [lower] and [upper] at 95% confidence; this suggests the process change [improves/worsens] performance by around [x̄Δ] on average.”

Misconception: treating before and after as independent samples. Stress that pairing removes between-unit variation and usually increases power.

Prompt: What is your Δ sign convention, and will a stakeholder interpret ‘negative’ as good or bad without explanation?

slides.title: Selecting the right simple t-test

content.title: Selecting the right simple t-test
content.notes:
Explain that test choice is determined by how the data were collected, not by which result you prefer.

Paired t-test: same units measured twice; analysis is on Δ. One-sample t-test: compare a single sample mean to a benchmark (e.g., target 50 seconds). Two-sample t-test: compare means from two independent groups.

Highlight the Welch version: in practice, equal variances are often not credible, so Welch is a safer default for independent groups.

Probing question: In your work context, what would make observations ‘independent’? What would break independence (e.g., repeated measures, batching, shared operator)?

slides.speakerNotes:
Explain that test choice is determined by how the data were collected, not by which result you prefer.

Paired t-test: same units measured twice; analysis is on Δ. One-sample t-test: compare a single sample mean to a benchmark (e.g., target 50 seconds). Two-sample t-test: compare means from two independent groups.

Highlight the Welch version: in practice, equal variances are often not credible, so Welch is a safer default for independent groups.

Probing question: In your work context, what would make observations ‘independent’? What would break independence (e.g., repeated measures, batching, shared operator)?

slides.title: Assumptions and sampling limits checklist

content.title: Assumptions and sampling limits checklist
content.notes:
Walk learners through using this as a pre-flight checklist before reporting any inference.

Independence: the most important and most overlooked. If you sample consecutive items from a drifting process, observations may be correlated.

Normality: for paired t-tests, we need Δ to be approximately normal, not necessarily before and after separately. With moderate n, the t procedure is fairly robust unless the distribution is very skewed.

Outliers: do not delete automatically. First ask: is it a data error, a special cause, or a legitimate extreme? Your decision should be documented.

Measurement stability: if the definition of ‘cycle time’ changed, your ‘improvement’ could be a reporting artefact.

Prompt: Which assumption is hardest to defend in your organisation, and what evidence could you collect to strengthen it?

slides.title: Statistical vs practical significance

content.title: Statistical vs practical significance
leftColumn: Statistical: is μΔ different from 0?
Tools: p-value, CI excludes 0
Sensitive to sample size
Answers: “Is change detectable?”
rightColumn: Practical: is change big enough to matter?
Tools: effect size, % change, threshold
Sensitive to business context
Answers: “Is change worth acting on?”
content.notes:
Explain that these are different questions and both must be addressed for quality decisions.

Give contrasting examples: (1) Very large n gives p<0.001 for a 0.1 second improvement—statistically real but operationally irrelevant. (2) Small n gives p=0.08 for a 5 second improvement—potentially valuable but inconclusive.

Teach uncertainty language: “evidence suggests…” when CI is entirely on one side of the threshold; “results are inconclusive…” when CI spans meaningful and non-meaningful values.

Probing question: What is your organisation’s ‘minimum worthwhile improvement’ for this metric, and who sets it?

slides.title: Worked example data (cycle time, seconds)

content.title: Worked example data (cycle time, seconds)
content.notes:
Set up the scenario: five comparable jobs were timed before and after a small process change (e.g., a new checklist). The same unit/job type is measured twice, so this is paired data.

Explain the sign convention explicitly: Δ = After − Before, so negative values indicate reduced cycle time (an improvement). Encourage learners to pick one convention and label it clearly.

Probing question: If Unit 3 had ‘After’ recorded for a different product variant, would it still be a valid pair? What would you do?

slides.title: Worked example results: CI and paired t-test

content.title: Worked example results: CI and paired t-test
content: n = 5 pairs; x̄Δ = −3.8 s; sΔ = 1.10 s
Paired t-test H0: μΔ = 0 vs H1: μΔ ≠ 0
Interpretation: mean cycle time decreased by ~2.4–5.2 s
Check threshold: if ≥2 s needed, evidence supports rollout
content.notes:
Talk through how each number is produced and what it means.

Excel pathway (paired):
- Create Δ column.
- Mean: AVERAGE(Δrange); SD: STDEV.S(Δrange); n: COUNT(Δrange).
- t critical: T.INV.2T(0.05, n-1).
- CI: mean ± tcrit*SD/SQRT(n).
- p-value: T.TEST(AfterRange, BeforeRange, 2, 1) where type=1 indicates paired.

Python pathway (typical):
- Compute delta = after - before.
- CI: use scipy.stats.t.interval with df=n-1 and scale=sd/sqrt(n).
- Test: scipy.stats.ttest_rel(after, before).

Stress reporting discipline: always include df, the alternative, and whether p is one- or two-sided.

Common misconceptions: rounding too early (can change CI endpoints), and interpreting p as “probability H0 is true”.

Probing question: With only n=5, what makes you trust or distrust these results? What extra data would you collect next?

slides.title: Communicating change with a mini-dashboard

content.title: Communicating change with a mini-dashboard
content: Use a paired dot plot or slope chart (Before → After)
Add mean change with 95% CI as an error bar
Label metric, units, timeframe, and n clearly
State decision vs threshold and uncertainty in text
Note key limitation(s) and what you will do next
Keep narrative ≤120 words; avoid statistical jargon
content.notes:
Explain why paired visuals work: they show both the overall shift and the individual variability (some units may worsen even if the mean improves).

CI visualisation options:
- Error bar around mean change (Δ) on a separate panel.
- Or show mean Before and mean After with CI for the mean (be careful: that is not the CI for change unless paired properly).

Teach narrative structure (suggested order): (1) what changed, (2) how much it changed with CI, (3) whether it meets threshold, (4) limitations, (5) next step.

Example limitation statements: small sample; convenience sampling; short time window; possible learning effect; measurement system not audited.

Probing question: Which one chart would you choose for a time-poor manager, and why?

slides.title: Review checklist for integrity and collaboration

content.title: Review checklist for integrity and collaboration
content.notes:
Position this as professional practice: statistical reporting is part of ethical decision-making. The goal is not to ‘win’ an argument but to support sound action.

How to use the checklist:
1) Self-check your draft once, then step away for 10 minutes.
2) Re-check as if you were an external reviewer.
3) If peer-checking, ask for two specific suggestions and record what you changed.

Require at least two implemented improvements (per the objective). Examples: clarify sign convention; add business threshold; add limitation about sampling; correct test selection; add CI visual.

Probing question: If a peer challenges your method choice, what evidence would you show to justify it?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Write a 1–2 sentence CI interpretation with parameter and units
Choose: one-sample, two-sample, or paired t-test (justify)
List 2 assumptions most at risk in your data source
Set a practical threshold and decide: act, pilot, or re-sample
Draft ≤120-word dashboard narrative with limitations
Apply the checklist and implement 2 improvements
content.notes:
Encourage learners to use their own dataset if available; otherwise, reuse the worked example and practise the writing.

Provide quick decision wording templates:
- Strong evidence + practical: “Evidence suggests the change reduces mean cycle time by …; likely exceeds the 2 s threshold; recommend rollout with monitoring.”
- Statistical but not practical: “Change is detectable but smaller than the threshold; do not prioritise rollout.”
- Inconclusive: “Results are inconclusive because the CI spans meaningful and non-meaningful values; collect more data.”

Common misconception: concluding ‘no effect’ when p>0.05. Stress that p>0.05 often means “insufficient evidence”, not “no change”.

Probing question: What additional sampling would most reduce uncertainty—more pairs, better measurement, or broader conditions?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: process-change report with CI, test, and dashboard
Common error: wrong test (paired vs independent)
Common error: missing units, parameter, or sign convention
Common error: only p-value, no effect size or threshold
Common error: claims beyond the sample scope
Common error: no limitations or assumption evidence
content.notes:
Explain how markers typically evaluate work: correctness of method, transparency of assumptions, clarity of communication, and decision relevance.

Elaborate on “claims beyond scope”: if you sampled one shift, do not generalise to all shifts without caveats. If the process was unstable, acknowledge that inference is fragile.

Remind learners to include reproducibility: Excel formulas shown or Python code cell outputs captured; state software used and versions if requested.

Probing question: Which of these mistakes have you seen in real reports, and how did it affect decisions?

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Use Δ = After−Before and a paired t-method for before/after
A 95% CI estimates μΔ with units and practical meaning
Pick tests based on design; document assumptions explicitly
Combine p-value with effect size and business threshold
Communicate with a clear chart, CI visual, and short narrative
content.notes:
Reinforce integration: computation, decision-making, and communication belong together.

Invite learners to revisit their own outputs: Does your dashboard tell a coherent story in under two minutes? Could a stakeholder repeat the conclusion correctly after reading it once?

Exit questions:
- If your CI crosses 0, what would you recommend next?
- If your CI excludes 0 but misses the threshold, what action is justified?
- What is the single most important label that prevents misinterpretation in your chart?

slides.title: Stakeholder-friendly charts and dashboards

content.title: Stakeholder-friendly charts and dashboards
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD105 Statistics for Quality Reporting
Lesson 12 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners to Lesson 12. Frame the purpose: you are moving from “doing statistics” to “reporting statistics for decisions”. Emphasise that stakeholders often care less about the full analysis and more about: (1) whether the data are trustworthy, (2) what has changed, (3) whether performance is within constraints, and (4) what to do next. Remind them this lesson is at Bloom’s ‘create’: you will produce a chart set and a one-page dashboard, not just calculations.

slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study
content: Outcome: clean data with missing, units, and outlier flags
Outcome: compute mean, median, SD, and IQR with units
Outcome: build distribution + over-time charts with annotations
Outcome: create a one-page dashboard + 80–150 word narrative
How to use: watch/read → practise → self-check → refine
content.notes: Set expectations: you should work alongside the lesson in Excel or Python. Encourage a ‘build, then polish’ workflow—get a correct first version quickly, then improve clarity. Prompt: which tool will you use today—Excel or Python? Either is acceptable, but you must produce the same deliverables: a cleaned dataset with an outlier flag, summary statistics for at least two variables, two chart types, and a one-page dashboard with a short narrative. Misconception to address: learners sometimes think presentation is ‘optional’. In quality reporting, communication quality is part of analytical quality.

slides.title: What stakeholders need vs what analysts like

content.title: What stakeholders need vs what analysts like
leftColumn: So what? What changed, and does it matter?
Is it in spec? What risks or constraints exist?
What should we do next, and by when?
Can I trust it? Clear units, scope, and caveats
rightColumn: All variables and all plots on one page
Unlabelled axes, no units, no definitions
P-values with no effect size or context
Raw output tables pasted without interpretation
content.notes: Explain that stakeholder-friendly reporting is not about ‘dumbing down’; it is about reducing cognitive load and foregrounding decisions. Give a mini-example: a production manager may only need to know that defect rate rose after a process change and that it exceeds an internal limit—then what action to take. Probing question: if your dashboard were printed and taken into a meeting without you, would it still be interpretable? Common misconception: more charts equals more insight. Often, more charts equals more confusion.

slides.title: Data cleaning for quality reporting

content.title: Data cleaning for quality reporting
content: Define units and valid ranges before editing data
Fix data types: numeric fields stored as text
Handle missing: remove, impute, or mark as unknown
Validate units: convert to a single agreed unit
Add an outlier flag using a stated rule (IQR or z-score)
content.notes: Walk through a practical cleaning order: (1) confirm variable definitions and units; (2) correct data types; (3) handle missing values; (4) validate ranges and units; (5) compute outlier flags. Excel tips: use Data Validation, VALUE(), TRIM(), and ISNUMBER(); avoid manual edits that cannot be audited. Python tips: use pandas dtypes, to_numeric(errors='coerce'), and explicit unit conversion. Stress ‘zero unresolved data-type errors’: if a column is ‘object’ due to stray strings, your stats and charts may silently break. Probing question: what is your rule for missing—are you allowed to impute, or must you report missingness separately?

slides.title: Missing values: options and trade-offs

content.title: Missing values: options and trade-offs
content.notes: Explain that the ‘best’ approach depends on why values are missing. Use a mini-scenario: temperature readings missing during a machine stop—this is not random and may indicate a process issue. Encourage learners to keep an audit trail: create a ‘CleanValue’ column rather than overwriting the original, and document decisions in a notes cell or README. Misconception: imputation is always more advanced; sometimes, dropping or flagging is more honest. Probing question: if you impute, how will you stop the stakeholder thinking the imputed values are real measurements?

slides.title: Outlier flags you can justify to non-specialists

content.title: Outlier flags you can justify to non-specialists
content: IQR rule: flag < Q1−1.5×IQR or > Q3+1.5×IQR
Z-score rule: flag |(x−mean)/SD| > 3 (approx.)
Always state the rule on the dashboard
Outlier flag ≠ delete: it is a prompt to investigate
Check units first, or you will flag false outliers
content.notes: Explain IQR in plain language: it looks at the middle 50% of values and flags points far beyond typical spread. It is robust to skewness and is often better for quality variables that are not normal. Explain z-scores as ‘how many standard deviations away’, but caution that SD is sensitive to outliers and skew. Excel implementation: compute Q1 and Q3 via QUARTILE.INC, IQR=Q3−Q1, then IF(value<lower OR value>upper,1,0). Python implementation: df['flag']=((x<lower)|(x>upper)).astype(int). Probing question: if a flagged outlier is a genuine extreme, what operational story might explain it (shift change, raw material batch, sensor issue)?

slides.title: Measures of centre and spread with units

content.title: Measures of centre and spread with units
content: Mean: average level; sensitive to extreme values
Median: typical value; robust under skewness
SD: overall spread around mean; unit matches the data
IQR: spread of middle 50%; robust and interpretable
Always report units and time window (scope) used
content.notes: Teach the ‘pairing’ idea: mean goes with SD, median goes with IQR. For skewed distributions (common in quality defects, lead times), median and IQR often communicate better. Give a quick example: if thickness is measured in mm, then SD and IQR are also in mm—this helps stakeholders interpret magnitude. Probing question: which measure would you trust if one reading is clearly a sensor glitch? Common misconception: SD is ‘more scientific’ than IQR; in fact, appropriateness depends on distribution shape and data quality.

slides.title: Charts that answer stakeholder questions

content.title: Charts that answer stakeholder questions
content: Distribution: histogram or box plot to show spread and outliers
Over-time: line chart with dates in true time order
Titles should state metric, unit, and period
Axes must have labels and units; avoid ambiguous abbreviations
Annotate one trend and one constraint or turning point
content.notes: Position charts as answers to questions. Distribution asks: ‘What is typical, and how variable is it?’ Trend asks: ‘Is it improving or deteriorating, and when did it change?’ Stress correct time handling: dates must be real date types (Excel serial dates; pandas datetime), not text. Demonstrate annotation ideas: add a vertical line for a process change date; add a horizontal line for a spec limit; call out a step change after maintenance. Misconception: stakeholders can infer context without labels—most cannot, especially when viewing quickly or on mobile.

slides.title: Worked example: cleaning and outlier flag

content.title: Worked example: cleaning and outlier flag
content.notes: Narrate a realistic dataset: e.g., ‘Viscosity (Pa·s)’ and ‘Fill weight (g)’ with some blanks, one value in the wrong unit, and a few extremes. Emphasise ‘keep the evidence’: retain original columns and add cleaned/standardised columns rather than overwriting. Demonstrate a QA habit: after cleaning, sort by the cleaned variable and inspect top/bottom 5; check that any unit conversion makes sense (e.g., 0.5 kg should become 500 g, not 5 g). Probing question: if your OutlierFlag count is unexpectedly high, what are the first two checks you run?

slides.title: Worked example: build the chart set

content.title: Worked example: build the chart set
content: Distribution: box plot of Fill weight (g) with outlier points
Trend: weekly mean Fill weight (g) line chart
Add spec lines: target and lower limit
Annotate a turning point: after calibration date
Add a note on missingness and outlier rule used
content.notes: Explain how to aggregate for the trend chart: daily or weekly means/medians, but be consistent and state it. In Excel, use a PivotTable with date grouping and a PivotChart; in Python, use resample('W') with mean/median. Show how to add spec lines: include constant series (target, LSL/USL) or add horizontal lines. Model an annotation: “Mean increases by ~2 g after 10 Jan calibration; variability reduces.” Warn against dual axes unless essential; they often confuse non-specialists. Probing question: would a median trend be more stable if your distribution is skewed?

slides.title: Practice and reflection: build your dashboard

content.title: Practice and reflection: build your dashboard
leftColumn: Choose 2 variables and confirm units
Create OutlierFlag using IQR or z-score
Compute mean, median, SD, IQR for both variables
Draft 80–150 word narrative + recommendation
rightColumn: Add one distribution chart + one trend chart
Show outlier count and missing count on the page
Label axes, titles, scope (dates) and assumptions
Self-check: can a non-specialist explain it back?
content.notes: Give learners a concrete build order: (1) clean and flag, (2) summary stats block, (3) charts, (4) narrative, (5) final polish. Encourage them to keep the dashboard to one page: prioritise what drives action. Provide a narrative template they can adapt: “Across [period], [metric] averaged [value unit] (median [value]). Variability was [SD/IQR]. After [event/date], the trend [increased/decreased] and [constraint/spec] was [met/breached] on [n] occasions. There were [n] flagged outliers (IQR rule) and [n] missing values. Recommended next step: [investigate/adjust] focusing on [cause], and review again by [date].” Probing question: what single decision should your dashboard enable?

slides.title: Choose the right distribution

content.title: Choose the right distribution
leftColumn: Count of successes in fixed n trials
Measured value around a mean
Time between events or to failure
Need fast approximation for large n
rightColumn: Binomial: X ~ Bin(n, p)
Normal: X ~ N(μ, σ²)
Exponential: T ~ Exp(λ)
Normal approx to binomial if np, n(1-p) large
content.notes: Walk through the decision logic with workplace cues. For binomial, stress: fixed number of opportunities (n), two outcomes per trial, constant probability p, and independence. For normal, stress: continuous measurement (e.g., demand, delivery time), symmetric variability, and using μ and σ in the same units as the variable. For exponential, stress: modelling waiting time with a constant rate λ and the memoryless property. Probing question: 'What exactly is being counted or measured, and what is the natural unit?' Misconception: treating 'number of breakdowns in a week' as exponential; that is typically Poisson for counts, while exponential is for the time between breakdowns.

slides.title: Binomial model: what it assumes

content.title: Binomial model: what it assumes
content: Random variable: X = number of successes in n trials
Parameters: n (trials), p (success probability per trial)
Assumptions: independent trials, constant p, two outcomes
PMF: P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k)
Mean np; variance np(1-p)
Normal approx: use when np and n(1-p) are both ≥ 10
content.notes: Expand on what a 'trial' means in practice: inspecting items, contacting customers, processing invoices. Clarify 'success' can mean a defect, a late delivery, or a sale—define it clearly to avoid sign errors later. When discussing the normal approximation, explain it is a speed/tractability tool and requires continuity correction if used carefully (e.g., P(X≤k) ≈ P(Y≤k+0.5)). Probing question: 'If p changes over time (learning curve, different suppliers), would binomial still be defensible?' Common misconception: using binomial when n is not fixed (e.g., number of arrivals today).

slides.title: Normal model: standardisation and intervals

content.title: Normal model: standardisation and intervals
content: Random variable: X is continuous (e.g., demand, lead time)
Parameters: μ (mean), σ (standard deviation)
Standardise: Z=(X-μ)/σ so Z ~ N(0,1)
Tail: P(X>a)=1-Φ((a-μ)/σ)
Interval: P(a≤X≤b)=Φ(zb)-Φ(za)
Check plausibility: negatives and strong skew may break fit
content.notes: Explain why standardisation works: it rescales any normal variable to the standard normal so we can use a single CDF table or calculator. Emphasise units: μ and σ must match X (e.g., units/day, minutes, £). Discuss model sense-checking: if the normal model implies a meaningful chance of negative demand or negative processing time, consider truncation or a different distribution. Probing question: 'Would you model waiting time with a normal distribution? What would go wrong?' Common misconception: confusing variance and standard deviation, or using σ² where σ is required in Z.

slides.title: Exponential model: waiting times and rate

content.title: Exponential model: waiting times and rate
content: Random variable: T = time to next event or failure
Parameter: rate λ (events per unit time)
Mean waiting time is 1/λ (same time unit as T)
Tail: P(T>t)=e^(-λt)
CDF: P(T≤t)=1-e^(-λt)
Memoryless: P(T>s+t|T>s)=P(T>t)
content.notes: Connect λ to how people speak at work: 'on average one breakdown every 2 hours' means mean=2 hours, so λ=1/2 per hour. Stress that exponential implies a constant hazard rate; if ageing or wear-out exists, exponential may be inappropriate (Weibull may be better later in the module). Probing question: 'If the machine is more likely to fail as it heats up, is memoryless reasonable?' Common misconception: mixing up λ and mean; learners often set λ=mean rather than λ=1/mean.

content.title: Monte Carlo outputs to risk metrics

slides.title: Worked example: binomial defects in a batch

content.title: Worked example: binomial defects in a batch
content: Scenario: 20 items, defect chance p=0.03 per item
Let X = number of defects; X ~ Bin(n=20, p=0.03)
Interpretation: chance of ≥2 defects in the batch
content.notes: Work through the logic: 'at least two' is easier via the complement of 0 or 1. Encourage calculator use but insist learners write the distribution statement and parameter definitions first. If time, approximate numerically: 0.97^20 ≈ 0.543; P(X=1) ≈ 20*0.03*0.97^19 ≈ 0.336; so P(X≥2) ≈ 1-0.879 ≈ 0.121 (about 12%). Ask: 'What assumption is most questionable here—independence, constant p, or two outcomes?' Misconception: forgetting the combination term C(20,1)=20 or misreading p as 3% per batch rather than per item.

slides.title: Worked example: normal demand interval probability

content.title: Worked example: normal demand interval probability
content: Scenario: daily demand D ~ N(100, 15²) units
Find P(80 ≤ D ≤ 120)
Probability = Φ(1.33) - Φ(-1.33)
Interpretation: chance demand stays within 80–120 units
content.notes: Explain symmetry: Φ(-a)=1-Φ(a), so the interval can be computed as 2Φ(1.33)-1. Using common values, Φ(1.33)≈0.908, giving probability ≈0.816. Discuss what the interval means operationally (e.g., staffing or inventory levels). Probing questions: 'If you hold 120 units of stock, how often do you stock out?' and 'What if demand is bounded below by zero—does the normal still make sense here?' Misconception: swapping σ and σ², or writing N(100,15) instead of N(100,15²) and then misusing the value.

slides.title: Worked example: exponential downtime tail risk

content.title: Worked example: exponential downtime tail risk
content: Scenario: downtime to repair T is exponential, mean 2 hours
Rate λ = 1/2 = 0.5 per hour; T ~ Exp(0.5)
Check units: t in hours, λ in per hour
Interpretation: risk of long outage vs quick fix
content.notes: Compute approximate values: P(T>3)=e^-1.5≈0.223; P(T≤1)=1-e^-0.5≈0.393. Emphasise that these are not symmetrical and reflect the skew of waiting times. Probing question: 'If the repair team is called out, does the chance of finishing in the next hour depend on how long it has already taken?' Use this to explain memorylessness in plain language. Misconception: treating λ as hours rather than per hour, leading to exponent errors.

slides.title: Worked example: interpret a simulation summary

content.title: Worked example: interpret a simulation summary
content: Output: P50=10.2 weeks, P90=12.5 weeks (project duration)
Baseline plan: 11.0 weeks
Estimate P(duration > 11.0) from CDF or counts in runs
If 320 of 1000 runs exceed 11.0, probability = 0.32
Contingency to reach 90% confidence: 12.5-11.0=1.5 weeks
Interpretation: overrun risk and a risk-based schedule
content.notes: Explain how the probability is estimated empirically: number of runs beyond the threshold divided by total runs. Clarify that P50 is the median (half the outcomes are below), while P90 is a planning value if you want a 90% chance of finishing by that time. Probing questions: 'Would you communicate P50 or P90 to a client, and why?' and 'What would make you distrust the simulation results (e.g., too few runs, missing correlations)?' Misconception: claiming 'we will finish in 10.2 weeks'—P50 is not a guarantee, it is a percentile.

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: For each scenario: define the random variable and its unit
Scenario A: 15 calls, each answered within 20s with p=0.8
Scenario B: delivery time mean 3.2d, SD 0.6d; P(>4d)?
Scenario C: time to next IT incident; average 10 days; P(<2d)?
Simulation: given P80 and P95, explain what each means
Reflection: which assumption is weakest in each scenario?
content.notes: Guide learners to map each scenario to a model: A is binomial count of successes out of n=15; B is normal tail probability using Z; C is exponential with λ=1/10 per day and CDF. Encourage writing one interpretation sentence per answer (e.g., 'There is a 9% chance delivery exceeds 4 days'). For the simulation prompt, push them to use correct language: '80% chance outcome is at or below P80.' Common misconception: interpreting percentiles as probabilities of a point value rather than a threshold.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD106 tasks on model choice and risk interpretation
Always state X~, parameters, units, and the event in words
Show approximations used (e.g., normal approx, continuity)
Avoid mixing up p, μ, σ, and λ across models
Do not report a number without context and direction (>, <, between)
Document assumptions as if a colleague must reproduce it
content.notes: Explain typical marking criteria: correct distribution selection with justification, correct setup (random variable + parameters), correct calculation, and interpretation in context. Highlight frequent errors: using the wrong tail (P(X>a) vs P(X<a)); forgetting continuity correction when claiming a normal approximation; using σ where σ² is required or vice versa; and omitting units (days vs hours). Probing question: 'If your result seems too large/small, what quick sanity checks can you do?' Suggest checks like bounding probabilities between 0 and 1, and comparing to the mean.

slides.title: MOD106 Lesson 2: Binomial, normal and exponential

content.title: MOD106 Lesson 2: Binomial, normal and exponential
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD106 — Probability, Distributions and Simulation for Risk | Lesson 2 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners. slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Select a model and justify assumptions and data needs

How to use: watch/read → practise → self-check → apply to work

Probing questions: What decision depends on this probability? What variable is random here? What is the time unit? What does independence mean in this context? Common misconception: treating model choice as purely mathematical rather than driven by the process and data generation mechanism.

slides.title: Choosing the right probability model

content.title: Choosing the right probability model

rows: Count of successes in fixed number of trials
Continuous measure with many small influences
Time between events in a Poisson process

content.notes: Talk through the decision tree: if the outcome is a count out of a fixed number of opportunities, binomial is usually the first candidate. If it is a continuous measurement (e.g., demand, lead time, strength) that varies around a mean due to many additive effects, normal may be suitable, often as an approximation. If the variable is a waiting time until an event (failure, call arrival, downtime start), exponential is a baseline model. Probe: Are the “trials” genuinely comparable? Does p stay stable across time, shifts, or suppliers? For normal: is negative demand possible in the model, and is that acceptable? For exponential: does maintenance or ageing make the rate change over time (violating constant hazard)?

slides.title: Binomial model: essentials for workplace risk

content.title: Binomial model: essentials for workplace risk
content: Random variable: X = number of successes in n trials
Parameters: n (count), p (probability per trial)
PMF: P(X=x)=C(n,x)p^x(1-p)^(n−x)
Mean = np; variance = np(1−p); SD = √(np(1−p))
Interpretation: “exactly/at most/at least x defects”
Data need: stable p from historical or test data
content.notes: Explain what “success” means: it can be a defect, a late delivery, a pass, etc. Stress that n is fixed in advance (e.g., 200 items inspected). Clarify independence: the outcome of one trial does not change the probability for the next; in practice, this is often only approximately true. Mini-example: if items come from the same machine setting drifting over time, p may change—binomial may then underestimate tail risk. Common misconception: using binomial when n is not fixed (e.g., number of calls in an hour—this is not binomial; it is better aligned with Poisson, with exponential inter-arrival times).

slides.title: Normal model: essentials for exceedance risk

content.title: Normal model: essentials for exceedance risk
content: Random variable: X is continuous (e.g., demand, duration)
Parameters: mean μ and standard deviation σ
Standardise: Z=(X−μ)/σ then use Normal(0,1)
Exceedance: P(X>k)=1−Φ((k−μ)/σ)
Units: μ and σ share X units; probabilities unitless
Check: extreme skew or hard bounds may break normal fit
content.notes: Give intuition: the normal distribution is often used when many small independent effects contribute to variability (measurement errors, aggregated demand). Explain that “standardise then look up Φ” is the core computational move. Probing questions: Does the variable have a natural lower bound (e.g., time cannot be negative)? If μ is close to zero relative to σ, the normal model may assign material probability to impossible negative values; you may then need truncation or a different distribution (lognormal, gamma). Common misconception: treating σ as “average error” rather than a measure of spread; also mixing up Φ(z) with 1−Φ(z) for exceedance.

slides.speakerNotes: Give intuition: the normal distribution is often used when many small independent effects contribute to variability (measurement errors, aggregated demand). Explain that “standardise then look up Φ” is the core computational move. Probing questions: Does the variable have a natural lower bound (e.g., time cannot be negative)? If μ is close to zero relative to σ, the normal model may assign material probability to impossible negative values; you may then need truncation or a different distribution (lognormal, gamma). Common misconception: treating σ as “average error” rather than a measure of spread; also mixing up Φ(z) with 1−Φ(z) for exceedance.

slides.title: Exponential model: essentials for downtime timing

content.title: Exponential model: essentials for downtime timing
content: Random variable: T = time to next event (failure/arrival)
Parameter: rate λ per unit time; mean time = 1/λ
CDF: P(T≤t)=1−e^(−λt) for t≥0
Survival: P(T>t)=e^(−λt) (no event by time t)
Memoryless: P(T>s+t|T>s)=P(T>t)
Check: ageing or maintenance breaks constant-rate assumption
content.notes: Explain the workplace reading: λ=0.2 per hour means an average of 0.2 events each hour, not “20% chance per hour” unless time is exactly one hour and you compute it via 1−e^(−0.2). Show the link between mean time between failures (MTBF) and λ: MTBF=1/λ. Probing questions: Is the hazard realistically constant? If equipment wears out, hazard increases; if preventive maintenance resets condition, hazard may drop after maintenance. Common misconception: confusing λ with a probability; λ has units (e.g., failures/hour).

slides.title: Monte Carlo outputs: what to report and why

content.title: Monte Carlo outputs: what to report and why
content: Percentiles: P50 median; P80/P90 “conservative” outcomes
Mean and SD: expected value and variability of outcomes
95% CI: uncertainty in the estimated mean (not a percentile)
Report units: days, £, defects, hours—match the variable
Decision link: choose contingency using P80/P90 as policy
Sense-check: compare simulated tails with model assumptions
content.notes: Differentiate clearly between (a) a distribution of possible outcomes (e.g., project cost) and (b) uncertainty in the estimated mean from a finite number of simulation runs. A 95% confidence interval (CI) here typically refers to the mean estimate: mean ± 1.96·SE, where SE=SD/√N for N simulation runs (assuming independence of runs). P80 is a percentile of the outcome distribution: 80% of outcomes are below it. Probing questions: If a sponsor asks for “a 95% figure”, do they mean P95 (percentile) or 95% CI (estimation uncertainty)? Common misconception: claiming “95% chance cost will be below the upper CI limit”—that confuses CI with a predictive percentile.

slides.title: Worked example 1: binomial defect probability

content.title: Worked example 1: binomial defect probability
content: Scenario: inspect n=200 items; defect rate p=0.03
Question: P(X≥10 defects) in the batch
Compute: 1−P(X≤9) using binomial CDF
Interpret: chance of “rework trigger” threshold being hit
Communicate: assumptions (independent items, stable p)
content.notes: Walk the learner through translation: X is the number of defects observed among 200 inspected items. The event “at least 10 defects” is a tail probability, so we compute 1−P(X≤9). Explain practical computation: in Excel use BINOM.DIST(9,200,0.03,TRUE) then take 1 minus that result; in R pbinom(9,200,0.03) similarly. Use the mean and SD to sanity-check: 10 is about (10−6)/2.41≈1.66 SD above the mean, so a modest tail probability is plausible. Probing questions: What happens if p is uncertain (e.g., between 2% and 4%)? Would a beta-binomial be more realistic? Common misconception: using P(X=10) when the decision threshold is “≥10”.

slides.title: Worked example 2: normal demand exceedance

content.title: Worked example 2: normal demand exceedance
content: Scenario: daily demand X~N(μ=120, σ=25) units
Question: P(X>160) demand exceeds capacity 160
Standardise: z=(160−120)/25=1.6
Interpret: about 5.5% of days exceed capacity
Communicate: consider rounding, non-negativity, seasonality
content.notes: Emphasise that the normal model is an assumption about the distribution of daily demand, not a statement that demand is “naturally normal”. Show how to obtain Φ(1.6): using standard normal tables or Excel NORM.S.DIST(1.6,TRUE). Then compute 1 minus the result. Discuss interpretation: if capacity exceedance triggers overtime or lost sales, 5.5% might be acceptable or not depending on service level targets. Probing questions: Is σ stable across weekdays vs weekends? Is demand skewed (promotions) such that normal underestimates high-demand days? Common misconception: reporting the z-score as if it were the probability.

slides.title: Worked example 3: exponential time to downtime

content.title: Worked example 3: exponential time to downtime
content: Scenario: failures occur at rate λ=0.2 per hour
Question: P(failure within next 3 hours)
Interpret: ~45% chance of failure within 3 hours
Communicate: constant-rate assumption; define the time unit
content.notes: Translate carefully: T is time until the next failure from now. Rate λ=0.2 per hour implies MTBF=5 hours. Show the computation step-by-step and stress the role of units: if time were in minutes, λ must also be per minute. Probing questions: What operational changes could alter λ (load, temperature, operator skill)? If a failure is more likely right after a repair (infant mortality) or later due to wear, exponential is not appropriate; consider Weibull. Common misconception: interpreting λ as “20% chance each hour” and multiplying by 3 to get 60%; the exponential model does not accumulate linearly.

slides.title: Risk register entry from model and simulation

content.title: Risk register entry from model and simulation

rows: Add flex capacity 20 units on peak days

content.notes: Explain that a risk register is a communication tool: it makes assumptions and limitations explicit so decisions can be audited and revisited. The “model & params” line should always include units and the data window used to estimate parameters. “Key metrics” should mix probability statements and operational thresholds (e.g., exceedance probability, P80 or P90 outcome). Probing questions: If challenged, can you justify why normal rather than empirical distribution? What evidence supports parameter stability? Common misconception: listing “risk score” without traceability to data, model, or decision threshold.

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
leftColumn: Identify model: 12 hires, each may fail probation
Identify model: time to next IT incident
Identify model: weekly demand around a mean
rightColumn: Compute: P(at least 3 fails) if p=0.15
Compute: P(no incident in 4 days) if λ=0.1/day
Compute: P(demand<80) if μ=100, σ=15
content.notes: Invite learners to pause and attempt each prompt without tools first: write down the random variable, distribution, parameters, and the probability event in words. Then compute using a calculator/Excel if available. For the right column, learners should produce both the numeric result and an interpretation sentence in context. Probing questions: What does “at least” mean in terms of a CDF complement? For the exponential question, do you recognise that “no incident in 4 days” is a survival probability e^(−λt)? For the normal question, do you standardise correctly and choose Φ(z) rather than 1−Φ(z)? Common misconception: switching time units (days vs hours) mid-calculation.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports: probability model selection and risk reporting tasks
Show assumptions and justify model choice with data structure
Include units for λ, μ, σ and for the random variable
Avoid mixing percentiles with confidence intervals
Use correct tail: at least vs at most; > vs <
State limitations and next data to collect
content.notes: Explain how assignments typically reward reasoning: marks come from model justification, correct parameter meaning, and interpretation, not only numeric accuracy. Stress common pitfalls: (1) using the wrong tail (e.g., computing P(X≤k) when asked for exceedance), (2) reporting λ without units, (3) treating SD as a “margin” rather than variability, (4) confusing P90 with a 90% CI, and (5) failing to document that p, μ, σ, or λ were estimated from limited data. Probing questions: If your result seems surprisingly high/low, what quick checks can you do (mean/SD sanity check, bounds, extreme cases)?

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Model choice follows data structure: count, continuous, or time
Parameters have meanings and units; state and interpret them
Tail probabilities answer decision questions (threshold risks)
Simulation summaries: percentiles for outcomes; CI for mean
Risk registers document assumptions, limits, and actions
content.notes: Close by reinforcing the workflow: define the random variable and decision threshold; pick the distribution that matches the process; compute the probability; interpret in plain language; then document the assumptions and actions. Encourage learners to revisit any scenario they meet at work and ask: “What is the random variable, and what is the decision threshold?” Probing question for reflection: Which assumption (independence, constant rate, approximate symmetry) is most fragile in your workplace context, and what data would you collect to test it?

slides.title: MOD106 Probability, Distributions and Simulation for Risk

content.title: MOD106 Probability, Distributions and Simulation for Risk
content.content: Lesson 3: Calculate probabilities using binomial, normal and exponential models (1h 30m)
content.notes: Welcome. In this lesson we connect three common probability models to workplace risk questions: counts of events (binomial), measured variation around a typical level (normal), and waiting times between events (exponential). The emphasis is on selecting an appropriate model by checking assumptions, computing probabilities with correct notation and units, and then interpreting simulation (Monte Carlo) outputs responsibly. As you work through, keep asking: what is the random variable, what are its units, and what assumptions am I making about how the process behaves?

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: You will choose a model and justify it using assumptions
You will compute and interpret binomial, normal and exp probs
You will interpret Monte Carlo summaries and 95% CIs
You will draft a brief risk register entry with uncertainty
You will check results for reasonableness and common errors
Suggested flow: read → watch/work → practise → self-check
content.notes: Treat the lesson as a cycle: (1) decide the model, (2) calculate, (3) interpret for a decision-maker, (4) document limits, and (5) sanity-check. A frequent learner trap is to jump straight to formulae. Instead, start by naming the random variable clearly, e.g. “X = number of defects in a sample of 20 items” or “T = time in days until the next failure”. Probing question: if you changed the units (minutes to hours), would your parameters and probability statement still make sense?

slides.title: Selecting a probability model

content.title: Selecting a probability model

rows: Binomial: fixed n, p constant, independent
Normal: approx symmetric; use μ, σ

content.notes: Model selection is about matching the story to the mathematics. Binomial fits when you have a fixed number of opportunities and each opportunity results in success/failure with the same probability, and trials are independent. Normal is often a pragmatic model for continuous measurements driven by many small influences; it can also be a useful approximation when distributions are roughly symmetric and unimodal. Exponential fits the time between events when the event rate is constant over time (a Poisson process assumption). Probing questions: What could break independence in your setting (e.g., batch effects)? Is the rate really constant (e.g., wear-out, maintenance cycles)?

slides.title: Binomial model essentials

content.title: Binomial model essentials
content: Use when X counts successes in n independent trials
Parameters: n (trials), p (success probability per trial)
PMF: P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k)
Typical risk queries: P(X≥k), P(X≤k), expected defects
Mean=np, SD=√(np(1-p))
State what counts as a “success” before calculating
content.notes: Be explicit about what “success” means; in quality control it might be “defective”, which feels negative but is mathematically fine. Clarify the trial unit (item, day, transaction) and whether n is fixed in advance. Common misconception: using binomial when p changes across trials (e.g., different suppliers) or when outcomes cluster (e.g., one machine setting causes many defects). Probing question: if you double the sample size n, should the expected count of defects double? If yes, binomial may be plausible.

slides.title: Normal model essentials and standardisation

content.title: Normal model essentials and standardisation
content: Use for continuous Y with mean μ and SD σ
Standardise: Z=(Y−μ)/σ to use standard normal tables
Tail probs: P(Y>y)=1−Φ((y−μ)/σ)
Intervals: P(a<Y<b)=Φ(zb)−Φ(za)
Check plausibility of negatives when Y must be ≥0
Interpret σ in units of Y (e.g., units/day, minutes)
content.notes: Standardisation is just a unit conversion: how many SDs away from the mean is your threshold? Learners often forget that Φ gives P(Z≤z), not the upper tail; always sketch a quick number line and mark the region. Another common error is mixing up σ and σ²; the normal model uses SD σ in the Z formula. Probing question: does the normal model assign meaningful probability to impossible values (like negative demand)? If that probability is not negligible, you may need a different model or a truncation/log transform in more advanced work.

slides.title: Exponential model essentials (waiting times)

content.title: Exponential model essentials (waiting times)
content: Use for time-to-event T with constant rate λ
Parameter links: mean=1/λ, median=(ln2)/λ
Survival: P(T>t)=e^(−λt) for t≥0
CDF: P(T≤t)=1−e^(−λt)
Units: λ is “per time” (e.g., per hour), t in same time
Memoryless: P(T>s+t|T>s)=P(T>t)
content.notes: The exponential model is best thought of as a model for “random arrivals” with no ageing: the chance of failure in the next hour does not depend on how long you have already waited. That is powerful but can be unrealistic if components wear out; in that case the hazard rate increases and exponential underestimates long-term risk. Units matter: if λ=0.1 per day, then t must be in days. Probing question: if you switch from days to hours, what happens to λ numerically (hint: it scales by 24)?

slides.title: Reading Monte Carlo output and 95% CIs

content.title: Reading Monte Carlo output and 95% CIs

rows: Central estimate and spread of simulated outcomes
Typical and “bad case” levels under the model
Estimated chance of breaching a threshold
Controls Monte Carlo error; more n narrows the CI

content.notes: Separate two uncertainties: (1) real-world variability in outcomes (captured by the simulation distribution and percentiles), and (2) Monte Carlo error because you used a finite number of runs (captured by a CI around an estimate such as a mean or a breach probability). A 95% CI for P(Outcome>T) does not mean “95% of outcomes lie in this interval”; it means that if you repeated the simulation process many times (with the same model and n), about 95% of such intervals would contain the true model-based probability. Common misconception: treating the CI as a guarantee about reality; it is conditional on the model assumptions and input distributions.

slides.title: Reasonableness checks and common sources of error

content.title: Reasonableness checks and common sources of error
content: Probabilities must be between 0 and 1 (inclusive)
Check units: λ per hour with t in hours; μ,σ in same units
Order-of-magnitude: does the answer fit rough intuition?
Use bounds: P(X≥k) ≤ 1 and ≥ 0; tails should be small/large
Common errors: wrong tail, wrong parameter, rounding z too early
State limitations: dependence, changing rates, poor fit to data
content.notes: Reasonableness checking is professional practice, not optional. For example, if you calculate P(Demand>Capacity)=0.7 when capacity is far above the mean, that should trigger a re-check of the Z calculation and tail direction. Another frequent issue is mixing up “at least” (≥) with “more than” (>) in discrete settings; for binomial these differ by P(X=k). Probing questions: what quick mental estimate would you expect? Can you approximate with symmetry (normal) or with exponential decay (exp) to see if your computed value is plausible?

slides.title: Worked example 1: defects (binomial tail)

content.title: Worked example 1: defects (binomial tail)
content: Scenario: n=20 items, defect rate p=0.05 per item
Let X = # defects in the sample; X~Bin(n=20,p=0.05)
Question: P(X≥2) = 1 − P(0) − P(1)
content.notes: This example uses a complement because “at least 2” is easier as 1 minus the small set {0,1}. Emphasise notation: X is a count, so the probability statement is dimensionless. Interpretation: even with only a 5% defect probability per item, a sample of 20 has a non-trivial chance (about 1 in 4) of containing at least two defects. Probing question: what happens to P(X≥2) if you double n to 40 while keeping p the same? Another check: compute mean np=1 defect; so “≥2” should not be extremely rare—26.5% feels plausible.

slides.title: Worked example 2: demand exceeds capacity (normal)

content.title: Worked example 2: demand exceeds capacity (normal)
content: Scenario: daily demand D ~ N(μ=120, σ=15) units/day
Capacity is 150 units/day; compute P(D>150)
Use table/software: Φ(2.00)=0.9772
Interpretation: about 2.3% of days exceed capacity
content.notes: Explain why normal is being used: demand is measured on a continuous-ish scale and fluctuates around a typical level. The key skill is the Z transformation and selecting the correct tail. Common misconception: using Φ(2)=0.9772 as the exceedance probability; remind learners Φ gives the lower tail. Probing questions: if capacity rose to 165, what z do you get and how should the probability change? Also ask: is it credible that demand could be negative under this model, and is that probability negligible given μ=120 and σ=15?

slides.title: Worked example 3: downtime (exponential + MC read)

content.title: Worked example 3: downtime (exponential + MC read)
content: Scenario: mean time to failure is 10 days ⇒ λ=0.1 per day
Let T = time to next failure; T~Exp(λ=0.1/day)
MC summary (n=10,000): P(T>15)=0.224 (close to 0.223)
95% CI (MC): [0.216, 0.232] for the estimated probability
CI meaning: simulation precision, not a 95% chance of survival
content.notes: First, reinforce the unit link: mean 10 days implies λ=1/10 per day, not per hour. Then show the survival function and interpret: roughly 22% chance the time to next failure exceeds 15 days. The Monte Carlo output is used here to illustrate that simulation estimates should align with analytic results when the model is correct; any small mismatch is Monte Carlo error. Clarify the CI: it quantifies uncertainty due to finite simulation runs, not uncertainty about the machine’s true failure rate in the real world. Probing question: if you increased runs from 10,000 to 100,000, what should happen to the CI width?

slides.title: Practice: choose model, compute, interpret

content.title: Practice: choose model, compute, interpret
content: A: 30 calls, p=0.08 escalate. Find P(X≥5). State model
B: Lead time ~ N(8,1.5) days. Find P(L<6) and interpret
C: Arrivals mean 20 min. Find P(wait>30 min). Use units
D: A report states p90=£2.1m. Explain “p90” to a manager
E: A CI for P(overrun)=0.12 is [0.10,0.14]. What is it not?

For D, clarify percentile language: p90 means 90% of simulated outcomes are at or below that value. For E, correct the common misinterpretation that the CI is a range where the true outcome will fall 95% of the time. Probing follow-up: what extra data would you want to test the assumptions (e.g., independence, constant rate, normality)?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Applies to MOD106 tasks on distributions and simulation for risk
Marks reward: justified model choice, not only correct arithmetic
Show working: define RV, parameters, units, and tail direction
Use clear notation: P(X≥k), P(Y>y), λ per time unit
Avoid: wrong tail, mixing σ and σ², ignoring dependence

content.notes: In assessed work, graders look for the full chain: assumptions → model → calculation → interpretation → limitations. A correct number with unclear modelling choices often earns limited credit because it is not auditable. Encourage learners to write short interpretive sentences: “There is a 2.3% chance demand exceeds capacity on a given day.” Also remind them that simulation outputs must be contextualised: the CI is about the estimate from the simulation, and both are conditional on the input model. Probing question: what would you write if you suspected dependence (e.g., demand is higher on Mondays) but were told to use a simple model?

slides.title: MOD106 Lesson 4: Binomial, normal and exponential models

content.title: MOD106 Lesson 4: Binomial, normal and exponential models
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD106 — Probability, Distributions and Simulation for Risk | Lesson 4 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners. Position this lesson as a decision-making toolkit: given a workplace scenario (defects, demand, downtime), your first task is to choose a model and state the assumptions that make the model defensible. Emphasise that at Bloom’s “analyse” level we are not only calculating, but explaining why the model fits, interpreting outputs for decisions, and identifying limitations. Remind learners that a small change in assumptions (e.g., independence) can invalidate a result more than an arithmetic slip.
