slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and study approach

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and study approach
content: Choose binomial/normal/exponential models and justify assumptions
Calculate and interpret workplace probabilities with correct units
Read Monte Carlo outputs: mean, percentiles, threshold probability
Compute and interpret a CI/uncertainty band; note limitations
Write a risk register entry: result, assumptions, uncertainty, action
Study cycle: watch → practise → self-check → reflect and apply
content.notes: Frame the learning objectives as a workflow you can reuse at work: (1) model choice, (2) parameterise, (3) calculate, (4) interpret, (5) quantify uncertainty, (6) document for governance. When learners “justify assumptions”, prompt them to explicitly mention: independence, identical probability, measurement scale (counts vs continuous), and constant rate. Ask: “If I showed this to a colleague, could they reproduce the logic and challenge the assumptions?” Common misconception: thinking model choice is about which formula is easiest; instead it is about the data-generating process and measurement scale.

slides.title: Selecting a probability model

content.title: Selecting a probability model

rows: Count of successes in n trials

content.notes:
Talk through model selection as a diagnostic. First ask: is the outcome a count (0,1,2,...) or a measurement on a continuous scale (time, cost, demand)? If it is a count of “successes” across a fixed number of opportunities, binomial is the natural starting point. If it is a continuous measurement influenced by many small factors, normal is often reasonable (or at least a workable approximation). If it is a waiting time until the next event, exponential is a standard baseline.

Probe: “What is the random variable here?” and “What is one ‘trial’?” Learners often misclassify because they focus on context words (e.g., ‘defects’) rather than the variable (count per batch vs time to next defect). Note also that simulation is not a distribution; it is a method that uses distributions plus process logic.

slides.title: Binomial model: when and how

content.title: Binomial model: when and how
content: Random variable: X = number of successes in n trials
Conditions: fixed n; independent trials; constant p
Parameters: n (count), p (probability per trial)
Probability: P(X=k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k)
Mean/SD: E[X]=np; SD[X]=sqrt(np(1-p))
Interpret k as a count, not a rate or proportion
content.notes:
Explain “success” is any defined outcome (e.g., “defective item”, “order arrives late”), so the word is neutral. Emphasise the three conditions: fixed number of opportunities, independence, and constant p. Discuss what breaks them: learning effects, clustering of defects, mixed suppliers, or changing inspection sensitivity.

Mini-example: “In a sample of 20 items, each has 2% chance of defect, what is P(0 defects)?” That is (1−0.02)^20. Ask: “Would p be the same for every item if two machines are involved?” Common misconception: using binomial when n is not fixed (e.g., ‘number of calls until first complaint’—that is geometric/negative binomial).

slides.title: Normal model: standardisation and interpretation

content.title: Normal model: standardisation and interpretation
content: Use for continuous measures: time, demand, cost, dimensions
Parameters: μ (mean), σ (standard deviation), same units as X
Standardise: Z=(X-μ)/σ; then use Φ(z) for probabilities
Tail events: P(X>a)=1-Φ((a-μ)/σ)
Check shape: extreme skew or bounds can mislead
Normal approx to binomial: np≥10 and n(1-p)≥10
content.notes:
Reinforce units: μ and σ are in the original units (minutes, £, units/week). When you compute z, you create a unitless standard score, enabling you to use normal CDF tables or software.

Probe: “What does a z-score of 2 mean in plain language?” (Two standard deviations above the mean.) Highlight the common error of mixing up σ with variance σ².

Discuss approximation: binomial can be approximated by normal for large n with p not too close to 0 or 1. Mention continuity correction conceptually (e.g., P(X≤k) ≈ P(Y≤k+0.5)), but keep focus on interpretation. Misconception: assuming normal just because data ‘looks random’; instead check plausibility (e.g., demand cannot be negative).

slides.title: Exponential model: waiting times and rates

content.title: Exponential model: waiting times and rates
content: Random variable: T = time until next event (e.g., breakdown)
Parameter: λ = rate per unit time (e.g., 0.2 per hour)
Survival: P(T>t)=e^(-λt); CDF: P(T≤t)=1-e^(-λt)
Mean time: E[T]=1/λ (same time unit as t)
Memoryless: P(T>s+t | T>s)=P(T>t)
Check: constant rate may fail with ageing or maintenance cycles
content.notes:
Translate λ carefully: “0.2 per hour” means on average 0.2 events each hour, not a probability. Clarify the connection between λ and mean time between events: if λ=0.2/hour, the mean time is 5 hours.

Use a mini-example: “If breakdowns occur at rate 1 per 10 hours (λ=0.1/hr), what is P(no breakdown in next 3 hours)?” Answer e^(−0.1·3). Ask learners why this is plausible only if the hazard is roughly constant.

Misconception: treating exponential as ‘the downtime distribution’. It is for time between events; downtime duration itself might be lognormal or gamma. Also, memoryless is often counterintuitive—invite learners to question whether “already running for 8 hours” changes risk; if yes, exponential may be inappropriate.

slides.title: Monte Carlo outputs: what to report

content.title: Monte Carlo outputs: what to report
content: Mean: expected value; sensitive to extreme outcomes
Median: typical outcome; robust to skewed distributions
Percentiles (P50/P80/P95): plan for service levels
P(X>threshold): probability of breach or delay
Expected shortfall: average severity beyond a threshold
Always report inputs and assumptions used in the simulation
content.notes:
Explain that Monte Carlo repeats the model many times to approximate the distribution of outcomes. Connect metrics to decisions: mean supports budgeting under risk neutrality; percentiles support conservative planning (e.g., P80 cost for contingency); P(X>threshold) supports compliance and SLA management.

Mini-example: If “project delay” is skewed, the mean may exceed the median; ask: “Which would you communicate to a sponsor and why?” Introduce expected shortfall as a way to summarise ‘how bad is bad’ beyond the threshold, not just how likely.

Misconception: believing more simulation runs automatically makes results ‘true’. The quality depends primarily on input distributions and process logic; more runs only reduce sampling noise.

slides.title: Uncertainty: confidence intervals for risk metrics

content.title: Uncertainty: confidence intervals for risk metrics
content: Simulated probability p̂ = (# exceedances) / N
Approx CI: p̂ ± 1.96 * sqrt(p̂(1-p̂)/N)
Report N and random seed (or replication approach)
Uncertainty band narrows as N increases
Limitations: input error; model form; dependence misspecification
Avoid false precision; round sensibly for decisions
content.notes:
Frame this as “uncertainty in the estimate”, not “uncertainty in reality”. When you estimate a probability from simulation, the count of exceedances behaves like a binomial with parameters N and true p, so the standard error formula follows.

Walk a quick numeric: if N=10,000 and p̂=0.12, SE≈sqrt(0.12*0.88/10000)=0.00325, so 95% CI ≈ 0.12±0.0064 → [0.114, 0.126]. Ask: “If management’s risk appetite threshold is 0.10, does this CI change the decision?”

Highlight limitations beyond sampling error: if input distributions are guessed, a narrow CI can still be misleading. Misconception: using a CI to claim the probability cannot be outside the interval; instead interpret as long-run coverage under assumptions.

slides.title: Risk register entry: minimum quantitative standard

content.title: Risk register entry: minimum quantitative standard

rows: Supplier delay → late parts → stop line
Escalate if P>0.10; add buffer stock

content.notes:
Explain that a risk register is an audit trail: someone else should be able to see what was modelled, how, and what decision follows. Encourage clear “cause-event-impact” wording so the metric aligns to the risk.

Probe: “Does your metric directly measure the impact described?” For example, if the impact is ‘financial penalty’, a pure delay probability may be insufficient; you may need expected penalty or expected shortfall.

Misconception: listing assumptions vaguely (“data is accurate”). Instead require specific modelling assumptions: independence, stationarity, parameter source, time window, and what was excluded.

slides.title: Worked example 1: binomial defects in a batch

content.title: Worked example 1: binomial defects in a batch
content: Scenario: 50 items, defect probability p=0.03 per item
Let X = number of defective items; X ~ Bin(n=50,p=0.03)
Interpret as chance the batch meets an “≤2 defects” rule
Check assumptions: constant p; independent items; same inspection
content.notes:
Walk the set-up slowly: define the random variable, then state the distribution and parameters. Emphasise that n is fixed (50 items) and p is per item. For Task A, highlight the logic: “no defects” means every trial is non-defective.

For Task B, learners can use software rather than hand-summing; the key is knowing what to sum and why. Ask: “Is ‘≤2 defects’ a quality gate, a rework threshold, or a customer acceptance criterion?” That drives interpretation.

Common errors: using p=3% as 3 (not 0.03), confusing P(X≤2) with P(X=2), or forgetting that binomial counts defects, not defect rate. Also challenge independence: if one tool is misaligned, defects cluster, increasing tail risk.

slides.title: Worked example 2: normal demand exceedance

content.title: Worked example 2: normal demand exceedance
content: Scenario: weekly demand X ~ N(μ=1200, σ=180) units
Task: probability demand exceeds 1500 units
Interpret: about 4.8% of weeks exceed capacity 1500
Sense-check: negative demand unlikely? Here μ-3σ=660 > 0
content.notes:
Explain the meaning: demand is treated as continuous for modelling convenience, even though units are discrete; normal can still be fine if counts are large. Show the structure: translate to z, then use a CDF.

Ask learners: “Is 1500 a hard capacity limit or a soft one with overtime?” If soft, you might instead compute expected overtime cost or expected exceedance beyond 1500.

Common mistakes: using Φ(1.67) as the answer (forgetting the upper tail), or mixing up σ and σ². Also highlight that normality is an assumption; if demand is strongly seasonal or skewed, consider alternative distributions or simulate with empirical data.

slides.title: Worked example 3: exponential downtime risk

content.title: Worked example 3: exponential downtime risk
content: Scenario: time to breakdown T ~ Exp(λ=0.25 per hour)
Task A: P(breakdown within 2h)=1-e^(-0.25*2)
Interpret: 39% chance of failure within 2h; 22% survive 6h
Units check: λ in per hour, so t must be in hours
content.notes:
Reinforce unit discipline: if someone supplies λ “per day” and you use hours, the result is wrong by a factor of 24. Invite learners to rewrite λ as an average time between failures: 1/0.25=4 hours.

Probe: “Does the hazard look constant?” If equipment wears out, hazard increases, so exponential underestimates late-life risk. If preventive maintenance resets the condition, a renewal process might fit better.

Common misconceptions: treating e^(−λt) as the probability of failure (it is survival), and assuming exponential implies frequent failures; in fact λ controls frequency.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: model choice and outputs

content.title: Practice and reflection: model choice and outputs
leftColumn: A: 30 calls/day; P(>40 calls)?
B: 12 deliveries; P(≥2 late) if p=0.1?
C: Waiting time to next outage; P(>3h) given λ?
D: Simulation: P(cost>£50k)=0.18 from N=5,000 runs
rightColumn: Pick a model and state assumptions for A–C
Compute one probability for B or C; show parameter units
For D, compute an approx 95% CI for the 0.18 estimate
Write one sentence: what decision the metric informs
content.notes:
Guide learners to treat A–C as classification first, calculation second. For A, discuss that call counts per day are often modelled with Poisson, but if they approximate demand as normal due to aggregation, they must justify it (mean/variance, symmetry). This is a deliberate prompt to practise model justification, not just formula recall.

For B, binomial is clear: fixed number of deliveries, late/not late, constant p. Encourage learners to compute P(≥2)=1−[P(0)+P(1)].

For C, exponential is plausible if outage rate is constant; ask what evidence would support or contradict that. For D, use SE=sqrt(p(1−p)/N); ask learners to interpret whether the CI crosses a policy threshold.

Common issue: learners write assumptions as generic statements. Push for concrete phrasing: “late deliveries are independent across routes and days within this week” rather than “assume independence”.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common errors

content.title: Assessment connection and common errors
content: Supports: quantitative risk write-up using models or simulation
Marks usually reward assumptions, units, and interpretation
Common error: wrong variable type (count vs continuous vs time)
Common error: incorrect parameter units (λ per day vs per hour)
Common error: report a number without decision meaning
Common error: omit uncertainty and limitations in the risk entry
content.notes:
Explain how typical assessment rubrics allocate credit: model selection and justification, correct parameterisation, correct probability calculation, and interpretation tied to a decision. Encourage learners to show the modelling chain: define variable → choose model → state assumptions → compute → interpret.

Offer quick checking questions learners can apply before submitting: “Have I written units on every parameter?” “Is my probability between 0 and 1?” “Did I compute the correct tail?” “If I change units, does the answer change sensibly?”

Highlight that risk communication is part of the maths: a technically correct probability that is not connected to an action is often graded as incomplete.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Model choice follows the random variable and assumptions
Binomial: fixed n and constant p for counts of successes
Normal: continuous outcomes; use z-scores and tail probabilities
Exponential: waiting times with constant rate; check units
Simulation outputs need interpretation and uncertainty reporting
content.notes:

Final probing question: “If your result changed materially when an assumption is relaxed, how would you explain that sensitivity to a non-technical stakeholder?” This sets up good practice for later lessons on model validation and sensitivity analysis.

Remind learners that the same context can sometimes be modelled in multiple ways; the skill is to justify the choice and be transparent about limitations.

Is an approximation being used (normal for binomial), and is it justified?

slides.title: Choosing a probability model

content.title: Choosing a probability model

rows: Count of successes in n trials
System too complex for closed form

content.notes: Talk through the decision logic using everyday workplace examples. Binomial: number of defective items in a sampled batch. Normal: daily demand or process time when many factors add up and the histogram looks roughly symmetric. Exponential: time-to-failure or time between breakdowns if the hazard rate is approximately constant. Monte Carlo: when the metric depends on multiple uncertain inputs or complicated rules (e.g., project finish date with correlated delays). Common misconception: using normal just because the variable is ‘large’; symmetry and scale matter more than size.

slides.title: Binomial model: counts with fixed n

content.title: Binomial model: counts with fixed n
content: Random variable: X = number of successes in n trials
Parameters: n (integer), p (0 to 1)
Mean and SD: μ=np, σ=√(np(1−p))
Typical probabilities: P(X≤k), P(X=k), P(X≥k)
Check: independence and constant p are plausible
Report with context: “defects per batch of n”
content.notes: Clarify what counts as a ‘trial’ and what counts as a ‘success’ (success can be a defect, a failure, a late delivery—define it explicitly). Walk through why independence matters: if defects cluster (machine misalignment), the binomial may understate risk. Mention practical computation: use cumulative binomial functions in Excel/Sheets or a calculator, rather than hand-calculating combinations for large n. Probing question: if the sampling is without replacement from a finite batch, is binomial still reasonable or should you consider hypergeometric (and is the batch large enough to approximate with binomial)?

slides.title: Normal model: continuous near-symmetric data

content.title: Normal model: continuous near-symmetric data
content: Random variable: X measured on a continuous scale
Parameters: μ (mean), σ (standard deviation), σ>0
Standardise: Z=(X−μ)/σ then use N(0,1)
Interval: P(a≤X≤b)=Φ(zb)−Φ(za)
Tail: P(X>c)=1−Φ((c−μ)/σ)
Check: symmetry; beware hard bounds (e.g., X≥0)
content.notes: Explain standardisation as a change of units to ‘standard deviations from the mean’. Remind learners to sketch where a, b, or c sits relative to μ before calculating—this prevents sign errors. Highlight bounded variables: demand cannot be negative; if μ is not far from 0 relative to σ, the normal model may assign non-trivial probability to impossible values. Mention continuity correction only if learners are converting a discrete count to a normal approximation; flag it as a possible improvement rather than always required.

slides.title: Exponential model: waiting times at a constant rate

content.title: Exponential model: waiting times at a constant rate
content: Random variable: T = time until next event
Parameter: rate λ (events per unit time)
Mean time: E[T]=1/λ (same unit as T)
Survival: P(T>t)=e^(−λt) for t≥0
Within time: P(T≤t)=1−e^(−λt)
Check: constant rate; memoryless property holds
content.notes: Interpret λ carefully: if λ=0.2 per hour, then the average waiting time is 5 hours. Emphasise unit consistency: if t is in minutes, convert λ to per minute or convert t to hours before substituting. Discuss memorylessness in plain language: ‘the chance of failing in the next hour does not depend on how long it has already run’. This is often unrealistic for wear-out, so ask learners to justify why constant rate is acceptable (e.g., random external interruptions rather than component ageing).

slides.title: Monte Carlo: from simulations to risk + 90% CI

content.title: Monte Carlo: from simulations to risk + 90% CI
content: Define output metric (e.g., cost, finish date, downtime)
Generate N runs from input distributions and rules
Estimate risk: p̂ = (# runs exceeding threshold)/N
Summarise: mean, median, percentiles (P90, P95)
State N, seed (if used), and key modelling assumptions
content.notes: Clarify that Monte Carlo produces an estimate with sampling error: if you rerun with a different seed or more runs, the estimate moves slightly. Use a quick numerical illustration: if N=10,000 and p̂=0.12, then SE≈sqrt(0.12·0.88/10,000)≈0.00325, so a 90% CI is roughly 0.12±0.0053. Stress that this CI is about Monte Carlo error, not about whether the input model is correct. Probing question: which uncertainty dominates—simulation sampling error or input data uncertainty/model form uncertainty?

slides.title: Worked example 1: binomial defects in a sample

content.title: Worked example 1: binomial defects in a sample
content: Scenario: sample n=20 items; defect probability p=0.08
Let X = number of defects; X~Bin(n=20,p=0.08)
Compute P(X≤2) to check risk of “too many defects”
Use cumulative binomial: P(X≤2)=BinomCDF(20,0.08,2)
Interpret: probability sample passes (≤2 defects)
State assumptions: independent items; stable defect rate
content.notes: Talk through why binomial fits: fixed number inspected (n fixed), each item either defective or not, and a stable defect probability p. If learners do not have a CDF function, outline that P(X≤2)=P(0)+P(1)+P(2), but discourage manual arithmetic for larger n. Ask: what operational reality could break independence (e.g., a single miscalibrated machine producing multiple defects)? Also ask: is p estimated from limited historical data, and should that be acknowledged as uncertainty in the risk register?

slides.title: Worked example 2: normal demand between two levels

content.title: Worked example 2: normal demand between two levels
content: Scenario: daily demand X~N(μ=500, σ=60) units
Find P(450≤X≤620) for capacity planning
Compute: Φ(zb)−Φ(za) using a z-table/tool
Sense-check: interval spans below and above the mean
Report result with units and rounding (e.g., 3 d.p.)
content.notes: Model justification: demand often aggregates many small independent factors, which supports an approximately normal shape. Work the standardisation slowly: za≈−0.833, zb≈2.000, so the probability should be well over 0.5 because most mass is between −0.83 and 2.00. Misconception to flag: learners often swap za and zb or drop the negative sign, giving impossible probabilities. Probing question: if demand is skewed (e.g., occasional very high spikes), what alternative might be more appropriate, and how would that affect risk assessment?

slides.title: Worked example 3: exponential time between breakdowns

content.title: Worked example 3: exponential time between breakdowns
content: Scenario: breakdowns average 1 every 10 hours
Rate: λ=0.1 per hour; T~Exp(λ=0.1)
Find P(T>6 hours): e^(−0.1×6)
Find P(T≤2 hours): 1−e^(−0.1×2)
Check units: t in hours matches λ per hour
Interpret as reliability over a time window
content.notes: Unpack the phrase ‘average 1 every 10 hours’: it implies mean waiting time 10 hours, hence λ=1/10 per hour. Show the numerical values: P(T>6)=e^(−0.6)≈0.549; P(T≤2)=1−e^(−0.2)≈0.181. Ask learners whether a constant breakdown rate is plausible: is this random external disruption, or wear-related failure (in which case exponential may understate late-life risk)? Remind them that exponential is often a first-cut model and should be justified as such.

slides.title: Worked example 4: simulation output to risk + 90% CI

content.title: Worked example 4: simulation output to risk + 90% CI
content.notes: Explain how to read a simulation summary table: the estimate is the proportion of runs beyond the threshold. Then connect the CI to the Monte Carlo standard error: CI≈p̂±1.645·sqrt(p̂(1−p̂)/N). Emphasise interpretation: ‘Given the model inputs and logic, the simulated probability of cost exceeding £120k is about 12%, with Monte Carlo uncertainty about ±0.5 percentage points.’ Probing question: what would you do if the CI is too wide for decision-making (increase N, simplify the metric, or improve input data)?

slides.title: Risk register entry: what to include

content.title: Risk register entry: what to include
content.notes: Make clear that a good risk register entry is both decision-useful and auditable. Encourage learners to separate ‘simulation uncertainty’ (finite N) from ‘model uncertainty’ (inputs may be wrong, independence may fail). Give a mini-example of a transparency note: ‘Failure rate inferred from 42 events; may be seasonally biased.’ Probing question: if an executive asks “How sure are you?”, which part of your entry answers that, and which part admits limitations?

slides.title: Critique a worked solution: spot and fix issues

content.title: Critique a worked solution: spot and fix issues
leftColumn: Issue 1: unit mismatch (minutes vs hours)
Issue 2: wrong parameter (λ vs mean time)
Issue 3: normal used with heavy skew
Issue 4: CI omitted from simulation claim
rightColumn: Fix: convert units before substituting
Fix: use λ=1/mean, then apply exp formula
Fix: justify normal or choose alternative
Fix: add N and 90% CI; avoid false precision
content.notes: Use this slide to model the mindset of an analyst reviewing someone else’s work. Provide a quick concrete correction: if λ=0.2 per hour and t=30 minutes, either use t=0.5 hours or λ=0.2/60 per minute. For parameter misuse, stress that exponential’s mean is 1/λ, not λ itself. For overconfident reporting, demonstrate improved wording: replace ‘Probability is 12.00%’ with ‘Estimated at 12% (90% CI 11.5%–12.5%) under stated assumptions’. Probing question: which error is most dangerous operationally—small arithmetic slips or unjustified assumptions?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Defects: n=50, p=0.03. Find P(X≥3). State assumptions.
Downtime: mean 4 days. Find P(T>7 days). Watch units.
Simulation: N=5,000, 410 overruns. Estimate p and 90% CI.
Reflection: which assumption is weakest in each scenario?
Self-check: do results pass a quick sanity test?
content.notes: Encourage learners to attempt each prompt without immediately reaching for formulas: first identify the model and parameters. For the simulation prompt: p̂=410/5000=0.082; SE≈sqrt(0.082·0.918/5000)≈0.00388; 90% CI≈0.082±0.0064 → about [0.076, 0.088]. Ask learners to write one sentence interpreting each answer in business terms (not just a number). Common misconception: mixing up P(X≥3) with P(X>3), or forgetting that ‘mean 4 days’ implies λ=0.25 per day.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
leftColumn: Match scenario to model and justify assumptions
Show parameter identification and unit checks
Compute and interpret probabilities clearly
Summarise simulation with CI and limitations
rightColumn: Wrong model: using normal for counts without justification
Sign errors in z-scores and tail probabilities
Exponential: mixing λ and mean; unit inconsistency
Simulation: reporting p̂ without N, CI, or caveats
content.notes: Link explicitly to likely assessment marking criteria: method selection, correct setup, correct computation, and professional interpretation. Stress that clear working is part of communication: define X/T, state distribution and parameters, then calculate. Encourage learners to annotate outputs (e.g., label z-values, indicate which tail). Probing question: if you had to defend your answer in a meeting, what would you point to as evidence that your method is appropriate?

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Choose model from data type: count, continuous, or waiting time
State assumptions explicitly; check units before calculating
Binomial: n and p; Normal: standardise; Exp: λ per time unit
Monte Carlo estimates need N and a 90% CI for transparency
Report results as decisions and risks, not just numbers
content.notes: Close by reinforcing transfer: the aim is not memorising formulas, but producing defensible risk statements. Invite learners to revisit the model-choice table when uncertain. Encourage a final metacognitive check: ‘What would make my result wrong?’ (wrong model, wrong parameter, wrong units, or unjustified certainty). Suggest that learners keep a personal checklist for future tasks: define variable, identify parameters, compute, interpret, then critique.

slides.title: Operational data and model outputs for evidence-based decisions

content.title: Operational data and model outputs for evidence-based decisions
content.content:
Programme: Maths Certification
Module: MOD108 — Integrated Workplace Maths Project (Capstone)
Lesson 1: Operational data and model outputs to produce evidence-based decisions
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Position this lesson as a bridge between ‘doing calculations’ and ‘making defensible workplace decisions’. Emphasise Bloom’s level (evaluate): learners are expected to judge competing options using evidence and uncertainty, not just compute statistics. Remind learners that the outputs they produce should be suitable for a manager: clear claims, clear evidence, clear limits.

slides.title: Orientation and learning outcomes

content.title: Orientation and learning outcomes
leftColumn: Identify 2 trends, 1 turning point, 1 constraint from data
Compute and interpret a 95% confidence interval (CI)
Compare recommendations: impact vs uncertainty and choose one
Document assumptions, uncertainty, and bias in a risk entry
rightColumn: 1) Review concepts (slides 3–8)
2) Follow worked examples (slides 9–10)
3) Practise prompts (slide 11)
4) Take the two short checks (slide 12)
content.notes: Explain how to study: first understand the vocabulary (trend/turning point/constraint; CI meaning), then practise making written judgements. Highlight that objective 1 includes a word-count and evidence standard: learners must cite specific values, changes, or thresholds rather than saying ‘it looks higher’. Probe: ‘If your chart disappeared, could your written claim still stand using numbers alone?’ Address a common misconception: that uncertainty is an optional add-on; in this module it is part of the decision quality.

slides.title: From operational data to evidence

content.title: From operational data to evidence
content: Operational data: time-stamped measures of process performance
Model outputs: forecasts, scenarios, or optimisation results
Evidence-based claim = statement + quantified evidence + context
Prefer rates and deltas: per hour, %, change per week
State constraints explicitly: capacity, SLA, safety, budget
Separate signal from noise before recommending action
content.notes: Clarify that ‘operational data’ often comes from systems (queues, tickets, sensors) and can be messy. ‘Model outputs’ might be as simple as an Excel forecast or as complex as a simulation—either way, you must validate whether they make operational sense. Give a mini-example: ‘Average waiting time fell from 14 to 9 minutes after staffing change’ is stronger than ‘waiting time improved’. Ask: ‘What decision would a manager make from your sentence?’ Misconception to flag: learners may treat a chart as proof; charts are summaries and can mislead if scales change or data are aggregated.

slides.title: Trend vs turning point vs constraint

content.title: Trend vs turning point vs constraint
content.notes: Talk through each row with an operational example. Trend: a gradual increase in call volume over several weeks. Turning point: after a system upgrade, error rate drops and stays lower. Constraint: ‘SLA requires 80% of calls answered within 20 seconds’ or ‘maximum 6 staff per shift’. Stress that learners must justify why they classify a pattern as trend vs noise; a single spike could be a reporting error or a one-off incident. Probing question: ‘What additional data would help you confirm a turning point is real?’

slides.title: 95% confidence intervals: what they are

content.title: 95% confidence intervals: what they are
content: CI estimates an unknown population value from a sample
Mean CI: x̄ ± t*·(s/√n) for unknown σ
Proportion CI: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1−p̂)/n)
95% refers to long-run method performance, not certainty
Wider CI means more uncertainty; narrower means more precision
Precision improves with larger n and lower variability
content.notes: Explain the intuition: a CI gives a plausible range for the true mean/proportion, given a sampling process. Emphasise the frequentist meaning: if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of intervals would contain the true value. Many learners incorrectly say ‘there is a 95% probability the true mean is in this interval’—correct that gently and offer an alternative phrasing: ‘Using this method, we are 95% confident…’. Remind them to choose t vs z appropriately and to keep units (minutes, £, %) consistent.

slides.title: Interpreting CIs: do and do not

content.title: Interpreting CIs: do and do not
leftColumn: Conclude the range of plausible true values
Compare options by overlap and practical significance
Describe precision and how sample size affects it
State assumptions behind the CI method used
rightColumn: Do not claim the CI proves causation
Do not treat 95% as a guarantee for one dataset
Do not ignore biased sampling or measurement error
Do not hide uncertainty when writing recommendations
content.notes: Expand with concrete examples. If CI for mean wait time is [8.5, 10.2] minutes, you can say the true mean is plausibly around 9–10 minutes, given assumptions. You cannot say ‘the new policy caused improvement’ without design evidence (e.g., control group, A/B test). Introduce three explicit limitations learners should routinely include: (1) sample representativeness (selection bias), (2) independence/identical distribution (e.g., repeat callers), (3) measurement quality (logging changes, rounding, missingness). Ask: ‘Which limitation is most likely in your workplace data, and why?’

slides.title: Evaluating recommendations under uncertainty

content.title: Evaluating recommendations under uncertainty
content: Define decision criterion: SLA, cost, safety, fairness
Estimate expected impact and attach uncertainty (CI/range)
Check sensitivity: do conclusions change under assumptions?
Prefer options robust to uncertainty, not just best-case
Write a risk statement: likelihood, impact, mitigations
State residual risk and monitoring plan after rollout
content.notes: Teach a practical evaluation workflow: (1) make the objective measurable, (2) compare options on the same metric, (3) include uncertainty, (4) decide with a rationale. Give a mini-scenario: Option A reduces wait time by 2 minutes ± 0.5; Option B reduces by 3 minutes ± 2.5. Discuss that B might be higher upside but riskier; the ‘better’ choice depends on SLA tolerance and risk appetite. Misconception: choosing the option with the largest point estimate without considering uncertainty. Probing questions: ‘What is the cost of being wrong?’ and ‘How would you detect early that the chosen option is failing?’

slides.title: Integrity in quantitative reporting

content.title: Integrity in quantitative reporting
content: Document assumptions: scope, time window, definitions
Record uncertainty sources: sampling, model, parameter error
Identify bias risks: missing data, self-selection, drift
Provide traceability: data source, version, and method
Use plain language: avoid false precision and overclaims
Create a risk-register entry linked to the decision

slides.title: Worked example: identify patterns from a short dataset

content.title: Worked example: identify patterns from a short dataset
content.notes:
Walk learners through what they could claim, and how to evidence it.

Possible trends (at least two):
- Volume trend: 820 → 930 from week 1 to 5 (increase of 110; about 13%).
- Wait-time trend: 12.4 → 16.2 minutes (increase of 3.8 minutes; about 31%).

Turning point (one):
- Utilisation crosses a plausible capacity threshold at week 3 (81% → 88%). If your operational rule-of-thumb is ‘above 85% leads to queues’, week 3 is a turning point where queuing becomes more likely.

Constraint (one):
- Operational constraint could be ‘utilisation should stay ≤85% to meet SLA’. Weeks 3–5 breach this.

Stress that the turning point must be justified as a change in regime, not just a high value. Ask: ‘If week 4 dips slightly, does that break the trend or is it noise?’ Highlight that learners should reference the chart (if provided) but still cite numbers from the dataset.

slides.title: Worked example: compute a 95% CI (mean or proportion)

content.title: Worked example: compute a 95% CI (mean or proportion)
content: Step 1: Choose parameter: mean wait or % within SLA
Step 2: Check n, outliers, and independence assumption
Step 3 (Excel mean): CONFIDENCE.T + AVERAGE()
Step 3 (Python mean): scipy.stats.t.interval(...)
Step 4: Report estimate and CI with units and n
Step 5: Add 3 limitations tied to the data collection
content.notes:
Provide a concrete walkthrough verbally.

Mean CI example (Excel): Suppose you have 30 daily mean wait times (minutes). Compute x̄ with AVERAGE(range) and s with STDEV.S(range). Use CONFIDENCE.T(0.05, s, n) to get the margin of error (MOE). Then CI is x̄ ± MOE.

Mean CI example (Python): Use numpy mean and standard deviation (ddof=1), then scipy.stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n-1, loc=mean, scale=s/√n).

Proportion CI example: If 210 of 300 calls met SLA, p̂=0.70. Use z=1.96 and compute MOE.

Interpretation script learners can reuse: ‘The estimated mean wait is 9.4 minutes (95% CI: 8.8 to 10.0; n=30). Under the assumptions of independent, representative days and stable measurement, the true mean is plausibly within this range.’

Limitations prompts: representativeness (only weekdays), autocorrelation (busy days cluster), measurement changes (clock start/stop definition).

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Write 150–250 words: 2 trends, 1 turning point, 1 constraint
Cite at least 4 numbers: values, differences, or % change
Compute a CI and add 3 limitations specific to your data
Choose between 2 recommendations and justify the trade-off
Draft one risk-register entry: risk, mitigation, residual risk
Reflect: what evidence would change your recommendation?
content.notes:
Guide learners to practise in a way that matches the assessment. Encourage them to timebox: 15 minutes for identifying patterns, 20 minutes for CI, 15 minutes for recommendation and risk entry.

Probing questions to deepen evaluation:
- ‘Is the turning point operationally meaningful or just statistical?’
- ‘If the CI were twice as wide, would your decision change?’
- ‘What is the opportunity cost of delaying action to collect more data?’

Common misconceptions: writing too many claims without evidence; including a CI but not explaining what it means; listing generic limitations not linked to the dataset (e.g., ‘human error’ without describing where it enters).

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
leftColumn: Supports MOD108 capstone evidence-based recommendations
Strengthens written justification using data and uncertainty
Builds a defendable CI interpretation with limitations
Develops risk-register language for quantitative decisions
rightColumn: Overclaiming causation from observational trends
Using a CI without stating assumptions or limitations
Reporting point estimates with no uncertainty context
Vague risks with no mitigations or residual risk stated
content.notes:
Make the connection explicit: in a capstone, markers look for decision quality, not just computation. Explain what ‘defendable’ looks like: another analyst should be able to reproduce your method and understand why you chose a recommendation.

Elaborate pitfalls with examples:
- Causation overclaim: ‘New rota caused the improvement’ without ruling out seasonality.
- CI misuse: mixing up standard deviation and standard error, or using z when n is small and σ is unknown.
- Risk writing: ‘There is a risk of failure’ is not useful—risk entries need a mechanism (‘If demand spikes, utilisation exceeds 85%, increasing waits’).

Ask: ‘If a stakeholder disagrees, which part of your argument can you defend with numbers, and which part is judgement?’

slides.title: Operational data and model outputs for evidence-based decisions

content.title: Operational data and model outputs for evidence-based decisions
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project (Capstone)
Lesson 2 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
Introduce this lesson as the bridge between “having outputs” and “using outputs responsibly”. Emphasise Bloom’s level: evaluate. Learners will practise judging which summaries are fit for a specific workplace decision, not merely producing charts.

Set expectations: we will work with operational datasets (often messy, limited, and time-bound) and typical model outputs (forecasts, distributions, simulations). Highlight that decision-quality evidence includes uncertainty and constraints, not just point estimates.

Probing question: Think of a recent workplace decision you have seen—what evidence was used, and what evidence was missing (e.g., uncertainty, capacity limits, assumptions)?

slides.title: Orientation: how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: how to use this lesson
content: You will learn to evaluate outputs for a stated decision
Watch/read: concepts and frameworks (slides 3–7)
Work through examples (slides 8–10) with your own tool
Practise prompts (slide 11) and compare to notes
Complete the two MCQ checks at the end of the lesson
Keep a log: assumptions, limits, and what you would verify
content.notes:
Explain the study loop for self-paced learning: concept → example → attempt → self-check → revise. Encourage learners to pause after each worked example to reproduce it in Excel or Python, even if only with small numbers.

Stress the “assumptions log” habit: in operational work, many errors come from silent assumptions (e.g., independence, stable process, no stockouts). Recording assumptions is part of professional integrity.

Probing questions: Which parts do you usually rush—visual choice, uncertainty, or interpretation? How will you check you are not over-claiming from limited data?

slides.title: Choosing outputs that support a decision

content.title: Choosing outputs that support a decision
content: Start with the decision: what action and what threshold?
Prefer visuals that show trend and turning points clearly
Surface constraints (capacity, policy, lead time, budget)
Include uncertainty where it could change the decision
Favour simple, traceable summaries over complex dashboards
Justify choices with evidence, not style preferences
content.notes:
Walk learners through the idea that “best chart” is decision-dependent. A weekly time series line chart might be best for detecting a turning point, whereas a histogram or box plot might be best for variability and risk. Stress that a visual is an argument: it should make the decision-relevant signal easy to see and the key caveats hard to ignore.

Mini-example: If the decision is “increase staffing next month if average call volume exceeds 1,200/day,” then a control chart or a time series with a 1,200 reference line is more decision-relevant than a pie chart of call types.

Common misconception: ‘More charts equals more evidence.’ In practice, too many views can hide the key conclusion and increase the risk of cherry-picking.

Probing question: What would need to be visible for a stakeholder to disagree with you (and be right)?

slides.title: 95% confidence intervals: what they mean

content.title: 95% confidence intervals: what they mean
leftColumn: A plausible range for a population mean/proportion
Built from a sample and a method (e.g., t-interval)
If repeated, ~95% of such intervals would contain truth
Wider CI = more uncertainty (often small n or high spread)
rightColumn: Not a 95% chance the true value is inside this one CI
Not proof the process is stable or unbiased
Not immunity to bad sampling or missing data
Not a substitute for operational constraints and context
content.notes:
Explain confidence intervals in plain language while keeping the statistical meaning accurate. The key is long-run coverage: the method, not the specific interval, has a 95% success rate under assumptions.

Add assumptions/limitations learners must mention: random or representative sampling, independence (or correct handling of time dependence), correct distributional model (or use of large-sample approximations), and no major measurement bias.

Mini-example phrasing (mean): “Based on 40 days of data, we estimate the mean is 118 units/day; a 95% CI of 112–124 means values in this range are consistent with the data and assumptions. This does not guarantee the true mean lies in the interval, and it does not address future changes in demand.”

Common misconception: Interpreting the CI as a probability about the parameter for this specific interval.

Probing question: Which assumption is most likely to fail in operational time-series data?

slides.title: Turning points: constraint vs correlation

content.title: Turning points: constraint vs correlation
leftColumn: Constraint-based: capacity limit creates a plateau
Policy change: new rules shift volumes abruptly
Lead time: delayed effects after an intervention
Budget cycle: end-of-quarter spend changes patterns
rightColumn: Correlation-only: co-moves with unrelated variable
Seasonality mistaken for a one-off turning point
Data artefact: system change, missing days, re-coding
Regression to mean misread as improvement
content.notes:
Clarify that a turning point is a change in level or slope. The evaluation task is to propose plausible explanations and separate mechanism-based constraints from ‘it moved with X’ stories.

Teach a practical test: ask “What mechanism would prevent the process from exceeding that level?” If the answer is capacity, policy, or supply limits, you likely have a constraint story. If the answer is ‘it seems related to…’, you may only have correlation.

Mini-example: A backlog stops growing after week 8. Constraint explanation: extra shift added (capacity). Correlation-only explanation: ‘temperature increased.’ The latter might be true but needs a mechanism and evidence.

Common misconceptions: Assuming every turning point is caused by the most recent event; ignoring reporting changes; not checking if the turning point aligns with a calendar boundary.

Probing questions: What additional data would help discriminate between a capacity constraint and a demand drop?

slides.title: Balanced risk statements for stakeholders

content.title: Balanced risk statements for stakeholders
content: State decision context: what is at stake and by when
Quantify uncertainty: CI, distribution, or simulation
Record assumptions and key limitations explicitly
Explain what could go wrong and the likely impact
Offer at least two practical mitigations
Maintain traceability: link claim to output and data
content.notes:
Explain that a risk statement is not a dramatic warning; it is a balanced, evidence-linked summary that supports action. It should be readable by non-technical stakeholders while still being auditable.

Give a template learners can reuse:
1) Decision + timeframe; 2) Best estimate; 3) Uncertainty (range/probability); 4) Assumptions/limitations; 5) Implications; 6) Mitigations.

Mini-example structure: “If we keep current staffing, we expect mean wait time of 6.2 min (95% CI 5.5–6.9). If demand returns to peak levels, there is a 25–35% chance wait time exceeds 8 min. Assumes call handling time remains stable and no system outages. Mitigations: add on-call cover for peak windows; trial call-back option; monitor daily with trigger thresholds.”

Common misconception: Reporting only the point estimate (‘6.2 minutes’) and hiding uncertainty.

Probing question: Which limitation, if true, would most change the decision?

slides.title: Collaborative integrity in a team review

content.title: Collaborative integrity in a team review
content: Explain reasoning step-by-step, not just conclusions
Invite challenge: “What would change your mind?”
Cite evidence: data source, method, and parameter choices
Use the critique checklist to find weak claims
Incorporate at least one improvement from feedback
Document changes so the work remains auditable
content.notes:
Frame integrity as a collaborative behaviour: making your work easy to scrutinise and improve. This is essential in capstone-style work where models inform real decisions.

Provide a micro-script for a review reply:
- “Here is what I did…” (data cleaning, assumptions)
- “Here is why…” (decision relevance)
- “Here is what I’m uncertain about…” (limitations)
- “Please challenge…” (specific questions)
- “Based on your checklist point, I changed…” (one concrete improvement)

Common misconception: Treating critique as a threat rather than a quality control mechanism.

Probing questions: What is the difference between defending your work and making it testable? What part of your process is hardest for others to reproduce?

slides.title: Worked example: compute a 95% CI (Excel/Python)

content.title: Worked example: compute a 95% CI (Excel/Python)
content: Mean CI: x̄ ± t* × (s/√n) using sample data
Proportion CI: p̂ ± z* × √(p̂(1−p̂)/n)
Excel: AVERAGE, STDEV.S, COUNT; T.INV.2T for t*
Python: scipy.stats.t.interval or statsmodels proportion CI
Report CI with units and sample window (e.g., last 30 days)
Interpret in 2–3 sentences, include assumptions/limits
content.notes:
Walk step-by-step with a concrete numerical mini-example for the mean:
- Suppose n=25 days, x̄=118, s=15 units/day.
- df=24, t*≈2.064 (two-sided 95%).
- SE = 15/√25 = 3.
- Margin = 2.064×3 ≈ 6.19.
- CI ≈ [111.8, 124.2] units/day.

Excel guidance: learners often misuse STDEV.P vs STDEV.S; remind them STDEV.S is typical for sample-based inference. Also remind them to use T.INV.2T(alpha, df) with alpha=0.05.

Proportion notes: mention the normal approximation works best when np̂ and n(1−p̂) are both sufficiently large; otherwise use an exact or Wilson interval.

Interpretation practice: learners must state what it does NOT mean (not a probability for this interval; not a guarantee about future).

Probing questions: What is your sample window, and why is it defensible? Is independence plausible across days, or is there autocorrelation that would widen uncertainty?

slides.title: Worked example: a balanced risk statement

content.title: Worked example: a balanced risk statement
content.content: Decision: set stock reorder point for next month. Model: demand mean 520/week with 95% CI 480–560; simulation shows 30% chance of stockout if reorder=500. Assumes stable demand pattern and current lead time; mitigate by raising reorder to 550 and adding a lead-time contingency plan.
content.notes:
Read this aloud as an example of concise stakeholder communication. Then unpack it:
- Decision context is explicit (reorder point, next month).
- Uncertainty is quantified in two ways: CI for the mean and a probability from simulation.
- The statement includes assumptions and a limitation (stability and lead time).
- Two mitigations are practical and aligned to the scenario.

Encourage learners to adapt the structure to their own workplace context. Highlight that the CI for mean demand and the simulation probability answer different questions: estimation uncertainty vs operational risk under variability.

Common misconceptions: Treating the CI as covering all future weeks; failing to specify the time horizon; giving mitigations that are not actionable (e.g., ‘monitor closely’ with no trigger).

Probing questions: What reorder point would you recommend if the lead time doubles? Which assumption would you validate first (demand stability or lead time reliability), and how?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Pick one decision: what metric and threshold defines success?
Choose 2 visuals; justify with trend, turning point, constraint
Compute one 95% CI and write a 2–3 sentence interpretation
List 2 constraint explanations for a turning point you see
Draft a risk statement with 2 mitigations and key limits
Write a team-review reply: invite challenge + 1 improvement

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Identify 2 trends + 1 turning point using an annotated graph

Evaluate model outputs: 3 limits + rate decision risk
Give a recommendation: finding, constraint, uncertainty, mitigations
Complete a risk register entry: bounds, assumptions, owner
Workflow: study → try the worked steps → practise → take quizzes
content.notes: Explain that these objectives are aligned to Bloom’s “evaluate”: learners will judge evidence quality and decision risk, not merely calculate. Clarify what “annotated” means: labels on the chart that explicitly reference axes, units, and time window, plus short callouts for trends/turning point. For the CI objective, stress that the key skill is interpretation in plain language, including what uncertainty is excluded (e.g., bias, non-stationarity, data quality issues). For model evaluation, frame it as: “Would you stake a decision on this output? Under what conditions?” Invite learners to keep a running list of common limitations (small n, missing data, process changes, unrealistic assumptions).

slides.title: From operational data to decision evidence

content.title: From operational data to decision evidence
content: Start with the decision question, not the dataset
Define metric, unit, time window, and data source
Describe patterns: level, trend, seasonality, turning points
Quantify uncertainty: CI, distribution spread, or simulation range
State assumptions and limitations that affect trust
Conclude with a recommendation and risk-managed next steps
content.notes: Talk through a simple evidence chain: (1) decision question (e.g., “Should we add a second shift?”), (2) operational metric (e.g., mean pick time in minutes), (3) pattern description (e.g., improving trend then deterioration), (4) uncertainty (CI around the mean, or a simulated throughput distribution), (5) caveats (process changes, missing observations, non-random sampling), and (6) recommendation plus mitigations. Probing questions: What decision will change if the metric is 5% higher? What is the cost of being wrong? Common misconception: presenting analysis without linking it to a decision threshold or action.

slides.title: Annotated graphs: trends and turning points

content.title: Annotated graphs: trends and turning points
content: Trend: sustained directional change over a stated period
Turning point: change in direction or slope after a specific time
Label axes with metric name, units, and time period
Call out 2 trends and 1 turning point with brief annotations
Check context: process change, policy change, or data artefact
Avoid overclaiming from noise or too few points
content.notes: Explain how to justify a trend: specify the start/end dates and describe magnitude (e.g., “from ~12 min to ~9 min between weeks 1–3”). For turning points, emphasise identifying the point and stating the nature of the change (direction or slope), then offering plausible explanations to test (new staff, system outage, demand surge). Encourage learners to distinguish signal vs noise: a single spike is not necessarily a turning point unless it is sustained. Probing questions: What would you need to see to confirm this is real? What operational event coincides with the change? Misconception: confusing seasonal variation with a turning point.

slides.title: 95% confidence intervals for decisions

content.title: 95% confidence intervals for decisions
leftColumn: Choose sample period and ensure observations are comparable
Compute mean, SD, n; use t-critical for small samples
Standard error = SD / SQRT(n)
CI = mean ± t*SE (for 95%, alpha = 0.05)
rightColumn: Meaning: plausible range for the population mean metric
Not a probability the true mean is “inside” for this dataset
Does not include bias, bad data, or process change impacts
Use CI to judge if differences are practically meaningful
content.notes: Walk learners through interpretation carefully. A 95% CI is a procedure that, under assumptions (independent, identically distributed errors; stable process), will cover the true mean 95% of the time in repeated sampling. In practice, we use it as an uncertainty band around an estimated mean. Stress decision relevance: if the CI straddles a decision threshold (e.g., SLA requires mean < 10 min), the evidence is weaker than if the entire CI is below threshold. Address common misconceptions: (1) thinking 95% means a 95% chance the true mean is in the interval; (2) treating CI as capturing all uncertainty; (3) using a CI for an individual forecast rather than a mean estimate.

slides.title: Evaluating model or simulation outputs

content.title: Evaluating model or simulation outputs

rows: Are inputs current, complete, and in correct units?
Data source, date range, missingness summary
Does it match known history or benchmarks?
Is output a point, CI, or distribution?

content.notes: Explain that model evaluation is not about finding a single ‘correct’ answer; it is about judging fitness for purpose. Expand each row with examples: Inputs—units mismatch (hours vs minutes) can create large errors; Assumptions—constant demand, no downtime, linear relationships; Validation—compare to last month’s throughput and compute error; Uncertainty—prefer distributions or scenario ranges when decisions involve tail risk. Probing questions: What is the simplest baseline this should beat (e.g., last-week average)? Which assumption, if wrong, would change the decision? Misconception: believing a complex model is automatically better than a transparent baseline.

slides.title: Recommendation statements for team review

content.title: Recommendation statements for team review
content: Main finding: one sentence with metric, unit, and period
Constraint: what you could not measure or control
Uncertainty: CI/range and what it covers (and excludes)
Decision risk rating: low/medium/high with rationale
Mitigations: 2 practical actions to reduce risk or impact
Close with a clear ask: approve, defer, or run a test
content.notes: Model a “recorded review” statement structure. Example: “Over weeks 1–5, mean pick time increased from 9–10 min to 13 min; the 95% CI for week 5 mean is 12.2–13.8 min.” Then add a constraint: “We lack scanner downtime logs, so we cannot separate labour from system effects.” Then uncertainty: “The CI reflects sampling variability only, not measurement bias or the process change in week 4.” Risk rating: “Medium, because the trend is consistent but causality is unclear.” Mitigations: “Add downtime tracking; run a two-day A/B test with additional staffing.” Probing questions: What is the smallest action that reduces uncertainty? What is reversible if the decision is wrong? Misconception: using vague language (“seems better”) rather than quantifying and bounding.

content.title: Workplace-style risk register entry

rows: No weekend data; training week included
Back-test vs last 8 weeks by Fri

content.notes: Explain that the risk register is a communication and accountability tool: it makes assumptions visible and assigns ownership for follow-up, preventing ‘analysis theatre’. Stress that uncertainty bounds must specify the method (CI, percentile range, scenario range) and the time window. Probing questions: If this risk materialises, what is the operational consequence (cost, safety, SLA)? Which action would most reduce uncertainty before committing? Misconception: writing generic risks without linking to the decision and without an owner or deadline.

slides.title: Worked example: trends and turning point

content.title: Worked example: trends and turning point
content: Metric: average pick time (min), weekly, Warehouse A
Annotate: trend 1 (W1–W3), turning point (W3→W4), trend 2 (W4–W5)
Use axis labels: week number on x; minutes on y
content.notes: Teach learners to translate the table into an annotated line chart. Trend 1: improvement from 12.0 to 9.6 minutes (W1–W3). Turning point: W3→W4 reverses direction (+2.3 min). Trend 2: continued deterioration from 11.9 to 13.1 (W4–W5). Ask learners to write annotations that connect to context: “W4 increase coincides with scanner outages.” Then challenge them: is it causal or coincidental? What extra data would you pull (downtime logs, volume, staffing, order mix)? Misconception: ignoring operational notes and over-interpreting numbers alone.

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI in Excel or Python

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI in Excel or Python
leftColumn: Excel: mean =AVERAGE(B2:B21); SD =STDEV.S(B2:B21)
n =COUNT(B2:B21); SE =SD/SQRT(n)
Lower/Upper = mean ± t*SE
rightColumn: Python: import numpy as np; from scipy import stats
mean=np.mean(x); sd=np.std(x,ddof=1); n=len(x)
se=sd/np.sqrt(n); t=stats.t.ppf(0.975,n-1)
ci=(mean-t*se, mean+t*se)
content.notes: Provide a concrete interpretation script learners can reuse: “The mean pick time is 11.2 minutes; the 95% CI is 10.6 to 11.8 minutes. This reflects sampling variability assuming a stable process during the sampled period. It does not capture bias from missing scans or a process change mid-period.” Probing questions: What happens to the CI width if n doubles? (It shrinks roughly with 1/sqrt(n).) When should you not compute a single CI across the whole period? (When the process is not stable—e.g., turning point or policy change.) Common mistakes: using STDEV.P instead of STDEV.S for a sample; mixing units; forgetting to use t-critical for small n.

slides.title: Worked example: model output critique and risk

content.title: Worked example: model output critique and risk
leftColumn: Output: simulated throughput mean 120 units/day
Range: P10–P90 is 105–135 units/day
Decision: commit to 130 units/day plan next month
Context: recent downtime not included in training data
rightColumn: Assumptions: no downtime; constant demand mix; stable staffing
Limitations: no weekend data; short calibration window
Validation gap: no back-test vs last month actuals
Risk: High if plan needs ≥130; tail risk exceeds buffer
content.notes: Demonstrate how to move from critique to a decision risk rating. If the plan requires 130 units/day, but the distribution shows material probability below 130 (since P90 is 135, much of the mass is below 130), the risk of failure may be unacceptable without mitigations. Ask learners to articulate risk in operational terms: missed SLA, overtime cost, customer impact. Then propose mitigations: incorporate downtime as an input, run scenario with 2%/5% downtime, or set a conservative plan at P50 (or P10) depending on risk appetite. Misconception: quoting the mean as if it is a guaranteed outcome; ignoring the consequence of underperformance.

Draft chart annotations: 2 trends + 1 turning point

If learners struggle to find turning points, remind them to look for operational events (system changes, staffing changes) and consider plotting rolling averages. Link explicitly to the formative MCQs: use them to check conceptual understanding (CI meaning, validation, risk statements), not only calculation steps.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD108 capstone: evidence-based workplace decision
Show traceability: data → method → outputs → recommendation
Common error: CI stated as “95% probability” of containing truth
Common error: model risk rated without linking to decision threshold
Common error: limitations missing from slides and risk register
Common error: mitigations vague or not actionable/owned
content.notes: Explain how assessors typically judge quality: clarity, correctness, and transparency. Traceability means a reviewer can reproduce outputs and see how they informed the decision. Give examples of threshold linkage: if SLA requires mean < 10 minutes, state whether the CI is entirely below 10, overlaps 10, or above 10. For model risk, insist on a rationale grounded in the data and uncertainty: “High because the P10 is below the minimum viable throughput.” For mitigations, require specificity: who will do what by when (which also ties to the risk register owner).

slides.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson
content: Study core ideas: trends, constraints, uncertainty, effect size
Follow worked examples: visuals → metrics → decision text

A common misconception is that a p-value or a model coefficient is a decision; it is not. The decision requires context, constraints, and an explicit statement of uncertainty.

slides.title: From data to decision: the evaluation workflow

content.title: From data to decision: the evaluation workflow
content: Clarify decision and success metric (KPI) upfront
Summarise data: levels, trends, turning points, anomalies
Validate model output against operational reality
Quantify uncertainty: confidence intervals, sensitivity
Judge practical meaning under constraints
Communicate: recommendation + risk statement + limitations
content.notes: This is a repeatable workflow you can evidence in your capstone: define the decision and KPI, then characterise the data (including turning points), then check whether model outputs make sense operationally (e.g., do predicted throughputs exceed capacity?), then quantify uncertainty (confidence intervals, not just point estimates), then evaluate practical importance with constraints in mind, and finally write decision artefacts. Probing question: if you removed the model completely, what evidence from the raw data would still support your decision?

slides.title: Trends and turning points vs noise and seasonality

content.title: Trends and turning points vs noise and seasonality
leftColumn: Trend: persistent direction over time
Turning point: slope change or level shift
Step change: abrupt, sustained change
Seasonality: regular cyclic pattern
rightColumn: Noise: short-lived fluctuations
Outlier: unusual point, may be data error
Regression to mean: extremes tend to normalise
Beware: smoothing can hide true turning points
content.notes: A turning point is not “any wiggle”. It should be supported by a visible slope change (e.g., pre/post intervention) or a level shift that persists. Discuss how seasonality can masquerade as improvement: for example, call volumes drop every August; if an intervention starts in July, you may mistakenly credit the intervention. Encourage learners to annotate charts: mark dates of policy changes, staffing changes, system upgrades. Misconception: “more data points” automatically resolves ambiguity; more points help, but only if they cover relevant cycles and are comparable.

slides.title: Operational constraints: what limits practical change?

content.title: Operational constraints: what limits practical change?
content: Capacity: max throughput, staffing, machine hours
Service levels: SLAs, queue targets, lead times
Quality: defect limits, rework rate, compliance thresholds
Data limits: missingness, measurement error, lagged data
Policy limits: budgets, contracts, safety requirements
Model limits: assumptions, feature drift, range extrapolation
content.notes: Constraints convert statistical change into operational meaning. For instance, a predicted 12% increase in throughput is irrelevant if the bottleneck is a downstream inspection station capped at 500 units/day. Ask: what is the binding constraint right now? Another common issue is data latency: if outcomes are recorded weekly, you cannot claim daily improvements. Also highlight model range: predictions outside the training range are often unreliable. Probing question: which constraint would you cite in a risk register as the first barrier to implementing your recommendation?

slides.title: Confidence intervals: what a 95% CI means

content.title: Confidence intervals: what a 95% CI means
content: CI gives a plausible range for the true value
95% CI: long-run, 95% of such intervals contain truth
Narrow CI: more precision; wide CI: more uncertainty
CI crossing 0 (difference) suggests weak evidence of change
Report CI with units and context, not just numbers
content.notes: Stress interpretation: a 95% CI is not “a 95% chance the true value is in this interval” in the strict frequentist sense; it is a procedure with 95% coverage in repeated sampling. For practical communication, say: “Based on this sample, a reasonable range for the true mean is …”. Show how CIs support evaluation: if the interval is wide, the decision may be to gather more data or pilot. Misconception: “If CI excludes 0 then it is important.” Statistical evidence is not the same as operational importance; you still need effect size and constraints.

slides.title: Compute a 95% CI: quick method choices

content.title: Compute a 95% CI: quick method choices
content.notes: Use this slide to help learners select an appropriate CI. For means with unknown population variance, use the t-distribution with df=n−1. For large n, t and z are similar, but teach correct practice. In Excel, emphasise computing standard error (SE) correctly, and using T.INV.2T(0.05, df) for the critical value. In Python, note that libraries differ: scipy gives t-intervals; statsmodels provides proportion intervals (e.g., Wilson) which are often better than normal approximations for small n. Probing question: what would make the normal approximation for a proportion unsafe (e.g., very small n, p near 0 or 1)?

slides.title: Practical meaning: effect size + CI + constraints

content.title: Practical meaning: effect size + CI + constraints
content: Effect size: magnitude (e.g., % change, Cohen’s d)
CI width: precision; wide CI weakens actionable claims
Operational threshold: minimum worthwhile improvement
Constraint check: does change fit capacity and policy limits?
Decision logic: benefit vs risk under uncertainty
State uncertainty explicitly in the recommendation text
content.notes: This is the core evaluative step. Define a minimum worthwhile change (MWC), for example a 2-minute reduction in mean handling time or a 5% reduction in defects, and compare your estimated effect and its CI to that threshold. Example: if the estimated improvement is 3% but the 95% CI is −1% to 7%, you cannot confidently claim improvement; you can say results are compatible with a small decline through to a moderate improvement. Misconception: “Non-significant means no effect.” It often means “inconclusive with current data”. Probing question: what additional data or design change would narrow the CI most efficiently?

slides.title: Worked example 1: trends, turning points, constraints

content.title: Worked example 1: trends, turning points, constraints
content.notes: Walk learners through how to justify each claim with a specific reference. They should be able to point to the chart element: the slope direction, the date marker, the plateau, the threshold line. Clarify that “3σ” is illustrative: if they use such a rule, they should define it and ensure it is appropriate for the distribution. Encourage triangulation: combine visuals with summary statistics (pre/post means, rolling averages). Probing questions: what alternative explanations exist for the turning point (seasonality, reporting change)? Which constraint is binding, and how do you know?

slides.title: Worked example 2: 95% CI for a mean (Excel/Python)

content.title: Worked example 2: 95% CI for a mean (Excel/Python)
content: Scenario: mean time (min) before vs after a change
Compute x̄, s, n for the key group(s)
SE = s/√n; critical t* = T.INV.2T(0.05, n-1)
CI = x̄ ± t*·SE; report with units
Interpret: plausible range for the true mean time
Avoid: claiming certainty from a single point estimate
content.notes: Provide a concrete mini-example verbally. Example numbers: after-change sample n=25, mean x̄=12.4 min, s=3.0 min. Then SE=3/√25=0.6. t* with df=24 is about 2.064. CI is 12.4 ± 2.064*0.6 = 12.4 ± 1.24, i.e., [11.16, 13.64] min. In Excel, show the cell formula pattern: =AVERAGE(range), =STDEV.S(range), =COUNT(range), =STDEV.S(range)/SQRT(COUNT(range)), =T.INV.2T(0.05,COUNT(range)-1). In Python, outline: import numpy as np; from scipy import stats; x=np.array(...); stats.t.interval(0.95, len(x)-1, loc=x.mean(), scale=stats.sem(x)). Misconception: using STDEV.P instead of STDEV.S for sample data.

slides.title: Worked example 3: recommendation with uncertainty

content.title: Worked example 3: recommendation with uncertainty
content.content: A defensible recommendation states the estimated effect, its uncertainty, and the operational conditions under which it holds. It avoids overclaiming and records key limitations that could change the decision.
content.notes:
Model a 100–150 word recommendation structure learners can imitate:

1) Decision context and KPI: “To reduce average handling time…”
2) Evidence and magnitude: “Post-change mean decreased by 1.8 minutes…”
3) Uncertainty: “95% CI suggests the true reduction is between 0.2 and 3.4 minutes…”
4) Practical meaning + constraints: “This meets the 1-minute MWC, but benefits may be capped by staffing limits on weekends…”
5) Recommendation + next step: “Proceed with a two-week pilot expansion, monitoring SLA breaches and queue growth…”

Probing question: if the CI included no improvement, what would you recommend instead (e.g., gather more data, change the intervention, segment analysis)?

slides.title: Balanced risk statement: what to include

content.title: Balanced risk statement: what to include
leftColumn: Assumptions: stability, comparability, no major confounders
Uncertainty: CI range, model error, data quality
Limitations: scope, timeframe, missing variables
Risk owner and review date for the register
rightColumn: Impacts: cost, SLA, safety, compliance, reputation
Likelihood: qualitative + evidence basis
Mitigations: monitoring, controls, rollback plan
Triggers: thresholds that prompt action
content.notes:
Explain that a risk statement is not an apology; it is governance. It protects decision-makers by recording what was assumed and what could invalidate the conclusion. Provide a 120–180 word template:

“Assuming demand mix remains similar and measurement definitions are unchanged, the model suggests X. However, the 95% CI indicates outcomes could range from A to B, and the model was trained on data excluding peak-period disruptions. Key limitations include missing staffing-skill data and potential reporting lag. If adopted, there is a risk of SLA breaches during high demand because throughput is constrained by inspection capacity. Mitigations: (1) implement a staged rollout with daily SLA monitoring and predefined trigger thresholds; (2) maintain a rollback plan and allocate contingency staffing during peak windows. Review after two weeks of operation or sooner if backlog exceeds Y%.”

Misconception: listing mitigations without stating triggers or owners reduces usefulness.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: self-check prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection: self-check prompts
content: Name 3 trends/turning points you would look for and why
List 2 constraints and how you would evidence each
Draft a plain-language CI interpretation in 2 sentences
Decide if change is meaningful using MWC + CI + constraints
Write 120–180 words: a risk register entry with 2 mitigations
Critique: find 3 integrity issues in a draft recommendation
content.notes: Encourage learners to answer in writing, not mentally, and to attach references (e.g., “plateau at 500/day”, “CI width 4.2 units”). For the critique prompt, suggest common issues to search for: overclaiming (“proves”, “guarantees”), missing limitations (no mention of sample size or confounders), ambiguous visuals (no axes/units, truncated y-axis), and selective reporting (only best-case scenario). Probing questions: what single sentence could you add to make the recommendation more transparent? Which limitation is most decision-relevant?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD108 capstone: evidence-based decision outputs
Use in: recommendation section, risk register, traceability
Avoid: confusing statistical with practical significance
Avoid: missing units, dates, baselines, and constraint evidence
Avoid: reporting only point estimates without CIs
Prepare for MCQs: uncertainty, validation, risk statements
content.notes: Link explicitly to capstone expectations: traceability from data → analysis → decision text, and professional integrity in communication. Clarify that markers will look for: (1) specific references to visuals/numbers; (2) correct CI computation and interpretation; (3) balanced judgement using effect size and constraints; (4) transparent limitations and mitigations. Common pitfalls include: using the wrong denominator for proportions; mixing time windows (pre vs post not comparable); ignoring seasonality; and writing recommendations that omit uncertainty. Suggest a final check: “Could a colleague reproduce my calculation and see exactly where each claim came from?”

slides.title: What a confidence interval represents

content.title: What a confidence interval represents
content.content: A CI is a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on a sample. A 95% CI comes from a method that would capture the true value in 95% of repeated samples. It does not mean a 95% probability the true value lies in this one interval.
content.notes: Emphasise the long-run frequency interpretation: the parameter is fixed; the interval is random across repeated sampling. A common misconception is treating the CI as a probability statement about the parameter for a single dataset; that is a Bayesian credible interval, which uses a different framework. Mini-example: if we repeatedly sample 50 calls and compute a 95% CI for mean handling time each day, about 95 out of 100 such intervals would contain the true mean handling time for that stable process. Ask learners: “If you widened the interval, what happens to confidence and usefulness for decisions?”

slides.title: Choosing a CI method for workplace metrics

content.title: Choosing a CI method for workplace metrics
content.notes: This slide is about method selection, not calculation detail. For means, the t-interval is standard when population standard deviation is unknown; it is robust with moderate n but can fail with extreme skew and tiny samples. For proportions, avoid the naive normal approximation when counts are small; Wilson is often better behaved. For difference in means, default to Welch unless you have strong evidence of equal variances. Probing questions: What is your parameter (mean, proportion, difference)? Are your data independent observations? Are there structural reasons the distribution is skewed (e.g., durations, costs)?

slides.title: Interpretation and uncertainty statement rules

content.title: Interpretation and uncertainty statement rules
content: State metric, population, time window, and units
Give point estimate and CI with confidence level
Explain meaning in plain language (repeat-sampling idea)
Round sensibly: CI ends to 1–2 decimal places (match units)
Avoid: “95% chance true value is in this interval”
Link uncertainty to a decision or threshold where relevant
content.notes: Learners often under-specify the population: a CI for ‘all staff’ differs from ‘staff on night shift last month’. Encourage a 3–5 sentence structure: (1) context and data (n, period, unit), (2) estimate + CI, (3) interpretation, (4) decision implication, (5) limitation/next step. Rounding: pick a precision that is meaningful operationally; for example, seconds for call handling time, £ for costs, percentage points for proportions. If the CI is wide, say what that means for decision confidence. Probing question: “If you removed the units, would the statement still be interpretable?”
