slides.title: Key assumptions that drive uncertainty quality

content.title: Key assumptions that drive uncertainty quality
content: Independence: observations not correlated or clustered
Distribution choice: normal/t/lognormal/binomial fit
Representativeness: sample matches target population
Stationarity: process stable across time/conditions
Measurement quality: definition, missingness, bias
Model validity: correct formula and correct inputs
content.notes: Assumptions affect both bias (wrong centre) and precision (wrong width). Independence is frequently violated at work: repeated measures per employee, multiple calls per customer, or batch production. Representativeness is also common: data from “best week” or “trained team only” will understate uncertainty for the full operation. Stationarity matters when there is seasonality or policy changes; you may need stratified analysis or separate CIs by period. Probing questions: Are there natural clusters (teams, sites, machines)? Has anything changed in the process during data collection?

leftColumn: Assumption: independence of rows
Assumption: normality / chosen distribution
Assumption: sample represents target group
Assumption: stable process over time
rightColumn: Impact: CI too narrow; Mitigation: cluster/stratify
Impact: wrong tails; Mitigation: transform/bootstrp
Impact: biased mean; Mitigation: broaden sampling frame
Impact: mixed regimes; Mitigation: segment by period

Encourage learners to record: assumption, evidence check (e.g., plot or test), likely direction of impact (bias high/low; interval too wide/narrow), and what they will do next. Clarify that you do not need perfection; you need transparency and proportionate mitigations. Example: if calls are nested within agents, you might compute per-agent means first, then CI across agents, or use a bootstrap that resamples agents rather than calls. Probing question: “Which assumption, if wrong, would most change your decision?”

slides.title: Reproducible workflow for CI or simulation

content.title: Reproducible workflow for CI or simulation
content: Inputs tab/cell block: data source, dates, filters, units
Data cleaning steps documented (missing, outliers, coding)
Method block: formula, confidence level, distribution choice
Outputs: table of estimates + CI; chart with labels and units
Audit trail: version, author, timestamp, and parameter notes
Re-run button/script: one action regenerates all outputs
content.notes: Reproducible means someone else can press run and get the same results from the same data. In Excel: separate inputs, calculations, and outputs; avoid hard-coded numbers in formulas; use named ranges; store confidence level in a single cell. In Python: keep a clear notebook/script structure (import → clean → analyse → report), pin package versions if possible, and write outputs to CSV/PNG with filenames that include dates. Misconception: a screenshot is not an audit trail; an audit trail includes the underlying data definitions, assumptions, and steps. Probing question: “If the input dataset is updated next month, what exactly will change and where will you see it?”

content.title: Worked example 1: mean CI (call handling time)
content: Scenario: mean handling time (seconds) for a support team
Sample: n=40 calls; x̄=312 s; s=48 s (last 2 weeks)
Choose 95% t-interval (σ unknown)
content.notes: Walk through the structure: identify parameter (true mean), confirm metric and units, then choose the method (t-interval). Emphasise that the critical value comes from t with df=n−1. Discuss rounding: it is acceptable to round to the nearest second here; ensure the interval endpoints match the same precision. Probing questions: What if there are repeat callers or the same agent appears many times—does independence hold? What would skewed handling time (a long right tail) do to the mean and CI?

slides.title: From CI to stakeholder-ready statements

content.title: From CI to stakeholder-ready statements

rows: If target is 300 s, current CI crosses target.

content.notes: Model how to expand each row into full 3–5 sentence writing. Example uncertainty statement: “Using 40 calls from the last two weeks (seconds), the estimated mean handling time is 312 s. A 95% confidence interval is 297 to 327 s, meaning that if we repeated this sampling process many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean for this team and period. The interval width (about 30 s) suggests moderate uncertainty; reporting to the nearest second is appropriate.” Example risk statement: “Against a 300 s target, the point estimate exceeds target and the CI spans both sides, so we cannot be confident the true mean meets the target. Results may be affected by repeated calls per agent and potential day-to-day variation. Mitigations: collect a larger, stratified sample across shifts and compute per-agent averages to reduce clustering effects.” Probing question: “What decision threshold exists in your workplace, and does your interval cross it?”

slides.title: Worked example 2: simulation-based uncertainty

content.title: Worked example 2: simulation-based uncertainty
content: Use when formula CIs are hard or assumptions are weak
Define input distributions (e.g., demand ~ Poisson, time ~ logn)
Run many trials (e.g., 10,000) to simulate outcome metric
Summarise with median and 5th–95th percentiles
Check sensitivity: which inputs drive output spread most?
Report limits: distributions are assumptions, not facts
content.notes: Simulation (Monte Carlo) is useful for combined uncertainty: for instance, monthly cost = demand × cost per item, where both vary. Give a mini-example: assume daily demand ~ Poisson(λ=120) and handling time ~ Lognormal with mean around 312 s; simulate staffing hours required and compute the 90% interval. In Excel, this can be done with RAND(), inverse CDF functions, and a data table; in Python with numpy.random and pandas summarisation. Emphasise that simulation outputs depend heavily on distribution choice and independence assumptions. Probing questions: “Which distribution did you choose and why?” “What real data would you collect next to validate the assumed distribution?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Pick a workplace metric: mean, proportion, or diff in means
Compute a 90% or 95% CI; show all inputs and units
Write a 3–5 sentence uncertainty statement (plain language)
Complete 3 rows in your Assumptions & Limitations log
Create one chart: estimate with CI/quantile bars and labels
Reflect: what decision changes if CI widens by 20%?
content.notes: Encourage learners to use their capstone dataset if available; otherwise, invent a small realistic dataset and state it is illustrative. For the chart, suggest an error-bar plot or a bar with whiskers; the key is correct labelling (confidence level, units, timeframe). For reflection, push beyond mechanics: wide intervals might justify more data collection, segmentation, or a conservative decision. Common misconception: treating the CI width as a ‘mistake’; it is information about data variability and sample size. Probing question: “What is the cheapest next piece of data you could collect that would reduce decision risk most?”

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
leftColumn: Supports MOD108: uncertainty + traceable outputs
Use in final report: CI/simulation + risk statement
Attach: workflow evidence and assumptions log
Use MCQs to check method selection and wording
rightColumn: Mistake: wrong CI type (e.g., z instead of t)
Mistake: CI stated without population/time window
Mistake: independence assumed despite clustering

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: A CI quantifies plausible values given a sampling method
Correct interpretation uses repeat-sampling, not 95% probability
Method choice must match metric, data conditions, and n
Reproducible workflows separate inputs, methods, and outputs

slides.title: Reproducible Excel or Python workbook for decisions

content.title: Reproducible Excel or Python workbook for decisions
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project | Lesson 6 | 1h 30m
content.notes: Position this lesson as a capstone skill: making your analysis rerunnable, auditable, and decision-ready. Emphasise that in workplace settings the main risk is not complex maths; it is untraceable logic, hidden assumptions, and outputs that cannot be reproduced when data updates. Explain that today’s focus is on building an end-to-end workflow (Excel or Python) that survives handover, review, and re-run. Prompt: “If someone reopened your file in 3 months, could they reproduce your numbers without asking you questions?”

slides.title: Orientation: what you will build and submit

content.title: Orientation: what you will build and submit
content: Build end-to-end workflow; pass a restart-and-run test
Create Assumptions & Limitations log (≥6 linked entries)
Implement ≥3 quality checks and record results centrally
Write 1-page technical report OR notebook narrative
Create 5-slide deck for non-specialists with a decision
Revise using ≥5 feedback items and log changes
content.notes: Explain how to use the lesson: (1) skim the framework slides, (2) implement the patterns in your own workbook/notebook, (3) run the restart-and-run test, then (4) produce the two communication outputs (technical + non-specialist). Clarify what “linked entries” means: each assumption should point to where it is applied (cell range, named range, tab, code function, or notebook section). Stress that quality checks are not optional ‘nice-to-haves’; they are evidence that your outputs are safe to act on. Probing question: “Which step in your current workflow would break if the raw data changed shape or units?”

slides.title: Reproducibility: the restart-and-run test

content.title: Reproducibility: the restart-and-run test
content: Reproducible = rerun from raw inputs to outputs, unchanged
No hard-coded intermediate values in formulas or code
One-click or one-command run path is clearly documented
All parameters live in a visible, editable place
Restart-and-run: close, reopen, rerun; outputs match
Evidence: timestamped run log and saved outputs
content.notes: Define reproducibility in practical terms: another person (or you, later) can generate the same results using the same raw data and documented settings. Explain that hard-coding often appears as ‘quick fixes’: typing totals over formulas, copy-pasting values to “freeze” them, or editing code outputs by hand. In Excel, this often hides in overwritten cells, untracked filters, or manual sorting. In Python, it shows up as undocumented data cleaning steps done interactively without saving code. Ask: “Where in your file do you currently ‘just type the answer’ to make it work?” Misconception to challenge: ‘If the number is correct once, it is correct.’ Correctness must be repeatable.

slides.title: A simple structure for workbook or notebook

content.title: A simple structure for workbook or notebook
content.notes: Walk through the layers as an engineering-style pipeline. Emphasise separation of concerns: inputs should not depend on downstream calculations; transformation should be deterministic; model logic should be transparent and testable; reporting should not contain hidden calculations. Excel guidance: use separate tabs, consistent naming, and avoid mixing raw data with formulas. Python guidance: use clear sections/cells, functions, and keep raw data immutable (read-only) while creating derived frames. Probing question: “If an auditor asked ‘where did this figure come from?’, could you point to one layer and trace it forward?” Common misconception: ‘More tabs = more structure.’ Structure is about clear responsibilities and minimal back-and-forth dependencies.

slides.title: Assumptions & limitations log: what it must contain

content.title: Assumptions & limitations log: what it must contain
content: Minimum 6 entries; include units, sources, rounding rules
State whether each item is an assumption or limitation
Explain why it is reasonable (or why it is a constraint)
Link to where it is used (cells, named ranges, functions)
Note direction of impact if wrong (over/under estimate)
Include date and owner for each entry
content.notes: Explain the difference: assumptions are chosen simplifications (e.g., constant rate), limitations are constraints you cannot remove (e.g., missing data, sensor accuracy). Give mini-examples: an assumption could be “electricity tariff constant over month”; a limitation could be “meter readings are only daily, not hourly.” Demonstrate what ‘link’ looks like: in Excel, a hyperlink to a cell/range or named range; in Python, a comment referencing a function name or notebook section heading. Probing questions: “Which assumption is doing the most work in your model?” and “If this were wrong, what decision would change?” Misconception: listing assumptions is enough; you must show where they enter the maths.

slides.title: Audit checks: build trust into your workflow

content.title: Audit checks: build trust into your workflow
content: Unit checks: confirm conversions and consistent units
Reasonableness bounds: flag impossible or extreme values
Reconciliation totals: inputs vs outputs must balance
Sensitivity checks: vary key parameters and note impact
Record checks in a dedicated sheet or notebook section
Fail loud: clear pass/fail and action taken
content.notes: Position checks as lightweight tests that prevent expensive errors. Provide examples: unit check—kWh vs Wh; reasonableness—negative headcount, efficiency >100%; reconciliation—sum of departmental totals equals grand total; sensitivity—±10% demand to see cost range. Stress that checks must be recorded, not just ‘eyeballed’: show date/time, result, and whether it blocks reporting. In Excel, use conditional formatting and a “Checks” tab with PASS/FAIL cells referencing formulas. In Python, use assertions, summary tables, or test cells that raise clear errors. Ask: “Which single check would have caught the biggest mistake you’ve ever made in a spreadsheet?”

slides.title: Decision outputs: technical vs non-specialist

content.title: Decision outputs: technical vs non-specialist
content: Technical: 1 page method, data, units, results, limits
Non-specialist: 5 slides focused on decision and impact
Include at least 1 visual with labelled units
State uncertainty: CI, error bars, or sensitivity range
Make a recommendation and the conditions for it to hold
Keep traceability: figure/table numbers link to outputs
content.notes: Explain the communication principle: different audiences need different levels of detail, but both need clarity, units, and uncertainty. Offer a structure for the 1-page technical note: problem statement; data and preparation; method; results; checks performed; limitations; recommendation. For the 5-slide deck: (1) decision question, (2) key results, (3) method at a high level, (4) visual + uncertainty, (5) recommendation + risks/next steps. Misconception: “Uncertainty makes us look weak.” In reality, uncertainty increases credibility and supports risk-aware decisions. Probing question: “What could a manager do differently tomorrow based on your outputs?”

slides.title: Implementation patterns: Excel vs Python

content.title: Implementation patterns: Excel vs Python
leftColumn: Excel: named ranges for parameters
Excel: tables for raw and tidy data
Excel: pivot/chart outputs pull from tidy table
Excel: Checks tab with PASS/FAIL cells
rightColumn: Python: config dict/YAML for parameters
Python: tidy dataframe from pure functions
Python: plots from final dataframe, no manual edits
Python: assertions + saved check summary
content.notes: Clarify that the goal is the same in both tools: a deterministic pipeline with explicit parameters and recorded checks. Expand with practical tips: in Excel, protect raw data ranges, avoid volatile functions if possible, and document refresh steps (e.g., Power Query refresh). In Python, separate data loading, cleaning, modelling, and reporting into functions; avoid ‘stateful’ notebook behaviour by restarting kernel and running all cells. Probing question: “Which tool better matches your workplace context and who needs to maintain it after you?” Misconception: Python is automatically reproducible; it is not if you rely on manual notebook edits or hidden environment dependencies.

slides.title: Worked example: passing the restart-and-run test

content.title: Worked example: passing the restart-and-run test
content: Step 1: move all inputs to a single Parameters area
Step 2: rebuild calculations to reference parameters only
Step 3: generate outputs from final model tables only
Step 4: add a Run log: date, user, data version, result
Step 5: restart (close/reopen or kernel restart) and rerun
Step 6: confirm outputs match and checks are all PASS
content.notes: Narrate a concrete walkthrough: take a workbook that currently has typed-in totals and scattered assumptions. Consolidate parameters (e.g., VAT rate, conversion factors, target thresholds) into one location. Then refactor formulas so that parameters are referenced by name (Excel) or config variables (Python). Explain how to build a run log: in Excel, a cell with NOW() and a manual “Run complete” checkbox; in Python, write a small cell that saves a timestamp and git commit hash if available. Emphasise what ‘match’ means: identical within rounding rules—so ensure rounding is itself an explicit assumption. Ask: “If results differ after rerun, where is the hidden state?” Common causes: filters left on, manual sorting, random seeds, or cached query results.

slides.title: Worked example: assumptions and checks (mini-log)

content.title: Worked example: assumptions and checks (mini-log)
content.notes: Use this mini-log to show the expected level of specificity. Explain that ‘Where used’ must be a traceable pointer: a named range like Tariff_GBP_per_kWh, a function like compute_cost(), or a cell block like Model!E5:E120. Probing question: “Which of your assumptions are actually data quality rules?” Misconception: limitations cannot be quantified; many can be expressed as an uncertainty range that flows through to the result.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: build your evidence pack

content.title: Practice and reflection: build your evidence pack
content: Draft your pipeline map: Inputs → Transform → Model → Report
Create Assumptions & Limitations log with 6 linked entries
Add 3 checks and capture PASS/FAIL plus notes
Run restart-and-run and screenshot or export run log
Write a 5-sentence method summary for your technical note
Complete the two MCQ quizzes to self-check understanding
content.notes: Set clear practice outputs: learners should leave with artefacts, not just ideas. Suggest a timebox: 20 minutes to restructure, 20 minutes for assumptions/log links, 15 minutes for checks, 10 minutes for restart-and-run, and the remainder for drafting communication. Encourage learners to treat screenshots/exports as evidence (useful in submission and peer review). Provide reflection prompts: “Which check is most convincing to a sceptical reviewer?” and “Which assumption, if challenged, would you need to replace with better data?” Point them to the formative MCQs as a diagnostic: if they miss uncertainty/validation questions, they should revisit the decision outputs slide.

content.title: Assessment connection: how this supports MOD108
content: Supports capstone submission: model + evidence of reliability
Markers look for traceability: data → logic → outputs
Common error: manual fixes that break reproducibility
Common error: assumptions listed but not linked to use
Common error: visuals without units or uncertainty statement
Common error: no change log showing response to feedback
content.notes: Explain explicitly what quality looks like in assessment terms: not just a correct answer, but a robust method that can be checked. Give examples of weak vs strong evidence: weak—“I checked it looks right”; strong—Checks tab with thresholds, results, and actions taken. Probing question: “If your result changed after applying feedback, did you explain why and whether the decision recommendation changed?”

slides.title: Summary: what to implement today

content.title: Summary: what to implement today
content: Design a clear pipeline from raw data to decision outputs
Make assumptions explicit, linked, and impact-aware
Add checks that fail loudly and are recorded as evidence

slides.title: Audience-first technical writing for non-specialists

content.title: Audience-first technical writing for non-specialists
content: Start with the decision to be made, not the method
Use plain language; define terms only when needed
Lead with quantified results (with units) and implications
Separate evidence, assumptions, and judgement calls
Include one clear recommendation with next step
Match detail to stakeholder risk and time constraints
content.notes: Frame ‘non-specialist’ as time-poor and outcome-focused, not incapable. Explain that method detail belongs in appendices/logs, while the main narrative should answer: What is happening? So what? Now what? Give mini-examples: replace ‘heteroscedastic residuals’ with ‘errors increase at higher volumes, so forecasts are less reliable there’. Highlight a common misconception: adding more equations makes work more credible to stakeholders; often it reduces credibility if it obscures the decision. Probing questions: ‘What is the stakeholder afraid of getting wrong?’ and ‘Which single number would they quote in a meeting?’

slides.title: Executive summary structure (150–250 words)

content.title: Executive summary structure (150–250 words)
content: Problem: context + decision + success metric
Key findings: 2–4 quantified results with units
Interpretation: what the numbers mean for the decision
Recommendation: action, scale, and timeframe if relevant

slides.title: Mini-deck narrative: context → evidence → recommendation

content: Slide 1: context, objective, decision question

slides.title: Audit-ready calculation log (traceability)

content.title: Audit-ready calculation log (traceability)
content: Record inputs, sources, and version/date
State assumptions and why they are reasonable

content.notes: Define ‘audit-ready’ as reproducible and defensible, not bureaucratic. Explain that the log can be spreadsheet notes, a separate tab, or a short appendix—what matters is traceability. Highlight rounding pitfalls: rounding intermediate values can materially change totals—recommend rounding at presentation stage, not within chained calculations. Probing question: ‘If you left the organisation, could someone rerun your numbers next month?’

slides.title: Uncertainty using confidence intervals and distributions

content.title: Uncertainty using confidence intervals and distributions
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project | Lesson 8 | 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners to Lesson 8, which focuses on expressing uncertainty in a way that is both mathematically defensible and workplace-auditable. Position this lesson as a bridge between “getting an answer” and “communicating decision-grade evidence”.

Probing questions to open with:
- When you report a single number at work, what could go wrong?
- Who might challenge your result, and what would they ask to see?

Common misconception to surface early: a 95% confidence interval (CI) is not a “guarantee” that the true value is inside the interval in 95% of cases for this specific dataset; it is about the long-run performance of the method under stated assumptions.

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Compute and report a 95% CI with assumptions stated
Build an auditable workbook/notebook: Inputs→Outputs trace
Compare CI vs simulation/distribution for uncertainty
Write a risk statement with mitigations for non-specialists
Self-audit and fix rounding, units, assumptions, reproducibility
How to use: study → build → run checks → complete MCQs
content.notes:
Explain that the lesson is designed for self-paced study: read the concepts, then implement them in Excel or Python, then use checks to find and fix issues.

Clarify what “auditable note” means: a short write-up that a colleague (or assessor) can follow without asking you questions. It should name the metric, the method, the data window, assumptions, and the computed interval.

Mini-example: “Average call handling time last week: mean 8.4 min, 95% CI [7.7, 9.1], assuming independent calls and approximately normal sampling distribution (n=25).”

Probing questions:
- If someone else opens your file, can they reproduce the same CI?
- Can they see where every number came from?

Misconception: “Reproducible” is not just “I saved the file”; it is separation of inputs/logic/outputs and traceable formulas or code.

slides.title: What uncertainty means in workplace metrics

content.title: What uncertainty means in workplace metrics
content.content: A workplace metric from a sample is an estimate, not a fixed truth. Uncertainty summarises how much the estimate could vary with new samples. A CI quantifies this sampling uncertainty under explicit assumptions.
content.notes:
Expand the idea of sampling variability: if you re-sampled a new week of calls, you would not get the same mean or defect rate. The question is “how different could it be, plausibly?”

Link to decision-making: uncertainty should change how confidently you act. A point estimate can be misleading if the uncertainty range crosses a decision threshold.

Mini-example: If the KPI target is defect rate < 5% and you estimate 6% with a wide interval (e.g., 3%–9%), the decision implication is different than a tight interval (e.g., 5.7%–6.3%).

Probing questions:
- What decision threshold exists for your metric?
- Would a plausible range cross that threshold?

Common misconception: CIs address sampling uncertainty, not measurement error, bias, or process changes unless explicitly modelled.

slides.title: Choose the right 95% confidence interval

content.title: Choose the right 95% confidence interval
content.notes:
Explain that the metric type drives the interval choice. For means, the t-interval is standard when population SD is unknown (which is almost always in workplace data).

For proportions, recommend Wilson for robustness, but allow normal approximation with explicit checks (expected successes and failures both at least ~10 is a common rule). Clarify that “defect rate” can mean either a proportion (defective units / units inspected) or a Poisson rate (defects per hour, per 1,000 units, etc.). Learners must define the denominator.

Probing questions:
- Is your denominator “items” or “time/exposure”?
- Are multiple defects per unit possible (suggesting a rate rather than proportion)?

Misconception: treating a rate (defects per hour) as a proportion can produce nonsensical bounds or incorrect standard errors.

slides.title: How a 95% CI is built (and when it fails)

content.title: How a 95% CI is built (and when it fails)
content: Estimate ± critical value × standard error
SE shrinks with n: more data → narrower interval
Assume random sampling or a defensible proxy
Assume independence (watch time series and batching)
Assume model fit: normal/t/Poisson as appropriate
State what is excluded: bias, drift, measurement error
content.notes:
Walk learners through the generic structure: centre (estimate) plus/minus a margin of error. Emphasise that the margin depends on both variability (SD) and sample size.

Discuss independence in practical terms: calls from the same agent in a row, measurements from the same machine shift, or daily totals across time are often autocorrelated.

Mini-example: If you sample 30 consecutive items from a single production run, you have n=30 but may have far fewer “independent pieces of information” because the process conditions are constant.

Probing questions:
- What is the sampling unit: item, batch, day, person?
- What could make observations similar to each other?

Common misconception: “Large n fixes everything.” Large n does not fix bias or non-representative sampling; it can make you confidently wrong.

slides.title: CI vs simulation: what each captures

content.title: CI vs simulation: what each captures
leftColumn: CI: sampling uncertainty for one parameter
Often analytic, quick, and explainable
Best for means/proportions with stable process
Weak on nonlinearity and complex dependencies
rightColumn: Simulation: uncertainty through a full calculation chain
Handles nonlinearity (e.g., costs, queues, ratios)
Can include distributions for inputs and scenarios
Depends on modelling choices; can be mis-specified
content.notes:
Explain that CIs are excellent for “one-step” estimates (mean, proportion, rate). Simulation becomes valuable when the workplace decision uses a formula combining uncertain inputs (e.g., demand × unit cost + overtime penalties).

Give an intuition: a CI tells you where the true mean might be; simulation tells you how the final decision metric (profit, staffing hours, risk of breach) varies after propagating uncertainty.

Probing questions:
- Is your output a simple parameter estimate, or a derived KPI?
- Does your calculation include maxima/minima, thresholds, or ratios?

Common misconceptions:
- Simulation is not automatically “more accurate”; it is only as good as its assumptions.
- A CI does not provide the probability the parameter lies in the interval for your realised data (frequentist interpretation).

slides.title: Risk statement template for non-specialists

content.title: Risk statement template for non-specialists
content: Metric and period: what was measured, where, when
Result with 95% CI: include units and denominator
Practical meaning: link to targets and decision thresholds
Limitations: key assumptions and what is not covered
Mitigations: 2+ actions tied to controllable levers
content.notes:
Teach a simple structure learners can reuse in the capstone. Stress that the audience is non-specialist: avoid statistical jargon without explanation.

Mini-example phrasing:
- “We estimate the defect proportion last month at 6.0% (95% CI: 3.3%–8.7%). If the true rate is near the upper end, we are likely to miss the 5% target. This CI assumes independent inspections and stable process conditions; it does not include measurement error or changes in supplier quality.”

Mitigations must be actionable and controllable, for example:
- increase in-process checks (lever: inspection frequency)
- operator refresher training (lever: process adherence)
- tighten supplier acceptance criteria (lever: incoming quality gates)

Probing questions:
- Which lever can you actually change next week?
- What evidence would show the mitigation is working?

Common misconception: writing a mitigation like “monitor closely” without specifying what will be monitored, how often, and what threshold triggers action.

slides.title: Audit-ready workbook/notebook structure

content.title: Audit-ready workbook/notebook structure
content: Separate tabs/sections: Inputs, Assumptions, Calcs, Outputs
Use named ranges or clearly labelled variables/functions
Unit checks: minutes vs hours, %, per 1,000, per month
Traceability: no hard-coded constants in formulas
Versioning: date-stamped data and change log comments
Outputs: CI, chart, and short auditable note block
content.notes:
Explain the goal: someone else can open your file and verify every step without guessing. For Excel, recommend:
- an Inputs tab with only data and parameter cells
- an Assumptions tab listing distribution choice, independence, sampling method
- a Calcs tab with formulas referencing inputs (avoid typing numbers into formulas)
- an Outputs tab with final results, clearly formatted

For Python, recommend:
- a top cell for imports and a random seed
- functions for CI calculations (e.g., ci_mean_t(x))
- a single “parameters” dictionary for assumptions

Probing questions:
- If I change one input, does the output update automatically?
- Could I identify all assumptions without reading your mind?

Common misconceptions:
- Copy/pasting values into outputs breaks auditability.
- “Hidden” intermediate steps increase error risk; make the chain visible.

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI for a mean (t-interval)

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI for a mean (t-interval)
content: Scenario: mean call time, n=25, x̄=8.4 min, s=1.6
t* for 95% with df=24 is about 2.064
Note assumptions: independent calls; stable process this week
content.notes:
Talk through each step slowly and model “auditable writing”: define each symbol and keep units in every line.

Excel implementation tips:
- mean: AVERAGE(range)
- SD (sample): STDEV.S(range)
- SE: =SD/SQRT(n)
- t*: =T.INV.2T(0.05, n-1)

Python tips (conceptually): compute mean and sample SD; use scipy.stats.t.ppf for t*.

Probing questions:
- What would happen to the CI if n doubled and variability stayed the same?
- If you suspect outliers, what diagnostic would you do before trusting the t-interval?

Common misconceptions:
- Using z=1.96 regardless of sample size and unknown SD.
- Reporting too many decimals; teach sensible rounding (e.g., 2 dp for minutes).

- SD (sample): STDEV.S(range)

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI for a defect proportion

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI for a defect proportion
content: Scenario: 18 defects in 300 items → p̂ = 0.060
Check: n·p̂=18 and n·(1−p̂)=282 (OK for normal approx)
If counts small, use Wilson or exact; state method used
content.notes:
Emphasise that “defect rate” must specify its denominator: here it is a proportion defective per item inspected.

Discuss why the normal approximation can be acceptable here (expected counts not small), but also why Wilson is often preferred in professional settings because it behaves better near 0 and 1.

Excel tips:
- p-hat: =defects/n
- SE: =SQRT(p*(1-p)/n)
- CI: =p ± 1.96*SE

Probing questions:
- If you observed 2 defects in 30 items, would you still use the normal approx?
- How would you phrase this result to avoid overclaiming certainty?

Common misconceptions:
- Reporting CI bounds as percentages without converting (0.033 is 3.3%).
- Forgetting to mention the data period or inspection method.

slides.title: Worked example: Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation

content.title: Worked example: Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation
content: Goal: monthly overtime cost from uncertain demand
Inputs: demand ~ Normal(μ=10,000, σ=800) units
Cost model: overtime = max(0, demand−9,500)×£2.10
Simulate 10,000 months; record overtime each run
Report P50 and P95 (e.g., £420 and £2,520) as a range
Compare: CI is for μ demand; sim is for cost distribution
content.notes:
Explain why simulation is needed: the output is a nonlinear function with a threshold (max(0, …)). A CI for mean demand does not directly tell you the distribution of overtime cost.

Teach good simulation hygiene:
- set a random seed for reproducibility
- keep inputs explicit and justified (why Normal? why σ=800?)
- run enough iterations to stabilise percentiles

Excel approach: use NORM.INV(RAND(), mu, sigma) for demand, compute overtime, copy down many rows, summarise with PERCENTILE.INC.

Python approach: generate random draws, compute overtime array, then np.quantile.

Probing questions:
- What assumption is most fragile here: distribution shape or parameter values?
- If demand cannot go below zero, does Normal still make sense?

Common misconceptions:
- Treating simulated percentiles as “guarantees”.
- Forgetting to label outputs as model-based and assumption-dependent.

slides.title: Practice and reflection

content.title: Practice and reflection
leftColumn: Pick one metric: mean, proportion, or rate
Draft a 95% CI and list 3 assumptions
Add a simulation for one derived KPI (optional)
Write a 5-line risk statement with 2 mitigations
rightColumn: Self-check: units consistent in every line
Self-check: formulas use references, not typed constants
Self-check: rounding is sensible and consistent
Self-check: methods named (t, Wilson, Poisson, sim)
content.notes:
Guide learners to choose a metric from their workplace or a plausible proxy dataset. Encourage them to keep scope small: one metric done well beats many metrics done superficially.

Offer a simple reflection routine:
1) compute the CI
2) interpret it against a threshold
3) write limitations
4) propose mitigations
5) run the self-audit checks and fix issues

Probing questions:
- What would convince an auditor that your inputs are correct?
- Which assumption would you test first if challenged?

Common misconception: learners often write assumptions but do not connect them to the data collection process (e.g., “random sample” without explaining how the sample was obtained).

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD108 capstone: uncertainty + decision narrative
Use the same structure for your final workbook/notebook
Pitfall: CI without assumptions or without a clear denominator
Pitfall: mixed units (%, fraction, per 1,000) in one model
Pitfall: non-reproducible results (manual edits, no seed/log)
Formative MCQs: model traceability; uncertainty and risk
content.notes:
Explicitly connect this lesson to the capstone expectations: assessors look for clear method selection, correct calculations, and credible communication of uncertainty.

Explain how the formative MCQs should be used: not as a memory test, but as a diagnostic for gaps (e.g., confusion between CI interpretation and probability statements).

Probing questions:
- If your result is challenged, what evidence will you show first?
- Where in your model is the “single source of truth” for each input?

Common misconceptions:
- Confusing “defect rate” (Poisson per exposure) with “defect proportion”.
- Reporting a CI but then making a categorical claim (“we meet target”) when the interval crosses the threshold.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: A CI quantifies sampling uncertainty under stated assumptions
Method choice depends on metric type and data conditions
Simulation propagates uncertainty through complex KPIs
Audit-ready builds separate inputs, assumptions, calcs, outputs
Risk statements must link uncertainty to actions and limits
content.notes:
Close by reinforcing that technical correctness and communication quality are equally important in workplace maths. Encourage learners to revisit their model after a break: fresh eyes often catch unit errors and hidden assumptions.

Quick recap questions:
- What does your CI method assume, and is it reasonable?
- What uncertainty does your analysis not include?
- What will you change operationally based on the result?

Final misconception to correct: uncertainty reporting is not a weakness; it is what makes your conclusion credible and decision-ready.

slides.title: MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project — Lesson 9

content.title: MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project — Lesson 9
content.content: A reproducible Excel or Python workbook for workplace decisions (1h 30m)
content.notes: Frame the lesson as a capstone-quality build task: you are not just “getting an answer”, you are producing an artefact that another analyst (or future you) can rerun, audit, and trust. Emphasise Bloom’s “create”: learners will design a reproducible model, checks, visuals, and concise communications. Prompt: “If your manager asked you to rerun this in six months with new data, could you do it in 5 minutes without guessing what you did?” Common misconception: reproducibility equals ‘saving the file’—it actually means separating inputs, making steps explicit, and ensuring outputs regenerate reliably.

slides.title: Orientation: what you will produce and how to study

content.title: Orientation: what you will produce and how to study
content: Build/refactor a reproducible workbook/notebook with traceable steps
Add an assumptions log (≥5) with units and sources
Implement ≥3 integrity checks with actions if checks fail
Create 2 visuals: summary + uncertainty/variation, stakeholder-ready
Write a 1-page tech report and a 5–7 slide results deck
Study loop: watch → build → self-check → MCQs → revise
content.notes: Explain the workflow: first, make the model rerunnable; second, make it trustworthy; third, make it communicable. Clarify what “stakeholder-ready” means: a non-specialist can read the chart and take the correct message without extra decoding. Suggest a practical approach in a 90-minute session: 20 minutes structure, 25 minutes checks, 20 minutes visuals, 15 minutes report/deck outline, 10 minutes review. Point to the formative MCQs as a quick diagnostic: do you understand traceability, validation language, and uncertainty statements? Probing question: “Which part of your current work is least reproducible: inputs, transformations, or reporting?”

slides.title: What “reproducible” means in workplace modelling

content.title: What “reproducible” means in workplace modelling
content: Inputs are separate, clearly labelled, and versioned
All steps are explicit: no hidden manual edits
Outputs regenerate by rerun/recalculate, not copy-paste
Logic is traceable: a reader can follow data → decision
Assumptions and limitations are documented and justified
Results are stable: same inputs give same outputs
content.notes: Expand with concrete examples. In Excel, reproducible means calculations are formula-driven, not dependent on “someone typed a number into an intermediate cell last week”. In Python, it means a notebook runs top-to-bottom from a clean kernel and produces the same tables/figures (including fixed random seeds when relevant). Highlight traceability: the ability to map each output back to the exact inputs and transformation steps. Common misconception: “I can explain it verbally, so it’s traceable.” Traceability must be present in the artefact itself. Probing questions: “Could a colleague audit your model without asking you questions?” and “What would break if an input column name changed?”

slides.title: A clean model architecture (Excel or Python)

content.title: A clean model architecture (Excel or Python)
content.notes: Talk through this as a design pattern rather than a rigid template. In Excel: consider separate tabs (Inputs, Model, Checks, Outputs) with consistent colour-coding for user-entered cells. In Python: separate cells/sections, or better, a script/module for functions plus a notebook for narrative and outputs. Emphasise that checks are a first-class layer, not an afterthought. Probing question: “Where would you place a manual override, if it must exist?” (Answer: in Inputs, explicitly logged, never embedded mid-calculation.) Misconception: checks belong only at the end—actually, checks should sit close to where risk is introduced (e.g., unit conversions, merges, constraints).

slides.title: Assumptions log template (minimum 5 required)

content.title: Assumptions log template (minimum 5 required)
content.notes: Explain the purpose: assumptions are not admissions of weakness; they are what make the model auditable and discussable. Stress units and sources: “unitless” is still a unit, and sources can be a dataset, a policy document, a meeting note, or an engineering specification—just be explicit. Teach learners to include an “impact if wrong” line to prioritise what to validate. Probing questions: “Which assumption, if violated, would change the decision?” and “Which assumptions are most uncertain versus most influential?” Common misconception: assumptions are only for inputs—assumptions also include modelling choices (e.g., linearity, independence, stationarity).

slides.title: Integrity checks: build trust into the model

content.title: Integrity checks: build trust into the model
content: Unit checks: confirm conversions and consistent dimensions
Reasonableness bounds: flag impossible or extreme values
Reconciliation totals: inputs match outputs after transforms
Constraint checks: optimiser/Solver respects limits
Change detection: highlight input schema or parameter shifts
Each check needs: threshold, message, and next action
content.notes: Explain that integrity checks are like automated “sanity tests” for analysis. Give a mini-example: if price is entered in pence but model assumes pounds, margins may be off by 100×—a unit check catches this. For reconciliation: after filtering or joins, totals should match expected counts or sums within tolerance. For optimisation: verify constraints are satisfied in the returned solution and that the solution status is optimal/feasible. Emphasise actions: a check is only useful if it triggers a clear response (stop, investigate, revert data, adjust constraints). Probing question: “If this check fails at 17:00 on deadline day, what exactly would you do?” Misconception: “If Solver returns a number, it must be correct.” Solvers can return infeasible, local, or constraint-violating solutions if poorly configured.

slides.title: Visual 1: a stakeholder-ready summary chart

content.title: Visual 1: a stakeholder-ready summary chart
content: Choose one message: what decision should change and why
Title states the takeaway, not the chart type
Axes include units; currency and time basis are explicit
Caption: data source, period, and key assumptions
Annotate the baseline and the recommended option
Avoid clutter: limit series and use consistent rounding
content.notes: Teach the difference between ‘a chart’ and ‘a decision graphic’. Encourage learners to write the title as a sentence: “Recommended price improves margin by 4.2% vs baseline”. Discuss common errors: missing units, ambiguous time basis (per day vs per month), and overloaded charts with too many categories. Mini-example: a bar chart of profit by scenario with a clear highlight on the recommended scenario and a thin reference line for baseline. Probing questions: “Could a non-specialist repeat your conclusion after 10 seconds?” and “What would you remove if you had to halve the ink?”

slides.title: Visual 2: show uncertainty and variation responsibly

content.title: Visual 2: show uncertainty and variation responsibly
content: Pick a form: CI bars, fan chart, box plot, or tornado chart
State what varies: data noise, parameter uncertainty, scenarios
Label interval meaning (e.g., 95% CI) and method briefly
Include units and the baseline reference for comparison
Write an interpretation sentence for non-specialists
Do not imply certainty: avoid over-precise decimals
content.notes: Explain uncertainty vs variation: uncertainty is about what we do not know (parameters, future demand), variation is dispersion in observed outcomes. Provide mini-examples: (1) confidence interval around mean defect rate; (2) scenario band showing profit range under low/medium/high demand; (3) tornado chart from one-way sensitivity. Stress interpretive language: a 95% CI is about repeated sampling, not “95% chance the true value is inside” unless using a Bayesian credible interval—use careful wording. Probing question: “If your uncertainty band overlaps the baseline, what does that mean for decision confidence?” Misconception: adding an interval makes the model ‘safer’; it must be connected to a decision threshold (risk tolerance).

slides.title: Worked example: refactor to a reproducible build

content.title: Worked example: refactor to a reproducible build
leftColumn: Before: inputs scattered across sheets/cells
Before: hard-coded fixes inside formulas
Before: manual chart edits and pasted results
Before: unclear run order and undocumented steps
rightColumn: After: Inputs tab or config cell, all units visible
After: functions/steps named; no hidden constants
After: outputs linked to model; one-click refresh/rerun
After: README + assumptions + run instructions
content.notes: Walk through a realistic ‘messy workbook/notebook’ pattern and how to refactor without changing the underlying logic (initially). In Excel: consolidate inputs into a single area, use named ranges, separate intermediate calculations, and remove “magic numbers” from formulas by referencing parameter cells. In Python: move parameters to a config section, create functions for repeated steps, and ensure the notebook runs from a clean kernel. Stress the principle: refactor first, then improve the model—otherwise you cannot tell whether results changed due to structure or logic. Probing question: “What is the smallest structural change you can make today that increases reproducibility by 50%?” Common misconception: refactoring is ‘cosmetic’; it directly affects auditability and error rates.

content.title: Worked example: three checks with actions

rows: GBP vs pence; kg vs g

content.notes: Model how to document checks: each has a purpose, a threshold, and a response. For unit checks, suggest explicit conversion cells/functions and a ‘unit expected’ field beside each input. For bounds, stress domain knowledge: what is plausible for your context (e.g., defect rate cannot exceed 1; capacity cannot be negative). For reconciliation, introduce tolerances and reasons for legitimate differences (e.g., removed invalid records) that must be documented. For constraint checks, show that you must verify both (a) solver status and (b) constraint satisfaction numerically. Probing question: “Which check would have caught your last real-world modelling error?” Misconception: conditional formatting alone is a check—it is only a visual flag unless it also triggers investigation and prevents silent use.

Suggest a quick self-check: change an input by 10%—do outputs update correctly and do checks behave sensibly?

content.title: Assessment connection: expectations and pitfalls
leftColumn: Mistake: mixed inputs and formulas in the same cells
Mistake: assumptions missing units or sources
Mistake: charts lack takeaway titles and captions
Mistake: no evidence of revision after feedback

Fix: add assumption table with impact and references
Fix: titles as conclusions; label units; add baseline

content.notes: Connect directly to the capstone deliverables: the model artefact, a one-page report, and a short results deck. Clarify that markers look for reproducibility evidence: can they rerun your work, follow your steps, and see that checks exist and are meaningful? For the report/deck, stress concise structure: method (what you did), results (what you found), assumptions/limitations (what could change the answer), and uncertainty (how confident you are). Probing question: “If I only read your one-page report, would I know what to do next?” Misconception: ‘limitations’ weaken the work; in professional practice, limitations increase credibility when they are specific and bounded.

slides.title: Summary: what good looks like

content.title: Summary: what good looks like
content: Reproducible means rerunnable, traceable, and regenerable outputs
Assumptions must be explicit, sourced, and unit-consistent
Integrity checks detect errors early and specify actions
Visuals must be decision-focused and uncertainty-aware
Revision is part of quality: document improvements from feedback
content.notes: Reinforce that this lesson is about building a professional standard artefact, not just meeting minimum criteria. Encourage learners to keep a simple ‘audit trail’: README, assumptions log, check log, and change log. Close with two reflective prompts: “What is the single highest-risk assumption in your model?” and “Which check would you bet your grade on catching a serious issue?” Common misconception: learners may believe ‘more complexity’ equals ‘more advanced’; emphasise that clarity, validation, and communication are what make work advanced in workplace analytics.

Lesson 10: Produce a concise technical report and slide deck for non-specialists
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
In this lesson you will practise turning model outputs into two professional artefacts used in workplace decision-making: (1) a concise technical report section (Findings + Recommendations) and (2) a short slide deck for non-specialists. The emphasis is on clarity, traceability, and responsible communication of uncertainty and limitations.

As you work, keep asking: “If a decision-maker only read this page or these slides, could they act appropriately, and would they understand what could be wrong?” A common misconception is that communication is a ‘presentation layer’ added at the end; in professional maths work, reporting is part of the analytical method because it makes assumptions, constraints, and uncertainty explicit.

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: By end: draft Findings+Recommendations with 3+ visuals
Include units, assumptions/constraints, and a limitations statement
Build 5–7 slides translating outputs into 2–3 actions
Add slides on uncertainty and on constraints/turning points
Work through: read → draft → QA → revise using rubric
Check learning via the two MCQ quizzes at the end
content.notes:
Treat the objectives as a checklist for your own submission readiness.

When drafting, prioritise: (a) decision relevance (what should change?), (b) evidential support (what output supports it?), and (c) transparency (what assumptions and limits apply?).

Probing questions:
- What decision is your report enabling, and for whom?
- Which numbers are “decision-critical” (if wrong, the decision changes)?
- Which uncertainties are material rather than trivial?

Misconception to avoid: writing everything you did. Your reader needs what you found, what you recommend, and how confident you are—not a full lab notebook.

slides.title: Deliverables and audience expectations

content.title: Deliverables and audience expectations
leftColumn: Technical report: evidence record
Assumptions explicit
Units, methods, and traceability
Limitations stated to avoid over-claim
rightColumn: Slide deck: decision support
Plain language and signposting
2–3 actions with rationale
Uncertainty and constraints made visible
content.notes:
You are producing two related but different products.

The technical report section is for reviewers who may check logic and credibility: it must be auditable (units, assumptions, and limitations are essential). The slide deck is for stakeholders who need to decide: it must be understandable quickly and should avoid technical detail unless it changes the decision.

A useful test: if you swapped the audiences, what would break? Typically:
- A technical report read by non-specialists overwhelms with method and caveats.
- A slide deck read by specialists often lacks evidence detail and traceability.

Probing questions:
- What does this audience already know?
- What do they need to do next?
- What is the risk of misunderstanding?

slides.title: Findings + recommendations: required structure

content.title: Findings + recommendations: required structure
content: Start with the question the project brief asks
State 3–5 findings as quantified, testable statements
Attach each finding to a numbered visual (Figure 1, etc.)
Give recommendations as actions, owners, and time horizon
Justify each recommendation using evidence from findings
Close with assumptions, constraints, and key limitations
content.notes:
A strong Findings section reads like a series of claims that can be checked. For each finding, include: metric, value, unit, timeframe, and comparison point (baseline, target, scenario).

Recommendations should be actionable, not descriptive. “We recommend increasing X by 10% next quarter” is actionable; “X seems important” is not.

Mini-example of a finding:
- “Under Scenario B, mean waiting time increases from 4.2 to 6.1 minutes (+45%), Figure 2.”
Then a recommendation:
- “Add one staff member during 12:00–14:00 to keep mean waiting time <5 minutes.”

Common misconception: treating recommendations as opinions. They must be traceable to evidence and framed within constraints (budget, staffing, policy, data coverage).

slides.title: Visuals, units, assumptions, and limitations

content.title: Visuals, units, assumptions, and limitations
content: Use 3+ visuals: trend, comparison, and uncertainty/sensitivity
Label axes, units, sample size/time window, and scenario
Define assumptions (fixed inputs) and constraints (hard limits)
State limitations: data gaps, model bias, and validity bounds
Apply rounding rules consistently; avoid false precision
Add captions: what to notice and why it matters
content.notes:
Visuals do not ‘speak for themselves’. Your caption should direct attention to the decision-relevant pattern.

Clarify units rigorously. Typical issues include mixing £ and £k, days and weeks, percentages and proportion units, or forgetting “per” (e.g., kWh per day vs total kWh).

Assumptions vs constraints:
- Assumption: a chosen simplification (e.g., “arrival rate constant within each hour”).
- Constraint: a boundary you cannot exceed (e.g., “maximum staffing = 6”).

Limitations should be aligned to your brief. They are not an apology; they are a risk-control mechanism. A high-quality limitation statement also indicates impact (what could change) and mitigation (what you would check next).

Probing questions:
- What would make this visual misleading?
- Which assumptions, if violated, would change the recommendation?

slides.title: Deck design for non-specialists

content.title: Deck design for non-specialists
content: Use a narrative arc: context → evidence → decision → next steps
One message per slide; remove jargon and equations
Translate metrics into meaning (impact, cost, time, risk)
Include one slide on uncertainty (CI, bands, scenario range)
Include one slide on constraints/turning points
Finish with 2–3 recommendations and a clear ask
content.notes:
Non-specialists need an explanation of what numbers mean, not how they were computed.

For uncertainty, choose a format that matches your model:
- Confidence interval for estimated mean/parameter.
- Error bands for forecasts.
- Scenario range if uncertainty is mainly structural or assumption-driven.

For constraints/turning points, show where conclusions change. Examples:
- “If demand grows above 8%, current capacity fails.”
- “Recommendation holds unless the unit cost exceeds £X.”

Common misconception: hiding uncertainty to appear confident. In practice, hiding uncertainty creates decision risk and can damage credibility.

slides.title: Quality assurance checklist (minimum set)

content.title: Quality assurance checklist (minimum set)
content.notes:
QA is not optional: it is part of professional mathematical practice. Your goal is to prevent avoidable errors and make remaining uncertainty explicit.

Focus QA effort on ‘decision-critical’ elements: numbers that drive the recommendation, and any boundaries where the decision changes.

Tolerances: decide what counts as ‘matching’ (e.g., recomputation within rounding tolerance). Document the tolerance if it matters.

Probing questions:
- Which single error would most damage the decision?
- Are you consistent across report, slides, and any appendices?

Common misconception: QA is only proofreading. It includes re-calculation, unit auditing, and checking that claims match evidence.

slides.title: Worked example: build a findings section

content.title: Worked example: build a findings section
content: Step 1: Identify 3 decision metrics from the brief
Step 2: Select 3 visuals that answer those metrics
Step 3: Write each finding as: metric + value + unit + context
Step 4: Link each finding to Figure/Table numbers
Step 5: Add assumptions/constraints that affect interpretation
Step 6: Draft limitations: what may change and likely direction
content.notes:
Imagine your brief asks for: cost impact, service level, and risk.

Step 1: choose metrics such as “weekly cost (£/week)”, “mean waiting time (minutes)”, “probability of breach (%)”.

Step 2: choose visuals to match:
- A comparison bar chart for cost by option.
- A time-series for service level over time.
- An uncertainty band or scenario fan chart for risk.

Step 3: write findings so they can be checked. Avoid vague terms (“significant”, “better”) unless defined.

Example finding template:
- “Option A reduces cost by £12k/year (±£3k), while keeping breaches <5%, Figure 3.”

Limitations should be specific: “Data excludes weekends, so peak-demand effects may be underestimated.” Explain direction where possible.

Misconception to avoid: listing outputs without interpretation. Decision-makers need meaning, not raw values.

slides.title: Worked example: 6-slide decision deck

content.title: Worked example: 6-slide decision deck
content: 1. Context: decision, scope, and what success means
2. What we modelled: inputs, scenarios, and time window
3. Key result: headline metric with a simple visual
4. Uncertainty: CI/bands/range and what it changes
5. Constraints: limits, turning points, and dependencies
6. Recommendations: 2–3 actions, rationale, and next steps
content.notes:
This is a practical ‘default deck’ structure. You may adjust order, but keep the logic: context → evidence → uncertainty/constraints → action.

For Slide 3 (key result), aim for one chart and one sentence that states the implication.

For Slide 4 (uncertainty), make the uncertainty decision-relevant:
- “Even at the upper bound, Option B stays under the risk threshold.”
or
- “If the demand growth exceeds 10%, the recommendation changes.”

For Slide 5 (constraints), include operational limits (capacity, staff), policy constraints, and data coverage. Turning points are especially valuable because they give stakeholders a monitoring trigger.

Common misconception: adding more slides for completeness. The constraint is a feature—prioritise what changes the decision.

slides.title: Worked example: audit log entries (5 minimum)

content.title: Worked example: audit log entries (5 minimum)
content.notes:
An audit log is your traceability record: it shows what you checked, what you found, and what you changed. This protects you and improves the reliability of your submission.

Encourage a habit: every time you fix something, add an entry. Every entry should be specific enough that another person could replicate the check.

Good practice:
- Include versioning (v3, v4) or a stable link reference.
- Record pass/fail honestly; ‘pass’ entries show diligence.

Probing questions:
- Can you demonstrate that your main numbers were independently verified?
- If a stakeholder challenged one figure, could you show the chain of evidence quickly?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
leftColumn: Draft 3 findings using the metric+unit+context pattern
Create 3 visuals with captions that state the takeaway
Write 3 assumptions and 2 constraints tied to your brief
Add a limitations statement with impact and mitigation
rightColumn: Outline a 6-slide deck using the template structure
Draft an uncertainty slide with one sentence: “So what?”
Draft a constraints slide with one turning point trigger
Run QA checklist and log 5 audit entries
content.notes:
Use these prompts as a self-study workflow. If you do not have your own project data available, use a previous assignment dataset or a provided sample model output from earlier lessons.

Reflection questions:
- Which finding is most likely to be questioned, and why?
- What is your ‘monitoring trigger’ (turning point) that indicates the decision should be revisited?
- Are your recommendations feasible under stated constraints?

Link to formative checks (do after drafting):
- Short Quiz: Integrated Model Build, Traceability and Decision Outputs.
- MCQ Knowledge Check: Uncertainty, Validation and Risk Statements.

Common misconception: believing that adding more caveats improves quality. The goal is relevant caveats that affect interpretation or action.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD108 capstone: report section + stakeholder deck
Common error: missing units or mismatched scales across outputs
Common error: recommendations not actionable or not evidenced
Common error: uncertainty hidden or described vaguely
Common error: constraints/limits not stated or not decision-linked
Common error: no QA record, so results are not auditable
content.notes:
Your capstone will be judged not only on correctness but on decision usefulness and professional transparency.

When reviewing your draft, look for alignment:
- Does each recommendation map to one or more findings?
- Does each finding map to a visual or a computed result?
- Do uncertainty and limitations affect the recommendation wording?

Misconception to avoid: “If my model is correct, I do not need limitations.” All models have validity boundaries; stating them demonstrates competence.

Practical tip: use a final ‘consistency pass’ across all artefacts—report, slides, and any appendices—checking that the same numbers and units appear everywhere.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Write findings as checkable claims with units and visual links
Make recommendations actionable, evidenced, and constraint-aware
Communicate uncertainty and turning points explicitly in the deck
Apply QA systematically and keep an audit log for traceability
content.notes:
If you remember one principle: make it easy for someone else to verify what you did and to act appropriately on what you found.

Before you finish, ask yourself:
- Could a non-specialist repeat back the recommendation accurately?
- Could a technical reviewer trace each headline number to a source?
- Have you avoided false precision and over-confident language?

A strong submission is not the one with the most content; it is the one with the clearest decision story, supported by transparent evidence.

content.content:

content.notes: In this lesson we move from producing single “best estimates” to producing decision-ready statements that include uncertainty. In workplace settings, uncertainty is not a weakness; it is essential context for risk, prioritisation, and stakeholder communication. Encourage learners to keep a running definition of: metric, sample, population, variability, and uncertainty. Remind them that the capstone expects evidence of traceability and diligence checks—not just an answer.

slides.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson
content: Goal: quantify uncertainty and communicate risk clearly
Watch/read: concepts and method choices (CI, fit, simulation)
Practice: build a reproducible workbook/notebook
Check: run diligence checks and document outcomes
Quiz: model traceability and uncertainty statements
Output: a stakeholder-ready risk statement with mitigations
content.notes: Guide learners through a simple workflow: (1) select an uncertainty method appropriate to the metric and data, (2) build a transparent model structure that can be rerun, (3) validate with diligence checks, (4) communicate uncertainty in plain language with limitations and mitigations. Ask: “Who will act on your results, and what decision will they make?” This keeps uncertainty analysis tied to decisions rather than mathematics alone.

slides.title: Uncertainty in workplace metrics

content.title: Uncertainty in workplace metrics
content: A sample estimate is not the same as the true process value
Uncertainty comes from randomness, measurement, and modelling
Confidence interval: range of plausible values at a confidence level
Distribution: model for variability of the metric or drivers
Simulation: propagate uncertainty through a calculation chain
Aim: support decisions, not to eliminate uncertainty
content.notes: Emphasise the distinction between variability (natural spread in data) and uncertainty (how sure we are about an estimate). A common misconception is that a 95% CI means “95% of data fall in this interval”; correct it: it is about the parameter estimate across repeated sampling. Probe: “If you had double the sample size, what happens to your interval width, and why?” Tie to workplace metrics: defect rate, cycle time, cost per unit, waiting times.

slides.title: Choosing an uncertainty method

content.title: Choosing an uncertainty method
content.notes: Walk through selection logic. Analytical CIs are efficient but rely on assumptions (normality, independence, constant variance). Distribution fitting is useful for skewed operational data (cycle times often lognormal/gamma), but can be misleading if the process has mixtures or truncation. Monte Carlo is powerful for end-to-end models but can hide errors unless traceability is strong; always fix a random seed for reproducibility. Bootstrap is a pragmatic fallback when theory is unclear, but it still assumes the observed sample reflects the underlying process. Probing question: “Which method would you trust for n=12 cycle times with a long right tail, and why?”

slides.title: 95% CI: what you must state

content.title: 95% CI: what you must state
content: Metric definition and units (e.g., minutes, %, defects per 100)
Sampling frame and independence assumptions
Distribution used (normal, t, binomial, etc.)
CI method (Wald, Wilson, t-based, bootstrap, etc.)
Rounding rules aligned to measurement resolution
Interpretation: parameter uncertainty, not individual outcomes
content.notes: Explain that the same “95% CI” label can hide different methods with different reliability. For proportions, highlight that the simple Wald interval can perform poorly when p is near 0/1 or n is small; Wilson or exact methods are often better. For means, clarify when to use z vs t: t is standard when population SD is unknown. Encourage learners to record rounding: e.g., cycle time measured to nearest 0.1 min, so report CI to 0.1 min; defect rates may be reported per 1,000 units. Ask: “If your data are in seconds but stakeholders use minutes, where can conversion errors creep in?”

slides.title: Reproducible model structure

content.title: Reproducible model structure
leftColumn: Inputs: raw data, source, date, filters
Assumptions: distributions, priors, exclusions
Calculations: formulas, code, intermediate tables
Outputs: charts, CI results, risk statement
rightColumn: Parameter table with named cells / constants
Formula map or cell tracing notes
Versioned code cells with fixed random seed
One-click rerun: refresh + regenerate outputs
content.notes: Explain that reproducibility is an assessment requirement and a professional standard. In Excel, this often means separate tabs and named ranges; avoid hard-coded constants inside formulas. In Python, this means a notebook/script with clear sections and a requirements note (library versions). Stress transparency: someone else should be able to follow how inputs become outputs. Common misconception: “A clean-looking dashboard is enough.” It is not—markers look for traceability, logs, and the ability to reproduce identical results. Probe: “If I change one input value, can I see exactly which outputs change and why?”

slides.title: Diligence checks to document

content.title: Diligence checks to document
content: Units check: consistent units across all steps and charts
Reasonableness check: compare to baseline or known ranges
Sensitivity check: vary key inputs and note output change
Spot-check: compute one case by hand or with a second tool
Data check: missing values, outliers, duplicates, time order
Record: what you checked, outcome, and any fixes made
content.notes: Frame diligence checks as risk controls against silent model failure. Units errors are common in operational data (seconds vs minutes, per shift vs per day). Reasonableness checks can use historical averages, physical constraints, or process capability limits. Sensitivity checks help identify which inputs matter; this supports mitigation planning. Spot-checking can be as simple as verifying one CI bound using an online calculator or alternate method. Ask: “What would be a ‘too good to be true’ result for your metric, and how would you detect it?”

slides.title: Worked example 1: defect rate CI (proportion)

content.title: Worked example 1: defect rate CI (proportion)
content: Scenario: 18 defects in 400 units; estimate defect rate
Point estimate: p̂ = 18/400 = 4.5%
Choose CI: Wilson 95% (better than Wald at low p)
Report: CI in % and defects per 1,000 units
Document: independence, stable process, random sample
Diligence: compare to last month’s defect rate range
content.notes: Teach the workflow: define metric (defects per unit), compute p-hat, choose method, compute CI, interpret. Explain why Wilson is preferred: it avoids negative lower bounds and has better coverage for small/medium samples. If learners use Python, they can use statsmodels proportion_confint(method='wilson'). In Excel, Wilson can be implemented with a parameter table (z, n, p-hat) and formulas; if learners use a normal approximation, require them to justify that np and n(1-p) are sufficiently large and to note the limitation. Probing question: “What process change could violate independence (e.g., batch defects), and what would that do to your CI?”

slides.title: Worked example 2: mean cycle time CI (t-based)

content.title: Worked example 2: mean cycle time CI (t-based)
content: Scenario: n=25 cycle times; mean=12.4 min; s=3.1 min
Assume approx normal or n large; use t with df=24
Report: 12.4 min (95% CI: 11.1 to 13.7 min)
Rounding: to 0.1 min if measurement is to 0.1 min
content.notes: Walk learners through each symbol and why it appears. Explain degrees of freedom and why t is wider than z for smaller n. Address skew: cycle times often have right tails; a t-based CI can be acceptable if the sample is not extremely skewed, but learners should check a histogram/QQ plot and state limitations. In Excel, a common approach is to compute t-critical via T.INV.2T(0.05, df). In Python: scipy.stats.t.ppf and standard error. Probing question: “If your data include two very long delays due to breakdowns, do they represent the same process? What are defensible options (keep, exclude with rule, separate process)?”

slides.title: Worked example 3: Monte Carlo with a fixed seed

content.title: Worked example 3: Monte Carlo with a fixed seed
content: Goal: P(cycle time > 15 min) given uncertain inputs
Fit a distribution (e.g., lognormal) or use empirical sample
Set seed for reproducibility (e.g., seed=10811)
Simulate N=10,000 runs; record output each run
Summarise: mean, 95% interval, and exceedance probability
Validate: compare simulated CI to t-based CI for consistency
content.notes: Explain that Monte Carlo turns uncertain inputs into an output distribution, enabling probability statements (e.g., chance of breaching an SLA). Stress two critical practices: (1) fixed seed so reruns match, (2) separation of distribution parameters from code so assumptions are visible. Discuss fit diagnostics briefly: visual fit (QQ plot), and that “best fit” does not guarantee correct process representation. Highlight convergence: N=10,000 is typical, but learners should check stability by repeating with N=20,000 and comparing key outputs. Probing question: “If your exceedance probability changes from 8% to 14% when you change the distribution family, what do you tell stakeholders?”

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Pick one metric: defect rate, mean time, or throughput
Build Inputs/Assumptions/Calculations/Outputs structure
Compute an analytical 95% CI with stated assumptions
Try a second method (fit, bootstrap, or Monte Carlo)
Run 3 checks: units, reasonableness, sensitivity
Draft a 3–6 sentence risk statement with 2 mitigations
content.notes: Encourage learners to use their own capstone data if available; otherwise, generate a small realistic dataset and clearly label it as synthetic. For the second method, suggest a practical pairing: t-based CI vs bootstrap CI for means, or Wilson CI vs bootstrap CI for proportions, or analytical CI vs Monte Carlo if there is a formula chain. For sensitivity, propose a simple ±10% variation of key parameters and a short note on which input dominates. Probing questions: “Which assumption is most fragile?” and “Which mitigation would reduce the biggest source of uncertainty (more data, better measurement, process stabilisation)?”

slides.title: MOD108 Capstone: Reproducible model deliverables

content.title: MOD108 Capstone: Reproducible model deliverables
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project
Lesson 12 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Introduce the lesson as the point where learners turn an analysis into a reproducible artefact that someone else can run without “invisible” steps. Emphasise the capstone context: markers and workplace stakeholders value repeatability, traceability, and clear communication as much as the final number. Set expectations: learners will leave with a model that runs end-to-end (Excel Refresh/Calculate or Python Run All), includes explicit assumptions, quantifies uncertainty with one confidence interval, and produces a short summary plus a small slide deck. Probing question: “If you were on annual leave, could your manager rerun your model tomorrow and get the same outputs?” Common misconception to surface early: reproducible does not mean complex—often it means simpler, more transparent structure.

slides.title: Orientation: objectives and learning loop

content.title: Orientation: objectives and learning loop
leftColumn: Build a 2-click end-to-end model (Excel/Python)
Document ≥6 assumptions + link to outputs
Create and interpret 1 confidence interval
Produce summary + mini-deck with visuals
Apply feedback and log ≥3 improvements
rightColumn: 1) Watch/read the steps and templates
2) Implement in your own project file
3) Run checks: trace, validate, label
4) Take MCQs to confirm understanding
5) Revise using change log entries
content.notes: Walk through the two columns: what learners will produce (left) and how they will work (right). Clarify that “2-click” is a practical standard: the model should run from raw inputs to final outputs without manual copy/paste, re-filtering, or hidden recalculations. For assumptions, explain that the goal is not to “cover yourself” but to make the model interpretable and auditable. For the confidence interval, remind learners it is an uncertainty statement about an estimated quantity, not a guarantee about single outcomes. Probing questions: “Where would a new user start?” and “What could they misinterpret if units or time period are missing?” Misconception: learners often think documentation is separate from the model; instead, it must be embedded and cross-referenced.
