slides.title: Reproducibility: what it means in practice

content.title: Reproducibility: what it means in practice
content: Same inputs + same run steps → same outputs
No hidden steps: no manual edits after running
Inputs, logic, outputs clearly separated
One-button run: Refresh/Calculate or Run All
Versioned file with a dated change log
content.notes: Define reproducibility operationally: a colleague can open the file, press the run action, and regenerate the outputs. Explain “hidden steps” with examples: manually sorting before a pivot updates, copying values from a web page, hard-coding a number that came from a filter, or running cells out of order in a notebook. Stress separation of concerns: inputs (raw + parameters), logic (transformations, formulas, model), outputs (tables, charts, decisions). Probing question: “If a stakeholder disputes the result, can you show exactly where it came from?” Common misconception: “It works on my machine” counts as reproducible—explain environment dependencies (Excel add-ins, Python package versions, file paths).

slides.title: A simple workbook/notebook architecture

content.title: A simple workbook/notebook architecture
content.notes: Explain that this structure is deliberately generic so it fits both Excel and Python. In Excel, these layers might map to separate sheets (e.g., Inputs, Calc, Output, Assumptions). In Python, map to notebook sections or scripts (e.g., 01_load, 02_clean, 03_model, 04_report). For each layer, give one concrete check: Inputs—confirm units and time period; Transform—reconcile row counts before/after joins; Model—test extreme values; Outputs—ensure axes and units; Audit—include a 'How to run' cell or box. Probing question: “Where would you place a manual override if it is genuinely required, and how would you flag it?” Misconception: adding more tabs or code automatically improves rigour; too many layers can hide errors unless checks exist.

slides.title: Assumptions and limitations: minimum standard

content.title: Assumptions and limitations: minimum standard
content: Units and measurement definition (e.g., mins, £/unit)
Data source and extraction date/version
Time period covered and forecast horizon
Constraints and boundary conditions
Rounding rule and presentation precision
Known limitations and when not to use results
content.notes: Clarify the difference: assumptions are choices you make to complete the model; limitations are reasons the model may fail or mislead in certain contexts. Give mini-examples: a demand model assumes stationarity over the last 12 weeks; a defect-rate estimate assumes independent observations; an optimisation assumes capacity constraints are fixed. Stress cross-referencing: each major output should point to relevant assumptions (e.g., a footnote: “Assumptions A2, A4 apply”). Probing questions: “Which assumption, if wrong, would change the decision?” and “Is the rounding rule applied consistently across tables and charts?” Common misconceptions: listing vague statements (“data is accurate”) and forgetting to include time period, which is often the most material assumption.

slides.title: Confidence intervals: build and interpret one

content.title: Confidence intervals: build and interpret one
content.notes: Teach CI interpretation carefully: a 95% CI is about the procedure’s long-run performance, not the probability the true mean is in this specific interval (unless adopting a Bayesian frame, which we are not here). Provide a plain-language script: “Based on our sample of n=40 jobs, we estimate mean cycle time at 12.4 minutes; a 95% CI is 11.6 to 13.2 minutes, meaning values in this range are plausible for the true average under our sampling assumptions.” Highlight the key distinction: CIs are for parameters (e.g., mean defect rate), not for predicting the next item (prediction intervals). Probing questions: “What is your sampling unit?” and “Are there seasonal effects that violate the sampling assumption?” Common misconception: reporting too many decimals—link back to rounding rules and stakeholder readability.

slides.title: Decision outputs and visuals: communicate clearly

content.title: Decision outputs and visuals: communicate clearly
content: State the decision: price, plan, or quality conclusion
Show 1–2 key visuals, not every chart you made
Label axes, units, time period, and sample size
Add a limitation/uncertainty statement on outputs
Keep outputs stable: no manual rearranging post-run
content.notes: Frame outputs as decision-support: the model exists to recommend or compare options. Explain what “stable outputs” means: charts and tables should update automatically when inputs change; avoid manual formatting that breaks on refresh. Provide examples of suitable visuals: line chart for demand over time with CI band; bar chart comparing options with error bars; scatter plot for relationship diagnostics. Stress audience: a non-specialist should be able to read a chart without verbal explanation. Probing question: “If someone only reads your output page, what could they misunderstand?” Misconception: more visuals implies better analysis—often it signals lack of prioritisation. Encourage learners to annotate the one key limitation directly on the figure or under it.

slides.title: Peer feedback and change log: make improvements visible

content.title: Peer feedback and change log: make improvements visible
content: Use a short rubric: clarity, correctness, traceability
Capture issues as actions, not vague comments
Implement ≥3 improvements and re-run end-to-end
Record: what changed, why, and what it affected
Keep older versions or use file naming conventions
content.notes: Explain structured feedback: it is not about preferences but about criteria that affect validity and usability. Offer an example rubric prompt: “Can you trace this output back to inputs in under 2 minutes?” or “Are units consistent everywhere?” For solo learners, present self-review as if they are a reviewer: run from a fresh open, follow the run steps, and see if anything breaks. Describe a simple change log format: date, change, reason, impacted outputs, retest result. Probing question: “Which change most reduces the risk of a wrong decision?” Common misconception: only logging big changes—small fixes (units, labels, rounding) often matter most for stakeholder interpretation.

slides.title: Worked example: Excel end-to-end build

content.title: Worked example: Excel end-to-end build
content: Inputs sheet: raw table + named parameter cells
Transform: Power Query clean steps, no manual edits
Model: formulas or Solver linked to named ranges
Outputs: dashboard with slicers, labels, limitation note
Run test: Data > Refresh All, then Calculate
content.notes: Talk through a realistic Excel workflow. Inputs: keep raw data in an Excel Table, avoid merged cells, and store parameters (e.g., cost per hour, target service level) as named cells with units in adjacent labels. Transform: use Power Query for cleaning so steps are recorded; explain why manual cleaning is risky (not repeatable and easy to forget). Model: link everything to named ranges so formulas remain readable; if using Solver, store the Solver model settings and ensure the objective and constraints reference the correct cells. Outputs: create a single output sheet where all stakeholder-facing numbers appear; include a limitation line such as “Assumes last 12 weeks representative; does not model seasonality.” Probing question: “If you copy this file to a new folder, does anything break due to external links?” Common misconception: leaving intermediate calculations scattered across many sheets without clear flow.

slides.title: Worked example: Python notebook end-to-end

content.title: Worked example: Python notebook end-to-end
content: Top cell: purpose, data source, and run instructions
Load: relative paths, schema checks, fixed random seed
Transform: functions with clear names and tests
Model + CI: compute estimate and 95% CI
Outputs: save tables/figures with units in filenames
content.notes: Explain notebook reproducibility standards: a short header cell should state what the notebook does and how to run it (e.g., “Kernel > Restart & Run All”). Emphasise relative paths and repository structure to avoid machine-specific file locations; show an example: data/raw/input.csv and outputs/figures/. Include schema checks (expected columns and types) and row-count assertions after merges to catch silent errors. If randomness is used (bootstrapping, train/test split), set and report a random seed. For CI, suggest a straightforward method aligned to the project: t-interval for a mean when appropriate, or bootstrap CI if distribution is non-normal (but remind learners to state this as an assumption). Probing question: “Could another learner run this on a clean environment and get the same outputs?” Misconception: thinking “Run All works” is enough—outputs must also be saved and clearly labelled for submission.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: your project checklist

content.title: Practice and reflection: your project checklist
leftColumn: List 6 assumptions with units and time period
Create 1 CI and write a 1-sentence interpretation
Make 2 visuals with axis labels and units
Write a limitation/uncertainty statement
rightColumn: Do a fresh-run test from closed file
Trace one output back to raw inputs
Ask: what breaks if inputs update next week?
Log 3 improvements you will implement
content.notes: Guide learners to apply the lesson immediately to their own capstone artefact. Encourage them to pick one key metric for the CI that aligns to their decision (defect rate, cycle time, demand level). For the fresh-run test, specify the discipline: close the file/notebook, reopen, then run using only the prescribed actions—no extra clicks. For traceability, set a time challenge: find the source of one output number and document the chain (input → transform → model → output). Reflection prompts: “What assumption is most contestable?” and “What would you tell a manager not to do with this model?” Common misconception: leaving interpretation until the end; writing plain language early often reveals missing units and unclear definitions.

slides.title: MOD108 Capstone: Lesson 13 technical reporting

content.title: MOD108 Capstone: Lesson 13 technical reporting
content.content: Produce a concise technical report and slide deck for non-specialists (1h 30m)
content.notes:
Welcome. This lesson focuses on communicating model outputs to non-specialists with technical accuracy and traceability. You will practise two deliverables: (1) a short technical report section (maximum 400 words) and (2) a five-slide recommendation deck. The emphasis is not on building a better model, but on explaining clearly what was done, what it means, and what to do next—while being explicit about units, assumptions, uncertainty, and constraints.

slides.title: What non-specialists need from your outputs

content.title: What non-specialists need from your outputs
content: The business question in plain language
What data were used and what was excluded
One clear result plus what it implies operationally
Uncertainty and risk, quantified where possible
Constraints/trade-offs that limit the decision
A specific next action with ownership and timing
content.notes:
Explain the difference between technical correctness and decision usefulness. Non-specialists rarely want model internals; they want confidence in the decision.

Mini-example: Instead of “ARIMA(1,1,1) minimised AIC”, say “We forecast demand for the next 8 weeks using the last 24 months of sales; the expected weekly demand is 1,200 units (95% CI: 1,050–1,350).”

Common misconception: “More detail builds trust.” Often it reduces clarity. Trust is built by transparency (data sources, assumptions, validation, uncertainty) and by traceability (how numbers were calculated).

Probing questions: If your manager only reads one sentence, what must it say? What risk would they worry about most (service level, cost, compliance, safety)?

rows: Decision to make; success metric; time horizon
Units for key values; ≥3 explicit checks
Bias, coverage gaps, model limits, impact on use

content.notes:
Walk learners through a practical template that forces concision. The goal is a report section that a reviewer can audit: what question, what data, what assumptions, what units, what limitations.

slides.title: Unit checks and rounding: minimum standard

content.title: Unit checks and rounding: minimum standard
content: State units for every headline figure (e.g., £/week, kWh)
Do 3 explicit unit checks (dimensional consistency)
Check scale: magnitudes match reality (order-of-magnitude)
Show conversions (mins→hours, kg→tonnes) not just results
Round to decision-useful precision (usually 2–3 sig figs)
Avoid false accuracy: align rounding with uncertainty
content.notes:
Explain what a unit check looks like in text: you write the equation and show units cancel. Provide three common checks learners can use:

1) Rate × time = quantity. Example: 20 orders/hour × 6 hours = 120 orders.
2) Price × quantity = cost. Example: £0.12/kWh × 5,000 kWh = £600.
3) Flow × distance = volume/usage. Example: 7 L/100km × 250 km = 17.5 L.

Add a scale check: “Does 17.5 L for a 250 km trip sound plausible?”

Rounding guidance: Teach that rounding is a communication decision. If the uncertainty is ±10%, reporting to the nearest penny is misleading. Prefer “£0.60k” or “~£600” depending on context.

Common misconception: “Unit checks are only for physics.” In workplace maths, they prevent costly errors (e.g., per day vs per week, net vs gross, VAT vs non-VAT).

Probing questions: Where do unit errors sneak in your work: data extracts, conversions, or chart labels? What rounding would you choose if the CI width is ±200 units?

slides.title: Recommendation deck: 5-slide blueprint

content.title: Recommendation deck: 5-slide blueprint
leftColumn: 1. Problem and decision
2. Evidence (visual)
3. Recommendation
4. Uncertainty and risk
rightColumn: 5. Constraints and trade-offs
Keep one message per slide
Use plain-language headings
End with clear next steps
content.notes:
Explain that the slide deck is not the report: it is an executive communication tool. It should be readable without narration.

Clarify each slide’s job:
- Slide 1 sets the decision context (what we are deciding, why now).
- Slide 2 shows one strong visual. Avoid multiple small charts.
- Slide 3 states a specific recommendation with quantified impact.
- Slide 4 states uncertainty (e.g., CI, scenario range) and what could go wrong.
- Slide 5 states constraints/trade-offs (capacity, budget, SLA, emissions, fairness) and proposes next steps.

Common misconception: “More slides = more professional.” The assessment requires five slides; the skill is prioritisation.

Probing questions: If you had to remove one slide, which would you keep and why? What is your single strongest visual—trend line, bar comparison, or scenario fan chart?

slides.title: Trends and turning points: how to justify them

content.title: Trends and turning points: how to justify them
content: Define the metric and time window before claiming a trend
Identify 2 patterns: trend, seasonality, step change, outlier
Locate turning points with dates and plausible causes
Quantify change: Δ, %, rate per period, before/after means
Use a simple check: compare 2 periods or segments
Link to action: why this pattern changes the decision
content.notes:
Teach disciplined interpretation. A “trend” is not a visual impression; it is a quantified change over a defined window.

Mini-example: “Average lead time rose from 2.1 days (Jan–Mar) to 3.0 days (Apr–Jun), +0.9 days (+43%). The increase begins mid-April, coinciding with staffing changes.”

Explain turning points: points where direction or level changes. You can detect them with simple methods (rolling averages, before/after comparison) without advanced statistics.

Common misconceptions:
- Confusing seasonality with trend.
- Choosing windows after seeing the data (cherry-picking).
- Ignoring operational explanations.

Probing questions: What is the minimum evidence you need to claim “improvement”? What alternative explanation could produce the same pattern (data quality, policy change, reporting lag)?

slides.title: Worked example: report paragraph (before → after)

content.title: Worked example: report paragraph (before → after)
content: Before: long, model-focused, missing units and limitations
After: question, data, units, checks, limits, and implication
Includes 3 unit checks embedded in sentences
Rounding aligned to CI width and decision threshold
Links to calculation log for reproducibility
content.notes:
Present a realistic ‘before’ and ‘after’ narrative verbally.

Before (describe): A paragraph that says “We used regression, R²=0.87, p<0.05” but does not specify the business decision, data dates, or units.

After (model answer outline learners can emulate):
- Business question: “Should we add a second delivery shift to maintain a 95% on-time rate next quarter?”
- Data: “Dispatch logs (Jan 2024–Dec 2025), 48,120 deliveries; excluded cancelled jobs (2.3%).”
- Units + checks: “Average load is 1.8 tonnes/vehicle; 12 vehicles × 1.8 tonnes = 21.6 tonnes/day capacity (tonnes/day). Fuel cost uses £/L × L/day = £/day.” Include a time-rate check too.
- Uncertainty and rounding: “Expected demand 20–23 tonnes/day (95% range); report to nearest 0.5 tonne.”
- Limitations: “No weather variable; risk of underestimating peaks.”
- Traceability: “See Calc Log tab ‘capacity_checks’.”

Probing questions: Which sentence in your ‘after’ paragraph most directly supports the decision? What would a reviewer need to recreate your capacity number?

slides.title: Worked example: uncertainty + constraint statements

content.title: Worked example: uncertainty + constraint statements

rows: Risk: stockout if upper CI persists 3+ weeks

content.notes:
Use this slide to teach precise language that non-specialists can act on. Explain that uncertainty must be quantified where possible: CI, prediction interval, scenario range, or sensitivity band.

Show how to tie uncertainty to an operational risk: not just “uncertain” but “what happens if we are at the top of the range?”.

Constraint vs trade-off:
- Constraint: a hard limit (capacity cap, legal requirement, SLA).
- Trade-off: a choice between competing objectives (cost vs service).

Common misconception: “Including uncertainty weakens the recommendation.” In reality it prevents overconfidence and supports contingency planning.

Probing questions: What is your main constraint: budget, staff time, storage, lead time, or compliance? Which uncertainty matters more: volume, timing, or unit cost?

slides.title: Practice and reflection: draft your two deliverables

content.title: Practice and reflection: draft your two deliverables
content: Write a ≤400 word report section using the template
Add 3 explicit unit checks (show units cancelling)
Choose 1 visual for the deck; remove all others
Write 1 recommendation with quantified impact
Add 1 CI/range statement and 1 constraint/trade-off
Record calculations in a log (link, cell refs, or steps)
content.notes:
Set expectations for independent practice. Learners should produce tangible outputs.

Guidance:
- Start by writing the business question as a yes/no or choose-between decision.
- Then list the minimum data fields needed (metric, date, unit, segment).
- Create a calculation log: this can be a spreadsheet tab listing inputs, formulas, and outputs; or a notebook section with numbered steps.

Reflection prompts:
- Which part took most time: editing for length, writing limitations, or making a clear visual?
- Does your recommendation answer the stated business question?
- Would a colleague be able to reproduce your headline number in under 10 minutes?

Common misconception: “A calculation log is extra work.” It often saves time when you revise and when you receive feedback.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports capstone outputs: report section + decision deck
Common issue: unclear business question and decision owner
Common issue: missing units on charts, axes, and tables
Common issue: no quantified uncertainty or vague risk wording
Common issue: no constraint/trade-off; recommendation unbounded
Common issue: no audit trail of feedback-led revisions
content.notes:
Explicitly connect to the MOD108 capstone expectations: decision-ready communication, reproducibility, and professional judgement.

Explain how markers typically interpret these mistakes:
- Unclear question: suggests you did not understand the stakeholder need.
- Missing units: suggests lack of technical control; can invalidate numbers.
- Vague uncertainty: suggests overconfidence or incomplete validation.
- No constraints: suggests an unrealistic recommendation.
- No audit trail: suggests you did not engage with feedback or cannot justify changes.

Audit trail guidance: Keep a short change log with three entries: “What changed / why / evidence”. Example: “Rounded outputs to nearest 10 units because PI is ±120 units.”

Probing questions: Which of these mistakes are you currently at risk of making? What one change would most improve clarity for a non-specialist reader?

slides.title: Uncertainty using confidence intervals and simulation

content.title: Uncertainty using confidence intervals and simulation
content.content:
Maths Certification | MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project
Lesson 14 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Introduce this lesson as a capstone-focused skill-builder: you will quantify uncertainty, communicate it clearly, and make your workbook auditable. Emphasise that uncertainty is not a weakness in analysis; it is information decision-makers need. Set expectations: we will use confidence intervals (CIs) for sampling uncertainty and Monte Carlo simulation for model/input uncertainty. Prompt: “Where, in your capstone workbook, do you currently show uncertainty rather than single-point answers?”

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce this lesson as a capstone-focused skill-builder: you will quantify uncertainty, communicate it clearly, and make your workbook auditable. Emphasise that uncertainty is not a weakness in analysis; it is information decision-makers need. slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to study
content: Compute and interpret a 95% CI with units, n, and level
Run Monte Carlo (≥1,000 iters) and report P5/P50/P95
Write a risk statement with assumptions and mitigations
Build reproducible Excel/Python steps with an audit log
Self-audit and fix ≥5 issues: units, rounding, assumptions
Study flow: learn → build → check (MCQs) → improve workbook
content.notes: Explain the learning loop for self-study: first understand concepts, then implement them in your own workbook, then test understanding via the MCQs, then return to improve traceability and communication. Clarify what “interpret” means: not just computing numbers, but stating what they mean in plain language, including the parameter (mean/proportion/difference), the unit, sample size, and the confidence level. Misconception to pre-empt: a 95% CI does not mean “95% chance the true value is in this interval” under a strict frequentist interpretation; it means the method covers the true value in 95% of repeated samples. Probe: “Which parts of your capstone are driven by sample data (CI) versus assumed variability (simulation)?”

Probe: “Which parts of your capstone are driven by sample data (CI) versus assumed variability (simulation)?”

slides.title: What uncertainty are we quantifying?

content.title: What uncertainty are we quantifying?
content.content: Workplace decisions are made with incomplete information. Confidence intervals quantify sampling uncertainty from data; Monte Carlo quantifies uncertainty from variable inputs and model assumptions.
content.notes: Expand the distinction with examples. Sampling uncertainty: you inspected 80 items, not all production. Input/model uncertainty: demand varies daily; yield is variable; lead time fluctuates. Emphasise that these tools answer different questions: a CI is about an unknown population parameter given a sample; simulation is about the distribution of outcomes given uncertain inputs. Ask: “If you collected more data, which uncertainty would shrink?” (sampling) and “Which would remain even with perfect measurement?” (intrinsic variability / scenario uncertainty).

slides.title: Confidence intervals: meaning and correct wording

content.title: Confidence intervals: meaning and correct wording
content: A CI is an interval estimate for a population parameter
95% CI = estimate ± (critical value × standard error)
Always report: metric, units, sample size (n), confidence
Interpretation: method would cover true value 95% of runs
Wider CI comes from higher variability or smaller n
Avoid: treating CI bounds as guaranteed limits
content.notes: Walk through the structure: point estimate (e.g., sample mean), uncertainty around it (standard error), and a multiplier (z or t critical value). Stress the difference between standard deviation (spread of individual values) and standard error (uncertainty in the estimate). Give a mini-example: mean handling time 6.2 minutes, 95% CI [5.8, 6.6] minutes, n=40. Common misconceptions: (1) CI is not the range of individual values; (2) 95% CI is not “95% of customers will be between…”. Probing question: “What would you change—n or process variability—if you need a narrower CI?”

Probing question: “What would you change—n or process variability—if you need a narrower CI?”

slides.title: Common 95% CI types and implementation

content.title: Common 95% CI types and implementation
content: Choose the CI that matches your metric and data structure
Use t when σ is unknown and n is small for means
content.notes: Explain how to select the right CI: one sample vs two samples; continuous (mean) vs binary (proportion). Clarify the ‘critical value’: for large samples, z≈1.96 for 95%; for means with unknown σ, use t with df. Mention practical guidance: for proportion CIs, the normal approximation can be poor when n is small or p is near 0 or 1; consider Wilson/Agresti–Coull in Python (statsmodels) if needed, but for this capstone a clear normal-approx CI may be acceptable if you justify assumptions. Prompt: “What is your metric in the capstone—mean, proportion, or difference—and what assumptions are you making about independence?”

Clarify the ‘critical value’: for large samples, z≈1.96 for 95%; for means with unknown σ, use t with df. Mention practical guidance: for proportion CIs, the normal approximation can be poor when n is small or p is near 0 or 1; consider Wilson/Agresti–Coull in Python (statsmodels) if needed, but for this capstone a clear normal-approx CI may be acceptable if you justify assumptions. Prompt: “What is your metric in the capstone—mean, proportion, or difference—and what assumptions are you making about independence?”

slides.title: Assumptions: distributions and data conditions

content.title: Assumptions: distributions and data conditions
leftColumn: Independence of observations
Random or representative sampling
Mean CI: approx normality of x̄
Proportion CI: n p̂ and n(1-p̂) large
rightColumn: Check for clustering (by shift, site, team)
Look for bias in who/what got measured
Use plots: histogram, boxplot, QQ plot
If assumptions fail, widen scope or change method
content.notes: Talk learners through how assumption failures show up at work: sampling only Monday mornings, counting defects only when a specific inspector is on duty, repeated measures from the same machine treated as independent. Provide a quick diagnostic routine: (1) segment results by key categories; (2) plot distributions; (3) sanity-check n and event counts for proportions. Emphasise that you can still proceed if you are transparent: document limitations and consider mitigations (e.g., stratified sampling, collecting more balanced data, using bootstrap or non-parametric methods if appropriate). Probe: “Which assumption is most fragile in your workplace data—and how would you test it quickly?”

slides.title: Monte Carlo simulation: when and why

content.title: Monte Carlo simulation: when and why
content: Use when inputs vary and outcomes are non-linear
Define uncertain inputs as distributions, not single values
Simulate many trials to approximate outcome distribution
Report percentiles (P5/P50/P95), not just the mean
Set iterations ≥1,000; increase if results are unstable
Fix a random seed for reproducibility
content.notes: Explain that Monte Carlo is a practical way to propagate uncertainty through a model: you sample inputs repeatedly and compute outputs. Give examples: profit depends on demand, price, and cost; quality depends on defect probability and volume; staffing depends on arrivals and service time. Highlight a misconception: more iterations do not fix a bad model—if input distributions are wrong or relationships are missing, simulation can produce precise nonsense. Teach a quick convergence check: run 1,000 then 5,000 iterations; see whether P50 and P95 materially change. Ask: “Which input in your model is both uncertain and influential enough to justify simulation?”

slides.title: Summarising uncertainty for decisions

content.title: Summarising uncertainty for decisions
content: Use P5/P50/P95 to show downside, typical, upside cases
Visuals: histogram, cumulative curve, or box-and-whisker
Include units and time basis (per day, per batch, per month)
Label clearly: what varies and what is held constant
Add decision thresholds (e.g., break-even, SLA target)
Connect uncertainty to actions: buffers, controls, triggers
content.notes: Explain why percentiles are decision-friendly: P5 approximates a ‘bad but plausible’ case, P95 a ‘good but plausible’ case; P50 is the median and often more robust than the mean when distributions are skewed. Demonstrate how to interpret: “P5 profit is -£10k” means 5% of simulated outcomes are at or below -£10k under the model assumptions. Encourage adding a vertical line for a threshold (e.g., profit=0, defect rate target, capacity limit) and reporting the probability of falling below it. Probe: “What threshold matters to your stakeholder, and can you express risk as a probability relative to it?”

slides.title: Worked example: 95% CI for a defect proportion

content.title: Worked example: 95% CI for a defect proportion
content: Scenario: 18 defects in 200 items sampled from a process
Report as a proportion and a percentage with clear units
content.notes: Talk through each row and narrate the ‘story’ you will write in a report: “Based on n=200 items, the estimated defect rate is 9.0%. A 95% CI is 5.0% to 13.0%.” Emphasise rounding discipline: keep calculations in full precision, round only for reporting, and ensure the CI bounds remain within 0–1 (or 0–100%). Mention a common pitfall: using population SD instead of sample SD for mean CIs, or confusing percentage points with percent changes. Probing questions: “Is the sample representative across shifts?” and “What does a 13% upper bound imply for expected scrap cost next month?”

slides.title: Worked example: Monte Carlo pricing risk in Excel/Python

content.title: Worked example: Monte Carlo pricing risk in Excel/Python
content: Output: monthly margin = (price-cost)×demand - fixed costs
Inputs: demand ~ Normal(μ,σ); cost ~ Tri(min,mode,max)
Step 1: set Assumptions table with sources and rationale
Step 2: simulate ≥1,000 rows; compute margin each row
Step 3: summarise P5/P50/P95; plot histogram or CDF
Step 4: report P(margin<0) and key drivers (sensitivity)
content.notes: Provide an implementation sketch. In Excel: use NORM.INV(RAND(), μ, σ) for demand; use a triangular generator for cost (or approximate with PERT if taught elsewhere); compute margin per row; use PERCENTILE.INC for P5/P50/P95; use COUNTIF to estimate probability of loss. In Python: numpy.random.normal, a custom triangular via numpy.random.triangular, then np.percentile and matplotlib for plots. Stress traceability: each distribution parameter should link back to a cell or a documented source. Misconceptions: (1) using RAND() without controlling recalc and then copying values without documenting; (2) interpreting simulated percentiles as guarantees rather than model-based scenarios. Probe: “If you could reduce uncertainty in only one input, which would most reduce the downside (P5)?”

content.title: MOD108 Capstone: Reproducible Excel/Python workbook
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD108 Integrated Workplace Maths Project | Lesson 15 | 1h 30m
content.notes: In this lesson you will move from a model that merely “works” to one that is defensible, repeatable, and easy for someone else to audit. In workplace maths, the credibility of your recommendation often depends less on clever calculation and more on traceability: what you assumed, where values came from, how results were produced, and how uncertainty is communicated. Keep your own capstone workbook/notebook open throughout so you can implement each component as we discuss it.

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content: Add an Assumptions Register (≥5 items with key fields)

content.notes: Work through the lesson in a cycle: (1) read the concept, (2) implement immediately in your model, (3) run a self-check, and (4) revise using critique prompts. Aim for “peer reproducible”: someone else should be able to re-run from raw inputs to key outputs without guessing steps. A common misconception is that reproducibility is only for code; Excel models also require version notes, named ranges, input controls, and a clear calculation chain.

slides.title: Assumptions Register: purpose and required fields

content.title: Assumptions Register: purpose and required fields
content: Make assumptions explicit, not hidden in cells or prose
Each row: name, value+units, source, rationale, impact dir.
Link assumptions to model inputs (named range or variable)
Separate assumptions from data (do not mix in one cell)
Review assumptions before sharing results externally
content.notes: An Assumptions Register is a structured list that makes your model’s “choices” inspectable. It should include at least: assumption name, numerical value with units, data source (e.g., policy document, invoice sample, benchmark), rationale (why this value is reasonable), and expected impact direction on the main result (e.g., increasing the rate increases cost). Encourage yourself to ask: if a colleague challenged this value, could you defend it quickly? Misconception to avoid: writing vague assumptions like “demand is stable” without units, timeframe, or measurable proxy.

slides.title: Audit trail: what reproducibility looks like

content.title: Audit trail: what reproducibility looks like
content: Inputs are clearly marked and separated from calculations
All transformations are visible, labelled, and repeatable
Key outputs have defined tolerance (e.g., ±0.5%)
A peer can run in one pass: data → model → outputs
Record version, date, and what changed since last run
content.notes: Reproducibility means someone else can follow your process and obtain the same results, within a stated tolerance. Tolerance matters because solver methods, rounding, and floating-point behaviour can cause tiny differences. In Excel, reproducibility is strengthened by consistent input sheets, named ranges, and documentation of macros or solver settings. In Python, it means deterministic code paths, captured package versions, fixed random seeds where relevant, and a clear run order. A frequent pitfall is relying on manual steps (copy/paste, filters) without documenting them; convert these into recorded steps, scripts, or clearly numbered instructions.

content.title: Audit trail methods: Excel vs Python
leftColumn: Named ranges for key inputs and outputs
Cell comments for assumptions and sources
Calculation sheet with step labels
Solver/Goal Seek settings recorded
rightColumn: Headed code cells and a clear run order
Version notes (packages, seed, data timestamp)
Logging key parameters and results
Save outputs to a results cell/table
content.notes: Choose techniques suited to your tool, but aim for the same outcome: a transparent chain from inputs to decision outputs. In Excel, named ranges reduce the risk of “wrong cell” errors and make formulas readable; comments or notes capture source and rationale at point of use. In Python, use markdown headings to separate stages (import, clean, model, validate, report) and ensure reruns are consistent by capturing package versions and data extract timestamps. Probing question: if you left the organisation and returned in six months, could you reproduce your own results without re-learning the model?

slides.title: Uncertainty statements: pick one and be precise

content.title: Uncertainty statements: pick one and be precise
content: Confidence interval: range for an estimated parameter
Sensitivity range: result change when inputs vary
Solver tolerance: acceptable numerical error in optimisation
State assumptions behind the statement (sample, model form)
Translate meaning for non-specialists without overclaiming
content.notes: Uncertainty is not a weakness; it is honest reporting. Select the uncertainty statement that matches your analysis. If you estimated a mean or rate from data, a confidence interval may be appropriate. If the model depends heavily on uncertain inputs (prices, demand, utilisation), a sensitivity range is often more meaningful. If you used an optimiser, state the solver tolerance and what it implies for the stability of the solution. Misconception to avoid: treating a confidence interval as “the probability the true value lies in the interval” (frequentist CIs do not mean that). Instead, explain it as a procedure that would capture the true value in a stated proportion of repeated samples.

slides.title: Limitations and next checks: a useful structure

content.title: Limitations and next checks: a useful structure
content: Limitations: what the model excludes or simplifies
Why it matters: likely direction of bias, if known
Next checks: specific data/tests to run next
Separate “unknown” from “out of scope for this task”
Keep it short: 100–150 words, plain language
content.notes: A strong limitations section is specific and action-oriented. Avoid generic lines like “more data is needed”; instead, name the exact dataset, timeframe, or validation test. When possible, state how a limitation might bias results (e.g., “Using list prices may overstate costs; negotiated rates likely reduce total cost”). ‘Next checks’ should be doable: reconcile with finance ledger totals, run out-of-sample validation, confirm unit conversions, check seasonality. Probing questions: what single additional check would most increase confidence? What is the highest-risk assumption if wrong?

content.title: Worked example: plain-language uncertainty statement
content.content: Based on sensitivity testing, total annual cost is £1.20m–£1.35m when utilisation varies from 0.78 to 0.86. This range shows how much the result could change if the utilisation assumption is wrong; it is not a guarantee that costs will fall within the range.

slides.title: Peer-style critique and revision prompts

content.title: Peer-style critique and revision prompts
content: Can I find every input value and its source within 2 mins?
Are units consistent end-to-end (hours, £, %, per year)?
Is any step manual? If yes, is it documented and repeatable?
Does uncertainty language avoid certainty or guarantee wording?
Revise one element based on critique (register, notes, slide)
content.notes: Use these questions to simulate a peer review. If possible, swap files with a classmate or ask a colleague to follow your run steps without coaching; note where they hesitate. Common issues: unit mismatches (monthly vs annual), silent conversions (percent entered as 5 vs 0.05), and hidden filters altering totals. For uncertainty, ban phrases like “will be” or “proves”; use “suggests”, “is consistent with”, and specify conditions. Your required revision can be small but concrete—e.g., add units to two assumptions, record the solver tolerance, or rewrite the uncertainty statement to remove overclaiming.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD108 capstone: model credibility + decision output
Aligns with MCQs on traceability and uncertainty statements
Mistake: assumptions implicit or duplicated across the model
Mistake: results not reproducible after restart/recalc
Mistake: uncertainty presented as a promise or precise truth
Mistake: limitations too vague; next checks not actionable
content.notes: In the capstone, markers look for technical correctness and professional decision support. Your recommendation slide is only credible if the model can be audited and rerun. Use the MCQs as retrieval practice: they test your ability to recognise good uncertainty phrasing and validation approaches. content.title: Produce a concise technical report and slide deck
content.content:
Maths Certification

Lesson 16: Produce a concise technical report and slide deck for non…
Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes:
In this lesson you will practise turning analysis outputs into decision-ready communication for a non-technical audience, without losing traceability. The emphasis is on (1) a tight executive-summary recommendation, (2) two clear visuals that carry the argument, (3) audit-ready documentation of assumptions and uncertainty, and (4) revising based on peer-style feedback.

As you work, keep two readers in mind: the decision-maker (needs clarity and consequences) and the reviewer/auditor (needs evidence, assumptions, and reproducibility). A common misconception is that “concise” means “vague”. In professional reporting, concision comes from prioritising what changes the decision, not from omitting definitions, units, or limitations.

slides.title: Orientation: what you will produce

content.title: Orientation: what you will produce
content: Executive summary ≤150 words with decision + evidence
Two visuals: trend + constraint/marginal view
Technical report ≤2 pages using module template
Slide deck 5–7 slides using module template
Revise using feedback; record changes in a change log
Self-check with the two MCQ quizzes at the end
content.notes:
Treat the outputs as a package: the executive summary and slide deck should align, and the report should provide the supporting detail. The two visuals are not decoration: they should each answer a specific question (e.g., “What is happening over time?” and “Where is the bottleneck/turning point?”).

When you complete the lesson, use the MCQ checks to test your understanding of traceability, decision outputs, and uncertainty statements. While working, pause after each component and ask: “If I removed this sentence or chart, would the decision change?” If not, it may be unnecessary.

Probing questions:
- Who is the primary decision-maker and what is the decision they control?
- What would a sceptical reviewer ask first (data source, units, assumptions, risk)?

slides.title: From analysis to decision: audience and purpose

content.title: From analysis to decision: audience and purpose
content: State the decision first, not the method
Use plain language; define unavoidable technical terms
Quantify impact using units and a time horizon
Separate facts, assumptions, and judgement
Include risks, constraints, and what could change the result
content.notes:
Non-technical does not mean non-rigorous. It means you must translate: replace internal model language (e.g., “objective function improved”) with operational meaning (e.g., “weekly cost reduces by £X”).

A useful structure is: Decision → Evidence → Implications → Limitations/Risks → Next action. Keep method details mostly in the report appendix area (or a short ‘Approach’ paragraph), not in the first lines.

Common misconceptions:
- “If I show enough equations/tables, it will be credible.” Credibility comes from traceable evidence and clear limitations.
- “Assumptions undermine confidence.” In fact, assumptions increase trust if stated transparently.

Probing questions:
- What is the smallest set of facts needed to justify the recommendation?
- What is the most decision-relevant uncertainty (demand, capacity, price, failure rate)?

slides.title: Executive summary: a 150-word blueprint

content.title: Executive summary: a 150-word blueprint
content: Open with a clear recommendation (do X by when)
Add 2–3 quantitative evidence points with units
Explain the key driver in one sentence (why X wins)
State at least one limitation or assumption explicitly
Close with the next step and owner (what happens next)
content.notes:
The executive summary is a mini-decision memo. Start with the verb: “Approve…”, “Adopt…”, “Prioritise…”, “Defer…”. Then add only the evidence that would change a reasonable person’s decision.

Evidence points should be measurable and comparable, e.g., “reduces mean waiting time by 18% (from 11.2 to 9.2 min)” or “keeps utilisation below 85% at peak”. Avoid naked numbers: always include units and context (baseline, time window, scenario).

Limitation examples:
- “Assumes arrival rate remains within ±10% of the last 8 weeks.”
- “Model does not include downtime >2 hours; results may overstate capacity.”

Probing questions:
- If a manager only reads 150 words, can they act safely?
- What assumption, if wrong, would flip the recommendation?

slides.title: Choosing evidence points that carry the argument

content.title: Choosing evidence points that carry the argument

rows: Percent with no CI or sample size
P(failure) 0.07 per week under scenario B

content.notes:
Use evidence that aligns with the decision criteria. If the decision is about service reliability, lead with service level and risk, then cost. If it is budget-driven, lead with cost but still include at least one operational constraint so the recommendation is safe to implement.

Explain confidence intervals (CI) in plain terms: “We expect the true on-time rate to fall between 92% and 96% most of the time, given this data.” If you do not have a CI, you can still communicate uncertainty using ranges or scenario bounds, but you must say where the range comes from.

Misconception to challenge: “More numbers = better.” In executive summaries, 2–3 strong, well-framed metrics beat a dense list.

Probing questions:
- Which metric would your stakeholder challenge first?
- What unit would make a non-technical reader trust the number (minutes, £/month, kWh/week)?

slides.title: Two visuals that do the heavy lifting

content.title: Two visuals that do the heavy lifting
content: Visual 1: trend over time with a labelled baseline
Visual 2: constraint or marginal view (turning point)
Label axes, units, timeframe, and scenario names
Annotate the key change point (knee, threshold, peak)
Add one-sentence interpretation under each visual
Avoid clutter: one message per chart
content.notes:
Your two visuals should be complementary. A typical pairing is:
1) Trend: demand, output, waiting time, defects, or costs over time.
2) Constraint/marginal: utilisation vs throughput, cost vs service level, or benefit vs investment showing diminishing returns.

A turning point (or ‘knee’) is where the decision changes: e.g., utilisation above 90% causes waiting time to increase sharply. Mark it explicitly with a vertical line or callout.

Interpretation sentence examples:
- “Waiting time rises steadily after week 6, coinciding with utilisation exceeding 85%.”
- “Beyond 3 staff per shift, the marginal reduction in delay is <1 min, indicating diminishing returns.”

Common misconceptions:
- “A legend is enough.” Non-technical readers need axis labels, units, and a plain-language caption.
- “More series on one plot is efficient.” Often it hides the message.

Probing questions:
- What would you want the reader to say after 5 seconds looking at the chart?
- Where is the decision boundary visible on the plot?

slides.title: Audit-ready reporting: traceability and uncertainty

content.title: Audit-ready reporting: traceability and uncertainty
content: Document data source, date, and any cleaning rules
List assumptions and constraints with rationale
State rounding policy and significant figures
Report uncertainty: CI, range, or scenarios
Version outputs; keep a reproducible calculation trail
Link each claim to a figure/table or model output ID
content.notes:
An audit-ready report allows a reviewer to reproduce the decision logic. That does not mean they can rerun your whole model, but they can track every claim back to a source.

Practical approaches:
- Data provenance: “Ops export v3, pulled 12/02/2026; removed 4 duplicate rows; imputed 2 missing values using median.”
- Assumption register: list each assumption, why it is needed, and how sensitive results are to it.
- Rounding: choose a consistent rule (e.g., costs to nearest £1k; times to 0.1 min). Inconsistency is a common source of mistrust.

On uncertainty: when you present a CI, avoid implying certainty. When you cannot compute a CI, use scenario comparisons (best/base/worst) and clearly label what drives the spread.

Probing questions:
- If someone challenged your numbers in 6 months, could you defend them?
- Which assumption is least defensible, and how will you flag it?

slides.title: Worked example: executive summary before and after

content.title: Worked example: executive summary before and after
leftColumn: Before: 'Model shows option A is best.'
No units or baseline; unclear decision
No limitations; sounds overconfident
Method-focused rather than outcome-focused
rightColumn: After: 'Adopt option A next quarter.'
Evidence: £9k/month saving; 94% on-time (CI 92–96%)
Constraint: keeps utilisation under 88% at peak
Limitation: assumes demand within ±10% of recent weeks
content.notes:
Walk through why the ‘before’ version fails: it asks the reader to trust the model without understanding the operational effect. The ‘after’ version works because it is decision-led, quantified, and appropriately cautious.

Mini-example phrasing (≤150 words target):
“Recommend adopting option A from Q3 to reduce monthly operating cost by ~£9k (from £51k to £42k) while maintaining a 94% on-time rate (92–96% CI). Peak utilisation remains below 88%, reducing the risk of queue instability observed above ~90% utilisation. This recommendation assumes demand remains within ±10% of the last 8 weeks and excludes downtime events longer than 2 hours; if either occurs, service levels may fall by 2–4 percentage points. Next step: run a two-week pilot with weekly KPI review and a rollback trigger if on-time rate drops below 90%.”

Probing questions:
- Which phrase in the ‘after’ version increases trust most?
- What would you remove to stay within 150 words without weakening the decision?

slides.title: Worked example: building two decision visuals

content.title: Worked example: building two decision visuals
content: Step 1: choose the question each chart must answer
Step 2: select the simplest chart type that fits
Step 3: label axes with units and timeframe
Step 4: add baseline/target lines and annotate threshold
Step 5: write a one-sentence interpretation
Step 6: check readability at 100% zoom
content.notes:
Provide an illustrative scenario: you have weekly throughput and utilisation from an operations model.

Trend visual example:
- Line chart of weekly cost (£/week) over 12 weeks for options A and B.
- Add a horizontal baseline line for the current process.
- Interpretation: “Option A stays below baseline cost from week 3 onwards; option B only briefly improves.”

Constraint/marginal visual example:
- Plot waiting time (minutes) vs utilisation (%) showing a sharp increase after ~90%.
- Add a vertical line at 90% to mark the turning point.
- Interpretation: “Above ~90% utilisation, delay increases nonlinearly, so plan for ≤88% at peak.”

Common misconceptions:
- Forgetting units on either axis.
- Using dual axes that confuse interpretation.
- Using 3D effects or dense gridlines that reduce clarity.

Probing questions:
- Where is the turning point and how will you visually cue it?
- Could a reader misread the chart and reach the opposite conclusion?

content.title: Practice and reflection: draft, check, refine
content: Write a 150-word recommendation using 2–3 metrics
Draft two chart captions: trend + turning point
List 5 assumptions/constraints and assign evidence sources
Add one uncertainty statement (CI or scenario range)
Create a 3-item change log from imagined peer feedback
Reflect: what would change your recommendation?
content.notes:
Use your own operational dataset/model outputs from the module, or a previous exercise. Timebox each task:
- 10 minutes: executive summary draft.
- 15 minutes: two visuals (or at least their structure and labels).
- 10 minutes: assumptions/constraints list.
- 5 minutes: uncertainty statement.

Peer-feedback prompts you can simulate:
1) “I cannot see the baseline or target; add it and explain.”
2) “Your cost savings lack a timeframe; state £/week or £/month.”
3) “You sound certain; add a limitation and what data you need next.”

Change log format example:
- Item: Added baseline line to Chart 1. Why: improves comparability.
- Item: Changed ‘significant’ to ‘£9k/month’. Why: removes ambiguity.
- Item: Added CI to on-time rate. Why: communicates uncertainty.

Probing questions:
- Which feedback would you prioritise if you could only fix one issue?
- Which assumption is most likely to be challenged by a supervisor?

slides.title: Model outputs: dimensional, tolerance and sensitivity

content.title: Model outputs: dimensional, tolerance and sensitivity
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD107 — Mathematical Modelling: Calibration, Validation and Sensitivity
Lesson 1 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners. This lesson focuses on evaluating model outputs for correctness and fitness-for-purpose, not on building a model from scratch. Emphasise that most stakeholder issues arise at the interface between the model and reporting: wrong units, inconsistent rounding, untracked fixes, and unjustified claims about sensitivity or validity. Signal that we will use simple but realistic output tables to practise: (1) unit/dimensional checking, (2) tolerance and rounding compliance, (3) one-parameter-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity ranking, (4) evidence-based fit-for-purpose decisions, and (5) reproducibility packaging.

slides.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: outcomes and how to use this lesson
content: You will evaluate outputs for units, tolerance and uncertainty
Objective 1: find and fix ≥5 dimensional/unit inconsistencies
Objective 2: apply reporting rules with 100% checklist compliance
Objective 3: run OAT sensitivity, rank ≥3 parameters by influence
Objective 4: decide fit-for-purpose with evidence (approve/conditional/reject)
Objective 5: produce a reproducibility package for audit readiness
content.notes: Explain how to study: (1) read each concept slide, (2) follow the worked examples step-by-step, (3) attempt the practice prompts without looking, (4) take the two formative MCQs at the end. Encourage learners to keep a running ‘change log’ while working; it is part of the skill, not admin. Probing questions: What does “evaluate” mean in Bloom’s terms here? (Judgement using criteria and evidence.) What would make an output table professionally unacceptable even if calculations are numerically correct? Common misconception: thinking validation is only statistical; here it includes documentation, units, reporting discipline, and decision justification.

slides.title: Dimensional consistency: what to check first

content.title: Dimensional consistency: what to check first
content: Write quantities as value × unit; never just the number
Check base dimensions: M, L, T, Θ, I, N, J as relevant
Derived units must reduce correctly (e.g., Pa = N/m²)
Convert early to a consistent unit system (often SI)
Check each equation term has identical dimensions
Flag unitless ratios: confirm they are genuinely dimensionless
content.notes: Talk through a fast workflow: start with the specification (what each symbol means and its units), then check every column header in outputs, then check equations. Demonstrate quick reductions: N = kg·m·s⁻², so Pa = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². Explain that many errors are “hidden” in derived units: mixing kPa with Pa, mm with m, hours with seconds. Probing questions: If two terms are added, what must be true about their units? If an exponent is applied, what should the base quantity be (usually dimensionless)? Misconception to address: treating “%” as always dimensionless without clarifying whether it is fraction or percentage points.

slides.title: Common inconsistencies and typical fixes

content.title: Common inconsistencies and typical fixes
content: Use this as a spotting checklist during audits
content.notes: Explain that this slide is not a memorisation task; it is a pattern library. Model review is efficient when you recognise recurring faults. Misconception: learners sometimes “fix” by changing numbers without recording the unit basis—this destroys reproducibility.

slides.title: Tolerance, rounding and uncertainty: reporting rules

content.title: Tolerance, rounding and uncertainty: reporting rules
content: Differentiate accuracy, precision and resolution
Rounding rule: keep extra digits until final reporting step
Use significant figures aligned to measurement uncertainty
State tolerance as interval: target ± tol, or [min, max]
Use uncertainty notation consistently (e.g., 12.3 ± 0.4)
Check units on every reported value and on the tolerance
content.notes: Clarify definitions with a mini-example: a sensor reads 10.0 with resolution 0.1; that does not guarantee accuracy 0.1. Explain why premature rounding can flip pass/fail against a tolerance boundary. Show a typical workflow: compute with full precision → compare to tolerance using unrounded values → then round for reporting. Probing questions: When would you use 2 s.f. vs 3 s.f.? If a stakeholder tolerance is ±2%, how do you represent it when the output is in kW? Misconception: interpreting “±” as the same as tolerance; uncertainty is about knowledge of the value, tolerance is an acceptance criterion.

slides.title: OAT sensitivity: a defensible quick check

content.title: OAT sensitivity: a defensible quick check
content: Select one key output (the decision-driving metric)
Choose parameters to test (≥3) and justify the choice
Perturb one parameter at a time (e.g., ±5% or ±10%)
Record change in output: absolute and percentage
Rank parameters by influence; note sign and nonlinearity
Recommend tighter control where influence meets tolerance
content.notes: Explain why OAT is useful: fast, interpretable, suitable for calibrated models when you need triage. Also explain limitations: it can miss interactions and non-linear coupling; it is not a full global sensitivity analysis. Provide a mini-example in words: if +10% in friction factor changes head loss by +12%, that parameter is influential. Probing questions: What perturbation size is appropriate, and why might ±1% be too small? How do you handle parameters that are bounded (e.g., efficiencies between 0 and 1)? Misconception: assuming sensitivity ranking is universal; it depends on the operating point and calibration context.

slides.title: Fit-for-purpose evaluation: decision framework

content.title: Fit-for-purpose evaluation: decision framework
leftColumn: Stakeholder use-case and tolerance requirements
Validation evidence (data match, residuals, tests)
Uncertainty sources and quantified bounds
Reproducibility and audit readiness
rightColumn: Model limitations and assumptions
Domain of validity (range of inputs/conditions)
Sensitivity risks and control feasibility
Decision: approve / conditional / reject
content.notes: Explain that fit-for-purpose is a structured argument, not a feeling. Walk learners through building a decision: start with the use-case and required tolerances, then weigh evidence against limitations and uncertainty. Give examples of “conditional”: approved only within a temperature range, or only after tightening measurement of a sensitive parameter. Probing questions: What evidence would justify approval if the model fails at extremes but the use-case is central range only? What would trigger rejection even with good fit (e.g., irreproducible workflow or untracked fixes)? Misconception: equating a high R² with fitness; stakeholders care about decision risk, not just goodness-of-fit.

slides.title: Worked example 1: fix unit inconsistencies

content.title: Worked example 1: fix unit inconsistencies
content: Before/after corrections with a reproducible change log
content.notes: Talk through each correction and explicitly show one conversion method in words: 120 L/min = 120×10⁻³ m³ / 60 s = 0.00200 m³/s. Emphasise that the corrected value should carry an appropriate number of significant figures based on the given data; do not invent precision. Demonstrate how to log: U-01 (Q conversion), U-02 (pressure scaling), etc., including where the change was applied (e.g., input sheet cell B4) and the impact (outputs shifted by factor). Probing questions: Which of these errors would silently pass a unit check if you only inspected column headers? Which correction changes both unit and magnitude? Common misconception: treating mm² to m² as 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶.

slides.title: Worked example 2: rounding and tolerance compliance

content.title: Worked example 2: rounding and tolerance compliance
content: Compute with full precision; round only for final report
content.notes: Explain each reporting rule as if you were writing a lab report: efficiency is often reported with an uncertainty; pressure drop might be specified to the nearest 0.1 kPa based on instrument resolution. Stress the pass/fail line: compare to tolerance using the unrounded calculation; then report the rounded value. Probing questions: Can the reported value ever appear to violate the tolerance even if the unrounded value passes (or vice versa)? How would you document the reporting checklist so a reviewer can verify compliance quickly? Misconception: learners sometimes round intermediate steps to match a display format; that can accumulate error and create inconsistent results across tools.

slides.title: Worked example 3: OAT sensitivity ranking

content.title: Worked example 3: OAT sensitivity ranking
content: Baseline output y0 = 100 units; perturb each parameter by +10%
content.notes: Explain how to compute Δy(%): (y_perturbed − y0)/y0 × 100. Stress that ranking should consider magnitude and direction; a parameter that can move the output negative/positive across a decision threshold may be more important than its average magnitude suggests. Link to stakeholder tolerances: if the acceptable band on y is ±5%, then k and α clearly threaten compliance, so they require tighter control, better measurement, or redesign. Probing questions: Would you use +10% for all parameters if one is already near a physical bound? What if the response is nonlinear (e.g., +10% gives +9% but −10% gives −15%)? Misconception: interpreting OAT results as proof of causality; it indicates local influence under current calibration.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: self-check prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection: self-check prompts
content: Find 5 likely unit issues in your last model output table
Write a 5-entry change log with IDs, location, rationale, impact
Apply a reporting checklist: units, s.f., dp, ± uncertainty
Run OAT on ≥3 parameters; rank and justify control priorities
Decide approve/conditional/reject for a stated use-case
Complete the two formative MCQs to test recall and judgement
content.notes: Guide learners to pause and do the tasks on their own artefact (or a provided dataset, if available in the wider module). Encourage them to treat the prompts as an audit rehearsal: could a third party reproduce the numbers and understand every fix? Suggest a simple template for the checklist (columns: item, rule, compliant Y/N, evidence link). Probing questions: Which step was hardest—finding inconsistencies, deciding rounding, or justifying the fit-for-purpose decision? What would you need from stakeholders to make the decision less ambiguous (e.g., explicit tolerances, operating range, consequences of error)? Misconception: thinking the MCQs only test memorisation; they also test whether you can apply criteria in short scenarios.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
leftColumn: Supports: MOD107 calibration/validation/sensitivity assignment
Include: units audit, tolerance table, sensitivity ranking
Attach: reproducibility package with version identifier
Justify: fit-for-purpose decision with evidence and limits
rightColumn: Mistake: silent unit conversions without log evidence
Mistake: rounding before tolerance check (boundary errors)
Mistake: sensitivity without stating baseline and perturbation
Mistake: approval with no domain-of-validity statement
content.notes: Make the bridge explicit: assignments typically require not only correct numbers but also traceability and defensibility. Explain what a ‘reproducibility package’ looks like: (1) inputs file, (2) assumptions list, (3) calculation steps or script/notebook, (4) parameter values and calibration source, (5) version ID (date/time, git hash, or revision number), (6) change log of corrective actions, and (7) final outputs with reporting rules. Probing questions: If a marker re-runs your work, what would they need to obtain identical results within tolerance? Which of the listed mistakes would cause a conditional pass versus a fail in a professional audit context? Misconception: treating reproducibility as optional “appendix material”; it is central to credibility.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Dimensional checks catch many high-impact errors quickly
Convert and document: fix units with a reproducible change log
Separate computation from reporting; round only at the end
Use OAT sensitivity to prioritise control and data quality
Fit-for-purpose is an evidence-based decision with stated limits

Invite learners to revisit their own modelling work and apply the same audit lens; most will find at least one unit labelling issue or premature rounding step. Probing questions: What is one habit you will change immediately (e.g., always storing SI internally, always comparing tolerances on unrounded values, always writing a change log)? content.title: Model outputs using dimensional, tolerance and sensitivity checks
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD107 — Mathematical Modelling: Calibration, Validation and Sensitivity | Lesson 2 | 1h 30m
content.notes: Introduce the lesson as a practical quality-check toolkit for judging whether model outputs are credible and usable. Emphasise the Bloom level (evaluate): learners are not just computing, but making defensible decisions based on evidence. Set expectations for self-paced study: pause frequently, replicate steps in a calculator/spreadsheet, and keep a simple calculation log as they go.

slides.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation: objectives and how to use this lesson
content: Find and fix ≥3 unit/dimension issues; log checks and assumptions
Check outputs vs tolerances; justify rounding aligned to limits
Run one-way sensitivity; rank parameters and define 'material'
Write a validation decision note with evidence and limitations
Build an audit-ready record: versions, changes, reproducibility
Workflow: study → replicate examples → practise → attempt MCQs
content.notes:
Explain that each objective maps to a common real-world failure mode: (1) wrong units silently corrupt outputs, (2) over-precise reporting hides non-compliance, (3) sensitivity tells you what to control, (4) validation is a decision, not a feeling, and (5) audit readiness protects you when results are questioned later.

Prompting questions: Which of these do you currently do informally? Which feels least familiar: tolerances/rounding, sensitivity ranking, or audit records? Reinforce that a 'reproducible calculation log' can be a simple dated document or spreadsheet tab that records: inputs, units, conversions, formulas, and checks.

slides.title: Dimensional consistency: what you are checking

content.title: Dimensional consistency: what you are checking
content: Dimensions: physical type (L, T, M, Θ), not the unit label
Units: chosen scale (m vs mm); conversions must be explicit
Every equation must balance dimensions on both sides
Red flags: mixed unit systems, hidden constants, copied formulae
Outputs must carry units and stated conventions
A unit check is a model test, not a formatting step
content.notes:
Clarify the distinction: dimensions are the underlying physical quantities; units are the measurement scales. A formula can be numerically 'working' in one unit system and fail in another if a constant embeds unit assumptions.

Mini-example: If you use Q = A·v, A in mm² and v in m/s gives Q in mm²·m/s, which is not a standard volumetric flow unit until you convert mm² to m². The numbers may look plausible but be off by 10^6.

Misconception to address: 'The software handles units automatically.' Many tools do not unless you explicitly use a unit-aware library. Ask learners: where could a unit error hide in your typical workflow—inputs, constants, or copied data?

slides.title: A practical unit-check workflow

content.title: A practical unit-check workflow
content: List each variable with name, definition, unit, expected range
State a unit convention (SI base, prefixes, temperature scale)
Convert all inputs to the convention before modelling
Check each equation dimensionally; isolate any constants
Spot-check with an order-of-magnitude estimate
Record fixes and evidence in a calculation log
content.notes:
Walk learners through a repeatable routine they can apply to any model, including spreadsheets.

Explain the value of 'expected range': it catches swapped units (e.g., 0.5 m vs 0.5 mm) because the output becomes implausible. When checking constants, challenge them to ask: is this constant empirical (unit-dependent) or dimensionless?

Probing questions: If your output is 1000× too large, which conversion is most likely missing? Which variables are most likely to be entered in non-SI units in your domain (e.g., kPa, °C, L/min)?

Common mistake: doing conversions in-line in formulas without documenting them; this makes review and audit difficult.

slides.title: Tolerance and rounding: evaluating acceptability

content.title: Tolerance and rounding: evaluating acceptability
content: Tolerance defines acceptable deviation from a target or spec
Compare unrounded model output to tolerance first
Choose rounding to avoid hiding non-compliance
Report precision consistent with tolerance (not with calculator)
Prefer rules: decimal places or significant figures, not ad hoc
Document the rounding rule and the reason for it
content.notes:
Frame tolerance checking as a compliance question: 'Is the output within limits?' not 'How many decimals can I show?'

Teach the sequence: evaluate against tolerance using full precision; only then decide how to present. Rounding can change a pass into a fail (or vice versa), so presentation must be defensible and aligned to the specification.

Mini-example: Spec 10.0 ± 0.1. If the model gives 10.14, rounding to 1 d.p. gives 10.1 (looks like a pass), but it is actually outside tolerance. Therefore, rounding must not conceal failure.

Ask: does your stakeholder need conservative rounding (towards worst case), or standard rounding? When would you report extra digits (e.g., for internal diagnostics) versus final reporting?

slides.title: One-way sensitivity: purpose and interpretation

content.title: One-way sensitivity: purpose and interpretation
content: Vary one parameter; hold others at calibrated baseline
Use a defined perturbation (e.g., ±1%, ±10%, 1 SD)
Measure output change: absolute, % change, or vs tolerance
Rank parameters by impact on the output(s) of interest
Define 'material' with a justified cutoff
Use results to prioritise data quality and monitoring
content.notes:
Explain that one-way sensitivity is a screening tool: it tells you which parameters drive uncertainty and which are relatively harmless.

Discuss choices of perturbation size: ±10% is common for a first pass, but domain knowledge may suggest tighter bounds (e.g., sensor accuracy) or statistical bounds (±1 SD). Materiality cutoffs should relate to decision context: exceeding tolerance, changing a decision category, or moving an output by more than a stakeholder-relevant threshold.

Misconception: 'Sensitivity proves causality.' It does not; it shows model responsiveness given the current structure.

Probing questions: Which output matters to your stakeholder? If an input is highly sensitive but poorly measured, what corrective action is available: better measurement, redesign, or model refinement?

slides.title: Validation decision: fitness-for-purpose

content.title: Validation decision: fitness-for-purpose
leftColumn: Clarify stakeholder requirement and acceptance criteria
Compare evidence: checks, residuals, tolerances, sensitivity
State limitations and uncertainty explicitly
Decide: accept / accept with conditions / reject
rightColumn: Conditions: constraints on use, ranges, or required monitoring
Corrective actions: data, recalibration, model change
Record what was tested and what was not tested
Make the decision traceable to evidence
content.notes:
Position validation as a judgement against a requirement brief, not an internal quality feeling. The decision must be justified by evidence gathered in this lesson: unit checks, tolerance checks, and sensitivity results.

Explain the three outcomes:
- Accept: evidence supports intended use within stated range.
- Accept with conditions: acceptable only if certain constraints hold (e.g., temperature range, recalibration frequency, or conservative rounding).
- Reject: evidence indicates it does not meet requirements, or uncertainty is too high.

Probing questions: What is the 'intended use' and what would be an unintended use? If the model passes tolerances but is extremely sensitive to an uncertain parameter, would you accept with conditions? What conditions would be meaningful and actionable?

slides.title: Audit-ready validation record: minimum set

content.title: Audit-ready validation record: minimum set
content: Identifiers: model version, data version, parameter set ID
Change notes: what changed, why, who approved, when
Reproducibility: environment, settings, random seeds if used
Evidence: logs of unit, tolerance, and sensitivity checks
Reporting rules: rounding, units, sign conventions
Checklist: inputs, outputs, tests run, and unresolved issues
content.notes:
Explain that audit readiness is about being able to recreate results later, possibly by someone else. Stress that 'version control' can be simple (semantic version labels and dated files) but must be consistent.

Mini-example: 'Model v2.1.0, Data 2026-02-14 export, Params set P03'. If a learner re-runs with a different dataset, they should expect different outputs; the record makes this explicit.

Common mistakes: forgetting to record environment details (solver settings, spreadsheet calculation mode, locale decimal separator), or changing rounding rules late without documenting it. Ask learners: if you were asked in six months to reproduce today’s result exactly, what would you be missing?

slides.title: Worked example: fixing unit and dimensional issues

content.title: Worked example: fixing unit and dimensional issues
content.notes:
Narrate a realistic scenario: a simple flow/energy model in a spreadsheet. Emphasise recognising symptoms: extreme magnitudes, negative values where impossible, or outputs that change when you change display units.

Walk through each row:
1) Area conversion: show how 1 mm² = 1e-6 m²; explain why the error factor is so large.
2) Temperature: many thermodynamic relations require absolute temperature; show the difference between 20°C and 293.15 K.
3) Constant k: copied constants are dangerous because they often assume a particular unit system. If the constant comes from regression, refitting may be required after unit changes.

Probing questions: Which of these errors would be caught by dimensional analysis alone? Which requires domain knowledge and range checking?

slides.title: Worked example: tolerance check and rounding choice

content.title: Worked example: tolerance check and rounding choice
content.notes:
Explain the method explicitly:
1) Compare the unrounded output to the tolerance limits.
2) Decide a rounding rule that matches the tolerance resolution.

Walk learners through each row:
- Pressure: 9.96 is within 9.9–10.1, so it passes. Reporting 10.0 at 1 d.p. is consistent with ±0.1.
- Flow: 15.07 is within 14.8–15.2, passes. Reporting 15.1 at 1 d.p. reflects the tolerance scale.
- Temperature: 79.94 is within 79.5–80.5, passes. Reporting 79.9 at 1 d.p. is fine.

Key teaching point: reporting is not the test; the tolerance comparison must use unrounded values. Misconception: 'More decimals is always better.' More decimals can imply unwarranted certainty.

- Flow: 15.07 is within 14.8–15.2, passes. Reporting 15.1 at 1 d.p. reflects the tolerance scale.
- Temperature: 79.94 is within 79.5–80.5, passes. Reporting 79.9 at 1 d.p. is fine.

Key teaching point: reporting is not the test; the tolerance comparison must use unrounded values. Misconception: 'More decimals is always better.' More decimals can imply unwarranted certainty.

slides.title: Worked example: one-way sensitivity and materiality

content.title: Worked example: one-way sensitivity and materiality
content.notes:
Explain how to run the one-way sensitivity:
- Start from the calibrated baseline parameter set.
- Change one parameter at a time, rerun, record the output difference.
- Use a consistent metric (here % change in the key output).

Interpretation:
- Rank by |ΔOutput|: f (6.5%), D (4.0%), b (2.2%), ρ (0.3%).
- Define 'material' with a cutoff. Example cutoffs:
  (a) Material if |ΔOutput| > 1% (decision-relevant threshold), or
  (b) Material if it can push outputs outside tolerance.

Probing questions: Why is D tested at +1% but f at +10%? (Because plausible uncertainty differs.) If D is highly sensitive, what action is best: improved measurement, tighter manufacturing control, or re-parameterisation?

Probing questions: If you can only do one check due to time, which reduces risk most for your context? Why?

content.title: Model outputs using dimensional, tolerance and sensitivity
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD107 Mathematical Modelling: Calibration, Validation and Sensitivity | Lesson 3 | 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners to Lesson 3 within MOD107. Position the lesson as the point where we move from “getting outputs” to “judging whether outputs are credible and usable”. Emphasise Bloom’s level: evaluate—learners will justify decisions using evidence, not intuition. Remind them that in professional modelling, most failures are not exotic mathematics, but unit mistakes, unclear tolerances, and weak audit trails.
