slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Use: read slides → replicate examples → attempt checks
Objective 1: fix ≥3 unit/scale issues with written justification
Objective 2: interpret tolerance/sensitivity vs acceptance limits
Objective 3: pass/conditional pass/fail with evidence log
Objective 4: record audit trail + link to version control and CI
content.notes: Explain how to study this lesson: (1) follow the concepts, (2) reproduce the worked steps in your own calculator/spreadsheet, (3) then attempt the quizzes as readiness checks. Clarify the difference between “correcting” and “explaining”: you must justify why a unit conversion or scaling is correct, not merely apply it. Probe: What would convince a stakeholder that your correction is trustworthy? Highlight that robustness and fitness-for-purpose are not the same: a model can be robust but still fail requirements. Common misconception: assuming that producing a plot or running a sensitivity tool automatically counts as validation—validation requires explicit criteria and evidence.

slides.title: Dimensional analysis as a validation gate

content.title: Dimensional analysis as a validation gate
content: Check every column: quantity, unit, scale, sign
Convert to a consistent base (e.g., SI) before comparing
Use order-of-magnitude tests to spot scale errors
Sanity checks: bounds, monotonicity, conservation
Document corrections: what changed, why, and impact
content.notes: Talk through dimensional analysis as a fast, high-yield check performed before deeper validation. Stress that “dimensionally consistent” does not mean “correct”, but “dimensionally inconsistent” is almost always wrong. Give a mini-example: if energy is reported in kWh but treated as kJ, the factor is 3600—large enough to break decisions. Probing questions: If two outputs disagree, is it a modelling error or a reporting/units error? What is your reference system of units? Misconception to address: relying on software defaults—tools may display units, but they do not enforce correct conversions or scaling.

slides.title: Tolerance, sensitivity and robustness

content.title: Tolerance, sensitivity and robustness
content: Tolerance: allowed deviation from a target or requirement
Sensitivity: how outputs change when inputs/params change
Local vs global sensitivity: small vs wide perturbations
Robust if outputs stay within limits across perturbations
Report both magnitude and direction of change
content.notes: Define tolerance as a stakeholder or engineering concept (acceptable error band), and sensitivity as a mathematical/empirical property of the model. Explain that a highly sensitive model is not automatically “bad”; it may reflect genuine system behaviour, but it increases risk if parameters are uncertain. Provide a mini-example: a 1% change in a friction coefficient causing a 15% change in stopping distance is a red flag for calibration and safety. Probing questions: Which parameters are uncertain in your setting? Which outputs matter most to stakeholders? Misconception: treating “sensitivity analysis” as a single method—learners should recognise multiple approaches (one-at-a-time, factorial, Monte Carlo) and choose proportionate effort.

slides.title: Fitness-for-purpose decision framework

content.title: Fitness-for-purpose decision framework
content: Start from requirements: outputs, accuracy, context of use
Define acceptance limits and evidence needed to judge them
Assess: assumptions, data quality, uncertainty, residuals
Decide: pass, conditional pass, or fail
Record rationale as a concise validation evidence log
content.notes: Emphasise that fitness-for-purpose is a decision relative to intended use, not an absolute label. Explain pass/conditional pass/fail: conditional pass often means “usable if constraints are met”, such as narrower operating ranges, added monitoring, or more calibration data. Probing questions: What would change your decision? What evidence is missing? Common misconception: trying to hide assumptions—assumptions are acceptable if they are explicit, justified, and tested for impact.

slides.title: Reproducible calculations and audit readiness

content.title: Reproducible calculations and audit readiness
content: Record inputs, sources, and preprocessing choices
State software, version, and environment details
Apply explicit rounding and significant-figure rules
Include verification steps and independent cross-checks
Link to commit hash and CI run status where applicable
content.notes: Frame reproducibility as a professional standard: someone else (or you in two weeks) should be able to regenerate the numbers. Explain a “minimal audit trail”: you do not need a novel, but you do need unambiguous traceability. Give concrete examples: pin package versions; capture random seeds; store the exact requirements brief version. Probing questions: If your output changes after an update, can you prove why? Misconception: believing screenshots are sufficient evidence—prefer scripts, saved notebooks, or exported logs linked to version control and CI.

slides.title: Worked example: fixing unit and scale mismatches

content.title: Worked example: fixing unit and scale mismatches
content.notes: Walk learners row-by-row and model the justification language. For each correction, state (1) the requirement or reference, (2) the conversion, and (3) the impact on downstream interpretation. Emphasise documenting ambiguity: for temperature, the key is noticing the missing unit and resolving it using context (sensor specification, typical ranges, solver settings). Probing questions: Which of these errors is most dangerous and why? How would you confirm the intended unit if documentation is weak? Misconception: assuming “no unit” means “dimensionless”; often it means “unit not recorded”, which is a quality issue requiring resolution.

slides.title: Worked example: tolerance and sensitivity decision

content.title: Worked example: tolerance and sensitivity decision
content.notes: Explain what the table demonstrates: a model can pass at baseline yet fail robustness because plausible parameter shifts breach limits. Clarify interpretation: sensitivity is asymmetric here (increases in k and c push the output over the limit). Show how to write an evidence-based judgement: “Given ±10% uncertainty in k, peak exceeds limit by 0.6; therefore not robust unless k uncertainty is reduced or design margin increased.” Probing questions: What is the source of the ±10% assumption? Would stakeholder limits be absolute or could they be negotiated with mitigation? Misconception: equating ‘small parameter change’ with ‘small output change’; the model structure can amplify effects.

slides.title: Worked example: concise validation evidence log

content.title: Worked example: concise validation evidence log
content.notes: Explain that this is not bureaucratic overhead: it is a decision record. Highlight good practice: each check has (a) what you did, (b) what happened, and (c) how to reproduce it. Clarify “conditional pass”: state the condition explicitly (e.g., restrict operating range; reduce parameter uncertainty; add monitoring). Probing questions: If audited, could you point to the exact run that produced the numbers? What would a ‘fail’ look like in your context? Misconception: thinking version control is only for code—spreadsheets, requirements briefs, and logs should also be versioned.

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
leftColumn: Find 3 unit/scale risks in your last model output
Write conversions and one-sentence justifications
Pick 2 uncertain parameters and set perturbation ranges
Check outputs against one explicit acceptance limit
rightColumn: Which assumption most affects your decision?
What evidence would reduce uncertainty fastest?
Would a stakeholder accept conditional pass? Why?
How would you make your results reproducible?
content.notes: Encourage learners to use their own work if available; otherwise, invent a small table of outputs and apply the prompts. Remind them that the goal is evaluative reasoning: ‘because X, therefore Y’. Offer scaffolding: if they struggle to choose perturbation ranges, use datasheet tolerances, literature ranges, or calibration confidence intervals. Probing questions: Are your acceptance limits stated before you look at results? If not, why is that risky? Misconception: doing sensitivity first and then inventing limits—limits should come from requirements and risk appetite.

slides.title: Formative checks: what to look out for

content.title: Formative checks: what to look out for
content: MCQ: Validation, Sensitivity and Audit Readiness
Quiz: Calibration and Parameter Fitting from Data
Focus: interpret evidence, not memorise definitions
Show workings for conversions and tolerance comparisons
If wrong: identify whether concept, maths, or reading error
content.notes: Frame quizzes as diagnosis. Advise learners to review explanations for incorrect answers and categorise the failure mode: misunderstanding (concept), arithmetic (calculation), or misreading units/limits (interpretation). Suggest a method: for each question, underline given units and acceptance limits before computing anything. Probing questions: Did you assume a unit that was not stated? Did you compare against the right limit (upper vs lower bound)? Misconception: rushing MCQs—many errors are avoidable with a 10-second ‘units-first’ scan.

leftColumn: Supports: validation report and robustness justification
Evidence log structure fits appendices and audit needs
Dimensional checks strengthen credibility of results
CI/commit links show reproducibility and traceability
rightColumn: Mistake: mixing °C/K or kPa/Pa without stating it
Mistake: sensitivity shown, but no acceptance limits
Mistake: decisions made with no written rationale
Mistake: results not reproducible (no versions, no inputs)

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Dimensional analysis is the first, fastest credibility check
Tolerance is a limit; sensitivity is behaviour under change
Robustness depends on staying within stakeholder limits

slides.title: Fitness-for-purpose: the evaluation frame

content.title: Fitness-for-purpose: the evaluation frame
content: Validation answers: can we use this output for this decision?
Start from stakeholder requirements, not model elegance
Evidence types: checks, comparisons, sensitivity, uncertainty
Decision options: pass, conditional-pass, fail
Always state at least one limitation or uncertainty
content.notes: Expand the idea of fitness-for-purpose: a model can be ‘correct’ mathematically yet unfit because it omits a key effect, has too much uncertainty, or reports outputs at the wrong precision. Give a mini-example: predicting annual energy use may be fit with ±10% error, but sizing a safety-critical component may require ±2% with conservative bounds. Ask: What decision will be made from this output? What is the cost of being wrong? Misconception: treating validation as a single universal standard rather than decision-dependent.

slides.title: Structured output validation checklist

content.title: Structured output validation checklist
content.notes: Walk learners through how to use the checklist as a repeatable process. Clarify the difference between ‘units’ (labels and conversions) and ‘dimensions’ (fundamental physical dimensions). Provide a short illustration: adding 5 m + 2 s is dimensionally invalid even if both are numbers. Explain rounding: retain full precision internally, round only for reporting; show how rounding intermediate values can accumulate error. For tolerances: distinguish measurement tolerance, manufacturing tolerance, and requirement tolerance; specify whether tolerances are symmetric or one-sided. For sensitivity: emphasise that it is not just about uncertainty—high sensitivity can signal the need for tighter control or better data.

slides.title: Dimensional consistency: quick diagnostics

content.title: Dimensional consistency: quick diagnostics
content: Write each variable with units and dimensions (e.g., m, kg, s)
Check each equation balances dimensions on both sides
Watch sums: only like dimensions can be added or subtracted
Check outputs: do magnitudes look plausible for the domain?
Flag any “magic constants” with unclear units
content.notes: Explain a practical method: annotate each term in an equation with dimensions, not just units; this catches hidden conversion errors. Give a mini-example: kinetic energy 0.5 m v^2 has dimensions kg·(m/s)^2 = kg·m^2/s^2, which matches Joules. Contrast with a common mistake: using v instead of v^2, which gives kg·m/s^2 (a force), clearly wrong. Probing questions: If you doubled length units from m to cm, would the numerical value change in a predictable way? Misconception: assuming a spreadsheet formula is correct because it ‘runs’ without errors.

slides.title: Rounding and reporting precision

content.title: Rounding and reporting precision
content: Keep full precision in calculations; round only at the end
Report to match measurement resolution and requirement tolerance
Use significant figures for multiplicative models
Use decimal places for additive models and fixed tolerances
Check that rounding cannot flip a pass/fail decision
content.notes: Explain why rounding matters in evaluation: rounding can change compliance status near a tolerance boundary. Provide a mini-example: a limit of 10.00 mm with output 10.004 mm should fail if the rule is strict; rounding to 10.00 mm would hide the exceedance. Discuss significant figures: when inputs have limited precision, outputs cannot be more certain than inputs allow. Encourage learners to state a rounding policy explicitly (e.g., ‘report to 3 s.f.; keep 10+ digits internally’). Misconception: thinking that more decimal places always means more accuracy.

slides.title: Tolerances and uncertainty: interpreting bands

content.title: Tolerances and uncertainty: interpreting bands
content: Distinguish spec tolerance from model uncertainty
Check worst-case and nominal cases where appropriate
State whether tolerance is absolute, relative, or both
Avoid mixing confidence levels (e.g., 1σ vs 95%)
Document assumptions on distributions and correlations
content.notes: Clarify that tolerance is typically a requirement (what is allowed), while uncertainty describes what we do not know about the true value. Explain worst-case reasoning: if inputs can vary within bounds and safety matters, worst-case may be required; in other contexts, statistical confidence may be acceptable. Give a mini-example: a sensor accuracy ±0.5% (often a bound) is not the same as a standard deviation. Probing questions: What confidence does the stakeholder need? Are uncertainties independent, or do they move together? Misconception: treating all uncertainty numbers as directly comparable without their statistical meaning.

slides.title: One-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity: the method

content.title: One-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity: the method
content: Choose baseline inputs and record baseline output y0
Vary one input by a defined step (e.g., ±5% or ±1 unit)
Hold other inputs fixed; compute new output y1
Quantify Δy and %Δy = (y1−y0)/y0 × 100%
Rank inputs by |%Δy| to identify influential parameters
content.notes: Explain OAT as a local sensitivity check: it tests behaviour near the baseline, not across all plausible combinations. Discuss step size: use a step that is meaningful relative to data quality (e.g., measurement tolerance) and small enough to stay in the same regime, but large enough to avoid numerical noise. Mention directionality: +5% and −5% may not be symmetric in nonlinear models. Probing questions: Does the ranking change if you use ±1% instead of ±10%? What would you do if the output is highly sensitive to a poorly measured input? Misconception: assuming OAT captures interaction effects between inputs—it does not.

slides.title: Worked example 1: unit and dimension check

content.title: Worked example 1: unit and dimension check
leftColumn: Given: Q = ρ·A·v
rightColumn: Units: (kg/m^3)(m^2)(m/s) = kg/s
So Q is mass flow rate, not volumetric flow
If volumetric flow needed: use q = A·v (m^3/s)
Issue: variable name and unit mismatch
content.notes: Narrate the example as a real validation moment: a formula may be correct, but the output label may be wrong for the stakeholder need. Here, Q computed with density is mass flow rate (kg/s). If the requirement is volumetric flow (m^3/s), the model output is not directly fit-for-purpose without conversion or reformulation. Ask learners: What would happen if someone assumed Q was m^3/s and sized equipment? Highlight that dimensional analysis quickly reveals the mismatch even before plugging numbers. Extend: show the conversion if needed—mass flow ÷ density gives volumetric flow.

slides.title: Worked example 2: tolerance and rounding decision

content.title: Worked example 2: tolerance and rounding decision
content.notes: Explain that both 9.996 mm and 10.004 mm are within ±0.005 mm, so they pass on a strict numeric check. The teaching point is about auditability and decision robustness: rounding to 2 d.p. masks proximity to the limit, and in other cases could flip the decision (e.g., 10.006 mm would fail but might display as 10.01 mm or 10.00 mm depending on rounding). Encourage learners to report: (1) unrounded internal value, (2) rounded display value, and (3) margin to limit (headroom). Probing question: If a stakeholder re-runs your numbers with slightly different rounding, will they reach the same decision?

slides.title: Worked example 3: OAT sensitivity ranking

content.title: Worked example 3: OAT sensitivity ranking
content.notes: Interpret the table: parameter a is the most influential under the chosen perturbation, then b, then c. Discuss what ‘influential’ means in practice: if a is uncertain or controllable, improving its estimate/control will most reduce output uncertainty. Also note sign: c reduces output when increased, which may matter for corrective actions. Ask learners: Would you also test −5% to check linearity and symmetry? What if y0 were near zero—how would you handle percent change? Misconception: assuming the largest absolute change always indicates a modelling error; it may simply reflect real physics or scaling.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: apply the checklist

content.title: Practice and reflection: apply the checklist
content: List 5 checks you would apply to a new model output
Write one example issue per area: units, dims, rounding, tol, sens
Draft a pass/conditional-pass/fail decision with 3 evidence points
State one limitation and its likely impact on the decision
Reflect: which check gives you most confidence, and why?
content.notes: Guide learners to practise without a provided dataset by using a ‘generic’ model output they have seen before (from earlier lessons, work, or a simple spreadsheet). Common misconception: thinking a limitation must invalidate the model; often it leads to conditional acceptance with clear boundaries.

slides.title: Audit-ready calculation trail and validation summary

content.title: Audit-ready calculation trail and validation summary
leftColumn: Inputs: values, units, source, timestamp
Assumptions: scope, simplifications, exclusions
Model version: file name, hash/ID, change note
Results: outputs, units, rounding policy
rightColumn: Validation: checks run + outcomes
Evidence: tables, screenshots, comparison benchmarks
Decision: pass/cond-pass/fail + rationale
Limitations: uncertainty, sensitivity, data gaps
content.notes: Explain that audit readiness is about reproducibility: another person should be able to recreate your result and understand why you trusted it. Provide a version-control style change note example: ‘v1.3: corrected density units kg/L → kg/m^3; recalculated Q; updated tolerance check’. Encourage learners to separate raw inputs from derived quantities and to cite sources (datasheet, measurement log, stakeholder brief). Probing question: If you were absent, could a colleague defend your decision to an external reviewer? Misconception: treating documentation as administrative overhead rather than part of technical quality.

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD107 validation and sensitivity write-ups
Use the checklist to structure your evidence and decision
Common pitfall: unit mismatch hidden by “reasonable” numbers
Common pitfall: OAT results reported without baseline y0

slides.title: Model outputs: dimensional, tolerance and sensitivity

content.title: Model outputs: dimensional, tolerance and sensitivity
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD107 Mathematical Modelling | Lesson 5 | 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners to Lesson 5, positioned late in the modelling workflow: once a model is calibrated, we must evaluate whether its outputs are trustworthy for decision-making. Emphasise the Bloom level (evaluate): the goal is not to compute more numbers, but to judge fitness-for-purpose using evidence. Briefly frame the three evidence strands used throughout: (1) dimensional consistency (units and scaling sanity), (2) sensitivity and tolerance checks (how outputs move when inputs move), and (3) audit readiness (reproducibility and version control). Invite learners to think of this lesson as the bridge from “I can run the model” to “I can defend the model in a review.”

slides.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson
content: Learning focus: evaluate model outputs against requirements
Step 1: check dimensional consistency (units, scales, conversions)
Step 2: run sensitivity and tolerance checks vs acceptance criteria
Step 3: decide fitness-for-purpose with quantified uncertainty
Step 4: create an audit-ready calculation record and version tag
Finish with two MCQ quizzes to self-check understanding
content.notes: Talk learners through a practical study path: first read the checklists/frameworks, then follow the worked examples, then attempt the practice prompts before taking the MCQs. Stress that evaluation requires explicit criteria: “acceptable” must be defined by stakeholders (or by a proxy if not provided). Encourage learners to keep a running record as they study: write down units, assumptions, and any rounding rules used in examples—this models the audit-ready habit. Probing questions: What evidence would convince a reviewer that your output variability is acceptable? What would make you reject a model even if it fits historical data?

slides.title: Dimensional consistency: checklist and intent

content.title: Dimensional consistency: checklist and intent
content: List units for every input, parameter, intermediate and output
Check each equation: both sides must have identical dimensions
Confirm constants are not hiding unit conversions
Verify scaling factors (k, 10^x) are documented and justified
Test with a unit change (e.g., m to cm) and compare outputs
Record fixes with evidence: before/after units and conversions
content.notes: Explain that dimensional consistency is a low-cost, high-yield validation step: many model failures are not “math errors” but unit/scale mismatches. Clarify: dimensional analysis is not the same as checking numerical plausibility—an answer can be plausible yet dimensionally wrong, or vice versa. Mini-example: if a flow rate is entered as L/min but treated as L/s, outputs shift by a factor of 60; calibration may still “fit” by distorting parameters, masking the defect. Probing questions: If you changed all lengths from metres to millimetres, what should happen to your dimensionless outputs? Which parameters should change, and which should remain invariant?

slides.title: Common unit and scaling inconsistencies

content.title: Common unit and scaling inconsistencies
content.notes: Walk through the idea that not all errors are multiplicative. Temperature is a key misconception: Celsius and Kelvin share scale but differ by an offset; using Celsius in equations requiring absolute temperature (e.g., ideal gas law) breaks the physics, not just the magnitude. Encourage learners to look for “hidden conversions”: a constant like 0.27778 might be km/h to m/s; if undocumented, it becomes a maintenance risk. Ask: Which of these errors could be ‘absorbed’ by calibration, and why is that dangerous? Highlight that the correction evidence must be auditable: show the original value, the conversion, and the updated run results.

slides.title: Sensitivity vs tolerance: what are we checking?

content.title: Sensitivity vs tolerance: what are we checking?
leftColumn: Sensitivity (OAT)
Purpose: rank influential inputs
Change one input, hold others fixed
Output: % change or elasticity
rightColumn: Tolerance-bound check
Purpose: worst-case within allowed ranges
Vary inputs within stated tolerances
Output: output range vs acceptance limits
content.notes: Clarify the distinction: sensitivity is about influence; tolerance is about compliance. One-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity is simple and interpretable, but it assumes local linearity and ignores interactions—state that limitation explicitly. Tolerance-bound checks align more directly with stakeholder risk: “Given allowed input uncertainty, will outputs remain acceptable?” Provide a mini-example: if an input has low sensitivity but very large tolerance, it can still dominate output risk. Probing questions: If two inputs interact (e.g., multiplied together), what does OAT miss? When would you need a more advanced method (e.g., factorial designs, Sobol indices)?

slides.title: Acceptance criteria and decision rules

content.title: Acceptance criteria and decision rules
content: Start with stakeholder limits: target, min/max, or error bands
Define metric: absolute error, relative error, or probability
State decision rule: accept, accept-with-limits, or reject
Separate calibration fit from predictive validity
Quantify uncertainty: intervals, bounds, or scenario ranges
Write limitations: domain, data gaps, known failure modes
content.notes: Explain that evaluation needs a clearly stated rule, otherwise results become subjective. Distinguish model fit (matching past data) from validity for purpose (reliable predictions under intended use). Introduce an explicit template: “Accept if output stays within ±X for all tolerance scenarios; otherwise reject or restrict domain.” Emphasise that “accept-with-limits” is often the professional outcome: you may accept the model only for a subset of conditions. Misconception to tackle: “If it matches historical data, it is valid.” Calibration can hide structural errors. Probing questions: What is the cost of false acceptance vs false rejection in your domain? How would that change the acceptance band?

slides.title: Audit-ready record and version control

content.title: Audit-ready record and version control
content: Record inputs, sources, and units for every run
List assumptions and rounding rules (and where applied)
Document run steps so another person can reproduce results
Store artefacts: data files, scripts, plots, parameter sets
Use commits/tags: what changed, why, and impact on outputs
Log corrective actions and link them to detected issues
content.notes: Frame audit readiness as both quality assurance and professional protection: if a result is challenged, you must show how you obtained it. Give a concrete example of a good commit message: “Fix: convert pressure kPa→Pa in Eq(3); outputs -0.8%.” Contrast with a poor message: “update.” Explain tagging: create a version tag for the evaluated release (e.g., v1.2-validation) so results are traceable. Common misconception: saving multiple spreadsheet copies is version control; it is not reliable or searchable. Probing questions: Could someone reproduce your result in six months with only your record? What would they need that you have not captured?

slides.title: Worked example: dimensional check and corrections

content.title: Worked example: dimensional check and corrections
content.notes: Narrate a realistic review workflow: start by listing each variable with units as provided in the data sheet, then check each equation’s dimensional balance. For each issue, show the evidence chain: where the unit was stated, where it was assumed differently, and the exact conversion used. Emphasise that “correction” includes re-running the model and noting output changes; learners should not stop at converting numbers. Ask learners to reflect: Which correction changes ratios (multiplying/dividing) and which changes offsets? Highlight that temperature is a classic trap: using 20 instead of 293.15 can catastrophically distort any formula involving T in a denominator.

slides.title: Worked example: OAT sensitivity in five steps

content.title: Worked example: OAT sensitivity in five steps
content: Choose output metric (e.g., cost per unit, error, peak value)
Select inputs and baseline values (document sources and units)
Perturb each input by a fixed % (e.g., ±10%) one at a time
Compute sensitivity: Δoutput / Δinput (or %/% elasticity)
Rank inputs and note nonlinearity (asymmetric +10% vs -10%)
content.notes: Teach the OAT procedure with an emphasis on documentation and interpretation. Suggest a sensible perturbation size: large enough to exceed numerical noise but small enough to remain in the local regime; ±10% is a common starting point, but use domain knowledge. Provide a mini-example verbally: if baseline output is 100 and +10% input gives 112, elasticity ≈ (12%)/(10%) = 1.2; that input is influential. Emphasise checking symmetry: if +10% causes +20% but -10% causes -5%, the model is nonlinear or constrained. Misconception: “highest sensitivity means highest risk”; risk also depends on tolerance/uncertainty of that input.

slides.title: Worked example: tolerance-bound vs acceptance

content.title: Worked example: tolerance-bound vs acceptance
content.notes: Explain how to interpret the table: acceptance is determined by the stated criterion (here, an example band of 100±10 with a hard cap at 110). Even if the nominal scenario passes, a credible worst-case failure can justify rejection or a restricted operating envelope. Highlight the modelling judgement: “worst-case” may be overly conservative if input extremes are unlikely to co-occur; however, if stakeholders require a hard guarantee, worst-case is appropriate. Probing questions: Are tolerances independent? If not, what correlation assumptions are you making? Would a probabilistic check (e.g., Monte Carlo) be more aligned with stakeholder needs?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
leftColumn: Find 3 unit/scale issues in your model
Write conversions and show before/after units
Run OAT: ±10% for 5 key inputs
List top 3 drivers and explain why
rightColumn: Define stakeholder criterion for one output

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports MOD107 tasks on validation, sensitivity and reporting
Evidence expected: units, conversions, plots/tables, decision rule
Common error: confusing calibration fit with validation evidence
Common error: reporting sensitivity without stating perturbations
Common error: no reproducibility steps or version tags
Use the two MCQ quizzes to check readiness for submission
content.notes: Explain how this lesson feeds into typical module submissions: learners must provide an evaluative narrative supported by artefacts. Clarify what “evidence” means in marking terms: not just statements, but traceable calculations and documented decisions. Unpack common errors: students often present a sensitivity chart without specifying whether they used ±1%, ±10%, or absolute changes; this makes results uninterpretable. Another frequent issue is omission of the decision rule—markers cannot infer what “good” means. Encourage learners to treat the MCQs as diagnostic: if they miss items on validation vs calibration, revisit the acceptance criteria slide.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Dimensional checks catch hidden model errors cheaply and early
Sensitivity ranks drivers; tolerance checks compliance vs criteria
Fitness-for-purpose needs an explicit decision rule and evidence
Quantify uncertainty and state limitations, not just point values
Reproducible records and version control make results auditable
content.notes: Close by reinforcing the evaluation mindset: the objective is defensible judgement, not perfect certainty. Encourage learners to adopt a repeatable workflow: unit audit → sensitivity screening → tolerance/acceptance test → recommendation → audit record and version tag. slides.title: Fitness-for-purpose: what you must demonstrate

content.title: Fitness-for-purpose: what you must demonstrate
content: Model meets stated use-case, not every possible use-case
Inputs/outputs, units, and assumptions are explicit
Accuracy is evaluated against stakeholder tolerances
Uncertainty and limitations are stated, not hidden
Evidence is reproducible from data + method description
content.notes: Fitness-for-purpose is a targeted claim: the model is adequate for a specified decision context. For example, a model may be acceptable for weekly planning but unacceptable for real-time control. Encourage learners to translate a brief into measurable criteria (e.g., ‘within ±5% for typical loads’). Ask: Which errors are more costly—overestimation or underestimation? Misconception: believing ‘more complex’ implies ‘more fit’. Often a simpler model is preferable if it is robust, explainable, and meets tolerances.

content.title: Model Card: minimum audit-ready structure
content.notes: Treat the Model Card as a one-page contract between you and the stakeholder: it states what the model is for, what it uses, what it assumes, and what evidence supports it. Emphasise that ‘Model’ must include variables, units, and parameter sources; ‘Validation’ must include explicit acceptance thresholds and outcomes. Probing question: If someone only read the Model Card, could they safely use the model? Misconception: using the Model Card as marketing—avoid claims without quantified evidence.

slides.title: Calibration workflow from operational data

content.title: Calibration workflow from operational data
content: Define target output and allowable error (tolerance)
Select model form justified by physics/process knowledge
Prepare data: filtering, missing values, outliers, units
Estimate parameters; record method and initial values
Check plausibility: signs, magnitudes, and constraints
Freeze baseline results before further iterations
content.notes: Calibration is not only parameter fitting; it is a documented sequence that links data to a decision-ready model. Highlight data hygiene: operational data often contains sensor faults, regime changes, and inconsistent units. Parameter estimation can be least squares, maximum likelihood, or constrained optimisation—what matters is that the method is stated and reproducible. Ask: What would you do if two parameter sets fit equally well? Misconception: adjusting data until the model looks good—any preprocessing must be justified and recorded.

slides.title: Validation checks: evidence and decisions

content.title: Validation checks: evidence and decisions
leftColumn: Residual inspection
Dimensional/unit check
Tolerance/rounding check
Holdout test
rightColumn: Look for bias, trends, heteroscedasticity
Confirm units consistent; no hidden conversions
Verify rounding does not breach tolerances
Test on unseen data; compare to acceptance criteria
content.notes: Explain each check as a different failure detector. Residual plots can reveal misspecification even when aggregate metrics look fine (e.g., systematic underprediction at high loads). Unit checks prevent ‘silent’ errors—especially when stakeholders combine data from multiple sources. Rounding/tolerance checks matter in operational settings where decisions are threshold-based (e.g., pass/fail, compliance). Holdout testing guards against overfitting to the calibration period. Probing question: Which check would most likely catch a mistaken unit conversion? Misconception: treating validation as one metric; fitness-for-purpose needs multiple complementary checks.

slides.title: Audit-ready version control options

content.title: Audit-ready version control options
content.notes: An auditor (or future you) must be able to reconstruct how results were produced and why they changed. For learners new to Git, a well-maintained change log plus consistent naming is acceptable, but it must still capture: what changed, why, who/when, and impact on results. Demonstrate a strong commit message structure: ‘Change: … Reason: … Impact: …’. Probing question: If a stakeholder disputes an output, how quickly can you identify which version produced it? Misconception: versioning is only for software—models and spreadsheets require the same discipline.

slides.title: Worked example 1: from brief to model choice

content.title: Worked example 1: from brief to model choice
content: Brief: predict daily energy use for planning, ±5% target
Data: daily production volume V, temperature T, energy E
Candidate model: E = a + bV + cT
Scope: valid for V in observed range; no extrapolation
Assumption: linear effects; interactions ignored initially
content.notes: Walk learners through translating a brief into a modelling statement. Emphasise specifying tolerance early: it defines ‘good enough’. Justify the model form: linear terms are a reasonable baseline when the goal is planning and interpretability, but note limitations (e.g., may miss nonlinear efficiency effects). Ask: What operational regimes might break linearity (start-up/shutdown, extreme temperatures)? Misconception: assuming the chosen features are automatically causal—state them as predictive drivers unless causal evidence exists.

slides.title: Worked example 2: variable and parameter register

content.title: Worked example 2: variable and parameter register
content.notes: This register is often the fastest way to prevent confusion and rework. Make learners check dimensional consistency: b must convert tonnes/day into kWh/day, so its unit is kWh/tonne; c is kWh/°C. Explain that ‘source’ distinguishes measured variables from estimated parameters and clarifies provenance. Probing questions: Do any variables require scaling or conversion (e.g., MWh to kWh)? Are there time alignment issues (temperature averaged over the same day)? Misconception: leaving units implicit because ‘everyone knows them’—in practice, mixed units are a leading cause of model failure.

slides.title: Worked example 3: when validation fails

content.title: Worked example 3: when validation fails
leftColumn: Residuals rise with V
Unit check shows V in kg
Holdout error > ±5%
Rounding flips pass/fail
rightColumn: Try log/interaction; check regimes
Convert to tonnes; re-fit; note change
Re-calibrate; reduce features; add constraints
Use higher precision; revise tolerance rule
content.notes: Use this slide to model diagnostic thinking: each failure signal implies specific corrective actions, not random tweaking. If residual variance increases with V, discuss heteroscedasticity and remedies (transformations, weighted least squares, segmented models). The unit error example shows why validation must include unit checks—fixing units is not ‘minor’; it changes parameter meaning and results. For holdout failure, highlight the difference between poor fit and poor generalisation; consider data drift or omitted variables. For rounding issues, stress that operational decisions can be threshold-based, so numerical precision and decision rules must be explicitly defined. Probing question: Which corrective action changes the model structure versus only the calibration? Misconception: believing you must always ‘force a pass’—sometimes the correct action is to narrow the intended use or state limitations.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: your turn

content.notes: Encourage learners to keep outputs short but complete: a Model Card should be readable in under two minutes. For residual inspection, suggest a simple plot or a brief description of patterns (e.g., ‘underpredicts above V=120’). For holdout, specify the split rationale (e.g., last month as holdout to mimic future use). For change logging, prompt them to quantify impact (e.g., RMSE, bias, number of records removed). Reflection questions: What is the single biggest risk if this model is used incorrectly? Which assumption is most fragile? Misconception: treating MCQs as separate from practice—the quizzes should reveal gaps to fix in your Model Card or validation evidence.

Evidence must be reproducible
Show thresholds tied to the brief
Keep an audit trail of changes
rightColumn: Mistake: report metrics but no pass/fail decision
Mistake: omit units or parameter sources

Probing question: If your stakeholder tolerance is ±5%, what does a 4% error mean if the model is biased high in one regime? Misconception: that a single strong plot can substitute for documented decisions and traceability.

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Fitness-for-purpose is defined by the brief and tolerances
Model Cards make assumptions, units, and scope explicit
Use multiple validation checks; record evidence + decisions
Version control is part of technical quality, not admin

Common misconception: that uncertainty statements weaken credibility—done properly, they strengthen it because they prevent misuse.

slides.title: Core concept: model spec and boundaries

content.title: Core concept: model spec and boundaries
content: State purpose: decision to support and audience
Define outputs (KPIs) and required accuracy/tolerance
List variables, parameters, and units for each
Assumptions: at least five, explicit and testable
Boundaries: time range, operating regime, exclusions
Parameter sources: data fields, literature, judgement
content.notes: Explain that a model spec is a contract: it tells others what the model is for, how it works at a high level, and when it should not be trusted. Give mini-examples of boundaries: “valid for throughput 50–120 units/hour”, “excludes start-up transients”, “assumes steady ambient temperature”. Stress that assumptions should be testable or at least reviewable; avoid vague phrases like “assume normal conditions” without defining normal. Common misconception: listing assumptions weakens a model; actually it strengthens credibility and speeds review. Probing questions: Which assumptions are about physics/operations, which are about data quality, and which are about simplifications for tractability?

slides.title: Core concept: variables vs parameters vs data

content.title: Core concept: variables vs parameters vs data
leftColumn: Variables: change within a run
Parameters: fixed per scenario/run
Data: observed values used to fit params
Outputs: modelled KPIs for decisions
rightColumn: Example: flow rate q(t), temperature T(t)
Example: loss factor k, efficiency η
Example: sensor readings, logs, meter totals
Example: cost, risk, capacity, emissions
content.notes: Use this slide to clean up terminology, because confusion here causes messy spreadsheets and unclear calibration. Explain: variables can be time-indexed or condition-indexed; parameters are constants within a run but can vary between scenarios. Data is not automatically “truth”: discuss measurement error, missingness, and sampling frequency mismatch. Mini-example: fitting a pump curve—flow and head are variables, curve coefficients are parameters, SCADA readings are data, predicted energy use is an output. Probing question: In your current project, what did you treat as a parameter that might actually be a variable (e.g., efficiency changing with load)?

slides.title: Core concept: calibration as an optimisation problem

content.title: Core concept: calibration as an optimisation problem
content: Choose objective: minimise error between model and data
Select error metric: SSE, MAE, MAPE, weighted error
Set constraints: bounds, monotonicity, physical limits
Split data: fit set vs check set when possible
Avoid overfitting: prefer parsimonious parameter sets
Record: initial guesses, final params, and fit quality
content.notes: Explain calibration as parameter estimation: you pick parameters to best match observed behaviour under a chosen criterion. Discuss why the error metric matters: MAE is robust to outliers; SSE penalises large errors; MAPE can misbehave near zero. Mention weighting when measurements have different reliability or variance. Address constraints: parameters should stay physically plausible (e.g., efficiencies between 0 and 1). Encourage a simple fit/check split or at least time-based hold-out if data is limited. Common misconception: a very low calibration error means the model is correct; it may simply be flexible enough to mimic noise. Probing question: What would make you choose MAE over SSE for your dataset?

slides.title: Core concept: reproducible workflow and audit trail

content.title: Core concept: reproducible workflow and audit trail
content: Separate inputs, parameters, calculations, outputs
Label every input/output with units (e.g., kW, kg/s)
Annotate formulas/code: purpose and source links
One path to rerun: button/macro or notebook 'Run all'
Version control: dated exports + change log notes
Freeze key outputs: tables/plots with run timestamp
content.notes: Make clear that reproducibility is both technical and procedural. In spreadsheets, recommend an Inputs tab, Parameters tab, Calculations tab, Outputs tab, and a Calibration tab; use named ranges and consistent unit conventions. In notebooks, recommend a top-to-bottom structure with parameter cells first, then functions, then calibration, then checks, then reporting. Explain what an audit trail looks like: parameter sources cited (dataset column name, document reference), calibration settings recorded (solver method, tolerance), and outputs time-stamped. Common misconception: comments are optional; in assessment and professional review, they are part of the evidence. Probing question: If someone else changes an input unit (e.g., minutes to seconds), where would the model catch that mistake?

slides.title: Core concept: validation checks you must submit

content.title: Core concept: validation checks you must submit

rows: Verify units balance in key equations
Apply rounding policy; test numeric stability

content.notes: Walk through each check as a different type of risk control. Dimensional consistency catches structural mistakes early (e.g., adding kW to kWh). Rounding/tolerance is about both reporting discipline and numerical robustness; define a rounding policy such as “store full precision, report to 2 d.p., compare decisions at full precision.” Sensitivity is not only ‘change inputs and see outputs’; it needs interpretation: why does a parameter matter, and what does that imply for data collection priorities? Reasonableness checks include extreme values, boundary conditions, and “back-of-envelope” comparisons. Common misconception: these checks are optional extras; they are core evidence for model credibility. Probing question: Which check would most likely catch a spreadsheet copy/paste error, and why?

slides.title: Core concept: uncertainty and transparency statement

content.title: Core concept: uncertainty and transparency statement
content: Pick one key output and quantify uncertainty (CI or band)
Separate sources: data error, parameter, model form error
Method options: analytic CI, bootstrap, scenario band
Report assumptions behind the uncertainty method
Interpretation: what the CI does and does not mean
State limits: when uncertainty may be understated
content.notes: Explain that uncertainty reporting is about decision quality, not decoration. Give a simple CI example: if output is predicted cost saving, provide a 95% CI and explain it as “range consistent with data and assumptions,” not a guarantee. Distinguish uncertainty sources: data error (measurement noise, missingness), parameter uncertainty (estimation error), model form error (wrong functional form, omitted variables). Emphasise transparency: explicitly state what was not included (e.g., regime shifts, unmodelled downtime). Common misconception: a narrow CI always means high certainty; it might mean the method ignored model form error. Probing question: Which uncertainty source is most likely to dominate in operational datasets with sensor drift?

slides.title: Worked example: calibration workflow (step-by-step)

content.title: Worked example: calibration workflow (step-by-step)
content: 1) Define KPI: energy per unit (kWh/unit) over 4 weeks
2) Choose model: KPI = a + b·load + c·temp
3) Set bounds: b≥0; plausible ranges for a,c
4) Fit a,b,c on weeks 1–3; check on week 4
5) Record fit: MAE, bias, and residual pattern notes
6) Save run: params, plots, timestamp, and data snapshot
content.notes: Narrate a realistic, generic scenario without needing a specific dataset: an operations team wants to predict energy intensity as conditions change. Explain why a simple linear model may be acceptable initially (interpretability and speed) but still requires calibration and checks. Discuss residual patterns: if residuals increase with load, consider heteroscedasticity or missing nonlinear terms. Reinforce documentation: include the dataset extract or a reproducible data query, not just copied numbers. Common misconception: a hold-out check is only for machine learning; it is equally valuable for simple regression-style calibration. Probing question: What would you do if week 4 shows a systematic bias compared with weeks 1–3?

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

Pitfall: missing units or mixed unit systems in equations
Pitfall: undocumented parameter sources and solver settings
Pitfall: calibration error reported without validation checks
Pitfall: CI reported with no method assumptions or meaning
Use the MCQs to diagnose gaps before submission
content.notes: Position this lesson as directly feeding the module’s expected deliverables: a spec, a runnable model, and evidence of checks. slides.title: Model fitness-for-purpose and stakeholder needs

content.title: Model fitness-for-purpose and stakeholder needs
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD107 Mathematical Modelling | Lesson 8 (1h 30m)
content.notes: Welcome. In this lesson we move beyond “can I fit the data?” to “is the model good enough for what a stakeholder needs it to do?”. You will build a calibrated model from operational data, test it with validation metrics, and produce audit-ready evidence (Model Card + version history). As you work, keep asking: what decision will this model inform, and what would be the cost of being wrong?

slides.title: Orientation: what you will do in this lesson

content.title: Orientation: what you will do in this lesson
content: Watch/read: calibration, validation, audit evidence
Practice: build a reproducible model with consistent units
Check: compute ≥2 validation metrics and interpret them
Write: 150–250 words on fitness-for-purpose
Record: Model Card, rounding policy, uncertainty, actions
Control: create a 3-entry version history with impacts
content.notes: Use the lesson in three passes: (1) first skim the concepts and frameworks, (2) then follow the worked examples and replicate them in a spreadsheet or notebook, (3) finally attempt the practice prompts and complete the two MCQ checks. A common mistake is to treat validation as a single number; instead, you will combine metrics, residual reasoning, and stakeholder tolerances. Another frequent issue is weak traceability: you must be able to show where parameters came from, what assumptions you made, and how changes affected outputs.

slides.title: Calibrated model: what it is and is not

content.title: Calibrated model: what it is and is not
content: A calibrated model matches parameters to operational data
Define inputs, outputs, and decision-relevant quantities
Separate calibration data from validation data where possible
Prefer simplest model that meets the requirement
Document what the model cannot represent
Reproducible calculation is part of the model
content.notes: Calibration means choosing parameter values so the model reproduces observed behaviour in operational data. Stress the distinction: calibration is fitting; validation is judging fitness for purpose. Encourage learners to explicitly name: (a) independent variables (inputs), (b) dependent variables (outputs), and (c) derived KPIs (e.g., cost, risk, time). If you only have one dataset, discuss pragmatic splits (time-based split; k-fold where sensible) and the risk of optimistic performance. Probe: If you made the model more complex, what new failure modes might you introduce?

slides.title: Assumptions, parameters, and unit discipline

content.title: Assumptions, parameters, and unit discipline
leftColumn: State ≥5 explicit assumptions
Each assumption: why needed, likely impact
Check dimensional consistency on every formula
Define boundary of validity (scope)
rightColumn: Parameter sources: dataset, handbook, expert
Record estimation method (fit, lookup, judgement)
Track uncertainty or plausible ranges
Set rounding policy for reporting
content.notes: Learners often write vague assumptions (“data is accurate”). Push them to be testable and specific, e.g., “ambient temperature is constant at 20°C during runs” or “sensor bias is negligible relative to ±0.5 units”. Explain unit discipline: convert early, label columns, and ensure every intermediate calculation has units. A quick check is to write units beside each term in an equation and confirm both sides match. Ask: Which assumption, if violated, would most distort the stakeholder decision? Misconception to address: rounding is not cosmetic; inconsistent rounding can change pass/fail decisions against a tolerance.

slides.title: Validation metrics: choose metrics that match use

content.title: Validation metrics: choose metrics that match use
content: MAE: average absolute error (same units as output)
RMSE: penalises large errors more than MAE
MAPE: percentage error; unstable near zero values
Residual checks: bias, patterns, outliers
Choose ≥2 metrics; justify choice from requirement
Report both metric values and what they mean
content.notes: Explain metric selection as a design choice. MAE is interpretable in output units; RMSE highlights occasional large misses (important for safety-critical or peak-load decisions). MAPE is intuitive but can explode when actual values are near zero; suggest alternatives (sMAPE) if appropriate, but keep the lesson focused. Residual checks are not optional: you can have an acceptable MAE but systematic bias (e.g., always underpredicting at high loads). Probing questions: What error matters more to the stakeholder—average error or worst-case spikes? Are errors symmetric in consequence (over vs under prediction)?

content.title: Fitness-for-purpose decision framework

rows: Accept, restrict scope, or improve model

content.notes: Walk through the framework as a repeatable checklist. Emphasise that “fitness-for-purpose” is contextual: a model can be unfit for forecasting peaks yet fit for approximate planning. Encourage learners to convert stakeholder language into measurable criteria: e.g., “within ±5% for typical operation between 10 and 80 units” or “RMSE under 2.0 units”. Highlight a key misconception: good historical fit does not imply the model captures true causality or will generalise under new conditions.

slides.title: Audit-ready validation record: the Model Card

content.title: Audit-ready validation record: the Model Card
content: Intended use and non-use (what it must not be used for)
Data: source, period, exclusions, quality notes
Assumptions, scope, and limitations
Validation: metrics, residual findings, acceptance decision
Uncertainty statement and rounding policy
Corrective actions after critique or test failure
content.notes: Introduce the Model Card as a compact artefact for governance: someone unfamiliar should understand what was built, why, and how much to trust it. Stress the “non-use” section: it prevents misuse and protects decision-makers. For uncertainty, learners can state parameter ranges, measurement error, or scenario variability; it need not be advanced statistics, but it must be explicit. Corrective actions should be specific (e.g., “added temperature term; reduced bias at high output; RMSE dropped from 3.1 to 2.4”). Ask: If a regulator or manager asked “why should I trust this?”, which Model Card lines answer them?

slides.title: Simple version control for modelling work

content.title: Simple version control for modelling work
content: Use consistent names: model_v1.0, model_v1.1, model_v2.0
Keep a change log: what changed, why, impact on outputs
Save inputs and outputs used for validation
Tag key decisions: assumptions, parameter updates, fixes
Avoid overwriting: keep prior versions for auditability
Minimum: 3 entries covering meaningful iterations
content.notes: Frame version control as risk management, not bureaucracy. In spreadsheets, a practical approach is dated folders plus a version history table in a ‘README’ tab. In notebooks, use a repository or at least sequential filenames and a markdown changelog. Impacts must be stated quantitatively where possible (e.g., “MAE improved by 0.3 units; peak error worsened by 1.2 units”). Common misconception: “I can remember what I changed.” In audit contexts, memory is not evidence.

slides.title: Worked example: calibrate a simple linear model

content.title: Worked example: calibrate a simple linear model
content: Goal: predict output y from driver x using y = a + b·x
1) Inspect data: ranges, missing values, outliers
2) Set units and convert columns (e.g., kW, hours, £)
3) Estimate a and b (least squares or spreadsheet LINEST)
4) Record ≥5 assumptions and parameter sources
5) Save reproducible file/notebook with inputs and formulas
content.notes: Talk through a realistic operational dataset: time-stamped x and y measured from a system. Demonstrate that calibration starts with data hygiene: if x is in minutes in one file and hours in another, your b parameter will be wrong by a factor of 60. For estimation, note that learners can use LINEST in Excel/Google Sheets or a simple regression in a notebook; the key is reproducibility. Example assumptions to model: linear relationship over the operating range; measurement noise is independent; no major regime changes; x measured without significant bias; training data representative of normal operation. Probing: Which assumption is most questionable given the domain? What plot would you draw first to test linearity?

slides.title: Worked example: compute validation metrics

content.title: Worked example: compute validation metrics

rows: plot e vs ŷ or x

content.notes: Explain how to compute each metric in a spreadsheet: create columns for ŷ, residual e, |e|, e^2, and optionally |e/y|. Then use AVERAGE and SQRT. Emphasise careful handling of missing values and zero denominators for MAPE. For residual checks, learners can do a simple scatter plot: if residuals fan out, variance may increase with x; if residuals curve, the model form may be wrong (consider quadratic or log). Ask: If RMSE is much larger than MAE, what does that suggest about error distribution? (Answer: occasional large errors.)

slides.title: Worked example: fitness-for-purpose justification

content.title: Worked example: fitness-for-purpose justification
content.content: Compare metrics and residual evidence to the stakeholder tolerance. Decide accept, restrict scope, or revise. Write a concise 150–250 word justification with limits and risk.
content.notes: Model a short justification structure learners can copy: (1) restate intended use and operating range, (2) report the metrics on validation data, (3) interpret against acceptance thresholds, (4) summarise residual checks (bias/patterns/outliers), (5) conclude acceptability and any constraints. Example prompts: “For planning decisions, an MAE of 1.2 units against a ±2.0 unit tolerance is acceptable; however, RMSE of 2.8 indicates occasional larger errors. Residuals show underprediction above x=70, so the model is restricted to x≤70 until revised.” Misconception: writing only “metrics are good” without linking to a decision threshold and consequences.

slides.title: Worked example: Model Card and critique response

content.title: Worked example: Model Card and critique response
leftColumn: Intended use: planning within range x=10–70
Limitations: not valid for peaks or new regime
Evidence: MAE, RMSE, residual plot summary
Uncertainty: parameter ranges + data quality note
rightColumn: Critique: bias at high x values
Action: add term or segment model by regime
Re-validate: metrics change and residual pattern
Log change: version bump + impact statement
content.notes: Demonstrate how audit readiness includes responding to critique. A critique scenario could be: “Model systematically underpredicts at high demand, risking understaffing.” Show a corrective action that is proportionate: add a quadratic term, piecewise model, or restrict scope. After the change, re-run validation and report what improved and what did not. Stress the importance of documenting both the fix and its side-effects (e.g., improved high-end bias but worse mid-range MAE). Ask: When is restricting scope better than increasing complexity? (Often when data is sparse or the use case does not require full range coverage.)

If the stakeholder tightened tolerance by 25%, would your decision change?

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: calibration + validation evidence in MOD107 tasks
You will be marked on clarity, traceability, and judgement
Mistake: mixing units or leaving units unstated
Mistake: validating on the same data used to fit
Mistake: no acceptance threshold linked to stakeholder need
Mistake: missing Model Card fields or no version history
content.notes: Link back to typical marking criteria in modelling modules: correctness, transparency, and appropriate evaluation. Explain how assessors look for auditability: parameter sources, assumptions, and reproducible workflows. Clarify that using the same dataset for calibration and validation is not always forbidden, but it must be acknowledged as a limitation and handled with care (e.g., time split or cross-validation). Ask: If you were auditing someone else’s model, what evidence would you demand before approving use?

content.title: Develop a calibrated mathematical model from data
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD107 — Mathematical Modelling: Calibration, Validation and Sensitivity | Lesson 9 | Duration: 1h 30m
content.notes: Welcome learners to Lesson 9, focused on creating a calibrated model from operational data with an emphasis on transparency and audit readiness. Frame this as an end-to-end workflow: define a model, estimate parameters, validate behaviour, ensure reproducibility, then analyse sensitivity to guide decisions. Remind learners that the expected level is ‘create’: you will not only apply methods but also justify choices and document assumptions clearly enough for another person to rerun and critique your work. Prompt: What makes a model “usable” in practice—accuracy, interpretability, traceability, or all three?

slides.title: Orientation and learning objectives

content.title: Orientation and learning objectives
content: Create a model card: variables, parameters, 5 assumptions, use
Calibrate 1–3 parameters; report units and 95% CI (or justified)
Validate: dimensional check + 2 feasibility/tolerance checks
Make a rerunnable spreadsheet/notebook with fixed steps/seeds
Run OAT sensitivity on 2 parameters and 1 input; rank influence
Use: study → practise → self-check quizzes
content.notes: Explain how to study this lesson in a self-paced mode: first skim the workflow slides, then follow the worked example as a template, then do the practice prompts and finally attempt the two MCQ quizzes. Clarify what ‘model card’ means: a one-page summary that communicates what the model is for, what it assumes, and how it should (and should not) be used. Emphasise that uncertainty reporting is not optional; if a 95% confidence interval is unsuitable (e.g., non-identifiable parameters), learners must justify an alternative (e.g., bootstrap interval, scenario bounds). Probing questions: If two people build models from the same dataset, what documentation would allow you to compare them fairly? What would you need to rerun their analysis?

slides.title: From operational data to a usable model

content.title: From operational data to a usable model
content: Define purpose: prediction, explanation, control, or planning
Select model form: empirical, mechanistic, or hybrid
Specify variables, inputs, parameters, and units
Calibrate parameters on data; quantify uncertainty
Validate behaviour with checks, then iterate if needed
Communicate and freeze: model card + reproducible artefact
content.notes: Walk through the modelling lifecycle as an iterative loop, not a linear checklist. Operational datasets often include noise, missing values, and regime changes; the model must be shaped around intended use and data limitations. Stress the difference between “fit” and “valid”: a model can fit calibration data well and still be physically impossible or dimensionally inconsistent. Mini-example: a fitted linear model might predict negative demand at low inputs—good fit near observed data, poor feasibility elsewhere. Misconception to address: learners may think validation means ‘high R²’; instead, validation also includes sanity checks and limiting-case behaviour.

slides.title: Model card: what must be documented

content.title: Model card: what must be documented
content.notes: Explain that the model card is a governance tool as much as a learning artefact: it makes the model inspectable. For assumptions, encourage specificity and testability where possible (e.g., “Flow is steady during each 10-minute interval” rather than “Flow is stable”). Give examples of assumptions: sensor calibration unchanged; ambient conditions constant; linearity in operating band; no interaction terms; independence of errors. Probing question: Which assumption, if violated, would most damage decisions based on the model? Common misconception: treating assumptions as “disclaimers” rather than hypotheses that can be checked or monitored.

slides.title: Variables, inputs and parameters: keep them distinct

content.title: Variables, inputs and parameters: keep them distinct
leftColumn: Inputs (measured): set by scenario or observed
Outputs: model predictions to compare or use
State variables: evolve internally over time
Units: define for every symbol
rightColumn: Parameters (unknown): calibrated from data
Constraints: physical or operational bounds
Initial conditions: starting values for dynamics
Identifiability: can data determine parameters?
content.notes: Use this slide to reduce a common source of confusion: learners may label anything unknown as a parameter. Clarify with a mini-example: in y = a x + b, x is an input, y is an output, and a and b are parameters; measurement noise is not a parameter unless explicitly modelled. For dynamic models, distinguish state variables (e.g., temperature in a tank) from parameters (e.g., heat loss coefficient). Introduce identifiability informally: if changing two parameters produces almost the same outputs, the data cannot uniquely pin them down, and confidence intervals may become huge or meaningless. Probing question: In your own context, which quantities are controllable inputs versus uncertain parameters?

slides.title: Calibration by least squares (and uncertainty)

content.title: Calibration by least squares (and uncertainty)
content: Choose residuals: observed minus predicted output
Define objective: minimise sum of squared residuals (SSE)
Estimate parameters; record units and constraints
Check residual patterns for bias or regime shifts
Compute 95% CI from covariance or use bootstrap if needed
Report: parameter values, CI, dataset window, method
content.notes: Explain least squares as fitting parameters to minimise SSE, and note when variants are needed: weighted least squares if measurement variance changes with magnitude; robust methods if outliers dominate; constrained optimisation if parameters must be positive. Provide a minimal formula verbally: residual r_i = y_i − ŷ_i(θ), choose θ to minimise Σ r_i². For confidence intervals, outline the idea: if assumptions about noise are reasonable, parameter covariance can be estimated; otherwise bootstrap resampling offers an alternative. Misconception: a narrow CI does not guarantee correctness; it may reflect overconfident assumptions or poor noise modelling. Probing questions: What is your residual telling you—random noise, systematic bias, or missing variables?

slides.title: Validation: dimensional and feasibility checks

content.title: Validation: dimensional and feasibility checks
content: Dimensional check: equations must balance units
Bounds: outputs within physical/operational limits
Sign checks: no negative mass, time, or energy where impossible
Limiting cases: behaviour as inputs → 0 or large values
Tolerance checks: within stated error bands for use
Document pass/fail and corrective action taken
content.notes: Emphasise validation as “is it plausible and fit for purpose?” not merely “does it fit?” Dimensional consistency is a fast, high-value check: if units do not match, the model is wrong regardless of calibration quality. For feasibility, give examples: predicted throughput cannot exceed equipment capacity; efficiency must lie between 0 and 1; concentration cannot be negative. Limiting-case behaviour is often overlooked—ask learners to test extremes even if they are outside observed data, because that is where models can produce nonsense. Corrective actions could include re-scaling variables, revising functional form, adding constraints, or narrowing the intended use in the model card.

slides.title: Reproducible and auditable calculation artefacts

content.title: Reproducible and auditable calculation artefacts
content: Single source of truth: raw data tab or file snapshot
Locked formulas or scripted notebook steps
Fixed random seeds; record software and versions
Clear rounding rules and output formatting
Automated checks: units, bounds, and flags where possible
Run log: who, when, dataset range, parameter set
content.notes: Explain reproducibility as enabling another learner to press ‘run’ and obtain the same outputs within defined rounding. For spreadsheets, recommend separating inputs, calculations, and outputs; lock formula cells; and provide a clear ‘run’ pathway. For notebooks, stress fixed seeds for any randomness (e.g., bootstrap), and a linear execution order with no hidden state. Misconception: copying results into a report is not reproducibility; the artefact must recreate results from the stored data and steps. Probing question: If you were audited in six months, could you reconstruct exactly what you did and why?

slides.title: Worked example: operational fit-for-use model

content.title: Worked example: operational fit-for-use model
content.content: Scenario: You have hourly operational records of throughput x (units/h) and energy use y (kWh). Build a simple predictive model y = a·x + b, calibrate a and b, and document a model card stating assumptions and valid operating range.
content.notes: Set expectations: this is a deliberately simple model to practise the workflow, not a claim that linearity is always correct. Explain the interpretation: a is marginal energy per unit throughput (kWh per unit), b is baseline energy use per hour at zero throughput (often representing standby loads). Discuss assumptions to anticipate: linear relationship within the observed band; stable equipment configuration; energy meter accuracy; no unmeasured confounders like ambient temperature; errors roughly independent over time. Ask: What would make b negative, and would that be physically plausible? If it appears, would you constrain b ≥ 0 or rethink the model form?

slides.title: Worked example steps and expected outputs

content.title: Worked example steps and expected outputs

rows: Fit least squares for a, b
Freeze artefact and write model card

content.notes: Teach learners how to operationalise each step. For cleaning, provide examples of ‘impossible’: negative throughput, energy spikes from sensor resets, duplicated timestamps. For least squares in a spreadsheet, show that built-in functions (e.g., LINEST) can return coefficients and standard errors; in code, use a standard regression routine and extract covariance. For CI sanity: a should likely be positive; if CI includes negative, discuss whether data are too noisy, range too narrow, or model mis-specified. For validation documentation, encourage a small checklist that records pass/fail and what changed: e.g., “b constrained ≥ 0; refit; updated CI; revised intended use to x in [x_min, x_max].”

slides.title: OAT sensitivity: how to run and interpret

content.title: OAT sensitivity: how to run and interpret
content: Pick baseline: parameters and a representative input level
Vary one factor at a time by ±10% (or justified range)
Recompute output metric: y, cost, error, or KPI
Compute sensitivity index: %Δoutput per %Δfactor
Rank factors by absolute influence and sign
Write one recommendation for use or data priorities
content.notes: Explain one-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity as a local method: it tells you which factors matter near a baseline, not across all possible combinations. Make the sensitivity index concrete: S = (Δy/y)/(Δp/p). For the linear example, show quick reasoning: y = a x + b, so sensitivity to a depends on x; at high throughput, a dominates; at low throughput, b dominates. Common misconception: “largest parameter value means most important”—importance depends on how the parameter affects outputs and on the operating point. Probing questions: Which baseline is defensible for your intended use? Would your ranking change at a different operating regime?

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
leftColumn: Draft 5 assumptions for your model card
List 3 variables with units and data sources
Choose 1–3 parameters and justify constraints
Define 2 feasibility checks for your context
rightColumn: Run a quick fit; inspect residual plot or table
State a 95% CI or justify an alternative
Do OAT: 2 parameters + 1 input; rank influence
Write one recommendation based on evidence
content.notes: Encourage learners to pause and apply prompts to a dataset they already have or to a provided practice dataset (if available in the module resources). Give guidance on ‘evidence-based recommendation’: it must reference the sensitivity ranking or a validation failure. Examples: “Prioritise better measurement of x because output uncertainty is dominated by x variance”; or “Restrict use to throughput above 20 units/h because b uncertainty dominates below this.” Direct learners to use the formative quizzes after attempting these prompts. Probing question: If you had budget to improve only one measurement, which would you choose and why?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes

content.title: Assessment connection and common mistakes
content: Supports: calibrated model + validation + sensitivity deliverable
Common error: missing units for variables and parameters
Common error: reporting fit without uncertainty statement
Common error: no pass/fail record for validation checks
Common error: non-reproducible steps (manual edits, no seeds)
Avoid: using the model outside stated operating range
content.notes: Connect this lesson explicitly to the kinds of artefacts typically graded: model card quality, calibration transparency, validation discipline, and reproducibility. Expand on each mistake: units missing leads to unusable parameters; uncertainty missing prevents decision-making; validation undocumented makes it impossible to trust results; manual edits break rerun-ability; and extrapolation beyond range is a frequent cause of failure in operational modelling. Offer a quick self-audit question set: Can someone else reproduce your numbers? Can they tell what you assumed? Can they see what checks you ran and what failed? Encourage learners to treat the quizzes as a diagnostic: wrong answers point to gaps in process, not just recall.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Start with intended use; let it constrain model form and checks
Separate inputs, outputs, and parameters; define units everywhere
Calibrate transparently and report uncertainty, not just point fits
Validate with units + feasibility/limiting checks; record actions
Make work reproducible; use sensitivity to guide decisions
content.notes: Close by reinforcing the end-to-end mindset: modelling is as much about disciplined documentation and checks as it is about optimisation. Encourage learners to revisit their model card after sensitivity analysis, because sensitivity often reveals which assumptions or data gaps matter most. Final probing question: If your model were handed to a colleague tomorrow, what single improvement would most increase their confidence in using it?

slides.title: Fitness-for-purpose: what it is and why it matters

content.title: Fitness-for-purpose: what it is and why it matters
content.content: A fitness-for-purpose statement links a model to a specific intended use, stating measurable acceptance criteria and explicit limitations/assumptions. It ensures stakeholders understand what decisions the model can support and what it cannot. It also defines the evidence needed for validation.
content.notes: Unpack “intended use” with examples: forecasting demand for staffing vs estimating energy consumption vs screening risk. Stress that the same model may be fit for one use and unfit for another. Introduce the idea that acceptance criteria must be testable (e.g., error thresholds, domain limits), while limitations must be explicit (e.g., assumes steady-state, ignores rare events). Probing question: “What decision will be made from this model output, and what could go wrong if the model is used outside scope?” Misconception to challenge: “High accuracy means fit-for-purpose.” Accuracy is only one criterion; interpretability, robustness, and domain validity can dominate.

slides.title: Acceptance criteria vs limitations (examples)

content.title: Acceptance criteria vs limitations (examples)
content.notes: Walk through how each acceptance criterion maps to a measurable test and a piece of evidence. Make explicit that limitations are not “weaknesses to hide”; they are conditions under which the model may mislead. Mini-example: if the dataset contains only 15–30°C, claiming validity at 80°C is unjustified; you must either restrict the domain or collect data. Probing question: “Which of these is easiest to test? Which is hardest to evidence, and why?” Misconception: learners sometimes write vague criteria such as “reasonably accurate”; insist on quantified thresholds and domains.
