slides.title: Calibration vs validation: keep them separate

content.title: Calibration vs validation: keep them separate
leftColumn: Calibration: fit parameters to data
Goal: minimise error on training/calibration set
Outputs: parameter values, units, sources
Risk: overfitting if unchecked
rightColumn: Validation: test on new or reserved evidence
Goal: confirm criteria met for intended use
Outputs: checks, uncertainty, pass/fail decision
Risk: circularity if you tune on test data
content.notes: Explain the “separation principle”: you calibrate once, then you validate without moving the goalposts. If validation fails, you can return to calibration, but you must record that as a new iteration (and treat it as model development, not validation). Give a concrete example: calibrating a heat transfer coefficient using historical runs; validating on later runs or a withheld subset. Probing question: “If you adjust a parameter after seeing validation results, what has happened to the validity of that test?” Common misconception: learners report only a single error value and call it validation; emphasise multiple checks and clear data partitioning.

slides.title: Reproducible calibration record: what to include

content.title: Reproducible calibration record: what to include
content: Variable definitions: names, units, transformations
Parameter list: symbol, unit, initial value, bounds
Parameter sources: measured, literature, estimated
Dataset: time window, filters, exclusions, missing rules
Fitting method: objective function and solver settings
Assumptions: simplifications and why they are acceptable
content.notes: Clarify what “another learner can reproduce results” means: with your dataset and notes, they should obtain the same fitted parameters to within rounding tolerance. Explain transformations with examples: log-scaling, normalisation, detrending, lag features. Discuss solver settings that matter: convergence tolerance, max iterations, random seed, regularisation. Probing question: “Which single missing detail would make your calibration impossible to reproduce?” (Often: units, filtering rules, or solver settings.) Misconception: learners may list parameter values but omit bounds/initial values; highlight that these can change the fitted solution.

slides.title: Worked example: from brief to fitness statement

content.title: Worked example: from brief to fitness statement
leftColumn: Brief: predict output within 5% for routine ops
Users need explanation for QA sign-off
Data: only routine days, no fault events
Decision: adjust setpoint if predicted drift occurs
rightColumn: Criteria: MAPE ≤5% on holdout routine data
Criteria: domain = routine ops; faults excluded
Criteria: interpretable coefficients or rules stated
Limits: not for fault diagnosis or shutdown periods
content.notes: Narrate how to translate stakeholder language into measurable criteria. Show the traceability: each criterion directly responds to a line in the brief. Explain that “routine ops” must be operationalised (e.g., define thresholds for temperature/pressure ranges, exclude maintenance flags). Probing question: “What exactly counts as ‘routine’, and where will that definition be recorded?” Misconception: learners may quietly assume faults are rare and ignore them; instead, explicitly exclude them and state the consequence (model not to be used for faults).

slides.title: Validation evidence package: minimum contents

content.title: Validation evidence package: minimum contents
content: Check 1: holdout error vs acceptance threshold
Check 2: residual pattern or tolerance/dimensional check
Uncertainty: quantified statement (e.g., ±X at 95%)
Rounding: significant-figures rule and justification
Decision: pass/conditional pass/fail for intended use
Traceability: link each check to a criterion
content.notes: Teach validation as a package, not a single metric. Provide examples of Check 2: residuals vs fitted values to spot heteroscedasticity; dimensional consistency checks; tolerance checks against known physical limits. For uncertainty, suggest practical approaches: prediction interval from residual standard deviation; bootstrap; propagation from sensor uncertainties (even approximate). For rounding, explain why it matters: overstated precision can mislead decisions and fails audit expectations. Probing question: “If your error metric passes but residuals show a trend, what does that imply about model structure?” Misconception: learners may confuse parameter uncertainty with prediction uncertainty; distinguish them explicitly.

slides.title: Learning objectives for this lesson

content.title: Learning objectives for this lesson
content: Construct a calibrated model with 95% CIs for parameters
Write a model card: use, variables, assumptions, limits
Perform unit checks; find and fix at least two errors
Run ±5–10% OAT sensitivity; rank top two drivers
Deliver a reproducible spreadsheet/notebook artefact
content.notes: Clarify what ‘calibrated’ means here: parameters are estimated from operational data using an explicit objective function, and uncertainty is reported as 95% confidence intervals—not just point estimates. Stress that the model card is part of the deliverable, not an optional add-on; it supports peer review and responsible use. For sensitivity: one-at-a-time perturbations are a pragmatic baseline; they do not capture interactions, but they are often sufficient to identify dominant drivers. For reproducibility: another person should be able to rerun the artefact and obtain the same outputs, including rounding and unit handling.

slides.title: From purpose to model: a minimal workflow

content.title: From purpose to model: a minimal workflow
content: State purpose and output(s) the model must predict
Define variables, parameters, and data sources
Choose a functional form consistent with physics/logic
Estimate parameters by fitting to operational data
Validate on hold-out or time-shifted data where possible
Document: model card, units, and reproducible artefact
content.notes: Walk through the end-to-end pipeline as a checklist. Emphasise that ‘purpose’ constrains everything: you do not select a complex form because it exists; you select it because it supports the decision and data available. Note the difference between variables (measured inputs/outputs) and parameters (to be estimated). Highlight a common misconception: calibration is not the same as validation. Calibration makes the model match the calibration dataset; validation tests performance on data not used for fitting (or at least on a different time period). If learners lack a hold-out set, discuss pragmatic alternatives: rolling-origin evaluation, cross-validation, or careful residual analysis.

slides.title: Variables vs parameters (and why it matters)

content.title: Variables vs parameters (and why it matters)
leftColumn: Variables: measured/controlled quantities (x, y)
Can change each run (e.g., load, temperature)
Often include noise and missing values
Need units, ranges, and data provenance
rightColumn: Parameters: fixed constants within a scope (θ)
Estimated from data (e.g., k, exponent, offset)
Reported with uncertainty (95% CI, SE)
May drift over time; track re-calibration triggers
content.notes: Explain that confusing variables and parameters leads to unstable models and poor documentation. Give a mini-example: modelling energy use E as a function of throughput q: q is a variable; the coefficient linking q to E is a parameter. Probe learners: ‘If throughput doubles tomorrow, do you expect the coefficient to change immediately?’ Usually not—unless operations have shifted. Introduce the idea of scope: parameters can be “fixed” only within a defined context (site, season, equipment configuration). Misconception to address: learners often treat parameters as universal truths; instead, treat them as estimated, context-bound quantities.

slides.title: Calibration: fitting and 95% confidence intervals

content.title: Calibration: fitting and 95% confidence intervals
content: Select an objective: SSE, RMSE, MAE, or log-likelihood
Fit parameters using solver/optimiser or regression
Check residual patterns: bias, trend, heteroscedasticity
Compute 95% CIs from SEs or bootstrap resampling
Report: estimates, CIs, dataset period, and exclusions
content.notes: Explain objective functions in plain language: SSE/RMSE penalise large errors; MAE is more robust to outliers; likelihood-based fitting supports statistical inference. Provide a mini-example: if operational sensors occasionally spike, MAE or robust regression may be preferable. For confidence intervals, briefly distinguish approaches: analytic (standard errors from regression assumptions) versus bootstrap (resample observations, refit, then take percentiles). Ask: ‘What would make you distrust a narrow CI?’ Answer: model misspecification, autocorrelation, or data leakage can create false certainty. Common misconceptions: (1) 95% CI means 95% of data fall inside—incorrect; it is about parameter uncertainty under assumptions. (2) High R² guarantees good prediction—incorrect, especially out of sample.

slides.title: Dimensional and unit-consistency checks

content.title: Dimensional and unit-consistency checks
content.notes: Teach units as a first-line debugging tool: many modelling ‘errors’ are actually unit or scale mistakes. Elaborate each row with a short explanation. For equation units: you cannot add a pressure term to an energy term; learners should enforce dimensional homogeneity. For input units: operational datasets often mix units across sites; the fix is not just conversion but locking and documenting units in the artefact. For scaling: Celsius versus Kelvin is a classic trap in exponential or Arrhenius-type relationships. For outputs: distinguish power (kW) from energy (kWh); emphasise time aggregation. Probe question: ‘If you changed from minutes to seconds, which parameters must change to keep the model identical?’ This reinforces dimensional thinking.

slides.title: Transparency: model card and audit readiness

content.title: Transparency: model card and audit readiness
content: Intended use and non-use (what decisions it supports)
Variables: definitions, units, valid ranges, data sources
Assumptions and known limitations (incl. boundary cases)
Calibration method, period, and parameter sources
Performance: error metrics and validation approach
Change control: versioning and re-calibration criteria
content.notes: Position the model card as the bridge between mathematics and professional accountability. Give examples of intended use/non-use: e.g., ‘forecast daily energy demand for planning’ versus ‘not suitable for fault detection’. Stress that limitations should be operationally meaningful: where does the model break (extreme loads, maintenance periods, new equipment)? Highlight a misconception: learners often omit ‘non-use’; however, stating what the model should not be used for prevents misuse. Encourage including a simple version identifier and a trigger for review (sensor replacement, process change, seasonal shift). Ask: ‘Could a peer reproduce your calibration from what you wrote?’ If not, the model card is incomplete.

slides.title: Worked example: calibrate a throughput–energy model

content.title: Worked example: calibrate a throughput–energy model
content: Goal: predict daily energy E from throughput q
Choose form: E = a + b·q (baseline + marginal use)
Prepare data: filter downtime; align units (kWh, tonnes)
Fit a, b by least squares; record estimates and 95% CIs
Check residuals vs q and time; note any structure
Create a first model card entry for this model
content.notes: Walk through a realistic scenario without needing a full dataset on screen. Explain why the linear form is a sensible starting point: baseline energy (a) plus variable energy per tonne (b). Clarify what filtering means: remove days with shutdowns or known anomalies, but record exclusions to avoid cherry-picking. Mention unit alignment: throughput in tonnes/day, energy in kWh/day. Explain how to compute CIs in a spreadsheet (using regression output) or a notebook (e.g., statsmodels). Probing questions: ‘What would a negative a mean operationally?’ (possible model misspecification or missing variable). ‘If residuals grow with q, what might you change?’ (transformations, weighted regression, nonlinear form).

slides.title: Worked example: OAT sensitivity and ranking

content.title: Worked example: OAT sensitivity and ranking
content.notes: Explain how to perform one-at-a-time sensitivity: hold all else constant, perturb one input/parameter by ±5–10%, and observe output change. Interpret the table: b is the strongest driver in this illustrative case, followed by q; a is less influential at this operating point because it is smaller relative to b·q. Emphasise that rankings can change with operating conditions (e.g., at very low q, a may dominate). Discuss implications for decision-making: if b is dominant, prioritise improving its estimate (better calibration data, better measurement of energy attributable to throughput). Misconception: sensitivity is not the same as uncertainty; a parameter can be highly sensitive but well-known, or low sensitivity but highly uncertain. Ideally combine both in prioritisation.

slides.title: Practice and reflection prompts

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
leftColumn: Define outputs and purpose for a model you know
List variables, parameters, and their units
Name two assumptions and one boundary case
Choose a fit metric and justify it
rightColumn: Find two unit/scale errors in a draft equation
Propose fixes and write the corrected equation
Plan a ±5–10% OAT sensitivity list (3 factors)
Identify top two likely drivers and why
content.notes: Invite learners to apply the workflow to their own context (or a chosen operational process). For unit/scale errors, suggest common candidates: mixing minutes and hours, °C versus K, percentage versus fraction, kW versus kWh, or using ‘per day’ data with ‘per hour’ parameters. Encourage learners to write justifications, not only corrections: ‘I converted kg to tonnes because throughput is recorded in tonnes/day.’ Probing questions: ‘Which variable is most uncertain in your dataset?’ and ‘Which parameter would you recalibrate first if the process changes?’ This promotes decision-focused modelling.

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports: MOD107 tasks on calibration and sensitivity evidence
Submit: model card + artefact + parameter table with 95% CIs
Avoid: calibrating and validating on the same data without note
Avoid: hidden unit conversions or hard-coded constants
Avoid: reporting only point estimates without uncertainty
Use MCQs to check gaps before final submission
content.notes: Make the link explicit: the module expects not only a working model but evidence of method and rigour. Emphasise documentation: parameter tables must include CIs, and artefacts must show inputs, formulas, and version/date. Expand on common pitfalls: ‘same data’ validation can be acceptable in constrained settings only if clearly labelled as in-sample and accompanied by limitations. Hidden conversions (e.g., multiplying by 1000 without comment) are audit failures; they also create irreproducible results when units change. Reinforce rounding rules: specify and apply consistently (e.g., parameters to 3 s.f., CIs to same decimal places). Direct learners to attempt the two formative MCQs after completing the worked example to confirm conceptual understanding.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Start with purpose; it constrains form, data, and evaluation
Calibrate with an explicit objective and report 95% CIs
Use unit checks to catch errors early and justify corrections
Rank drivers via OAT sensitivity to guide data priorities
Deliver transparency: model card + reproducible artefact
content.notes: Close by reinforcing the ‘triangle’ of good practice: statistical fit, physical/units coherence, and transparent documentation. Encourage learners to keep a running log of assumptions, exclusions, and unit decisions as they work—this becomes the model card and audit trail. Final probing question: ‘If a colleague took your file today, could they reproduce your numbers and understand your model’s limits?’ If the answer is not clearly yes, the next iteration should focus on documentation and reproducibility rather than additional complexity.

content.title: Model fitness-for-purpose against stakeholder needs
content.content: Maths Certification | MOD107 Mathematical Modelling | Lesson 12 | 1h 30m
content.notes:
Welcome learners to Lesson 12 within MOD107. Frame the session as a capstone-style workflow: moving from a stakeholder brief and operational data to a calibrated model, then demonstrating that the model is fit-for-purpose through validation evidence, and finally packaging the work so someone else can reproduce it.

Emphasise Bloom’s level “create”: learners are not only applying techniques, but producing an artefact (model + documentation + audit trail) suitable for handover. A common misconception is that modelling ends when the curve “looks right”; in professional settings, the deliverable is the documented, reproducible model with a defensible validation argument.

slides.title: Fitness-for-purpose: what it means

content.title: Fitness-for-purpose: what it means
content.content: A model is fit-for-purpose when it supports the stakeholder decision within agreed accuracy, scope, and operational constraints. The goal is not maximum complexity, but justified adequacy for the intended use and data quality.
content.notes:
Unpack the phrase “fitness-for-purpose”: it is conditional on (a) intended use, (b) operating range, (c) acceptable error, and (d) consequences of error. A simple model can be fit-for-purpose, and a complex model can be unfit if it is fragile or undocumented.

Mini-example: A linear demand forecast may be adequate for weekly stock planning within a stable range, but unfit for promotional spikes.

Ask learners: What would make your model unfit—extrapolation beyond data, missing key variables, or unstable parameters?

Common misconception: “If it predicts well on my dataset, it is validated.” Clarify the difference between calibration fit and validation evidence for the intended context.

content.title: Model specification from a stakeholder brief
content.notes:
Walk through each specification item as a documentation checklist. Stress that your LO1 requires a ≤200-word intended use statement that addresses every checklist item.

Explain “evidence/source”: you should be able to point to where each choice came from (brief, data dictionary, engineering judgement). This becomes crucial when the model is reviewed later.

Probing questions: What range of inputs is expected operationally? Which inputs are controllable vs measured? What would be an unacceptable model error, and why?

Common misconception: treating assumptions as admissions of weakness. Reframe assumptions as explicit boundaries that make the model interpretable and testable.

slides.title: Calibration workflow from operational data

content.title: Calibration workflow from operational data
content: Define objective function and error metric aligned to intended use
Split data: fit vs test; avoid leakage from future information
Estimate parameters; constrain by physics, units, or business rules
Inspect residuals, outliers, and regime changes in operations
Quantify uncertainty: confidence intervals or bootstrap where feasible
Record settings: data version, filters, solver, and initial values
content.notes:
Explain that calibration is an optimisation task with choices that must match the decision context. For example, minimising absolute error may be preferable to squared error when large errors are particularly harmful, or when outliers exist.

Discuss data leakage in operational datasets: future values or derived features can inadvertently enter the calibration.

Residual inspection: teach learners to look for structure (trend, seasonality, heteroscedasticity) which indicates missing mechanisms.

Mini-example: If residuals grow with throughput, you may need a non-linear term or a variance model.

Common misconception: “More data always fixes it.” Sometimes more data reveals multiple regimes; the correct response may be segmenting the model or narrowing the scope.

slides.title: Validation: pick checks that match the risk

content.title: Validation: pick checks that match the risk
leftColumn: Residual analysis
Dimensional consistency
Sensitivity/tolerance checks
Hold-out or cross-validation
rightColumn: Look for bias, structure, non-constant variance
Verify units and scaling; sanity-check magnitudes
Change inputs/params; test stability of conclusions
Test on unseen data; report performance range
content.notes:
Position validation as an argument, not a single statistic. Learners must select and justify at least three checks. The selection should reflect model purpose and operational risk.

Expand each check briefly:
- Residual analysis: a good fit can still be wrong if errors are systematic.
- Dimensional consistency: catches silent errors (e.g., minutes vs seconds).
- Sensitivity/tolerance: reveals whether decisions flip under small changes.
- Hold-out testing: estimates generalisation, but must respect time ordering.

Probing questions: If the model is used for scheduling, which errors matter most—peak periods or average conditions? What is the cost of false confidence?

Common misconception: “Validation means matching the past perfectly.” Emphasise robustness and transparency about limitations.

slides.title: Sensitivity and tolerance: showing robustness

content.title: Sensitivity and tolerance: showing robustness
content: Define tolerances: acceptable input noise and output error bounds
Run one-at-a-time and scenario sensitivity around baseline inputs
Check rank of drivers: which inputs dominate the output?
Test boundary cases: min/max operating conditions and constraints
Report non-linearities or thresholds where behaviour changes
Link sensitivity findings to decisions and monitoring needs
content.notes:
Teach the difference between parameter sensitivity (model structure) and input sensitivity (operational variability). Explain tolerances as negotiated: stakeholders often care about decision stability more than perfect accuracy.

Mini-example: If staffing recommendations change by ±2 people when demand varies by 1%, the model may be too sensitive for operational planning.

Encourage learners to interpret sensitivity: high sensitivity can be acceptable if that input is well-measured and controllable; it is risky if the input is noisy.

Common misconception: “Sensitivity is optional.” For fitness-for-purpose, sensitivity often provides the most actionable evidence: where to improve measurement, where to monitor drift, and where to set guardrails.

slides.title: Audit readiness: change control and traceability

content.title: Audit readiness: change control and traceability
content: Use Git commits or structured filenames with dates and versions
Record ≥3 changes with rationale and link to evidence
Keep raw data read-only; document transformations separately
Capture run settings: environment, library versions, random seeds
Use clear tags: bugfix, calibration, validation, refactor
Ensure outputs can be regenerated within stated rounding rules
content.notes:
Explain why version control is part of modelling competence: it protects you from “unknown unknowns” when results change. Even a simple naming convention can be sufficient if it preserves traceability.

Give examples of meaningful changes:
1) “Changed loss from MSE to MAE due to outlier-heavy residuals.”
2) “Added unit conversion after dimensional check flagged mismatch.”
3) “Removed sensor readings during maintenance windows; documented filter.”

Probing questions: If a stakeholder challenges a number, can you explain which dataset and settings produced it? Can someone else rerun it without you?

Common misconception: “Git is only for programmers.” Clarify that it is an audit tool; the goal is reproducibility and accountability.

content.title: Worked example: calibrating a simple linear model

rows: Define y = a + b x + e
No trend with x or time

content.notes:
Narrate this as a template learners can adapt to their own model form (linear, exponential, mass-balance, queueing approximation, etc.).

Explain key choices:
- Time-ordered split matters for operational data with drift or seasonality.
- Parameter plausibility is not optional: if b implies impossible behaviour, revisit units or scope.

Mini-example numbers (verbal): Suppose b is 0.02 hours per unit throughput; sanity-check against known cycle times. If the implied cycle time exceeds operating limits, the model is mis-specified.

Ask: What would you do if residuals show curvature—add a quadratic term, transform variables, or restrict the valid range? Emphasise that any change must be recorded and justified (links back to version control slide).

slides.title: Worked example: a 1-page validation note structure

content.title: Worked example: a 1-page validation note structure
content: Purpose and scope: intended use, bounds, and acceptance criteria
Data and calibration summary: dataset version, key settings
Validation checks (≥3): method, results, and interpretation
Limitations and risks: where model may fail or mislead
Actions: fixes applied and monitoring recommendations
Decision statement: fit-for-purpose yes/no, with conditions
content.notes:
Explain that the validation note is a persuasive but evidence-based document. It should let a reviewer understand what was tested, what passed, what did not, and what that means for use.

Guide learners on wording: avoid absolute claims (“validated”) and use conditional statements (“fit-for-purpose for X within Y range”).

Provide a mini-example of limitations: “Model assumes steady-state; during start-up/shut-down, errors increase and outputs should not be used.”

Probing questions: Which limitation is most critical to your stakeholder decision? What monitoring signal would indicate model drift (e.g., increasing MAE, biased residuals)?

Common misconception: hiding weaknesses. In professional practice, explicit limits increase trust and reduce misuse.

slides.title: Practice and reflection: apply to your own model

content.title: Practice and reflection: apply to your own model
content: Draft your ≤200-word intended use statement using the checklist
List variables, parameters, and 5 key assumptions with rationale
Choose 3 validation checks and state what “pass” looks like
Describe 3 versioned changes you would expect during modelling
Write a reproducibility plan: inputs, steps, outputs, rounding rules
Complete the two MCQ checks on calibration and validation
content.notes:
Direct learners to produce tangible artefacts, not just notes. Encourage them to timebox: 15 minutes for intended use, 15 minutes for validation plan, 10 minutes for reproducibility plan.

Give prompting questions:
- Intended use: Who is the user? What decision threshold will they apply?
- Assumptions: Which are structural (physics/logic) vs convenience (data gaps)?
- Validation: What failure mode worries you most—bias, extrapolation, instability?

Mention the MCQs as quick feedback loops: use incorrect answers to identify weak areas (e.g., confusing calibration vs validation, misunderstanding sensitivity).

Common misconception: writing assumptions after the fact. Encourage writing assumptions early, then revising with versioned changes.

slides.title: Assessment connection: technical handover pack

content.title: Assessment connection: technical handover pack
leftColumn: Deliverables
Reproducibility
Evidence trail
Communication
rightColumn: Model file + readme + validation note
Run steps yield same outputs within rounding rules
Links from changes to checks and corrective actions
Clear limits, acceptance criteria, and conditions of use
content.notes:
Explain how this lesson supports typical modelling assessments: you are evaluated on the quality of the artefact and the defensibility of your reasoning, not only numeric performance.

Common mistakes to warn against:
- Overfitting: too many parameters for the data quality.
- Incomplete scope: not stating bounds leads to misuse.
- “Metric-only” validation: reporting RMSE without residual patterns or unit checks.
- Non-reproducible runs: missing seed, missing package versions, or unclear data prep.

Probing question: If a peer tried to run your work next week on a clean machine, what would break first? Use that to prioritise readme content.

slides.title: Summary: key takeaways

content.title: Summary: key takeaways
content: Fitness-for-purpose is defined by intended use, bounds, and risk
Calibration must be documented: data, objective, constraints, results
Validation is a multi-check argument, not a single performance score
Sensitivity shows robustness and clarifies where monitoring is needed
Version control and reproducibility turn a model into a handover-ready asset
content.notes:
Reinforce the thread running through the lesson: modelling is a disciplined workflow that ends with a reproducible package and a justified claim of fitness-for-purpose.

Invite learners to self-audit against the learning objectives:
- Can you describe intended use within 200 words and cover all checklist items?
- Do you have at least three validation checks with evidence and limitations?
- Are there at least three traceable changes with rationales and links to evidence?
- Could another learner reproduce your outputs without your help?

Close by reminding them to use the MCQs diagnostically: the goal is not merely a score, but identifying which part of the workflow needs strengthening.

slides.title: How to use this lesson

content.title: How to use this lesson
content: 1) Read the core concepts for a modelling workflow
2) Follow the worked example end-to-end
3) Replicate in a spreadsheet or notebook
4) Complete the two MCQ knowledge checks
Keep an audit trail: data, steps, assumptions, outputs
content.notes:
Explain that self-study works best when learners actively reproduce the calculations rather than only reading them. Encourage pausing after each worked example slide to implement the step in their own tool.

Stress the audit trail expectation: a future marker (or colleague) should be able to start from the same data file and obtain the same parameter estimates within rounding tolerance.

Common misconception: learners often treat modelling as a narrative write-up. In this module, modelling is also a computational artefact that must be testable and repeatable.

slides.title: Learning objectives for this lesson

content.title: Learning objectives for this lesson
content: Build a model with defined I/O, parameters, assumptions, use
Calibrate parameters and report values with 95% CI (or justify)
Check dimensional consistency and correct a unit mismatch risk
Run tolerance/sensitivity checks and identify key drivers
Package as a reproducible calculation with full audit trail
content.notes:
Clarify the performance level: Bloom’s “create” means learners produce an original calibrated model from a dataset, not just answer questions about calibration.

Explain what counts as evidence for each objective:
- Objective 1: explicit variable list, at least three assumptions, and a use statement (3–5 sentences).
- Objective 2: method description (e.g., least squares), parameter table with units, and uncertainty.
- Objective 3: term-by-term unit check, and at least one identified mismatch risk.
- Objective 4: at least two factors varied over stated ranges, with summary outputs.
- Objective 5: another learner can rerun it and match within ±1 rounding unit.

Probing question: Which objective would fail if your spreadsheet had hard-coded numbers in formulas?

slides.title: A practical modelling workflow

content.title: A practical modelling workflow
content: Define purpose and output(s) to predict or explain
Select inputs, parameters, and a functional form
State modelling assumptions and expected validity range
Calibrate parameters using operational data
Check units, then test sensitivity and tolerances
Package for reproducibility and review
content.notes:
Walk through the workflow as an iterative loop rather than a linear checklist. After calibration, learners often discover they need to revisit assumptions or the chosen functional form.

Mini-example: If you fit a linear model and residuals show curvature, that is evidence the functional form may be wrong, not merely that the parameter estimates are ‘noisy’.

Common misconception: validation is not the same as calibration. Calibration uses the data to estimate parameters; validation checks performance on unseen or withheld data, or checks plausibility against domain knowledge.

Probing question: At which step would you document a sensor reliability issue—and why?

slides.title: Specify the model before fitting

content.title: Specify the model before fitting
leftColumn: Inputs x: measured drivers (e.g., temperature, speed)
Outputs y: target (e.g., demand, consumption, yield)
Parameters θ: unknown constants to estimate from data
Assumptions: simplifications you will rely on
rightColumn: Intended use: decision, forecasting, monitoring, control
Scope: operating range and time period covered by data
Data context: source, sampling, cleaning, exclusions
Risks: confounders, bias, missing variables, drift
content.notes:
Explain that a model is a claim about how quantities relate, within a defined context. “Operational data” is typically messy: changing regimes, maintenance events, seasonal effects, and sensor bias.

Guide learners to be explicit:
- Inputs and outputs must be measurable with stated units.
- Parameters should be interpretable (where possible) and stable within scope.
- Assumptions should be testable or at least discussable.

Examples of suitable assumptions (choose at least three in learner work):
- Linearity within the observed range.
- Errors are independent with constant variance.
- Input measurements are sufficiently accurate relative to output noise.
- No major process change during the calibration window.

Probing questions:
- Which variable is under your control, and which is merely observed?
- What operating condition would invalidate your assumptions?

slides.title: Calibration and parameter uncertainty

content.title: Calibration and parameter uncertainty
content: Choose an objective: minimise squared residuals (least squares)
Fit parameters: linear regression or nonlinear optimisation
Check residuals: bias, curvature, outliers, heteroscedasticity
Report θ with units and rounding justified by uncertainty
Uncertainty: 95% CI, bootstrap, or a justified alternative
Document method, software/tool, and key settings
content.notes:
Explain least squares in plain language: pick parameters that make the model’s predictions as close as possible to observed outputs, measured by squared differences.

Clarify uncertainty reporting:
- For linear regression under standard assumptions, use standard errors and a t-based 95% CI.
- If assumptions are doubtful (non-normal errors, small n, clear heteroscedasticity), bootstrap intervals can be more defensible.
- If you cannot compute a CI (e.g., insufficient data), you must provide a justified uncertainty statement (e.g., sensitivity bounds, instrument accuracy-based bounds) and explain limitations.

Common misconception: a 95% CI is not “a 95% chance the true value is inside this interval” in a frequentist interpretation; it is a procedure with 95% long-run coverage under assumptions.

Probing question: What would residual curvature suggest about your chosen functional form?

slides.title: Dimensional (units) checking

content.title: Dimensional (units) checking
content: List units for every variable and parameter
Check each term: additions require identical units
Check multiplications/divisions: derived units match output
Convert units early and consistently (e.g., kW vs W)
Flag mismatch risks: time bases, % vs fraction, °C vs K
Record the check and any corrections made
content.notes:
Teach dimensional checking as a fast, high-impact quality gate. It often detects errors that calibration can hide (because parameters compensate for unit mistakes).

Mini-examples of common traps:
- Using temperature in °C inside a thermodynamic expression requiring Kelvin.
- Mixing hourly and daily rates (e.g., kWh vs kW).
- Treating efficiency written as “90” rather than 0.90.
- Using litres when the model expects cubic metres.

Probing question: If your output is in kWh/day, what must the time unit be in each rate term?

slides.title: Sensitivity and tolerance checks

content.title: Sensitivity and tolerance checks
content.notes:
Explain the distinction:
- Tolerance analysis propagates plausible uncertainty ranges through the model to produce output uncertainty.
- Sensitivity analysis ranks which factors most influence the output.

Encourage learners to select ranges that are defensible (instrument specs, historical variation, operational limits). “±10%” is acceptable only if justified.

Common misconception: varying one factor at a time can miss interactions; it is still useful as a first diagnostic, but scenario checks help reveal combined effects.

Probing question: If two inputs are correlated in reality, what does one-at-a-time sensitivity fail to capture?

slides.title: Worked example: operational demand model

content.title: Worked example: operational demand model
content.content: We model daily energy demand D (kWh/day) from mean outdoor temperature T (°C). Proposed model: D = a + b·(Tref − T), with Tref = 15 °C. Intended use: quick forecasting and monitoring; within T ∈ [0, 20] °C and similar occupancy patterns.
content.notes:
Set expectations: this is a deliberately simple, transparent model that learners can fully audit. Explain the choice of a heating-degree style formulation: when outdoor temperature drops below a reference, demand tends to rise.

Clarify the model components:
- Output D: daily energy demand.
- Input T: daily mean outdoor temperature.
- Parameter a: baseline demand at T = Tref.
- Parameter b: sensitivity of demand to temperature deficit.

Provide at least three example assumptions explicitly (learners should include these in their own work):
1) Linear relationship over the stated temperature range.
2) Other drivers (occupancy, wind, internal gains) are approximately constant or absorbed in residuals.
3) Temperature measurements are unbiased and represent the site.
4) No step change in equipment performance during the period.

Probing question: What operational changes could cause the same temperature to yield different demand?

slides.title: Example dataset and derived variable

content.title: Example dataset and derived variable
content.notes:
Explain why we compute H = (Tref − T): it simplifies the model to D = a + bH, which is a standard linear regression form.

Make the operational-data point: even this tidy dataset would typically require cleaning steps (missing days, holiday effects, abnormal events). Encourage learners to document any exclusions.

Probing questions:
- Why keep Tref fixed rather than calibrating it as another parameter?
- What happens if T exceeds Tref (negative H) in this formulation?

slides.speakerNotes:
Explain why we compute H = (Tref − T): it simplifies the model to D = a + bH, which is a standard linear regression form.

Make the operational-data point: even this tidy dataset would typically require cleaning steps (missing days, holiday effects, abnormal events). Encourage learners to document any exclusions.

Probing questions:
- Why keep Tref fixed rather than calibrating it as another parameter?
- What happens if T exceeds Tref (negative H) in this formulation?

slides.title: Fit parameters using least squares

content.title: Fit parameters using least squares
content: Model: D = a + bH, residual ei = Di − (a + bHi)
Choose a,b to minimise SSE = Σ ei² across all days
In a spreadsheet: use LINEST or Solver for a,b
In Python/R: fit linear regression of D on H
Record n, SSE/RMSE, and any excluded observations
content.notes:
Explain the mechanics at a conceptual level, then point to tooling:
- For linear models, closed-form solutions exist, but learners can use standard regression tools.
- Emphasise documenting the method: function name, options (e.g., include intercept), and any data transformations.

Mini-example (interpretation): If b = 35 kWh/day per °C, then each 1 °C colder than Tref increases daily demand by ~35 kWh/day, on average.

Common misconceptions:
- Forgetting the intercept (forcing through zero) changes meaning and often biases results.
- Using H in °C but later interpreting b as “per Kelvin” without noting equivalence for differences.

Probing question: If residuals increase in variance as H increases, what might you do next?

slides.title: Report parameters with units and 95% CI

content.title: Report parameters with units and 95% CI
content: Example fit: a = 1085 kWh/day, b = 43.0 kWh/day/°C
Round to reflect uncertainty, not calculator precision
State assumptions behind CI (independent, approx normal errors)
If violated, use bootstrap CI or justify an alternative statement
content.notes:
Explain what to include in a parameter report:
- Point estimates with correct units.
- Uncertainty: CI for each parameter (or at least the key sensitivity parameter).
- Brief method statement: “ordinary least squares on (H, D), with intercept”.

Provide a concrete worked explanation of CI computation (no need to derive fully):
- Regression software outputs SE(b).
- For small samples, use a t-multiplier with n−2 degrees of freedom.

Clarify rounding practice:
- If the 95% CI half-width is ~5 kWh/day/°C, reporting b = 43.027 is misleading.

Probing question: If your CI includes b = 0, what does that imply about temperature as a driver in your dataset?

slides.title: Units check and a mismatch risk

content.title: Units check and a mismatch risk
leftColumn: D has units kWh/day
a must be kWh/day
H is °C (difference), treated as K difference
b must be (kWh/day)/°C
rightColumn: Mismatch risk: D recorded in MWh/day, not kWh/day
Mismatch risk: b reported per K but H entered in °C
Fix: convert D to kWh/day (×1000) before fitting
Fix: document H as temperature difference (°C ≡ K)
content.notes:
Demonstrate the rule: you can only add terms with identical units. Since D = a + bH, both a and bH must be in kWh/day.

Explain why °C vs K can be subtle:
- Absolute temperatures require Kelvin.
- Temperature differences can be expressed in °C or K with identical magnitude, but you must document this to avoid confusion.

Describe how unit errors contaminate calibration:
- If D was in MWh/day but treated as kWh/day, the fitted parameters would be scaled by 1000. The model may still fit the data well but be unusable when applied correctly.

Probing question: Which is more dangerous: a unit mismatch that breaks the fit, or one that still fits? Why?

slides.title: Sensitivity/tolerance check on predicted demand

content.title: Sensitivity/tolerance check on predicted demand
content.notes:
Explain how the numbers are produced using the example fit (a = 1085, b = 43, Tref = 15):
- For T = 8, H = 7, so D = 1085 + 43×7 = 1386 kWh/day.
- For T = 10, H = 5, so D = 1085 + 43×5 = 1300.

Interpretation:
- In this local neighbourhood, a ±2 °C temperature change shifts demand by ±86 kWh/day.
- A ±10% change in b shifts demand by ±30 kWh/day at T = 8 °C.
- Therefore, in this scenario, temperature uncertainty (or variability) is the dominant driver.

Common misconception: sensitivity depends on the operating point; at different T, the influence of b changes because H changes.

Probing question: At T = 14 °C, would b uncertainty matter more or less? Show why.

content.title: Practice and reflection prompts
content: Write 3–5 sentences stating intended use and validity range
List inputs, outputs, parameters, and 3+ assumptions
Fit a,b on your dataset and compute a 95% CI for b
Perform a term-by-term units check and note one risk
Vary two factors and summarise output changes in a table

content.notes:
Encourage learners to use their own operational dataset if provided elsewhere in the module, or to reuse the worked example structure with different values.

Guide them on what “good” looks like:
- Intended use should be specific (e.g., “flag abnormal consumption days”) rather than generic (“predict demand”).

Common misconception: learners often list assumptions but do not connect them to limitations. Prompt them to state what would break each assumption.

Probing question: If you had to remove one assumption, which would most damage model credibility?

slides.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls

content.title: Assessment connection and common pitfalls
content: Supports MOD107 assignment: calibrated model + audit-ready artefact
Pitfall: unclear variable definitions or missing units
Pitfall: calibration with no method description or uncertainty
Pitfall: unit inconsistency hidden by fitted parameters
Pitfall: sensitivity ranges not justified or not recorded
Pitfall: irreproducible files (manual edits, hidden steps)
content.notes:
Make explicit how marking typically works: clarity, correctness, and reproducibility are graded alongside mathematical content.

Provide practical avoidance strategies:
- Put a variable dictionary at the top of the spreadsheet/notebook.
- Keep raw data on a separate tab or read-only cell range.
- Use named ranges or clearly labelled columns.
- Avoid “magic numbers” inside formulas; reference parameter cells.
- Record software versions or library versions when relevant.

Connect to the MCQs: these checks often target conceptual errors such as interpreting CIs, distinguishing calibration vs validation, and recognising unit traps.

slides.title: Model fitness-for-purpose against stakeholder requirement

content.title: Model fitness-for-purpose against stakeholder requirement
content.content:
Maths Certification
MOD107 — Mathematical Modelling: Calibration, Validation and Sensitivity
Lesson 14 (1h 30m)
content.notes:
Set expectations for this lesson: we move beyond “a model that runs” to “a model that is defensible for a stated decision”. Emphasise Bloom’s level (create): learners will produce a purpose statement, calibrate a model, assemble validation evidence, and package it in an audit-ready form.

Prompt: “When you say a model is ‘good’, good for what decision, and good for whom?” Highlight that fitness-for-purpose is contextual and cannot be judged without explicit requirements.

slides.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson

content.title: Orientation and how to use this lesson
content: Outcome: justify model fitness-for-purpose using evidence
1) Draft purpose + 5+ assumptions (tag testable/untestable)
2) Calibrate with two metrics and reproducible calculations
3) Validate vs requirements and conclude pass/conditional/fail
4) Record v0.1→v0.2 changelog with data/code references
5) Revise after peer-review and document what changed
content.notes:
Explain the suggested learning flow for self-study: (1) read the core concepts, (2) follow the worked examples by replicating calculations, (3) attempt the practice prompts, (4) complete the MCQs, and (5) revisit any section where you could not justify a decision in writing.

Clarify that evidence must be traceable: someone else should be able to reproduce the metrics and see why the decision (pass/conditional/fail) follows from the requirements.

Probing question: “If you handed your model to a colleague today, what would they need to trust it?”

slides.title: Purpose statement and assumptions

content.title: Purpose statement and assumptions
content: State intended use and decision to be supported
Name stakeholders and who signs off results
Define scope: system boundary, horizon, granularity
List assumptions/constraints and tag testable/untestable
Record known exclusions and when model must not be used
content.notes:
Coach learners to write a purpose statement that is operational, not aspirational. Good purpose statements include: the decision context (e.g., scheduling, capacity, pricing), the operating conditions (e.g., weekdays only, normal demand), and the output quantities that will be acted upon.

Explain testable vs untestable assumptions: testable assumptions can be checked against data or observable behaviour (e.g., “sensor error is unbiased”). Untestable assumptions are normative or lack data access (e.g., “customers behave rationally”), but they still must be documented and stress-tested through sensitivity or scenario analysis.

Common misconception: listing assumptions is not “admitting weakness”; it is how you delimit claims.

Probing questions: “What decision would be wrong if this assumption fails?” and “What data would you need to test it?”

slides.title: Calibration from operational data

content.title: Calibration from operational data
content: Choose variables: inputs, states, outputs aligned to purpose
Estimate parameters and report source, unit, plausible range
Split data: fit vs check (time split or cross-validation)
Compute metrics: RMSE, MAPE, R² (report rounding rules)
Keep calculations reproducible (formulae and data filters)
content.notes:
Explain calibration as parameter fitting to reduce discrepancy between model outputs and observed operational outputs. Stress that “best fit” is not the same as “best for decision”: overfitting can harm generalisation.

Give quick metric intuition:
- RMSE penalises large errors; units match the output.
- MAPE expresses relative error; problematic near zero values.
- R² indicates variance explained; can be misleading for biased fits.

Highlight reporting discipline: specify the dataset window, any cleaning rules, and parameter units. Encourage including parameter bounds and justifications.

Common misconceptions: using the same data for fitting and claiming validation; reporting metrics without stating the evaluation set.

Probing question: “If your output can be zero, is MAPE appropriate? What alternative would you use (e.g., MAE, sMAPE)?”

slides.title: Validation evidence: what counts

content.title: Validation evidence: what counts
content: Dimensional check: units and magnitudes make sense
Tolerance check: errors within stakeholder thresholds
Residual diagnostics: bias, trends, autocorrelation, outliers
Sensitivity check: outputs respond plausibly to key inputs
Conclude pass/conditional pass/fail against requirements
content.notes:
Position validation as an argument supported by evidence, not a single statistic. Walk through each evidence type:

Dimensional checks: verify units consistency and order-of-magnitude plausibility (e.g., energy in kWh, rates per hour). A model that “fits” but violates units is not credible.

Tolerance checks: link directly to stakeholder-defined acceptable error (e.g., “forecast within ±5% weekly”). Without thresholds, you cannot conclude pass/fail—only describe performance.

Residual diagnostics: show whether errors are random. If residuals trend with time or input magnitude, the model is structurally wrong or missing variables.

Sensitivity: vary one input/parameter at a time to test directional correctness and robustness. Stress that sensitivity is not optional when assumptions are untestable.

Probing questions: “Where could hidden bias sit?” and “Which requirement would fail first under stress?”

slides.title: Audit readiness and version control

content.title: Audit readiness and version control
content: Use semantic versions: v0.1 draft, v0.2 revised
Changelog: change, rationale, impact, corrective action
Reference data version and code/spreadsheet version
Freeze inputs: keep raw data read-only and hash/ID it
Peer-review checklist: clarity, maths, evidence, reproducibility
content.notes:
Explain that audit readiness is about traceability and accountability: a reviewer should be able to reconstruct exactly what was run and why changes were made.

Discuss minimal but sufficient version control: even if learners are using spreadsheets, they can still implement versioned filenames, a changelog tab, and a clear ‘data snapshot’ identifier.

Give examples of “impact on results”: metric changed from RMSE 12.4 to 10.9; parameter estimate changed units; validation conclusion changed from conditional pass to pass.

Common misconception: a changelog is only for code—stress it is equally for model structure, assumptions, dataset filters, and documentation changes.

Probing question: “If a stakeholder challenges your conclusion, what artefact would you show first?”

slides.title: Worked example: calibrate and report metrics

content.title: Worked example: calibrate and report metrics
content: Step 1: select output y and inputs X consistent with purpose
Step 2: choose parameters θ and record units and bounds
Step 3: fit θ on training window; keep test window untouched
Step 4: compute RMSE and MAPE on test window
Step 5: document formulae and rounding (e.g., 2 d.p.)
Step 6: interpret: which errors matter for the decision?
content.notes:
Provide a concrete walkthrough learners can mirror.

Mini-example (illustrative numbers): Suppose actual y = [100, 110, 90] and predicted ŷ = [95, 120, 92].
- Errors e = ŷ − y = [-5, 10, 2].
- RMSE = sqrt(mean(e²)) = sqrt((25+100+4)/3) = sqrt(43) = 6.56.
- MAPE = mean(|e|/y)×100 = (5/100 + 10/110 + 2/90)/3×100 ≈ 5.42%.
Explain why you would report the calculation steps (and not just the final value), so another person can reproduce it.

Common misconception: reporting R² alone. Emphasise that a high R² can coexist with unacceptable bias.

Probing question: “If staffing decisions change when error exceeds 8 units, is RMSE 6.56 sufficient evidence?”

slides.title: Worked example: map requirements to evidence

content.title: Worked example: map requirements to evidence
leftColumn: Req 1: Units correct and plausible magnitudes
Req 2: Weekly forecast error ≤ ±5%
Req 3: No systematic bias across demand levels
Req 4: Robust to ±10% demand shift
rightColumn: Dimensional check passed; rates and totals consistent
MAPE = 4.8% on test window (n=52 hours)
Residuals trend upward at high demand; bias present
Sensitivity: +10% demand raises output by +9.7%
content.notes:
Explain that fitness-for-purpose is a structured argument: each requirement needs corresponding evidence. Learners should avoid generic statements like “validated” without referencing which requirement is satisfied.

Demonstrate how to conclude: With Req 3 failing (bias at high demand), you might issue a conditional pass if the decision context rarely enters high-demand regimes, or fail if high demand is precisely when the decision is most critical.

Teach learners to note sample size and evaluation period (e.g., n=52 hours), because metrics without context can mislead.

Probing questions: “Which requirement is most critical to stakeholders?” and “Would you accept conditional pass if the risk occurs during peak periods?”

rows: Initial fit; used all data for calibration

Explain that the changelog is not a diary; it is a decision record. Each entry should allow an auditor to see: what changed, why it changed, what it changed in outputs/metrics, and what you did in response.

Common misconception: hiding adverse impacts (e.g., metrics worsening). Emphasise that transparent degradation after fixing leakage is a sign of improved validity.

Probing question: “If v0.2 gives worse headline metrics, why might it still be the better model?”

brief.studentFacingIntro: You will build an audit-ready Excel workbook for a small workplace planning task. The workbook must use correct units, appropriate significant figures and rounding, and clearly show how calculations are produced and checked. You will also demonstrate that you can rearrange formulae to isolate key variables (e.g., price or quantity) and use linear equations/inequalities to test whether simple production targets are feasible under stated constraints. You must present your workbook in class and answer short questions about your assumptions, rounding decisions and how you ensured traceability.
brief.workplaceContext: You work in operations support for a small manufacturer producing two products (Product A and Product B). Your manager needs a transparent spreadsheet that (1) prices products consistently using a margin rule, (2) calculates material and labour requirements with correct units and rounding, (3) records assumptions and changes for audit, and (4) checks whether a weekly production target is feasible given machine-time and labour constraints. The workbook will be reviewed during an internal audit, so it must be easy to follow and to verify.
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1 — Set up the workbook structure (Excel): Create a single .xlsx file with separate sheets named exactly: 01_Inputs, 02_Calculations, 03_Feasibility, 04_ChangeLog, 05_Checks. Use a consistent layout: inputs clearly separated from calculations; units shown next to every input and key output.
Step 2 — Enter the provided scenario data (in class handout): Enter all given values into 01_Inputs only. Do not hard-code numbers inside formulas on other sheets (except 0/1 flags if needed).

Step 3 — Apply referencing standards (MLO 3): Use named ranges for key inputs (e.g., LabourHoursPerUnit_A) and/or an Excel Table for input data with structured references. Use absolute/relative references correctly. Include a short 'How to use this file' note at the top of 01_Inputs (3–6 bullet points).

Step 4 — Units and rounding plan (MLO 1): On 05_Checks, create a small table titled 'Units and Rounding Rules' stating: (a) base units used (e.g., minutes, hours, kg, £), (b) rounding rules you apply to intermediate steps vs final outputs, and (c) the significant figures/decimal places used for each key output. Apply these rules consistently in the workbook.

Step 5 — Multi-step calculation with error/rounding propagation explanation (MLO 1): In 02_Calculations, build a multi-step calculation chain (minimum 4 linked steps) that produces a final cost and/or requirement output. Then, on 05_Checks, explain (in plain English) how rounding at intermediate steps could change the final result, and demonstrate this with a clear comparison (e.g., 'round at each step' vs 'round at the end').

Step 6 — Algebraic rearrangement and implementation (MLO 2): From the pricing and/or production formulae provided in the handout, show your algebraic rearrangement to isolate a variable (e.g., solve for SellingPrice given target margin and cost; or solve for RequiredUnits given revenue target and price). Include the rearrangement in your PDF report and implement the rearranged formula in Excel using referenced inputs (not typed numbers). Record the units, rounding choices and assumptions used.

Step 7 — Feasibility using linear equations and inequalities (MLO 4): On 03_Feasibility, model the weekly constraints as linear equations/inequalities (e.g., total labour hours available; total machine minutes available; minimum/maximum units). Use Excel formulas to compute left-hand sides and compare against limits. Provide a clear 'Feasible? YES/NO' output and a brief explanation of what constraint fails if infeasible. Document assumptions clearly on the sheet.

Step 8 — Audit trail and change notes (MLO 3): Complete 04_ChangeLog with at least 6 entries. Each entry must include: date, your initials, what changed, where (sheet/cell range), and why. Use Excel’s formula auditing where appropriate (trace precedents/dependents) and include screenshots in the PDF report showing at least two examples of traceability.

Step 9 — In-class audit demonstration (in-person): Bring a printed copy of 01_Inputs, 03_Feasibility summary area, and 04_ChangeLog to class. You will deliver an 8-minute live walkthrough of your workbook and answer up to 4 minutes of questions focusing on units, rounding, referencing/named ranges, algebraic rearrangement, and feasibility constraints.
deliverables: Deliverable 1: Excel workbook (.xlsx) with the required sheets and a working model that meets the brief (submitted via LMS).

Deliverable 2: Short technical commentary (PDF) including: your algebraic rearrangement working, units/rounding decisions, error/rounding propagation explanation with a demonstrated comparison, and traceability screenshots (submitted via LMS).
Deliverable 3: Printed pack for in-class audit (hard copy): 01_Inputs (1–2 pages), 03_Feasibility summary area (1 page), 04_ChangeLog (1 page).
Deliverable 4: In-class live demonstration (8 minutes) plus Q&A (up to 4 minutes).

rubric.criterionName: Units, significant figures, rounding and error/rounding propagation explanation
rubric.fail: Units are missing or inconsistent for multiple key inputs/outputs; rounding is applied inconsistently or not stated; explanation of significant figures/rounding is absent or incorrect; no clear demonstration of how rounding affects a multi-step spreadsheet outcome.
rubric.pass: Units are shown for key inputs and key outputs; rounding rules and significant figures are stated and mostly applied consistently; provides a basic explanation and a simple comparison showing that rounding can change the final result in a multi-step calculation chain.
rubric.merit: Units are consistently recorded next to inputs and outputs; rounding choices are clearly justified (intermediate vs final rounding) and applied consistently; provides a clear, correct explanation of how rounding/error can propagate through linked steps and includes an organised comparison that a reviewer can reproduce.
rubric.distinction: Units are comprehensive and unambiguous throughout; rounding/significant-figure rules are precise, consistently applied, and appropriate for workplace reporting; provides a robust, clearly presented demonstration of propagation across multiple steps, highlighting where the spreadsheet is most sensitive to rounding and how the design mitigates risk of misleading outputs.

rubric.criterionName: Algebraic rearrangement and correct Excel implementation with documented assumptions
rubric.fail: Rearrangement is missing or incorrect; the isolated variable does not match the stated goal; Excel implementation is incorrect or uses hard-coded numbers in formulas; units/rounding/assumptions are not recorded.
rubric.pass: Provides a correct rearrangement that isolates the required variable; Excel formula produces a plausible output using referenced inputs; documents basic units and at least one assumption and rounding choice.
rubric.merit: Rearrangement is clearly shown step-by-step and correctly isolates the variable; Excel implementation is correct, readable and uses referenced inputs/named ranges appropriately; units, rounding choices and assumptions are recorded clearly and align with the workbook results.
rubric.distinction: Rearrangement is accurate, clearly communicated and tightly linked to the workplace decision being made; Excel implementation is robust (readable structure, no unnecessary complexity, consistent referencing); assumptions, units and rounding are complete, explicit and make audit checking straightforward.

rubric.criterionName: Excel transparency: referencing, named ranges/structured layout, and traceable change notes for audit
rubric.fail: Workbook layout is confusing; inputs and calculations are mixed; references are inconsistent or break when copied; no named ranges/structured references used where appropriate; change log is missing or not meaningful; traceability evidence is absent.
rubric.pass: Workbook separates inputs from calculations; uses basic good referencing practice (appropriate absolute/relative references); includes some named ranges or structured references; change log includes at least 6 entries with basic details; includes at least one traceability screenshot or example.
rubric.merit: Workbook is consistently structured and easy to navigate; named ranges and/or tables are used effectively for key inputs; formulas are readable and minimise hard-coding; change log entries are specific and support audit review; includes at least two clear traceability examples (e.g., trace precedents/dependents) that connect outputs to inputs.
rubric.distinction: Workbook demonstrates audit-ready transparency: consistent layout standards, clear labelling, effective use of named ranges/structured references, and high formula readability; change log is thorough and supports an audit narrative; traceability evidence is clear, well-chosen and makes verification efficient.

rubric.criterionName: Feasibility testing using linear equations and inequalities with clear assumptions
rubric.fail: Constraints are not expressed as linear equations/inequalities, or are incorrect; feasibility conclusion is missing/incorrect; assumptions are absent or unclear; spreadsheet does not clearly show which constraint(s) pass/fail.
rubric.pass: Represents the stated constraints with linear equations/inequalities; calculates and compares totals to limits; outputs a clear feasible/not feasible decision; documents basic assumptions used.
rubric.merit: Constraints are correctly and clearly expressed; the spreadsheet shows each inequality with left-hand side, right-hand side, and pass/fail status; feasibility conclusion is correct and explained; assumptions are clearly documented and consistent with the model.
rubric.distinction: Feasibility modelling is clear, complete and audit-friendly: each constraint is correctly represented, transparently calculated, and clearly interpreted; includes a concise explanation identifying the binding/failed constraint(s) under the stated target; assumptions are explicit, well-structured and support decision-making.

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Excel workbook implementing the full model (with required sheet names and structure)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include sheets: 01_Inputs, 02_Calculations, 03_Feasibility, 04_ChangeLog, 05_Checks. Inputs must be entered on 01_Inputs only. Use named ranges and/or structured references. No hard-coded numbers inside calculation formulas except where explicitly justified in the PDF.

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Technical commentary covering algebraic rearrangement, units/rounding choices, propagation explanation, and audit traceability evidence
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include: (1) algebraic rearrangement working with the isolated variable clearly identified; (2) a brief list of units and rounding rules used; (3) a demonstrated comparison showing the impact of rounding through a multi-step chain; (4) at least two screenshots showing formula traceability (e.g., trace precedents/dependents or clearly highlighted referenced cells) and a short explanation of what each screenshot demonstrates.

Print: 01_Inputs, 03_Feasibility summary area, and 04_ChangeLog. Ensure your name and student ID appear on each page (header or footer). You may redact any personal data beyond what is required for assessment.

evidenceRequirements.wordCountOrDuration: 8 minutes presentation + up to 4 minutes Q&A
evidenceRequirements.fileType: In-person performance (no recording required unless agreed as an adjustment)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: You must be able to navigate your workbook, show where units and rounding rules are stated, point to the rearranged formula in Excel, and explain the feasibility constraints. You may use printed notes (1 side of A4) during the demonstration.

in_person.academicIntegrity: This is an individual assignment. You may discuss the scenario and general Excel techniques with peers during workshops, and you may receive tutor guidance on interpreting the brief and improving spreadsheet transparency. However, your workbook structure, formulas, algebraic rearrangement working, written explanations, and change log must be your own work. Do not copy another learner’s spreadsheet (in whole or in part), do not share your completed file, and do not submit work produced by someone else. If you use any external resources (e.g., Excel documentation, textbooks, websites), you must acknowledge them briefly in the PDF (e.g., a short 'Resources used' section). You must include a declaration of authenticity in your PDF stating that the submission is your own work and that all sources have been acknowledged. Suspected misconduct will be handled under the programme’s academic integrity procedures.
in_person.accessibilityOptions: Reasonable adjustments are available without lowering academic standards. Examples include: additional time for the in-class demonstration; an alternative time slot; presenting to the tutor only rather than the full class; providing the demonstration as a recorded screen capture with live follow-up questions if speaking in front of the group is a barrier; accessible templates (larger fonts/high contrast); permission to use assistive technology; printed materials provided in advance; and flexibility in the PDF format (e.g., structured headings for screen readers). Any adjustment must still allow you to evidence the same module learning outcomes (units/rounding and propagation explanation, algebraic rearrangement in Excel with documented assumptions, transparent referencing/named ranges and change log, and feasibility testing using linear equations/inequalities).

Apply algebraic rearrangement to isolate variables in pricing and production formulae within Excel, recording units, rounding choices and assumptions.
