brief.studentFacingIntro:
You will build an audit-ready Excel workbook for a realistic workplace pricing and production scenario. The focus is on (1) correct handling of units and rounding, (2) algebraic rearrangement to isolate required variables, (3) transparent spreadsheet standards (referencing, named ranges, structured layout, change notes), and (4) linear feasibility checks against constraints.

This is a self-study assessment. You must work independently and submit a digital workbook, a short technical note, and a brief recorded walkthrough of how your spreadsheet works and how you controlled units, rounding, and assumptions.
brief.workplaceContext:
Scenario: You are supporting a small manufacturing business producing bottled cleaning solution in 750 mL bottles.

The business needs a spreadsheet that:
- calculates unit cost and a selling price based on a target gross margin,
- calculates the production hours required to meet a weekly target output, allowing for scrap,
- checks whether the target is feasible under simple capacity constraints (time, materials, and labour), and
- is auditable: a colleague can follow the logic, see units, see rounding, and understand changes.

You are given a set of baseline inputs (you may add clearly-labelled assumptions where required):
- Bottle volume: 750 mL per bottle
- Weekly demand target: 4,800 bottles
- Scrap rate: 3.5% of bottles produced are scrapped (assume scrap affects finished bottles)
- Machine fill rate: 22.5 bottles/minute
- Available machine time: 34.0 hours/week
- Labour staffing: 2 operators available, each up to 16.0 hours/week on this line
- Labour required: 0.60 labour-hours per machine-hour (operators can support more than one task; treat as proportional)
- Ingredients (concentrate) usage: 55 mL concentrate per bottle (assume no process loss unless you state one)
- Concentrate available: 260 litres/week
- Packaging (caps) available: 5,200 caps/week
- Costs:
  - Concentrate cost: £3.40 per litre
  - Bottle + cap packaging cost: £0.18 per bottle
  - Label cost: £0.04 per bottle
  - Labour cost: £14.50 per labour-hour
  - Overhead: £62.00 per machine-hour
- Pricing rule: Set selling price per bottle (ex VAT) to achieve a gross margin of 38% on selling price.

You must keep all units explicit (mL, L, bottles, min, hour, £/L, £/hour, etc.).
stepByStepInstructions:
1) Set up your workbook structure (minimum required sheets):
   a) README (purpose, how to use, version/date)
   b) Inputs (all inputs in one place with units, source/assumption, and last-updated date)
   c) Calculations (core computations only; no hard-coded numbers inside formulas except 0/1 flags)
   d) Checks_Audit (self-checks, error/rounding demonstrations, and reasonableness checks)
   e) Change_Log (date, change description, cells/areas affected, reason, author)

2) Apply spreadsheet standards (required):
   - Use named ranges for key inputs (e.g., Bottle_mL, Demand_bottles, Scrap_rate, Fill_rate_bpm, Machine_hours_available, Concentrate_cost_per_L).
   - Use consistent cell styles: inputs (one colour), calculated cells (another), headings, and units.
   - Use a clear calculation flow top-to-bottom.
   - Use absolute/relative referencing appropriately; avoid copying errors.
   - Add cell comments or short notes where an assumption is made.

3) Units, significant figures, and rounding (MLO 1):
   a) Create a small section in Checks_Audit that lists at least 8 quantities from your model with:
      - value,
      - unit,
      - rounding rule applied (e.g., money to 2 dp; hours to 2 dp; bottles to whole numbers), and
      - the unrounded value used for internal calculations (where applicable).
   b) Demonstrate error propagation in a multi-step spreadsheet:
      - Choose a chain of at least 4 steps (e.g., demand -> required production -> required machine minutes -> machine hours -> labour hours -> labour cost).
      - Compute the final result using (i) rounding at each step and (ii) rounding only at the final output.
      - Report the absolute difference and percentage difference and explain, in plain English, what caused the difference.

4) Algebraic rearrangement to isolate variables (MLO 2):
   You must include at least TWO algebraic rearrangements written out in your technical note and implemented in Excel:
   a) Pricing: Given gross margin g on selling price, selling price P and unit cost C satisfy: (P - C) / P = g.
      - Rearrange to make P the subject in terms of C and g.
      - Implement P in Excel using named ranges, with unit cost computed from your cost model.
   b) Production hours: Define good bottles produced as Good = Rate * Time * (1 - Scrap_rate), using consistent units.
      - Rearrange to make Time the subject given a good-bottle target.
      - Implement required machine time in Excel.
   For each rearrangement, record units, rounding choices, and any assumptions (e.g., whether scrap increases required production quantity).

5) Build the cost and price model in Excel:
   a) Compute concentrate litres required, packaging quantities, labour hours, overhead cost, and total weekly cost.
   b) Compute unit cost per bottle (£/bottle) based on weekly production needed to meet demand after scrap.
   c) Compute selling price per bottle (ex VAT) using the rearranged margin formula.

6) Feasibility checks using linear equations/inequalities (MLO 4):
   a) Translate the constraints into inequalities, using your defined variables and units. Minimum required constraints to include:
      - Machine time: Required_machine_hours ≤ Available_machine_hours
      - Labour: Required_labour_hours ≤ Available_labour_hours (2 operators × 16 hours/week)
      - Concentrate: Required_concentrate_L ≤ Available_concentrate_L
      - Caps: Required_caps ≤ Available_caps
   b) In your spreadsheet, produce a clear PASS/FAIL indicator for each constraint and an overall feasibility result.
   c) If not feasible, calculate (using linear reasoning) the maximum feasible weekly good-bottle output given each single constraint and identify the binding constraint (the tightest limit).

7) Create self-checks (must be included before submission):
   a) Add at least 6 automated checks in Checks_Audit, such as:
      - negative values not permitted for rates/costs,
      - scrap rate between 0 and 0.20 (or your justified range),
      - units consistency checks (e.g., mL to L conversion correctness),
      - reconciliation checks (e.g., total weekly cost equals sum of components),
      - reasonableness checks (e.g., selling price > unit cost).
   b) Provide a short checklist (tick boxes) in README confirming you have: used named ranges, documented rounding, demonstrated error propagation, included change notes, and included feasibility constraints.

8) Record a short walkthrough (recorded presentation replacement):
   - Screen-record a 6–8 minute walkthrough explaining where inputs are, how calculations flow, where you documented rounding/units, and how to interpret feasibility results.
   - You must show at least one example of tracing a key output back to inputs (auditability).

9) Export and submit:
   - Submit the Excel workbook (.xlsx) with all formulas intact.
   - Submit a PDF technical note addressing the required explanations and showing your algebraic rearrangements.
   - Submit your MP4 walkthrough recording.
deliverables: Excel workbook (.xlsx) containing the required sheets, named ranges, calculations, checks, and change log.
Technical note (PDF) including algebraic rearrangements, units/rounding explanation, and error propagation demonstration results.
Recorded walkthrough (MP4) demonstrating use of the workbook, audit trail, and feasibility logic.

rubric.criterionName: Units, significant figures, rounding rules, and error propagation explanation
rubric.fail: Units are missing or inconsistent across multiple calculations; rounding is applied arbitrarily or not stated; no clear demonstration of how rounding affects multi-step results; explanation is absent or incorrect.
rubric.pass: Units are stated for key inputs/outputs and are mostly consistent; rounding rules are stated for key quantities (e.g., £ to 2 dp; hours to 2 dp; whole bottles); includes a worked comparison of stepwise rounding vs end-only rounding with a basic explanation of the difference.
rubric.merit: Units are consistently shown and conversions are correct (e.g., mL↔L, minutes↔hours); rounding rules are justified in a workplace context; error propagation example includes absolute and percentage differences and identifies which steps contribute most to divergence.
rubric.distinction: Units, rounding and significant figures are applied consistently and professionally throughout; the error propagation demonstration is clearly structured, replicable, and includes interpretation of operational impact (e.g., cost impact per week) while keeping within stated assumptions; checks make rounding/precision effects visible for audit.

rubric.criterionName: Algebraic rearrangement and correct Excel implementation of isolated-variable formulae (with units, rounding, assumptions)
rubric.fail: Rearrangements are missing or incorrect; Excel formulas do not match stated rearrangements; units/assumptions not recorded; outputs are not credible or do not respond correctly to input changes.
rubric.pass: Provides at least two correct rearrangements (pricing margin and production time) written clearly; implements them in Excel so outputs change appropriately when inputs change; records basic units, rounding choices, and assumptions.
rubric.merit: Rearrangements are correct, clearly presented, and linked to workbook cell logic; assumptions are explicit and reasonable; rounding choices are applied consistently (e.g., internal precision vs displayed rounding) with notes explaining why.
rubric.distinction: Rearrangements and implementations are robust and audit-ready: formulas are transparent, use named ranges, avoid hard-coded constants, and include clear assumption notes; the model behaves correctly under test changes and edge conditions (e.g., scrap rate changes) without breaking logic.

rubric.criterionName: Spreadsheet standards: referencing, named ranges, structured layout, and traceable change notes for audit
rubric.fail: Workbook is difficult to follow; inconsistent or incorrect referencing; hard-coded numbers embedded in formulas without explanation; named ranges not used; no structured layout; no change log or change log is not meaningful.
rubric.pass: Workbook has a clear Inputs and Calculations separation; uses appropriate absolute/relative references; uses named ranges for key inputs; layout is readable; includes a change log with at least three meaningful entries.
rubric.merit: Workbook is transparent and professionally structured: consistent formatting for inputs/calculations, clear headings and units, minimal duplication; named ranges used widely and correctly; includes traceable notes/comments for assumptions; change log entries link to specific areas and reasons.
rubric.distinction: Workbook meets audit-ready expectations: a third party can trace outputs to inputs using structured layout, named ranges, and checks; change log is complete, specific, and supports reproducibility; checks are well-labelled and highlight issues clearly without manual searching.

rubric.criterionName: Linear equations and inequalities for feasibility testing under constraints (with documented assumptions)
rubric.fail: Constraints are missing, incorrect, or not expressed as inequalities; feasibility conclusion is unsupported; assumptions are unclear; PASS/FAIL indicators are absent or unreliable.
rubric.pass: Includes the required constraints as inequalities with correct units; provides a PASS/FAIL indicator per constraint and an overall feasibility statement; assumptions are stated at a basic level.
rubric.merit: Constraints are correctly implemented and clearly explained; identifies maximum feasible output for each constraint and correctly identifies the binding constraint; assumptions are explicit and consistent with the model structure.
rubric.distinction: Feasibility analysis is clear, correct, and decision-useful: constraints, binding constraint, and implications are stated plainly; workbook allows quick scenario testing (e.g., changing available hours or scrap) while maintaining correct inequality logic and documentation standards.

evidenceRequirements.wordCountOrDuration: N/A (all required sheets and features must be present)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Workbook must include (minimum): README, Inputs, Calculations, Checks_Audit, Change_Log. Formulas must remain live (no paste-as-values for calculated areas). Use named ranges for key inputs. Include PASS/FAIL constraint indicators and automated checks.

Must include: (1) two algebraic rearrangements written out and linked to workbook, (2) units and rounding rules used (with examples), (3) error propagation demonstration (stepwise rounding vs end-only rounding) with absolute and % difference and explanation, (4) list of assumptions used in the model.

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Recorded walkthrough (screen recording with voice or captions)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must show: where inputs are, how key outputs are calculated, where named ranges are used, where rounding/units are documented, where checks and feasibility constraints are shown, and how to trace one output back to inputs.

self_study.academicIntegrity:
You must complete this assessment independently. You may use: Microsoft Excel help resources, openly available reference materials on units and rounding, and your own notes. You may use spelling/grammar tools to improve writing quality. If you use any generative AI tool, you must (a) use it only for language clarity or formatting support, not to generate the model logic or calculations, and (b) include a short disclosure in your technical note stating what tool was used and how.

You must not: submit someone else’s spreadsheet or text as your own; share your completed workbook for others to copy; contract someone to produce the work; falsify results by hard-coding outputs to match expectations; remove formulas to hide method.

By submitting, you confirm the work is your own and that all sources and tools used have been appropriately acknowledged.
self_study.accessibilityOptions: Reasonable adjustments are available without lowering academic standards. You may request: extra time if time-limited conditions apply to you; permission to submit an accessible alternative to the MP4 (e.g., a narrated PowerPoint exported to MP4, or an MP4 with captions only, or an audio recording with a structured PDF of screenshots); use of assistive technology (screen readers, speech-to-text) and accessible colour choices in Excel (do not rely on colour alone—also use labels/icons). If you have a documented need, you may submit the technical note in an alternative accessible format (DOCX instead of PDF) provided the content requirements are met.

stepByStepInstructions: Step 1 — Download and read the assignment template pack from the LMS (or collect a printed copy in class). The pack contains: (a) scenario data tables, (b) required sheet structure, (c) a change log table format, and (d) a self-audit checklist.

Step 2 — Set up your Excel workbook structure with separate tabs (minimum): Inputs, Calculations, Outputs, Audit_Log, and Feasibility. Use a consistent layout, clear headings, and cell styling that distinguishes inputs from calculated cells.

Step 3 — Define units for every input and key output (e.g., £/hr, kg/unit, units/week). Record units next to inputs and in output tables. Where you convert units (e.g., minutes to hours; grams to kg), show the conversion clearly in the calculations.

Step 4 — Implement significant figures and rounding rules appropriate to a workplace context (e.g., money to 2 d.p.; measured quantities to a stated precision). Create a short “Rounding & Precision Policy” section in your workbook (either on Outputs or Audit_Log) explaining your choices.

Step 5 — Demonstrate error propagation through a multi-step spreadsheet: choose at least two measured inputs with tolerances/uncertainty (provided in the scenario pack), and show how these tolerances affect a final output (e.g., unit cost or contribution margin). Use clear formulas and show intermediate steps so the propagation is traceable.

Step 6 — Apply algebraic rearrangement to isolate variables in pricing/production formulae. You must include at least two rearrangements (e.g., solve for required selling price given target margin; solve for required output quantity given fixed costs and desired profit). Implement each rearranged formula in Excel and label it clearly. Record units, rounding choices and assumptions alongside each.

Step 7 — Build the model using robust Excel practices: (a) use correct relative/absolute referencing, (b) create named ranges for key inputs, and (c) use structured layout so the calculation logic can be followed. Avoid hard-coded numbers inside formulas (except 0/1 flags where justified).

Step 8 — Create an audit trail: complete the Audit_Log tab with traceable change notes. Include at least five change entries (e.g., correction of a unit, update to a rounding rule, renamed range, fixed reference, revised assumption). Each entry must include date/time (or version), what changed, why, and impact.

Step 9 — Feasibility check: using linear equations and inequalities, test whether a proposed production target is feasible under constraints provided (e.g., labour hours, material availability, machine time). Show the inequalities and the logic used to determine feasibility. If infeasible, show at least one feasible alternative plan (e.g., revised mix or reduced total) and explain it.

Step 10 — Prepare your written audit note and walkthrough. Your audit note should explain how your workbook works, highlight units/rounding decisions, summarise the error propagation demonstration, and present the feasibility conclusion with assumptions.

Step 11 — Peer review (collaborative element) OR asynchronous alternative: Option A (collaborative): exchange your workbook (or PDF printout) with one peer in your seminar group and provide structured feedback using the checklist (upload your feedback as evidence). Option B (asynchronous): complete the self-audit checklist yourself and write a brief note identifying at least three risks or improvements you would make if this were a live business tool.

Step 12 — Submit all required deliverables by the deadline using digital submission (LMS upload) or physical submission (printed report and spreadsheet printouts) as agreed with the tutor. If submitting physically, you must also provide the Excel file on a USB drive or via LMS upload unless a reasonable adjustment is in place.
deliverables: Deliverable 1: Excel workbook (.xlsx) with required tabs (Inputs, Calculations, Outputs, Audit_Log, Feasibility), using named ranges, correct referencing, and a structured layout.

Deliverable 2: Audit note (PDF) explaining units, significant figures, rounding rules, error propagation demonstration, algebraic rearrangements implemented, and feasibility conclusion (with assumptions).
Deliverable 3: Walkthrough presentation (live 5–7 minutes in class/online OR recorded video 5–7 minutes) demonstrating key features and how to audit the workbook.
Deliverable 4: Peer-review feedback form (if completing Option A) OR completed self-audit checklist with improvement note (if completing Option B).

rubric.criterionName: Units, significant figures, rounding rules and error propagation
rubric.fail: Units are missing or inconsistent for multiple inputs/outputs; rounding is applied inconsistently or not justified; explanations are absent or incorrect; error propagation is not demonstrated, is conceptually incorrect, or cannot be traced through the spreadsheet steps.
rubric.pass: Units are stated for key inputs and outputs with only minor omissions; rounding and significant figures are generally appropriate for money and measured quantities and are stated in a brief policy; an error propagation example is included and mostly traceable, showing how input tolerance affects at least one final output.
rubric.merit: Units are consistently recorded for all relevant inputs and outputs; rounding/significant figures choices are clearly justified with workplace rationale; error propagation is clearly set out with traceable intermediate steps and a correct explanation of how rounding/precision affects final figures.
rubric.distinction: Units are comprehensive and include clear conversions where needed; rounding/significant figures policy is precise, consistently implemented, and explicitly linked to decision-making (e.g., pricing impact); error propagation is demonstrated clearly across multiple steps with a well-explained sensitivity/tolerance impact and transparent auditability.

rubric.criterionName: Algebraic rearrangement and implementation in Excel with documentation
rubric.fail: Rearrangements are missing or incorrect; Excel formulas do not reflect correct rearranged relationships; units, rounding choices, and assumptions are not recorded or are contradictory; the model cannot be used to isolate variables reliably.
rubric.pass: At least two correct algebraic rearrangements are included and implemented in Excel; variables are isolated to support pricing/production questions; units and key assumptions are recorded, with rounding choices stated but not always fully justified.
rubric.merit: Rearrangements are correct, clearly labelled, and implemented using good Excel practice (e.g., named ranges, no hard-coded constants unless justified); units, rounding choices, and assumptions are clearly documented next to the relevant calculations.
rubric.distinction: Rearrangements are correct and used effectively for realistic scenarios (e.g., target margin/profit, break-even-style reasoning); documentation is thorough and audit-ready (units, rounding, assumptions, and limits of validity are explicit); Excel implementation supports easy what-if changes without breaking logic.

rubric.criterionName: Spreadsheet transparency, referencing, named ranges, structured layout and audit change notes
rubric.fail: Workbook layout is confusing; formulas contain hard-coded values without explanation; referencing is incorrect or fragile (e.g., broken relative/absolute references); named ranges are absent or misused; change notes are missing or not traceable.
rubric.pass: Workbook follows a mostly clear structure with separate inputs/calculations/outputs; referencing is mostly correct; some named ranges are used; an Audit_Log is included with at least five entries that broadly describe changes.
rubric.merit: Workbook is clearly structured and readable; inputs are clearly separated and protected/marked; referencing is robust (appropriate absolute/relative use); named ranges are used for key inputs; Audit_Log entries are specific (what/why/impact) and enable traceability for review.
rubric.distinction: Workbook demonstrates strong spreadsheet engineering: consistent layout conventions, transparent calculation flow, reliable referencing throughout, well-chosen named ranges, and outputs designed for quick checking; Audit_Log is detailed and supports an audit narrative (including versioning and clear impact statements).

rubric.criterionName: Linear equations/inequalities feasibility testing and clear assumptions
rubric.fail: Feasibility test is missing or incorrect; constraints are not expressed as linear equations/inequalities or are misapplied; assumptions are absent; feasibility conclusion is unsupported or contradictory to the model’s numbers.
rubric.pass: Constraints are expressed as linear equations/inequalities and used to test feasibility of the target plan; conclusion (feasible/infeasible) is mostly correct; assumptions are stated but may be brief or incomplete; at least one feasible adjustment is suggested if infeasible.
rubric.merit: Feasibility test correctly applies linear equations/inequalities with clear working; assumptions are clearly documented and consistent with the spreadsheet; conclusion is well supported; where infeasible, an alternative feasible plan is shown with clear reasoning.
rubric.distinction: Feasibility analysis is rigorous and clearly communicated: constraints are correctly defined and checked, assumptions are explicit and well-justified, and the feasibility conclusion is presented in a way suitable for team review (including a clear alternative plan and explanation of trade-offs).

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Excel workbook with required tabs and features
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include: named ranges, robust referencing, structured layout, documented units, rounding/significant figures policy, error propagation example, algebraic rearrangements, feasibility tab with inequalities, and Audit_Log with at least five traceable change entries.

Should be written for a workplace audience. Must reference specific cells/tabs (e.g., ‘Outputs!F12’) or include screenshots to support explanations. Include a short assumptions list and a brief conclusion for a manager.

brief.studentFacingIntro: In this assignment you will work with a realistic operational dataset and produce clear graphs and a short decision note suitable for a team review meeting. You will model relationships using linear, quadratic and exponential functions, present plots for non-specialist readers, and calculate key thresholds such as gradients, intercepts and break-even points. You will then interpret trends and constraints and propose a recommendation supported by evidence from your graphs and calculations.
brief.workplaceContext: You are supporting an Operations Manager in a small manufacturing and fulfilment business. The team is reviewing whether to (a) adjust unit price, and (b) add capacity during peak periods. You have been given recent operational data (sales volume, unit price, variable cost, fixed cost, and throughput/capacity observations). The manager needs a short, evidence-based note and clear visuals to use in a face-to-face team meeting with colleagues who are not mathematicians.
stepByStepInstructions: 1) Attend the in-class briefing and collect the assignment data pack (dataset + scenario notes). Confirm which tool you will use: Excel or Python.
2) Import the dataset into Excel or Python. Check for missing values or obvious data issues. Do not change raw values; if you clean or filter data, keep a clear log of what you did and why.

3) Create at least three graphs that relate directly to the scenario, including: one linear relationship, one quadratic relationship, and one exponential relationship. For each, show the observed data and an appropriate fitted function (trendline/model) that you will use for interpretation.

4) For each function used, write brief statements explaining what the input(s) and output represent in the workplace scenario (e.g., what x means, what y means, and what a change in x implies operationally). Keep explanations in plain English for non-specialist readers.

5) Ensure every graph is presentation-ready: labelled axes, units, appropriate scale choices, legend if needed, and a descriptive title. Make sure a non-specialist could understand what is being compared and why it matters.

6) Use your graphs/functions to compute and clearly show: (a) gradients where relevant, (b) intercepts where relevant, and (c) at least one break-even calculation that identifies a performance threshold (e.g., units required to cover fixed costs, or throughput required to avoid backlog). Show working and report units.

7) Analyse your graphs to identify trends, turning points (where applicable), and operational constraints (e.g., capacity limits, diminishing returns, non-linear effects). Link each point to evidence (a feature on the graph and/or a calculated threshold).

8) Draft a short recommendation note for a team review meeting. It must summarise: what the graphs show, the key threshold(s), the implications for pricing/throughput decisions, and a clear recommended action with assumptions and limitations.

9) Prepare and deliver a 5-minute in-class briefing summarising your recommendation using 1–3 slides or a printed one-page visual summary. You should be prepared to answer 2–3 questions from peers/tutor about your graphs and thresholds.
10) Submit your final files to the LMS by the deadline: a single PDF report pack plus your source file(s) (Excel workbook or Python notebook).
deliverables: A) Graph and calculations pack (PDF) containing: dataset summary, your three required plots (linear, quadratic, exponential) with fitted functions, and clearly presented threshold calculations (gradients, intercepts, break-even).
B) Recommendation note (included in the PDF; typically 600–800 words) written for a team review meeting, referencing the graphs and calculations as evidence.
C) Source file(s): Excel workbook (.xlsx) or Python notebook (.ipynb) used to produce the graphs and calculations (including formulas/code).
D) In-class live 5-minute briefing (not recorded unless an agreed accessibility adjustment is in place). Optional: slides (.pptx) or a one-page printed visual handout.

rubric.merit: Accurately explains inputs/outputs and links them explicitly to operational meaning (e.g., what an increase in input implies in practice); demonstrates sound understanding of how the function form relates to the relationship (e.g., linear rate, curvature/turning behaviour, exponential growth/decay).
rubric.distinction: Provides precise, well-structured interpretations for all three function types, explicitly connecting function behaviour to operational reasoning (e.g., why the relationship is plausibly linear/quadratic/exponential in context); clearly communicates implications for decision-making without relying on specialist jargon.

rubric.criterionName: Plotting operational datasets and fitted functions for non-specialist readers (Excel or Python)

rubric.distinction: Plots are publication-ready for a workplace pack: excellent clarity, consistent design conventions, correct and transparent display of data and fitted functions; scale choices are explicitly justified where they affect interpretation; visuals directly support the operational message without clutter or ambiguity.

rubric.criterionName: Threshold quantification using gradients, intercepts and break-even calculations

brief.studentFacingIntro: You will work independently with a small operational dataset to model typical workplace relationships using linear, quadratic and exponential functions. You will produce clearly labelled graphs (suitable for non-specialists), quantify key thresholds (including break-even), and write a short recommendation note based on what the graphs show. You may use either Excel or Python. Your submission must be reproducible (a marker should be able to follow your steps and obtain the same results).
brief.workplaceContext: You are supporting a team review meeting for a small operations unit that sells a service product. The team needs evidence-based visuals to understand (a) how cost changes with volume, (b) how revenue and profit behave, and (c) how demand is affected by price changes. You have been given a dataset extract and asked to prepare graphs and a short note recommending an operational decision (e.g., a volume target and a pricing point), with clear assumptions and any limitations.
stepByStepInstructions: Download the assessment pack from the LMS: (1) Operational_Data.csv, (2) Template_Report.docx, and either (3a) Excel_Template.xlsx or (3b) Python_Starter.ipynb. Use only these files and standard Excel/Python functionality.
Choose your tool: Excel OR Python. You must use one tool consistently for the charts and calculations you submit (you may use the other for checking, but submit one primary set of workings).

Part A — Interpret functions (MLO 1): In your report, write short, workplace-focused interpretations (2–4 sentences each) for: a linear function, a quadratic function, and an exponential function. For each, state what the input and output represent in an operational setting (use units), and give one example relationship (e.g., cost vs units, time vs distance, demand vs price). Do not use purely abstract explanations.

Part B — Plot dataset(s) and fitted functions (MLO 2): Import Operational_Data.csv. Create at least THREE charts that combine: (i) the operational dataset points and (ii) a fitted function/line/curve. Your three charts must include one linear fit, one quadratic fit, and one exponential fit. Each chart must include: title, labelled axes, units, appropriate scale, legend (if needed), and a short caption explaining what a non-specialist should notice.

For Excel: use scatter plots; add trendlines (linear, polynomial order 2, exponential) where appropriate; display the equation on the chart and record the fitted equation in your report. For Python: use a clear plotting library (e.g., matplotlib) and show the code for fitting (e.g., numpy.polyfit for linear/quadratic; log-transform or curve_fit for exponential).

Part C — Gradients, intercepts, and break-even (MLO 3): Using one of your fitted relationships, calculate and clearly show: (1) the gradient and intercept (for a linear relationship), and interpret both in context with units; (2) at least one break-even or threshold calculation (e.g., where revenue equals cost, or where profit crosses zero). You must show your method (Excel formulas or Python code) and state the final answer with units and sensible rounding.

Part D — Graph analysis and recommendation note (MLO 4): Analyse your graphs to identify trends, turning points, and constraints (e.g., capacity limit, diminishing returns, maximum/minimum point of a quadratic, or practical domain restrictions such as non-negative volume). Then write a short recommendation note intended for a team review meeting. Your note must: (i) reference at least TWO of your charts, (ii) state a recommended action and a justification based on the graph evidence, (iii) include at least one quantified threshold (e.g., break-even volume or critical price point), and (iv) state assumptions/limitations.

Self-check before submission (required): Use the provided Self-Check List (in the template report) and confirm you have met all items. Ensure your charts are readable at 100% zoom and that your workings are reproducible.
deliverables: A short report (PDF) containing: Part A interpretations; Part B chart captions and fitted equations; Part C calculations and interpretations; Part D recommendation note; plus a completed self-check list and an academic integrity declaration.
Your workings file: either an Excel workbook (XLSX) with data, calculations, and charts, OR a Python notebook (IPYNB) with code, outputs, and charts.
A short recorded walkthrough (MP4) explaining where to find your three charts, your threshold calculation, and your final recommendation (screen recording with voice-over is sufficient).

brief.studentFacingIntro: In this assignment you will use a small operational dataset to create clear graphs, fit suitable functions (linear, quadratic and exponential), and use those graphs to calculate and explain practical decision points such as thresholds and break-even. You will then write a short recommendation note suitable for a team review meeting. You may complete the work in Excel or Python, and you may work independently or as part of a pair/small group as long as what you submit is your own work (see Academic Integrity).
brief.workplaceContext: You are supporting an operations team deciding whether to scale a service offer over the next quarter. The team needs a simple, evidence-based view of (1) how input changes affect output (e.g., staffing hours to daily throughput), (2) where performance thresholds sit (e.g., break-even point for a pricing or throughput decision), and (3) what constraints or turning points appear in the data (e.g., diminishing returns or a capacity limit). Your audience is non-specialist stakeholders at a weekly review meeting.
stepByStepInstructions: 1) Choose your data source (one option): (A) Use the dataset provided by your tutor via the LMS (recommended), or (B) use your own workplace dataset only if you have permission to use it and can anonymise it (remove names, IDs, confidential figures). Your dataset must include at least 12 data points and at least two measurable variables with units.

2) Identify three relationships to model and justify the choice of function type: one linear relationship, one quadratic relationship, and one exponential relationship. For each relationship, clearly define the input variable (independent variable) and output variable (dependent variable), including units.

3) Create three separate plots (one per relationship) in Excel or Python: scatter plot of the observed operational dataset plus a fitted function curve/line. Each plot must have a clear title, labelled axes, units, and an appropriate scale for a non-specialist reader. Include a legend if more than one series appears.

4) For each fitted function, write a short interpretation of what the inputs and outputs represent in the workplace relationship. Keep the explanation grounded in the scenario and your variable definitions (e.g., what does a 1-unit increase in input mean operationally).

5) Use your graphs and/or fitted equations to calculate and report (as applicable across your models): (i) gradients (where the model is linear or you are considering a local slope), (ii) intercepts, and (iii) at least one break-even point relevant to pricing or throughput discussions. Show your method clearly in the workbook/notebook and report units, rounding, and any assumptions.

6) Analyse each graph to identify trends, turning points and constraints. For example: increasing/decreasing trends, a maximum/minimum turning point for a quadratic model, or rapid growth/decay patterns in an exponential model. Identify at least one operational constraint (e.g., capacity limit, minimum viable volume, staffing restriction) that is supported by the plotted evidence.

7) Draft a short recommendation note for a team review meeting (non-specialist audience). Your note must reference the graphs and calculations and make a clear recommendation (e.g., proceed/do not proceed, change a threshold, focus on a range of inputs). Include a brief statement of limitations/assumptions.

8) Hybrid collaboration option (choose one route): (A) Live/in-person peer check: swap one draft plot with a peer and record their feedback in 3–5 bullet points; or (B) Asynchronous: upload one draft plot to the LMS discussion board and summarise feedback received; or (C) No-peer alternative: complete the provided self-check checklist and include it as an appendix. This step supports quality but is not separately graded; you must include evidence of completion.

9) (Optional communication extension for hybrid learners) Prepare a 3–5 minute briefing that summarises your recommendation note. You may deliver it live in class/online or submit a recording. This does not replace the written recommendation note.
deliverables: A concise report (PDF) containing: variable definitions with units; three labelled plots with fitted functions; interpretation of inputs/outputs; gradient/intercept/break-even calculations with units and assumptions; brief analysis of trends/turning points/constraints; and a short recommendation note for a team review meeting.

brief.studentFacingIntro: In this assignment you will use Excel to model marginal change (derivatives) and accumulation (integrals) in a realistic workplace setting. You will build a clear, auditable workbook that calculates marginal cost and total resource use from polynomial and exponential functions, and you will justify your results using unit checks, plausibility checks and a structured calculation log. You will also give a short in-class explanation of what your derivative and integral results mean for operations.
brief.workplaceContext:
You work as an analyst supporting a small manufacturing site. The Operations Manager wants a simple Excel tool to answer two recurring questions:
1) If we increase the production rate slightly, how much does cost increase at that point (marginal cost)?
2) Over a shift, how much total energy is used when the energy-use rate changes over time (accumulation)?
The manager also needs the calculations to be transparent for audit: units must be shown, rounding decisions recorded, and results checked for plausibility.
stepByStepInstructions: 1) Set up your Excel workbook structure with three sheets named exactly: (a) Inputs, (b) Calculus, (c) Outputs. Add a short note at the top of each sheet describing its purpose.

2) Inputs (given functions): Enter the following workplace models, including units in nearby cells:
   a) Cost as a function of production rate q (units/hour): C(q) = 0.02q^2 + 5q + 100, where C is in £/hour.
   b) Energy-use rate as a function of time t (hours): E(t) = 20 * EXP(0.05t), where E is in kWh/hour.
   Define the evaluation points: q0 = 120 units/hour; shift length T = 8 hours.

3) Differentiation task (marginal cost):
   a) In the Calculus sheet, compute the analytic derivative dC/dq and implement it as an Excel formula.
   b) Evaluate marginal cost at q0 = 120.
   c) Interpret the result in words in the Outputs sheet: what does your marginal cost number mean operationally and what are its units?

4) Integration task (total resource use):
   a) In the Calculus sheet, compute the analytic integral of E(t) from t = 0 to t = T and implement it as an Excel formula to compute total energy used over the shift.
   b) Report total energy in kWh in the Outputs sheet.
   c) Interpret the result in words: what does the total represent, and what would happen to the total if T increased?

5) Spreadsheet quality and transparency:
   a) Use named cells (or clearly labelled cell references) for q0 and T.
   b) Show units beside every key input and output (e.g., £/hour, units/hour, kWh/hour, kWh).
   c) Use consistent rounding: state your chosen rounding rule (e.g., 2 d.p. for £, 1 d.p. for kWh) and apply it consistently only at the reporting stage (not inside the calculus formulas).

6) Plausibility and dimensional consistency checks (required):
   a) Dimensional check: write the expected units for dC/dq and for the integral of E(t) and confirm your outputs match.
   b) Plausibility check for marginal cost: compute C(q0) and C(q0 + 1) and compare C(q0 + 1) − C(q0) to your marginal cost value at q0 (explain why they are close but not identical).
   c) Plausibility check for energy: compare your total-energy result to a simple estimate using E(0)*T and/or E(T)*T and explain whether your exact total is reasonable.

7) Calculation log (audit trail): Complete a calculation log (template permitted—see Evidence Requirements) that documents: assumptions, definitions of variables, steps for differentiation and integration, units, rounding decisions, limitations, and the results of your plausibility checks.

8) In-class presentation (individual): Deliver a 5-minute in-person presentation to the tutor and peers summarising:
   a) What derivative and integral represent in your scenario (rate of change and accumulation).
   b) Your key results (marginal cost at q0; total energy over T).
   c) One dimensional check and one plausibility check and what they tell you.
   You may use up to 4 slides (or a single printed A4 page) as a visual aid.
deliverables: Excel workbook (.xlsx) containing Inputs, Calculus and Outputs sheets with working formulas (not screenshots).
Calculation Log (PDF) documenting assumptions, units, rounding, limitations, and plausibility/dimensional checks.
Presentation slides/handout file (PDF or PPTX) submitted to the LMS, plus live in-class delivery.

brief.studentFacingIntro:
In this self-study assignment you will model marginal change (derivatives) and accumulation (integrals) in a practical workplace-style scenario using Excel. You will: (1) explain what derivatives and integrals mean in context (rates and totals), (2) compute marginal cost from a cost function and total energy use from a power-demand function, and (3) check whether your outputs are plausible and dimensionally consistent, keeping an audit-ready calculation log.

You must complete the work independently and submit digital evidence. Your Excel file must be reproducible: formulas must be visible and the steps must be clear to a reviewer.
brief.workplaceContext:
You work as an analyst for a small manufacturing site preparing an internal audit pack. Management needs a transparent method to (a) estimate marginal cost at different production volumes and (b) estimate total energy used during a shift when power demand increases as equipment warms up.

The audit team requires: clear units, clear assumptions, consistent rounding, and basic plausibility checks (e.g., costs and energy totals should have reasonable magnitudes and correct units).
stepByStepInstructions: 1) Set up your Excel workbook (XLSX): Create three sheets named (i) Inputs, (ii) Calculations, (iii) Summary. On the Inputs sheet, add a table of units you will use (e.g., £, units, hour, kW, kWh) and define your rounding rule (e.g., money to 2 dp, energy to 1 dp).

2) Task A (Polynomial – marginal cost): Use the total cost function C(q) = 0.004q^3 + 0.60q^2 + 18q + 5000 where q is the weekly output in units and C(q) is in £ per week. (a) Differentiate C(q) to obtain marginal cost MC(q) = dC/dq in £ per unit. (b) In Excel, create a column of q values (at least 10 values spanning 0 to 500 units). (c) Compute C(q) and MC(q) for each q using Excel formulas (not typed values).

3) Self-check A (must be included in your workbook): At q = 100, your formulas should give C(100) = 135000 and MC(100) = 258. (If you do not get these values, fix your differentiation and/or Excel formulas before proceeding.)

4) Task B (Exponential – total resource use): During an 8-hour shift, power demand is modelled by P(t) = 12 + 4·EXP(0.30t) where t is hours since shift start (0 ≤ t ≤ 8) and P(t) is in kW. (a) Integrate P(t) to obtain an expression for total energy use E(0→T) in kWh for any T in hours. Use a definite integral from 0 to T. (b) Implement E(0→T) in Excel and compute total energy for T = 8.
5) Self-check B (must be included in your workbook): At T = 0, E(0→0) must equal 0 kWh. At T = 1, your model should give approximately E(0→1) ≈ 18.54 kWh (allow ±0.05 due to rounding).

6) Interpretation (rate of change and accumulation): In the Summary sheet, write brief notes (bullet points are acceptable) explaining: (a) what MC(q) means operationally (rate of cost increase per extra unit), and (b) what E(0→T) means operationally (accumulated energy use over time). Your explanation must reference the workplace context (cost and energy use).

7) Plausibility and dimensional consistency checks: In your calculation log (PDF), include: (a) unit checks for C(q), MC(q), P(t), and E(0→T), (b) at least two plausibility checks (examples: MC(q) should be positive over the chosen q range if costs increase with output; energy over 8 hours should be greater than 8×12 = 96 kWh because the exponential term adds extra demand), and (c) a short note on limitations (e.g., model form, range validity, assumptions like continuous output).

8) Calculation log: Create a calculation log that documents your steps as if for audit. It must include: assumptions, units, rounding rules, key formulas used, checks performed, and any issues encountered and resolved. Ensure it is understandable without you present.

9) Recorded walkthrough (asynchronous): Record a short screen-and-voice walkthrough (MP4) showing your workbook tabs and explaining your main results and checks. If you cannot submit audio/video, submit the written alternative described in the evidence requirements.

10) Finalise and export: Ensure formulas are visible (use Excel’s ‘Show Formulas’ view for at least one screenshot included in the PDF log). Save the workbook as XLSX and export the calculation log as PDF. Upload all required files to the LMS.
deliverables: Completed Excel workbook (XLSX) with Inputs, Calculations, Summary sheets, containing formula-based computations for C(q), MC(q), P(t), and E(0→T), plus the required self-checks.
Calculation log (PDF) documenting assumptions, units, rounding, differentiation/integration steps, plausibility checks, and limitations.

rubric.criterionName: Conceptual explanation: differentiation and integration as rate of change and accumulation (workplace meaning)
rubric.fail: Explanation is missing or largely incorrect; does not link derivatives/integrals to workplace meanings (marginal cost, energy use) or confuses rate with total; minimal or no use of units and context.
rubric.pass: Provides a correct explanation of derivative as rate of change and integral as accumulation, linked to marginal cost and total energy use; uses workplace terms and includes at least one correct unit statement (e.g., £/unit, kWh).
rubric.merit: Clear, accurate explanation that connects mathematical objects (dC/dq and ∫P(t)dt) to operational decisions; distinguishes clearly between instantaneous rate and accumulated total; uses correct units consistently throughout the explanation.
rubric.distinction: Concise, audit-ready explanation with strong workplace interpretation: explicitly states what changes when q or t increases, and what the derivative/integral outputs represent; highlights at least one practical implication (e.g., how marginal cost trend affects scaling decisions) without introducing new methods or topics.

rubric.criterionName: Technical accuracy in Excel: differentiation and integration of polynomial and exponential functions to compute outputs
rubric.fail: Derivative and/or integral set-up is incorrect; Excel implementation contains hard-coded values in place of formulas or yields incorrect self-check values; outputs for marginal cost and/or total energy are missing or not reproducible.
rubric.pass: Correctly differentiates the polynomial cost function and integrates the exponential power function; Excel formulas compute MC(q) and E(0→T) correctly and reproduce the stated self-check values (within tolerance); outputs are presented for the specified ranges/inputs.
rubric.merit: As pass, plus workbook is well-structured: clear input cells, relative/absolute references used appropriately, outputs clearly tabulated; includes a simple chart or table in Summary that helps interpret how MC(q) changes with q and/or how energy accumulates with T (no additional topics required).
rubric.distinction: As merit, plus implementation is robust and audit-friendly: named ranges or clearly labelled input cells, consistent rounding strategy applied, and formulas are easy to trace; demonstrates correct handling of definite integrals (baseline at 0) and communicates final numeric results unambiguously.

rubric.criterionName: Analysis quality: plausibility, dimensional consistency, and calculation log (assumptions, rounding, limitations)
rubric.fail: Calculation log is missing or not usable; units are absent or incorrect; no meaningful plausibility checks; assumptions/rounding/limitations are not stated or are contradictory.
rubric.pass: Calculation log documents assumptions, units, rounding rules, and key steps; includes correct unit reasoning for derivative and integral outputs (e.g., £/unit and kWh) and at least two basic plausibility checks; limitations are stated at a basic level.
rubric.merit: As pass, plus checks are specific and justified (e.g., compares energy to a baseline, comments on magnitude and sign of MC across the range); rounding choices are applied consistently and explained; limitations are linked to how results should be used (range validity, model simplifications).
rubric.distinction: As merit, plus analysis is audit-standard: dimensional consistency is explicitly shown for each main quantity; plausibility checks include at least one cross-check using an alternative viewpoint consistent with the same content (e.g., comparing energy to average power × time, or checking C(q) increases with q and MC aligns with the slope); log is clear, structured, and reproducible.

rubric.criterionName: Communication and presentation of evidence (clarity, organisation, reproducibility)
rubric.fail: Files are incomplete, poorly labelled, or difficult to follow; key results are not clearly identified; recording/written alternative is missing; reviewer cannot readily locate formulas, assumptions, or final answers.
rubric.pass: All required files are submitted and readable; workbook tabs and outputs are labelled; final answers (e.g., MC at selected q, total energy at 8 hours) are clearly stated; recording/written alternative explains what was done at a basic level.

assessedOutcomes.mloStatement: Explain differentiation and integration as rate of change and accumulation using workplace examples such as throughput, cost and energy use.

brief.studentFacingIntro: This assignment assesses your ability to use calculus to interpret marginal change (derivatives) and accumulation (integrals) in a realistic workplace-style scenario. You will build an Excel worksheet that calculates marginal cost and total resource use from given polynomial and exponential models, and you will justify your results with checks for plausibility and dimensional consistency. You must document your assumptions, rounding and limitations in a clear calculation log suitable for audit.
brief.workplaceContext:
You work as an operations analyst supporting a small manufacturing site. The site manager wants a simple Excel tool to (1) estimate marginal cost at different production volumes and (2) estimate total energy consumption over a production range. The manager will use your outputs in a weekly planning meeting, so your worksheet must be transparent, checked, and accompanied by a short briefing.

Use the following models (treat them as calibrated planning models for this task):

A) Total weekly cost as a function of weekly output q (units/week):
C(q) = 12000 + 15q + 0.02q^2 + 0.000015q^3  (C in £)

B) Electricity use per unit as a function of weekly output q (units/week):
e(q) = 0.6 + 0.00004q + 0.18·exp(0.0002q)  (e in kWh/unit)

Your manager needs:
1) Marginal cost MC(q) at q = 6000, 9000 and 12000 units/week.
2) Total electricity use between q = 6000 and q = 12000 units/week, using the accumulation of e(q) over output.

You must also explain, in workplace terms, what the derivative and integral mean for throughput/cost/energy decisions.
stepByStepInstructions: Set up your Excel workbook with clearly labelled input cells (including units) and separate sections/tabs for: Inputs, Differentiation (marginal cost), Integration (total energy), Checks, and Calculation Log.
Enter the cost model C(q) exactly as given. In Excel, implement it using cell references (not hard-coded numbers inside formulas wherever possible). Clearly label q (units/week) and C(q) (£/week).
Differentiate the cost model analytically to obtain MC(q) = dC/dq. Implement MC(q) in Excel and compute MC at q = 6000, 9000 and 12000. Present results with units (£/unit).
Enter the energy-per-unit model e(q) exactly as given, using Excel’s EXP() function. Clearly label e(q) (kWh/unit).

Integrate e(q) with respect to q to compute total electricity use between q = 6000 and q = 12000:
Total kWh = ∫(from 6000 to 12000) e(q) dq.
Implement the definite integral in Excel by first creating an antiderivative E(q) and then calculating E(12000) − E(6000). Present results with units (kWh).

Add at least two independent checks for your derivative and integral outputs, such as:
(a) A reasonableness check using magnitudes (e.g., compare total kWh against a simple average e(q) × (12000−6000)).
(b) A dimensional consistency check that explicitly states the units before and after differentiation/integration.
(c) A sensitivity check (e.g., how much MC changes between 6000 and 12000; whether e(q) increases as expected).

Maintain a calculation log (within the workbook or as a separate document) that records: assumptions, units, rounding approach, formula locations (cell references), limitations of the model, and any issues encountered and resolved.

Prepare a short briefing for the manager explaining differentiation as marginal change and integration as accumulation, using this case (throughput, cost, energy). You may deliver this as either:
(a) a live 5–7 minute briefing in class/online session, or
(b) a 5–7 minute recorded video/screen recording, or
(c) an accessibility alternative: a structured written briefing note (maximum 650 words) covering the same points.

Hybrid collaboration requirement (formative, not co-authored): obtain one piece of feedback on your draft workbook from a peer (in-person or via the discussion board). If you cannot access a peer, complete the self-check version instead. Include evidence of either peer feedback or self-check in your submission.
deliverables: Excel workbook containing: models, derivative and integral calculations, results table, and built-in checks (with units and clear labels).
Calculation log (can be a workbook tab or separate PDF) documenting assumptions, rounding, limitations, dimensional checks and plausibility checks, with cell references to key formulas.
Short written report (briefing report) summarising outputs and interpretation for a non-specialist manager, including what the derivative and integral represent in this scenario.
Live or recorded briefing (or approved written alternative) explaining your method and checks.
Evidence of peer feedback or self-check (e.g., screenshot of discussion post, emailed comments, or completed self-check checklist).

brief.studentFacingIntro: In this assignment you will build and defend a constrained optimisation model using Excel Solver. You will: (1) structure a clear and auditable spreadsheet model (decision variables, objective, constraints), (2) run Solver and interpret key outputs including sensitivity information, and (3) test alternative scenarios and justify a recommended option using transparent calculation logs, a clear constraints rationale, and concise risk notes. This is an individual practical task completed through in-person lab/workshop sessions with a short live presentation at the end.
brief.workplaceContext:
You work as an operations analyst for a small manufacturer producing two product lines: Product A and Product B. Each unit requires time on two shared resources (Assembly and Finishing) and uses a constrained raw material. Demand limits mean there is an upper bound on units that can be sold. Management wants a weekly production plan that maximises contribution (profit) while respecting operational constraints and providing an auditable record of assumptions. You must also advise how robust the chosen plan is if capacity or demand changes, and identify bottlenecks and trade-offs using Solver sensitivity information.

Base data (use exactly as provided below for your baseline model):
- Decision variables: xA = units of Product A; xB = units of Product B
- Contribution per unit: A = £45; B = £60
- Assembly hours per unit: A = 1.5; B = 2.0; Weekly Assembly capacity = 180 hours
- Finishing hours per unit: A = 1.0; B = 1.5; Weekly Finishing capacity = 120 hours
- Material (kg) per unit: A = 0.8; B = 1.2; Weekly Material availability = 120 kg
- Demand limits: xA ≤ 110; xB ≤ 90
- Non-negativity: xA ≥ 0; xB ≥ 0

Scenarios to evaluate (use these to create and compare alternative optimisation runs):
Scenario 1 (Overtime option): Assembly capacity increases by 15% (cost already accounted for, so keep the same contributions).
Scenario 2 (Supplier delay): Material availability decreases to 95 kg.
Scenario 3 (Demand shift): Demand limits change to xA ≤ 80 and xB ≤ 120.
stepByStepInstructions: 1. Create a new Excel workbook named using the required convention (see Deliverables). Add separate worksheets titled: Inputs, Model, Solver_Setup, Results, Sensitivity, Scenarios, and Audit_Log.
2. In Inputs, enter the baseline data exactly as given (contributions, resource use per unit, capacities, demand limits). Use clearly labelled cells and consistent units.

3. In Model, create cells for the decision variables xA and xB. Create formulas for: (a) total contribution (objective), (b) total Assembly hours used, (c) total Finishing hours used, (d) total Material used, and (e) checks for demand limits and non-negativity. Ensure formulas reference Inputs cells (no hard-coded numbers inside formulas).

4. In Solver_Setup, document (in your own words) the Solver configuration you will use: objective cell, variable cells, constraints list, and Solver method (e.g., Simplex LP if linear). Include a screenshot of the Solver Parameters window pasted into this sheet after your baseline solve.
5. Run Solver for the baseline case to maximise total contribution. Save the final solution values for xA and xB, and the objective value. Copy results into Results in a tidy table.

6. Generate and capture sensitivity output (where available). Paste the Sensitivity Report output into the Sensitivity sheet (or copy key tables). If sensitivity reporting is not available for your chosen method/settings, explain why and provide equivalent marginal interpretation using Solver reports available to you (e.g., constraints report) and clear, quantitative reasoning.

7. In Sensitivity, interpret: (a) which constraint(s) are binding at the optimum, (b) the bottleneck resource(s), (c) marginal values/shadow prices (where provided) in practical terms, and (d) at least two trade-offs (e.g., what must be reduced to increase a product, which resource becomes limiting). Use numbers from your output.

8. Build three scenario variants (Scenario 1–3) by changing only the relevant input(s) in Inputs. For each scenario: re-run Solver, record the new optimal xA, xB, objective value, and which constraints bind. Keep a clear record of each run in Scenarios and Audit_Log (date/time, what changed, and key outputs).

9. Evaluate the baseline and three scenarios. Choose one option to recommend to management (this may be the baseline or a scenario). Justify your choice using: quantitative comparisons, your constraints rationale (why constraints are appropriate and realistic), and risk notes (what could break the plan, what uncertainty matters, and what checks you would run next).

10. Prepare a short in-class presentation (5 minutes + 2 minutes Q&A) summarising your model, the baseline results, sensitivity insights, scenario comparison, and final recommendation. Use 5–8 slides. Be ready to point to specific cells/tables in your workbook during Q&A.
11. Submit the required files via the LMS by the deadline. Bring your workbook accessible on your device for the live presentation session.
deliverables: Deliverable 1: Excel workbook (.xlsx) containing all required worksheets, formulas, Solver setup documentation, pasted Solver outputs/reports, scenarios, and a complete Audit_Log.

Deliverable 2: Written report (PDF) presenting the model overview, results, sensitivity interpretation, scenario evaluation, final recommendation, constraints rationale, and risk notes (including references to specific workbook locations).
Deliverable 3: Live in-class presentation (5 minutes + 2 minutes Q&A) supported by submitted slides (PPTX or PDF).

Risk notes are specific and include at least one mitigation/check (e.g., monitoring material availability, validating demand limits).
rubric.distinction: Evaluation demonstrates strong judgement and transparency. Documentation is presentation-ready and reproducible.

You will then interpret Solver outputs (including sensitivity information) to explain bottlenecks, marginal values and operational trade-offs. Finally, you will test alternative scenarios and justify a recommended option using clear calculation logs, stated constraint rationale and concise risk notes. This task is designed for hybrid study: you can work and submit digitally or with a physical printout (plus file link), and you can present live or via a short recording.
brief.workplaceContext: You work as an operations analyst for a small manufacturer producing three products (A, B, and C). Each product requires limited resources: machine time, skilled labour hours, and a key raw material. There are also contractual minimums for at least one product, maximum demand limits for others, and a waste/stock constraint (e.g., limited storage or scrap disposal capacity). Management wants a plan for next month that either (a) maximises profit, or (b) minimises waste cost while meeting demand and operational constraints. They also want to understand what is limiting production, how much extra capacity is worth (marginal value), and how sensitive the plan is if conditions change.
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1: Download the provided dataset/template (or create your own structured sheet if a template is not provided). Set up a clearly labelled input section (profits/costs, resource usage rates, available capacities, minimum/maximum requirements). Ensure units are stated (e.g., hours, kg, £ per unit) and kept consistent.

Step 2: Define your decision variables (e.g., quantities of products A, B, C to produce). Place them in a dedicated decision variable range with clear labels and (if relevant) non-negativity and/or integer restrictions stated.

Step 3: Build the objective function cell: either total profit to maximise or total waste cost to minimise. Show the formula using transparent spreadsheet logic (e.g., SUMPRODUCT) and label it clearly as the objective.

Step 4: Build constraint calculations in the sheet (left-hand side and right-hand side). For each constraint, show how resource consumption is calculated from decision variables, and compare against available capacity or requirement (e.g., machine hours used ≤ machine hours available). Include at least one minimum requirement and one maximum limit constraint (demand/capacity), plus non-negativity constraints.

Step 5: Configure Solver: set the objective cell, choose Max/Min as appropriate, set decision variable cells, and add constraints. Select an appropriate solving method (e.g., Simplex LP for linear models). Record key Solver settings (e.g., method, options) in a short log within the workbook.

Step 6: Run Solver and capture the solution. Save the Solver Answer Report and (where applicable) the Sensitivity Report. Ensure the workbook includes the final solution values and the objective value.

Step 7: Analyse results (Sensitivity/Shadow Prices/Reduced Costs where applicable): identify which constraints are binding (bottlenecks), interpret at least two marginal values (e.g., shadow prices) in operational terms, and describe at least two trade-offs (what increases/decreases when a constraint is relaxed/tightened).

Step 8: Create and evaluate two alternative scenarios. Examples include: (i) increase one resource capacity by a stated amount; (ii) change unit profit/cost for one product; (iii) impose a tighter demand cap; (iv) introduce a new minimum requirement. For each scenario, re-run Solver, summarise the new optimum, and compare to the base case (objective value, decision variables, binding constraints).

Step 9: Decide on your recommended option (base case or one scenario). Justify your choice with: (a) constraint rationale (why those constraints are appropriate and how they reflect the workplace context), (b) a transparent calculation log (what you changed and where), and (c) risk notes (key uncertainties, operational risks, and limitations of the model/sensitivity interpretation).

Step 10 (collaboration element, non-assessed but required participation): complete one peer review activity. Option A (live): bring a printed one-page model summary to class and exchange feedback with a peer using the peer checklist. Option B (asynchronous): upload your one-page model summary to the LMS discussion board and provide structured feedback to one peer using the same checklist. Include a short note in your report confirming which option you completed and one improvement you made as a result.
deliverables: Deliverable 1: Excel workbook containing the optimisation model (inputs, decision variables, objective, constraints), Solver configuration details, and results for base case and two scenarios.

Deliverable 2: PDF report summarising the model, results interpretation (including sensitivity/marginal values), scenario comparison, recommendation, constraint rationale, calculation log, and risk notes.
Deliverable 3: Short presentation (live or recorded) summarising the recommendation and key evidence (objective, bottlenecks, marginal values, scenarios).
Deliverable 4: Peer review completion note (embedded in the report appendix or workbook notes), stating the mode (live/asynchronous) and one implemented improvement.

rubric.criterionName: Solver model set-up: decision variables, objective, constraints, and configuration
rubric.fail: Decision variables, objective and/or constraints are missing or incorrectly defined; formulas do not correspond to the stated problem; Solver is not correctly configured (wrong objective, wrong variable range, missing constraints), or the model cannot be solved reproducibly.
rubric.pass: Decision variables, objective and constraints are defined and solvable; spreadsheet formulas correctly compute objective and constraint LHS/RHS; Solver configuration is appropriate and produces a feasible optimum; labels and units are mostly clear.
rubric.merit: Model is well-structured and audit-friendly: clear separation of inputs/variables/outputs; constraints are correctly implemented and comprehensively listed; Solver method choice is appropriate and justified briefly; configuration details are logged so the run is reproducible.
rubric.distinction: Model is exemplary and robust: clean, professional layout; consistent units; constraints are complete and clearly tied to the scenario; Solver settings and assumptions are documented for audit; built-in checks (e.g., constraint slack indicators, feasibility checks) support reliability without obscuring the core model.

rubric.criterionName: Results and sensitivity analysis: marginal values, bottlenecks, and trade-offs
rubric.fail: Results are reported without analysis; sensitivity outputs are missing or misinterpreted; binding constraints/bottlenecks are not identified correctly; marginal values are stated without operational meaning or are incorrect.
rubric.pass: Correctly identifies the optimum and at least one binding constraint; provides a basic interpretation of sensitivity outputs (e.g., at least one shadow price or reduced cost) with a plausible operational meaning; describes at least one trade-off based on the results.
rubric.merit: Provides clear interpretation of multiple sensitivity outputs (e.g., at least two marginal values) and links them to operational decisions (e.g., value of extra capacity, product mix implications); correctly identifies bottlenecks and explains trade-offs using the model evidence (binding/slack constraints, changes in objective).
rubric.distinction: Analysis is precise and decision-oriented: interprets marginal values and bottlenecks with correct units and scope (e.g., within allowable ranges where relevant); articulates nuanced trade-offs and limitations of sensitivity interpretation; validates conclusions with cross-checks from the worksheet calculations and constraint status.

rubric.criterionName: Scenario evaluation and justified recommendation with constraints rationale and risk notes
rubric.fail: Fewer than two scenarios are evaluated, or scenarios are not implemented correctly; recommendation is unsupported or contradictory; constraint rationale and risk notes are absent or not relevant; calculation changes are not traceable.
rubric.pass: Two scenarios are implemented and compared to the base case; a recommendation is stated and supported by basic comparison (objective value and/or feasible plan); includes some constraint rationale and at least one relevant risk/limitation; calculation changes are partially logged.
rubric.merit: Two scenarios are well-designed, implemented correctly, and compared using clear metrics (decision variables, objective, binding constraints); recommendation is justified with transparent reasoning; constraints rationale is clear and plausible; risk notes cover multiple uncertainties/limitations and operational implications; calculation log is clear enough to audit.
rubric.distinction: Scenario evaluation is thorough and defensible: scenarios are realistic, clearly parameterised, and comparison is systematic; recommendation is strongly justified, including operational feasibility considerations and sensitivity-informed reasoning; constraint rationale is explicit and well-evidenced; risk notes are structured (assumptions, uncertainties, mitigations) and show strong model validation awareness; calculation log is complete and reproducible.

rubric.criterionName: Communication, audit trail, and hybrid professionalism (reporting, presentation, and peer review reflection)
rubric.fail: Submission is unclear, disorganised, or incomplete; files are not readable or key outputs are missing; report does not communicate the model and findings; no evidence of peer review participation.
rubric.pass: Report and workbook are understandable and include the required sections; presentation (live or recorded) summarises the recommendation and key results; peer review participation is confirmed with one improvement noted; referencing of any external sources/tools is acceptable.
rubric.merit: Communication is clear and concise: tables/figures are labelled; assumptions, units, and results are easy to follow; presentation is well-structured and aligned to evidence; peer review reflection is specific and shows a meaningful improvement; submission is professionally packaged for hybrid viewing (e.g., readable fonts, accessible layout).
rubric.distinction: Communication is exceptionally clear and decision-ready: executive-style summary plus technical appendix; well-designed visuals/tables support interpretation; presentation is confident, within time, and directly addresses bottlenecks/marginal values/scenarios; peer review reflection demonstrates substantive refinement; artefacts are highly accessible and audit-ready.

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Excel workbook with Solver model, base case, two scenarios, and calculation/log notes
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include: labelled decision variables, objective formula, constraint calculations, Solver settings log (method, objective, variable cells, constraints list), and saved Solver reports (Answer Report and Sensitivity Report where applicable). Use clear sheet names (e.g., Inputs, Model, Results, Scenarios).

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Written report (model summary, interpretation, scenario comparison, recommendation, constraints rationale, calculation log, risk notes, peer review note)
evidenceRequirements.wordCountOrDuration: 1500–2000 words (excluding tables, figure captions, and appendices)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Include: (1) brief context and objective; (2) model structure; (3) base case results; (4) sensitivity interpretation (marginal values, bottlenecks, trade-offs); (5) two scenario summaries and comparison; (6) recommendation; (7) constraints rationale; (8) calculation log (what changed, where, and why); (9) risk notes (assumptions, uncertainties, limitations).

evidenceRequirements.fileType: MP4 (recorded) OR live presentation (in class or online) with slides (PPTX/PDF) uploaded
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Live option: present during scheduled session (in-person or online). Recorded option: upload MP4 and slides to LMS. Slides should show objective value, key constraints/bottlenecks, at least one marginal value interpretation, and scenario comparison headline results.

hybrid.academicIntegrity: You must submit work that is your own. You may discuss the case context and general Excel/Solver techniques with peers, and you may participate in the peer review activity, but you must not share completed spreadsheets, Solver outputs, or scenario solutions for copying. If you use any external resources (textbooks, websites, tutorials) you must cite them in your report. If you use generative AI tools, this is permitted only for improving clarity of writing and formatting; you must not use AI to generate the model structure, formulas, Solver configuration, results, or interpretation. You must keep an audit trail (calculation log) so your work can be checked. Include a declaration of authenticity in your report: 'I confirm that this submission is my own work and that all sources and permitted support have been acknowledged.'
hybrid.accessibilityOptions: Reasonable adjustments are available. You may request: alternative submission formats (e.g., accessible Word instead of PDF), additional time where supported by evidence, captions/transcripts for recorded presentations, and permission to submit a narrated slide deck instead of video. If you have limited access to Excel, contact the module team early to arrange access via institutional licensing or an on-campus workstation. Adjustments will not lower academic standards: you must still demonstrate the same optimisation model, analysis of Solver outputs, and scenario evaluation evidence mapped to the assessed learning outcomes.
