brief.studentFacingIntro: You are working as a quality analyst supporting routine reporting and improvement decisions. You have been given a dataset of quality measurements collected before and after a process change. Your task is to clean the data, produce a robust summary for routine reporting, test whether the change is associated with a meaningful difference, and communicate the results clearly to non-specialist stakeholders using charts or a simple dashboard. You may complete the analysis using either Excel or Python, but your work must be reproducible and clearly explained.
brief.workplaceContext: A site manager has introduced a process change to reduce defects and stabilise a critical-to-quality (CTQ) measurement. Weekly samples are taken from the line (or service process) and recorded with timestamps, product/service type, shift/team, and the CTQ metric (e.g., fill weight, response time, thickness, defect count per batch). Stakeholders need a one-page view that shows typical performance, variation, and whether the change has led to a statistically supported and practically meaningful improvement. The manager will use your report in a team review meeting.
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1: Choose your tool (Excel or Python) and set up a clearly named project folder with: (a) raw data file (read-only), (b) working file(s), and (c) outputs (figures/dashboard/report).

Step 2: Import the dataset provided by your tutor (or an approved workplace dataset). Create a short data dictionary in your report: each variable name, description, units, and allowable values (e.g., shift codes).

Step 3: Clean the data and document what you did. Minimum cleaning requirements: (a) handle missing values (state rule used), (b) check data types (dates as dates, numbers as numbers), (c) identify and treat obvious data entry errors (e.g., negative values where impossible), and (d) remove or flag duplicates if present (state criteria).

Step 4: Produce routine summary measures for the CTQ metric for the overall dataset and split by period (pre-change vs post-change). Include measures of centre and spread appropriate to the data (e.g., mean/median; standard deviation/IQR).

Step 5: Create an outlier flag and explain your method (e.g., IQR rule, z-score threshold, or a clearly justified alternative). Report how many points were flagged in each period and how you treated them in subsequent analysis (retain with flags, sensitivity check with/without, etc.).
Step 6: Build at least one table suitable for routine quality reporting that a non-specialist could read (clear labels, units, rounding, and brief notes).

Step 7: Construct confidence intervals relevant to the question (e.g., CI for mean CTQ pre and post; CI for mean difference; CI for proportion defective if applicable). State assumptions used (e.g., independence, approximate normality, sample size considerations) and any sampling limits (e.g., convenience samples, shift imbalance).

Step 8: Run one simple hypothesis test for process change aligned to your data (e.g., two-sample t-test with equal/unequal variance justification, paired t-test if matched, Mann–Whitney if justified, or a test for proportions). Clearly state: null and alternative hypotheses, chosen significance level, test statistic/p-value, and decision.

Step 9: Explain practical significance alongside statistical significance. Include an effect size or an operationally meaningful comparison (e.g., change relative to tolerance, target, customer limit, or cost impact proxy).

Step 10: Create stakeholder-friendly charts or a simple dashboard (one page/single screen view). Minimum visual requirements: (a) a comparison of pre vs post, (b) a view of variation (e.g., box plot, control-style run chart with limits if appropriate, histogram), and (c) clear annotations/labels and units. Avoid clutter; ensure accessibility (readable fonts, colour-blind-safe palette).
Step 11: Write concise narrative commentary (for non-specialists) that explains what was found, what it means, and what should be checked next. Keep it evidence-based and aligned to your outputs.

Step 12 (In-person): Deliver a short in-class presentation using your dashboard/figures, focusing on: the key metric, whether the change improved performance, confidence/uncertainty, assumptions/limits, and recommended next steps. Be prepared to answer questions.
deliverables: A cleaned and reproducible analysis file: either (a) one Excel workbook with clearly named tabs and formulae, or (b) one Python notebook (.ipynb) that runs end-to-end without missing steps.

A short Quality Reporting Brief (PDF) containing: data dictionary, cleaning summary, descriptive statistics, outlier approach, confidence interval(s), hypothesis test results, assumptions and sampling limits, and practical significance.
A one-page dashboard or set of stakeholder charts (embedded in the PDF and also provided as a separate page/tab/image where relevant).
An in-class presentation (slides optional) delivering the key findings and answering questions.

rubric.criterionName: Data cleaning, summarisation and outlier flags for routine reporting
rubric.fail: Data are not reliably cleaned (e.g., missing values/errors not addressed or not described). Summary measures are missing or inappropriate (e.g., no clear measures of centre and spread). Outlier flags are absent or unjustified. Outputs are not suitable for routine reporting (unclear labels/units, inconsistent rounding).
rubric.pass: Data cleaning steps are completed and described (missing values and basic errors handled with stated rules). Routine summaries include appropriate measures of centre and spread for overall and pre/post periods. An outlier flag method is applied and briefly justified, with counts reported. Tables/outputs have clear labels, units, and consistent rounding.
rubric.merit: Cleaning is systematic and well documented (clear rationale for decisions; duplicates/type issues addressed where relevant). Summaries are accurate and include sensible breakdowns (e.g., by shift/product where relevant) without overcomplication. Outlier approach includes a brief sensitivity check (e.g., flagged vs unflagged comparison) or clear justification for retention/removal. Reporting tables are well formatted and immediately usable by stakeholders.
rubric.distinction: Cleaning and summarisation are robust, auditable, and reproducible (clear separation of raw vs processed data; transparent steps). Summary measures are well chosen and interpreted (e.g., median/IQR when skewed) with clear implications for routine reporting. Outlier flagging is methodologically sound and communicated clearly, with a thoughtful sensitivity/impact discussion on key metrics. Outputs demonstrate professional-quality reporting conventions (consistent naming, units, rounding, and notes).

rubric.criterionName: Confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for process changes (assumptions, sampling limits, practical significance)
rubric.fail: Confidence intervals and/or tests are missing, incorrect, or not aligned to the question/data. Hypotheses and conclusions are unclear or wrong. Assumptions, sampling limits, and practical significance are not stated or are inaccurate.
rubric.pass: At least one relevant confidence interval and one simple hypothesis test are carried out correctly and aligned to pre vs post comparison. Hypotheses and conclusions are stated clearly. Key assumptions and sampling limits are identified at a basic level. Practical significance is addressed with a clear statement (even if brief).
rubric.merit: Confidence intervals and tests are correct, well chosen, and interpreted accurately in context. Assumptions are explicitly checked or reasonably justified (e.g., sample size considerations; distributional notes). Sampling limits are clearly described with implications for decision-making. Practical significance is supported by an effect size or operational comparison (e.g., against tolerance/target) and linked to the recommendation.
rubric.distinction: Inference is rigorous and well communicated: confidence intervals and tests are correctly specified with clear rationale for the chosen method (including variance/paired/alternative choices where applicable). Assumptions and sampling limits are critically evaluated (what could bias results, what data would strengthen the conclusion). Practical significance is convincingly argued with quantified impact, and conclusions balance statistical evidence with operational constraints.

rubric.criterionName: Stakeholder-friendly charts/dashboard and narrative commentary
rubric.fail: Charts/dashboard are unclear or misleading (missing units/labels; inappropriate chart types; cluttered visuals). Narrative commentary is absent, overly technical, or unsupported by the outputs. Stakeholders cannot readily understand what changed or what to do next.
rubric.pass: Charts/dashboard clearly show pre vs post and variation with appropriate chart types. Labels, units, titles, and basic annotations are present and readable. Narrative commentary explains the main findings in plain English and links to the visuals, with a clear overall message.
rubric.merit: Visuals are well designed for stakeholder decision-making (clean layout, consistent scales, meaningful annotations such as targets/limits). Commentary is concise and well structured (what we measured, what changed, how confident we are, what it means). Limitations and next steps are stated clearly and proportionately for a non-specialist audience.
rubric.distinction: Dashboard/visuals are polished and highly effective: strong visual hierarchy, minimal cognitive load, accessibility-aware formatting, and precise labelling/units. Commentary is executive-ready: accurate, concise, and persuasive without overclaiming, integrating uncertainty, assumptions/limits, and practical significance into a clear recommendation suitable for a team review meeting.

evidenceRequirements.wordCountOrDuration: 1200–1500 words (excluding tables/figures and references, if used)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include: data dictionary; cleaning summary; descriptive stats; outlier method and counts; confidence interval(s); hypothesis test (H0/H1, alpha, result, interpretation); assumptions and sampling limits; practical significance; brief recommendation. Figures/tables must be numbered and titled with units.

Excel: include clearly named tabs (e.g., Raw_Data (read-only copy), Cleaned_Data, Summary, Inference, Dashboard) and show key formulae (no unexplained hard-coded values). Python: notebook must run top-to-bottom; include package imports and any random seed; reference the provided dataset file path clearly. Do not submit only screenshots.

evidenceRequirements.fileType: PDF (embedded in report) plus optional PNG/PDF export or Excel dashboard tab
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include clear labels, units, and at least: (a) pre vs post comparison, (b) variation view. Ensure readable font sizes for printed review.

evidenceRequirements.wordCountOrDuration: 6 minutes presentation + up to 4 minutes Q&A
evidenceRequirements.fileType: Live in person (slides optional: PPTX or PDF if used)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Use your dashboard/figures to explain: what changed, how confident we are, assumptions/limits, and practical significance. Your tutor may ask you to show specific parts of your workbook/notebook during Q&A to confirm understanding and authorship.

in_person.academicIntegrity: You must submit work that is your own. You may discuss the task in class and take part in peer feedback on draft charts/tables, but you must not share files containing calculations/code, copy another learner’s outputs, or divide the work between learners. If you use workplace data, you must have permission and remove personal/confidential identifiers. You may use Excel help, official documentation, and tutor-provided materials. If you use AI tools for language polishing or to explain functions/concepts, you must (a) ensure all analysis choices and calculations are your own, (b) verify correctness, and (c) include a short disclosure in an appendix stating what tool was used and for what purpose. Fabrication (invented data/results), falsification (manipulating results without explanation), and plagiarism (including copying code/analysis without attribution) are prohibited. By submitting, you confirm an authenticity declaration: the submission is your own work and all sources/tools are acknowledged.
in_person.accessibilityOptions: Reasonable adjustments are available without lowering academic standards. Examples include: additional time or a smaller-room setting for the in-class presentation; permission to present seated; use of speaker notes; alternative presentation format (e.g., 1:1 viva-style explanation to the tutor covering the same content and Q&A expectations); accessible colour palettes and larger fonts in dashboards; submitting the report in an accessible format (tagged PDF or DOCX) where needed; assistive technology for Excel/Python. If you require adjustments, contact the tutor/student support as early as possible and provide any required evidence so arrangements can be confirmed before the presentation date.

brief.studentFacingIntro: You are completing an individual quality reporting task using either Excel or Python. You will clean a provided quality dataset, produce routine statistical summaries (including outlier flags), analyse whether a process change produced a meaningful improvement using confidence intervals and a simple hypothesis test, and communicate findings in a stakeholder-friendly dashboard with short narrative commentary. Your submission must be clear, reproducible, and suitable to share with non-specialist operational stakeholders.
brief.workplaceContext: You work as a Quality Analyst for a manufacturing site. The site monitors a critical-to-quality continuous measurement (e.g., fill weight, thickness, cycle time) and a binary defect indicator (pass/fail). A process adjustment (e.g., new calibration routine, supplier change, or revised operator guidance) was introduced on a known change date. Your manager needs a short, evidence-based report and a simple dashboard for the monthly quality meeting, showing: (1) the current process performance, (2) any outliers that require investigation, and (3) whether the change produced a statistically supported improvement and whether that improvement is practically meaningful against the site specification.
stepByStepInstructions: 1) Download the dataset from the LMS: (a) quality_data_raw.csv and (b) data_dictionary.pdf. Use either Excel or Python for the full analysis (do not mix tools unless you clearly explain what was done where).

2) Set up your analysis file: (a) Excel workbook with clearly named sheets (e.g., RAW, CLEAN, SUMMARY, TESTS, DASHBOARD), or (b) a Python notebook with clear headings and code cells that run from top to bottom without errors. Include your name and learner ID on the first page/cell.

3) Import the raw dataset and complete an initial data audit. As a minimum, report: number of rows, number of columns, key fields, duplicates (if any), missing values by column, and any obvious invalid values (e.g., non-numeric entries in numeric columns, impossible dates).

4) Clean the dataset. Apply appropriate cleaning steps such as: converting data types (dates/numbers), standardising categories (e.g., shift names), handling missing values (state your rule: remove, impute, or flag), and removing or resolving duplicates (justify your decision). Keep a clear log of what you changed and why. Preserve the original raw data unchanged.

5) Produce routine summary statistics for the key quality measure(s). At a minimum, include measures of centre and spread (e.g., mean, median, standard deviation, IQR, min/max). Provide summaries overall and segmented by at least one operational category from the dataset (e.g., production line, product, shift, or operator) suitable for routine reporting.

6) Create an outlier flag field for the main continuous quality measure. Use a clear and defensible method (e.g., 1.5×IQR rule within a relevant subgroup, or a z-score rule). State the method, show the threshold calculation, and output an OutlierFlag (e.g., TRUE/FALSE) in the cleaned dataset. Summarise how many outliers were flagged and where they occur (by line/shift/product, if available).

7) Define the process change comparison. Use the change date provided in the dataset documentation to split data into ‘Before’ and ‘After’ periods. State your sample sizes for each period and any exclusions (e.g., removed missing values).

8) Confidence intervals: Calculate and interpret a 95% confidence interval relevant to the process change. As a minimum, provide a 95% CI for the mean (or mean difference) of the main continuous measure for Before vs After. Clearly state what the CI means in context (plain English).

9) Hypothesis test: Conduct one simple hypothesis test for the process change using the main continuous measure (e.g., two-sample t-test with clearly stated choice of equal/unequal variance; or an appropriate alternative if justified). Report the test statistic, p-value, decision at a stated alpha (e.g., 0.05), and your conclusion in context.

10) State assumptions, sampling limits, and practical significance. Explicitly address: independence/representativeness, approximate distributional assumptions (and what you checked), any sampling constraints (e.g., convenience samples, missingness), and practical significance (e.g., compare the estimated change to the site tolerance/specification or an agreed operational threshold).

11) Create stakeholder-friendly visuals and a dashboard. Include at least three visuals that help a non-specialist understand process performance and the process change. Your charts must have clear titles, labelled axes, correct units, and legible scales. Include concise narrative commentary (short paragraphs or callouts) explaining what each visual shows and what actions (if any) are suggested.

12) Complete the self-check before submission: (a) your cleaned dataset has consistent types and an OutlierFlag, (b) your summaries match the cleaned data (not the raw), (c) your CI and hypothesis test inputs use the same Before/After definitions, (d) all figures have units and labels, (e) your workbook/notebook reruns without errors, and (f) your report conclusions match your calculations.

13) Export and submit all required files to the LMS by the deadline. Ensure your report is readable as a standalone document (a manager should understand what you did and what you found without opening your workbook/notebook).
deliverables: A) Quality Report (PDF) containing: data cleaning summary and decisions; routine summary tables (centre/spread); outlier method and results; confidence interval(s); hypothesis test; assumptions, sampling limits, and practical significance; and brief recommendations.
B) Reproducible analysis file: either (i) Excel workbook (XLSX) with formulas/steps and a dashboard sheet, or (ii) Python notebook (IPYNB) plus exported HTML or PDF showing outputs.
C) Cleaned dataset (CSV) including the OutlierFlag field and any derived fields used for analysis (e.g., BeforeAfter indicator).
D) Dashboard export (PDF or image embedded in the report) showing key KPIs and charts for stakeholders.
E) Recorded briefing (MP4) summarising findings and recommendations for non-specialists.

rubric.criterionName: Data cleaning, summarising, and outlier flagging for routine reporting
rubric.fail: Cleaning steps are missing or not evidenced; raw and cleaned data are confused; summary statistics are incorrect, incomplete, or not based on the cleaned dataset; measures of centre/spread are absent or inappropriate; outlier flag is missing, unjustified, or incorrectly implemented; outputs are not suitable for routine reporting.
rubric.pass: Dataset is cleaned with basic evidence (e.g., type fixes, missing values handled, duplicates addressed) and a brief rationale; routine summary statistics include appropriate measures of centre and spread and are correct for the cleaned dataset; an outlier flag is implemented using a stated method and correctly applied; summaries are adequate for routine reporting.
rubric.merit: Cleaning is systematic and well-documented (clear audit of missingness/duplicates/invalid values and defensible handling); summaries are correctly segmented by relevant operational categories and presented clearly; outlier method is well-justified (including thresholds) and results are meaningfully summarised (counts and where they occur); outputs are clearly formatted for routine quality reporting.
rubric.distinction: Cleaning decisions demonstrate strong professional judgement and transparency (clear data quality issues identified, handling choices justified, and implications noted); summary statistics are comprehensive yet focused for stakeholders (clear tables, correct rounding/units, and insightful segmentation); outlier flagging is robust (method appropriate to context, thresholds shown, and outlier patterns interpreted with plausible operational explanations or follow-up questions).

rubric.criterionName: Confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for a process change (assumptions, sampling limits, practical significance)
rubric.fail: Confidence intervals and/or hypothesis test are missing, incorrect, or not connected to the process change; assumptions are absent or wrong; sampling limits are not stated; interpretation is incorrect or purely technical with no practical meaning; practical significance is not addressed.
rubric.pass: At least one relevant 95% confidence interval is computed correctly and interpreted in context; one simple hypothesis test for the process change is conducted and reported (test choice stated, p-value reported, decision at a stated alpha); key assumptions and sampling limits are stated at a basic level; practical significance is considered in relation to a stated operational threshold/specification.
rubric.merit: Confidence interval(s) and hypothesis test are clearly linked to the Before/After definition with correct sample sizes and handling of exclusions; assumptions are explicitly stated and briefly checked/justified (e.g., comments on distribution/outliers/independence); sampling limitations are explained with likely impacts on conclusions; practical significance is evaluated using a defensible comparison (spec, tolerance, or operational impact) and communicated clearly.
rubric.distinction: Inferential analysis is accurate, well-structured, and professionally interpreted: confidence intervals and hypothesis test reinforce each other; assumptions are discussed with evidence from the data (appropriate diagnostic checks or summaries); sampling limits and uncertainty are critically evaluated; practical significance is convincingly argued (including magnitude, direction, and operational relevance) with clear recommendations and caution where warranted.

rubric.criterionName: Stakeholder-friendly dashboard/visuals with clear labels, units, and concise narrative commentary
rubric.fail: Charts/dashboard are missing or unclear; visuals lack titles/labels/units; visuals are inappropriate for the message (misleading scales or cluttered presentation); commentary is absent, overly technical, or does not explain findings for non-specialists.
rubric.pass: Includes at least three appropriate visuals and a simple dashboard or equivalent layout; charts have clear titles and labelled axes with units; visuals align with the statistical findings; short commentary explains what is shown and the main takeaway in plain English.
rubric.merit: Dashboard is well-organised with a clear story (performance, outliers, and change impact); visuals are consistently formatted with readable scales, correct units, and informative legends; commentary is concise and decision-focused, linking visuals to conclusions and indicating any cautions.
rubric.distinction: Dashboard and visuals are highly effective for stakeholders: the narrative is coherent and action-oriented; chart choices maximise clarity (e.g., appropriate comparisons, uncertainty shown where relevant); labelling, units, and annotations prevent misinterpretation; commentary communicates statistical findings accurately without unnecessary jargon and supports evidence-based recommendations.

rubric.criterionName: Reproducibility, structure, and professional reporting (digital evidence and traceability)
rubric.fail: Work is difficult to follow or not reproducible; files are incomplete or cannot be opened; formulas/code are not traceable to outputs; figures/tables are not referenced; conclusions do not match calculations; required artefacts are missing.
rubric.pass: Submission is complete and readable; workbook/notebook is organised and outputs can be reproduced; tables/figures are referenced in the report; calculations are traceable; conclusions align with the presented results; basic referencing is provided for any external sources or tools.
rubric.merit: Strong structure and traceability: clear sectioning, consistent naming, and logical flow; workbook/notebook includes notes or comments enabling another person to rerun the analysis; rounding/units are consistent; limitations are appropriately signposted; any external sources are cited consistently.
rubric.distinction: Excellent reproducibility and professional standard: analysis runs end-to-end with clear documentation; data transformations are transparent (cleaning log or equivalent); outputs are presentation-ready; report is concise but complete, with strong alignment between evidence and recommendations; high-quality referencing and an explicit audit trail from raw data to decisions.

evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Include tables/figures with captions; use clear units and rounding; include a short reference list for any external sources (e.g., dataset documentation, software documentation).

brief.studentFacingIntro:
You will produce a quality-reporting pack using either Excel or Python. You will take a realistic quality dataset, clean it for reporting, summarise process performance, analyse whether an observed change is statistically and practically meaningful, and communicate findings through stakeholder-friendly visuals and brief narrative commentary.

This is an applied assessment: marks are awarded for correct methods, clear assumptions, and communication that a non-specialist audience could act on. You may choose Excel or Python, but you must make your work reproducible (i.e. a marker can follow what you did and re-run it).
brief.workplaceContext:
You work as a quality analyst supporting a team that monitors a key quality metric (for example: defect rate, rework minutes, fill volume, response time, or calibration error). A process change (new supplier, training, equipment adjustment, revised inspection method, etc.) was introduced part-way through the reporting period. Your manager needs a short routine report that (a) summarises current performance and flags unusual observations, and (b) assesses whether the process change produced a meaningful improvement or deterioration.

You will be given a dataset by your tutor (or you may use a workplace dataset with tutor approval). The dataset will include at least: a date/time or batch identifier, a measurable quality characteristic (numeric), and an indicator of 'Before change' vs 'After change' (or equivalent grouping variable).
stepByStepInstructions: Choose your tool: Excel or Python. Set up your working file(s) so that another person can reproduce your results (named tabs/cells with formulas in Excel; or a single runnable Jupyter notebook/script in Python).
Import/load the dataset and create a clear data dictionary section (briefly define each variable used in your analysis, including units).

Clean the data for reporting: handle missing values, incorrect data types, duplicates (if present), and clearly justify any exclusions or corrections. Keep an audit trail (e.g. a 'Cleaning log' tab or a notebook section).

Produce routine summary statistics for the key quality metric, including measures of centre and spread. At minimum include: a measure of centre (e.g. mean/median) and a measure of spread (e.g. standard deviation/IQR). Ensure units are shown and rounding is consistent.

Create outlier flags suitable for routine reporting. State the rule used (e.g. IQR rule, z-score threshold, or business-defined thresholds) and present a table of flagged records (identifier, value, reason flagged).

Define a clear comparison for process change (e.g. Before vs After). Check and state assumptions relevant to your chosen confidence interval and hypothesis test (e.g. independence, approximate normality/large-sample conditions, equal/unequal variance where applicable).

Compute and interpret at least one confidence interval relevant to the process change question (for example: difference in means, difference in proportions, or mean before vs after with appropriate method).

Conduct one simple hypothesis test aligned to the same process change question. State: null and alternative hypotheses, chosen significance level, test statistic and p-value (or equivalent), and conclusion in plain English.

Discuss sampling limits and practical significance: explain what the sampling method/time window allows you to conclude, and quantify whether the estimated change is operationally meaningful (not only statistically significant).

Create stakeholder-friendly charts or a simple dashboard to communicate: (a) current level and variation, (b) before/after comparison, and (c) any notable outliers or special-cause signals. Ensure labels, units, legends and short narrative commentary are clear for non-specialists.

Collaborative element (required, but not graded): share one draft chart/dashboard screenshot to the class forum or in-class review and provide brief constructive feedback to at least one peer. If you cannot attend live, complete this asynchronously via the forum within the same week. Summarise in one paragraph how you used any feedback (or why you did not).

Finalise your report pack and submit the required artefacts (see Deliverables). Ensure your submission is anonymous where required by your institution’s policy, and that files open without specialist permissions.
deliverables: A short statistical quality report (PDF) that includes: context and question, data cleaning decisions, summary statistics with outlier flags, confidence interval(s) and hypothesis test results, assumptions and sampling limits, and practical significance. Include brief narrative commentary suitable for stakeholders.

A reproducible analysis file: either (a) Excel workbook (.xlsx) containing the cleaned dataset (or a clear link to it), calculations and outputs; or (b) Python notebook (.ipynb) or script with requirements and runnable code to produce the same outputs.
A stakeholder-friendly dashboard or set of charts: embedded in the PDF and also provided as image exports (PNG/JPG) or as an Excel dashboard tab.
A short presentation (live or recorded) summarising your findings for a non-specialist audience (key results, what changed, how confident you are, and what action is recommended).

rubric.criterionName: Data cleaning, summarisation and outlier flagging for routine quality reporting
rubric.fail: Data are not cleaned to a usable standard (e.g. unresolved missing/invalid values or unclear exclusions). Summary statistics are missing/incorrect or not linked to the dataset. Measures of centre/spread are inappropriate or incorrectly calculated. Outlier flags are absent or based on an unstated/invalid rule. Outputs are not suitable for routine reporting (unclear units/rounding, no identifiers for flagged points).
rubric.pass: Data are cleaned with basic checks (missing values and types addressed) and key exclusions/corrections are stated. Correct measures of centre and spread are produced and clearly reported with units and sensible rounding. Outlier flags are generated using a stated rule and a list of flagged records is provided for follow-up.
rubric.merit: Cleaning decisions are well-justified and traceable (clear cleaning log/audit trail). Summaries are accurate and organised for reporting (e.g. overall and by relevant groups such as before/after). Outlier approach is appropriate for the data and reporting purpose, with clear thresholds and practical follow-up notes (e.g. likely data error vs special cause).
rubric.distinction: Cleaning and summarisation are robust, efficient and fully reproducible. Summary statistics directly support stakeholder decisions (e.g. includes comparative summaries and highlights meaningful changes in centre/spread). Outlier flagging is both statistically sensible and operationally relevant, with clear, defensible rules and well-presented flagged cases ready for action.

rubric.criterionName: Confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for process change (assumptions, sampling limits, practical significance)
rubric.fail: Confidence interval and/or hypothesis test is missing, incorrect, or mismatched to the question/data type. Hypotheses are not stated or are incorrect. Assumptions are not stated or are inappropriate. Interpretation is wrong or purely mechanical (e.g. p-value with no conclusion). Sampling limits and practical significance are not addressed.
rubric.pass: At least one appropriate confidence interval and one appropriate simple hypothesis test are carried out for the process change question. Null/alternative hypotheses and significance level are stated. Key assumptions are stated at a basic level. Results are interpreted correctly in plain English. Sampling limits and practical significance are addressed in a brief, relevant way.
rubric.merit: Methods are well-chosen and clearly aligned to the data and process change question. Assumptions are stated and checked where feasible (e.g. graphically or via sample size reasoning) and any violations are discussed. Practical significance is quantified (e.g. effect size in units, relative change, or comparison to a tolerance/target) alongside statistical significance. Sampling limits are clearly explained and linked to decision risk.
rubric.distinction: Inference is technically accurate, clearly justified, and communicated for decision-making. Assumptions and sampling limits are analysed with insight (e.g. independence concerns, measurement system considerations, time-related confounding, representativeness). Practical significance is convincingly argued using operational thresholds, costs, or service impact, and conclusions appropriately balance statistical evidence with real-world constraints.

rubric.criterionName: Stakeholder-friendly visualisation/dashboard with clear narrative commentary
rubric.fail: Charts/dashboard are missing or unsuitable (wrong chart type, unclear axes, missing units/labels/legend, misleading scales). Visuals do not support the statistical findings or contain errors. Narrative is absent or confusing, overly technical, or fails to explain what the audience should understand/do.
rubric.pass: Charts/dashboard are present, readable and relevant to the question (e.g. distribution/variation and before/after comparison). Labels, units and legends are clear. A concise narrative explains the main statistical findings and the direction of change in a way a non-specialist can follow.
rubric.merit: Visual choices are appropriate and help stakeholders interpret variation and change (e.g. clear comparison views, sensible scales, annotations for change point/outliers). Narrative commentary is concise, accurate and linked to the visuals (what changed, how certain, and why it matters).
rubric.distinction: Visuals and narrative form a coherent stakeholder report: clear hierarchy of information, excellent labelling/annotation, and no unnecessary complexity. The dashboard/charts anticipate stakeholder questions (e.g. targets, tolerances, context for outliers) and the narrative makes an evidence-based recommendation grounded in the statistical results.

rubric.criterionName: Reproducibility, transparency and professional presentation of analysis pack
rubric.fail: Work cannot be followed or reproduced (broken links, missing data, opaque steps). Files are poorly organised or do not open reliably. Key outputs in the report do not match the workbook/notebook. Referencing of sources/tools is missing where needed. Collaborative reflection is missing.
rubric.pass: Analysis steps are organised and broadly reproducible (clear tabs/sections, consistent naming). Report matches the submitted workbook/notebook outputs. Files open and run with reasonable effort. A brief note summarises peer feedback received/given (or asynchronous equivalent).
rubric.merit: Reproducibility is strong: clear structure, well-commented formulas/code, and a reader can trace from raw data to outputs. Assumptions and parameter choices (e.g. outlier thresholds, alpha) are transparent. Presentation is clear and professional with consistent formatting and readable tables/figures.
rubric.distinction: Submission is audit-ready: fully traceable workflow, excellent documentation, and high reliability (e.g. clear run instructions/requirements for Python; robust formula design and protection against accidental edits in Excel). Commentary is concise and precise. Reflection shows how feedback improved the final communication.

evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Include: context and question; data cleaning and any exclusions; summary statistics (centre/spread) and outlier flags; confidence interval(s) and hypothesis test with assumptions, sampling limits and practical significance; stakeholder-friendly visuals with brief narrative commentary; short paragraph on peer feedback used (or why not).

evidenceRequirements.fileType: XLSX or IPYNB (or .py plus outputs if agreed)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Excel route: include a clearly labelled 'Raw/Imported Data' tab, 'Cleaned Data' tab, calculations, and dashboard/outputs. Python route: include code to load data, clean, summarise, flag outliers, run CI/test, and generate the submitted charts; include a brief 'How to run' section and any package requirements used.

evidenceRequirements.fileType: PNG or JPG (or embedded in PDF plus separate image exports)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Provide at least 2–4 visuals suitable for stakeholders (e.g. histogram/boxplot, time/batch plot with change point, before/after comparison plot, outlier highlight). Ensure all have titles, axis labels and units.

evidenceRequirements.fileType: MP4 (or LMS recording link) or live delivery if scheduled
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Audience: non-specialist stakeholders. Cover: what data were used, what changed, confidence interval and test conclusion, practical significance, and recommended next step. Slides are optional; if used, submit PPTX/PDF.

brief.studentFacingIntro:
In this assignment you will complete a workplace-style risk modelling portfolio. You will (1) calculate probabilities for defects, demand and downtime using standard distribution models and (2) build and interpret a Monte Carlo simulation to quantify either schedule risk or financial risk. You will document assumptions and uncertainty in a risk register and then explain your modelling decisions and findings to a non-specialist audience in a short in-person briefing.

You may use Excel or Python. Your work must be reproducible (another person should be able to re-run your model and obtain the same results using your stated settings/seed).
brief.workplaceContext:
You work as a risk analyst in an operations team for a small manufacturer-distributor. Senior staff need a quick, evidence-based view of operational risk for the next month. Key uncertainties are: (a) defects in output, (b) daily customer demand, and (c) machine downtime due to breakdowns. The operations manager also needs a simple simulation-based estimate of monthly profit risk (or schedule risk for a small improvement project) to support decision-making.

You have the following baseline information (use as given unless you clearly justify an alternative in your evaluation section):

1) Defects (binomial context)
- A shift produces n = 200 units.
- Historical defect probability per unit: p = 0.03.
- A quality intervention is triggered if defects exceed 8 in a shift.

2) Demand (normal context)
- Daily demand (units) is approximately normal with mean μ = 450 and standard deviation σ = 60.
- Daily available capacity is 520 units.

3) Downtime / time-to-failure (exponential context)
- Time between breakdowns is modelled as exponential with mean 120 operating hours.
- If a breakdown occurs, repair time is a fixed 6 hours (assume this for simulation unless you justify an alternative).

4) Monthly financial model for simulation (choose this option unless your tutor approves the schedule-risk option)
- Planning horizon: 20 working days.
- Unit selling price: £55.
- Variable cost per unit produced: £32.
- Any unmet demand is lost (no backorders).
- If defects occur, defective units are scrapped (no rework), costing the variable cost only.
- If a breakdown occurs during a day, you lose 6 hours of production time that day. Assume an 8-hour working day and a nominal production rate of 65 units per full day when no downtime occurs.

Your task is to quantify risk and communicate it clearly to non-specialists, including your assumptions, uncertainty and limitations.
stepByStepInstructions:
Part A — Distribution-based probability calculations (MLO 1)
1. Binomial (defects): State the model and parameters. Calculate:
   a) P(defects > 8) in a 200-unit shift.
   b) The expected number of defects and a brief operational interpretation (1–2 sentences).
2. Normal (demand): State the model and parameters. Calculate:
   a) P(demand > 520) in a day.
   b) The demand level exceeded only 10% of the time (the 90th percentile) and interpret what that means for capacity planning.
3. Exponential (downtime): State the model and parameters. Calculate:
   a) P(a breakdown occurs within the next 40 operating hours).
   b) The expected number of breakdowns in a 160-hour operating month (assume 20 working days × 8 hours).

Part B — Monte Carlo simulation model (MLO 2)
4. Build a Monte Carlo simulation to estimate monthly profit risk over 20 working days using the context data. Your simulation must:
   a) Include demand uncertainty (normal model) and defect uncertainty (binomial model per day, based on that day’s production).
   b) Include breakdowns using an exponential time-to-failure model and the stated repair-time impact.
   c) Be run for a suitable number of iterations (minimum 5,000) and include a method to reproduce results (e.g., fixed random seed or documented Excel approach).
5. Define and calculate at least four simulation outputs that quantify risk, including:
   a) Mean monthly profit.
   b) Probability monthly profit is below a chosen threshold (you must justify the threshold as a meaningful operational concern).
   c) A percentile-based risk measure (e.g., P10 or P90 profit).
   d) A clear statement of uncertainty and what drives variability in outcomes.
6. Create a workplace risk register entry set (minimum 6 entries) that records assumptions and uncertainty used in your probability models and simulation. Each entry must include: risk/assumption description, distribution choice, parameter values, source/basis, uncertainty notes, and a control/mitigation action.

Part C — Evaluation, limitations, and communication (MLO 3)
7. Evaluate your distribution choices and simulation settings for fitness-for-purpose. You must address:
   a) Why binomial/normal/exponential are appropriate here (or where they are only approximate).
   b) At least three limitations of your modelling (e.g., independence assumptions, normality, parameter uncertainty, truncation/negative demand handling, constant defect rate, fixed repair time).
   c) Simulation settings and their impact (iterations, seed/reproducibility, any truncation rules, time-step assumptions, how breakdowns are mapped to days).
8. Sensitivity drivers: Identify at least two key drivers of profit risk and show evidence from your work (e.g., simple one-at-a-time sensitivity, alternative parameter scenario, or comparison of outcomes when varying a key input such as defect rate, demand variability, or mean time between failures). Keep the method simple and clearly explained.

Part D — In-person stakeholder briefing (MLO 3)
9. Prepare 4–6 slides (or one A3 poster) summarising: your model purpose, key assumptions, key results, main limitations, and recommendations. Deliver a 5-minute in-class briefing to a non-specialist audience (your peers and tutor), followed by up to 3 minutes of questions.
deliverables: A PDF report presenting Part A–C (recommended 1,800–2,200 words, excluding tables/figures).
A completed risk register (template allowed) included in the PDF report and also submitted as a separate file (Excel/PDF). Minimum 6 entries.
Your simulation model file: either an Excel workbook with workings visible and clearly labelled tabs, or a Python notebook/script with instructions to run. Must be reproducible.
Slides (PDF) or a one-page A3 poster (PDF scan) used for the in-person briefing.
In-person 5-minute briefing presentation delivered during the scheduled class assessment window.

rubric.criterionName: Distribution-based probability calculations and workplace interpretation
rubric.fail: Uses incorrect distribution models and/or parameters; key probability results are wrong or missing; working is unclear or not shown; interpretations are absent or not connected to defects/demand/downtime decisions.
rubric.pass: Correctly applies binomial, normal and exponential models with appropriate parameters; provides the required probabilities/percentile with sufficient working for checking; provides brief workplace interpretations that relate to defect triggers, capacity exceedance, and breakdown likelihood.
rubric.merit: Calculations are correct and clearly structured; units, notation and assumptions are stated; interpretations show operational relevance (e.g., relating probabilities to expected frequency per month/shift) and include a short comment on model appropriateness (e.g., normal approximation caveats, independence).
rubric.distinction: Calculations are correct, well-communicated and audit-ready; interpretations are concise and decision-focused, including practical implications (e.g., trigger frequency, buffer/capacity implications, maintenance planning); demonstrates strong control of assumptions and highlights where parameter uncertainty could matter.

rubric.criterionName: Monte Carlo simulation build, outputs, and risk register documentation
rubric.fail: Simulation model is missing, not runnable, or does not reflect the stated workplace context; insufficient iterations or outputs; results are not quantified clearly; assumptions/uncertainty are not recorded or risk register is incomplete.
rubric.pass: Simulation is runnable and reflects demand, defects and downtime using the stated distribution models; uses at least 5,000 iterations and provides the required outputs (mean, threshold probability, percentile measure, uncertainty statement); a risk register with at least 6 entries records assumptions and uncertainty in a workplace-appropriate format.
rubric.merit: Simulation logic is clear and traceable; outputs are well-presented with appropriate charts/tables; threshold choice is justified; risk register entries are specific and include basis/source and mitigation/control actions; includes a reproducibility method (seed or clearly documented Excel method) and basic validation checks (e.g., sense checks against expected values).
rubric.distinction: Simulation is robust and professionally documented; outputs include clear risk statements (e.g., probability of unacceptable outcome) and decision-relevant summaries; risk register demonstrates strong practice with well-formed assumptions, uncertainty notes, and actionable mitigations; includes thoughtful validation and error-checking (e.g., extreme-case tests, comparison to analytic expectations where possible).

rubric.criterionName: Evaluation of distribution choices and simulation settings; limitations and sensitivity drivers
rubric.fail: Little or no evaluation of why distributions/settings were chosen; limitations are missing or incorrect; no credible identification of sensitivity drivers; statements are generic and not supported by evidence from the model.
rubric.pass: Explains why the chosen distributions and key simulation settings are reasonable for the scenario; states at least three limitations; identifies at least two sensitivity drivers and provides some evidence from model outputs or simple scenario changes.
rubric.merit: Evaluation is specific to the workplace context and includes discussion of fitness-for-purpose; limitations are explained in terms of likely impact on results; sensitivity evidence is clearly shown and interpreted, identifying which inputs most influence outcomes and why.
rubric.distinction: Evaluation demonstrates strong judgement and model governance: clear rationale, clear statement of what the model can/cannot support, and how settings affect reliability; limitations are prioritised and linked to decisions; sensitivity work is convincing, well-organised, and highlights the main drivers of risk with clear implications for data collection or controls.

rubric.criterionName: Non-specialist communication and in-person briefing effectiveness
rubric.fail: Briefing is unclear, over-technical, or does not communicate results/assumptions/limitations; slides/poster are confusing or unreadable; unable to answer basic questions about model purpose and findings.
rubric.pass: Delivers a clear 5-minute summary with readable slides/poster; communicates purpose, key assumptions, key results and at least one limitation; answers questions adequately using plain English.
rubric.merit: Briefing is well-structured and targeted to non-specialists; highlights the most decision-relevant results and uncertainty; handles questions confidently and explains limitations without excessive technical detail.
rubric.distinction: Briefing is concise, authoritative and stakeholder-ready; communicates risk using clear measures and simple visuals; transparently explains assumptions, limitations and sensitivity drivers; responds to questions with clarity and maintains alignment to decision needs.

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Report (Parts A–C) including figures/tables and embedded risk register
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must show workings or provide references to where calculations are implemented (e.g., appendix screenshots or cell references). Use clear headings for Part A–C. Include any truncation rules (e.g., negative demand handling) if used.
May use a provided template or your organisation’s format. Must include: distribution, parameters, basis/source, uncertainty note, and mitigation/control.
