brief.studentFacingIntro: In this capstone you will build and evidence a complete, workplace-style mathematical solution using either Excel or Python. You will work from a provided operational dataset and a business problem statement to (1) create a reproducible model with clear assumptions and traceable calculations, (2) analyse outputs to identify trends, turning points and constraints, (3) quantify uncertainty and communicate risk with limitations and mitigations, and (4) communicate your recommendations to non-specialists using a concise report, slide deck and recorded team-review presentation. This is an individual, self-study assessment completed asynchronously; all outputs are submitted digitally via the LMS.
brief.workplaceContext:
Scenario: You are a quantitative analyst supporting an operations manager at a small manufacturing-and-fulfilment business producing a single main product line. The business must decide (a) a pricing approach and/or (b) a production and resource plan that meets demand while controlling cost and quality. You are provided with operational data (historic sales/prices, production capacity, labour and machine availability, defect/return rates, and key process measures). Management wants a reproducible model they can audit and re-run, plus clear recommendations and a risk statement explaining what could go wrong and how to mitigate it.

You may choose ONE focus problem type (choose the one best supported by the dataset you pick):
1) Pricing: model demand/revenue/profit vs price and identify an evidence-based pricing recommendation under operational constraints.
2) Optimisation: allocate resources (e.g. labour hours, machine hours, batch sizes) to optimise an objective (e.g. maximise contribution, minimise cost, meet service level) subject to constraints.
3) Quality: model defect/return behaviour, quantify process stability and propose actions to reduce quality risk while considering cost/capacity impacts.

Datasets: Select ONE dataset from the LMS ‘Capstone Data Pack’ (Dataset A, B, or C). Each dataset includes a README describing columns, units and any known data quality issues.
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1 — Choose tools and dataset: Choose Excel (with Solver) OR Python (e.g. pandas/numpy/scipy/matplotlib). Download ONE dataset (A, B, or C) and its README from the LMS ‘Capstone Data Pack’. Save a clean copy of the original data unchanged.

Step 2 — Define the business question and success measure: Write a short problem statement (3–6 sentences) specifying: objective (what you are optimising/deciding), decision variables (e.g. price, hours, batch size), constraints (capacity, quality, service level), and success metric(s) (e.g. profit, cost per unit, defect rate threshold).

Step 3 — Create an assumptions register: Create a clearly labelled assumptions table (Excel tab or Python markdown/text output) listing each assumption, rationale, and impact. Include units and rounding approach (e.g. currency rounding, units sold as integers).

Step 4 — Build a reproducible model: Build the full calculation chain from inputs → transformations → outputs. Requirements:
- Traceability: every reported output must link back to source data and/or stated assumptions.
- Reproducibility: a third party can open/run your workbook/script and reproduce the same outputs.
- Documentation: include a ‘READ ME’ section/tab with how to run, required files, and where key outputs are found.
- Auditability: include clear intermediate calculations; avoid hard-coded numbers in formulas (use named cells/parameters).

Step 5 — Include optimisation or decision logic (where relevant):
- Excel route: use Solver with a clearly defined objective cell, variable cells, and constraint cells. Save Solver settings and describe them in your READ ME.
- Python route: implement optimisation/decision logic (e.g. grid search, scipy.optimize) and clearly show objective and constraints.
If your chosen focus is Quality rather than Optimisation, include a decision rule (e.g. threshold, control limit, accept/reject, or prioritisation logic) that leads to an operational recommendation.

Step 6 — Validate and sense-check your model (required): Implement at least THREE validation checks, for example:
- Unit/dimensional checks (e.g. currency per unit, hours per week)
- Tolerance/rounding checks (e.g. totals reconcile, constraints not violated beyond tolerance)
- Sensitivity checks (e.g. small changes in inputs produce plausible output changes)
- Back-testing check against a holdout period (if available)
Document results of checks and any fixes made.

Step 7 — Analyse data and outputs for trends, turning points and constraints: Produce at least THREE visuals (charts) and at least THREE quantified findings. Your analysis must include:
- At least one identified trend (directional change)
- At least one turning point or non-linear feature (e.g. optimum, threshold effect, diminishing returns)
- At least one constraint that binds or strongly affects the result (e.g. capacity, quality limit, budget)
Ensure visuals have titles, labelled axes, units, and brief interpretation.

Step 8 — Evaluate uncertainty and risk (required): Use at least ONE of the following and justify your choice:
- Confidence interval(s) for a key metric (e.g. mean defect rate, mean demand)
- Distribution-based modelling (fit/assume a distribution and quantify probability of adverse outcomes)
- Simulation (e.g. Monte Carlo) to estimate variability of profit/cost/service level
Produce a balanced risk statement: what might vary, how much it could matter, limitations, and practical mitigations (operational actions).

Step 9 — Write the technical report (non-specialist audience): Produce a concise report that explains the problem, method, outputs, recommendations, assumptions, uncertainty, limitations and mitigations. You must reference your model artefacts (workbook tabs or script sections) so the reader can audit key results.

Step 10 — Create slides and record the team review: Create a short slide deck and record a presentation for a ‘team review meeting’ (screen recording with voice). Your recording must present: the problem, your key evidence (charts), the recommendation, constraints, and the risk statement.

Step 11 — Respond to peer feedback (asynchronous): Use the LMS peer-review tool if enabled. If peer review is enabled, you must: (a) submit by the peer-review deadline, (b) provide feedback to peers as allocated, and (c) include a short ‘Response to Feedback’ section in your report explaining what you changed or why you did not change it. If peer review is not enabled, complete the provided ‘Self-Review Checklist’ (LMS download) and include a ‘Response to Review’ section addressing at least FIVE checklist items.
deliverables: A reproducible Excel workbook (.xlsx) OR Python project (.ipynb preferred, or .py plus outputs) implementing the pricing/optimisation/quality solution with traceable calculations, assumptions, and validation checks.
A concise technical report for non-specialists (PDF) including visuals, units, assumptions, uncertainty/risk statement, limitations and mitigations, and response to peer/self review.
A slide deck (PDF) suitable for a team review meeting.
A recorded team review presentation (MP4) with screen share of slides and (briefly) the model outputs.

rubric.criterionName: Reproducible model build, traceability, and documentation (Excel/Python)
rubric.fail: Model is not reproducible (missing data links/files, cannot run/open without errors), calculations are not traceable (hard-coded numbers without explanation), assumptions are missing or unclear, and outputs cannot be audited to source data. Documentation (READ ME/how-to-run) is absent or insufficient for a third party to reproduce results.
rubric.pass: Model runs/opens and produces stated outputs using the provided dataset. Key calculations are traceable to inputs/assumptions with mostly clear structure. Assumptions are documented with units and basic rounding stated. A READ ME/how-to-run section is provided and a third party could reproduce the main outputs with reasonable effort.
rubric.merit: Model is clearly structured (inputs/parameters, calculations, outputs separated), with strong traceability and minimal hard-coding. Assumptions register is complete with rationale and units; rounding/precision is applied consistently. Documentation is clear and includes where to find key outputs, how to rerun, and any dependencies (Solver settings or Python environment notes).
rubric.distinction: Model is fully audit-ready: comprehensive traceability, well-labelled variables, consistent units, robust structure, and clear calculation lineage. Assumptions are explicit, justified, and impact-aware. Documentation enables straightforward reproduction (including Solver setup/exported settings or a requirements/environment file and run instructions). Model design supports reuse (parameters easy to change, outputs update cleanly).

rubric.criterionName: Operational analysis, trends/turning points/constraints, and evidence-based recommendation (recorded team review focus)
rubric.fail: Findings are largely descriptive or unsupported by data/model outputs. Trends, turning points or constraints are missing, incorrect, or not evidenced. Recommendation is absent, not actionable, or not linked to quantified results. Recording does not clearly communicate the evidence and decision logic.
rubric.pass: Analysis uses dataset and model outputs to produce an actionable recommendation. At least one trend, one turning point/non-linear feature, and one constraint are identified with supporting evidence (numbers and/or charts). Recording explains the recommendation and the main evidence in a way a team could follow.
rubric.merit: Analysis is well-evidenced and coherent: multiple findings are quantified and correctly interpreted. Turning points/optima/thresholds are identified and connected to operational decisions. Constraints are clearly explained (what binds, when, and why it matters). Recording presents a structured narrative (problem → evidence → recommendation → constraints) with clear visuals.
rubric.distinction: Analysis is decision-grade: strong synthesis of data and model outputs; clear identification of key drivers, turning points, and binding constraints with credible interpretation. Recommendation includes practical operational implications (e.g. expected impact, trade-offs) and is defended against alternatives using evidence. Recording is concise, well-paced, and stakeholder-appropriate, demonstrating confident command of the analysis.

rubric.criterionName: Uncertainty evaluation and balanced risk statement (with limitations and mitigations)
rubric.fail: Uncertainty is not evaluated or is incorrect/misapplied (e.g. inappropriate confidence intervals, unclear simulation). Risk statement is missing, one-sided, or not linked to quantified uncertainty. Limitations and mitigations are absent or generic.
rubric.pass: At least one valid uncertainty method is applied (confidence intervals and/or distributions and/or simulation) with correct interpretation. A risk statement is provided describing what could vary and plausible impact on the decision. Limitations are acknowledged and at least one practical mitigation is proposed.
rubric.merit: Uncertainty method choice is justified and implemented correctly, with clear outputs (e.g. interval estimates, probability of adverse outcomes, simulated distribution). Risk statement is balanced and decision-relevant (likelihood/impact where appropriate), with specific limitations tied to data/model assumptions. Mitigations are practical and linked to identified risks.
rubric.distinction: Uncertainty evaluation is rigorous and integrated into the decision: outputs are clearly communicated and used to qualify the recommendation (e.g. confidence in achieving targets, probability of constraint violation). Limitations are specific, prioritised, and technically accurate. Mitigations are operationally credible, with monitoring/trigger suggestions (e.g. thresholds, leading indicators) and acknowledgement of residual risk.

rubric.criterionName: Professional technical communication: report + slide deck + response to peer/self review
rubric.fail: Report/slides are unclear or incomplete, with missing units, visuals, assumptions, or limitations. Structure does not support a non-specialist audience. Visuals are poorly labelled or misleading. No meaningful response to peer/self review is provided.
rubric.pass: Report and slides are complete and understandable for non-specialists. Includes relevant visuals with labels/units, key assumptions, limitations, and a clear recommendation. Response to peer/self review is present and identifies at least one change made (or provides a reasonable justification for not changing).
rubric.merit: Communication is concise and well-structured (executive summary, method, findings, recommendation, risk/limitations). Visuals are well-designed and interpreted. Units, assumptions, and constraints are integrated consistently. Response to peer/self review is specific and shows thoughtful improvement (what changed, why, and the impact).
rubric.distinction: Communication is stakeholder-ready: highly clear, concise, and persuasive without overselling. Visuals and narrative align tightly with the decision, including trade-offs and constraints. Assumptions/limitations are transparent and appropriately framed. Response to peer/self review demonstrates reflective practice and measurable enhancement to clarity, correctness, or robustness.

evidenceRequirements.artefactType: Model artefact (choose ONE): Excel workbook OR Python project
evidenceRequirements.fileType: XLSX (Excel) OR IPYNB (preferred) / PY + exported outputs (PDF/HTML) (Python)
evidenceRequirements.additionalNotes: Must include: assumptions register; traceable calculations; clear inputs/outputs; at least three validation checks with recorded results; optimisation/decision logic (Solver settings for Excel or documented objective/constraints in Python). If using Python, include a short README in the notebook or as a text cell describing how to run, required packages, and where outputs are generated.

Must include: problem statement; dataset used; method overview; key results with visuals; identified trend(s), turning point(s), and constraint(s); recommendation; uncertainty method and results; balanced risk statement; limitations; mitigations; response to peer/self review. Use UK academic conventions for referencing any external sources (e.g. software documentation, statistical references).
Slides should be readable and not overloaded. Include: aim, key visuals, recommendation, constraints, risk statement, and next steps. Ensure units and chart labels are visible.

Screen recording with voice. Show slides throughout and briefly demonstrate where model outputs come from (e.g. key output tab/cell or notebook output). Audio must be clear. If you appear on camera, this is optional. Include captions if available via your recording tool.

If LMS peer review is enabled: summarise feedback received and what you changed. If not enabled: complete the LMS ‘Self-Review Checklist’ and respond to at least five items (what you checked, what you changed, and why). Do not include personal data from peers.

self_study.academicIntegrity: You must submit work that is your own and created for this assessment. Permitted support: (1) standard software help resources (Microsoft Support, Python library documentation), (2) textbooks/online references with appropriate citation, (3) spelling/grammar tools, and (4) optional use of generative AI for language editing or debugging guidance only, provided you (a) verify all mathematics and outputs independently, (b) do not paste confidential/personal data into external tools, and (c) include a brief AI-use statement in an appendix (what tool, what it was used for, and what you verified). Prohibited conduct includes: copying another learner’s workbook/script/report; submitting someone else’s code; fabricating data or results; editing screenshots to misrepresent outputs; using AI to generate the full analysis without understanding and verification; or colluding on a ‘shared’ model. You must include an authenticity declaration in the report: 'I confirm this submission is my own work and that all sources (including any tools) have been acknowledged.'
self_study.accessibilityOptions: Reasonable adjustments are available without lowering academic standards. Options include: submitting an accessible report format (tagged PDF or DOCX converted to PDF), alternative colour palettes and larger fonts on charts, providing a transcript in place of captions (or alongside), and using audio-only recording with slides if video is not feasible. If you use assistive technology, ensure the workbook/notebook is navigable (clear headings, labelled tabs/sections). If you cannot use Excel Solver or cannot record video due to access needs, you may submit an equivalent Python optimisation/decision implementation and an audio narration over slides (MP3) plus the slide PDF, subject to the same evidence requirements. Contact the programme team via the LMS support route in advance to confirm the adjustment.

overview.title: Integrated Workplace Maths Project (Capstone): Workplace Modelling, Analysis and Communication Portfolio
overview.moduleTitle: Integrated Workplace Maths Project (Capstone)

assessedOutcomes.mloStatement: Create a reproducible Excel or Python workbook solving a workplace-style pricing, optimisation or quality problem, with traceable calculations and documented assumptions.
Analyse operational data and model outputs to produce evidence-based recommendations, identifying trends, turning points and constraints for a recorded team review.
Evaluate uncertainty using confidence intervals, distributions or simulation, producing a balanced risk statement with limitations and practical mitigations.
Produce a concise technical report and slide deck for non-specialists, integrating visuals, units, assumptions and limitations, and responding to peer feedback.

brief.studentFacingIntro: You will complete an end-to-end workplace-style maths project that demonstrates how you build, check and communicate a practical model using Excel or Python. You will work from an operational dataset (provided by the tutor or approved by the tutor if you propose your own) and address a realistic business question in one of these categories: pricing, optimisation, or quality. Your submission must be reproducible (another person can run it and obtain the same outputs), transparent (traceable calculations and clear assumptions), and suitable for non-specialist stakeholders (clear visuals, units, and limitations). This is a hybrid assessment: you may attend live sessions or engage asynchronously, and you may present live or via a recording.
brief.workplaceContext:
Scenario (choose ONE track):
A) Pricing track: You work for a service business that offers three service tiers. You have historical monthly demand, price, cost and capacity data. Management wants a revised pricing structure that meets a profit target without exceeding capacity, and they need to understand how sensitive profit is to demand changes.
B) Optimisation track: You work for a small manufacturer that produces two or more products using shared resources (machine hours, labour hours, materials). You have unit contribution margins, resource limits, and quality/tolerance constraints. Management wants the best production plan and an explanation of binding constraints and trade-offs.
C) Quality track: You work for an operations team monitoring a measured characteristic (e.g., fill volume, processing time, defect rate). You have sample data over time and need to assess process performance, identify trends/turning points, and quantify uncertainty to support a quality improvement decision.
Your tutor will provide a dataset and a short case brief for each track (or you may propose an equivalent workplace dataset/problem for approval).
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1 — Select your track and dataset: Choose pricing, optimisation, or quality. Confirm with your tutor which dataset and case brief you are using (tutor-provided or tutor-approved).

Step 2 — Define the business question and scope: State the decision to be supported (e.g., price changes, production plan, or quality intervention). Specify what is in scope/out of scope. List required outputs (e.g., recommended price/plan/thresholds).

Step 3 — Build a reproducible workbook (Excel or Python): Implement the model with transparent structure and traceable calculations. Include documented assumptions, units, rounding approach, and a clear input–process–output layout. Ensure another user can run and reproduce results (no hidden steps).

Step 4 — Validate and check your model: Carry out dimensional/unit checks, tolerance/reasonableness checks, and at least one sensitivity check (e.g., effect of changing a key input). Record checks and outcomes inside the workbook and/or in an appendix.

Step 5 — Analyse outputs to generate recommendations: Use graphs/tables to identify trends, turning points and constraints (e.g., binding capacity constraints, break-even or diminishing returns, changes over time). Convert findings into evidence-based recommendations that address the business question.

Step 6 — Evaluate uncertainty and risk: Quantify uncertainty using confidence intervals, distributions or simulation (as appropriate to your dataset and track). Produce a balanced risk statement including limitations and practical mitigations.

Step 7 — Prepare stakeholder communication: Write a concise technical report and create a slide deck for non-specialists. Integrate visuals, units, assumptions and limitations. Ensure recommendations are clear and actionable.

Step 8 — Peer feedback and response (hybrid): Exchange feedback with at least one peer (or use the asynchronous alternative). Record what feedback you received and what changes you made (or justify why no changes were made).

Step 9 — Recorded team review (hybrid): Deliver your team review either live (in-class or online) or via a recording. Your review must explain the model, evidence, uncertainty and recommendations, and it must explicitly identify trends, turning points and constraints.
deliverables: A reproducible Excel workbook (.xlsx) OR Python notebook/script (.ipynb and/or .py) implementing the model, including assumptions, traceable calculations and checks.
A concise technical report for non-specialists (PDF) summarising context, method, outputs, uncertainty, limitations, and recommendations.
A slide deck (PPTX or PDF) used for the team review.
A recorded team review presentation (video or narrated slides) OR confirmation of a live presentation (tutor will record/confirm attendance where applicable).
Peer feedback evidence and your response (e.g., completed feedback form, annotated draft changes, or short reflection note).

rubric.criterionName: Reproducible model/workbook with traceable calculations, assumptions and validation checks
rubric.fail: Workbook/notebook is incomplete or cannot be run to reproduce stated outputs; calculations are opaque (e.g., hard-coded values without explanation, missing formulas/steps); assumptions are missing or undocumented; units and rounding are inconsistent or absent; little/no evidence of checking (dimensional/tolerance/sensitivity).
rubric.pass: Workbook/notebook runs and reproduces the main outputs; structure is generally clear with traceable calculations; key assumptions are stated and mostly aligned to the case; units and rounding are mostly consistent; includes at least basic checks (e.g., reasonableness or simple sensitivity) with outcomes noted.
rubric.merit: Workbook/notebook is clearly structured (inputs/processing/outputs) and reliably reproducible; calculations are fully traceable and auditable; assumptions are explicit, justified and documented in the file; units and rounding are consistently applied; includes dimensional/tolerance checks and at least one meaningful sensitivity check with interpretation.
rubric.distinction: Workbook/notebook is highly professional and audit-ready: reproducible from a clean run; transparent calculation log/notes and clear parameterisation; assumptions are comprehensive, justified and linked to data sources; units/rounding conventions are rigorous; validation is strong (dimensional, tolerance, sensitivity) and clearly demonstrates model credibility and limits.

rubric.criterionName: Analysis of operational data and model outputs leading to evidence-based recommendations (team review focus)
rubric.fail: Analysis is minimal, incorrect, or not linked to the workplace question; trends/turning points/constraints are not identified or are misidentified; recommendations are missing, unsupported, or contradictory to outputs; team review content is unclear or absent.
rubric.pass: Uses data/model outputs to support recommendations that address the workplace question; identifies at least one relevant trend and at least one constraint; provides a coherent explanation suitable for a team review, though interpretation may be limited in depth or specificity.
rubric.merit: Analysis is well-supported with appropriate tables/graphs; clearly identifies multiple relevant trends and/or turning points and explains their operational meaning; constraints and trade-offs are explicitly described (e.g., binding constraints, capacity limits); recommendations are specific, feasible and evidence-based for the team review.
rubric.distinction: Analysis is insightful and decision-focused: trends, turning points and constraints are clearly demonstrated and convincingly interpreted; recommendations are prioritised with rationale, quantified impacts and clear operational implications; demonstrates strong linkage between data, model behaviour and stakeholder decision needs in the team review.

rubric.criterionName: Uncertainty evaluation and balanced risk statement with limitations and mitigations
rubric.fail: Uncertainty is not evaluated or is applied incorrectly (e.g., inappropriate method, incorrect interpretation); risk statement is missing or one-sided; limitations are ignored; mitigations are absent or impractical.
rubric.pass: Applies at least one appropriate uncertainty method (confidence interval, distribution-based approach or simulation) and interprets it at a basic level; provides a risk statement that recognises uncertainty and includes at least one limitation and one practical mitigation.
rubric.merit: Uses appropriate uncertainty methods correctly and reports results clearly (including parameters/assumptions); explains how uncertainty affects the recommendation; provides a balanced risk statement with relevant limitations and multiple practical mitigations (e.g., monitoring plan, contingency thresholds).
rubric.distinction: Uncertainty evaluation is robust and well-communicated: methods are well-justified and correctly executed; results are clearly visualised and interpreted for decision-making; risk statement is nuanced, explicitly ties uncertainty to outcomes (financial/schedule/quality), and includes realistic mitigations and clear limitations/assumption boundaries.

rubric.criterionName: Professional communication: report + slide deck for non-specialists, with visuals, units, assumptions/limitations and response to peer feedback
rubric.fail: Report/slide deck is missing, unclear, overly technical for non-specialists, or poorly organised; visuals are absent or misleading; units/assumptions/limitations are not integrated; peer feedback is not evidenced or not addressed.
rubric.pass: Report and slides communicate the purpose, method and recommendations to a non-specialist audience with generally clear structure; includes some relevant visuals and mostly correct units; states key assumptions and limitations; shows evidence of receiving and responding to peer feedback at a basic level.
rubric.merit: Report and slides are concise, well-structured and accessible to non-specialists; visuals are appropriate, labelled and support interpretation; units, assumptions and limitations are integrated throughout (not just listed); peer feedback is documented and responses lead to clear improvements or justified decisions.
rubric.distinction: Communication is exemplary and stakeholder-ready: report and slides are highly clear, concise and persuasive without losing technical accuracy; visuals are well-designed and correctly annotated with units; assumptions/limitations are integrated and linked to decisions and risk; peer feedback process is clearly evidenced and responses materially strengthen clarity, validity and usefulness.

overview.examPurpose: Validate program-level competence across all PLOs in workplace mathematics, including algebra, functions/graphs, calculus, optimisation, statistics, probability/risk, and mathematical modelling validation, with transparent and auditable working suitable for spreadsheet- or code-based workflows.
